concepts.title: Java is a language and a platform
concepts.question: What two things does the phrase Java technology cover, and how does a platform differ from an ordinary one?

paragraphs: Java technology names two things at once. One is a high-level programming language, the thing you write programs in. The other is a platform, the environment in which those programs run.

A platform is usually a combination of hardware and an operating system. The Java platform is different: it is made only of software and sits on top of the platform underneath it. It has two components, the Java Virtual Machine (the Java VM) and the Application Programming Interface (the API).

The API is a large collection of ready-made components, organised into packages, which are libraries of related classes and interfaces. The tutorial also lists ten buzzwords for the language, such as simple, portable and secure, but it leaves them undefined and points to a white paper.
card.example: A team writes a payroll tool in the Java language. It later runs on a Windows laptop and on a Linux server, because each machine has the Java platform installed above its own operating system. The tool talks to the platform, not to the machine below it.
card.rule: Java is a language for writing programs plus a software-only platform, made of a VM and an API, that runs them on top of other platforms.
card.limits: The buzzword list is a label list, not a specification, since the tutorial gives no definitions for it. Treat each buzzword as a claim to look up elsewhere.

concepts.title: From source to bytecode to running
concepts.question: What happens to a Java source file on its way to running, and why can the result run on many systems?

paragraphs: You write source code in plain text files whose names end in .java. The javac compiler turns a source file into a .class file. You then start the program with the java launcher, which creates an instance of the Java VM to run it.

A .class file does not hold instructions for your processor. It holds bytecodes, the machine language of the Java VM. Because a Java VM exists for Windows, Linux, Solaris and Mac OS, the same class files run on all of them.
Some VMs, such as HotSpot, also watch the running program, spot busy places, and recompile frequently used code to native code for speed.
card.example: Ana saves Greeter.java and runs javac Greeter.java, which creates Greeter.class. She copies only the class file to a friend's Linux laptop that has Java installed and runs java Greeter there. The same bytecode runs unchanged.
card.rule: Compile once with javac to bytecode, then run that bytecode with java on any system that has a Java VM.
card.limits: Bytecode travels only to systems that have a Java VM. And if javac finds errors in the source, it creates no class file, so there is nothing to run.

concepts.title: What the Java platform provides
concepts.question: Which kinds of ready-made parts does a full Java platform provide, and which tools will a beginner use first?

paragraphs: The platform ships with development tools for compiling, running, monitoring, debugging and documenting applications. A beginner mainly uses three: javac compiles source, java launches a program, and javadoc generates API documentation from comments in the source.
The API gives the core library of ready-to-use classes: basic objects, networking and security, XML generation, database access and more.

Around these sit deployment technologies (Java Web Start and Java Plug-In), three toolkits for graphical user interfaces (JavaFX, Swing and Java 2D), and integration libraries such as JDBC for databases, JNDI, RMI and Java IDL for reaching other systems.
card.example: Sam needs a window with buttons and menus. By the tutorial's grouping, that need falls under the user interface toolkits, so Sam looks at JavaFX or Swing rather than at the deployment technologies or the integration libraries.
card.rule: Match a need to its group: tools, core API, deployment technologies, user interface toolkits or integration libraries.
card.limits: The tutorial was written for JDK 8, so its list may not match a current JDK. Check current documentation before relying on a named technology.

concepts.title: Reading the benefit claims
concepts.question: What does the tutorial claim Java will do for a programmer, and which of those claims rest on its own figures?

paragraphs: The page promises no fame, fortune or job. Its argument is narrower: learning Java should improve your programs and take less effort than many other languages.

It lists seven benefits: a quick start (especially for people who know C or C++), less code, better code, faster development, no platform dependencies, write once and run anywhere through machine-independent bytecode, and easier distribution. Better code is tied to good practices, automatic garbage collection against memory leaks, and reuse of tested code.

Two claims carry numbers: program metrics suggest a Java program can be about four times smaller than the same C++ program, and development can be up to twice as fast. The page gives no further detail on how these were measured.
card.example: A teammate says Java cuts our code to a quarter. The tutorial says about four times smaller, as a suggestion from program metrics. So the sentence is a claim worth checking: for which programs was it measured?
card.rule: Separate what the page asserts from the evidence it gives, and treat figures as claims until you know what was measured.
card.limits: A missing source does not make a figure false; it only means you cannot yet rely on it. Some claims, such as the one-click distribution, have since aged.

concepts.title: Setting up and choosing a route
concepts.question: What must you install before writing Hello World, and which three routes does the tutorial offer for building it?

paragraphs: Before you begin you need the Java SE Development Kit (the JDK), not just the JRE, because the JDK contains the javac compiler. You also need a text editor, such as Notepad on Windows or Pico on Unix-like systems, or an integrated development environment (IDE).

The tutorial gives three routes for the same program: the NetBeans IDE, the Windows command prompt, and a terminal on Solaris, Linux or Mac OS X. It recommends NetBeans over the command line whenever possible, because an IDE greatly simplifies development.
All routes follow the same cycle: write the source, compile it, run it. If a step fails, the tutorial sends you to its page of common problems.
card.example: Priya has a Mac and likes tidy tools. Following the tutorial's advice she installs a JDK and NetBeans and follows the IDE page. A friend who prefers Terminal uses a text editor and follows the Unix page instead.
card.rule: Install a JDK, choose an IDE or a text editor with a command line, then follow the page for that route.
card.limits: The pages name older versions of the JDK, NetBeans and operating systems, so exact menus, versions and screens may differ today.

concepts.title: Compile and run on the command line
concepts.question: Which exact commands compile and run HelloWorldApp from a command line, and what name does each command expect?

paragraphs: Save the code in a file named HelloWorldApp.java. In a command window, change to that folder and compile with javac HelloWorldApp.java. When it succeeds the compiler prints nothing and a new HelloWorldApp.class appears beside the source. You can check with dir on Windows or ls on Unix-style systems.

Run the program with java HelloWorldApp. The launcher wants a class name, so you leave off the .class ending. The Windows page adds -cp . to set the classpath to the current folder; the Unix page omits it.
Both tools are case sensitive, so HelloWorldApp is not the same name as helloworldapp. Type names exactly as shown.
card.example: For a file Welcome.java, the commands are javac Welcome.java and then java Welcome. After the first, a Welcome.class appears. The second never mentions an extension.
card.rule: javac takes the source file name with .java; java takes the class name without an extension.
card.limits: These steps fit a single class with no package line. The tutorial handles bigger programs in later lessons, so do not assume the same typing applies.

concepts.title: Build and run in NetBeans
concepts.question: How do you create, build and run HelloWorldApp in NetBeans, and what do the build messages tell you?

paragraphs: In NetBeans you start with a project, an environment for building and running applications that removes much command-line setup. Choose File, New Project, then Java Application, and name the main class helloworldapp.HelloWorldApp. The IDE generates a skeleton source file that you edit.

Replace the placeholder comment line inside main with the println statement, then save. Choose Run, Build Project. The Output window reports BUILD SUCCESSFUL, or BUILD FAILED with errors shown as links that jump to the faulty line. A successful build writes HelloWorldApp.class.
Choose Run, Run Main Project. The IDE calls the java launcher, and Hello World! appears in the Output window.
card.example: Tom mistypes a semicolon. The build reports BUILD FAILED and lists a clickable error. He double-clicks it, fixes the line, builds again and sees BUILD SUCCESSFUL, then runs the project.
card.rule: In an IDE, create a project, build it, read the Output, then run the main project.
card.limits: Menu names come from an older NetBeans version and may differ today. The build-then-run cycle is the part that holds.

concepts.section: A Closer Look at the "Hello World!" Application
concepts.title: Three kinds of comments
concepts.question: What are the three kinds of comments in Java, and which one does the javadoc tool read?

paragraphs: Comments are notes for human readers, and the compiler ignores them. Java has three forms.

A block comment starts with /* and ends with */. A doc comment starts with /** and ends with */; the compiler skips it as it skips a block comment, but the javadoc tool uses it to build documentation. A line comment starts with // and runs to the end of that line.
In HelloWorldApp, a doc comment above the class describes the program, and a line comment after the println statement explains that line.
card.example: /* old note */ describes a block. /** Counts the words. */ before a method feeds javadoc. int total = 0; // start at zero ends with a line comment that stops at the end of the line.
card.rule: Use block and line comments to explain code to readers and doc comments for javadoc; the compiler ignores all three.
card.limits: A block comment must be closed with its ending marker to be valid. Comments never change what the program does, so they cannot fix a compile error.

concepts.section: A Closer Look at the "Hello World!" Application
concepts.title: The class and the println statement
concepts.question: What must every Java application begin with, and what does System.out.println do?

paragraphs: Every application begins with a class definition. Its basic shape is the keyword class, a name, and the class's code between an opening brace and a closing brace. In HelloWorldApp the name is HelloWorldApp, and the tutorial's pages say the class name must match the file name.

The statement System.out.println, followed by text in parentheses and a semicolon, prints that text on standard output and then moves to a new line. System is a class from the core library, the API; out is the standard output stream; println does the printing.
The tutorial postpones the full story of classes. For now, treat the class as the container for the program's code.
card.example: In a class Greeter, main can call println once with the word Hi and once with the word Bye. The output is two lines: Hi, then Bye.
card.rule: Put the program's code inside a class, and use System.out.println to print a line to standard output.
card.limits: This card shows only the shape of a class; classes are covered in later lessons. println is one output tool among many in the API.

concepts.section: A Closer Look at the "Hello World!" Application
concepts.title: The main method and its arguments
concepts.question: What exact signature must a Java application's starting method have, and what does each part mean?

paragraphs: Every Java application must contain a main method with the signature public static void main(String[] args). It is the entry point: it runs first and calls any other methods the program needs, much as main does in C and C++.
The words public and static are modifiers; void says the method returns no value; main is the required name. The modifiers may come in either order, though convention puts public first.

The one parameter is an array of String. Programmers usually call it args or argv, but any name works. The runtime fills it with command-line arguments, which are strings typed after the class name, as in java MyApp one two.
card.example: A sorting program started as java Sorter -descending receives the string -descending in args. The program can read it and sort in descending order, so users change behaviour without recompiling.
card.rule: Give the starting class a method public static void main(String[] args); everything else runs from there.
card.limits: The parameter name and the order of the modifiers are free. The method name, the void return type and the String array parameter are fixed.

concepts.title: Matching an error to its cause
concepts.question: Given an error message from javac or java, how do you find its cause and fix it?

paragraphs: First note which tool printed the message. Compiler problems come from javac; runtime problems come from java. If javac reports errors, whether a syntax typo such as a missing semicolon or a semantic problem such as using a variable before it has a value, no class file is created until you fix them and recompile.

A message saying javac is not recognized or not found means the system cannot find the compiler. Type the full path to it, or add the JDK's bin folder to PATH. A message saying class names are only accepted if annotation processing is requested means you left off .java.
NoClassDefFoundError means java cannot find the class. Change to the folder holding the class file and check with dir or ls. If it still fails, clear CLASSPATH for the session and retry.

A message such as Could not find or load main class HelloWorldApp.class means you gave a file name instead of a class name. NoSuchMethodError: main means the class lacks public static void main(String[] args).
card.example: A run prints Exception in thread main java.lang.NoSuchMethodError: main. The program compiled, so the fault is at run time: the class that was started has no public static void main(String[] args).
card.rule: Read which tool printed the error, match the message to its cause, and fix that one thing before trying again.
card.limits: The messages belong to the JDK 8 era, and newer JDKs word them differently. Clearing CLASSPATH is a test to try after the folder check, not a first step.

concepts.title: Objects bundle state and behavior
concepts.question: What two features describe any object, and where does a software object keep each?

paragraphs: Everyday things such as a dog, a desk or a lamp can be described by two features. State is the condition the thing is in right now. Behavior is what the thing can do.

A software object follows the same plan. Its state is stored in fields, which some languages call variables. Its behavior is offered through methods, which some languages call functions. Methods work on the fields, and objects communicate with each other by calling methods.
Objects differ in size. A radio has more states and more behaviors than a lamp, and some objects contain other objects.
card.example: Picture a kettle object. Its fields might hold the water temperature and whether it is switched on. Its methods could switch it on, switch it off and report the temperature.
card.rule: Describe an object by its state, stored in fields, and its behavior, offered as methods.
card.limits: Fields and methods are the Java names for these parts. A single stored value with nothing bundled around it is state without related behavior, so it is not yet an object in this sense.

concepts.title: Encapsulation and the benefits of objects
concepts.question: Why does an object keep its fields behind methods, and what does bundling code into objects gain?

paragraphs: Data encapsulation means hiding an object's internal state and allowing all interaction to go through its methods. The tutorial calls it a fundamental principle of object-oriented programming.
The gain is control. A bicycle with six gears can have a gear-changing method that refuses any request below 1 or above 6, so the stored gear always stays valid.

The tutorial names benefits of bundling code into objects. Modularity: an object can be written and kept up independently, then passed around the system. Information hiding: outsiders do not see the details. Code reuse: objects built and tested by others can be used.
card.example: A parking-garage object holds a count of free spaces. Its enterCar method checks that the count is above zero before lowering it, so outside code cannot push the count below zero.
card.rule: Keep state behind methods, so the object itself decides which changes are allowed.
card.limits: Hiding a field protects it only as far as the methods check what they accept. A method that stores any value it receives guards nothing, and the listed benefits are design claims, not guarantees.

concepts.title: A class is a blueprint; objects are its instances
concepts.question: How do many separate objects relate to the one class they are made from?

paragraphs: Many objects are of one kind. Thousands of bicycles can be built from the same plans, so each has the same components. In object-oriented terms, each bicycle is an instance of the class of bicycles. A class is the blueprint from which individual objects are created.
A class declares the fields and methods that each of its instances will have. Every instance gets its own copy of the state, so changing the speed of one bicycle leaves other bicycles alone.
In Java the keyword new creates an instance of a class, and dot notation on a variable holding the instance calls its methods.
card.example: Take a class Lamp with a field on. Two statements, Lamp a = new Lamp(); and Lamp b = new Lamp();, make two lamps. Calling a.turnOn() changes the state of a only, and b is untouched.
card.rule: A class is the shared blueprint, and each object made from it with new is an instance holding its own state.
card.limits: A class only describes what its instances will have. Changing one instance does not change the class or any other instance.

concepts.title: Tracing the Bicycle and BicycleDemo classes
concepts.question: How do you work out what two bicycle objects print after different method calls?

paragraphs: The tutorial's Bicycle class has three fields: cadence starting at 0, speed at 0 and gear at 1. Its methods set the cadence or gear, add to or subtract from the speed, and print all three values. It has no main method.
A second class holds main, the place where a Java application starts. It creates two Bicycle objects with new and calls their methods using dot notation.

To predict the printed result, keep a separate tally for each object. Start from the initial values, apply that object's calls in order, then read the tally. Setting methods replace a value; speedUp and applyBrakes change it by an amount.
card.example: A fresh bicycle receives changeGear(2), speedUp(5), speedUp(3) and applyBrakes(4). Its tally ends with gear 2 and speed 5 plus 3 minus 4, which is 4. Cadence is still 0.
card.rule: Trace each object on its own tally from its starting values, applying its calls in order.
card.limits: A trace is only as good as your knowledge of each method body. A method that replaces a value behaves differently from one that adds to it, so read the bodies before assuming.

concepts.title: Inheritance: superclasses and subclasses
concepts.question: How can one class reuse another class's fields and methods, and what rules limit this in Java?

paragraphs: Different kinds of objects share some features. Mountain, road and tandem bikes all have speed, cadence and gear, yet each adds something of its own. Inheritance lets a class take over the fields and methods of another class, so shared code is written once.

The class being inherited from is the superclass. The class that inherits is the subclass. A subclass is declared with the keyword extends followed by the superclass name, and its own body holds only what makes it different.
Java sets two rules. A class may have only one direct superclass. A superclass may have any number of subclasses.
card.example: Class Vehicle holds a speed field and a brake method. Class Ferry extends Vehicle adds a field for the number of decks. A Ferry object has speed and brake as well as decks.
card.rule: A subclass, declared with extends, receives the fields and methods of its one direct superclass and adds its own.
card.limits: A class cannot have two direct superclasses. A subclass's own source does not show inherited code, so the superclass's state and behavior need clear documentation. Beyond the tutorial: private members and constructors are not inherited.

concepts.title: Interfaces as contracts the compiler checks
concepts.question: What does an interface promise, and how is a class held to it?

paragraphs: The methods an object exposes are its interface to the outside world. Like the buttons on a television, they let you use the device without knowing what is behind the casing.
In the tutorial, an interface in its most common form is a group of related methods with empty bodies. It says what an object can do, not how.

A class takes on an interface with the keyword implements. This is a formal promise, a contract. The compiler checks it: every method in the interface must appear in the class, or the code does not compile.
card.example: Interface Playable lists start() and stop(). Class Radio implements Playable must write a body for both. If it has only start(), the compiler rejects it.
card.rule: An interface lists methods without bodies, and a class that implements it must supply all of them, which the compiler enforces.
card.limits: The tutorial's own sample class needs the keyword public added to each implemented method before it compiles, a point later lessons explain. Interfaces beyond this common form come later.

concepts.title: Packages and the Java API
concepts.question: What is a package for, and where should you look before building something the platform may already offer?

paragraphs: A package is a namespace that organizes a set of related classes and interfaces, much as folders keep related files on a computer. A Java program can have hundreds or thousands of classes, so grouping them keeps it manageable.

The Java platform ships with a large class library made of packages. It is called the Application Programming Interface, or API. Its examples include String for text, File for working with files, Socket for network connections, and classes for buttons and other graphical controls.

Using the library lets you focus on your application's design instead of building the supporting infrastructure. The Java Platform API Specification lists every package, interface, class, field and method, and the tutorial advises bookmarking it.
card.example: A school program might keep its student classes in one package and its timetable classes in another, while using String and File from the platform library.
card.rule: Group related classes and interfaces in packages, and consult the Java API specification before building something general.
card.limits: The tutorial's list of API classes is a sample, not the whole library. The tutorial was written for JDK 8, so later releases bring features it does not show.

concepts.title: Putting the lesson's vocabulary together
concepts.question: Which term names each piece of the lesson, from state to package?

paragraphs: The lesson's terms form a chain. Objects have state and behavior. Fields hold state and methods expose behavior. Hiding state behind methods is data encapsulation. A class is the blueprint for objects.

Common behavior can be defined in a superclass and inherited into a subclass with the keyword extends. A collection of methods with no implementation is an interface, which a class takes on with implements. A package is a namespace organizing classes and interfaces by function.
The tutorial closes with two exercises: write classes for real objects you observed, then give each an interface, make the class implement it, and leave out a method to see the compile error.
card.example: A library program might have a class Book with fields title and borrowed, an interface Lendable listing lend and giveBack, the line class Book implements Lendable, and all of it in a package named library.
card.rule: Link each term to its role: fields to state, methods to behavior, class to blueprint, extends to inheritance, implements to contract, package to namespace.
card.limits: These definitions are the introductory ones from this lesson. Later lessons add detail to terms such as class, interface and package, so treat them as a starting point.

concepts.title: Fields, variables and the four kinds
concepts.question: Which four kinds of variable does Java distinguish, and why is a parameter called a variable but not a field?

paragraphs: Java uses two overlapping words. A field is a variable that belongs to a type and holds the state of an object. The word variable is wider: it covers fields, local variables and parameters. Every field is a variable, but not every variable is a field.

Four kinds exist. An instance variable is a field declared without static. A class variable is a field declared with static. A local variable is declared inside a method body to hold temporary state. A parameter is a variable listed in a method signature, such as args in main.
The kind is settled by where the declaration sits. Nothing marks a local variable except its location. Fields, methods and nested types together are called the members of a type.
card.example: In class Cup, int ml = 250; sits outside any method, so it is a field. In the method pour(int amount), amount is a parameter. Inside pour, int left = ml - amount; declares a local variable that no other method can see.
card.rule: Classify a variable by where it is declared: fields belong to the type, while locals and parameters belong to one method.
card.limits: The tutorial reserves field for the general case and counts locals and parameters as variables only. Other writers may blur the two words, so check which sense is meant.

concepts.title: Instance variables and class variables
concepts.question: How many copies of an instance variable and of a class variable exist, and who sees a change?

paragraphs: An instance variable is created again for every object, so two objects keep separate values and changing one leaves the other alone. A class variable is declared with static and exists once for the whole class, however many objects are made, so every object sees the same value.

Choose an instance variable for state that differs object by object, such as the current speed of one bicycle. Choose a class variable for a fact shared by all, such as the number of gears every model has.
card.example: Class Ticket declares int seat; and static int sold = 0;. Two Ticket objects can hold seat 12 and seat 40. If each constructor adds 1 to sold, both objects report the same total, because only one copy of sold exists.
card.rule: Use an instance variable for per-object state and a static class variable for a value all objects share.
card.limits: Static does not mean unchangeable. A class variable can still change, and the one copy then changes for every object at once.

concepts.title: Rules for legal variable names
concepts.question: Which requirements must a Java variable name meet, as opposed to recommended style?

paragraphs: A name must be a run of letters and digits with no length limit, and it must not contain white space. The first character may be a letter, a dollar sign or an underscore; later characters may also be digits. Names are case-sensitive, so total and Total are two variables.
A name also cannot be a keyword or reserved word, because the language already uses those. Breaking any of these rules is a compile-time error, not only poor style.
card.example: Legal: speed, _cache, max2, Total. Illegal: 2fast (starts with a digit), my-var (hyphen is not allowed), top speed (contains a space), class (reserved word).
card.rule: A legal name starts with a letter, dollar sign or underscore, continues with letters, digits and those two symbols, has no spaces, and is not a reserved word.
card.limits: Legal does not mean advisable. A name can obey every rule and still break the style conventions, which the compiler does not check.

concepts.title: Naming conventions
concepts.question: Which naming habits does the tutorial recommend even though the compiler would accept other legal names?

paragraphs: Conventions are style advice that the compiler does not enforce. Begin names with a letter, and avoid dollar signs and leading underscores. Prefer full descriptive words to cryptic abbreviations, so cadence beats c.

Write a one-word name in lowercase. Write a name of several words in camel case: first word lowercase, each later word starting with a capital, as in gearRatio. Write a constant, meaning a static final field, in capitals with underscores between the words, as in NUM_GEARS. Use underscores nowhere else.
card.example: A game keeps a fixed level cap and a changing score. Following the conventions: static final int MAX_LEVEL = 50; for the constant and int currentScore; for the field. The name currentscore is legal but harder to read, and cs is legal but cryptic.
card.rule: Write one-word names in lowercase, multi-word names in camel case, and constants in capitals with underscores.
card.limits: Conventions are advice, not law. A team may add its own, and the compiler accepts a legal name that ignores them.

concepts.title: The eight primitive types
concepts.question: What are the eight primitive types, and what kind of value and size does each hold?

paragraphs: Java has eight primitive types. Four hold whole numbers and are signed: byte (8 bits), short (16), int (32) and long (64). Two hold fractions: float (32 bits) and double (64 bits). boolean holds true or false. char holds one 16-bit Unicode character and is unsigned.

Ranges grow with size. A byte covers -128 to 127 and a short covers -32,768 to 32,767. An int reaches about 2.1 billion either way and is the default for whole numbers; a long is for anything larger. A char runs from 0 to 65,535.
A String is not a primitive. It is a class, although the language gives it special support. A String object cannot be changed once it exists.
card.example: int age = 36; holds a person age. long seconds = 5_000_000_000L; holds a big count. boolean on = true; holds a flag. char grade = 'B'; holds one character. String name = "Asha"; holds text and is an object, not a primitive.
card.rule: Pick the primitive that matches the value: an integral type by size, float or double for fractions, boolean for flags, char for one character.
card.limits: String is written like a simple value but is a class. Size and range describe storage only, and the size of boolean is not precisely defined.

concepts.title: Choosing a number type
concepts.question: Which number type should you pick by default, when do you narrow or widen it, and why not float or double for money?

paragraphs: For whole numbers the tutorial favours int unless there is a reason not to. Use byte or short mainly to save memory in large arrays, where the small range also tells readers the values stay small. Use long when int is too small. For fractions, double is the default, and float is for saving memory in large arrays.

Neither float nor double should hold exact values such as currency, because they only approximate. For exact decimal work the tutorial points to the BigDecimal class, which it covers in a later lesson.
card.example: A shop stores five million item ratings from 1 to 5 in an array, so byte is a sensible way to save memory. A single loop counter is fine as an int. A price total uses BigDecimal, because a double can drift slightly when many small amounts are added.
card.rule: Default to int and double, narrow to byte, short or float only to save memory in big arrays, widen to long when needed, and use BigDecimal for exact money.
card.limits: Saving memory matters only for large arrays; for a few variables a smaller type gains nothing. BigDecimal itself is outside this lesson.

concepts.title: Default values and uninitialised locals
concepts.question: What does a field hold if you never assign it, and what happens when you read an unassigned local variable?

paragraphs: The compiler gives an unassigned field a default: 0 for the whole-number types (0L for long), 0.0 for float and double, the null character for char, false for boolean, and null for any object, a String included. The tutorial calls relying on these defaults poor style, so assign values explicitly.
Local variables get no default at all. Reading a local before it has been assigned is a compile-time error, so initialise it at declaration or assign it before it is used.
card.example: class Tank { int litres; boolean full; String label; } starts with litres 0, full false and label null. Inside a method, int used; followed by printing used does not compile, since used was never assigned.
card.rule: Fields start with a default set by their type; locals start with nothing and must be assigned before they are read.
card.limits: A default is a placeholder, not a meaningful value for your program. null can be assigned only to a variable of an object type, never to a primitive.

concepts.title: Number, character and text literals
concepts.question: How do you write a long, a float, a hexadecimal or binary number, a char and a String as literals?

paragraphs: A literal is the source-code form of a fixed value, and primitives take literals directly without new. A whole-number literal is an int unless it ends in L, which makes it a long; prefer the capital L, since a lowercase l looks like the digit one. Plain digits are decimal, 0x starts hexadecimal and 0b starts binary.

A decimal literal is a double unless it ends in F or f, which makes it a float. The letter e writes a power of ten. A char literal sits in single quotes and a String literal in double quotes, and the two are not interchangeable.
card.example: int a = 26; int b = 0x1a; int c = 0b11010; all hold 26. long big = 3000000000L; float f = 2.5f; double d = 2.5; char z = 'Z'; String s = "Z"; keeps the text in an object.
card.rule: Show a number literal's type with its marks: L for long, F for float, 0x for hexadecimal, 0b for binary, single quotes for char and double quotes for String.
card.limits: A suffix changes the type, not the quantity. A value too large for its type is still an error, and a plain decimal literal cannot be stored in a float without the f.

concepts.title: Underscores and escape sequences
concepts.question: Where may underscores go inside a number literal, and what do escape sequences let a char or String hold?

paragraphs: Since Java 7 you may put underscores between digits to make long numbers readable, as in 1_000_000. Any count works and the value is unchanged. They must sit between digits: not at the start or end, not beside a decimal point, not before a suffix such as F or L, and not inside or right after a 0x or 0b prefix.

An escape sequence writes a character that is hard to type inside a char or String. A backslash with t, n, r, b or f gives tab, line feed, carriage return, backspace or form feed. A backslash before a quote or a backslash gives that character itself. A Unicode escape is backslash, u and four hexadecimal digits.
card.example: long phone = 555_0142L; is legal and equals 5550142. The forms 555_, 3_.14 and 0x_FF are illegal. Inside a String, backslash-n starts a new line and backslash-u00E9 writes an accented e.
card.rule: Place underscores only between digits for readability, and use a backslash escape for characters you cannot type directly.
card.limits: Underscores change nothing about the value, so they cannot repair a wrong number, and they do not work where a digit is not expected, such as straight after a prefix.

concepts.title: Declaring, creating and reading arrays
concepts.question: How do you declare, create and read an array, and what stays fixed about its size?

paragraphs: An array is a container holding a fixed number of values of one type. The length is set when the array is created and cannot change. Each value is an element found by its index, and indexing starts at 0, so ten elements have indexes 0 to 9.

Declaring int[] scores; only says the variable will refer to an array; it creates nothing. Create one with new, as in scores = new int[10];, or use a braced initializer such as int[] scores = {5, 8, 9};, where the count of values sets the length. Read the size from scores.length, a field with no parentheses.
card.example: int[] temps = {18, 20, 21}; gives temps.length equal to 3, temps[0] equal to 18 and temps[2] equal to 21, which is the last element.
card.rule: Declare with type[], create with new or a braced initializer, count from index 0, and read the size with the length field.
card.limits: A declaration alone gives no array, the length cannot grow afterwards, and an index outside 0 to length minus 1 is invalid. For a size that changes, a different structure is needed.

concepts.title: Arrays of arrays
concepts.question: What is a multidimensional array in Java, and how do you reach one element of it?

paragraphs: A multidimensional array has more than one pair of brackets, such as String[][] names. In Java it is an array whose elements are themselves arrays. To reach one value you give one index for each pair of brackets.

Because every row is its own array, rows can have different lengths. If names holds a row of three titles and a row of two surnames, names[0] has three elements and names[1] has two. The expression names[0][2] picks the third element of the first row.
card.example: int[][] grid = {{1, 2, 3}, {4, 5}}; makes grid.length equal to 2 and grid[0].length equal to 3. grid[1][1] is 5, and grid[1][2] does not exist because the second row has two elements.
card.rule: Treat a two-dimensional array as an array of rows: the first index picks a row and the second picks an element within it.
card.limits: Rows need not match in length, so a rectangle is not guaranteed. Check the length of the row you are reading before indexing it.

concepts.title: Copying arrays
concepts.question: How do System.arraycopy and Arrays.copyOfRange differ in setup and in how they treat the range ends?

paragraphs: System.arraycopy takes five arguments: the source array, the start index in the source, the destination array, the start index in the destination, and the number of elements to copy. The destination must already exist and be big enough, because the method fills it and returns nothing.

Arrays.copyOfRange takes the source, a from index and a to index. It builds a new array and returns it, so nothing is created first. The from index is included and the to index is excluded, so 2 and 9 copy indexes 2 to 8.
The Arrays class also offers sort, fill, equals, toString and binarySearch, which needs a sorted array.
card.example: With src = {10, 20, 30, 40, 50}, System.arraycopy(src, 1, dst, 0, 3) fills a ready-made dst of size 3 with 20, 30, 40. Arrays.copyOfRange(src, 1, 4) returns a new array holding the same three values.
card.rule: Use arraycopy when a destination exists and you know a start and a count; use copyOfRange to get a new array from a start index up to, but excluding, an end index.
card.limits: Neither call lengthens an array; the result has a fixed size. The end index of copyOfRange is excluded, so pass the last wanted index plus one.

concepts.title: Arithmetic, remainder and joining text
concepts.question: What do the arithmetic operators do, and how does the plus sign behave when a String is involved?

paragraphs: The arithmetic operators are +, -, *, / and %. The last is the remainder operator: it divides one operand by another and gives what is left over, so 10 % 7 is 3. The plus sign has a second job. Between strings it joins them into a longer string, which is called concatenation.
The single = is different from all of these. It stores the value on its right in the variable on its left, so result = result - 1; reads the old value, subtracts one and stores the new value back.
card.example: int r = 10 % 7; stores 3. String a = "Hi, "; String b = "Sam"; String c = a + b; makes c hold Hi, Sam. int total = 1 + 2; stores 3.
card.rule: Use + - * / for arithmetic, % for a remainder, = to store, and + between strings to join them.
card.limits: One symbol does two jobs, so check the operand types. And = stores a value; it does not test equality.

concepts.title: Prefix and postfix increment
concepts.question: What value does ++i produce compared with i++, and what do both do to i?

paragraphs: The operators ++ and -- add one to or subtract one from a variable. Each can be written before the variable (prefix) or after it (postfix). Either way, the variable changes by one.

They differ in the value the expression yields. Prefix ++i increases first and yields the new value. Postfix i++ yields the old value and then increases. As a standalone statement the difference is invisible; inside a larger expression it matters.
card.example: int i = 5; int a = ++i; leaves a and i both 6. int j = 5; int b = j++; leaves b at 5 and j at 6.
card.rule: Prefix yields the updated value, postfix yields the original value, and both leave the variable changed.
card.limits: The two forms differ only when the value is used. Packing an increment inside a larger expression makes code harder to read.

concepts.title: Precedence and associativity
concepts.question: In what order does Java evaluate an expression with several operators, and what do parentheses change?

paragraphs: Precedence decides which operator is applied first. In the tutorial table, operators nearer the top bind tighter: multiplication, division and remainder come before addition and subtraction, then comparisons, equality, && , || , the ternary operator, and finally assignment.

Operators in the same row are settled by associativity. Binary operators other than assignment run left to right, so 10 - 4 - 3 means (10 - 4) - 3. Assignment runs right to left, so in a = b = 5 the variable b is assigned first. Parentheses override both rules, and the tutorial recommends them for clarity.
card.example: 2 + 3 * 4 is 14 because * goes first. 10 - 4 - 3 is 3 because of left-to-right order. (2 + 3) * 4 is 20 because parentheses force the sum first.
card.rule: Higher rows go first, equal rows go left to right except assignment, and parentheses make the order explicit.
card.limits: Remembering the whole table invites mistakes. Parentheses cost nothing and help the next reader, even where the default order already gives the right result.

concepts.title: Equality and relational operators
concepts.question: Which operators compare values, what do they produce, and how does == differ from =?

paragraphs: The comparison operators are == (equal), != (not equal), >, >=, < and <=. Each takes two operands and produces a boolean, true or false. Use == to ask whether two values are equal.
The single = is assignment: it stores the right-hand value in the left-hand variable. Writing an assignment where a test was intended is a classic mistake.
card.example: With int a = 1; int b = 2; the test a == b is false, a != b is true, a < b is true and a >= b is false. The statement a = b; changes a to 2 and tests nothing.
card.rule: Use == and != to test equality, the ordering operators to test order, and keep = for storing.
card.limits: These examples use primitive values. Comparing objects is a different matter that the tutorial treats later.

concepts.title: Short-circuit logic
concepts.question: How do && and || decide whether to evaluate their right operand, and why does that protect code?

paragraphs: The conditional AND, &&, is true only when both sides are true. The conditional OR, ||, is true when at least one side is. Both stop early: the right operand is evaluated only if it can still change the result.

So with && a false left side skips the right side, and with || a true left side skips it. That lets you put a safety check first, for example testing that a value exists before using it in the second condition.
card.example: In name != null && name.length() > 0, a null name makes the left side false, so name.length() is never called and no error occurs. Reversing the order would call length() on null and fail.
card.rule: Put the guard on the left, because the right operand runs only when the left side has not already settled the result.
card.limits: Skipping applies to side effects on the right as well, so do not hide needed actions there. The order of the operands changes the behaviour.

concepts.title: The conditional operator ?:
concepts.question: What does the three-part conditional operator do, and when is it better than an if-else?

paragraphs: The ternary operator ?: has three operands: a condition, a value for the true case and a value for the false case. The form condition ? a : b gives a when the condition is true and b otherwise. It is shorthand for a simple if-then-else that chooses a value.
The tutorial favours it when it makes code more readable, usually with compact expressions that have no side effects. When the branches are long or do several things, an if-else is clearer.
card.example: int speed = isRaining ? 40 : 60; stores 40 when isRaining is true and 60 otherwise. The long form needs an if, an else and two assignments.
card.rule: Use ?: to pick one of two values with a compact, side-effect-free test; use if-else for anything longer.
card.limits: It yields a value, so each branch must supply one; it cannot hold a sequence of actions. Nesting several of them quickly becomes hard to read.

concepts.title: The type test instanceof
concepts.question: What does instanceof test, and does it look at the declared type or at the actual object?

paragraphs: The instanceof operator checks whether an object is an instance of a given type: a class, a superclass of its class, or an interface its class implements. The result is true or false.

The test uses the real type of the object, not the declared type of the variable holding it. An object created as a Child but held in a Parent variable still passes the tests for Child, Parent and any interface Child implements. An object created as a plain Parent fails the Child test.
card.example: Suppose Dog extends Animal and implements Pet. With Animal a = new Dog(); both a instanceof Dog and a instanceof Pet are true. With Animal b = new Animal(); b instanceof Dog is false.
card.rule: x instanceof T is true when the object x refers to has type T, a subtype of T, or implements T, whatever the declared type of x.
card.limits: The test is about the actual object, so it can be true even when the variable has a broader declared type. It checks type, not equality of values.

concepts.title: Bitwise and shift operators
concepts.question: What do the bitwise and shift operators do to the bits of a whole number?

paragraphs: Bitwise operators work on the individual bits of whole-number values. The operator ~ flips every bit. The operator & keeps a bit only when both operands have it set. The operator | keeps a bit when either has it set. The operator ^ keeps a bit when exactly one has it set.

Shift operators slide the bits. The operator << shifts left and fills with zeros. The operator >> shifts right and copies the sign bit into the gap, so negative numbers stay negative. The operator >>> shifts right and fills with zeros whatever the sign. The tutorial notes that these operators are less common.
card.example: 0x2222 & 0x000F keeps only the lowest four bits of 0x2222, which gives 2. Because & keeps only matching bits, it is the usual way to mask out the part of a value you want.
card.rule: Use & to mask, | to set bits, ^ to find differences, ~ to flip, << and >> to shift, and >>> to shift in zeros.
card.limits: Rarely needed, and unclear when used for ordinary arithmetic. Reach for them for flags and low-level data.

concepts.title: Expressions and their types
concepts.question: What is an expression, what type does it have, and how do you control the order inside it?

paragraphs: An expression is a construct built from variables, operators and method calls that evaluates to a single value. Its type depends on its parts: an assignment to an int variable yields an int, a comparison yields a boolean, and joining text yields a String.

A compound expression combines smaller expressions, as in 1 * 2 * 3. When the order could change the meaning, as in x + y / 100, say what you intend. The tutorial recommends parentheses because they make the grouping explicit and the code easier to maintain.
card.example: In count + 1 > limit, the part count + 1 is an int expression and the whole is a boolean expression. Writing (x + y) / 100 divides the sum, while x + y / 100 divides only y, since division ranks higher than addition.
card.rule: An expression computes one value of a definite type; use parentheses to make the grouping of a compound expression explicit.
card.limits: Parentheses control grouping but not the meaning of the parts. An expression can stand alone as a statement only in a few cases.

concepts.title: Statements and their kinds
concepts.question: What turns an expression into a statement, what are the three kinds, and which expressions qualify?

paragraphs: A statement is a complete unit of execution, roughly like a sentence, and ends with a semicolon. Java has three kinds: expression statements, declaration statements and control flow statements.

Only four kinds of expression become a statement when a semicolon is added: an assignment, any use of ++ or --, a method call, and an object creation. A declaration statement introduces a variable. Control flow statements, such as if and for, decide the order in which other statements run.
card.example: aValue = 8933.234; is an assignment statement. aValue++; is an increment statement. System.out.println(aValue); is a method call. Bicycle b = new Bicycle(); creates an object. double c = 1.5; is a declaration. The line 3 + 4; is not a statement.
card.rule: End an assignment, an increment or decrement, a method call or an object creation with a semicolon to make a statement; declare variables with declaration statements.
card.limits: Not every expression can stand alone: a bare sum or comparison with a semicolon is rejected, since it does nothing.

concepts.title: Blocks
concepts.question: What is a block, and where may it appear?

paragraphs: A block is a group of zero or more statements enclosed in balanced braces. Wherever Java accepts a single statement, it also accepts a block, so a block lets one place hold several statements.
The most familiar use is with if and else: each branch can be a block holding as many statements as needed. Braces must balance, so every opening brace needs a closing one.
card.example: In if (ok) { count++; log(count); } else { reset(); } each branch is a block. With ok true, the first block runs both statements and the else block is skipped.
card.rule: Wrap statements in braces to use a group of them wherever one statement is allowed.
card.limits: Without braces an if governs only the next single statement. A block groups statements but does not decide whether they run; the controlling statement does.

concepts.title: if, else and else-if chains
concepts.question: How does an else-if chain choose a branch, and why does the order of its tests matter?

paragraphs: The if-then statement runs its block only when a boolean test is true. The if-then-else statement adds a second path for when the test is false. To choose among several options, chain further tests with else if.

The tests are checked from the top down, and the first true one wins: its block runs and every remaining test, including the final else, is skipped. A value that satisfies several tests still takes only the first matching branch, so range tests must be ordered with care.
card.example: With score 76 and tests >= 90, >= 80, >= 70, >= 60 and a final else, the first two fail and the third passes, so the grade is C. The test >= 60 is also true for 76 but is never evaluated.
card.rule: In an else-if chain only the first true test runs, so order range tests from the most restrictive to the least.
card.limits: Reordering the tests can change the result even though each test is still correct alone. Use separate if statements, not a chain, when several branches should all run.

concepts.title: Which if an else belongs to
concepts.question: Which if does an else belong to, and how do braces make the meaning obvious?

paragraphs: An else pairs with the nearest earlier if that does not yet have an else. The compiler ignores indentation completely, so a layout that suggests another pairing is misleading to the reader.

Braces remove the doubt. If the then clause is a single statement the braces may be left off, but when a second statement is added later only the first one stays under the if, and the compiler gives no warning. Many programmers therefore always use braces.
card.example: In if (n >= 0) if (n == 0) first(); else second(); third(); with n equal to 3, the else belongs to the inner if, so second() and third() run. With braces around the inner if, the pairing is visible at a glance.
card.rule: Pair each else with the nearest unmatched if, and use braces so the layout and the meaning agree.
card.limits: Indentation helps readers but does not decide meaning. Braces do not change the default pairing; they let you choose it explicitly.

concepts.title: The switch statement
concepts.question: What can a switch test, how does it choose a path, and when is if-else the better tool?

paragraphs: A switch statement selects one of many paths according to a single expression. That expression may be a byte, short, char or int, an enum, or a String, and the wrappers Character, Byte, Short and Integer also work. Each possible value gets a case label, and default covers every other value.

Use switch when one expression is compared with single values. An if-else chain is better for ranges and general conditions. A String is matched as if by equals, and a null expression throws a NullPointerException, so guard against null.
card.example: switch (month) { case 1: name = January; break; case 2: name = February; break; default: name = Invalid; break; } with month equal to 2 gives February. Labels can share a block: case 4: case 6: days = 30; break;
card.rule: Use switch to select among single values of one expression, with default for the rest; use if-else for ranges.
card.limits: A switch cannot test ranges, or long, boolean, float or double expressions, and a null String expression fails at run time. This lesson covers the classic colon form of switch.

concepts.title: break and fall-through in switch
concepts.question: What does break do inside a switch, and what happens when it is left out?

paragraphs: After the switch finds a matching case label, it runs the statements from that label onward. A break statement ends the switch, and control continues after the switch block.

Without break, execution falls through: the statements of each following case run in order, ignoring those labels, until a break or the end. This is occasionally wanted, as when collecting a month and all later months, but usually it is a bug. The tutorial suggests a break at the end of the last case too, which makes later edits safer.
card.example: With n equal to 2 in switch (n) { case 1: out(a); case 2: out(b); case 3: out(c); break; case 4: out(d); }, the output is b then c. A break after out(b) would stop it at b.
card.rule: End each case with break unless you want execution to continue into the next case.
card.limits: Fall-through starts only at the matched label and runs onward, not backward. Stacked labels with no statements between them are not a bug; they share one block.

concepts.title: while and do-while loops
concepts.question: When does a while loop test its condition compared with do-while, and how often must each body run?

paragraphs: The while statement repeats a block as long as its condition, which must be a boolean, is true. The condition is tested before each pass, so if it is false at the start the body never runs.

The do-while statement tests its condition at the bottom, so its body always runs at least once, and a semicolon follows the condition. Writing while (true) makes an infinite loop, which needs an exit inside the body, such as break or return.
card.example: int n = 5; while (n < 3) { show(n); } shows nothing. int m = 5; do { show(m); } while (m < 3); shows 5 once.
card.rule: Use while when the body may need to run zero times, and do-while when it must run at least once.
card.limits: Both repeat only while the condition stays true, so the body must change something the condition reads, or the loop never ends. A do-while runs once even if the condition is false at the start.

concepts.title: The for statement and enhanced for
concepts.question: In what order do the parts of a for statement run, and how does the enhanced for differ?

paragraphs: The for statement has three parts in its header. The initialization runs once at the start. The termination test is checked before every pass and ends the loop when false. The increment runs after every pass. Any part may be left out, and for (;;) loops forever.

A variable declared in the initialization is visible only inside the loop. The enhanced for, written for (int item : numbers), visits each element of an array or collection in turn. The tutorial recommends it whenever possible, because it is compact and easy to read.
card.example: for (int i = 1; i < 4; i++) show(i); shows 1, 2 and 3, since the test fails when i reaches 4. With int[] a = {5, 6}; the loop for (int v : a) show(v); shows 5 then 6.
card.rule: In a for loop initialise once, test before each pass and increment after each pass; use the enhanced for to visit every element.
card.limits: The enhanced for supplies each element but not its index. A counter declared in the header cannot be used after the loop.

concepts.title: break and continue, plain and labeled
concepts.question: How do break and continue alter a loop, and what do labels add?

paragraphs: An unlabeled break ends the innermost switch or loop at once, and execution continues after it. An unlabeled continue skips the rest of the current pass: in a for loop the increment runs next, and in a while loop the condition is tested next.

In nested loops an unlabeled statement affects only the innermost one. A labeled break names an outer statement and ends it, continuing after it. A labeled continue moves to the next pass of the named outer loop. A label is an identifier and a colon placed before the loop.
card.example: outer: for (i = 1; i <= 3; i++) for (j = 1; j <= 3; j++) if (i * j == 4) break outer; ends both loops at once. A plain break would end only the inner loop, and the outer loop would carry on.
card.rule: Use break to leave a loop early, continue to skip to the next pass, and a label to aim either at an outer loop.
card.limits: Unlabeled forms reach only the innermost loop. A labeled break resumes after the labeled statement, not at the label. Overuse makes the flow hard to follow.

concepts.title: The three families of control flow, and return
concepts.question: Which family of control flow fits a task, and what does return do?

paragraphs: Statements normally run from top to bottom, and control flow statements change that. The tutorial groups them into three families: decision-making (if-then, if-then-else, switch), looping (for, while, do-while) and branching (break, continue, return).

The return statement leaves the current method at once and hands control back to the caller. In a method with a return type it carries a value of a matching type; in a void method it is written with no value, often as an early exit. Code after it on the same path does not run.
card.example: static void show(int n) { if (n <= 0) return; print(n); } shows nothing for -3 and 7 for 7. static int square(int x) { return x * x; } gives 16 for 4.
card.rule: Pick a decision statement to choose a path, a loop to repeat, and a branching statement to jump out or skip; return leaves the method.
card.limits: The families overlap: loops contain decisions, and a return inside a loop ends the whole method, not only the loop. Choose the simplest statement that states the intent.

concepts.title: What a class holds
concepts.question: What three kinds of member does a class hold, and what job does each one do?

paragraphs: A class is a template for objects. Its body can hold three kinds of things: fields, which record the state of each object; methods, which give the object its behaviour; and constructors, which set up a new object at the moment it is created.

A bicycle class, for instance, would have fields for gear, cadence and speed, methods that change them, and a constructor that supplies starting values. Keeping data together with the operations on that data is the point of a class.

A class can also build on another one with the extends keyword. The subclass inherits the fields and methods of its parent and adds its own. Its constructor can pass the inherited setup to the parent constructor by calling super with the needed values.
card.rule: A class declares fields for state, methods for behaviour and constructors for setting up new objects.
card.limits: A class is only a template: no state exists until an object is made from it. A subclass adds to its parent and cannot remove what it inherits.
card.example: class Lamp { boolean on; Lamp(boolean start) { on = start; } void toggle() { on = !on; } }  The field on is state, toggle is behaviour, and the constructor gives each new lamp its first value.

concepts.title: Parts of a class declaration
concepts.question: In what order do the parts of a class declaration appear, and which parts are required?

paragraphs: Only three things are required to declare a class: the class keyword, a name and a body in braces. Everything else is optional, so a very short declaration is already valid.

When the optional parts are present they come in a fixed order: modifiers such as public, then the class name, then extends and one parent class, then implements and a comma-separated list of interfaces, then the body. By convention the name starts with a capital letter.
A class can extend only one parent, but it may implement several interfaces.
card.rule: Write modifiers, the name, an optional extends with one parent, an optional implements with a list, then the braced body.
card.limits: The order is fixed, so implements cannot come before extends. Single inheritance applies to parent classes only. What extends and implements mean in depth is left to a later lesson.
card.example: public class Gadget extends Device implements Chargeable, Trackable { }  Read left to right: a modifier, the name, a single parent, then two interfaces separated by a comma.

concepts.title: Fields, locals and parameters
concepts.question: What are the three kinds of variable in Java, and where is each one declared?

paragraphs: Java uses the word variable for three different things. A field is declared in a class, outside any method. A local variable is declared inside a method or another block of code. A parameter is declared in the parentheses of a method's signature.

Every variable also has a type, which falls into one of two groups. Primitive types such as int, float and boolean hold a plain value. Reference types, such as strings, arrays and objects, give access to something held elsewhere.
card.rule: Tell the three kinds apart by where each is declared: in the class, in a block, or in a method signature.
card.limits: The three kinds follow the same naming rules, so a name does not reveal its kind. Only the place of declaration does.
card.example: class Meter { int total; void add(int amount) { int doubled = amount * 2; total += doubled; } }  Here total is a field, amount is a parameter and doubled is a local variable.

concepts.title: Private fields, public methods
concepts.question: Why does the tutorial recommend private fields with public methods, and how does an outside class then reach the data?

paragraphs: A field declaration has up to three parts in order: any modifiers, the type, then the name. The leftmost modifier controls access. A public field can be reached from every class, while a private field can be reached only from inside its own class.

The tutorial recommends private fields as a matter of encapsulation. Other classes cannot then read or change them directly. The class offers public methods instead: getters that return a value, and setters or action methods that change it.
Methods can also protect the object. A bicycle can offer a getter for speed and methods to speed up or brake, but no setter, so outside code can change speed only through those controlled actions.
card.rule: Keep fields private and let other classes work with the object through public methods.
card.limits: The tutorial's own early examples use public fields only to stay short. Private is a recommendation about design: it does not make a field unreadable to its own class or to nested classes inside it.
card.example: class Thermostat { private int target; public int getTarget() { return target; } public void raise(int by) { target += by; } }  Outside code reads the target through getTarget and changes it only through raise.

concepts.title: Naming conventions
concepts.question: What naming conventions does the tutorial give for classes and methods?

paragraphs: Fields, local variables and parameters follow the same naming rules, which the earlier lesson on language basics covers. Class names and method names follow those rules too, plus one extra convention each.

A class name starts with a capital letter, as in Bicycle. A method name is a verb in lower case, or a name that begins with a lower-case verb followed by adjectives or nouns, with each later word capitalized, as in applyBrake, speedUp, getSpeed or isEmpty.
card.rule: Start class names with a capital letter and method names with a lower-case verb.
card.limits: These are conventions, not rules enforced by the compiler: a method named Total would compile. They exist so that readers can tell what a name stands for.
card.example: A class that models a parking meter might be called ParkingMeter, with methods insertCoin, resetTimer and isExpired.

concepts.title: Anatomy of a method
concepts.question: Which parts make up a method declaration, which are required, and what is the signature?

paragraphs: A method declaration can have six parts in order: modifiers, a return type (or void if nothing is returned), a name, a parameter list in parentheses, an exception list, and a body in braces. Only the return type, the name, the parentheses and the body are required.
The signature of a method is its name plus the types of its parameters, in order. Modifiers, the return type, the exception list and the parameter names are not part of the signature.
card.rule: A method needs a return type, name, parentheses and body, and it is identified by its signature of name plus parameter types.
card.limits: Signature covers only name and parameter types, so two methods can look alike in other ways yet clash. The exception list is explained in a later lesson.
card.example: public double scale(double value, int times) { return value * times; }  The signature is scale(double, int). The return type double and the names value and times are not in it.

concepts.title: Overloading methods
concepts.question: When may two methods in one class share a name, and how does the compiler tell them apart?

paragraphs: Overloading means that several methods in the same class share one name. It is allowed when their parameter lists differ in number, in types, or in both. A drawing class could offer draw for a string, draw for an int, and draw for an int together with a double.

The compiler tells overloaded methods apart by their signatures. It ignores the return type, so two methods with the same name and the same parameter types clash even when they return different things.
The tutorial adds a caution: use overloading sparingly, because many methods behind one name can make code much harder to read.
card.rule: Methods may share a name only when their parameter lists differ in number or types.
card.limits: Different parameter names or a different return type do not create an overload. Even legal overloads can hurt readability, which is why the tutorial recommends restraint.
card.example: void log(String text), void log(int code) and void log(String text, int code) can sit side by side. A method int log(String text) could not join them, since its signature repeats the first.

concepts.title: Declaring constructors
concepts.question: How does a constructor declaration differ from a method declaration, and how does a call choose among several?

paragraphs: A constructor declaration looks like a method declaration with two differences: it is named exactly like its class, and it has no return type. Its parameters carry starting values, which its body assigns to the fields.

A constructor runs when new is used with the class name, as in new Bicycle(30, 0, 8). A class may have several constructors, including one that takes no arguments and sets fixed defaults, as long as their parameter lists differ. Two constructors with the same parameter types cause a compile-time error.
Java chooses among them by the arguments in the call, just as it does for overloaded methods.
card.rule: A constructor has the class's name and no return type, and the arguments of the new call select which one runs.
card.limits: Two constructors with the same parameter types cannot coexist, whatever the parameter names. A constructor is part of making a new object, so it is not a way to change one that already exists.
card.example: class Badge { int level; Badge(int start) { level = start; } Badge() { level = 1; } }  The call new Badge(3) starts at level 3, while new Badge() uses the fixed default of 1.

concepts.title: The default constructor
concepts.question: What happens when a class declares no constructor, and when can that cause a compile error?

paragraphs: You are not required to write a constructor. If a class declares none, the compiler supplies a default constructor that takes no arguments. It calls the no-argument constructor of the superclass.

A class with no declared parent has Object as its parent, and Object has a no-argument constructor, so nothing goes wrong. If the parent is another class that lacks a no-argument constructor, the compiler reports an error.
Constructors also carry access modifiers, which decide which classes may call them. If other classes cannot call any constructor of a class, they cannot create its objects directly.
card.rule: With no declared constructor a no-argument default is added, and it needs the parent to have a no-argument constructor.
card.limits: The compiler adds it only for a class that declares no constructor at all. It takes no arguments, so it cannot receive starting values from a caller.
card.example: class Empty { } still has one constructor, supplied by the compiler. A class Child that extends Parent fails to compile when Parent declares only Parent(int size), until Child declares a constructor that passes a size up.

concepts.title: Parameters, arguments and varargs
concepts.question: How do parameters differ from arguments, and how does a varargs parameter work?

paragraphs: Parameters are the variables listed in a method or constructor declaration. Arguments are the actual values supplied in a call. Arguments must match the parameters in type and order. Any type may be a parameter, primitive or reference, including arrays and objects.

Varargs let a method accept any number of values of one type, including none. Put an ellipsis after the type of the last parameter. Inside the method the parameter acts like an array, and a caller may pass separate values or an array.
Because a caller may pass few values, code that indexes into the varargs array should check its length first.
card.rule: Parameters are the names in the declaration, arguments are the values in the call, and a final ellipsis parameter takes any number of values.
card.limits: The ellipsis form belongs to the last parameter only. A method that uses it cannot assume how many values will arrive.
card.example: int sum(int... nums) can be called as sum(), sum(4) or sum(1, 2, 3). Inside the method, nums.length tells how many values arrived.

concepts.title: Parameters that shadow fields
concepts.question: What does it mean for a parameter to shadow a field, and which name refers to which?

paragraphs: A parameter name must be unique in its scope: it cannot repeat another parameter of the same method or a local variable declared inside it. A parameter may, however, share its name with a field.

In that case the parameter shadows the field: inside the method the plain name refers to the parameter. The field can still be reached through a qualified name such as this.x, where this stands for the current object.
Shadowing makes code harder to read, so the tutorial says it is conventionally used only in constructors and in methods that set a field.
card.rule: A parameter that shares a field's name hides the field inside the method, and this.name reaches the field.
card.limits: Shadowing hides the field only inside that method. A parameter cannot share a name with another parameter or a local of its own method, and convention limits shadowing to constructors and setters.
card.example: class Circle { int x; void setOrigin(int x) { x = x; } }  Both x names are the parameter, so the field never changes. Writing this.x = x stores the argument in the field.

concepts.title: Passing arguments by value
concepts.question: When a method changes its parameter, what does the caller see for primitive arguments and for objects?

paragraphs: Java passes every argument by value, which means the method receives a copy. For a primitive argument the copy is the number itself, so assigning a new value to the parameter changes only the local copy. When the method returns, the caller's variable still holds its old value.

For an object or array argument the copy is of the reference. The method can follow that reference and change the object's fields, and the caller sees those changes afterwards. But if the method assigns a different object to the parameter, only its local copy of the reference moves.
The caller's variable therefore keeps pointing at the original object, even though that object may have been changed.
card.rule: Arguments are copied: a method can change the object a reference points to, but it cannot repoint the caller's variable.
card.limits: Changing an object through a parameter needs access to its fields or methods, so private fields stay protected. Reassigning the parameter never reaches the caller, whatever the type.
card.example: void shift(Point p) { p.x = p.x + 5; p = new Point(0, 0); }  After the call, the caller's point has x raised by 5, and the caller's variable still points to that same point, not to the new one.

concepts.title: Declare, instantiate, initialize
concepts.question: What three jobs does a statement like Point origin = new Point(23, 94) perform?

paragraphs: A program usually creates many objects, and they do their work by calling one another's methods. An object's life has three stages: it is created, it is used, and it is cleaned up once it is no longer needed.

A creation statement such as Point origin = new Point(23, 94); does three jobs. Declaration associates a variable name with a type. Instantiation uses the new keyword to create the object. Initialization is the constructor call after new, which sets the object's starting values.
Creating an object is also called instantiating its class, and the object is an instance of that class.
card.rule: A creation statement declares a variable, instantiates the class with new, and initializes the object through a constructor call.
card.limits: The three jobs can be split over separate statements, with the declaration first and new used later. A declaration on its own performs only the first job.
card.example: Rectangle box = new Rectangle(50, 100);  The words Rectangle box declare the variable, new brings the object into being, and Rectangle(50, 100) initializes its width and height.

concepts.title: A declaration creates no object
concepts.question: Does declaring a reference variable create an object, and what happens if you use it before assigning one?

paragraphs: Declaring a variable of a class type, such as Point origin;, tells the compiler that the name will refer to a Point. It does not create one. Until you assign an object, the variable has no determined value and refers to nothing.

Using such a variable before it is assigned is a compiler error. Only the new operator creates an object. A primitive declaration is different, because it reserves memory for the value itself, while a reference declaration reserves nothing for an object.
card.rule: Declaring a reference variable creates no object, so assign one made with new before you use it.
card.limits: The rule is about reference variables. A primitive declaration is different because it reserves space for the value itself.
card.example: Rectangle shape; shape.width = 40;  fails to compile, because shape refers to nothing yet. After shape = new Rectangle(); the assignment is fine.

concepts.title: What the new operator does
concepts.question: What does the new operator do, and where can the reference it returns be used?

paragraphs: The new operator does three things: it allocates memory for a new object, it invokes the constructor named after it, and it returns a reference to the memory it allocated. Its single operand looks like a constructor call, such as Point(23, 94).

Usually the returned reference is stored in a variable of a suitable type. It can also be used directly inside an expression. For example, new Rectangle().height creates a rectangle, reads its height field, and keeps no variable for the object.
card.rule: new allocates memory, runs a constructor and returns a reference that can be stored or used straight away.
card.limits: A reference that is neither stored nor kept is gone after the expression, so that object cannot be reached again afterwards.
card.example: int a = new Rectangle(100, 50).getArea();  This builds a 100 by 50 rectangle, calls its getArea method and stores 5000. No variable ever holds the rectangle.

concepts.title: Several names for one object
concepts.question: If two variables refer to the same object, what happens when one of them changes it?

paragraphs: An object can have more than one reference. When one variable is assigned another variable's reference, or a reference is stored in a field, both names lead to the same object rather than to copies.
