In the tutorial's demo, the variable originOne is passed to a Rectangle constructor and stored as the rectangle's origin. The origin field and originOne now refer to one Point, so a change made through either name is visible through the other.
Separate uses of new, in contrast, give separate objects.
card.rule: Variables that hold the same reference share one object, so a change through one is seen through the others.
card.limits: Only variables given the same reference share an object. Each separate new makes a fresh object, and assigning a different object to a variable ends the sharing for that variable.
card.example: Point a = new Point(1, 1); Rectangle r = new Rectangle(a, 3, 3); r.move(5, 5);  After the move, a.x is 5, because the rectangle's origin and a are the same Point.

concepts.title: Reaching fields with the dot
concepts.question: How is a field referred to inside its class and outside it, and does each object have its own copy?

paragraphs: Inside its own class, a field is referred to by its simple name, such as width. From outside the class you need an object reference, a dot and the field name, such as rectOne.width. Using the simple name from another class is a compiler error, because the field exists only inside objects.
Objects of one class each have their own copy of the instance fields. Reading or writing rectOne.width touches only that object's width, and rectTwo has a separate width of its own.
Outside code can use a field this way only if the field's access modifier permits it.
card.rule: Use the simple name inside the class and reference.field outside it, and remember that each object keeps its own copy of instance fields.
card.limits: Private fields cannot be reached this way from other classes. The dot also needs a reference that actually refers to an object.
card.example: If Rectangle declares public int width, other code writes rectOne.width = 40 to change one rectangle, and rectTwo.width stays as it was.

concepts.title: Calling methods on objects
concepts.question: How do you call a method on an object, and what can you do with the value it returns?

paragraphs: To call a method, write an object reference, a dot, the method name and the arguments in parentheses, with empty parentheses when there are none. The tutorial likens this to sending the object a message.

The part before the dot can be any expression that yields an object reference, including a new expression. If the method returns a value, the call can be used wherever that value fits: assigned to a variable, tested in a decision, or used to control a loop.
card.rule: Call methods with reference.method(arguments), and use any returned value like any other value of its type.
card.limits: A call on a variable that refers to no object cannot work, and from outside the class only the methods its access modifiers allow can be called.
card.example: int area = rectOne.getArea(); rectTwo.move(40, 72);  The first call asks rectOne for its area and stores it. The second tells rectTwo to change its origin and returns nothing.

concepts.title: Cleaning up unused objects
concepts.question: When is an object eligible for garbage collection, and who decides when it is actually removed?

paragraphs: Java programs do not destroy objects themselves. The runtime does it automatically, a process called garbage collection. An object becomes eligible for collection when no references to it remain.

References usually disappear when the variable holding them goes out of scope. You can also drop one deliberately by setting the variable to null. When several references lead to one object, every one of them must be dropped.
The collector runs periodically and frees memory when it judges the time is right. A program does not control when.
card.rule: An object is eligible for collection once no references to it remain, and the runtime reclaims it at a time of its own choosing.
card.limits: Being eligible is not the same as being removed, since the collector picks the moment. Dropping one reference does nothing while another still reaches the object.
card.example: Tray t = new Tray(); Tray u = t; t = null;  The Tray is still reachable through u. Setting u = null as well makes it eligible.

concepts.title: Returning from a method
concepts.question: When does a method return to its caller, and what must it hand back?

paragraphs: A method returns to its caller when it completes all its statements, reaches a return statement, or throws an exception, whichever happens first. Exceptions are covered in a later lesson.

The declared return type decides what must come back. A void method returns no value, needs no return statement, and may use a bare return; to leave early. Returning a value from a void method is a compiler error.

Any other method must return a value of its declared type. A method declared to return an int cannot return a boolean. The value can be a primitive, such as the int from getArea, or a reference to an object, such as a Bicycle.
card.rule: A void method returns nothing, and every other method must return a value of its declared type.
card.limits: A bare return; belongs to void methods. A return statement ends the method at once, so statements after it on that path never run.
card.example: int abs(int n) { if (n < 0) { return -n; } return n; }  has two return statements. A void method such as void log(int n) may stop early with return; but may not hand back a number.

concepts.title: Returning classes and interfaces
concepts.question: When a method's return type is a class or an interface, which objects may it actually return?

paragraphs: When the return type is a class, the returned object must be an instance of that class or of one of its subclasses. If ImaginaryNumber extends Number, a method declared to return Number may return an ImaginaryNumber. It may not return a plain Object, because an Object might be something unrelated, such as a string.
An overriding method in a subclass may narrow the return type to a more specific class. This is called a covariant return type. The narrowing goes toward subclasses, not the other way.
When the return type is an interface name, the returned object must be an instance of a class that implements that interface.
card.rule: A returned object must be an instance of the declared class or a subclass, or of a class that implements the declared interface.
card.limits: The tutorial marks this as an advanced topic that builds on inheritance, covered later. A broader type than the declared one is not accepted.
card.example: Trucks and Bikes both extend Vehicle. A method declared to return Vehicle may return either. A method declared to return Truck may not return a Bike or a plain Vehicle.

concepts.title: The current object
concepts.question: What does this refer to, and where can it be used?

paragraphs: Inside an instance method or a constructor, this is a reference to the current object, the one whose method or constructor is running. Through it you can reach any member of that object.

Its most common use is to separate a field from a parameter with the same name. In a constructor Point(int x, int y), the statement this.x = x; copies the parameter into the field. If the parameters were named a and b instead, plain x = a would do the same job with no this.
card.rule: this names the current object, and this.name reaches that object's member when a plain name is shadowed.
card.limits: Without shadowing, the plain name already reaches the field. this is unavailable in static methods, and this(...) as the first statement of a constructor calls another constructor of the same class.
card.example: class Score { int points; void add(int points) { this.points = this.points + points; } }  Here this.points is the field, while points alone is the amount passed in.

concepts.title: Constructors calling constructors
concepts.question: How can one constructor reuse another in the same class, and where must that call appear?

paragraphs: Inside a constructor, the word this followed by an argument list in parentheses calls another constructor of the same class. The compiler chooses the target by the number and types of the arguments, as for any constructor call.

A common pattern puts the real initialization in one full constructor and lets shorter ones call it. In the tutorial's Rectangle, the no-argument constructor calls the four-argument one with 0, 0, 1, 1, and the two-argument one passes 0, 0 for the position.
Such a call must be the first statement in the constructor.
card.rule: Start a constructor with this(...) to hand its work to another constructor of the same class.
card.limits: This form reuses constructors within one class; reaching a parent's constructor uses super instead. Placing the call after other statements is an error.
card.example: class Box { int w; int h; Box() { this(1, 1); } Box(int w, int h) { this.w = w; this.h = h; } }  A call new Box() ends up with w and h both 1, by way of the second constructor.

concepts.title: The four access levels
concepts.question: Which code can reach a member under public, protected, no modifier and private?

paragraphs: Access modifiers decide which other code may use a class or a member. A top-level class is either public, visible everywhere, or has no modifier, which makes it visible only inside its own package, a named group of related classes.

Members have four levels. Public: all classes. Protected: the same package, plus subclasses in other packages. No modifier, called package-private: the same package only. Private: only the declaring class.

Ordered from widest to narrowest, public reaches the class, its package, its subclasses and the world; protected reaches all but the world; no modifier reaches the class and its package; private reaches the class alone.
card.rule: Each access level opens a smaller circle of code, from public for everyone down to private for the declaring class only.
card.limits: Protected reaches a subclass in another package, but a non-subclass there gets nothing. No modifier is easily confused with public, since it has no keyword. Subclasses are covered in a later lesson.
card.example: Alpha has a method with no modifier. Beta, in the same package, can call it, but Gamma, in another package, cannot. Declared protected, it can also be called from a subclass of Alpha in another package, while Gamma itself still cannot.

concepts.title: Choosing an access level
concepts.question: What does the tutorial advise when choosing an access level, and why should public fields be rare?

paragraphs: The tutorial advises the most restrictive access level that still makes sense for each member. Unless there is a good reason for something else, use private. This protects your class from misuse.

Avoid public fields except for constants. They tie other code to one particular implementation and limit your freedom to change the class later. The tutorial's early examples use public fields only to keep their code short, not as a model for real programs.
A method that guards a private field can check a rule each time the field changes, which a public field cannot.
card.rule: Start with private and widen access only when a real need appears.
card.limits: Restrictive does not mean unusable: the operations that other classes must call still need wider access. The advice is about fields, not about hiding the whole class.
card.example: A deposit method on an Account can reject a negative amount. If balance were public, any class could assign a negative balance directly and skip the check.

concepts.title: Class variables and instance variables
concepts.question: What separates an instance variable from a class variable, and how is a class variable referred to?

paragraphs: An instance variable gets a separate copy in each object. A class variable is declared with the keyword static: there is a single copy for the whole class, shared by every instance, and any object can change it.

Take a Bicycle class that gives each bike a unique id. The id is an instance variable, one per bicycle. The count of bicycles made so far must be shared, so it is a class variable. The constructor increases the count and gives the new bicycle its id.
Refer to a class variable through the class name, as in Bicycle.numberOfBicycles. Using an object reference compiles too, but the tutorial discourages it because it hides that the variable is static.
card.rule: static marks a member as belonging to the class and shared by all; without it each object has its own copy.
card.limits: A shared variable can be changed by every object, so it is shared state that any caller can disturb. A member without static is an instance member by default.
card.example: static int created = 0; int id; Bicycle() { id = ++created; }  The first bicycle gets id 1 and the second gets id 2, because created is shared while id belongs to each object.

concepts.title: Class methods and what they can use
concepts.question: What can class methods and instance methods use directly, and why can a class method not use instance variables by plain name?

paragraphs: A class method is declared with static and called on the class, as in Bicycle.getNumberOfBicycles(), with no object needed. A common use is to give access to a class variable. Calling it through an object reference compiles but is discouraged.
Instance methods can directly use instance variables, instance methods, class variables and class methods. Class methods can directly use only class variables and class methods.
A class method may be running with no object at all, so there is no object whose instance values a plain name could mean. To use an instance member it needs an object reference.
card.rule: A class method can directly use only class members, and instance members need an object reference.
card.limits: The restriction runs one way: instance methods may freely use class members, but class methods may not return the favour by plain name.
card.example: static int total() { return created; } is fine, since created is a class variable. Replacing the body with return id; fails to compile, because id belongs to individual bicycles and none is available.

concepts.title: Constants with static final
concepts.question: How is a constant declared, and how are constants named?

paragraphs: Combining static and final creates a constant. The keyword final means the value cannot be changed once it is set, and trying to assign to it again is a compile-time error. The keyword static gives the whole class a single copy.
By convention, constant names are written in uppercase, with underscores between words, such as MAX_SPEED. The tutorial's example is static final double PI = 3.141592653589793;.
card.rule: Declare a constant with static final and an uppercase name; it cannot be reassigned.
card.limits: A constant cannot be reassigned while the program runs. The programmer can still edit its source value, and what other classes then see depends on how they were compiled.
card.example: static final int MAX_USERS = 50;  declares one shared value. A statement MAX_USERS = 60; elsewhere is rejected by the compiler.

concepts.title: Ways to initialize fields
concepts.question: Which tools can initialize a field, and which problem does each one solve?

paragraphs: The simplest way is to give a field a value where it is declared, such as private boolean full = false;. This suits values that are known and fit in one expression. It falls short when initialization needs logic, such as error handling or a loop that fills a complex array.

Instance variables can be initialized in a constructor, where any logic is possible. Class variables use a static initialization block: the keyword static followed by a block of statements. A class can have any number of them, placed anywhere in the body, and they run in the order they appear.
Alternatively, a class variable can be initialized by calling a private static method from the field's declaration.
card.rule: Use a declaration initializer for simple values, a constructor for instance logic, and a static block or private static method for class logic.
card.limits: Fields need not be declared at the top, but they must be declared and initialized before use. Only the private static method can be called again later.
card.example: static int[] table; static { table = new int[5]; for (int i = 0; i < 5; i++) { table[i] = i * i; } }  The loop is logic that a one-line initializer could not hold.

concepts.title: Instance initializer blocks and final methods
concepts.question: How do instance initializer blocks and final methods help initialize instance fields?

paragraphs: Besides constructors, instance variables can be initialized with an initializer block, which looks like a static block without the static keyword. The compiler copies the block into every constructor, so one piece of code can be shared by several constructors.
Another option is to initialize a field by calling a method, as in private int size = computeSize();. The tutorial suggests making that method final, which means subclasses cannot override it.
card.rule: Share initialization code across constructors with an instance initializer block, or call a final method from the field's declaration.
card.limits: Constructors remain the usual place for instance initialization. The block suits code that every constructor needs.
card.example: class Grid { int[] cells; { cells = new int[9]; } Grid() { } Grid(int n) { } }  Both constructors get the block's work without repeating it.

concepts.title: Nested, inner and static nested classes
concepts.question: What are nested, inner and static nested classes, and why would you nest a class?

paragraphs: A nested class is a class declared inside another class. There are two kinds. A nested class declared without static is an inner class, and one declared with static is a static nested class. The tutorial keeps these two names apart.
A nested class is a member of its enclosing class, so it can be private, public, protected or package-private, while a top-level class can only be public or package-private.

The tutorial gives three reasons to nest: to group a class that is useful to only one other class, to increase encapsulation (a class B inside A can use A's private members while B itself stays hidden), and to keep small classes near where they are used, which helps readability and maintenance.
card.rule: A class declared inside another is nested: with static it is a static nested class, and without static it is an inner class.
card.limits: Nested is the general term, and inner names only the non-static kind, so calling every nested class inner mixes up two kinds that behave differently.
card.example: class Outer { class InnerClass { } static class StaticNestedClass { } }  Both are nested classes. The first is an inner class and the second is a static nested class.

concepts.title: Inner classes
concepts.question: What can an inner class use, how is one created, and what can it not declare?

paragraphs: An inner class is tied to an instance of its enclosing class. It has direct access to that object's fields and methods, including private ones. Because it is tied to an instance, an inner object exists only within an outer object, and according to the tutorial an inner class cannot declare static members of its own.
To create one, first create the outer object and then use it to create the inner one, as in OuterClass.InnerClass inner = outer.new InnerClass();.
card.rule: An inner class needs an outer instance, can use that instance's members directly even when private, and has no static members.
card.limits: Without an enclosing object no inner object can exist, so code with no outer instance must create one first or use a static nested class.
card.example: Outer o = new Outer(); Outer.Inner i = o.new Inner();  The inner object i belongs to o and can read o's private fields directly.

concepts.title: Static nested classes
concepts.question: How does a static nested class differ from an inner class in how it is created and what it can reach?

paragraphs: A static nested class is associated with its outer class, not with an outer instance, much as static methods and variables are. It is created like a top-level class, with no outer object: StaticNestedClass obj = new StaticNestedClass();.

Like a static method, it cannot refer directly to the outer class's instance variables or instance methods; it reaches them only through an object reference. It can use the outer class's static members directly. In this respect it behaves like a top-level class that happens to be nested for packaging convenience.
card.rule: A static nested class needs no outer instance, uses outer static members directly, and reaches outer instance members only through a reference.
card.limits: Being nested gives it no outer object, so any plain-name use of an outer instance member is a compiler error, just as for a top-level class.
card.example: static class Helper { void show(Outer o) { use(o.name); } }  The instance field name is reached through the reference o. A static field of Outer could be used by its plain name.

concepts.title: Shadowing across nested scopes
concepts.question: When the same name is declared in nested scopes, which declaration does each form of the name refer to?

paragraphs: If a declaration in an inner scope, such as a method or an inner class, has the same name as one in an enclosing scope, it shadows the outer one. The outer declaration can no longer be named by its simple name.

The tutorial's ShadowTest declares x three times: a field of the outer class, a field of the inner class, and a parameter of a method in the inner class. Inside that method, plain x is the parameter, this.x is the inner class's field, and ShadowTest.this.x is the outer class's field.
So ClassName.this reaches the enclosing instance of that class.
card.rule: The innermost declaration wins by simple name; use this.name for the current object's member and Outer.this.name for the enclosing object's.
card.limits: Shadowing can make code confusing, so distinct names are often clearer. Outer.this works only when an enclosing instance exists.
card.example: Outer has int x = 0. Inner has int x = 1 and a method f(int x). When f is called with 23, x is 23, this.x is 1, and Outer.this.x is 0.

concepts.title: A hidden helper: the iterator
concepts.question: What problem does the tutorial's private inner class EvenIterator solve?

paragraphs: The tutorial's example stores 15 integers in a private array and wants to print the values at even positions. The outer class DataStructure holds the array. A private inner class, EvenIterator, steps through it and implements a small nested interface that narrows the standard Iterator type to integers.

EvenIterator reads the outer object's private array and size directly. Its hasNext method tests that the index is still inside the array, and its next method returns the current value and then moves the index forward by two. The outer method creates it with this.new EvenIterator() and loops until hasNext is false.
Because the inner class is private, outside code sees only the interface type. The tutorial adds that inner classes are heavily used for event handling in graphical interfaces.
card.rule: A private inner class can act as a hidden helper that walks through its outer object's private data.
card.limits: The helper works only together with an outer object. Small single-purpose helpers like this can often be written more briefly with lambdas, which the tutorial introduces later.
card.example: With the array holding 0 to 14, the loop in printEven prints 0 2 4 6 8 10 12 14.

concepts.title: Local classes
concepts.question: Where can a local class be declared, which enclosing variables can it use, and what can it not declare?

paragraphs: A local class is declared inside a block, meaning statements between braces, most often a method body. It can also sit in a for loop or an if clause. Like an inner class, it can use the members of its enclosing class.

It can capture local variables and parameters of the enclosing block, but only if they are final or effectively final, meaning never changed after initialization. Before Java SE 8 the final keyword itself was required. Assigning to a captured variable anywhere makes the compiler reject its use.
Local classes are non-static. They cannot declare an interface inside a block, nor static methods or static initializers.
card.rule: A local class is declared in a block and may use enclosing local variables only if they are final or effectively final.
card.limits: Capturing needs a value that does not change after it is set. A local class is also more limited than a full nested class in what it may declare.
card.example: void check(int limit) { class Rule { boolean ok(int v) { return v < limit; } } }  The parameter limit is captured. If limit were given a new value anywhere in check, Rule could no longer use it.

concepts.title: Anonymous classes
concepts.question: How does an anonymous class differ from a local class, and what does its syntax look like?

paragraphs: An anonymous class declares and creates a class in a single step and has no name. It is an expression, whereas a local class is a declaration. It suits a class needed only once.

The syntax has four parts: the new operator, the name of an interface to implement or a class to extend, parentheses holding constructor arguments (empty for an interface), and a class body in braces. Because it is an expression, the statement ends with a semicolon after the closing brace.
It can capture enclosing variables under the same final-or-effectively-final rule. It may declare fields, extra methods, instance initializers and local classes, but not constructors.
card.rule: An anonymous class is new Type(args) { body }, an expression that defines and creates a one-off class.
card.limits: With no name it can have no constructor. When the interface has just one method to implement, a lambda expression is shorter, as later ideas show.
card.example: Greeter g = new Greeter() { public void greet() { print(1); } };  creates an unnamed class that implements Greeter, and one object of it, in a single statement.

concepts.title: Why lambda expressions exist
concepts.question: Why do lambda expressions exist, and how does the tutorial's roster example improve step by step?

paragraphs: Anonymous classes are bulky when the class has one simple method. A lambda expression lets you treat functionality as a method argument, or code as data, in a compact form. It can stand for an implementation of any interface with exactly one abstract method, called a functional interface.

The tutorial works on one task: print the roster members that meet some criteria. A separate method for each characteristic is brittle and restrictive. Moving the criteria into an object that implements a one-method interface fixes that, first as a named local class, then as an anonymous class.

A lambda then shrinks the anonymous class to just the test. Standard interfaces in java.util.function, such as Predicate for a yes-or-no test, Consumer for an action and Function for a transformation, mean you rarely declare your own.
card.rule: A lambda is a compact implementation of a functional interface, so behaviour can be passed to a method as an argument.
card.limits: A lambda stands in only for an interface with a single abstract method. An interface with several abstract methods still needs a class.
card.example: printPersons(roster, p -> p.getAge() >= 18);  passes the criterion as a lambda. A Predicate of Person describes it: it takes a Person and answers true or false.

concepts.title: Writing a lambda
concepts.question: What are the three parts of a lambda expression, and which shortcuts are allowed?

paragraphs: A lambda has three parts: a parameter list in parentheses separated by commas, the arrow token ->, and a body. You may leave out the parameter types, and you may leave out the parentheses when there is exactly one parameter. An empty list is written ().

The body is either a single expression, whose value is returned automatically, or a block in braces. A block needs an explicit return statement to give back a value, because return is a statement, not an expression. A call to a void method needs no braces.
Think of a lambda as an anonymous method.
card.rule: A lambda is parameters, an arrow and a body, and a single-expression body returns its value automatically.
card.limits: A lambda gets its meaning only from a functional interface. Braces are needed when the body is a block of statements, including one with return.
card.example: (a, b) -> a + b  returns the sum without braces. The block form would be (a, b) -> { return a + b; }. And s -> print(s) takes one parameter and needs no parentheses.

concepts.title: Lambda scope and target types
concepts.question: How do lambdas treat names and local variables from the enclosing code, and how does the compiler decide a lambda's type?

paragraphs: A lambda can capture local variables and parameters of its enclosing code, but only if they are final or effectively final, just as for local and anonymous classes. Assigning to a captured variable inside the lambda is a compile error.

Unlike those classes, a lambda does not create a new scope or inherit names from a supertype; it is lexically scoped. A lambda parameter therefore cannot reuse the name of an enclosing local variable.

A lambda has no type of its own. The compiler infers it from the target type, the type expected where the lambda appears, such as a declared variable, an assignment, a return statement or a method argument. The same lambda text can be one interface type in one place and another elsewhere.
card.rule: Lambdas capture only effectively final locals, share their enclosing scope's names, and take their type from where they are used.
card.limits: A lambda needs a context that supplies a target type. With overloaded methods the compiler picks by overload resolution and type inference.
card.example: int base = 10; Show c = n -> print(n + base);  captures base (Show is an interface with one method taking an int). Naming the lambda parameter base would be rejected, because base already names a local variable.

concepts.title: Method references
concepts.question: When can a method reference replace a lambda, and what are its four kinds?

paragraphs: When a lambda does nothing except call an existing method, a method reference can name that method directly. Person::compareByAge means the same as (a, b) -> Person.compareByAge(a, b). The parameters come from the functional interface, not from the reference.

There are four kinds. A static method: Type::staticMethod. An instance method of a particular object: object::method. An instance method of an arbitrary object of a given type: Type::method, where the interface method's first parameter becomes the object the method is called on. A constructor: ClassName::new.
If the lambda does more than forward its arguments, keep the lambda.
card.rule: Use a method reference when a lambda only forwards its parameters to an existing method or constructor.
card.limits: A reference needs a functional interface and a compatible method. The Type::method form is easy to misread as static.
card.example: String::compareToIgnoreCase stands for (a, b) -> a.compareToIgnoreCase(b). It looks like a static reference, but the method is an instance method called on the first parameter.

concepts.title: Choosing the simplest construct
concepts.question: Given a need, which of lambda, anonymous class, local class or nested class does the tutorial suggest?

paragraphs: All four help group code, increase encapsulation and improve readability. They differ in what each offers. The tutorial suggests choosing the simplest construct that meets your needs.

Use a lambda to pass a single unit of behaviour to other code, or as a simple instance of a functional interface when you need no constructor, named type, fields or extra methods. Use an anonymous class when you need fields or additional methods. Use a local class when you need several instances, its constructor, or a new named type.

Use a nested class when your needs resemble a local class's, you want the type more widely available, and you need no local variables or parameters. Make it an inner class if you need an enclosing instance's non-public members, otherwise a static nested class.
card.rule: Pick the simplest construct that meets the need: lambda first, then anonymous class, local class, and nested class as requirements grow.
card.limits: This is the tutorial's guidance, not a compiler rule, and the choices overlap. Lambdas are the most concise, while nested classes are the most widely visible.
card.example: Sorting once with a comparison rule: a lambda. The same rule with a counter field: an anonymous class. A helper type used in one method, created many times: a local class.

concepts.title: Enum types and switch
concepts.question: What is an enum type, when should you use one, and how does it work with switch?

paragraphs: An enum type is a special data type whose variables can hold only one of a fixed set of predefined constants, such as the days of the week or the compass directions. By convention the constant names are written in uppercase.

Declare one with the enum keyword followed by the constants, as in public enum Day { SUNDAY, MONDAY, and so on }. Use an enum whenever you need a fixed set of constants known when the program is written, such as menu choices or command-line flags.

Enums work naturally with switch. A variable of the enum type is tested, and each case label uses the constant's bare name, such as MONDAY rather than Day.MONDAY. Labels can be stacked to share code, and default covers the rest.
card.rule: Use an enum for a fixed set of named constants, and write the bare constant names as switch case labels.
card.limits: An enum suits values known when the program is written. A set that must grow while the program runs is not a fit.
card.example: enum Size { SMALL, MEDIUM, LARGE }  A variable of type Size holds one of these three. A switch on it can handle SMALL and LARGE and let default cover MEDIUM.

concepts.title: Enums are classes
concepts.question: What can an enum do beyond holding names, and which rules govern how it is declared?

paragraphs: An enum declaration defines a class, so its body can contain fields, methods and a constructor. Each constant can carry data: in the tutorial's Planet enum, every constant passes a mass and a radius to the constructor. The constructor runs by itself to create the constants listed at the top of the body, and you cannot call it yourself.
The constants must come first in the body. When fields or methods follow, the constant list ends with a semicolon. An enum constructor must be private or package-private.
The compiler adds a static method values() that returns an array of all the constants in the order they were declared. It is usually used with a for-each loop to visit every constant.
card.rule: An enum is a class whose constants are created by its constructor, listed first, and visited with values().
card.limits: The constant list and the constructor are fixed in the declaration: other code cannot create new constants or call the constructor.
card.example: enum Coin { PENNY(1), DIME(10); private final int cents; Coin(int cents) { this.cents = cents; } }  Each constant is built with its own value, and for (Coin c : Coin.values()) visits PENNY, then DIME.

concepts.title: What an annotation is
concepts.question: What does an annotation add to a program, and does it change how the annotated code runs?

paragraphs: An annotation is metadata: information about a piece of a program that is not itself part of the program. By itself it has no direct effect on the operation of the code it marks.

Other parties do the acting. The compiler can read annotations to detect errors or silence warnings. Tools can read them while building or deploying, to generate code or files such as XML. Some annotations stay available so the running program can examine them.
So an annotation is a label plus a reader. The label says something about the code; whoever reads it decides what follows.
card.example: A method that adds two numbers carries a marker saying it was reviewed. Removing the marker leaves the sum unchanged. A build tool that reads the marker could still list every reviewed method in a report.
card.rule: An annotation is metadata about code; it does not change what the code does, but a compiler, tool or running program can read it and act.
card.limits: The label alone never alters the annotated code's logic, yet its readers can still change outcomes, for example a compiler refusing to build. Do not conclude that annotations never matter.

concepts.title: Writing and placing an annotation
concepts.question: How do you write an annotation, and where on a program may it appear?

paragraphs: An annotation is an at sign followed by its type name. Elements are name-value pairs in parentheses. When there are no elements, the parentheses may be left out.
If the type has just one element and it is called value, you may drop the name and the equals sign. The short and long forms mean the same thing. With several elements, write each one with its name.

A declaration can carry several different annotations, usually one per line. Since Java SE 8 the same type may also be repeated. Annotation names are case-sensitive, so they must match their declarations.
Annotations sit on declarations such as classes, fields and methods. Since Java SE 8 they can also mark a use of a type, for instance after new, in a cast, in an implements clause or after throws.
card.example: A type Limit has one element, int value(). Both @Limit(5) and @Limit(value = 5) set it to 5. A type Stable with no elements is written @Stable. A cast can carry one too: (@Stable Box) item.
card.rule: Write the at sign, the type name, and name-value pairs in parentheses; drop value = only when value is the single element.
card.limits: The shorthand fails when the single element has another name, or when you give several elements. Brackets or hashes are not annotation syntax, and a misspelt or wrongly cased name will not match its type.

concepts.title: Declaring your own annotation type
concepts.question: How do you define an annotation type, and which of its elements must a user supply?

paragraphs: Notes such as author or revision kept in comments are free text that tools cannot process. An annotation type turns them into structured data. Declare it with @interface; the body lists elements that look like methods: a type, a name, then empty parentheses.
An element with no default must receive a value at every use. Adding default and a value makes it optional, and users who omit it get that value.
An element may have an array type. At the use site, its values go inside braces, separated by commas.
Generated Javadoc leaves annotations out unless the annotation type itself is marked with Documented, which lives in java.lang.annotation and needs importing.
card.example: @interface Ticket { int id(); int priority() default 3; int[] codes(); } is used as @Ticket(id = 7, codes = {4, 9}). The id and codes values are required; priority takes 3.
card.rule: Declare with @interface, give each element a type and optionally a default, and supply a value for every element that has none.
card.limits: A default only relieves the user of writing a value. Documented affects generated documentation, not behaviour, and goes on the annotation type, not on the classes that use it.

concepts.title: Annotations the compiler acts on
concepts.question: Which predefined annotations does the compiler act on, and what does each make it do?

paragraphs: Deprecated marks a class, method or field that should no longer be used; the compiler warns at every use. By convention it is paired with a Javadoc deprecated tag that explains why. The tag starts with a lowercase letter, the annotation with a capital.

Override states that a method is meant to override one from a superclass. It is optional, but if the method does not really override, the compiler reports an error. That exposes misspelt names and wrong parameter lists.

SuppressWarnings silences named warning categories in the marked code. Two categories exist: deprecation, for use of deprecated items, and unchecked, which can arise when code meets legacy code from before generics. List several in braces.
FunctionalInterface, added in Java SE 8, states that an interface is meant to have a single abstract method.
card.example: Base has void run(). Child extends Base and declares @Override void runn() { }. The compiler stops with an error, because runn overrides nothing; without the annotation the typo would quietly create a new method.
card.rule: Deprecated yields a warning on use, Override yields an error when nothing is overridden, and SuppressWarnings hides named warning categories.
card.limits: Suppressing hides a warning without fixing its cause, and only the categories you name. Override guards only where you write it. A warning does not stop the build; an Override mismatch does.

concepts.title: Meta-annotations
concepts.question: Which annotations control how another annotation is kept, placed, documented, inherited or repeated?

paragraphs: Meta-annotations are annotations placed on annotation types. Retention says how long the annotation survives. SOURCE keeps it only in source, ignored by the compiler. CLASS has the compiler store it in the class file, ignored by the JVM. RUNTIME has the JVM keep it, so the running program can read it, for example through reflection.
Target limits which kinds of element can carry the annotation, using ElementType values such as METHOD, FIELD, PARAMETER, CONSTRUCTOR, LOCAL_VARIABLE, PACKAGE, TYPE and ANNOTATION_TYPE.

Documented makes uses appear in Javadoc. Inherited means that, when a class has no such annotation, a query also checks its superclass; by default that does not happen. Repeatable, added in Java SE 8, allows more than one use on the same element.
card.example: @Retention(RetentionPolicy.RUNTIME) @Target(ElementType.METHOD) @interface Timed { } declares an annotation that can mark only methods and that the running program can read.
card.rule: Place Retention, Target, Documented, Inherited or Repeatable on an annotation type to set how long it lives, where it goes, and how it is documented, inherited or repeated.
card.limits: Target restricts placement but does not change meaning. Annotations kept at SOURCE or CLASS retention are not available to the JVM at run time.

concepts.section: Type Annotations and Pluggable Type Systems
concepts.title: Type annotations and pluggable checkers
concepts.question: How do type annotations and pluggable checkers work together to catch errors before a program runs?

paragraphs: Before Java SE 8, annotations could mark only declarations. Since then they can mark any use of a type. The goal is stronger analysis and type checking.

Java SE 8 supplies no checking framework. Instead you write or download a checker as a pluggable module that runs with the compiler. Several modules can run together, each looking for a different kind of error.

With a non-null checker: obtain the module, annotate the variable as non-null, compile with the module named on the command line, and read the warnings the compiler prints for each place null might get in. Edit the code until no warnings remain; the null error should then not occur at run time.
You need not write modules yourself. The Checker Framework offers ready-made ones, including non-null and regular-expression checkers.
card.example: A method parameter is annotated as non-null. Compiled with the checker, a call passing a value that might be null gets a warning. The programmer adds a guard until the warning goes away.
card.rule: Annotate type uses with the property to enforce, compile with a pluggable checker, and fix every warning it reports.
card.limits: The annotation alone enforces nothing; without a checker module on the compile it is just a label. A checker covers only the property it was built for.

concepts.title: Repeating annotations
concepts.question: What two declarations let an annotation be written twice on the same element?

paragraphs: Since Java SE 8 the same annotation type can be written more than once on one declaration or type use, for example two schedule entries on one cleanup method. Without the right declarations, repeating is a compile-time error.

The compiler stores repeats inside a container annotation it generates. Two declarations make that possible. First, mark the annotation type with Repeatable, naming the container type. Second, declare the container type.
The container needs an element named value, of array type, whose component type is the repeatable annotation.

To read repeats, getAnnotation still returns one annotation only when exactly one is present, which keeps old code working. For repeats, retrieve the container, or call getAnnotationsByType, added in SE 8, which scans the container and returns them all.
card.example: @Repeatable(Shifts.class) @interface Shift { int hour(); } and @interface Shifts { Shift[] value(); } allow @Shift(hour = 9) @Shift(hour = 17) on one method.
card.rule: To make an annotation repeatable, mark it Repeatable naming a container type whose value element is an array of the repeatable type.
card.limits: Repeatable alone is not enough; the container must be well formed. Old getAnnotation calls do not hand back repeats directly. Repetition is a design choice, not something every annotation needs.

concepts.title: An interface as a contract
concepts.question: What does an interface let two separate groups of programmers agree on without seeing each other's code?

paragraphs: An interface is a contract between groups of programmers. One group publishes a list of methods that may be called; the other group writes code that calls them. Neither side has to read the other side's code.

Because the published list is all that is shared, either side may rewrite its internals at any time, provided it still honours the published interface. The tutorial's picture is a robotic car: car makers publish operations such as start, stop and turn, and guidance-instrument makers call them.

The word interface carries two meanings here. In general it is an agreed boundary between parties. In Java it is also a specific reference type, similar to a class, with a restricted set of members. A vendor can even sell such an interface as an API.
card.example: A weather company publishes one method that returns today's forecast text. An app developer writes code that calls that method. Next year the company changes its data source. The app keeps working, because the published method did not change.
card.rule: An interface is a published contract that lets callers and implementers change their own code independently as long as the contract itself holds.
card.limits: The promise holds only while the published interface stays the same. If its methods change, every party relying on it can break.

concepts.title: What an interface may hold
concepts.question: Which five kinds of member may an interface contain, and what can you never do with an interface?

paragraphs: In the tutorial's JDK 8 terms, an interface is a reference type, similar to a class, that can contain only constants, method signatures, default methods, static methods and nested types. Nothing outside that list is allowed, so an interface has no instance fields.
A method signature gives a return type, a name and parameters, and ends with a semicolon instead of a body. Such a method is abstract. Only default methods and static methods carry a body.
You cannot create an object from an interface. It is used in two ways: a class implements it, or another interface extends it.
card.example: Interface Greeter holds a constant PREFIX, a signature greet with no body, a default method shout that calls greet and adds an exclamation mark, and a static method polite that builds a Greeter. Writing new Greeter() is an error.
card.rule: An interface holds only constants, method signatures, default methods, static methods and nested types, and it cannot be instantiated.
card.limits: According to the tutorial, which targets JDK 8, this list is complete. Later Java releases may allow other members, which this lesson does not cover.

concepts.title: Declaring an interface
concepts.question: What parts make up an interface declaration, and what decides which packages may use it?

paragraphs: An interface declaration has these parts in order: optional modifiers such as public, the keyword interface, the name, an optional extends clause naming parent interfaces separated by commas, and the body in braces.
If the interface is public, any class in any package may use it. Without public, only classes in the same package may use it.
An interface may extend any number of interfaces. A class, by contrast, may extend only one class.
card.example: Public interface Playable extends Pausable, Stoppable has a body with the single signature play. Any package may use it, and it carries the methods of both parents. Remove the word public and only classes in its own package may use it.
card.rule: An interface declaration is optional modifiers, the interface keyword, a name, an optional comma-separated extends list of any length, and a body, and public decides whether other packages may use it.
card.limits: The extends list of many parents belongs to interfaces only. A class still has at most one extends parent and uses implements for interfaces.

concepts.title: Implied modifiers
concepts.question: Which modifiers can be left out of interface members because the language implies them?

paragraphs: Inside an interface, every abstract, default or static method is implicitly public, so writing public is optional. A method with neither default nor static is implicitly abstract.
Every constant is implicitly public, static and final, so those three words may be left out. A constant is therefore a value fixed for the whole interface, not stored separately in each object.
In short, the declarations a reader sees are shorter than the rules behind them. Know the implied modifiers when reading an interface.
card.example: Inside an interface, int MAX = 10; means the same as public static final int MAX = 10;. Likewise void stop(); means the same as public abstract void stop();.
card.rule: In an interface, methods are implicitly public, plain ones are also abstract, and constants are implicitly public, static and final.
card.limits: These shortcuts apply to members declared inside an interface. In a class, leaving out public changes the access, and leaving out static or final changes what the field is.

concepts.title: Implementing an interface
concepts.question: What must a class do once it names an interface in an implements clause, and where does that clause go?

paragraphs: To make a class implement an interface, add an implements clause to the class header. A class may implement several interfaces by listing their names with commas. By convention the implements clause comes after any extends clause.
The class must then provide a body for every abstract method the interface declares, with a matching signature. A class that does not do so would have to be declared abstract.

Implementing is a promise to callers. The tutorial's Relatable has one method, isLargerThan, returning 1, 0 or -1; any implementing class promises its objects can be compared by size, whatever size means for that class.
card.example: Class Tablet extends Device implements Chargeable, Foldable lists its parent class first. If Chargeable declares charge and Foldable declares fold, then Tablet must contain a body for both methods.
card.rule: A class names its interfaces after implements, after any extends, and must give a body to every abstract method they declare.
card.limits: A class that leaves some methods undone is acceptable only if it is declared abstract. The duty to finish the methods then passes to its concrete subclasses.

concepts.title: An interface as a type
concepts.question: Where can an interface name be used as a type, and what may a variable of that type hold?

paragraphs: Defining an interface creates a new reference type name. It may be used anywhere a type name is allowed, such as for variables, parameters, return types and array elements.
A variable of an interface type may hold only an object whose class implements that interface. The compiler then permits calls to the interface's methods on it, and no method that only the class has.

Through the interface type, objects of different classes can be handled in one way. A class can keep behaviour from its superclass and still be treated as the interface type, which the tutorial says gives some advantages of multiple inheritance.
card.example: Chargeable c = new Tablet(); then c.charge() is accepted. Calling c.fold() would be rejected if fold is not in Chargeable. An array of Chargeable can hold a Tablet, a Phone and a Torch, if each class implements Chargeable.
card.rule: An interface name is a type: a variable of that type may refer to any object of an implementing class, and it exposes only the interface's methods.
card.limits: The declared type decides which methods the compiler allows. To use a method that only the class has, you must cast, and a cast to the wrong class fails at run time.

concepts.title: Writing code once against an interface
concepts.question: How can one helper method work for objects of many unrelated classes?

paragraphs: Once a method depends only on an interface, it serves every implementing class, whatever its place in the class hierarchy. The tutorial's findLargest takes two Object parameters, casts both to Relatable, calls isLargerThan, and returns the original argument that is larger.
findSmallest reverses the test, and isEqual counts a result of 0 as equal. All three rest on the single contract method.
Their safety depends on a condition from the contract comment: the two objects must be of the same class. The interface itself does not enforce it.
card.example: A Recipe class and a Book class both implement Relatable, using steps and pages. findLargest works for two recipes or for two books. Passing one recipe and one book breaks the same-class condition.
card.rule: Code written against an interface method works for any implementing class, provided callers honour the conditions stated in the contract.
card.limits: The interface cannot enforce a condition that lives only in a comment, such as comparing objects of one class, so a mixed call can fail when the program runs.

concepts.title: Why published interfaces are hard to change
concepts.question: Why can adding one abstract method to a published interface break other people's code?

paragraphs: Once an interface is published, other programmers write classes that implement it. If you then add a new abstract method, each of those classes lacks a body for it. They no longer meet the contract, so their code stops compiling.
The tutorial's example adds a method named didItWork to an interface named DoIt. Programmers relying on DoIt would, as the tutorial puts it, object loudly.
The advice is to anticipate all uses of an interface and specify it completely from the start. After publishing, avoid changing its abstract methods.
card.example: A library interface Exporter has one method, export. Thousands of apps implement it. The authors add a second abstract method, exportAll. Every existing implementer now lacks exportAll and fails to meet the contract.
card.rule: Adding an abstract method to a published interface breaks every existing implementer, so specify an interface fully before publishing it.
card.limits: The break comes from adding an abstract method. The tutorial offers other ways to grow an interface that leave existing implementers working, covered in the next idea.

concepts.title: Ways to grow an interface safely
concepts.question: What three ways does the tutorial give for adding behaviour to a published interface without breaking implementers?

paragraphs: The first way is a sub-interface. Create a new interface that extends the original and adds the new method, as DoItPlus extends DoIt. Existing users keep the old interface; users who want the new method move to the new one.
The second way is a default method: give the new method a body inside the existing interface. Classes already implementing it need no change and no recompilation, because they inherit the body.

The third way is to add static methods to the existing interface, which also leaves implementers working. With a sub-interface, users choose when to upgrade; with a default method, the new method reaches every implementer at once.
card.example: Interface Exporter has export. Instead of adding an abstract exportAll, the authors either write interface ExporterPlus extends Exporter with exportAll, or give Exporter a default exportAll that calls export for each file. Old classes stay untouched.
card.rule: To grow a published interface safely, add a sub-interface, a default method or a static method rather than a new abstract method.
card.limits: Each way has a price. A sub-interface leaves old classes without the new method, and a default method needs a body that behaves sensibly for every existing implementer.

concepts.title: Default methods
concepts.question: What is a default method, and how does it let a library add behaviour without forcing implementers to change?

paragraphs: A default method is a method in an interface that has a body and is marked with the keyword default. Classes implementing the interface inherit it without writing anything. Here the word default means the interface supplies the method, not a preset value.

The tutorial's TimeClient interface has four abstract methods, implemented by SimpleTimeClient. Adding getZonedDateTime as abstract would force SimpleTimeClient to change. As a default method it uses getLocalDateTime and a helper, and SimpleTimeClient is untouched.
The helper getZoneId is a static method in the same interface. For an invalid zone name it prints a message to the error stream and falls back to the system default zone.
card.example: An interface Stack has push and pop. The authors add a default method pushAll that calls push once for each item. Every existing Stack class gains pushAll with no edits.
card.rule: A default method gives an interface a method with a body, so a library can add behaviour without forcing implementers to change.
card.limits: A default method can use only what the interface already offers, such as its other methods. Behaviour that needs an implementer's own state or special knowledge cannot be supplied this way.

concepts.title: Extending an interface that has a default method
concepts.question: What three choices does a sub-interface have for a default method it inherits from its parent?

paragraphs: When an interface extends another interface that has a default method, it can leave the method alone. Implementing classes then get the parent's default body.
It can redeclare the method as a plain signature with no body. This makes the method abstract again, so every implementing class must write its own body.
It can override the method with a new default body. Implementing classes then get the new body instead of the parent's.
card.example: TimeClient has a default getZonedDateTime. AnotherTimeClient extends TimeClient and says nothing, so it inherits. AbstractZoneTimeClient redeclares the signature, so implementers must supply a body. HandleInvalidTimeZoneClient gives a new default body.
card.rule: A sub-interface may inherit a parent's default method, redeclare it as abstract, or override it with a new default.
card.limits: These choices bind the sub-interface and its own implementers. A class that implements only the parent interface keeps the parent's default untouched.

concepts.title: Conflicting default methods
concepts.question: When a class inherits the same method from several places, which one wins, and when must the class decide?

paragraphs: The compiler applies two principles. First, an instance method inherited from a class is preferred over an interface default. Second, a default that another candidate has already overridden is ignored, so a more specific interface's version counts.
If two independently defined defaults conflict, or a default conflicts with an abstract method of the same signature, the compiler reports an error. The class must then override the method itself.

Inside that override you may call one interface's version by writing the interface name, a dot, the word super, and the call. The name must be a direct superinterface. This form also works outside conflicts. Static interface methods are never inherited.
card.example: Pegasus extends Horse and implements Flyer and Mythical, each with a default identifyMyself. Horse's own method wins. FlyingCar implements OperateCar and FlyCar, both with a default startEngine, so it must override and may call FlyCar.super.startEngine.
card.rule: A class method beats interface defaults, a more specific default beats a less specific one, and unrelated conflicting defaults must be settled by overriding in the class.
card.limits: These tests apply to methods with the same signature. Methods with different names or parameter lists do not conflict with each other.

concepts.title: Static methods and Comparator
concepts.question: What are static methods in an interface for, and how do they work with default methods in Comparator?

paragraphs: A static method in an interface is a helper with a body that belongs to the interface itself. Keeping helpers there ties them to the interface they support. Static methods of an interface are never inherited.
The tutorial shows how Java 8 enhanced Comparator this way. The static method comparing builds a comparator from a key extractor such as a reference to a getRank method.
Default methods then chain onto a comparator. The method thenComparing adds a second criterion, and reversed flips the order of the comparator it follows.
card.example: To sort a deck by rank, highest first, and break ties by suit, write Comparator.comparing of the rank getter, then reversed, then thenComparing with a comparator built from the suit getter.
card.rule: A static interface method is a helper owned by the interface, and static factories plus default combinators build many orderings from a few small methods.
card.limits: Static interface methods are not inherited, so an implementing class does not get them as its own methods. They are reached through the interface.

concepts.title: What an implementer owes, and marker interfaces
concepts.question: Which methods must a class write when it implements an interface, and what is an interface with no members for?

paragraphs: To know what to write, list the interface's abstract methods. Default and static methods need no body from the implementer, though default methods may be overridden. The lesson's CharSequence exercise asks exactly this question for a library interface.
An interface method written with a body but without default or static is an error. There are two fixes: replace the body with a semicolon, or mark the method default.

An interface with no members at all is valid. It is called a marker interface: implementing it labels a class as having some property, shown only through its type. Cloneable is an example the lesson mentions.
card.example: Interface Shape has an abstract area, a default describe and a static unit. A class implementing Shape must write area. It may use describe as it is, or override it.
card.rule: An implementer owes a body for each abstract method only, and an interface with no members is a legal marker whose value is its type.
card.limits: A marker interface says nothing about behaviour by itself. Other code must check for the type before the label has any effect.

concepts.title: Subclasses and superclasses
concepts.question: What do subclass, superclass and inherit mean, and how many direct superclasses can a class have?

paragraphs: A class can be derived from another class and inherit its fields and methods, reusing code instead of writing it again. The derived class is the subclass, also called a derived, extended or child class. The class it comes from is the superclass, also called a base or parent class.

Except for Object, every class has exactly one direct superclass. A class with no extends clause is implicitly a subclass of Object. Descent runs through the whole chain back to Object, so a class inherits from all its ancestors.

The keyword extends declares the relation. In the tutorial, MountainBike extends Bicycle, gains all of Bicycle's fields and methods, adds a seatHeight field and a setHeight method, and calls the superclass constructor with super.
card.example: Class Puppy extends Dog, and Dog extends Animal, which has no extends clause. Puppy's direct superclass is Dog. Animal and Object are its further ancestors. A Puppy object can use methods from Dog, Animal and Object.
card.rule: A class extends exactly one direct superclass, which is Object when none is named, and it inherits from every class in the chain above it.
card.limits: Inheriting does not give access to everything above. Which members are inherited depends on access modifiers, as the next idea explains.

concepts.title: What a subclass inherits
concepts.question: Which members does a subclass inherit, and which does it not?

paragraphs: A subclass inherits the fields, methods and nested classes of its superclass that it is allowed to see. Public and protected members are inherited whatever package the subclass is in. Package-private members are inherited only when the subclass is in the same package.
Private members are not inherited. Constructors are not inherited either, although a subclass constructor can call a superclass constructor.

A private field can still be used indirectly. If the superclass has public or protected methods that read and write it, the subclass can call them. An inherited public or protected nested class can also reach its enclosing class's private members.
card.example: Account has a private balance, a public deposit and a protected audit. Savings extends Account. Savings inherits deposit and audit but not balance. It changes the balance by calling deposit.
card.rule: A subclass inherits public and protected members, package-private ones only from its own package, and neither private members nor constructors.
card.limits: Not inheriting a private field does not make the data vanish. The inherited public methods of the superclass still work on it.

concepts.title: Casting and instanceof
concepts.question: When is a cast needed between a class and its superclass, and how does instanceof guard it?

paragraphs: A MountainBike is a Bicycle and an Object, so it can be used wherever those types are required. Moving up the hierarchy needs no cast: Object obj = new MountainBike() is accepted.

Moving down needs an explicit cast. MountainBike bike = obj is a compile-time error, because the compiler does not know obj holds a MountainBike. Writing (MountainBike) obj promises that it does, and adds a check at run time that throws an exception if the promise is false.
The instanceof operator tests an object's type first, so the cast runs only when it is safe.
card.example: Object o holds some value. The code if (o instanceof Bicycle) followed by a cast of o to Bicycle is guarded. Without the test, a String held in o would make the cast fail when the program runs.
card.rule: Moving up the hierarchy is implicit and safe, while moving down needs an explicit cast with a run-time check, which instanceof can guard.
card.limits: A cast does not convert an object. It changes only the compiler's view, and the run-time check accepts only what the object really is.

concepts.title: Three meanings of multiple inheritance
concepts.question: What are the three kinds of multiple inheritance, and which of them does Java allow?

paragraphs: The phrase multiple inheritance covers three things. Multiple inheritance of state is inheriting fields from several classes. Multiple inheritance of implementation is inheriting method definitions from several classes. Multiple inheritance of type is a class implementing more than one interface.

Java does not let a class extend more than one class. One reason is to avoid inheriting state from several superclasses, where it is unclear which constructor or method sets a shared field. Another is name conflicts: a compiler may be unable to tell which inherited method to use. Interfaces have no fields, so no state comes from them.

Multiple inheritance of type is allowed: an object has its own class type and the type of every interface its class implements. Default methods bring a limited form of implementation inheritance, and when they clash, the compiler or the programmer must decide.
card.example: Class Duck extends Bird and implements Swimmer and Flyer. Duck gets its fields and method bodies from Bird, plus any defaults from the interfaces. Duck objects can be used as Bird, Swimmer or Flyer.
card.rule: Java allows several interfaces, which is multiple inheritance of type, but only one superclass, so state comes from a single line of ancestors.
card.limits: Default methods let interfaces contribute implementation. When two supply the same method, the compiler or the programmer must choose which one to use.

concepts.title: Overriding, hiding and overloading
concepts.question: What is the difference between overriding, hiding and overloading a method?

paragraphs: An instance method in a subclass with the same signature (name and parameter types) and return type as a superclass instance method overrides it. The return type may be a subtype of the original, called a covariant return type. The annotation @Override makes the compiler complain if nothing is overridden.

A static method in a subclass with the same signature as a superclass static method hides it. With overriding, the subclass version runs for a subclass object. With hiding, the version used depends on whether the call is made through the superclass or the subclass. Mixing an instance method and a static method of the same signature is a compile-time error.

Overloading is different: a method with the same name but a different parameter list is a new method that neither overrides nor hides. An overriding method may allow more access than the original, but not less.
card.example: Animal and Cat both define an instance method testInstanceMethod and a static method testClassMethod. With Animal myAnimal = new Cat(), the call myAnimal.testInstanceMethod() runs Cat's version, while Animal.testClassMethod() runs Animal's.
card.rule: Same-signature instance methods override, same-signature static methods hide, an instance and static mix fails to compile, and a different parameter list is an overload.
card.limits: The choice by actual object applies only to overriding. Hiding and overloading are different relations, and an override may widen access but not narrow it.

concepts.title: Polymorphism
concepts.question: When a superclass-typed variable refers to a subclass object, which version of an overridden method runs?

paragraphs: Polymorphism means subclasses can define their own behaviour while sharing the parent's functionality. In the tutorial, Bicycle has a printDescription method. MountainBike and RoadBike override it, each calling super.printDescription() first and then printing its own extra data.

A variable declared as Bicycle may refer to a Bicycle, a MountainBike or a RoadBike. When printDescription is called, the Java virtual machine runs the version belonging to the object, not the version of the variable's declared type. The tutorial calls this virtual method invocation.
The shared part is written once in the parent, and each subclass adds only what is special.
card.example: Bicycle b = new RoadBike(...) followed by b.printDescription() prints the general bike details and then the tire width, because the object is a RoadBike.
card.rule: For an overridden instance method, the version that runs is chosen by the object's actual class at run time, not by the variable's declared type.
card.limits: This holds for overridden instance methods. A static method hidden by a subclass is not chosen by the object, as the previous idea showed.

concepts.title: Hiding fields
concepts.question: What happens when a subclass declares a field with the same name as a superclass field, and what does the tutorial advise?

paragraphs: A field in a subclass with the same name as a superclass field hides the superclass field. This holds even when the two fields have different types.
Inside the subclass, the hidden field cannot be reached by its simple name. It must be reached through super.
The tutorial does not recommend hiding fields, because it makes code difficult to read.
card.example: Base has a String field label. Child extends Base and declares its own String label. Inside Child, label means Child's field, and super.label means Base's field.
card.rule: A same-named field in a subclass hides the superclass field, which is then reachable only through super, and the tutorial advises against hiding.
card.limits: Hiding goes by name alone, whatever the types. The usual fix is a different field name, not a clever use of super.

concepts.title: Reaching the superclass's version with super
concepts.question: How does a subclass run the superclass's version of a method it has overridden?

paragraphs: Inside a subclass, super followed by a dot and a method name calls the superclass's version of that method. Without super, the simple name refers to the subclass's own version.

In the tutorial, Subclass overrides printMethod. Its version first calls super.printMethod() and then prints its own line, so the output shows the superclass line and then the subclass line. The same dot form reaches a hidden field.
The keyword super has a second job in constructors, covered in the next idea. A dot after super points to the first job; parentheses point to the second.
card.example: Class Cat extends Animal and overrides describe. Its body is: return super.describe() plus the text purrs. The result is the Animal description followed by purrs.
card.rule: Super followed by a dot and a member name reaches the superclass's version of an overridden method or a hidden field.
card.limits: The super form works only for the call written with it. Other code that calls the method on the same object still gets the subclass's override.

concepts.title: Constructors and super
concepts.question: How does a subclass constructor reach the superclass constructor, and what happens when it says nothing?

paragraphs: A subclass constructor can call a superclass constructor with super and a parenthesised argument list, choosing the constructor whose parameters match. A bare super() calls the no-argument one. This call must be the first line of the constructor.

If the constructor does not call one, the compiler adds a call to the superclass's no-argument constructor. If the superclass has no such constructor, that is a compile-time error. Object has a no-argument constructor, so a class whose only superclass is Object has no trouble.
A superclass constructor may call its own superclass's constructor in turn, and so on up to Object. The tutorial calls this constructor chaining.
card.example: Vehicle has only a constructor taking a String id. Car extends Vehicle and has an empty constructor. The compiler inserts super() and finds no such constructor, so Car fails to compile. Writing super of a text value on the first line fixes it.
card.rule: Every constructor starts with a call to a superclass constructor, either written first or implied as the no-argument one, and the calls chain up to Object.
card.limits: The implied call works only if the superclass has a no-argument constructor. Otherwise the subclass constructor must call a matching one itself.

concepts.title: Overriding equals and hashCode
concepts.question: Why override equals, and what else must be overridden along with it?

paragraphs: Object's version of equals uses the identity operator, so it reports whether two references point to the very same object. When objects holding the same information should count as equal, you must override equals.
The tutorial's Book class overrides equals to compare ISBN numbers. Two separate Book objects with the same ISBN are then equal. The cast must wrap obj before the ISBN getter is called.
If you override equals, you must also override hashCode. Equal objects must have equal hash codes, and Object's hashCode no longer matches the new meaning of equal.
card.example: Book has an ISBN. Its equals returns true when the other object is a Book with the same ISBN, and its hashCode is built from the ISBN. Two Book objects with ISBN 0201914670 are equal and share a hash code.
card.rule: Override equals when identity is the wrong test, and override hashCode with it so that equal objects have equal hash codes.
card.limits: Keep identity-based equals where two objects with the same data should still count as different things. Override only when equal information means equal objects.

concepts.title: toString, getClass, clone and finalize
concepts.question: What do toString, getClass, clone and finalize do, and what does the tutorial advise about each?

paragraphs: The method toString returns a text form of the object. The tutorial advises considering an override in every class, because the default is meant for debugging. The method getClass returns the object's runtime class as a Class object, and it cannot be overridden.

The method clone makes a copy. The class must implement Cloneable, or Object's version throws CloneNotSupportedException. The default copy gives the clone the same member values, so if the object refers to another object, both share it. Override clone when the copy needs its own version of that other object.

The method finalize may be called by the garbage collector when an object becomes garbage, but when, or whether, is uncertain. Do not rely on it for cleanup. The tutorial recommends try-with-resources to close resources.
card.example: A Book's toString returns its ISBN and title. A Playlist whose songs field refers to one list object is copied by default clone. Both playlists then share that list, so a song added through one shows in the other.
card.rule: Override toString for readable output, remember getClass is fixed, make clone copy referenced objects when copies must be independent, and do not rely on finalize.
card.limits: Default clone is fine when the object's fields hold only plain values. The extra work is needed only when the object refers to other objects that must not be shared.

concepts.title: Final methods and classes
concepts.question: What do final methods and final classes prevent, and when does the tutorial suggest using them?

paragraphs: A method declared final cannot be overridden by subclasses. Use it when the implementation must not change and is critical to the object's consistent state. The tutorial's chess example makes getFirstPlayer final because it returns a fixed value that should not vary. Object has several final methods.
The tutorial also says methods called from constructors should generally be final. Otherwise a subclass may redefine one of them, with surprising or undesirable results.
A final class cannot be subclassed. This is useful for immutable classes, such as String.
