card.example: Account declares audit as final and calls only final methods from its constructor. No subclass can replace them. A class declared final, like String, cannot have subclasses at all.
card.rule: A final method blocks overriding, a final class blocks subclassing, and methods called from constructors should be final.
card.limits: Final removes flexibility. Use it where a change would damage the object's consistency, not as a default.

concepts.title: Abstract classes and methods
concepts.question: What is an abstract class or method, and what must a subclass of an abstract class do?

paragraphs: An abstract method is declared without an implementation: no braces, only a semicolon. An abstract class is declared with the keyword abstract and may or may not contain abstract methods. It cannot be instantiated but can be subclassed. A class that has an abstract method must itself be declared abstract.

A subclass usually implements all the abstract methods it inherits. If it does not, it must be declared abstract too. An abstract class can hold fields and ordinary methods that its subclasses share, and may have static members used through the class name.
An abstract class may implement an interface without implementing all of its methods, provided the class is declared abstract. A concrete subclass can then finish the job.
card.example: Abstract GraphicObject has fields x and y, a concrete moveTo, and abstract draw and resize. Circle and Rectangle extend it and each writes draw and resize.
card.rule: An abstract class cannot be instantiated; a class with an abstract method must be abstract, and a subclass must implement inherited abstract methods or be abstract itself.
card.limits: An abstract class need not contain any abstract method; the keyword alone blocks instantiation. In an interface, methods are implicitly abstract, so the keyword is unnecessary there.

concepts.title: Abstract class or interface
concepts.question: When does the tutorial favour an abstract class, and when an interface?

paragraphs: Neither can be instantiated. In an abstract class, fields may be non-static and non-final, and methods may be public, protected or private. A class extends only one class. In an interface, fields are public static final, methods are public, and a class may implement any number.

Use an abstract class to share code among closely related classes, when subclasses need common fields or non-public members, or when you want non-static, non-final fields that hold each object's state.

Use an interface when unrelated classes will implement it, as with Comparable and Cloneable, when you want to specify behaviour without caring who implements it, or when you want multiple inheritance of type. Libraries often use both: HashMap extends AbstractMap and implements Map.
card.example: A family of related shapes that share position fields suits an abstract class. A Printable contract that invoices, photos and shapes must all meet suits an interface.
card.rule: Choose an abstract class to share state and code among closely related classes and an interface to give unrelated classes a common type, and combine them when both needs exist.
card.limits: These are guidelines. A class that already extends another class cannot also extend an abstract class, which can force the interface choice.

concepts.title: Primitive numbers and their wrapper classes
concepts.question: What is the difference between an int and an Integer, and how does Java move between them?

paragraphs: Most number work in Java uses primitive types such as int, float and byte. A primitive is a bare value, not an object. For every primitive there is also a wrapper class, an object type that holds one primitive value: Integer for int, Float for float, Byte for byte, and so on.

The compiler converts between the two forms by itself. Wrapping a primitive into its object is boxing, and taking the primitive back out of the object is unboxing. The numeric wrapper classes (for byte, short, int, long, float and double) all extend one abstract parent class, Number.
Literals show the primitive side: an int can hold 500, a float literal needs the suffix f as in 3.65f, and a byte can be set from the hexadecimal literal 0x7f, whose decimal value is 127.
card.example: int level = 12 holds the bare number. Integer boxed = level creates an Integer object that wraps 12, which is boxing. int again = boxed pulls the value back out, which is unboxing. All three variables carry the same number; only the kind of thing holding it differs.
card.rule: Numbers are primitives by default, each primitive has a wrapper class, and the numeric wrappers extend Number, with the compiler boxing and unboxing automatically.
card.limits: Only the numeric wrappers extend Number; the wrapper for a single character is not a number type. Wrappers are objects, so use them when you need object behaviour, not as the everyday way to store a number.

concepts.title: Three reasons to use a wrapper object
concepts.question: When is it worth using a Number object instead of a primitive?

paragraphs: According to the tutorial, three reasons justify a Number object. First, a method may expect an object as its argument; a Number is accepted there, which comes up often when numbers are kept in collections.

Second, the wrapper classes define constants such as MIN_VALUE and MAX_VALUE, the smallest and largest values the type can hold. Third, they carry class methods that convert values to and from other primitive types, to and from strings, and between number systems such as decimal, octal, hexadecimal and binary.
card.example: A grade tool needs the largest value an int can hold as a sentinel. It reads Integer.MAX_VALUE, which is 2147483647, instead of typing digits. Later it saves scores into a collection that accepts only objects, so each int is boxed on the way in.
card.rule: Choose a wrapper object when an API needs an object, when you need the type's bounds, or when you need its conversion methods; otherwise keep the primitive.
card.limits: The three reasons are a list of needs, not a ban on primitives. For plain arithmetic and local variables a primitive does the job and no object is needed.

concepts.title: What every Number object can do
concepts.question: Which instance methods do all Number subclasses share, and when does equals say true?

paragraphs: Every Number subclass gives you methods that convert the object's value to a primitive type: byteValue, shortValue, intValue, longValue, floatValue and doubleValue. Each returns the value as the primitive its name states.

compareTo compares this object to an argument and returns an int. equals returns true only when the argument is not null, is an object of the same type, and holds the same numeric value. Two objects with equal numbers but different types are therefore not equal.
card.example: Integer n = 7. n.doubleValue() gives 7.0. n.equals(Integer.valueOf(7)) is true: same type, same value. n.equals(Short.valueOf((short) 7)) is false, because the type differs even though both hold seven.
card.rule: Use xxxValue to read a Number as a primitive, and remember that equals needs the same type as well as the same value.
card.limits: The plain equals rule is a baseline: Double and Float carry extra requirements described in the API documentation. Equal-looking numbers of different wrapper types still fail equals.

concepts.title: Turning strings into numbers, in any base
concepts.question: How do Integer methods read a string as a number, and how do you choose the number system?

paragraphs: The Integer class converts text to numbers in several ways. parseInt(String) reads a decimal string and returns a primitive int. parseInt(String, radix) reads the string in the number system you name: radix 10 is decimal, 2 binary, 8 octal and 16 hexadecimal. valueOf does the same reading but returns an Integer object.
decode(String) accepts a decimal, octal or hexadecimal representation. toString and the static toString(int) go the other way, from number to string. The other numeric wrappers have similar methods.
card.example: Integer.parseInt("11", 2) reads the digits 11 in base 2 and gives 3. Integer.parseInt("11") reads the same digits in decimal and gives 11. The radix is the only difference between those two calls.
card.rule: Pass a radix to parseInt or valueOf to read a string in another base; without one the string is read as decimal.
card.limits: The radix names the base the text is written in, not the base of the result: the result is just a number. The tutorial shows these methods for Integer and says the other wrappers have similar ones.

concepts.title: printf, format specifiers and the newline
concepts.question: How does a format string with percent specifiers turn arguments into printed text?

paragraphs: The methods printf and format are equivalent; both belong to PrintStream, so they work wherever print or println does. The first argument is a format string holding plain text and format specifiers, and the arguments after it fill the specifiers in order. Because the argument list can vary in length, it is declared as varargs.

A specifier begins with a percent sign, may have flags, a width and a precision, and ends with a converter naming the argument type. Converter d prints a decimal integer, f a floating-point number (six decimal places by default), s a string, and n the platform's newline. Use %n rather than the escape for a newline.
card.example: With int n = 42 and double r = 2.5, System.out.printf("n=%d r=%f%n", n, r) prints n=42 r=2.500000 and then ends the line. The %d took n, the %f took r, and %n added the newline.
card.rule: A format string mixes plain text with percent specifiers, each ending in a converter such as d, f, s or n that is filled by the next argument.
card.limits: Specifier and argument must agree: a converter for integers cannot take a floating-point value. The tutorial lists only some converters and refers readers to java.util.Formatter for the full set.

concepts.title: Flags, width and precision
concepts.question: What do the parts between the percent sign and the converter change about the printed number?

paragraphs: Between the percent sign and the converter you can put flags, a width and a precision. The width is how many characters the value should take; the value is right-justified in that space unless told otherwise. A flag of 0 before the width pads with zeros, so 08 means eight characters wide, filled with zeros.

The plus flag always shows the sign, the comma flag adds grouping separators for the locale, and the minus flag left-justifies. A precision such as .3 sets the digits after the decimal point for f, rounding as needed. Width and precision can be combined, as in 10.3.
card.example: With long n = 461012, %08d prints 00461012 and %+,8d prints +461,012. With pi, %.3f prints 3.142 and %10.3f prints 3.142 right-justified in ten columns, so five spaces come first.
card.rule: Flags, width and precision go between the percent sign and the converter, and each shapes the output without changing the argument.
card.limits: The tutorial shows only a handful of flags and defers the full set to java.util.Formatter. A flag only helps with a converter it fits: a precision shapes f output, and the zero flag is shown with d.

concepts.title: DecimalFormat patterns
concepts.question: How does a pattern string tell DecimalFormat what digits, separators and symbols to show?

paragraphs: DecimalFormat, in the java.text package, formats a number according to a pattern string. The pattern controls leading and trailing zeros, prefixes and suffixes, grouping separators and the decimal separator. Its format method takes a double and returns a String.

In a pattern, 0 is a digit that is always shown, padded with a zero when needed, while # is a digit that is not forced. A comma marks grouping and a point marks the decimal separator. Other characters, such as a dollar sign, are literal text.
card.example: The value 123.78 with the pattern 000000.000 gives 000123.780, because every 0 is a forced digit. The value 123456.789 with ###.## gives 123456.79: only two fractional digits are allowed, so the number is rounded.
card.rule: A DecimalFormat pattern uses 0 for forced digits, # for optional digits, a comma for grouping, a point for decimals and other characters as literal text.
card.limits: The pattern shapes the text you get back; the double itself is not changed. A pattern fixes how many digits can appear, so a number that is too long is rounded to fit.

concepts.title: The Math class: rounding, powers, angles and random numbers
concepts.question: Which Math methods and constants go beyond the basic operators, and what rules govern their arguments?

paragraphs: Math, in java.lang, supplies constants (E and PI) and more than 40 static methods, so you call them on the class, as in Math.sqrt(16). Basic methods include abs, min, max and the rounding family: ceil gives the smallest whole number not below the argument, floor the largest not above it, rint the closest, each as a double. Powers and logs come from pow, sqrt, exp and log.

The trigonometric methods sin, cos and tan take angles in radians; toRadians and toDegrees convert. Math.random returns a double from 0.0 up to but not including 1.0, so multiplying by 10 and casting to int gives 0 through 9.
card.example: Math.ceil(43.74) gives 44.0 and Math.floor(43.74) gives 43.0, both doubles. Math.sin(Math.toRadians(90)) gives 1.0, while Math.sin(90) treats 90 as radians. (int)(Math.random() * 10) is a whole number from 0 to 9.
card.rule: Call Math methods on the class, give trigonometric methods radians, and treat random as at least 0.0 and below 1.0.
card.limits: Math.random fits a single random number; for a series the tutorial suggests a java.util.Random object. Math methods are chosen by argument type, so pass the type you intend.

concepts.title: char, Character and escape sequences
concepts.question: When do you use the primitive char and when the Character object, and what does a backslash do inside a text literal?

paragraphs: A single character is held in the primitive type char by default. The Character class wraps a char in an object, and you use it when an object is required, for example a method parameter typed as an object. A Character holds one char and is immutable: once created, its value cannot change. The compiler boxes and unboxes between the two.

A backslash begins an escape sequence, which the compiler reads specially. A tab is backslash t, a newline backslash n, a carriage return backslash r, a backspace backslash b, a form feed backslash f. Backslash plus a single quote, a double quote or another backslash inserts that character itself.
card.example: char initial = 'R' stores one letter. Character boxed = initial wraps it. System.out.println("She said \"Hi\"") prints She said "Hi", because each backslash-quote inserts a double quote inside the text.
card.rule: Use char for single characters, Character when an object is needed, and a backslash to insert special characters into text.
card.limits: A Character is not a general text type; it holds exactly one char and cannot be changed. An escape sequence is written as two characters in source code but stands for one character in the result.

concepts.title: Character methods for testing and converting
concepts.question: Which static Character methods test or convert a single char?

paragraphs: The Character class has more than fifty methods; the tutorial lists a few. Test methods take a char and give true or false: isLetter, isDigit, isWhitespace, isUpperCase and isLowerCase. Conversion methods give a new value: toUpperCase and toLowerCase return a char, and toString returns a one-character String.
These are static, so you call them on the class, as in Character.isDigit(c). They return a result and do not alter the variable you pass in.
card.example: To count digits in some text, step over each char c and add one whenever Character.isDigit(c) is true. For a letter k, Character.toUpperCase('k') gives K, and Character.isLetter('7') gives false.
card.rule: Test or convert one char with the static Character methods and use the value they return.
card.limits: The tutorial lists only some of the Character methods. They work on one char at a time; to change a whole String you use String methods instead.

concepts.title: Strings are objects that never change
concepts.question: What does it mean that a String cannot be changed, and what do methods like concat do instead?

paragraphs: A string is a sequence of characters, and in Java a string is an object of the String class. Writing text in double quotes creates one, and so does a constructor; the class has thirteen, and new String(charArray) builds a string from an array of chars. length() returns how many characters the string holds.

A String is immutable: it cannot be changed after it is created. A method that seems to modify it, such as concat, builds and returns a new string, and the original stays exactly as it was. To keep the result, you must store the returned string.
card.example: String s = "Dot" holds Dot. Calling s.concat(" saw") on its own line returns a new string, Dot saw, and throws it away; s still holds Dot. String t = s.concat(" saw") keeps the result in t.
card.rule: A String never changes; every method that seems to change it returns a new String, which you must keep.
card.limits: Immutability belongs to each String object, not to a variable name: a variable can be pointed at a different String. Beyond the tutorial: when text must change many times, a mutable StringBuilder, covered later, is the tool.

concepts.title: Joining strings and building formatted strings
concepts.question: How do you join strings, mix in other values, and build a formatted String you can reuse?

paragraphs: Two tools join strings. The concat method returns a new string with the argument added at the end. The plus operator does the same and is more common; with it, a non-String operand is converted to text by calling its toString method, so numbers and other objects can sit in the chain.
String.format is a static method that works like printf but returns a String instead of printing. Use it when you need the formatted text more than once or somewhere other than the console.
card.example: int n = 3; the expression with the text Items, a colon and space, plus n gives Items: 3. String line = String.format with %d items and n stores the text 3 items in line, ready to reuse; printf with the same arguments would only print it.
card.rule: Join with concat or plus, which converts non-String operands, and use String.format when you need the formatted text as a value.
card.limits: Both joins make new strings and leave the originals alone. String.format returns text but prints nothing, so a call whose result is ignored has no visible effect.

concepts.title: From text to number: valueOf and parse methods
concepts.question: How do you turn a String such as user input into a number you can calculate with?

paragraphs: Numeric data often arrives as text, such as a value typed by a user or given on the command line. Each numeric wrapper offers a class method valueOf that converts a string to an object of that wrapper type. To get the primitive, call a method like floatValue on that object.
The wrappers also provide parseXXXX methods, such as parseFloat or parseInt, which return the primitive directly. The tutorial calls this more direct than valueOf, and it gives the same results.
card.example: String in = a text holding 12. int n = Integer.parseInt(in) gives the number 12, so n + 1 is 13. Without conversion, in joined with 1 by plus would give the text 121, not 13.
card.rule: Convert text with parseXXXX to get a primitive, or valueOf to get a wrapper object, before doing arithmetic.
card.limits: The tutorial's demo only checks that two arguments were given, not that they are valid numbers. Beyond the tutorial: text that is not a valid number makes these methods throw NumberFormatException, so check or catch.

concepts.title: From number to text
concepts.question: What are the ways to turn a number into a String, and what can you do with the text afterwards?

paragraphs: The tutorial shows three ways to convert a number to a String. Join it with an empty string using plus, as in the empty string plus i. Call String.valueOf(i). Or call the class method toString on the number's wrapper, such as Integer.toString(i) or Double.toString(d).
All three give a String. Once you have text, you can use String methods on it, for instance length(), to look at the digits.
card.example: int i = 255. Integer.toString(i) gives the String 255, whose length() is 3. The same text comes from String.valueOf(i). A primitive int has no methods of its own, but the String does.
card.rule: Convert a number with String.valueOf, the wrapper's toString, or plus with an empty string, then use String methods on the result.
card.limits: Converting does not change the number, and the text is only as precise as the conversion shows. The tutorial gives no rule for choosing between the three ways; each yields a String.

concepts.title: Indexes, charAt and substring
concepts.question: How are characters in a String numbered, and which characters does substring return?

paragraphs: Characters in a String are numbered from 0, so the last valid index is length() minus 1. charAt(i) returns the character at index i. substring(begin, end) returns the characters from begin up to but not including end, that is, up to index end minus 1. substring(begin) returns everything from begin to the end.
Counting carefully is the skill: the first number is where the piece starts, the second is where it stops, and that stopping point is excluded.
card.example: String word = "stationery" has length 10 and indexes 0 to 9. charAt(5) is o. substring(2, 6) is atio: indexes 2, 3, 4 and 5. substring(7) is ery, from index 7 to the end.
card.rule: Index from 0; substring includes the start index and excludes the end index.
card.limits: Reading a character at index length is out of range, because the last valid index is length minus 1. Indexes outside the String are rejected with an exception, so check positions that come from a search before using them.

concepts.title: Searching and replacing inside a String
concepts.question: How do you find where something occurs in a String, and how do you replace parts of it?

paragraphs: indexOf searches forward from the start of a String and lastIndexOf searches backward from the end. Both take a character or a substring, and both return minus 1 when nothing is found. When you only need to know whether a piece is present, contains returns true or false.

For replacing, the String class has four methods. replace swaps every occurrence of a character, or of a literal piece of text. replaceAll and replaceFirst treat the first argument as a regular expression, a pattern, and replace every match or only the first. Each returns a new String.
card.example: String fruit holds banana. indexOf with the char a returns 1 and lastIndexOf returns 5. indexOf with the char z returns -1. fruit.replace('a', 'o') returns bonono, and fruit itself is unchanged.
card.rule: indexOf and lastIndexOf give a position or minus 1, contains gives true or false, and the replace family returns new Strings.
card.limits: The tutorial's Filename example does no error checking: if the name has no period, lastIndexOf returns minus 1 and the following substring call throws an exception. Always test a search result before using it as an index.

concepts.title: Comparing Strings and parts of Strings
concepts.question: Which methods test equality, order and matching regions of Strings, and what do they return?

paragraphs: equals returns true only when the argument is a String with the same characters in the same order, and equalsIgnoreCase does the same while ignoring case. startsWith and endsWith test the ends of a String. These all return boolean.

compareTo compares two Strings in dictionary order and returns an int: positive if this String is greater, 0 if equal, negative if less. compareToIgnoreCase ignores case. regionMatches compares a stretch of this String, given a start index and length, with a stretch of another; a version with a leading boolean can ignore case.
card.example: String a holds apple and b holds banana. a.compareTo(b) is negative, since apple comes first. a.startsWith with app is true. a.equals with Apple is false, but a.equalsIgnoreCase with Apple is true.
card.rule: equals and its relatives answer yes or no, while compareTo answers with the sign of an int; ignore-case versions differ only in case handling.
card.limits: regionMatches needs both start indexes and the length, and the region must fit inside both Strings. Case matters in equals, compareTo and regionMatches unless an ignore-case version is used.

concepts.title: StringBuilder: length, capacity and when to use it
concepts.question: How is StringBuilder different from String, and what are its length and capacity?

paragraphs: A StringBuilder is like a String that can be modified. Inside, it is a variable-length array of characters whose content and length change through method calls. The tutorial says to use String by default, and a StringBuilder when it gives simpler code or better performance, notably when you join a large number of strings.

length() is the number of characters in the sequence. capacity() is the number of character spaces allocated; it is at least the length and grows automatically. StringBuilder() starts with capacity 16, and StringBuilder(String s) holds s plus 16 spare spaces.
card.example: new StringBuilder("abc") has length 3 and capacity 19: three characters plus 16 spare spaces. A builder can hold more characters than three; its capacity is just the room currently reserved.
card.rule: Use String by default and StringBuilder for repeated changes; length counts characters while capacity counts allocated space.
card.limits: Capacity is not content: only length tells how many characters are present. For a one-off join of a few Strings, the tutorial's default of String remains the simpler choice.

concepts.title: Editing a StringBuilder
concepts.question: Which StringBuilder methods add, remove, replace and reverse characters?

paragraphs: append and insert are overloaded for many data types. They convert the argument to text and add its characters: append at the end, insert before a chosen offset. delete(start, end) removes from start up to but not including end, and deleteCharAt removes one character. replace(start, end, text) swaps a range for text, setCharAt changes one character, reverse flips the order, and toString returns a String.

The String methods are reached by calling toString first; StringBuilder(String) converts back. setLength shortens the content or pads it with null characters. StringBuffer is the same class of tool with synchronized, thread-safe methods.
card.example: sb holds hello. sb.append('!') makes hello!. sb.insert(0, 'o') puts o before everything. sb.delete(0, 1) removes the first character again. sb.reverse() gives !olleh. Each call changes sb itself.
card.rule: Edit a StringBuilder in place with append, insert, delete, replace, setCharAt and reverse, and call toString when you need a String.
card.limits: Ranges follow the substring convention: the end index is excluded. A StringBuilder has few methods of its own, so for other String operations convert with toString first.

concepts.title: Autoboxing and unboxing in practice
concepts.question: When does the compiler wrap a primitive in an object or unwrap one, and what does it do for operators?

paragraphs: Autoboxing is the compiler's automatic conversion of a primitive to its wrapper object. It applies when a primitive is passed to a method expecting the wrapper, or assigned to a variable of the wrapper type. Unboxing is the reverse: it applies when a wrapper is passed to a method expecting the primitive or assigned to a primitive variable.
The pairs are boolean and Boolean, byte and Byte, char and Character, float and Float, int and Integer, long and Long, short and Short, double and Double.
card.example: Character ch = 'a' boxes a char. Passing an int to a method with an Integer parameter boxes it. double pi = list.get(0), where the list holds Double objects, unboxes the Double into a primitive double.
card.rule: The compiler boxes when a wrapper is expected and unboxes when a primitive is expected, in assignments and method arguments.
card.limits: The tutorial's autoboxing page does not cover comparison of wrapper objects. Beyond the tutorial: constructors such as new Integer(-8), used in its example, are deprecated in newer Java releases.

concepts.title: Types as parameters
concepts.question: What does a type parameter receive, compared with the formal parameter of a method?

paragraphs: Generics let a class, an interface or a method take types as parameters. A formal parameter of a method stands for a value that arrives when the method is called. A type parameter stands for a type that arrives when the generic code is used. In both cases one definition serves many inputs.
So you write the logic once and supply different types where you use it, such as a list of String in one place and a list of Integer in another.
card.rule: A type parameter is to types what a formal parameter is to values: one definition, many inputs.
card.limits: The comparison covers reuse only. A type argument has to be an object type, never a primitive, and it is checked by the compiler rather than passed around as an ordinary value.
card.example: A greeting method takes a name as text, and each call passes a different name. A class Crate with a type parameter takes a kind of item, and Crate of Apple and Crate of Wrench are both made from the one definition.

concepts.title: Checks at compile time, no casts
concepts.question: Why is a wrong item caught while compiling with a typed collection, but only while running with an Object collection?

paragraphs: Without generics, a collection holds plain Object values. Anything can be put in, so a wrong item is accepted. The mistake shows only when a later line takes the item out and assumes it is something else, and that failure happens while the program runs.

With a type argument, such as a list of String, the compiler knows what the list may hold. It rejects a wrong item at the line that adds it, and it lets you take items out with no cast. Compile-time errors are easier to fix than run-time errors, which can be hard to find.
card.rule: Declare the element type so the compiler, not a later run, finds wrong items and removes the need for casts.
card.limits: The checks apply where the compiler sees the generic type. Raw types and old code can bypass them, so a cast-free line is no guarantee by itself.
card.example: Old style: a list holds anything, so you add the number 5, later cast the first item to String, and the program stops with an error. New style: a list of String refuses the number 5 at the add line, before the program ever runs.

concepts.title: Generic algorithms
concepts.question: How can one algorithm serve collections of many element types and still be type safe?

paragraphs: A third benefit is generic algorithms. A procedure such as counting or searching often works the same way whatever the elements are. With a type parameter you write it once for collections of any element type, and each caller gets its own element type back, checked by the compiler.
Such code can be customized, is type safe and is easier to read, because the types it works with appear in its signature instead of hiding behind casts.
card.rule: Write the procedure once over a type parameter instead of once per element type.
card.limits: An unbounded type parameter allows only operations that every object has. Tasks that need more, such as ordering items, need extra help from a bound, covered in a later idea.
card.example: A method that counts how often an item occurs in an array can be written once with a type parameter T. Given a String array and a String, it works. Given an Integer array and a String, the compiler refuses the call.

concepts.title: Making a class generic
concepts.question: How does replacing Object with a type variable in a class change what the compiler can check?

paragraphs: A non-generic Box stores Object, so it can hold anything and the compiler cannot verify what comes out. To make it generic, put a type parameter section after the class name and replace each Object with the type variable. Box of T then reads: set takes a T and get returns a T.
The type variable can be used anywhere inside the class. The same technique works for interfaces, so a generic type is simply a class or interface that has type parameters.
card.rule: Add a type parameter list after the class name and use it wherever the class said Object.
card.limits: Inside the class the type variable stands for an unknown type, so the code can use only what every object has unless a bound adds more.
card.example: Plain Box: set takes Object and get returns Object, so one part of a program may store an Integer while another stores a String, and the mismatch appears at run time. Generic Box with T: a Box of Integer accepts and returns only Integer.

concepts.title: Naming type parameters
concepts.question: Which single letters do programmers conventionally use for type parameters, and why not longer names?

paragraphs: By convention a type parameter name is a single uppercase letter. This keeps a type variable visibly apart from the longer, mixed-case names of ordinary classes and interfaces.
The common letters hint at the role: E for an element (heavily used in the collections), K for a key, V for a value and T for a general type.
card.rule: Name type parameters with a single uppercase letter whose meaning matches its role.
card.limits: This is a convention for readability, not a rule about meaning: a letter that does not fit the role makes readers guess, and the letter alone says nothing about any bound.
card.example: A lookup table from words to counts uses K for the word type and V for the count type. A list-like class uses E for what it holds. A one-off helper class uses T.

concepts.title: Type parameter and type argument
concepts.question: In Box of Integer, what is Integer called, and what is T called in the declaration?

paragraphs: Two terms are easy to blur. In the declaration of Box of T, the T is a type parameter. In a use such as Box of String, the String is a type argument. Many developers use the words interchangeably, but the tutorial keeps them apart.
Replacing T with a type argument is a generic type invocation, and the result, such as Box of Integer, is a parameterized type. It is like a method call that passes a type instead of a value.
card.rule: Parameters appear where a generic is defined; arguments appear where it is used.
card.limits: The distinction matters for exact talk, but people mix the words. Judge by where the name sits, in a declaration or in a use, not by the word someone chose.
card.example: A class Cell has the type parameter T. The line declaring a variable of type Cell of Date uses the type argument Date, and Cell of Date is a parameterized type.

concepts.title: The diamond
concepts.question: When may the type arguments in a constructor call be replaced by an empty pair of angle brackets?

paragraphs: Since Java SE 7 you may leave the type arguments out of a constructor call and write only an empty pair of angle brackets, informally called the diamond, when the compiler can infer them from the context.
The declared type on the left tells the compiler which arguments the new object needs, so repeating them on the right adds nothing.
card.rule: Use the diamond when the declared type already tells the compiler the type arguments.
card.limits: The diamond is not the same as writing no brackets: a construction with no brackets at all creates a raw type, while the diamond keeps the full parameterized type.
card.example: A variable is declared as a Map of String and List of String. On the right, new HashMap followed by the diamond lets the compiler fill in String and List of String.

concepts.title: Several and nested type arguments
concepts.question: How can a generic type take several parameters, and can one argument itself be a generic type?

paragraphs: A generic class or interface may list several type parameters, separated by commas. A Pair has K for the key type and V for the value type. Using it supplies one argument for each, in order: Pair of String and Integer makes K a String and V an Integer.
A type argument may itself be a parameterized type. Replacing V with Box of Integer gives a pair whose value is a box of integers.
card.rule: Supply one type argument for each type parameter, in order, and an argument may itself be a parameterized type.
card.limits: Order matters: swapping the arguments swaps the roles, so Entry of Integer and String is a different type from Entry of String and Integer.
card.example: A class Entry with parameters K and V is used as Entry of String and Integer for a word count. Another use, Entry of String and List of String, passes a list type as the value argument.

concepts.title: Raw types
concepts.question: What is a raw type, and why does the tutorial advise avoiding it?

paragraphs: A raw type is the name of a generic class or interface used with no type arguments. For Box of T, plain Box is the raw type, while Box of Integer is a parameterized type. A class that is not generic is not a raw type.
A raw Box behaves the pre-generics way and hands out Object values. Raw types skip the generic checks, so wrong items can be caught only at run time, and the tutorial advises avoiding them.
card.rule: Name the type argument; use a raw type only where old code forces it.
card.limits: A plain non-generic class name is not a raw type, so it is fine. Raw types cannot always be avoided at the edge of old code, so the aim is to keep them out of new code.
card.example: A generic class Crate has a parameter T. A variable of type Crate of Fruit is parameterized. A variable of type Crate with no argument is raw, and its get method gives a plain Object.

concepts.title: Unchecked warnings
concepts.question: Which assignments and calls involving raw types draw warnings, and which stay silent?

paragraphs: Assigning a parameterized type to its raw type is allowed with no warning, so old code keeps working. Assigning a raw type to a parameterized type gives an unchecked conversion warning. Calling a generic method through a raw reference gives an unchecked invocation warning.
Unchecked means the compiler lacks the type information to promise safety. By default it prints only a short note that unchecked operations exist.
card.rule: Parameterized to raw is silent; raw to parameterized, or a call through a raw reference, draws an unchecked warning.
card.limits: A warning is not an error. The code compiles and the mistake may surface only at run time, and the default short note is easy to overlook.
card.example: A Box of String is assigned to a raw Box variable: silent. A new raw Box is assigned to a Box of Integer variable: unchecked conversion. A set call with the number 8 through the raw variable that refers to the Box of String: unchecked invocation, because the check that would reject 8 is skipped.

concepts.title: Generic methods
concepts.question: Where do a generic method's type parameters go, and where can they be used?

paragraphs: A generic method declares its own type parameters. The list goes in angle brackets before the return type, so a static method returning a boolean writes K and V first, then the word boolean. The scope of those parameters is that one method.
Static and non-static methods can both be generic. A static generic method cannot use the type parameters of its class, because those belong to instances, so it declares its own.
card.rule: Declare the method's type parameters in angle brackets before the return type.
card.limits: The parameters exist only inside that method. They are not the class's parameters, and a static method cannot borrow the class's.
card.example: A utility class has a static method that takes two Pair objects, declares K and V before the word boolean, and reports whether their keys and values are equal. A caller just passes two pairs, and K and V come from the arguments.

concepts.title: Generic types and subtyping
concepts.question: Why can a Box of Integer not be used where a Box of Number is expected?

paragraphs: Ordinary objects follow the is-a relationship: an Integer can be used wherever a Number is expected. It is natural to expect a Box of Integer to work where a Box of Number is expected. It does not. For two different arguments A and B, Box of A and Box of B have no relationship, whether or not A and B are related.
So a method declared to take a Box of Number rejects a Box of Integer or a Box of Double, with a compile error saying one cannot be converted to the other.
card.rule: Related type arguments do not make related generic types: a Box of Integer is not a Box of Number.
card.limits: Subtyping still works for the generic class itself with the same argument, as with ArrayList of String and List of String. Wildcards, covered later, create relationships between different arguments.
card.example: A method boxTest takes a Box of Number. Passing a Box of Number works. Passing a Box of Integer or a Box of Double is a compile error, although Integer and Double are subtypes of Number.

concepts.title: Subtyping through extends and implements
concepts.question: When is one parameterized type a subtype of another, if not through its arguments?

paragraphs: A generic class or interface is subtyped by extending or implementing it, and the clauses decide how parameters line up. ArrayList of E implements List of E, which extends Collection of E. So an ArrayList of String is a List of String, which is a Collection of String.
The relationship holds only while the type argument passed along stays the same. An ArrayList of String is a List of String, but it is not a List of Object.
card.rule: A generic type is a subtype of what it extends or implements, as long as the type argument passed along stays the same.
card.limits: Changing the argument that is passed along breaks the relationship. Only parameters that the supertype does not use can vary freely.
card.example: A box-like class Stack of E extends List of E. A Stack of Book can be used wherever a List of Book is expected, and so wherever a Collection of Book is expected. It is not accepted where a List of Object is expected.

concepts.title: Type inference
concepts.question: How does the compiler choose type arguments for a call when none are written?

paragraphs: Type inference is the compiler's ability to examine each call and its declaration and choose the type arguments that make the call valid. It uses the types of the arguments and the type the result is assigned to or returned as, and it picks the most specific type that suits all the arguments.
It never uses anything from later in the program. An explicit type argument, called a type witness, overrides inference when you write one.
card.rule: Let the compiler infer type arguments from the call's arguments and target; write a type witness only when it cannot decide.
card.limits: Inference looks only at the call, its arguments and where the result goes, never at later code, so a call whose context gives no information can fall back to a broad type.
card.example: A method pick takes two values of the same type T and returns one. It is called with the text d and an ArrayList of String. Both are Serializable, so T becomes Serializable, and the result can be assigned to a Serializable variable.

concepts.title: Generic constructors
concepts.question: How are a constructor's own type parameters different from its class's, and how are both filled in?

paragraphs: A constructor can declare its own type parameters, in a generic or a non-generic class, just as a method can. In a class MyClass with the parameter X, a constructor may declare a separate parameter T.

So two sets of parameters may be in play: the class's X and the constructor's T. When an object is created, X comes from the type written or the declared target, and T is inferred from the constructor's arguments.
card.rule: A constructor's own type parameters are separate from the class's and are inferred from the constructor's arguments.
card.limits: The constructor's parameter exists only for that constructor, as a method's parameter does for its method. It is not available elsewhere in the class.
card.example: Creating a MyClass of Integer with the empty text as the argument gives X as Integer by writing it, and T as String inferred from the argument. With the diamond, X comes from the declared variable type and T still comes from the argument.

concepts.title: Upper bounds on type parameters
concepts.question: How does an upper bound limit a type parameter, and what does it let the code do?

paragraphs: A bounded type parameter restricts which types may be used as type arguments. Write the parameter name, the word extends, and the upper bound, as in U extends Number. Only Number and its subtypes are accepted; any other type is a compile-time error. Here extends is used in a general sense: it means extends for classes and implements for interfaces.
A bound also gives the code something. Since every U is known to be a Number, the code may call the methods that Number defines on a U value. An unbounded parameter offers only what every object has.
card.rule: Put extends and a bound after a type parameter to limit the arguments and to unlock the bound's methods.
card.limits: A bound limits callers: a type that neither extends nor implements it cannot be used. Methods the bound lacks are still unavailable.
card.example: A Box with the parameter T has a generic method inspect with the parameter U extends Number. Calling inspect with the text some text is rejected at compile time, because a String is not a Number. Calling it with an Integer works.

concepts.title: Bounding by Comparable
concepts.question: Why does a generic counting method need a Comparable bound, and what replaces the greater-than operator?

paragraphs: The greater-than operator works only on primitive numeric types, so a generic method cannot use it on objects of type T. Comparing objects needs a method. Bounding T by Comparable of T guarantees that every T value has the method compareTo.

Comparable of T declares compareTo, which takes a T and returns an int. A method that counts the elements greater than a given one declares T extends Comparable of T and tests each element with compareTo.
card.rule: To order or compare generic items, bound the parameter by Comparable of itself and use compareTo, not an operator.
card.limits: The bound restricts callers to types that implement Comparable of themselves, and the result is only as meaningful as that type's own compareTo.
card.example: A method countGreaterThan takes an array of T and one element, declared with T extends Comparable of T. With a String array it counts the strings that come after the given string. With an array of a class that is not Comparable, the call is rejected.

concepts.title: Several bounds
concepts.question: How are several bounds written on one type parameter, and which one must come first?

paragraphs: A type parameter may have several bounds, joined with an ampersand: T extends B1 and B2 and B3. Then T is a subtype of all of them at once.
If one of the bounds is a class, it must be listed first. Putting a class bound after an interface bound is a compile-time error.
card.rule: List the class bound first, then the interfaces, and remember that a type argument must satisfy all bounds.
card.limits: Every bound must be met at once, so each extra bound narrows the types allowed.
card.example: Take a class A and interfaces B and C. The header T extends A & B & C compiles. The header T extends B & A & C does not, because the class A is not first.

concepts.title: The wildcard
concepts.question: What does the question mark stand for in generic code, and where is it used?

paragraphs: In generic code the question mark, called the wildcard, stands for an unknown type. It can be the type of a parameter, a field or a local variable. It can sometimes be a return type, but it is better practice to be more specific.
Think of it as a type whose exact identity does not matter to this code. That makes it a tool for flexibility in what a method accepts.
card.rule: Use the wildcard for a type that is unknown and does not matter, in parameters, fields and local variables.
card.limits: A wildcard says what you do not know. It fits places that accept or hold values, but a return type that callers must then use is better stated precisely.
card.example: A method parameter declared as a List of question mark accepts a list of any element type. A local variable of that type may refer to any list.

concepts.title: Upper bounded wildcards
concepts.question: How does a wildcard with extends let one method accept lists of several element types?

paragraphs: An upper bounded wildcard is written as the question mark, extends and a bound: question mark extends Number. It matches Number and every subtype. So a List of question mark extends Number accepts a List of Integer, a List of Double and a List of Number, where a List of Number alone accepts only the last.
Inside the method, items read from the list are treated as the bound type. As elsewhere, extends covers implements for interfaces.
card.rule: Use question mark extends Bound for a list you only read from, when it may hold the bound or any subtype.
card.limits: This form suits reading from a list. It does not suit storing items into it, which a later idea explains.
card.example: A method sumOfList takes a List of question mark extends Number, loops over Number items, adds the doubleValue of each, and returns the total. For the Integers 1, 2, 3 the total is 6.0. For the Doubles 1.2, 2.3, 3.5 it is 7.0.

concepts.title: The unbounded wildcard
concepts.question: When is a List of question mark the right parameter type, and how does it differ from a List of Object?

paragraphs: The unbounded wildcard, a lone question mark, gives a list of unknown type. Use it in two cases: when the method needs only what Object offers, or when it calls methods of the generic class that do not depend on the type parameter, such as size or clear.

A List of Object is not the same thing. A method taking List of Object accepts that exact type, not a List of Integer or a List of String. A method taking List of question mark accepts a list of any element type, because every List of A is a subtype of it.
card.rule: Use a list of the unbounded wildcard when the code needs nothing from the element type beyond Object.
card.limits: Items come out only as Object, so it is no use when the code needs more from the elements.
card.example: A printList method takes a List of question mark and loops with an Object variable, printing each item. It works for a list of Integer and for a list of String alike.

concepts.title: Lower bounded wildcards
concepts.question: What does a wildcard with super allow a method to do, and which list types does it accept?

paragraphs: A lower bounded wildcard restricts the unknown type to a given type or any of its supertypes: question mark super Integer. A List of question mark super Integer matches a List of Integer, a List of Number and a List of Object, all of which can hold Integer values.
Use the lower bound when the goal is to put values of that type into a collection whose exact element type may be the type or a supertype.
card.rule: Use question mark super Type when the code puts values of Type into a collection.
card.limits: A wildcard takes one bound, upper or lower, never both. The tutorial's page covers putting values in, not reading them back.
card.example: A method addNumbers takes a List of question mark super Integer and adds the numbers 1 to 10, each boxed to an Integer. It works for a list of Integer, a list of Number and a list of Object.

concepts.title: Wildcards and subtyping
concepts.question: How do wildcards create subtype relationships between lists whose arguments differ?

paragraphs: Wildcards give back relationships that fixed arguments lack. A List of Integer and a List of Number are unrelated, but a List of question mark extends Integer is a subtype of a List of question mark extends Number. Upper bounded wildcards follow the direction of the arguments.

Lower bounded wildcards run the other way: a List of Number is a subtype of a List of question mark super Integer, and a List of question mark super Number is a subtype of a List of question mark super Integer. A List of the bare wildcard sits above all of them.
card.rule: Extends wildcards follow the direction of the arguments, super wildcards run the opposite way, and the bare wildcard sits on top.
card.limits: The plain pair stays unrelated even with wildcards around: a List of Integer is still not a List of Number. Wildcards add relationships only to the wildcard types.
card.example: A List of Integer fits under List of question mark extends Integer, then under List of question mark extends Number, then under List of the bare wildcard. A List of Number fits under List of question mark super Number and under List of question mark super Integer.

concepts.title: Wildcard capture and helper methods
concepts.question: What does an error mentioning capture of mean, and when does a helper method fix it?

paragraphs: Sometimes the compiler gives an unknown wildcard type a temporary specific name; this is wildcard capture. You rarely think about it, except when an error message contains the words capture of. That message means the compiler cannot prove an operation type safe.

If the operation really is safe, move it into a private generic helper method. The public method passes its wildcard argument to the helper, whose type parameter names the captured type. By convention the helper takes the method's name plus Helper. If the operation is truly unsafe, no helper will fix it.
card.rule: When a capture-of error blocks code that is truly safe, route it through a private generic helper; if it is unsafe, redesign.
card.limits: A helper only helps the compiler see what is already correct. Two wildcard arguments are captured separately, and mixing them stays an error.
card.example: A method foo takes a List of the bare wildcard, reads the first item and writes it back to the same position. The direct code is rejected. A private fooHelper that takes a List of T and does the same with T compiles, and foo simply calls it.

concepts.title: Choosing extends or super
concepts.question: How do you decide between extends, super and no wildcard for a parameter?

paragraphs: Classify each variable by its role. An in variable supplies data to the code: in a copy method, the source list. An out variable receives data for use elsewhere: the destination list.
The guideline: give an in variable an upper bounded wildcard with extends, and give an out variable a lower bounded wildcard with super.
card.rule: In means extends, out means super, Object-only in means the bare wildcard, and both in and out means no wildcard.
card.limits: A variable used as both in and out gets no wildcard, and the guideline does not cover return types.
card.example: A method copies items from a source list to a destination list. The source is read, so it is an in variable. The destination is written, so it is an out variable. Each gets the matching wildcard.

concepts.title: Read-only lists and wildcard returns
concepts.question: Is a list with an extends wildcard really read-only, and should a wildcard be a return type?

paragraphs: A list typed with an extends wildcard is informally called read-only, but the tutorial notes this is not strictly true. Say ln is a List of question mark extends NaturalNumber that refers to a List of EvenNumber. Adding a new NaturalNumber is a compile-time error, since the list might hold only even numbers.
The guidelines also do not apply to return types. A wildcard as a return type is best avoided, because it forces the callers to deal with wildcards.
card.rule: Treat an extends list as read-only for new items, know that some changes still work, and avoid wildcard return types.
card.limits: Read-only is only informal, because some operations that change the list remain possible.
card.example: A List of EvenNumber is assigned to a List of question mark extends NaturalNumber variable. Adding an ordinary NaturalNumber is refused, because it could be odd and break a list of even numbers.

concepts.title: What type erasure does
concepts.question: What does the compiler do to generic code when it erases types, and why do generics still help?

paragraphs: Generics exist to give tighter type checks at compile time and to support generic programming. To implement them, the compiler applies type erasure. It replaces every type parameter with its bound, or with Object if there is no bound, so the compiled code contains only ordinary classes, interfaces and methods.
Erasure also inserts casts where needed to keep type safety, and generates bridge methods to keep polymorphism working in extended generic types.
card.rule: Erasure replaces type parameters with bounds or Object, adds casts where needed, and adds bridge methods.
card.limits: Erasure removes type arguments from compiled code, so the running program cannot see them. That is why some operations on generic types are restricted, as the last section shows.
card.example: A class Box with T extends Number is compiled with Number in place of T. A class Crate with an unbounded T is compiled with Object in place of T. Code that reads a value gets a cast added where needed.

concepts.title: Erasing classes and methods
concepts.question: What do bounded and unbounded type parameters become after erasure, in classes and in methods?

paragraphs: In a generic class, each type parameter is replaced by its first bound, or by Object if it has none. A Node with an unbounded T ends up with a data field of type Object. If T extends Comparable of T, the field becomes the raw Comparable, and Node of T itself becomes the raw type Node.

Generic methods are erased the same way. A method taking an array of T and one T, with T unbounded, ends up taking an Object array and an Object. With T extends Shape, a parameter of type T ends up as Shape.
card.rule: Erasure turns each type parameter into its first bound, or Object when there is none.
card.limits: With several bounds, erasure uses the first. The erased signature is what exists at run time, and the type argument is gone from it.
card.example: A class Tray with T extends Fruit has a field of type T and a method get returning T. After erasure the field has type Fruit and get returns Fruit.

concepts.title: Bridge methods
concepts.question: Why does the compiler add a bridge method, and how can a ClassCastException still appear?

paragraphs: Suppose Node of T has a setData method taking a T, and MyNode extends Node of Integer with a setData taking an Integer. After erasure Node's method takes Object while MyNode's takes Integer, so MyNode's method would no longer override; it would only overload.

To keep overriding working, the compiler adds a bridge method to MyNode. It takes an Object, casts it to Integer and calls the Integer version. Bridge methods are synthetic: you do not write or call them.
card.rule: A bridge method keeps overriding working after erasure by casting and then delegating to the real method.
card.limits: Bridge methods are made by the compiler. They cannot stop misuse through raw types: the cast inside fails at run time.
card.example: A class Pack of T has a put method taking T, and BookPack extends Pack of Book with put taking Book. After erasure Pack's put takes Object, so BookPack gets a bridge put taking Object that casts to Book and calls put with the Book.

concepts.title: Reifiable types and heap pollution
concepts.question: What makes a type reifiable, and what does heap pollution mean?

paragraphs: A reifiable type is one whose full type information is available at run time: primitives, non-generic types, raw types, and uses of unbounded wildcards such as List of the bare wildcard. A non-reifiable type has had information removed by erasure. List of String and List of Number are examples, and the runtime cannot tell them apart.

Heap pollution happens when a variable of a parameterized type refers to an object that is not of that parameterized type. It comes from operations that give an unchecked warning, such as mixing raw and parameterized types.
card.rule: Non-reifiable types lose their arguments at run time, and unchecked warnings are the warning signs of heap pollution.
card.limits: The guarantee that clean code cannot pollute the heap holds for code compiled together. Code compiled in separate pieces can hide the risk.
card.example: A variable of type List of String ends up, through a raw reference, referring to a list that holds Integer values. Reading an item as a String later fails with a ClassCastException.

concepts.title: Generic varargs and SafeVarargs
concepts.question: Why does a varargs parameter of a generic type produce a warning, and when is it honest to hide it?

paragraphs: A varargs parameter is compiled into an array, and Java cannot create arrays of parameterized types. After erasure the array becomes an Object array, so a method with a generic varargs parameter can pollute the heap. The compiler warns at the method declaration.

A method that only reads its varargs and adds them to a list is safe. The annotation SafeVarargs declares a method safe and removes the declaration warning; use it only if the body cannot cause a ClassCastException.
card.rule: Use SafeVarargs only on a method whose body merely reads its generic varargs.
card.limits: The annotation is a promise you must keep. Hiding the warning another way is less desirable.
card.example: A method addToList takes a List of T and varargs of T, and only adds each element to the list: safe. A method faultyMethod takes varargs of List of String, stores a List of Integer into the array through an Object array alias and reads it back as a String: it fails with a ClassCastException.

concepts.title: No primitives, no new E
concepts.question: Why can a type argument not be a primitive, and why can you not write new E?

paragraphs: A type argument cannot be a primitive type. A Pair of int and char is rejected; a Pair of Integer and Character works, and autoboxing converts values such as 8 and the letter a for you.
You also cannot create an instance of a type parameter with new. The type is erased at run time, so there is no class to create from.
card.rule: Use wrapper types as type arguments, and obtain instances of a type parameter some way other than new.
card.limits: Only the type argument is restricted. Primitive values still work as ordinary values, and autoboxing lets them be passed where the wrapper is expected.
card.example: A Pair of int and char fails to compile, while a Pair of Integer and Character compiles. Inside a generic method, a line that creates an object of the type parameter E with new also fails to compile.

concepts.title: No static fields of the parameter type
concepts.question: Why can a generic class not have a static field whose type is its type parameter?

paragraphs: A static field belongs to the class and is shared by every instance, whatever type argument the instance has. So a static field whose type is the class's type parameter is a compile-time error.
If it were allowed, one field os in a class MobileDevice would have to be a Smartphone, a Pager and a TabletPC at the same time, once objects of each kind exist.
card.rule: Static members cannot use the class's type parameters.
card.limits: The ban concerns types that use the class's parameter. A static field of a type such as int, or a static method with its own type parameter, is fine.
card.example: A class Singleton with the parameter T declares a private static T instance and a static method returning T. Neither line compiles.

concepts.title: No instanceof, casts or arrays of parameterized types
concepts.question: Why can you not test, cast to or create arrays of types with arguments?

paragraphs: Because parameterized types are erased, the runtime cannot tell an ArrayList of Integer from an ArrayList of String. So instanceof with a parameterized type is a compile-time error, and so is a cast between different parameterizations, such as List of Integer to List of Number.

For the same reason you cannot create arrays of parameterized types. Arrays check element types at run time and throw ArrayStoreException on a mismatch, but erased generics give the runtime nothing to check.
card.rule: Do not test, cast to or build arrays of types whose arguments erasure removes.
card.limits: Some forms are still allowed, because they ask for nothing that erasure removed.
card.example: A test asking whether a list is an ArrayList of Integer is rejected. Creating an array of List of Integer with two slots is rejected.

concepts.title: Exceptions and clashing overloads
concepts.question: Why can a generic class not extend Throwable, and why can two overloads differing only in type arguments not coexist?

paragraphs: A generic class cannot extend Throwable, directly or indirectly. A catch clause cannot use a type parameter, because matching an exception depends on its run-time class, which erasure removes. A type parameter may appear in a throws clause.

You also cannot overload methods whose parameter types erase to the same raw type. A method taking a Set of String and one taking a Set of Integer would both become a method taking a Set, so the compiler rejects them.
card.rule: Exception matching and overloading depend on run-time types, so type arguments erased away cannot tell cases apart.
card.limits: Overloads whose parameter types differ even after erasure, such as a Set and a List, stay legal.
card.example: A class Parser with T extends Exception can declare a method parse that throws T. A second print method taking a Set of Integer next to print taking a Set of String is rejected.

concepts.title: What a package is for
concepts.question: What does a package give you that a plain list of related classes does not?

paragraphs: A package groups related types into one unit. Types here means classes and interfaces and their close relatives. Programmers can see that the grouped types belong together, which is the first benefit.
A package also forms its own namespace, a space in which names are looked up. Two packages can each hold a type with the same simple name, because the package keeps them apart.
The second job of a package is access protection. Types inside one package can share access freely, while access from outside the package can be restricted.
card.example: A clinic library keeps Patient, Appointment and Doctor together in one package. A bakery library, written elsewhere, also has a class called Appointment for pickup times. Both libraries can be used in one program, because each package supplies its own namespace.
card.rule: A package groups related types into one namespace and controls how outside code may reach them.
card.limits: A namespace only separates names that sit in different packages; nothing in the compiler stops two independent authors from choosing the same package name.

concepts.title: Declaring a package in a file
concepts.question: What must a source file contain, and where, for its types to belong to a named package?

paragraphs: To place a type in a package, write a package statement naming it as the first statement of the source file. The statement covers every type in that file, and a file can hold only one such statement.
A file may contain at most one public top-level type, and the file must carry that type's name. A public class Invoice therefore lives in Invoice.java.

Other top-level types may share the file, but they are package private: only code in the same package can use them. The tutorial discourages sharing unless those types are small and closely tied to the public one. A file with no package statement puts its types in the unnamed package.
card.example: File Invoice.java begins with package billing; then declares public class Invoice and, below it, a small class Rounding without public. Invoice is visible outside billing. Rounding can be used only by other billing types.
card.rule: Start each file with one package statement, and give each file at most one public top-level type named like the file.
card.limits: Putting several types in one file is allowed for non-public types, but the tutorial advises it only for small types closely tied to the public one.

concepts.title: Naming packages
concepts.question: How should a package name be built so that two organisations are unlikely to pick the same one?

paragraphs: A type's full name is its package name followed by its own name. So graphics.Rectangle and java.awt.Rectangle can both exist and the compiler tells them apart.
Trouble starts only when two programmers choose the same package name. The compiler cannot prevent that, so a naming convention does the work instead.

By the convention, package names use lower case only, which keeps them distinct from type names that start with a capital. They begin with your organisation's internet domain written in reverse. Inside one organisation, add a region or project name to separate teams.
card.example: A firm that owns tulip.example.org starts all its packages with org.example.tulip, for instance org.example.tulip.billing. Two teams that both want a package called orders can use org.example.tulip.emea.orders and org.example.tulip.asia.orders.
card.rule: Begin package names with your reversed domain name in lower case, and add region or project names to separate teams.
card.limits: The compiler does not enforce this convention, so it protects you only as far as everyone follows it.

concepts.title: Three ways to reach a type in another package
concepts.question: Which way of reaching a type from another package suits how often you use it?

paragraphs: Code outside a package can use only the package's public types. It may write a simple name only if the type is in its own package or has been imported. Otherwise it needs one of three routes.

Route one is the fully qualified name, such as pets.Dog, written at each use. Route two imports a single type, after which the simple name works. Route three imports the whole package with an asterisk, so every type in it can be used by simple name.
The tutorial matches the route to how often you use the package. Rare use calls for the qualified name, a few types for single imports, and many types for the asterisk.
card.example: A class in package kennel uses pets.Dog once, so it writes the qualified name there. Another kennel class works with Dog, Cat and Hamster all over the file, so it begins with import pets.asterisk, written as the pets package followed by dot star.
card.rule: Use the qualified name for rare references, a single import for a few types, and a package import for many.
card.limits: These routes change only how names are written; a type that is not public stays out of reach whichever route you pick.

concepts.title: What the asterisk and the dots mean
concepts.question: What does an import with an asterisk bring in, and what does a shared name prefix tell you?

paragraphs: The asterisk means all types directly in the named package. It cannot select a subset, so a pattern such as import shop.Ca asterisk is a compile error rather than a way to import names starting with Ca.

Package names look like a tree, but the tree is only a naming habit. The package java.awt does not contain java.awt.color. Importing java.awt.asterisk brings in only types sitting directly in java.awt, so you import both packages if you need both.
A shared prefix hints that packages are related; it does not mean one contains the other.
For every source file the compiler imports two packages without being asked: java.lang and the package that the file belongs to.
card.example: A file uses Item from package shop and Coupon from package shop.promo. It needs import shop.asterisk; and import shop.promo.asterisk; as two separate lines, one per package.
card.rule: An asterisk import covers every type directly in one package, and a shared name prefix shows a relation, never containment.
card.limits: The asterisk never filters by name pattern and never reaches into related packages beneath the named one.

concepts.title: Name clashes and static import
concepts.question: What happens when two imported packages share a simple name, and what does static import cost?

paragraphs: A simple name can stand for two different types. If two imported packages each contain a type called Rectangle, using the simple name is ambiguous and the compiler rejects it. Writing the qualified name, such as graphics.Rectangle, settles which one you mean.

Static import lets code use a class's static members, its constants and static methods, without the class name in front. One line can import a single member, as with the constant PI of Math, or all static members with an asterisk.
The tutorial urges care. When many members are used without a class name, readers cannot tell which class defines them. Used lightly it removes repetition; used heavily it hurts readability.
card.example: Packages maps and geom both contain Point, and a file imports both with asterisks. Writing Point p; is rejected, while maps.Point p; is accepted. In a geometry file, one import static of the Math constant PI saves typing it forty times.
card.rule: When two imported packages share a simple name, qualify it; use static import sparingly because it hides where a member is defined.
card.limits: Ambiguity arises only where the shared simple name is used, and static import pays off for a few often-used members, not for everything.

concepts.title: Where source and class files go
concepts.question: Given a package name and a type, in which directory do its source file and class file belong?

paragraphs: Most implementations store a package as a directory tree. Each part of the package name becomes one directory level, so com.example.graphics.Rectangle has its source in com/example/graphics/Rectangle.java.
The compiler writes one class file for each type in a source file, named after the type, even for non-public helper types. Class files also belong in directories that match the package name.
The Java language itself does not require a hierarchical file system; the directory mapping is what most implementations use.
card.example: Package com.example.pets holds public class Dog and a package-private class Leash in Dog.java, found at com/example/pets/Dog.java. Compiling it gives com/example/pets/Dog.class and com/example/pets/Leash.class.
card.rule: Mirror the package name as directories for both source and class files, with one class file per type.
card.limits: The mapping describes what most implementations do; the language does not demand a hierarchical file system.

concepts.title: How compiled types are found: the class path
concepts.question: How do the compiler and the virtual machine find the compiled types a program uses?

paragraphs: The problem: a program names types by package, but class files live somewhere on disk. The solution is the class path, a root directory or list of root directories where the search begins.
From a root, the tools add the package parts as directories. For package com.example.graphics and class path /work/classes, they look in /work/classes/com/example/graphics.
A list of roots separates entries with a semicolon on Windows and a colon on UNIX. You can set it with the CLASSPATH environment variable, and display or clear that variable as well.
card.example: Class files for package shop.cart sit under /work/out/shop/cart. The class path must name /work/out, the root, so that the search adds shop and cart itself.
card.rule: The class path names the root directories under which the package tree of every used type is searched.
card.limits: An entry must be the directory that holds the top of the package tree, not the package directory itself.

concepts.title: An exception is an event that gets thrown
concepts.question: What is an exception, and what does a method do at the moment one occurs?

paragraphs: An exception is an event that happens while a program runs and disrupts the normal flow of its instructions. The word is short for exceptional event.
When an error occurs inside a method, the method builds an exception object and hands it to the runtime system. That act is called throwing an exception.
The exception object holds information about the problem: its type, and the state of the program when the problem occurred.
card.example: A method that turns a typed-in quantity into a number meets the text 'abc'. It cannot go on, so it builds an exception object that records the kind of failure and the program state, and hands that object to the runtime system.
card.rule: An exception is an event that disrupts normal flow, and throwing it means building an exception object and handing it to the runtime system.
card.limits: The object only describes the problem; it repairs nothing. Something else must deal with it. Also, ordinary expected events, such as a read reaching the planned end of a stream, are not exceptions.

concepts.title: The search for a handler along the call stack
concepts.question: In what order does the runtime system look for a handler, and what happens if none is found?

paragraphs: After a method throws, the runtime system looks for something to deal with the exception. It searches the call stack: the ordered list of methods that were called to reach the method where the error happened.

The search starts in the method where the error occurred and moves back through its callers, in the reverse order of the calls. A block of code that can deal with the exception is an exception handler.

A handler is appropriate when its type matches the type of the thrown object. The handler that is chosen is said to catch the exception. If the whole stack is searched without success, the runtime system and the program terminate.
card.example: main calls load, and load calls parse. parse throws. The runtime checks parse, then load, then main. Only main has a handler of a matching type, so main's handler catches it. If main had none either, the program would end.
card.rule: The runtime searches the call stack from the failing method back toward the first caller for a handler of a matching type, and the program ends if there is none.
card.limits: The order is the order of the calls, not the order of methods in the source file. A handler of an unrelated type is passed over, so having some handler is not enough.

concepts.title: The Catch or Specify requirement
concepts.question: What must code that might throw certain exceptions do so that it compiles?

paragraphs: Valid Java code must honor the Catch or Specify Requirement. Code that might throw certain exceptions must either sit inside a try statement that has a handler for the exception, or sit in a method whose declaration specifies the exception in a throws clause.
Code that breaks the requirement does not compile. The check happens before the program runs.
The requirement does not cover every exception. The next idea sorts out which ones it covers.
