card.example: A method opens a file with a FileReader constructor that can throw a missing-file exception. Option one: put the call in a try statement with a catch block for it. Option two: add a throws clause naming it after the parameter list. With neither, the compiler rejects the method.
card.rule: Code that might throw a covered exception must either catch it in a try statement or specify it with a throws clause, or it will not compile.
card.limits: Only some exceptions are covered. Neither option is better in itself: catching suits a method that can respond, and specifying hands the decision to a caller.

concepts.title: Checked exceptions, errors and runtime exceptions
concepts.question: Which exceptions fall under Catch or Specify, and which may be left alone?

paragraphs: A checked exception is a condition a well-written application should anticipate and recover from, for example a missing file named by a user. Every exception is checked unless it is an Error, a RuntimeException, or a subclass of one of those.

An error is a condition outside the application that it usually cannot foresee or recover from, such as a hardware fault while reading. A runtime exception is a condition inside the application, usually a bug such as passing null where a value is required.
Errors and runtime exceptions together are called unchecked exceptions. Only checked exceptions are subject to Catch or Specify.
card.example: A user types a file name and the file is missing: checked, so the code must handle it. A disk fault interrupts a read: an error. Code passes null to a constructor that needs a value: a runtime exception, and the sensible move is to fix the bug.
card.rule: Only checked exceptions must be caught or specified; errors and runtime exceptions, together called unchecked, need neither.
card.limits: Unchecked does not mean harmless: such exceptions can still be thrown and can still end a program. The tutorial adds that using unchecked types only to avoid the requirement is generally not recommended.

concepts.title: The try block marks the risky code
concepts.question: What goes inside a try block, and does a try block handle anything by itself?

paragraphs: The first step in writing a handler is to enclose the code that might throw an exception in a try block. The block can hold a single risky statement or a group of statements.
You choose the grain. You can give each risky statement its own try block and its own handler, or put several statements in one try block and attach several handlers to it.
A try block handles nothing alone. It needs catch blocks after it, or a finally block. A variable that a later cleanup block must see is often declared before the try and set to null.
card.example: A method that writes numbers to a file declares a writer variable set to null, then opens the file and writes inside one try block. The whole method body fits in a single try because it is short.
card.rule: Enclose the code that might throw in a try block, then attach handlers to it.
card.limits: A try block does not handle anything by itself: the summary says a try statement needs at least one catch block or a finally block.

concepts.title: Catch blocks and handler matching
concepts.question: How does a catch block receive an exception, and which handler does the runtime choose?

paragraphs: A catch block follows its try block directly, with no code between them. It has one parameter whose type must be a class inheriting from Throwable. Inside the block the parameter name refers to the exception object.
A try can have several catch blocks. The runtime chooses the first handler whose parameter type fits the thrown object, meaning the object could legally be assigned to that parameter.
The code of a handler can do more than print a message. It can recover from the error, ask the user to decide, or pass the problem to a higher-level handler by chaining exceptions.
card.example: A try is followed by one catch with an IndexOutOfBoundsException parameter e that prints e.getMessage(), and one catch with an IOException parameter e that prints a different line. A thrown IOException skips the first and runs the second.
card.rule: Each catch block has one parameter of a Throwable type, and the first handler whose type can accept the thrown object runs.
card.limits: Matching is by type, not by message text or name. A handler for a general type also accepts its subclasses, so it may catch more than intended.

concepts.title: One handler for several types
concepts.question: How can a single catch block handle more than one exception type?

paragraphs: Since Java 7 a single catch block can handle several exception types. List the types in the catch clause, separated by the vertical bar character.
This removes duplicated handler code and lessens the temptation to catch an overly broad type just to save typing.
When a block handles more than one type, its parameter is implicitly final, so the block cannot assign a new value to it.
card.example: catch (NumberFormatException | IndexOutOfBoundsException ex) prints a line using ex.getMessage(). One block now serves both types where two copies of the same body were needed before.
card.rule: List the types separated by a vertical bar in one catch clause to share one handler, and do not reassign its parameter.
card.limits: Share a block only when the same response suits every listed type. If the types need different recovery, separate catch blocks fit better.

concepts.title: Catch order: specific before general
concepts.question: Why does the order of catch blocks matter, and what goes wrong with a broad handler first?

paragraphs: Since the first fitting handler wins, the order of catch blocks matters. A subclass object fits a superclass parameter, so a handler for a superclass accepts every subclass object.

If a catch for a general type comes before a catch for a more specific subclass, the specific block can never be reached. According to the tutorial's exercise, a catch for Exception followed by a catch for ArithmeticException does not compile.
Write the more specific handlers first and the more general ones after them.
card.example: Wrong order: catch Exception first, then catch ArithmeticException. The second is unreachable and the code is rejected. Swapping them, ArithmeticException first and Exception second, lets each fit the objects meant for it.
card.rule: Write catch blocks for more specific types before catch blocks for more general types.
card.limits: Order matters only between related types. Handlers for unrelated types never compete for the same object, so they can appear in either order.

concepts.title: The finally block runs on every way out
concepts.question: What does a finally block promise, and when can that promise fail?

paragraphs: A finally block runs whenever its try block exits, whether the exit is normal or abrupt because of an exception. It lets cleanup code run even when something unexpected happens.
It also keeps cleanup from being bypassed by a return, continue or break inside the try block. The tutorial calls putting cleanup in a finally block good practice even when no exception is expected.
There is one caveat. If the JVM exits while the try or catch code is running, the finally block may not execute.
card.example: A method opens a file inside a try block and writes lines. The try can end three ways: opening fails, a write fails, or everything works. A finally block closes the file in all three cases, so the cleanup is written once.
card.rule: Put cleanup in a finally block so that it runs on every way out of the try block, except when the JVM itself exits.
card.limits: Not guaranteed if the JVM exits during try or catch code. Also, for closing files and similar resources the tutorial prefers try-with-resources to a finally block.

concepts.title: The try-with-resources statement
concepts.question: How does try-with-resources close things automatically, and in what order?

paragraphs: A resource is an object that must be closed when the program has finished with it. A try-with-resources statement declares one or more resources in parentheses after try. Each one is closed when the statement ends, whether it finishes normally or abruptly.

Any object that implements java.lang.AutoCloseable can be a resource, which includes everything that implements java.io.Closeable. Several resources are separated by semicolons and are closed in the reverse order of their creation.
A try-with-resources statement can have catch and finally blocks like an ordinary try. They run after the resources have been closed.
card.example: try (BufferedReader in = new BufferedReader(new FileReader(path))) { first = in.readLine(); } closes in after the line is read, or when readLine throws. No finally block and no null check is needed.
card.rule: Declare resources in parentheses after try and they are closed automatically, the last opened first, before any catch or finally block runs.
card.limits: The resource must implement AutoCloseable. Closing can itself throw, so the surrounding code still has to catch or specify what close declares.

concepts.title: Why try-with-resources beats finally for closing
concepts.question: Why does the tutorial prefer try-with-resources to a finally block for closing resources?

paragraphs: Closing in a finally block can leak a resource. If the body throws and the first close in the finally block also throws, the second close is skipped. A leak means a resource was not released to the operating system.
With the finally approach, if both the body and a close throw, the exception from the finally block propagates and the exception from the body is lost.

With try-with-resources the exception from the body propagates, and exceptions from closing are suppressed. They stay attached to the main exception and can be read with getSuppressed. The tutorial concludes: use try-with-resources to close resources.
card.example: Old style: try { return br.readLine(); } finally { br.close(); fr.close(); }. If readLine throws and br.close() also throws, fr.close() never runs and the caller sees only the close failure. The same task with both readers declared as resources loses nothing.
card.rule: Prefer try-with-resources to finally for closing, because it closes every resource and keeps the body's exception, recording close failures as suppressed.
card.limits: Finally still serves cleanup that is not resource closing. A suppressed exception is recorded, not thrown, so it is seen only if you call getSuppressed on the main exception.

concepts.title: Tracing try, catch and finally together
concepts.question: In what order do try, catch and finally run when the try block fails or succeeds?

paragraphs: When an exception is thrown inside the try block, the runtime stops the try block at once. It checks the handlers in the order they are written, and the first one that matches runs. Then the finally block runs, and execution goes on after the finally block.
When the try block completes without an exception, no catch block runs. The finally block runs, and execution goes on after it.
So the finally block runs in both cases. After an early failure, a variable that the try block would have assigned later still has its starting value when finally runs.
card.example: A try block opens a writer and writes numbers. Handlers exist for a bad index and for an I/O failure. The finally block closes the writer if it is not null, otherwise prints that it was never opened. If the open fails: the I/O handler runs, then the not-open message. If all works: only the closing path runs.
card.rule: After an exception the first matching catch runs and then finally; after normal completion only finally runs; either way execution continues after the finally block.
card.limits: Statements after the failing line inside the try block do not run once an exception is thrown, so no later step in that block can be counted on.

concepts.title: Specifying exceptions with a throws clause
concepts.question: When should a method declare an exception instead of catching it, and how is the clause written?

paragraphs: A method does not have to catch every exception itself. Sometimes it should pass the exception up the call stack to a caller better placed to handle it. A method in a package for unknown users cannot guess how each user wants errors handled, so it should declare the exception rather than catch it.
To declare, add a throws clause: the word throws followed by a comma-separated list of exceptions. It goes after the method name and parameter list and before the opening brace.
A checked exception that the method does not catch must be listed. Listing an unchecked exception is allowed but not required.
card.example: A writeList method whose body calls a constructor that throws IOException compiles with the header public void writeList() throws IOException. Adding IndexOutOfBoundsException to the list is allowed but not needed, because it is unchecked.
card.rule: Declare with throws the checked exceptions a method does not catch, so that callers can decide how to respond.
card.limits: A throws clause handles nothing; it moves the duty to the caller, who must then catch or specify in turn. Unchecked exceptions may be listed but need not be.

concepts.title: Throwing with the throw statement
concepts.question: How does code throw an exception, and what kinds of object can be thrown?

paragraphs: Any code can throw an exception: code you write, code in packages such as those of the Java platform, or the Java runtime. All of them use the throw statement.
A throw statement takes one argument, a throwable object: an instance of Throwable or of one of its subclasses. The object is usually created with new in the same statement.
A common use is to guard a condition: test for a bad state first, and throw before any damage is done.
card.example: A pop method for a stack first tests whether the size is zero. If so it executes throw new EmptyStackException(). Otherwise it removes and returns the top item. No throws clause is needed, because EmptyStackException is unchecked.
card.rule: Throw with a throw statement whose single argument is a Throwable object, as soon as the bad state is detected.
card.limits: Only Throwable objects can be thrown, not text or numbers. And throwing a checked exception obliges the method to catch or specify it, even when you wrote the throw yourself.

concepts.title: The Throwable family tree
concepts.question: Where do Error, Exception and RuntimeException sit under Throwable, and what does each stand for?

paragraphs: Everything that can be thrown descends from Throwable. It has two main branches: Error and Exception.

Errors are thrown by the JVM for hard failures, such as a failure in dynamic linking. Simple programs typically do not catch or throw them. Exception covers problems that are not serious system failures, and most programs throw and catch subclasses of Exception.

RuntimeException is a branch of Exception, reserved for incorrect use of an API, such as dereferencing a null reference. The tutorial says most applications should not throw runtime exceptions or subclass RuntimeException.
card.example: NullPointerException sits under RuntimeException, so it is unchecked. A class that extends Exception but not RuntimeException is checked. A dynamic linking failure belongs to the Error branch.
card.rule: Throwable splits into Error for serious JVM failures and Exception for problems a program can handle, with RuntimeException inside Exception for misuse of an API.
card.limits: A class's position in the tree decides whether it is checked, so look at its ancestry instead of guessing from its name.

concepts.title: Chained exceptions and stack traces
concepts.question: How can a new exception carry the one that caused it, and what does a stack trace show?

paragraphs: A handler often catches one exception and responds by throwing a different one. The first exception caused the second. Chained exceptions keep that link, so the whole story is visible when debugging.
Throwable supports chaining. Constructors can take a cause, either with a message or alone. The method initCause sets a cause, and getCause returns the exception that caused this one.

A stack trace is the execution history of the current thread when an exception was thrown: the classes and methods that were called. getStackTrace returns an array of StackTraceElement, each describing one frame, so a handler can format the trace itself.
card.example: catch (IOException e) { throw new ReportException('Could not load settings', e); } A higher-level handler holding the ReportException can call getCause to reach the original IOException.
card.rule: When a handler throws a new exception, pass the original as its cause so that getCause can recover it.
card.limits: Chaining records the link only; it does not choose which handler runs. If the original is left out, the link is lost.

concepts.title: When and how to write your own exception class
concepts.question: When should you write your own exception class, and how should it be placed and named?

paragraphs: The platform has many exception classes, so reuse is the default. Write your own if the answer is yes to any of these questions. Do you need a type the platform lacks? Would users gain by telling your exceptions from those of other vendors? Does your code throw several related exceptions? Should your package be self-contained, since users may lack access to the exceptions you would reuse?
When several related exceptions are thrown, give them a common base class so a caller can catch the family with one handler.
Make Exception the superclass of that base class; Error is for serious system failures. Give every class that inherits from Exception, directly or indirectly, a name ending in Exception.
card.example: A linked list class can fail in three ways: a bad position, an empty list, an item not found. LinkedListException extends Exception and is the base. Each specific failure is a subclass, and every name ends in Exception.
card.rule: Reuse a platform exception unless one of the four questions says otherwise, then build a family under Exception with names ending in Exception.
card.limits: If all four answers are no, use an existing exception. A class that extends Exception directly is checked, so methods that throw it must catch or specify it.

concepts.title: Checked or unchecked: the tutorial's rule
concepts.question: How does the tutorial say to choose between a checked and an unchecked exception?

paragraphs: Unchecked exceptions escape Catch or Specify, so a programmer may be tempted to throw only unchecked exceptions, or to make all of their own exception classes extend RuntimeException. The tutorial says this sidesteps the intent of the requirement and can cause problems for the people who use your classes.

The exceptions a method can throw are part of its public interface. Runtime exceptions are treated differently because they usually come from programming errors, can occur anywhere, and clients cannot reasonably recover from them. Declaring them everywhere would reduce clarity.
The tutorial's rule: if a client can reasonably be expected to recover from an exception, make it checked. If a client cannot do anything to recover, make it unchecked.
card.example: A loader whose settings file may be missing lets callers fall back to defaults, so its failure is checked. A method given null for a required argument has a caller bug nobody can recover from at run time, so an unchecked exception fits.
card.rule: According to the tutorial, make an exception checked if callers can reasonably recover from it and unchecked if they cannot, and do not choose unchecked just to avoid writing throws clauses.
card.limits: This is the tutorial's guideline, and the topic is called a controversy for a reason: some programmers regard Catch or Specify as a serious flaw. The rule rests on judging what a caller can reasonably do.

concepts.title: Advantage one: regular code apart from error handling
concepts.question: What problem does separating error handling from regular code solve, and what does it leave unsolved?

paragraphs: A method that reads a file has a simple core: open the file, find its size, allocate memory, read, close. But each step can fail, and the plain version ignores that.

With error codes, every step needs a check and the checks nest. The few lines of real work get buried, and the flow is hard to follow. For example, it is unclear whether the file gets closed when memory allocation fails.

With exceptions, the steps sit together in one try block and each failure gets its own catch block. The tutorial cautions that exceptions do not remove the work of detecting and handling errors; they help you organize it.
card.example: Pseudocode: try { open; find size; allocate; read; close } catch (open failed) {...} catch (size failed) {...} catch (memory failed) {...} catch (read failed) {...} catch (close failed) {...}. The normal path reads from top to bottom.
card.rule: Exceptions let the normal path read straight through while the catch blocks gather the error handling in one place.
card.limits: Exceptions do not do the error handling for you: each failure still needs detecting and a decision. The gain is organization, not less thinking.

concepts.title: Advantage two: errors travel up the call stack
concepts.question: How do exceptions spare the methods in the middle from passing error codes along?

paragraphs: An exception can travel up the call stack to a method that knows how to handle it. Suppose method1 calls method2, method2 calls method3, and method3 calls readFile. Only method1 cares about readFile failures.

With error codes, method2 and method3 must each check the code and return it upward. With exceptions, the runtime searches back through the calls for a handler, and method2 and method3 only declare the exception in a throws clause. The tutorial calls this ducking the exception.
The cost is that a checked exception must be listed in the throws clause of every method in the middle. Only the methods that care about an error have to deal with it.
card.example: method1 holds try and catch around its call to method2. method2 and method3 are each marked throws, with a body that only calls the next method. readFile throws, and the exception passes both middle methods to reach method1's handler.
card.rule: Let an exception travel to the method that can handle it, and let the methods in between only declare it.
card.limits: The methods in the middle still pay in throws clauses when the exception is checked. And a handler must exist somewhere on the stack, or the program ends.

concepts.title: Advantage three: grouping and telling apart error types
concepts.question: How does the class hierarchy let a handler be as narrow or as broad as needed?

paragraphs: Exceptions are objects in a class hierarchy, so they can be caught narrowly or broadly. In java.io, IOException is the general case for input and output errors, and its subclasses are more specific, such as FileNotFoundException.

A handler for FileNotFoundException catches only that case, since it has no subclasses. A handler for IOException catches it and also EOFException and other I/O exceptions as a group. The handler can inspect the object, for example with printStackTrace, to learn what happened.

A handler for Exception itself is acceptable when the program only prints a message and exits. Otherwise it is discouraged, since it also catches exceptions nobody anticipated. The tutorial advises choosing the most specific type that fits the situation.
card.example: A program reading a user-chosen file wants to ask for another name when the file is missing, but only report any other I/O trouble. It uses catch for FileNotFoundException first, then catch for IOException.
card.rule: Catch the most specific exception type that fits the situation, and avoid the broadest types unless the program only reports and exits.
card.limits: Broad handlers are convenient but hide differences between the problems they receive. Exception is the extreme, since it also receives problems nobody anticipated.

concepts.title: Processes and threads
concepts.question: What separates a process from a thread, and why does that matter for sharing data?

paragraphs: A process is a self-contained execution environment with its own private set of run-time resources, above all its own memory space. A single application on screen may really be several cooperating processes, which talk through inter-process communication (IPC) such as pipes or sockets, on one machine or across machines.
A thread is often called a lightweight process. It lives inside a process, and every process has at least one. Creating a thread takes fewer resources than creating a process.

The threads of one process share that process's resources, including its memory and open files. That makes communication between them efficient, but it also opens the door to the shared-data bugs the rest of the lesson addresses.
card.example: A music player might run its audio decoder in one process and its window in another, passing samples through a pipe. Inside the window process, one thread could redraw the screen while another loads a playlist file, both seeing the same playlist object in memory.
card.rule: A process has private memory and talks to other processes through IPC, while the threads inside one process share its memory and files.
card.limits: The tutorial calls multiprocess applications beyond its scope, so the lesson concentrates on threads. Sharing makes threads cheap to coordinate, yet it is also the very thing that makes them risky.

concepts.title: Time slicing and the main thread
concepts.question: How can one core run many threads, and which thread does every Java program start with?

paragraphs: Even a computer with a single execution core has many active processes and threads. Only one executes at any instant, and the operating system shares processor time among them by time slicing. Machines with several processors or cores can run more at once, but concurrency does not depend on that hardware.
Most Java Virtual Machine implementations run as a single process. From the programmer's point of view an application begins with one thread, the main thread, which can create further threads.
card.example: A laptop with one core plays music, downloads a file and shows a clock. Each gets short turns on the core, switching so fast that all three seem to move together. On a four-core machine, up to four of them could genuinely execute at the same instant.
card.rule: Time slicing lets one core share its time among many threads, and every Java program begins with the main thread.
card.limits: On one core only one thread executes at any instant, so slicing gives the appearance of simultaneity. Truly simultaneous execution needs more processors or cores.

concepts.title: Starting a thread with a Runnable
concepts.question: How do you give a new thread its code, and what call actually launches it?

paragraphs: Runnable is an interface with a single method, run, which holds the code a thread should execute. Write a class implementing Runnable, pass an instance to the Thread constructor, and call start on the Thread. The new thread then executes your run method.

The tutorial prefers this idiom. It separates the task, the Runnable, from the thread that executes it. That is more flexible, and the same separation carries over to the high-level thread management APIs met later in the lesson.
It is also more general: a class implementing Runnable remains free to extend some other class.
card.example: A class Ping implements Runnable, and its run method prints the word ping. In main, new Thread(new Ping()).start() creates the thread object and launches it, so the printing happens on the new thread rather than on main.
card.rule: Put the task in a Runnable, hand it to a Thread, and call start so that the new thread executes run.
card.limits: Creating the Runnable and even the Thread object runs no task until start is called. Later pages add Callable for tasks that must return a value.

concepts.title: Subclassing Thread
concepts.question: When is extending Thread enough, and when is the Runnable idiom the better choice?

paragraphs: The second way to supply a thread's code is to subclass Thread and override its run method. The Thread class does implement Runnable, but its own run method does nothing, so the subclass supplies the work. You create an instance of the subclass and call start, exactly as in the other idiom.

This version is shorter and suits simple applications. Its limit is that the task class must descend from Thread, so it cannot also extend some other class. The Runnable idiom has no such limit, which is why the lesson uses it.
card.example: A class Beeper extends Thread and overrides run to print a beep. main creates new Beeper() and calls start on it. The output matches a Runnable version; only the way the task and the thread are tied together differs.
card.rule: Subclassing Thread works for simple cases, but Runnable is more general because the task stays free to extend another class.
card.limits: Neither idiom starts a thread by itself: both rely on start. The preference for Runnable is the tutorial's recommendation, and for a tiny program the choice does not change what the new thread prints.

concepts.title: Pausing with sleep
concepts.question: What does Thread.sleep pause, and how exact is the pause?

paragraphs: Thread.sleep suspends the thread that calls it for a given time. While it sleeps, processor time is available to other threads or other programs. The tutorial lists three uses: freeing the processor, pacing actions over time, and waiting for another thread that has time requirements.

There are two forms, one taking milliseconds and one taking milliseconds plus nanoseconds. The time is a request only, since sleep times are limited by the facilities of the operating system, so a program must not assume the thread sleeps exactly as long as asked.
Another thread may interrupt a sleeping thread. Sleep then throws InterruptedException, a checked exception, so the calling code must catch it or declare it with throws.
card.example: A loop prints four lines of a poem. Before each line it calls Thread.sleep(4000), so each line appears about four seconds after the last. main declares throws InterruptedException because no other thread in that program interrupts it, so the exception is passed on rather than handled.
card.rule: Thread.sleep pauses only the calling thread for about the requested time, and its InterruptedException must be caught or declared.
card.limits: Because the time is approximate, sleep alone cannot promise that a given amount of work elsewhere has finished by the time it returns.

concepts.title: Interrupts as requests
concepts.question: What does interrupt() do to a thread, and what must the target do for it to matter?

paragraphs: An interrupt is a signal telling a thread to stop what it is doing and do something else. What the thread does next is the programmer's choice, but the most common response, and the one the lesson stresses, is to terminate. Another thread sends the signal by calling interrupt on the Thread object of the target.

Sending an interrupt forces nothing. The target must support its own interruption, by noticing the signal and acting on it. A thread that ignores interrupts is unaffected by them. In that sense interruption is cooperative, not a kill switch.
card.example: A downloader thread loops over a list of files. The main thread calls interrupt on the downloader when the user presses Cancel. If the downloader's code checks for interrupts and returns, the download stops; if its code never checks, it carries on to the end.
card.rule: Interrupt only asks; the interrupted thread must be written to notice the request and respond.
card.limits: If a thread's code ignores interrupts, calling interrupt has no visible effect. Terminating is common, but it is not the only response the programmer may choose.

concepts.title: Interrupts and blocking calls
concepts.question: How does a thread that keeps calling sleep support interruption?

paragraphs: When a thread often calls methods that throw InterruptedException, supporting interruption is easy: catch the exception and return from run. Methods such as sleep are designed to cancel what they are doing and return at once when interrupted, throwing the exception to tell the caller.
Without that catch block the thread would carry on after being interrupted. The catch is where the thread decides what to do, and in the lesson's examples it simply ends the task.
card.example: A loop prints four messages with sleep(4000) before each. The sleep call sits inside a try block, and the catch for InterruptedException contains a return. If another thread interrupts during a sleep, the loop stops and run ends, so the thread terminates.
card.rule: If a thread calls blocking methods often, handle InterruptedException by returning from run.
card.limits: This works only while the thread reaches such a call. A thread that never blocks never sees the exception. The catch block also decides what happens; returning is the usual choice, not a requirement.

concepts.title: Polling for interrupts
concepts.question: How does a thread that never blocks notice an interrupt, and how can handling be centralised?

paragraphs: A thread that spends a long time without calling any method that throws InterruptedException will never see that exception. It must check for itself, calling the static method Thread.interrupted, which returns true if an interrupt has been received. A typical loop does one unit of work, then checks, and returns if the answer is true.

In a more complex application it can be tidier to turn a detected interrupt into an exception: when Thread.interrupted returns true, throw a new InterruptedException. All interrupt handling then happens in one catch clause, whether the signal arrived during a sleep or was found by polling.
card.example: A loop processes 1,000 images, calling a heavy resize method on each. After every image it tests Thread.interrupted; when the test is true the method returns, leaving the remaining images untouched. A single catch clause could serve the same loop if the test threw InterruptedException instead.
card.rule: A thread that rarely blocks should poll Thread.interrupted between units of work, and may throw InterruptedException to centralise the handling.
card.limits: Polling reacts only when the check runs, so a very long unit of work delays the response. Calling Thread.interrupted also clears the interrupt status, which matters if other code needs to see it afterwards.

concepts.title: The interrupt status flag
concepts.question: What is the interrupt status, and which calls set it, read it or clear it?

paragraphs: Interruption is implemented with a boolean flag in each thread, the interrupt status. Calling interrupt on a thread sets it. The static method Thread.interrupted reads the current thread's flag and clears it. The instance method isInterrupted lets one thread read another's flag without changing it.
Because another thread may call interrupt at any moment, the flag can be set again straight after it has been cleared.
card.example: Thread T is interrupted, so its flag is true. T calls Thread.interrupted and gets true; the flag is now false, so a second call returns false. A watcher thread that calls t.isInterrupted() before T's first check sees true, and the flag stays true after that call.
card.rule: Interrupt sets the flag, Thread.interrupted reads and clears it, and isInterrupted reads it without clearing.
card.limits: A cleared flag can be set again at once, so a false reading is no promise that no interrupt will arrive later.

concepts.title: Waiting with join
concepts.question: How does one thread wait for another to finish, and what can cut that wait short?

paragraphs: If t is a Thread object whose thread is executing, t.join() makes the calling thread pause until t's thread terminates. That lets one thread wait for another to finish its work before it goes on.

There are overloaded versions of join that take a waiting period. As with sleep, join depends on the operating system for timing, so you should not assume that it waits exactly as long as you specify.
card.example: A main thread starts a worker that builds a report, then calls worker.join(). Main sits idle until the worker terminates, and only then prints that the report is ready.
card.rule: t.join() pauses the caller until thread t terminates, and a timed version limits how long it waits.
card.limits: The timed form can return when its period ends while the thread is still running, so the caller cannot assume the thread has finished.

concepts.title: The SimpleThreads program
concepts.question: How do sleep, join, isAlive and interrupt fit together in the SimpleThreads program?

paragraphs: SimpleThreads has two threads: main, and a message thread that main creates from a Runnable. The message thread prints four messages, sleeping four seconds before each. If it is interrupted, it prints that it was not done and returns, which ends the thread.

Main starts it, then loops while the thread isAlive. Each pass it prints a waiting note and calls join with a one-second limit, so it checks in about once a second. If more than the patience period has passed and the thread is still alive, main interrupts it and calls join with no limit.
Patience defaults to one hour and may be given in seconds on the command line. A helper prints each message with the current thread's name, so you can see which thread spoke.
card.example: With a patience of 10 seconds, main reports after about ten seconds that it is tired of waiting and interrupts. The message thread is asleep, so sleep throws, it prints that it was not done, and exits. Main's untimed join returns and main prints its closing line.
card.rule: Main polls with a timed join and isAlive, interrupts when patience runs out, then waits fully with an untimed join.
card.limits: The pattern works because the message thread supports its own interruption. A thread that ignored the interrupt would leave main waiting in its untimed join.

concepts.title: Why shared data needs care
concepts.question: Why does sharing data between threads need care, and what does that care cost?

paragraphs: Threads communicate mainly by sharing access to fields and to the objects those fields refer to. This is very efficient, but it allows two kinds of error: thread interference and memory consistency errors. The tool for preventing both is synchronization.

Synchronization has a price. It can cause thread contention, which occurs when two or more threads try to access the same resource at the same time and the Java runtime slows one or more of them, or suspends them.
card.example: Two threads update the same shopping cart object. With nothing coordinating them they may overwrite each other (interference), or one may not see the other's change (inconsistency). Locking the cart prevents both, but a thread that wants the cart while another holds it must wait.
card.rule: Shared fields make communication cheap but invite interference and inconsistency, which synchronization prevents at the cost of possible contention.
card.limits: Synchronization is a remedy with a cost, not something to add everywhere: it can slow or suspend threads, and later pages show it can also lead to liveness problems.

concepts.title: Thread interference
concepts.question: How can two correct-looking operations on one counter still lose an update?

paragraphs: Thread interference happens when two operations in different threads act on the same data and their steps interleave. Even a single statement may be several steps for the virtual machine. The increment c++ is three: retrieve the current value of c, add one to it, and store the result back in c. A decrement is the same with a subtraction.

Suppose c starts at 0. Thread A retrieves 0, thread B retrieves 0, A computes 1, B computes minus 1, A stores 1, then B stores minus 1. A's result is lost, overwritten by B. This is one possible interleaving; others lose B's result or cause no error, so the bugs are unpredictable and hard to find.
card.example: A page-view counter runs views++ on every request, handled by many threads. Two requests read 41 at the same moment, each adds one and stores 42, so two visits count as one. On another run the steps happen not to overlap, the count is right, and the bug stays hidden.
card.rule: A compound statement such as c++ is several steps, and if threads interleave them an update can be lost.
card.limits: The error depends on timing, so a test that passes proves little. A class like Counter works as designed in single-threaded use; interference appears only when several threads reach the same object.

concepts.title: Memory consistency and happens-before
concepts.question: What does a happens-before relationship guarantee, and why might a reader thread still see an old value?

paragraphs: A memory consistency error occurs when different threads hold inconsistent views of what should be the same data. The causes are complex, but the programmer needs only a strategy to avoid them: establish a happens-before relationship between the statement that writes and the statement that reads.

Happens-before is a guarantee that the memory writes of one specific statement are visible to another specific statement. Without it, nothing promises that a write in one thread can be seen in another.

Take a shared int counter that starts at 0. Thread A runs counter++, and shortly afterwards thread B prints counter. In one thread you could assume the output is 1. In separate threads the output might be 0, because nothing guarantees A's change is visible to B.
card.rule: Without a happens-before relationship between a write and a later read, the reader has no guarantee of seeing the write.
card.limits: Source order within one thread is enough, but across threads it is not. The tutorial leaves the detailed causes out of scope and gives a strategy instead.

concepts.title: Start and join create happens-before
concepts.question: Which two thread calls create happens-before, and what does each make visible?

paragraphs: Besides synchronization, some thread actions themselves establish happens-before. First, Thread.start: statements that happen before the call to start also happen before everything the new thread executes. The new thread therefore sees the effects of the code that led up to its creation.

Second, Thread.join: when a thread terminates and another thread's join on it returns, everything the terminated thread did happens before the statements after the join. The joining thread therefore sees the effects of the finished thread's work.
card.example: Main sets a config field, then starts a worker: the worker sees the configuration. The worker computes a total into a field and ends. Main joins the worker and then reads the field: it sees the total, because join returned after the worker terminated.
card.rule: Writes made before start are visible to the new thread, and writes by a finished thread are visible to the thread whose join on it returns.
card.limits: These two actions are only part of the list; the tutorial points to the java.util.concurrent package summary for the rest, and synchronization, covered next, is another way.

concepts.title: Synchronized methods
concepts.question: What does marking a method synchronized change for the threads that call it?

paragraphs: To make a method synchronized, add the keyword synchronized to its declaration. Suppose count is an instance of a SynchronizedCounter whose increment, decrement and value methods are all synchronized. Two effects follow.

First, two calls to synchronized methods on the same object cannot interleave. While one thread runs such a method, other threads that call synchronized methods on that object block, meaning they suspend, until the first thread is finished with it.

Second, when a synchronized method exits, it establishes a happens-before relationship with every later call of a synchronized method on the same object. Changes to the object's state are then visible to all threads.
card.example: A class SynchronizedCounter has a private int c and public synchronized increment, decrement and value methods. While thread A is inside increment on one counter, thread B calling value on that same counter waits until A is done.
card.rule: Synchronized methods of one object run one thread at a time, and each exit makes its changes visible to later calls.
card.limits: Protection depends on every access going through synchronized methods: a method left unsynchronized can still run alongside them, and synchronization costs waiting time when many threads want one object.

concepts.title: Constructors, leaks and the strategy
concepts.question: What rule keeps a shared object safe, and what must a constructor avoid?

paragraphs: The tutorial's strategy: if an object is visible to more than one thread, every read or write of its variables goes through synchronized methods. The one exception is final fields, which cannot change after construction and may be read through unsynchronized methods once the object is built. The price is that the strategy can cause liveness problems, treated later.
Constructors cannot be synchronized; adding the keyword is a syntax error. The reasoning is that only the thread creating an object should have access to it while it is under construction.
So take care that a new object does not escape early. A constructor that adds this to a shared list lets other threads reach the object before construction is finished.
card.example: A class Account has a private final String owner and a private int balance. getOwner may be unsynchronized, because owner is final. deposit and getBalance are synchronized. A constructor that did registry.add(this) would expose a half-built Account to other threads.
card.rule: Route every access to shared changeable state through synchronized methods, read final fields freely, and do not let this escape from a constructor.
card.limits: The strategy protects single method calls and says nothing about sequences of calls, and heavy use of it risks liveness problems. Final fields are safe to read freely only after construction.

concepts.title: Intrinsic locks
concepts.question: What is an intrinsic lock, who holds it during a synchronized method, and when is it released?

paragraphs: Every object has an intrinsic lock, also called a monitor lock. A thread that needs exclusive, consistent access to an object's fields must acquire the lock before touching them and release it afterwards. From acquiring until releasing, the thread owns the lock: no other thread can acquire it, and any that try block.

Releasing a lock establishes a happens-before relationship with every later acquisition of the same lock. Calling a synchronized method acquires the lock of its object, and the lock is released when the method returns, even if it returns because of an uncaught exception.
A static synchronized method belongs to a class, not an object, so it acquires the lock of the Class object. Static fields are therefore guarded by a lock distinct from any instance's lock.
card.example: Class Sensor has a synchronized instance method read and a static synchronized method calibrate. Thread A inside read on sensor1 owns sensor1's lock. Thread B calling calibrate takes the Sensor class's lock and is not blocked by A, while thread C calling read on sensor1 is.
card.rule: A synchronized method owns its object's lock, or the Class object's lock if static, until it returns or fails.
card.limits: A lock holds back only threads that try to acquire the same lock. Code that locks a different object, or none, is not held back.

concepts.title: Synchronized statements
concepts.question: How does a synchronized statement differ from a synchronized method, and why keep calls to other objects outside it?

paragraphs: A synchronized statement is a block that must name the object whose intrinsic lock it uses. Unlike a synchronized method, it can protect just the lines that need it.

In the tutorial's addName method, a block synchronized on this covers the update of lastName and nameCount. The call that adds the name to a separate list stays outside the block. That way no other object's methods are invoked while the lock is held, which could cause liveness problems described later.
Without synchronized statements, the tutorial notes, you would need a separate unsynchronized method just to make that list call.
card.example: In void log(String line), the block synchronized on this holds the lock only while lastLine is set and count is incremented. The slow call archive.add(line) comes after the block, so it runs without the lock.
card.rule: A synchronized statement locks a named object around only the lines that need it, keeping calls to other objects outside.
card.limits: A smaller block protects less: anything left outside is no longer guarded. Fields that must change together belong in one block, under the same lock other users of that data take.

concepts.title: Separate locks for independent fields
concepts.question: When can two fields use separate locks, and why does the tutorial urge extreme care?

paragraphs: Sometimes one object holds fields that are never used together, such as two counters c1 and c2. Synchronizing every update on this, or through synchronized methods, makes the updates share one lock and needlessly block each other.

The tutorial's alternative gives each field its own lock object, created just for the purpose, and synchronizes each update on its own lock. An update to c1 can then interleave with an update to c2 without harm, which improves concurrency.
The tutorial warns that the idiom needs extreme care: you must be absolutely sure it is safe to interleave access to the fields involved.
card.example: A class Gauges has int rain and int wind, with lock objects lockRain and lockWind. addRain synchronizes on lockRain, addWind on lockWind. Two threads can add rain and wind at once, but two threads adding rain still take turns.
card.rule: Independent fields may be guarded by separate lock objects so their updates can overlap, but only if interleaving them is certainly safe.
card.limits: If any operation uses both fields, or needs to see them change together, separate locks no longer protect it. Such fields need one common lock.

concepts.title: Reentrant synchronization
concepts.question: Can a thread take a lock it already owns, and why does that matter?

paragraphs: A thread cannot acquire a lock owned by another thread. It can, however, acquire a lock it already owns. This is reentrant synchronization.

It matters when synchronized code calls another method that contains synchronized code needing the same lock. Without reentrancy, such code would need many extra precautions to stop a thread from blocking itself.
card.example: A synchronized method report() calls another synchronized method of the same object, format(). The thread already owns the object's lock when it reaches format(), so it simply carries on. Without reentrancy it would wait on itself.
card.rule: A thread may acquire an intrinsic lock it already owns, so synchronized code can call other synchronized code on the same lock.
card.limits: Reentrancy lets a thread past its own lock only. Another thread's ownership still blocks it, and a thread holding one lock while waiting for a lock another thread owns can still be stuck, as the liveness pages show.

concepts.title: Atomic access
concepts.question: What makes an action atomic, which accesses are atomic, and what does atomicity not give you?

paragraphs: An atomic action happens all at once. It cannot stop in the middle: it either happens completely or not at all, and none of its effects is visible until it is complete. An expression that looks simple, such as c++, may hide several steps, so it is not atomic.

Reads and writes are atomic for reference variables and for most primitive variables, meaning all types except long and double. They are also atomic for every variable declared volatile, including long and double.
Atomic actions cannot be interleaved, so they are free of thread interference. But atomicity does not remove the need for synchronization, because memory consistency errors are still possible.
card.example: A field Node head is assigned by one thread and read by another. Each assignment and each read of a reference is a single atomic action, so a reader never sees a half-written reference. By contrast, hits++ on an int is a read-modify-write and is not atomic.
card.rule: Single reads and writes of references and most primitives are atomic, but compound actions such as c++ are not, and atomicity alone does not guarantee visibility.
card.limits: A non-volatile long or double is not covered by the atomic rule for reads and writes. Atomic does not mean visible, so synchronization or a happens-before link may still be needed.

concepts.title: Volatile variables
concepts.question: What does volatile add to a variable beyond atomic reads and writes?

paragraphs: A write to a volatile variable establishes a happens-before relationship with every later read of that same variable. So changes to a volatile variable are always visible to other threads.

More than that, a thread that reads a volatile variable sees not only the latest change to it but also the side effects of the code that led up to the change. Using volatile variables reduces the risk of memory consistency errors.
card.example: Thread A prepares a settings object, then sets a volatile boolean ready to true. Thread B reads ready and sees true, so B also sees everything A did before that write, including the finished settings.
card.rule: A write to a volatile variable happens before later reads of it, so readers also see what the writer did earlier.
card.limits: Volatile covers individual reads and writes. The tutorial does not claim it makes a compound action such as c++ atomic, which is why it also offers synchronization and atomic variables.

concepts.title: Liveness and deadlock
concepts.question: What does liveness mean, and what is a deadlock?

paragraphs: Liveness is a concurrent application's ability to execute in a timely manner. A liveness problem means the program stops making progress when it should not. The most common liveness problem is deadlock.

Deadlock is a situation where two or more threads are blocked forever, each waiting for another. It typically arises from threads that hold locks others need: each thread owns one resource and waits for one that another thread owns, so none can move.
card.example: Thread 1 owns lock P and needs lock Q. Thread 2 owns lock Q and needs lock P. Each waits for the other to release, and neither can, so both stay blocked for good.
card.rule: Liveness is timely progress, and deadlock, its most common failure, leaves threads blocked forever waiting for one another.
card.limits: Waiting alone is not deadlock: a thread waiting for a lock that its owner will soon release is only slow. Deadlock needs a cycle of waiting in which no thread can ever release what the next one needs.

concepts.title: The bowing friends deadlock
concepts.question: Why do two polite friends who both start to bow end up blocked forever?

paragraphs: In the tutorial's story, Alphonse and Gaston follow a rule of courtesy: when you bow to a friend, you stay bowed until the friend has returned the bow. The rule does not allow for two friends bowing to each other at the same moment.

In the code, Friend has a synchronized bow method, which prints and then calls bower.bowBack(this), and a synchronized bowBack. One thread runs alphonse.bow(gaston) and another runs gaston.bow(alphonse). Each is inside its own friend's bow, holding that friend's lock, and each now calls bowBack on the other friend, whose lock is held.
Each thread waits for the other to leave bow, which neither can do. The tutorial calls this outcome extremely likely when the program runs.
card.example: Two accounts each have a synchronized send method that calls a synchronized receive method on the other account. One thread runs a.send(b) while another runs b.send(a). Each holds one account and waits for the other, the same trap.
card.rule: Deadlock arises when each thread holds one object's lock and, while holding it, calls a synchronized method of another object whose lock the other thread holds.
card.limits: The threads must overlap in time: if one bow finishes before the other starts, nothing sticks. Timing makes the deadlock likely here, which the tutorial calls extremely likely, rather than certain.

concepts.title: Starvation
concepts.question: What is starvation, and how does a greedy thread cause it?

paragraphs: Starvation is a situation where a thread cannot gain regular access to shared resources and so cannot make progress. It happens when shared resources are held for long periods by greedy threads.

For example, suppose an object has a synchronized method that often takes a long time to return. If one thread calls this method frequently, other threads that also need frequent synchronized access to the same object will often be blocked.
The tutorial adds that starvation is much less common than deadlock, but every concurrent software designer is likely to meet it.
card.example: A report object has a synchronized method export that takes ten seconds. One thread calls export again and again. A second thread needs the object for a one-millisecond read, but finds the lock taken almost every time, so it makes very little progress.
card.rule: Starvation means a thread rarely gets the shared resource it needs because other threads hold it for long stretches.
card.limits: Starvation differs from deadlock: nothing waits in a circle. The trouble is uneven access over time, so a starved thread is held back by repeated long holds rather than by one permanent block.

concepts.title: Livelock
concepts.question: How does livelock differ from deadlock, even though neither makes progress?

paragraphs: A thread often acts in response to another thread's action. If that other thread's action is itself a response to the first thread's, livelock may result.
Like deadlock, livelocked threads cannot make further progress. Unlike deadlock, they are not blocked: they are too occupied with responding to each other to resume their work.

The tutorial's picture is two people in a corridor. Alphonse steps left to let Gaston pass; Gaston steps right to let Alphonse pass. They still block each other, so Alphonse steps right and Gaston steps left, and the cycle goes on.
card.example: Two services each retry a failed call the moment they see the other retrying, and each retry triggers another retry from the other. Both keep running and sending, yet no real work gets done.
card.rule: In livelock the threads stay active, responding to each other, but make no progress; in deadlock they are blocked.
card.limits: Livelock needs threads that react to one another. A thread waiting passively for a lock is blocked, not livelocked, and the tutorial calls both livelock and starvation much less common than deadlock.

concepts.title: Guarded blocks and busy waiting
concepts.question: What is a guarded block, and why is spinning in a loop a poor way to wait?

paragraphs: Threads often need to coordinate. The most common idiom is the guarded block: a block that begins by polling a condition that must be true before the block can go on.

One way to write the guard is a loop that spins until the condition becomes true, such as a while loop on a flag with an empty body. It works, but the tutorial says it wastes processor time while it waits, and that you should not do it.
A better guard suspends the thread until another thread signals that the condition may have changed. The next idea shows how wait does this.
card.example: One thread waits for a flag done to become true by running while(!done) with nothing inside the loop. It uses processor time on every pass, even though nothing changes until another thread sets done.
card.rule: A guarded block waits for a condition before going on, and spinning in an empty loop to do so wastes processor time.
card.limits: Spinning gives the right result, only wastefully. The condition being polled is also shared data, so it needs the visibility care of the earlier ideas.

concepts.title: wait and notifyAll
concepts.question: How do wait and notifyAll work, and why must wait sit in a loop inside a synchronized method?

paragraphs: Object.wait suspends the current thread until another thread issues a notification. To call d.wait, a thread must own d's intrinsic lock, or an error results; calling wait inside a synchronized method is a simple way to own it. The call releases the lock and suspends the thread.
Another thread then acquires the same lock and calls notifyAll, which wakes every thread waiting on that lock. A woken thread reacquires the lock and resumes after its wait call returns.

Always call wait inside a loop that tests the condition. Do not assume the wake-up was for your condition, or that the condition still holds. The notify method wakes one unspecified thread; the tutorial finds it useful only in massively parallel programs whose threads do similar work, so the examples use notifyAll.
card.example: synchronized void waitForJoy() { while (!joy) { try { wait(); } catch (InterruptedException e) { } } } and synchronized void setJoy() { joy = true; notifyAll(); }. The waiter re-tests joy after every wake-up.
card.rule: Inside a synchronized method, wait in a loop that re-tests the condition, and have the other thread set the condition and call notifyAll.
card.limits: Wait works only while the caller owns the lock, and a notification wakes threads but proves nothing about the condition, which is why the loop re-tests it. Notify wakes one unspecified thread, so it suits only interchangeable workers.

concepts.title: Producer-consumer with Drop
concepts.question: How do put and take in the Drop class hand a message from producer to consumer?

paragraphs: In producer-consumer, a producer thread makes data and a consumer thread uses it. They must coordinate: the consumer must not take data before the producer has delivered it, and the producer must not deliver new data before the consumer has taken the old.

The tutorial's Drop object holds a message and a flag, empty, that starts true. take waits while empty is true, then sets empty to true, calls notifyAll and returns the message. put waits while empty is false, then sets empty to false, stores the message and calls notifyAll. Both are synchronized and use the loop guard.
The producer sends four messages with random pauses, then a DONE marker. The consumer takes until it sees DONE.
card.example: With empty true, a consumer calling take finds nothing and waits. The producer's put stores a message, sets empty to false and wakes everyone. The consumer wakes, sees empty false, takes the message, and wakes the producer for the next put.
card.rule: A shared object with a full-or-empty flag, synchronized put and take, wait loops and notifyAll lets one thread hand data to another in turn.
card.limits: Drop exists only to demonstrate guarded blocks; for real work the tutorial points to the Collections Framework instead of a hand-written class. A one-slot object also makes the two threads proceed in strict turns.

concepts.title: Why immutable objects help
concepts.question: Why does the tutorial favour immutable objects for concurrent code, and what is the usual objection?

paragraphs: An object is immutable if its state cannot change after it is constructed. The tutorial says that relying heavily on immutable objects is a widely accepted strategy for creating simple, reliable code.
For concurrent programs the point is that immutable objects cannot be corrupted by thread interference and cannot be observed in an inconsistent state.

Programmers often resist them because creating a new object looks costly compared with updating one in place. The tutorial says this cost is often overestimated, and can be offset by reduced garbage-collection overhead and by not needing code that protects mutable objects from corruption.
card.example: A date range class stores start and end once, in its constructor. A thread reading both can never see a start from one version and an end from another, because there is only one version. To change the range, code creates a new object.
card.rule: Immutable objects need no protection from interference or inconsistent views, and their extra object creation is often cheaper than feared.
card.limits: Immutability concerns the object's own state after construction; it does not remove every other concurrency problem in the program that uses it. The cost argument is the tutorial's judgement that the cost is often overestimated, not a guarantee.

concepts.title: Inconsistent reads in a mutable class
concepts.question: Why can two individually synchronized getters still give a caller a mismatched colour and name?

paragraphs: The tutorial's SynchronizedRGB class stores red, green and blue values, each from 0 to 255, and a name. Its getRGB, getName and invert methods are synchronized, and its set method updates all four fields inside a block synchronized on this.

The trouble lies in the caller. If one statement calls getRGB and the next calls getName, another thread may call set in between. The caller then holds a colour from the old state and a name from the new one.
The fix is for the caller to lock the object around both calls, with a block synchronized on the colour object. Such inconsistency is possible only for mutable objects.
card.example: A Pair object has synchronized getLeft and getRight, and a synchronized setBoth. A reader calls getLeft, then getRight; setBoth runs in between. The reader sees a left value from before and a right value from after. A block synchronized on the pair around both calls avoids it.
card.rule: Synchronizing each method does not make a sequence of calls atomic; a caller that needs related values together must hold the object's lock across the calls.
card.limits: The caller's lock works only because the object's own synchronized methods use the same lock. The problem exists only for mutable objects: with an immutable object no change can fall between the calls.

concepts.title: Rules for immutable classes
concepts.question: What four rules does the tutorial give for making a class immutable?

paragraphs: The tutorial gives a simple strategy of four rules for making a class immutable, and notes that not every class documented as immutable follows it. The first rule: provide no setter methods, meaning no methods that change fields or the objects fields refer to. The second: make every field final and private.

The third rule: do not let subclasses override methods. The simplest way is to declare the class final; a more refined way is a private constructor with instances made in factory methods. The fourth rule, about fields that refer to mutable objects, is the next idea.
card.example: A class Money has a private final long cents and a private final String currency, no setters, and is declared final. A method plus(Money other) returns a new Money. Nothing can change a Money after construction, and no subclass can add a method that does.
card.rule: For an immutable class provide no setters, make all fields final and private, and prevent overriding, for example with a final class.
card.limits: These are the tutorial's simple strategy; other classes can be immutable for good reasons by methods needing sophisticated analysis. Fields that hold mutable objects need the fourth rule on top of these three.

concepts.title: Mutable objects inside immutable ones
concepts.question: What must an immutable class do when one of its fields refers to a mutable object?

paragraphs: The fourth rule concerns instance fields that refer to mutable objects. Do not provide methods that modify those objects, and do not share references to them.

In particular, never store a reference to an external mutable object passed to the constructor. If necessary, create a copy and store a reference to the copy. Likewise create copies of internal mutable objects when necessary, so that methods do not return the originals.
card.example: A class Playlist holds a list of titles. Its constructor receives a list from the caller and copies the titles into its own list rather than keeping the caller's list. Its getter returns a fresh copy. Without both copies, the caller could still change the Playlist's contents.
card.rule: Keep no reference to a mutable object that outsiders can reach: copy on the way in and copy on the way out.
card.limits: No copy is needed for fields that hold immutable objects, such as a String. The rule applies when the referred object can change, and copying costs memory, so it is used when necessary.

concepts.title: From SynchronizedRGB to ImmutableRGB
concepts.question: How does the tutorial turn SynchronizedRGB into an immutable class, and what happens to invert?

paragraphs: The tutorial applies the rules to SynchronizedRGB. It has two setter-like methods. set transforms the object arbitrarily, so it has no place in an immutable version. invert can be adapted. The fields were already private and are now also final, and the class is declared final.
The fourth rule needs no special care here: the only field that refers to an object is the name, a String, and a String is itself immutable.

invert changes meaning. Instead of altering the object, it returns a new ImmutableRGB holding the inverted values and the name Inverse of followed by the old name. The original object is left unchanged.
card.example: ImmutableRGB sky = new ImmutableRGB(0, 100, 255, skyName); ImmutableRGB opposite = sky.invert(); afterwards sky still holds 0, 100, 255, and opposite holds 255, 155, 0.
card.rule: Remove setters, make the class and fields final, and let operations such as invert return new objects instead of modifying the old one.
card.limits: Returning new objects moves the cost to creating them, which the tutorial argues is often modest. A caller who wants the new state must use the returned object, since the original never changes.

concepts.title: Why higher-level tools
concepts.question: Why does the tutorial move beyond the low-level thread API, and which tools does it name?

paragraphs: The low-level thread APIs, part of Java from the beginning, are adequate for very basic tasks. More advanced tasks call for higher-level building blocks, above all in massively concurrent applications that make full use of multiprocessor and multi-core systems.

These features arrived with version 5.0 of the Java platform. Most live in the java.util.concurrent packages, and the Java Collections Framework gained concurrent data structures too. The lesson covers lock objects, executors, concurrent collections, atomic variables, and ThreadLocalRandom.
card.rule: Reach for the java.util.concurrent tools when low-level threads and locks are not enough, especially in large, multi-core applications.
card.limits: The higher-level tools aim at needs beyond the basics. ThreadLocalRandom came later, in JDK 7, while the other features arrived with version 5.0.

concepts.title: Lock objects
concepts.question: What can a Lock object do that an intrinsic lock cannot?

paragraphs: Synchronized code relies on a simple kind of reentrant lock. It is easy to use but has many limitations. The java.util.concurrent.locks package offers more sophisticated locking idioms, and the lesson looks only at its most basic interface, Lock.
Lock objects work much like implicit locks: only one thread can own a Lock at a time. They also support wait and notify, through associated Condition objects.

The main advantage is the ability to back out of an attempt to acquire a lock. The tryLock method backs out if the lock is not available immediately or before a timeout expires. The lockInterruptibly method backs out if another thread sends an interrupt before the lock is acquired.
card.example: A thread tests if (lock.tryLock()) and, when true, updates shared data and unlocks; otherwise it takes an else branch and skips this round. If another thread owns the lock, the caller does not wait. A synchronized block would have waited.
card.rule: A Lock object behaves like an intrinsic lock but can give up: tryLock and lockInterruptibly let a thread back out of acquiring.
card.limits: The tutorial covers only the basic Lock interface, leaving the package's other locking idioms outside the lesson. Backing out is an extra ability; for simple cases the intrinsic lock is easier to use.

concepts.title: Safelock: avoiding the deadlock
concepts.question: How does the Safelock version avoid the bowing deadlock?

paragraphs: The tutorial applies Lock objects to the earlier deadlock. Alphonse and Gaston have learned to notice when a friend is about to bow, and the model requires each Friend to acquire the locks of both participants before bowing.

Each Friend has a ReentrantLock. impendingBow calls tryLock on its own lock and on the bower's lock. If it gets only one, it releases that one in a finally block. It returns true only if it holds both.

bow goes ahead only when impendingBow succeeds, then bows and unlocks both locks in a finally block. Otherwise it reports that the other friend was already bowing. A loop in each thread repeats this after a short random pause.
No thread holds one lock while waiting indefinitely for the other, so the cycle of waiting cannot form.
card.example: A thread gets its own lock, but tryLock on the other friend's lock fails. It releases its own lock at once and skips the bow. The other thread can now take both locks, bow and finish. Neither waited for a lock it could not get.
card.rule: Acquire all needed locks with tryLock, and if any attempt fails, release what you hold and back out instead of waiting.
card.limits: Backing out removes the deadlock but does not make every bow happen: a thread may fail and skip. The program must tolerate skipped attempts, which is why the tutorial's loops try again.

concepts.title: Executors
concepts.question: Why separate thread management from the rest of the application, and what is an executor?

paragraphs: So far a task, the Runnable, has been tied closely to the thread that runs it, the Thread object. That is fine for small programs. In a large application it makes sense to separate thread creation and management from the rest of the application.
Objects that encapsulate these functions are called executors. Instead of creating Thread objects each time, the application hands tasks to an executor.

The Executor interface has one method, execute, designed as a drop-in replacement for the idiom new Thread(r).start(). With e.execute(r), the executor might start a new thread, but is more likely to use an existing worker thread, or to queue r until a worker is free.
card.example: Instead of new Thread(task).start() in twenty places, the code calls executor.execute(task). Later the team can switch to an executor that reuses ten worker threads without touching those twenty lines.
card.rule: Hand tasks to an executor with execute instead of creating threads yourself, so thread management lives in one place.
card.limits: execute is less specific than starting a thread: it does not promise a new thread, or an immediate start. Whether tasks run at once, reuse workers or queue is the implementation's choice.

concepts.title: Executor interfaces
concepts.question: How do ExecutorService and ScheduledExecutorService extend Executor?

paragraphs: java.util.concurrent defines three executor interfaces, each extending the one before. Executor launches tasks. ExecutorService adds management of the life cycle of individual tasks and of the executor itself. ScheduledExecutorService adds future and periodic execution.

ExecutorService adds a versatile submit method beside execute. It accepts Runnable objects and also Callable objects, which let a task return a value, and it returns a Future. A Future is used to retrieve a Callable's result and to manage the status of Callable and Runnable tasks.
ExecutorService also has methods to submit large collections of Callable objects and to shut the executor down. To allow immediate shutdown, tasks should handle interrupts correctly.
ScheduledExecutorService adds schedule, which runs a task once after a delay, and scheduleAtFixedRate and scheduleWithFixedDelay, which run a task repeatedly at defined intervals.
card.example: A task that counts lines in a file is written as a Callable and passed to submit. The call returns a Future at once. Later, the code asks the Future for the count, which is the Callable's result.
card.rule: Use execute for plain Runnables, submit when you want a Future or a result, and a scheduled executor for delayed or repeating tasks.
card.limits: Immediate shutdown depends on the tasks: they must handle interrupts correctly for the executor to stop them. The interface to use depends on what the tasks need: results, status, shutdown or timing.

concepts.title: Thread pools
concepts.question: Why reuse worker threads, and what does a fixed thread pool do when tasks outnumber threads?

paragraphs: Most executor implementations in java.util.concurrent use thread pools, made of worker threads. A worker thread exists apart from the Runnable and Callable tasks it runs, and is often used for many tasks. Reusing workers minimises the overhead of thread creation, which matters because Thread objects use a significant amount of memory.

In a fixed thread pool a given number of threads is always running. If one ends while still in use, it is automatically replaced. Tasks go through an internal queue, which holds the extras whenever there are more active tasks than threads.

A fixed pool degrades gracefully. A web server that makes a new thread for every request can suddenly stop responding to all requests if more arrive than it can handle. With a limit on threads, requests are served more slowly but as quickly as the system can sustain.
card.example: A pool of four workers receives ten tasks. Four start at once and six wait in the queue. As each worker finishes, it takes the next queued task, so no more than four tasks run at any moment.
card.rule: A fixed thread pool runs tasks on a set number of reusable workers and queues the rest, so heavy load slows the service instead of collapsing it.
card.limits: A bounded pool trades speed for stability, since queued tasks must wait their turn. The factory methods cover common cases; other needs call for the custom pool classes.

concepts.title: The fork/join framework
concepts.question: What is the fork/join framework for, and what does work stealing add?

paragraphs: The fork/join framework is an ExecutorService implementation for work that can be broken into smaller pieces recursively. Its aim is to use all the available processing power to improve performance.

Like other executors, it hands tasks to worker threads in a pool. It is distinct in using a work-stealing algorithm: worker threads that run out of work can steal tasks from other threads that are still busy. The centre of the framework is the ForkJoinPool class, which runs ForkJoinTask objects.

The logic is: if my part of the work is small enough, do it directly; otherwise split it in two, invoke both pieces and wait for the results.
