You put this in a subclass of ForkJoinTask: RecursiveTask when a result is returned, RecursiveAction when not. Then you pass the task to the invoke method of a ForkJoinPool.
card.example: Summing a huge array: a task for the whole array splits itself into two tasks for the halves, until a piece is small enough to add directly. A RecursiveTask suits this, since each piece returns its partial sum.
card.rule: Split work recursively until pieces are small enough to run directly, run them in a ForkJoinPool, and let idle workers steal queued tasks.
card.limits: Fork/join suits work that splits into independent pieces and is built for using multiple processors. Splitting has overhead, so pieces must not be too small, a point the blur example makes with a threshold.

concepts.title: The ForkBlur example
concepts.question: How does the ForkBlur example decide between computing directly and splitting?

paragraphs: ForkBlur blurs an image stored as an int array, one int per pixel. Each destination pixel is the average of the red, green and blue parts of the source pixels around it. Because images are large arrays, the work is slow, so the tutorial spreads it over processors with fork/join.

ForkBlur extends RecursiveAction because it writes into the destination array and returns nothing. Each task handles a segment given by a start index and a length. The blur window width should be odd, so that it is centred on a pixel.

compute checks the length. If it is below a threshold, 100,000 in the example, it blurs the segment directly. Otherwise it splits the segment in half and runs both halves with invokeAll. To run it, create the task for all the work, create a ForkJoinPool, and call invoke on the pool.
card.example: An image with 400,000 pixels: the first task splits into two of 200,000, then four of 100,000, then eight of 50,000. Only the 50,000-pixel pieces are below the 100,000 threshold, so only those are blurred directly.
card.rule: Below the threshold a task works directly; at or above it, the task splits in half and runs both halves with invokeAll.
card.limits: The threshold is a tuning choice that keeps pieces large enough to be worth splitting. The odd window width and the index clamping belong to this example, not to fork/join in general.

concepts.title: Concurrent collections
concepts.question: Which concurrent collection interfaces does the tutorial describe, and what do they guarantee?

paragraphs: The java.util.concurrent package adds several collections to the Java Collections Framework, grouped by interface. BlockingQueue is a first-in-first-out structure that blocks or times out when you add to a full queue or retrieve from an empty one.

ConcurrentMap is a subinterface of Map. It defines atomic operations that remove or replace a pair only if the key is present, and add a pair only if the key is absent. This helps avoid explicit synchronization. ConcurrentHashMap is the general implementation, a concurrent analog of HashMap.
ConcurrentNavigableMap is a subinterface of ConcurrentMap that supports approximate matches. Its general implementation is ConcurrentSkipListMap, a concurrent analog of TreeMap.
card.example: A producer thread puts jobs into a BlockingQueue and a worker takes them out. If the queue is empty the worker waits for a job; if the queue is full the producer waits for room. Neither writes any wait or notifyAll code.
card.rule: Use the concurrent collections instead of hand-made locking: queues that block, and maps with atomic conditional operations.
card.limits: The atomic operations are single calls; a program that combines several separate calls must still reason about what can happen between them.

concepts.title: Atomic variables
concepts.question: How do atomic variables let a counter avoid interference without synchronized methods?

paragraphs: The java.util.concurrent.atomic package has classes supporting atomic operations on single variables. Their get and set methods work like reads and writes of volatile variables: a set has a happens-before relationship with any later get of the same variable.

The tutorial revisits its Counter. The plain int version suffers interference. Making all methods synchronized fixes it, and for a simple class that is acceptable. AtomicCounter keeps its value in an AtomicInteger and uses incrementAndGet, decrementAndGet and get, with no synchronized keyword.
For a more complicated class, atomic variables let you prevent interference while avoiding the liveness impact of unnecessary synchronization.
card.example: class Hits has a private AtomicInteger n created with 0. hit() calls n.incrementAndGet() and count() returns n.get(). Two threads calling hit never lose an update, and no lock is involved.
card.rule: Replace a plain shared variable by an atomic variable and update it with its atomic methods instead of locks.
card.limits: Atomic variables protect single variables. A rule that spans several variables still needs a lock, and for a simple class the tutorial considers synchronized methods acceptable.

concepts.title: ThreadLocalRandom
concepts.question: Why use ThreadLocalRandom instead of Math.random for concurrent code, and how do you get one?

paragraphs: ThreadLocalRandom, in the java.util.concurrent package since JDK 7, is a convenience class for applications that use random numbers from several threads. For concurrent access it is preferred over Math.random(), because it causes less contention and therefore gives better performance.

You get the generator by calling ThreadLocalRandom.current(), and then call one of its methods to retrieve a number. For example, ThreadLocalRandom.current().nextInt(4, 77) gives an int between the two bounds.
card.example: Each of eight worker threads picks a random delay by calling ThreadLocalRandom.current().nextInt(10, 20), instead of all of them sharing Math.random(), so the threads rarely compete for one random source.
card.rule: In multi-threaded code, take random numbers from ThreadLocalRandom.current() rather than Math.random() to reduce contention.
card.limits: The advantage the tutorial names is less contention, which matters when several threads draw numbers. It does not describe a different kind of randomness.

concepts.title: Pattern, Matcher and the syntax exception
concepts.question: Which three classes of java.util.regex do the work, and what does each one do?

paragraphs: A regular expression describes a set of strings by what they share. You use one to search, edit or change text. Its syntax is its own, separate from Java, and the Java version is closest to Perl's.

Three classes in java.util.regex do the work. A Pattern is a compiled regular expression. It has no public constructors; you get one by calling the static compile method with the expression as a string.
A Matcher is the engine that applies a Pattern to an input string; you get one by calling matcher on the Pattern. A PatternSyntaxException is the exception that reports a malformed expression.
card.example: Pattern p = Pattern.compile("[0-9]+"); Matcher m = p.matcher("rows 12 and 345"); while (m.find()) { System.out.println(m.group()); } prints 12 and then 345. Compile first, ask for a matcher, then loop on find.
card.rule: Compile the expression into a Pattern, ask it for a Matcher on your input, and let the Matcher do the searching.
card.limits: These classes only run the expression. A malformed expression fails when it is compiled, and a well-formed one can still fail to match what its writer had in mind.

concepts.title: Reading a match: start and end indexes
concepts.question: What do the start and end numbers of a match report, and why is the end larger than expected?

paragraphs: The simplest regular expression is a plain string; it matches input that contains exactly that text. The expression foo finds foo in the input foo, and the match comes with two numbers: a start index and an end index.

Picture each character in its own cell, with the index numbers on the lines between cells. The text foo fills cells 0, 1 and 2, so it starts at index 0 and ends at index 3. A match range includes its start and excludes its end, so its length is end minus start.
A search can return several matches. In foofoofoo the expression foo matches at 0 to 3, 3 to 6 and 6 to 9. Each match begins where the previous one ended, so the ranges touch but do not overlap.
card.example: In the input a-foo-foo (a, hyphen, foo, hyphen, foo) the expression foo matches at 2 to 5 and at 6 to 9. Each length is end minus start, which is 3.
card.rule: A match covers its start index up to but not including its end index, so its length is end minus start.
card.limits: The end index points at the position after the match, not at a character inside it. Matches reported by one search do not overlap.

concepts.title: Metacharacters and escaping
concepts.question: How can one character be ordinary in one expression and special in another, and how do you make it ordinary?

paragraphs: Most characters in an expression stand for themselves. A metacharacter is a character with a special meaning for the matcher. The expression cat. matches cats, because the dot means any one character, and here it matches s even though the input has no dot.

The tutorial lists these as metacharacters: angle, round, square and curly brackets, the backslash, caret, hyphen, equals sign, dollar sign, exclamation mark, vertical bar, question mark, star, plus and dot. Some are not special in every position. Characters such as @ and # are never special.
To make a metacharacter ordinary, put a backslash before it, so \. matches only a real dot. Or enclose the text between \Q and \E, with \Q first, so \Qcat.\E matches the text cat. including its dot.
card.example: In the input 'v2.5 v2x5', the expression v2.5 matches both v2.5 (0 to 4) and v2x5 (5 to 9), because the dot accepts any character. The expression v2\.5 matches only the first, since \. demands a real dot.
card.rule: A metacharacter keeps its special meaning unless you escape it with a backslash or enclose it between \Q and \E.
card.limits: The list says which characters can be special, not which always are, because some lose their meaning in certain positions. Letters, digits, @ and # need no escape.

concepts.title: Character classes: sets of one character
concepts.question: How do you describe a set of acceptable single characters, and combine, negate or subtract such sets?

paragraphs: A character class is a set of characters inside square brackets; it has nothing to do with Java class files. It matches exactly one character of the input, any member of the set. The expression [bcr]at matches bat, cat and rat, but not hat.

A caret right after the opening bracket negates the set: [^bcr]at matches hat but not bat, cat or rat. A hyphen between two characters gives an inclusive range, so [a-c] means a, b or c, and ranges can sit side by side, as in [a-zA-Z].

Classes can nest. A nested class makes a union: [0-4[6-8]] matches 0 to 4 and 6 to 8. Two ampersands make an intersection: [0-9&&[345]] matches only 3, 4 and 5. An intersection with a negated class subtracts: [0-9&&[^345]] is every digit except 3, 4 and 5.
card.example: The class [a-z&&[^m-p]] means the lower-case letters except m through p. It describes the same set as [a-lq-z], written in a different way.
card.rule: A class matches one character from its set: a caret negates, a hyphen spans a range, nesting joins, && intersects, and && with a negated class subtracts.
card.limits: A class matches a single character, so matching several characters needs a quantifier. The caret negates only when it opens the class.

concepts.title: Predefined classes and backslashes in Java
concepts.question: Which shorthand classes cover digits, whitespace and word characters, and how are their opposites and Java backslashes written?

paragraphs: Predefined character classes are short names for common sets. The dot is any character. \d is a digit, the same as [0-9]. \s is a whitespace character, such as a space, tab or newline. \w is a word character, the same as [a-zA-Z_0-9]: letters, digits and the underscore.

A capital letter gives the opposite: \D is a non-digit, \S a non-whitespace character, \W a non-word character. The tutorial advises using these shorthands whenever you can, since they are shorter and cut mistakes from hand-made classes.

A construct starting with a backslash is an escaped construct. In Java source, a backslash inside a string literal is already an escape, so you write each one twice: the string holding the expression \d is written with two backslashes. In the console harness you type a single one.
card.example: In the input 'id_7 ok!', the expression \w+ finds id_7 at 0 to 4 and ok at 5 to 7. The spaces and the exclamation mark are not word characters, so they end the runs.
card.rule: Use \d, \s and \w, with capitals for the opposites, and write each backslash twice inside a Java string.
card.limits: Taking the tutorial's equivalent class as written, \w covers only ASCII letters, digits and underscore, so accented letters are not word characters. The dot may not match line terminators.

concepts.title: Quantifiers repeat one element
concepts.question: How do you say how many times an element repeats, and which element does a quantifier repeat?

paragraphs: A quantifier says how many times the element just before it may occur. In the plain (greedy) forms: X? means once or not at all, X* zero or more times, X+ one or more times, X{n} exactly n times, X{n,} at least n times, and X{n,m} from n to m times.

The count must be met. The expression a{3} fails on aa and matches aaa; in aaaa it matches the first three and ignores the leftover a. On nine a characters, a{3} matches three times, a{3,} matches once with all nine, and a{3,6} matches six and then the remaining three.

A quantifier attaches to a single element: one character, one class or one group. So abc+ repeats only the c. To repeat a longer piece, wrap it in parentheses, as in (dog){3}, or use a class, as in [abc]{3}.
card.example: In the input abab, the expression (ab){2} matches the whole text, 0 to 4. The expression ab{2} does not match abab; it would need abb, because the 2 repeats only the b.
card.rule: A quantifier repeats only the single element before it, so use parentheses to repeat a longer piece.
card.limits: Parentheses also capture text, which later ideas explain. A class can repeat a choice of characters but not a fixed multi-character sequence. This card covers the greedy forms; other forms differ in how much they take.

concepts.title: Zero-length matches
concepts.question: Can a match be empty, where can empty matches appear, and why do a* and a+ differ on text with no a?

paragraphs: A zero-length match consumes no characters, so its start and end index are equal. It can occur in an empty input, at the start of the input, after the last character, and between any two characters. Quantifiers that allow zero repeats, such as ? and *, can produce one; + cannot, because it needs at least one.

On empty input, a? and a* each match the empty string at 0 to 0, and a+ finds nothing. On the single character a, both a? and a* report a at 0 to 1 and then an empty match at 1 to 1, while a+ reports only the a.

On aaaaa, a? finds five single a matches and then an empty match at 5, while a* finds one match of all five and then the empty match at 5. At positions holding something other than a, a? and a* report empty matches and a+ skips them.
card.example: In the input bab the expression a* reports an empty match at 0 to 0, the a at 1 to 2, an empty match at 2 to 2 and another at 3 to 3. The expression a+ reports only the a.
card.rule: A quantifier that allows zero repeats can match nothing, so it may report empty matches wherever the element is absent.
card.limits: An empty match is still a match, with equal start and end. A quantifier that needs at least one repeat, such as + or {1,}, cannot report one.

concepts.title: Greedy, reluctant and possessive
concepts.question: How do greedy, reluctant and possessive quantifiers differ when the input can be matched in several ways?

paragraphs: Each quantifier has three flavors. Greedy is the plain form, such as X*. Reluctant adds a question mark, as in X*?. Possessive adds a plus, as in X*+. They accept the same counts but differ in how much text they take when the input offers a choice.

A greedy quantifier first takes as much as it can, possibly the whole input; if the rest of the expression then fails, it gives back one character at a time until the rest fits. A reluctant one starts with as little as possible and takes one more character at a time. A possessive one takes as much as it can and never gives anything back.
The tutorial adds that a possessive quantifier suits cases where you want everything that fits and never need to back off, and that it can be faster than the greedy form when no match is found.
card.example: On the input xfooxxxxxxfoo, .*foo matches the whole text, 0 to 13. The reluctant .*?foo matches xfoo at 0 to 4 and xxxxxxfoo at 4 to 13. The possessive .*+foo finds nothing, since .*+ takes everything and leaves no room for foo.
card.rule: Greedy takes the most and gives back, reluctant takes the least and adds, possessive takes the most and never gives back.
card.limits: When the rest of the expression leaves no choice, all three give the same result. A possessive quantifier can fail where a greedy one succeeds.

concepts.title: Capturing groups and their numbers
concepts.question: How do parentheses build groups, how are groups numbered, and which Matcher methods read their text?

paragraphs: Parentheses make a capturing group. A group treats several characters as one unit, so a quantifier can apply to the whole unit, and the text it matches is stored for later use.

Groups are numbered by their opening parentheses, counted left to right. In ((A)(B(C))), group 1 is the whole thing, group 2 is (A), group 3 is (B(C)) and group 4 is (C). Group 0 always means the entire match and is not counted by groupCount, which returns 4 here. A group opened with (? is non-capturing: it is not numbered and keeps no text.
After a successful match, group(n) returns the text captured by group n, start(n) its start index and end(n) the index after its last character.
card.example: The expression (\d{4})-(\d{2}) on the input 2026-10 gives group(0) as 2026-10, group(1) as 2026 and group(2) as 10. The value groupCount is 2, start(2) is 5 and end(2) is 7.
card.rule: Count opening parentheses from left to right for group numbers; group 0 is the whole match, and groupCount leaves it out.
card.limits: Groups starting with (? do not capture and get no number. Numbers follow the opening parentheses, not the order in which groups close or the meaning of their contents.

concepts.title: Backreferences
concepts.question: How can an expression require the same text to appear twice?

paragraphs: The text a group captured is kept, and a backreference matches that exact text again later in the same expression. You write a backslash followed by the group number, such as \1 for group 1.

The expression (\d\d)\1 means two digits followed by those same two digits. It matches 1212, from 0 to 4, but not 1234, because 34 differs from 12. Backreferences work with nested groups too: use the number of the group whose text you want to repeat.
card.example: The expression (\w)\1 finds doubled letters. In the input 'book keeper' it matches oo at 1 to 3 and ee at 6 to 8, because each second letter must equal the first.
card.rule: A backreference \n matches the exact text that group n captured, not just anything the group could match.
card.limits: A backreference can only repeat text that its group has already captured, and it repeats that same text, so it cannot match something merely similar.

concepts.title: Boundary matchers: where a match sits
concepts.question: How do you require a match to sit at a line edge, at a word edge, or exactly where the last match ended?

paragraphs: Boundary matchers take no characters; they limit where a match may sit. The caret is the beginning of a line and the dollar sign the end of a line. So ^dog$ matches only a line that is exactly dog. With leading spaces it fails, while \s*dog$ accepts them.

\b is a word boundary and \B is a place that is not one. The expression \bdog\b matches the word dog in 'The dog plays' but not inside doggie, since a word character follows. The expression \bdog\B does the reverse: it matches the start of doggie but not the word dog.

\G matches at the end of the previous match, so \Gdog on 'dog dog' finds only the first dog: the second starts at index 4, but the previous match ended at 3. Also, \A is the start of the input, \z its very end, and \Z its end except a final line terminator.
card.example: In the input 'a cat; cats' the plain expression cat matches at 2 to 5 and again at 7 to 10, inside cats. The expression \bcat\b matches only the first, because the second cat is followed by the letter s.
card.rule: Use ^ and $ to pin lines, \b to pin whole words, and \G to continue exactly where the last match stopped.
card.limits: A boundary matcher uses no characters, so the match length is unchanged. The caret and dollar sign concern lines, while \A and \z concern the whole input.

concepts.title: Flags that change how matching works
concepts.question: How do flags change the way an expression is matched, and how can they be set inside the expression?

paragraphs: Pattern.compile accepts a second argument of flags, combined with the bitwise or operator. CASE_INSENSITIVE ignores case, for US-ASCII only unless UNICODE_CASE is added. DOTALL lets the dot match line terminators. MULTILINE lets ^ and $ work at every line, not only at the ends of the input. COMMENTS ignores whitespace and # comments in the expression.

LITERAL treats the whole expression as plain text. UNIX_LINES makes only the newline count as a line terminator. UNICODE_CASE adds Unicode-aware case matching. CANON_EQ matches characters by their canonical decomposition.

Most flags have an embedded form written inside the expression: (?i) for CASE_INSENSITIVE, (?s) for DOTALL, (?m) for MULTILINE, (?x) for COMMENTS, (?u) for UNICODE_CASE and (?d) for UNIX_LINES. CANON_EQ and LITERAL have none.
card.example: The expression [az]$ on the input az, newline, bz, newline, ca (indexes 0 to 7) matches only the final a, at 7 to 8. With MULTILINE it also matches the z at 1 to 2 and the z at 4 to 5, because each line now has its own end.
card.rule: Pass flags to compile joined with the or operator, or embed their letter forms such as (?i) in the expression.
card.limits: CANON_EQ and LITERAL cannot be embedded. Case-insensitive matching covers US-ASCII only unless UNICODE_CASE is also set, and some flags may cost speed.

concepts.title: Shortcuts: matches, split and quote
concepts.question: Which shortcuts test a whole input, split text or quote user text, and what do the String versions mirror?

paragraphs: Pattern.matches(regex, input) is a static shortcut that tests whether the whole input fits the expression. With the expression \d, the input 1 gives true and the input 12 gives false. String.matches(regex) gives the same result.

The split method returns the pieces of text between matches. The delimiter can be any expression, not only fixed text: splitting on a digit expression cuts one9two4three into one, two and three. String.split(regex) matches Pattern.compile(regex).split(input) and drops trailing empty strings.

Pattern.quote(s) returns a pattern string that matches s literally, which suits text typed by users. By contrast, String.replace(target, replacement) is not regex-based: it replaces literal text only.
card.example: Calling split on the text 2026-10-11 with the hyphen as delimiter gives the three parts 2026, 10 and 11. The expression Pattern.quote(a.b) matches only the text a.b, not axb, while plain a.b matches both.
card.rule: The static and String shortcuts test whole inputs or split text, and quote turns user text into a literal pattern.
card.limits: matches demands the whole input, so it cannot find a pattern inside longer text; that needs find. String.replace is literal text replacement, not a regex tool.

concepts.title: matches, lookingAt and find
concepts.question: Which Matcher method needs the whole input, a prefix or any part to match, and where does each start?

paragraphs: A Matcher offers three ways to test. matches() needs the entire input to fit the expression. lookingAt() needs the expression to match at the beginning of the input, and anything may follow. find() scans forward for the next match anywhere, starting where the previous match ended; find(int start) resets the matcher and searches from that index.
For the expression foo and the input fooooooooo, lookingAt returns true and matches returns false: the input starts with foo but has more characters after it.

After a successful match, start() gives where it begins and end() the index after its last character, so end minus start is its length. start(group) and end(group) report the same for a capturing group.
card.example: With the expression \d+, the input '42 apples' gives lookingAt true, matches false and find true at 0 to 2. The input 'apples 42' gives lookingAt false, matches false and find true at 7 to 9.
card.rule: Use matches when all the input must fit, lookingAt when the start must fit, and find to look anywhere.
card.limits: matches and lookingAt do not search past the start, so they miss a match found later in the text; only find moves on to later matches.

concepts.title: Replacing matched text
concepts.question: Which methods replace matched text, and when do you need appendReplacement and appendTail?

paragraphs: replaceAll(replacement) swaps every match for the replacement, and replaceFirst swaps only the first. Both take an expression, not only literal text. Replacing dog with cat in 'The dog says meow. All dogs say meow.' also turns dogs into cats, since dog has no boundaries.
The expression a*b with the replacement - turns aabfooaabfooabfoob into -foo-foo-foo-. The matches are aab, aab, ab and the last b, each replaced by one dash.

For custom logic, loop with find. For each match, appendReplacement(sb, text) copies the text since the previous match and adds your replacement; after the loop, appendTail(sb) copies the rest. Matcher.quoteReplacement escapes backslash and dollar in replacement text. String.replaceAll and replaceFirst do the same for one-off jobs.
card.example: With the expression \d+ and the replacement #, replaceAll turns 'a1 b22 c333' into 'a# b# c#', while replaceFirst gives 'a# b22 c333'.
card.rule: Use replaceAll or replaceFirst for a fixed replacement, and find with appendReplacement and appendTail when each replacement needs logic.
card.limits: The replacement text has its own special characters, backslash and dollar, so user text needs quoteReplacement. An expression without boundaries also changes text inside longer words.

concepts.title: PatternSyntaxException: reading the error
concepts.question: What does PatternSyntaxException tell you about a bad expression, and when should you catch it?

paragraphs: PatternSyntaxException is unchecked: the compiler does not force you to catch it. Pattern.compile throws it when an expression is malformed, so wrap compile in try and catch whenever the expression comes from a user or a configuration.

Four methods describe the fault. getDescription gives the error text, getIndex the position in the expression (or -1 if unknown), getPattern the faulty expression, and getMessage a multi-line report with the description, the index, the pattern and a caret under the error.

In the tutorial's example, the text ?i) typed instead of (?i) gives the description Dangling meta character '?' at index 0. A metacharacter with nothing to modify often signals a missing opening parenthesis.
card.example: Pattern.compile of the text (abc fails, because a group is opened and never closed. A catch block can print getDescription to say what went wrong and getIndex to say where.
card.rule: Catch PatternSyntaxException around compile for expressions you do not control, and use getDescription and getIndex to report the problem.
card.limits: Being unchecked, the exception comes with no compiler reminder. A fixed expression in your own source needs fixing rather than catching. Only malformed syntax raises it; a valid expression that finds nothing does not.

concepts.title: Writing a character by its code point
concepts.question: How do you write a specific Unicode character in an expression, even when it needs more than four hex digits?

paragraphs: The tutorial says expression matching supports Unicode, with version 6.0 supported since JDK 7. A character can be named by its code point. The escape \uFFFF names the code point with exactly four hexadecimal digits, so it reaches only values up to FFFF.

The escape \x{h...h} accepts any number of hexadecimal digits, so it can name supplementary characters above FFFF, such as the grinning face with code point 1F600. In a Java string literal, both need doubled backslashes.
card.example: The expression \x{6771} and the expression \u6771 both match the single Han character with code point 6771. Only \x{1F600} can name code point 1F600, which has five digits.
card.rule: Use \uFFFF for a code point written with four hex digits, and \x{...} when it may need more.
card.limits: \u needs exactly four hexadecimal digits, so it cannot write a supplementary character. Writing a code point is a way to name one character, not a set of characters.

concepts.title: Unicode properties: scripts, blocks and categories
concepts.question: How do you match characters by script, block or category, and how do you negate the test?

paragraphs: The construct \p{prop} matches one character that has a Unicode property, and \P{prop} matches one that lacks it. Three kinds of property are supported: scripts, blocks and general categories.

A script is named with script=Name, sc=Name or the prefix Is, as in \p{IsHiragana}. A block is named with block=Name, blk=Name or the prefix In, as in \p{InMongolian}. The names are those accepted by Character.UnicodeScript.forName and Character.UnicodeBlock.forName.

A general category groups characters by kind: \p{L} or \p{IsL} is any letter, and \p{gc=Lu} is an upper-case letter. The capital P negates, so \P{IsL} is any character that is not a letter, such as a digit.
card.example: Pattern.matches of \p{gc=Lu} succeeds on A and fails on a. Pattern.matches of \P{IsL} succeeds on the digit 7, because 7 is not a letter.
card.rule: Use \p{...} with a script, block or category name to match by property, and \P{...} for the opposite.
card.limits: Each \p or \P construct tests one character, so add a quantifier to match words. Names must be ones the Java classes accept, and which characters have a property depends on the Unicode version in use.

concepts.title: What a collections framework is
concepts.question: What are the three parts of a collections framework, and what does each contribute?

paragraphs: A collection, also called a container, is an object that groups several elements into one unit. You use it to store, retrieve, manipulate and pass around data that forms a natural group, such as a hand of cards, a mail folder or a phone directory.

A collections framework is a unified architecture for representing and handling collections. According to the tutorial it has three parts. Interfaces are abstract data types that let you use a collection without depending on how it is represented. Implementations are the concrete classes, in effect reusable data structures. Algorithms are methods such as searching and sorting that work on any implementation of the right interface.

The tutorial lists the payoff: less programming effort, faster and better programs because implementations of one interface can be swapped to tune a program, a shared language that lets unrelated APIs exchange collections, less to learn for each new API, and easier reuse of new data structures and algorithms that follow the standard interfaces.
card.rule: A collections framework is interfaces, implementations and algorithms working together, so code written against an interface can swap implementations and reuse algorithms.
card.limits: The framework tells you how groups of objects are organised, not which implementation is fastest for your program. That still needs judgment, and measurement when you are unsure.
card.example: A network tool returns node names as a collection and a separate GUI toolkit wants column headings as a collection. Both follow the standard interfaces, so the names pass straight across with no adapter code.

concepts.title: The two interface trees
concepts.question: Which core interface is not a Collection, and how does each branch of the hierarchy differ?

paragraphs: The core interfaces form two separate trees. Collection is the root of the first. Under it are Set, List, Queue and Deque, and SortedSet is a special kind of Set. Map is the root of the second tree, and SortedMap is a special kind of Map.

Map is not a true Collection. It holds mappings from keys to values, not a plain group of elements. Collection itself is the least common denominator: use it as a type when you want to pass groups of elements around with maximum generality.

Each branch adds one rule. A Set holds no duplicates. A List is an ordered sequence that allows duplicates and access by position. A Queue holds elements before processing, usually first in first out. A Deque can be used at both ends. A Map holds each key at most once. The sorted variants keep ascending order.
card.rule: Collection roots one tree and Map roots a separate one, and each interface adds one rule about duplicates, order or keys.
card.limits: The tree shows what each interface promises, not how fast it works. Two interfaces can look alike on the diagram yet need quite different implementations.
card.example: A shop keeps a List of order numbers in arrival order, repeats allowed. It keeps a Set of postcodes it delivers to. It keeps a Map from each postcode to a delivery fee.

concepts.title: Generic element types
concepts.question: Why does the tutorial say to specify the element type of a collection when declaring it?

paragraphs: All the core collection interfaces are generic. The declaration Collection of E means the interface is parameterised by the type of its elements. When you declare a collection you should name that type, for example a List of String.

According to the tutorial, naming the element type lets the compiler check at compile time that you insert only elements of the right type. Mistakes that would otherwise show up while the program runs are reported when it is built.
Beyond the tutorial pages: because the type is known, elements also come back out as that type, so reading them needs no cast.
card.rule: Declare a collection with its element type so the compiler, not a failing run, finds wrong insertions.
card.limits: The check happens at compile time. The tutorial later notes that this static checking can be defeated, for example through raw types, which is why checked wrappers exist.
card.example: A List of String called names accepts add of a text value. Adding the number 42 is rejected by the compiler. Without the element type, the same mistake would surface only when some later code treated the number as text.

concepts.title: Optional operations
concepts.question: What does it mean that modification operations are optional, and what happens when one is not supported?

paragraphs: The framework does not define separate interfaces for every variant of collection, such as immutable, fixed-size or append-only ones. That would multiply the number of interfaces.

Instead the operations that modify a collection are optional. An implementation may decide not to support some of them. If you call an unsupported operation, the collection throws UnsupportedOperationException.
Implementations must document which optional operations they support. According to the tutorial, all the general-purpose implementations of the Java platform support all of them.
card.rule: Modification operations are optional, and calling one the collection does not support throws UnsupportedOperationException.
card.limits: Optional applies to modification operations. Reading operations such as size or contains work on every collection, and general-purpose implementations support every modification.
card.example: A list obtained from Arrays.asList on an array of three names allows set, which replaces an element. It is fixed in size, so add and remove throw UnsupportedOperationException.

concepts.title: Basic Collection operations
concepts.question: What do add and remove return, and what does Collection guarantee about them?

paragraphs: Collection provides size, isEmpty, contains, add, remove and iterator. The word add is general enough for collections that allow duplicates and those that do not. After add, the collection is guaranteed to contain the element.

add returns true if the collection changed as a result. For a Set, adding an element already present returns false. remove deletes a single instance of the element, if there is one, and returns true if the collection was modified.
General-purpose collections also have a conversion constructor that takes any Collection and copies its elements, which converts one kind of collection into another.
card.rule: add returns whether the collection changed, and remove takes out one instance and reports whether anything was removed.
card.limits: The return value says whether the collection changed, not whether the call worked. In a Set, a false from add means the element was already there.
card.example: Adding the word red to an empty Set of String returns true. Adding it again returns false and the set is unchanged. A List with the word red twice and one remove of red keeps one red.

concepts.title: Bulk operations
concepts.question: What do the bulk operations do, and which of them change the collection they are called on?

paragraphs: Bulk operations act on a whole collection at once. containsAll tests whether the target holds every element of another collection. addAll adds them all. removeAll removes every element that is also in the other collection. retainAll keeps only the elements that are also in it. clear empties the target.

addAll, removeAll and retainAll return true if the target was modified. These classic bulk operations are mutative: they change the collection they are called on. The aggregate operations of JDK 8 are not mutative.

A handy idiom uses Collections.singleton, which makes an immutable set of one element: removeAll with a singleton removes every instance of that element, and removeAll with a singleton of null removes every null.
card.rule: addAll, removeAll, retainAll and clear change the target, and removeAll with a singleton removes every instance of one value.
card.limits: These bulk operations modify the target. To keep the original you must copy it first. Do not confuse them with JDK 8 aggregate operations, which do not change the source.
card.example: A List holds 3, 4, 3, 5. Calling removeAll with a singleton of 3 leaves 4, 5 and returns true. A second identical call leaves the list alone and returns false.

concepts.title: Three ways to traverse
concepts.question: Which three ways can you traverse a collection, and when is each the right tool?

paragraphs: The tutorial lists three ways to traverse a collection. In JDK 8 the preferred way is aggregate operations: obtain a stream and chain operations, usually with lambda expressions. The other two are the for-each construct and explicit iterators.

The for-each construct is concise and hides the iterator, but it cannot remove elements, so it cannot be used for filtering. An Iterator lets you walk through the collection and remove the current element.

Use an Iterator instead of for-each when you need to remove the current element or to iterate over several collections in parallel. Lambdas passed to aggregate operations should avoid side effects, so that the code still works if it later runs on a parallel stream.
card.rule: Prefer aggregate operations to read or transform, for-each for plain loops, and an Iterator when you must remove while walking.
card.limits: These are options, not a strict ranking for every job. An Iterator is the only one of the three that removes the current element from the collection safely.
card.example: To print the names of the red shapes, call stream, then filter on color, then forEach with print. To delete every shape whose weight is zero from the collection itself, use an Iterator and call remove.

concepts.title: Iterator and safe removal
concepts.question: Under what conditions does Iterator.remove work, and why is it the only safe way to change a collection during iteration?

paragraphs: An Iterator has hasNext, next and remove. hasNext tells you whether more elements remain, and next returns the next one. remove deletes from the underlying collection the element that next last returned.

remove can be called only once per call to next. Calling it more often than that throws an exception. The remove operation is optional, so an iterator for a collection that does not support removal throws UnsupportedOperationException.
The tutorial states that Iterator.remove is the only safe way to modify a collection during iteration. Any other change to the collection while an iteration is in progress has unspecified behaviour.
card.rule: Call next first, then remove at most once per next, and make no other change to the collection while the loop runs.
card.limits: Iterator.remove is about removing during iteration. If the changes are made outside any loop, ordinary collection methods are fine, and a modifiable Map offers Map.Entry.setValue for changing values safely.
card.example: To keep only even numbers in a collection, loop with hasNext. Inside, call next and test it. If the number is odd, call remove once. The method works on any Collection, which makes it polymorphic.

concepts.title: Collections and arrays
concepts.question: How do you turn a collection into an array, and what type does each form of toArray return?

paragraphs: toArray is the bridge between collections and older APIs that expect arrays. Called with no argument it creates a new array of Object whose length equals the number of elements in the collection.

The second form takes an array as an argument and creates a new array of that array's type with the same length as the collection. For a collection known to hold only strings, passing a String array of length zero produces a String array of the right size.
In both forms the caller can supply an array or choose the runtime type of the result.
card.rule: toArray() gives an Object array, and passing an array of the wanted type gives an array of that type.
card.limits: The result is a new array, so changing an element slot of the array does not change the collection. The typed form suits a collection known to hold only elements of that type.
card.example: A Collection of String called c holds three words. Calling c.toArray() gives an Object array of length 3. Calling c.toArray(new String[0]) gives a String array of length 3 that an older method can accept.

concepts.title: The Set interface
concepts.question: What does Set add to Collection, and which implementation gives speed, value order or insertion order?

paragraphs: A Set is a Collection that cannot contain duplicate elements. It models the mathematical set. According to the tutorial it adds no methods beyond those of Collection; it only adds the no-duplicates restriction.

The platform has three general-purpose implementations. HashSet keeps elements in a hash table, guarantees no order and performs best. TreeSet keeps them in a red-black tree, sorted by value, and is substantially slower. LinkedHashSet is a hash table with a linked list through it, iterates in insertion order, and is only slightly slower than HashSet.
Copying any collection into a Set removes the duplicates, for example new HashSet of c. Declare the variable with the type Set so the implementation can be changed later.
card.rule: A Set is a Collection without duplicates: use HashSet for speed, TreeSet for value order and LinkedHashSet for insertion order.
card.limits: No duplicates says nothing about order. A plain HashSet may list its elements in any order, so code must not depend on one.
card.example: Given the words i came i saw i left, a HashSet reports four distinct words in no guaranteed order. A TreeSet reports came, i, left, saw. A LinkedHashSet reports i, came, saw, left.

concepts.title: Bulk operations as set algebra
concepts.question: How do the bulk operations compute union, intersection and difference of two sets, and when is it destructive?

paragraphs: With two sets s1 and s2, bulk operations give set algebra. s1.containsAll(s2) tests whether s2 is a subset of s1. addAll turns s1 into the union. retainAll turns s1 into the intersection. removeAll turns s1 into the asymmetric difference, the elements of s1 that are not in s2.

All of these change s1. To get a result without damaging s1, first copy it, as in new HashSet of s1, and then apply the operation to the copy. The symmetric difference, the elements in exactly one of the sets, is the union minus the intersection.

The result of add also helps: add returns false when the element was already present. A program can add each word to a set called uniques and, whenever add returns false, put the word in a second set called dups. Finally uniques.removeAll(dups) leaves words that occurred once.
card.rule: containsAll is subset, addAll is union, retainAll is intersection and removeAll is difference, and each changes the set it is called on.
card.limits: Difference depends on order: s1 minus s2 differs from s2 minus s1. The operations are destructive, so copy first when you need the original.
card.example: s1 holds 1, 2, 3 and s2 holds 3, 4. Union is 1, 2, 3, 4. Intersection is 3. The difference s1 minus s2 is 1, 2. The symmetric difference is 1, 2, 4.

concepts.title: The List interface
concepts.question: What does List add to Collection, and what do its positional and search operations return?

paragraphs: A List is an ordered collection, also called a sequence, that may contain duplicates. It adds positional access (get, set, add and remove by index), search (indexOf and lastIndexOf), a richer iterator (listIterator) and a range view (subList). The platform offers ArrayList, usually the better performer, and LinkedList.

set and remove by index return the old element. indexOf and lastIndexOf return the first or last index of an element, or minus one if it is absent. add and addAll append at the end, and remove of an object removes its first occurrence. addAll with an index inserts a collection at that position.
List strengthens equals: two lists are equal if they hold the same elements in the same order, whatever their implementation.
card.rule: A List keeps elements in position, allows duplicates, and its set and remove by index return the old element.
card.limits: Ordered means by position, not sorted: a List keeps elements where they were put, not in ascending value order.
card.example: names holds Ann, Bob, Ann. indexOf of Ann is 0, lastIndexOf is 2, indexOf of Zed is minus one. set at index 1 with Cy returns Bob, and the list becomes Ann, Cy, Ann.

concepts.title: ListIterator and its cursor
concepts.question: Where does a ListIterator's cursor sit, and what do next, previous, add, set and remove act on?

paragraphs: A ListIterator extends Iterator with backward traversal (hasPrevious and previous), modification (set and add) and position queries (nextIndex and previousIndex). listIterator starts at the beginning; listIterator with an index starts there, so index size starts at the end.
The cursor sits between elements, so a list of n elements has n plus 1 cursor positions, numbered 0 to n. next and previous move the cursor and return the element they cross.

remove and set act on the last element returned by next or previous. add inserts a new element just before the cursor. nextIndex is always previousIndex plus 1; previousIndex is minus one before the first element, and nextIndex is the size after the last.
card.rule: The cursor sits between elements, and remove and set act on whichever element next or previous returned last.
card.limits: nextIndex and previousIndex only report the cursor position; they do not move it. set and remove need a recent next or previous to act on.
card.example: On the list A, B, C, a ListIterator started at index 3 calls previous twice and returns C then B. Now nextIndex is 1 and previousIndex is 0. A call to remove deletes B, the last element returned.

concepts.title: Range views with subList
concepts.question: What does subList return, and why should a sublist be used only briefly?

paragraphs: subList with a from index and a to index returns a view of that range: from is included and to is excluded, matching an ordinary for loop. The view is backed by the original list, so a change in either shows up in the other.

Because it is a live window, any list algorithm works on part of a list, for example list.subList(a, b).clear() removes a range. indexOf and lastIndexOf on a sublist return indexes relative to the sublist.

The tutorial advises using a sublist only as a short-lived object. If the backing list is structurally changed in any way other than through the sublist, the sublist's behaviour is undefined. To get an independent list, copy the view.
card.rule: subList is a live window with an included start and an excluded end; use it briefly and copy it if you need an independent list.
card.limits: A copy is independent. The view is not, and it must not outlive structural changes made to the backing list from outside it.
card.example: letters holds A to F. subList(1, 4) shows B, C, D. Clearing it leaves A, E, F in letters. To deal a hand from a deck, copy the view of the last cards into a new list, then clear the view.

concepts.title: Queue operations in two forms
concepts.question: Which Queue methods throw an exception on failure, and which return a special value instead?

paragraphs: A Queue holds elements before processing. Besides the Collection operations it has insertion, removal and examination operations. Each exists in two forms: one throws an exception when it fails, the other returns a special value, null or false depending on the operation.

For insertion, add throws IllegalStateException if the queue's capacity would be exceeded, while offer returns false. For removal, remove throws NoSuchElementException on an empty queue, while poll returns null. For examination, element throws NoSuchElementException on an empty queue, while peek returns null.
card.rule: Each queue operation has a throwing form (add, remove, element) and a special-value form (offer, poll, peek).
card.limits: The special values are null and false, which can be confused with real contents. A queue that allows null elements makes a null from poll or peek ambiguous.
card.example: A Queue of String is empty. Calling poll returns null. Calling remove throws NoSuchElementException. Calling peek returns null and element throws.

concepts.title: Queue ordering and the head
concepts.question: What decides which element is the head of a queue, and what do FIFO and priority queues have in common?

paragraphs: Queues typically order elements first in, first out (FIFO), but not necessarily. A priority queue orders elements by their values, using natural ordering or a comparator. Whatever the policy, the head is the element that remove or poll would return. In a FIFO queue new elements go at the tail.

Every Queue implementation must specify its ordering properties. A queue may be bounded, limiting how many elements it holds. Some queues in java.util.concurrent are bounded, while those in java.util are not.

Queue implementations generally do not allow null elements. LinkedList is a historical exception, but null should still be avoided in it. Blocking methods that wait for elements or space are not part of Queue; they belong to the BlockingQueue subinterface in java.util.concurrent.
card.rule: The head is whatever remove or poll would return, and the queue's ordering policy decides which element that is.
card.limits: FIFO is typical, not guaranteed. Do not assume arrival order for a queue until its documentation says so, and do not assume a java.util queue ever blocks.
card.example: A LinkedList used as a Queue is loaded with 3, 2, 1, 0 and drained with remove, giving 3, 2, 1, 0. A PriorityQueue loaded with 7, 2, 9 and drained with remove gives 2, 7, 9, least first by natural order.

concepts.title: The Deque interface
concepts.question: What can a Deque do that a Queue cannot, and how do its methods name the two ends?

paragraphs: A Deque, pronounced deck, is a double-ended queue: elements can be inserted, retrieved and removed at both ends. It can be used as a first-in first-out queue or as a last-in first-out stack, so the tutorial calls it a richer abstract data type than either Stack or Queue. ArrayDeque and LinkedList implement it.

The methods fall into three groups, each for the first and the last element. Insert: addFirst, offerFirst, addLast, offerLast. Remove: removeFirst, pollFirst, removeLast, pollLast. Retrieve without removing: getFirst, peekFirst, getLast, peekLast.

As with Queue, the add, remove and get forms throw an exception when they fail, and the offer, poll and peek forms return false or null. removeFirstOccurrence and removeLastOccurrence remove an element by value and return true if one was found.
card.rule: A Deque works at both ends, so the same structure serves as a queue or as a stack depending on which ends you use.
card.limits: First and Last name the ends of the deque, not the age of an element. Whether you get queue or stack behaviour depends on which pair of ends you insert and remove at.
card.example: On an ArrayDeque, addFirst of B, addLast of C and addFirst of A leave A, B, C. removeFirst returns A, and getLast returns C.

concepts.title: The Map interface
concepts.question: What does a Map store, what happens when you put an existing key, and which implementations order the keys?

paragraphs: A Map maps keys to values. It cannot contain duplicate keys, and each key maps to at most one value; it models the mathematical function. The basic operations are put, get, remove, containsKey, containsValue, size and isEmpty. putAll and clear are the bulk operations.
HashMap, TreeMap and LinkedHashMap parallel HashSet, TreeSet and LinkedHashSet: HashMap is fastest with no order, TreeMap iterates in key order, and LinkedHashMap in insertion order.

In the tutorial's frequency program, each word is looked up with get. A null means no mapping yet, so the program puts 1; otherwise it puts the old count plus 1, which replaces the earlier value for that key.
card.rule: A Map holds each key once, put on an existing key replaces its value, and get gives null when the key has no mapping.
card.limits: A Map pairs one value with each key. To keep several values for a key you need a different structure. A null from get may also be a stored null, depending on the implementation.
card.example: Counting the words to, be, to with a Map from word to count: after the first to the map holds to=1, after be it also holds be=1, and the second to replaces the count, giving to=2, be=1.

concepts.title: Collection views of a Map
concepts.question: How do keySet, values and entrySet let you iterate and edit a Map, and what can and cannot you do through them?

paragraphs: A Map offers three collection views. keySet is a Set of the keys. values is a Collection of the values; it is not a Set because several keys can share a value. entrySet is a Set of Map.Entry objects, each holding a key and a value. The views are the only way to iterate over a Map.

The views are backed by the map. Removal through a view, with remove, removeAll, retainAll, clear or Iterator.remove, removes the entries from the map. Adding is not supported through a view; use put or putAll. During iteration, the safe changes are Iterator.remove and Map.Entry.setValue.

Bulk operations on views give map algebra. m1.keySet().equals(m2.keySet()) tests for the same keys. m1.keySet().removeAll(m2.keySet()) deletes from m1 the entries whose keys are in m2. m1.entrySet().containsAll(m2.entrySet()) tests whether m2 is a submap of m1.
card.rule: Iterate and edit a map through its views: removal through a view changes the map, but there is no way to add through one.
card.limits: Only removal writes through. A view has no add, so new entries need put. The values view may hold repeats, since different keys can share a value.
card.example: A map called job pairs people with occupations. Calling job.values().removeAll(Collections.singleton(LAWYER)) removes every entry whose value is LAWYER, because the values view writes through to the map.

concepts.title: Multimaps from Map and List
concepts.question: How do you give one key several values when the framework has no multimap?

paragraphs: A multimap maps each key to several values. The framework does not include a multimap interface, so the tutorial's technique is a Map from each key to a List of values. Each key then owns its own list.

The anagram example builds one. For each word it sorts the letters to make a key, so bad becomes abd. It looks up the list for that key, creates and stores a new list if get returned null, and adds the word. All words under one key are anagrams.
Streams can build the same shape in one pipeline: groupingBy with a classifier function produces a Map from each key to a List of the matching elements.
card.rule: For several values per key, store a list as the value and create the list the first time a key is used.
card.limits: get returns null for a key with no list yet, so adding straight to it fails. The map does not create lists by itself; your code, or groupingBy, must.
card.example: Grouping cat, act and dog by sorted letters gives a map with the key act holding cat and act, and the key dgo holding dog.

concepts.title: Natural ordering with Comparable
concepts.question: What gives a class a natural ordering, and what does compareTo return?

paragraphs: Collections.sort can sort a List because the elements implement Comparable. String sorts alphabetically and Date chronologically. A class that implements Comparable has a natural ordering, and the sort uses it automatically. If the elements are not Comparable, Collections.sort throws ClassCastException.

Comparable declares compareTo, which returns a negative integer, zero or a positive integer when the receiving object is less than, equal to or greater than the argument. Number classes sort numerically, Boolean puts false before true, and String sorts lexicographically.
To compare objects with several parts, compare the most significant part first and move to the next only on a tie. The tutorial's Name class compares last names, then first names.
card.rule: Implement Comparable so compareTo gives the natural ordering, and compare the most significant field first, using later fields only on a tie.
card.limits: A class has one natural ordering. For another order, or for classes that do not implement Comparable, a Comparator is needed.
card.example: Four Name objects John Smith, Karl Ng, Jeff Smith and Tom Rich sort to Karl Ng, Tom Rich, Jeff Smith, John Smith: last names first, and first names settle the Smith tie.

concepts.title: Custom ordering with Comparator
concepts.question: How does a Comparator give a different ordering, and how do you reverse or write one safely?

paragraphs: A Comparator encapsulates an ordering. Use one to sort in a way other than the natural order, or to sort objects that are not Comparable. Its compare method takes two objects and follows the same sign rules as compareTo. Pass it to Collections.sort along with the list.

To reverse an order, swap the two arguments in the comparison. The tutorial warns against negating the result: compare may return any negative integer, and negating the smallest int gives the same number back.

Do not compare integers by subtraction unless negative values are impossible. If one value is a large positive and the other a large negative, the difference can overflow and flip sign, which breaks transitivity. Compare explicitly instead.
card.rule: A Comparator supplies an ordering from outside the class; reverse it by swapping arguments, and compare ints explicitly instead of subtracting.
card.limits: A comparator must still give a consistent ordering: if a is before b and b is before c, then a is before c. Subtraction on ints that may be large breaks that.
card.example: A seniority comparator compares e2's hire date to e1's. Swapping the arguments puts the earliest hire first, with no negation involved.

concepts.title: Ordering consistent with equals
concepts.question: Why can a comparator that works for sorting a list make a TreeSet lose elements?

paragraphs: The seniority comparator compares only hire dates. Sorting a List with it is fine. But two different employees hired on the same day compare as equal, and when both go into a TreeSet the second is treated as a duplicate and silently dropped. Sorted collections judge equality by the ordering.
The fix is a two-part comparison. Compare by hire date first and, on a tie, by a unique value such as the employee number. Then only objects that are equal under equals compare as equal.

The tutorial adds related rules for elements and keys. Override hashCode whenever you override equals. Make such classes immutable, because changing an element or key while it is stored corrupts a Set or Map. equals returns false for null or a wrong type, while compareTo throws an exception.
card.rule: An ordering used by a sorted set or map should call two objects equal only when equals does, so break ties with a unique field.
card.limits: A tie is harmless when you only sort a List. The problem appears in sorted sets and maps, where the comparator decides what counts as a duplicate.
card.example: Ana Smith and Bo Smith are different people, but a comparator on last name alone says they are equal. A TreeSet holding Ana then offered Bo keeps one and drops Bo. Adding a first-name tiebreak keeps both.

concepts.title: SortedSet and SortedMap
concepts.question: What do SortedSet and SortedMap add, and how do their range views and constructors behave?

paragraphs: A SortedSet is a Set kept in ascending order, by natural ordering or by a Comparator. It adds range views (subSet, headSet, tailSet), endpoints (first and last) and comparator access. Its iterator and toArray follow the order. SortedMap is the Map analogue, with subMap, headMap, tailMap, firstKey and lastKey.

A range view is a live window. subSet from and to includes from and excludes to. headSet of x holds elements less than x, and tailSet of x holds elements greater than or equal to x. The endpoints are values, not positions, so the view stays valid when the backing set changes.

For a closed range, ask for the successor of the high end; for strings, add a null character. Constructors: TreeSet from a Collection uses natural ordering, TreeSet from a SortedSet keeps its ordering, and the choice is made from the compile-time type of the argument.
card.rule: Sorted collections give ordered iteration and live, half-open range views whose ends are values, not positions.
card.limits: The constructor taking a Collection loses a comparator. The tutorial calls that behaviour probably a mistake. The choice is made by the static type, so a SortedSet held as a Collection takes the natural-ordering path.
card.example: With a SortedSet of dictionary words, dictionary.subSet of f and g clears the words beginning with f. headSet of n and tailSet of n split the dictionary into two disjoint volumes.

concepts.title: Pipelines and streams
concepts.question: What are the three parts of an aggregate-operation pipeline, and what does a stream store?

paragraphs: Collections are mostly used to retrieve and process elements, and aggregate operations express that processing as a pipeline. A pipeline has a source, such as a collection, an array, a generator function or an I/O channel; zero or more intermediate operations; and one terminal operation.

Each intermediate operation, such as filter or mapToInt, produces a new stream. The terminal operation produces a result that is not a stream: a primitive, a collection, or nothing at all, as with forEach.
A stream is a sequence of elements, but unlike a collection it stores none. It carries values from the source through the pipeline.
card.rule: A pipeline is a source, zero or more intermediate operations that each yield a stream, and a terminal operation that produces the result.
card.limits: A stream is not a data structure: it holds nothing, and the data stays in the source. Methods called on the result of the terminal operation belong to that result, not to the stream.
card.example: roster.stream().filter(male).mapToInt(age).average() has roster as its source, filter and mapToInt as intermediate operations, and average as the terminal operation. average returns an OptionalDouble, and calling getAsDouble on that is not a stream operation.

concepts.title: Internal versus external iteration
concepts.question: How do aggregate operations differ from iterators in who controls the traversal and what they can parallelise?

paragraphs: With an iterator or a for-each loop, your code controls both what is iterated and how: this is external iteration, and it can only proceed sequentially. Aggregate operations have no next method. You say what to do with each element, and the library decides how to traverse: internal iteration.

Internal iteration can more easily be split into subproblems that run in parallel and then be combined. Aggregate operations process elements from a stream, take behaviour as parameters, usually lambda expressions, and keep no storage of their own.
They do not modify the collection they read from, unlike the classic bulk operations.
card.rule: With aggregate operations you state what happens to each element and the library controls how the traversal runs.
card.limits: For a plain loop the stream form is longer; the gain shows up in multi-step pipelines. Aggregate operations also do not replace an Iterator when you must remove elements from the collection itself.
card.example: A for-each loop printing each name sets the loop itself. roster.stream().forEach with a lambda that prints a name hands only the action to the library, which chooses how to walk the elements.

concepts.title: Reduction with reduce
concepts.question: What are the identity and the accumulator in reduce, and why is reduce costly for building collections?

paragraphs: A reduction operation is a terminal operation that combines the contents of a stream into one result. Examples are average, sum, min, max and count. For general reductions the JDK offers Stream.reduce and Stream.collect.

reduce takes two arguments. The identity is the initial value of the reduction. The accumulator takes a partial result and the next element and returns a new partial result. To total ages: map to the age, then reduce with 0 and a function that adds its two arguments.

reduce produces a new value every time the accumulator runs. When the result is a collection, that means a new collection for every element, which the tutorial calls inefficient and answers with collect.
card.rule: reduce folds a stream into one value from an identity and an accumulator that returns a new partial result each time.
card.limits: The new value per step is cheap for numbers and costly for collections. For results that are containers, the tutorial prefers collect.
card.example: Ages 20, 30 and 40 with reduce(0, plus): start at 0, then 0 plus 20, then 20 plus 30, then 50 plus 40, giving 90.

concepts.title: Mutable reduction with collect
concepts.question: How does collect differ from reduce, and what do supplier, accumulator, combiner and downstream collector do?

paragraphs: collect is a mutable reduction: it modifies a result container instead of creating a new value for each element. The three-argument form takes a supplier that creates new containers, an accumulator that adds one element to a container, and a combiner that merges two containers. The combiner matters when the stream runs in parallel.

The one-argument form takes a Collector, which bundles those three. The Collectors class has ready-made ones. Collectors.toList gathers elements into a List. Collectors.groupingBy takes a classifier function and returns a Map from each key to a List of its elements.

groupingBy can take a second argument, a downstream collector, applied to each group. Collectors.mapping, averagingInt and reducing are examples. A collector with downstream collectors is called a multilevel reduction.
card.rule: Use collect to accumulate into a mutable container, and groupingBy with a downstream collector to group and reduce in one pass.
card.limits: A custom three-argument collect is worth writing when one pass must compute several values. For a single average the built-in operation is simpler.
card.example: groupingBy of Person::getGender gives a Map from gender to List of Person. Adding averagingInt of Person::getAge as the downstream collector gives a Map from gender to the average age, as a Double.

concepts.title: Parallel streams
concepts.question: How do you request parallel execution, and what does it change about ordering and speed?

paragraphs: Parallel computing divides a problem into subproblems, solves them at the same time in separate threads and combines the results. With aggregate operations, the runtime does the partitioning and combining. The tutorial stresses that parallelism is not automatically faster: it needs enough data and processor cores, and you must judge whether it suits your application.

Collections are not thread-safe, but parallel streams work with them as long as the collection is not modified while the operation runs. Streams are serial by default. Request a parallel one with Collection.parallelStream or BaseStream.parallel.

Ordering changes. A parallel forEach does not keep the stream's order and may differ from run to run. forEachOrdered keeps the encounter order, but may reduce the benefits of parallelism. For grouping, groupingByConcurrent returns a ConcurrentMap and avoids the costly merging of maps.
card.rule: Ask for parallel execution with parallelStream or parallel; the runtime splits and combines, but speed is not guaranteed and parallel forEach is unordered.
card.limits: Parallel is a choice to measure, not a default. It needs enough data and cores, and ordered operations give up part of the gain.
card.example: Printing 1 to 8 from a parallel stream with forEach might give 3 4 1 6 2 5 7 8 on one run and a different order on the next. With forEachOrdered it prints 1 to 8 in order.

concepts.title: Laziness, side effects and interference
concepts.question: Why must lambdas in a pipeline avoid side effects and never touch the source, and when do intermediate steps run?

paragraphs: Intermediate operations are lazy: they do not process the stream until a terminal operation starts. Laziness lets the runtime optimise, for example by pulling only the elements it needs through the chain.

A side effect is a change to program state beyond returning a value. A mutable reduction with collect is handled safely by the JDK. forEach and peek are designed for side effects, but in a parallel stream their lambdas may run at the same time on several threads. Do not pass side-effecting lambdas to operations such as filter and map.

Interference: a lambda must not modify the stream's source while the pipeline runs. The tutorial's example adds to the source inside peek and gets ConcurrentModificationException. A stateful lambda, whose result depends on state that can change during execution, gives unpredictable results, especially in parallel.
card.rule: Keep lambdas stateless and free of side effects, leave the source alone, and remember nothing runs until the terminal operation starts.
card.limits: forEach and peek exist for side effects, but under a parallel stream they can run concurrently, so any shared state they touch needs protection. Even debugging prints are side effects.
card.example: A pipeline ends with peek and has no terminal operation: nothing runs. A map lambda that adds each element to a shared list works in serial but fills the list in a different order on each parallel run.

concepts.title: Kinds of implementation
concepts.question: What kinds of implementation exist, what do general-purpose ones have in common, and what are the usual defaults?

paragraphs: Implementations are the data objects behind the interfaces. The tutorial names six kinds: general-purpose, special-purpose (unusual performance, restrictions or behaviour), concurrent (in java.util.concurrent, built for high concurrency), wrapper (add or restrict behaviour), convenience (small ones from static factories) and abstract (skeletons for your own).
The usual defaults are HashSet, ArrayList and HashMap. For Queue the general-purpose choices are LinkedList for first in first out and PriorityQueue for value order; ArrayDeque is the usual Deque.

General-purpose implementations support all optional operations, permit null elements, keys and values, are not synchronized, and have fail-fast iterators, which throw on illegal concurrent modification instead of behaving unpredictably. The choice mostly affects performance. When in doubt, measure.
card.rule: Start from the default implementation behind the interface you need, and change it only when measurement says to.
card.limits: Individual pages add exceptions: ArrayDeque and PriorityQueue do not permit null. Nominal speed ratings are guides, and the nominally slower implementation is sometimes faster.
card.example: A program declares its collection as a List and creates an ArrayList. If a test shows poor speed, only the constructor changes to try another List implementation.

concepts.title: Choosing and sizing a Set
concepts.question: Which Set implementation suits which need, and how does initial capacity affect a HashSet?

paragraphs: HashSet has constant-time operations and no ordering; the tutorial expects you to use it most of the time. Use TreeSet when you need sorted operations or value-ordered iteration; its operations take log time and it has no tuning. LinkedHashSet is nearly as fast as HashSet and iterates in insertion order.

HashSet and LinkedHashSet have a tuning parameter, initial capacity, 16 by default. Iterating a HashSet takes time linear in the number of entries plus the capacity. Too large a capacity wastes space and iteration time; too small wastes time on copying as the table grows.

A rule of thumb is a capacity about twice the expected size. Capacity is always rounded up to a power of two, so the old advice about prime numbers no longer applies. LinkedHashSet iteration time is not affected by capacity.
card.rule: Use HashSet by default, TreeSet for sorted needs and LinkedHashSet for insertion order, and size a HashSet at about twice the expected number of elements.
card.limits: The capacity advice is a rule of thumb, and wrong guesses are unlikely to cause big problems. It also does not apply to TreeSet, which has no capacity parameter.
card.example: A set will hold about 500 words. new HashSet with capacity 1000 avoids repeated growth without leaving the table far too large.

concepts.title: EnumSet and CopyOnWriteArraySet
concepts.question: What are EnumSet and CopyOnWriteArraySet for, and what does each cost or require?

paragraphs: EnumSet is a high-performance Set for the values of an enum type. All its members must come from the same enum. Internally it is a bit vector, typically a single long. It supports range iteration and is a typesafe replacement for traditional bit flags: EnumSet.range of MONDAY and FRIDAY covers the weekdays, and EnumSet.of of BOLD and ITALIC makes a set of flags.

CopyOnWriteArraySet is backed by a copy-on-write array. Every change copies the whole array, so no locking is needed, and iteration can safely run while others insert and delete. The price is that add, remove and contains take time proportional to the size of the set.
Use it only for sets that are rarely modified but frequently iterated, such as event-handler lists that must not hold duplicates.
card.rule: Use EnumSet for sets of enum values and CopyOnWriteArraySet for rarely changed, often iterated sets that several threads share.
card.limits: EnumSet holds the values of one enum only. CopyOnWriteArraySet copies its array on every change, so it is a poor fit for write-heavy sets.
card.example: A word processor keeps the active text styles as an EnumSet of Style values. A list of listeners that is read thousands of times and changed a few times a day suits a CopyOnWriteArraySet.

concepts.title: ArrayList or LinkedList
concepts.question: When does ArrayList beat LinkedList, and when might LinkedList be worth measuring?

paragraphs: ArrayList gives constant-time positional access and is usually just fast. It allocates no node per element and can move many elements at once with an array copy. Its only tuning parameter is the initial capacity. The tutorial treats it as the default List.

LinkedList is good for frequent additions at the beginning and for deleting interior elements while iterating, which are constant time there but linear in an ArrayList. Positional access is linear, the constant factors are much worse, and ArrayList is usually faster. If you think you want a LinkedList, measure with both first.

LinkedList also offers addFirst, getFirst, removeFirst, addLast, getLast and removeLast, and implements Queue. CopyOnWriteArrayList suits rarely changed lists that are iterated often. Vector is slightly faster than a synchronized ArrayList and should be used through the List interface.
card.rule: Start with ArrayList, and consider LinkedList only for frequent front insertions or interior deletions during iteration, after measuring.
card.limits: The growth rates are only a guide: LinkedList's cheap insertion means little if you first have to walk to the position, and the constant factors favour ArrayList.
card.example: A report reads 10,000 rows by index and rarely changes them: ArrayList. A queue of jobs that always inserts at the front and removes from the middle during a scan might justify measuring LinkedList.

concepts.title: Choosing a Map, and LinkedHashMap as a cache
concepts.question: Which Map implementation fits which need, and how does LinkedHashMap support a cache?

paragraphs: For maps the situation parallels sets, and what was said about set implementations applies. Use TreeMap when you need SortedMap operations or key-ordered iteration of the views. Use HashMap for maximum speed when order does not matter. Use LinkedHashMap for near-HashMap speed with predictable iteration order.

LinkedHashMap has two features that LinkedHashSet lacks. It can order by access instead of insertion, so looking up a key moves it to the end. And it has a protected method removeEldestEntry that you can override to drop stale mappings automatically when new ones are added, which makes a custom cache easy.
