The tutorial's override returns true when the size exceeds a maximum such as 100. The map then grows to 100 entries and stays at 100, deleting the eldest on every further addition. Because the method is protected, it is overridden in a subclass.
card.rule: Pick HashMap for speed, TreeMap for key order and LinkedHashMap for insertion order or cache-style eviction through removeEldestEntry.
card.limits: removeEldestEntry only answers whether to drop the eldest entry. With the default insertion order the eldest is the oldest inserted, not the least recently used; access order must be turned on for that.
card.example: A LinkedHashMap subclass overrides removeEldestEntry to return size() greater than 3. After four puts, the first key put is gone and three entries remain.

concepts.title: Special-purpose and concurrent maps
concepts.question: What do EnumMap, WeakHashMap, IdentityHashMap and ConcurrentHashMap each offer?

paragraphs: EnumMap is implemented as an array, for keys that are enum values. It joins the richness of the Map interface with speed close to an array. The tutorial says to prefer an EnumMap to an array when mapping an enum to a value.

WeakHashMap keeps only weak references to its keys, so an entry can be garbage-collected once its key is no longer referenced outside the map. It suits registry-like structures where an entry is useless after its key is unreachable.

IdentityHashMap compares keys with == instead of equals. It is used for graph transformations such as serialization and deep copying, which need a table of nodes already seen, and for object-to-metadata maps in tools such as debuggers. It is not fooled by odd equals methods.
ConcurrentMap adds atomic putIfAbsent, remove and replace. ConcurrentHashMap implements it with highly concurrent hashing, never blocks retrievals, and can replace Hashtable.
card.rule: Use EnumMap for enum keys, WeakHashMap for entries that should vanish with their keys, IdentityHashMap for reference-based keys and ConcurrentHashMap for shared maps.
card.limits: Each of these changes the usual map contract: weak entries can disappear without a remove call, and an identity map treats equal but distinct keys as different.
card.example: A calendar maps each Day value to its schedule with an EnumMap. A debugger records one note per live object in an IdentityHashMap, so two distinct objects that are equal under equals still get separate notes.

concepts.title: Queue and Deque implementations
concepts.question: Which implementations serve FIFO, priority, blocking and double-ended needs?

paragraphs: LinkedList implements Queue with FIFO operations and permits null elements. PriorityQueue is a heap-based queue ordered by natural ordering or a Comparator; its head is the least element, ties are broken arbitrarily, it forbids null, and its iterator does not promise any order. For ordered traversal sort its toArray result.

Concurrent queues implement BlockingQueue, which waits for the queue to be non-empty when retrieving and for space when storing. They include LinkedBlockingQueue (optionally bounded), ArrayBlockingQueue (bounded), PriorityBlockingQueue, DelayQueue (an element is taken only after its delay expires), SynchronousQueue (zero capacity hand-off) and LinkedTransferQueue.

For Deque, ArrayDeque is a resizable array, forbids null, is more efficient than LinkedList at both ends and uses less memory. LinkedList implements all optional list operations, permits null and is best at removing the current element during iteration. LinkedBlockingDeque is the concurrent one.
card.rule: Pick LinkedList or ArrayDeque for plain FIFO or double-ended use, PriorityQueue for value order and a BlockingQueue when threads must wait for each other.
card.limits: None of the java.util queues block or is thread-safe. PriorityQueue's iterator order is not the priority order, so do not print or iterate it expecting sorted output.
card.example: A job runner shared by threads uses an ArrayBlockingQueue of fixed capacity so producers wait when it is full. A stack inside one thread uses an ArrayDeque.

concepts.title: Wrapper implementations
concepts.question: What do synchronized, unmodifiable and checked wrappers add, and what must you do to use them correctly?

paragraphs: Wrapper implementations delegate to another collection and add or restrict behaviour, in the manner of the decorator pattern. They are anonymous: instead of public classes there are static factory methods in the Collections class, such as synchronizedList, unmodifiableSet and checkedList.

A synchronization wrapper makes the collection thread-safe. All access must go through the wrapper, so keep no reference to the backing collection. Iterating takes many calls, so lock on the wrapper yourself and call iterator inside the block. For a map's view, lock the map, not the view.

An unmodifiable wrapper throws UnsupportedOperationException on every modification. Use it to freeze a collection after building it, dropping the backing reference, or to give clients read-only access while you keep the backing collection. A checked wrapper is a dynamically type-safe view: wrong-typed insertions throw ClassCastException.
card.rule: Wrap with the Collections factory methods to add thread safety, read-only access or run-time type checks, and keep no stray reference to the backing collection when the guarantee matters.
card.limits: A synchronized wrapper makes each call atomic, not a whole loop, so iteration still needs your own synchronized block. A read-only wrapper is a view of the backing collection, so changes made to that show through.
card.example: A class keeps a private list. Its getter returns Collections.unmodifiableList of the list, so callers can read but not change it, while the class keeps editing the list.

concepts.title: Convenience implementations
concepts.question: What do Arrays.asList, nCopies, singleton and the empty constants provide, and which of them can be changed?

paragraphs: Convenience implementations are mini-implementations from static factory methods. Arrays.asList returns a fixed-size list view of an array: changes write through in both directions, and add and remove throw UnsupportedOperationException. It is a bridge between array-based and collection-based APIs.

Collections.nCopies returns an immutable list of n references to one element. Use it to initialise a list, as in new ArrayList of nCopies(1000, null), or to grow one with addAll. Collections.singleton returns an immutable set of one element, handy for c.removeAll(Collections.singleton(e)).

Collections.emptySet, emptyList and emptyMap return immutable empty collections. Their main use is passing no values to a method, as in declarePurchases(Collections.emptySet()), without creating a new collection.
card.rule: Arrays.asList is a fixed-size writable view, and nCopies, singleton and the empty constants are immutable.
card.limits: Only asList allows changing elements, and it cannot grow. The others refuse every change, so copy them into an ArrayList if you need to modify the contents.
card.example: A list from Arrays.asList on a String array allows set, which also changes the array. A list from nCopies of 3 and a word is immutable, but new ArrayList of that list is a modifiable copy.

concepts.title: Sorting a List
concepts.question: What does Collections.sort guarantee, and why does stability matter when you sort twice?

paragraphs: The Collections class holds polymorphic algorithms: static methods whose first argument is the collection to work on. Most apply to lists. Collections.sort reorders a list in ascending order, using natural ordering, or a Comparator if you pass one.

The algorithm is a slightly optimised merge sort. It is fast: it is guaranteed to take n log n time and runs much faster on nearly sorted lists. It is also stable, which means equal elements are never reordered.

Stability matters when you sort repeatedly on different attributes. A mail program that sorts the inbox by date and then by sender keeps each sender's messages in date order, because the second sort does not disturb equal senders.
card.rule: Collections.sort is fast and stable, so sort first by the secondary key and then by the primary key to get a two-level order.
card.limits: Stability preserves the earlier order only among elements that the later sort calls equal. It cannot restore an order that the later sort changes.
card.example: Messages are sorted by date. Sorting again by sender groups each sender together. Within one sender the messages stay in date order, since the sort is stable.

concepts.title: Shuffling and routine manipulation
concepts.question: Which Collections algorithms shuffle, reverse, fill, copy and swap a list, and what does copy require?

paragraphs: Collections.shuffle does the opposite of sort: it destroys any order in a list. With a fair source of randomness every permutation is equally likely. shuffle(list) uses a default source; shuffle(list, random) uses a Random you supply. Uses include games of chance and generating test cases.

Five routine operations are provided. reverse reverses the order. fill overwrites every element with a given value. swap exchanges the elements at two positions. addAll adds the given elements, singly or as an array, to a Collection.
copy takes a destination and a source and copies the source over the destination. The destination must be at least as long as the source, and any extra destination elements are left unchanged.
card.rule: Use shuffle to randomise, reverse, fill and swap to rearrange or reset, and copy to overwrite a destination that is at least as long as the source.
card.limits: copy overwrites in place and cannot grow the destination. To append elements to a collection, use addAll.
card.example: A deck list is shuffled before dealing. A destination list of five elements receives a source of three through copy: the first three are overwritten and the last two are unchanged.

concepts.title: Searching with binarySearch
concepts.question: What does binarySearch require, and how do you read its return value when the key is missing?

paragraphs: Collections.binarySearch finds an element in a sorted list. The list must already be sorted in ascending order, so sort it first if necessary. It takes the list and a key, using natural ordering, or a Comparator as a third argument.

If the key is found, the result is its index, zero or more. If it is not found, the result is minus the insertion point, minus one. The insertion point is the index of the first element greater than the key, or the list size if every element is smaller. The result is nonnegative exactly when the key is found.
To insert a key if absent: pos is the binarySearch result, and if pos is negative, call add at index minus pos minus one.
card.rule: A nonnegative result is the index of the key; a negative result n means not found, and the insertion point is minus n minus one.
card.limits: The list must be sorted by the same ordering the search uses. On a list that is not sorted the result cannot be relied on.
card.example: For the list 1, 3, 5: key 3 returns 1; key 4 returns minus 3 (insertion point 2); key 0 returns minus 1; key 6 returns minus 4. Inserting 4 with add at index 2 gives 1, 3, 4, 5.

concepts.title: Frequency, disjointness and extremes
concepts.question: Which algorithms count occurrences, test for overlap, and find the smallest or largest element?

paragraphs: Some Collections algorithms test the makeup of collections. frequency takes a collection and an element and counts how many times the element occurs. disjoint takes two collections and tells you whether they have no elements in common.

min and max return the smallest and largest elements of a collection. The simple form uses natural ordering; the other form takes a Comparator and uses its ordering. These algorithms work on any Collection, not only on lists.
card.rule: frequency counts occurrences, disjoint tests for no overlap, and min and max find extremes by natural ordering or a Comparator.
card.limits: min and max need an ordering: elements must be Comparable, or you must supply a Comparator. They do not sort or change the collection.
card.example: Guest lists a and b share nobody if Collections.disjoint(a, b) is true. With a Comparator on name length, min of a word collection returns a shortest word.

concepts.title: Why write your own collection
concepts.question: When is a custom collection justified, and which abstract class should you extend for each storage style?

paragraphs: The built-in collections live in main memory and vanish when the program ends. The tutorial gives reasons to write your own. Persistent: a veneer over a database. Application-specific: an unmodifiable map of live sensor data. High-performance: a run-length-encoded list. Enhanced functionality: a bag built on a HashMap. Convenience: a list of a range of integers. Adapter: a legacy API presented as a collection.

Abstract implementations are skeletons that leave you only the core methods. AbstractCollection and AbstractSet need iterator and size. AbstractList suits random-access storage: supply get and size, plus set, add and remove if modifiable. AbstractSequentialList suits linked storage: supply listIterator and size. AbstractQueue needs offer, peek, poll, size and an iterator with remove. AbstractMap needs entrySet, and put if modifiable.
card.rule: Write a custom collection only for a need the built-ins do not meet, and extend the abstract class that matches your storage so you write only the core methods.
card.limits: A custom collection means extra work to test and maintain. Abstract classes supply most methods, but those defaults may be slow, so override them only after measuring.
card.example: A list that presents the integers 1 to n without storing them extends AbstractList. Its get computes the value from the index, and its size returns n.

concepts.title: Building a list on AbstractList
concepts.question: What must you write to turn an array into a List with AbstractList, and what do you get for free?

paragraphs: The tutorial's example is a list that views an array, close to the real Arrays.asList. A private class extends AbstractList and holds the array. get returns the element at the index. set stores the new element and returns the old one. size returns the array length.

That is all. AbstractList supplies the ListIterator, bulk operations, search operations, hash code, equality and string form. The list is a fixed-size, write-through view: add and remove were not implemented, so they are unsupported.

AbstractList does toArray element by element, so cloning the array is faster. The tutorial's process is: pick the abstract class, implement its abstract methods, test, and optimise only if needed, measuring each override.
card.rule: Extend the abstract class that matches your storage, implement its few core methods, and optimise only after measuring.
card.limits: A skeleton gives correct but not always fast methods. Override an inherited method only if measurement shows it is too slow, and measure again after the change.
card.example: Wrapping the array a with the class above and calling set at index 0 changes a[0] and returns the previous value. Calling add throws UnsupportedOperationException.

concepts.title: Old APIs feeding new ones
concepts.question: How do you pass arrays, Vectors, Hashtables and Enumerations from older APIs into code that expects collections?

paragraphs: The framework was designed to work with the early Java types: arrays, Vector, Hashtable and Enumeration. The tutorial names two directions. Upward compatibility is what you need when an old API feeds a new one, so the old type must be seen as a collection.

An array becomes a List through Arrays.asList. A Vector needs no conversion, because it was retrofitted to implement List. A Hashtable needs none either, because it was retrofitted to implement Map. An Enumeration becomes a Collection through Collections.list, which is less common.
card.rule: Arrays go through Arrays.asList, Vector and Hashtable pass straight in, and an Enumeration goes through Collections.list.
card.limits: The tutorial's snippets use raw types for brevity. An array view is fixed-size, so a new method that adds elements to it fails; copy it into an ArrayList first if that is needed.
card.example: An old method returns a Vector. A new method taking a Collection accepts it directly, with no copying or wrapping.

concepts.title: New collections feeding old APIs
concepts.question: How do you pass a Collection or Map to an older API that expects an array, Vector, Hashtable or Enumeration?

paragraphs: Backward compatibility is the opposite problem: a new API produces a collection and an old API wants an older type. To get an Object array use the collection's toArray. To get an array of a given type, use toArray with an array of that type as the argument.

To get a Vector, use the Vector constructor that takes a collection. To get a Hashtable from a Map, use the Hashtable constructor that takes a map, the same way. To get an Enumeration, use the static factory Collections.enumeration.
card.rule: Use toArray for arrays, a constructor for Vector and Hashtable, and Collections.enumeration for an Enumeration.
card.limits: A conversion hands the old API the elements in the old type. The tutorial's snippets use raw types; with generics, state the element type in the typed toArray call.
card.example: A newMethod returns a Collection of String called c. An old routine that needs a String array receives c.toArray(new String[0]). One that needs a Vector receives new Vector(c).

concepts.title: Designing APIs with collections
concepts.question: What types should an API accept as parameters and return, according to the tutorial?

paragraphs: The tutorial's guidance on API design starts with parameters. Use an interface type, never an implementation type, because the framework exists so collections can be handled without regard to implementation. Use the least specific type that makes sense: take Collection or Map unless the method needs a property of List or Set, such as ordering. Do not invent your own collection class for input.

Return values are more flexible. Any type that implements a collection interface may be returned, including special-purpose ones. Return the most specific interface that is always true: if you always return a sorted map, declare SortedMap, so the caller gets more power and can still pass it where a Map is accepted.
The tutorial's example is a class ImageList that implements List and adds an indexImage operation. Even if methods return ImageList, they should accept general collections as input.
card.rule: Accept the most general interface that does the job and return the most specific interface you can promise.
card.limits: General input is not always right: a method that truly depends on order or uniqueness should say so by asking for a List or a Set. A narrower return type is a commitment that you must keep.
card.example: A method that only counts distinct words takes a Collection of String. A method that always builds its answer in key order returns a SortedMap of String to Integer.

concepts.title: The four design principles
concepts.question: Which four design qualities shape the Date-Time API, and what does each one promise the programmer?

paragraphs: The Date-Time API was built around four principles: clear, fluent, immutable and extensible. Clear means each method does one well-defined, predictable thing. A null passed as an argument usually triggers a NullPointerException at once, so a misuse shows up where it happens instead of producing a quietly wrong date.

Fluent means calls can be chained into readable lines. That works because most methods neither accept nor return null, so one call's result is safe to feed to the next. Extensible means you may add your own adjusters and queries, or even a whole calendar system.
The third principle, immutable, shapes every method name and gets its own idea next.
card.example: LocalDate.of(2024, Month.JUNE, 10).with(TemporalAdjusters.lastDayOfMonth()).minusDays(2) reads left to right. Start at 10 June 2024, move to 30 June, step back two days: the result is 2024-06-28. Each call returns a new date that the next call receives.
card.rule: Expect Date-Time methods to be predictable, chainable, safe against null, and open to adjusters and queries you write yourself.
card.limits: The tutorial says most methods avoid null, not all of them, and it describes design intent rather than a guarantee for your own code. Check a method before relying on how it treats null.

concepts.title: Immutable values and no setters
concepts.question: How do you obtain a changed date from an object that never changes?

paragraphs: Most Date-Time classes are immutable: once an object exists, its value never changes. A method that looks like an edit, such as plusYears, builds and returns a new object with the changed value, and the original keeps its old value. The tutorial adds that this makes the API inherently thread-safe.

Two consequences follow. There are no set methods, because a setter would change an existing object. And values are created through factory methods whose names start with of, from or with instead of constructors. The practical habit is to keep the value a call returns.
card.example: LocalDate born = LocalDate.of(2012, Month.MAY, 14); LocalDate first = born.plusYears(1); Afterwards first is 2013-05-14 and born is 2012-05-14. A bare statement born.plusYears(1) with the result thrown away changes nothing at all.
card.rule: Treat every date-time value as fixed, and capture the result of any change in a variable.
card.limits: The tutorial says most classes are immutable, not all. Immutability protects the object, not your variable: you may point a variable at a newer value. Older java.util date classes are mutable.

concepts.title: The Date-Time packages
concepts.question: Which of the five Date-Time packages holds the everyday classes, and what are the other four for?

paragraphs: The everyday classes live in java.time: dates, times, combined date-times, time zones, instants, durations and clocks. It uses the ISO-8601 calendar, and its classes are immutable and thread-safe. Four subpackages hold the specialised parts.

java.time.format converts between values and text. java.time.zone holds zone rules and offsets, though most developers need only ZonedDateTime, ZoneId and ZoneOffset. java.time.chrono supports calendars other than ISO and lets you define your own.
java.time.temporal is mainly for framework and library writers. It supports querying, adjusting and mixing classes, and it defines the fields and units that dates are built from.
card.example: Task: print a date in a custom layout, so look in java.time.format. Task: represent a birth date, so use java.time. Task: name the day-of-week field as a value, so look in java.time.temporal. Task: model a lunar calendar, so look in java.time.chrono.
card.rule: Start in java.time and open a subpackage only for formatting, zone rules, other calendars, or low-level fields and units.
card.limits: A package name tells you where a class is declared, not how often you will use it. The tutorial does not cover chrono in depth, and temporal is aimed at framework authors, so everyday code can stay in java.time.

concepts.title: Naming: of, from and parse
concepts.question: What do the prefixes of, from and parse each promise about how a new date-time value is created?

paragraphs: Date-Time method names follow a small vocabulary, so the first word tells you what a method does. Because values are immutable, new ones come from static factory methods. Three prefixes create values: of, from and parse.

Of builds a value from parts you supply and mainly checks that they are valid. From converts an object of another type into the target type and may lose information on the way. Parse reads a string and produces a value, using a formatter if you give one.
card.example: LocalDate.of(2024, Month.MARCH, 15) builds a date from parts. LocalDate.from(someZonedDateTime) converts a value of another type. LocalDate.parse applied to the text 2024-03-15 reads a string. Each call starts with the target class and returns a new value.
card.rule: Use of to build from parts, from to convert another type, and parse to read text.
card.limits: The prefixes are conventions from the tutorial's naming table, not rules the compiler enforces. From can lose information, so converting back may not restore the original. Of checks its input, so a day that does not exist fails.

concepts.title: Naming: get, is, with, plus, minus, to, at
concepts.question: What do get, is, with, plus, minus, to, at and format promise about a method called on an existing value?

paragraphs: Instance methods use the same vocabulary. Get returns part of the object's state, and is asks a yes-or-no question about it. Format uses a formatter to produce a string from the value.

With returns a copy that has one element replaced, the immutable counterpart of a setter. Plus and minus return a copy with an amount added or subtracted. To converts the value to another type, and at combines it with another object to make a richer one.
card.example: Starting from 2024-03-15: getYear gives 2024; isLeapYear answers true; withDayOfMonth(1) gives 2024-03-01; plusDays(20) gives 2024-04-04; atTime(10, 30) gives the date-time 2024-03-15T10:30.
card.rule: Pick the prefix by what you want back: a part, an answer, a replaced value, a shifted value, another type, or a richer combination.
card.limits: With replaces a field by a value you name, while plus and minus shift by an amount, so the two are not interchangeable. The prefix tells you the family of a method, not its exact name; check the class for the precise method.

concepts.title: Human time and machine time
concepts.question: Is the value I want to store a point on a continuous timeline, or a reading in the units people use?

paragraphs: The tutorial separates two kinds of time. Human time is expressed in the units people use: year, month, day, hour, minute and second. Machine time is a continuous timeline measured from an origin called the epoch, with nanosecond resolution. Some Date-Time classes model one kind and some the other.

To choose a class, first decide whether you need human or machine time. Then ask what else you need: a time zone or not, date and time or only the date, and which parts of the date. Classes that capture or work with date or time values, such as Instant, LocalDateTime and ZonedDateTime, are called temporal-based.
card.example: A birth date that people celebrate on the same calendar day wherever they are is human time, so LocalDate fits. A log entry stamped when an event happened, to be compared with other events, is machine time, so Instant fits.
card.rule: Choose machine time for stamping and comparing moments, and human time for what people read on a calendar and a clock.
card.limits: One moment can be described both ways: an Instant and a ZonedDateTime can name the same moment, so the split is a choice of viewpoint. Helper types such as the TemporalAdjuster interface and the DayOfWeek enum are not called temporal-based.

concepts.title: Choosing the right class
concepts.question: Given what I need to store, which class holds exactly those parts: zone, date, time, or only part of a date?

paragraphs: After choosing human or machine time, narrow the choice by the parts you need. Date only: LocalDate. Time of day only: LocalTime. Date and time with no zone: LocalDateTime. Date and time with a zone: ZonedDateTime. A stamp on the machine timeline: Instant.

Partial dates have their own classes: Year for a year, YearMonth for a month in a year, and MonthDay for a recurring month and day such as a birthday. OffsetDateTime and OffsetTime attach a fixed offset from UTC instead of a full zone.
card.example: A library card expires on one date: LocalDate. A monthly bill period such as 2024-08: YearMonth. An anniversary that repeats each year: MonthDay. A meeting at 15:00 in Tokyo that others convert: ZonedDateTime.
card.rule: List the parts you need, then take the class that holds exactly those parts.
card.limits: The table offers candidates, not a verdict. A class that holds more than you need, such as LocalDateTime for a plain birth date, works but carries parts you must ignore. Choose by meaning first and convenience second.

concepts.title: The DayOfWeek and Month enums
concepts.question: What do the DayOfWeek and Month constants give you that plain numbers do not, and how do you print a name?

paragraphs: DayOfWeek has constants MONDAY through SUNDAY, and Month has JANUARY through DECEMBER. They are typed names, so code reads better than raw numbers. Their numeric values follow the ISO convention: Monday is 1 and Sunday is 7; January is 1 and December is 12.
Plus on a day of the week wraps around: MONDAY plus 3 is THURSDAY. The maxLength method of Month gives the most days a month can have, so FEBRUARY reports 29 whatever the year.

To print a name, call getDisplayName with a TextStyle and a Locale. FULL gives Monday, SHORT gives Mon, NARROW gives one letter such as M. STANDALONE styles serve languages where the form differs inside a date and on its own.
card.example: DayOfWeek.SATURDAY.plus(2) gives MONDAY. Month.APRIL.maxLength() gives 30. Month.AUGUST with the SHORT style and an English locale prints Aug.
card.rule: Use the enum constants instead of numbers, and choose the style and locale that getDisplayName should use.
card.limits: maxLength gives the greatest possible length, so it cannot tell you how long February is in a given year. The output of getDisplayName depends on the locale you pass.

concepts.title: LocalDate
concepts.question: What does a LocalDate hold, and how do of, getDayOfWeek and with act on it?

paragraphs: A LocalDate holds a year, month and day in the ISO calendar, with no time of day and no zone. It suits dates people attach to a day, such as a birth date or a wedding date. Create one with of, giving the year, a Month constant and the day.

A TemporalAdjuster describes a rule for moving to another date, and the with method applies it and returns a new LocalDate. With TemporalAdjusters.next(DayOfWeek.WEDNESDAY) you land on the first Wednesday after the date. getDayOfWeek returns the weekday as a DayOfWeek constant.
card.example: LocalDate d = LocalDate.of(2024, Month.MAY, 15); d.getDayOfWeek() gives WEDNESDAY; d.with(TemporalAdjusters.next(DayOfWeek.THURSDAY)) gives 2024-05-16. The printed form of a LocalDate is year-month-day.
card.rule: A LocalDate is a calendar day only: ask it for its weekday with getDayOfWeek and move it with with and an adjuster.
card.limits: A LocalDate has no time or zone, so it cannot say when during a day something happens or in which place the day applies. It prints in the ISO form year-month-day.

concepts.title: YearMonth, MonthDay and Year
concepts.question: How do YearMonth, MonthDay and Year differ from a LocalDate, and which questions can each one answer?

paragraphs: YearMonth is a month of a particular year, such as 2024-02. Its lengthOfMonth tells how many days that month has, so it knows February 2024 has 29 days and February 2023 has 28. Year is just a year, and isLeap tests whether it is a leap year.

MonthDay is a month and a day with no year, such as a birthday or New Year's Day. Because it has no year, isValidYear tells whether that month and day exist in a given year: 29 February is valid for 2024 and not for 2023.
card.example: YearMonth.of(2024, Month.SEPTEMBER).lengthOfMonth() gives 30. MonthDay.of(Month.FEBRUARY, 29).isValidYear(2023) gives false. Year.of(2028).isLeap() gives true.
card.rule: Choose the class whose fields match the question: YearMonth for month lengths, MonthDay for recurring days, Year for leap-year tests.
card.limits: These classes hold only part of a date, so they cannot be placed on a timeline. A MonthDay valid in one year may be invalid in another, so 29 February cannot be treated as a usable day every year.

concepts.title: LocalTime and LocalDateTime
concepts.question: What does Local mean in LocalTime and LocalDateTime, and which information do these classes leave out?

paragraphs: LocalTime holds only a time of day: hour, minute, second and fraction. It suits movie times, library hours, or the display of a digital clock. It carries no zone and no daylight saving information.

LocalDateTime is a date plus a time, still with no zone. A race that starts at 1:10 p.m. on a given day is described in local time: the clock in the place where it happens. Add a zone with ZonedDateTime or OffsetDateTime when you need to compare across places.
Create one with now, of, or from, and shift it with plus and minus methods: plusMonths(6) moves six months forward. ofInstant combines an Instant with a zone to give a local reading.
card.example: LocalDateTime.of(1994, Month.APRIL, 15, 11, 30) prints 1994-04-15T11:30. Its plusMonths(6) gives 1994-10-15T11:30. The printed text has no zone marker because none is stored.
card.rule: Local in a class name means a reading on a wall clock and calendar with no zone attached.
card.limits: A local value alone does not say which moment it names: 11:30 in two cities are two different moments. Do not use LocalDateTime to compare times across places. ofInstant needs a zone because an Instant has none.

concepts.title: Time zones: ZoneId and ZoneOffset
concepts.question: How does a ZoneId differ from a ZoneOffset?

paragraphs: A time zone is a region where the same standard time is used. Zones have identifiers, usually in region/city form such as Asia/Tokyo, and an offset from Greenwich/UTC. Tokyo's offset is +09:00.
ZoneId holds the identifier and supplies the rules for converting between an Instant and a LocalDateTime. ZoneOffset holds only a fixed offset from UTC, such as +09:00 or -08:00.

Offsets are usually whole hours, but not always. The tutorial's listing of zones found offsets such as +05:30 for Asia/Calcutta and +05:45 for Asia/Kathmandu, so code must not assume a whole number of hours.
card.example: ZoneId.of with the text Asia/Tokyo names a zone and brings its rules. ZoneOffset.of with the text +05:30 is a fixed offset whose total is 19800 seconds. The offset stays the same wherever it is applied.
card.rule: Use a ZoneId when a place's rules matter and a ZoneOffset when only a fixed distance from UTC matters.
card.limits: A region can have more than one offset during a year, so an identifier alone does not give one offset; it needs a moment to look up. Do not assume whole-hour offsets when computing with them.

concepts.title: ZonedDateTime, OffsetDateTime and OffsetTime
concepts.question: Which of ZonedDateTime, OffsetDateTime and OffsetTime knows daylight saving rules, and when would you choose the others?

paragraphs: Three classes carry zone information. ZonedDateTime is a LocalDateTime plus a ZoneId, so it can use zone rules. OffsetDateTime is a LocalDateTime plus a ZoneOffset, and OffsetTime is a LocalTime plus a ZoneOffset. The offset classes have no access to zone rules.

Most zones jump forward, usually by an hour, when daylight saving begins, which leaves a gap in local times. When it ends, the last hour before the change repeats, which makes an overlap. ZonedDateTime handles both through its rules. The offset classes cannot.

OffsetDateTime suits software that models its own location rules, and database timestamps that track only absolute offsets from UTC. The tutorial adds that XML and other network formats carry date-times as OffsetDateTime or OffsetTime.
card.example: A ticket stamped 2024-07-10T09:00-08:00 is an OffsetDateTime: a fixed offset and nothing about daylight saving. A concert in New York next summer is a ZonedDateTime, so the rules decide whether the offset is -05:00 or -04:00.
card.rule: Use ZonedDateTime when daylight saving rules must apply, and an offset class when a fixed distance from UTC is all you store.
card.limits: A fixed offset records what the clock said then, but cannot compute later dates across a daylight saving change. A ZonedDateTime needs a zone identifier, which some data sources do not give, so an offset may be all you have.

concepts.title: Converting between zones
concepts.question: Which call re-reads the same moment on another zone's clock, and which call adds the travel time?

paragraphs: The tutorial's flight example leaves San Francisco at 7:30 p.m. on 20 July 2013 for a flight of 10 hours 50 minutes to Tokyo. It builds a ZonedDateTime from a LocalDateTime and the zone America/Los_Angeles.

The call withZoneSameInstant keeps the moment and changes the clock reading to another zone, which moves the departure onto Tokyo's clock. Then plusMinutes(650) adds the flight time. The arrival reads 10:20 p.m. on 21 July in Tokyo.

The example then asks the arrival zone's rules, through getRules and isDaylightSavings, whether daylight saving time is in effect at the arrival instant. For Tokyo in that example it reported standard time.
card.example: Leave London at 09:00 on 10 July 2024 (Europe/London) on an 8-hour flight to New York. withZoneSameInstant moves the departure to 04:00 on New York's clock, and plusHours(8) gives an arrival of 12:00 New York time.
card.rule: Convert the departure to the arrival zone with withZoneSameInstant, then add the travel time, so the arrival reads on the destination clock.
card.limits: withZoneSameInstant changes the clock reading, not the moment. Keeping the same clock digits and swapping the zone would name a different moment, so decide which of the two you mean.

concepts.title: Instant
concepts.question: What does an Instant represent, and how do you get human units from it?

paragraphs: An Instant is a point on the machine timeline, with nanosecond resolution, counted from the epoch 1970-01-01T00:00:00Z. Instants after the epoch are positive and those before it negative. It is the natural stamp for events you want to order or compare.

toString gives ISO-8601 text ending in Z, which marks UTC, such as 2013-05-30T23:38:23.085Z. You can add or subtract with plus and minus and a unit such as ChronoUnit.HOURS, compare with isBefore and isAfter, and measure with until.

An Instant does not understand human units such as months, years or days. To read them, convert it with a zone, for example with LocalDateTime.ofInstant and a ZoneId. A ZonedDateTime or OffsetDateTime converts to an Instant directly; the reverse needs a zone or offset.
card.example: Instant.ofEpochSecond(3600) prints 1970-01-01T01:00:00Z. Instant.ofEpochSecond(-86400) prints 1969-12-31T00:00:00Z. The instant 2024-03-15T23:30:00Z read with the zone Asia/Tokyo gives the local reading 2024-03-16T08:30.
card.rule: Use Instant to stamp and compare moments, and supply a zone before asking for any human unit.
card.limits: An Instant is not wrong about human units, it holds none: units such as months and years are unsupported on it. The text ending in Z is UTC, not your local time, so do not read it as your clock.

concepts.title: Parsing and formatting
concepts.question: How do you turn text into a date-time value and a value into text, and what happens when it fails?

paragraphs: Date-Time classes convert between values and text with a DateTimeFormatter. The parse method reads text into an object, and format writes an object as text. LocalDate.parse with one argument expects the ISO layout; to read another layout, give parse a formatter as the second argument.

A pattern describes the layout. In MMM d yyyy, MMM is a short month name, d is the day and yyyy is a four-digit year, so Jan 3 2003 matches. Writing dd instead of d demands two characters, so the day must be zero-padded, as in Jun 03 2003.

A failed parse throws DateTimeParseException, and a failed format throws DateTimeException. A DateTimeFormatter is immutable and thread-safe, so the tutorial advises assigning it to a static constant where appropriate.
card.example: LocalDate.of(2024, Month.MARCH, 15).format with the pattern dd/MM/yyyy gives 15/03/2024. Parsing the text 19590709 with BASIC_ISO_DATE gives 1959-07-09. Plain LocalDate.parse applied to 15/03/2024 fails, because that text is not in ISO layout.
card.rule: Choose a formatter whose pattern matches the text exactly, and catch the exceptions that parse and format can throw.
card.limits: The pattern must match the text: dd rejects a one-digit day. A formatter fixes the layout only; choosing the right class to parse into is still your job.

concepts.title: Fields, units and the temporal interfaces
concepts.question: What role does each low-level interface in java.time.temporal play for application code?

paragraphs: The java.time.temporal package holds low-level building blocks, mainly for framework and library writers. Temporal is the framework for temporal objects such as Instant and ZonedDateTime, with methods to add and subtract units. TemporalAccessor is its read-only form. TemporalField names a field, TemporalUnit names a unit, and TemporalAmount is the parameter type for arithmetic.

ChronoField is an enum of fields, such as DAY_OF_WEEK, MONTH_OF_YEAR and MINUTE_OF_HOUR. ChronoUnit is an enum of units from milliseconds to millennia. Not every class supports every field or unit, and isSupported tells you. A LocalDate does not support CLOCK_HOUR_OF_DAY, and an Instant does not support MONTHS or YEARS.
Declare variables with concrete types such as LocalDate or ZonedDateTime, not Temporal, just as you declare a String instead of a CharSequence. IsoFields adds ISO fields such as QUARTER_OF_YEAR.
card.example: LocalDate d = LocalDate.of(2024, Month.MARCH, 15). Then d.isSupported(ChronoField.DAY_OF_WEEK) is true and d.isSupported(ChronoField.MINUTE_OF_HOUR) is false. Reading d.get(IsoFields.QUARTER_OF_YEAR) gives 1.
card.rule: Ask isSupported before using a field or unit on an unfamiliar class, and declare variables with concrete types.
card.limits: These interfaces matter mostly to framework and library authors, and everyday code rarely names them. Support is decided class by class, so a field that works on LocalDateTime may not work on LocalDate.

concepts.title: Predefined temporal adjusters
concepts.question: How do I move a date to a calendar landmark, such as the end of the month, without doing the arithmetic myself?

paragraphs: A TemporalAdjuster takes a temporal value and returns an adjusted one. The TemporalAdjusters class, with an s, provides ready-made adjusters as static methods: firstDayOfMonth, lastDayOfMonth, firstDayOfNextMonth, firstDayOfYear, firstDayOfNextYear, firstInMonth and lastInMonth with a weekday, and next and previous with a weekday.
Apply one with the with method. Adjusters work on any temporal-based class, and applied to a ZonedDateTime the result keeps the time and the zone and changes only the date.
card.example: For 2024-02-15, a Thursday: lastDayOfMonth gives 2024-02-29; firstInMonth(MONDAY) gives 2024-02-05; lastInMonth(FRIDAY) gives 2024-02-23; firstDayOfNextYear gives 2025-01-01.
card.rule: To land on a calendar landmark, pass the matching TemporalAdjusters method to with.
card.limits: An adjuster only moves the date; it keeps the time and zone, and it returns a new value rather than editing the old. For a rule the library does not provide, you write your own adjuster.

concepts.title: Writing your own adjuster
concepts.question: What problem does a custom TemporalAdjuster solve, and which single method must it implement?

paragraphs: When no predefined adjuster matches a business rule, write your own by implementing TemporalAdjuster. It has one method, adjustInto, which receives a Temporal and returns the adjusted Temporal.

The tutorial's PaydayAdjuster expresses a rule: pay falls on the 15th and the last day of each month, and if that day is a weekend, pay moves to the previous Friday. If the day of month is before 15, the target is the 15th; otherwise it is the last day of the month.
You use it exactly like a built-in one: date.with(new PaydayAdjuster()). This is the extensible principle at work, because your rule plugs into the same with call.
card.example: Under the payday rule, 2024-08-12 gives 2024-08-15, a Thursday. 2024-06-10 gives 2024-06-14, because the 15th is a Saturday. 2024-09-20 gives 2024-09-30, the last day of the month, a Monday.
card.rule: Encode a repeated date rule once in an adjustInto method, then apply it with with.
card.limits: A rule written as a branch on the day of month has edge cases: in the tutorial's logic a date that is already the 15th takes the other branch and moves to month end. Test boundary days, and remember that the adjuster returns a new value.

concepts.title: Temporal queries
concepts.question: How does a TemporalQuery differ from a TemporalAdjuster?

paragraphs: A TemporalQuery asks a question of a temporal object and returns an answer, instead of producing a changed date. You call it with the query method. TemporalQueries holds ready-made queries, such as precision, which reports the smallest unit an object can represent.

Precision examples: LocalDate reports Days, LocalDateTime reports Nanos, Year reports Years, YearMonth reports Months, and Instant reports Nanos. Such queries help when a program does not know the exact type of the object it holds.

To write your own, implement queryFrom, which receives a TemporalAccessor and returns a result, for example a Boolean saying whether a date falls inside a family vacation. A static method with the same shape can be passed as a method reference.
card.example: A query that reads the DAY_OF_WEEK field and answers true for Saturday and Sunday could be called as date.query(Weekend::check). It answers a yes-or-no question and leaves the date unchanged.
card.rule: Use an adjuster to get a different date, and a query to get information about a date.
card.limits: A query reads and does not change the temporal. The fields it reads must be supported by the object: a query that reads month and day works on any type that has them.

concepts.title: Duration and Period
concepts.question: When do I use a Duration, and when a Period, to hold an amount of time?

paragraphs: Duration measures time in seconds and nanoseconds and suits machine time, such as the gap between two Instants. It has no years, months or days of its own, though it offers methods that convert to days, hours or minutes. A Duration can be negative when the end comes before the start.
Period measures date-based amounts in years, months and days, read with getYears, getMonths and getDays. It suits human time.

They behave differently with zones. Adding a Duration of one day to a ZonedDateTime adds exactly 24 hours. Adding a Period of one day moves the calendar date by one day, which can differ from 24 hours near a daylight saving change.
card.example: Duration.ofMinutes(90) prints as PT1H30M. Period.of(1, 2, 3) prints as P1Y2M3D. In New York at 12:00 on 9 March 2024, adding Period.ofDays(1) gives 10 March at 12:00, while adding Duration.ofDays(1) gives 10 March at 13:00, because clocks moved forward that night.
card.rule: Use Duration for exact elapsed time and Period for calendar-based amounts.
card.limits: A Duration of one day is exactly 24 hours, so it does not follow the calendar. A Period is not a fixed number of seconds, because a day or a month can span different amounts of time. Neither is a point on the timeline.

concepts.title: Measuring the gap between two points
concepts.question: How do Period.between and ChronoUnit.between differ in what they report about the gap between two dates?

paragraphs: To measure a gap you have three tools: Duration, Period and ChronoUnit.between. ChronoUnit.between reports the amount in a single unit, such as days or seconds, and works with all temporal-based objects.

Period.between reports years, months and days together. From 2024-01-15 to 2024-03-20 it gives 2 months and 5 days, while ChronoUnit.DAYS.between gives 65 days, because 2024 is a leap year and its February has 29 days.

The tutorial's age example prints both forms, years-months-days and total days. It notes that these calculations ignore time zone differences; for exact results across places, use a Period with ZonedDateTime.
card.example: Birthday on 15 September and today is 2024-06-10, so the next birthday is 2024-09-15. Period.between gives 3 months and 5 days. ChronoUnit.DAYS.between gives 97 days. Both describe the same gap in different shapes.
card.rule: Take a Period for a calendar-style answer in years, months and days, or ChronoUnit.between for one total in a single unit.
card.limits: The two answers describe the same gap in different shapes, so do not add or compare them directly. The tutorial's calculations ignore time zone differences, so they are approximate for people in different zones.

concepts.title: The Clock class
concepts.question: What problem does passing a Clock to now solve?

paragraphs: Most temporal classes have a no-argument now method that reads the system clock and the default time zone. They also have now(Clock), which takes the clock to read.

The date and time depend on the zone, so global applications need a Clock to be sure values use the right zone. Using one is optional, but it also lets you test code for other time zones, or against a clock where time does not move.

Clock is abstract, so you get one from factories. Clock.systemUTC reads UTC, Clock.fixed(Instant, ZoneId) always returns the same instant, and Clock.offset(Clock, Duration) shifts a clock by an amount.
card.example: Clock c = Clock.fixed(Instant.parse of 2024-01-15T20:00:00Z, ZoneId.of Asia/Tokyo). LocalDateTime.now(c) always gives 2024-01-16T05:00, so a test can check code that depends on today's date.
card.rule: Give now a Clock when the result must not depend on the machine's own clock and zone.
card.limits: A Clock is optional: the no-argument now is fine when the system clock and default zone are what you want. A fixed clock does not advance, so it is for tests, not for real timestamps.

concepts.title: Non-ISO calendars
concepts.question: How do you convert an ISO date to a Japanese, Hijrah, Minguo or Thai Buddhist date, and back?

paragraphs: The java.time.chrono package provides calendar systems other than ISO: Japanese, Hijrah, Minguo and Thai Buddhist. You can also define your own. The tutorial does not cover the package in depth, only how to convert.

To go from ISO to a non-ISO date, call from on the date class: JapaneseDate.from, HijrahDate.from, MinguoDate.from or ThaiBuddhistDate.from. To go back, call LocalDate.from with the non-ISO date. Both directions throw DateTimeException when the conversion cannot be done.

The same day gets different numbering. For 29 October 1996 the tutorial's output shows year 0008 in the Japanese calendar, 0085 in Minguo, 2539 in Thai Buddhist and 1417 in Hijrah. Converting each back gives 1996-10-29 again.
card.example: LocalDate iso = LocalDate.of(1996, Month.OCTOBER, 29). ThaiBuddhistDate.from(iso) shows year 2539. LocalDate.from of that Thai date gives 1996-10-29 again, so the day is unchanged and only the numbering differs.
card.rule: Convert with from in either direction, and treat the ISO LocalDate as the common form between calendars.
card.limits: Conversion changes how a day is numbered, not which day it is. Year numbers are not interchangeable between calendars, and a conversion that cannot produce a valid date fails with an exception.

concepts.title: Legacy date-time code
concepts.question: How do you move values between the old java.util date classes and the java.time classes?

paragraphs: Before Java SE 8, dates used java.util.Date, Calendar, TimeZone and GregorianCalendar. The tutorial lists their problems: Calendar was not type safe, the classes were mutable and so unsafe in multithreaded code, and odd month numbering plus weak typing caused bugs.

JDK 8 added bridge methods: Date.toInstant and Date.from(Instant); Calendar.toInstant; GregorianCalendar.toZonedDateTime and GregorianCalendar.from(ZonedDateTime); TimeZone.toZoneId. Turning an Instant into a ZonedDateTime needs a zone, such as ZoneId.systemDefault().

The mapping is approximate, not one-to-one: Date matches Instant, GregorianCalendar matches ZonedDateTime, TimeZone matches ZoneId or ZoneOffset, and a GregorianCalendar used for only a time or only a date matches LocalTime or LocalDate. The easiest route is to bridge with toInstant or toZonedDateTime; otherwise rewrite the code.
card.example: Date legacy = new Date(0); legacy.toInstant() gives 1970-01-01T00:00:00Z. That instant with the zone Asia/Tokyo gives 1970-01-01T09:00+09:00. Date.from of the instant returns an equal Date.
card.rule: Bridge with toInstant or toZonedDateTime at the edge of old code, and prefer rewriting to java.time where you can.
card.limits: The mapping has no one-to-one correspondence. A GregorianCalendar set to midnight as a date-only value was already flawed, because some places skip midnight on some days at a daylight saving change.

concepts.title: A declared element type is a guarantee
concepts.question: What does declaring a list's element type give the compiler that a cast at the point of use does not?

paragraphs: Before generics, a list could hold any object. Code that took an item out had to cast it to the type the programmer believed was inside, and that cast was only the programmer's claim.

Declaring the list as holding one type moves the claim into the declaration. The compiler then knows the type of every item wherever that variable is used, so the cast disappears from the reading line.

The check also moves in time. A cast is verified at one spot while the program runs. A declared element type is verified at every use before the program runs. The tutorial credits this with more readable and more robust code, especially in large programs.
card.example: Old style: a list of names is created raw, a String is added, and the first item is read with a cast to String. New style: the variable is declared as a List of String, and the same reading line needs no cast.
card.rule: State the element type in the declaration so the compiler guarantees it at every use and no cast is needed.
card.limits: The guarantee covers only code the compiler checks. A raw type or a legacy method can still hand over a wrong item, and that shows up as a ClassCastException at run time.

concepts.title: Formal parameters, actual arguments, and no copies
concepts.question: When a generic is used with a real type, what is substituted for what, and is any code copied?

paragraphs: A generic type lists formal type parameters after its name. In the tutorial's List, the parameter E is used for the argument of add and the result of next, anywhere an ordinary type could appear. Using List with a real type, as in List of Integer, makes a parameterized type, and each E becomes the actual type argument.
This mirrors methods. A method has formal value parameters, and each call substitutes actual arguments. A generic has formal type parameters, and each use substitutes actual type arguments.

The tutorial calls it helpful but misleading to picture the declaration copied out into one class per argument. The methods of List of Integer do look copied, but the declaration is never expanded. It is compiled once into one class file, with no copies in source, binary, disk or memory. This differs from C++ templates.
card.example: A declaration Crate of E has a put method taking an E and a take method returning an E. Writing Crate of Apple supplies Apple for E, so put takes an Apple and take returns an Apple. Only one compiled Crate exists, however many element types a program uses.
card.rule: Formal type parameters stand in the definition and actual type arguments replace them at each use, without any copy of the code being made.
card.limits: The expansion picture predicts method signatures well but wrongly suggests a separate class for each argument. The next ideas show what the single shared class means at run time.

concepts.title: Why a list of String is not a list of Object
concepts.question: Why does the compiler refuse to treat a list of String as a list of Object even though String is an Object?

paragraphs: Intuition says that since String is a kind of Object, a list of String is a kind of list of Object. The tutorial poses this as a key legality question and answers no: assigning a list of String variable to a list of Object variable is a compile-time error.

The reason is aliasing. If the assignment were allowed, both names would point to one list. Through the Object name you could add a plain Object, and reading through the String name would then hand an Object to a String variable, which is the failure generics exist to prevent.

General rule: when Foo is a subtype of Bar and G is a generic, G of Foo is not a subtype of G of Bar. The tutorial calls this the hardest part of generics. Its analogy: a motor-vehicle office gives a census bureau a list of drivers. The bureau gets a copy, because the original could be corrupted by adding non-drivers.
card.example: Take a list of Cat and a list of Animal. If a list of Cat could be used as a list of Animal, code holding the Animal view could add a Dog, and the Cat owner would later find a Dog among the Cats.
card.rule: A generic of a subtype is not a subtype of the generic of the supertype, because a shared writable list could be corrupted through the wider view.
card.limits: The ban protects writing. For code that only reads, the wildcard forms in later ideas give back flexibility without the danger, so the rule does not make generic types unrelatable.

concepts.title: Wildcards: read as the bound, add only null
concepts.question: What can a method safely read from, and add to, a collection whose element type is a wildcard?

paragraphs: A method that prints a collection with the parameter type collection of Object accepts only that exact type. The wildcard, written as a question mark, means a collection of unknown element type, and it accepts every collection.

What you can do follows from what you know. Every element is at least an Object, so reading elements as Object is safe. The add method wants an item of the unknown element type, and no value is known to fit it, so nothing can be added except null, which belongs to every type.

An upper bound narrows the unknown: question mark extends Shape means Shape or some subtype. A method reading such a list accepts lists of Circle or Rectangle, and reads give Shape. Adding a Rectangle still fails, since the list may hold another kind of Shape. A map can be bounded too, such as a map from String to question mark extends Person.
card.example: A method taking a list of question mark extends Shape may loop over it and call draw on each item. Inside it, adding a new Rectangle to that list is rejected; adding null is accepted.
card.rule: With a wildcard type you can read items as the bound (Object when unbounded) but can add only null, so use extends for a structure the method only reads.
card.limits: Wildcards fit methods that only read. A method that must also add items of the element type needs a named type parameter, which the next ideas introduce.

concepts.title: Generic methods: use a name only for a dependency
concepts.question: When does a method need a named type parameter, and when is a wildcard the better choice?

paragraphs: A method can declare its own type parameters. The tutorial's array-to-collection copier shows why. A collection of Object as the target is too restrictive, and a collection of unknown cannot be added to. Declaring one parameter T for an array of T and a collection of T lets the add compile.

The compiler infers T from the arguments, usually the most specific type that makes the call valid. An Integer array with a Collection of Number infers Number, and a String array with a Collection of Object infers Object. A Number array with a Collection of String fails, because no T fits both.

Choose by how often the parameter appears. If it ties argument types or the return type together, it is a dependency and needs a name. If it appears once, it only buys flexible subtyping, and the tutorial recommends a wildcard. Its copy method uses T for the destination and question mark extends T for the source.
card.example: A method firstOf takes a list of T and returns a T. The T links the argument to the result, so it needs a name. A method countNonNull takes a list of question mark: the element type is used once, so a wildcard fits.
card.rule: Use a type parameter on a method where it relates several types, and use a wildcard where it would appear only once.
card.limits: The count test guides clarity: single-use parameters work either way, though the tutorial prefers wildcards. A wildcard cannot express a tie to the return type, such as returning the element type the argument holds.

concepts.title: Where generic code meets legacy code
concepts.question: Where do unchecked warnings arise when generic and legacy code meet, and who must vouch for safety?

paragraphs: A great deal of code predates generics, so the two must work together. A generic type used without type arguments is a raw type, and legacy methods use raw types. The tutorial's example is an inventory API whose methods take and return a raw Collection.

Generic code calling legacy code: passing a collection of Part into a raw parameter is fine. Storing the raw collection that a legacy method returns into a collection of Part compiles with an unchecked warning, because the compiler cannot confirm the legacy code returns only Parts. Raw types are checked less strictly than wildcards, on purpose, to allow this.

Legacy code calling converted generic code: passing a raw collection to a parameter of type collection of Part also draws an unchecked warning. Safety then rests on the method's documented contract, not its signature. The tutorial advises studying each warning and being able to justify it. An old source level hides warnings but blocks newer features.
card.example: A team's old class returns a raw List documented as holding Double values. A new class assigns it to a List of Double and gets one unchecked warning. Its author checks the documentation and notes why the warning is safe.
card.rule: Treat each unchecked warning at a generic and legacy boundary as a claim you must be able to justify from the legacy method's documented contract.
card.limits: Warnings appear where raw meets parameterized in the unsafe direction. Passing a parameterized collection into a raw parameter is silent. A warning marks a claim only the programmer can check; it does not prove an error.

concepts.title: An ignored warning becomes a run-time cast failure
concepts.question: Why does an ignored unchecked warning end in a ClassCastException, and why does the JVM stay safe?

paragraphs: The tutorial shows an ignored warning hiding a real bug. A method builds a list of String, aliases it with a raw list variable, adds an Integer through the raw variable (an unchecked warning at compile time), then returns the first item of the String list as a String.

Generics are implemented by erasure, a translation by the compiler's front end. Type arguments are removed, type variables become their upper bound (usually Object), and casts are inserted where needed. After translation the method reads the first item with a cast to String.

So the failure is a ClassCastException at that inserted cast, in the reading code, not at the add. The tutorial stresses that the type safety and integrity of the JVM are never at risk: the wrong value is caught at a cast. Code that compiles without unchecked warnings is, by the tutorial's design goal, type safe.
card.example: A List of Integer named ids is aliased by a raw list, and the text x is added through the raw one (warning). Later a line reads the first id into an Integer variable. After translation that line casts to Integer and throws there.
card.rule: An unchecked warning marks a place where the casts erasure inserts may fail later, so code without such warnings is type safe, and code with them fails safely at a cast.
card.limits: A cast fails only when the item is read through the parameterized type. A wrong item never read that way causes no exception, so a quiet test run does not prove a warning was harmless.

concepts.title: One run-time class for every type argument
concepts.question: If a list of String and a list of Date share a run-time class, what cannot be asked about them while running?

paragraphs: The first fine-print point: comparing the run-time classes of an ArrayList of String and an ArrayList of Integer shows they are equal. All instances of a generic class share one run-time class, whatever their type arguments, because the class behaves the same for all of them and can be seen as many types.

Statics belong to that single class, so a static variable is shared by every parameterization. A static method, a static initializer, or the declaration of a static variable may not refer to the type parameter.

Asking whether an object is a particular parameterization has no run-time meaning. An instanceof test against Collection of String is illegal. A cast to it compiles with an unchecked warning, since the run time does not check the argument. A cast to a type variable T warns too. Type variables do not exist at run time.
card.example: Two lists come from the same class, one declared as a List of String and one as a List of Date. Asking each for its class gives the same answer. A test asking whether an object is a List of String cannot be written, because a List of Date is the same class.
card.rule: A generic class is one run-time class, so run-time questions about the type argument (instanceof, reliable casts, static use) have no answer.
card.limits: This restricts only code that needs the argument at run time. Compile-time checking of the arguments applies in full, and a cast to a parameterized type is legal, though unchecked.

concepts.title: Why generic arrays cannot be created
concepts.question: Why can a program create an array of unbounded wildcard lists but not an array of lists of String?

paragraphs: You may declare an array type whose element type is a type variable or a parameterized type, but you cannot create an array object with such an element type. The exception is an array whose element is an unbounded wildcard type.

The ban closes a hole. Suppose an array of List of String could be created. Through an Object array view you could store a List of Integer in it, since the run-time store check sees only List, and no warning appears. Reading an item as a String would then throw ClassCastException. The tutorial wants unwarned code to be type safe, so this must be refused.

Arrays of lists of the wildcard are allowed because reading needs an explicit cast, so the risk is visible. Creating an array of a type variable is also an error: the type variable does not exist at run time, so the array type is unknown. The tutorial names class literals as the way out.
card.example: A generic class tries to build its storage as an array of its type parameter with size 10. That line is an error. A variable declared with such an array type is legal, but no array object of that type can be created.
card.rule: Arrays of wildcard-only lists can be created, but arrays of type variables or of lists with named arguments cannot.
card.limits: The ban covers creating the array, not declaring a variable of such a type. Wildcard arrays are allowed, but reading from them needs an explicit cast, and that cast can still fail.

concepts.title: Class literals as run-time type tokens
concepts.question: How does passing a class literal let one method return a correctly typed collection?

paragraphs: The Class type is generic: its parameter is the type the Class object stands for. The literal String.class has type Class of String. Methods such as newInstance return that type, so code built on reflection gets precise static types.

The tutorial's problem: a utility runs a database query and returns objects of a requested type. A factory object, an interface with one make method, works, but each caller writes an anonymous class or a factory class per type. Passing a class literal is more natural, but before generics the result was an untyped collection.

With the generic Class, the method declares a type parameter T, takes a Class of T, and returns a Collection of T. Calling it with EmpInfo.class binds T to EmpInfo, so the result is a Collection of EmpInfo and no cast is needed. The class literal serves as a run-time type token, an idiom common in annotation APIs.
card.example: A method loadAll takes a Class of T and returns a List of T. Calling it with Invoice.class returns a List of Invoice, and with Customer.class returns a List of Customer. One method serves both.
card.rule: Pass the class literal as a Class of T argument so the compiler fixes T and the run-time object can still make instances of it.
card.limits: A class literal fixes T to one concrete class and supplies the type for creating objects. The tutorial's database code is only a sketch, so treat it as showing the typing idea, not a finished query tool.

concepts.title: Super wildcards for consumers
concepts.question: When should a parameter be declared with super rather than extends, and why does it help?

paragraphs: The tutorial's example is a write-only sink with a flush method taking a T. A method writeAll takes a collection of T and a sink of T, flushes each item and returns the last. With a collection of String and a sink of Object, no single T fits both, so the call is illegal.

Loosening the collection to question mark extends T makes the call legal, but T is then inferred as Object from the sink, so assigning the result to a String fails. The fix is a sink of question mark super T: the sink may accept T or any supertype. T is String and the result stays String.

The same idea appears elsewhere. A TreeSet of String should accept a comparator of Object, so its constructor takes a comparator of question mark super E. The tutorial's rule of thumb: a parameter that only consumes T uses super, and one that only produces T uses extends.
card.example: A method pourAll takes a list of Tea and a holder of question mark super Tea. A holder of Drink or of Object works. A holder of Coffee does not.
card.rule: Use question mark super T on a parameter that only consumes values of T, and question mark extends T on one that only produces them.
card.limits: A parameter that both gives values out and takes values in needs the exact type, with no wildcard. The producer or consumer label depends on how the method uses the parameter, not on the interface's name.

concepts.title: Wildcard capture
concepts.question: Why does a generic method accept a wildcard-typed set when adding one value to that set is refused?

paragraphs: A set whose element type is a wildcard might hold Strings at run time, but the compiler sees only an unknown element type. The tutorial's method addToSet takes a set of T and a T. Called with such a set and the string abc, the call is illegal, since abc may not fit the unknown type.

Contrast unmodifiableSet, a generic method taking a set of T and returning a set of T. Called with the same unknown set, it compiles and returns a set of wildcard. It works for any element type and adds nothing, so nothing can go wrong.

The rule behind this is wildcard capture: the compiler may treat the unknown type as the type argument of a generic method call, but only where it can prove the call safe. Calls that merely pass the structure along qualify; calls that insert a separate value do not.
card.example: A tray of unknown pastries may be relabelled as a whole, but nobody may slip in a chosen pastry. Likewise unmodifiableSet may be applied to a set of wildcard, but addToSet with a chosen String may not.
card.rule: A wildcard-typed value can be passed to a generic method that works for every element type, because the compiler captures the unknown type; a separate value cannot be tied to it.
card.limits: Capture is applied by the compiler, not written by you. It does not make the unknown type known, so a call needing a particular value to fit the element type is refused even if the set really holds that type.

concepts.title: Converting a published API to generics
concepts.question: What three things must a generified library method preserve for the callers and binaries that already exist?

paragraphs: Retrofitting generics must not break existing users. The tutorial gives three rules. First, do not be stricter than the old contract: the old containsAll accepted any collection, so a version requiring a collection of E would refuse calls it used to accept. Wildcards fix this, and addAll should take a collection of any subtype of E.

Second, keep the erasure identical, so old compiled code still links. A max method with the bound Comparable of question mark super T would erase to a method returning Comparable, but the original returned Object. Adding Object as the first bound makes the erasure take that first bound and match the original.

Third, avoid covariant returns in published APIs. Narrowing an override's return type to the subclass makes the compiler add a bridge method. An outside class that overrode the old version with the old return type then no longer overrides properly and stops compiling. The tutorial calls these cases rare.
card.example: Original: max takes a raw Collection and returns Object. Generic: T extends Object and Comparable of question mark super T, taking a Collection of T. The first bound makes the erasure return Object, as before.
card.rule: When generifying a published method, keep every call it used to accept, keep its erasure identical, and do not narrow return types.
card.limits: These rules protect published APIs that have existing users, and the tutorial calls the cases rare. A brand-new method has no old signature or binary to preserve.

concepts.title: The compile-and-run cycle
concepts.question: What does each tool and file in the classic write, compile, run cycle do, and what are the JDK and JRE?

paragraphs: Java source code lives in plain text files whose names end in .java, written in a plain text editor (a word processor does not work). A compiler named javac checks the source and turns it into bytecode, stored in a file ending in .class. The tutorial leaves bytecode details aside; treat it as the compiled form of your program.

To run, you use the java command with the class name, written without .java. So the classic cycle is: write the .java file, compile it with javac and the full file name including .java, then run it with java and the class name. If the code is incorrect, compilation fails.

Both tools come from the JDK, the Java Development Kit. The JRE is an older, smaller set with run-time tools only; it cannot compile, and OpenJDK and Oracle no longer distribute it. The tutorial also notes that Java SE 11 and later can run a .java file directly, merging compile and run into one step.
card.example: A file Counter.java is compiled with javac Counter.java, which creates Counter.class. Then java Counter runs it.
card.rule: Compile the .java file with javac to get a .class file of bytecode, then run it by giving java the class name.
card.limits: The two separate steps are the classic path, not a law: from Java SE 11 a single .java file can be launched directly, and a JRE alone cannot do the compile step.

concepts.title: Telling compile errors from run errors
concepts.question: Which failures happen at the compile step and which at the run step, and what does the tutorial advise for each?

paragraphs: Problems split by step. At compile time: javac not found, because the system cannot locate it (type the full path or add the JDK bin directory to PATH); javac given a name without .java; syntax errors; and semantic errors. For a syntax or semantic error, javac reports the kind, line and position, and creates no .class file.
A syntax error is something like a missing semicolon. A semantic error is a mistake in meaning, such as using a variable before it is initialized. Both stop the class file from being created.

At run time: java cannot find the class file (it looks in the current directory first, so move to the folder holding it, and check CLASSPATH if that fails); java given Name.class instead of the class name; or a class with no main method, where the JVM has no place to start.
card.example: Typing java Hello.class fails because java wants the class name Hello. Typing javac Hello fails because javac wants Hello.java.
card.rule: Match the symptom to the step: compile errors mean no class file exists; run errors mean the class file or its start point is wrong.
card.limits: Setup problems such as PATH and JAVA_HOME can look like either kind, and a program that compiles may still not run: compiling does not prove a main method exists.

concepts.title: Launching a source file directly
concepts.question: What can the java launcher do with source files directly, and what conditions does it set?

paragraphs: According to the tutorial, since JDK 11 the java launcher can compile and run a source file in one go. It compiles in memory and keeps the compiled classes there, so there is no separate compile step. The tutorial presents this for learning Java and trying out API features.
The first class defined in the file must contain the main method. A file may hold several classes. Command-line arguments are passed as for a normally compiled class.

JDK 22 (JEP 458) lets the launcher find other source files, provided each file's directory path matches its package name. Core JDK classes need no setup, but outside libraries must be on the classpath. On Unix-like systems, a file with a first line naming java and a source version, no .java extension, and execute permission runs like a script.
card.example: A file Greeter.java has class Greeter first, with main, and a helper class below. java Greeter.java runs it with no class file on disk.
card.rule: For quick runs, hand a source file to the launcher; keep the main class first and put extra source files and libraries where it can find them.
card.limits: Multi-file launching needs JDK 22 and directories matching package names; libraries outside the JDK need the classpath. This is for learning and small trials, as the tutorial frames it.

concepts.title: Exploring Java in JShell
concepts.question: What is JShell, how do snippets and commands differ, and how do you manage a session?

paragraphs: JShell is an interactive tool for learning Java, trying out APIs and prototyping. You type snippets: statements, variable, method and class definitions, imports, or expressions. A missing semicolon is added for you, and an expression without a name gets a scratch variable. Redefining a method, variable or class replaces the old one.

Commands start with a slash and manage the session. /list shows snippets with IDs, /vars and /methods show what is defined, /drop makes a snippet inactive, /history shows all you typed, /edit opens an editor, and /exit leaves. Tab completes names and shows method parameters.

/reset discards all snippets and does not replay history, while /reload restarts and replays it. Feedback modes set how much output follows each snippet: verbose, normal (the default), concise, silent, and custom. Errors are always shown. Only custom modes can be changed.
card.example: After typing int pass = 80, entering int pass = 85 replaces it. /list shows the current snippets by ID.
card.rule: Type snippets to try Java directly, use slash commands to inspect or change the session, and pick the feedback mode that fits.
