card.limits: JShell state is for exploring, not saved code: /reset discards snippets, and built-in modes cannot be edited. Use /save to keep work, or make a custom mode to change feedback.

concepts.title: From occasional releases to a six-month rhythm
concepts.question: Why did Java move to feature releases every six months, and what did that change for developers?

paragraphs: Java first appeared in 1995. For years a new feature release arrived only every two to three years, and its date followed feature readiness.

Since 2017 the platform uses time-based releases: a feature release every six months, in March and September. Mark Reinhold proposed this in a post titled Moving Java Forward Faster. Java 9 came in 2017, Java 10 followed in 2018 and delivered var, and Java 12 in 2019 made significant improvements to the G1 garbage collector.

According to the tutorial, developers now get features every six months instead of after years. Large efforts such as Project Loom and Project Panama can arrive step by step. Teams can test upgrades automatically in their build and delivery pipelines instead of facing one disruptive event, and a release has become a routine non-event for the platform team.
card.example: A team with an automated pipeline adds the newest JDK to its test runs each March and September. Each upgrade carries only the changes of six months, so a failing test points to a small, recent change.
card.rule: Java ships time-based feature releases every six months, so features and upgrades arrive in small, routine steps rather than in rare large ones.
card.limits: The tutorial describes the rhythm and its benefits but not support lifetimes or which releases get long-term support, so questions about how long a release is maintained need another source.

concepts.title: Preview features and early-access builds
concepts.question: How does Java let developers try upcoming features before they are final, and what should they expect from them?

paragraphs: Some features are released as previews before they become standard. A preview feature is shipped so that developers can try it and send feedback, and it may change before it is finalized. The tutorial also mentions early-access builds, which are time-based builds published at jdk.java.net.

Project Amber is the effort that brings new language features. According to the tutorial, many of them start as previews and sometimes change before becoming standard. A timeline of Amber's features across recent releases ties the preview process to the six-month rhythm.
Once a feature does become standard, the tutorial expects it to remain for a long time. Two words therefore need to be kept apart: preview means open to change, and standard means expected to last.
card.example: A developer tries a language feature that is marked as a preview in the current release, writes a small experiment and shares feedback. In a later release the feature is adjusted before it is finalized, so the experiment needs a small edit.
card.rule: Treat a preview feature as an invitation to try and give feedback that may still change, and a standard feature as one expected to stay.
card.limits: The tutorial gives no list of which features are currently previews and no steps for enabling them, so check the documentation of the specific release.

concepts.title: Evidence that Java keeps evolving
concepts.question: What evidence does the tutorial offer that moving beyond Java 8 brings real gains?

paragraphs: The tutorial argues that Java only seems to stand still. Java 8, released in 2014, brought lambda expressions, the Stream API and the Optional class, and it is still widely used. Staying there, the tutorial says, means missing progress in the language, the JVM and the tooling.

It then lists features since Java 8 by purpose. Records, sealed classes and pattern matching serve data-oriented, maintainable code. Virtual threads serve concurrency at scale. The Foreign Function and Memory API serves safer work with non-Java code and data. Helpful NullPointerExceptions serve debugging.

It also reports a SPECjbb 2015 benchmark with a fixed 16 GB heap and no collector tuning. Average pauses of Parallel and G1 in Java 17 were about 60 percent of their Java 8 averages, and ZGC held sub-millisecond pauses at a 128 GB heap. ZGC pays for low latency with a larger footprint, meaning more native memory used by collector structures; the tutorial expects this to improve.
card.example: G1 overhead in this benchmark fell from about 10 percent in Java 8 to about 5 percent in Java 17. The tutorial adds that this benchmark is relatively favorable and that earlier G1 overhead was about 20 percent.
card.rule: Weigh the tutorial's claim that Java keeps improving against its evidence: feature groups listed by purpose and benchmark results measured under stated conditions.
card.limits: The benchmark used one setup, a 16 GB heap with no tuning, so its numbers show a pattern, not a promise for every application.

concepts.title: What a preview feature is
concepts.question: What does the label preview promise about a Java feature, and what does it ask of the people who use it?

paragraphs: According to the tutorial, a preview feature is a new language or API feature that the JDK team believes is fully specified and implemented, yet may still change before it becomes permanent. Developer feedback is what drives those changes.

A feature usually moves through one or more preview rounds and then a final phase that makes it permanent. Between rounds the feature and its documentation can change. Only the final version falls under long-term compatibility rules.

Preview features are off by default, so both compiling and running code that uses one needs special switches. The tutorial adds that such features belong to one specific Java feature release, so output built with them should not be distributed, for example to a public repository.
card.example: A team writes a small tool with a language feature that is in its second preview in some release. Compiling it the ordinary way fails. Compiling with preview switched on works and prints a warning that preview features are in use. Starting the program also needs preview switched on.
card.rule: A preview feature is believed complete but may change, is off by default, and is tied to one feature release.
card.limits: The tutorial does not give the switch spellings or say how class files record preview use, so check the JDK documentation for those. Preview status says a feature can change, not that it is half built.

concepts.title: Preview, experimental and incubating
concepts.question: Which of the three kinds of nonfinal feature is this, and what switch turns it on?

paragraphs: The tutorial names three kinds of nonfinal feature. Preview covers new language or API features. Experimental mainly covers new features of the HotSpot JVM. Incubating covers potentially new APIs and JDK tools, and these live in incubator modules.

An experimental feature is disabled by default. You first enable the mechanism with the option -XX:+UnlockExperimentalVMOptions, then turn on the specific feature with its own option. The tutorial's example is the ZGC collector: experimental from JDK 11, started before Java 15 with -XX:+UseZGC, and a production feature in Java 15.

Incubating APIs and tools sit only in the jdk.incubator namespace, and you must ask for them explicitly. On the classpath you pass --add-modules. In a modular application you declare requires, or requires transitive, for the incubating module.
card.example: To try a hypothetical experimental collector you would pass the unlock option plus the collector's own option. To use a hypothetical incubating module named jdk.incubator.demo from a modular program, you would add a requires line for it to the module descriptor.
card.rule: Match the kind to its switch: preview needs preview enabled, experimental needs the unlock option plus its own option, incubating needs the module requested.
card.limits: The three labels describe how the JDK stages a feature, not how good it is. The tutorial says incubating APIs may change, and only a final version gets long-term compatibility rules.

concepts.title: How features moved to final, and early access builds
concepts.question: What do the tutorial's examples show about how previews change a feature, and where do early access builds fit?

paragraphs: The tutorial traces three features. Switch expressions were previewed in Java 12 and 13 and became final in Java 14; feedback replaced break with yield as the way to produce a value. Records had a second preview and became final in JDK 16. Sealed classes had a second preview in JDK 16 and became final in JDK 17.

The sealed example also shows the switches at work. On JDK 16, compiling a sealed interface with the ordinary command fails because permits is unavailable. With preview enabled the compile works but warns, and running the program needs preview enabled too. The permitted types must share a package or module with the sealed type.

Some novel work, such as Projects Loom, Panama and Valhalla, arrives over several releases and may be too unstable for the regular feedback process. For that, expert users can download feature-specific early access builds from jdk.java.net. Such builds can break compatibility, and their APIs can change drastically between builds.
card.example: Reading the history as a timeline: a feature appears in one or two preview releases, feedback reshapes it, and a later release makes it final. An early access build sits before that line, for work not yet ready even for a preview release.
card.rule: Features reach final through preview rounds shaped by feedback, while early access builds serve novel, unstable work outside that process.
card.limits: The three examples are a sample, not a schedule: the tutorial says a feature goes through one or more preview rounds. Early access builds follow their own download pages and feedback lists, not the regular preview rules.

concepts.title: Four kinds of variable
concepts.question: Which of the four kinds is this variable, and how many copies of it exist?

paragraphs: Java uses both field and variable. According to the tutorial, fields means the ones that belong to a type, leaving out local variables and parameters, while variables means every kind together. The fields, methods and nested types of a type are its members.

An instance variable (non-static field) is declared without static, and each object gets its own copy, so changing it in one object leaves the others alone. A class variable (static field) is declared with static and has exactly one copy, however many objects exist.

A local variable is declared inside a method body with no special keyword: its position makes it local, and only that method can see it. A parameter is a variable named in a method signature, such as args in main. Parameters count as variables, not fields.
card.example: class Counter { static int created = 0; int ticks = 0; void add(int step) { int before = ticks; ticks = before + step; } } Here created is a class variable, ticks an instance variable, step a parameter and before a local variable.
card.rule: Decide the kind from where and how the variable is declared: static field, plain field, inside a method body, or in a signature.
card.limits: Position and the static keyword decide the kind, not the type or the spelling of the declaration, so the same text can mean different kinds in different places.

concepts.title: Legal names and conventions
concepts.question: What makes a name legal, and what does good style add on top of that?

paragraphs: A legal name is case-sensitive and of any length. It starts with a letter, a dollar sign or an underscore, and continues with letters, digits, dollar signs or underscores. It cannot contain whitespace and cannot be a keyword or reserved word.

Convention goes beyond legality. Start with a letter, leave the dollar sign out of your own names, and use full words instead of cryptic abbreviations. A single-word name is all lowercase; a multi-word name is in camel case: first word lowercase, each later word capitalised, as in gearRatio.
A constant, which is a static final field, is written in capitals with underscores between the words, such as NUM_GEARS. According to the tutorial, the underscore is used only in this role.
card.example: Legal and conventional: cadence, currentGear, NUM_GEARS. Legal but discouraged: _speed, $total, s. Not legal: 2ndGear (starts with a digit), my speed (whitespace), class (a keyword).
card.rule: First check that a name is legal, then shape it with the conventions: camel case for variables and capitals with underscores for constants.
card.limits: Legality is enforced by the compiler; conventions are advice. A discouraged name still compiles, and capital letters mark a constant only for human readers.

concepts.title: The eight primitive types
concepts.question: Which of the eight primitive types fits a value, and which things only look primitive?

paragraphs: Java is statically typed: a variable is declared with a type and a name before use, and the type decides which values it can hold and which operations apply. Primitive types are built into the language, named by reserved keywords, and a primitive value shares no state with any other value.

There are eight. The signed whole-number types are byte (8 bits), short (16), int (32) and long (64). The decimal types are float (32-bit) and double (64-bit). The other two are boolean, for true or false, and char, a single 16-bit Unicode character. The tutorial treats int as the default whole-number choice and double as the default decimal.

Byte and short can save memory in large arrays. Floating-point types should not hold precise values such as currency; the tutorial points to the BigDecimal class instead. String is not primitive but a class: a double-quoted literal creates a String object, and Strings are immutable.
card.example: int pages = 320; double price = 4.5; char grade = 'B'; boolean passed = true; String title = "Notes"; The first four are primitives; title refers to a String object.
card.rule: Choose int and double by default, a smaller or larger type only for a reason, and remember that String is an object.
card.limits: Ranges are fixed by the language, so a value beyond int needs long. The tutorial does not describe conversions between types, and it says the size of boolean is not precisely defined.

concepts.title: Literals and default values
concepts.question: How does the way a value is written fix its type, and what does an unset variable hold?

paragraphs: A literal is a value written directly in code, and primitives need no new. A whole-number literal is long when it ends in L (uppercase is preferred) and int otherwise. The prefix 0x gives hexadecimal and 0b gives binary. A decimal literal ending in F is float; otherwise it is double, and a trailing D is optional.

Underscores may separate digits for readability, as in 1_000_000. They are not allowed at the start or end of a number, beside a decimal point, or before an F or L suffix. A char literal uses single quotes and a String literal uses double quotes.

A field that you do not initialise gets a default from the compiler: zero for byte, short and int, 0L for long, 0.0f for float, 0.0d for double, false for boolean, the null character for char and null for objects. A local variable gets no default, and using it before assigning is a compile-time error.
card.example: long views = 3_000_000_000L; int mask = 0b1010; float rate = 2.5f; The three are valid. int bad = 1_; is not, because it ends with an underscore.
card.rule: Read the suffix and prefix to know a literal's type and base, and give every local variable a value before using it.
card.limits: Defaults apply to fields only, and the tutorial calls relying on them poor style. Underscores change nothing about a value.

concepts.title: Arrays: fixed length, zero-based index
concepts.question: What does an array hold, how is it created, and what cannot change after creation?

paragraphs: An array is a container object that holds a fixed number of values of one type. Its length is fixed when it is created and cannot change afterwards. Elements are reached by an index that starts at 0, so the sixth element has index 5.

The type is the element type followed by square brackets, as in int[] scores. This declaration only tells the compiler the variable will refer to an array; it creates none. Brackets after the name are legal but discouraged. Creation uses new with a size, such as new int[10], and must happen before use.

A shortcut lists the values in braces, separated by commas, which creates and fills the array at once; the number of values sets the length. Every array has a length property. A for-each loop visits each element without managing an index.
card.example: int[] scores = new int[3]; scores[0] = 70; scores[2] = 95; String[] days = {"Mon", "Tue"}; Here days.length is 2, and 3 is one past the last valid index of scores.
card.rule: Declare with brackets after the type, create with a fixed length, and use indexes from 0 up to length minus one.
card.limits: A fixed length means a bigger collection needs a new array. Declaring alone creates nothing. The tutorial does not describe what happens with an invalid index.

concepts.title: Jagged arrays and copying
concepts.question: How are arrays of arrays built, and which tools copy part of an array?

paragraphs: A multidimensional array uses two or more bracket pairs, such as String[][], and needs one index per dimension. In Java it is an array whose elements are themselves arrays, so rows may have different lengths. Such arrays are called irregular or jagged, and code should read each row's own length.

System.arraycopy takes five arguments in this order: the source array, the start position in the source, the destination array, the start position in the destination, and the number of elements to copy. The destination must already exist.

The Arrays class saves manual loops. copyOfRange(array, from, to) returns a new array, with from included and to excluded. It also offers equals, fill, sort, parallelSort, binarySearch, stream, and toString, which produces bracketed, comma-separated text.
card.example: int[] src = {4, 5, 6, 7, 8}; int[] part = Arrays.copyOfRange(src, 1, 3); part holds 5 and 6. int[] dst = new int[5]; System.arraycopy(src, 0, dst, 2, 3); dst holds 0, 0, 4, 5, 6.
card.rule: Count arraycopy's five arguments in order, treat the end index of copyOfRange as excluded, and read each row's own length.
card.limits: The tutorial describes these tools but not their failure cases, such as ranges that do not fit. With jagged rows, no single length describes the whole array.

concepts.title: Local variable type inference with var
concepts.question: Where may var replace a type name, and what must the compiler be able to see?

paragraphs: Since Java SE 10, var declares a local variable whose type the compiler infers from its initializer. The inferred type is fixed from then on. The tutorial's case for var is readability: when the explicit type is redundant, var makes the code simpler to read.
var is allowed for local variables in methods, constructors and initializer blocks. It is not allowed for fields, and not for the parameters of methods or constructors.
The compiler must pick a type at the point of declaration, so a var variable needs an initializer. The value null alone has no type, so it cannot be the initializer either.
card.example: var title = "Notes"; gives String. var pages = 320; gives int. var later; does not compile, since it has no initializer. var nothing = null; does not compile, since null has no type.
card.rule: Use var for local variables with a typed initializer, and keep explicit types for fields and parameters.
card.limits: var cannot be used for fields or parameters. Readability is the only style guidance the tutorial gives, so it says nothing more about when to avoid var.

concepts.title: Precedence, associativity and increments
concepts.question: In what order does Java evaluate one expression, and what do compound and increment operators do?

paragraphs: Operators act on one, two or three operands and give a result. Precedence says which operator is evaluated first: multiplicative before additive, then shift, relational, equality, the bitwise operators, logical AND, logical OR, the ternary and last assignment. Operators in the same row have equal precedence.

Associativity breaks ties: binary operators other than assignment run left to right, and assignment runs right to left. Parentheses fix the order explicitly, and the tutorial recommends them in compound expressions for readability and maintenance.

A compound assignment such as += joins an operator to =, so x += 1 has the same effect as x = x + 1. Prefix ++x gives the new value and postfix x++ gives the original; both change x by one. The difference shows only inside a larger expression. The % operator gives the remainder.
card.example: int a = 10; int b = a++ + 2; gives b = 12 and a = 11. With int c = 10; int d = ++c + 2; d = 13 and c = 11. Also 8 + 6 / 2 is 11, while (8 + 6) / 2 is 7.
card.rule: Work out the order from precedence, then associativity, and add parentheses wherever a reader might doubt it.
card.limits: Prefix and postfix differ only inside a larger expression; as a lone statement they do the same. Parentheses that match the default order change nothing in the result.

concepts.title: Comparing and combining conditions
concepts.question: How do equality, the conditional operators and the ternary behave, and when is work skipped?

paragraphs: Equality and relational operators give a boolean. Use == to compare primitive values for equality; writing a single = by mistake assigns instead of comparing. The unary ! inverts a boolean.
The conditional operators && and || combine two boolean expressions and short-circuit: the second operand is evaluated only if the first does not already settle the result.

The ternary operator has three operands: condition ? value1 : value2 gives value1 when the condition is true and value2 otherwise. It is shorthand for if-then-else. The tutorial prefers it for compact expressions with no side effects, and otherwise recommends a regular if-else.
The instanceof operator tests whether an object is an instance of a given type, which can be a class, a superclass or an interface implemented by the object's class.
card.example: int stock = 0; boolean ready = stock != 0 && check(stock); The method check is not called, because the left side is false. String label = stock != 0 ? "in" : "out"; gives out.
card.rule: Let the first operand of && or || decide whether the second runs, and use the ternary only for compact choices without side effects.
card.limits: Short-circuiting means a call on the right side may never run, so it cannot be relied on for side effects. The tutorial describes the ternary and instanceof briefly.

concepts.title: Expressions, statements and blocks
concepts.question: Is this piece of code a value, a complete instruction, or a group of instructions?

paragraphs: An expression is built from variables, operators and method invocations, and evaluates to a single value. Its type follows from its parts: the assignment cadence = 0 is an int expression, because an assignment gives a value of its left operand's type. Small expressions combine when their types fit together.

A statement is a complete unit of execution, like a sentence. There are three kinds: expression statements, which are expressions ended with a semicolon, though only certain expressions qualify; declaration statements, which declare variables; and control-flow statements, which regulate the order of execution.

A block is zero or more statements within balanced braces, and it can be used anywhere one statement is allowed. Floating-point arithmetic can surprise: the tutorial shows a sum compared with an expected value printing false because of rounding, and treats the details as beyond its scope.
card.example: int total = 0; is a declaration statement. total = total + 5; is an expression statement. { int bonus = 3; total += bonus; } is a block. The expression total + 5 has type int.
card.rule: Ask whether code yields a value (expression), does one complete thing (statement), or groups statements (block).
card.limits: Adding a semicolon does not turn every expression into a statement. Floating-point details are outside the tutorial, which only warns that results can surprise.

concepts.title: Choosing, repeating and jumping
concepts.question: Which statement chooses a path or repeats code, and how do break, continue and labels change the flow?

paragraphs: if-then runs its block only when a boolean test is true; if-then-else adds a path for false. In a chain, conditions are checked in order and the first true one wins; the rest are skipped. Braces may be left off for a single statement, but the tutorial calls that brittle: a second statement added later falls outside without any error.

while tests at the top, so its body may never run; do-while tests at the bottom, so its body runs at least once. A for loop has an initialization run once, a termination test checked before each pass, and an increment run after each pass. The enhanced for visits each element of an array or collection without an index, and the tutorial recommends it whenever it fits.

break ends the innermost switch or loop and continues after it; continue skips the rest of the current iteration. A labeled break ends the outer statement carrying the label, and control resumes right after that statement, not at the label. return leaves the current method.
card.example: int found = -1; for (int i = 0; i != data.length; i++) { if (data[i] == 7) { found = i; break; } } The loop stops at the first 7 and the code after the loop runs.
card.rule: Choose the loop by when the test must run, and use break, continue or a label to leave or skip only the construct you mean.
card.limits: Unlabeled break and continue touch only the innermost loop, so nested loops need a label to reach an outer one. A for loop with all three parts left empty repeats forever.

concepts.title: The switch statement and fall-through
concepts.question: How does a classic switch pick what to run, and why does a missing break matter?

paragraphs: A switch statement evaluates a selector and runs the statements after the matching case label. The tutorial lists the allowed selectors: byte, short, char and int, the wrappers Character, Byte, Short and Integer, enumerated types, and String. boolean, long, float and double cannot be selectors.

Without a break, execution falls through: every statement after the matching label runs in order until a break. The last break is technically optional, but the tutorial recommends it. The default section handles values that match no case, and several case labels can share one set of statements.

Compared with if-then-else, a switch tests one value against fixed labels, while if-then-else can test ranges and general conditions, including boolean ones. The tutorial says the choice depends on readability and on the expression being tested.
card.example: char out; int day = 2; switch (day) { case 1: out = 'A'; case 2: out = 'B'; case 3: out = 'C'; break; default: out = 'Z'; } For day 2, out becomes B and then C, so it ends as C.
card.rule: End each group of statements with break unless fall-through is meant, and give the switch a selector of an allowed type.
card.limits: A switch cannot test ranges or boolean conditions; use if-then-else for those. The statement form need not cover every value. This card does not cover the arrow form.

concepts.title: Switch expressions, arrows and yield
concepts.question: What does the arrow form change, and how does a switch expression produce its value?

paragraphs: Java SE 14 added a new form of switch. A case label can use an arrow, and then only the code to its right runs: there is no fall-through. That code is a single expression, a block or a throw statement, and one arrow label can list several constants separated by commas. A variable declared in the block is local to it.

A switch expression produces a value, so it can be assigned. With a single expression, that expression is the result. In a block, the tutorial uses yield to supply the value, because a plain return would be ambiguous: it is unclear whether it leaves the switch or the method.

A switch expression must be exhaustive: every possible selector value needs a label. For an enum, labels for all constants need no default; otherwise default usually supplies exhaustiveness. A switch statement need not be exhaustive, and an unmatched value silently does nothing.
The older colon form can also be used in a switch expression; fall-through then applies, and values are supplied with yield.
card.example: With arrow labels, a switch on a day number from 1 to 7 can set a String to weekend for the labels 6 and 7 together, and to weekday for 1 to 5 listed with commas, with default for anything else. No break is needed.
card.rule: Use arrow labels to avoid fall-through, yield to give a value from a block, and cover every possible selector value.
card.limits: Exhaustiveness is required of expressions only. The tutorial does not list every allowed selector type for expressions, and null handling was a preview feature in Java SE 17.

concepts.title: Number wrappers and text conversion
concepts.question: Why would code use an Integer object rather than an int, and how do strings and numbers convert?

paragraphs: Every primitive number type has a wrapper class in java.lang, and the numeric wrappers all extend the abstract class Number. According to the tutorial, an object is worth having when a method asks for one (collections are the usual case), when you want a type's bounds from constants such as MIN_VALUE and MAX_VALUE, or when you want class methods that convert values.

Text conversion has two families. A parse method such as parseInt takes a string and hands back a primitive. The valueOf method hands back a wrapper object instead. Both work on strings and each can take a radix, so the text can be read as binary, octal, hexadecimal or decimal. The decode method also reads decimal, octal and hexadecimal text.

Going the other way, toString turns a value into text, and valueOf can also wrap an existing primitive. Every Number object offers conversion methods such as intValue and doubleValue that return a primitive of another numeric type.
card.example: Integer.parseInt of the text 1010 with radix 2 returns the primitive int 10. Integer.valueOf of the same text and radix returns an Integer object holding 10. Integer.toString of the int 10 returns the text 10.
card.rule: Use a parse method when you need a primitive from text, valueOf when you need a wrapper object, and pass a radix when the text is not decimal.
card.limits: Wrappers cover ordinary fixed-size values only; the tutorial notes other Number subclasses that it does not cover. A parse method also needs text that really is written in the stated radix.

concepts.title: Formatting numbers and using Math
concepts.question: How do printf specifiers, DecimalFormat patterns and the Math rounding and random methods control what a number looks like?

paragraphs: The printf and format methods of System.out are equivalent. They take a format string followed by any number of arguments. A specifier starts with a percent sign and ends with a converter: d for a decimal integer, f for a floating-point number, n for the platform's line break. According to the tutorial, prefer the n specifier to a backslash-n escape.

Optional settings sit between the percent sign and the converter. A width with a leading zero, such as 08, pads with zeros to eight characters. A plus shows the sign, a comma adds grouping separators, a minus left-justifies, and a dot with a number, such as .3, sets the digits after the decimal point.

DecimalFormat, from java.text, takes a pattern and formats a double. In a pattern a hash sign marks an optional digit, a zero marks a required digit, a comma is the grouping separator and a dot is the decimal separator. Digits beyond the pattern's decimals are rounded.

Math offers static methods. Floor gives the largest whole number not above the argument, and ceil the smallest not below it, both as doubles. Round returns a long for a double argument and an int for a float argument. Random returns a pseudo-random double that is at least 0.0 and below 1.0; multiply it to change the range.
card.example: printf with the specifier 08.2f and the value 3.14159 prints 00003.14, which is eight characters wide with two decimals. A DecimalFormat with pattern 000.00 turns 5.5 into 005.50. Math.random times 10 gives a value from 0.0 up to, but not including, 10.0.
card.rule: Use printf for one-off formatted output, DecimalFormat for reusable digit patterns, and Math for rounding and scaled random values.
card.limits: The tutorial suggests a java.util.Random object when you need a series of random numbers, not repeated Math.random calls. Full details of specifiers live in java.util.Formatter, which the lesson only points to.

concepts.title: Characters, code points and escapes
concepts.question: What does a Java char hold, when do you need Character or an int instead, and what do escape sequences insert?

paragraphs: The primitive char holds one character and suits most code. The Character wrapper is for places that need an object, and its objects cannot be changed once made. The class has static helpers such as isLetter, isDigit, isWhitespace, isUpperCase, isLowerCase, toUpperCase, toLowerCase, and toString, which gives a one-character String.

A char is 16 bits, covering 0000 to FFFF in hexadecimal, a range called the Basic Multilingual Plane. Unicode code points run up to U+10FFFF, and those above FFFF are supplementary characters. An int can hold any code point. Methods that accept only a char cannot support supplementary characters and treat their surrogate values as undefined characters.

A backslash in a literal starts an escape sequence that the compiler interprets. Backslash t inserts a tab, n a newline, b a backspace, r a carriage return, f a form feed, s a space. A backslash before a quote mark inserts that quote, and two backslashes insert one backslash.
card.example: Character.isDigit applied to the char 7 gives true. Character.toUpperCase applied to the char q gives Q. A string literal with a backslash t between two words prints them separated by a tab.
card.rule: Use char for single characters, the Character helpers to test and convert them, and an int when a code point may exceed FFFF.
card.limits: A method that takes only a char cannot treat a supplementary character as one unit. Escape sequences matter only inside literals, where the compiler reads the backslash.

concepts.title: Strings are unchangeable text objects
concepts.question: What does it mean that a String cannot change, and how do concat, plus and text blocks build new text?

paragraphs: A string literal makes the compiler create a String object, and the String class also has thirteen constructors. A String cannot be changed after creation: a method that seems to modify one actually returns a new String, so you must keep that value. The length method counts characters, and charAt reads one by a zero-based index.

The concat method returns the first string with its argument added at the end. The plus operator does the same job and is more common; when one operand is not a string, its toString method supplies the text. String.format is the static partner of printf and returns a String instead of printing.

Before Java SE 15 a string literal could not span lines, so authors joined pieces with plus at each line end. From Java SE 15, a text block opens with a triple quote mark, closes with another triple quote, and holds the lines between them.
card.example: String a is tea. The statement a.concat with the string literal pot builds teapot but throws it away, so a is still tea. Only an assignment such as b = a.concat with the string literal pot keeps the result.
card.rule: Every String method that appears to change text returns a new String, so assign the result if you want to keep it.
card.limits: Immutability applies to String objects, not to variables: a variable can be pointed at a different String. Building text in many steps creates many objects, which is where the tutorial brings in StringBuilder.

concepts.title: Slicing, searching, replacing and comparing
concepts.question: How do substring, indexOf, replace and the comparison methods behave at their edges, such as end positions and missing matches?

paragraphs: Indexes start at 0. Substring with a begin and an end returns the characters from begin up to but not including end, and substring with only a begin runs to the end of the string. A begin equal to the length is accepted and reaches the end.

The indexOf method searches forward and lastIndexOf searches backward. Both return -1 when nothing is found, and both can start from a given index. The contains method answers only whether a sequence is present. Replace changes every occurrence of a char or a literal sequence, replaceAll every regular-expression match, and replaceFirst only the first such match.

Equals tests for the same characters and equalsIgnoreCase ignores case. CompareTo compares lexicographically and returns a value below, at, or above zero. StartsWith and endsWith test the ends, regionMatches compares regions, and matches tests whether the whole string fits a regular expression.
card.example: In the String notes.final.txt, lastIndexOf of the dot char is 11, so substring of 12 returns txt.
card.rule: Treat the end index as exclusive, check for -1 before using a search result, and pick the replace or compare method whose scope fits the job.
card.limits: These methods never edit the original String; inserting needs a new string built from pieces. The regex-based methods rely on regular expressions, which this lesson leaves to another lesson.

concepts.title: StringBuilder: text you edit in place
concepts.question: How does a StringBuilder differ from a String, and what do its length and capacity measure?

paragraphs: A StringBuilder holds characters that can be changed after creation, like a variable-length array of characters. According to the tutorial, use String by default and a builder when it makes code simpler or faster. Before Java SE 9 appending could beat joining many strings with plus, but Java SE 9 optimized plain concatenation, which now outperforms appending.

Length is the number of characters present. Capacity is the number of slots allocated; it is never smaller than length and grows automatically when append or insert needs more. An empty builder has capacity 16. A builder made from a String holds its characters plus 16 extra slots, and a constructor taking an int sets the capacity.

Editing methods change the builder itself. Append converts any primitive or object and adds it at the end, insert adds at an offset, delete removes from start through end minus one, deleteCharAt removes one character, replace swaps a range for a String, setCharAt swaps one character, and reverse flips the order. The toString method returns a String copy.
card.example: A builder made from abcdef: delete of 1 and 3 leaves adef, appending the int 9 leaves adef9, and reverse leaves 9feda. Its length is now 5, and its capacity is at least 5.
card.rule: Use a StringBuilder to edit text in place: length counts characters, capacity counts reserved slots, and delete and replace treat the end index as exclusive.
card.limits: For a handful of joins on Java SE 9 or later, the tutorial's better choice is plain concatenation. To use a String method on a builder, call toString first.

concepts.title: Autoboxing and unboxing
concepts.question: When does the compiler convert between a primitive and its wrapper by itself, and which primitive goes with which wrapper?

paragraphs: Autoboxing is the compiler's automatic conversion of a primitive value into an object of its matching wrapper class. Unboxing is the reverse conversion. The pairs are boolean with Boolean, byte with Byte, char with Character, float with Float, int with Integer, long with Long, short with Short and double with Double.

Boxing happens when a primitive is passed to a method that expects the matching wrapper, or assigned to a variable of that wrapper type. Unboxing happens when a wrapper object is passed to a method that expects the matching primitive, or assigned to a variable of that primitive type.
card.example: Integer box = 8 boxes the int 8 into an Integer. Then int plain = box unboxes that Integer back into a primitive.
card.rule: The compiler boxes and unboxes on its own when a primitive meets its matching wrapper in an assignment or method argument.
card.limits: Boxing links each primitive to its own matching wrapper only, such as int to Integer. The compiler performs the conversion by writing the conversion calls into the program.

concepts.unitTitle: Objects, Classes, Interfaces, Packages and Inheritance (dev.java)
concepts.title: Objects, encapsulation and classes
concepts.question: What do an object's state and behavior mean, and how does a class relate to the objects built from it?

paragraphs: According to the tutorial, an object is a bundle of related state and behavior. A dog has state such as name and color, and behavior such as barking. An object keeps its state in fields and offers its behavior through methods. Methods work on the fields and are the main way objects talk to each other.

Data encapsulation means hiding the internal state and making every interaction go through methods. The object then controls how it is used: a gear method on a six-gear bicycle can refuse values below 1 or above 6. The tutorial lists four gains from bundling code: modularity, information hiding, code reuse, and easy plugging or debugging of replaceable objects.

A class is the blueprint from which objects are created, and each object is an instance of its class. The tutorial's Bicycle class has fields for cadence, speed and gear plus methods that change them. It has no main method because it is a blueprint, not a whole application; another class creates and uses Bicycle objects.
card.example: Take a Thermostat class. Its field holds the target temperature, and a setTarget method accepts only values from 5 to 30. Code elsewhere calls setTarget and never touches the field. One instance runs the hall, another the kitchen, each with its own target, and both were made from the same blueprint.
card.rule: Model a thing as fields for its state and methods for its behavior, let outside code act only through the methods, and write the shared design once as a class.
card.limits: Protection holds only while all interaction goes through methods. A class by itself does not run: something else must create instances and call their methods.

concepts.unitTitle: Objects, Classes, Interfaces, Packages and Inheritance (dev.java)
concepts.title: Inheritance, interfaces and packages
concepts.question: How do extends, implements and packages each help organise and reuse code?

paragraphs: Inheritance lets a class build on another. In Java each class has exactly one direct superclass, while a superclass may have any number of subclasses. The word extends, placed at the start of the subclass declaration, names the superclass. The subclass receives its fields and methods and only adds what makes it special. Because inherited code is not written in the subclass file, the tutorial advises documenting the superclass well.

An interface is a group of related methods with empty bodies; it is the boundary between an object and the outside. A class adopts it with implements and so commits to the contract. The compiler checks that every interface method is present, and the tutorial says the implementing methods must be declared public.

A package is a namespace that groups related classes and interfaces, much as folders group files. This matters when a program has thousands of classes. The Java platform supplies its library in packages, such as String, File and Socket classes, so you can concentrate on your own application; the tutorial recommends bookmarking the API specification.
card.example: Suppose Truck extends Vehicle, so it gains the Vehicle fields and methods. Truck also implements Loadable, which lists load and unload; Truck must then define both, with public. The classes Truck, Vehicle and Loadable could sit together in a package named fleet.
card.rule: Use extends to reuse state and behavior from one superclass, implements to promise the methods of an interface, and packages to group related types.
card.limits: The tutorial postpones details: why interface methods must be public and how interfaces and inheritance interact are left to later lessons. Packages only organise names; they do not supply behavior.

concepts.title: What a class declaration holds
concepts.question: What goes into a class declaration and its body, and how do fields, local variables and parameters differ?

paragraphs: A class declaration lists optional modifiers, the class name (capitalized by convention), an optional extends clause naming one superclass, an optional implements clause listing any number of interfaces, and a body in braces. A minimal declaration needs only the class keyword, a name and a body.

The body holds three kinds of member: constructors that initialize new objects, fields that hold state, and methods that define behavior. Variables come in three kinds: a field is a member of the class, a local variable is declared inside a method or block, and a parameter is declared in a method signature.

The modifier public makes a member reachable from every class; private limits it to its own class. Common practice is to make fields private and let other classes use public methods, such as getters. This practice is called encapsulation.
card.example: A class Lamp declares a private int brightness and a public method getBrightness that returns it. Code in other classes cannot touch brightness directly; it asks the method.
card.rule: A class bundles state, behavior and constructors in one body, and private fields are reached through public methods.
card.limits: Other access levels exist and come later. The extends clause allows only one parent, while implements allows several.

concepts.title: Methods, signatures and overloading
concepts.question: What does the compiler use to tell two methods in one class apart, and what does it ignore?

paragraphs: A method declaration needs a return type (void when nothing comes back), a name, parentheses and a body in braces. Modifiers, parameters and an exception list are optional extras. By convention a method name starts with a lowercase verb, with later words capitalized.
The method signature is the name plus the parameter types in order. The return type and modifiers are not part of the signature.

Overloading lets several methods in one class share a name when their parameter lists differ in number or type; the compiler picks by the arguments at the call. Two methods whose signatures match cannot coexist, even when their return types differ. The tutorial advises using overloading sparingly, since it can hurt readability.
card.example: A Printer class may have print(String s) and print(int n). It may not also have int size() and long size(), since both have the signature size with no parameters.
card.rule: Overloads must differ in parameter types or count, because the signature leaves out the return type.
card.limits: Overloading is legal but the tutorial urges restraint for readability. Methods that differ in parameters may still have different return types.

concepts.title: Constructors and the default constructor
concepts.question: What does a constructor look like, and what happens when a class has none?

paragraphs: A constructor runs when the new operator creates an object, allocating memory and initializing its fields. It is declared like a method but carries the class name and has no return type.

A class may have several constructors if their parameter counts or types differ, the same overloading idea as for methods. Two constructors with identical parameter types in one class are a compile error. Access modifiers on a constructor decide which classes may call it.

If a class declares no constructor, the compiler supplies a default one that takes no arguments and calls the superclass no-argument constructor. A class with no extends clause implicitly extends Object, which has such a constructor. If the superclass has no usable no-argument constructor, the code does not compile.
card.example: A Mug class declares Mug() and Mug(int ml). The call new Mug(250) runs the second constructor; new Mug() runs the first.
card.rule: A constructor has the class name and no return type; if you write none, the compiler adds a no-argument one that calls the parent's.
card.limits: The default constructor only helps when the parent offers a usable no-argument constructor. Without one, compilation fails.

concepts.title: Parameters, arguments and pass by value
concepts.question: When a method changes its parameter, what does the caller's variable see?

paragraphs: Parameters are the variables named in a method or constructor declaration; arguments are the values supplied at the call. Arguments must match the parameters in type and order. A parameter may be a primitive or a reference type.

A varargs parameter accepts any number of values of one type, including none. It is written with an ellipsis after the type, must come last, and is treated as an array inside the method. A caller may pass either a comma-separated list or an array.

Every argument is passed by value, meaning the method receives a copy. A primitive copy changes only inside the method. A reference copy still points to the same object, so changes to that object's fields are visible to the caller, but reassigning the parameter to a new object changes only the local copy.
card.example: A method reset(Counter c) runs c.count = 0, then c = new Counter(), then c.count = 99. Back in the caller, the original counter shows count 0, not 99.
card.rule: Java copies every argument; a copied reference still reaches the same object, but reassigning the copy leaves the caller's variable alone.
card.limits: Changing an object through a parameter works only where access rules let the method reach those fields.

concepts.title: Creating, using and freeing objects
concepts.question: What are the three parts of creating an object, and when does the runtime free it?

paragraphs: Creating an object has three parts. Declaration gives a variable a type and a name; a reference variable declared alone refers to no object, and using it before assignment is a compile error. Instantiation uses the new operator, which allocates memory, runs a constructor and returns a reference. Initialization is the constructor setting the starting state.

Inside the class, fields are named simply; outside, you write a reference, a dot and the member, such as rect.width or rect.area(). Each object has its own copy of its instance fields. A returned value can be stored or used in a condition.

Java has no manual destruction. The garbage collector reclaims an object once no references to it remain; a reference goes away when its variable leaves scope or is set to null. An object with several references becomes eligible only after all are gone, and the collector decides itself when to run.
card.example: Cup a = new Cup(250); Cup b = a; a = null; The Cup still has the reference b, so it stays in use. After b = null as well, it becomes eligible.
card.rule: New creates the object and hands back a reference; an object stays alive until its last reference is gone.
card.limits: Eligible does not mean freed at once; the collector runs when it decides to.

concepts.title: this, shadowing and constructor chaining
concepts.question: How can code reach a field hidden by a parameter, and how can one constructor reuse another?

paragraphs: Inside an instance method or constructor, this refers to the current object. When a parameter has the same name as a field, the parameter shadows the field: the plain name means the parameter. Writing this.name reaches the field, which is why constructors and setters often contain this.x = x.
A constructor can call another constructor of the same class with this followed by an argument list, so that setup code is shared. The compiler picks the target by argument count and types.

According to the tutorial, before JDK 25 such a call must be the first statement of the constructor. From JDK 25 on, some code may come before it, but it may not use the instance under construction except to initialize its fields, and may not call instance methods.
card.example: class Seat { int row; int col; Seat(int row, int col) { this.row = row; this.col = col; } Seat(int row) { this(row, 1); } }
card.rule: Use this.field to reach a field hidden by a parameter, and this with arguments to reuse another constructor of the same class.
card.limits: this exists only in instance code, and the placement rule for the constructor call depends on the JDK version.

concepts.title: Access levels
concepts.question: Which code can see a member declared private, with no modifier, protected or public?

paragraphs: A top-level class is either public or package-private (no modifier). A member may be public, protected, package-private or private. A class can always use its own members.

Private members are visible only in their own class. With no modifier, the class and its package can see the member. Protected adds subclasses in other packages. Public opens the member to every class.

The tutorial advises using the most restrictive level that makes sense, with private as the starting point, and avoiding public fields except for constants. Public fields tie other code to one implementation and make later changes harder.
card.example: In package shop, class Order has a package-private method and a private field. Report in shop can call the method but not read the field. Mailer in package mail can use neither.
card.rule: Choose the most restrictive access level that still lets the code that needs a member use it.
card.limits: The Java Module System can restrict public classes further, and reflection can sometimes reach members that are not visible, so access modifiers are not the only protection.

concepts.title: Class members and constants
concepts.question: Which data is shared by every object of a class, and what can a class method reach directly?

paragraphs: Instance variables get a separate copy in every object. A class variable, declared static, has one copy shared by all objects and lives with the class. Both class variables and class methods are reached through the class name, such as Counter.total; the tutorial discourages using an object reference instead.

Instance methods can use instance and class members directly. Class methods can directly use only class variables and class methods; to reach an instance member they need an object reference. They cannot use this.

A constant is declared static final and cannot be reassigned. By convention its name is uppercase with underscores between words. A static initialization block sets up class variables and runs in source order; an instance initializer block is copied into every constructor.
card.example: class Ticket { static int issued; int number; Ticket() { issued++; number = issued; } } After three tickets exist, issued is 3 and the numbers are 1, 2 and 3.
card.rule: Static members belong to the class and are shared; instance members belong to each object, and static code needs an object to reach them.
card.limits: Calling a static member through a reference compiles but is discouraged. If a static initializer fails, objects of the class cannot be created.

concepts.title: Inner and static nested classes
concepts.question: What can an inner class reach that a static nested class cannot?

paragraphs: A nested class is a class declared inside another class, and it is a member of the enclosing class. It may be private, public, protected or package-private, while a top-level class may only be public or package-private. Reasons to nest: group classes used in one place, let a helper reach the private members of its outer class, and keep small helpers close to their use.

An inner class (non-static) is tied to an instance of the outer class and can use that instance's fields and methods directly, even private ones. You create the outer object first, then the inner object within it.

A static nested class is tied to the outer class, not to an instance. Like a static method, it cannot use the outer instance members directly and needs an object reference. It is created the way a top-level class is, with no outer object.
Shadowing applies here too: a declaration in an inner scope hides a same-named one outside, so the innermost name wins. Qualify with this, or with the enclosing class name, to reach a hidden one.
card.example: A DataStructure holds an int array. Its inner class EvenIterator reads that array directly while stepping through the even positions.
card.rule: Use an inner class when the helper needs a particular outer object; use a static nested class when it does not.
card.limits: The tutorial strongly discourages serializing inner classes, because compiler-generated parts can differ between compilers.

concepts.title: Local and anonymous classes
concepts.question: What can a local or anonymous class capture, and what can it not declare?

paragraphs: A local class is a named class declared inside a block, such as a method body. It can use members of its enclosing class, and also local variables and parameters of the enclosing method, but only if they are final or effectively final, meaning never reassigned after initialization. Such a class is said to capture the variable.

An anonymous class is declared and instantiated in one expression, with no name, and suits a one-time use. It is written as new, then an interface or class name, then parentheses for constructor arguments, then a body in braces. Because it is an expression, the statement ends with a semicolon.

An anonymous class body may declare fields, extra methods, instance initializers and local classes, but not constructors. Both kinds follow the same capture rule, and neither may declare static initializers or member interfaces.
card.example: Greeter g = new Greeter() { public void greet() { System.out.println(5); } }; creates an unnamed implementation of the interface Greeter, used once.
card.rule: Use a local class for a named helper inside a block and an anonymous class for a one-off; both read only final or effectively final locals.
card.limits: In a static method a local class can use only static members of the enclosing class. Constant variables are the exception to the ban on static members.

concepts.title: Enums
concepts.question: What makes an enum different from an ordinary class, and what happens to switches when its constants change?

paragraphs: An enum is a class whose instances are all known to the compiler. It is declared with the enum keyword; the body begins with comma-separated constants, which are the only instances. You cannot create others with new. Every enum implicitly extends java.lang.Enum and has no named subclasses.

Compare constants with ==. A switch can branch on an enum, and a switch expression must cover every constant or the code does not compile, a property called exhaustiveness. After the constants, a semicolon introduces fields, constructors and methods; constructor arguments follow each constant name.

Built-in methods: name() and ordinal() on an instance, and static values() and valueOf(String). Changing constants later can cause compile errors, runtime errors when a default branch silently handles a new constant, and stored values that no longer match.
card.example: enum Light { RED, AMBER, GREEN } Light.GREEN.ordinal() is 2, and Light.values() returns an array of the three constants.
card.rule: An enum fixes its instances at compile time, so switch expressions over it can be checked for completeness.
card.limits: Adding a constant can break code that a default branch hides. With very many constants, the tutorial suggests a configuration file.

concepts.title: Choosing the right construct
concepts.question: Given what a piece of code needs, which of nested, local, anonymous or lambda is the lightest that works?

paragraphs: Nested classes, local classes, anonymous classes and lambda expressions all group code, encapsulate it and improve readability. The tutorial gives rules for choosing, based on what the code needs.

Use a local class when you need more than one instance, its constructor, or a new named type. Use an anonymous class when you need fields or extra methods. Use a lambda expression for one unit of behavior to pass to other code, or for a simple instance of a functional interface (an interface with one abstract method) when you need no constructor, named type, fields or extra methods.

Use a nested class when your needs resemble a local class's, you want the type more widely available, and you need no access to local variables or parameters. Choose an inner class if you need non-public members of an enclosing instance, and a static nested class if not.
card.example: Run an action on each element: lambda. A one-off object holding a call counter and an extra method: anonymous class. A type used by several methods of one class with no locals: nested class.
card.rule: Pick the lightest construct that supplies what you need: lambda for one behavior, anonymous for fields or methods, local for a named multi-instance type, nested for wider reach.
card.limits: These are guidelines from the tutorial, and real needs can overlap, so more than one choice may work.

concepts.unitTitle: Using Records to Model Immutable Data (dev.java)
concepts.title: What a record declaration gives you
concepts.question: What does the compiler build from a record header, and what may a record body still contain?

paragraphs: A record is declared with the record keyword and a header in parentheses. Each entry in the header is a component. For every component the compiler creates a private final field with the same name and an accessor method with the same name, so a component named x is read with x().

The compiler also supplies a canonical constructor that takes every component and stores it, plus toString, equals and hashCode in the default style an IDE would generate. You may override these generated methods. Because the compiler regenerates them from the components, they cannot fall out of date when you change the header.

The generated class is final and extends java.lang.Record, so a record cannot extend another class, but it may implement any number of interfaces. The body is restricted: no extra instance fields, no instance field initializers, no instance initializers. Static fields and static initializers are allowed.
card.example: A one-line declaration of a record named Pair with components String left and String right gives two private final fields, the accessors left() and right(), a constructor taking both values, and equals, hashCode and toString.
card.rule: A record header declares components, and the compiler derives the fields, accessors, canonical constructor and the three Object methods from them.
card.limits: The generated accessor returns the field as it is, so a mutable component such as a list can still be changed from outside unless you copy it. The body cannot hold extra instance state.

concepts.unitTitle: Using Records to Model Immutable Data (dev.java)
concepts.title: Canonical, compact and additional constructors
concepts.question: How do you validate or copy components in a record, and what must every other constructor do?

paragraphs: The canonical constructor takes all components and copies them into the fields. Override it for two reasons: to validate the state, and to make defensive copies of mutable components.

A compact canonical constructor has no parameter list. Your code runs first and the compiler assigns the fields afterwards. You cannot assign the fields yourself, but you may reassign the parameters, for example to an unmodifiable copy, and the new values are what get stored. An explicit canonical constructor has the full parameter list, and you must assign every field yourself.

A record may have more constructors, but each must call the canonical one with this(...). According to the tutorial, JDK 25 allows some statements before that call, with restrictions. Delegating means validation in the canonical constructor covers every way of creating the record.
card.example: A record Playlist with components String name and List of String tracks has a compact constructor that reassigns tracks to an unmodifiable copy. A second constructor taking only the name calls this(name, List.of()) to start with no tracks.
card.rule: Put validation and defensive copying in the canonical constructor, in compact form when you only check or reassign parameters, and have every other constructor delegate to it with this(...).
card.limits: A compact constructor cannot assign fields, so use the explicit form when you prefer to assign them yourself. A copy made at construction does not help if an accessor later hands out a mutable internal object; then copy there too.

concepts.unitTitle: Using Records to Model Immutable Data (dev.java)
concepts.title: Records in use: local records and serialization
concepts.question: Where do records pay off beyond a short declaration?

paragraphs: Records are handy for small throwaway data shapes. The tutorial counts cities per state with a stream, which yields a Map from state to count. Finding the maximum over raw Map.Entry objects reads badly because an entry carries no business meaning.

The tutorial fixes this with a local record, declared inside a method, that pairs a state with its count. It has a constructor taking a Map.Entry, and a static factory method supplies a comparator ordering by count. The maximum is then easy to read. The tutorial notes that on ties only one state is reported.

Records can implement Serializable with special rules. The methods writeObject and readObject have no effect, and Externalizable is not available. A record can be a serialization proxy through readResolve or writeReplace. Deserialization invokes the canonical constructor, so its validation also applies to incoming data, which suits data transport objects.
card.example: To rank products by sales, map each product entry to a local record named Ranked with the product name and total, then sort or take the maximum on the total instead of reading entry getters.
card.rule: Use a local record to give an intermediate result meaningful names, and rely on the canonical constructor to validate deserialized records.
card.limits: A local record is only visible inside its method, so it suits one-off shapes. The tutorial's maximum reports a single winner, so ties need extra handling. Serialization rules listed here are the tutorial's; it does not cover other cases.

concepts.title: What a subclass inherits
concepts.question: Which members does a subclass receive from its one superclass, and which does it not?

paragraphs: A subclass is a class derived from another class, its superclass. By inheriting, it receives the fields, methods and nested classes of the superclass, so tested code is reused instead of rewritten. Other names are child or derived class, and parent or base class.

Every class has exactly one direct superclass, except Object, which has none. A class that names no superclass becomes a subclass of Object, so every class sits at the end of a chain of ancestors that reaches Object.

Constructors are not members, so they are not inherited, although a subclass constructor may call the superclass constructor. Public and protected members are always inherited. Package-private members are inherited only inside the same package. Private members are not inherited directly, but public or protected accessor methods give access to them.
card.example: Class Vehicle, in package fleet, has a public method start, a private field serial and a public method getSerial. Class Truck extends Vehicle from package depot. A Truck method may call start and getSerial, but it cannot name serial.
card.rule: A subclass inherits the members that access rules let it see, never constructors, from exactly one direct superclass.
card.limits: Inheriting a member is different from being able to name it: private fields are reached only through accessors. Constructors need an explicit call. Single inheritance applies to classes; interfaces can be many.

concepts.title: Upcasting, downcasting and instanceof
concepts.question: When may a variable of a superclass type be treated as its subclass, and what protects that step?

paragraphs: A MountainBike is a Bicycle and an Object, so a MountainBike may be used wherever either type is expected. Assigning it to a variable of a superclass type needs no cast. This direction is called upcasting and is implicit.

The reverse is not guaranteed: a Bicycle variable may hold a MountainBike or may not. Assigning it to a MountainBike variable without a cast is a compile-time error, because the compiler cannot confirm the type.

An explicit cast, called downcasting, tells the compiler you expect that type. It adds a runtime check, and an exception is thrown if the object is of another type. Testing with instanceof first avoids the exception.
card.example: Object o = new Truck(); Truck t = o; fails to compile. Truck t = (Truck) o; compiles and works, since o really holds a Truck. if (o instanceof Truck) guards the cast.
card.rule: Upcast freely, and downcast only with an explicit cast guarded by instanceof, because the runtime checks the real type.
card.limits: The compiler accepts a cast on trust; only the runtime check protects you. A cast does not turn an object into another type, and a wrong guess throws an exception.

concepts.title: Overriding and hiding methods
concepts.question: How do overriding an instance method and hiding a static method differ in which version runs?

paragraphs: An instance method in a subclass with the same name, parameter types and return type overrides the superclass method. The return type may be a subtype of the original, which is a covariant return. A call runs the subclass version even through a superclass-typed variable. The annotation Override is optional but recommended: the compiler reports an error if nothing is overridden.

A static method with the same signature hides the superclass method. Which version runs depends on the class used in the call: a call through the superclass gives the superclass version, through the subclass the subclass version.

An overriding method may allow more access but not less, so protected may become public but not private. Turning an instance method into a static one, or the reverse, is a compile-time error. Changing the parameters creates an overload, a new method that neither overrides nor hides.
card.example: Light has turnOn and a static method kind returning light. Lamp extends Light and redefines both, kind returning lamp. With Light x = new Lamp(), x.turnOn() runs the Lamp version, but Light.kind() still returns light.
card.rule: Instance methods are overridden and chosen by the object; static methods are hidden and chosen by the class named in the call.
card.limits: A matching name is not enough: different parameter types make an overload, less access is an error, and mixing static with instance is a compile-time error.

concepts.title: Inherited interface methods: who wins
concepts.question: When a class inherits the same method from a class and from interfaces, which version is used?

paragraphs: Default and abstract interface methods are inherited much like instance methods. When a class inherits an instance method from a superclass and a default method with the same signature from an interface, the class method wins.
If two supertypes share an ancestor and one default method already overrides the other, the overridden one is ignored.

If two independent defaults conflict, or a default conflicts with an abstract method, the compiler reports an error and the class must override the method. Inside it, InterfaceName.super.method() calls the default of a chosen direct superinterface. Static interface methods are not inherited.
card.example: Interfaces Boat and Car each have a default move. Class Amphibian implements both, so it must declare move itself, and its body may call Boat.super.move() to reuse the Boat version.
card.rule: A class method beats a default, an overridden default is ignored, and any other clash must be resolved by overriding.
card.limits: Interface.super works only for a direct superinterface. Static interface methods are not inherited, so they do not take part in these conflicts.

concepts.title: Polymorphism, super and constructors
concepts.question: Which method runs when a superclass-typed variable holds a subclass object, and how do super and final fit in?

paragraphs: Polymorphism lets subclasses define their own behavior while sharing what the parent offers. With virtual method invocation, the JVM runs the method of the object's actual class, not of the variable's declared type. A Bicycle variable holding a RoadBike runs the RoadBike version of an overridden method.

Inside a subclass, a plain call to an overridden method runs the subclass version, and super.method() calls the superclass version. A field with the same name as an inherited field hides it, and super.field reaches the hidden one. The tutorial advises against hiding fields.

A constructor calls the superclass constructor with super() or super(arguments), as its first statement. According to the tutorial this holds until Java 25, which allows code before it. If none is written, the compiler adds super(), an error if the superclass has no no-argument constructor. Constructors chain up to Object.

A final method cannot be overridden, and a final class cannot be subclassed; String is one. The tutorial says methods called from constructors should generally be final, so a subclass cannot change what they do.
card.example: Staff has describe; Manager overrides it and calls super.describe() first. Staff s = new Manager(); s.describe() runs the Manager version, which then runs the Staff version.
card.rule: The object's class chooses the instance method, super reaches the parent version, and constructors chain upward starting with a super call.
card.limits: Choosing by the actual class applies to overridden instance methods. Hidden fields and hidden static methods are not overridden, so the declaration decides them.

concepts.title: Object methods worth overriding
concepts.question: Which methods does every class inherit from Object, and which of them should you override?

paragraphs: Object, in java.lang, is the root of the hierarchy, so every class inherits its instance methods: clone, equals, finalize, getClass, hashCode and toString, besides the thread methods wait and notify. The tutorial says to consider always overriding toString, since the default output helps mainly debugging.

By default equals compares identity, so it is true only for the same object. Override it when two objects with the same information should count as equal, as with two books sharing an ISBN. Equal objects must have equal hash codes, so overriding equals means overriding hashCode too.

getClass is final and returns a Class object describing the real class. clone needs the Cloneable interface, else it throws CloneNotSupportedException; the default copy shares referenced objects, so override clone to copy them as well.
finalize is deprecated, and deprecated for removal since Java 18. Its timing is uncertain, so do not use it for cleanup; the tutorial points to AutoCloseable.
card.example: Book overrides equals to compare ISBN. Two separate Book objects with the same ISBN are then equal, though they are different objects.
card.rule: Override toString, and override equals together with hashCode whenever identity is the wrong test; getClass cannot be overridden.
card.limits: Default equals is right when identity is the right test. Default clone makes a shallow copy. finalize is not a reliable way to release resources.

concepts.title: Abstract classes and interfaces
concepts.question: What can an abstract class do that an interface cannot, and when is each the better choice?

paragraphs: An abstract class is declared with abstract. It cannot be instantiated but can be subclassed, and it may or may not contain abstract methods, which have no body and end with a semicolon. A class with an abstract method must itself be abstract. A subclass usually implements all inherited abstract methods; otherwise it must be abstract too.

Neither abstract classes nor interfaces can be instantiated, and both may mix methods with and without bodies. Abstract classes can hold non-static, non-final fields and methods of any access. Interface fields are public static final. A class extends one class but implements many interfaces.

Use an abstract class to share code among closely related classes, or when subclasses need shared state or non-public members. Use an interface when unrelated classes implement it, when you describe behavior regardless of who provides it, or when you want multiple inheritance of type.
card.example: Abstract class Sprite holds position fields, a concrete moveTo method and an abstract draw method. Circle and Square extend Sprite and each write their own draw.
card.rule: Share code and state among related classes with an abstract class; describe behavior for any class with an interface.
card.limits: An abstract class implementing an interface need not implement every method; it stays abstract. Abstract classes can also have static members, called through the class name.

concepts.title: An interface as a contract
concepts.question: What does it mean to call an interface a contract between groups of programmers?

paragraphs: An interface is a reference type, much like a class, that works as a contract between groups of programmers. One group promises certain methods; another group writes code that calls them. Neither needs to see how the other side's code works.

According to the tutorial, a robotic car shows this. Car makers publish an interface listing control methods such as turning, braking and accelerating. Makers of guidance software call those methods without knowing how any particular car carries them out.

The same idea makes an interface an API. A company publishes the interface, and customers rely on its method signatures and return types. The company keeps its implementation private and may change it later, as long as it still implements the same interface.
card.example: A bank publishes an interface named PaymentGateway with a method pay that takes an amount. A shop's checkout code calls pay. The bank rewrites its internals next year, and the shop's code stays as it is.
card.rule: Treat an interface as a published promise of methods: callers depend on the signatures, and implementers stay free to change how they work.
card.limits: The contract fixes signatures and return types only. It says nothing about what happens inside a method, and changing the interface itself can still disturb the classes that implement it.

concepts.title: What an interface holds and how a class implements it
