concepts.question: What may an interface contain, which modifiers can be left out, and what must an implementing class do?

paragraphs: An interface body may hold constants, method signatures, default methods, static methods, private instance methods with a body, and nested types. Bodies appear only in default, private and static methods. An abstract signature ends with a semicolon and has no braces.

Some modifiers are implied. Abstract, default and static methods are implicitly public, and constants are implicitly public, static and final, so writing those words is optional. The interface itself is usable from any package only if you declare it public; otherwise it stays within its own package.

A class meets the contract with an implements clause. It can list several interfaces separated by commas, and the clause follows any extends clause. A class extends only one class, but an interface may extend any number of interfaces.
card.example: interface Counter { int START = 0; int next(); } and interface Resettable { void reset(); }. Then class Ticket extends Base implements Counter, Resettable. START is public static final without being written, and next is public and abstract.
card.rule: Write abstract signatures with a semicolon, rely on the implied modifiers, and list a class's interfaces after its extends clause.
card.limits: Implied public covers abstract, default and static methods and constants. A private interface method is marked private explicitly, and the interface declaration itself is public only when you write it.

concepts.title: Evolving an interface without breaking implementers
concepts.question: How can an interface gain new behavior without breaking the classes that already implement it?

paragraphs: Once classes implement an interface, changing it is risky. According to the tutorial, adding a new abstract method breaks the existing implementers, because each must now supply a body that it never wrote.

Two safer routes exist. One is a new sub-interface that extends the original and adds the method, so users pick the old or the new interface. The other is a default method, which carries a body, so existing implementers receive it unchanged. A static method with a body is also a safe addition.
card.example: interface Timer has void start(). The team wants stop. Writing void stop(); inside Timer breaks every implementer. Writing default void stop() { } keeps them compiling, and a new interface TimerPlus extends Timer { void stop(); } lets new code opt in.
card.rule: To grow a published interface, add a default or static method or a sub-interface, not a new abstract method.
card.limits: A default method needs a sensible body to be worth adding. According to the tutorial, it must not clash with a method that a class gets from another interface it implements.

concepts.title: Using an interface as a type
concepts.question: What does it mean that an interface is a type, and what can a variable of that type hold?

paragraphs: Defining an interface creates a new reference data type. Its name can be used anywhere another data type name can be used.

A variable of an interface type can hold only an object whose class implements that interface. So a method with a Relatable parameter accepts objects of any class that implements Relatable, whatever that class inherits from.

Such an object has two types: its own class, or superclass, and the interface. According to the tutorial, this gives some of the advantages of multiple inheritance, because an object can draw behavior from both a superclass and an interface.
card.example: interface Priced { double price(); }. A method cheaper(Priced a, Priced b) returns the one with the lower price. It works for a Book, a Ticket or a HotelStay, even though the three classes have unrelated parents.
card.rule: Declare variables and parameters with the interface type to accept any implementer, and call only what the interface promises.
card.limits: An interface-typed variable offers the interface's methods only, so the tutorial casts to the class before calling a class-specific method. Its comparison example also works only when both objects come from the same class.

concepts.title: Type parameters, type arguments and raw types
concepts.question: What is the difference between a type parameter and a type argument, and what changes if you leave the argument out?

paragraphs: According to the tutorial, generics let classes, interfaces and methods take types as parameters, much as a method takes values. The payoff is stronger compile-time checks, no casts when values are read back, and one algorithm that works over collections of many element types.

A generic class lists its type parameters, or type variables, after its name and uses them where a plain class would use Object. In a declaration of Foo with parameter T, T is the type parameter. In a use of Foo with String, String is the type argument. Supplying it is a generic type invocation, giving a parameterized type. Declaring such a variable creates no object; new does.

By convention a type parameter is one uppercase letter: E for element, K for key, V for value, N for number, T for type, and S or U for a second or third type. A class may have several parameters, and an argument can itself be a parameterized type.

A raw type is a generic name used with no arguments, such as plain Box. It exists for legacy code from before JDK 5 and behaves like the old class, returning Object. Assigning a parameterized value to a raw variable gives no warning; the reverse gives an unchecked warning. Avoid raw types, says the tutorial.
card.example: Imagine a class Crate with one type parameter T that stores one item. Here T is the type parameter. A variable declared as Crate of String, built with new Crate of String (angle brackets in real code), supplies String as the type argument, so reading the item gives a String with no cast. A plain Crate variable is raw and would hand back Object.
card.rule: A type parameter is the placeholder in a generic declaration, a type argument is the concrete type supplied at use, and omitting the argument gives an unsafe raw type.
card.limits: People often use the two terms loosely, but the tutorial keeps them apart. Raw types are legal for legacy code, yet they switch off generic checks, so mistakes surface only at run time.

concepts.title: Generic methods and bounded type parameters
concepts.question: How does a generic method declare its own type parameter, and what does a bound let the method body do?

paragraphs: A generic method declares its own type parameters in angle brackets placed before the return type. Their scope is that method alone, unlike a generic class whose parameters cover the whole class. Static and non-static methods can be generic, and so can constructors. Callers usually write no type argument because the compiler infers it.

A bounded type parameter limits which arguments are allowed. Write the parameter name, then extends, then the upper bound; here extends covers both extending a class and implementing an interface. A parameter bounded by Number accepts Number and its subclasses and rejects a String at compile time.

A bound also gives the body the bound's methods. With T bounded by Number, the body can call intValue on a T value. Without a bound only Object methods are available. A parameter may have several bounds, and then the type must be a subtype of all of them.

Bounds are what make generic algorithms possible. To count array elements greater than a given element, the greater-than operator cannot be used because it works only on primitive numeric types. Bounding T by Comparable of T and calling compareTo fixes it.
card.example: A static method largest takes two values of type T and returns the larger one. Its type parameter list comes before the return type and bounds T by Comparable of T (angle brackets in real code). The body calls a.compareTo(b). Without the bound, T is known only as Object and that call would not compile.
card.rule: Declare a method's own type parameters before its return type, and bound them with extends when the body needs the bound's methods.
card.limits: A bound admits only subtypes of the bound, and the parameter exists only inside its method. It unlocks only the bound's methods, not those of a more specific type.

concepts.title: Type inference, the diamond and target types
concepts.question: What information does the compiler use to infer type arguments, and when might you still write them yourself?

paragraphs: Type inference is the compiler's ability to look at a method call and its declaration and pick type arguments that make the call valid. It weighs the argument types, the type the result is assigned to or returned as when that is known, and the most specific type that fits all arguments. Writing the arguments yourself, before the method name, gives what the tutorial calls a type witness.

The diamond is an empty pair of angle brackets used in place of a constructor's type arguments; the compiler infers them from context. Leaving out even the diamond is a different thing: the call then names the raw type, and assigning it to a parameterized variable gives an unchecked conversion warning.

The target type of an expression is the type the compiler expects from the place where the expression appears. If a generic method returning a list of T is assigned to a variable of type list of String, the compiler infers String for T.

A lambda expression has no type of its own and takes its target type from its context. With overloaded methods, the compiler combines overload resolution with inference. If one overload takes Runnable, whose run method returns nothing, and another takes Callable, whose call method returns a value, a lambda that yields a value selects the Callable overload.
card.example: A generic method pick returns the first of two values of type T. The call pick with the Strings a and b needs no witness: both arguments are String, so T is inferred as String. Writing String as an explicit type argument before the method name states the same thing by hand. A diamond on new HashMap would likewise let the map's declared type fill in its arguments.
card.rule: Let the compiler infer from the arguments and the target type, use the diamond for constructors, and add a witness only when inference cannot decide.
card.limits: Inference uses only the call's arguments and target type, and an obvious expected return type, not code that appears later in the program. Where those do not settle a type argument, a witness is needed.

concepts.title: Why generics are not subtypes, and the three wildcards
concepts.question: Why is a list of Integer not a list of Number, and which wildcard forms bridge the gap?

paragraphs: Ordinary inheritance does not carry over to type arguments. Integer is a subtype of Number, yet Box of Integer is not a subtype of Box of Number. For two concrete types A and B, MyClass of A and MyClass of B are unrelated whatever A and B are. A method that takes Box of Number therefore rejects Box of Integer.

A wildcard is a question mark standing for an unknown type. An upper bounded wildcard, a question mark followed by extends and a bound, accepts that bound and its subtypes. A list with an upper bounded wildcard on Number matches lists of Integer, Double or Float, so one method can total any of them, reading each element as a Number.

An unbounded wildcard, a bare question mark, means a list of unknown type, and every list of some type is a subtype of it. Use it when the code needs only Object methods, or methods such as size and clear that do not depend on the type parameter. It differs from a list of Object, which accepts only lists declared as exactly that.

A lower bounded wildcard, a question mark followed by super and a bound, accepts that bound and its supertypes. A list with a lower bounded wildcard on Integer matches lists of Integer, Number or Object, so a method can add integers to any of them. A wildcard has an upper bound or a lower bound, not both.
card.example: A method printAll takes a list with an upper bounded wildcard on Number. It is called with a list of Integer holding 1, 2, 3 and then with a list of Double holding 0.5. Both calls compile, because each list type is a subtype of the wildcard type. A parameter declared as a list of Number would reject both.
card.rule: Generic types with different type arguments are unrelated; use extends for a family of subtypes, super for a family of supertypes, and a bare wildcard when the type does not matter.
card.limits: Wildcards buy flexibility at the price of operations: when the exact element type is unknown, not every value can be stored. The next idea shows what that means for reading and writing.

concepts.title: In and out variables, capture and helper methods
concepts.question: How do you choose between extends, super, a bare wildcard and no wildcard, and what is wildcard capture?

paragraphs: The tutorial frames each variable as an in variable, which supplies data to the code, or an out variable, which receives data. In a copy method with a source and a destination, the source is in and the destination is out. A variable can also be both.

Its guidelines: an in variable gets an upper bounded wildcard (extends); an out variable gets a lower bounded wildcard (super); an in variable that needs only Object methods gets the bare wildcard; a variable used as both in and out gets no wildcard. The guidelines are not for return types, where the tutorial advises avoiding wildcards because callers must then handle them.

Wildcard capture is the compiler giving an unknown type a temporary name while checking an expression. It matters mostly when an error message mentions capture of. Setting an element in a list of unknown type fails to compile, since the type cannot be confirmed. A private helper with its own type parameter lets the compiler capture the wildcard. By convention it takes the original name plus Helper.

A list with an extends wildcard is often called read-only, but the tutorial says that is not a strict guarantee. A capture helper also cannot rescue code that is itself unsafe, such as moving an Integer from a list of Integer into a list of Double.
card.example: A method copies temperature readings from a source list into a target list. The source is read, so it is typed with an upper bounded wildcard on Number. The target is written, so it is typed with a lower bounded wildcard on Number. A caller can copy from a list of Integer into a list of Object.
card.rule: Use extends for what you read from, super for what you write to, a bare wildcard when only Object methods matter, and no wildcard when a variable does both.
card.limits: The in and out advice is for parameters, not return types. It does not make extends lists strictly read-only, and a capture helper cannot make logically unsafe code safe.

concepts.title: Type erasure, bridge methods and heap pollution
concepts.question: What does the compiler change when it erases generic types, and how can erasure leave a variable pointing at the wrong type?

paragraphs: To implement generics the compiler applies type erasure. It replaces each type parameter with its first bound, or with Object when there is none; it inserts casts where needed for type safety; and it generates bridge methods to keep polymorphism in extended generic types. No new classes are made for parameterized types, so generics add no run-time overhead. Method type parameters are erased the same way.

A bridge method is a synthetic method the compiler creates when a class extends a parameterized class or implements a parameterized interface. Say a node class has setData taking T and a subclass for Integer overrides setData taking Integer. After erasure the parent method takes Object, so the compiler adds an Object-taking bridge in the subclass that casts and calls the real one.

A reifiable type has all its type information available at run time. A non-reifiable type lost information to erasure; a list of String and a list of Number look the same to the JVM. Heap pollution happens when a variable of a parameterized type refers to an object that is not of that type, usually after operations that raise unchecked warnings.

If code compiles with no unchecked warnings, the tutorial says heap pollution cannot occur. A generic varargs parameter becomes an array which, after erasure, is an Object array, so it can come to hold the wrong kind of list. The method then warns. If its body handles the parameter safely, SafeVarargs asserts that; SuppressWarnings on the declaration is less desirable and leaves call sites warning.
card.example: A class Bag has an unbounded T and a field of that type. In the compiled form the field has type Object, and the compiler adds a cast wherever a caller reads it as a String. Another class Ranked bounds its T by Comparable, so there the field is compiled as Comparable.
card.rule: Erasure turns each type parameter into its first bound or Object, adds casts and bridge methods, and leaves non-reifiable types without run-time type information.
card.limits: Warning-free code cannot pollute the heap. Reifiable types keep their information, and SafeVarargs is only honest for a method that really handles its varargs parameter safely.

concepts.title: What generic code is not allowed to do
concepts.question: Which operations does Java forbid on generic types, and which fact about erasure explains each ban?

paragraphs: Most restrictions on generics follow from erasure. You cannot create an instance of a type parameter with new T, because the real type is unknown at compile time; the tutorial's workaround is reflection. You cannot declare a static field whose type is a type parameter: the field is shared by all instances, yet different instances may use different type arguments.

Casts and instanceof tests with parameterized types are restricted because the runtime cannot tell a list of Integer from a list of String. An instanceof test against a type with an unbounded wildcard is allowed, since it checks only the raw type. A cast to a parameterized type is allowed with unbounded wildcards, or when the compiler can prove it valid.

You cannot create arrays of parameterized types. An array throws ArrayStoreException when the wrong kind of element is stored, which depends on the element type being known at run time. With erasure the same attempt on a generic list throws nothing, so allowing such arrays would open a gap in type safety.

A generic class cannot extend Throwable, directly or indirectly, and a method cannot catch an instance of a type parameter. Finally, two overloads cannot have parameter types that erase to the same raw type, such as one method taking a list of String and another a list of Integer.
card.example: A class Registry with parameter T tries four things: calling new T, declaring a static field of type T, creating an array of Lists of String, and declaring two overloads taking a list of String and a list of Integer. All four are rejected at compile time. The tutorial's way around the first is to create the object through reflection.
card.rule: Generic code cannot depend on run-time type arguments, so new T, static fields of type T, instanceof or casts on parameterized types, arrays of them, catching them and erased-identical overloads are forbidden.
card.limits: The bans concern type parameters and parameterized types, not everything generic. An instanceof test with an unbounded wildcard is allowed, and a cast the compiler can prove valid is accepted.

concepts.title: The type a lambda needs: a functional interface
concepts.question: What must be true of an interface before a lambda can be written for it?

paragraphs: A lambda always has a type known at compile time, taken from where it is used: a variable, a field, a method parameter or a return value. That type must be a functional interface, which is an interface with exactly one abstract method. An anonymous class whose type is not such an interface cannot be rewritten as a lambda.

Only abstract methods count toward the one. Default methods (instance methods with a body) and static methods are not counted. According to the tutorial, Runnable has one abstract method, Consumer has one plus a default method, and Predicate has one plus several default and static methods; all three qualify.

The annotation FunctionalInterface is optional. Adding it asks the compiler to verify the shape and to report an error when the interface is not functional. Without the annotation, an interface with the right shape is still functional.
card.example: Interface Shouter declares one abstract method that takes a String and returns a String, plus a default method whisper. A lambda that upper-cases its parameter can be assigned to a Shouter variable. If a second abstract method were added, the lambda would no longer compile, and a class would be needed.
card.rule: A lambda can only be written where the target type is an interface with exactly one abstract method, and the lambda supplies the body of that method.
card.limits: Counting abstract methods is the whole test: default and static methods are free, but two abstract methods rule a lambda out. The annotation only checks the shape; it does not create it.

concepts.title: Writing the lambda: parts, shortening and capture
concepts.question: How is a lambda written from the method it implements, and which outside variables may it use?

paragraphs: Writing a lambda takes three steps: identify its type, find the single abstract method, then implement that method. A lambda has three parts: a parameter block copied from the method, the arrow, and a body. The arrow in Java is the thin one made of a hyphen and a greater-than sign.

The compiler can infer parameter types, so they can be dropped. With exactly one parameter, its parentheses can go as well; zero parameters, or two or more, keep them. When the body is a single expression, the braces and the return keyword can be left out.

A lambda may read a local variable of the surrounding code only when that variable is final or effectively final, meaning it is never changed after its initialization. The lambda cannot change it. Otherwise the compiler reports an error.
card.example: To test whether a String has exactly five characters, the target is a Predicate of String. Its method takes a String and returns a boolean. Full form: a parameter String s, the arrow, then a body checking that s.length() equals 5. Shortened: s, the arrow, the same body. A Runnable that prints a message has no parameters, so it keeps empty parentheses.
card.rule: Copy the parameter list from the single abstract method, add the arrow and a body, drop what the compiler can infer, and only read outside locals that are effectively final.
card.limits: Parentheses can go only for exactly one parameter, and braces with return only for a single-expression body. Captured locals cannot be changed from inside, so a running total cannot be a plain local variable.

concepts.title: The four families of functional interfaces
concepts.question: How do Supplier, Consumer, Predicate and Function differ in what they take and return?

paragraphs: The package java.util.function holds about 40 functional interfaces, built around four. A Supplier takes nothing and returns an object, through get. A Consumer takes an argument and returns nothing, through accept. A Predicate takes an argument and returns a boolean, through test. A Function takes an argument and returns a result, through apply.

The rest are variations. Bi versions take two arguments: BiConsumer, BiPredicate and BiFunction. UnaryOperator is a Function whose input and result share one type; BinaryOperator does the same for two inputs. Primitive versions, such as IntPredicate or IntSupplier, avoid boxing; some rename the method, for example getAsInt and applyAsInt.
card.example: A lambda that reads the current temperature with no input is a Supplier. One that writes a log line is a Consumer. One that checks whether a name is blank is a Predicate. One that turns a name into its length is a Function. One that replaces every list element by its upper-case form fits UnaryOperator.
card.rule: Choose the family by shape: nothing in and a value out is a Supplier, a value in and nothing out is a Consumer, a value in and a boolean out is a Predicate, and a value in and a result out is a Function.
card.limits: The families describe shapes, not meaning; a Predicate is a Function that returns boolean. Primitive versions help only with primitive values, and boxing matters mostly in hot code, not around database or network calls.

concepts.title: Reading the four kinds of method reference
concepts.question: How do you read a method reference and rebuild the lambda it stands for?

paragraphs: When a lambda only calls an existing method, a method reference can take its place. It is written with a double colon. There are four kinds: static, unbound, bound and constructor. The functional interface the reference is assigned to decides how many arguments the call receives.

A static reference names a type and a static method, so Math::sqrt stands for a lambda that passes its argument to Math.sqrt. An unbound reference names a type and an instance method, such as String::length. The object is not written in the reference; it arrives as the first argument of the lambda.

A bound reference names an object and an instance method, such as System.out::println: the object is fixed in advance. A constructor reference ends in new, as in ArrayList::new. A constructor reference cannot be read without knowing the target type.
card.example: A Function from String to Integer set to String::length is the lambda with parameter s and body s.length(). With a local String variable greeting, the reference greeting::length is bound: no argument arrives and the receiver is fixed. A Supplier of a list of String set to ArrayList::new calls the no-argument constructor.
card.rule: To read a method reference, look at the target functional interface and rebuild the lambda: a type before the colons with an instance method means the first argument is the receiver, an object before them means the receiver is fixed.
card.limits: A reference fits only when the lambda does nothing but call one existing method. Unbound references can look confusing at first, so rebuild the lambda from the target type. Constructor references cannot be read without it.

concepts.title: Combining predicates, consumers and functions
concepts.question: How can small predicates, consumers and functions be joined into bigger ones?

paragraphs: A functional interface has one abstract method, so its helpers for combining are default methods that the JDK already supplies. Predicate gives and, or and negate. Each takes or returns a Predicate, so small tests such as not null, not empty and shorter than five characters can be chained into one test.

Consumer has a default method that joins two consumers: the first runs, then the second. For functions, f1.andThen(f2) and f2.compose(f1) both apply f1 first and f2 second, and give the same function; the first reads left to right, the second right to left. The result type of f1 must fit the input type of f2.
card.example: With isLong (length over eight) and startsWithA, the test isLong.and(startsWithA) accepts only long names that begin with A. With trim and upper as functions, trim.andThen(upper) trims first and then upper-cases, and upper.compose(trim) is the same function.
card.rule: Chain predicates with and, or and negate, run consumers one after the other, and join functions with andThen or compose, which both run the inner function first.
card.limits: Chains help only while they stay readable; the tutorial says a chain of or and negate can go a little too far. Function chains need each result type to fit the next input type.

concepts.title: The comparator contract and the subtraction trap
concepts.question: What must a comparator return, and why is subtracting two integers a risky shortcut?

paragraphs: Comparator is a functional interface whose one abstract method, compare, takes two objects and returns an int. It returns a negative number when the first is smaller, a positive number when the first is larger, and zero when they rank equal. Swapping the arguments must flip the sign.

For integers, the tutorial recommends the static method Integer.compare, usable as the reference Integer::compare. It warns against returning the first minus the second: this seems to work but has corner cases where it fails. The tutorial does not name the cause.
card.example: Beyond the tutorial: with the first value 2000000000 and the second minus 2000000000, the true difference 4000000000 does not fit in an int and wraps to a negative number, so the larger value would be reported smaller. Integer.compare returns a positive number here.
card.rule: A comparator returns negative, zero or positive for first smaller, equal or larger, with opposite signs when the arguments are swapped, and for integers it should use Integer.compare rather than subtraction.
card.limits: Returning zero for objects that are equal is not strictly required by the tutorial. The subtraction warning concerns numeric differences; a comparator over any other key must still follow the sign contract.

concepts.title: Building comparators with comparing, thenComparing and reversed
concepts.question: How do comparing, thenComparing, reversed and the null helpers build comparators from small parts?

paragraphs: Comparator.comparing takes a function that extracts a sort key and returns a comparator ordering by that key; the key must be Comparable. So comparing with User::getName orders users by name. The method thenComparing adds a second comparator that is consulted only when the first returns zero; an overload takes a key function such as User::getLastName.

The variants comparingInt, comparingLong and comparingDouble, and thenComparingInt and its siblings, avoid boxing for primitive keys. Comparator.naturalOrder uses compareTo for any Comparable. Calling reversed on any comparator gives the opposite order, and List.sort takes the comparator.
Comparing a null can throw a NullPointerException. The wrappers nullsFirst and nullsLast take an existing comparator and place nulls at the start or end; the wrapped comparator orders the rest.
card.example: To sort Book objects by page count, then by title, write comparingInt with Book::getPages, then thenComparing with Book::getTitle. For books whose title may be null, wrap the title comparator with nullsLast around naturalOrder.
card.rule: Build a comparator from a key function with comparing, break ties with thenComparing, flip it with reversed, and wrap with nullsFirst or nullsLast when keys may be null.
card.limits: thenComparing is consulted only on a tie. The key given to comparing must be Comparable. The primitive variants matter only for primitive keys, and the wrappers matter only when nulls can occur.

concepts.title: Type patterns with instanceof
concepts.question: What three elements does every pattern match have, and what does a type pattern give you once it succeeds?

paragraphs: Pattern matching tests a target against a pattern and reports a result. Regular expressions are the familiar case: the tutorial searches a poem for a whole word, so the text is the target, the expression is the pattern, and the result is where the word starts and ends. Every pattern match has these three elements: a matched target, a pattern and a result.

Since Java 16 the instanceof operator accepts a pattern. The target is its left operand, which can be any object. The pattern is a type followed by a new variable, such as String s, and is called a type pattern. The type may be a class, an abstract class or an interface, so a String target also matches a pattern that names CharSequence.

On success the new variable, called a pattern variable, holds a reference to the target with the matched type, so no cast is needed. It exists only when the match succeeded. That is why it may be used on the right of an and operator, which runs only after the test passed. It also stays in scope after an if statement whose branch always leaves by return or exception.

The compiler rejects impossible matches. String is final, so a variable of an unrelated type can never hold a String, and testing it against String does not compile. The tutorial also rewrites the equals method of a Point class: the classic cast-and-test version becomes much shorter and easier to read with a pattern.
card.example: static int length(Object o) { if (!(o instanceof String s)) { return 0; } return s.length(); } The if branch always returns, so s is in scope on the last line.
card.rule: A type pattern tests the type and, on success, gives a typed variable that is valid only where the match is known to have succeeded.
card.limits: The variable is not available where the match may have failed, for example after an if branch that can finish normally. Impossible matches do not compile.

concepts.title: Type patterns and guards in switch
concepts.question: How can a switch pick a branch by the type of its selector, and how do you add a condition to one case?

paragraphs: Pattern matching for switch is final in JDK 21 and was a preview feature in Java 17 to 20. The target is the selector expression, and each case label may now be a type pattern, written like the one after instanceof. A chain of if statements that each test one type can become one switch with a type pattern per case, which the tutorial finds more readable.

According to the tutorial, an if-else-if chain takes time proportional to its number of branches, while a switch is described as constant time. Before type patterns, a selector could be a byte, short, char or int, one of the wrappers Byte, Short, Character or Integer, a String, or an enumerated type. A long was not accepted.

A case label cannot be a plain boolean condition. To add one, follow the type pattern with the word when and a boolean expression. That expression is a guard, and the whole label is a guarded case label. A label for a String that is not empty combines the type pattern String s with the guard that s is not empty.
card.example: A switch statement over Object o declares int size. The label case String s when !s.isEmpty() sets size to s.length() and then breaks. The label case Integer i sets size to i and breaks. The default label sets size to 0.
card.rule: Put a type pattern in a case label to branch on type, and add a when guard when the type alone is not enough.
card.limits: A guard comes only after a type pattern; a bare condition cannot be a case label. Selector types outside the tutorial's list, such as long, are not covered.

concepts.title: Record patterns and deconstruction
concepts.question: How does a record pattern take a record apart, and which rules govern the patterns for its components?

paragraphs: A record is an immutable class, introduced in Java 16, whose declared parts are its components. A record pattern takes such a record apart. It is final in Java 21 and was a preview feature in 19 and 20. It is the record name followed by one type pattern per component, such as Point(int x, int y) for a record with components x and y.

If the target is a Point, the pattern variables are created and filled by calling the record's accessor methods, so an accessor that returns a defensive copy changes what you receive. The component patterns follow the canonical constructor's signature, whatever other constructors the record declares. A pattern that does not fit that signature does not compile.

A component pattern may use var, or a type that extends the component's declared type; a type unrelated to the component does not compile. Record patterns do not apply boxing or unboxing, so an int component needs an int pattern. Patterns can be nested: a component can itself be taken apart by another record pattern.

The tutorial names three places where patterns apply, as final or preview features: the instanceof operator, the switch statement and expression, and the enhanced for loop. All three accept type patterns and record patterns. It adds that more kinds of pattern and more constructs are expected, and that the page will change.
card.example: record Range(int low, int high) {} then: if (o instanceof Range(int lo, int hi)) { System.out.println(hi - lo); } The variables lo and hi hold the two components when o is a Range.
card.rule: A record pattern names the record and gives one fitting pattern per component, binding each component value to a variable.
card.limits: Every component needs a pattern of a compatible type, and no boxing or unboxing happens. The tutorial covers only type and record patterns, and says the feature set was still growing.

concepts.unitTitle: Refactoring from the Imperative to the Functional Style (dev.java)
concepts.title: Imperative versus functional style
concepts.question: What does imperative code spell out that functional code leaves to the library?

paragraphs: According to the tutorial, imperative style tells the computer both what to do and how to do it, step by step. Functional style is declarative: you state what you want and delegate the mechanics to library code.

A classic index loop has two layers. The essence is the range of values and the action done on each. The ceremony is the loop syntax and the manual stepping of the index variable. Refactoring keeps the essence and sheds the ceremony.

A for loop is an external iterator: your own code controls the stepping. A stream method such as forEach is an internal iterator: the stream steps through the values and you supply only the action for each one.

The tutorial advises refactoring opportunistically, when you fix a bug or make an enhancement, rather than in one sweeping rewrite. After each change, confirm behaviour is unchanged, ideally with existing automated tests.
card.example: A loop declares n, tests n against 5, bumps n after each pass and sends n to a printer. The essence is the numbers 0 to 4 and the printing. Declaring, testing and bumping n are ceremony that a stream would handle itself.
card.rule: Keep the essence (values and action), drop the ceremony (index handling), and verify behaviour after each change.
card.limits: The tutorial grants that imperative code is easier to write at first because it is familiar, and functional code takes practice. Convert when you are already touching the code, not as a goal in itself.

concepts.unitTitle: Refactoring from the Imperative to the Functional Style (dev.java)
concepts.title: Index loops become range and rangeClosed
concepts.question: Which IntStream factory matches a loop that excludes its end value, and which one includes it?

paragraphs: According to the tutorial, an index loop that steps by one over a known range can be written with IntStream.range. Its first argument is included, its second is excluded, and forEach then supplies the action for each value.

If the loop test allows the final value, with less-than-or-equal, the tutorial maps it to IntStream.rangeClosed, which includes both ends. The clue to look for is an index running over a range of values.
A method reference such as System.out::println can replace a lambda when the action passes each value straight to one existing method.
card.example: A loop starts month at 1, keeps going while month is at most 12, and calls show with month. The end is included, so use IntStream.rangeClosed with 1 and 12 and pass each value to show with forEach.
card.rule: Strictly-below test with step one maps to range; at-most test with step one maps to rangeClosed; the action goes in forEach.
card.limits: Both factories walk upward by one. A loop that skips values or leaves through a break needs a different tool, which the next idea covers.

concepts.unitTitle: Refactoring from the Imperative to the Functional Style (dev.java)
concepts.title: Stepped loops use iterate, and break becomes takeWhile
concepts.question: How do the three parts of a for header map onto iterate, and what takes the place of break?

paragraphs: According to the tutorial, a loop that skips values is best converted with IntStream.iterate rather than by filtering a range. The header parts map directly: the start becomes the seed, the loop test becomes an IntPredicate, and the step becomes an IntUnaryOperator.

So a loop starting at 0, continuing while the value is below 15 and adding 3 each pass becomes iterate with seed 0, a test saying below 15, and a step adding 3, followed by forEach. The semicolons turn into commas and the test and step become lambdas.

A loop with no test that leaves through break maps to the two-argument iterate, with only a seed and a step, which yields an endless stream. Adding takeWhile ends the stream at the first value failing its predicate; this is the functional break.
card.example: A loop starts s at 5, adds 5 each pass and breaks once s exceeds 22. The rewrite is iterate with seed 5 and step add 5, then takeWhile with a predicate keeping s at most 22. The values seen are 5, 10, 15 and 20.
card.rule: Seed, test and step become the three arguments of iterate; a break becomes takeWhile with the keep-going condition, which is the opposite of the break test.
card.limits: takeWhile stops at the first failing value, so write the condition to keep going, not the one to break. Loops stepping by one belong to range or rangeClosed.

concepts.unitTitle: Refactoring from the Imperative to the Functional Style (dev.java)
concepts.title: foreach becomes forEach, and an if becomes filter
concepts.question: Where does the if inside a foreach loop go when the loop is rewritten with streams?

paragraphs: According to the tutorial, the enhanced for loop is sugar for a while loop over an iterator. A plain one converts directly: call forEach on the collection and pass a lambda that receives each element. The collection advances itself, so this is an internal iterator.
A variant calls stream first and then forEach, since forEach exists on both Collection and Stream.
The method filter lives only on streams. The tutorial says this is by design, so that several intermediate operations can be chained before a terminal one such as forEach or findFirst.
An if that selects elements inside the loop becomes filter with a predicate. Elements for which it gives true pass on; the rest are discarded.
card.example: A loop goes over cities and prints each city whose name has more than five letters. The stream version calls stream on cities, filter with a test of length above five, then forEach to print.
card.rule: A plain foreach becomes forEach on the collection; a foreach with a selecting if becomes stream, filter, forEach.
card.limits: filter only selects and passes elements on unchanged. If the loop body also changes the element, filter alone is not enough; the next lesson adds map.

concepts.unitTitle: Refactoring from the Imperative to the Functional Style (dev.java)
concepts.title: Transformation becomes map, with filter first
concepts.question: Which stream operation replaces a transformation inside a loop, and where does filter sit relative to it?

paragraphs: According to the tutorial, wherever a loop body transforms each value, use map in the functional style. map takes a function and produces a stream of the results, which later steps such as forEach then use.

Moving a loop that uppercases and prints names straight into one forEach lambda keeps both jobs in one place. The tutorial calls that version not cohesive, hard to read and hard to change. First split the work into separate steps, then convert: map for the change, forEach for the printing.
If an if also chooses which values get transformed, the order is stream, filter, map, then the terminal action. Method references can shorten the lambdas.
card.example: A loop goes over product codes, skips codes whose length is not 6, and prints the lowercase form of the others. The stream version is stream, filter on length equal to 6, map to lowercase, forEach to print.
card.rule: A selecting if becomes filter, a transforming statement becomes map, and filter comes before map.
card.limits: map changes values one for one and decides nothing about which to keep; filter decides which to keep and changes nothing. Splitting the work first matters when one lambda does both.

concepts.unitTitle: Refactoring from the Imperative to the Functional Style (dev.java)
concepts.title: Reading an external source as a stream
concepts.question: How can a loop that reads a file line by line and counts matches be replaced?

paragraphs: According to the tutorial, before looping over data from an external resource, ask whether there is a way to get a stream over its contents. The JDK or a library may already provide one. Ranges suit fixed numbers, but much real data comes from files.

An imperative line counter opens a buffered reader and runs a while loop that reads one line at a time. An if increments a counter when the line contains the word. This is an external iterator and it mixes reading with checking.

The functional version gets a stream of lines from Files.lines in java.nio.file, applies filter for the word test and ends with count. The reading boilerplate disappears, filter replaces the if, and count replaces the counter variable.
card.example: To count log lines holding a given level text, take Files.lines on the log path, apply filter with a test that the line contains the level text, and end with count. No reader, loop or counter variable is written.
card.rule: Look first for a stream over the resource, then express the if as filter and the counter as count.
card.limits: This works where the JDK or a library offers a stream for the resource. Without such a source the pipeline has nothing to start from, so the search for one comes first.

concepts.unitTitle: Refactoring from the Imperative to the Functional Style (dev.java)
concepts.title: Matching loop cues to stream operations
concepts.question: Which cue in a loop points to which stream operation?

paragraphs: Across the lessons the tutorial links loop cues to operations. An index over a range points to range or rangeClosed. A step other than one points to iterate. A break points to takeWhile. A foreach points to forEach on the collection.

Inside the body, an if that selects points to filter, and a statement that transforms data points to map. Counting matches points to count. Data from an external resource calls for a search for a stream over it.
Cues can combine, so one loop may need several operations in order: source, then filter, then map, then a terminal step. Apply the mapping one cue at a time and recheck behaviour after each change.
card.example: A loop starts y at 2000, adds 4 while y is at most 2024, and prints y when y is not a multiple of 100. Cues: step and test give iterate; the if gives filter; the print gives forEach.
card.rule: Read the loop for its cues, map each to its operation, and chain them as source, filter, map, terminal.
card.limits: The mapping covers the loop shapes the tutorial shows; it does not say every loop should be converted. Refactor when touching the code and verify behaviour each time.

concepts.title: Annotations as metadata, and how they are written
concepts.question: What does an annotation do to the code it is attached to, and how is one written?

paragraphs: An annotation is metadata: information about a program that is not part of its logic. According to the tutorial it has no direct effect on the code it marks. Its value comes from what reads it: the compiler (to report errors or hide warnings), tools at build or deployment time (to generate code or XML files), and sometimes the running program.

An annotation starts with an at sign followed by its name. It may carry elements, each a name and a value. If the only element is called value, the name may be left out. If there are no elements, the parentheses may be left out. Several annotations can sit on one declaration, and by convention each goes on its own line.

Annotations go on declarations such as classes, fields and methods. Since Java SE 8, according to the tutorial, they can also go wherever a type is used: in a new expression, a cast, an implements clause or a throws clause.

The tutorial lists predefined ones: Override (the method must override a superclass method, or the compiler reports an error), Deprecated (the compiler warns when the element is used), SuppressWarnings (hides named warning categories) and FunctionalInterface (the type is meant to be a functional interface).
card.example: A class Report has a method render marked with Override. The marking changes nothing about how render runs. If render misspells the superclass method name, the compiler reads the annotation and reports an error, so the mistake shows up early.
card.rule: Treat an annotation as information for readers such as the compiler and tools, written with an at sign, and short forms apply only when elements are named value or absent.
card.limits: The no-effect statement is about the annotated code itself. The build can still change, since tools act on annotations. The short form for a lone element works only when that element is named value.

concepts.title: Declaring annotation types and controlling them
concepts.question: Which settings decide how long an annotation is kept, where it may go, and who inherits it?

paragraphs: You declare your own annotation type like an interface, with an at sign before the interface keyword. Elements are declared like methods and may have default values. Once defined, the annotation is applied with values filled in. Many such annotations replace a comment header that a team would otherwise copy at the top of each class.

Annotations placed on annotation types are meta-annotations. Retention says how long it is kept: SOURCE (source code only), CLASS (kept by the compiler but ignored by the JVM) or RUNTIME (kept by the JVM, so running code can read it). Documented makes the annotation appear in generated Javadoc, which leaves it out by default.

Target limits where the annotation can be applied, for example to METHOD, FIELD, PARAMETER, TYPE or TYPE_USE. Inherited lets a subclass pick up the annotation from its superclass; it is off by default and, according to the tutorial, applies only to class declarations.
card.example: A team writes an annotation type Owner with an element name, then marks it with Retention RUNTIME and Target TYPE. A tool can now read, while the program runs, which person owns each class, and the compiler stops the annotation from being placed on a field.
card.rule: Define an annotation type with at sign interface, then use Retention, Target, Documented and Inherited on it to set how long it lives, where it goes, whether Javadoc shows it and whether subclasses inherit it.
card.limits: Each meta-annotation controls one thing. Inherited covers class declarations only, so it does not carry an annotation from an overridden method to its override, and Retention does not limit where the annotation may be placed.

concepts.title: Repeating annotations and type annotations
concepts.question: What must be declared to apply one annotation twice, and what are type annotations for?

paragraphs: Repeating annotations (Java SE 8) let the same annotation type appear more than once on one declaration, such as a schedule applied once for the last day of the month and once for Fridays. For compatibility the compiler stores the repeats inside a generated container annotation.

Two declarations make this work. First mark the annotation type with Repeatable, naming the container type. Second declare the container, with an element called value whose type is an array of the repeatable type. Repeating without the Repeatable marking causes a compile-time error.
To read repeats through reflection, getAnnotation returns a single annotation and works only when one is present, while getAnnotationsByType returns all of them.

Type annotations may be placed wherever a type is used. Java SE 8 ships no type-checking framework; instead, checkers can be plugged into the compiler. With a NonNull-style annotation on a variable and a checker included, the compiler warns about possible null use.
card.example: Alert is marked Repeatable with container Alerts, and Alerts has a value element holding an array of Alert. A class Office can then carry two Alert annotations, one for managers and one for admins, and getAnnotationsByType on Office returns both.
card.rule: To repeat an annotation, mark it Repeatable naming a container whose value is an array of it, and read the repeats with getAnnotationsByType.
card.limits: A type annotation records a claim and checks nothing until a checker is plugged into the compiler. The getAnnotation call returns a single annotation only when one use exists; with repeats, the container or getAnnotationsByType is needed.

concepts.title: What an exception is and how it travels
concepts.question: What happens, step by step, between the moment an error occurs and the moment something handles it?

paragraphs: An exception is short for exceptional event: something that happens while a program runs and breaks the normal order of its instructions. When an error occurs inside a method, the method builds an exception object that records the kind of problem and the state of the program at that moment.

Creating that object and handing it to the runtime system is called throwing. The runtime then looks for a handler, a block of code able to deal with the problem. It starts in the method where the error happened and works backward through the call stack, the ordered list of methods that were called to get there.

A handler fits when its declared type matches the type of the thrown object. When the runtime passes the exception to it, the handler is said to catch it. If the search ends with no match, the thread ends; when that thread is the main thread, the whole program ends.
card.example: Method a calls b, and b calls c, and c fails. The runtime checks c first, then b, then a. If only a has a matching handler, a catches the exception, and c and b are abandoned. If none of them has one, the thread stops.
card.rule: A thrown exception object is passed back along the call stack to the first method with a handler whose type matches.
card.limits: Matching is by type, so a nearer handler for an unrelated type is skipped. With no match anywhere, the thread ends, and the program ends too if it was the main thread.

concepts.title: Checked, error and runtime: the catch or specify rule
concepts.question: How do the three kinds of exception differ, and which of them must be caught or declared?

paragraphs: Java sorts exceptions into three kinds. A checked exception is a condition a well-written application should expect and recover from, such as a mistyped file name. An error is external to the application, such as a hardware fault while reading, and the program usually cannot foresee or recover from it. A runtime exception is internal, usually a bug, such as null passed where it is not allowed.

Errors and runtime exceptions, with their subclasses, are together called unchecked. Every other exception is checked. Checked ones fall under the catch or specify requirement: code that may throw one must sit inside a try statement that catches it, or inside a method whose throws clause lists it. Code that breaks the requirement does not compile.
Unchecked exceptions are exempt from the requirement. For a runtime exception such as an unexpected null, the tutorial says it makes more sense to fix the bug than to catch the exception.
card.example: A program asks for a file name and opens that file. A mistyped name is a checked case: catch it and ask again. A disk failing in the middle of reading is an error. A coding slip that passes null as the name is a runtime exception.
card.rule: Checked exceptions must be caught or declared; errors and runtime exceptions need neither.
card.limits: The requirement is a compile rule, not a safety net: unchecked exceptions can still be thrown and can still end a thread. The tutorial adds that using unchecked types only to dodge the rule is generally not recommended.

concepts.title: Catching: try, catch, finally and resources
concepts.question: When an exception strikes inside a try block, which catch block runs, and what still runs afterward?

paragraphs: Risky code goes in a try block, followed directly by one or more catch blocks, with no code between them. Each catch declares an exception type that must be Throwable or a subclass. The first catch that matches the thrown object, tested in order, runs. A broader type may not come before a narrower one, because the narrower catch could never run, and the compiler rejects that.
One catch can list several types separated by a vertical bar, when the handling is the same. The listed types may not be related by subclassing, and the catch parameter is implicitly final.

A finally block runs whenever the try block exits: normally, by exception, or through return, continue or break. It suits cleanup. It is not guaranteed if the JVM exits during try or catch. If finally itself throws, that exception replaces an earlier one.

Try-with-resources declares resources in parentheses after try. Each must implement AutoCloseable, and its close method runs automatically, in reverse order of creation. If the body and a close both throw, the body's exception surfaces and the close failures are attached as suppressed ones.
card.example: A method opens a writer inside try, with a catch for IOException and a finally that closes the writer. If opening fails, the catch runs, then finally. If all goes well, finally still runs and closes the writer. With try-with-resources, the writer is declared in parentheses and no finally is needed for closing.
card.rule: Put narrow catches before broad ones, and do cleanup in finally or with try-with-resources.
card.limits: Finally does not run if the JVM exits in try or catch, and an exception thrown from finally hides the one from try. Try-with-resources avoids that hiding: the body's exception surfaces and close failures become suppressed.

concepts.title: Declaring, throwing and chaining exceptions
concepts.question: When should a method declare an exception instead of catching it, and how do you throw, chain or define one?

paragraphs: A method need not handle every exception itself. A caller higher in the stack may know better how to respond, especially when the method is library code. A method that does not catch the checked exceptions it can meet must list them in a throws clause: the word throws and comma-separated types, after the parameter list and before the opening brace. Listing unchecked ones is optional.

Any code may raise an exception with a throw statement, which takes one argument: an object of Throwable or a subclass. Throwable has two direct children: Error, for hard failures of the JVM that simple programs leave alone, and Exception, for problems most programs deal with.

Chaining records that one exception caused another. A handler that throws a different exception can pass the original into the new one, and getCause later returns it. A stack trace, read with getStackTrace, lists the classes and methods that were active, which makes it a main debugging aid.

Write your own exception class when the platform has no fitting type, when users should tell your errors apart from other packages', when you throw several related exceptions, or when your package should stand alone. The tutorial advises extending Exception directly, not Error, and ending the class name with Exception.
card.example: A method readConfig reads a file. It catches the low level IOException, wraps it in a new ConfigException with the original as the cause, and throws that. Its header declares throws ConfigException, so its callers must catch or declare it in turn.
card.rule: Declare checked exceptions you do not handle, raise with throw, and chain the original when you translate one.
card.limits: Throws is required only for checked exceptions. A custom class is worth writing only for the listed reasons; otherwise, the tutorial says, a platform class is probably enough.

concepts.title: The unchecked exception controversy
concepts.question: What does the tutorial argue about choosing between checked and unchecked, and what rule does it end with?

paragraphs: Because unchecked exceptions need no catching or declaring, it is tempting to throw only those, or to make every custom exception extend RuntimeException. Both silence the compiler. According to the tutorial, both sidestep the purpose of the catch or specify rule and can cause problems for people who use your classes.

Its argument for checked: any exception a method can throw is part of its public interface, like parameters and return value, so callers must know what to expect in order to choose a response. Its argument for unchecked: runtime exceptions signal programming errors such as dividing by zero or a bad index, clients usually cannot recover, and declaring them everywhere would clutter code.

Its bottom line: if a client can reasonably be expected to recover, make it checked; if not, make it unchecked. Throwing a runtime exception such as NullPointerException is common when a caller misuses a method, for instance by passing null where it is forbidden.
card.example: A payment method gets a card the bank declined. The caller can ask for another card, so the failure is checked. The same method gets a null amount because of a caller bug. Nothing at run time can repair that, so an unchecked exception fits.
card.rule: Make an exception checked when the caller can reasonably recover and unchecked when it cannot, not by what is shorter to write.
card.limits: This is the tutorial's recommendation on a contested design point. Whether a caller can reasonably recover is a judgment, not a test the compiler applies, and recovering means handling at run time, not fixing the code.

concepts.title: Two roots and a side category: the shape of the framework
concepts.question: Which interfaces are the roots of the framework, and how do queues, stacks and iterators fit around them?

paragraphs: According to the tutorial, the Collections Framework is a set of interfaces that model containers, with at least one implementation for each interface. Knowing the implementations matters as much as knowing the interfaces, because the right choice depends on the task.

There are two main categories. A collection stores objects and lets you iterate over them; its root interface is Collection, which extends Iterable. A map stores key and value pairs, where the key identifies the object much like a primary key in a database; its root is Map. The two hierarchies have no direct relationship.

Queues and stacks are interfaces inside the Collection hierarchy, so they can be iterated even though iteration is not their main job. An iterator is an object that walks over a collection, and the tutorial treats the Iterator hierarchy as a side category. Iterable is not part of the framework, but Collection inherits from it.
card.example: A program keeps invoices that are looked up by invoice number, and also a waiting line of print jobs. The invoices fit the Map category, because each number identifies one invoice. The print jobs fit Queue, which sits inside the Collection hierarchy, so the jobs can also be iterated.
card.rule: Place any container first as a Collection (with Queue inside it) or as a Map, and remember that the two hierarchies are unrelated.
card.limits: This is a map of interfaces, not a ranking and not a choice of implementation. A Map is not a Collection, even though the tutorial later shows that a map has parts that behave like sets and collections.

concepts.title: Choosing an interface and implementation, and when an array is enough
concepts.question: What decides the interface and the implementation you pick, and when is a plain array still the better tool?

paragraphs: According to the tutorial, you choose the interface by the functionality you need: storing and iterating, pushing and popping through a queue, retrieving by key, accessing by index, sorting, or preventing duplicates or nulls. You then choose the implementation by how it will be used: iteration or random access, fixed or changing contents, many membership checks, and concurrent access.

The tutorial lists legacy classes kept for backward compatibility. Vector is replaced by ArrayList in non-concurrent code, and Stack, which extends Vector, by ArrayDeque. Enumeration is replaced by Iterator, and Hashtable by HashMap, or by ConcurrentHashMap in concurrent code.

If a simple solution you have mastered, such as an array, fits your needs, keep it. A collection earns its place when you need it to know its own size, to have no fixed capacity, to reject elements such as null, to test whether an element is present, or to intersect or merge with another collection.
card.example: A checkout screen always shows exactly three payment buttons, so a three-slot array is enough. A list of customers waiting for refunds grows and shrinks and must answer whether a given name is present, so a collection suits that job better.
card.rule: Pick the interface from the functionality you need, then the implementation from how you will use it, and keep a mastered array when it already fits.
card.limits: The legacy list says what the tutorial advises against in new applications. It does not say those classes are removed, and the array advice is a guideline: a fixed, simple need gives no reason to switch.

concepts.title: What each interface in the hierarchy adds
concepts.question: What does each interface from Iterable down to NavigableSet add to the one above it?

paragraphs: Iterable sits above the framework: any object that implements it works in a for-each loop, and to implement it you supply an Iterator. Collection extends Iterable and models a container of elements, with adding, removing, testing presence, counting, clearing, set operations such as union and intersection, iterators and streams.

List extends Collection and adds order and positions. Iterating a list yields elements in insertion order, the same each time, and index operations let you get, delete, insert or replace by position, or take a range. Set extends Collection and adds one promise: no duplicates. It adds no operations beyond Collection.

SortedSet extends Set and keeps elements ascending by a comparison rule, either the elements' own compareTo or a Comparator you pass. It adds first, last, and head and tail views. NavigableSet extends SortedSet and adds navigation, including descending iteration.
card.example: Add the names Maya, Ravi, Maya to three containers. A list holds all three, in the order added. A set holds two names, because the second Maya is a duplicate. A sorted set also holds two, kept in ascending order whatever order they arrived in.
card.rule: Read the hierarchy by what each level adds: Iterable gives loops, Collection gives element operations, List gives order and indexes, Set gives uniqueness, SortedSet gives sorted order, and NavigableSet gives navigation.
card.limits: Some Set implementations happen to iterate in a consistent order, but that is incidental. Unless an implementation guarantees a stable order, do not rely on it, and do not read a Set as if it were a List.

concepts.title: Adding, removing and bulk operations on a Collection
concepts.question: What do add, remove and the bulk methods on a Collection promise, and how do they fail?

paragraphs: add returns a boolean, but the tutorial stresses a stronger promise: once add returns, true or false, the element must be in the collection. A collection that refuses an element must throw: UnsupportedOperationException if it cannot be modified, NullPointerException if it rejects null, ClassCastException for a wrong type, IllegalArgumentException if it dislikes the element's properties. remove returns false when the element is absent.

Four methods take another collection and model set operations. containsAll tests inclusion and can be true for an empty argument. addAll is union and returns true if the collection changed, which means at least one element was added. removeAll removes the elements found in the other collection (complement), and retainAll keeps only those (intersection). The other collection may have a different element type.

size, isEmpty and clear work on the collection itself. toArray with an array argument fills that array when it is big enough, with a null after the last element if room remains; if the array is too small, a new array of the exact size is made. removeIf takes a Predicate and removes every matching element.
card.example: A Collection of String named names, backed by ArrayList, holds Ana and Bo. Calling addAll with a list holding Bo and Cy gives Ana, Bo, Bo, Cy and returns true. Then retainAll with a list holding Bo keeps only the two Bo entries.
card.rule: Trust that add leaves the element in the collection or throws, and read addAll, removeAll and retainAll as union, complement and intersection.
card.limits: Bulk behaviour depends on the implementation: the same addAll call gives a different result on a HashSet than on an ArrayList. Also, contains accepts any type, so a check that can never be true still compiles.

concepts.title: Iterating, removing safely, and implementing Iterable
concepts.question: How do you remove elements while looping over a collection without triggering an exception?

paragraphs: The for-each loop is the simplest way to go over a collection and suits read-only passes. When you must remove elements during the pass, use an Iterator, an object you get by calling iterator() on any type in the Collection hierarchy. hasNext() checks whether another element exists, and next() moves on and returns it. Calling next() with nothing left throws NoSuchElementException.

An iterator's remove() deletes the element most recently returned by next(). Some iterators do not support it and throw UnsupportedOperationException, for example those of immutable collections; the tutorial names the iterators of ArrayList, LinkedList and HashSet as supporting it.

Changing a collection's contents directly while iterating over it can throw ConcurrentModificationException, even in single-threaded code. To drop elements by condition, call removeIf with a Predicate or use the iterator's own remove(). You can also make your own class iterable; the tutorial builds a Range class of integers for this.
card.example: To drop empty strings from a list named words, call words.removeIf with a predicate that tests for emptiness. The same job with an iterator calls next(), checks the value, and calls remove() on the iterator, not on the list.
card.rule: Read with for-each, remove through the iterator's remove or through removeIf, and do not change the collection directly while a loop is running.
card.limits: Iterator removal works only where the iterator supports it; an immutable collection's iterator throws UnsupportedOperationException. The tutorial says a direct change during iteration can throw ConcurrentModificationException, which can happen without any second thread.

concepts.title: Index operations, sublist views and sorting on a List
concepts.question: What do the index operations do to the elements around them, and which results are views rather than copies?

paragraphs: A List adds a predictable order and indexes to Collection. add(index, element) inserts at a position and shifts later elements; get(index) reads; set(index, element) replaces; remove(index) removes and shifts. An invalid index throws IndexOutOfBoundsException. indexOf and lastIndexOf give the first or last position of an element, or -1 if it is absent.

subList(start, end) returns the elements from start up to end minus one. The result is a view: changes to the sublist show in the original list and the other way round, so clearing a sublist removes that range from the original. addAll(index, collection) inserts a whole collection at a position.

sort takes a Comparator and was added to List in JDK 8, replacing Collections.sort(list). Passing null asks for natural order, which needs Comparable elements or a ClassCastException follows. A ListIterator, from listIterator(), extends Iterator with backward moves, index queries, add and set. List.reversed() returns a view, not a copy.
card.example: A list holds A, B, C, D, E. Calling subList(1, 3) shows B and C. Calling clear() on that sublist leaves A, D and E in the original list, because the sublist is a view and not a copy.
card.rule: Index operations insert, replace or remove by position and shift neighbours, and subList and reversed give views tied to the original list.
card.limits: Indexes belong to List only, and each implementation decides how it finds a position. A view stays tied to its original, so it is not a snapshot to keep after the original changes.

concepts.title: HashSet, LinkedHashSet, TreeSet and their range views
concepts.question: Which Set implementation suits unordered, reproducible or sorted storage, and what do TreeSet range views allow?

paragraphs: HashSet is the main Set implementation and wraps a HashMap internally. Its iteration order is not guaranteed and will very likely differ from insertion order. LinkedHashSet adds an internal linked list to the set, which gives a reproducible iteration order. TreeSet implements SortedSet; it needs elements that implement Comparable or a Comparator passed at construction, and a Comparator wins if both exist.

first and last return the lowest and greatest elements. headSet(to) holds elements lower than to, tailSet(from) holds elements greater than or equal to from, and subSet(from, to) includes from and excludes to. The bounds need not be elements of the set. These results are views, and adding through a view an element outside its bounds throws IllegalArgumentException.

As a NavigableSet, TreeSet adds boolean overloads of headSet, tailSet and subSet that choose whether each bound is included. ceiling returns the lowest element greater than or equal to the argument, floor the greatest less than or equal, higher the lowest strictly greater, lower the greatest strictly less; each gives null if none exists. pollFirst and pollLast remove an end. descendingIterator and descendingSet iterate in reverse.
card.example: A TreeSet holds 10, 20, 30, 40. floor(25) gives 20 and ceiling(25) gives 30. higher(30) gives 40 while ceiling(30) gives 30. headSet(30) is a view of 10 and 20, and adding 35 through it throws IllegalArgumentException.
card.rule: Choose HashSet when order does not matter, LinkedHashSet for a reproducible order, and TreeSet for sorted order with neighbour queries and range views.
card.limits: Range views stay tied to the main set and keep their bounds, so they neither copy the data nor accept any element. TreeSet depends on a comparison rule, so its elements must be comparable by Comparable or by a Comparator.

concepts.title: Unmodifiable factories, copies, Arrays.asList and read-only wrappers
concepts.question: Which of List.of, copyOf, Arrays.asList and the unmodifiable wrappers cannot change, and which only restrict changes?

paragraphs: List.of and Set.of (Java SE 9) build unmodifiable collections from the elements you pass. Treat the result only as a List or a Set. You cannot add, remove or replace elements, though mutable element objects can still change internally. Null elements are rejected, and Set.of treats a duplicate as a probable bug and fails.

List.copyOf and Set.copyOf (Java SE 10) return unmodifiable copies of an existing collection. The source must not be null or contain null, or NullPointerException follows. Set.copyOf accepts duplicates and keeps one. The copy is independent: later changes to the source do not reach it.

Arrays.asList wraps an array in a fixed-size list. You may replace elements, even with null, but adding or removing throws UnsupportedOperationException. The unmodifiableX wrappers of the Collections class are different again: they are read-only views backed by the original collection, so changes to the original show through. For a snapshot, copy first.
card.example: Given a list named scores, List.copyOf(scores) is a snapshot: later adds to scores do not appear in it. Collections.unmodifiableList(scores) is a read-only window: later adds to scores do appear through it, although you cannot add through the window itself.
card.rule: Fixed contents come from of and copyOf, a read-only window comes from an unmodifiable wrapper, and Arrays.asList only restricts size.
card.limits: Unmodifiable describes the collection, not its elements: a mutable element can still change. A wrapper is only as stable as the collection behind it, so copy before wrapping when you need a snapshot.

concepts.title: Collections class helpers: extremes, reordering and synchronized wrappers
concepts.question: Which Collections helpers search or reorder a list, and when do min and max fail?

paragraphs: The Collections class holds helpers that work on collections. min and max each have an overload that takes a Comparator. Without one, the elements must implement Comparable or a ClassCastException follows. On an empty collection both throw NoSuchElementException.

indexOfSublist(source, target) returns the first index where target appears in source, or -1, and lastIndexOfSublist gives the last. Reordering helpers change a list in place: sort (since Java SE 8, List.sort is preferred), shuffle (pass a Random for a repeatable result), rotate (shift with wrap-around), reverse, and swap (exchange two indexes).

The synchronizedX wrappers, such as synchronizedList, return thread-safe views. All access must go through the wrapper, and iterating or streaming over one must be synchronized by hand, or race conditions can occur. The tutorial suggests that java.util.concurrent offers better options.
card.example: For a list of the numbers 4, 9, 2, Collections.max gives 9. On an empty list it throws NoSuchElementException. Collections.swap(list, 0, 2) exchanges the first and last values, giving 2, 9, 4.
card.rule: Use the Collections helpers for extremes, sublist search and in-place reordering, and remember their two failure cases: elements that are not Comparable and empty input.
card.limits: A synchronized wrapper protects its individual calls, not a loop over it: the loop needs manual synchronization. The tutorial also points to java.util.concurrent for better thread-safe options.

concepts.title: Queue and Deque methods, and ArrayDeque, PriorityQueue and Stack
concepts.question: How do Queue and Deque methods report a full or empty structure, and which implementation fits which job?

paragraphs: Queue (Java SE 5) extends Collection and models first in, first out. Deque (Java SE 6) extends Queue and is double-ended, so it can act as a queue or as a stack, which is last in, first out. peek looks at the element pop or poll would return without removing it.

Two corner cases need defined behaviour: the structure is full, or it is empty. Each Queue operation comes in a pair. Insert: add throws IllegalStateException, offer returns false. Remove: remove throws NoSuchElementException, poll returns null. Examine: element throws NoSuchElementException, peek returns null. Deque names methods by end, such as addFirst, offerLast, pollFirst, peekLast and getFirst, and adds push and pop for stack use at the head.

ArrayDeque is array-backed, grows automatically, and is the tutorial's replacement for Stack when thread safety is not needed. LinkedList also implements Queue and Deque.
