PriorityQueue implements only Queue, orders by natural order or a Comparator, and its head is the least element; non-Comparable objects without a Comparator cause ClassCastException. Stack and Vector are thread-safe but discouraged.
card.example: On an empty ArrayDeque named jobs, jobs.poll() and jobs.peek() return null, while jobs.remove() and jobs.element() throw NoSuchElementException. Pushing A then B and then popping returns B first, as a stack should.
card.rule: Among the paired methods, add, remove and element throw on a problem, while offer, poll and peek return false or null.
card.limits: The tutorial leaves BlockingQueue, BlockingDeque and TransferQueue to concurrent programming. A Deque used as a stack pushes and pops at its head, so the same structure behaves as FIFO or LIFO depending on which methods you call.

concepts.title: Entries, unique keys and the map hierarchy
concepts.question: What makes a key different from a value, and how do the keys, values and entries of a map behave as collections?

paragraphs: A map stores key and value pairs, called entries. Values can be any object; keys are usually simple objects such as a string or a number. Given a key, you retrieve its value. A key is unique in a map, a value need not be, every value is bound to a key, and each key is bound to one value, while one value may be bound to several keys.

These rules have consequences. The set of keys has no duplicates, so it behaves like a Set. The set of entries has no duplicates either, so it also behaves like a Set. The values can repeat, so they form a plain Collection. A Map.Entry gives getKey, getValue and setValue; entries are views, so changing an entry's value changes the map, but a key cannot be changed.

Map is the base interface; SortedMap extends it and keeps pairs sorted by key; NavigableMap extends SortedMap. HashMap is the most widely used implementation, and LinkedHashMap keeps insertion order when iterating keys or entries. IdentityHashMap compares keys by reference with == instead of equals and hashCode, and the tutorial says to use it only in very specific cases.
card.example: A map from student ID to grade holds 101 to B, 102 to A and 103 to B. Each ID appears once, so the keys form a Set. Two students share the grade B, which is allowed because values can repeat, so the grades form a plain Collection.
card.rule: A key is unique and identifies one value, so a map's keys and entries behave like sets while its values behave like a plain collection.
card.limits: Unique keys do not make values unique. A map is also not part of the Collection hierarchy, so its parts reach you as separate set and collection views, not as a Collection of the map itself.

concepts.title: put, get, remove and the key, value and entry views
concepts.question: What do put, putIfAbsent and remove return, and how do the keySet, values and entrySet views behave?

paragraphs: put(key, value) adds the pair if the key is absent and replaces the value if it is present; either way it returns the value previously bound, null for a new key. putIfAbsent (Java SE 8) adds the pair only if the key is absent or bound to null. get(key) reads a value, and getOrDefault (Java SE 8) returns a default for a missing key.

remove(key) deletes the pair and returns the value that was bound, which may be null. remove(key, value) (Java SE 8) deletes only if both match and returns a boolean; it avoids the risk of removing a pair whose value you do not know. containsKey and containsValue test presence. putAll copies another map's pairs, and for shared keys the other map's values win.

keySet() returns a Set of keys, values() returns a Collection, and entrySet() returns a Set of entries. They are views backed by the map, so changes show both ways. Removing from keySet removes the pair, while adding to keySet or values throws UnsupportedOperationException. To iterate over pairs, loop over entrySet, which the tutorial says is much more efficient than looping over keys and calling get for each.
card.example: A map holds apple to 3. put of apple to 5 returns 3, and the map now holds apple to 5. put of pear to 2 returns null, because pear is a new key. remove of apple with the value 9 returns false and changes nothing, since the value does not match.
card.rule: put returns the old value, and the key, value and entry views are windows on the map that accept removal but not addition.
card.limits: Removing through values() removes only one of several equal values, and you cannot predict which pair goes. The two-argument remove is the safer form when you are not sure which value is bound to the key.

concepts.title: Replacing, computing and merging map values with lambdas
concepts.question: Which Map method fits creating a value on demand, updating one, or combining values, and what does a null result do?

paragraphs: Map.forEach takes a BiConsumer of key and value. replace(key, value) replaces only if the key is present and returns the removed value. replace(key, old, new) replaces only if the current value equals old and returns a boolean. replaceAll(BiFunction) applies a function to every pair and stores the results.

compute(key, BiFunction) receives the key and the current value, or null if there is none. computeIfPresent runs only when the key has a non-null value. computeIfAbsent(key, Function) runs only if the key is absent or bound to null, and gets just the key. If the function returns null, the key is removed. They return the new value, unlike put, which returns the old one.

computeIfAbsent suits creating a value on demand, such as grouping words: the lambda builds an empty list only when needed, and the returned list receives the word. For immutable values such as String, use merge(key, value, BiFunction): if the key is absent or null, the value is bound without calling the function; otherwise the function gets the old and new values, and a null result removes the key.
card.example: To count words, call counts.merge(word, 1, Integer::sum). A new word gets 1 and the function is not called. A repeated word calls the function with the old count and 1, so the count rises by one.
card.rule: Use computeIfAbsent to create a mutable value on demand and merge to combine values, and expect a null result to remove the key.
card.limits: computeIfAbsent cannot build up an immutable value such as a String, which is why merge exists. The tutorial also advises preferring non-capturing lambdas over capturing ones for performance.

concepts.title: SortedMap and NavigableMap: ordering, neighbours and views
concepts.question: How do SortedMap and NavigableMap order keys, and what do their neighbour methods and views do?

paragraphs: SortedMap and NavigableMap extend Map and keep entries sorted by key; NavigableMap extends SortedMap. TreeMap, a red-black tree, implements both, and ConcurrentSkipListMap is a thread-safe sorted alternative. Keys must be comparable through Comparable or through a Comparator passed at creation, and a Comparator wins even for Comparable keys.

SortedMap adds firstKey, lastKey, headMap (keys strictly below the argument), tailMap (keys at or above it) and subMap (from included, to excluded). These are views backed by the original map: changes show both ways, and you cannot insert a key outside a view's bounds.

NavigableMap adds firstEntry, lastEntry, and ceiling, floor, higher and lower in Key and Entry forms; ceiling and floor can match the given key, while higher and lower cannot. pollFirstEntry and pollLastEntry return and remove an end. descendingKeySet and descendingMap give reverse views that support removal but not addition. Overloads of subMap, headMap and tailMap take inclusion flags.
card.example: A TreeMap holds keys 10, 20, 30. ceilingKey(20) returns 20, while higherKey(20) returns 30. headMap(30) is a view with keys 10 and 20, and a put of key 35 into that view is refused because 35 is outside its bounds.
card.rule: Treat a sorted map like a sorted set over its keys: neighbour methods answer nearest-key questions, and range and descending results are live views.
card.limits: Views stay tied to the original map and keep their bounds, so they are not copies. The descending views allow removal but not addition, and keys must be comparable by Comparable or by a Comparator.

concepts.title: Why mutating keys and set elements breaks lookups
concepts.question: What goes wrong when a key or set element changes after it has been stored, and what is the safer choice?

paragraphs: The tutorial calls mutable map keys an antipattern, because mutating a key can make the map's contents unreachable. Its example is a Key class wrapping a String, with equals and hashCode generated from that text. Before any mutation, the map works correctly.

Mutate a stored key to a value no other key uses, and lookups fail: the mutated key cannot retrieve its value even through the same reference, and looking up the original value fails too, so the pair is effectively lost. Mutate it to a value another key already uses, and a lookup with the mutated key returns the other key's value, while its own value cannot be retrieved.

A HashSet is built on an internal HashMap: add stores the element as a key, with a placeholder value. So the same problem applies to sets, and mutating an element after adding it can cause hard-to-diagnose bugs. The best choice is an unmodifiable key type; if you cannot avoid a mutable one, do not mutate it after insertion.
card.example: A Key object wrapping the text cat is stored in a map with a value. The code then changes that Key's text to dog. A lookup with the same Key reference now fails, although it is the very object that was stored, because the key's hash code changed.
card.rule: Use unmodifiable keys and set elements, or at least do not change them after they are stored.
card.limits: The tutorial shows the failure for hash-based containers whose equals and hashCode follow the changed content. It does not discuss sorted maps or records, so claims beyond that are outside the tutorial.

concepts.title: The complexity table and why the tutorial also measures
concepts.question: Why does the tutorial benchmark ArrayList and LinkedList instead of trusting the complexity table alone?

paragraphs: The tutorial starts from a textbook table. Read first and read last: constant for both. Read middle: constant for ArrayList, linear for LinkedList. Add last: constant for both. Insert first: linear for ArrayList, constant for LinkedList. Insert middle: linear for both. LinkedList keeps references to its first and last nodes, which is why reading the last element is constant.

Big-O describes growth beyond some threshold, so constant factors matter. The tutorial's example: 10n plus 1 behaves like n from about 10 elements, but n plus 10 behaves like n only from about 1,000. Compare the threshold with your real data size. Theory alone is not enough, because hardware effects, notably pointer chasing, can dominate.

The tutorial uses JMH benchmarks and warns that absolute numbers differ between machines; only relative comparisons on the same machine mean anything. Benchmark your own workload in an environment close to production. In its measurement, reading linked nodes scattered in memory was about three times slower than reading nodes that sit together.
card.example: Two engineers compare a LinkedList and an ArrayList of 50 elements. Theory says inserting at the front is cheaper for LinkedList, but with a list this small the constant factors and memory layout may outweigh the difference, so a measurement on their own workload decides.
card.rule: Use the complexity table as a first guide, then confirm with a benchmark on your own workload, because constant factors and pointer chasing can reverse the ranking.
card.limits: The numbers quoted in the tutorial come from its own machine and JVM, and are comparable only with each other. They show a pattern, not a figure to expect elsewhere.

concepts.title: Reading, iterating and inserting: what the benchmarks showed
concepts.question: For reading, iterating and inserting, where does LinkedList beat ArrayList and where does the theory mislead?

paragraphs: Reading: the first and last elements are fast for both, with LinkedList slower at the last by a negligible fraction of a nanosecond. The middle element is constant for ArrayList but grows with size for LinkedList, which walks references from the nearer end, so the middle is its worst case.

Iterating: for ArrayList, an index loop and an iterator perform about the same. For LinkedList, indexed iteration is quadratic and should not be used: the tutorial measured about 0.5 ms for 1,000 elements by index against about 4 microseconds with an iterator. Copying a LinkedList into an array-based list cost about 4 percent of one iteration; the tutorial suggests Stream.toList() for it.

Inserting: LinkedList wins at the beginning, where ArrayList must shift every element. In the middle, LinkedList must first traverse to the position, and despite its better theoretical complexity, ArrayList beat it on almost every insertion benchmark. A full ArrayList grows by a factor of 1.5 and copies, which is rare and averages out; pre-sizing avoids it. Reallocation is no good reason to choose LinkedList.
card.example: To process a 1,000-element LinkedList three times, an index loop walks the nodes for every element on every pass. Copying it once into an ArrayList costs about 4 percent of one iteration, and each later pass is cheap. An iterator loop on the LinkedList avoids the index walks too.
card.rule: Loop over a LinkedList with an iterator rather than by index, and expect ArrayList to win on reads and on almost all insertions except at the front.
card.limits: These figures come from the tutorial's benchmark setup and are meant for relative comparison. A LinkedList can also win at the end in some cases, so the front is the only clear exception to remember.

concepts.title: Memory footprint of ArrayList, LinkedList and small lists
concepts.question: Why does a LinkedList use more memory than an ArrayList, and how can small lists be kept compact?

paragraphs: Each element of a LinkedList lives in a Node object holding three references (previous, next and item) plus an object header, which the tutorial estimates at about 24 bytes of overhead per element. For 1,000 elements it measured about 24 KB for LinkedList against about 5 KB for ArrayList. The JOL measurements depend on the JVM and heap setup.
In a fixed heap, an ArrayList can store several times more elements than a LinkedList. LinkedList has no unused capacity, since every element has its own node, but the node overhead outweighs that.

For a single-element list the tutorial reports about 76 to 80 bytes for a default ArrayList, 44 to 48 after trimToSize, 56 for LinkedList and 26 for List.of. Many small lists add up. An ArrayList created with initial capacity 2 takes 48 bytes for zero to two elements, below LinkedList at every nonzero size. List.of suits small immutable lists, and trimToSize suits a list that has finished growing.
card.example: A service holds a hundred thousand lists of one or two names each. Creating each ArrayList with capacity 2 costs about 48 bytes per list, where a default ArrayList with one element costs around 76 to 80 bytes and a LinkedList costs 56.
card.rule: Expect an ArrayList to be much lighter than a LinkedList, and shrink or pre-size small lists when many of them are kept.
card.limits: The byte counts are the tutorial's measurements for its JVM and settings, and its two tables differ slightly for the default ArrayList. Treat them as magnitudes, and note that List.of lists cannot be modified.

concepts.title: Defaults and exceptions when choosing an implementation
concepts.question: Which default does the tutorial give for lists and why, and when does it point elsewhere?

paragraphs: According to the tutorial, ArrayList is the default List: it wins on most operations and on memory, and its iteration is much faster. It is also the default when you model a plain Collection, since the framework has no direct Collection implementation. Pre-size an ArrayList when the expected size is known.

LinkedList is preferable only when you mainly operate at the ends, as in stack or queue behaviour. If you keep a LinkedList, iterate with an iterator, not by index, or copy it into an array-based list. Use List.of or trimToSize for small or finished lists when memory is tight.

Choosing is about the task: pick the interface for the functionality, then the implementation for the usage pattern. Benchmark with JMH in conditions close to production before trusting any rule of thumb.
card.example: A buffer of recent events needs adding at one end and removing at the other, in single-threaded code: that points to a double-ended queue. A list of 10,000 names read by index and appended to points to a pre-sized ArrayList.
card.rule: Default to ArrayList for lists, pre-size it when you can, look to other structures for end-only work, and confirm with a benchmark.
card.limits: These defaults come from the tutorial's benchmarks and stated workloads. Concurrency, sorted order, uniqueness or key lookup send you to other interfaces, and the tutorial says to measure your own workload.

concepts.title: Map, filter and reduce
concepts.question: What are the three steps of map-filter-reduce, and how does each one change the count and type of elements?

paragraphs: A stream pipeline describes data processing with three kinds of step. Mapping turns each element into another value, one for one, so the count and the order stay the same while the type may change. Filtering keeps or drops each element using a yes-or-no test, so the count can shrink while the type stays the same.

Reducing combines many elements into one result, such as a single total or a built structure like a list or map. According to the tutorial, this style is declarative, like a SQL query: you state what result you want and leave the how to the runtime, instead of writing each loop step yourself.
card.rule: Describe the result as filter, map and reduce steps, and let the stream decide how to run them.
card.limits: The tutorial gives readability and room for runtime optimisation as the goals. A step that must change a variable outside the stream does not fit these three shapes, and the tutorial says such side effects can be avoided.
card.example: Goal: the total of the amounts of sales made in October. Filter keeps only the sales made in October. Map turns each remaining sale into its integer amount. Reduce adds the amounts into one number. Ten sales go in, four are kept, four amounts come out of the map, and one total comes out of the reduction.

concepts.title: Lazy pipelines and single-use streams
concepts.question: What happens when a pipeline has intermediate operations but no terminal operation, and why can a stream be used only once?

paragraphs: A stream is an object that does not store data; it describes steps over a source. An intermediate operation, such as map or filter, returns another stream and processes nothing. A terminal operation returns anything that is not a stream, including void, and triggers the work. According to the tutorial, a pipeline with no terminal operation processes no data.

Once triggered, elements are pulled through the whole pipeline one at a time: an element is mapped, then filtered, then consumed before the next element starts. This is the order an equivalent for loop would use, so no intermediate storage is needed.

A stream instance accepts only one intermediate or terminal call; a second call on the same instance throws IllegalStateException. So create and consume a stream on the spot, do not change its source during processing, and avoid side effects inside operations.
card.rule: Nothing runs until a terminal operation, elements flow one at a time, and each stream instance is used once.
card.limits: Laziness applies to intermediate operations only; a terminal operation does the work at once. After a terminal operation runs, that stream instance is used up and cannot take another call.
card.example: Words: one, two, three. Pipeline: map to the length, keep lengths equal to 3, then count. Writing the map and filter calls prints and computes nothing. Adding count starts the run: one is mapped to 3 and kept, two is mapped to 3 and kept, three is mapped to 5 and dropped. The result is 2.

concepts.title: Creating streams from sources
concepts.question: Which factory or source fits a given kind of data, and what must you do with infinite or file-backed streams?

paragraphs: Streams can start from many sources. A collection has stream; a map has none, so stream its keySet, entrySet or values. Stream.of takes varargs and Arrays.stream takes an array. IntStream.range excludes its upper bound and rangeClosed includes it; mapToObj turns the numbers into objects.

Stream.generate calls a supplier for each new element, and Stream.iterate starts from a seed and applies a unary operator to the previous element. Both give infinite streams, so cut them off with a short-circuiting operation such as limit; an iterate overload with a predicate stops by itself. Random offers ints, longs and doubles, and String.chars gives an IntStream.

Files.lines and BufferedReader.lines stream the lines of a file; a stream can be closed, so use try-with-resources. Pattern.splitAsStream splits text straight into a stream. A stream builder collects elements first and builds the stream once.
card.rule: Pick the factory that matches the data source, limit infinite streams, and close streams that hold files.
card.limits: Closing matters for streams backed by files; the tutorial shows try-with-resources there. A stream builder is single use: adding elements after building, or building again, throws IllegalStateException.
card.example: To count the lines of a log file that contain the word warn, open Files.lines on the path inside a try-with-resources block, keep lines containing warn, and call count. For the numbers 1 to 5 use rangeClosed with 1 and 5; for the numbers 0 to 4 use range with 0 and 5.

concepts.title: Mapping, filtering and primitive streams
concepts.question: How do map, mapToInt and filter differ, and what do primitive streams add?

paragraphs: map applies a Function to every element and may change the type, giving a stream of the new type. mapToInt, mapToLong and mapToDouble give primitive streams, which avoid boxing and unboxing. The same method reference, such as String::length, works for both map and mapToInt; what differs is the kind of stream you get back.

filter keeps the elements that match a Predicate and works on object and primitive streams. IntStream, LongStream and DoubleStream add sum, min, max, average and summaryStatistics, which gives count, min, max, sum and average in a single pass.
card.rule: Map to a primitive stream when you need numeric results such as a sum, an average or summary statistics.
card.limits: Primitive streams hold only numbers; for objects use map, and go back with mapToObj or boxed. A filter keeps the type and leaves the elements it lets through unchanged.
card.example: Words: tree, sun, moon. mapToInt with String::length gives an IntStream of 4, 3, 4. Adding sum gives 11. Replacing sum with summaryStatistics gives count 3, min 3, max 4, sum 11 and an average of about 3.67 in one pass. Using map instead of mapToInt gives a stream of Integer objects, which has no numeric sum.

concepts.title: flatMap and mapMulti for one-to-many
concepts.question: How do you turn each element into zero, one or many elements, and when is mapMulti a better fit than flatMap?

paragraphs: Mapping is one-to-one, but flatMap handles one-to-many relations. Its function returns a stream for each element, and the results are merged into one stream. Where a nested loop adds up the cities of every country, flatMap over the countries, with a function that returns each country's city stream, flattens all cities into one stream.

flatMap can also validate. Parsing strings with Integer.parseInt throws NumberFormatException on bad input. A function that returns a one-element stream for a good string and an empty stream for a bad one drops the bad ones. According to the tutorial, filtering first would parse every string twice, and returning from a catch block is a bad idea.

The cost is one stream per element. mapMulti (Java SE 16) takes a BiConsumer of the element and a consumer: calling the consumer emits a value, not calling it emits nothing, and no stream is created. The compiler needs the output type, so declare the lambda parameter types or give an explicit type argument before mapMulti.
card.rule: Use flatMap to flatten one-to-many results, and mapMulti when you emit zero or a few values per element without building streams.
card.limits: If the compiler cannot infer the output type, mapMulti yields a stream of Object. mapMulti exists only from Java SE 16, so code for older versions uses flatMap with empty streams.
card.example: Strings: 12, x, 7. For each string, a function returns a one-element stream holding the parsed number if parsing works and an empty stream otherwise. flatMap over it gives 12 and 7. With mapMulti, the lambda calls the consumer for each valid number and does not call it for bad input, giving the same two values without creating streams.

concepts.title: Sorting, slicing and peeking
concepts.question: Which operations hold elements back, skip them, stop early or only observe them, and what traps do skip and limit have?

paragraphs: distinct removes duplicates using hashCode and equals and passes each new element on at once. sorted uses natural order or a supplied Comparator, and it holds all elements before emitting any. So on an infinite stream, distinct followed by limit can finish, but sorted never emits anything.

skip and limit each create a new stream, so limit counts from where skip left off: to pick the 3rd to 8th integers, use skip(2) then limit(6). dropWhile drops elements while a predicate holds and then passes everything; takeWhile passes elements while it holds and then stops. Both make sense only on ordered streams.

peek hands each element to a consumer as it flows past; it is for debugging, not for production side effects. Because elements move one at a time through the whole pipeline, peek output interleaves with the other steps. Put debugger breakpoints inside lambdas.
card.rule: Know which operation holds elements back (sorted), which stops (limit, takeWhile) and which only observes (peek).
card.limits: takeWhile and dropWhile need an ordered stream; on an unordered one any subset may pass. And skip(2) then limit(8) gives 3 to 10, not 3 to 8, because limit counts after the skip.
card.example: Numbers 1 to 10 in order. skip(2) then limit(6) gives 3 to 8. takeWhile for numbers below 4 gives 1, 2, 3. dropWhile for numbers below 4 gives 4 to 10. For the values 5, 1, 3, 1, distinct gives 5, 1, 3, and sorted afterwards gives 1, 3, 5.

concepts.title: Stream characteristics
concepts.question: Which characteristics does a stream carry, and which operations keep or erase them?

paragraphs: A stream gets its characteristics from its spliterator (split plus iterator), which also controls how the stream is split for parallel work. Each characteristic is set or unset when the stream is created, and it depends on the source, or on the parent stream plus the operation applied. You can test one with hasCharacteristics.

ORDERED means processing order matters: lists have it, sets do not, and unordered removes it. DISTINCT means no duplicates (HashSet, distinct). SORTED means sorted data (TreeSet, sorted). NONNULL means no null elements. SIZED means the count is known, as with any collection. SUBSIZED means splitting gives two SIZED parts.

Operations keep or erase them. Mapping or flatMapping erases DISTINCT, SORTED and NONNULL. Filtering keeps DISTINCT and NONNULL but erases SIZED and SUBSIZED. Mapping keeps SIZED and SUBSIZED; flatMap erases them. SIZED and SUBSIZED streams are better for parallel computation.
card.rule: Ask what the source and each operation do to ORDERED, DISTINCT, SORTED, NONNULL, SIZED and SUBSIZED.
card.limits: IMMUTABLE and CONCURRENT also exist, but the tutorial does not cover them. Characteristics are rarely used directly, and the implementation does not always apply an optimisation that a characteristic would allow.
card.example: A stream from a list of strings is ORDERED, SIZED and SUBSIZED but not DISTINCT. After distinct it is DISTINCT. Mapping to the lengths erases DISTINCT again. A stream from a HashSet is DISTINCT and SIZED but not ORDERED and not SUBSIZED.

concepts.title: Reducing: associativity and identity
concepts.question: What must a binary operator and an identity satisfy for reduce to be correct, including in parallel?

paragraphs: reduce combines elements with a binary operator, which turns two values into one. A sum loop that adds each element to a running partial sum is such a reduction, and an operator that keeps the larger value gives a maximum. A parallel stream splits the source, reduces each part with the same operator, and merges the partial results with it.

So the operator must be associative: any way of splitting the data must give the same result, as when 3+(6+2+1), (3+6)+(2+1) and (3+6+2)+1 agree. Nothing checks this for you. Random tests can prove an operator wrong, but passing tests never prove it right.

An identity element lets an empty part reduce to something: 0 for a sum. reduce with an identity and an operator starts from the identity and works on empty input. The API does not verify the identity, and a wrong one gives a wrong result silently. reduce with only an operator returns an Optional, because minimum and maximum have no identity.
card.rule: Use reduce only with an associative operator and a true identity; otherwise the result depends on how the data is split.
card.limits: Passing tests does not prove associativity or an identity, because an untried counterexample may exist. The tutorial also advises avoiding reduce where sum, min or max on a number stream already does the job.
card.example: Strings: ab, c, def. reduce with identity 0, an accumulator that adds a string's length to the partial sum, and a combiner that adds two sums gives 6. Subtraction is not associative: (10-4)-3 is 3, but 10-(4-3) is 9, so a parallel split could change the answer.

concepts.title: Terminal operations: finding, matching and collecting
concepts.question: Which terminal operation fits when you need a count, a match test, one element or a collected result, and which can stop early?

paragraphs: Prefer ready-made terminal operations to reduce. count works on every stream interface. sum, min, max and average on number streams replace reduce calls; min and max on object streams need a Comparator and return an Optional, and so do findFirst and findAny. anyMatch, allMatch and noneMatch return a boolean without building an Optional.

On an empty stream anyMatch is false, while allMatch and noneMatch are true, because the predicate never runs. findFirst honours encounter order, which is costly in parallel; findAny does not. anyMatch, allMatch, noneMatch, findFirst and findAny can stop early, while count, max, min, average, forEach, toList and toArray read every element.

forEach with a side effect, such as adding to a list declared outside the stream, is a bad pattern: it captures a variable and is unsafe in parallel. Collect instead. Since Java SE 16, Stream.toList gives an unmodifiable list. toArray() gives an Object array, while toArray with String[]::new keeps the element type.
card.rule: Choose the terminal operation that states the question directly, and remember what an empty stream gives.
card.limits: Opening an empty Optional with get or orElseThrow throws NoSuchElementException, so confirm that a value can exist first. A print inside forEach is a side effect, which is acceptable for output but a poor way to build results.
card.example: Prices 12, 30 and 7. anyMatch for above 25 is true, allMatch for above 5 is true, noneMatch for above 100 is true. On an empty stream, the same three calls give false, true and true. max on an IntStream of these prices needs no comparator and returns an optional result.

concepts.title: Collectors for collections, strings and partitions
concepts.question: Which collector builds a list, set, string or true-or-false split, and what can you rely on about the result type?

paragraphs: collect takes a Collector, usually built by the Collectors factory class. toList, toSet and toCollection with a supplier build collections, and toUnmodifiableList and toUnmodifiableSet build immutable ones. Do not rely on the concrete List or Set type these methods return, because it is not part of the specification; use toCollection with a supplier to choose a type.

joining works only on streams of strings, and takes an optional separator, or a separator with a prefix and a suffix. partitioningBy takes a predicate and gives a map from Boolean to a list: one group passes the test and one fails it. A primitive stream has no collect method that takes a collector.

counting does the same as count, but it becomes useful when it is placed inside another collector. Mapping values into a HashSet drops duplicates the mapping produces. String.join or a StringJoiner avoids stream overhead when the data is small or not a stream.
card.rule: Pick the collector that builds the structure you need, and do not rely on its concrete type unless you supply it.
card.limits: A primitive stream has no collect that takes a collector, so box it first or build the pieces yourself. joining requires a stream of strings.
card.example: Words: tree, sun, moon. toList keeps all three. joining with a comma, the prefix open bracket and the suffix close bracket gives the text [tree,sun,moon]. partitioningBy with the test length above 3 puts tree and moon under true and sun under false.

concepts.title: Grouping, toMap and downstream collectors
concepts.question: How do groupingBy and toMap build maps, how do they treat duplicate keys, and what does a downstream collector do?

paragraphs: groupingBy takes a classifier function and gathers elements with the same key into a list, giving a map from key to list. The classifier must not return null. A downstream collector, passed as a second argument, replaces each list: counting gives a count per key (a histogram), joining gives a string per key, and mapping, filtering and flatMapping apply a step before another downstream collector.

toMap takes a key mapper and a value mapper. Unlike groupingBy, a duplicate key throws IllegalStateException unless you pass a merge function as the third argument; a fourth argument supplies the map type. Do not rely on the map type that groupingBy or toMap returns unless you supply one.

A Map has no stream method, so to find the most frequent key of a histogram, stream its entrySet and take max with a comparator on the values. If several keys tie for the maximum, one extraction returns only one of them; invert the histogram by grouping on the count to see all tied keys.
card.rule: Use groupingBy when many elements may share a key, and toMap only when keys are unique or a merge function resolves clashes.
card.limits: The classifier of groupingBy must not return null. Taking the maximum of a histogram hides ties, and the entry values must be Comparable for the comparison to work.
card.example: Words: ant, bee, tiger, lion. groupingBy on length gives 3 to ant and bee, 5 to tiger and 4 to lion. With counting as downstream collector: 3 to 2, 5 to 1, 4 to 1. toMap with the length as key and the word as value throws IllegalStateException, because ant and bee share the key 3; a merge function that joins them with a comma resolves it.

concepts.title: Custom collectors, collectingAndThen and teeing
concepts.question: What are the four components of a collector, and how do a finisher, collectingAndThen and teeing extend what a collector can do?

paragraphs: A collector has four parts. The supplier creates the mutable container, the accumulator adds one element to it, the combiner merges two containers when a parallel stream fills several, and the finisher optionally turns the container into the final result. Collector.of builds a collector from these parts, with characteristics as hints to the implementation.

On primitive streams you call collect with a supplier, an accumulator and a combiner directly, because the Collectors factory serves object streams only. To join primitives, the container is a mutable StringBuffer, and a finisher that converts it to a String saves the caller a toString call. For toList and toSet the finisher does nothing: it is the identity function.

collectingAndThen applies a finisher to another collector's result, so a collector that extracts the maximum entry of a histogram can be used as a downstream collector. teeing (Java SE 12) runs two collectors over the same data in one pass and merges their results with a BiFunction. Implementing the Collector interface yourself is the most flexible but most technical option.
card.rule: Build a collector from supplier, accumulator, combiner and optional finisher, and reuse existing collectors with collectingAndThen or teeing.
card.limits: The combiner is needed only for parallel streams. Characteristics are hints to the implementation: IDENTITY_FINISH for an identity finisher, UNORDERED when order is not preserved, and CONCURRENT when the container supports concurrent access.
card.example: Collecting numbers into a list: the supplier creates an empty ArrayList, the accumulator adds one number, the combiner adds all elements of the second list to the first, and the finisher is the identity. To gather electric cars and trucks, teeing filters cars into one list and trucks into another, and its merging function adds the second list to the first.

concepts.title: Using Optional safely
concepts.question: How do you create, read and transform an Optional, and which usage rules does the tutorial give?

paragraphs: An Optional models a method that may not return a result, so callers need not handle null. It is final with factory methods: empty makes an empty one, of wraps a value that must not be null (null throws NullPointerException), and ofNullable turns null into an empty Optional. A nonempty Optional never holds null. OptionalInt, OptionalLong and OptionalDouble wrap primitives.

To read it: isPresent and isEmpty test; orElseThrow (preferred since Java 10) and the older get throw NoSuchElementException when empty; orElse returns a default that is always evaluated, while orElseGet runs a supplier only if needed; or supplies another Optional. ifPresent and ifPresentOrElse consume the value.

map, filter and flatMap work like their stream namesakes: on an empty Optional they return an empty one and ignore the function. stream gives a stream of zero or one element, so Stream.flatMap with Optional.stream drops empty results. Use Optional for return values, not for fields, parameters, collections or maps.
card.rule: Return Optional from methods that may have no result, transform it with map and filter, and open it only when a value is certain or a default is supplied.
card.limits: According to the tutorial, do not use Optional for fields, parameters, collections or maps, and do not create one only to test a reference for null. Avoid get and orElseThrow unless a value is certain.
card.example: A list of customers is searched for the one with a given id. findFirst returns an Optional of customer; map to the customer's name stays empty if nothing matched; orElse with the text unknown yields a printable name either way. No explicit emptiness check is needed.

concepts.title: Parallel streams: when they help
concepts.question: When does parallel help, what makes a source split well, and which rules does the tutorial give for using it safely?

paragraphs: Any stream can run in parallel through parallel, but it is not always faster. It uses recursive decomposition on the Fork/Join common pool: split the data, process small parts sequentially, and merge the partial results. Splitting, coordination and merging are overhead, which must be small compared to the gain.

How well a source splits matters. ArrayList and IntStream.range split fast and evenly; a LinkedList needs a walk to its middle; HashSet buckets split unevenly; generate and iterate are hard to split because elements depend on earlier ones. Data locality counts too: an int array sits together in cache, while linked nodes force pointer chasing.

Pool threads run in any order, so changing external state, such as adding to an ArrayList, causes race conditions. limit, skip and findFirst depend on encounter order and are costly in parallel. The tutorial's rules: do not optimise for its own sake, choose the source with care, share no mutable state, and measure instead of guessing.
card.rule: Go parallel only for a measured need, with a source that splits well and operations that share no mutable state.
card.limits: A small stream, such as the sum of a few numbers, is too small to show a speedup. In a web server, parallel work competes with the threads that serve requests. Merging hash maps is costly, while merging sums or collections is cheap.
card.example: A web server wants to speed up summing 1,000 prices in an ArrayList. Before adding parallel, ask: is there a measured requirement that is unmet, are spare cores and threads available, and can the gain be measured under production-like conditions? If the prices sat in a LinkedList, splitting would be slower and the gain smaller.

concepts.title: Gatherers: custom intermediate operations
concepts.question: What is a gatherer, which parts does it have, and how does an integrator tell upstream that downstream wants no more elements?

paragraphs: According to the tutorial, Gatherers are available starting with JDK 24, as the intermediate-operation counterpart of collectors: Stream.gather applies a Gatherer. Use one only for operations the Stream API lacks, such as fixed windows or a distinct-like operation; for plain map, filter or flatMap use the existing methods. Upstream supplies elements; downstream receives what the gatherer pushes.

The integrator is called per upstream element with the state (if any), the element and the downstream, and returns a boolean. An initializer creates mutable state once per run, a finisher runs after the last element and cannot return a value, and a combiner merges states in parallel runs. Gatherer.of builds a parallel-capable gatherer; ofSequential builds one that runs on a single thread.

Downstream push returns false when the downstream is rejecting, meaning it wants no more elements, and isRejecting tells the same. A downstream starts non-rejecting and can turn rejecting only after a push. An integrator should return the push result, or true when nothing was pushed; once it returns false it is never called again.
card.rule: Return the result of push from the integrator, so that upstream stops as soon as downstream is full.
card.limits: A placeholder return of true is wrong once a gatherer can interrupt a stream, and pushing to a rejecting downstream is silently ignored, which wastes work. Prefer the existing operations for plain map, filter and flatMap.
card.example: A limit-like gatherer keeps a counter as state. For each element it increments the counter, pushes the element, and returns the push result; when the limit is reached it returns false so that upstream stops. A distinct-like gatherer keeps a HashSet as state and pushes only elements that Set.add reports as new.

concepts.title: Ready-made gatherers, finishers and parallel gatherers
concepts.question: Which ready-made gatherers does the Gatherers class offer, and when do you need a finisher, a combiner or andThen?

paragraphs: The Gatherers class provides five ready-made gatherers. fold reduces left to right from an initial value and emits a single element, with no restriction on empty streams. scan emits every intermediate result. mapConcurrent maps elements concurrently. windowFixed groups elements into disjoint lists, the last possibly shorter, and windowSliding makes overlapping windows that move one element at a time. Window gatherers need an ordered stream.

A finisher is called once after the last element, with the state and the downstream. Use it when the gatherer must see all elements before pushing, as when sorting distinct values: the integrator adds them to a TreeSet and pushes nothing, and the finisher pushes them in order. Check for a rejecting downstream in the finisher, not in the integrator.

In a parallel stream, a gatherer made with of can run in parallel, with one state per thread merged by the combiner; a stateful gatherer without a combiner must be sequential. A sequential gatherer in a parallel stream runs on one thread, while steps before and after it can still run in parallel. andThen chains two gatherers when the first output type matches the second input type.
card.rule: Use a ready-made gatherer when one fits, a finisher when all elements are needed before output, and a combiner only when the gatherer should run in parallel.
card.limits: Window gatherers need an ordered stream, because unordered streams can give inconsistent results. For fused map, filter and flatMap gatherers the tutorial says to measure before relying on a performance gain.
card.example: Elements 1, 2, 3. fold with addition emits the single value 6; scan with addition emits a running total after each element: 1, 3, 6. For the numbers 0 to 4, windowFixed(3) gives [0,1,2] and [3,4], and windowSliding(3) gives [0,1,2], [1,2,3] and [2,3,4].

concepts.title: Off-heap memory and memory segments
concepts.question: What is a memory segment, and why would Java code want memory outside the heap?

paragraphs: Java objects normally live on the heap. The garbage collector decides when that memory is reclaimed, and the heap can grow or shrink while the program runs. Off-heap memory lies outside the heap: the garbage collector does not reach it, so your own code controls when it is released. According to the tutorial, arguments given to a C function must be in off-heap memory, which is the main motivation.

A MemorySegment is the object through which Java code works with one contiguous region of memory. A heap segment is backed by on-heap memory, and a native segment is backed by off-heap memory. This lesson concentrates on native segments.

You read or write a segment by passing a value layout to its get and set methods. A value layout describes the size, byte order, bit alignment and Java type of the access. For instance, the layout JAVA_BYTE has the size of a Java byte, an alignment of 1 and the hardware's native byte order.
card.example: In a confined arena, the String hi is copied into a new native segment with the arena's allocateFrom method, which stores it as a null-terminated UTF-8 C string. Calling get with JAVA_BYTE and offset 0 on that segment returns 104, the byte for the letter h. The offset counts bytes from the start of the segment.
card.rule: To give native code data, copy it into a native segment and read or write it through a value layout that states the size and type of each access.
card.limits: Off-heap memory is not free-floating: a native segment can be used only while the scope of its arena is alive, so the data cannot outlive that arena.

concepts.title: Arenas: who may use a segment and for how long
concepts.question: Which arena kind fits which sharing and lifetime need, and what happens when a segment outlives its arena?

paragraphs: An arena controls the lifecycle of native segments. Its scope decides when the memory is released and becomes invalid, and a segment can be accessed only while its scope is alive.

A confined arena lives from creation until it is closed. It has an owner thread, usually its creator, and only that thread may access its segments; closing it from another thread throws an exception. A shared arena has no owner thread, so many threads can use its segments, and any thread can close it safely and atomically.

An automatic arena is managed by the garbage collector, any thread can access its segments, and calling close throws UnsupportedOperationException. The global arena also allows access from any thread, never deallocates its memory, and its close method throws the same exception.

Put an arena in try-with-resources. When the block ends, the scope is no longer alive, every segment is invalidated and the memory is freed. Accessing such a segment afterwards throws IllegalStateException.
card.example: A method opens a confined arena in try-with-resources, allocates a segment, and returns it. When the method exits, the arena closes. The caller's first read of the returned segment then throws IllegalStateException, because the segment's scope ended with the block.
card.rule: Pick the arena by who may touch the segments and who decides when they die, and close confined or shared arenas with try-with-resources.
card.limits: Automatic and global arenas cannot be closed: calling close throws UnsupportedOperationException, so try-with-resources cannot release their memory early.

concepts.title: Struct layouts, VarHandles and slicing
concepts.question: How do you model a C struct in Java, read its fields, and cut one big segment into pieces?

paragraphs: Working with structured native data byte by byte gets complicated and hard to maintain. A MemoryLayout describes the data instead. MemoryLayout.structLayout takes member layouts and returns a StructLayout. A C fraction with a numerator and a denominator becomes a struct layout of two named JAVA_INT members.

To reach a field, build a VarHandle, a typed reference to a variable that can be a part of an off-heap structure, from a path element such as groupElement with the member name. Calling set takes the segment, a base offset and the value. Calling get takes the segment and a base offset.

For an array of structs, define a SequenceLayout with the count. A slicing allocator, made by SegmentAllocator.slicingAllocator on an existing segment, hands out consecutive contiguous slices, each starting right after the previous one.

The method asSlice with an offset and a size returns a slice from any place in a segment, but only when the slice stays within the bounds of the original. When several threads work on slices in parallel, the tutorial associates the segment with a shared arena.
card.example: A point struct has two JAVA_INT members, x and y, so it takes 8 bytes. A slicing allocator over a 24-byte segment gives the first point bytes 0 to 7, the second bytes 8 to 15 and the third bytes 16 to 23. Asking for a fourth slice would go past the end.
card.rule: Describe a struct once with a struct layout, reach fields through VarHandles built from named path elements, and split a segment with a slicing allocator or asSlice.
card.limits: A slice must stay within the original segment, and a slicing allocator only moves forward; use asSlice when you need a slice at an arbitrary offset.

concepts.title: Calling a C function: the downcall steps
concepts.question: What steps turn a C function such as strdup into a Java method handle you can call?

paragraphs: A downcall is a Java call into native code. The tutorial's steps: copy arguments into off-heap memory, obtain the native Linker, locate the function's address, describe its signature, build a method handle, and invoke it. The Linker gives Java code access to foreign functions and gives foreign code access to Java code.

To find an address, Linker.defaultLookup searches the standard C library, so strdup needs no library name. SymbolLookup.loaderLookup finds symbols in libraries loaded with System.loadLibrary. SymbolLookup.libraryLookup loads a named library, with an arena controlling the lookup's lifetime.

A FunctionDescriptor records the layouts of the return value and arguments, with the return layout first. Each layout maps to a Java type; JAVA_FLOAT maps to float. Pointers use ADDRESS, and GroupLayout, with subtypes StructLayout and UnionLayout, models structs and unions. Sizes vary by platform: size_t is JAVA_LONG on 64-bit x64 and JAVA_INT on 32-bit x86. Linker.canonicalLayouts shows the layouts on your platform.

Giving the address and the descriptor to the linker yields a MethodHandle for the C function. Invoke it with the segment holding the argument. The tutorial warns that invokeExact needs the call-site types to match the handle's type exactly.
card.example: For C strlen on a 64-bit x64 platform, the descriptor is FunctionDescriptor.of(JAVA_LONG, ADDRESS), because size_t is returned and a pointer is taken. The handle comes from the linker's downcallHandle with the address found by defaultLookup. The call is long n = (long) handle.invokeExact(segment).
card.rule: Allocate native arguments, find the symbol, describe the C signature in a FunctionDescriptor, create the downcall handle, and invoke it with exactly matching types.
card.limits: The descriptor must match the real C signature, and layout sizes depend on the platform: the tutorial's size_t choice holds for 64-bit x64 only.

concepts.title: Upcalls: letting C call Java
concepts.question: How can Java code be handed to a C function that expects a function pointer, as qsort does?

paragraphs: Some C functions take a pointer to another function. qsort takes four arguments: a pointer to the first array element, the element count, the element size in bytes, and a pointer to a comparison function. Java code can act as that function pointer through an upcall stub.

First, write the comparison as a static Java method. It receives the two elements as MemorySegment objects, reads each with get and a byte offset, and compares with Integer.compare. Then obtain a method handle for it with MethodHandles.Lookup.findStatic, giving the class, the method name and the method type.

Next, describe the comparator's C-level signature with a FunctionDescriptor and call Linker.upcallStub with the method handle, the descriptor, an arena and optional options. The arena controls the stub's lifetime; the tutorial uses Arena.ofAuto, which the garbage collector manages.
Finally, copy the int array into an off-heap segment, call the qsort downcall handle with the segment, count, element size and stub, and copy the sorted values back into a Java array.
card.example: To sort in descending order, write a static method that compares the second value with the first, so larger numbers come first. Wrap it with findStatic and upcallStub as before. The qsort call and the copy back to a Java array stay the same.
card.rule: Turn a static Java method into a method handle, wrap it with upcallStub and a matching descriptor, and pass the resulting segment wherever C expects a function pointer.
card.limits: The stub is only as safe as your descriptor: the tutorial says the linker cannot verify that the pointer is correct for the downcall it is passed to, and the arena bounds how long the stub lives.

concepts.title: Pointers returned from C: zero-length segments
concepts.question: Why can't Java read the memory behind a pointer returned by malloc directly, and how does reinterpret fix that?

paragraphs: Some native functions allocate memory and return a pointer to it, as malloc does. The Java runtime knows neither the size nor the lifetime of the memory behind that pointer. The FFM API therefore represents it as a zero-length memory segment.

Accessing a zero-length segment throws IndexOutOfBoundsException, because the JVM cannot validate accesses to memory of unknown size. Such segments are mainly meant to be passed to other native functions, for example free, and their scope is always alive, so the JVM does not manage their lifetime.

To read the memory safely, call MemorySegment.reinterpret. The overload with three arguments takes the new size in bytes, an arena to associate the segment with, and an action to run when the arena closes, such as calling free. The arena then manages the memory's lifetime.
card.example: A downcall to malloc with 16 as the argument returns a zero-length segment p. Reading p fails. Calling p.reinterpret(16, arena, cleanup) gives a 16-byte segment tied to the arena, where cleanup is an action that calls free. Closing the arena runs it.
card.rule: Treat a returned pointer as a zero-length segment: pass it on to native code unchanged, or reinterpret it with a size, an arena and a cleanup action before reading it.
card.limits: reinterpret trusts the size you supply: the tutorial warns that too large a size can cause out-of-bounds access, a JVM crash or silent memory corruption, because the JVM cannot verify it.

concepts.title: Reading errno and granting native access
concepts.question: How do you read a C error code after a downcall, and what makes the runtime print native-access warnings?

paragraphs: Some C functions signal failure by setting the thread-local errno. The fopen function returns a null pointer on failure and sets errno. To read it, create the downcall handle with the option Linker.Option.captureCallState and the name errno. It captures that thread-local state right after the foreign function returns. The function strerror turns an errno value into text.

Opening a nonexistent file with fopen in mode r sets errno to 2 in the tutorial. Some FFM methods are unsafe and so are restricted; using one makes the runtime print a warning. The tutorial lists libraryLookup, the reinterpret methods, upcallStub, downcallHandle, AddressLayout.withTargetLayout and ModuleLayer.Controller.enableNativeAccess.

To use them without warnings, pass --enable-native-access=M for code in module M, with a comma-separated list for several modules, or --enable-native-access=ALL-UNNAMED for all class-path code. An executable JAR may instead declare Enable-Native-Access: ALL-UNNAMED in its manifest; a module name cannot go in that attribute.
card.example: A launcher runs java --enable-native-access=ALL-UNNAMED -cp app.jar Main, so class-path code calls restricted methods without warnings. If the same code were packaged as module com.shop on the module path, the flag would read --enable-native-access=com.shop.
card.rule: Capture errno in the downcall handle when a C function reports failure through it, and grant native access explicitly instead of ignoring the warnings.
card.limits: Granting native access silences the warning but does not make the calls safe: the linker still cannot check that a descriptor matches the real function.

concepts.title: Generating bindings with jextract
concepts.question: What does jextract produce from a C header, and how do you keep its output manageable?

paragraphs: Writing descriptors and handles by hand is repetitive. jextract reads C header files and generates Java bindings that use the FFM API, which according to the tutorial became final in JDK 22. Prebuilt binaries are published periodically, or you can build it from source.

Common options: -t sets the target package, -I adds an include directory, -l names the shared library that the header class loads (a leading colon marks a path), --output sets where files go, and --header-class-name sets the header class name. Without it, foo.h gives foo_h; the option is required for several headers.

Big headers produce far more code than needed. Run --dump-includes to list every symbol, edit the file, and pass it back with the at-file syntax, or use the --include options such as --include-function. If you remove a declaration that a kept struct depends on, jextract reports the missing dependency, stops and generates nothing.

The header class holds most static members: functions, global variables, macros, enums, primitive typedefs and layouts such as C_INT; import it statically. Structs, unions, function types and typedefs get their own classes; import them with a wildcard. Adding -Djextract.trace.downcalls=true prints call parameters. C++ and Rust need a C interface first.
card.example: A command with --output src, -t org.demo, -I inc, -l with a colon and the path to libdemo.so, and the header demo.h generates a header class demo_h in package org.demo. Client code then adds import static org.demo.demo_h.* and import org.demo.*.
card.rule: Point jextract at a header with a target package, include directories and library, then import the header class statically and the other generated classes with a wildcard.
card.limits: Filtering must keep dependencies intact: if a kept struct needs a declaration you removed, jextract stops and writes nothing. C++ and Rust need a C interface in between.

concepts.title: Why date and time are hard
concepts.question: What makes date and time handling tricky, and which standards does the API lean on?

paragraphs: According to the tutorial, time only looks simple. Adding one month to 31 January gives a different outcome in a leap year than in a non-leap year. Time zones add more trouble: a country can change its daylight saving rules at short notice, change them more than once a year, or skip daylight saving for a year.

The API defaults to the ISO-8601 calendar, which is built on the Gregorian system and is the de facto world standard. The core classes LocalDateTime, ZonedDateTime and OffsetDateTime use it. Other calendars, such as Hijrah or Thai Buddhist, live in the package java.time.chrono, and you may define your own.

Two outside data sources feed the API. Locale text comes from the Unicode CLDR, which covers hundreds of languages. Zone information comes from the Time-Zone Database (TZDB), which records zone changes around the world since 1970.
card.example: A billing program adds one month to 31 January. Whether the answer lands in late February depends on the year, and which local clock applies depends on zone rules that governments may change.
card.rule: Date and time arithmetic depends on calendar and zone rules, so the API uses the ISO calendar by default and takes locale text from CLDR and zone rules from TZDB.
card.limits: The ISO calendar is only the default; java.time.chrono offers other calendars. The data sources describe what exists, they do not remove the need to pick the right class.

concepts.title: Four design principles and the packages
concepts.question: Which four principles shape java.time, and what do they mean for how you call it?

paragraphs: The tutorial names four principles. Clear: methods are well defined and behave as expected; passing null normally throws NullPointerException. Fluent: most methods reject null and never return null, so calls chain and read easily.

Immutable: most objects cannot change after creation, so a change returns a new object, and that makes the API thread-safe. You use factory methods starting with of, from or with rather than constructors, and there are no set methods. Extensible: you can write your own adjusters and queries, or a whole calendar.

The classes sit in packages. java.time holds the core classes; java.time.chrono other calendars; java.time.format formatting and parsing; java.time.temporal the extended API for library writers (fields and units); java.time.zone zone and rule support, which most developers meet only through ZonedDateTime, ZoneId or ZoneOffset.
card.example: Calling plusDays on a LocalDate does not alter it. It returns a second LocalDate, so you must keep the returned value.
card.rule: A java.time object never changes in place; every change method returns a new object.
card.limits: Immutability is described for most objects; the tutorial does not claim every type in every package is immutable. It also does not cover java.time.chrono in detail.

concepts.title: Method name prefixes
concepts.question: What does each method prefix, such as of, from, with or at, tell you the method does?

paragraphs: The API names methods consistently, so a prefix tells you the kind of operation. Static factories: of creates an instance and mainly validates its inputs; from converts from another type and may lose information; parse reads text. now captures the current moment.
Instance methods: format turns the object into text; get returns part of the state; is queries the state; to converts to another type; at combines the object with another one.
Three prefixes make copies: with returns a copy with one element changed (the immutable counterpart of a setter), plus returns a copy with time added, and minus returns a copy with time subtracted.
card.example: A call such as someDate.withDayOfMonth(15).plusWeeks(2).isAfter(other) reads in sequence: copy with the 15th, copy two weeks later, then a boolean query.
card.rule: The prefix tells the kind of operation: of validates, from converts, with replaces one element, plus and minus shift, is asks, to converts type and at combines.
card.limits: The prefix names the intended kind of operation, not the exact return type. Check the documentation of a specific method before relying on a guess.

concepts.title: Choosing a class: human or machine time
concepts.question: How do you choose between the date and time classes for a given job?

paragraphs: The tutorial separates two ways to see time. Human time uses year, month, day, hour, minute and second. Machine time counts continuously along a timeline from an origin called the epoch, with nanosecond resolution. The API has classes for both.

To choose a class, decide whether you need human or machine time, then which aspects: a time zone or not, date and time or date only, and which parts of a date. Then pick the class that matches. Classes that capture date or time values, such as Instant, LocalDateTime and ZonedDateTime, are called temporal-based classes.

The tutorial's examples: a birth date fits LocalDate; a birth moment for astrology fits LocalDateTime, or ZonedDateTime to include the zone; a timestamp fits Instant. Duration and Period hold amounts of time, not points.
card.example: A bakery records the day a customer's loyalty card expires (LocalDate) and the exact time an order was placed on the till (Instant).
card.rule: Pick the class from two questions: human or machine time, and which parts (zone, date, time) you need.
card.limits: The tutorial's scenarios are guidance, not a complete list. Needs that combine several requirements, such as zone plus daylight saving behaviour, call for a closer look at the zone classes.

concepts.title: DayOfWeek and Month enums
concepts.question: How do the DayOfWeek and Month enums store values, do arithmetic and produce readable names?

paragraphs: DayOfWeek has seven constants, MONDAY to SUNDAY, with integer values 1 to 7. Month has twelve constants, JANUARY to DECEMBER, with values 1 to 12. The tutorial recommends using the constants, such as DayOfWeek.FRIDAY or Month.SEPTEMBER, rather than raw integers, for readability and type safety.
The enums have methods like the temporal classes. Adding 3 days to MONDAY gives THURSDAY. Month.maxLength() reports the longest the month can be; for February it is 29.

getDisplayName takes a TextStyle and a Locale and returns a name in the user's language. FULL is the full name, SHORT an abbreviation, NARROW typically one letter, and STANDALONE variants suit languages where the word changes when a name stands alone. For a Month without a defined style, you get the numeric value as text.
card.example: In a roster tool, DayOfWeek.SATURDAY.plus(2) gives MONDAY, and Month.FEBRUARY.getDisplayName(TextStyle.SHORT, locale) gives a short February name in that locale.
card.rule: Use the enum constants, let plus wrap around the week or year, and ask getDisplayName for a localized name in the style you need.
card.limits: Display names depend on locale and style. Some styles may be undefined for a month, and then the method returns the number as text. maxLength is the maximum, not the length in a given year.

concepts.title: Date-only classes
concepts.question: Which classes hold only date information, and what can each tell you?

paragraphs: Four classes hold dates without a time or time zone: LocalDate, YearMonth, MonthDay and Year. LocalDate is a year, month and day in the ISO calendar, suited to dates such as a birth date or a wedding date. You create one with of methods, and get a changed copy with with methods.
LocalDate can tell the day of the week with getDayOfWeek. YearMonth is a month within a given year, and lengthOfMonth gives how many days it has. MonthDay is a day within a month, such as 1 January.
MonthDay.isValidYear(int) asks whether a day exists in a year; February 29 is not valid in 2010. Year.isLeap tells whether a year is a leap year; 2012 is.
card.example: A library stores each reader's membership start as a LocalDate, billing cycles as YearMonth, and the yearly book-sale day as MonthDay.
card.rule: Choose the date class that holds exactly the parts you need: LocalDate, YearMonth, MonthDay or Year.
card.limits: None of these classes carries a time of day or a zone. If you need either, use LocalTime, LocalDateTime or a zoned class.

concepts.title: LocalTime and LocalDateTime
concepts.question: What do LocalTime and LocalDateTime represent, and what do they leave out?

paragraphs: LocalTime works like the other Local classes but holds only a time of day. It suits showtimes, opening hours and digital clocks. It stores no zone or daylight saving information.

LocalDateTime combines a date and a time to the nanosecond: conceptually, a LocalDate joined to a LocalTime. It also carries no zone. Its value is local time: 1:10 p.m. on 17 August means that on a local clock, not at one moment of the world timeline.

Like every temporal class they offer now(), several of methods, and from to convert another temporal type. Arithmetic methods add or subtract hours, minutes, days, weeks and months. For a zone, use ZonedDateTime or OffsetDateTime.
card.example: A cinema lists a film at LocalTime 19:30. An exam notice says LocalDateTime 15 June 10:00 at the hall, meaning the hall's own clock.
card.rule: LocalTime and LocalDateTime hold local clock values with no zone, so they name a clock reading, not a moment on the timeline.
card.limits: A LocalDateTime cannot identify one moment, because the same reading is a different moment in each zone. Use a zoned class, or an Instant, when the moment matters.

concepts.title: ZoneId, ZoneOffset and the zoned classes
concepts.question: How do ZoneId and ZoneOffset differ, and which class should carry a zone?

paragraphs: A time zone is a region using the same standard time. Its identifier usually has the region/city form, such as Asia/Tokyo, and it has an offset from Greenwich/UTC (Tokyo is +09:00). Offsets are usually whole hours but not always.

ZoneId identifies a zone and supplies the rules for converting between an Instant and a LocalDateTime. ZoneOffset is a fixed offset from UTC. ZoneRules, in java.time.zone, describe how a zone's offset changes over time.

ZonedDateTime is a LocalDateTime plus a ZoneId and uses the rules. OffsetDateTime is a LocalDateTime plus a ZoneOffset; OffsetTime is a LocalTime plus a ZoneOffset; neither uses rules. Only ZonedDateTime can handle daylight saving gaps and overlaps.
card.example: A flight leaves Los Angeles at 14:00 local time. Build a ZonedDateTime with the Los Angeles zone, move it to Tokyo with withZoneSameInstant, and add the flight minutes.
card.rule: Use ZonedDateTime when zone rules such as daylight saving matter, and OffsetDateTime or OffsetTime when only a fixed offset from UTC is needed.
card.limits: OffsetDateTime is right for database timestamps in absolute offsets and for network formats such as XML, but it cannot handle daylight saving changes, because it holds no rules.

concepts.title: Instant: a point on the timeline
concepts.question: What is an Instant, what can you do with it, and what must you add to see a calendar date?

paragraphs: An Instant is the start of a nanosecond on the timeline and is meant for machine timestamps. Values count from the epoch, 1970-01-01T00:00:00Z. An instant before the epoch is negative, one after it positive. The constants EPOCH, MIN and MAX give the reference point and the extreme past and future.
toString gives ISO-8601 text. plus and minus add or subtract time, isAfter and isBefore compare, and until measures the time between two instants.

According to the tutorial, an Instant does not work with years, months or days (months and years are indeed rejected). To use them, attach a zone and convert to a LocalDateTime or ZonedDateTime, for example with LocalDateTime.ofInstant and a zone. A ZonedDateTime or OffsetDateTime converts to an Instant directly, but the reverse needs a zone or offset.
card.example: To show a log timestamp as local time: take the Instant, choose a ZoneId, convert with ofInstant, then format the result.
card.rule: An Instant is a zone-free point on the timeline; add a zone to get human date fields.
card.limits: According to the tutorial an Instant does not support years, months or days; in practice months and years are rejected. Use zoned or local types for calendar arithmetic. An Instant needs a zone before it gives a readable date.

concepts.title: Parsing and formatting with DateTimeFormatter
concepts.question: How do you turn text into a date or a date into text, and what do pattern letters mean?

paragraphs: Parsing turns a string into a temporal object; formatting turns a temporal object into a string. Both use a DateTimeFormatter, which is immutable and thread-safe and may be kept in a static constant. It offers predefined formatters and lets you define your own pattern.

LocalDate.parse with one argument uses ISO_LOCAL_DATE. With a second argument you pass your own formatter, for example BASIC_ISO_DATE for text like 19590709. Pattern letters are case-sensitive: MMM is a month abbreviation, d allows one digit, dd needs two characters with padding, and yyyy is a four-digit year.

format(DateTimeFormatter) exists on ZonedDateTime, OffsetDateTime, OffsetTime, LocalDateTime, LocalDate and LocalTime. parse can throw DateTimeParseException and format can throw DateTimeException, so catch them where text may be wrong.
card.example: A formatter built from MMM d yyyy accepts text like Jan 3 2003. A formatter built from MMM dd yyyy needs Jun 03 2003 with a padded day.
card.rule: Build a formatter whose pattern matches the text shape, and expect DateTimeParseException when it does not.
card.limits: Parsing fails when text does not match the pattern in order and shape. A one-digit day text does not fit dd.

concepts.title: The temporal package: fields, units and amounts
concepts.question: What are Temporal, TemporalField, TemporalUnit and TemporalAmount, and how do you ask what an object supports?

paragraphs: The package java.time.temporal supports calculations. The tutorial says application code should declare variables as concrete types such as LocalDate or ZonedDateTime, not as Temporal. Temporal is implemented by Instant, LocalDateTime and ZonedDateTime and adds add and subtract methods; TemporalAccessor is its read-only version.

A TemporalField defines a value of a temporal object. ChronoField supplies constants such as DAY_OF_WEEK, MONTH_OF_YEAR, CLOCK_HOUR_OF_DAY and DAY_OF_YEAR. IsoFields, WeekFields and JulianFields supply further fields.

A TemporalUnit measures amounts, and ChronoUnit implements it, from milliseconds to millennia. TemporalAmount is implemented by Period and Duration. isSupported asks whether an object supports a field or unit: LocalDate does not support CLOCK_HOUR_OF_DAY.
card.example: Before reading the hour-based field from a value of unknown type, check isSupported first.
card.rule: Fields name parts, units name measures, amounts such as Period and Duration are applied to temporal objects, and isSupported tells what an object can do.
card.limits: Not every class supports every field or unit. For example, an Instant rejects months and years (the tutorial also lists days, which the Java documentation treats as exactly 24 hours, so check before relying on that).

concepts.title: Adjusters and queries
concepts.question: How do you move a date by a rule, and how do you ask a question about a date?

paragraphs: A TemporalAdjuster takes a temporal object and returns an adjusted one, working with all temporal types. With a ZonedDateTime the result keeps the original time and zone. TemporalAdjusters has predefined ones: first or last day of the month or year, the last Wednesday of the month, the first Tuesday after a date. You apply them with with().
You can write your own by implementing adjustInto. The tutorial's PaydayAdjuster sets paydays on the 15th and the last day of the month, and moves a weekend payday to the previous Friday.

A TemporalQuery retrieves information instead of changing the value. TemporalQueries has predefined ones, such as precision(), which returns the smallest unit an object supports. A custom query implements queryFrom and, for instance, returns true when a date is in a holiday range. A plain method can also be used as a lambda.
card.example: Starting from a date, with(TemporalAdjusters.lastDayOfMonth()) returns the last day of that month, keeping the same type.
card.rule: Adjusters return a changed temporal; queries return information about it.
card.limits: An adjuster expresses one rule; the tutorial's custom payday adjuster assumes the current calendar year. A query does not change the object.

concepts.title: Duration, Period and ChronoUnit.between
concepts.question: When should you measure time with Duration, with Period, or with ChronoUnit.between?

paragraphs: Duration is time-based: seconds and nanoseconds, suited to machine time with Instant objects. It has no years, months or days, can be negative, and ignores zones and daylight saving. A Duration of one day is exactly 24 hours, so adding it to a ZonedDateTime adds 24 hours.

Period is date-based: years, months and days, read with getYears, getMonths and getDays. A one-day Period added to a ZonedDateTime can vary with the zone, for instance on a daylight saving change day, because it accounts for local time.

ChronoUnit.between works on any temporal object but gives one total in one unit, such as days. For an age as years, months and days use Period; for the whole span in days use between. Both ignore zones unless you combine Period with a ZonedDateTime.
card.example: Age from a birth date: Period gives years, months and days; ChronoUnit.DAYS.between gives the total days.
card.rule: Use Duration for elapsed machine time, Period for calendar amounts, and between when one total in one unit is needed.
card.limits: Neither Period nor between knows about zones unless the values are zoned. A Period cannot be turned into a fixed number of days, since months differ in length.

concepts.title: Clock: controlling what now means
concepts.question: How can you control which zone or moment the now methods use?

paragraphs: The no-argument now() on temporal classes uses the system clock and the default time zone. A one-argument now(Clock) accepts another Clock. The current date and time depends on the zone, so a global application may need a Clock to get the correct one. Using a Clock is optional but helps when testing other zones or a time that does not advance.

Clock is abstract, so you obtain one from a factory. Clock.systemUTC() gives a clock in UTC. Clock.fixed(Instant, ZoneId) always returns the same instant, so time does not advance. Clock.offset(Clock, Duration) gives a clock shifted from a base clock by a Duration.
card.example: A test creates Clock.fixed with a chosen Instant and a zone, then passes it to now(clock) so that a deadline check gives the same answer every run.
