card.rule: Pass a Clock to now when the zone or the moment must be controlled, especially in tests.
card.limits: Clock is optional. The tutorial does not say a Clock is needed for ordinary code that uses the default zone and system time.

concepts.title: Non-ISO calendars and conversion
concepts.question: How do you convert dates between the ISO calendar and other calendars?

paragraphs: The package java.time.chrono provides non-ISO chronologies: Japanese, Hijrah, Minguo and Thai Buddhist, and you can create your own. The tutorial does not cover the package in detail.

To go from ISO to a non-ISO date, use the from(TemporalAccessor) factory of the chronology's date class, for example JapaneseDate.from. To go back, use LocalDate.from, which other temporal classes also offer. Both throw DateTimeException when the date cannot be converted.

A DateTimeFormatterBuilder can build a format for printing a date in a given chronology. The tutorial's round trip converts a LocalDate to a chronology date, to text and back, and gets October 29, 1996 again.
card.example: Convert a LocalDate to a ThaiBuddhistDate with ThaiBuddhistDate.from, and back to ISO with LocalDate.from.
card.rule: Use the target type's from method to convert between calendars; both directions may throw DateTimeException.
card.limits: The tutorial does not cover java.time.chrono in detail, so rules of individual calendars, such as year numbering, are beyond it.

concepts.title: Legacy date classes and conversion methods
concepts.question: Why replace the old java.util date classes, and how do you move between old and new objects?

paragraphs: The tutorial calls the pre-Java 8 classes Date, Calendar, TimeZone and GregorianCalendar problematic. They are not type safe, they are mutable and so unsafe across threads, and they are error-prone, with unusual month numbering and weak typing.

Java 8 added methods so old code can work with java.time. Calendar.toInstant gives an Instant. GregorianCalendar.toZonedDateTime gives a ZonedDateTime and GregorianCalendar.from(ZonedDateTime) goes back using the default locale. Date.from(Instant) and Date.toInstant convert between Date and Instant. TimeZone.toZoneId gives a ZoneId.
An Instant has no zone, so converting it to a ZonedDateTime needs a zone.
card.example: Given a Date, call toInstant, add a ZoneId to get a ZonedDateTime, and use that for formatting or arithmetic.
card.rule: Use the conversion methods at the boundary with old code: toInstant, toZonedDateTime, Date.from, GregorianCalendar.from and toZoneId.
card.limits: The conversion methods do not make old and new objects the same: Instant needs a zone to become a ZonedDateTime, and old classes remain mutable.

concepts.title: Mapping old code to java.time
concepts.question: How should you replace common old date and time patterns with java.time types?

paragraphs: There is no one-to-one replacement for old methods, so most code needs rewriting unless the conversion methods are enough. The tutorial says to try the conversions first, and otherwise rewrite with java.time classes, using the Standard Calendar table as a starting point.

Date and Instant both are points on the UTC timeline, independent of zone and stored as seconds and nanoseconds from the epoch. GregorianCalendar corresponds to ZonedDateTime, which is made of a LocalDate, a LocalTime, a ZoneId and a ZoneOffset. TimeZone corresponds to ZoneId, which has rules, while ZoneOffset is only a fixed offset.

Old code with a fake date of 1970-01-01 just to hold a time of day should use LocalTime. Old code that uses midnight to hold a date should use LocalDate; the tutorial says the midnight approach is flawed because midnight does not exist on some days in some countries when daylight saving begins. For formatting use DateTimeFormatter, or Formatter and String.format.
card.example: A legacy class set a Calendar to midnight to store a date of birth. The new code stores a LocalDate.
card.rule: Try the conversions first; otherwise map the purpose: moment to Instant, calendar with zone to ZonedDateTime, time of day to LocalTime, date to LocalDate.
card.limits: The mapping follows what the old object was used for, not its class. Several old uses map to different new types.

concepts.title: Regex, Pattern and Matcher
concepts.question: Which classes does Java use to work with a regular expression, and how do you get each one?

paragraphs: A regular expression describes a set of strings that share some feature. You use one to search text, edit it or pull data out of it. Its syntax is a small language of its own that must be learned apart from ordinary Java. The tutorial says Java's flavor is most similar to Perl's.

Two classes do the work. A Pattern is a compiled regular expression. It has no public constructor, so you call the static method compile and pass the regex text. A Matcher applies a Pattern to one input string. It also has no public constructor, so you ask the Pattern for one by calling matcher.

A third class, PatternSyntaxException, is unchecked and reports a malformed pattern. Regexes can also name Unicode characters. Backslash u plus four hex digits gives one code point. Backslash p with a property in braces matches one character in a category, and backslash capital P matches one character outside it.
card.example: Pattern p = Pattern.compile("\\p{Lu}"); Matcher m = p.matcher("aBc"); The Matcher m can now be asked about the text aBc; an uppercase letter is present, namely B.
card.rule: Compile the regex text into a Pattern, ask the Pattern for a Matcher for each input, and read results from the Matcher.
card.limits: This lesson covers the java.util.regex flavor only, so a pattern written for another tool may need changes. Unicode property names depend on the Unicode version used by the JDK.

concepts.title: Literal text, indexes and metacharacters
concepts.question: How does a literal match report its position, and how do you make a special character ordinary?

paragraphs: The simplest regex is plain text: foo matches the input foo. A match reports a start index and an end index. The start is included and the end is excluded, so foo found in foo runs from 0 to 3. Picture the indexes as the gaps between character cells. A repeated search starts the next match at the previous end index.

Some characters are metacharacters with a special meaning. The dot means any one character, so cat. matches cats. Others include the star, plus, question mark, parentheses, brackets, braces, caret, dollar and backslash. Characters such as the at sign and the hash are never special.

To read a metacharacter as ordinary text, put a backslash before it, or wrap a stretch of text between backslash Q and backslash E. The Q comes before the E, and the pair can sit anywhere in the pattern. Everything between them is plain text.
card.example: To find the text a.b exactly, write a\.b or \Qa.b\E. The plain regex a.b would also match axb, because the dot accepts any character.
card.rule: Plain characters match themselves, a metacharacter needs a backslash or a Q to E quote to be literal, and a match includes its start index but excludes its end index.
card.limits: Whether a character is special depends on context, so the metacharacter list is not a list of characters that are special everywhere. The hyphen matters inside a bracketed class but is ordinary in plain text.

concepts.title: Character classes
concepts.question: How do you build a set of allowed characters, and how are sets combined?

paragraphs: A character class is a set of characters inside square brackets. It matches exactly one character of the input, and it has nothing to do with Java classes. In [bcr]at the class governs only the first character, so the pattern matches bat, cat or rat. The letters after the class must still follow.

A caret as the first character negates the class: [^bcr]at accepts any one character except b, c and r before at. A hyphen between two characters makes a range, as in [1-5] or [a-h]. Ranges can sit side by side, so [a-zA-Z] accepts any letter.

Classes combine. A union nests one class in another: [0-4[6-8]] accepts 0 to 4 and 6 to 8. An intersection uses a double ampersand and keeps shared characters: [0-5&&[3-9]] accepts 3, 4 and 5. A subtraction intersects with a negated class: [0-9&&[^345]] accepts every digit except 3, 4 and 5.
card.example: [a-z&&[^bc]] accepts the letters a to z except b and c, which is the same as [ad-z].
card.rule: A bracketed class matches one character: caret negates, hyphen makes ranges, nesting makes unions, and double ampersand gives intersections and subtractions.
card.limits: A class always consumes a single character, so it cannot match a whole word without help from a quantifier. Inside the brackets the caret, hyphen and ampersand follow class rules rather than their usual meanings.

concepts.title: Predefined classes and doubled backslashes
concepts.question: Which shorthand classes exist, and how do you write them inside Java source code?

paragraphs: The tutorial advises using predefined classes whenever possible, because they are easier to read and prevent mistakes in hand-built classes. The dot means any character. Backslash d is a digit, the same as 0 to 9. Backslash s is a whitespace character such as space, tab or newline. Backslash w is a word character: a letter, a digit or an underscore.
A capital letter reverses the class. Backslash D is a non-digit, backslash S a non-whitespace character and backslash W a non-word character. Each shorthand still matches exactly one character.

Constructs that start with a backslash are called escaped constructs. Inside a Java string literal each backslash must be typed twice so the code compiles, but the regex that results still holds a single backslash. Text typed at a console prompt needs no doubling.
card.example: The regex \d\d:\d\d fits times like 09:45. In Java source it is written as the literal "\\d\\d:\\d\\d".
card.rule: Prefer the predefined classes, use capitals to negate them, and type every regex backslash twice inside a Java string literal.
card.limits: A word character is a letter, digit or underscore, so a hyphen or an apostrophe in a word is not matched by backslash w. Doubling applies to Java string literals, not to text read while the program runs.

concepts.title: Quantifiers and zero-length matches
concepts.question: How do quantifiers set repeat counts, which element do they apply to, and what is a zero-length match?

paragraphs: A quantifier says how often the element before it may repeat. X? means zero or one time, X* zero or more, X+ one or more, X{n} exactly n times, X{n,} at least n times, and X{n,m} between n and m times.

A quantifier applies only to the single element just before it. abc+ repeats only the c. Wrap text in a group to repeat all of it: (abc)+. A class such as [abc]+ repeats any mix of those letters. Likewise dog{3} repeats only the g, while (dog){3} needs the whole word three times.

A zero-length match starts and ends at the same index. It can occur in empty input, at the start, between any two characters and after the last character. So a* on aaaaa gives one match of all five letters and then a zero-length match at index 5, while a+ gives only the first.
card.example: The regex a* on the input baab reports four matches: zero-length at 0, aa from 1 to 3, zero-length at 3, and zero-length at 4.
card.rule: A quantifier repeats the single element before it, and forms that allow zero repeats can produce zero-length matches.
card.limits: Braces count repeats of one element only, so grouping is needed for longer pieces. A quantifier that allows zero repeats can match nothing at all, so it cannot demand that something is present.

concepts.title: Greedy, reluctant and possessive quantifiers
concepts.question: How do the three quantifier styles differ in how much text they take and whether they give any back?

paragraphs: Each quantifier has three styles. Greedy is the default: it takes as much as it can and gives characters back one at a time if the rest of the pattern fails. Reluctant adds a question mark, as in X*?: it starts with little and takes more only when needed. Possessive adds a plus, as in X*+: it takes as much as it can and gives none back.

On the input xfooxxxxxxfoo, the greedy .*foo takes everything, backs off to the last foo and finds one match covering the whole input. The reluctant .*?foo finds two matches, xfoo from 0 to 4 and xxxxxxfoo from 4 to 13. The possessive .*+foo finds none, because .*+ swallows all the text and leaves nothing for foo.
According to the tutorial, possessive quantifiers skip backtracking and so can run faster when a match is not found right away. Choose one when you want to take everything and return none of it.
card.example: On the input (red) and (blue), the regex \(.*\) matches the whole input, while \(.*?\) finds (red) and (blue) as two separate matches.
card.rule: Greedy takes the most and backs off, reluctant takes the least and grows, and possessive takes the most and never backs off.
card.limits: When only one length can succeed, all three styles give the same result. Possessive is not a safe default, because it can turn a working pattern into one that never matches.

concepts.title: Capturing groups and backreferences
concepts.question: How are capturing groups numbered, what does group zero mean, and how does a backreference reuse captured text?

paragraphs: Parentheses make a capturing group. It treats several characters as one unit, so a quantifier can repeat all of them, and it saves the text it matched. Groups are numbered by their opening parentheses from left to right. In ((A)(B(C))) there are four groups: the outer one is 1, (A) is 2, (B(C)) is 3 and (C) is 4.

Group 0 always means the whole expression, and groupCount on a Matcher does not count it. A group whose opening parenthesis is followed by a question mark does not capture and is not counted. After a match, group(n) gives the captured text, start(n) where it began, and end(n) the index just past its last character.

A backreference is a backslash followed by a group number. It matches the very same text that the group captured, not just any text the group could match. The regex (\d\d)\1 accepts 1212 but not 1234, because the second pair must repeat the first.
card.example: In (\w)\1 the group captures one word character and \1 demands the same character again, so the regex finds the double letter ll in hello.
card.rule: Count opening parentheses to number groups, remember that group 0 is the whole match, and use a backreference to repeat captured text exactly.
card.limits: The tutorial does not cover named groups. It says only that groups starting with a question mark do not capture and are not counted.

concepts.title: Boundary matchers
concepts.question: Which constructs test a position, and how do they pin a match to a line, a word or the previous match?

paragraphs: Boundary matchers match a position, not a character. Caret is the start of a line and dollar its end. Backslash A is the start of the input and backslash z its end; backslash capital Z also ends the input but ignores one final line terminator. Backslash b is a word boundary and backslash B a position that is not one.

Putting caret and dollar around a pattern forces it to cover the whole line. If the input has extra leading whitespace, ^dog$ fails. Writing caret, dog and word characters anchors the word to the start of the line; word characters, dog and dollar anchor it to the end.

A bare dog matches inside dogs and hotdog. Wrapping it as \bdog\b accepts only the standalone word. Backslash G matches where the previous match ended, so a search using it finds consecutive matches only: a second dog that does not directly follow the first is missed.
card.example: On the input dog dogs hotdog, the regex dog finds three matches, but \bdog\b finds only the first word at index 0.
card.rule: Boundary matchers test positions, so use them to pin a pattern to a line, to the input, to a word edge or to the end of the previous match.
card.limits: According to the tutorial, the MULTILINE flag, shown with the Pattern class, changes whether caret and dollar also match at line terminators. Word boundaries rely on the word character definition, so punctuation counts as a boundary.

concepts.title: Compile flags and embedded flags
concepts.question: Which flags change how a pattern is read, and how can they be set inside the regex itself?

paragraphs: Pattern.compile accepts a second argument, an int bit mask of flags that change how the regex is read. Combine flags with the bit-or operator, or store the mask in an int. CASE_INSENSITIVE ignores case, assuming only US-ASCII letters by default; add UNICODE_CASE for Unicode-aware folding.

DOTALL lets the dot match line terminators. MULTILINE makes caret and dollar match at line terminators as well as at the start and end of the input. COMMENTS ignores whitespace in the pattern and treats a hash to the end of the line as a comment. UNIX_LINES recognizes only the newline as a line terminator. LITERAL reads the whole pattern as plain characters.

CANON_EQ matches characters whose canonical forms agree; it is off by default and may cost speed. Most flags have an embedded form written inside the regex: (?i) for CASE_INSENSITIVE, (?x) COMMENTS, (?s) DOTALL, (?m) MULTILINE, (?u) UNICODE_CASE and (?d) UNIX_LINES. CANON_EQ and LITERAL have none.
card.example: Pattern.compile("^dog$", Pattern.CASE_INSENSITIVE) and the regex (?i)^dog$ behave alike: both accept DOG.
card.rule: Pass flags as a bit mask to compile, or write the matching embedded flag inside the regex.
card.limits: CANON_EQ and LITERAL have no embedded form, and case folding beyond US-ASCII needs UNICODE_CASE as well. With LITERAL on, the other flags become superfluous, apart from the case flags.

concepts.title: Pattern shortcuts, split, quote and String twins
concepts.question: Which shortcut methods exist on Pattern and String, and which of them read their argument as a regex?

paragraphs: Pattern.matches(regex, input) is a static shortcut that checks whether the whole input matches; Pattern.matches with the regex backslash d and the input 1 is true. A Pattern also has split, which returns the text between matches, and quote, which turns any string into a pattern that matches it literally. toString returns the regex the Pattern was built from.

Splitting one:two:three:four:five on a colon gives the five words. String has twins: str.matches(regex) behaves like Pattern.matches, and str.split(regex, limit) behaves like compile followed by split with a limit. Calling str.split(regex) alone uses a limit of zero, which removes trailing empty strings.
The String method replace takes plain text, not a regex, and works from left to right. Replacing aa with b in aaa gives ba, not ab. It differs from replaceAll, which reads a regex.
card.example: Pattern.quote("1+1") returns a string that, used as a pattern, finds the text 1+1 itself instead of one or more ones followed by a one.
card.rule: Use the shortcuts for one-off checks, use quote to match text literally, and remember that replace is literal while matches, split and replaceAll read regexes.
card.limits: The matches shortcut tests the whole input, so it cannot find a part of it; a Matcher is needed for that.

concepts.title: Study methods and index methods of Matcher
concepts.question: How do matches, lookingAt and find differ, and how do you read where the last match sat?

paragraphs: A Matcher has study methods that return a boolean. matches() asks whether the whole input fits the pattern. lookingAt() asks whether the pattern matches starting at the beginning, but the match may stop early. find() looks for the next matching part anywhere and can be repeated to walk through the input. find(int start) first resets the matcher and then searches from the given index.

Both matches and lookingAt begin at the start of the input; the difference is that matches must use all of it. The index methods describe the last match: start() gives its first index and end() gives the offset just after its last character. start(group) and end(group) do the same for a captured group.
A loop such as while (m.find()) visits each match in turn, and inside it start() and end() give the position. Since each search resumes at the previous end, matches do not overlap.
card.example: Pattern cat on the input catalog: lookingAt is true, matches is false, find is true. On concat: lookingAt is false, find is true, start() is 3 and end() is 6.
card.rule: matches needs the whole input, lookingAt needs a match at the start, and find looks anywhere and can be repeated.
card.limits: The index methods describe the previous match, so call a study method first. The end value is one past the last character, not the index of the last character.

concepts.title: Replacing matches
concepts.question: Which Matcher methods replace matches, and how does the append pair compare with replaceAll?

paragraphs: replaceFirst(String) swaps the first match for the replacement, and replaceAll(String) swaps every match. The pattern can be any regex. With the pattern a*b, the input aabfooaabfooabfoob and the replacement -, replaceAll gives -foo-foo-foo-.

appendReplacement and appendTail do the same job in steps. For each match you call appendReplacement(sb, replacement), which appends the text since the last match plus the replacement. After the loop, appendTail(sb) adds the rest of the input. The result equals replaceAll, with room to change each replacement.

The replacement string treats backslash and dollar sign specially, so for literal text use the static Matcher.quoteReplacement. The String methods replaceFirst and replaceAll are shortcuts for compile, matcher, and then the Matcher method of the same name.
card.example: Pattern.compile("\\d+").matcher("a1b22").replaceAll("#") gives a#b#.
card.rule: replaceAll changes every match, replaceFirst only the first, the append pair does the same in steps, and literal replacement text needs quoteReplacement.
card.limits: The replacement is not a regex, but it still treats backslash and dollar sign as special, so text such as a price needs quoteReplacement.

concepts.title: PatternSyntaxException and its diagnostics
concepts.question: What does PatternSyntaxException report, and which methods locate the fault?

paragraphs: PatternSyntaxException is unchecked, so the compiler does not force you to catch it. It signals a syntax error in a pattern. getDescription returns a description of the error, getIndex the position in the pattern, getPattern the faulty regex, and getMessage a multi-line text that combines the description, the index, the pattern and a marker pointing at the problem.

The tutorial's example pattern is ?i)foo. The programmer meant the embedded flag (?i) but forgot the opening parenthesis. The error reported is a dangling metacharacter, the question mark, at index 0. Reading the index and the marker leads to the missing parenthesis.
card.example: Catching the exception around Pattern.compile of (abc and printing getDescription and getIndex shows an unclosed group and the position where the pattern ended.
card.rule: Use getDescription, getIndex and getPattern, or the multi-line getMessage, to learn what is wrong and where.
card.limits: The exception reports only a malformed pattern. A well-formed regex that matches the wrong text raises nothing.

concepts.title: Class objects and class loaders
concepts.question: What does a Class object stand for, and how do you get one without knowing the type at compile time?

paragraphs: Reflection means a running program looks at its own structure: it can discover fields, methods and constructors, read and write fields, call methods and build objects. The entry point is the Class object, an instance of the class named Class that describes one type.

You can reach it in three ways. Call getClass on any object, a method inherited from Object that reports the real runtime class, whatever the variable was declared as. Write a class literal, the type name followed by dot class. Or load a type from a String, which works even when the name is only known at run time.

Every class is loaded by a class loader. According to the tutorial, JDK classes come from the bootstrap loader, whose getClassLoader result is null, while ordinary application classes come from the application loader. Loaders partition classes for security, so classes in different loaders cannot see each other.
card.example: Suppose Object thing holds a new StringBuilder. Then thing.getClass describes StringBuilder, not Object. The literal StringBuilder.class gives the same Class object, and its loader is null because it is a JDK class.
card.rule: Use getClass for what an object really is, a class literal for a type you can name, and remember that a null loader marks a JDK class.
card.limits: getClass needs an instance, and a literal needs the name written in source. A single-file launch uses a different loader than a compiled run, so classes mixed between the two can fail to see each other.

concepts.title: Shallow reflective access: finding and invoking methods
concepts.question: Which members can shallow reflection reach, and how do you find and call a method?

paragraphs: According to the tutorial, shallow reflective access covers public members, superclasses and implemented interfaces. For a sealed type you can also discover its permitted subtypes. This level needs no special permission.

To call a method, get the Class, find the Method by name and parameter types, then invoke it with the target object followed by the arguments. For a static method there is no target, so the first argument to invoke is null.

Lookups can fail. A missing method gives NoSuchMethodException and a forbidden one gives IllegalAccessException. Since Java 7 both fall under ReflectiveOperationException, so one catch handles them. The tutorial loops with for-each rather than streams because streams cope poorly with checked exceptions.
Do not depend on the order in which methods come back. The tutorial notes that the order is not guaranteed and differs between JDK builds.
card.example: To reverse a list of names, find the static method named reverse on the Collections class that takes a List, then call invoke with null as the first argument and the list as the second.
card.rule: Find a method by name and parameter types, pass the target (or null for static) plus arguments to invoke, and catch ReflectiveOperationException.
card.limits: Shallow access reaches only public members; private ones need deep access. Lookup order is unspecified, so code that assumes the first method found is the one you want can break on another JDK.

concepts.title: Deep reflective access, modules and records
concepts.question: What lets reflection change a private field, and what can stop it?

paragraphs: Deep reflective access goes beyond public members to private ones. The tutorial shows reflection changing a private final field of an ordinary class, which the compiler would never allow in plain code.

Two things can block it. First, the module system: deep access works only when the package's module is open to your module. Module authors are usually unwilling to open packages, because doing so exposes internal details that later changes could break. The command-line option add-opens is described as a last resort.
Second, records: according to the tutorial, if the class is turned into a record, deep reflection can no longer change its properties.
Because reflection works through names held as Strings, compile-time checks do not cover it. A missing or inaccessible member shows up only when the program runs.
card.example: A class Wallet has a private final field named coins. Reflection can overwrite coins on a Wallet object if its package is open to the caller. If Wallet becomes a record, the same attempt no longer works.
card.rule: Deep access to private state needs an open package, fails on records, and any problem appears at run time.
card.limits: Success on an ordinary class in an open package does not carry over to a closed module or a record. Options such as add-opens are a last resort, and the tutorial does not explain their use further.

concepts.title: What reflection is for and what it costs
concepts.question: When is reflection worth using, and what does it cost?

paragraphs: Reflection lets a running program examine, and sometimes change, how applications behave inside the Java virtual machine. According to the tutorial, it is an advanced feature meant for developers who already know the language fundamentals well.

The tutorial names typical users: programs that create objects from class names supplied later, class browsers and development environments that list members, debuggers that must look at private members, and test tools that call every discoverable method of a class.

It also lists costs. Reflected types are resolved dynamically, so some JVM optimizations cannot apply and calls run slower. Modules can block reflective access. Private members can be reached, which can cause side effects, hurt portability, and break after a platform upgrade.
card.example: A team writes a plug-in loader that receives the text name of a class from a settings file and must create an object of it. The class does not exist when the loader is compiled, so ordinary construction cannot be written. The tutorial calls this extensibility. If the class were known at compile time, plain code would be preferred.
card.rule: Use reflection when ordinary code cannot do the job, because it is slower, can be blocked, and exposes internals.
card.limits: The tutorial advises plain code whenever an operation can be done without reflection. Its performance warning targets frequently called code in performance-sensitive applications.

concepts.title: Getting a Class object
concepts.question: How can you obtain the Class object for a type, and which route works for primitives?

paragraphs: According to the tutorial, java.lang.Class is the entry point for all reflection. The classes in java.lang.reflect have no public constructors, so you obtain them by calling methods on a Class. The JVM keeps one immutable Class instance for each type: a class, interface, enum, record, array, or one of the eight primitives.

Calling getClass() on an object works for any reference type but not for primitives. A class literal, a type name followed by .class, needs no instance and is the easy way to reach a primitive. Class.forName takes a fully qualified name as text and throws ClassNotFoundException if no such class exists.

Each wrapper class has a static field TYPE holding the Class of its primitive, so Double.TYPE is the Class for double. According to the tutorial, Class.forName cannot be used for primitive names, but it does accept array names.
card.example: A variable holds some list implementation and you want its runtime class: call getClass() on the variable. For the Class of int write int.class, because calling a method on the keyword int does not compile. To load a class named by a configuration string, pass the full name to Class.forName and be ready for ClassNotFoundException.
card.rule: Use getClass() for an object, a class literal for a type known at compile time, and forName for a name held as text.
card.limits: getClass() cannot be called on primitives, and forName rejects primitive names. According to the tutorial, Class.forPrimitiveName, added in Java SE 22, accepts them, so older platforms lack it.

concepts.title: Parents, interfaces and nested classes
concepts.question: Which Class methods reach parents, interfaces and nested classes, and how do the near-twins differ?

paragraphs: From a Class you can reach related classes. getSuperclass() returns the single parent, or null for Object. getInterfaces() returns only the interfaces the class itself lists, not those inherited from parents; for an interface it returns the interfaces it extends directly.

For nested types, getClasses() returns the public member classes, interfaces, records, and enums of the class and its superclasses. getDeclaredClasses() returns every member type declared in the class itself, whatever its access, but none inherited. The tutorial's example is Character, whose private cache class shows up only in the declared list.

getDeclaringClass() returns the class in which a member class is declared, or null if the class is not a member class, as with an anonymous class. getEnclosingClass() returns the immediately enclosing class, so for an anonymous class it names the class where that code is written.
card.example: Class Order has a public nested class Line and a private nested class Audit. getClasses() on Order lists Line only; getDeclaredClasses() lists both. Line.class.getDeclaringClass() is Order. An anonymous class written inside Order has a null declaring class but Order as its enclosing class.
card.rule: Methods with Declared in the name look only at the class itself at any access level, and an anonymous class has a null declaring class but a non-null enclosing class.
card.limits: For an ordinary member class, getDeclaringClass and getEnclosingClass return the same class. They differ only for classes that are not members. getInterfaces ignores interfaces inherited from superclasses.

concepts.title: Simple, canonical, type and coded names
concepts.question: Which name does each Class method return, and when is the answer null or a coded string?

paragraphs: A Class can be asked for several names. getSimpleName() gives the name as written in source, without a package; anonymous classes have none. getCanonicalName() gives the fully qualified name defined by the Java Language Specification, and is null for local, anonymous, hidden, and lambda classes.

getTypeName() is an informative string defined by the Type interface, and anonymous and lambda classes do have one, the name the compiler generated. For classes that are not arrays, getName() gives the same text as getTypeName().

Arrays differ for getName(). It writes one opening square bracket per dimension, then a letter for a primitive element: Z boolean, B byte, S short, I int, J long, C char, F float, D double. A reference element is written as L, the name, and a semicolon. That string works with Class.forName.
card.example: For a one-dimensional array of String, getName() gives a bracket, L, java.lang.String and a semicolon, while getSimpleName() gives String followed by brackets and getCanonicalName() gives java.lang.String followed by brackets. For a two-dimensional long array, getName() gives two brackets and J.
card.rule: Simple and canonical names follow the source, the type name exists even for anonymous classes, and getName encodes arrays with brackets and letter codes.
card.limits: A null canonical name is normal for local, anonymous, hidden, and lambda classes, so check for null before printing it. According to the tutorial, the simple name of a lambda class may vary.

concepts.title: Reading modifiers
concepts.question: How are modifiers read from a Class or a member, and what do the number and access flags mean?

paragraphs: Classes, fields, methods, constructors, and parameters can carry modifiers such as public, private, abstract, static, final, sealed, and non-sealed. Not every modifier fits every element: the tutorial notes that an interface cannot be final and an enum cannot be abstract.

getModifiers() on a Class, or on a Field, Method, or Constructor (each is a Member), returns an int in which each bit stands for one modifier; bit 0 is public and bit 3 is static. The helper class java.lang.reflect.Modifier has static methods that decode the number. It has no constants for sealed or non-sealed.

According to the tutorial, Java SE 20 added accessFlags(), which returns a set of AccessFlag values and is easier to read. Modifiers and access flags do not map one to one. The compiler also adds abstract to every interface, so reflecting on Collection reports it as abstract.
card.example: To test a class Invoice, call getModifiers() and pass the int to Modifier.isFinal. A final class gives true. The same check on String reports final and not abstract, while Collection reports abstract although no one wrote that keyword.
card.rule: Read modifiers with getModifiers() and decode the int with Modifier, or call accessFlags() on newer platforms for a readable set.
card.limits: Modifier lacks sealed and non-sealed constants, and modifiers and access flags are not fully one to one. According to the tutorial, accessFlags() needs Java SE 20 or later.

concepts.title: Finding fields and their types
concepts.question: Which Class call finds a field, and how do getField and getDeclaredField differ in what they can see?

paragraphs: A Field object describes one field and can read or write its value on an object. Class offers four lookups. getDeclaredField(name) and getDeclaredFields() look only at the class itself but see every field, private ones included. getField(name) and getFields() include fields inherited from superclasses up to Object, but return public fields only.

The singular forms return one Field, and getDeclaredField can throw NoSuchFieldException. The tutorial's example is ArrayList: getDeclaredFields() lists its own fields whatever their modifiers, while getFields() returns nothing, because neither ArrayList nor its superclasses have a public field.

A field's type comes from getType(), a Class that is erased for generic fields, so a field of type T reports Object. getGenericType() returns a Type whose getTypeName() shows the declaration as written in source, but it does not reveal the actual type arguments used at run time.
card.example: Account has a private field balance and extends Base, which has a public field id. getDeclaredField(balance) finds balance. getField(id) finds id because it is public and inherited. getField(balance) fails because balance is private. getDeclaredFields() returns only Account's own fields, not id.
card.rule: Declared lookups see every access level of one class; plain lookups see the public fields of the class and its parents.
card.limits: getType reports the erased type for generic fields, and getGenericType shows only what the source declared, not the type arguments of a particular object at run time.

concepts.title: Reading and writing field values
concepts.question: How do you read and write a field value reflectively, and what stops you from doing so?

paragraphs: Field.get(object) reads and set(object, value) writes. You must pass the instance, because one Field belongs to the Class and is shared by all instances. Both use Object, so you cast results and primitives are boxed. getInt, setInt and their relatives avoid boxing, but the wrong one for the field's type throws an exception.

Access rules still apply: touching a private field from outside the class fails. setAccessible(true), defined by AccessibleObject, which Field, Method, and Constructor extend, suppresses the checks without changing declared visibility. A named module is closed to reflection unless it or the package is opened; the unnamed module is reachable.

According to the tutorial, setAccessible(true) also suppresses the final check, so a private final instance field can be changed. A static final field and an instance field of a record still cannot be written. From JDK 26 a warning appears, since code cannot assume a final field stays unchanged.
card.example: A User object has a private final String name. Get the Field with getDeclaredField, call setAccessible(true), then read with get(user) and replace with set(user, newName). Without setAccessible the call from another class throws an access exception. If User were a record, the write would fail anyway.
card.rule: Pass the instance to get and set, use setAccessible(true) to pass access checks, and expect records and static final fields to stay unwritable.
card.limits: setAccessible fails for closed modules unless the package is opened, and it changes only the checks, not the visibility. Writing final fields draws warnings from JDK 26 and can defeat optimizations.

concepts.title: Finding methods and their signatures
concepts.question: How do you locate one method or all methods, and what must the parameter types look like?

paragraphs: A Method object describes a method and can run it. Lookup mirrors fields: getDeclaredMethod(name, parameter types) and getDeclaredMethods() see the class's own methods at any access level; getMethod(name, parameter types) and getMethods() include inherited methods, but public ones only.

The parameter types must match exactly. List.get takes an int, so the lookup needs int.class, and Integer.class throws NoSuchMethodException. Type parameters are erased, so a lookup for add on a List of String must use Object.class, not String.class.

getReturnType() gives the raw Class, while getGenericReturnType() keeps generic information. getParameters() lists formal parameters, but class files do not store names unless compiled with javac -parameters. getExceptionTypes() returns the declared exceptions.
card.example: To find the String method substring that takes two ints, call getMethod with substring, int.class, int.class. Passing Integer.class raises NoSuchMethodException. To list public methods including those inherited from Object, call getMethods(); an overridden toString appears once, from the subclass.
card.rule: Name the method and give the exact erased parameter types; use Declared forms for own methods at any access, plain forms for public ones including inherited.
card.limits: Parameter names are not stored by default. Generic return information comes from declarations, and erasure changes what a lookup must pass.

concepts.title: Invoking methods
concepts.question: How does invoke run a method, and how are results, static targets, and failures handled?

paragraphs: Method.invoke(target, args...) runs the method on the target object with the given arguments and returns an Object, so you cast the result when you know its type. A method with no parameters needs only the target. For a static method the target is null.

If the invoked method throws, reflection wraps the exception in InvocationTargetException, and getTargetException() returns the original. A varargs parameter is passed as an array of the right type, an empty array when there are no values.

Calling a non-visible method, such as a private one, from outside throws IllegalAccessException. setAccessible(true) suppresses the check without making the method public, with the same module restrictions as for fields. After erasure the compiler's type safety is lost: invoking add with a string works, but nothing checks it.
card.example: To call text.length() reflectively, find length with no parameter types, invoke it on text, and cast the Integer result. For the static Math.max with two ints, pass null as the target and two numbers. If a method throws, catch InvocationTargetException and inspect getTargetException().
card.rule: Pass the target first, then the arguments, cast the returned Object, and unwrap InvocationTargetException to see the real failure.
card.limits: The null target is for static methods. Private methods need setAccessible(true), and closed modules can still refuse it. Because generics are erased, invoke gives no compile-time type checking.

concepts.title: Creating objects with constructors
concepts.question: How do you create an object reflectively, and why prefer Constructor.newInstance to Class.newInstance?

paragraphs: A Constructor object describes a constructor and can run it to create an object. Constructors are not inherited, so there is no inherited lookup. getDeclaredConstructor(types) and getDeclaredConstructors() see every constructor of the class, private ones included; getConstructor(types) and getConstructors() return public ones only.

Class.newInstance() is deprecated since Java SE 9 and should be avoided: it can call only the no-argument constructor, it passes on any exception the constructor throws, even checked ones, bypassing compile-time checking, and it needs a visible constructor. Constructor.newInstance(args) can call any constructor and may reach private ones.

Four exceptions matter: NoSuchMethodException when no such constructor exists, InvocationTargetException wrapping what the constructor throws, InstantiationException for abstract classes and interfaces, and IllegalAccessException when the constructor is not accessible. setAccessible(true) skips the check on a private constructor without making it public.
card.example: To build a Customer with a String name, call getConstructor(String.class), then newInstance with a name. For a private constructor, look it up with getDeclaredConstructor and call setAccessible(true) first. If Customer is abstract, newInstance throws InstantiationException.
card.rule: Look up the constructor by its exact parameter types and call Constructor.newInstance, avoiding the deprecated Class.newInstance.
card.limits: Constructors are not inherited, so look them up on the declaring class. Private constructors need setAccessible(true), which can still be refused, and abstract classes and interfaces cannot be instantiated.

concepts.title: Recognising and creating arrays
concepts.question: How does reflection recognise an array type and create an array when the type is known only at run time?

paragraphs: An array is a reference-type object holding a fixed number of components of one type. The length cannot change after creation and is not part of the array's type. Components may be primitives, references, or other arrays, and a multi-dimensional array is an array whose components are arrays. The JVM implements arrays, and their only methods are those inherited from Object.

Class.isArray() tells whether a Class is an array class, and getComponentType() returns the element type. java.lang.reflect.Array.newInstance(type, length) creates an array of any type and dimension at run time, and Array.getLength(array) reads its length.
Array.get(array, index) and Array.set(array, index, value) read and write elements, with values boxed. An index at or beyond the length throws ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException.
card.example: To build an int array of 10 elements without writing new int, call Array.newInstance(int.class, 10). Calling getClass().isArray() on the result gives true and getComponentType() gives int. Array.set(arr, 3, 6) stores 6 at index 3, and Array.get(arr, 3) returns it boxed.
card.rule: Use Array.newInstance when the element type or length is known only at run time, and Array.get, set, and getLength to work with the result.
card.limits: The length is fixed once created and is not part of the type, so Array.getLength reports it for each object. An index outside zero to length minus one throws ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException.

concepts.title: Typed array accessors
concepts.question: Which typed Array accessors avoid boxing, and which stores are rejected?

paragraphs: Array has typed methods such as getInt, setInt, getDouble, and setDouble that read and write primitive elements without boxing and unboxing. Field has the same family, so the pattern of typed accessors repeats.

The setters follow widening. Storing an int through setInt into a long array is allowed, because no precision is lost, while calling setLong on an int array is illegal, because it would narrow the value.

A further trap is the same rule applied to another type: Array.setFloat on an int array is rejected with IllegalArgumentException, because a float would narrow into an int. And any index at or beyond the length throws ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException.
card.example: A long array made with Array.newInstance(long.class, 3) accepts Array.setInt(arr, 0, 5), because int widens to long. Array.setLong on an int array is rejected. Array.getDouble reads an element of a double array without creating a Double object.
card.rule: Choose the typed accessor that matches the element type or widens into it, and avoid one that would narrow the value.
card.limits: Typed accessors avoid boxing only on primitive arrays; Array.get and Array.set still box values. Bounds are still checked, so a bad index throws ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException.

concepts.title: Enums through reflection
concepts.question: What does reflection add for enums, and what can it not do with them?

paragraphs: Enums are classes, so reflection has no separate enum class. Three APIs are enum specific: Class.isEnum() tests whether a Class is an enum type, Class.getEnumConstants() returns the constants in declaration order, and Field.isEnumConstant() tests whether a field is an enum constant. Without an instance, getEnumConstants() is the way to list the possible values.

The compiler generates members. Each constant becomes a public static final field named after it, a private static array named $VALUES holds all constants, and methods values(), valueOf(String), and a private $values() are created. Static fields are read with get(null).

An enum constructor is private, and its reflected parameter list is longer than the source one, because the compiler adds the constant's name and index. Reflection cannot add constants: invoking that constructor to make a new one fails.
card.example: For an enum Color with constants RED and GREEN, Color.class.isEnum() is true and getEnumConstants() returns RED then GREEN, like values(). Reading the static field named RED with get(null) also gives RED. An attempt to call the constructor to make BLUE fails.
card.rule: Use isEnum and getEnumConstants to list the constants of a Class, expect compiler-generated members, and do not expect to create new constants.
card.limits: Constants cannot be added at run time. The generated names seen in the tutorial's output, like $VALUES, come from the compiler, and other members behave as in any ordinary class.

concepts.title: Records through reflection
concepts.question: How does reflection describe record components, and why are record fields read-only?

paragraphs: Records strongly enforce non-modifiability and have record components. Class.isRecord(), added with other record support in Java SE 16, tells whether a class is a record. A RecordComponent models one component and offers getName(), getType(), getGenericType(), getGenericSignature(), getAccessor() for the accessor Method, and getDeclaringRecord().

A RecordComponent has no method that returns its Field. To get the Field objects, use getDeclaredFields(). Reading a private field works after setAccessible(true), and getInt avoids unboxing for an int component.

Writing differs: record fields cannot be changed through reflection, even after setAccessible(true), and the attempt throws IllegalAccessException. The compiler generates the canonical constructor implicitly, so it is not in the source, but it can be found and invoked to create a record.
card.example: For a record Point with int components x and y, isRecord() is true. Each RecordComponent reports its name and type, and getAccessor() gives the method x(). getDeclaredFields() lists the private fields x and y. Setting x reflectively throws IllegalAccessException; invoke the canonical constructor to build a new Point instead.
card.rule: Use RecordComponent for metadata and getDeclaredFields for fields; read freely, but create a new record instead of modifying one.
card.limits: Ordinary final fields can be changed after setAccessible(true), according to the tutorial, but record fields cannot. JDK 26 adds warnings for the ordinary final case.

concepts.title: Reading annotations
concepts.question: How do you read annotations at run time, and which calls see inherited or repeated ones?

paragraphs: Frameworks for persistence, injection, validation, and security read annotations at run time. The AnnotatedElement interface, implemented by Class, Field, Method, and Constructor, gives access. isAnnotationPresent(type) tests for one annotation. Returned annotations are instances of the annotation type, so you can call their attribute methods.

getAnnotations() and getAnnotation(type) may include inherited annotations; getDeclaredAnnotations() and getDeclaredAnnotation(type) return only those written on the element itself. An inheritable annotation on a class or abstract class passes to its subclasses. According to the tutorial, enums and records are final and cannot be extended, so nothing inherits from them. Beyond the tutorial: Java does not pass annotations from interfaces to implementing classes.

A repeated annotation is stored in a container annotation, so getAnnotations() finds only the container and you must call its value() to reach the repeats. getAnnotationsByType(type), added in Java SE 8, unwraps the container and returns the repeated annotations directly.
card.example: Bean is an inheritable annotation with run-time retention, and Person carries it. User extends Person with no annotation of its own: User.class.getAnnotations() lists Bean, while getDeclaredAnnotations() is empty. On a field with two Validator annotations, getAnnotationsByType(Validator.class) returns both.
card.rule: Use the Declared forms for annotations written on the element, the plain forms to include inherited ones, and getAnnotationsByType for repeatable annotations.
card.limits: Enums and records are final, so no subtype can inherit their annotations. Repeated annotations sit inside a container, so getAnnotations alone shows only the container; getAnnotationsByType unwraps it.

concepts.title: An annotation-driven interceptor
concepts.question: How can an annotation redirect a service method call to another class, using reflection?

paragraphs: The tutorial builds a small interception system. A service method carries an annotation whose attribute names an interceptor class. When the method is called through a factory, the interceptor's method runs in its place. It may validate or change the arguments, enforce security, decide whether to call the service at all, change the result, or handle exceptions. Proxy objects could do this but are left out.

For simplicity every interceptor implements one interface whose parameterized types describe the intercepted object and the return type. The factory takes the service class, method name, and arguments. It creates the service with its empty constructor, finds the method from the name and the argument classes, checks for the annotation, and returns the result.

If the annotation is present, the factory reads the interceptor class from its value, creates an interceptor, and calls intercept directly, passing the Method, the service object, and the arguments, so the interceptor can call the service reflectively. If absent, the factory invokes the service method with no interception.
card.example: An interceptor for a method greet(String) checks that exactly one String argument arrives and throws otherwise, so the service does not run. It then invokes greet reflectively and appends a note to the returned text. A second service without the annotation runs untouched.
card.rule: Read the annotation's class attribute, build that interceptor, and let it decide whether and how the real method runs.
card.limits: The tutorial calls this code complex and not type-safe at compile time. The method lookup uses the runtime argument classes, so a method declared with CharSequence is not found when a String is passed.

concepts.title: A small dependency injection framework
concepts.question: How does a small framework create beans, share singletons, and fill injected fields reflectively?

paragraphs: A dependency injection framework creates objects for your application instead of your code doing it. A factory inspects a class reflectively, finds fields needing values, and sets them, so business objects start properly initialized and collaborators are created in the right order. The tutorial's BeanFactory is itself a singleton, suggested as an enum.

Its getInstanceOf method takes the class and constructor arguments, builds an array of their classes, finds the matching constructor, and invokes it. Types must match exactly: passing a String when the constructor takes CharSequence leads to NoSuchMethodException. A Singleton annotation marks classes with one instance, kept in a ConcurrentMap registry.

putIfAbsent is atomic, but its returned value may not be the one stored, since another thread may have won, so the factory calls get afterwards. An Inject annotation marks fields: after constructing the bean, the factory gets all declared fields, keeps the annotated ones, obtains an instance of each field's type through itself, and sets the field.
card.example: AppService has a field marked Inject of type DbService, which is marked Singleton. Asking the factory for AppService constructs it with that field null, finds the field, asks the factory for a DbService, and sets it. Asking for AppService twice gives two apps, but both share one DbService.
card.rule: Construct through the factory, check the Singleton annotation for reuse, then set every Inject field with an instance obtained from the same factory.
card.limits: Constructor lookup needs exact types. Several threads may build extra instances before one is registered, unless the whole block is synchronized, which adds contention. The tutorial calls setAccessible even for public fields, which is unnecessary.

concepts.title: Method handles and when access is checked
concepts.question: What is a method handle, and why does the moment its access is checked matter?

paragraphs: According to the tutorial, a method handle is a directly invocable reference to a method, a constructor or a field. Like reflection, it can call methods and constructors and reach fields, but it is a low-level tool, and the API can also adapt the reference, for example by inserting or reordering arguments.

Reflection checks the caller's access on every call. A method handle is checked once, when it is created. A handle built where private members are reachable keeps that reach wherever it travels, so whoever receives it can use it without further checks.

Handles come from a Lookup object, a factory whose access level decides which members it can find. Keeping the lookup and its handles private makes it safe to reach any member. The lookup from MethodHandles.publicLookup finds only public members of public classes in packages that are exported unconditionally.

Reflection and handles can be converted. Lookup.unreflect turns a Method into a handle, and MethodHandles.reflectAs turns a handle back into a Member, but only if no transformation was applied. Reflection can list the members of a class; handles cannot.
card.example: A class builds a handle to its own private method with its own lookup. If it stores the handle in a public field, any other code can call the private method through it. Storing the handle in a private field keeps the reach inside the class.
card.rule: Access is checked when a method handle is created, so use the narrowest lookup that works and keep powerful handles confined.
card.limits: The one-time check makes calls cheaper but moves the responsibility to you, because nothing re-checks the caller later. A public lookup is safe to share only because it can find public members alone.

concepts.title: Finding handles and calling them
concepts.question: How do you find a handle for a method, constructor or field, and how do invokeExact and invoke differ?

paragraphs: A MethodType describes a signature: the return type comes first, then the parameter types. A Lookup finds a handle from a class, a name and a MethodType: findVirtual for instance methods, findStatic for static methods. For a constructor, findConstructor needs only the class and a type.

invokeExact is the core call and demands arguments that match the handle's type exactly. invoke is more forgiving: it adapts the handle to the supplied arguments with asType, then performs the exact call. invokeWithArguments adapts in the same way but takes its arguments as an array or a list.

Fields have their own finders: findGetter and findSetter for instance fields, findStaticGetter and findStaticSetter for static ones. They take the field's type instead of a MethodType. MethodHandles also supplies ready-made array handles, such as arrayConstructor, arrayElementGetter, arrayElementSetter and arrayLength, which need no Lookup.

Both invoke and invokeExact declare Throwable, so the caller must catch it or declare it. An instance field handle needs an instance of the owner when invoked, and the tutorial says VarHandles are generally more suitable for fields.
card.example: To reach a static method named max that takes two ints and returns an int, build a type with int as the return type followed by two int parameters, then call findStatic with the class, the name max and that type.
card.rule: Build a MethodType with the return type first, pick the finder that matches the member, and use invokeExact when types match exactly or invoke when they may need adapting.
card.limits: Field finders take the field's type, not a MethodType, and the preset array handles need no Lookup at all. Adaptation by invoke has limits too: when a conversion is impossible, the call fails.

concepts.title: Adapting handles and handling exceptions
concepts.question: How can you reshape an existing handle without rewriting the method it points to?

paragraphs: Adapters build a new handle around an existing one. asType converts a handle to a new type, for instance one taking Object into one taking String, and throws WrongMethodTypeException if the conversion is impossible. permuteArguments reorders arguments using a new MethodType and an index array. insertArguments pre-binds leading arguments, so callers supply only the rest.

filterArguments runs filter handles on chosen arguments before the call, starting at a position, where null means skip that argument. foldArguments runs a combiner on the trailing arguments and feeds its result into the target at a given position (default 0), so callers omit that argument. filterReturnValue passes the result through another handle.

For exceptions, catchException wraps a handle with a handler for one exception type. The handler returns the target's return type and takes the exception first, then the original arguments. Exceptions of other types still propagate.
card.example: A handle takes a unit cost and then a quantity and returns a price. insertArguments with unit cost 5 yields a handle that takes only the quantity. filterReturnValue with a handle that adds a fee turns the price into a final total.
card.rule: Wrap an existing handle with the adapter that matches the change you need: type, order, fixed values, filtered values or exception handling.
card.limits: Each adapter changes only what it names: a pre-bound argument must not be supplied again, and a catchException handler covers one exception type, so others still propagate.

concepts.title: Platform threads versus virtual threads
concepts.question: What problem do virtual threads solve, and which kind of work do they suit?

paragraphs: A platform thread is a Java thread backed by one operating system thread. According to the tutorial, starting one costs thousands of CPU instructions and each holds several megabytes of memory, so a server cannot give every concurrent request its own.

A virtual thread is a lightweight Java thread that runs on top of a platform thread. Many virtual threads share a smaller number of platform threads. When a virtual thread blocks, it is unmounted, and the platform thread under it goes on to run a different virtual thread. According to the tutorial, they were introduced in Java 19, previewed in Java 20 and finalized in Java 21.

Because blocking is cheap, code can use ordinary branches, loops and try blocks instead of nested callbacks. According to the tutorial, virtual threads fit many concurrent tasks that mostly wait on network input and output, and fit CPU-intensive work poorly, where parallel streams or fork-join tasks are suggested.
card.example: A shop service gets 10000 requests, and each spends about 200 milliseconds waiting for a stock database. Giving each request its own virtual thread is cheap, and while one waits, its platform thread serves another. A program that multiplies huge matrices keeps every core busy and gains little.
card.rule: Use virtual threads for many tasks that mostly block, and other tools for work that mostly computes.
card.limits: The tutorial presents the gain as higher throughput for waiting tasks. A single task does not run faster, and CPU-bound work is a poor fit.

concepts.title: Creating virtual threads and not pooling them
concepts.question: How are virtual threads created and used, and why does the tutorial advise against pooling them?

paragraphs: According to the tutorial, one way is an executor from the Executors class that starts a new virtual thread for each submitted task. Another is a Thread.Builder, which can supply a ThreadFactory for APIs that want one, or create a single thread, unstarted or started. Only the executor route handles tasks that return results.

A virtual thread is still a Thread, so the familiar API applies. Cancellation uses interrupt, and the code must check the interrupted flag or call methods that do. The method isVirtual tells the two kinds apart.
Some details differ. All virtual threads share one thread group, have normal priority and are daemon threads. Calls to setPriority and setDaemon are ignored.

Do not pool virtual threads. Pooling is a tuning tool for scarce platform threads, and queuing virtual threads for a pool only adds overhead. To limit load, guard the scarce resource itself, for example with a Semaphore, whose blocking acquire is acceptable here.
card.example: A crawler fetches 3000 pages. It submits each fetch to a virtual-thread-per-task executor and lets a Semaphore with 20 permits cap the requests in flight against one site.
card.rule: Make one virtual thread per task and limit the resource, not the number of threads.
card.limits: The tutorial's advice targets virtual threads. Pools still make sense for platform threads. Which limit fits depends on the resource, so a rate limit for a web service is not a connection limit. Beyond the tutorial: asking for a non-daemon virtual thread with setDaemon false throws IllegalArgumentException.

concepts.title: Pinning and thread-local variables
concepts.question: When does a virtual thread stop being cheap to block, and what should you do about it?

paragraphs: Virtual threads are mounted on carrier threads, which are platform threads; by default there is one carrier per CPU core. A virtual thread is pinned while it runs a synchronized method or block, or a native method or foreign function. A pinned thread cannot unmount.

Pinning alone does no harm. The trouble comes when a pinned thread blocks, because it then holds its carrier idle. According to the tutorial, JDK 21 starts no extra carrier in that case, so the carriers can run out and other virtual threads wait.

According to the tutorial, if synchronized guards only in-memory work, leave it. If blocking calls occur inside it and you control the source, switch to ReentrantLock. The tutorial says pinning is fixed in JDK 24 and later. A JVM option and Java Flight Recorder events can reveal pinning.

Thread-local variables give each thread its own value. Virtual threads far outnumber pooled threads, so you get far more instances, and the tutorial says to rethink how values are shared. A VM flag can print a stack trace when a virtual thread sets one.
card.example: On JDK 21 a service has four carriers. Four virtual threads each sleep for a minute inside a synchronized method. Every other virtual thread must now wait for a carrier, even if it has almost no work.
card.rule: Do not block while inside synchronized on JDK 21; use ReentrantLock where you control the code, and keep thread-locals few.
card.limits: Pinning without blocking is harmless, and synchronized around brief in-memory work can stay. The tutorial ties the fix to JDK 24 and later, so the advice depends on the version.

concepts.unitTitle: Reading the tutorials as a whole
concepts.title: The five lessons as a chain
concepts.question: How does each of the five lessons build on the one before it?

paragraphs: The five lessons form a chain. Getting Started produces one working program: a class with a main method, compiled and run. Object-Oriented Programming Concepts then explains what objects, classes, inheritance, interfaces and packages are, with little syntax to master.

Language Basics supplies the small parts that every method body is made of: variables, primitive types, arrays, operators, expressions and control flow. Classes and Objects goes back to the class of the first lesson and shows how to declare it fully and create objects from it.
Annotations comes last because it labels declarations. It needs classes, fields and methods to exist before it has anything to attach to.
card.example: The bicycle first appears as an idea in the concept lesson. Language Basics gives its fields types and a range test on the gear. Classes and Objects gives it a constructor and private fields. Annotations lets a subclass method carry an Override label that the compiler checks.
card.rule: Read the lessons as a chain: a running program, the concepts behind it, the parts it is built from, full declarations, and labels on those declarations.
card.limits: The chain is a teaching order, not a lock. Lessons reach back and forward: the concept lesson shows code before the syntax lesson explains it, and a reader can follow parts of a later lesson early.

concepts.unitTitle: Reading the tutorials as a whole
concepts.title: Stating what the lessons are about
concepts.question: How do I say in a sentence what the five lessons are about without listing topics or naming their type?

paragraphs: The unity of a whole is what it is about, stated briefly in one sentence or a short paragraph. It differs from the kind of thing it is, and from a list of its contents.

For the five Java lessons, a kind statement says they are introductory tutorials. A list says they cover a program, objects, variables, classes and annotations. A unity says what they do together: they lead a reader from running a first program to writing classes of their own and labelling them.
A good unity works as a test. Every lesson should be explainable under it, and a sentence that would fit any tutorial at all says too little.
card.example: For Lesson 3 alone: Language Basics gives the small parts, variables, types, operators and control flow, from which every method body is built. This says what the lesson does, and each of its sections fits beneath it.
card.rule: State the unity in a sentence or two that says what the whole does, not what type of material it is and not a list of topics.
card.limits: More than one wording can be right, as long as every part fits under it. A unity is the reader's own statement and can be revised when later parts show a different emphasis.

concepts.unitTitle: Reading the tutorials as a whole
concepts.title: The question each lesson answers
concepts.question: How do I find the question a lesson is answering when the lesson never states it?

paragraphs: Each lesson is an answer to a question. The authors rarely state the question outright, so the reader formulates it, as precisely as possible, from the title, the headings and the exercises.

Read this way, Getting Started asks how to get a program written, built and run. The concept lesson asks what the pieces of an object-oriented program are. Language Basics asks which small parts every method is made of. Classes and Objects asks how to declare classes and create objects. Annotations asks how to attach information to code that tools can check.

A lesson's main question splits into smaller ones, and its sections answer them. The section on the new operator, for example, answers a smaller question inside the main question of Classes and Objects.
card.example: The heading on repeating annotations suggests: how can the same annotation be used twice on one declaration, and what must be declared for the compiler to allow it? That is sharper than asking what annotations are.
card.rule: Write down, as precisely as you can, the question each lesson and each section answers before you study the answer.
card.limits: Some sections only list items or point elsewhere, such as the buzzword list in Lesson 1, and answer no question of their own. A formulated question is a hypothesis and may need revising.

concepts.unitTitle: Reading the tutorials as a whole
concepts.title: Finding the joints between ideas
concepts.question: Which earlier idea does each new idea stand on, and where are those joints in the lessons?

paragraphs: An author starts with a skeleton of ideas and covers it with examples and prose. A reader works the other way: uncover the skeleton by finding the joints, the places where one idea rests on another.

Many joints run across lessons. A private field with public methods rests on encapsulation from the concept lesson. A constructor rests on the idea of a class as a blueprint. A lambda rests on an interface with one abstract method. The Override label rests on a subclass changing an inherited method.
To find a joint, ask of any sentence: what must I already know to follow this? The answer names the earlier idea.
card.example: A static nested class needs the idea of a class, then of a class declared inside another class, then the choice between needing the enclosing object (inner) and not needing it (static nested).
card.rule: For each idea, name the earlier idea it rests on; the joints, not the page order, show how the lessons fit together.
card.limits: Presentation order can differ from dependency order: the first program uses public, static and the System class before later lessons explain them. Such forward uses are open joints to close later.

concepts.unitTitle: Reading the tutorials as a whole
concepts.title: Tracing one example through the lessons
concepts.question: How does following a single example, such as a bicycle, show what each lesson adds to it?

paragraphs: One way to see the lessons as a whole is to follow a single example and ask what each lesson adds to it. The bicycle works well.

In the concept lesson it is an idea: state such as cadence, speed and gear, behavior to change them, a class as the blueprint, and a demo class that creates two objects. In Language Basics its fields get types and default values, and an if test can keep the gear in range.

In Classes and Objects it gets private fields, a constructor and methods that other code calls. In Annotations a subclass method can carry an Override label, so the compiler checks that it replaces an inherited one.
card.example: Take a Light. Lesson 2 gives it on and off states and two behaviors. Lesson 3 makes the state a boolean that starts false. Lesson 4 adds a constructor and a switching method. Lesson 5 marks the switchOn method of a DimmableLight subclass with Override.
card.rule: Follow one example through the lessons and write, for each, the single thing that lesson adds to it.
card.limits: The tutorials do not use one example throughout; Lesson 1 runs a greeting program and other lessons use other examples. When they differ, build your own small example and carry it through.

concepts.unitTitle: Reading the tutorials as a whole
concepts.title: Choosing a construct from the need
concepts.question: Given a need, which construct fits: enum, interface, subclass, lambda, class, annotation or a control-flow statement?

paragraphs: Across the lessons, each construct exists to meet a particular need. Start from the need, not from the construct.

A fixed set of named values known in advance calls for an enum. A promise that the compiler enforces on any implementing class calls for an interface. Shared state and behavior with a specialised child calls for a subclass. A short piece of behavior handed to other code calls for a lambda. A reusable named type with its own state calls for a class.

Information about code, for the compiler or tools to read, calls for an annotation rather than a comment, because a comment cannot be checked or processed. When two constructs both meet the need, take the simpler one.
card.example: A game needs the four directions north, east, south and west. The need is a fixed set known in advance, so an enum fits. Four loose integers, or a class with four flags, would allow meaningless values.
card.rule: Name the need first, then choose the simplest construct whose stated purpose matches it.
card.limits: The categories overlap: an enum is a class, and an annotation type is a form of interface. The lessons give explicit guidance for only some choices, so others rest on your judgment.

concepts.unitTitle: Reading the tutorials as a whole
concepts.title: Placing a problem at the right stage
concepts.question: When something goes wrong, how do I decide whether it came from writing, building or running, and what to try first?

paragraphs: A Java program passes through three stages: writing the source, compiling it to bytecode, and running that bytecode on the virtual machine. A problem belongs to the stage that reports it.

The compiler reports mistakes in the source with a line number, and if it reports any, no class file is made. Examples are a missing semicolon, a local variable that might not be initialized, and a repeated annotation without the repeatable marking. The launcher reports a class it cannot find, or a class without a main method of the right form.

A first useful question is therefore whether a class file appeared. If not, read the compiler message and its line. If it did, read the launcher message, then check the file name, the folder and the classpath setting.
card.example: The launcher prints a class-not-found error although javac finished silently. A class file exists, so the compile stage passed. Check that the shell is in the folder holding it, and that you typed the class name and not the file name.
card.rule: Decide first which stage reported the problem, then apply the fixes that belong to that stage, changing one thing at a time.
card.limits: A logic error, such as a wrong total, produces no message at any stage. Placing the stage only narrows the search; tracing the code by hand is then needed.

concepts.unitTitle: Reading the tutorials as a whole
concepts.title: The order of the reading steps
concepts.question: In what order do I apply the reading steps to a lesson, and why does that order matter?

paragraphs: The reading steps fall into groups. First inspect: skim the title, headings and summary to see what the lesson covers and whether it needs a careful read. Then find the structure: classify the lesson, state its unity, outline its parts and write the questions it answers.

Next comes content: fix the key terms, find the key sentences and the claims in them, follow the reasoning, and see which of the lesson's problems it solves. Last comes judgment: what holds, and what is missing.
The order matters because each group feeds the next. The structure shows which words carry weight, and terms and claims must be clear before there is anything fair to judge.
card.example: Opening a new lesson on interfaces and inheritance: skim the headings; state in a sentence what it is about; outline its sections and write its questions; list key terms such as superclass; trace the claims; only then ask what it leaves out.
card.rule: Inspect, then find the structure, then the content, and judge only when you can state what the lesson says.
