card.limits: The groups are not strictly chronological: a hard term can send you back to the outline. With a short familiar lesson you may merge steps, but you still do not judge before you understand.

concepts.unitTitle: Reading the tutorials as a whole
concepts.title: Preparing the terms for a later lesson
concepts.question: How do I spot the words a new Java lesson uses in a special way, and settle what each means?

paragraphs: Before reading a later lesson in detail, scan its title, headings and first sentences for words that carry its meaning. Look for the ones used in a special way: everyday words with a fixed technical sense, and new names the lesson introduces.

The five lessons show how many there are. A package is a namespace for related classes. A field holds state in an object. A block is statements inside braces. Interface has two senses: the methods an object exposes, and the Java construct that lists methods with empty bodies.

For each term, settle one meaning from the lesson's own sentences and note what it contrasts with, such as field against local variable against parameter. Hold that meaning while reading on. If the lesson uses a word without defining it, mark the meaning as provisional.
card.example: In a lesson on generics you meet type parameter. Entry: a name standing for a type, supplied later; it contrasts with a method parameter, which stands for a value. Keep the contrast in mind when the lesson uses the word parameter for both.
card.rule: Collect the words the lesson uses in a special way, fix one meaning for each from the lesson's own sentences, and note the terms each contrasts with.
card.limits: Not every new word is a term: names of single examples, or words used in their ordinary sense, need no entry. A term may also be defined further on, so keep early meanings open.

concepts.unitTitle: Reading the tutorials as a whole
concepts.title: What a finished understanding looks like
concepts.question: What can I do once I have understood the five lessons, and how do I name what they leave out?

paragraphs: Having read the lessons is not the same as understanding them. Understanding can be shown without the page: state in a sentence what the lessons are about, outline the five in order, give the question each answers, and explain the key terms with their contrasts.

It also shows in use. You can trace one example through the lessons, choose a construct from a described need, place an error message at its stage, and predict what a short program does before you run it.

Only then is judgment fair. Judging completeness means naming what the lessons leave undone, as a specific gap. The lessons were written for JDK 8 and point to newer material, and later topics lie beyond them. A gap is not an error, and dislike is not a gap.
card.rule: Understanding is finished when you can do the tasks without the page, and the lessons are called incomplete only by naming a specific gap.
card.limits: These notes are condensed, so a gap may lie in the notes and not in the original lessons. A gap shows what to read next; it does not show that the lessons said anything false.

questions.q: Which statement about Java technology is closest to the truth?
options: It is both a language and a platform that runs on top of other platforms
It is a language only; the runtime belongs to the operating system
It is a platform only; programmers write in other languages
It is a compiler that is rebuilt for each operating system
optionExplain: Right: the language and the platform together make up the technology.
Tempting because many languages lean on the operating system, but Java brings its own software runtime layer.
Programmers do write in a Java language, so it is more than a platform.
A compiler is one tool in the platform, not the whole technology.
questions.explain: Java names both a language and a software platform. The card next shows how the two fit together.
questions.rule: Java is a language and a platform.

questions.q: The Java platform has two components: the Java Virtual Machine and a library of ready-made classes known by the three-letter name ____.
questions.explain: The library is the Application Programming Interface, shortened to API.
questions.rule: The platform is the VM plus the API.

questions.q: A Java program runs well on Dana's Linux server. She now wants it on a Windows desktop. According to the tutorial's model, what must the desktop have?
options: A copy of the Linux operating system
A rewrite of the source in another language
The Java platform installed on top of Windows
Hardware identical to the server
optionExplain: Java platforms run on top of existing systems, so the host keeps its own operating system.
Rewriting is the work that a portable platform is meant to avoid.
Right: the platform layer is what the program talks to.
The platform is software-only, so matching hardware is not needed.
questions.hint: Think about which layer the program speaks to.
questions.explain: The platform sits on top of each machine's own system, so Windows needs the Java platform installed. The program does not need rewriting.
questions.rule: A new host needs the Java platform, not a rewrite.

questions.q: True or false: because the Java platform is only software, a Java program loses no speed at all compared with native code.
questions.teaches: A software layer between program and machine can cost some speed, and VM improvements narrow that gap.
questions.explain: According to the tutorial, being platform-independent can make the platform somewhat slower than native code, though improvements in compilers and VMs bring it close.
questions.rule: Portability has a cost that technology narrows rather than removes.

questions.q: Sort each item: does it belong to the Java language side or to the Java platform side?

items.t: Source files saved with a .java ending
The Java Virtual Machine
Packages of related classes and interfaces
Rules for writing statements
The software layer above the operating system
The object-oriented style of the program text

questions.explain: The language is what you write; the platform is what runs it and supplies ready-made parts.
questions.rule: Language is the writing; platform is the running and the library.

questions.q: A console emulator is software that runs on a PC and imitates an older console, so that old games run unchanged on the PC. Which part of the Java idea does it most resemble?
options: The javac compiler producing native code for each CPU
The ten buzzwords describing the language
The API's packages of ready-made classes
A software-only layer above the host that runs unchanged programs
optionExplain: Java compiles to bytecode, not to native code for each CPU.
The buzzwords describe qualities, not a mechanism.
The API is library content, not the layer that runs programs.
Right: the VM-plus-API layer plays the role the emulator plays.
questions.teaches: A software layer that imitates a machine is what lets one program run on many hosts, which is the idea behind a virtual machine.
questions.explain: An emulator is a software layer on top of an existing machine that lets the same programs run there, which is how the Java platform treats each host.
questions.rule: A software layer on top of a host lets unchanged programs run.

questions.q: What does the javac compiler produce from a Java source file?
options: Machine code for the processor in your computer
A class file of bytecodes
A shorter copy of the source file
A running program
optionExplain: Natural to expect, but the output is for the Java VM, not for a specific processor.
Right: bytecodes are the machine language of the Java VM.
Compilation translates; it does not just shorten.
Running is done later by the java launcher.
questions.explain: It produces a class file of bytecodes. The card next explains what bytecodes are.
questions.rule: javac turns source into bytecode.

questions.q: Put the stages of a Java program's life in order.
items: Write the source in a .java file
Compile it with javac
Start it with the java launcher
The Java VM runs the bytecode
questions.explain: You write the source first, compile it with javac, start it with the java launcher, and the VM then executes the bytecode.
questions.rule: Write, compile, launch, execute.

questions.q: Ben compiled a program on a Mac and has the .class file. What does the pipeline say he needs in order to run it on a Windows laptop?
options: To recompile the source with a compiler built for Mac
A converter from Mac machine code to Windows machine code
A Java VM on the laptop; the class file itself can be reused
The original Mac operating system installed
optionExplain: Recompiling is not required, because the output is not tied to one processor.
The class file holds no Mac machine code, so no conversion is needed.
Right: the VM is the part that differs per system.
The VM, not the operating system, is what runs bytecode.
questions.explain: The class file can be reused because it holds bytecode; the laptop only needs a Java VM.
questions.rule: Move the class file, and make sure a Java VM is there.

questions.q: True or false: if javac reports a syntax error in a source file, it still writes a class file that you can run.
questions.teaches: Compilation is all or nothing: until the reported errors are fixed, no class file exists to run.
questions.explain: According to the tutorial, when compile errors occur no class file is created until you fix them and recompile.
questions.rule: Fix every compile error before expecting a class file.

questions.q: Match each item to what it is or does.
pairs: Plain-text source code that you write
The launcher that starts a VM and runs the program
questions.explain: Source files are written by you, class files hold bytecode, javac compiles and java launches.
questions.rule: Each artifact and tool has one job.

questions.q: A translator turns a book into a neutral shorthand, and each country has a reader who turns the shorthand into its own language. Which Java part matches the shorthand?
options: The bytecode in the class file
The .java source file
The java launcher
The Java VM on each system
optionExplain: Right: bytecode is the neutral form that each VM reads.
The source is the original book, not the shorthand.
The launcher starts the reader; it is not the shorthand.
Each VM matches the reader in a country.
questions.teaches: With a neutral middle form, one compile serves every system, because only each reader (VM) has to be written per system.
questions.explain: The shorthand sits between the writer and every reader, just as bytecode sits between the source and each Java VM.
questions.rule: Bytecode is the neutral middle form.

questions.q: Which tool generates documentation for classes from comments in the source?
options: javac
java
jar
javadoc
optionExplain: javac compiles source into bytecode.
java launches a compiled program.
A jar tool is not part of the three the tutorial presents for beginners.
Right: javadoc reads documentation comments.
questions.explain: That job belongs to javadoc. The card next gives each tool's task.
questions.rule: javadoc builds documentation from comments.

questions.q: Match each beginner tool to its job.
pairs: Builds API documentation from source comments
questions.explain: Compile, launch and document are the three jobs the tutorial highlights.
questions.rule: Three tools, three jobs.

questions.q: Lee wants a program with windows, buttons and menus. Which group of the platform should Lee check first?
options: Integration libraries such as JDBC
User interface toolkits such as Swing
Development tools such as javac
Deployment technologies
optionExplain: Those reach databases and remote systems.
Right: Swing, JavaFX and Java 2D build graphical interfaces.
Tools compile and run; they do not draw windows.
Deployment is about delivering finished applications.
questions.explain: Windows, buttons and menus make up a graphical user interface, which the user interface toolkits cover.
questions.rule: GUI needs point to the user interface toolkits.

questions.q: True or false: Java Web Start, which the tutorial presents as a way to deliver applications, is still part of current JDKs.
questions.teaches: A tutorial's feature list can age: Java Web Start was deprecated in JDK 9 and removed in JDK 11.
questions.explain: The tutorial's own note says Java Web Start was deprecated in JDK 9 and removed in JDK 11, so current JDKs lack it.
questions.rule: Check the JDK version before using a delivery technology.

questions.q: Sort each item: is it part of the class library (the API) or a development tool?

items.t: Classes for networking
The javac compiler
Classes for XML generation
The javadoc documentation generator
Packages of related classes and interfaces
The java launcher

questions.explain: Tools act on your files; the API is a library of classes your program uses.
questions.rule: Tools work on programs; the API is used inside programs.

questions.q: A restaurant kitchen has knives and ovens, a pantry of ready-made sauces, and a delivery service. Which Java group matches the pantry?
options: The javac compiler
The deployment technologies
The core API of ready-to-use classes
The javadoc tool
optionExplain: The compiler is a tool, like an oven.
Deployment matches the delivery service.
Right: ready-made classes are reused, like sauces.
javadoc writes documentation; it supplies no ready-made parts.
questions.teaches: Grouping a toolkit by role (tools, parts, delivery) helps you find the right place to look when you need something.
questions.explain: A pantry holds ready-made items you reuse, as the API holds ready-made classes.
questions.rule: The API is the pantry of reusable parts.

questions.q: True or false: the tutorial promises that learning Java will bring a better job.
questions.explain: The page says it makes no promise about fame, fortune or employment. The card next lists what it does argue.
questions.rule: Read what a page promises, not what you assume.

questions.q: Which memory-related benefit does the tutorial give for Java?
options: Programmers must free every block of memory by hand for speed
Programs never use memory
A fixed memory budget set by the language
Automatic garbage collection that helps avoid memory leaks
optionExplain: Manual control is the opposite of the claim.
Programs use memory; the claim is about managing it.
No fixed budget is mentioned.
Right: the tutorial credits it with fewer leaks.
questions.explain: Automatic garbage collection is listed under better code, as help against memory leaks.
questions.rule: Garbage collection helps avoid memory leaks.

questions.q: Which statements match the page's claims about Java? Select all that apply.
options: A Java program can be about four times smaller than the same C++ program
Development can be up to twice as fast
The language is especially approachable for people who know C or C++
Learning Java guarantees employment
A program must be rewritten for each operating system
optionExplain: Right: this is the size claim.
Right: this is the speed claim.
Right: the page says so.
The page explicitly makes no such promise.
Bytecode is meant to avoid that.
questions.explain: The page claims a size gain of about four times, up to twice as fast development, and an easy start for C and C++ programmers. It promises no employment and says bytecode avoids rewriting per system.
questions.rule: Check each statement against what the page claims.

questions.q: A blog post says: the Java tutorial proves Java code is four times smaller than C++. Which flaw does this sentence contain?
options: The tutorial gives it as a claim based on metrics, not as a proof
The tutorial says eight times, not four
The figure refers to speed, not size
The tutorial compares Java with C, not C++
optionExplain: Right: the figure is a metrics-based claim.
The tutorial says four times.
It concerns size; speed has a separate figure.
The comparison is with C++.
questions.hint: Look at the verb the tutorial uses for its metrics.
questions.teaches: A figure given without its method is something to check, not a proof; ask what was measured and on which programs.
questions.explain: The tutorial offers the figure as a suggestion from program metrics, not as a proof.
questions.rule: Do not upgrade a claim into a proof.

questions.q: True or false: a claim based on program metrics could come out differently if a different set of programs were measured.
questions.explain: Metrics depend on the programs measured, so a different sample can change the figure. That is why the method matters.
questions.rule: A figure is only as good as its sample.

questions.q: A phone advert says its battery lasts up to twice as long. Using the habit this page's figures call for, what is the best first question?
options: Which shop sells it?
Twice as long as what, and measured how?
Is twice better than four times?
Does the advert use the words up to?
optionExplain: A shop does not test the claim.
Right: this is the same pair of questions as for the four-times figure.
The two figures are about different things.
The wording matters less than the missing baseline.
questions.teaches: Comparative claims need a baseline and a method before you can weigh them.
questions.explain: A comparison needs a baseline and a method: twice as long as what, and measured how.
questions.rule: Ask for the baseline and the method.

questions.q: Which of these must be installed to compile Java source files?
options: The Java SE Development Kit
The JRE only
A web browser plug-in
A graphics toolkit
optionExplain: Right: the JDK includes javac.
The tutorial says to choose the JDK instead of the JRE.
A plug-in is for deployment, not compiling.
A toolkit builds interfaces, not class files.
questions.explain: The compiler javac comes with the JDK. The card next explains the setup.
questions.rule: Compiling needs the JDK.

questions.q: True or false: the tutorial recommends using the NetBeans IDE instead of the command line whenever possible.
questions.explain: The tutorial says an IDE greatly simplifies development and should be used whenever possible.
questions.rule: The tutorial prefers the IDE.

questions.q: Omar uses Ubuntu and does not want an IDE. Which route in the tutorial fits him?
options: The Windows command prompt page
The NetBeans page, after removing the IDE
The Solaris, Linux and Mac OS X terminal page
None, because Linux is not covered
optionExplain: That page is written for Windows.
The NetBeans route needs the IDE.
Right: Linux is covered by the terminal route.
Linux is named on the Unix-style page.
questions.explain: He wants a terminal and an editor, which is the route for Solaris, Linux and Mac OS X.
questions.rule: Pick the route that matches system and tools.

questions.q: According to the tutorial's checklist, why must you download the JDK rather than the JRE?
options: The JRE cannot run any Java program
The JRE only works on Windows
The JDK is needed only for NetBeans
The JDK includes the javac compiler you need
optionExplain: The JRE can run programs; the issue is compiling.
The JRE is not tied to Windows.
The command-line routes need it too.
Right: javac comes with the JDK.
questions.teaches: A runtime environment is for running existing programs, while compiling your own source needs the development kit.
questions.explain: The checklist says the JDK includes the compiler you need, which is how you turn source into bytecode.
questions.rule: The compiler lives in the JDK.

questions.q: Match each route to what you use on it.
pairs: A project with Build and Run menu items
Pico or another editor in a terminal
questions.explain: Each route has its own working tools, but all follow write, compile, run.
questions.rule: Routes differ in tools, not in the cycle.

questions.q: A baking class teaches one bread recipe on a gas oven, an electric oven and a wood-fired oven. Applying the way the tutorial treats its three routes, what stays the same across them?
options: The oven temperature dial
The order of the stages: prepare, bake, taste
The brand of flour
The sound the oven makes
optionExplain: Dials differ between the ovens.
Right: the stages are the shared cycle.
Flour is not part of what the routes share.
Sounds are irrelevant.
questions.teaches: Changing the tool changes the keystrokes but not the underlying cycle, so learn the cycle first.
questions.explain: The tutorial changes the tools but keeps the cycle of writing, compiling and running, as the class keeps its stages.
questions.rule: Tools change; the cycle stays.

questions.q: To run a compiled program you type java followed by the ____ of the class.
questions.explain: The launcher expects the class name rather than a file name. The card next shows the exact commands.
questions.rule: java takes a class name.

questions.q: Put the command-line steps for HelloWorldApp in order.
items: Save the source as HelloWorldApp.java
Run javac HelloWorldApp.java
Check that HelloWorldApp.class exists
Run java HelloWorldApp
questions.explain: Save, compile, check for the class file, then run.
questions.rule: Save, compile, verify, run.

questions.q: Kim has a file named Greet.java containing a class Greet. Which pair of commands compiles and then runs it?
options: javac Greet and then java Greet.class
java Greet.java and then javac Greet
javac Greet.java and then java Greet
javac Greet.class and then java Greet.java
optionExplain: Both names are in the wrong form.
The tools are swapped.
Right: this is the order and form the tutorial shows.
The class file is not compiled again.
questions.explain: javac takes the source file name with its ending, and java takes only the class name.
questions.rule: Source file name to javac, class name to java.

questions.q: Kim types java greet in lowercase, but the class is named Greet. What does the tutorial's case rule predict?
options: The launcher treats greet as another name and does not find the class Greet
It runs, because case is ignored
It runs, but prints in lowercase
javac recompiles the file automatically
optionExplain: Right: names must match exactly.
Case is not ignored by either tool.
Output text is a separate matter.
The launcher does not compile.
questions.teaches: Because names must match exactly, a wrong-case class name behaves like a name that does not exist, so the class cannot be found.
questions.explain: The tools are case sensitive, so greet is a different name from Greet and the launcher does not find the class Greet.
questions.rule: A wrong-case name is a different name.

questions.q: A learner types javac HelloWorldApp and the compiler refuses. The source file name is missing its ____ ending.
questions.hint: Think of what the file is called on disk.
questions.explain: The compiler needs the source file name including the .java ending. Leaving it off produces an error.
questions.rule: Include .java when compiling.

questions.q: A music app plays a track when you give it the track title, not the name of the file that stores it. Which Java rule works the same way?
options: javac needs the source file name with an ending
Both tools are case sensitive
The Windows route sets the classpath
java takes the class name, not the class file's name
optionExplain: True, but this is the opposite case, where the file name is required.
True, but unrelated to name versus file.
That is about where to look, not about name versus file.
Right: the launcher is asked for a name.
questions.teaches: A launcher looks up a thing by its name and finds the file that stores it, so you give the name, not the file.
questions.explain: The java launcher asks for a class by its name and finds the matching class file itself.
questions.rule: Ask by name; the system finds the file.

questions.q: True or false: in an IDE project you must type the javac command yourself to compile.
questions.explain: The IDE runs the compiler when you build the project. The card next walks through the menus.
questions.rule: An IDE can run the compiler for you.

questions.q: A successful compile in NetBeans shows the message BUILD ____ in the Output window.
questions.explain: The Output window reports BUILD SUCCESSFUL when compilation worked.
questions.rule: Read the Output after each build.

questions.q: Jo builds the project, sees BUILD SUCCESSFUL, but sees no greeting yet. What is the next step?
options: Build again until the greeting appears
Choose Run, Run Main Project
Delete the class file
Rename the project
optionExplain: Repeating the build does not run the program.
Right: running is a separate menu item.
The class file is the result of the build.
Renaming has no bearing on running.
questions.explain: Building creates the class file; running is a separate step done with Run Main Project.
questions.rule: Build compiles; run executes.

questions.q: A project holds classes Main and Helper. Helper is selected in the Projects window, and Tom picks Run Main Project. What runs, according to the tutorial's tips?
options: Helper, because it is selected
Whichever class was edited last
The project's designated main class
Both classes, one after another
optionExplain: Selection does not decide it.
Edit order does not decide it.
Right: Run File is the way to run another class.
Only one class is started.
questions.teaches: Run Main Project always starts the project's main class; use Run File to run a different class.
questions.explain: Run Main Project always runs the project's designated main class, whichever file is selected. To run another class you use Run File.
questions.rule: Run Main Project runs the main class.

questions.q: Match each NetBeans menu item to what it does.
pairs: Compiles the source into a class file
Starts the project's main class through the launcher
questions.explain: Build compiles source to a class file; Run Main Project starts the project's main class through the java launcher; Run File runs one chosen class.
questions.rule: Build compiles; run executes.

questions.q: A writer renames Chapter 3 by retyping its title, and cross-references elsewhere still show the old title. Which NetBeans habit from the tutorial would avoid the matching problem with a class?
options: Turning off code completion
Creating a separate project per file
Pressing F9 to compile the file
Using Refactor, Rename instead of renaming by hand
optionExplain: Completion has no bearing on references.
That tip is about multi-file samples.
Compiling does not update names.
Right: references are updated together.
questions.teaches: Renaming by hand leaves stale references, while a refactoring tool updates all of them together.
questions.explain: Using Refactor, Rename updates references to the class, where renaming by hand leaves stale references.
questions.rule: Rename through the refactoring tool.

questions.section: A Closer Look at the "Hello World!" Application
questions.q: Which comment form is read by the javadoc tool?
options: A block starting with /**
A line starting with //
A block starting with /*
A line starting with #
optionExplain: Right: the second star marks a doc comment.
A line comment is for notes beside code.
A block comment is ignored by javadoc.
A hash is not a Java comment form.
questions.explain: The doc comment, which starts with /**. The card next shows all three forms.
questions.rule: Doc comments feed javadoc.

questions.section: A Closer Look at the "Hello World!" Application
questions.q: Match each comment form to its name.
pairs: Line comment to the end of the line
questions.explain: Three forms, three names.
questions.rule: Know the three forms.

questions.section: A Closer Look at the "Hello World!" Application
questions.q: Write the marker that completes this line so that a note follows the statement and ends with the line: int total = 0; ____ start at zero
questions.explain: A line comment is meant to run from its marker to the end of the line.
questions.rule: Use // for a note that ends with the line.

questions.section: A Closer Look at the "Hello World!" Application
questions.q: Which of these is not a valid comment?
options: /** note */
/* note
/* note */
// note
optionExplain: A closed doc comment is valid.
Right: it never closes.
A closed block comment is valid.
A line comment needs no closing.
questions.teaches: Every block-style comment needs its closing marker; only line comments end on their own at the end of the line.
questions.explain: A block-style comment that is opened must be closed. Only the line comment ends by itself.
questions.rule: Close every block comment.

questions.section: A Closer Look at the "Hello World!" Application
questions.q: A programmer deletes every comment from HelloWorldApp, then compiles and runs it. What happens?
options: It behaves exactly as before
It fails to compile
It prints nothing
It prints Hello World! with a warning
optionExplain: Right: the compiler ignored the comments anyway.
Comments are not needed to compile.
The println statement is unchanged.
Nothing in the tutorial suggests a warning.
questions.explain: The compiler ignores comments, so removing them does not change the output.
questions.rule: Comments do not change behaviour.

questions.section: A Closer Look at the "Hello World!" Application
questions.q: A recipe card has margin notes for the cook and a printed summary line that a cookbook-indexing machine collects. Which Java form matches the summary line?
options: A line comment
A block comment
A doc comment
A statement
optionExplain: Line comments are notes beside code for readers.
Block comments are notes for readers, ignored by javadoc.
Right: a tool collects it into documentation.
Statements run; they are not notes.
questions.teaches: A comment can have a program as its audience, which is why doc comments are written in a form that javadoc can read.
questions.explain: The summary is meant for a tool that gathers it, like a doc comment is for javadoc.
questions.rule: Doc comments have a tool as audience.

questions.section: A Closer Look at the "Hello World!" Application
questions.q: In a Java application, where does the code that does the work sit?
options: In a loose file with no class
Inside the class file name
After the closing brace of the program
Between the braces of a class definition
optionExplain: The tutorial says every application begins with a class.
A file name holds no code.
Nothing follows the class.
Right: braces mark where the class's code sits.
questions.explain: It sits inside a class definition. The card next shows the shape.
questions.rule: Code lives inside a class.

questions.section: A Closer Look at the "Hello World!" Application
questions.q: System.out.println prints the text and then adds a ____.
questions.explain: The statement prints the text followed by a new line.
questions.rule: println ends the line.

questions.section: A Closer Look at the "Hello World!" Application
questions.q: A main method holds two statements in order: one println call that prints the letter A, and then one that prints the letter B. What appears?
options: AB on one line
A and B on two lines
Only B
Nothing, since two statements clash
optionExplain: That would happen without the new line after A.
Right: the new line follows each text.
Both statements run in order.
Statements may follow one another.
questions.explain: Each println prints its text and then moves on, so the two texts appear on separate lines.
questions.rule: Each println uses its own line.

questions.section: A Closer Look at the "Hello World!" Application
questions.q: True or false: you must write the definition of System yourself before println can be used.
questions.teaches: Classes of the core library such as System are available to every program without being defined in it.
questions.explain: System belongs to the core library, so it is available without being defined in your program.
questions.rule: Library classes are ready to use.

questions.section: A Closer Look at the "Hello World!" Application
questions.q: Kai writes Class HelloWorldApp { ... } with a capital C and the compiler complains. What is the likely fix?
options: Add a semicolon after the name
Rename the file to end in .class
Write the keyword class in lowercase
Move println outside the braces
optionExplain: A semicolon is not the issue.
Source files end in .java.
Right: case matters.
println belongs inside the braces.
questions.explain: The keyword is class in lowercase, and the tools are case sensitive.
questions.rule: Keywords must be typed exactly.

questions.section: A Closer Look at the "Hello World!" Application
questions.q: A letter template has a page frame that holds all the content, and a print command that writes a line to the printer and then moves to the next line. Which pair matches Java?
options: Frame is the class; command is println
Frame is println; command is the class
Frame is the comment; command is the API
Frame is main; command is javac
optionExplain: Right: container and line output.
The roles are swapped.
Comments hold notes, not the work.
javac is a tool, not a statement.
questions.teaches: Output statements write to a stream and move on, while the containing unit holds the program's code.
questions.explain: The frame holds the work, as a class does; the print command writes a line and moves on, as println does.
questions.rule: Container holds the work; the print statement writes a line.

questions.section: A Closer Look at the "Hello World!" Application
questions.q: Which of these is the correct signature of the method where a Java application starts?
options: public static void Main(String[] args)
public static void main(String args)
public void main(String[] args, int n)
public static void main(String[] args)
optionExplain: Case matters: Main is not main.
The parameter must be an array of String.
A second parameter changes the signature.
Right: this is the required form.
questions.explain: Only one of them has the required name, return type and parameter. The card next explains each part.
questions.rule: Know the exact signature.

questions.section: A Closer Look at the "Hello World!" Application
questions.q: The String[] args parameter receives the ____ arguments typed after the class name.
questions.explain: Those strings are called command-line arguments.
questions.rule: args carries command-line arguments.

questions.section: A Closer Look at the "Hello World!" Application
questions.q: Rita writes static public void main(String[] args). According to the tutorial, what happens?
options: The compiler rejects it because public must come first
It is valid, since modifier order is free and public static is only convention
It is valid only if the method is renamed Main
It works only on Windows
optionExplain: Nothing forces public first.
Right: the tutorial states this.
Main in capitals is a different name.
The rule is not tied to a system.
questions.explain: Modifiers may appear in either order; public static is only the convention.
questions.rule: Modifier order is free; the convention is public static.

questions.section: A Closer Look at the "Hello World!" Application
questions.q: Which changes to the signature still leave a valid starting method? Select all that apply.
options: Rename args to argv
Write static public instead of public static
Change void to int
Rename main to start
Rename the parameter to options
optionExplain: Right: any parameter name works.
Right: the order of modifiers is free.
The return type must be void.
The entry point must be called main.
Right: it is only a parameter name.
questions.teaches: Names that a programmer chooses, such as a parameter name, are free, while the words the runtime looks for are fixed.
questions.explain: The parameter name and the modifier order are free. The return type void and the method name main are fixed.
questions.rule: Names the programmer picks are free; fixed words are not.

questions.section: A Closer Look at the "Hello World!" Application
questions.q: A learner runs java HelloWorldApp one two using the tutorial's program. What is printed?
options: Hello World! one two
An error, because the arguments are unused
Hello World!
one two
optionExplain: The program never prints its arguments.
Unused arguments cause no error.
Right: the arguments exist but are ignored.
The greeting is still printed.
questions.explain: The program ignores its arguments, so it prints only its greeting.
questions.rule: Unused arguments do no harm.

questions.section: A Closer Look at the "Hello World!" Application
questions.q: A command-line tool for converting photos changes its behaviour with an option typed after its name, such as tool --small. Which Java feature plays the same role?
options: The doc comment
The class keyword
The println statement
The String array parameter of main
optionExplain: A comment is not read by the program.
The keyword declares a class.
println prints; it does not receive input.
Right: this is where such options arrive.
questions.teaches: Passing settings after a program's name is a general convention, and Java hands them to the program as an array of strings.
questions.explain: Options typed after a program's name arrive in Java as strings in the array parameter of main.
questions.rule: args carries what the user types after the name.

questions.q: A student types javac and the shell answers that the command is not found. What is the most likely cause?
options: The folder holding javac is not on the search path
The source file has a typo
The class has no main method
The class file is in the wrong folder
optionExplain: Right: the shell looks for commands only in folders on the search path.
A typo would produce a compiler error with a line number, which needs javac to run first.
That is a runtime message.
That is a runtime issue, after compiling.
questions.explain: The shell cannot find the compiler, usually because its folder is not on PATH. The card next gives this and other causes.
questions.rule: Command not found points to the search path.

questions.q: Match each message to its cause.
pairs: The system cannot find the compiler
A syntax typo in the source
The class lacks the required main method
Could not find or load main class HelloWorldApp.class
The file name was given instead of the class name
questions.explain: Each message points at one cause.
questions.rule: Match message to cause.

questions.q: Leo types javac Report and sees a message that class names are only accepted if annotation processing is requested. What is the fix?
options: Add the JDK folder to CLASSPATH
Type javac Report.java
Rename the class to report
Run java Report instead
optionExplain: That would not change how the argument is read.
Right: the compiler needs the source file name.
Case is not the problem.
Nothing has been compiled yet.
questions.explain: The message means the .java ending was left off, so the compiler read Report as a class name.
questions.rule: Compile with the file name and its ending.

questions.q: javac prints: cannot find symbol, pointing at the name cuont in a statement where the variable is called count. What kind of problem is this, and what is the fix?
options: A misspelled name caught by the compiler; correct the spelling and recompile
A runtime error; delete the class file
A path error; add bin to PATH
A missing main method; add one
optionExplain: Right: the compiler reports it before any class file is made.
It is reported by the compiler, not at run time.
PATH is about finding the tool, not about names in source.
That would give NoSuchMethodError at run time.
questions.teaches: The compiler reports unknown names with the exact spot, so the message itself tells you what to correct.
questions.explain: The compiler could not match the name to any declared variable. Correct the spelling and compile again.
questions.rule: Compilers also catch semantic errors.

questions.q: Put these steps for a NoClassDefFoundError in order.
items: Change to the folder that holds the class file
Confirm the files with dir or ls
Run java with the class name
If it still fails, clear CLASSPATH and retry
questions.explain: Go to the right folder, confirm the files, try the run command, and only then test CLASSPATH.
questions.rule: Check the simple causes before the CLASSPATH test.

questions.q: Mia says: javac printed nothing, so the compile must have failed. What is wrong with this reasoning?
options: The compiler always prints a success message
Silence means the class file is empty
Silence means success, and a class file should now exist
Silence means java must be run twice
optionExplain: The tutorial says it prints nothing on success.
The class file holds bytecode.
Right: check for the class file with dir or ls.
One run is enough.
questions.explain: On success the compiler prints nothing and creates the class file, so silence is a good sign.
questions.rule: No message from javac means success.

questions.q: A parcel is returned with a note. Tags can say address unreadable, which happens before dispatch, or recipient not at home, which happens after. Applying the tutorial's approach, what helps first?
options: Reprint the label in every case
Send the parcel again at once
Ignore the note
Identify which stage reported the problem
optionExplain: That fixes only one of the causes.
Repeating blindly risks the same result.
The note is the clue.
Right: the stage narrows the likely causes.
questions.teaches: The stage that printed an error narrows its causes, so read an error as a clue to match with a cause and not as a verdict.
questions.explain: Knowing which stage reported the problem narrows the causes, as knowing whether javac or java printed the message does.
questions.rule: Identify the stage before choosing a fix.

questions.q: Which pair of things does a software object bundle together?
questions.explain: A guess is fine here. The card next shows the two parts every object has.
options: A blueprint and a finished copy of it
A list of packages and a list of interfaces
State kept in fields and behavior offered through methods
Data kept in variables and a main method for starting
optionExplain: These two ideas come up later, and they relate classes to objects, not the parts of one object.
These organise and describe code; they are not the two parts of an object.
Right: that pairing is what the card teaches next.
A main method starts a program; it is not part of what makes up every object.
questions.rule: Describe an object by its state, stored in fields, and its behavior, offered as methods.

questions.q: A software object keeps its state in ____.
questions.explain: State is the object's current condition, and a software object stores it in fields.
questions.rule: State lives in fields; behavior lives in methods.

questions.q: A desk lamp object has the states on and off. Its designer adds a brightness setting from 1 to 3. How does the description of the object change?
questions.explain: Brightness is a condition the lamp is in at a given moment, which makes it state. Changing it would be a method.
questions.rule: Ask what the object is (state) and what it can do (behavior).
options: Nothing changes, because the lamp already has state
Only the behaviors change, because brightness is an action
State is replaced by behavior, because the lamp does more
It gains another piece of state, brightness, and probably a method to change it
optionExplain: Having some state does not stop new state from being added.
Brightness is a condition the lamp is in, so it is state; an action would be changing it.
Objects keep both; adding features does not swap one for the other.
A new setting is something the lamp holds, so it is state, and a way to adjust it is behavior.

questions.q: True or false: A software object can contain other objects as part of what it holds.
questions.explain: The tutorial notes that some objects contain other objects and says this carries over to software.
questions.teaches: Objects can be built from other objects, so a large object such as a bicycle can be described partly by smaller ones.
questions.rule: Describe an object by its state, stored in fields, and its behavior, offered as methods.

questions.q: A coffee machine is modelled as a software object. Sort each item as state or behavior.
questions.explain: Stored values are state. Actions are behavior, including an action that only reports a stored value.
questions.teaches: A method that merely reads and reports a value is still behavior; the value it reports is the state. This is a modelling convention, not tutorial text.

items.t: Amount of water in the tank
Brew one cup
Whether the machine is switched on
Report the bean level
Number of cups brewed today
Switch itself off

questions.rule: Describe an object by its state, stored in fields, and its behavior, offered as methods.

questions.q: A teammate says a lone number named total in a script is a software object, because it holds a value. What is missing from that claim?
questions.explain: The tutorial describes a software object as state together with related behavior, so one stored value alone falls short.
questions.rule: An object needs both halves: state and related behavior.
options: Nothing is missing, because any stored value counts as an object
The value has no related behavior bundled with it
The value has no name that a method could use
The value needs a package to count as an object
optionExplain: Storing a value gives state only; the second half is absent.
An object pairs state with related behavior; a lone value has state only.
A name exists here; the gap is the missing related behavior.
Packages group classes; they do not turn a value into an object.

questions.q: True or false: Letting outside code change an object's fields directly is the way the tutorial recommends keeping an object under control.
questions.explain: The tutorial recommends the opposite: outside code works through methods. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: Keep state behind methods, so the object itself decides which changes are allowed.

questions.q: Hiding internal state and allowing access only through methods is called data ____.
questions.explain: That practice is data encapsulation.
questions.rule: Encapsulation: state hidden, methods as the only door.

questions.q: A thermostat object accepts targets from 10 to 30 through its setTarget method, which rejects other values. What if the target field is made directly writable by outside code?
questions.explain: Encapsulation works by forcing changes through methods that can check them. Open the field and the guard is bypassed.
questions.rule: No guard method in the path, no control.
options: setTarget would still check every change
Outside code could store 80, because no method checks it
The field becomes read-only for everyone
The range check moves into the field automatically
optionExplain: The method only checks calls made through it, not writes that bypass it.
The check lived in the method; going around the method removes it.
Making a field writable does the opposite of read-only.
A field holds a value; checks come from methods the designer writes.

questions.q: A payment object in a program keeps failing. According to the tutorial's bolt analogy, which benefit lets the team swap in a working replacement?
questions.explain: The fourth benefit the tutorial lists is easy debugging and pluggability: remove the problem object and put another in its place.
questions.teaches: Pluggability and easy debugging: a problem object can be replaced without rebuilding the rest of the system.
options: Information hiding: failures cannot be seen from outside
Modularity: an object that is well written cannot fail
Pluggability: a faulty object can be removed and replaced by another
Code reuse: the team must then write a new object from scratch
optionExplain: Hiding concerns details of implementation, not the ability to swap parts.
Modularity eases separate writing and maintenance; it does not rule out failure.
The tutorial compares this to replacing a broken bolt instead of the whole machine.
Reuse means using existing objects; replacing a part is a different benefit.
questions.rule: Keep state behind methods, so the object itself decides which changes are allowed.

questions.q: A vending machine is built from objects. Match each situation to the benefit it shows.
questions.explain: Each situation names what one party no longer has to do or know: touch other code, build the part, see the details, or rebuild the machine.
questions.teaches: A benefit can be recognised by what someone no longer has to touch, build, know or rebuild.
pairs: One member rewrites the coin counter without touching the display code
The owner installs a card reader built and tested by a specialist
Customers press buttons without knowing how change is worked out
A broken coin counter is swapped for a working one
questions.rule: Keep state behind methods, so the object itself decides which changes are allowed.

questions.q: A colleague argues: the setGear method stores whatever number it is given, so encapsulation guarantees that the gear is valid. Which part of this reasoning fails?
questions.explain: Funnelling every change through a method gives a place to check, but the check must be written. A method that accepts anything protects nothing.
questions.rule: Encapsulation gives you a checkpoint; the method has to do the checking.
options: A method cannot be used to change a field at all
The gear is stored in a field, and fields cannot hold numbers
Hiding access alone guards nothing unless the method checks the value
Encapsulation only applies to objects with more than six gears
optionExplain: Methods are exactly how state is changed under encapsulation.
Fields can hold numbers; that is not the problem.
The tutorial's six-gear example works because the method rejects bad values.
The six gears were an example; encapsulation does not depend on that number.

questions.q: Two bicycle objects are built from the same class. One of them speeds up. What happens to the other one's speed?
questions.explain: A guess is fine. The card next shows how objects relate to their class.
options: It speeds up by the same amount
It slows down to balance the first
It becomes unknown until it is next used
It stays as it was
optionExplain: Objects from one class do not share their state.
Nothing links the two objects' speeds.
The value is held by that object and is unchanged.
Right: each object has its own state. The card next explains why.
questions.rule: A class is the shared blueprint, and each object made from it with new is an instance holding its own state.

questions.q: The blueprint from which individual objects are created is called a ____.
questions.explain: A class is the blueprint; objects made from it are its instances.
questions.rule: A class is the plan, an instance is a thing built from it.

questions.q: A class Counter has a field count that starts at 0 and a method increase. Code creates c1 and c2 with new, then calls c1.increase() three times. What does c2 hold afterwards?
questions.explain: Each instance holds its own copy of count, starting at 0. Calls on c1 change c1 only.
questions.rule: State belongs to the instance, not to the class.
options: 3, because all instances of one class share one count
6, because each instance adds its own three
It has no value until c2.increase() is called
0, because c2 keeps its own count and only c1 changed
optionExplain: The state is not shared; every instance has its own copy of count.
Nothing is added to c2, because only c1 received calls.
Fields get their starting value from the class when the object is created, so c2 holds 0 already.
Right: c2 has its own count, still at its starting value.

questions.q: True or false: A class such as the tutorial's Bicycle must contain a main method before objects can be created from it.
questions.explain: The Bicycle class has no main method. It is a blueprint, and a different class with main creates and uses Bicycle objects.
questions.teaches: A class need not be a runnable program; another class, with a main method, can create and use its instances.
questions.rule: A class is the shared blueprint, and each object made from it with new is an instance holding its own state.

questions.q: In a furniture shop, sort each item as the class (the shared plan) or an instance (one particular thing made from a plan).
questions.explain: A plan that applies to every item of a kind is the class. A particular item carrying its own values is an instance.
questions.teaches: A class names what all items of a kind share, while an instance is one particular item with values of its own.

items.t: The design drawing for the Oslo chair model
The Oslo chair standing in my kitchen
The template for a customer record
The customer record for order 1042
The layout of a library card
Library card number 77, issued to Sam

questions.rule: A class is the shared blueprint, and each object made from it with new is an instance holding its own state.

questions.q: A learner reasons: step 1, class Lamp has a field on set to false. Step 2, I create lamp a and turn it on. Step 3, so the Lamp class now has on set to true, and a new lamp b will start on. Which step is wrong?
questions.explain: The class describes what each new object starts with. Turning on lamp a changes a's own state, so b starts with the class's original value.
questions.rule: Changes happen in instances; the blueprint stays as written.
options: Step 1, because a class cannot declare a field
Step 2, because an object cannot be turned on after creation
Step 3, because changing one instance does not change the class
None, because a class follows its most recent instance
optionExplain: Classes do declare fields; that is how they set out an instance's state.
Methods can change an object's state after creation.
The blueprint stays as written; only instance a changed.
A class does not follow its instances.

questions.q: A new Bicycle starts with speed 0. Its speedUp method adds the given increment to speed. Code calls speedUp(10) twice. What is the speed?
questions.explain: A guess is fine. The card next shows how to trace a series of calls.
optionExplain: This takes only the last call into account.
Right: the speed grows by 10 each time. The card next shows how to trace this.
The starting value is changed by each call.
The increments are added, not multiplied.
questions.rule: Trace each object on its own tally from its starting values, applying its calls in order.

questions.q: True or false: The tutorial's Bicycle class can be run on its own as an application.
questions.explain: Bicycle has no main method, so it is a blueprint. The BicycleDemo class holds main.
questions.rule: The class with main starts the program.

questions.q: Code runs: Bicycle b = new Bicycle(); b.changeGear(3); b.speedUp(6); b.applyBrakes(2); b.changeCadence(30); b.speedUp(1); b.printStates(); What is printed?
questions.explain: Trace the speed: 0 plus 6 is 6, minus 2 is 4, plus 1 is 5. The other fields were replaced by their setting methods.
questions.rule: Setters replace; speedUp adds; applyBrakes subtracts.
options: cadence:30 speed:1 gear:3
cadence:30 speed:9 gear:3
cadence:30 speed:5 gear:3
cadence:0 speed:5 gear:3
optionExplain: This treats speedUp as a setter that replaces the value; it adds.
This adds the braking amount; applyBrakes subtracts it.
Speed goes 0, 6, 4, 5; cadence and gear were set.
This ignores changeCadence; the setting method replaced 0 with 30.

questions.q: class Bicycle declares int cadence = 0; int speed = 0; int gear = 1;. A brand-new Bicycle has had no method called on it. Calling printStates on it shows gear ____.
questions.explain: Each field has a starting value declared in the class, and the gear starts at 1.
questions.teaches: A new object starts with the values written in its class's field declarations, so an untouched object prints those values.
questions.rule: Trace each object on its own tally from its starting values, applying its calls in order.

questions.q: A Wallet class has a field coins starting at 5, a method spend(n) that subtracts n and a method find(n) that adds n. Code makes w1 and w2 with new, then calls w1.spend(2), w2.find(4), w1.find(1), w2.spend(3). How many coins do w1 and w2 hold?
questions.explain: Each object has its own tally. The order of calls between different objects does not matter; only the order within one object does.
questions.teaches: Interleaved calls on different objects do not affect each other; only the order of calls on one object matters.
options: w1 holds 6 and w2 holds 4
Both hold 5, because the calls cancel out
w1 holds 3 and w2 holds 7
w1 holds 4 and w2 holds 6
optionExplain: This swaps the objects; each call belongs to the object it is written on.
The calls to the two objects never cancel each other.
This applies only the first call of each object.
w1: 5 minus 2 plus 1. w2: 5 plus 4 minus 3.
questions.rule: Trace each object on its own tally from its starting values, applying its calls in order.

questions.q: A class Dial has a method setLevel(int n) that stores n in level, starting at 0. Code calls setLevel(4) and then setLevel(2). A learner says level is 6. Which assumption fails?
questions.explain: Whether a method replaces or adds decides the trace. The method body, not its name, tells you.
questions.rule: Read what each method does to its field before tracing.
options: That level starts at 0
That 4 plus 2 is 6
That setLevel adds to the old value instead of replacing it
That the calls run in order
optionExplain: The start at 0 is correct and does not change the final value.
The sum is correct; it is just not what the method does.
A setting method replaces the stored value, so the answer is 2.
The order is correct; the second call simply overwrites the first.

questions.q: Which keyword declares that one class is a subclass of another?
questions.explain: A guess is fine. The card next shows the keyword and the rules around it.
options: implements
inherits
extends
import
optionExplain: This keyword connects a class to an interface, a different idea from a superclass.
It sounds natural, but it is not the keyword Java uses.
Right: the card next shows how it is used.
This brings in names from a package; it does not create a subclass.
questions.rule: A subclass, declared with extends, receives the fields and methods of its one direct superclass and adds its own.

questions.q: In the declaration class RoadBike extends Bicycle, the class Bicycle is the ____.
questions.explain: The class named after extends is the superclass, and RoadBike is its subclass.
questions.rule: The class after extends is the superclass.

questions.q: Class Animal has a field age and a method sleep. Class Cat extends Animal and adds a method purr. The team later adds a method feed to Animal. What is the effect on Cat?
questions.explain: A subclass receives what its superclass defines, so a new superclass method reaches every subclass.
questions.rule: Shared code is written once, in the superclass.
options: Cat must be edited before it can use feed
Cat loses purr, since Animal has changed
Only newly written classes receive feed
Cat gains feed as well, with no change to Cat's own source
optionExplain: The point of inheritance is that shared code lives in the superclass only.
Adding to the superclass does not remove anything from the subclass.
Existing subclasses inherit from the superclass too.
Inherited methods come from the superclass, so new ones arrive automatically.

questions.q: MountainBike's source is short because most of its behavior is defined in Bicycle. What responsibility does the tutorial attach to this arrangement?
questions.explain: The trade-off for short subclasses is that readers cannot see inherited code there, so the superclass needs good documentation.
questions.teaches: Because inherited code is not shown in the subclass, superclasses should be documented carefully.
options: Subclass authors should copy superclass methods into the subclass
Developers should document carefully the state and behavior each superclass defines
Subclasses should be avoided whenever the superclass is long
Inherited methods should be listed only in comments of the subclass
optionExplain: Copying removes the benefit of writing shared code once.
The inherited code is not visible in the subclass's file, so readers need documentation.
The tutorial lists short, focused subclasses as a benefit.
Comments in the subclass do not replace documenting the superclass.
questions.rule: A subclass, declared with extends, receives the fields and methods of its one direct superclass and adds its own.

questions.q: A company models staff in Java. Which designs follow the tutorial's inheritance rules? Select all that apply.
questions.explain: Many subclasses per superclass are allowed. A class may not name two direct superclasses.
questions.teaches: A class that seems to belong to two families, such as an amphibious vehicle, must choose one direct superclass.
options: Manager, Engineer and Intern each extend Employee
Amphibian extends both Car and Boat as direct superclasses
Truck extends Vehicle and nothing else
Fifty different classes each extend Shape
optionExplain: A superclass may have any number of subclasses.
A class may have only one direct superclass.
One direct superclass is allowed.
The number of subclasses of a superclass is unlimited.
questions.rule: A subclass, declared with extends, receives the fields and methods of its one direct superclass and adds its own.

questions.q: True or false: Because Bicycle already has three subclasses, a fourth class cannot extend it.
questions.explain: The number of subclasses a superclass can have is unlimited. The limit applies to superclasses per class, which is one.
questions.rule: The limit is one direct superclass, not one batch of subclasses.

questions.q: A class declares that it implements an interface but leaves out one of the interface's methods. What happens?
questions.explain: A guess is fine. The card next shows how the contract is enforced.
options: The compiler reports an error
The missing method is created automatically
The class compiles and the method is skipped when called
The interface drops that method from its list
optionExplain: Right: the card next explains this contract.
The compiler does not write methods for you.
The class does not compile at all.
Interfaces do not change to suit classes.
questions.rule: An interface lists methods without bodies, and a class that implements it must supply all of them, which the compiler enforces.

questions.q: A group of related methods with empty bodies is called an ____.
questions.explain: An interface lists what an object can do without saying how.
questions.rule: Interface: the what, without the how.

questions.q: Interface Sensor lists read() and reset(). A class Thermometer implements Sensor with both. The team then adds calibrate() to Sensor. What happens when Thermometer is compiled?
questions.explain: Changing the contract changes what every implementing class must provide.
questions.rule: The contract is the whole list of methods in the interface.
options: It fails until Thermometer supplies calibrate
It compiles, since the old two methods are still there
It compiles and calibrate is added to Thermometer automatically
It fails because read and reset are no longer allowed
optionExplain: The contract now has three methods, and all must be present.
The compiler checks against the whole current contract.
No method is added for the class.
Those two stay part of the contract.

questions.q: True or false: A class that implements an interface may also declare methods the interface does not list.
questions.explain: The tutorial's ACMEBicycle has a printStates method that the Bicycle interface does not list.
questions.teaches: The contract sets a minimum: a class may add extra methods beyond those the interface requires.
questions.rule: An interface lists methods without bodies, and a class that implements it must supply all of them, which the compiler enforces.

questions.q: A shop app has interface PaymentMethod with charge(amount) and refund(amount). CardPayment and GiftVoucher both implement it. Checkout code calls only charge and refund. What follows from the contract?
questions.explain: Code that relies only on the contract does not need to know which class stands behind it.
questions.teaches: Code that relies only on an interface's methods can work with any class that implements it.
options: Checkout must read each class's source before using it
The two classes must have identical fields
Checkout can use either class, since both must provide those two methods
Checkout works only with the class written first
optionExplain: The point of the contract is to avoid that.
The contract covers methods; fields can differ.
The contract guarantees the methods, as the buttons guarantee how a TV is used.
Any class that meets the contract will do.
questions.rule: An interface lists methods without bodies, and a class that implements it must supply all of them, which the compiler enforces.

questions.q: A learner copies the tutorial's ACMEBicycle sample unchanged and the compiler complains. According to the tutorial, what must be added to make it compile?
questions.explain: Interface methods are implicitly public, so an implementation with weaker access is rejected.
questions.rule: The tutorial's sample needs public on each implemented method.
options: The keyword public at the start of each implemented interface method
A main method, since every class needs one
Removal of printStates, since it is not in the interface
A second interface, to share the work
optionExplain: The tutorial says this is needed and explains why in later lessons.
Classes such as Bicycle compile without main.
Extra methods are allowed.
One interface is enough for the sample.

questions.q: In Java, what does the abbreviation API stand for?
questions.explain: A guess is fine. The card next defines the term.
options: Applied Package Index
Application Programming Interface
Automatic Program Installer
Abstract Programming Instance
optionExplain: The letters fit, but this is not the expansion.
Right: the platform's library of packages is called the Application Programming Interface.
Nothing in the Java platform is called this.
This mixes terms from this lesson into a made-up phrase.
questions.rule: Group related classes and interfaces in packages, and consult the Java API specification before building something general.

questions.q: A namespace that organizes related classes and interfaces is called a ____.
questions.explain: A package groups related classes and interfaces, like a folder.
questions.rule: A package is a namespace for related classes and interfaces.

questions.q: Match each task to the API class the tutorial lists for it.
questions.explain: Each class in the tutorial's list covers one general-purpose job, so you can reuse it instead of building it.
questions.rule: Look for an existing API class before writing your own.
pairs: Hold and work with a string of characters
Delete or inspect a file on the filesystem
Create and use a network connection
Control a button or check box on screen

questions.q: The tutorial was written for JDK 8. How should a reader treat its examples when working with a much later Java release?
questions.explain: The pages say they may not use later improvements and point to Dev.java, Java Language Changes and the JDK release notes.
questions.teaches: The tutorial points readers to Dev.java, Java Language Changes and the JDK release notes for features added after JDK 8.
options: As a base, checking newer resources for features added later
As complete for every release, since the basics do not change
As wrong, and to be ignored completely
As valid only for file handling
optionExplain: The tutorial itself points to newer guides for later releases.
The tutorial warns that later releases bring improvements it lacks.
The tutorial's core ideas still stand; it warns only about newer features.
The warning covers the whole tutorial.
questions.rule: Group related classes and interfaces in packages, and consult the Java API specification before building something general.

questions.q: Two teams each write a class called Report for the same large program. Based on what a namespace is, why do packages help here?
questions.explain: Because a package is a namespace, the same simple name can live in different packages without confusion.
questions.teaches: A namespace lets the same simple class name exist in different packages.
options: Packages merge the two classes into one
Each Report can sit in its own package, so the two can be told apart
Packages make a class run faster
Packages stop a class from having a name
optionExplain: Grouping keeps classes apart; it does not merge them.
Right: a package is a namespace, so the two names live in separate spaces.
The tutorial presents packages as organisation, not speed.
Every class keeps its name; packages only give it a space.
questions.rule: Group related classes and interfaces in packages, and consult the Java API specification before building something general.

questions.q: Suppose the Java platform shipped with only ten classes. What would programmers have to do more of?
questions.explain: The tutorial says using the library lets you concentrate on design rather than infrastructure, so a thin library returns that work to you.
options: Write fewer classes, since there is less to choose from
Group classes less, since packages would not apply
Document less, since the specification would be short
Build the supporting infrastructure themselves, which the API normally saves
optionExplain: With less provided, more work falls to the programmer, not less.
Packages also organise your own classes, whatever the platform ships.
Your own code still needs documentation.
Right: the API saves the programmer from building general-purpose infrastructure.
questions.rule: Reuse the platform library to avoid rebuilding general infrastructure.

questions.q: A collection of methods with no implementation is called an ____.
questions.explain: That collection is an interface. The card next puts it with the other terms.
questions.rule: Link each term to its role: fields to state, methods to behavior, class to blueprint, extends to inheritance, implements to contract, package to namespace.

questions.q: Match each description to its term.
questions.explain: Each term has one job in the lesson's chain of ideas.
questions.rule: Know which term does which job.
pairs: Blueprint from which objects are created

questions.q: If a design uses these keywords, which does each described action need?
questions.explain: Extends relates a subclass to its superclass. Implements ties a class to an interface, which the compiler then checks.
questions.rule: extends is for inheritance, implements is for a contract.

items.t: Inherit fields from one superclass
Promise to supply every method a contract lists
Name the single direct superclass
Let the compiler flag a missing method body

questions.q: True or false: An object that was not declared with the interface keyword still has an interface in the tutorial's general sense.
questions.explain: The tutorial first calls the methods an object exposes its interface, and only then describes the common Java form of a group of empty methods.
questions.teaches: The word interface has two uses: the methods an object exposes in general, and the Java construct that lists methods without bodies.
questions.rule: Link each term to its role: fields to state, methods to behavior, class to blueprint, extends to inheritance, implements to contract, package to namespace.

questions.q: A bakery program has class Loaf, interface Sellable with price and wrap, and package bakery. Sourdough must reuse Loaf's fields and methods. Which line does that?
questions.explain: A keyword tells you the relationship: extends means inherit, implements means keep a contract, package means grouping.
questions.teaches: Reading the keyword in a declaration shows which relationship it creates.
options: class Sourdough implements Loaf
class Sourdough extends Loaf
class Sourdough implements Sellable
package Sourdough extends bakery
optionExplain: Implements connects a class to an interface, and Loaf is a class.
Right: extends makes Sourdough a subclass that receives Loaf's fields and methods.
This promises price and wrap but does not reuse Loaf's fields and methods.
A package is a namespace, not something a class inherits from.
questions.rule: Link each term to its role: fields to state, methods to behavior, class to blueprint, extends to inheritance, implements to contract, package to namespace.

questions.q: A student says an interface and a class are the same thing, because both list methods. Where does the lesson's introductory form of an interface differ?
questions.explain: A class describes fields and methods with bodies and can be used to create objects. An interface only states what must be provided.
options: A class lists methods but an interface lists only fields
An interface can create objects directly, while a class cannot
There is no difference apart from the keyword used
An interface lists methods with empty bodies, while a class can hold fields and method bodies to make objects
optionExplain: Interfaces in this lesson list methods, not fields.
Objects are created from classes, so this is reversed.
Their roles differ: one is a contract, the other a blueprint.
Right: the interface sets what must be provided, and the class gives the blueprint with bodies.
questions.rule: A class is a blueprint; an interface is a contract.

questions.q: A class declares int price; at the top, outside every method. Which description fits it best?
options: A field, and therefore also a variable
A local variable, because it holds a temporary value
A parameter, because it is declared once and used later
A variable but not a field, because it has no value yet
optionExplain: Right: a field is a variable that belongs to the type, so both words apply.
Locals live inside a method body; this declaration sits outside every method.
Parameters appear in a method signature, not at the top of a class.
Having no value yet does not change the kind; location does.
questions.explain: Declarations outside any method are fields, and fields are one kind of variable. The card next sets out all four kinds.
questions.rule: Location decides the kind of variable.

questions.q: A variable declared inside a method body to hold temporary state is called a ____ variable.
questions.explain: Local variables exist only inside the method (or block) where they are declared.
questions.rule: Locals are temporary and method-bound.

questions.q: In class Lamp { int watts; void set(int level) { int half = level / 2; watts = half; } }, which name is a parameter?
options: watts
level
half
set
optionExplain: watts is declared outside the method, so it is a field.
Right: it sits in the method signature.
half is declared in the body, so it is a local variable.
set is the method name, not a variable.
questions.explain: Only level is listed in the signature, so it is the parameter. half is local and watts is a field.
questions.rule: Parameters appear in the signature.

questions.q: A class declares static final int MAX = 6;. What does the word final add to this class variable?
options: Each object receives its own separate copy
It becomes a local variable of every method
Its value cannot be changed after it is set
It is treated as a parameter of the constructor
optionExplain: Separate copies per object come from omitting static, not from final.
Locals are decided by position inside a method, not by final.
Right: final fixes the value, which is what makes it a constant.
Parameters come from signatures; final does not create one.
questions.explain: The modifier final forbids reassignment. A static final field is therefore a single, fixed value shared by the whole class.
questions.rule: static final means one fixed value for the whole class.
questions.teaches: Combining static with final makes a constant: one copy that never changes after it is set.

questions.q: A banking app has an Account class. Sort each item: is it a field of the class, or something that is not a field?

items.t: The owner name stored inside each Account object
The interest rate shared by all accounts, declared static
The amount listed in the signature of deposit(double amount)
A temporary total declared inside the deposit method
The balance stored inside each Account object
A loop counter declared inside a method body

questions.explain: Fields are declared in the class body, whether static or not. The amount is a parameter and the other two are locals, so they count as variables but not as fields.
questions.rule: Fields sit in the class body; parameters and locals sit in a method.
questions.teaches: Whether a value is a field depends on where it is declared, not on how important it is: a loop counter is a local variable even though the whole method depends on it.

questions.q: In class Lamp from earlier, suppose int half is moved out of the method and written at the top of the class beside watts. What kind of variable is half now?
options: A class variable, because it is shared now
A parameter, because the method still reads it
A local variable, because it holds a half of level
An instance variable, which is a field
optionExplain: Sharing needs the static keyword; moving it changes only the position.
Parameters must appear in the signature.
The role it plays does not matter; a declaration outside methods is not local.
Right: without static it is a per-object field.
questions.explain: Moving the declaration to class level makes it a field. With no static modifier it is an instance variable.
questions.rule: Change the position and the kind changes.

questions.q: True or false: If a class declares a field with the static keyword, each object made from the class gets its own copy of it.
questions.explain: A static field has a single copy for the whole class. The card next explains what that means for objects.
questions.rule: Static means one copy.

questions.q: A field declared with the keyword ____ has exactly one copy, however many objects exist.
questions.explain: The keyword static makes the field belong to the class.
questions.rule: Static fields belong to the class.

questions.q: Class Mug has the field int sips; (not static). After Mug x = new Mug(); Mug y = new Mug(); x.sips = 4; y.sips = 7; x.sips++; what do x.sips and y.sips hold?
options: x.sips is 5 and y.sips is 7
Both are 8, since the totals are added together
Both are 7, since the last assignment wins
x.sips is 4 and y.sips is 7, since ++ affects nothing
optionExplain: Right: each object has its own sips.
Separate copies are never added together.
The last assignment only changed y.sips.
The ++ operator did change x.sips, from 4 to 5.
questions.explain: Each Mug object keeps its own sips. The increment changes only the one reached through x.
questions.rule: Instance variables are independent per object.

questions.q: Now sips is declared static int sips; and the same three statements run (x.sips = 4; y.sips = 7; x.sips++;). What does y.sips show afterward?
optionExplain: 7 forgets that x.sips++ changed the same copy.
Right: there is one shared copy: 4, then 7, then incremented to 8.
4 treats the first assignment as the final state.
5 assumes x has its own copy, as in the non-static case.
questions.explain: With one shared copy, the final statement raised 7 to 8, and either reference reads the same value.
questions.rule: What if static is added: separate copies become one.

questions.q: A school app stores each student grade, plus the school name that is the same for every student. Which design suits Java fields best?
