options: Both as instance variables, so every student object is complete
Both as class variables, so memory use stays small
Grade as an instance variable, school name as a class variable
Grade as a class variable, school name as an instance variable
optionExplain: This works but stores the identical name again in every object.
A shared grade would give every student the same grade.
Right: differing data per object, shared data once.
This reverses the roles of the two values.
questions.explain: The grade differs per student, so each object needs its own copy. The school name is shared, so one static copy is enough.
questions.rule: Separate what varies per object from what is shared.
questions.teaches: A class variable exists even before any object is created, so it suits totals and settings that describe the whole group.

questions.q: True or false: A static field cannot change value once the program has started.
questions.explain: Static only means one copy. Any code can assign to it unless it is also final, and the change is seen by every object.
questions.rule: Static means shared, not fixed.

questions.q: Which of these is a legal Java variable name?
options: 2nd_cost
cost-2
cost 2
cost_2
optionExplain: A name cannot start with a digit.
A hyphen is read as a minus sign, so it cannot be part of a name.
A space separates two tokens, so it cannot sit inside a name.
Right: it starts with a letter and uses only letters, digits and an underscore.
questions.explain: Only cost_2 follows the rules. The card next lists them all.
questions.rule: Start with a letter, dollar or underscore; no spaces.

questions.q: True or false: In Java, the names count and Count refer to the same variable.
questions.explain: Names are case-sensitive, so these are two different names.
questions.rule: Case matters in names.

questions.q: Which declaration compiles?
options: int $total = 0;
int total! = 0;
int float = 0;
int 9lives = 0;
optionExplain: Right: a dollar sign is allowed as the first character.
An exclamation mark is not a letter, digit, dollar sign or underscore.
float is a reserved word, so it cannot name a variable.
A digit cannot be the first character.
questions.explain: The dollar sign is legal at the start of a name, although style advice discourages it. The other three each break a rule.
questions.rule: Check first character, allowed characters, and reserved words.

questions.q: Suppose you rename a variable. Which new names would the compiler reject? Select all that apply.
options: _1st
final
data set
1st
dataSet
optionExplain: An underscore may begin a name and digits may follow.
Right: final is a reserved word.
Right: The space splits it into two tokens.
Right: A name cannot begin with a digit.
Letters only, so it is legal.
questions.explain: Reserved words, spaces and a leading digit each break a rule. dataSet and _1st obey every rule.
questions.rule: Three things break a name: reserved word, space, leading digit.

questions.q: A programmer writes a variable named Total and later uses total in the same scope. What happens?
options: Both refer to one variable, so the program works
The program compiles but prints a warning at run time
The compiler reports an unknown name, since the two differ by case
The second name silently creates a new default variable
optionExplain: That would be true only if names were case-insensitive.
Unknown names are caught when compiling, not at run time.
Right: case-sensitivity makes total a different, undeclared name.
Java does not create variables by use; each must be declared.
questions.explain: Because names are case-sensitive, total was never declared and the compiler rejects the use.
questions.rule: Using an undeclared name is a compile-time error.
questions.teaches: Rule violations and undeclared names are caught by the compiler before the program runs.

questions.q: A plain-text config file format says: a key must start with a letter, may then contain letters, digits and underscores, and may not equal a reserved word such as end. Which key fails?
options: port_8
Host
timeout2
end
optionExplain: It starts with a letter and uses an underscore and digit.
Capital letters are allowed in this format.
Digits after the first character are allowed.
Right: it equals a reserved word.
questions.explain: The key end is a reserved word, so it is rejected, just as keywords are rejected as Java names. The same pattern, start rule plus allowed-character rule plus reserved list, describes many identifier systems.
questions.rule: Identifier rules usually combine a start rule, an allowed-character rule and a reserved list.
questions.teaches: Identifier rules in many languages and file formats share the same three parts: a start rule, an allowed-character rule and a list of reserved words.

questions.q: Which is the usual Java way to name a field holding the number of seats booked?
options: seatsBooked
SeatsBooked
seats_booked
SEATSBOOKED
optionExplain: Right: camel case starts lowercase and capitalises later words.
A leading capital is not the convention for a field.
Underscores between words are reserved for constants.
All capitals signal a constant, which a changing count is not.
questions.explain: Fields use camel case. The card next lists the conventions.
questions.rule: Fields: camel case.

questions.q: Names made of several words, such as gearRatio, follow a style called ____ case.
questions.explain: The first word is lowercase and each later word begins with a capital.
questions.rule: Camel case joins words with capitals.

questions.q: Which declaration follows the tutorial convention for a constant?
options: static final int maxUsers = 10;
static final int MAX_USERS = 10;
static int MAX_USERS = 10;
static final int max_users = 10;
optionExplain: This is camel case, which suits ordinary fields, not constants.
Right: it is static final and uses capitals with underscores.
Capitals suggest a constant, but without final the value can still change.
Lowercase with underscores matches neither the field nor the constant convention.
questions.explain: The constant convention applies to static final fields and uses capitals with underscores.
questions.rule: Constants: static final, capitals, underscores.

questions.q: A reviewer flags the field int numOfGears_Total. Which complaint matches the tutorial?
options: It is illegal, because underscores are not allowed in names
It is illegal, because a name cannot contain capital letters
It breaks the convention: camel case joins words, with no underscore
It breaks the rule that a field name must be one word
optionExplain: Underscores are allowed by the rules; the problem is style.
Capitals are allowed anywhere in a name.
Right: underscores are legal but conventionally reserved for constants.
There is no one-word rule; camel case exists for multi-word names.
questions.explain: The name obeys the rules, so it compiles. It violates the style advice, which keeps underscores for constants.
questions.rule: Rule versus convention: legal can still be unconventional.

questions.q: Sort each declaration: does it cause a compile error, or is it legal but against the conventions?

items.t: int 2ndTry;
int total_amount;
int class;
int $fee;
int my-count;
int a;

questions.explain: The compiler rejects a leading digit, a reserved word and a hyphen. The other three compile, but an underscore in a field, a dollar sign and a cryptic one-letter name go against the style advice.
questions.rule: The compiler enforces rules; reviewers enforce conventions.

questions.q: A team style guide for database columns says to write lowercase words joined by underscores. Does that contradict Java camel case?
options: Yes; only one of the two styles can be legal
Yes; the compiler rejects whichever style the language does not use
No; both styles have the same meaning to every tool
No; each community agrees its own conventions, and consistency within one code base is the aim
optionExplain: Both are only styles; neither is a legal or illegal form.
The compiler checks rules, not conventions.
Tools do not treat the two styles as the same name.
Right: conventions are choices a community makes.
questions.explain: Style conventions differ between languages and teams without conflict, because they are agreements, not rules of the language.
questions.rule: Follow the convention of the code base you are in.
questions.teaches: Conventions are agreed by communities, so different languages and teams legitimately choose different ones.

questions.q: Which type is the best fit for a flag recording whether a door is open?
options: boolean
int
char
String
optionExplain: Right: a flag has exactly two states, true and false.
int could store 0 and 1, but it would allow many meaningless values.
char holds a single character, not a state.
String holds text and is an object, not a primitive.
questions.explain: boolean exists for true and false values. The card next covers all eight types.
questions.rule: boolean is for flags.

questions.q: Match each whole-number type to its size.
questions.explain: Sizes double at each step: 8, 16, 32 and 64 bits.
questions.rule: Whole-number sizes: 8, 16, 32, 64.

questions.q: A sensor count can reach 3,000,000,000. Which type holds it without overflow?
options: int
long
short
byte
optionExplain: int tops out near 2.1 billion, below the sensor limit.
Right: int stops near 2.1 billion, so only long is large enough here.
short stops at 32,767.
byte stops at 127.
questions.explain: The value is larger than int allows, so long is the choice.
questions.rule: Check the largest value against the range.

questions.q: The same sensor limit is lowered to 3,000,000. Which is the smallest of byte, short, int and long that still fits?
options: byte
short
int
long
optionExplain: byte stops at 127.
short stops at 32,767.
Right: 3 million exceeds short but is far below 2.1 billion.
long would work but is larger than needed.
questions.explain: Three million exceeds short, so int is the smallest that fits.
questions.rule: The right type shrinks when the limit shrinks.

questions.q: True or false: A String holds text, so it counts as the ninth primitive type.
questions.explain: Java has exactly eight primitives. String is a class with special language support, and its objects cannot be changed once created.
questions.rule: String is special but not primitive.

questions.q: A recipe app stores four data items. Match each to the fitting Java type.
questions.explain: A count is a whole number, a measurement can have a fraction, a yes-or-no is boolean and text is a String object.
questions.rule: Ask: count, measurement, yes-or-no, or text.
questions.teaches: Choosing a type starts with asking whether a value is a count, a measurement, a yes-or-no or text.

questions.q: A checkout system must add prices to the cent exactly. What does the tutorial advise?
options: Use double, the default decimal type
Use float, which needs less memory
Use char, which stores exact digits
Use the BigDecimal class
optionExplain: double approximates many decimal values, so it is not exact.
float is even less precise than double.
char holds characters, not exact sums.
Right: BigDecimal does exact decimal arithmetic.
questions.explain: The tutorial warns that float and double are for approximate values and names BigDecimal for exact ones. The card next sets out the full advice.
questions.rule: Money needs exact decimals.

questions.q: For whole numbers the default type is ____.
questions.explain: int is the default whole-number type, with byte, short and long as variants.
questions.rule: Default whole number: int.

questions.q: A program keeps 5 million ratings between 1 and 5 in an array and memory is tight. Which type does the tutorial favour for the elements?
options: byte
long
double
int
optionExplain: Right: byte saves memory in large arrays and its small range documents the intent.
long is larger than needed and wastes memory.
double stores fractions and is larger still.
int is the default but uses four times the space of byte.
questions.explain: With millions of small values, byte reduces memory and signals that the values are small.
questions.rule: Narrow types pay off in large arrays.

questions.q: Only a handful of ratings are stored instead of millions. What changes in the advice?
options: byte becomes illegal for small counts
Little: the memory saving is negligible, so the default int is fine
double becomes required
long becomes required
optionExplain: byte stays legal at any scale; the benefit simply shrinks.
Right: the benefit of byte comes from scale.
Ratings are whole numbers, so double is not needed.
The values are small, so long is not needed.
questions.explain: The memory saving grows with the number of elements. For a handful, readability and simplicity favour int.
questions.rule: Memory-saving choices depend on scale.

questions.q: True or false: Choosing byte for a single local variable in a small program gives a meaningful memory saving.
questions.explain: One variable saves a negligible amount. The tutorial ties the narrow types to large arrays.
questions.rule: Narrow types matter in bulk.

questions.q: Which description explains why double is a poor choice for money?
options: It is too small to hold large sums
It cannot store a fractional part
It stores approximations of many decimal values, so small errors can build up
It rounds every value to a whole number
optionExplain: double has a very wide range.
double exists to store fractions.
Right: approximate storage is the problem.
double keeps a fractional part.
questions.explain: Many decimal fractions, such as 0.1, have no exact double form, so repeated addition can drift from the exact total.
questions.rule: Approximate types are wrong for exact amounts.
questions.teaches: These types store binary approximations, so many decimal fractions have no exact form and small errors can accumulate.

questions.q: A fitness app has three data items. Match each to the type the tutorial advice suggests.
pairs: Steps in a day, up to about 50,000
questions.explain: Fifty thousand exceeds the short limit of 32,767, so int is needed. A measurement uses double, and exact money uses BigDecimal.
questions.rule: Check the biggest value against the range.
questions.teaches: Choosing a type means testing the largest expected value against the range, not only the kind of value: 50,000 overflows short.

questions.q: True or false: If a method declares int total; and prints total before assigning anything, the program prints 0.
questions.explain: Locals have no default, so the compiler rejects the read. The card next explains the difference between fields and locals.
questions.rule: Locals get no default.

questions.q: An unassigned boolean field starts as ____.
questions.explain: The default for boolean is false.
questions.rule: boolean field default: false.

questions.q: A class declares double width; String name; char tag; and a new object is created. What do the three fields hold?
options: 0, empty text and a space
0.0, null and a space
Nothing; reading them is a compile error
0.0, null and the null character
optionExplain: An int-style 0 and empty text are not the defaults; String defaults to null.
The default char is the null character, not a space.
That is the rule for local variables, not fields.
Right: defaults follow the type: 0.0, null and the null character.
questions.explain: Fields take their type default: 0.0 for double, null for String and the null character for char.
questions.rule: Fields: default by type.

questions.q: Suppose the same three variables are declared inside a method instead of the class. What happens when the method reads them before assigning?
options: The compiler rejects each read
They keep the same defaults
They all start as null
They get defaults only if declared final
optionExplain: Right: locals have no defaults.
Defaults belong to fields, not locals.
null applies only to object types, and not even to those when they are locals.
final does not create defaults.
questions.explain: Moving a declaration into a method removes the default and makes an early read a compile-time error.
questions.rule: Position decides whether a default exists.

questions.q: Which field declaration could be assigned the literal null?
options: int count;
String label;
boolean full;
double rate;
optionExplain: A primitive such as int cannot hold null.
Right: null belongs to object types.
boolean is a primitive, so null is not allowed.
double is a primitive, so null is not allowed.
questions.explain: null stands for no object, so only object types accept it, and a primitive cannot.
questions.rule: null goes with object types only.
questions.teaches: null is a value for any object type but cannot be assigned to a primitive; mostly you can only test whether something is null.

questions.q: True or false: The tutorial recommends relying on default values instead of assigning fields explicitly.
questions.explain: It calls reliance on defaults poor style. Assign values you mean.
questions.rule: Assign fields explicitly.

questions.q: A Person class has int age; and nobody sets it for some people. A report averages the ages and the result looks too low. What is the likely cause?
options: The unset ages hold null and are skipped
The compiler would have refused to build the unset objects
The unset ages hold the default 0 and are counted in the average
The unset ages hold -1, the standard unknown marker
optionExplain: An int cannot hold null, so nothing is skipped.
Fields may stay unassigned; only locals are checked.
Right: int fields start at 0, a real value.
No default marks unknown; the default for int is 0.
questions.explain: A default is a genuine value, so unset records look like newborns and pull the average down.
questions.rule: A default can pass for real data.
questions.teaches: A default is a real value that can be mistaken for genuine data, which is why explicit assignment is better style.

questions.q: What type is the literal 3.7 when it has no suffix?
options: float
int
long
double
optionExplain: float needs the f suffix.
int cannot hold a fractional part.
long holds whole numbers only.
Right: decimal literals default to double.
questions.explain: A decimal literal without a suffix is a double. The card next covers the marks that change a literal's type.
questions.rule: Unmarked decimal literal: double.

questions.q: Match each literal to what it is.
questions.explain: The prefixes 0x and 0b select the base, plain digits are decimal and the suffix L makes a long.
questions.rule: Prefix = base, suffix = type.

questions.q: Which declaration compiles?
options: float price = 4.5f;
char grade = "A";
float rate = 2.5;
long total = 3000000000;
optionExplain: Right: the f suffix makes the literal a float.
A char literal needs single quotes.
2.5 is a double and does not fit into a float variable.
3000000000 is an int literal and is too large for int.
questions.explain: Only the first line uses literals of the right types. The others use the wrong quotes, miss the f, or miss the L.
questions.rule: Match the literal type to the variable.

questions.q: Given int a = 0x10; and int b = 0b10;, what is a + b?
optionExplain: This reads 0x10 as ten.
Right: 0x10 is sixteen and 0b10 is two.
This reads both as ten.
This reads the digits as one and two.
questions.explain: Hexadecimal 10 is 16 and binary 10 is 2, so the sum is 18.
questions.rule: The prefix changes the value.

questions.q: The literal 1.234e2 equals ____.
questions.explain: The digit after e is the power of ten, so 1.234 times 100.
questions.rule: e gives the power of ten.
questions.teaches: The number after e is the power of ten, so 1.234e2 is 1.234 times 100, which is 123.4.

questions.q: Web colours are written in hexadecimal. In Java, the literal 0xFF equals ____ in decimal.
questions.explain: F is fifteen, so FF is 15 times 16 plus 15, which is 255.
questions.rule: Hex FF is 255.
questions.teaches: Each hexadecimal digit holds four bits, so two digits fill one byte; that is why hexadecimal suits byte-sized values such as colour channels.

questions.q: Which of these number literals is legal?
options: 0x_1F
optionExplain: An underscore cannot end a number.
An underscore cannot touch a decimal point.
Right: the underscore sits between two digits.
An underscore cannot come right after the 0x prefix.
questions.explain: Only an underscore between digits is allowed. The card next gives the full list.
questions.rule: Underscores go between digits.

questions.q: True or false: Underscores in a numeric literal change its value.
questions.explain: They are for readability only.
questions.rule: Underscores are cosmetic.

questions.q: Which line compiles?
options: float f = 3_.14f;
int mask = 0x_FF;
optionExplain: An underscore may not sit right before the L suffix.
An underscore may not touch the decimal point.
An underscore may not follow the 0x prefix directly.
Right: the underscore sits between digits, and L follows a digit.
questions.explain: In the legal line every underscore has a digit on both sides. Each other line breaks one placement rule.
questions.rule: Digit on both sides of each underscore.

questions.q: A String holds the characters ok, then backslash-n, then done. What does printing it show?
options: ok and done on two separate lines
ok, a backslash, the letter n, then done on one line
okdone on one line
A compile error
optionExplain: Right: the escape backslash-n is a line feed.
That would only happen if the backslash itself were escaped.
The line feed is not dropped; it ends the line.
The escape is valid in a String.
questions.explain: The escape sequence is replaced by a line feed, so the output breaks after ok.
questions.rule: Backslash-n is one character, a line feed.

questions.q: To put one real backslash character inside a String you write ____ backslashes in the source.
questions.explain: The first backslash starts an escape and the second is the character produced.
questions.rule: A double backslash yields one backslash.
questions.teaches: A backslash makes the next character special, so a literal backslash or a literal double quote needs its own escape instead of ending or altering the String.

questions.q: You need an accented e in a String but your keyboard cannot type it. Its code is 00E9. Which escape writes it?
options: backslash, e, then 00E9
backslash, u, then 00E9
backslash, x, then 00E9
backslash, 0, then E9
optionExplain: There is no backslash-e form of Unicode escape.
Right: a Unicode escape is backslash-u plus four hexadecimal digits.
There is no backslash-x form in Java.
The u is what introduces four hexadecimal digits.
questions.explain: Backslash-u00E9 writes the character with code 00E9.
questions.rule: Backslash-u plus four hex digits.
questions.teaches: A Unicode escape lets plain keyboard characters write any 16-bit character by its code.

questions.q: After the single line int[] data; inside a method, what exists?
options: An array of zero elements
An array of one element
A variable that can refer to an array, but no array yet
An array whose length is chosen later
optionExplain: A zero-length array would need new.
No element has been created.
Right: declaring does not create.
The length is fixed when an array is created, not later.
questions.explain: A declaration names a variable and its type only. The card next shows how to create the array.
questions.rule: Declare, then create.

questions.q: The first element of an array has index ____.
questions.explain: Indexing starts at 0.
questions.rule: Index 0 is first.

questions.q: Given int[] a = {4, 8, 15, 16, 23, 42};, what are a.length and the index of the last element?
options: 6 and 6
5 and 5
42 and 5
6 and 5
optionExplain: The last index is one less than the length.
Length counts elements, so it is 6.
42 is a value, not the length.
Right: six values, indexes 0 to 5.
questions.explain: There are six values, so length is 6 and the last index is 5.
questions.rule: Last index = length - 1.

questions.q: If one more value is added to the initializer, making seven values, the last index becomes ____.
questions.explain: Seven values occupy indexes 0 to 6.
questions.rule: Last index = length - 1.

questions.q: A student writes int n = a.length(); for an array a. What is wrong?
options: length is a field of an array, so the parentheses do not belong
length is a static method and needs the class name
Arrays have no length at all
length can be read only after the array is sorted
optionExplain: Right: array length is a field.
It is neither static nor a method.
Every array knows its length.
Sorting is unrelated to length.
questions.explain: Write a.length without parentheses.
questions.rule: Array length: field, no parentheses.

questions.q: True or false: The compiler accepts the two lines int[] a; a[0] = 5; inside a method.
questions.explain: The variable a was never assigned an array, so the compiler reports an error.
questions.rule: Create the array before using it.
questions.teaches: A local array variable obeys the same rule as other locals: it must be assigned an array before it is used.

questions.q: A cinema row has 12 seats labelled 1 to 12 and the program stores them in an array of 12. Which index holds seat 12?
optionExplain: Index 12 does not exist in an array of 12.
Right: labels start at 1 and indexes at 0.
Index 13 is further out of range.
Index 10 holds seat 11.
questions.explain: Labels start at 1 but indexes start at 0, so a label k sits at index k - 1.
questions.rule: Index = label - 1.
questions.teaches: When human labels start at 1, the matching index is the label minus one, and the valid indexes run from 0 to 11.

questions.q: In Java, a two-dimensional array is best described as
options: a single block of memory with equal rows
two separate arrays sharing one name
an array whose elements are arrays
a table in which every row must have the same length
optionExplain: Java does not force one rectangular block.
There is one array of rows, not two named separately.
Right: each row is itself an array.
Rows may differ in length.
questions.explain: It is an array of arrays. The card next shows what that allows.
questions.rule: Two-dimensional = array of rows.

questions.q: In int[][] grid, the expression grid[1] is itself an ____.
questions.explain: Each element of grid is a row, which is an array.
questions.rule: grid[i] is a row.

questions.q: Given int[][] grid = {{7, 8, 9}, {1, 2}};, what is grid[0][2]?
optionExplain: 8 is grid[0][1].
2 is grid[1][1].
1 is grid[1][0].
Right: row 0, third element.
questions.explain: The first index picks row 0, {7, 8, 9}, and the second picks its third element, 9.
questions.rule: Row first, then element.

questions.q: If the first row is changed to {7, 8}, grid[0].length becomes ____.
questions.explain: The row now has two elements.
questions.rule: Each row has its own length.

questions.q: Given int[][] g = {{7, 8, 9}, {1, 2}};, what happens when g[1][2] is read?
options: It is out of range, because row 1 has only indexes 0 and 1
It returns 9, the value at the same position in row 0
It returns 0 as padding for the missing element
It reads the first element of the next row
optionExplain: Right: index 2 needs a row of at least three elements.
Each row is a separate array; positions are not shared between rows.
Java does not pad shorter rows.
There is no spill-over from one row to another.
questions.explain: Row 1 is {1, 2}, which has indexes 0 and 1, so index 2 does not exist there even though it exists in row 0.
questions.rule: Check against the row you read.
questions.teaches: Each row must be checked against its own length, because an index that is valid in one row can be out of range in another.

questions.q: A timetable has one row per weekday: Monday has 5 lessons and Friday has 3. Which Java structure fits without padding?
options: A one-dimensional array of 8
A two-dimensional array with rows of different lengths
A two-dimensional array padded so every row has 5
Two unrelated variables for Monday and Friday
optionExplain: One array loses the weekday grouping.
Right: rows may differ in length.
Padding wastes space and invents lessons.
Separate variables cannot be indexed by day.
questions.explain: Each weekday is a row array sized to its lessons.
questions.rule: Uneven data fits uneven rows.
questions.teaches: Uneven data can be stored with one row array per group, each sized to fit, so no padding is needed.

questions.q: True or false: In names[0][2] the first index, 0, chooses a column.
questions.explain: The first index chooses the row; the second chooses the element within that row.
questions.rule: First index = row.

questions.q: True or false: Arrays.copyOfRange(a, 2, 5) includes the element at index 5.
questions.explain: The to index is excluded. The card next explains both copy methods.
questions.rule: The to index is excluded.

questions.q: System.arraycopy returns nothing, so the destination array must be ____ before the call.
questions.explain: The method only fills a destination that already exists with enough room.
questions.rule: arraycopy needs a ready destination.

questions.q: Given src = {5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10}, what does Arrays.copyOfRange(src, 1, 4) return?
optionExplain: This starts at index 0.
This includes index 4, the excluded end.
Right: indexes 1, 2 and 3.
This starts at 0 and includes 4.
questions.explain: Index 1 is 6, index 2 is 7 and index 3 is 8; index 4 is excluded.
questions.rule: From included, to excluded.

questions.q: True or false: If the call is changed to Arrays.copyOfRange(src, 1, 5), the result has 5 elements.
questions.explain: The length is to minus from, which is 4 here.
questions.rule: Length = to - from.

questions.q: int[] dst = new int[2]; System.arraycopy(src, 0, dst, 0, 4); What is wrong?
options: arraycopy returns the new array, which was not stored
A start index of 0 is not allowed
dst must be given the same name as src
Four elements are requested but dst has room for only two
optionExplain: arraycopy returns nothing.
0 is a valid start index.
Names are unrelated.
Right: the count exceeds the destination size.
questions.explain: The destination must have room for every copied element; here it does not.
questions.rule: Check the destination size.

questions.q: What does Arrays.toString applied to an array holding 6, 7, 8 produce?
options: Bracketed, comma-separated text: [6, 7, 8]
The text 6 7 8 with no brackets
The text {6, 7, 8} with braces
The memory address of the array
optionExplain: Right: it formats the elements between square brackets.
Separators are commas and there are brackets.
Braces are used in initializers, not in this output.
That is not what the method returns.
questions.explain: Arrays.toString gives a readable text of the elements.
questions.rule: toString shows the elements.
questions.teaches: Printing an array variable directly does not show its elements; Arrays.toString turns them into readable bracketed text.

questions.q: A playlist array has 12 songs and positions are numbered from 1. You want songs 4 to 7 as a new array. Which call fits?
options: Arrays.copyOfRange(songs, 4, 7)
Arrays.copyOfRange(songs, 3, 7)
Arrays.copyOfRange(songs, 3, 6)
Arrays.copyOfRange(songs, 4, 8)
optionExplain: Index 4 is song 5.
Right: position 4 is index 3, and position 7 is index 6, so the excluded end is 7.
The end 6 would drop song 7.
This begins at song 5 and ends at song 8.
questions.explain: Subtract one for the start index and take the last index plus one for the end.
questions.rule: Start = first position - 1; end = last position.
questions.teaches: Convert human positions to indexes by subtracting one, then set the end to the last wanted index plus one.

questions.q: What does 17 % 5 evaluate to?
optionExplain: 3 is the quotient, not the remainder.
% does not divide into decimals.
Right: 17 is three fives plus 2 left over.
12 is 17 minus 5.
questions.explain: The remainder operator returns what is left after dividing. The card next covers it.
questions.rule: % gives what is left over.

questions.q: The % operator gives the ____ of a division.
questions.explain: It returns what is left over after the division.
questions.rule: % = remainder.

questions.q: After int n = 29; n = n % 7; what does n hold?
optionExplain: 4 is the quotient.
7 is the divisor.
22 is 29 minus 7.
Right: 29 is four sevens (28) plus 1.
questions.explain: The statement divides 29 by 7 and stores the remainder, 1, back into n.
questions.rule: Assignment stores the remainder.

questions.q: If both operands are Strings, a holding the character 4 and b holding the character 5, what does a + b give?
options: The text 45
The number 9
A compile error
The text 4 5
optionExplain: Right: with strings, + joins.
Adding needs numeric operands.
Joining strings is legal.
Nothing inserts a space.
questions.explain: Because both operands are Strings, + concatenates them into the text 45.
questions.rule: Operand types decide what + does.

questions.q: A day counter holds 0 to 6. When day is 6, the expression (day + 1) % 7 gives ____.
questions.explain: 7 divided by 7 leaves no remainder.
questions.rule: Remainder wraps counters.
questions.teaches: For non-negative values the remainder is smaller than the divisor, so % can wrap a counter back to 0 after its top value.

questions.q: Sort each use of the plus sign: does it add numbers or join text?

items.t: Two int variables, a + b
A String variable plus an int variable
Two String variables
Two int literals, 7 + 8
A String literal and another String literal
A double variable plus an int variable

questions.explain: Plus adds when both operands are numbers. As soon as a String is involved, it joins text.
questions.rule: A String operand makes + join.

questions.q: A receipt line is joined with plus signs from, in order, the text Item followed by a colon and a space, a String name holding pen, a space and the letter x, and an int qty holding 3. What does the line contain?
options: Item: pen x 3
Item: pen x3
Item: penx3
A compile error, since a number is mixed with text
optionExplain: No spaces are added automatically.
Right: the number is converted to text when joined.
The text parts supply what is written; nothing removes the spaces inside them.
Joining a String with a number is allowed.
questions.explain: Once a String is involved, the int is converted to its text form and joined.
questions.rule: Mixed values can be joined into messages.
questions.teaches: When one operand of + is a String, a number joined to it is turned into text, so messages can be built from mixed values.

questions.q: If i holds 3, what does System.out.println(i++) print?
options: Nothing, because i++ has no value
optionExplain: 4 is what i holds afterwards.
++ increases; it does not decrease.
Right: postfix yields the old value.
i++ is an expression with a value.
questions.explain: The old value is used first, then i grows. The card next sets out the two forms.
questions.rule: Postfix yields the old value.

questions.q: In ++i the increase happens ____ the expression produces its value.
questions.explain: Prefix increments first and then yields the new value.
questions.rule: Prefix: change, then use.

questions.q: After int n = 10; int m = n++ % 5; what do n and m hold?
options: n is 11 and m is 1
n is 10 and m is 0
n is 10 and m is 1
n is 11 and m is 0
optionExplain: This uses the new value 11 in the remainder.
n does change to 11.
n does change and 10 % 5 is 0.
Right: the old value 10 is used, then n becomes 11.
questions.explain: n++ yields 10, so m is 10 % 5, which is 0, and n ends as 11.
questions.rule: Postfix uses the old value.

questions.q: True or false: If the code is changed to int m = ++n % 5; with n starting at 10, then m ends up as 1.
questions.explain: Prefix raises n to 11 first, so m is 11 % 5, which is 1.
questions.rule: Prefix uses the new value.

questions.q: With int k = 4; System.out.println(k++); System.out.println(++k); the third line System.out.println(k); prints ____.
questions.explain: k becomes 5 after the first line and 6 after the second.
questions.rule: Each increment changes the variable for good.
questions.teaches: Each increment changes the variable permanently; the operator position only decides which value the expression yields.

questions.q: A ticket machine keeps int next = 100;. A customer receives the number with int mine = next++;. What do mine and next hold?
options: mine is 100 and next is 101
mine is 101 and next is 101
mine is 100 and next is 100
mine is 101 and next is 100
optionExplain: Right: take the current value, then advance.
That would be prefix.
next must advance.
This has the two roles reversed.
questions.explain: Postfix hands out the current number and then moves the counter on.
questions.rule: Postfix suits take-then-advance.
questions.teaches: Postfix fits take the current value, then advance, as when handing out sequential numbers.

questions.q: What is 2 + 3 * 4?
optionExplain: 20 adds first, which the precedence rules do not do.
Right: multiplication happens before addition.
24 multiplies all three numbers.
9 adds all three numbers and ignores the multiplication.
questions.explain: The product 12 is computed before the sum. The card next lists the order.
questions.rule: * before +.

questions.q: Of * and +, the operator with the higher precedence is ____.
questions.explain: Multiplication ranks above addition.
questions.rule: Multiplicative beats additive.

questions.q: What is 20 - 6 - 4?
optionExplain: 18 would come from 20 - (6 - 4).
14 stops after the first subtraction.
Right: left to right: (20 - 6) - 4.
2 mixes up the operands.
questions.explain: Equal-precedence binary operators run left to right, giving 14 and then 10.
questions.rule: Same row: left to right.

questions.q: What if parentheses are added as 20 - (6 - 4)? The value becomes ____.
questions.explain: Inside the parentheses 6 - 4 is 2, so 20 - 2 is 18.
questions.rule: Parentheses change grouping.

questions.q: True or false: The expression true || false && false evaluates to false.
questions.explain: The && ranks above ||, so false && false is evaluated first and gives false; then true || false is true.
questions.rule: && binds tighter than ||.
questions.teaches: Logical AND ranks above logical OR, so a mixed condition groups its AND parts first even without parentheses.

questions.q: A colleague says the parentheses in (a + b) * c can be dropped because + comes first. Who is right?
options: The colleague is right: left-to-right order makes the sum go first
The colleague is right: the parentheses do not matter
The colleague is wrong: parentheses are required around every sum
The colleague is wrong: * ranks higher, so without parentheses b * c would go first
optionExplain: Left-to-right applies only among operators of equal rank.
Parentheses change the grouping when ranks differ.
Parentheses are not required everywhere.
Right: precedence beats left-to-right order.
questions.explain: Without parentheses, b * c is computed first, which changes the result.
questions.rule: Parentheses override precedence.

questions.q: A calculator app follows the same precedence as Java. For the key presses 8 + 2 * 5 - 4 / 2, what does it show?
optionExplain: This evaluates strictly left to right.
This groups the first sum before multiplying.
This misapplies the final division.
questions.explain: Multiplication and division go first, giving 10 and 2; then the additions and subtractions run left to right: 8 + 10 - 2.
questions.rule: Higher rows first, then left to right.
questions.teaches: Operators that share a row, like * and /, run left to right among themselves once the higher rows have been resolved.

questions.q: True or false: In Java, the expression a = b tests whether a and b are equal.
questions.explain: A single equals sign assigns. The card next shows the operator that tests.
questions.rule: == tests; = assigns.

questions.q: Match each operator to its meaning.
questions.explain: Each comparison operator produces true or false.
questions.rule: Comparisons produce booleans.

questions.q: With int x = 7; int y = 7;, which expression is false?
options: x == y
x != y
x >= y
x <= y
optionExplain: This is true.
Right: both hold 7, so they are not different.
This is true because they are equal.
This is true because they are equal.
questions.explain: Equal values make == true and != false, while >= and <= are both true.
questions.rule: Equal values: != is false.

questions.q: If x is changed to 5 while y stays 7, which expression is true?
options: x == y
x >= y
x < y
x > y
optionExplain: They differ now.
5 is not at least 7.
Right: 5 is less than 7.
5 is not greater than 7.
questions.explain: With x smaller than y only < (and !=, <=) hold.
questions.rule: Compare after the values change.

questions.q: A programmer writes if (score = 10) hoping to test for a score of ten. What is the mistake?
options: The operator == is reserved for strings
The number 10 must be written in quotes
An if statement cannot compare numbers
The single = assigns instead of comparing; the test needs ==
optionExplain: == compares primitives such as numbers.
Numbers need no quotes.
if tests any boolean, including comparisons.
Right: assignment is not comparison.
questions.explain: The tutorial singles out this mistake: = stores a value, == compares.
questions.rule: == compares; = stores.

questions.q: The expression age >= 18 has the type ____.
questions.explain: Every comparison produces true or false.
questions.rule: Comparisons give booleans.
questions.teaches: Because a comparison is an expression with a boolean value, it can be stored in a boolean variable or combined with other conditions, not only placed in an if.

questions.q: A pool admits children aged up to and including 12. Which test admits a child?
options: age <= 12
age < 12
age == 12
age > 12
optionExplain: Right: it includes 12 and everything below.
This turns away a 12-year-old.
This admits only one age.
This admits older children.
questions.explain: The edge value 12 is admitted, so <= is right.
questions.rule: Check the boundary value.
questions.teaches: Choosing between < and <= decides what happens at the boundary, so test the exact edge value.

questions.q: In a != 0 && 10 / a > 2, the variable a holds 0. What happens to 10 / a?
options: It runs and causes an error
It is skipped, because the left side is false
It runs but its result is ignored
The compiler rejects the expression
optionExplain: That would happen only without the guard.
Right: a false left side settles &&.
Nothing is run once the result is settled.
The expression is legal.
questions.explain: The left side is false, so the right side is never evaluated. The card next explains the rule.
questions.rule: Guard on the left.

questions.q: With ||, the right operand is skipped when the left operand is ____.
questions.explain: A true left side settles an OR.
questions.rule: || stops on true.

questions.q: After int x = 1; boolean r = (x > 5) && (x++ > 0); what does x hold?
optionExplain: That assumes the right side ran.
x was never lowered.
Right: the left side is false, so x++ never runs.
x was never set to 6.
questions.explain: The false left side skips the right operand, so the increment does not happen.
questions.rule: Skipped operands have no effect.

questions.q: True or false: If the operator is changed to || so the line is (x > 5) || (x++ > 0), with x starting at 1, then x ends as 2.
questions.explain: With || a false left side does not settle the result, so the right side runs and x becomes 2.
questions.rule: The operator decides what is skipped.

questions.q: if (s.length() > 0 && s != null) is meant to guard against a null s. What is wrong?
options: && cannot be used with strings
The null check should use = instead of !=
The guard works as written
The null check is on the right, so s.length() runs first and fails when s is null
optionExplain: && works on any booleans.
= would assign.
The right operand is reached only after s.length() has run.
Right: the guard must come first.
questions.explain: Put s != null first, so a null s makes the left side false and skips the length call.
questions.rule: Guard first.

questions.q: A mailer should send only when the address list is not empty and its first entry is valid, where checking the first entry of an empty list fails. Which order of the two checks is safer with &&?
options: Check that the list is not empty first, then the first entry
Check the first entry first, then that the list is not empty
Either order, because && evaluates both sides
Use || so that the second check is skipped
optionExplain: Right: the guard must come first.
The first entry would be read from an empty list.
&& skips the right side when the left is false, so the order matters.
|| would not express both conditions being needed.
questions.explain: The cheap protective check goes on the left; if it is false, the risky check on the right is skipped.
questions.rule: Guard first.
questions.teaches: Place the protective check on the left of && so the risky check on the right runs only when it is safe; a true left side still needs the right.

questions.q: Given boolean ok = false; choose the value that int r = ok ? 1 : 2; stores in r.
optionExplain: 1 is the value for a true condition.
Right: a false condition picks the value after the colon.
There is no third default.
Nothing adds the two values.
questions.explain: The second value is chosen when the condition is false. The card next explains the operator.
questions.rule: false picks the last operand.

questions.q: The ?: operator is called the ____ operator because it has three operands.
questions.explain: Unary has one operand, binary two and ternary three.
questions.rule: ?: is the ternary operator.

questions.q: Which if-else does the same job as label = big ? 'L' : 'S';
options: if (big) label = 'S'; else label = 'L';
if (label) big = 'L'; else big = 'S';
if (big) label = 'L'; else label = 'S';
label = 'L'; if (big) label = 'S';
optionExplain: This swaps the two values.
This tests the wrong variable.
Right: the true branch gets the first value.
This assigns S when big is true.
questions.explain: The value before the colon belongs to the true case and the value after it to the false case.
questions.rule: condition ? when-true : when-false.

questions.q: With int y = x > 3 ? x * 2 : x + 1;, if x is 2 then y becomes ____.
questions.explain: The test 2 > 3 is false, so the false value x + 1 is used.
questions.rule: Evaluate the test, then pick.

questions.q: A coder wants one message when logged in, and three separate actions otherwise, and reaches for the conditional operator. Why would if-else suit better?
options: The ?: operator cannot test booleans
The ?: operator is slower than if-else
The ?: operator only works with numbers
The ?: operator yields one value per branch, so it cannot carry several actions
optionExplain: It tests a boolean condition.
Speed is not the issue here.
It can produce any type of value.
Right: branches of ?: are values, not action lists.
questions.explain: Use ?: to choose between values; use if-else for multi-step branches.
questions.rule: ?: chooses values.

questions.q: True or false: Because the conditional operator has a value, an expression such as n > 0 ? 1 : -1 can be used directly as the argument of a method call.
questions.explain: Any expression can be an argument, and ?: is an expression with a value.
questions.rule: ?: can sit wherever a value fits.
questions.teaches: Since ?: is an expression, it can appear anywhere a value fits, such as inside a method call or a text join, which an if statement cannot do.

questions.q: True or false: A variable declared as Animal that refers to a new Dog object, where Dog extends Animal, passes the instanceof Dog test.
questions.explain: The test looks at the actual object, which is a Dog. The card next explains this.
questions.rule: Actual object type counts.

questions.q: The instanceof operator produces a value of type ____.
questions.explain: It answers yes or no, as true or false.
questions.rule: instanceof gives a boolean.

questions.q: Car extends Vehicle and implements Insurable. Given Vehicle v1 = new Vehicle(); and Vehicle v2 = new Car();, which expression is false?
options: v1 instanceof Insurable
v1 instanceof Vehicle
v2 instanceof Car
v2 instanceof Insurable
optionExplain: Right: a plain Vehicle is not insurable.
A Vehicle object is a Vehicle.
v2 refers to a Car object.
The Car object implements the interface.
questions.explain: Only the plain Vehicle lacks the interface; v2 refers to a Car, which has it.
questions.rule: Check the object, not the variable.

questions.q: True or false: If v1 is reassigned with v1 = new Car();, then v1 instanceof Car becomes true.
questions.explain: The variable now refers to a Car object, and the test looks at that object.
questions.rule: Reassigning changes the object under test.

questions.q: With Vehicle v3 = null;, what does v3 instanceof Vehicle give?
options: true
false
A run-time exception
A compile error
optionExplain: There is no object to be a Vehicle.
Right: null refers to no object.
The test is safe on null.
The code compiles.
questions.explain: null is not an instance of any type, so the test yields false.
questions.rule: null fails every instanceof test.
questions.teaches: null is not an instance of any type, so instanceof gives false on it and does not fail.

questions.q: A drawing app has an interface Shape. Circle and Square implement it; Label does not. Which of these pass the test item instanceof Shape? Select all that apply.
options: A Label object
A variable holding null
A Circle object
A Square object
optionExplain: It does not implement Shape.
It refers to no object, so it fails every type test.
Right: It implements Shape.
Right: It implements Shape.
questions.explain: Every object whose class implements the interface passes, whatever the class; labels and null fail.
questions.rule: Test the interface, not the class.
questions.teaches: A mixed collection can be filtered by type with instanceof, picking out everything that offers an interface regardless of its class.

questions.q: Which operator keeps a bit only when it is set in both operands?
optionExplain: OR keeps a bit set in either.
Exclusive OR keeps a bit set in exactly one.
Complement flips one operand.
Right: AND needs both.
questions.explain: The bitwise AND is the masking operator. The card next covers all of them.
questions.rule: & keeps common bits.

questions.q: Match each operator to its name.
questions.explain: Each works bit by bit.
questions.rule: Four bitwise operators.

questions.q: What is 0b1100 & 0b1010?
options: 0b1000, which is 8
0b1110, which is 14
0b0110, which is 6
0b1010, which is 10
optionExplain: Right: only the top bit is set in both.
That is the OR result.
That is the exclusive OR result.
That copies the second operand.
questions.explain: Only the leftmost bit is 1 in both numbers, so the result is 1000 in binary, which is 8.
questions.rule: AND keeps shared bits.

questions.q: If the operator in 0b1100 & 0b1010 is changed to |, the result in decimal is ____.
questions.explain: OR keeps bits set in either, giving 1110 in binary, which is 14.
questions.rule: OR keeps any set bit.

questions.q: The value of 3 << 2 is ____.
questions.explain: The bits 11 become 1100, which is twelve.
questions.rule: Left shifts multiply by powers of two.
questions.teaches: When no bits are lost, shifting left by n places multiplies a number by 2 to the power n.

questions.q: True or false: The expressions -8 >> 1 and -8 >>> 1 give the same result.
questions.explain: The signed shift copies the sign bit and stays negative, while the unsigned shift fills with zero and gives a large positive number.
questions.rule: >> keeps the sign; >>> fills with zeros.

questions.q: A file system stores permissions in one int, with READ as 1, WRITE as 2 and EXEC as 4. Which expression gives a value with READ and WRITE both set?
options: READ & WRITE
READ | WRITE
~READ
READ << WRITE
optionExplain: AND of two different single bits is 0.
Right: OR sets both bits.
Complement flips every bit.
Shifting READ by 2 gives 4, which is EXEC.
questions.explain: Combining flags with | sets each flag bit, giving 3.
questions.rule: Flags combine with |.
questions.teaches: Giving each option its own bit lets one int store many on-off choices: | sets flags and & tests them.

questions.q: What is the type of the expression score >= 50?
options: int
String
boolean
char
optionExplain: Comparing numbers does not give a number.
No text is involved.
Right: a comparison produces true or false.
No character is involved.
questions.explain: Comparisons yield a boolean. The card next covers expression types.
questions.rule: Comparison gives boolean.

questions.q: An expression evaluates to a single ____.
questions.explain: Every expression produces exactly one value.
questions.rule: One expression, one value.

questions.q: With int x = 3; int y = 4;, what is (x + y) * 10?
optionExplain: 43 would be x + y * 10.
7 drops the multiplication.
34 is y + x * 10: it multiplies only x.
Right: the parentheses force the sum first.
questions.explain: The sum 7 is computed first, then multiplied by 10.
questions.rule: Parentheses set the order.

questions.q: If the parentheses are removed so the expression is x + y * 10, the value becomes ____.
questions.explain: The product 40 is computed first, then 3 is added.
questions.rule: Precedence applies without parentheses.

questions.q: With int count;, what value and type does the assignment expression count = 7 have?
options: The int 7
No value, since assignment is only an action
The boolean true
The String count
optionExplain: Right: an assignment yields the stored value.
It does yield a value.
It is not a comparison.
The variable name is not the value.
questions.explain: An assignment is itself an expression, with the type of the variable on its left.
questions.rule: Assignments have values.
questions.teaches: An assignment is an expression with a value, which is why a chain such as a = b = 5 works.

questions.q: Sort each expression by the type of value it produces.

items.t: age >= 18
age - 18
name != null
count * 2
a < b
price + tax

questions.explain: Comparisons yield booleans; arithmetic yields numbers.
questions.rule: Comparison gives boolean; arithmetic gives numbers.

questions.q: A spreadsheet uses the same precedence as Java. With A1 holding 5 and B1 holding 3, what does the formula A1 + B1 * 2 give?
optionExplain: 16 adds first.
Right: the product goes first.
13 miscomputes the product.
10 ignores the addition.
questions.explain: B1 * 2 is 6 and then 5 + 6 is 11.
questions.rule: Same precedence rules, different tool.
questions.teaches: Precedence conventions are shared by many tools, so grouping habits carry over; add parentheses wherever readers may differ.

questions.q: Which line is a complete, valid statement?
options: count + 1;
count > 1;
count++;
count == 1;
optionExplain: A bare sum does nothing.
A bare comparison does nothing.
Right: an increment can stand alone.
A bare test does nothing.
questions.explain: Only a few expression kinds may stand alone. The card next lists them.
questions.rule: Standalone expressions must do something.

questions.q: A statement ends with a ____.
questions.explain: The semicolon ends a Java statement, as a full stop ends a sentence.
questions.rule: Statements end with a semicolon.

questions.q: Match each statement to its kind.
questions.explain: These four forms are the expression statements the card lists.
questions.rule: Assignment, increment, call, creation.

questions.q: If a line x + 1; is written by itself, what happens?
options: It adds one to x
It compiles and does nothing
It stores x + 1 in a hidden variable
The compiler rejects it, since a plain sum is not an allowed expression statement
optionExplain: Adding does not change x.
The rule rejects the line instead of ignoring it.
Nothing is stored anywhere.
Right: a bare sum has no effect and is not allowed.
questions.explain: Only assignments, increments, method calls and object creations may stand alone.
questions.rule: A statement must do something.

questions.q: A student writes age >= 18; to check an age. What is wrong?
options: A bare comparison is not a valid statement; it must be used inside something like an if or be stored
The semicolon must be removed
The operator >= is not allowed in Java
Comparisons must be written in capital letters
optionExplain: Right: a comparison gives a value but does nothing alone.
A statement needs the semicolon.
>= is a valid operator.
Case is irrelevant here.
questions.explain: The test needs to feed a control flow statement or be assigned to a variable.
questions.rule: Use a comparison inside an if or store it.

questions.q: Sort each line: is it a valid statement or not?

items.t: new Box();

questions.explain: An assignment, a decrement and an object creation can stand alone. A product, a comparison and a negation only produce values.
questions.rule: Standalone lines must act.

questions.q: A rule engine accepts a rule line only if it does something, such as changing a setting or calling an action, and rejects lines that only compute a value. Which Java idea does this mirror?
options: Declaration statements, which every line must be
Expression statements: only assignments, increments, calls and creations may stand alone
Blocks, which require braces around each line
Operators, which forbid a semicolon
optionExplain: Declarations introduce variables and are not required for every line.
Right: standalone lines must have an effect.
Blocks group statements; they do not decide what counts as one.
Statements end with a semicolon.
questions.explain: Java rejects lines that merely compute a value for the same reason.
questions.rule: A statement has an effect.
questions.teaches: Lines that only produce a value are rejected because a statement must perform an action; the allowed forms are the ones that do.

questions.q: True or false: A block may be used anywhere Java allows a single statement.
questions.explain: That is what makes a block useful. The card next explains it.
questions.rule: A block can replace a statement.

questions.q: A block is a group of statements enclosed in balanced ____.
questions.explain: The braces mark where the block starts and ends.
questions.rule: Blocks use braces.

questions.q: Which if statement runs both calls only when ready is true?
options: if (ready) start(); log();
if (ready) { start(); } log();
if (ready) { start(); log(); }
if ready { start(); log(); }
optionExplain: Only start() is controlled.
Only start() is inside the block.
Right: the braces gather both calls.
The test needs parentheses.
questions.explain: A block makes the two calls one unit controlled by the test.
questions.rule: Group with braces.

questions.q: In if (ready) start(); log(); with no braces, ready is false. Which calls run?
options: Neither call
Both calls
Only start()
Only log()
optionExplain: log() is not controlled by the if.
Only start() is controlled.
start() is skipped when ready is false.
Right: the if governs only the next statement.
questions.explain: Without a block the second call stands outside the if and runs regardless.
questions.rule: Without braces, one statement only.

questions.q: True or false: A method body with three opening braces and two closing braces compiles.
questions.explain: Braces must balance, so the compiler reports an error.
questions.rule: Balance every brace.

questions.q: A contract clause with several sub-points is treated as one clause in a longer document. Which Java construct plays the same part for statements?
options: A block
A declaration statement
A parameter
A literal
optionExplain: Right: it groups several statements as one.
It introduces one variable, not a group.
It is a variable in a method signature.
It is a fixed value.
questions.explain: A block bundles statements so the group counts as one statement.
questions.rule: A block acts as one statement.
questions.teaches: Because a block counts as a single statement, blocks can nest inside other blocks, building structure of any depth from the same piece.

questions.q: Given int s = 76; if (s >= 60) g = 'D'; else if (s >= 70) g = 'C'; else g = 'F'; what does g hold?
options: C
D
F
Nothing, because two tests are true
optionExplain: The test for C is never reached.
Right: the first true test wins.
The final else runs only when every test fails.
Java takes the first true test; it does not reject the code.
questions.explain: The first test is true, so its branch runs and the rest are skipped. The card next explains the rule.
questions.rule: First true test wins.

questions.q: In an else-if chain the tests are checked from the ____ down.
questions.explain: Evaluation starts at the first test.
questions.rule: Top-down, first true wins.

questions.q: With int t = 85;, the chain tests t >= 90 for A, then t >= 80 for B, then t >= 70 for C, otherwise F. What grade results?
options: A
C
B
F
optionExplain: 85 is below 90.
C is skipped once B matched.
Right: 85 fails the first test and passes the second.
F applies only if every test fails.
questions.explain: The second test is the first true one, so the grade is B.
questions.rule: Stop at the first true test.

questions.q: True or false: If t is changed to 70 in the same chain, the grade becomes C.
questions.explain: The tests for 90 and 80 fail, and t >= 70 is true.
questions.rule: The first passing threshold decides.

questions.q: A programmer writes grade tests as >= 60 first, then >= 70, then >= 90, each followed by else if. What happens for a score of 95?
options: The >= 90 branch runs, because it is the best match
All three branches run in turn
The compiler rejects the order
The >= 60 branch runs, because it is true first and ends the chain
optionExplain: Java does not look for the best match.
A chain runs only one branch.
The order is legal; it is the result that is wrong.
Right: the first true test wins, not the best.
questions.explain: Tests ordered from least to most restrictive make the broadest test win.
questions.rule: Order tests from most restrictive down.

questions.q: True or false: With int a = 6; int count = 0; and two separate statements if (a > 5) count++; if (a > 3) count++; the value of count ends as 2.
questions.explain: Separate if statements are tested independently, and both tests are true.
questions.rule: Separate ifs are independent.
questions.teaches: Two separate if statements are tested independently, unlike the branches of a chain, so several of them can run.

questions.q: A shipping rule charges 15 for parcels over 20 kg, 8 for parcels over 5 kg and 3 otherwise, written as an else-if chain. Which order of tests gives the right charge for 8 kg?
options: Test over 20 kg first, then over 5 kg, then the else
Test over 5 kg first, then over 20 kg, then the else
Any order, since only one test can be true
Use separate if statements in any order
optionExplain: Right: start with the most restrictive range.
An 8 kg parcel would match the first test and be right, but a 25 kg parcel would also match it and be charged 8.
More than one test can be true for large values.
Separate ifs could add two charges.
questions.explain: Putting the biggest threshold first means a larger parcel is caught before the broader test.
questions.rule: Narrowest range first.
questions.teaches: In a chain of threshold tests, each later test relies on the earlier ones having failed, so start from the extreme end.

questions.q: In if (a > 0) if (a > 10) big(); else other(); with a equal to 5, which call runs?
options: big()
other()
Neither call
Both calls
optionExplain: The inner test is false, so big() is skipped.
Right: the else belongs to the inner if.
The else attached to the inner if runs.
Only one branch runs.
questions.explain: The inner if fails, so its else runs. The card next explains the pairing.
questions.rule: Nearest if.

questions.q: An else pairs with the ____ unmatched if before it.
questions.explain: The nearest earlier if without an else owns it.
questions.rule: Nearest unmatched if.

questions.q: Given if (n >= 0) if (n == 0) first(); else second(); third(); with n equal to -2, which calls run?
options: second() and third()
first() and third()
Only third()
All three calls
optionExplain: second() belongs to the inner if, which is skipped.
first() needs n to be 0.
Right: the outer test fails, so the whole inner statement is skipped.
The outer test is false.
questions.explain: The outer test is false, so the entire inner if and its else are skipped; third() is outside.
questions.rule: An outer false skips the inner block.

questions.q: True or false: If braces make the else pair with the outer if in the same code, then n equal to -2 runs both second() and third().
questions.explain: The outer test fails, so its else runs, and third() follows.
questions.rule: Braces choose the pairing.

questions.q: A programmer indents an else under the outer if and expects it to run when n is negative, but it is attached to the inner if. Why?
options: Indentation is read only for else clauses
Negative numbers cannot be tested
The else must belong to the inner if
The compiler ignores indentation and pairs the else with the nearest unmatched if
optionExplain: Indentation is never read.
Negative numbers can be tested.
Either pairing is possible when written with braces.
Right: layout does not decide pairing.
questions.explain: The default pairing is syntactic, so the indentation was only a hint to readers.
questions.rule: Braces beat indentation.

questions.q: In a method, if (isMoving) speed--; is followed on the next line by a print statement at the same indentation, added later. When does the print run?
options: Whenever the method runs, regardless of isMoving
Only when isMoving is true
Only when isMoving is false
It does not run, because the compiler rejects it
optionExplain: Right: without braces the if controls one statement only.
That would need braces around both lines.
Nothing makes it run on false only.
The compiler accepts it with no warning.
questions.explain: The print stands outside the if, so it is unconditional.
questions.rule: Braces protect later edits.
questions.teaches: Omitting braces is brittle: adding a second statement later puts only the first under the if, and the compiler does not warn.

questions.q: A policy says: if the visitor is staff then if they hold a badge, let them in; otherwise call security. It does not say which condition the otherwise belongs to. What is the best fix?
options: Add more indentation to the second line
Add explicit grouping, as braces do, to show which condition the otherwise follows
Remove the word otherwise
Trust readers to apply the nearest-if habit
optionExplain: Layout does not carry meaning.
Right: say the pairing outright.
That changes the policy.
Readers may disagree about the intended pairing.
questions.explain: Explicit grouping removes the ambiguity in policies just as braces do in code.
questions.rule: Make pairing explicit.
questions.teaches: Natural-language rules suffer the same ambiguity as nested ifs, and explicit grouping is the fix there too.

questions.q: A program must pick a message for ages 0 to 12, 13 to 19, and 20 or more. Which structure fits best?
options: A switch, because it has a default
A switch on a boolean value
An if-else chain, because the tests are ranges
Either, because they read identically
optionExplain: default does not make ranges possible.
boolean is not an allowed switch type.
Right: switch tests single values, not ranges.
Ranges would need a case for every age.
questions.explain: Ranges call for conditions, which if-else handles. The card next lays out what a switch can do.
questions.rule: Ranges: if-else.

questions.q: Values not matched by any case label are handled by the ____ label.
questions.explain: default is the catch-all.
questions.rule: default catches the rest.

questions.q: Which expression types may a switch statement test, according to the tutorial? Select all that apply.
options: double
int
String
An enum value
long
boolean
optionExplain: double is not in the list.
Right: int is allowed.
Right: String is allowed since Java 7.
Right: Enums are allowed.
long is not in the list.
boolean is not in the list.
questions.explain: The tutorial lists the small integral types, enums, String and the matching wrapper classes.
questions.rule: Single values of a few types.

questions.q: Given switch (d) { case 6: case 7: type = 1; break; default: type = 0; break; }, if d changes from 3 to 7, what does type hold?
options: Nothing, because 7 has no statements of its own
optionExplain: Right: the stacked labels share one block.
0 is the default value used for 3.
7 is a case label, not the stored value.
Labels with no statements simply share the next statements.
questions.explain: Case 7 shares the block that follows it, so type is 1.
questions.rule: Stacked labels share a block.

questions.q: With String s = null;, what happens when switch (s) is reached?
options: The default label runs
A NullPointerException is thrown
Execution skips the switch silently
The first case label runs
optionExplain: null does not select default.
Right: a null expression is not treated as a non-matching value.
The switch does not skip itself.
No label matches null.
questions.explain: The switch needs a real String to compare, so null fails at run time.
questions.rule: Check for null before switching.
questions.teaches: A switch on a null String does not fall to default; it throws a NullPointerException, so null must be handled beforehand.

questions.q: True or false: A switch statement can test whether a double lies between 1.0 and 2.0.
questions.explain: Switch compares an expression with single values, and double is not an allowed type.
questions.rule: No ranges, no doubles.

questions.q: A vending machine reads a char button code such as A, B or C and must run a different action for each, with a message for unknown codes. What fits best?
options: An if-else chain testing ranges of codes
A switch on a boolean flag
A switch on the char, with a case for each button and default for unknown codes
A while loop that tests each code
optionExplain: The codes are single values, not ranges.
A boolean has only two values.
Right: each button is one value of an allowed type.
A loop repeats work; it does not choose.
questions.explain: A char is an allowed type, and one case per button is the shape switch is built for.
questions.rule: Single values: switch.
questions.teaches: A char works in a switch because it is among the allowed small integral types, and a fixed set of single values is the shape switch fits.

questions.q: In a switch, case 3 has no break and case 4 follows. For the value 3, what runs?
options: Only case 3
Only case 4
Nothing
The statements of case 3, then those of case 4
optionExplain: That would need a break after case 3.
The match is case 3, so it runs too.
A match always runs its statements.
Right: without a break, execution continues.
questions.explain: Execution continues into the next case. The card next explains this.
questions.rule: No break: keep going.

questions.q: Without a break, execution ____ through into the next case.
questions.explain: The statements keep executing downward.
questions.rule: No break means fall-through.

questions.q: Given switch (n) { case 1: out(a); case 2: out(b); case 3: out(c); break; case 4: out(d); } and n equal to 1, what is output?
options: a, b and c
a only
a and b
a, b, c and d
optionExplain: Right: the break after case 3 stops it.
a only would need a break after case 1.
b is followed by c with no break between.
The break after case 3 prevents d.
questions.explain: Case 1 falls through case 2 and case 3, then the break ends the switch.
questions.rule: Follow the cases until a break.

questions.q: If a break is added right after out(a) in the same switch, what is output for n equal to 1?
options: a and b
a only
a, b and c
Nothing
optionExplain: b would need fall-through.
Right: the break ends the switch immediately.
c would need fall-through.
The matched case runs.
questions.explain: A break after the first statement ends the switch at once.
questions.rule: Break stops the cascade.

questions.q: Put the steps in the order the original switch takes when n is 2.
items: Jump to the label case 2
Run the statement of case 2
Fall into case 3 and run its statement
Reach break and leave the switch
questions.explain: The switch runs statements, not labels, so the label of case 3 is ignored while falling through.
questions.rule: Labels are entry points only.
questions.teaches: Once running, a switch does not stop at later labels; it only stops at break or the end of the block.

questions.q: A troubleshooting guide has levels 1 to 4, and level n must run its own fix and every higher level fix. Which switch design fits?
options: One case per level, each ending with break
Cases in descending order with breaks
Cases in ascending order with no breaks, entering at level n
A default label only
optionExplain: Breaks would stop after one level.
Descending order with breaks still stops after one.
Right: fall-through gives cumulative behaviour.
default has no levels.
questions.explain: Entering at level n and falling through runs that fix and everything after it.
questions.rule: Fall-through means from here onward.
questions.teaches: Ordering cases on purpose and leaving out break gives cumulative behaviour: do this step and every later one.

questions.q: True or false: A while loop whose condition is false at the start still runs its body once.
questions.explain: The condition is tested first. The card next contrasts while and do-while.
questions.rule: while tests first.

questions.q: A do-while loop tests its condition at the ____ of the loop.
questions.explain: That is why its body always runs once.
questions.rule: do-while tests at the bottom.

questions.q: After int c = 10; do { c++; } while (c < 5); what does c hold?
optionExplain: That would need the body to be skipped.
5 is the limit in the condition.
6 ignores the starting value.
Right: the body runs once before the test.
questions.explain: The body runs once, making c 11; the test then fails and the loop ends.
questions.rule: do-while runs at least once.

questions.q: True or false: If the loop is rewritten as while (c < 5) { c++; } with c starting at 10, then c ends as 10.
questions.explain: The condition is false at the start, so the body never runs.
questions.rule: while may run zero times.

questions.q: In while (true) { work(); if (done) break; }, what ends the loop?
options: The break, once done becomes true
The condition true, which turns false
The end of the block
Nothing, so it runs forever
optionExplain: Right: the exit is inside the body.
true never turns false.
Reaching the end only starts another pass.
The break provides the way out.
questions.explain: An infinite loop with an explicit exit inside the body is a legitimate pattern.
questions.rule: while (true) needs an exit.
questions.teaches: A loop that is infinite by its header can still be finite by design, when the body contains an exit such as break or return.

questions.q: In int i = 0; while (i < 3) { show(i); } the loop cannot end because nothing ____ i.
questions.explain: The condition reads i, but the body leaves it at 0.
questions.rule: The body must change what the condition reads.

questions.q: An app must ask for a password at least once and ask again while the entry is wrong. Which loop fits best?
options: while, because the check comes first
do-while, because the first entry must happen before the test
for, because it counts
switch, because it picks one case
optionExplain: A while would test an entry that does not exist yet.
Right: the test depends on input the body obtains.
Counting is not the need.
switch does not repeat.
questions.explain: The condition depends on what the body obtains, so the body must run first.
questions.rule: Use do-while when the test depends on the first pass.
questions.teaches: Prompt-then-validate patterns suit do-while because the condition depends on data the body gathers.

questions.q: How many times does the body of for (int i = 0; i < 3; i++) run?
optionExplain: The test passes for 0, 1 and 2.
The value 3 fails the test.
Right: i takes the values 0, 1 and 2.
The first test is true.
questions.explain: The loop runs while i is below 3, so for i equal to 0, 1 and 2. The card next gives the order.
questions.rule: Count the passes of the test.

questions.q: Put the parts of a for loop in the order they run for each cycle, starting from the first.
items: Run the initialization
Check the termination test
Run the loop body
Run the increment
questions.explain: The initialization runs once; then the test, body and increment repeat in that order.
questions.rule: Initialise once; test, body, increment repeat.

questions.q: What does for (int i = 2; i <= 8; i += 3) show(i); display?
options: 2 and 5
5 and 8
3, 6 and 9
2, 5 and 8
optionExplain: 8 satisfies the test i <= 8.
The loop starts at 2.
The loop starts at 2, not 3.
Right: i takes 2, 5, 8 and then 11 fails the test.
questions.explain: The counter steps by three from 2, and 8 still satisfies the test.
questions.rule: Walk the counter through the test.

questions.q: If the test <= is changed to <, the last value shown is ____.
questions.explain: 8 now fails the test, so 5 is the last.
questions.rule: A stricter test drops the last value.

questions.q: A counter is declared in the for header. Can the code after the loop use it?
options: No: its scope ends with the loop
Yes, it stays available in the method
Yes, but only after a break
Only if it is also declared final
optionExplain: Right: the variable lives inside the loop.
That is true only for a variable declared before the loop.
break does not change scope.
final does not extend scope.
questions.explain: Declaring the counter in the header limits its lifetime.
questions.rule: Header variables are loop-scoped.
questions.teaches: A value needed after the loop must be declared before it; loop-scoped counters cannot be reused by later code by accident.

questions.q: A student wants the position of each element but writes int[] a = {4, 5, 6}; for (int v : a) ... What is the limitation?
options: It can only visit the first element
The enhanced for supplies the elements but no index
It requires a count variable declared outside
It cannot be used with arrays
optionExplain: It visits every element.
Right: the loop variable is the element itself.
No counter is needed.
It was designed for arrays and collections.
questions.explain: When you need positions, use the classic for with a counter.
questions.rule: Element, not index.

questions.q: You must total every value in a double array named prices, and positions do not matter. Which loop does the tutorial recommend whenever possible?
options: A classic for with a counter
while (true) with break
The enhanced for
do-while with an index
optionExplain: It works but adds code you do not need here.
It is needlessly complex.
Right: it is compact and readable for a pass over all elements.
It adds an index for no reason.
questions.explain: A read-through with no use for the index is the enhanced for case.
questions.rule: Visit-all: enhanced for.
questions.teaches: Choose the enhanced for for a read-through, and the classic for when you need positions or a stepped range.

questions.q: In a for loop, a break runs in the middle of the body on pass 3 of 10. What happens next?
options: Pass 4 begins
The rest of pass 3 is skipped and pass 4 begins
The program ends
The loop ends and the code after it runs
optionExplain: That is not what break does.
That describes continue.
Only the loop ends.
Right: break leaves the loop.
