questions.explain: break leaves the loop entirely. The card next sets break beside continue.
questions.rule: break leaves; continue skips.

questions.q: Match each statement to its effect.
pairs: leaves the innermost loop or switch
moves to the next pass of a named outer loop
questions.explain: The labeled forms do the same jobs on an outer statement.
questions.rule: Labels aim break and continue outward.

questions.q: What does for (i = 1; i <= 5; i++) { if (i == 3) continue; show(i); } display?
options: 1 and 2
4 and 5
optionExplain: Right: only the pass for 3 is skipped.
That would be break.
The pass for 3 is skipped.
Passes before 3 run too.
questions.explain: continue skips only the remainder of the pass where i is 3.
questions.rule: continue skips one pass.

questions.q: True or false: If continue is changed to break in the same loop, it displays 1 and 2 only.
questions.explain: The break ends the loop when i reaches 3.
questions.rule: break stops everything.

questions.q: In int i = 0; while (i < 4) { if (i == 2) continue; i++; } what happens?
options: It ends after i reaches 4
The loop does not end: when i is 2, continue skips i++ on every pass
It ends when i is 2
It skips only the pass where i is 2 and then carries on
optionExplain: i never gets past 2.
Right: continue jumps back to the condition without running i++.
continue does not end the loop.
The update is skipped on every pass after 2.
questions.explain: In a while loop continue goes straight to the condition, so an update placed after it is skipped.
questions.rule: Updates after continue can be skipped.
questions.teaches: In a while loop continue jumps to the condition, so an update written after it is skipped and the loop can stall; in a for loop the header increment still runs.

questions.q: A programmer uses a plain break inside the inner of two nested loops, intending to stop both. What happens?
options: Both loops end
The program ends
Only the inner loop ends and the outer loop carries on
The compiler rejects the break
optionExplain: That needs a labeled break.
break never ends the program.
Right: unlabeled break reaches the innermost loop only.
It is legal.
questions.explain: Use a label on the outer loop to end both.
questions.rule: Unlabeled: innermost only.

questions.q: A theatre program searches rows and seats for the first free seat and must stop all searching as soon as one is found. Which statement does that?
options: A plain break in the inner loop
A continue in the inner loop
A return from the outer loop
A labeled break naming the outer loop
optionExplain: That would continue with the next row.
That skips to the next seat.
A return would also leave the method, which may skip later work.
Right: it leaves both loops at once.
questions.explain: The label lets the inner statement end the outer loop as well.
questions.rule: Label the outer loop.
questions.teaches: Searches over nested structures commonly use a labeled break to stop every level once a result is found.

questions.q: Which family does a for statement belong to?
options: Looping
Decision-making
Branching
Declaration
optionExplain: Right: it repeats a block.
Decision-making statements choose a path.
Branching statements jump out or skip.
Declarations introduce variables.
questions.explain: for repeats work, so it is a loop. The card next names all three families.
questions.rule: for is a loop.

questions.q: Match each statement to its family.
questions.explain: if-then chooses, do-while repeats and break jumps out.
questions.rule: Decide, repeat, jump.

questions.q: A task must repeat until the user types quit and must run at least once. Which statement fits best?
options: if-then-else
do-while
switch
return
optionExplain: It chooses a path once.
Right: it repeats and always runs once.
It selects among values once.
It leaves a method.
questions.explain: The repeat-at-least-once shape is do-while.
questions.rule: Pick the family, then the statement.

questions.q: True or false: If show(0) is called in static void show(int n) { if (n <= 0) return; print(n); }, nothing is printed.
questions.explain: The return leaves the method before the print.
questions.rule: return exits at once.

questions.q: A return statement sits inside a for loop within a method. What does it end?
options: Only the current pass
Only the loop
The whole method, not only the loop
Only the enclosing if
optionExplain: That describes continue.
That describes break.
Right: return leaves the method.
return does not stop at an if.
questions.explain: return hands control to the caller at once, wherever it appears.
questions.rule: return leaves the method.
questions.teaches: A return inside a search loop can end the method with a found position in one step.

questions.q: A void method contains return x * x; What is wrong?
options: The loop is missing
x must be an int
The statement needs a label
A void method returns no value, so return must stand alone
optionExplain: No loop is needed.
The type of x is not the issue.
Labels are unrelated.
Right: void means no value.
questions.explain: In a void method write return; with no value.
questions.rule: void: bare return.

questions.q: An elevator controller has three jobs. Match each to the family that fits.
pairs: Choose which floor button was pressed
Keep checking floors until the door closes
Stop checking early when an alarm fires
questions.explain: Choosing is a decision, repeating is a loop and stopping early is a jump out.
questions.rule: Name the job, then the family.
questions.teaches: Most real tasks combine all three families, and naming each job as choose, repeat or jump out is a way to plan code.

questions.q: Which set of things can appear inside the body of a Java class?
options: Fields, methods and constructors
Only methods, since data is kept elsewhere
Only fields and methods, since objects start themselves
Only constructors, since they create everything else
optionExplain: Right: these three cover state, behaviour and set-up.
Data does live in the class, in fields.
A constructor is how a new object is given its first values.
Constructors only initialize; fields and methods are separate members.
questions.explain: A class body can hold fields, methods and constructors. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: A class declares fields for state, methods for behaviour and constructors for setting up new objects.

questions.q: Match each class member to its job.
pairs: Records the state of an object
Defines something the object can do
Makes the class a subclass of another
questions.explain: State lives in fields, behaviour in methods, set-up in constructors, and extends links a subclass to its parent.
questions.rule: Fields are state, methods are behaviour, constructors are set-up.

questions.q: A class Account must remember a balance, let callers add money, and start each new account at zero. Which assignment of these jobs to class members fits best?
options: A balance method, a deposit constructor, and a field that sets the start value
A balance field, a deposit method, and a constructor that sets the balance to zero
A balance constructor, a deposit field, and a method holding the start value
A balance field, a deposit constructor, and a method that sets the start value
optionExplain: Mixes up all three: constructors run at creation, not for each deposit.
Right: each job goes to the member type built for it.
Fields store data and cannot perform a deposit.
A constructor runs once per new object, so it cannot handle every later deposit.
questions.explain: State is a field, the repeatable action is a method, and the starting value is set when the object is created.
questions.rule: Match each requirement to field, method or constructor.

questions.q: True or false: A subclass declares one extra field. Objects of that subclass still carry the fields they inherit from the parent.
questions.explain: Inheritance adds: a subclass object has the parent's members plus its own new ones.
questions.rule: A subclass adds to what it inherits.

questions.q: True or false: A constructor can be called on an object that already exists, in the same way as a method, to reset it.
questions.explain: A constructor runs as part of creating a new object. Resetting an existing object needs an ordinary method.
questions.rule: Constructors create; methods act on existing objects.
questions.teaches: A constructor runs only when a new object is created with new; it is not called on an object that already exists.

questions.q: A Window class stores a width, a height and a title. Sort these items by whether the class would keep them in a field or offer them through a method.

items.t: the width
the height
the title text
the area worked out from width and height
a resize action
a close action

questions.explain: Width, height and title are stored state. The area can be computed from stored values, as the tutorial's Rectangle does with its area method, so it is offered by a method.
questions.rule: Store the basics; compute what follows from them.
questions.teaches: A value that follows from stored fields, such as an area, is normally offered by a method that computes it rather than stored as another field.

questions.q: What is the smallest valid way to declare a class?
options: A name, braces and at least one field
A modifier, a name and an extends clause
The class keyword, a name and a pair of braces
The class keyword, a name, a constructor and a main method
optionExplain: A body may be empty.
Modifiers and extends are both optional.
Right: everything else is optional.
Neither is required by the declaration itself.
questions.explain: Only the keyword, the name and the body are required. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: Write modifiers, the name, an optional extends with one parent, an optional implements with a list, then the braced body.

questions.q: Put the parts of a full class declaration in the order they must appear.
items: Modifiers such as public
The class name
The extends clause with one parent
The implements clause with a list of interfaces
The body in braces
questions.explain: The tutorial lists modifiers, name, extends, implements, then the body.
questions.rule: Modifiers, name, extends, implements, body.

questions.q: Which class header follows the tutorial's rules?
options: public class Invoice implements Printable, Taxable extends Document
public class Invoice extends Document, Report implements Printable
public class Invoice extends Document implements Printable Taxable
public class Invoice extends Document implements Printable, Taxable
optionExplain: implements comes after extends, not before.
A class may extend only one parent.
The interfaces must be separated by a comma.
Right: one parent, then a comma-separated interface list.
questions.explain: Only the first header has the clauses in order, one parent and a comma between interfaces.
questions.rule: One parent, many interfaces, fixed order.

questions.q: True or false: If the extends clause is deleted from a valid declaration that also has an implements clause, the declaration is still valid.
questions.explain: Both clauses are optional and independent of each other, so one may be present without the other.
questions.rule: extends and implements are each optional.

questions.q: A class written on its own, not inside another class, is given the modifier private. What does the tutorial say about this?
options: It is not allowed: private applies to classes only when they are nested
It is allowed and hides the class from every other class
It is allowed only when the class also extends a parent
It is allowed but then the class cannot declare fields
optionExplain: Right: the tutorial restricts private to nested classes.
That is what private does for members, but not for a class on its own.
The extends clause plays no part in this rule.
Access to a class and the members it may declare are unrelated.
questions.explain: The tutorial says private can be applied to nested classes only.
questions.rule: Private on a class means the class is nested.
questions.teaches: The modifier private can be applied to a class only when that class is nested inside another class.

questions.q: A designer wants class Seaplane to act as an Aircraft (a class) and as Floatable (an interface). Which header fits the tutorial's rules?
options: class Seaplane extends Aircraft, Floatable
class Seaplane extends Aircraft implements Floatable
class Seaplane extends Floatable implements Aircraft
class Seaplane implements Floatable extends Aircraft
optionExplain: Only one parent class is allowed after extends.
Right: the one parent is the class, the other role is an interface.
The roles are swapped: Floatable is an interface and Aircraft a class.
implements must come after extends.
questions.explain: A class gets one parent through extends and any number of further roles through implements.
questions.rule: Spend the single extends on a class, and use implements for the other roles.
questions.teaches: When a class needs several roles, one can come from its single parent class and the rest from interfaces.

questions.q: A method receives a number from its caller. Where is the variable that holds that number declared?
options: Inside the method body as a local variable
In the class body outside every method
In the parentheses after the method name
In the modifiers at the start of the declaration
optionExplain: Locals are declared in the body, but the received value arrives through the signature.
That would be a field shared by the whole object.
Right: that is where parameters are declared.
Modifiers describe access, not variables.
questions.explain: Parameters are declared in the method signature. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: Tell the three kinds apart by where each is declared: in the class, in a block, or in a method signature.

questions.q: Match each kind of variable to where it is declared.
pairs: In a class, outside any method
Inside a method or other block
In the parentheses of a method signature
questions.explain: The place of declaration decides the kind.
questions.rule: Kind follows place of declaration.

questions.q: In class Tank { double level; double cap; void fill(double litres) { double room = cap - level; level += litres; } }, which names are fields?
options: room
litres
level
cap
optionExplain: It is declared inside fill, so it is a local variable.
It is declared in the parentheses of fill, so it is a parameter.
Right: declared in the class body.
Right: also declared in the class body.
questions.explain: level and cap are declared in the class body. litres is a parameter and room is a local variable.
questions.rule: Fields sit in the class body.

questions.q: True or false: In class Tank above, moving the declaration of room out of fill and into the class body would turn it into a field.
questions.explain: The kind depends only on where the declaration sits, so moving it to the class body makes it a field.
questions.rule: Move the declaration and the kind changes.

questions.q: In void log(String message), what is message?
options: A parameter whose type is a primitive type
A field whose type is a reference type
A local variable whose type is a primitive type
A parameter whose type is a reference type
optionExplain: String is not a primitive type; it is an object type.
It is declared in the signature, not the class body.
It is neither in the body nor a primitive.
Right: it sits in the signature, and strings are reference types.
questions.explain: Kind (field, local, parameter) and type group (primitive, reference) are two separate questions about one variable.
questions.rule: Kind and type group are separate questions.
questions.teaches: Kind (field, local or parameter) and type group (primitive or reference) are independent: any kind can have either type group.

questions.q: In class Shelf { Book[] books; int count; void place(Book item) { int slot = count; books[slot] = item; count = slot + 1; } }, which description is correct?
options: books and count are fields, item is a parameter, slot is a local
books, count and slot are fields; there is no parameter
books is a reference-type local; count is a primitive field
count and item are fields; books and slot are locals
optionExplain: Right: place of declaration gives the kinds.
slot is declared inside place, so it is local, and item is a parameter.
books is declared in the class body, so it is a field.
item sits in the signature, which makes it a parameter.
questions.explain: Declaration place decides the kind; the array books is a reference-type variable that is still a field.
questions.rule: Apply the place test to every name.
questions.teaches: Reference-type variables, such as an array or an object, can be fields, locals or parameters just as primitive variables can.

questions.q: A class marks its fields private and gives them public methods. What is the main idea behind this?
options: The fields become quicker to read from other classes
Other classes can reach the data only through methods the class offers
The fields can then be shared by all objects of the class
The class no longer needs a constructor
optionExplain: Access level has nothing to do with speed.
Right: that is encapsulation.
Sharing is what static does, not private.
Constructors are unrelated to access modifiers.
questions.explain: Private fields with public methods hide the data and control how it changes. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: Keep fields private and let other classes work with the object through public methods.

questions.q: A field marked ____ can be accessed only from inside its own class.
questions.explain: Private limits access to the class that declares the field.
questions.rule: Private means only inside the declaring class.

questions.q: Class Ticket has a private field seat. The designers want outside code to read the seat but not to change it. Which public methods fit?
options: A setSeat method that assigns it, and no getter
Both getSeat and setSeat, since outside code needs full control
A getSeat method that returns it, and no method that assigns it
No methods, with the field changed to public
optionExplain: That allows writing but not reading.
A setter would let outside code change the seat.
Right: a getter without a setter gives read-only access.
Public lets any class change it directly.
questions.explain: A getter with no setter lets others read the value while the class alone controls changes.
questions.rule: A getter without a setter is read-only access.

questions.q: True or false: The class Ticket above later changes how it stores the seat internally, but keeps its public methods the same. Code in other classes that used only those methods still works.
questions.explain: Callers depended on the methods, not on the stored form, so internal changes stay hidden.
questions.rule: Private fields leave the class free to change inside.

questions.q: In a Bicycle class, speed has a getter but no setter, yet the class has applyBrake and speedUp methods. What does this design achieve?
options: Outside code has no way to change speed at all
Outside code can set speed to any value it wants
Speed becomes a class variable shared by all bicycles
Outside code can change speed only through the class's own actions
optionExplain: applyBrake and speedUp change it.
Without a setter it cannot assign an arbitrary value.
Sharing comes from static, not from missing setters.
Right: the class decides how speed may change.
questions.explain: A public method can change a private field by a controlled amount without handing over the field itself.
questions.rule: Expose actions, not raw assignment, when the class must control change.
questions.teaches: A public method can change a private field in controlled steps, such as braking by an amount, without giving callers a way to assign any value.

questions.q: A class Thermostat in a smart-home app keeps a private field target. A tester wants to check the temperature limit logic. What should the class offer?
options: A public setTarget method that applies the limit before storing
A public target field, so tests can assign any value freely
A private setTarget method that only the tests may call
Nothing, since a private field cannot have limit logic at all
optionExplain: Right: the method is the single place where the rule is enforced.
Direct assignment skips the limit logic.
Private methods are not reachable from other classes.
The logic lives in the class's methods.
questions.explain: Routing writes through a public method lets the class check or limit every change.
questions.rule: Put rules in the methods that guard the field.
questions.teaches: Because every change goes through a method, that method is a single place where the class can check or limit new values.

questions.q: Which method name best follows common Java style for a method that tells whether a list has no entries?
options: Empty
isEmpty
is_empty_list
IsEmpty
optionExplain: A method name should start with a lower-case verb.
Right: lower-case verb start, camel case.
Underscores in words are not the style; later words are capitalized instead.
Method names do not start with a capital letter.
questions.explain: Method names begin with a lower-case verb. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: Start class names with a capital letter and method names with a lower-case verb.

questions.q: By convention the first letter of a class name is ____.
questions.explain: The tutorial says class names are capitalized, as in Bicycle.
questions.rule: Class names start with a capital.

questions.q: A class models a library loan. Which pair of names fits the tutorial's conventions for the class and for a method that extends the due date?
options: loan and ExtendDueDate
Loan and due_date_extension
Loan and extendDueDate
LOAN and extenddatedue
optionExplain: Both are the wrong way round.
The method name is a noun phrase with underscores.
Right: capitalized class, lower-case verb method with camel case.
Neither follows the capitalization pattern.
questions.explain: Class: capital letter. Method: lower-case verb, later words capitalized.
questions.rule: Capital class, verb-first method.

questions.q: True or false: If a developer names a method Total instead of getTotal, the program stops compiling.
questions.explain: The names are conventions that help readers. The compiler accepts any legal identifier.
questions.rule: Conventions guide readers; they are not compiler rules.

questions.q: Which method name does the tutorial's pattern suggest for a boolean question about a player's turn?
options: turn
MyTurn
player_turn_state
isMyTurn
optionExplain: A noun alone does not begin with a verb.
It begins with a capital letter.
It uses underscores and no verb.
Right: a lower-case verb opens the name.
questions.explain: Names such as isEmpty show that a boolean-style question is also written verb first.
questions.rule: Questions about state can start with a verb like is.
questions.teaches: Methods that answer a yes-or-no question about an object are named like other methods, opening with a lower-case verb such as is.

questions.q: A team is reviewing names in a small shopping app. Sort them by whether they follow the tutorial's conventions.

items.t: class Basket
method addItem
method removeAll
class basket
method Checkout
method totalprice

questions.explain: Basket, addItem and removeAll follow the pattern. basket lacks the capital, Checkout has one it should not, and totalprice has no verb at the start.
questions.rule: Capital for classes, lower-case verb for methods.
questions.teaches: A name that is a bare noun, such as totalprice, breaks the verb-first convention even when it is lower case.

questions.q: Which of these is part of a method's signature?
options: Its name and the types of its parameters
Its name and its return type
Its modifiers and parameter names
Only its name
optionExplain: Right: A signature is the name plus parameter types. The card next shows why.
The return type is not part of the signature.
Neither is part of the signature.
The parameter types are included too.
questions.explain: A signature is the name plus parameter types. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: A method needs a return type, name, parentheses and body, and it is identified by its signature of name plus parameter types.

questions.q: Put the parts of a full method declaration in order.
items: Modifiers
Return type
Method name
Parameter list in parentheses
Exception list
Body in braces
questions.explain: The tutorial lists these six parts in this order.
questions.rule: Modifiers, return type, name, parameters, exceptions, body.

questions.q: What is the signature of public String label(int id, boolean full) { ... }?
options: label(int id, boolean full)
label(int, boolean)
String label(int, boolean)
public label(int, boolean)
optionExplain: Parameter names are not part of the signature.
Right: name plus parameter types.
The return type is not included.
Modifiers are not included.
questions.explain: Drop the modifier, return type and parameter names, and keep the name and ordered parameter types.
questions.rule: Signature: name plus ordered parameter types.

questions.q: True or false: Renaming the parameter value in scale(double value, int times) to amount changes the method's signature.
questions.explain: Parameter names are not part of the signature; the types and their order are.
questions.rule: Renaming a parameter does not change the signature.

questions.q: A method does its work but hands nothing back to the caller. What goes where the return type would be?
options: Nothing; the return type may be left out
The word null
The word void
The word empty
optionExplain: The return type position must be filled.
null is a value, not a return type.
Right: void marks a method with no return value.
There is no such keyword.
questions.explain: The return type is required, and void stands for no value.
questions.rule: No result means void, not blank.
questions.teaches: The return type position is never left blank: a method that returns nothing says so with void.

questions.q: A checkout app has void apply(String code) and also int apply(String code). What does the tutorial predict?
options: Both compile, since their return types differ
Only the int version compiles, since it returns a value
Both compile, since the packages of the two differ
A compile-time error, since the return type cannot separate them
optionExplain: Return type is ignored when telling methods apart.
The compiler treats the two as the same signature and rejects the pair.
They are declared in the same class, so the clash still applies.
Right: the compiler tells methods apart by signature.
questions.explain: Same name and same parameter types means the same signature, so the pair is rejected.
questions.rule: Return type cannot rescue a repeated signature.
questions.teaches: Two methods in one class that share a signature are an error even when their return types differ.

questions.q: True or false: Two methods in the same class can have the same name when the types of their parameters differ.
questions.explain: Overloading is permitted when the parameter lists differ. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: Methods may share a name only when their parameter lists differ in number or types.

questions.q: Methods that share a name in one class but differ in their parameter lists are called ____ methods.
questions.explain: The tutorial calls this overloading; the compiler tells the methods apart by their signatures.
questions.rule: Same name, different parameter lists.

questions.q: A class already has int area(int side). Which of these methods can be added without a clash?
options: double area(int length)
double area(int width, int height)
int area(double radius)
void area(int size)
optionExplain: Same name and parameter types as the existing method; the return type is ignored.
Right: a different number of parameters.
Right: a different parameter type.
Only the parameter name differs, so the signature repeats.
questions.explain: A new method needs a different number or type of parameters. A different return type or parameter name does not help.
questions.rule: Change the parameter list, not the return type or names.

questions.q: A class has void send(String to) and void send(String to, int priority). A third method void send(String to, int level) is added. What happens?
options: A compile-time error, since it repeats the signature of the second method
It compiles, because level and priority are different names
It compiles, and calls pick whichever was written last
It compiles, but only if its body differs from the second method
optionExplain: Right: the names of parameters do not count.
Parameter names are not part of the signature.
The compiler never tolerates two identical signatures.
The body plays no part in telling methods apart.
questions.explain: Only the types and their order count, so the third method duplicates the second.
questions.rule: A repeated signature is an error.

questions.q: A class DataArtist has draw(String), draw(int), draw(double) and draw(int, double). Which version runs for the call draw(5, 2.5)?
options: The draw(int) version, ignoring the second value
The draw(int, double) version
The draw(double) version, since 2.5 is the last value
None of them, since the call matches more than one
optionExplain: The count of arguments must match too.
Right: the argument types and count match it.
That version takes only one argument.
Only one parameter list fits this call.
questions.explain: The compiler picks the version whose number and types of parameters match the call.
questions.rule: The call's arguments select the overload.
questions.teaches: For a call to an overloaded method, the compiler picks the version whose parameter types and count match the arguments.

questions.q: A reviewer finds twelve methods named process in one cashier class, each with a different parameter list. All compile. Which tutorial advice applies?
options: Overloading is unsafe, since the compiler cannot tell the methods apart
Give them different return types, to keep them distinct
Use overloading sparingly, since many same-name methods make code much harder to read
A class may have only one method for each name
optionExplain: The compiler can tell them apart by signature.
Return types never separate methods.
Right: the tutorial warns about readability.
Overloading exists to allow several.
questions.explain: Legal does not mean wise: the tutorial recommends restraint because readability suffers.
questions.rule: Overload with restraint.
questions.teaches: Overloading is a readability trade-off: a distinct method name can be clearer than reusing one name for twelve parameter lists.

questions.q: Which feature turns a declaration into a constructor rather than an ordinary method?
options: It has void as its return type and any name
It is declared public
It has no parameters
It uses the class name and has no return type
optionExplain: A constructor has no return type at all, not even void.
Methods can be public too.
Constructors may have parameters, and methods may have none.
Right: A constructor is named like its class and has no return type. The card next shows why.
questions.explain: A constructor is named like its class and has no return type. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: A constructor has the class's name and no return type, and the arguments of the new call select which one runs.

questions.q: A constructor declaration has the name of its class and no ____ type.
questions.explain: The class name and the missing return type mark a constructor.
questions.rule: Class name, no return type.

questions.q: class Pin { int code; Pin() { code = 1234; } Pin(int c) { code = c; } }. What is code after new Pin(9)?
options: The program does not compile
optionExplain: Right: the call has one int argument, so Pin(int c) runs.
That value is set only by the no-argument constructor.
Neither constructor leaves the field at its starting value here.
The two constructors differ in their parameter lists, so both are legal.
questions.explain: The argument list in the call selects the constructor, and that one assigns 9.
questions.rule: The arguments pick the constructor.

questions.q: True or false: Adding a third constructor Pin(int value), next to Pin(int c), compiles because the parameter names differ.
questions.explain: Both take one int, so the parameter lists match and the compiler rejects the pair.
questions.rule: Same parameter types means a clash.

questions.q: Rectangle has the constructors (), (Point), (int, int) and (Point, int, int). Which one runs for new Rectangle(origin, 4, 6), where origin is a Point?
options: The (int, int) constructor, which takes the two numbers
The (Point, int, int) constructor
The (Point) constructor, which takes the origin
The () constructor, which ignores them
optionExplain: It cannot accept a third argument.
Right: the arguments are a Point and two ints.
It takes only one argument.
A call with arguments cannot select the no-argument version.
questions.explain: The three arguments match the longest constructor, and an object can itself be an argument.
questions.rule: Match count and types, including object types.
questions.teaches: A constructor parameter can be an object, such as a Point, so a new object can be built from an object that already exists.

questions.q: A recipe app has class Recipe with Recipe(String name) and Recipe(String name, int servings). Which statements are true?
options: A call that passes a name and a number runs the second constructor
A third constructor Recipe(String title) could be added next to them
The two constructors must have different names
Both constructors can coexist, since their parameter lists differ in number
optionExplain: Right: the arguments select it.
It repeats the type list of the first one.
Constructors share the class name.
Right: The count and types of arguments select the constructor; the class name is shared, and a repeated type list is rejected.
questions.explain: The count and types of arguments select the constructor; the class name is shared, and a repeated type list is rejected.
questions.rule: Shorter constructors can leave details to defaults.
questions.teaches: A constructor with fewer parameters lets callers leave details out, with the class supplying the missing values itself.

questions.q: True or false: A class that declares no constructors can still be used to create objects with new.
questions.explain: The compiler supplies a default constructor. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: With no declared constructor a no-argument default is added, and it needs the parent to have a no-argument constructor.

questions.q: If a class declares no constructor, the compiler adds a no-argument ____ constructor.
questions.explain: The compiler-supplied constructor is called the default constructor.
questions.rule: No constructor declared means a default is added.

questions.q: class Base { Base(int size) { } } and class Derived extends Base { }. What does the compiler do with Derived?
options: It accepts it, passing 0 as the size on its own
It accepts it, since Derived declares no constructor to check
It reports an error, since Base has no no-argument constructor
It accepts it, because Object is the real parent
optionExplain: The compiler never invents arguments.
Derived gets a default constructor, and that is what fails.
Right: Derived's default constructor must call Base(), which does not exist.
Derived names Base as its parent, not Object.
questions.explain: Derived's default constructor must call Base(), which does not exist.
questions.rule: The default constructor calls the parent's no-argument constructor.

questions.q: True or false: If Base also gains a no-argument constructor, the class Derived above compiles.
questions.explain: The default constructor of Derived can then call Base(), so the error disappears.
questions.rule: A no-argument parent constructor removes the problem.

questions.q: A class Hub has one constructor, declared private. Another class contains new Hub(). What does the access rule predict?
options: The call works, since new always has access
The call works, but the created object has no fields
The compiler quietly adds a second, public constructor
The code cannot call it, so it cannot create the object directly
optionExplain: new does not bypass access modifiers.
Access does not affect the fields.
Defaults are added only when no constructor is declared.
Right: only code allowed to call a constructor can create objects with it.
questions.explain: If other classes cannot call any constructor, they cannot create the object directly.
questions.rule: A constructor's access decides who can build the object.
questions.teaches: Making every constructor private stops other classes from creating the objects directly.

questions.q: In a game, Enemy declares only Enemy(int hp) and Boss extends Enemy with no constructor, so Boss fails to compile. Which changes repair it?
options: Rename Boss so its name differs from Enemy
Add a no-argument constructor to Enemy
Give Boss a constructor that passes an hp value to the parent
Add a public field to Boss
optionExplain: The name of the child is not the cause.
Right: Boss's default constructor can then call it.
Right: the explicit call supplies the argument.
Fields are not involved in the failing call.
questions.explain: The failure is that no parent constructor accepts zero arguments. Either give the parent one or have the child pass an argument.
questions.rule: Fix the missing link between child and parent constructors.
questions.teaches: There are two repairs: give the parent a no-argument constructor, or give the child a constructor that passes arguments up to the parent.

questions.q: In the call area(3.0, 4.0), what are 3.0 and 4.0?
options: Arguments
Parameters
Signatures
Return values
optionExplain: Right: values supplied in a call.
Parameters are the variables in the declaration.
A signature is a name plus parameter types.
Return values come out of the method.
questions.explain: Values in a call are arguments. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: Parameters are the names in the declaration, arguments are the values in the call, and a final ellipsis parameter takes any number of values.

questions.q: Match each term to its meaning.
pairs: A variable named in the method declaration
A value supplied in a method call
The last parameter, which accepts any number of values
questions.explain: Declarations hold parameters, calls hold arguments, and an ellipsis marks a varargs parameter.
questions.rule: Parameters declare, arguments supply.

questions.q: A method is declared void total(int... prices). Which calls are valid?
options: total()
total(4, 8)
total(new int[] {1, 2})
total(2.5, 3)
total(true)
optionExplain: Right: zero values are allowed.
Right: separate values.
Right: an array is accepted too.
2.5 is a double, not an int.
A boolean is not an int.
questions.explain: The values must match the declared element type, but their number is free, and an array also works.
questions.rule: Varargs accept any count of matching values.

questions.q: A call total() with no arguments gives a varargs array whose length is ____.
questions.explain: No values arrived, so the array inside the method is empty.
questions.rule: No arguments means an empty array.

questions.q: The same printf method accepts printf(fmt, a, b) and printf(fmt, a, b, c, d). What makes this possible?
options: It is overloaded once for every possible number of values
Its last parameter is a varargs parameter that collects the extra values
Java fills the unused arguments with null
The format string tells the compiler how many arguments follow
optionExplain: A single declaration handles all counts.
Right: The tutorial names printf as a common varargs method.
Java does not invent arguments.
The compiler relies on the declaration, not on the text.
questions.explain: The tutorial names printf as a common varargs method.
questions.rule: One varargs parameter replaces many overloads.
questions.teaches: The familiar method printf takes a format string followed by a varargs parameter, which is why it accepts as many values as the format needs.

questions.q: A recipe helper must take a serving count and then any number of ingredient names. Which declaration follows the tutorial's rule for the ellipsis?
options: void mix(String... items, int count)
void mix(String... items, String... more)
void mix(int count, String... items)
void mix(...String items, int count)
optionExplain: The ellipsis parameter must be last.
Only the last parameter may use it.
Right: the ellipsis parameter is last.
The ellipsis follows the type and goes on the last parameter.
questions.explain: Only the final parameter can be varargs, so any fixed parameters come before it.
questions.rule: Fixed parameters first, varargs last.
questions.teaches: A method can have at most one varargs parameter, because that parameter has to be the last one.

questions.q: A setter is written void setSize(int size) { size = size; } for a field also called size. What is the effect of a call?
options: The field receives the argument
The compiler reports a duplicate name
The parameter is set to the field's value
The field is unchanged, since both names mean the parameter
optionExplain: The plain name refers to the parameter, so nothing reaches the field.
A parameter may share a field's name.
Nothing is copied from the field here.
Right: The parameter hides the field. The card next shows why.
questions.explain: The parameter hides the field. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: A parameter that shares a field's name hides the field inside the method, and this.name reaches the field.

questions.q: When a parameter has the same name as a field, the parameter ____ the field.
questions.explain: The tutorial says the parameter shadows the field.
questions.rule: Shadowing hides the field's plain name.

questions.q: In class Tag { String text; Tag(String text) { ____ } }, which statement stores the argument in the field?
options: this.text = text;
text = text;
this.text = this.text;
text = this.text;
optionExplain: Right: field on the left, parameter on the right.
Both sides are the parameter.
This copies the field onto itself.
This copies the field into the parameter, the wrong way round.
questions.explain: Qualify the field with this, and let the plain name stand for the parameter.
questions.rule: this.field = parameter.

questions.q: True or false: If the parameter is renamed newText and the body reads text = newText, the field is set correctly without this.
questions.explain: With distinct names there is no shadowing, so the plain name text means the field.
questions.rule: Different names remove the need for this.

questions.q: class Meter { int x = 5; int add(int x) { return this.x + x; } }. What does add(2) return?
optionExplain: That would use the parameter twice: 2 + 2.
Right: this.x is the field 5 and x is the parameter 2.
That would use the field twice: 5 + 5.
The field is also included in the sum.
questions.explain: One expression can use both names: this.x for the field and plain x for the parameter.
questions.rule: Plain name: parameter. this.name: field.
questions.teaches: Inside one expression, this.x reads the field while the plain x reads the shadowing parameter, so both values can be used together.

questions.q: In an order system, class Order { int qty = 2; void setQty(int qty) { if (qty > 0) this.qty = qty; } }. What is the field after setQty(-3)?
options: -3, since the assignment always runs
0, since a rejected value resets the field
2, since the check uses the parameter and fails
An error, since a rejected value stops the program
optionExplain: The assignment is guarded by the condition.
A failed check leaves the field alone.
Right: the plain qty in the condition is the incoming -3.
A failed condition simply skips the assignment.
questions.explain: The plain name inside the condition is the parameter, so a negative value fails the check.
questions.rule: Test the incoming value by its plain name; store with this.
questions.teaches: A check on an incoming value uses the plain parameter name, while the guarded assignment reaches the field through this.

questions.q: int n = 3; bump(n); where void bump(int p) { p = 10; }. What does n hold after the call?
optionExplain: The method works on a copy of the value.
Values are not added together.
Nothing resets the variable.
Right: the method changed only its copy.
questions.explain: Primitive arguments are copied. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: Arguments are copied: a method can change the object a reference points to, but it cannot repoint the caller's variable.

questions.q: A method that assigns 10 to its int parameter leaves the caller's variable ____.
questions.explain: The parameter is a copy, so the caller's variable is not affected.
questions.rule: Primitive arguments are copied.

questions.q: void grow(Box b) { b.size = b.size * 2; } is called with a Box whose size is 4. What is box.size afterwards?
optionExplain: Right: the method changed the object that the reference points to.
That is the result for a primitive argument, not an object.
The size is doubled, not halved.
The doubling happens once.
questions.explain: The copied reference leads to the same object, so the field change is visible.
questions.rule: A changed field is visible to the caller.

questions.q: Change the body of grow to b = new Box(100); instead. The caller's box had size 4. What is box.size afterwards?
options: 100, since the parameter is the caller's variable
4, since only the local reference was repointed
0, since the old object is discarded
The call does not compile
optionExplain: The parameter is a separate copy of the reference.
Right: Reassigning the parameter changes the copy only, so the original object is untouched.
The caller's reference still reaches the old object.
Assigning to a parameter is legal.
questions.explain: Reassigning the parameter changes the copy only, so the original object is untouched.
questions.rule: Reassigning a parameter is invisible to the caller.

questions.q: A student writes that Java passes objects by reference, so a parameter reassigned inside a method moves the caller's variable. Where is the flaw?
options: Objects are passed as full copies, so nothing is shared
Reassigning a reference parameter is not allowed
The method gets a copy of the reference, so the two variables are separate
The caller's variable moves, but only after a delay
optionExplain: Only the reference is copied, so the object is shared.
It is allowed, with no effect on the caller.
Right: Java has one passing mode, by value. For objects, the value copied is the reference.
No such delay exists.
questions.explain: Java has one passing mode, by value. For objects, the value copied is the reference.
questions.rule: Two separate references can lead to one object.
questions.teaches: During a call the caller's variable and the parameter are two separate references to the same object, which is why changes show but repointing does not.

questions.q: In a grading app, void reset(int[] marks) { marks[0] = 0; marks = new int[5]; } is called with an array holding 70 and 80. What does the caller's array hold afterwards?
options: 70 and 80, unchanged
Five zeros
0 and 0
0 and 80, with length 2
optionExplain: The element assignment reached the shared array.
The new array was bound only to the local parameter.
Only the first element was changed.
Right: the element change shows, the repointing does not.
questions.explain: An array argument behaves like an object: its contents can change through the copy, but the caller's variable cannot be repointed.
questions.rule: Contents change; the variable stays.
questions.teaches: Arrays follow the same rule as objects: element changes made through a parameter are visible to the caller, but a new array assigned to the parameter is not.

questions.q: Sort these actions inside a method by whether the caller can see the effect after the call.

items.t: Setting a field of a Box object passed in
Assigning a new number to an int parameter
Assigning a new Box to a Box parameter
Calling a setter on the Box passed in
Changing one element of a passed array
Assigning a new array to an array parameter

questions.explain: Changes made through the shared object show up; assignments to the parameter itself disappear.
questions.rule: Through the reference: visible. To the parameter: lost.

questions.q: In Point p = new Point(1, 2);, which part actually brings the object into existence?
options: The new keyword
The declaration Point p
The semicolon at the end
The variable name p
optionExplain: Right: new instantiates the class.
A declaration only associates a name with a type.
The semicolon only ends the statement.
A name does not create anything.
questions.explain: Instantiation is done by new. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: A creation statement declares a variable, instantiates the class with new, and initializes the object through a constructor call.

questions.q: Match each job in a creation statement to what it does.
pairs: Associates a variable name with a type
The new keyword creates the object
A constructor call sets the starting values
questions.explain: Each of the three jobs has its own part of the statement.
questions.rule: Declare, instantiate, initialize.

questions.q: In Cup mug = new Cup(250); the keyword that creates the object is ____.
questions.explain: new instantiates the class. Cup mug declares the variable, and Cup(250) initializes the object.
questions.rule: new instantiates.

questions.q: True or false: Splitting the statement into Cup mug; and later mug = new Cup(250); still performs all three jobs.
questions.explain: The declaration comes first, and the later assignment instantiates and initializes. The same jobs are done in two statements.
questions.rule: The jobs can be split across statements.

questions.q: In Rectangle r = new Rectangle(new Point(1, 1), 3, 4);, how many objects does this one statement create?
options: One, since there is a single statement
Two: a Point and a Rectangle
Three: a Point, a Rectangle and the numbers
None until a method is called
optionExplain: Each new expression creates its own object.
Right: each new creates one object.
Plain numbers are values, not objects.
The objects exist as soon as new runs.
questions.explain: The inner new makes the Point, and the outer new makes the Rectangle around it.
questions.rule: Count the new expressions to count the objects.
questions.teaches: One statement can create several objects when the arguments of a constructor call are themselves new expressions.

questions.q: A game shows ten enemies on screen, all built from one Enemy class. How many classes and how many instances are involved?
options: Ten classes and ten instances
One class and one instance shared by all
One class and ten instances
Ten classes and one instance
optionExplain: The class is the single blueprint.
Each new makes a separate instance.
Right: A class is declared once, and each new produces another instance of it.
Neither count is right.
questions.explain: A class is declared once, and each new produces another instance of it.
questions.rule: One blueprint, many instances.
questions.teaches: Any number of instances can be created from one class, and each instance has its own state.

questions.q: After the single statement Rectangle r; how many Rectangle objects exist because of it?
options: One, with width and height at zero
One, with all its fields empty
Two: one for r and one held in reserve
None
optionExplain: That would need new.
No object has been made.
No object is held in reserve.
Right: a declaration creates no object.
questions.explain: A declaration only introduces a name. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: Declaring a reference variable creates no object, so assign one made with new before you use it.

questions.q: True or false: The statement Point origin; creates a Point object.
questions.explain: It only declares a variable that will refer to a Point; new creates the object.
questions.rule: Declaring is not creating.

questions.q: The code Rectangle myRect; myRect.width = 40; does not compile. Which change repairs it?
options: Assign myRect = new Rectangle(); before the first use
Declare width as a public int
Write Rectangle myRect = null; instead of the declaration
Swap the two lines
optionExplain: Right: the variable then refers to an object.
The trouble is the variable, not the field.
null still refers to no object.
Using the variable before declaring it is worse.
questions.explain: The variable must refer to an object before its fields are used.
questions.rule: Assign an object before the first use.

questions.q: True or false: If the first line becomes Rectangle myRect = new Rectangle();, the second line myRect.width = 40; compiles, assuming width is accessible.
questions.explain: The variable now refers to an object, so its field can be reached through the dot.
questions.rule: A new object makes the dot usable.

questions.q: After Point p = new Point(1, 2); the statement p = null; runs. What does p refer to?
options: A Point whose x and y are both 0
No object
The same Point, now hidden from other variables
A new empty Point
optionExplain: null does not create a new Point.
Right: null means the variable refers to nothing.
Nothing is hidden; the variable simply no longer refers to it.
No object is created by assigning null.
questions.explain: Assigning null clears the variable's reference.
questions.rule: null means refers to nothing.
questions.teaches: Assigning null to a reference variable makes it refer to no object.

questions.q: A UI snippet declares Button save; and then calls save.show(), which fails to compile. Which additions before the call would fix it?
options: Assign save from another variable that already refers to a Button
Write save = 0;
Declare save as public
save = new Button();
optionExplain: Right: copying an existing reference also works.
A number is not a Button reference.
Access is not the trouble.
Right: new creates an object for the variable.
questions.explain: The variable needs a reference to an object, which can come from new or from another variable that already has one.
questions.rule: Give the variable an object before use.
questions.teaches: A reference variable can be given an object by copying a reference from another variable that already refers to one, not only by new.

questions.q: What does the new operator hand back?
options: The size of the object in memory
A copy of the constructor's code
A reference to the newly allocated object
The value of the object's first field
optionExplain: new returns a reference, not a size.
Code is not returned.
Right: new returns a reference. The card next shows why.
No field value is returned.
questions.explain: new returns a reference. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: new allocates memory, runs a constructor and returns a reference that can be stored or used straight away.

questions.q: Put the steps that new performs into order.
items: Memory is allocated for the object
The constructor is invoked
A reference to the object is returned
questions.explain: The tutorial describes allocating memory, invoking the constructor, then returning a reference.
questions.rule: Allocate, construct, return a reference.

questions.q: A Rectangle class has a constructor Rectangle(int w, int h) and a method getArea(). To read the area of a fresh 4 by 5 rectangle with no variable, write new Rectangle(4, 5).____().
questions.explain: The new expression yields a reference, so a method can be called on it directly.
questions.rule: Call methods straight on a new expression.

questions.q: True or false: After int h = new Rectangle().height; the program can still reach that Rectangle through a variable.
questions.explain: No variable was ever given the reference, so the rectangle cannot be reached again.
questions.rule: An unstored reference is lost.

questions.q: In new Rectangle(100, 50).getArea(), what does the part before the dot supply?
options: The constructor's return type
A copy of the class that is then discarded
A variable name chosen by the compiler
A reference to the new Rectangle object
optionExplain: Constructors have no return type.
The expression yields an object reference, not a class copy.
No variable is involved.
Right: Any expression that yields an object reference may stand before the dot, and new is such an expression.
questions.explain: Any expression that yields an object reference may stand before the dot, and new is such an expression.
questions.rule: A new expression is an object reference.
questions.teaches: Any expression that yields an object reference, including a new expression, can stand to the left of the dot.

questions.q: Which line builds a Cup of 250 units, calls its fill method, and keeps no variable for it?
options: new Cup(250).fill();
Cup(250).fill();
new Cup.fill(250);
Cup c = Cup(250);
optionExplain: Right: new first, then the dot.
Without new there is no constructor call.
This does not name a constructor call.
Again new is missing.
questions.explain: Only new followed by a constructor call creates the object; the dot then calls a method on it.
questions.rule: No new, no object.
questions.teaches: Writing a class name and arguments without new does not create an object; the new operator must precede the constructor call.

questions.q: Point a = new Point(1, 1); Rectangle r = new Rectangle(a, 3, 3); r.move(5, 5); Assume move sets the origin's x and y to its arguments. What is a.x afterwards?
optionExplain: That would hold if the rectangle had its own copy of the point.
Right: the rectangle's origin is the same Point as a.
3 is the width, not a coordinate.
Nothing resets the point to zero.
questions.explain: The rectangle stored the same Point that a refers to. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: Variables that hold the same reference share one object, so a change through one is seen through the others.

questions.q: True or false: Two variables that refer to the same object see the same field values.
questions.explain: There is only one object, so both names show the same state.
questions.rule: One object, one state.

questions.q: Cup c = new Cup(100); Cup d = c; d.level = 40; After these lines the value of c.level is ____.
questions.explain: d and c refer to one Cup, so the change through d shows through c.
questions.rule: A change through one name shows through the other.

questions.q: Change the second line to Cup d = new Cup(100); and keep d.level = 40;. What is c.level now?
options: 40, since the variable names are similar
0, since c is no longer in use
100, since d refers to a separate Cup
The code no longer compiles
optionExplain: Names play no part; only the references matter.
c is still in use and unchanged.
Right: A second new creates a second object, so a change to it does not touch the first.
Creating two cups is perfectly legal.
questions.explain: A second new creates a second object, so a change to it does not touch the first.
questions.rule: A new new means a separate object.

questions.q: A Rectangle stores the Point it receives in its constructor, without copying it. The caller later changes that Point. What happens to the rectangle's origin?
options: It stays as it was, since the rectangle took its own copy
It becomes null, since the caller changed the Point
The program stops, since two owners are not allowed
It changes too, since both hold the same Point
optionExplain: The class stored the reference it was given.
Changing a Point does not clear references.
An object may have many references.
Right: Storing a received reference, rather than copying the object, shares that object with the caller.
questions.explain: Storing a received reference, rather than copying the object, shares that object with the caller.
questions.rule: A stored reference stays shared with its source.
questions.teaches: A class that stores an object it was given, instead of copying it, shares that object with the caller.

questions.q: In a to-do app, sort these statements by whether they create a second object or only a second name for an existing one.

items.t: Board b2 = b1;
Cup d = c;
Point p2 = firstPoint;
Board b2 = new Board();
Cup d = new Cup(100);
Point p2 = new Point(0, 0);

questions.explain: Assigning one variable to another copies the reference, while each new makes an object.
questions.rule: Only new makes an object.
questions.teaches: Plain assignment between reference variables never creates an object: only a new expression does.

questions.q: In a different class, how do you read the width of the rectangle held in variable box?
options: box.width
width
Rectangle.width
box(width)
optionExplain: Right: reference, dot, field name.
The simple name works only inside the class.
The class name does not choose which rectangle.
That is not field syntax.
questions.explain: Outside the class, use reference.field. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: Use the simple name inside the class and reference.field outside it, and remember that each object keeps its own copy of instance fields.

questions.q: Outside its class, a field is reached with an object reference, a ____, and the field name.
questions.explain: The dot joins the reference to the field name, as in rectOne.width.
questions.rule: reference.field

questions.q: Class Runner is a different class from Rectangle. Rectangle r = new Rectangle(); is in scope and its fields are public. Which statements compile?
options: int w = width;
r.height = 5;
Rectangle.height = 5;
int w = r.width;
optionExplain: The simple name works only inside Rectangle.
Right: the same form on the left of an assignment.
A class name does not pick out one rectangle's instance field.
Right: reference, dot, field.
questions.explain: Outside the class each access needs an object reference before the dot.
questions.rule: Outside, name the object first.

questions.q: True or false: If Runner writes width = 70; with no object reference, the code compiles.
questions.explain: The simple name refers to a field only inside the class, so the compiler reports an error.
questions.rule: No simple names for foreign fields.

questions.q: In rectTwo.origin.x, what is origin?
options: A method of rectTwo that returns the value x
A field of rectTwo that refers to a Point whose x is read
A class named origin that holds a field x
A second copy of rectTwo
optionExplain: There are no parentheses, so it is not a call.
Right: The first dot reaches the field origin, which refers to an object, and the second dot reaches a field of that object.
Class names are not reached through an object.
It refers to a Point, not a rectangle.
questions.explain: The first dot reaches the field origin, which refers to an object, and the second dot reaches a field of that object.
questions.rule: A field can lead on to another object.
questions.teaches: Dot notation can be chained: a field that refers to another object lets you reach that object's fields in the same expression.

questions.q: class Song { public int length = 180; } Song s1 = new Song(); Song s2 = new Song(); s1.length = 200; What are s1.length and s2.length?
options: 200 and 0
optionExplain: Each object has its own copy of the field.
The assignment changed s1.
Right: the change touched only s1's copy.
s2 keeps the starting value from the declaration.
questions.explain: Every new Song starts with its own length of 180, and the assignment changes only one of them.
questions.rule: Per-object copies change independently.
questions.teaches: A field initializer in the declaration gives every new object its own starting value for that field.

questions.q: A method is called on an object with the object reference, a dot, and the method ____.
questions.explain: The reference, a dot, then the method name and its arguments. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: Call methods with reference.method(arguments), and use any returned value like any other value of its type.

questions.q: Which call asks the object held in rectOne for its area?
options: getArea(rectOne)
rectOne:getArea
Rectangle(rectOne).area
rectOne.getArea()
optionExplain: That passes the object as an argument instead of calling a method on it.
This is not Java syntax.
This is not a method call.
Right: The object comes first, then a dot and the method call.
questions.explain: The object comes first, then a dot and the method call.
questions.rule: reference.method()

questions.q: Rectangle a has int getArea() and void move(int x, int y). Which statements are valid?
options: int s = a.move(3, 4);
int s = a.getArea();
a.move(3, 4);
a.getArea = 5;
optionExplain: move returns nothing, so there is no value to store.
Right: the returned int fits an int.
Right: a void method is called as a statement.
getArea is a method, not a field to assign.
questions.explain: A returned value can be stored; a void method has none, and a method is not assigned to.
questions.rule: Void calls give no value.

questions.q: True or false: The expression new Rectangle(100, 50).getArea() is legal, and its value is 5000.
questions.explain: The new expression yields a reference, getArea multiplies the two sides, and 100 times 50 is 5000.
questions.rule: A new expression can start a call.

questions.q: Rectangle a is 100 by 50 and rectangle b is 10 by 20. What do a.getArea() and b.getArea() return?
options: Neither, since the class decides one value
optionExplain: Right: each uses its own width and height.
The second object has different fields.
The first object has different fields.
A method works with the fields of the object it is called on.
questions.explain: The same method, called on two objects, reads each object's own fields.
questions.rule: The object on the left decides which fields a method uses.
questions.teaches: The same method call can give different results on different objects, since each call uses the fields of the object it is made on.

questions.q: class Counter has int value() and void bump(), which adds 1. A counter c holds 3, and this runs: if (c.value() < 5) c.bump(); What does c.value() return afterwards?
options: The code does not compile
optionExplain: The test passes, so bump runs.
Right: the decision used a returned value, then bump changed the state.
bump adds only 1.
A returned value may be tested in a decision.
questions.explain: The returned 3 passes the test, bump raises the state to 4, and value() now reports 4.
questions.rule: A returned value can steer what the next call does.
questions.teaches: A method's returned value can drive a decision about whether to call a second method that changes the object's state.

questions.q: How does a Java program destroy an object it no longer needs?
options: It calls a destroy method on the object itself
It sets the object's size to zero bytes first
It does not; the runtime reclaims objects nothing refers to
It closes the constructor that created the object
optionExplain: Java has no such step for programmers.
Sizes are not set by the program.
Right: Cleanup is automatic. The card next shows why.
Constructors do not own their objects.
questions.explain: Cleanup is automatic. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: An object is eligible for collection once no references to it remain, and the runtime reclaims it at a time of its own choosing.

questions.q: An object is eligible for garbage collection when no ____ to it remain.
questions.explain: Eligibility depends on whether any reference still reaches the object.
questions.rule: No references, eligible.

questions.q: Cup c = new Cup(); Cup d = c; c = null; Is the Cup eligible for garbage collection?
options: Yes, since c was set to null
Yes, since two variables made it a duplicate
Only after the program ends
No, since d still refers to it
optionExplain: Another reference remains.
There is only one Cup.
Eligibility depends on references, not on the program ending.
Right: Every reference must be dropped before the object is eligible.
questions.explain: Every reference must be dropped before the object is eligible.
questions.rule: One surviving reference keeps the object.

questions.q: True or false: If d = null is also executed, the Cup becomes eligible for garbage collection.
questions.explain: No references remain, which is the condition for eligibility.
questions.rule: Drop them all and the object is eligible.

questions.q: Student[] students = new Student[10]; Student s = new Student(); students[0] = s; s = null; Is the Student object eligible for garbage collection?
options: No, since students[0] still refers to it
Yes, since s was set to null
Yes, since an array only stores copies of objects
No, since null protects the object
optionExplain: Right: An array element is a reference too, and it keeps the object reachable.
The array element is another reference.
Arrays hold references, not copies.
null only clears one variable.
questions.explain: An array element is a reference too, and it keeps the object reachable.
questions.rule: Array elements count as references.
questions.teaches: Array elements hold references, so an object stored in an array stays reachable while that element refers to it.

questions.q: In a photo app, which statement creates an object that is eligible for garbage collection as soon as the statement finishes?
options: Photo p = new Photo();
int w = new Photo().width;
Photo[] album = { new Photo() };
Photo q = p;
optionExplain: The variable p still refers to the Photo.
Right: nothing keeps a reference to the Photo.
The array element refers to the Photo.
No new object is created here.
questions.explain: A new expression whose result is never stored leaves no reference behind.
questions.rule: No stored reference, instantly eligible.
questions.teaches: An object made by a new expression whose reference is never stored becomes eligible for collection right away.

questions.q: True or false: Once an object is eligible for garbage collection, the program can count on it being removed at once.
questions.explain: Eligible means the collector may reclaim it. The collector chooses when, and the program has no control over that moment.
questions.rule: Eligible does not mean removed now.

questions.q: Which method does the compiler reject?
options: void reset() { return; }
int one() { return 1; }
void reset() { return 0; }
boolean ok() { return true; }
optionExplain: A bare return is allowed in a void method.
The returned int matches the declared type.
Right: a void method cannot hand back a value.
The returned boolean matches the declared type.
questions.explain: A void method cannot return a value. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: A void method returns nothing, and every other method must return a value of its declared type.

questions.q: A method returns to its caller when which of these happens? Select all that apply.
options: It throws an exception
It completes all of its statements
It reaches a return statement
Its caller declares another variable
It declares a parameter
optionExplain: Right: the tutorial lists this as a third way.
Right: falling off the end returns.
Right: A method ends by finishing its statements, by a return statement, or by throwing an exception, whichever comes first.
Unrelated to the method's own run.
Having parameters does not end a method.
questions.explain: A method ends by finishing its statements, by a return statement, or by throwing an exception, whichever comes first.
questions.rule: Three ways out of a method.

questions.q: A student writes int total(int a, int b) { int sum = a + b; } with nothing else in the body. What is wrong?
options: Nothing; the last variable is returned automatically
The method should be void, because it declares a local variable
The parameters need modifiers such as public
A method with a non-void type must return a value of that type
optionExplain: Java does not return a variable by itself.
Locals do not decide the return type.
Parameters do not take access modifiers here.
Right: The body needs return sum; or an equivalent, since the declared type is int.
questions.explain: The body needs return sum; or an equivalent, since the declared type is int.
questions.rule: Non-void means a value must come back.

questions.q: True or false: If int total is changed to void total, the same body with no return statement compiles.
questions.explain: A void method needs no return statement, and there is no value to produce.
questions.rule: void removes the duty to return.

questions.q: int sign(int n) { if (n < 0) { return -1; } return 1; } What does sign(-4) return, and does the last line run?
options: -1, and the last line does not run
1, because the last line always runs
-1 first and then 1, because both returns run
It does not compile, because there are two returns
optionExplain: Right: the first return reached ends the call.
The earlier return ends the method.
A method returns once per call.
Several return statements are fine.
questions.explain: The first return reached ends the method, so later lines are skipped.
questions.rule: The first return reached wins.
questions.teaches: A method may contain several return statements, and the first one reached ends that call.

questions.q: In a racing app, Car faster(Car a, Car b) { return a; } is used as Car winner = faster(carA, carB);. Does winner refer to the same Car as carA?
options: No, because the method returns a copy of the car
Yes, because a reference to the same object was returned
No, because objects cannot be returned from methods
Yes, but only if Car is a primitive type
optionExplain: Only a reference comes back, not a copy.
Right: Returning an object hands back a reference, so the caller can end up sharing the object it passed in.
Methods may return objects.
Car is a class, which is a reference type.
questions.explain: Returning an object hands back a reference, so the caller can end up sharing the object it passed in.
questions.rule: A returned object is a returned reference.
questions.teaches: A method that returns an object returns a reference to it, so the caller may share the very object that was passed in.

questions.q: A method is declared to return Number, and ImaginaryNumber extends Number. Which object may it return?
options: A plain Object
Any object whatsoever
An ImaginaryNumber
A String
optionExplain: An Object might not be a Number at all.
Only Numbers and their subclasses qualify.
Right: a subclass instance is a Number.
A String is not a Number.
questions.explain: Subclass instances are accepted. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: A returned object must be an instance of the declared class or a subclass, or of a class that implements the declared interface.

questions.q: A method declared to return a class may return an instance of that class or of one of its ____.
questions.explain: A subclass instance is also an instance of the parent class.
questions.rule: Declared class or subclass.

questions.q: Truck and Bike extend Vehicle; Lamp is unrelated. A method is declared Vehicle pick(). Which objects may it return?
options: A Truck
A plain Object
A Lamp
A plain Vehicle
A Bike
optionExplain: Right: a subclass of Vehicle.
An Object may not be a Vehicle.
Lamp is unrelated to Vehicle.
Right: the declared class itself.
Right: also a subclass.
questions.explain: Anything that is a Vehicle qualifies, and nothing that might not be one.
questions.rule: Declared class or below.

questions.q: True or false: A method declared to return Truck may return a Vehicle that is not a Truck.
questions.explain: A plain Vehicle might be a Bike, so it need not be a Truck. Only a Truck or its subclasses fit.
questions.rule: Narrower declared types demand narrower objects.

questions.q: A parent class declares Number get(). A subclass overrides it. Which return type may the override declare?
options: Object, a superclass of Number
String, which is unrelated
Any class, since overriding replaces the method
ImaginaryNumber, a subclass of Number
optionExplain: The type may not widen.
Unrelated types are not covariant.
The override must still fit the parent's return type.
Right: a covariant return type.
questions.explain: An override may narrow the type toward subclasses but not widen it.
questions.rule: Covariant means narrowing toward subclasses.
questions.teaches: An overriding method may promise a more specific return type than the parent's, which makes things easier for callers.

questions.q: interface Playable; class Song implements Playable; class Photo does not. A method is declared Playable next(). Which object may it return?
options: A Song
A Photo
A plain Object
Any class that has a method called play
optionExplain: Right: Song implements the interface.
Photo does not implement Playable.
An Object need not implement Playable.
Only declared implementation counts, not method names.
questions.explain: For an interface return type, the object's class must implement the interface.
questions.rule: Implementing is what counts.
questions.teaches: For an interface return type, only objects of classes that implement the interface qualify, however similar the methods of other classes may look.

questions.q: Inside an instance method, what does this refer to?
options: The class itself
The object on which the method was called
The variable name used by the caller
The method's first parameter
optionExplain: this stands for an object, not the class.
Right: this is the current object. The card next shows why.
this is a reference, not a name.
Parameters are named separately.
questions.explain: this is the current object. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: this names the current object, and this.name reaches that object's member when a plain name is shadowed.

questions.q: True or false: In a constructor Point(int x, int y), the statement this.x = x; copies the parameter into the field.
questions.explain: this.x is the field and the plain x on the right is the parameter.
questions.rule: this.field = parameter.

questions.q: class Score { int points; void add(int points) { this.points = this.points + points; } } A Score holds 10, then add(5) is called. The field then holds ____.
questions.explain: this.points is 10 and the parameter is 5, so the field becomes 15.
questions.rule: this.points is the field; points is the argument.

questions.q: Remove both this. prefixes, so the line reads points = points + points;. With the field at 10, what does the field hold after add(5)?
options: 15, since the sum is still stored in the field
20, since the field is added to itself
10, since every name now means the parameter
5, since the argument replaces the field
optionExplain: The assignment now targets the parameter.
The field is not used at all.
Right: the parameter doubles and the field is untouched.
The field keeps its old value.
questions.explain: Shadowing hides the field, so the whole statement works on the parameter.
questions.rule: Without this, the parameter wins.

questions.q: True or false: A method declared static belongs to the class rather than to any object, and it can use this to reach the current object.
questions.explain: A static method belongs to the class and has no current object, so this has no meaning there.
questions.rule: No current object, no this.
questions.teaches: Because this stands for the current object, it is not available in static methods, which have no current object.

questions.q: class Meter { int reading; } Which constructor leaves the field reading unset without any error message?
options: Meter(int r) { reading = r; }
Meter(int reading) { this.reading = reading; }
Meter() { this.reading = 0; }
Meter(int reading) { reading = reading; }
