optionExplain: Different names, so the field is set.
this.reading is the field.
This sets the field explicitly.
Right: both names are the parameter.
questions.explain: A self-assignment of a parameter compiles quietly and never touches the field.
questions.rule: Check which name the left-hand side really means.
questions.teaches: Assigning a shadowing parameter to itself compiles without complaint, so the mistake shows up only as a field that never changes.

questions.q: A class has Box() and Box(int w, int h). How can Box() reuse the second constructor?
options: By starting its body with this(1, 1);
By calling Box(1, 1); as an ordinary statement
By calling super(1, 1);
By ending its body with new Box(1, 1);
optionExplain: Right: this(...) is the call between constructors of one class. The card next shows why.
A constructor is not called by name like a method.
super reaches the parent's constructor, not one in this class.
That makes a separate object and discards it.
questions.explain: this(...) is the call between constructors of one class. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: Start a constructor with this(...) to hand its work to another constructor of the same class.

questions.q: A this(...) call must be the ____ statement of the constructor.
questions.explain: The tutorial requires the call to come first.
questions.rule: this(...) comes first.

questions.q: Rectangle() { this(0, 0, 1, 1); } delegates to the constructor with x, y, width and height. What size is new Rectangle()?
options: 0 by 0, positioned at 1, 1
1 by 1, positioned at 0, 0
0 by 1, positioned at 0, 1
It does not compile, because Rectangle() has no body statements of its own
optionExplain: The values are in the order x, y, width, height.
Right: The four arguments become x = 0, y = 0, width = 1, height = 1.
Width and height are both 1.
A delegating call is a complete body.
questions.explain: The four arguments become x = 0, y = 0, width = 1, height = 1.
questions.rule: Read the arguments in the target constructor's order.

questions.q: True or false: If this(1, 1); is moved below another statement in Box(), the class still compiles.
questions.explain: The call must be the first statement, so the compiler rejects the new order.
questions.rule: Move it and the compiler objects.

questions.q: In a Rectangle with fields x, y, width and height, which constructor should hold the assignments, while shorter ones call it?
options: The no-argument constructor
Each constructor, so none depends on another
The full four-argument constructor
A private method that the compiler adds
optionExplain: It has no values to assign from.
That repeats the same assignments.
Right: one place does the real work.
The compiler adds nothing here.
questions.explain: Shorter constructors can supply defaults and pass them to the full one.
questions.rule: Put the real work in one constructor.
questions.teaches: Putting every field assignment in one full constructor lets the shorter constructors supply defaults without repeating code.

questions.q: class Coffee { int shots; int milk; Coffee(int shots, int milk) { ... } } The default drink should have 2 shots and no milk. Which line, as the first statement of Coffee(), fits?
options: Coffee(2, 0);
this.Coffee(2, 0);
super(2, 0);
this(2, 0);
optionExplain: A constructor is not called like a method.
A constructor is not a method of the object.
super leads to the parent's constructor.
Right: Another constructor of the same class is reached only by this(...).
questions.explain: Another constructor of the same class is reached only by this(...).
questions.rule: Use this(...) between sibling constructors.
questions.teaches: Another constructor is reached with this(...) or super(...), or by a new expression; its name cannot be called like a method.

questions.q: A method is declared with no access modifier. Which code may call it?
options: Classes in the same package as its class
Every class in every package
Only its own class
Its subclasses anywhere, but nothing else in its package
optionExplain: Right: package-private.
That would be public.
That would be private.
Same-package classes are included.
questions.explain: No modifier means same package only. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: Each access level opens a smaller circle of code, from public for everyone down to private for the declaring class only.

questions.q: Match each access level to the code it allows.
questions.explain: Each level reaches a smaller group than the one before.
questions.rule: Public down to private.

questions.q: Alpha declares a protected method. Beta is in Alpha's package. Alphasub is a subclass of Alpha in another package. Gamma is in another package and is not a subclass. Which can call the method?
options: Alphasub
Beta
Gamma
Alpha itself
optionExplain: Right: protected reaches subclasses.
Right: same package.
Different package and not a subclass, so no access.
Right: a class can use its own members.
questions.explain: Protected covers the class, its package and its subclasses, but not the wider world.
questions.rule: Protected = package plus subclasses.

questions.q: The protected method is changed to have no modifier. Which of the callers above loses access?
options: Beta, since it is in the package
Alphasub, since it is outside the package
Alpha, since it is the declaring class
Gamma, since it is outside the package
optionExplain: Beta stays in the package.
Right: Dropping protected removes only the subclass-in-another-package group.
A class always keeps its own members.
Gamma had no access before the change either.
questions.explain: Dropping protected removes only the subclass-in-another-package group.
questions.rule: No modifier loses the outside subclasses.

questions.q: A programmer only uses the Java platform classes and writes no class of their own. Why do access levels still matter?
options: They decide how quickly those classes run
They are needed to compile the platform classes again
They decide which members of those classes your code can use
They matter only to the authors of the classes
optionExplain: Access levels have no effect on speed.
Nothing is recompiled by using them.
Right: Access levels govern both writing your own classes and using classes from other sources.
Users meet them whenever a member is out of reach.
questions.explain: Access levels govern both writing your own classes and using classes from other sources.
questions.rule: Access levels bind users as well as authors.
questions.teaches: Access levels matter when you use classes written by others, since they decide which of those classes' members your code can reach.

questions.q: In a hospital system, class Records has a method with no modifier. A subclass SpecialRecords in a different package must call it. What change is needed?
options: Make the method private
Nothing, since subclasses can reach every member
Move the call into a class outside both packages
Make the method protected or public
optionExplain: That narrows the access further.
Package-private members stay inside the package.
That has even less access.
Right: the narrowest level that opens it is protected.
questions.explain: Subclass status alone does not open a package-private member to another package.
questions.rule: Across packages, protected or public.
questions.teaches: Being a subclass does not grant access to a package-private member from another package; protected is the narrowest level that opens it.

questions.q: Which choice follows the tutorial's advice for a field that only its own class uses?
options: private
public, so tests can see it
protected, in case someone extends the class
No modifier, to keep options open
optionExplain: Right: the most restrictive level that makes sense.
Public fields are discouraged.
That opens more than the field needs.
That is wider than needed.
questions.explain: Use private unless there is a reason not to. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: Start with private and widen access only when a real need appears.

questions.q: The tutorial advises using the most ____ access level that makes sense.
questions.explain: The narrowest level that still works protects the class from misuse.
questions.rule: Most restrictive that works.

questions.q: Class Library keeps a list of books, offers addBook to other classes, and has a helper checkIsbn used only inside. Which assignment of access follows the advice?
options: Books public, addBook public, checkIsbn public
Books private, addBook public, checkIsbn private
Books private, addBook private, checkIsbn private
Books public, addBook private, checkIsbn public
optionExplain: Everything is open and nothing is protected.
Right: only the operation others need is opened.
Other classes could then not add a book.
The data is exposed and the operation hidden.
questions.explain: Open only what other classes must use.
questions.rule: Open the operations, close the data.

questions.q: True or false: If the books field becomes public, other classes can bypass the checks inside addBook.
questions.explain: They could change the list directly, so the guard in addBook would no longer apply.
questions.rule: A public field skips the guard method.

questions.q: A class changes how its public field stores a temperature, switching units. What is the consequence?
options: Nothing; field changes never affect other classes
Only the declaring class has to change
Every class that used the field directly may need to change too
The compiler converts the old uses automatically
optionExplain: Users of a public field depend on its form.
Code that used the field directly also depends on it.
Right: they depended on the old form.
No such conversion exists.
questions.explain: A public field ties other code to the implementation, so it limits later changes.
questions.rule: Public fields freeze the implementation.
questions.teaches: With a public field, changing how the data is stored forces changes in every class that touched the field, whereas a private field with methods lets the class change inside.

questions.q: A fixed maximum of 120 is the same for every object and cannot be reassigned. Which access follows the tutorial's advice?
options: Private only, since every field must be private
Public, but only if it is not final
No modifier, since constants are always package-private
Public is acceptable, since it is a constant
optionExplain: The tutorial makes an exception for constants.
Reassignable public fields are the discouraged kind.
No such rule exists.
Right: constants are the stated exception.
questions.explain: A value that cannot be reassigned cannot be used to break the class's rules.
questions.rule: Constants are the exception.
questions.teaches: A public constant is safe because other classes cannot reassign it, so it cannot be used to break the class's rules.

questions.q: In class IdentifyMyParts { public static int x = 7; public int y = 3; }, which variable is a class variable?
options: x
y
Both x and y
Neither, since both are public
optionExplain: Right: it is declared static.
y has no static keyword, so each object has its own copy.
Only one of them is static.
public is about access, not sharing.
questions.explain: static makes a class variable. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: static marks a member as belonging to the class and shared by all; without it each object has its own copy.

questions.q: Match each term to its meaning.
pairs: A separate copy in each object
One copy shared by all objects
The keyword that makes a member belong to the class
questions.explain: static means shared by the class; no static means one copy per object.
questions.rule: static = shared.

questions.q: With IdentifyMyParts a and b created by new, the code runs a.x = 1; b.x = 2;. What does IdentifyMyParts.x hold afterwards?
optionExplain: The second assignment overwrote the first.
Right: both assignments write the same shared variable, and the second wins.
The assignments changed the initial value.
Nothing adds the two values.
questions.explain: There is only one x, so a.x, b.x and IdentifyMyParts.x are the same variable.
questions.rule: One shared copy means last write wins.

questions.q: If x were declared without static, then after a.x = 1; b.x = 2; the value of a.x would be ____.
questions.explain: Without static each object has its own x, so b.x = 2 would not touch a.x.
questions.rule: No static, no sharing.

questions.q: In the Bicycle example, numberOfBicycles starts at 0. Before any bicycle is created, can code read Bicycle.numberOfBicycles (assuming access)?
options: No, since a variable needs an object to exist
Yes, but only through an object reference
Yes, since a class variable can be reached with no instance
No, since the constructor sets it up first
optionExplain: Class variables belong to the class.
The class name is the preferred route.
Right: it would read 0.
The declaration already gives it a value.
questions.explain: A class variable is tied to the class, not to any object.
questions.rule: Class variables need no object.
questions.teaches: A class variable can be read before any object exists, because it belongs to the class itself.

questions.q: A school app tracks students. Sort each piece of data by whether it is stored per object or once for the class.

items.t: a student's name
a student's roll number
a student's personal grade
the total number of students enrolled
the school's founding year
the counter that hands out roll numbers

questions.explain: Data that differs from student to student is per object, and data that is the same for the whole school is shared.
questions.rule: Same for everyone means static.
questions.teaches: Data that is identical for every object, such as a founding year, belongs in a class variable, not only counters.

questions.q: True or false: A static method can use an instance variable of its class by its plain name.
questions.explain: A static method may run with no object, so a plain instance name has nothing to refer to. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: A class method can directly use only class members, and instance members need an object reference.

questions.q: Inside a class method, sort these by whether the plain name can be used directly.

items.t: a static field
another static method
an instance field
an instance method

questions.explain: Class methods reach class members directly and need an object for instance members.
questions.rule: Static reaches static directly.

questions.q: class Bike { private int gear; private static int made; static int made() { return made; } static int gear() { return gear; } } Which method fails to compile?
options: made(), since it returns a class variable
Both, since static methods return nothing
Neither, since fields are reachable anywhere
gear(), since it uses an instance field in a class method
optionExplain: A class method may use class variables.
Static methods may return values.
Instance fields need an object reference in a class method.
Right: A class method cannot name an instance field directly.
questions.explain: A class method cannot name an instance field directly.
questions.rule: No plain instance names in static code.

questions.q: True or false: If made() in the same class were not static, it could still return the class variable made.
questions.explain: Instance methods can use class variables directly.
questions.rule: Instance methods may use static members.

questions.q: Inside class Bike, does static int gearOf(Bike b) { return b.gear; } compile?
options: Yes, since the instance field is reached through an object reference
No, since a class method cannot use instance fields in any way
Only if gear is public
No, since b is a parameter
optionExplain: Right: The restriction is on plain names, not on instance data as such.
A reference makes the access legal.
Inside the class itself, private fields are reachable.
Parameters may be used freely.
questions.explain: The restriction is on plain names, not on instance data as such.
questions.rule: Go through a reference to use instance data.
questions.teaches: A class method can use instance members when it works through an object reference it has been given.

questions.q: class Counter { static int total; int mine; static void report() { ... } } Which statements may appear inside report()?
options: mine = 0;
Counter c = new Counter(); c.mine = 0;
this.total = 0;
total = 0;
optionExplain: A plain instance name needs an object.
Right: an instance field through a reference.
A class method has no this.
Right: a class variable by plain name.
questions.explain: Plain class members and instance members reached through a reference are allowed, but plain instance names and this are not.
questions.rule: Static code needs a reference for instance data.
questions.teaches: A class method can make its own objects with new and then use their instance members through those references.

questions.q: Which declaration creates a constant?
options: static int maxUsers = 50;
static final int MAX_USERS = 50;
int MAX_USERS = 50;
public int MAX_USERS;
optionExplain: static alone is only a shared variable.
Right: static and final together.
Without final the value can change.
Neither static nor final.
questions.explain: A constant needs static and final. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: Declare a constant with static final and an uppercase name; it cannot be reassigned.

questions.q: A constant is declared with the keywords static and ____.
questions.explain: final forbids reassigning the value.
questions.rule: static final.

questions.q: Which name follows the tutorial's convention for a constant holding the maximum number of retries?
options: maxRetries
MaxRetries
MAX_RETRIES
max_retries
optionExplain: Camel case is the style for methods.
That style is for classes.
Right: uppercase with an underscore.
Lower case is not the convention for constants.
questions.explain: Constants are uppercase with underscores between words.
questions.rule: UPPER_CASE for constants.

questions.q: True or false: Assigning a new value to a static final field elsewhere in the program compiles and changes the value.
questions.explain: Reassigning a constant is a compile-time error.
questions.rule: final forbids reassignment.

questions.q: Class Config has static final int PORT = 80, a value known at compile time, and Client uses Config.PORT. Config is edited to 8080 and only Config is recompiled. What does Client use?
options: 8080, since names are looked up when the program runs
Zero, since the link is broken
It fails to start, since the two classes disagree
Still 80, since the compiler copied the value into Client
optionExplain: Compile-time constants are replaced by their values.
The old value is still in Client.
Both classes still run, with mismatched values.
Right: Client must be recompiled too.
questions.explain: For a primitive or String constant known at compile time, uses of the name are replaced by the value itself.
questions.rule: Recompile users of a changed constant.
questions.teaches: The compiler may copy a compile-time constant's value into every class that uses it, so those classes must be recompiled after the value is edited.

questions.q: A bakery program needs fields. Which are good candidates for static final?
options: The number of days in a week
The legal limit on the weight of one loaf, fixed for all orders
The id number of each order
The running total of loaves sold today
optionExplain: Right: shared and never changing.
Right: same for all objects and fixed.
It differs per order.
It changes during the program.
questions.explain: A constant is a value shared by all and never changed.
questions.rule: Shared and unchanging means constant.
questions.teaches: A value that is the same for every object and never changes is a constant, while a value that differs per object or changes at run time is not.

questions.q: A class variable must be filled by a loop when the class is first set up. Which tool fits?
options: A static initialization block
A one-line initializer at the declaration
A constructor, which runs for each new object
A getter method on the class
optionExplain: Right: it holds logic for class variables.
A loop does not fit in one expression.
That would redo the work per object.
Getters read values; they do not set them up.
questions.explain: Class-level logic goes in a static block. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: Use a declaration initializer for simple values, a constructor for instance logic, and a static block or private static method for class logic.

questions.q: Match each tool to its use.
pairs: An alternative way to set a class variable
questions.explain: Each tool suits a different kind of field and amount of logic.
questions.rule: Pick the tool by field kind and logic.

questions.q: A class has static { x = 2; } and later in the body static { x = x * 10; }. What is x once both have run?
optionExplain: The second block also ran.
Right: the blocks run in source order.
Nothing is added to the product.
Both blocks assign a nonzero value.
questions.explain: Static blocks run in the order they appear, so 2 is set first and then multiplied by 10.
questions.rule: Static blocks run in source order.

questions.q: If the two static blocks were written in the opposite order, the final value of x would be ____.
questions.explain: x = x * 10 would run first on the starting value, then x = 2 would overwrite it.
questions.rule: Order matters.

questions.q: A class variable is set by a private static method called from its declaration. What can that method do that a static block cannot?
options: Run before the class exists
Hold more than one statement
Be called again later to reinitialize the variable
Set instance variables of every object
optionExplain: Neither runs before the class is set up.
A block can hold many statements too.
Right: A method has a name and can be called again, which a block cannot.
A static method cannot name instance variables directly.
questions.explain: A method has a name and can be called again, which a block cannot.
questions.rule: A named method can be rerun.
questions.teaches: A private static method can be called again later to reinitialize a class variable, which a static block cannot.

questions.q: A game needs a table of eight start positions filled by a loop once for the class, and a per-player flag alive that starts true. Which choices fit the tools?
options: A constructor fills the table
private boolean alive = true; at the declaration initializes the flag
A static block sets alive for each player
A static block fills the table
optionExplain: That would redo the class-level work for each player.
Right: a simple per-object value.
A static block runs at class level, not per player.
Right: class-level logic.
questions.explain: Class-level logic goes in static blocks and simple per-object values go in declarations.
questions.rule: Match the tool to class-level or object-level data.
questions.teaches: Choose the tool by the level of the data: class-level logic belongs in static initializers and object-level values in declarations or constructors.

questions.q: Three constructors all need the same ten lines of set-up. Which feature avoids repeating them?
options: A static initialization block
A private constructor
A varargs parameter
An instance initializer block
optionExplain: That belongs to the class and runs in class set-up.
That restricts creation and does not share code.
That accepts values; it does not share code.
Right: the compiler copies it into each constructor.
questions.explain: An instance block is copied into every constructor. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: Share initialization code across constructors with an instance initializer block, or call a final method from the field's declaration.

questions.q: The compiler copies an instance initializer block into every ____.
questions.explain: That is how the block's code runs for every new object.
questions.rule: Copied into each constructor.

questions.q: class Grid { int[] cells; { cells = new int[9]; } Grid(int n) { } } What is cells.length after new Grid(4)?
options: The code does not compile
optionExplain: Right: the block ran as part of construction.
The constructor argument is not used to size the array.
The block gave the array nine slots.
An initializer block in a class body is legal.
questions.explain: The block runs for every new object, whatever the constructor body does.
questions.rule: The block runs on every creation.

questions.q: True or false: If a second constructor Grid() is added, it also gets the block's work.
questions.explain: The compiler copies the block into every constructor.
questions.rule: All constructors share the block.

questions.q: Why does the tutorial suggest that a method called from a field initializer be final?
options: A final method runs faster while fields are set up
Subclasses cannot override it, yet they can still reuse it
A final method may be called without an object
A final method is invisible to subclasses entirely
optionExplain: Speed is not the reason given.
Right: Calling a method that subclasses could override during initialization can cause problems.
That describes static methods.
Subclasses can still use it.
questions.explain: Calling a method that subclasses could override during initialization can cause problems.
questions.rule: Make initialization helpers final.
questions.teaches: Calling an overridable method during initialization can cause problems, and a final method avoids them while still being reusable by subclasses.

questions.q: A developer writes plain statements in a bare block { ... } in a class body and expects them to run once when the class is first loaded. What actually happens?
options: They run once, since any block runs only once
They never run, since blocks must be called
They run for every new object, being copied into each constructor
They run once per class, but only when the class is public
optionExplain: Without static, the block runs per object.
An initializer block runs by itself.
Right: Only a static block runs at class level, so a bare block repeats per object.
Access does not decide this.
questions.explain: Only a static block runs at class level, so a bare block repeats per object.
questions.rule: Run-once class set-up needs static.
questions.teaches: A bare block runs for every object created, so setup that should happen only once for the class needs a static block.

questions.q: A class is declared inside another class and has no static keyword. What is it called?
options: A static nested class
A top-level class
A package class
An inner class
optionExplain: That kind has the static keyword.
A top-level class is not inside another class.
No such kind exists in this lesson.
Right: Nested without static is inner. The card next shows why.
questions.explain: Nested without static is inner. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: A class declared inside another is nested: with static it is a static nested class, and without static it is an inner class.

questions.q: Match each term to its meaning.
pairs: Any class declared inside another class
A nested class declared without static
A nested class declared with static
A class not declared inside another class
questions.explain: Nested is the broad term, and inner and static nested are its two kinds.
questions.rule: Nested covers inner and static nested.

questions.q: Which are reasons the tutorial gives for nesting a class?
options: To let the class extend several parents
To let the class use private members of the outer class while it stays hidden
To group a class that only one other class uses
To make the class run faster
optionExplain: Nesting does not change inheritance rules.
Right: increased encapsulation.
Right: logical grouping.
Speed is not one of the reasons.
questions.explain: The tutorial lists grouping, encapsulation, and readability or maintainability.
questions.rule: Nest to group, to encapsulate, to keep code close.

questions.q: True or false: A nested class can be declared private, even though a top-level class cannot.
questions.explain: A nested class is a member of its enclosing class, so all four access levels are open to it.
questions.rule: Nested classes are members, so private works.

questions.q: A team wants to save inner-class objects to disk and read them back with a different Java runtime. What does the tutorial advise?
options: Avoid it, since compiler-made pieces differ between implementations
Go ahead, since every runtime reads such files the same way
It works only for static nested classes
It works if every field is public
optionExplain: Right: serializing inner classes is strongly discouraged.
The generated constructs may differ, causing compatibility problems.
The tutorial does not draw that line.
Access levels are not the cause of the problem.
questions.explain: Inner classes, including local and anonymous ones, rely on compiler-generated constructs that may differ between compilers.
questions.rule: Avoid serializing inner classes.
questions.teaches: Serializing inner classes, including local and anonymous ones, is strongly discouraged because compiler-generated constructs can differ between Java implementations.

questions.q: In an invoicing app, TaxCalculator is used only by Invoice and needs Invoice's private rate field. Which design follows the tutorial's reasoning?
options: Make rate public so TaxCalculator can read it
Nest TaxCalculator inside Invoice, so it can use rate and stay hidden
Make TaxCalculator a separate top-level class with its own copy of rate
Merge both into one huge class with no helpers
optionExplain: That exposes the field to everyone.
Right: Nesting lets a helper reach private members without widening access.
That duplicates the data and exposes the helper.
The tutorial prefers grouping related classes, not merging them.
questions.explain: Nesting lets a helper reach private members without widening access.
questions.rule: Nest a helper to share private members safely.
questions.teaches: Nesting is a way to give a helper class access to private members without making those members public.

questions.q: True or false: An inner class can read the private fields of its enclosing object directly.
questions.explain: Direct access to the outer object's members, private ones included, is the main feature of inner classes. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: An inner class needs an outer instance, can use that instance's members directly even when private, and has no static members.

questions.q: An inner object exists only within an ____ object.
questions.explain: An inner class is tied to an instance of its enclosing class.
questions.rule: No outer object, no inner object.

questions.q: Given Outer o = new Outer();, which statement creates an Inner object tied to o?
options: Outer.Inner i = new Outer.Inner();
Outer.Inner i = Outer.new Inner();
Outer.Inner i = o.new Inner();
Inner i = new Inner();
optionExplain: That is the form for a static nested class.
There is no outer object in this form.
Right: the outer object creates the inner one.
Outside Outer, the bare name Inner does not name the class and no outer object is given.
questions.explain: An inner object is always created through an outer object.
questions.rule: outer.new Inner()

questions.q: True or false: According to the tutorial, an inner class may declare a static method.
questions.explain: The tutorial says an inner class cannot define static members, since it is tied to an instance.
questions.rule: Inner classes have no static members.

questions.q: Inside an instance method of DataStructure, which expression creates the inner EvenIterator tied to the current object?
options: new this.EvenIterator()
DataStructure.new EvenIterator()
EvenIterator.new(this)
this.new EvenIterator()
optionExplain: The outer reference goes before new, not after it.
A class name does not identify an outer object.
This is not creation syntax.
Right: this refers to the current outer object, and the .new form ties the inner object to it.
questions.explain: this refers to the current outer object, and the .new form ties the inner object to it.
questions.rule: Use this.new inside outer instance code.
questions.teaches: Inside the outer class's instance code, this.new Inner() creates an inner object tied to the current outer object.

questions.q: class Game { private int score; class Player { void win() { score += 10; } } } Game g1 = new Game(); Game g2 = new Game(); Game.Player p = g1.new Player(); p.win(); Which score changed?
options: Only g1's score
Only g2's score
Both scores
Neither, since score is private
optionExplain: Right: p is tied to g1.
p was created through g1.
Each inner object belongs to one outer object.
An inner class may use private members of its outer object.
questions.explain: Each inner object works on the particular outer object that created it.
questions.rule: An inner object is bound to one outer object.
questions.teaches: Each inner object is bound to the one outer object it was created through, and its changes affect that outer object only.

questions.q: Inside Outer, which code creates an object of its static nested class StaticNestedClass?
options: outerObject.new StaticNestedClass()
new StaticNestedClass()
new Outer().StaticNestedClass()
Outer.new StaticNestedClass()
optionExplain: That is the form for an inner class.
Right: no outer object is needed.
This is not creation syntax.
A class name cannot supply an outer object.
questions.explain: Static nested classes are created like top-level classes. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: A static nested class needs no outer instance, uses outer static members directly, and reaches outer instance members only through a reference.

questions.q: True or false: A static nested class can name an instance field of the outer class directly, without an object reference.
questions.explain: It has no outer object, so a plain instance name has nothing to refer to.
questions.rule: Instance members need a reference.

questions.q: From a static nested class, sort these outer members by how they are reached.

items.t: an outer static field
an outer static method
an outer instance field
an outer instance method

questions.explain: Static members need no object, while instance members need one to say whose values are meant.
questions.rule: Static direct, instance by reference.

questions.q: True or false: In a static nested class method that takes an Outer parameter o, the expression o.name compiles when name is an instance field of Outer.
questions.explain: The reference o supplies the object whose field is meant.
questions.rule: A reference makes instance access legal.

questions.q: TopLevelClass is declared outside OuterClass. How does its access to OuterClass's instance field outerField compare with that of a static nested class?
options: Better: a top-level class may use the plain name
Worse: it cannot reach the field at all
The same: both need an object reference
The same: both use the plain name since they share a package
optionExplain: Neither may use the plain name.
A reference gives access, as in the tutorial's example.
Right: In the tutorial's example, a static nested class and a top-level class reach the outer instance field in the same way.
A shared package does not allow plain names.
questions.explain: In the tutorial's example, a static nested class and a top-level class reach the outer instance field in the same way.
questions.rule: Static nested is like top-level here.
questions.teaches: For reaching the outer class's instance members, a static nested class gets no advantage over an ordinary top-level class.

questions.q: In a maps app, Route has an instance field distance and a static field UNIT. A static nested class Marker has a method that uses both. Which is correct?
options: Both by plain name, since Marker is nested
Both through a Route reference only
distance by plain name, UNIT through a reference
UNIT by its plain name, distance through a Route reference
optionExplain: Plain instance names are not allowed.
Static members can be used by plain name.
The two kinds are swapped.
Right: The nested class has no outer object, so only static members are plain-name reachable.
questions.explain: The nested class has no outer object, so only static members are plain-name reachable.
questions.rule: Static: plain name. Instance: reference.
questions.teaches: Choosing between an inner and a static nested class depends on whether the nested class must work directly with one particular outer object.

questions.q: An inner class method has a parameter x, the inner class has a field x, and the outer class has a field x. What does plain x mean inside the method?
options: The parameter
The inner class's field
The outer class's field
It is a compile error, since three x names clash
optionExplain: Right: the innermost declaration wins.
The parameter is closer.
That one is two scopes away.
Shadowing across scopes is legal.
questions.explain: The innermost declaration hides the others by simple name. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: The innermost declaration wins by simple name; use this.name for the current object's member and Outer.this.name for the enclosing object's.

questions.q: Match each expression in ShadowTest's method to what it names.
questions.explain: The simple name is the parameter, this reaches the current inner object, and ClassName.this reaches the enclosing object.
questions.rule: Plain, this, Outer.this.

questions.q: In a method where the parameter x is 7, the inner field x is 5 and the outer field x is 3, the expression this.x + Outer.this.x produces ____.
questions.explain: this.x is the inner field 5 and Outer.this.x is the outer field 3, giving 8.
questions.rule: Choose the form for each variable.

questions.q: Rename the parameter to y in that method. What does plain x refer to now?
options: The method parameter
The inner class's field
The outer class's field
Nothing, which is a compile error
optionExplain: That parameter is called y now.
Right: it now shadows the outer field.
The inner field hides it.
A closer declaration exists.
questions.explain: With the parameter gone, the next closest x is the inner class's field.
questions.rule: The closest declaration wins.

questions.q: After the call, is the outer class's x still 0 and still part of the outer object?
options: No, since the parameter replaced it
No, since the inner field overwrote it
Yes: shadowing hides the name, not the variable
Yes, but only if it was declared static
optionExplain: The parameter is a different variable.
They are separate variables.
Right: All three variables exist side by side; only the simple name x is claimed by the closest one.
Instance fields are unaffected too.
questions.explain: All three variables exist side by side; only the simple name x is claimed by the closest one.
questions.rule: Shadowing hides names, not variables.
questions.teaches: Shadowing hides a name but does not change or remove the hidden variable, which can still be reached by a qualified name.

questions.q: class Library { int branches = 3; class Desk { int branches = 1; int total(int branches) { return branches + this.branches + Library.this.branches; } } } What does total(10) return for a Desk of a Library?
optionExplain: That would use the parameter three times.
That leaves out the library's value.
That leaves out the parameter.
questions.explain: Each form picks a different variable, and a single expression can use all three.
questions.rule: Use the form that names the variable you want.
questions.teaches: One expression can combine a parameter, an inner field and an outer field that share a name, by using the plain name, this.name and Outer.this.name.

questions.q: Why is EvenIterator declared private inside DataStructure?
options: Outside code needs only the interface, so the helper stays hidden
So that it can declare static members
So that it can be created without any outer object around
Because private classes run faster
optionExplain: Right: A private helper is invisible outside its owner. The card next shows why.
Inner classes cannot declare static members.
An inner class always needs one.
Access modifiers do not affect speed.
questions.explain: A private helper is invisible outside its owner. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: A private inner class can act as a hidden helper that walks through its outer object's private data.

questions.q: Put the steps of the DataStructure example in order.
items: main creates a DataStructure, which fills the array
printEven creates an EvenIterator tied to this object
hasNext checks the index is inside the array
next returns a value and moves the index forward by two
The loop ends when hasNext reports false
questions.explain: The example builds the data, creates the iterator, then loops with hasNext and next.
questions.rule: Create, test, fetch, repeat.

questions.q: With the array holding 0 to 14, the last value that EvenIterator returns is ____.
questions.explain: Indexes 0, 2, 4 up to 14 are visited, and each value equals its index.
questions.rule: The last even index is 14.

questions.q: Suppose next advanced the index by 3 instead of 2. Which values would print?
optionExplain: That is the output for steps of two.
Right: the indexes 0, 3, 6, 9, 12 are inside the array.
Index 15 is outside the array, so hasNext stops before it.
The first value at index 0 is still printed.
questions.explain: hasNext stops the loop when the index passes the last position, 14.
questions.rule: Step size sets which indexes are visited.

questions.q: True or false: Code outside DataStructure can declare a variable of the type EvenIterator.
questions.explain: EvenIterator is private, so outside code can name only the interface type DataStructureIterator.
questions.rule: Callers use the interface type.
questions.teaches: A private nested class cannot be named outside its owner, so callers work with an interface type that it implements.

questions.q: A Playlist class keeps its songs in a private array and needs a helper that visits every second song. Which design matches the tutorial's example?
options: Make the array public so that any class can loop over it directly
A static nested class that reads the array by its plain name
A private inner class implementing an iterator interface over the array
A top-level class that reads the private array directly by name
optionExplain: That exposes the data to everyone.
A static nested class needs an object reference.
Right: An inner class can use private data directly while staying hidden.
A top-level class cannot reach private members.
questions.explain: An inner class can use private data directly while staying hidden.
questions.rule: Inner helper, private data, public interface.
questions.teaches: Private data can be traversed by a helper without being made public when the helper is an inner class.

questions.q: A local class uses a local variable limit from its enclosing method. What must be true of limit?
options: It is declared public
It is a class variable
It is assigned inside the local class
It is final or effectively final
optionExplain: Local variables take no access modifier.
Locals can be captured; class variables are not required.
Assignment would break the rule.
Right: Captured locals must not change after being set. The card next shows why.
questions.explain: Captured locals must not change after being set. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: A local class is declared in a block and may use enclosing local variables only if they are final or effectively final.

questions.q: A variable whose value is not changed after initialization is called effectively ____.
questions.explain: Effectively final variables may be captured even without the final keyword.
questions.rule: Effectively final = unchanged.

questions.q: void f(int n) { int k = 5; class A { int g() { return k + n; } } n = 7; } Does this compile?
options: No, since n is captured but later reassigned
Yes, since k and n are both fine
No, since a local class cannot use parameters
No, since A has no constructor
optionExplain: Right: The assignment n = 7 anywhere in f ruins the effectively final status of n.
n is reassigned, so it is not effectively final.
Parameters can be captured when effectively final.
A default constructor is supplied.
questions.explain: The assignment n = 7 anywhere in f ruins the effectively final status of n.
questions.rule: One reassignment blocks capture.

questions.q: True or false: If the line n = 7; is removed, the method f above compiles.
questions.explain: Both k and n are then effectively final and can be captured.
questions.rule: Unchanged variables can be captured.

questions.q: Which static member may a local class declare?
options: Any static method that returns a value
A final constant with a compile-time value
A static initializer block of statements
A static member interface of its own
optionExplain: Static methods are not allowed.
Right: the constant-variable exception.
Static initializers are not allowed.
Interfaces cannot be declared in a block.
questions.explain: Static members are allowed only when they are constant variables.
questions.rule: Only constants may be static.
questions.teaches: A local class may declare static members only if they are constant variables: final primitives or Strings initialized with compile-time constants.

questions.q: class Shop { int tax = 5; static int total(int p) { class Calc { int add() { return p + tax; } } return new Calc().add(); } } Why does this fail to compile?
options: p is a parameter, and local classes cannot capture parameters
Calc has no constructor, and every class must declare one
tax is an instance field, which a local class in a static method cannot use
A local class cannot be created with new inside a static method
optionExplain: Effectively final parameters can be captured.
A default constructor is supplied.
Right: A static method has no enclosing instance, so a local class inside it sees only static enclosing members.
Local classes are created with new like others.
questions.explain: A static method has no enclosing instance, so a local class inside it sees only static enclosing members.
questions.rule: Static context, static members only.
questions.teaches: A local class inside a static method can use only the static members of the enclosing class.

questions.q: What mainly distinguishes an anonymous class from a local class?
options: It is static, so it needs no outer object
It can declare constructors
It can only be declared at the top of a file
It has no name and is written as an expression
optionExplain: Anonymous classes are not static in that sense.
It cannot.
It appears inside other code.
Right: No name, an expression. The card next shows why.
questions.explain: No name, an expression. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: An anonymous class is new Type(args) { body }, an expression that defines and creates a one-off class.

questions.q: Match each part of an anonymous class expression to its role.
pairs: Constructor arguments, empty for an interface
The class body with member declarations
questions.explain: The four parts make up the expression.
questions.rule: new Type(args) { body }

questions.q: A statement that creates an anonymous class must end with a ____ after the closing brace.
questions.explain: The class is an expression, which forms part of a statement, so the statement needs its own end.
questions.rule: Expressions end in a semicolon.

questions.q: True or false: An anonymous class can declare its own constructor.
questions.explain: It has no name, so it cannot have a constructor, although it may use instance initializers.
questions.rule: No name, no constructor.

questions.q: Where can an anonymous class expression appear?
options: Anywhere an expression fits, such as a method argument
Only as a statement standing on its own line
Only at the very top of a class body
Only inside methods declared static
optionExplain: Right: Because it is an expression, it can be passed straight into a call.
It is an expression and can sit inside others.
It appears inside code.
No such limit exists.
questions.explain: Because it is an expression, it can be passed straight into a call.
questions.rule: An expression can be an argument.
questions.teaches: Because an anonymous class is an expression, it can be written directly as an argument in a method call.

questions.q: A music app needs a click handler for one button. The handler must count clicks in its own field and has a small helper method. Which construct fits the tutorial's reasoning?
options: A local class used once, since anonymous classes cannot have fields
An anonymous class, since it can declare fields and extra methods
An inner class with static members, since handlers need shared state
A top-level class with a public counter field
optionExplain: Anonymous classes can have fields.
Right: An anonymous class is a one-off class that may carry its own state and helpers.
Inner classes cannot declare static members.
That widens access for a one-off need.
questions.explain: An anonymous class is a one-off class that may carry its own state and helpers.
questions.rule: One-off plus fields or helpers: anonymous.
questions.teaches: An anonymous class suits a one-off object that needs its own state or helper methods, which a bare single-method body does not offer.

questions.q: A method must print the members that match a rule, and the rule changes often. Which design best keeps the method itself unchanged?
options: Write a new printing method for each rule
Copy the method and edit the copy for each rule
Pass the rule in as an argument, such as an object or lambda
Add a yes-or-no parameter for each new rule
optionExplain: That is the brittle, restrictive approach.
That duplicates the iteration logic.
Right: Separate the criterion from the iteration. The card next shows why.
The method would keep changing.
questions.explain: Separate the criterion from the iteration. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: A lambda is a compact implementation of a functional interface, so behaviour can be passed to a method as an argument.

questions.q: Match each standard interface to its job.
pairs: Takes a T and answers true or false
Takes a T and performs an action
Takes a T and returns an R
questions.explain: These three cover testing, acting and transforming.
questions.rule: Test, act, transform.

questions.q: The standard interface for a yes-or-no test on one object is called ____.
questions.explain: Predicate has a test method that takes one object and returns a boolean.
questions.rule: Predicate = yes-or-no test.

questions.q: True or false: A lambda expression can implement an interface that declares two abstract methods.
questions.explain: A lambda needs a functional interface, which has exactly one abstract method.
questions.rule: One abstract method only.

questions.q: An interface declares one abstract method and two default methods. Can a lambda implement it?
options: No, since the interface declares three methods in total
No, since default methods require a class to hold them
Yes, but only if the default methods are removed
Yes, since default and static methods are not counted as abstract
optionExplain: Only abstract methods are counted.
The interface remains functional.
They can stay.
Right: A functional interface has exactly one abstract method; other kinds of method do not matter.
questions.explain: A functional interface has exactly one abstract method; other kinds of method do not matter.
questions.rule: Count abstract methods only.
questions.teaches: Default and static methods do not count against the one abstract method, so an interface that has them can still be a functional interface.

questions.q: A program must pick orders over 100, take each order's customer email, and print it. Which interfaces supply the three steps?
options: Predicate for the filter, Function for the email, Consumer for the printing
Consumer for the filter, Predicate for the email, Function for the printing
Function for the filter, Consumer for the email, Predicate for the printing
Predicate for all three steps
optionExplain: Right: Filter with a test, transform with a function, act with a consumer.
Each interface is matched to the wrong job.
A filter needs a yes-or-no answer.
Only the first step is a yes-or-no test.
questions.explain: Filter with a test, transform with a function, act with a consumer.
questions.rule: Filter, map, act.
questions.teaches: The same three steps, filter, transform and act, appear in stream pipelines as operations that take lambdas, such as filter, map and forEach.

questions.q: Which of these is a valid lambda that adds two ints?
options: (a, b) => a + b
(a, b) -> a + b
a, b -> a + b
(a, b) -> return a + b
optionExplain: Java uses the arrow ->, not =>.
Right: Parameters, arrow, body. The card next shows why.
Two parameters need parentheses.
return needs braces because it is a statement.
questions.explain: Parameters, arrow, body. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: A lambda is parameters, an arrow and a body, and a single-expression body returns its value automatically.

questions.q: The token that separates a lambda's parameters from its body is the ____ ->.
questions.explain: The arrow token joins parameters to the body.
questions.rule: Parameters -> body.

questions.q: The lambda (int x) -> x * 2 can also be written in which of these ways?
options: (int x) -> { return x * 2; }
int x -> x * 2
x -> return x * 2
optionExplain: Right: the block form with return.
Right: the type may be left out.
A typed parameter needs parentheses.
Right: one parameter needs no parentheses.
return is a statement and needs braces.
questions.explain: Types and single-parameter parentheses are optional, and a block body needs return.
questions.rule: Shorten with care.

questions.q: True or false: The lambda x -> { x * 2 } still returns the doubled value.
questions.explain: A block body needs an explicit return statement to give back a value.
questions.rule: Block body, explicit return.

questions.q: int operateBinary(int a, int b, IntegerMath op) calls op.operation(a, b). What does operateBinary(20, 10, (x, y) -> x - y) return?
options: It does not compile, since the parameter names differ from a and b
optionExplain: That would come from an addition lambda.
Nothing is multiplied.
Right: The method hands 20 and 10 to the lambda, which subtracts.
Lambda parameter names are free.
questions.explain: The method hands 20 and 10 to the lambda, which subtracts.
questions.rule: The same method gives different results for different lambdas.
questions.teaches: A lambda can be passed to an ordinary method that runs it through the interface's single method, so different lambdas give different behaviour from the same method.

questions.q: An interface has one method void show(String text). Which lambda implements it for a console logger?
options: () -> print(text)
(String text) -> void print(text)
text -> { print(text) }
text -> print(text)
optionExplain: The lambda has no parameter to supply text.
A lambda body does not declare a return type.
A block needs a semicolon after the statement.
Right: one parameter and a void call as the body.
questions.explain: The number of lambda parameters must match the interface method.
questions.rule: Match the parameter count of the interface method.
questions.teaches: The number of parameters in a lambda must match the interface's single method, and an empty list is used only when that method takes none.

questions.q: A local variable count is changed after initialization elsewhere in the method. Can a lambda in that method read count?
options: No: captured locals must be final or effectively final
Yes, lambdas can capture any local variable
Yes, but only if the lambda has a block body
No, lambdas cannot read locals at all
optionExplain: Right: Captured locals must not change. The card next shows why.
The rule is the same as for local classes.
The body form does not matter.
They can, when the locals are effectively final.
questions.explain: Captured locals must not change. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: Lambdas capture only effectively final locals, share their enclosing scope's names, and take their type from where they are used.

questions.q: A lambda has no type of its own; the compiler infers its type from the ____ type, which is the type expected where the lambda appears.
questions.explain: The target type comes from the context, such as a declared variable or a method parameter.
questions.rule: Context supplies the target type.

questions.q: int x = 5; Show c = x -> print(x); where Show is an interface with one method taking an int. What does the compiler do?
options: Accepts it, and x inside the lambda is the parameter
Rejects it, since the lambda parameter x redeclares a local variable
Accepts it, and x inside the lambda is the local 5
Rejects it, since Show cannot take an int
optionExplain: Shadowing is not allowed here.
Right: A lambda shares its enclosing scope, so its parameter cannot repeat a local name.
The parameter declaration is the problem.
A one-method interface taking an int is a valid target.
questions.explain: A lambda shares its enclosing scope, so its parameter cannot repeat a local name.
questions.rule: Use a fresh name for a lambda parameter.

questions.q: True or false: If z is a captured local and the lambda body says z = 99;, the code compiles.
questions.explain: Assigning to a captured variable breaks the effectively final rule.
questions.rule: Do not assign to captured locals.

questions.q: A lambda sits inside a method of the inner class FirstLevel. In its body, what does this.x mean?
options: A field of the lambda object itself
The outer class's field x
FirstLevel's field x, since this still means the enclosing object
A compile error, since this cannot appear in a lambda
optionExplain: A lambda has no object of its own for this to name.
this is the nearest enclosing object, FirstLevel.
Right: A lambda adds no scope level, so this means the same as it does just outside the lambda.
It is allowed and means the enclosing instance.
questions.explain: A lambda adds no scope level, so this means the same as it does just outside the lambda.
questions.rule: this inside a lambda is the enclosing object.
questions.teaches: Inside a lambda, this refers to the enclosing object, since the lambda is not an object with a this of its own.

questions.q: Two overloads exist: void run(Task t), where Task has void act(), and void run(Maker m), where Maker has int make(). The call run(() -> 42) is made. Which overload does the compiler pick?
options: run(Task t), since it is declared first
Neither, since a lambda cannot be passed to overloaded methods
Both are called, one after the other
run(Maker m), since the lambda returns a value
optionExplain: Order of declaration does not decide it.
Overload resolution handles lambdas.
A call picks exactly one method.
Right: A lambda that produces a value fits an interface whose method returns a value, not one returning nothing.
questions.explain: A lambda that produces a value fits an interface whose method returns a value, not one returning nothing.
questions.rule: The lambda's shape helps pick the overload.
questions.teaches: When overloads accept different functional interfaces, whether the lambda returns a value helps the compiler choose between them.

questions.q: Person::compareByAge names a static method. Which lambda could it replace?
options: (a, b) -> Person.compareByAge(a, b)
(a, b) -> a.compareByAge(b)
(a, b) -> new Person(a, b)
a -> Person.compareByAge(a)
optionExplain: Right: it only forwards its two parameters.
That calls the method on the first parameter instead.
That is a constructor call.
That passes one parameter, not two.
questions.explain: A reference replaces a lambda that only forwards. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: Use a method reference when a lambda only forwards its parameters to an existing method or constructor.

questions.q: Match each kind of method reference to an example.
questions.explain: Each example shows one of the four kinds.
questions.rule: Static, particular object, arbitrary object, constructor.

questions.q: Which method reference is equivalent to the lambda (a, b) -> a.concat(b) for strings?
options: String.concat
String::concat
concat::String
new String::concat
optionExplain: The double colon is required.
Right: the first parameter becomes the receiver.
The type goes before the colons.
That is not a valid reference.
questions.explain: The arbitrary-object form passes the first parameter as the object and the rest as arguments.
questions.rule: Type::method uses the first parameter as the receiver.

questions.q: True or false: In transferElements(roster, HashSet::new), where the factory parameter is a Supplier, the reference stands for a lambda that takes no arguments and returns a new HashSet.
questions.explain: The factory parameter is a Supplier, and the constructor reference fits it.
questions.rule: ::new can be a supplier.

questions.q: Arrays.sort(roster, p::compareByName) uses an object p of class ComparisonProvider. On which object does compareByName run for each comparison?
options: On the first element being compared
On a new ComparisonProvider each time
On p, the object named before the colons
On no object, since the method is static
optionExplain: That is the arbitrary-object form.
No object is created per comparison.
Right: With object::method, the named object receives every call.
p names an object, so the method is an instance method.
questions.explain: With object::method, the named object receives every call.
questions.rule: object::method fixes the receiver.
questions.teaches: With object::method the method is always called on that specific object, not on the elements being processed.

questions.q: A mapper that takes a String and returns a StringBuilder, a Function of String and StringBuilder, is currently written as a lambda. Which lambda could become StringBuilder::new?
options: () -> new StringBuilder()
s -> s.append(s)
(a, b) -> new StringBuilder(a, b)
s -> new StringBuilder(s)
optionExplain: That has no parameter, so it does not fit a Function.
That calls a method on the parameter.
That has two parameters.
Right: it only forwards the one parameter to a constructor.
questions.explain: The interface's parameters decide which constructor the reference stands for.
questions.rule: The interface shape picks the constructor.
questions.teaches: With a constructor reference, the parameters of the functional interface decide which constructor is meant.

questions.q: Which construct does the tutorial suggest for a single unit of behaviour passed to other code?
options: A lambda expression
An anonymous class
A local class
A static nested class
optionExplain: Right: Lambdas for one unit of behaviour. The card next shows why.
It is heavier than the need.
It is heavier than the need.
It is the widest-visibility choice, not the simplest.
questions.explain: Lambdas for one unit of behaviour. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: Pick the simplest construct that meets the need: lambda first, then anonymous class, local class, and nested class as requirements grow.

questions.q: Match each need to the construct the tutorial suggests.
pairs: Several instances of a named helper inside one method
A one-off object with its own fields
A single behaviour to pass along
A type used widely, needing no local variables
questions.explain: Each need points to the lightest construct that provides it.
questions.rule: Match need to construct.

questions.q: A method needs one comparison rule for sorting, used once, with no state. Which construct fits best?
options: An anonymous class with a comparison method
A lambda expression
A local class with a constructor
An inner class in another file
optionExplain: It works but is heavier than needed.
Right: a single unit of behaviour.
No constructor or name is needed.
It is much heavier than the need.
questions.explain: No fields, no constructor, no extra methods: the lambda suffices.
questions.rule: Choose the simplest that works.

questions.q: A one-off comparison rule is written as a lambda. It must now also keep a field counting comparisons. Which construct does the tutorial's guidance choose as the simplest that meets the need?
options: Stay with the lambda, since lambdas can hold fields
To a static nested class with no instance
To an anonymous class, since it can declare fields
To a top-level class with public fields
optionExplain: Lambdas cannot declare fields; the tutorial gives that as a reason to move on.
A static nested class could hold the field, but the tutorial reserves it for wider visibility; for a one-off need that declares a field it points to an anonymous class.
Right: an anonymous class can declare fields and extra methods, which a lambda cannot.
That widens access unnecessarily.
questions.explain: Needing fields moves the choice from a lambda to an anonymous class.
questions.rule: Needing state outgrows the lambda.

questions.q: Sort these needs by whether a lambda is enough or the tutorial points to a class-based construct.

items.t: Run an action on each element of a list
Respond when a process reports an error
Create three separate objects of a named helper type
Give a one-off object its own fields
Add extra methods to a one-off object
Supply a simple instance of a one-method interface

questions.explain: One unit of behaviour suits a lambda. A constructor, a named type, fields or extra methods call for a class.
questions.rule: Any heavier need rules the lambda out.
questions.teaches: A single heavier need, such as a constructor, a named type, fields or extra methods, is enough to rule a lambda out.

questions.q: A game-level class needs a helper type used by many of its methods. It needs no local variables and does not touch any level instance data. Which construct fits?
options: A local class in one of the methods
An anonymous class in each method
An inner class
A static nested class
optionExplain: It would be visible only in that method.
It would repeat the code and cannot be named.
It would need an enclosing instance that it does not use.
Right: widely available, no locals, no enclosing instance needed.
questions.explain: A nested class is for widely available types, and static suffices without an enclosing instance.
questions.rule: Wide use, no locals, no outer data: static nested.
questions.teaches: A type used across several methods, without local variables or outer instance data, is the case for a static nested class.

questions.q: A program needs a variable that can hold only NORTH, SOUTH, EAST or WEST. Which is the best fit?
options: An enum type with those four constants
An int where 0 to 3 stand for the directions
A free-text string that the user types
A boolean field named direction
optionExplain: Right: A fixed set of named values is what enums are for. The card next shows why.
Any int could then be stored.
Any text could then be stored.
Four values do not fit two states.
questions.explain: A fixed set of named values is what enums are for. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: Use an enum for a fixed set of named constants, and write the bare constant names as switch case labels.

questions.q: By convention, the names of enum constants are written in ____ case.
questions.explain: Constants are conventionally uppercase.
questions.rule: Uppercase constants.

questions.q: According to the tutorial, which case label is used in a switch on a Day variable?
options: case Day.MONDAY:
case MONDAY:
case 1:
case Day:
optionExplain: The tutorial uses the bare name.
Right: the bare constant name.
The switch tests an enum, not a number.
That names the type, not a constant.
questions.explain: The tutorial's EnumTest writes the plain constant names as labels.
questions.rule: Bare names in case labels.

questions.q: True or false: In a switch with cases for MONDAY, FRIDAY, and the two weekend days, plus default, a Day of WEDNESDAY runs the default branch.
questions.explain: No label matches WEDNESDAY, so default covers it.
questions.rule: default catches the rest.

questions.q: A method takes a Day parameter. A caller tries to pass the number 3 instead of a constant. What happens?
options: It is accepted, since 3 stands for the fourth day of the week
It is accepted and quietly converted to THURSDAY
It is rejected, since only a Day constant fits that parameter
It is accepted, but only when used inside a switch
optionExplain: Numbers have no automatic meaning for an enum.
No conversion exists.
Right: A variable of an enum type must equal one of its declared constants.
A switch does not change the rule.
questions.explain: A variable of an enum type must equal one of its declared constants.
questions.rule: Enum types admit only their constants.
questions.teaches: An enum-typed variable or parameter can hold only one of the declared constants, so a number cannot be passed in its place.

questions.q: Sort these sets by whether the tutorial's reasoning makes them good candidates for an enum.

items.t: The three states of a traffic light
The suits of a deck of cards
The planets of the solar system
The names of today's website visitors
Amounts typed into a form
The items in a shopping basket

questions.explain: Sets fixed when the program is written fit enums; data that arrives at run time does not.
questions.rule: Fixed at write time means enum.
questions.teaches: A small set that is natural to the problem, such as card suits, is a sensible enum even when it has only a few members.

questions.q: True or false: An enum type can have fields and a constructor.
questions.explain: An enum declaration defines a class, so it can hold more than names. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: An enum is a class whose constants are created by its constructor, listed first, and visited with values().

questions.q: The compiler-added static method that returns all the constants of an enum in declaration order is ____().
questions.explain: values() returns an array of the constants in the order declared.
questions.rule: values() lists the constants.

questions.q: In enum Coin { PENNY(1), DIME(10) ... } followed by fields and a constructor, what must end the constant list?
options: A comma
A closing brace
Nothing; the list ends by itself
A semicolon
optionExplain: A comma separates constants and does not end the list.
The brace ends the whole enum.
The semicolon is required when members follow.
Right: fields or methods follow, so the list is closed with a semicolon.
questions.explain: A semicolon separates the constant list from the members that follow.
questions.rule: Constants first, then a semicolon.

questions.q: True or false: If Coin declared DIME before PENNY, then Coin.values() would return DIME first.
questions.explain: values() follows declaration order.
questions.rule: Order of declaration is order of values().

questions.q: True or false: An enum type can be a subclass of String.
questions.explain: Every enum implicitly extends java.lang.Enum, and a class can have only one parent, so an enum cannot extend another class such as String.
questions.rule: Enums extend Enum, so nothing else.
questions.teaches: Every enum implicitly extends java.lang.Enum, and because a class has only one parent, an enum cannot extend any other class.

questions.q: In a delivery app, enum Speed { STANDARD(5), EXPRESS(2); ... } has a constructor taking days. Another class writes new Speed(3). Why is it rejected?
options: Only the declaration creates enum constants
The constructor needs an extra name argument
The call works only inside a switch statement
The number 3 is not a valid count of days
optionExplain: Right: The constants listed in the declaration are the only instances that will exist.
The number of arguments is not the problem.
A switch does not create enum objects.
The value is irrelevant to the rule.
questions.explain: The constants listed in the declaration are the only instances that will exist.
questions.rule: No new instances from outside the enum.
questions.teaches: The constants listed in the declaration are the only instances of the enum that will ever exist.

questions.q: In the Planet example, if Earth weight 175 is converted to a mass and then back, the EARTH line printed by the loop shows a weight of ____.
questions.explain: The mass was derived from the Earth weight, so converting back for Earth gives the original 175.
questions.rule: The loop over values() covers every constant.

questions.q: True or false: Adding an annotation to a method changes the logic that runs when the method is called.
questions.explain: An annotation is information about code, not code that runs in its place. The card next shows who does act on annotations.
questions.rule: Annotations describe code; they do not rewrite it.

questions.q: Which of these is one of the uses of annotations that the lesson lists?
options: Replacing a method body with generated code while the program runs
Changing the access level of a field when the program starts
Giving the compiler information, for example to find errors or hide warnings
Choosing which Java version a source file may be compiled with
optionExplain: Annotations are metadata, so they do not swap in new method bodies.
Annotations do not alter access levels; they only describe code.
This is one of the three listed uses: compiler information, build or deployment processing, and runtime examination.
Version choice is a build setting, not a listed use of annotations.
questions.explain: The lesson names three uses: information for the compiler, compile-time and deployment-time processing by tools, and runtime examination.
questions.rule: Three uses: compiler, build or deployment tools, runtime.

questions.q: A build script scans source files for methods tagged with an owner annotation and prints a table of owners. Which use of annotations is this?
options: Processing by a tool at build or deployment time
Information the compiler uses to detect errors
Examination of the annotation by the running program
A direct change to how the tagged methods behave
optionExplain: A tool reads the annotations outside the compiler and produces output, which is the build-time processing use.
The script prints a table; it does not look for errors in the code.
The script reads source files before the program runs at all.
Tagging only labels the methods; their behaviour is untouched.
questions.explain: The script is a separate tool reading the labels to produce a report, so it is tool processing, not compiler checking or runtime inspection.
questions.rule: Match the reader to the use: compiler, tool, or running program.

questions.q: A method total() adds two numbers. Someone deletes a Reviewed annotation from it, and no tool in the project reads that annotation. What happens to the value total() returns?
options: It changes, because the method loses a safety check
The code fails to compile without the annotation
It drops to zero until the annotation is restored
It stays the same, since the label was not part of the logic
optionExplain: Annotations are not checks that run inside the method.
Nothing requires a custom marker to be present for compilation.
There is no mechanism that zeroes a result when a label is removed.
The sum comes from the method body; with no reader, the label affected nothing.
questions.explain: Removing a label that nothing reads changes no behaviour, because the annotation never took part in the computation.
questions.rule: No reader, no effect.

questions.q: True or false: A compiler can turn an annotation into a build failure even though the annotation does not change what the code does.
questions.explain: The Override annotation is read by the compiler, which reports an error when the marked method does not override anything. The method body is untouched, yet the build stops.
questions.rule: The reader, not the label, produces the effect.
questions.teaches: Effects come from readers: the compiler reads Override and stops the build on a mismatch, although the annotated code itself is unchanged.

questions.q: A test framework examines methods at run time for a marker annotation and calls each marked method. Which statements fit this setup? Select all that apply.
options: The framework is the reader that acts on the annotation
The marked methods keep the same code they had without the marker
This is runtime examination, one of the listed uses
The marker makes the method run, with no reader needed
Annotations can be examined only before the program starts
optionExplain: Right: the framework looks for the marker and then decides what to call.
Right: the marker is only a label on code that is otherwise unchanged.
Right: the lesson lists runtime examination as a use.
Tempting because the marker seems to cause the call, but the framework causes it.
Some annotations are kept so the running program can read them.
questions.explain: The marker is a selector: the framework reads it while running and chooses what to call. The methods themselves stay unchanged.
questions.rule: A framework can use annotations purely as selection labels.
questions.teaches: A framework can use an annotation as a selector: the label decides which code it acts on, while the labelled code stays unchanged.

questions.q: True or false: An annotation that has no elements can be written without any parentheses.
questions.explain: With no elements there is nothing to put in parentheses, so they may be left off. The card next shows the other short forms.
questions.rule: No elements, no parentheses needed.

questions.q: An annotation type named Stable has no elements. Which line applies it to a class?
options: Stable() class Box { }
@Stable class Box { }
@Stable[] class Box { }
#Stable class Box { }
optionExplain: Without the at sign this is not an annotation.
The at sign plus the name is the whole annotation when there are no elements.
Square brackets are for arrays, not annotation syntax.
The hash sign has no meaning here; annotations begin with an at sign.
questions.explain: Annotations begin with an at sign; a type without elements needs nothing more.
questions.rule: At sign, name, optional element pairs.

questions.q: An annotation type Limit has one element, int value(). Complete the short form that sets it to 5: @Limit(____)
questions.explain: Because the only element is named value, its name and equals sign can be dropped, leaving just the value.
questions.rule: A sole element named value needs no name at the use site.

questions.q: A type Cap declares one element, int max(). What happens with the line @Cap(8)?
options: It compiles and sets max to 8, since there is only one element
It compiles and leaves max at its default
It does not compile, since the shorthand needs the element to be named value
It compiles but prints a warning about the missing name
optionExplain: A single element is not enough; the element must be named value.
Nothing makes a bare number fall back to a default.
The nameless form is allowed only for an element called value; here the name max must be written out.
This is an error, not a warning.
questions.explain: Renaming the element from value to max removes the shorthand: the use must read @Cap(max = 8).
questions.rule: The shorthand depends on the element name value.

questions.q: Type Window has elements int width() default 1 and int height() default 1. Exactly one of these uses breaks a syntax rule. Which one?
options: @Window(width = 4, height = 3)
@Window(width = 4)
@Window(height = 3)
@Window(4, 3)
optionExplain: Both elements are named, which is fine.
Omitting height is fine since it has a default.
