Omitting width is fine since it has a default.
With several elements, each value needs its element name; the nameless form works only for a single element called value.
questions.explain: Only the bare numbers break the rule, because neither element is called value and there are two of them.
questions.rule: Several elements always need names.

questions.q: Sort each placement by what the annotation labels.

items.t: Owner before a class declaration
Entity before a field declaration
NonNull on the type inside a cast
Readonly on a type argument in an implements clause
Critical on the exception type after throws
Deprecated before a method declaration

questions.explain: Declaration annotations label a class, field or method being declared. Type annotations label where a type is used, including the argument inside angle brackets of an implements clause.
questions.rule: Where the annotation sits tells you whether it labels a declaration or a type use.
questions.teaches: An annotation can sit on a type argument inside angle brackets, not only on a whole type, as in List with a marked type parameter.

questions.q: Which declaration starts a new annotation type named Audit?
options: annotation Audit { }
@interface Audit { }
interface @Audit { }
@annotation Audit { }
optionExplain: Java has no plain keyword annotation for this.
The keyword interface preceded by an at sign begins an annotation type. The card next shows what goes inside.
The at sign goes before interface, not before the name.
There is no annotation keyword after the at sign.
questions.explain: The keyword interface preceded by an at sign begins an annotation type. The card next shows what goes inside.
questions.rule: @interface starts an annotation type.

questions.q: Match each piece of an annotation declaration to its job.
pairs: Starts the declaration of an annotation type
Lets users leave that element out
An element that takes several values
Shows its uses in generated Javadoc
questions.explain: Each piece does one job: @interface declares the type, default makes an element optional, an array type allows several values, and Documented affects Javadoc.
questions.rule: Know the job of each piece of a declaration.

questions.q: Task is declared as @interface Task { int id(); int priority() default 3; int[] codes(); }. Which use is valid?
options: @Task(id = 1)
@Task(id = 1, codes = {4, 9})
@Task(id = 1, codes = [4, 9])
@Task(codes = {4, 9})
optionExplain: codes has no default, so it must be given.
id and codes lack defaults, so both are required; the array uses braces; priority may be omitted.
Square brackets are not how array values are written.
id has no default, so it must be given.
questions.explain: A valid use supplies every element without a default and writes array values in braces.
questions.rule: Check required elements, then array syntax.

questions.q: True or false: If the default is removed from priority in Task, an existing use that omits priority stays valid.
questions.explain: Without a default, priority becomes a required element, so every use that leaves it out stops being valid.
questions.rule: Removing a default makes the element required.

questions.q: A team wants every use of their Ticket annotation to appear in generated Javadoc. Where does Documented belong?
options: Above each class that carries a Ticket
Above the import line for Ticket
On the declaration of the Ticket annotation type
On every element inside Ticket
optionExplain: Putting it on each user class would repeat work and does not describe the type.
Imports are not annotated.
Documented describes the annotation type itself, so it is placed on the type's definition.
The annotation type as a whole is marked, not its elements.
questions.explain: Marking the type once makes all of its uses appear in Javadoc.
questions.rule: Documented goes on the annotation type.

questions.q: Which element declaration inside an annotation type is written wrongly?
options: int id();
int level() default 2;
String[] labels();
int retries default 3;
optionExplain: This is a normal required element.
This is well formed: parentheses first, then the default value.
An array element is declared with the array type and parentheses.
Elements are written like methods, so the empty parentheses are required before default.
questions.explain: The retries line lacks the parentheses that every element needs.
questions.rule: Elements need a type, a name and parentheses.

questions.q: A recipe app defines an annotation for dishes. Every dish must state its servings. Most dishes have heat level 1, and a few are hotter. Which declaration fits that plan?
options: @interface Dish { int servings(); int heat() default 1; }
@interface Dish { int servings() default 1; int heat(); }
@interface Dish { int servings() default 1; int heat() default 1; }
@interface Dish { int servings(); int heat(); }
optionExplain: Servings has no default so each use must state it; heat has the common value as its default.
This makes heat required and servings optional, the reverse of the plan.
Nothing would be required, so a dish could omit servings.
Every dish would have to spell out heat even when it is the usual 1.
questions.explain: A default suits the value most uses share; leaving it off forces users to decide.
questions.rule: Defaults for shared values; none for values each use must state.
questions.teaches: Giving or withholding a default is a design choice: use a default for the value most uses share, and none for a value every use must decide.

questions.q: A method marked Override does not match any method in its superclass. What does the compiler do?
options: It ignores the mark and continues
It prints a warning and continues
It reports an error
It compiles, and fails when the method is called
optionExplain: Ignoring would defeat the purpose of the mark.
A warning would let the mismatch slip through; it is stricter than that.
A failed override is a compile error. The card next shows why this is useful.
The check happens at compile time, not at call time.
questions.explain: A failed override is a compile error. The card next shows why this is useful.
questions.rule: A mismatched Override is an error.

questions.q: Match each predefined annotation to what it does.
pairs: Compiler warns at each use of the marked element
Compiler errors when nothing is overridden
Hides the warning categories you name
States an interface is meant to have one abstract method
questions.explain: Deprecated warns, Override errors on mismatch, SuppressWarnings hides named categories, and FunctionalInterface states intent for a single abstract method.
questions.rule: Each annotation has its own compiler reaction.

questions.q: A subclass author meant to replace the parent method speak() but typed speek(). Name the annotation, written without the at sign, that on the subclass method would make the compiler report the slip: ____
questions.explain: With Override, the compiler checks that some superclass method matches, and reports an error for speek.
questions.rule: Override is the check against the superclass.

questions.q: A method carries a SuppressWarnings naming only the deprecation category. It calls a deprecated method and also uses a raw list from pre-generics code. What does the compiler report?
options: No warnings at all, since one category silences the whole method
An unchecked warning for the raw list use, and none for the deprecated call
A deprecation warning, since the annotation does not cover calls
An error, since the other category was left unnamed
optionExplain: The annotation hides only the categories it names.
Suppression is per category: deprecation is hidden, but unchecked is a separate category and still shows.
The named category covers the deprecated call.
Missing categories are not errors; they stay warnings.
questions.explain: Naming one category does not hide the other, so the unchecked warning remains.
questions.rule: Suppress only what you name.

questions.q: A learner reasons: Step 1, I put Override on a method that has no match in the parent. Step 2, the compiler will only print a warning. Step 3, so the build still succeeds. Which step is wrong?
options: Step 1, since Override cannot go on a method in a subclass
Step 3, since a warning always stops the build
Step 2, since an Override mismatch is a compile error
None of the steps; all three hold
optionExplain: Override is meant for subclass methods.
A warning does not stop a build; the real problem is that this is not a warning.
A mismatch is an error, so the build fails; Step 3 follows from a false Step 2.
Step 2 is false, so not all steps hold.
questions.explain: The false claim is Step 2; Deprecated warns, but Override errors.
questions.rule: Override mismatch is an error, not a warning.

questions.q: A generic helper method takes a varargs parameter. Its author states that the body does nothing unsafe with that parameter, so callers get no related unchecked warnings. Which predefined annotation expresses this?
options: Deprecated
FunctionalInterface
Override
SafeVarargs
optionExplain: Deprecated warns callers off the method.
FunctionalInterface concerns interface shape.
Override concerns superclass methods.
SafeVarargs, placed on a method or constructor, asserts that its varargs parameter is not used unsafely and hides the related unchecked warnings.
questions.explain: SafeVarargs is an assertion by the method's author, placed on a method or constructor.
questions.rule: SafeVarargs asserts safe varargs use.
questions.teaches: SafeVarargs goes on a method or constructor and asserts that its varargs parameter is not used unsafely, which hides the related unchecked warnings.

questions.q: Which retention policy keeps an annotation in a form the running program can read through reflection?
options: SOURCE
CLASS
TYPE
RUNTIME
optionExplain: Source-only annotations are gone before the program runs.
CLASS keeps them in the class file, but the JVM ignores them.
TYPE is a target value, not a retention policy.
RUNTIME is kept by the JVM and readable by reflection.
questions.explain: Only RUNTIME makes the JVM keep the annotation for the running program. The card next lays out all three policies.
questions.rule: RUNTIME retention makes an annotation readable while the program runs.

questions.q: Match each meta-annotation to what it controls.
pairs: Which kinds of element may carry it
Whether a class query checks the superclass
questions.explain: Each meta-annotation governs one aspect of the annotation it marks.
questions.rule: One meta-annotation, one aspect.

questions.q: A framework will scan methods at run time for a marker annotation named Job and must reject Job on fields. Which pair of meta-annotations on Job achieves this?
options: Retention set to SOURCE and Target set to METHOD
Retention set to RUNTIME and Target set to METHOD
Retention set to RUNTIME and Target set to FIELD
Documented together with Inherited
optionExplain: SOURCE would vanish before the program runs.
RUNTIME lets the framework read it while running, and METHOD limits placement to methods.
FIELD would allow fields and exclude methods.
These affect Javadoc and class inheritance, not retention or placement.
questions.explain: Retention decides whether the framework can see the annotation; Target decides where it may appear.
questions.rule: Pair Retention with Target for runtime markers.

questions.q: Which statements about the CLASS retention policy match the tutorial? Select all that apply.
options: Running code can read it through reflection
The compiler records it in the class file
The JVM ignores it
It is discarded by the compiler, like SOURCE
It is the same policy as RUNTIME
optionExplain: That is RUNTIME; the JVM ignores CLASS annotations.
Right: that is what separates CLASS from SOURCE.
Right: the JVM does not keep it for the running program.
SOURCE is discarded earlier; CLASS survives into the class file.
RUNTIME differs because the JVM keeps it.
questions.explain: CLASS sits between the two others: it reaches the class file but is not kept for the running program.
questions.rule: CLASS is stored but ignored by the JVM.

questions.q: Annotation Tag is not marked Inherited. Base carries Tag, and Sub extends Base without writing Tag. What does a query for Tag on Sub find?
options: Nothing, since Tag is not inherited by default
The Tag from Base, since subclasses automatically copy annotations
The Tag from Base, but only at run time
A compile error, since Sub lacks the annotation
optionExplain: Without Inherited, the query looks only at Sub. Marking Tag as Inherited would let the query find the Tag on Base.
Copying happens only for Inherited annotations.
Runtime does not change the default.
Omitting an annotation is not an error.
questions.explain: Inheritance of an annotation must be requested with Inherited.
questions.rule: No Inherited, no superclass lookup.

questions.q: True or false: Marking an annotation type Inherited makes an overriding method in a subclass pick up the annotation from the parent method.
questions.explain: Inherited applies only to class declarations, so method annotations are not carried down to overriding methods.
questions.rule: Inherited covers class declarations only.
questions.teaches: Inherited is limited to class declarations; it does not pass annotations from a method to the methods that override it.

questions.section: Type Annotations and Pluggable Type Systems
questions.q: True or false: Java SE 8 itself includes a framework that checks type annotations for you.
questions.explain: Java SE 8 provides the annotation hooks, but the checking comes from separate modules. The card next shows how they plug in.
questions.rule: Checking comes from pluggable modules, not from SE 8 itself.

questions.section: Type Annotations and Pluggable Type Systems
questions.q: Put the steps of the non-null checking workflow in order.
items: Obtain a non-null checker module
Annotate the variable as non-null
Compile with the module named on the command line
Read the warnings the compiler prints
Edit the code until the warnings stop
questions.explain: The module and the annotation must exist before compiling; the warnings then guide the edits, repeated until none remain.
questions.rule: Checker and annotation first, compile, then fix warnings.

questions.section: Type Annotations and Pluggable Type Systems
questions.q: A developer wants the compiler to warn when a text variable might hold something that is not a valid regular expression. Which approach matches the tutorial?
options: Mark the annotation type with Retention set to RUNTIME and recompile
Annotate the variable and compile with a regular-expression checker module
Wait for the SE 8 compiler's built-in regex check
Place Override on the variable declaration
optionExplain: Retention decides how long an annotation lives and does not check anything.
A regular-expression checker is one of the ready-made pluggable modules, used the same way as the non-null one.
SE 8 ships no checking framework.
Override applies to methods, not variables.
questions.explain: Choose a checker module for the property, annotate, and compile with it.
questions.rule: Pick the module that matches the property.

questions.section: Type Annotations and Pluggable Type Systems
questions.q: A developer annotates a variable as non-null but compiles without any checker module. What does the annotation achieve at compile time?
options: The compiler itself rejects every possible null assignment
A warning for each null, since SE 8 ships a null checker
Nothing beyond a label, since no module is there to check it
A runtime guard that blocks null values
optionExplain: The compiler has no built-in null analysis here.
SE 8 includes no such checker.
Checking is done by modules that run with the compiler; with none, no analysis happens.
The annotation does not insert code at run time.
questions.explain: Without a module the annotation changes nothing.
questions.rule: No checker, no checking.

questions.section: Type Annotations and Pluggable Type Systems
questions.q: Which statements about the pluggable checking approach match the tutorial? Select all that apply.
options: Several modules can be used at once
Each module can look for a different kind of error
Java SE 8 includes the checking framework itself
The modules run together with the compiler
The warnings appear only after the program is run
optionExplain: Right: modules can be combined.
Right: one may check for null, another for something else.
SE 8 does not include one; modules are written or downloaded.
Right: they run alongside the compiler.
The warnings appear at compile time.
questions.explain: Modules are add-ons that run with the compiler, so several can run at once, each for a different property.
questions.rule: Modules are add-ons run with the compiler.

questions.section: Type Annotations and Pluggable Type Systems
questions.q: A team wants warnings when shared data is touched without holding a lock. According to the tutorial, what kind of module exists for that?
options: A mutex lock module from the Checker Framework, used like the non-null one
A built-in Java SE 8 lock checker enabled by a compiler flag
A Retention policy that records lock use
A Target value that limits the data to one thread
optionExplain: The Checker Framework includes a mutex lock module, so the same annotate-and-compile pattern covers locking.
SE 8 has no built-in checker framework.
Retention controls annotation lifetime, not lock tracking.
Target controls placement of annotations, not threads.
questions.explain: The pattern is general: each property has its own module.
questions.rule: Same pattern, different module.
questions.teaches: The annotate-and-compile pattern works for properties beyond null: the Checker Framework also provides a mutex lock module for lock discipline.

questions.q: True or false: Writing the same annotation type twice on one method compiles without any special declaration.
questions.explain: Repeating needs the type to be declared repeatable, with a container. The card next shows the two declarations.
questions.rule: Repeating needs explicit support.

questions.q: The container annotation must have an array element named ____.
questions.explain: The container's element must be called value, be an array, and hold the repeatable annotation type.
questions.rule: The container element is named value.

questions.q: Annotation Tag has one element, int level(), and is marked Repeatable naming Tags. Which container declaration is correct?
options: @interface Tags { Tag value(); }
@interface Tags { Tag[] items(); }
@interface Tags { Tag[] value(); }
@interface Tags { int[] value(); }
optionExplain: Not an array, so it cannot hold several Tag uses.
Wrong name; the element must be called value.
The element is called value and is an array of Tag.
The component type must be Tag, not int.
questions.explain: Name, array shape and component type must all match the rule.
questions.rule: value, array, repeatable type.

questions.q: Tag is marked Repeatable naming Tags, but Tags is declared with the single element Tag item(). The compiler complains. What is the best diagnosis?
options: The container element must be named value and be an array of Tag
Repeatable can be placed only on container types
Tag needs a Retention policy before it can be repeated
The container must appear before Tag in the file
optionExplain: Item is both misnamed and not an array, so it breaks the container rule.
Repeatable goes on the repeatable type, not the container.
Retention is not what makes repeating possible.
Order of declarations in a file is not the rule.
questions.explain: The container shape is fixed by rule.
questions.rule: Check the container shape first.

questions.q: True or false: Calling getAnnotation with the Tag class returns every repeated Tag on an element in one go.
questions.explain: That call returns one annotation only when exactly one is present, which keeps old code working. The Java SE 8 call getAnnotationsByType scans the container and returns all the repeats.
questions.rule: Use getAnnotationsByType for repeats.

questions.q: A designer adds an annotation Approved that may mark methods and fields. Approving twice makes no sense there. Which design fits the tutorial's view of how often an annotation may appear?
options: Mark Approved repeatable, then ignore any extra uses
Add a container type anyway, since every annotation needs one
Use Inherited so duplicate uses get merged
Restrict Target to methods and fields and leave Repeatable off, so each element has at most one
optionExplain: That invites the duplicates the designer wants to prevent.
Only repeatable annotations need a container.
Inherited concerns superclasses, not duplicates.
Without Repeatable an annotation appears zero or one time per element, and Target limits where it goes.
questions.explain: Leaving Repeatable off keeps the limit; Target narrows placement.
questions.rule: Repeatable is a design choice.
questions.teaches: Cardinality is a design choice: an annotation appears zero or one time unless marked Repeatable, and Target can narrow where it may go.

questions.q: Two teams build programs that must work together without reading each other's code. What is the most workable way to let them cooperate?
options: Agree on a published list of operations both sides rely on
Share all source code so each side can read the other's logic
Let one team write both halves of the program
Make every method in both programs available to the other team
optionExplain: Right: a shared list of operations is the idea behind an interface.
Reading everything would work for two people, but it ties each side to the other's internals.
This removes the cooperation problem instead of solving it.
Exposing everything means any change on either side can break the other.
questions.explain: A fixed list of agreed operations lets each side work alone. The card next explains this idea.
questions.rule: An interface is a published contract that lets callers and implementers change their own code independently as long as the contract itself holds.

questions.q: In Java, a(n) ____ is the kind of reference type that the tutorial compares to a contract listing methods a class agrees to provide.
questions.explain: The tutorial presents the interface as the contract; classes that implement it fulfil the contract.
questions.rule: An interface is the contract; a class is one way of keeping it.

questions.q: A bank publishes a Java interface for looking up account balances, and a shop app calls it. The bank wants to move to a new database. What does the contract idea say about this change?
options: The shop must be recompiled with the bank's new database code before it can run
The bank may change its internals if it still implements the published interface
The bank must first ask the shop to approve the new database
The bank may not change anything until the shop releases a new version of its app
optionExplain: The shop never saw the database, so it has no reason to take on the bank's new code.
Right: callers depend on the interface, not on the bank's internals.
Approval is not needed when the published contract stays unchanged.
Both sides are meant to be free to change their own code.
questions.explain: Hiding the implementation behind the interface is what lets both sides evolve separately.
questions.rule: Change the inside freely; keep the published interface stable.

questions.q: Two car makers each write a class implementing the same published OperateCar interface, and they code its signalTurn method very differently. What follows for a guidance program that calls signalTurn?
options: It must be rewritten for each maker's version of the method
It works with only the maker that wrote the interface
It works with both makers' cars, whoever built them
The two makers must agree to code signalTurn in the same way
optionExplain: The caller sees only the shared signature, so the internal differences stay hidden.
Any class that implements the interface can be used by the caller.
Right: the caller depends only on the signature, so each implementation is free to differ.
The contract fixes what the method is called and takes, not how it does its work.
questions.explain: Many classes can honour one contract in different ways, and callers need not care which one they get.
questions.rule: One contract, many implementations.
questions.teaches: Many different classes can implement the same interface, each in its own way, and a caller written against the interface works with all of them.

questions.q: True or false: If a vendor renames one method in its published interface, customer code that calls the old name keeps working.
questions.explain: Customers depend on the published signatures, so a renamed method changes the contract and breaks them.
questions.rule: The freedom to change covers internals, not the interface.

questions.q: Wall sockets follow a published standard of plug shape and voltage. Appliance makers and power suppliers do not see each other's designs. Which feature of a Java interface does the standard match, and what does it leave open?
options: The implementing class; the standard leaves the plug shape open
The shared boundary; how the plug is shaped stays open
The method body; the standard leaves the voltage open
The shared boundary; each side's inner workings stay open
optionExplain: The plug shape is the boundary itself, which the standard fixes.
The shape and voltage are what the standard fixes.
A contract lists what is offered, and the voltage belongs to what is fixed.
Right: the standard fixes only the boundary, so appliances and power plants can each vary inside.
questions.explain: The standard plays the role of the interface: what is fixed is small, and everything else is free.
questions.rule: Fix the boundary, free the rest.
questions.teaches: The smaller and more precise the shared boundary, the more freedom each side keeps; anything not written into the interface can vary between implementations.

questions.q: True or false: An interface can declare an ordinary instance field that each implementing object stores separately.
questions.explain: An interface holds constants, not per-object state. The card next lists what it may contain.
questions.hint: Think about what an interface cannot do.
questions.rule: An interface holds only constants, method signatures, default methods, static methods and nested types, and it cannot be instantiated.

questions.q: Which of these can appear in an interface body, according to the tutorial? Select all that apply.
options: A constant
A method signature with no body
A static method with a body
A constructor
A field that differs for each object
optionExplain: Right: constants are on the allowed list.
Right: abstract method signatures are the core of an interface.
Right: static methods may have bodies.
Constructors build objects, and an interface is never instantiated, so none is listed.
Per-object state needs instance fields, which interfaces do not have.
questions.explain: Constants, signatures, default methods, static methods and nested types make up the list.
questions.rule: Learn the five kinds of member.

questions.q: A developer writes interface Logger with a method log(String msg) followed by braces that print msg. The compiler rejects it. Which change keeps the body and fits the tutorial's rules?
options: Add the abstract modifier to log
Add the final modifier to log
Add the default modifier to log
Move the braces into a constructor of Logger
optionExplain: An abstract method has no body, so the braces would still be rejected.
Final stops overriding; it does not allow a body in an interface method.
Right: a default method may carry a body in an interface.
Interfaces have no constructors.
questions.explain: Only default and static methods may have a body. A plain signature must end with a semicolon.
questions.rule: Body means default or static.

questions.q: True or false: An interface may declare a nested type, such as an enum for its method signatures to use.
questions.explain: Nested types are on the list of allowed members, so an enum such as a turning direction can live inside the interface that needs it.
questions.rule: Nested types are allowed in interfaces.
questions.teaches: Nested types, such as an enum used by the interface's own method signatures, may be declared inside the interface that needs them.

questions.q: Greeter is an interface. Its only method is then changed from an abstract signature to a default method with a body. Can the programmer now write new Greeter() to get an object?
options: Yes, because with no abstract methods nothing is missing from the type
Yes, but only from code in the same package as the interface
Yes, if the interface is declared public
No; interfaces cannot be instantiated, whatever their members
optionExplain: Missing methods are not the reason; an interface is a type to implement, not to instantiate.
Package access does not change the rule.
Public controls who can see the interface, not whether it can be instantiated.
Right: the ban on instantiation does not depend on whether methods have bodies.
questions.explain: Instantiation is ruled out for every interface, whatever its members.
questions.rule: Interfaces are never instantiated.

questions.q: An interface CoffeeMachine is being designed. Sort each proposed member by whether the tutorial's list allows it in the interface body.

items.t: A constant for the maximum water temperature
A default method that prints a standard greeting
A signature brew with no body
A static method that returns a standard machine
A constructor that takes the tank size
A field holding how many cups this machine has made

questions.explain: Constants, signatures, default and static methods are listed. A constructor or a per-object counter would need an object, and interfaces are not instantiated.
questions.rule: Ask whether the member needs an object of its own.
questions.teaches: A constructor has no place in an interface because there is never an object of the interface type to initialise; only classes build objects.

questions.q: How many parents can a class extend, and how many parents can an interface extend?
options: A class one class; an interface any number of interfaces
A class any number of classes; an interface one interface
Both exactly one parent
Both any number of parents
optionExplain: Right: the two rules differ.
This reverses the rules.
Interfaces are allowed to list several parents.
A class is limited to a single parent class.
questions.explain: Interfaces may list many parents while a class may extend one class. The card next gives the whole declaration.
questions.rule: An interface declaration is optional modifiers, the interface keyword, a name, an optional comma-separated extends list of any length, and a body, and public decides whether other packages may use it.

questions.q: Put the parts of an interface declaration in the order the tutorial gives them.
items: Optional modifiers such as public
The keyword interface
The interface name
The optional extends list of parent interfaces
The body in braces
questions.explain: The header runs from modifiers to the name and any parents, and the braces hold the members.
questions.rule: Modifiers, keyword, name, extends list, body.

questions.q: An interface Report is declared without the public modifier in package billing. A class in package shipping tries to implement Report. What does the tutorial's rule say?
options: It can, because an interface is visible to every package by default
It cannot, since only billing classes may use a non-public interface
It can, once shipping imports every class of billing
It can, but only through the extends keyword
optionExplain: Visibility to all packages needs the public modifier.
Right: without public, use is limited to the same package.
Importing does not widen who may use a non-public interface.
The keyword used does not change the access rule.
questions.explain: The public modifier is what opens an interface to other packages.
questions.rule: No public, no use outside the package.

questions.q: True or false: A concrete class that implements an interface which extends two parent interfaces, each with only abstract methods, must supply the methods of both parents as well as those of the child.
questions.explain: Extending passes the parents' signatures on, so the child interface carries all of them. The tutorial's DoItPlus extends one parent, DoIt, and must be implemented with all three methods; the two-parent case follows the same rule and goes beyond the tutorial.
questions.rule: A child interface carries its parents' methods.
questions.teaches: An interface that extends others inherits their method signatures, so implementing the child interface means supplying the methods of every parent too.

questions.q: Interface Hybrid extends Car and Boat, both interfaces, and compiles. A programmer rewrites Hybrid as a class: class Hybrid extends Car, Boat, where Car and Boat are now classes. What does the tutorial predict?
options: It compiles, since extends accepts a list of parents for any type
It compiles but inherits only from Car
It compiles if Car and Boat are in the same package
It is not allowed, because a class extends only one class
optionExplain: The list is allowed after extends only in an interface.
Java rejects the declaration rather than inheriting from the first parent.
Package does not change the single-parent limit.
Right: the many-parents freedom is only for interfaces.
questions.explain: Changing from interfaces to classes removes the permission to list several parents.
questions.rule: Many parents are allowed for interfaces only.

questions.q: A student writes: public interface Shape extends Drawable, Resizable implements Serializable { }. Which statement about it fits the tutorial?
options: It is correct, since an interface may implement any number of interfaces
Only the word public is wrong, because interfaces must be package-private
Interfaces use extends for parents, so implements has no place here
Only the two-name extends list is wrong, since it allows one parent
optionExplain: Implementing is what classes do; interfaces extend.
The tutorial allows public interfaces.
Right: an interface extends other interfaces, while a class is the one that implements.
An interface may list any number of parents.
questions.explain: The two verbs split the roles: classes implement interfaces, and interfaces extend interfaces.
questions.rule: Classes implement; interfaces extend.
questions.teaches: The verb implements belongs to classes; even when an interface builds on several interfaces it uses extends, never implements.

questions.q: True or false: A constant declared in an interface as int LIMIT = 5; can be reassigned by a class that implements the interface.
questions.explain: Interface constants are implicitly final. The card next explains which modifiers are implied.
questions.rule: In an interface, methods are implicitly public, plain ones are also abstract, and constants are implicitly public, static and final.

questions.q: A constant declared inside an interface is implicitly public, static and ____.
questions.explain: Public, static and final are all implied for an interface constant.
questions.rule: Interface constants are public static final.

questions.q: Inside an interface, which declaration means the same as double RATE = 0.2; with no modifiers written?
options: private static final double RATE = 0.2;
public static final double RATE = 0.2;
public double RATE = 0.2;
protected final double RATE = 0.2;
optionExplain: Private would hide the constant from implementers, but the implied access is public.
Right: constants are implicitly public, static and final.
Without static and final it would describe a changeable per-object field.
Protected is not the implied access, and the constant is also static.
questions.explain: Reading an interface means filling in the three implied words.
questions.rule: Constants are public static final.

questions.q: True or false: A constant declared in an interface is stored separately in each object of every class that implements the interface.
questions.explain: Because a constant is static, one value belongs to the interface, not to any object.
questions.rule: Static means one shared value.
questions.teaches: Since interface constants are static, there is one value belonging to the interface itself, shared by every implementing class instead of copied into each object.

questions.q: Interface Settings, declared public, contains int SIZE = 3; with no modifiers. Code in a different package reads Settings.SIZE. What happens?
options: It fails, because a field without a modifier is package-private
It fails, because SIZE needs an implementing object first
It works, because the constant is implicitly public and static
It works only if the other package's class implements Settings
optionExplain: In a class that would be so, but interface constants are implicitly public.
A static constant is read through the interface name, with no object.
Right: public lets the other package see it, and static lets it be read through the interface name.
Public access does not depend on implementing the interface.
questions.explain: Both implied words matter here: public for the other package, static for reading it without an object.
questions.rule: Implied public and static make interface constants easy to reach.

questions.q: A game-rules interface writes its members with no modifiers. Match each member to what the language implies for it.
pairs: Implicitly public, and has a body
questions.explain: What is implied depends on the member's kind: constant, plain method or default method.
questions.rule: Identify the kind of member first.
questions.teaches: The implied modifiers depend on the kind of member, so decide whether it is a constant, a plain method or a default or static method before saying what is implied.

questions.q: Class Kettle extends class Appliance and must also follow the Heater and Timer contracts, which are interfaces. Which header is written correctly?
options: class Kettle implements Heater, Timer extends Appliance { }
class Kettle extends Appliance, Heater, Timer
class Kettle extends Appliance implements Heater, Timer
class Kettle implements Appliance, Heater, Timer
optionExplain: The conventional order is extends first, then implements.
A class cannot extend several types, and interfaces go after implements.
Right: the extends clause comes first, then implements with commas.
Appliance is a class, so extends is the keyword for it.
questions.explain: Superclass first, interfaces after. The card next gives the rules.
questions.rule: A class names its interfaces after implements, after any extends, and must give a body to every abstract method they declare.

questions.q: By convention, the ____ clause of a class header follows the extends clause.
questions.explain: Extends comes first, and implements follows it.
questions.rule: Extends first, implements second.

questions.q: A concrete class Song implements Playable, which declares play and pause. Song defines only play. What does the tutorial's rule require?
options: Nothing, because a class implements only the first method listed
Song must define pause only if someone calls it
The interface must be changed to hold one method
Song must also define pause, or be declared abstract
optionExplain: A class takes on every method the interface declares.
The duty exists whether or not anyone calls the method.
The interface is the contract; the class has to meet it.
Right: every abstract method must get a body unless the class is abstract.
questions.explain: Implementing means meeting the whole contract, or admitting the class is unfinished by declaring it abstract.
questions.rule: Every abstract method needs a body, or the class is abstract.

questions.q: In RectanglePlus, the method isLargerThan(Relatable other) calls other.getArea() directly, and getArea exists only in RectanglePlus. Why does the compiler reject the call?
options: getArea is not public, so no other class may call it, not even this one
The compiler sees only Relatable's methods on that parameter
An interface method cannot call methods of its own class
The method must return an int and cannot call getArea
optionExplain: The method may well be public; the issue is the declared type of the parameter.
Right: the declared type decides what the compiler allows.
isLargerThan is in the class, and the class may call its own methods.
The return type does not stop a call to getArea.
questions.explain: A cast to RectanglePlus tells the compiler what the object really is, and then getArea is available.
questions.rule: Cast to reach class-specific members.
questions.teaches: A parameter declared with the interface type exposes only the interface's methods to the compiler; to use class-specific members, cast the parameter to the class.

questions.q: True or false: If a class implements two interfaces, it must supply bodies only for the methods of the interface listed first.
questions.explain: The clause lists every interface the class promises to honour, so all their abstract methods need bodies.
questions.rule: Every listed interface counts.

questions.q: A Recipe class implements Relatable and uses its number of steps as its size. This recipe has 8 steps and the other recipe has 12. Which return value of isLargerThan follows the convention?
optionExplain: Right: this recipe is smaller, and the convention returns -1 for less.
One means this object is larger, which is wrong here.
Zero means equal sizes.
The convention uses -1, 0 and 1, not the size difference.
questions.explain: The compiler checks only that the method exists with the right signature. The return convention lives in the comment, so the programmer must follow it.
questions.rule: Honour the convention in the contract.
questions.teaches: The compiler checks only the signature of an implemented method; conventions written in the contract's comment, such as returning -1, 0 or 1, are kept by the programmer.

questions.q: Pet is an interface and Dog is a class that implements Pet. Which statement is accepted by the compiler?
options: Pet p = new Dog();
Pet p = new Pet();
Dog d = new Pet();
Pet p = new Object();
optionExplain: Right: an object of an implementing class may be held in an interface-typed variable.
An interface is not instantiated.
Same problem: the interface cannot be instantiated.
Object does not implement Pet.
questions.explain: A variable of the interface type can refer to objects of implementing classes. The card next states the rule.
questions.rule: An interface name is a type: a variable of that type may refer to any object of an implementing class, and it exposes only the interface's methods.

questions.q: Where may an interface name appear as a type? Select all that apply.
options: A local variable
A method parameter
A method return type
An array element type
After new, to create an object of the interface itself
optionExplain: Right: variables may have an interface type.
Right: parameters may too.
Right: return types may too.
Right: arrays of an interface type are allowed.
An interface cannot be instantiated, so it cannot follow new.
questions.explain: An interface name is usable wherever a type name is allowed, except as the class to instantiate.
questions.rule: Use interface names as types, never to build objects.

questions.q: Chargeable declares charge(). Phone implements Chargeable and also has ring(). Given Chargeable c = new Phone(); which statement does the compiler reject?
options: c.charge();
((Phone) c).ring();
c.ring();
Phone p = (Phone) c;
optionExplain: charge belongs to Chargeable, so it is accepted.
The cast tells the compiler the object is a Phone, so ring is available.
Right: the declared type Chargeable does not offer ring.
An explicit cast to the implementing class is accepted.
questions.explain: What you can call depends on the variable's declared type, not only on the object it holds.
questions.rule: Declared type limits the calls.

questions.q: Phone and Torch are unrelated classes that both implement Chargeable, and Lamp is a class that does not. With Chargeable[] items = new Chargeable[3]; which statement is rejected?
options: items[0] = new Phone();
items[2] = new Lamp();
items[1] = new Torch();
items[1] = items[0];
optionExplain: Phone implements Chargeable.
Right: Lamp does not implement Chargeable.
Torch implements Chargeable, even though it has no relation to Phone.
Both sides have the type Chargeable.
questions.explain: Implementing the interface, not sharing a superclass, is the entry ticket.
questions.rule: Implementing is the entry ticket.
questions.teaches: An array of an interface type can mix objects of unrelated classes, as long as each of their classes implements the interface.

questions.q: True or false: Once Lamp is edited to implement Chargeable and given a charge method, assigning a Lamp to a Chargeable variable is accepted.
questions.explain: The rule depends on the class implementing the interface. After the edit Lamp does, so the assignment is accepted.
questions.rule: Implementing changes what may be assigned.

questions.q: A method largerOf(Object a, Object b) casts both arguments to Relatable. It is called with a Recipe that implements Relatable and a String that does not. What does the tutorial's cast rule suggest?
options: The call is rejected before the program runs, at compile time
The String is quietly skipped and the Recipe is returned
The cast succeeds because every object has the type Object
The cast of the String throws an exception when it runs
optionExplain: Casts from Object are accepted by the compiler, and the check moves to run time.
Java does not skip a failed cast.
The cast is to Relatable, not to Object.
Right: an explicit cast is checked at run time, and the String is not a Relatable.
questions.explain: Declaring the parameters as Relatable would let the compiler reject the String before the program runs.
questions.rule: Typed parameters catch mistakes earlier.
questions.teaches: Taking Object parameters and casting moves the type check from compile time to run time; declaring the parameters with the interface type lets the compiler catch a wrong argument earlier.

questions.q: You need one helper that picks the larger of two objects, and the objects come from several unrelated classes. Which design lets a single helper serve all of them?
options: Write a separate helper for every class and overload them
Each class promises one comparison method that the helper relies on
Copy the comparison logic into each class and call it from there directly
Make all the classes subclasses of one large class
optionExplain: This works but needs a new helper whenever a class is added.
Right: a shared promise lets the helper ignore the classes behind it.
Copies drift apart, and the caller still has to know every class.
Unrelated classes cannot all share one superclass, and they have only one parent each.
questions.explain: A shared contract is the way to serve unrelated classes. The card next shows the tutorial's version.
questions.rule: Code written against an interface method works for any implementing class, provided callers honour the conditions stated in the contract.

questions.q: In the tutorial's findLargest, a positive result from isLargerThan on the first object means the ____ argument is the larger one.
questions.explain: A positive result means the first object is larger than the second, so it is returned.
questions.rule: Positive means the first is larger.

questions.q: Two Recipe objects each have 7 steps. The tutorial's isEqual treats a result of 0 from isLargerThan as equal. What does isEqual return for them?
options: false, because they are two different objects
false, because recipes need different names to be equal
true, because isLargerThan returns 0 for equal sizes
true, but only if both variables refer to the same object
optionExplain: Different objects can still have equal sizes; isEqual compares sizes, not identity.
Names play no part in the comparison.
Right: equal sizes give 0, and isEqual reports true.
Identity is not what isEqual tests.
questions.explain: isEqual means equal in size, as the contract defines it, not the same object.
questions.rule: Equal here means equal by the contract.

questions.q: True or false: In findLargest, the object returned to the caller is the very same object that the Relatable reference obj1 or obj2 refers to.
questions.explain: A cast changes only how the compiler views a reference, so the original object comes back unchanged.
questions.rule: A cast changes the view, not the object.
questions.teaches: Casting changes only how the compiler sees a reference; the object itself and its class are unchanged, which is why the original object can be returned.

questions.q: True or false: If a Recipe and a Book are passed to a findLargest whose Recipe code casts its argument to Recipe, the compiler rejects the call before the program runs.
questions.explain: The parameters are typed Object, so the compiler accepts the call. The cast of the Book fails only when the program runs.
questions.rule: Conditions in comments are the programmer's duty.

questions.q: A program holds five Relatable Essay objects in a list and has a findLargest helper that compares two. Which plan finds the largest essay?
options: Call findLargest once on the first two essays and return the result it gives
Keep a current best and compare it with each next essay in turn
Call findLargest on the first and last essays only
Call isEqual on each neighbouring pair of essays
optionExplain: The other three are never looked at.
Right: reusing the two-way helper along the list covers every essay.
Essays in the middle are skipped.
Equality says nothing about which is larger.
questions.explain: A two-way comparison can be repeated to cope with any number of items.
questions.rule: Reuse a pairwise helper along a list.
questions.teaches: A helper that compares two objects can be reused along a list: keep the current winner and compare it with each next item.

questions.q: True or false: Adding a new abstract method to a widely used interface leaves every class that implements it unaffected.
questions.explain: Each implementing class lacks a body for the new method. The card next explains the problem.
questions.rule: Adding an abstract method to a published interface breaks every existing implementer, so specify an interface fully before publishing it.

questions.q: Adding a new ____ method to a published interface breaks the classes that already implement it.
questions.explain: An abstract method has no body, so existing implementers have nothing to satisfy it.
questions.rule: New abstract methods break existing implementers.

questions.q: A team is about to publish an interface for plug-ins that outside developers will implement. What does the tutorial recommend before publishing?
options: Publish a minimal interface and add methods as users ask
Think through all expected uses and specify every method now
Publish an empty interface and let each plug-in add its own methods
Publish quickly and fix breakages in later versions
optionExplain: Each added abstract method would break the plug-ins already written.
Right: the advice is to anticipate uses and specify completely from the start.
The shared contract would then say nothing that callers could use.
The tutorial treats breakage as the cost to avoid, not accept.
questions.explain: The cheapest time to fix an interface is before anyone implements it.
questions.rule: Specify completely before publishing.

questions.q: True or false: A class can stop compiling after a change to an interface it implements, even though nobody edited the class itself.
questions.explain: The class depends on the interface. If the interface gains an abstract method, the unchanged class no longer provides everything its contract demands.
questions.rule: The dependency runs through the interface.
questions.teaches: Breakage can reach a class without any edit to it, because the interface it depends on changed beneath it.

questions.q: The authors of an interface have not published it, and no class implements it yet. They now add one more abstract method. What does the tutorial's reasoning predict?
options: Every future class breaks, because the method was added late
The same breakage as for a published interface
No outside code breaks, since nobody depends on it yet
The compiler refuses the change until the interface is published
optionExplain: Future classes will simply be written with the method in mind.
Breakage needs existing implementers.
Right: the harm comes from existing implementers, and there are none.
The compiler does not track publishing.
questions.explain: The cost of changing an interface grows with the number of classes that already depend on it.
questions.rule: Change before publishing is cheap.

questions.q: A city publishes a standard form that two hundred businesses file by software, then adds a new mandatory field. Which lesson about interfaces does this match?
options: Forms should have no fixed fields, so that nobody can come to depend on them
Only the city is affected, because only it wrote the form
New fields can be added freely, because a form is not code
A published contract binds many parties, so changing it costs everyone
optionExplain: A contract with no content gives callers nothing to rely on.
The businesses must change what they file.
The analogy is to a contract: adding a required item breaks existing filers.
Right: the more parties depend on the form, the more costly the change becomes.
questions.explain: The form plays the interface, the businesses play the implementers, and the new mandatory field plays the new abstract method.
questions.rule: More dependants, costlier change.
questions.teaches: The cost of changing a published interface grows with the number of parties that depend on it, so the decision to publish is also a decision to keep the contract steady.

questions.q: An interface used by hundreds of classes needs one more operation. Which approach breaks none of those classes?
options: Add the operation as a default method with a body
Add the operation as another abstract method
Change an existing abstract method so that it also covers the operation
Replace the interface with a class of the same name
optionExplain: Right: implementers inherit the body and need no change.
Every existing class would lack a body for it.
Changing an existing signature breaks the classes that implemented the old one.
Implementers would have to be rewritten to extend the class.
questions.explain: A body supplied inside the interface is the safe route. The card next lists the tutorial's options.
questions.rule: To grow a published interface safely, add a sub-interface, a default method or a static method rather than a new abstract method.

questions.q: Match each way of growing an interface to its effect on existing users.
pairs: Existing users keep the old interface and upgrade when they choose
Existing implementers inherit a body and need no recompiling
New helper added without breaking existing implementers
questions.explain: All three leave existing implementers working, in different ways.
questions.rule: Three safe options: sub-interface, default, static.

questions.q: Interface Notifier has send. A team wants new classes to be able to opt in to a sendAll operation, while old classes stay untouched and unaware. Which option fits?
options: A default sendAll inside Notifier
An abstract sendAll inside Notifier
Removing send from Notifier and adding sendAll to take its place
A new interface NotifierPlus extending Notifier with sendAll
optionExplain: This gives sendAll to every implementer, with no opt-in.
Old classes would break.
Old classes lose the method they implement.
Right: a sub-interface lets users choose whether to upgrade.
questions.explain: The wording opt in points to the sub-interface, where users choose whether to upgrade.
questions.rule: Sub-interface when users should choose.

questions.q: True or false: An object of a class that implements DoItPlus, which extends DoIt, may be passed to a method that takes a DoIt parameter.
questions.explain: A sub-interface is also its parent type, so the object counts as a DoIt.
questions.rule: A sub-interface is also its parent type.
questions.teaches: A sub-interface type is also a kind of its parent interface, so code written for the old interface still accepts classes that implement the new one.

questions.q: Interface Exporter gains a default method exportAll. LegacyExporter, which implements Exporter, is not edited or recompiled. What happens when exportAll is called on a LegacyExporter?
options: The call fails, because LegacyExporter has no body for exportAll
The call fails until LegacyExporter is recompiled
The call works and runs the default body
The call runs a body of LegacyExporter's choosing
optionExplain: The default method supplies the body.
The tutorial says implementers need not be recompiled.
Right: the class inherits the default method without any change.
LegacyExporter has no such body; the default one runs.
questions.explain: This is the whole point of a default method: old classes gain it for free.
questions.rule: Defaults reach old classes automatically.

questions.q: A game-console maker publishes a Controller interface used by thousands of games and wants to add vibration. Sort each possible change by what happens to existing games that implement Controller.

items.t: Add a default method vibrate with a body
Add a sub-interface VibratingController
Add a static helper to Controller
Add an abstract method vibrate to Controller
Rename the abstract method press to push
Change press so it takes one more parameter

questions.explain: Additions with bodies or in a new interface leave old classes alone. Adding, renaming or re-typing an abstract method changes what implementers must provide.
questions.rule: Ask whether implementers must write something new.
questions.teaches: Renaming or changing the parameters of an existing abstract method breaks implementers just as adding one does, because their methods no longer match the contract.

questions.q: TimeClient has four abstract methods that SimpleTimeClient implements. The authors want a fifth operation available to SimpleTimeClient without editing it. Which approach does that?
options: Add the new operation to TimeClient as another abstract method
Declare the new operation final inside TimeClient
Give it a body inside TimeClient with the keyword default
Write a static copy of it inside SimpleTimeClient
optionExplain: SimpleTimeClient would have to change.
Final does not give an interface method a body.
Right: SimpleTimeClient inherits the body.
That edits SimpleTimeClient, which the authors wanted to avoid.
questions.explain: Writing the body in the interface is the idea. The card next explains it.
questions.rule: A default method gives an interface a method with a body, so a library can add behaviour without forcing implementers to change.

questions.q: A method inside an interface that has a body and the keyword ____ is inherited by implementing classes automatically.
questions.explain: The default keyword marks an interface method that carries a body.
questions.rule: Default marks a method with a body.

questions.q: Interface Playlist has abstract methods size and get. The authors want a default method isEmpty. Which body uses only what the interface offers?
options: Return whether an implementer's private count field equals 0
Return whether the list stored by one implementer has no items
Return true without calling anything
Return whether size() equals 0
optionExplain: A default method cannot see fields of implementing classes.
Only one implementer has that list.
That would be wrong for any playlist that has songs.
Right: size is an abstract method of the interface itself.
questions.explain: A default method is built from the interface's own methods.
questions.rule: Build defaults from the interface's own methods.

questions.q: In getZonedDateTime, a default method calls getLocalDateTime, an abstract method, and getZoneId, a static method of the interface. Which of these two calls runs code written by the implementing class?
options: getZoneId, the static method
getLocalDateTime, the abstract method
Both of them, since both are called from the implementer's object
Neither, because a default method runs only code in the interface
optionExplain: This one has its body in the interface itself.
Right: the abstract method is filled in by whichever class implements the interface.
The static helper's body is fixed in the interface.
A default method calls into the implementer through the abstract methods.
questions.explain: This is why a default can behave differently for each implementer even though it is written only once.
questions.rule: A default calls the implementer through abstract methods.
questions.teaches: A default method can call the interface's abstract methods, which run each implementer's own code, so one default body can behave differently for different implementing classes.

questions.q: True or false: If the keyword default is removed from getZonedDateTime while its body in braces stays, the interface method is still valid.
questions.explain: Without default or static, an interface method counts as abstract, and abstract methods have no body.
questions.rule: Body requires default or static.

questions.q: A logging library has an interface Sink with the abstract method write. Which proposed default method can be written using only what Sink offers?
options: flushToDisk, which empties the buffer inside one implementing class
writeAll, which calls write once for each line it is given
close, which releases the file held by one implementing class
rotateFile, which renames the log file of one implementing class
optionExplain: A default cannot see an implementer's buffer.
Right: it is built from the interface's own method.
The interface does not know what resource any implementer holds.
File names belong to the implementer.
questions.explain: Operations that need the implementer's own state or resources have to stay abstract.
questions.rule: Defaults cannot reach implementer state.
questions.teaches: A default method must be assembled from the interface's own methods; behaviour that needs an implementer's hidden state or resources must stay abstract for the implementer to supply.

questions.q: Interface Child extends Parent, and Parent has a default method greet. Child lists greet again as a signature ending in a semicolon. What do you expect for classes that implement Child?
options: They inherit Parent's greet body anyway
They must write their own greet
The compiler rejects Child
They inherit an empty greet that does nothing
optionExplain: Redeclaring without a body removes the default for Child's implementers.
Right: redeclaring makes the method abstract again.
The tutorial lists this as an allowed choice.
No empty body is created.
questions.explain: A signature alone means abstract. The card next gives all three choices.
questions.rule: A sub-interface may inherit a parent's default method, redeclare it as abstract, or override it with a new default.

questions.q: Match what a sub-interface does with an inherited default method to the result for its implementers.
pairs: Implementers get the parent's default body
Redeclares it as a signature only
Implementers must write their own body
Overrides it with a new default
questions.explain: Each choice decides who supplies the body, and which one.
questions.rule: Inherit, redeclare, or override.

questions.q: A library wants every class that implements its new sub-interface Greeter2 to decide its own greeting instead of using the generic default greet from the parent interface. What should Greeter2 do?
options: Say nothing at all about greet in the sub-interface
Override greet with a new default body
Redeclare greet as a bare signature
Declare greet static
optionExplain: Implementers would get the parent's generic body.
Implementers would get that body without a choice.
Right: this forces every implementer to write its own.
A static method is a different kind of method and does not force implementers.
questions.explain: Making a method abstract again turns a convenience into a duty.
questions.rule: Redeclare abstract to force a choice.

questions.q: True or false: When a sub-interface redeclares an inherited default method as abstract, classes that implement only the parent interface must also write their own body.
questions.explain: The change affects the sub-interface and its implementers. A class that implements only the parent still inherits the parent's default.
questions.rule: Sub-interfaces do not change the parent.
questions.teaches: A change made in a sub-interface does not reach back to the parent interface, so classes that implement only the parent keep inheriting the parent's default body.

questions.q: Child overrides the default greet with a new default body. A class implements Child and does not define greet. Which body runs when greet is called on it?
options: The default body in Parent
Both bodies, one after the other
None, because the class must define greet
The new default body in Child
optionExplain: Child's override replaced it for Child's implementers.
Only one body runs unless a method calls the other.
A default body is available, so the class need not.
Right: the sub-interface's override replaces the parent's default for its implementers.
questions.explain: The more specific interface's default is the one its implementers receive.
questions.rule: The sub-interface's override wins.

questions.q: A payments interface has a default method fee that returns 0. A sub-interface for premium cards must make sure every premium card class states its own fee instead of silently using 0. Which choice does that?
options: Override fee with a new default that returns 0
Leave fee alone
Add a second default method fee2
Redeclare fee with no body
optionExplain: Implementers would still get a silent 0.
Implementers would get the parent's body of 0.
The old fee would still return 0.
Right: it turns the convenient default into a duty.
questions.explain: Choosing between inherit, override and redeclare means choosing who is responsible for the behaviour.
questions.rule: Redeclare to require a decision.
questions.teaches: Redeclaring a default method as abstract is a design tool: it removes a convenient fallback and forces each implementer to make a decision.

questions.q: Class Pegasus extends Horse, which defines identifyMyself, and implements two interfaces that each give identifyMyself a default body. Which version does a Pegasus object use?
options: Horse's version, from the class
The version from the first interface listed
The version from the last interface listed
None; the compiler reports an error
optionExplain: Right: a method inherited from a class is preferred.
Interface defaults rank below class methods.
Order of interfaces does not beat a class method.
The class method settles the matter.
questions.explain: Class methods rank above interface defaults. The card next gives the full rules.
questions.rule: A class method beats interface defaults, a more specific default beats a less specific one, and unrelated conflicting defaults must be settled by overriding in the class.

questions.q: Writing FlyCar.____.startEngine(key) inside an overriding method calls the FlyCar interface's default version.
questions.explain: The form is the interface name, a dot, the word super, and the method call.
questions.rule: Interface.super.method() picks a version.

questions.q: Unrelated interfaces Printer and Scanner each define a default method id. Class Copier implements both and does not mention id. What does the compiler do?
options: Uses Printer's id because it is listed first
Uses an empty id with no behaviour
Accepts it and picks one at run time
An error; Copier must override id
optionExplain: Order of listing does not settle a conflict.
No empty body is made up.
The conflict is reported at compile time.
Right: independent defaults with the same signature conflict.
questions.explain: When neither default is more specific, the class must decide.
questions.rule: Unrelated conflicts need an override.

questions.q: Interface Animal has a default identifyMyself. EggLayer extends Animal and overrides it. FireBreather extends Animal without overriding. Dragon implements EggLayer and FireBreather. Which version does Dragon use?
options: Animal's version, since both interfaces extend Animal
EggLayer's version
None; it is a conflict and Dragon must override
FireBreather's version, since it is listed last
optionExplain: EggLayer's override takes Animal's version out of the running.
Right: Animal's version has been overridden by EggLayer, so it is ignored.
FireBreather only inherits Animal's version, which is ignored.
FireBreather has no version of its own.
questions.explain: Sharing an ancestor does not create a conflict when one branch has refined the ancestor's method.
questions.rule: Overridden defaults drop out.
questions.teaches: A default method that another candidate has already overridden is ignored, so two interfaces with a shared ancestor do not conflict when only one of them has refined its method.

questions.q: True or false: If both EggLayer and FireBreather override Animal's default identifyMyself, Dragon, which implements both without mentioning the method, must override it.
questions.explain: Neither override is more specific than the other, so the two unrelated defaults conflict and the class must decide.
questions.rule: Two refinements conflict.

questions.q: Class Boat extends Vessel, which has a concrete method sail. Boat also implements Moving, which declares sail as abstract. Boat itself does not define sail. According to the tutorial, what happens?
options: Boat must be declared abstract
The compiler reports a conflict that Boat must resolve
Moving's sail is ignored, so Boat has no sail
Vessel's sail fills Moving's abstract sail
optionExplain: Vessel's method already provides the body.
Conflicts arise between two defaults or a default and an abstract method, not here.
The method is not lost; Vessel's body fills it.
Right: an inherited class method can implement an abstract interface method of the same signature.
questions.explain: The tutorial's Mustang example is the same pattern: Horse's method fills the interface's abstract one.
questions.rule: Inherited class methods can fill interface slots.
questions.teaches: A concrete method inherited from a superclass can satisfy an interface's abstract method of the same signature, so the implementing class need not write it.

questions.q: A helper method exists only to support one interface. Where does the tutorial suggest keeping it, so it travels with that interface?
options: In the interface, as a static method
In every implementing class, as a copy
In the interface as an abstract method
In a class far away in another package
optionExplain: Right: the tutorial keeps helpers with the interface they serve.
Copies drift apart and clutter every class.
Abstract methods have no bodies, so they cannot be helpers.
This separates the helper from the interface it supports.
questions.explain: The card next explains static methods in interfaces.
questions.rule: A static interface method is a helper owned by the interface, and static factories plus default combinators build many orderings from a few small methods.

questions.q: Match each Comparator method to what it does in the tutorial's sorting example.
pairs: Static method that builds a comparator from a key extractor
Default method that adds a second criterion
Default method that flips the order of the comparator before it
questions.explain: One static method starts the chain, and default methods adjust it.
questions.rule: Static starts, default chains.

questions.q: A list of Person objects must be sorted by age, oldest first. Which expression builds the comparator, assuming the getter getAge?
options: Comparator.comparing of the getAge getter, with nothing after it
Comparator.comparing of the getAge getter, followed by reversed
Comparator.reversed of the getAge getter
Comparator.thenComparing of the getAge getter
optionExplain: This sorts youngest first.
Right: comparing gives youngest first, and reversed flips it.
reversed is a default method that follows an existing comparator, not a starting point.
thenComparing needs a first comparator to follow.
questions.explain: Start with the static factory, then apply default methods to the result.
questions.rule: Factory first, adjustments after.

questions.q: Cards are sorted with comparing by rank followed by thenComparing by suit. Two cards share a rank, one hearts and one spades. What decides their order?
options: The rank comparison, again
Their positions in the original list, always
The suit comparison
A random choice made at each sort
optionExplain: Their ranks are equal, so rank cannot separate them.
The suit criterion was added to settle exactly this case.
Right: the second criterion matters when the first finds the two equal.
A comparator gives a repeatable order.
questions.explain: Chained criteria work like a tie-breaker.
questions.rule: Later criteria break ties.
questions.teaches: Beyond the tutorial's text: a thenComparing criterion is consulted only when the earlier criteria treat two items as equal, which makes it a tie-breaker.

questions.q: The chain comparing of rank, then thenComparing of suit, then reversed is built. The tutorial says reversed flips the comparator before it. What order results?
options: Rank descending, with ties broken by suit ascending
Rank ascending, with ties broken by suit descending
Unchanged, because reversed only works at the start of a chain
Rank descending, with ties broken by suit also descending
optionExplain: Reversed flips the whole preceding comparator, including the suit part.
The rank part is flipped too.
The tutorial uses reversed mid-chain to flip the part before it.
Right: reversed flips the whole combined comparator before it.
questions.explain: Position in the chain decides how much gets flipped.
questions.rule: reversed flips everything before it.

questions.q: To sort products by price and, for equal prices, by name, chain Comparator.comparing of the price getter with ____ built from the name getter.
questions.explain: thenComparing adds the name as the second criterion.
questions.rule: Add criteria with thenComparing.
questions.teaches: Each added criterion costs one more thenComparing call, so complex orderings are built from small parts instead of a new comparator class for every combination.

questions.q: Interface Shape has an abstract area, a default describe and a static unit. A concrete class implements Shape. Which method must the class write?
options: area only
area and describe
area and unit
All three methods
optionExplain: Right: only abstract methods need a body from the implementer.
describe already has a body.
Static methods have bodies already and are not inherited.
Default and static methods come with bodies.
questions.explain: Only the abstract methods are missing. The card next says more about this.
questions.rule: An implementer owes a body for each abstract method only, and an interface with no members is a legal marker whose value is its type.

questions.q: True or false: An interface with no methods and no constants is a valid interface.
questions.explain: An empty interface is legal. It is called a marker interface.
questions.rule: Empty interfaces are legal.

questions.q: An interface has two abstract methods open and read, and one default method skip. A concrete class that implements it must write ____ methods.
questions.explain: Only the abstract methods need bodies, which here are open and read.
questions.rule: Count the abstract methods.

questions.q: Why would a library define an interface such as Cloneable with no methods at all?
options: To give implementers a default clone method to inherit from it
To label classes so that other code can check for the label
To force each implementer to write a clone method
To prevent the class from being used as a type
optionExplain: A marker interface has no members, so it supplies no method.
Right: the type is the whole message.
It declares no methods to force.
An interface name can be used as a type like any other.
questions.explain: The lesson's Object page says that clone checks for Cloneable and refuses to copy an object whose class does not implement it.
questions.rule: Marker types carry meaning through checks.
questions.teaches: Object's clone method checks whether the class implements Cloneable and throws an exception if it does not, so the empty interface acts as permission.

questions.q: A class that implements Shape overrides the default method describe with its own body. Which describe runs for objects of that class?
options: The interface's default describe, since defaults cannot be replaced
Both describe bodies in turn
The class's own describe
Neither, because describe must be abstract in the class
optionExplain: The summary of the lesson says defaults can be used as they are or overridden.
Only one body runs unless the override calls the other.
Right: defaults may be overridden by the implementing class.
The class's override is a normal concrete method.
questions.explain: The interface offers a fallback, and the class may replace it.
questions.rule: Defaults are fallbacks that can be overridden.

questions.q: A security library has an interface Trusted with no members. Vault, a class, implements Trusted. The library checks whether a class implements Trusted before opening it. What role does Trusted play?
options: It forces Vault to write an open method
It gives Vault default behaviour for opening
It does nothing, because an empty interface cannot affect a program
A label that library code checks on the class
optionExplain: Trusted declares no methods to force.
An empty interface has no default methods.
The type can still be tested, and the program can act on the answer.
Right: the check on the type gives the empty interface its meaning.
questions.explain: The marker works only because some code looks for it.
questions.rule: A marker needs code that checks it.
questions.teaches: Code can check whether a class implements a marker interface and branch on the answer, so an empty interface can act as a yes-or-no label.

questions.q: Class Puppy extends Dog, and Dog extends Animal, which has no extends clause. From which classes is Puppy descended?
options: Dog, Animal and Object
Dog only, its direct superclass
Dog and Animal, the two named classes
Dog and Object, skipping Animal
optionExplain: Right: the chain runs through every ancestor up to Object.
Dog is only the direct superclass.
Animal has no extends clause, so it descends from Object.
Animal sits between them in the chain.
questions.explain: Descent covers the whole chain to Object. The card next sets out the rules.
questions.rule: A class extends exactly one direct superclass, which is Object when none is named, and it inherits from every class in the chain above it.

questions.q: Match each term from the tutorial to its meaning.
pairs: The class that is derived from another class
The class another class is derived from
The implicit superclass of a class with no extends clause
questions.explain: These four terms describe the same relation from different sides.
questions.rule: Learn the four terms together.
