questions.q: True or false: A Kayak object has the public method launch of Vessel when Kayak extends Boat, Boat extends Vessel, and neither Kayak nor Boat mentions launch.
questions.explain: A class inherits from every class in its chain.
questions.rule: Inheritance is transitive.

questions.q: True or false: Because every class descends from Object, a variable of type Object can hold a Puppy object.
questions.explain: A subclass object may be used wherever a superclass type is expected, and every class has Object at the top of its chain.
questions.rule: Subclass objects fit superclass-typed variables.
questions.teaches: An object of a subclass can be used wherever any type in its chain is expected, from its direct superclass all the way up to Object.

questions.q: Class Animal gains a new public method groom. Puppy extends Dog extends Animal, and none of Dog or Puppy mentions groom. What is the effect on Puppy objects?
options: Nothing, until Puppy is edited to add groom
They can use it only if Dog repeats the declaration
They can use groom without any change to Puppy
They can use it only after being recompiled as Animal objects
optionExplain: Inheritance passes it down automatically.
No repeating is needed.
Right: new public members of an ancestor pass down the chain.
They stay Puppy objects.
questions.explain: Inherited members follow changes higher in the chain, which is both a benefit and a risk.
questions.rule: Ancestors' additions flow down.

questions.q: A company has class Employee. Manager extends Employee, and Director extends Manager. Which statements are true? Select all that apply.
options: Director inherits from Manager and from Employee
Director's direct superclass is Employee
A Director object may be used where an Employee is expected
Employee has no superclass at all
optionExplain: Right: a class inherits from every ancestor.
Director's direct superclass is Manager.
Right: a subclass object counts as each ancestor type.
Employee has Object as its implicit superclass.
questions.explain: The chain is Director, Manager, Employee, Object, and a Director counts as every type in it.
questions.rule: Know the chain, direct versus indirect.
questions.teaches: An object of a subclass counts as an instance of every class in its chain, so a Director can be used wherever a Manager or an Employee is expected.

questions.q: A subclass lives in a different package from its superclass. Which superclass members does it inherit? Select all that apply.
options: A public method
A protected method
A package-private method
A private field
A constructor
optionExplain: Right: public members are inherited from any package.
Right: protected members are inherited from any package.
Package-private members are inherited only inside the package.
Private members are not inherited.
Constructors are not inherited.
questions.explain: Guess from the access levels. The card next gives the rules.
questions.rule: A subclass inherits public and protected members, package-private ones only from its own package, and neither private members nor constructors.

questions.q: A subclass does not inherit the ____ members of its superclass.
questions.explain: Private members are the ones that stay behind.
questions.rule: Private members are not inherited.

questions.q: Account has a private balance, a public getBalance and a protected audit. Savings extends Account and is in a different package. Which line inside a Savings method is accepted by the compiler?
options: balance = balance + 10;
return balance;
audit();
Account(5);
optionExplain: balance is private, so it is not inherited and cannot be named.
Same problem: private balance is not inherited and cannot be named in Savings.
Right: protected members are inherited by subclasses even in a different package.
Constructors are not inherited, so they cannot be called like methods.
questions.explain: Protected members are inherited by subclasses even in a different package; private ones are not inherited and cannot be named.
questions.rule: Reach private data through inherited methods.

questions.q: Account has a private balance and a public nested class Statement that reads balance. Savings extends Account. How might Savings reach balance's value in a way that the rules allow?
options: Directly, by using the name balance inside Savings
By making Savings a nested class of Account
It cannot be reached in any way
By using the inherited Statement nested class
optionExplain: Private members are not inherited.
Savings is a subclass, not a nested class.
Indirect routes exist.
Right: an inherited public or protected nested class can reach private members of its enclosing class.
questions.explain: Access to private data can be indirect, through methods or nested classes.
questions.rule: Indirect access exists.
questions.teaches: Besides inherited public or protected methods, an inherited public or protected nested class gives a subclass indirect access to the private members of the superclass.

questions.q: Bike has a package-private method brake. Racer extends Bike and is in the same package, so it inherits brake. What if Racer is moved to a different package?
options: It still inherits brake, since subclasses inherit everything but private members
It no longer inherits brake
It inherits brake only if brake is also static
The compiler moves brake into Racer
optionExplain: Package-private members are an exception.
Right: package-private members are inherited only inside the package.
Static does not change the access rule.
Nothing is moved.
questions.explain: Package-private inheritance depends on location.
questions.rule: Same package, or no inheritance.

questions.q: A library class Item has a private id, a package-private shelf, a protected title, a public checkout method and a constructor. DigitalItem extends Item and lives in a different package. Sort the members by what DigitalItem inherits.

items.t: The public checkout method
The protected title field
The private id field
The package-private shelf field
Item's constructor

questions.explain: Public and protected members cross packages. Private members, package-private members from another package, and constructors are not inherited.
questions.rule: Check access level, then package.
questions.teaches: Constructors belong to their own class, so a subclass must declare its own constructors, even if only to call the superclass's.

questions.q: A variable obj of type Object refers to a MountainBike object. How do you get a MountainBike variable that refers to it?
options: Write a cast: MountainBike m = (MountainBike) obj;
Assign it directly: MountainBike m = obj;
Call a method named toMountainBike on obj
Create a new MountainBike and pass obj to its constructor
optionExplain: Right: the cast tells the compiler what the object is.
The compiler rejects this.
Object has no such method.
That makes a different object, not a view of this one.
questions.explain: A downward move needs an explicit cast. The card next explains it.
questions.rule: Moving up the hierarchy is implicit and safe, while moving down needs an explicit cast with a run-time check, which instanceof can guard.

questions.q: True or false: Object obj = new MountainBike(); is accepted with no cast.
questions.explain: Moving up the hierarchy is implicit.
questions.rule: Up needs no cast.

questions.q: Dog extends Animal and has a method bark. With Animal a = new Dog(); the call that reaches bark is ((____) a).bark().
questions.explain: The cast to Dog gives the compiler a Dog view, and then bark is available.
questions.rule: Cast to reach subclass members.

questions.q: True or false: A cast from an Object variable to MountainBike that compiles is certain to succeed when the program runs.
questions.explain: The compiler cannot see what the variable holds. If it holds a String, the run-time check of the cast fails.
questions.rule: The compiler cannot see what o holds.
questions.teaches: A cast compiles when the types could be related, so the compiler cannot prove it right; only the run-time check can reject a wrong one.

questions.q: The code if (o instanceof MountainBike) { MountainBike m = (MountainBike) o; } runs while o holds a String. What happens?
options: The cast runs and throws an exception
The String is converted into a MountainBike
The block is skipped; no exception
The compiler rejects the code
optionExplain: The cast is inside the guarded block.
Casts and tests do not convert objects.
Right: the test is false, so the cast never runs.
The code is accepted; only the run-time value differs.
questions.explain: The test turns a possible failure into a skipped block.
questions.rule: instanceof guards the cast.

questions.q: A mail sorter receives items typed as Object. Parcel extends Mail and has a weigh method. Which code calls weigh safely on an item that may be a Letter?
options: ((Parcel) item).weigh();
item.weigh();
if (item instanceof Mail) { ((Parcel) item).weigh(); } else { }
if (item instanceof Parcel) { ((Parcel) item).weigh(); }
optionExplain: This fails when the item is a Letter.
Object has no weigh method.
A Letter passes the Mail test but fails the Parcel cast.
Right: the test names the same type that the cast uses.
questions.explain: The test must be at least as specific as the cast.
questions.rule: Test for the type you cast to.
questions.teaches: The instanceof test must name the type you cast to; testing a broader type, such as the common superclass, does not make the cast safe.

questions.q: Which kind of multiple inheritance does Java permit?
options: A class implementing several interfaces
A class extending several classes
A class inheriting fields from several classes
A class inheriting several constructors
optionExplain: Right: implementing several interfaces is allowed.
A class may have only one direct superclass.
Fields come from one superclass chain.
Constructors are not inherited at all.
questions.explain: Several interfaces are fine, several classes are not. The card next separates the kinds.
questions.rule: Java allows several interfaces, which is multiple inheritance of type, but only one superclass, so state comes from a single line of ancestors.

questions.q: Match each kind of multiple inheritance to its meaning.
pairs: Inheriting method definitions from several classes
A class implementing more than one interface
questions.explain: The word covers three different things, and Java treats them differently.
questions.rule: Say which kind you mean.

questions.q: Class Robot extends Machine and implements Walker and Talker. From where can Robot inherit fields?
options: From Machine, Walker and Talker alike, as each supplies fields
From Machine only; interfaces have no fields
From Walker and Talker only
From nowhere, since a class never inherits fields
optionExplain: Interfaces have only constants, not per-object fields.
Right: state comes from the one superclass chain.
The superclass supplies the state.
Inheriting fields is what subclasses do.
questions.explain: One line of classes means one source of stored state.
questions.rule: One superclass chain supplies state.

questions.q: The tutorial calls inheriting implementation from several classes risky even for careful programmers. Which reason does it give?
options: Method bodies from two classes cannot be compiled into one class
Superclasses may not contain methods with bodies
Adding a method to a superclass can create a conflict unnoticed
Names of methods must be different in every class
optionExplain: The problem is ambiguity, not compilation of bodies.
Classes may have method bodies.
Right: a conflict can appear without anyone intending it.
Different classes may reuse names; the trouble is ambiguity in a subclass.
questions.explain: Hidden conflicts are the cost of inheriting implementation from many parents.
questions.rule: Conflicts can appear unseen.
questions.teaches: A programmer can create a name conflict by accident simply by adding a method to a superclass, which is part of why Java limits a class to one superclass.

questions.q: Duck implements Swimmer and Flyer. Both interfaces now gain a default method move with the same signature, and Duck does not define move. What does the compiler do?
options: Uses Swimmer's move because it is listed first
Accepts it and runs both moves
Accepts it and leaves move undefined for Duck
Reports an error, so Duck must override move
optionExplain: Order does not settle the conflict.
One body runs unless the override calls both.
An undefined method is not a state the compiler allows.
Right: two unrelated defaults conflict and the class must decide.
questions.explain: Default methods bring the old conflict back in a limited way.
questions.rule: Conflicting defaults need an override.

questions.q: Sort each class design for a game by whether Java allows it.

items.t: A class implements three interfaces
An interface extends two interfaces
A class extends one class and implements one interface
A class extends two classes
A class takes its stored fields from two superclasses

questions.explain: Types may come from many interfaces, but stored state comes through a single line of classes.
questions.rule: Many types, one state source.
questions.teaches: However many types an object has, its stored fields are laid out by a single line of ancestors, which keeps the state of an object unambiguous.

questions.q: Class B extends class A. Both declare a static method log with no parameters. Which term does the tutorial use for the relation of B's log to A's log?
options: B's log hides A's log
B's log overrides A's log
B's log overloads A's log
The code does not compile
optionExplain: Right: static methods with the same signature hide.
Overriding is for instance methods.
Overloads differ in their parameter lists.
Static with static is allowed.
questions.explain: Static pairs hide, instance pairs override. The card next gives the terms.
questions.rule: Same-signature instance methods override, same-signature static methods hide, an instance and static mix fails to compile, and a different parameter list is an overload.

questions.q: Match each pair of methods in a subclass and its superclass to the tutorial's term or result.
pairs: One instance and one static, same signature
questions.explain: Four pairings, four outcomes.
questions.rule: Know the table.

questions.q: ClassA declares public static void methodThree(int i). ClassB extends ClassA and declares public void methodThree(int i) as an instance method. What happens?
options: ClassB's method overrides ClassA's
A compile-time error
ClassB's method hides ClassA's
ClassB's method overloads ClassA's
optionExplain: Overriding needs two instance methods.
Right: a static method cannot be replaced by an instance method of the same signature.
Hiding needs two static methods.
The parameter lists are identical, so it is not an overload.
questions.explain: Mixed kinds with one signature are rejected.
questions.rule: Instance and static do not mix.

questions.q: A subclass defines tostring() in lower case, intending to override toString. What does adding the annotation @Override above it change?
options: Nothing, because the annotation is ignored
The method now overrides toString after all
A compile error, because nothing is overridden
The compiler renames the method for you
optionExplain: The annotation asks the compiler to check.
Names must match exactly.
Right: the annotation turns a silent mistake into an error.
It does not rewrite code.
questions.explain: Without the annotation, the misspelt method compiles as an unrelated new method.
questions.rule: @Override catches slips.
questions.teaches: Without @Override, a misspelt name or a wrong parameter list silently creates a new method; the annotation makes the compiler flag the slip.

questions.q: True or false: Cat.testClassMethod() runs Animal's version, because Cat's static method hides it.
questions.explain: With hiding, the class named in the call decides, so naming Cat runs Cat's version.
questions.rule: Hiding follows the class named.

questions.q: Shape declares an instance method draw(), a static method count() and an instance method resize(int). Subclass Square declares draw(), a static count(), and resize(double). Match each Square method to its relation.
pairs: Overloads: a new method beside Shape's resize(int)
questions.explain: Only the parameter type differs for resize, so it is a new method, not an override.
questions.rule: Check the full signature.
questions.teaches: Changing one parameter type turns an intended override into an overload, so the superclass version still exists beside the new one.

questions.q: Bicycle b = new RoadBike(...) where RoadBike overrides printDescription. Which version runs for b.printDescription()?
options: RoadBike's version
Bicycle's version, because b is declared as Bicycle
Both versions in turn automatically
Neither; the call is rejected
optionExplain: Right: the object is a RoadBike.
The declared type does not decide.
Only an explicit super call adds the parent's version.
The call is accepted, since Bicycle has the method.
questions.explain: The object decides, not the variable. The card next names this.
questions.rule: For an overridden instance method, the version that runs is chosen by the object's actual class at run time, not by the variable's declared type.

questions.q: The tutorial calls the run-time choice of method by the actual object ____ method invocation.
questions.explain: The Java virtual machine picks the object's own version.
questions.rule: Virtual method invocation.

questions.q: Animal has speak printing three dots. Dog overrides it to print Woof and Cat to print Meow. An array typed Animal holds a Dog, a Cat and a plain Animal, and a loop calls speak on each. What is printed?
options: Three dots, three dots, three dots
Woof, Meow, then three dots
Woof, Woof, Woof
Woof, Meow, Meow
optionExplain: The declared type does not choose the version.
Right: each object runs its own version.
The first object does not set the behaviour of the others.
The plain Animal has no override to use.
questions.explain: One loop, three behaviours.
questions.rule: Each object runs its own version.

questions.q: Inside RoadBike's printDescription, the first line is super.printDescription(). Beyond the tutorial's text, what would happen if that line were a plain printDescription() call instead?
options: It would call Bicycle's version once, as before
The compiler would reject the call
The method would call itself again and again
It would call the version in the variable's declared type
optionExplain: Only the super form reaches the parent's version.
The call is legal, just endless.
Right: the plain name refers to the current object's version, which is this very method.
The call refers to the object's version.
questions.explain: The super form is the way to reach the parent's version from inside an override.
questions.rule: Use super to reach the parent's version.
questions.teaches: Beyond the tutorial's text: inside an override, a plain call to the same method runs the object's own version again, so reaching the parent's version needs the super form.

questions.q: True or false: If MountainBike does not override printDescription, then for Bicycle b = new MountainBike(...), the call b.printDescription() runs Bicycle's inherited version.
questions.explain: With no override, the version the object has is the one it inherited.
questions.rule: No override means the inherited version.

questions.q: True or false: Adding a new Contractor subclass that overrides pay requires changing a payroll loop that calls pay on Employee-typed elements.
questions.explain: The call picks each object's own version at run time, so the loop stays as it is.
questions.rule: New subclasses plug in without edits.
questions.teaches: New subclasses can be added without changing code that calls the method through the superclass type, because each object supplies its own version at run time.

questions.q: Base declares int size. Child extends Base and also declares String size. What is the relation between the two fields?
options: Child's size hides Base's, though the types differ
The code is rejected, because the two field types differ
Child's size overrides Base's size
They are one field whose type has changed
optionExplain: Right: hiding goes by name.
The tutorial says the types may differ.
Fields are hidden, not overridden.
Two separate fields exist.
questions.explain: Hiding depends on the name. The card next gives the rule.
questions.rule: A same-named field in a subclass hides the superclass field, which is then reachable only through super, and the tutorial advises against hiding.

questions.q: True or false: According to the tutorial, hiding fields is a good way to keep subclass code readable.
questions.explain: The tutorial says the opposite: hiding makes code difficult to read.
questions.rule: Avoid hiding fields.

questions.q: Child extends Base and hides Base's field label. Inside a method of Child, which expression reads Base's label?
options: label
this.label
super.label
Child.label
optionExplain: The simple name means Child's field.
this refers to the current object's view in Child, which is Child's field.
Right: super reaches the hidden field.
That names Child's own field, which is not Base's.
questions.explain: The simple name now means the subclass's field.
questions.rule: Reach hidden fields through super.

questions.q: True or false: Beyond the tutorial's text, if Base has a method show that prints its label field, and Child hides label without overriding show, then new Child().show() prints Child's label value.
questions.explain: Code written in Base refers to Base's field, so the Base value is printed.
questions.rule: Hiding does not reach the parent's code.
questions.teaches: Beyond the tutorial's text: a hidden field is not overridden, so methods written in the superclass keep using the superclass's field even on a subclass object.

questions.q: Child renames its field so that it no longer matches Base's label. Inside Child, the simple name label then refers to ____'s field.
questions.explain: With no hiding, the inherited field is reachable by its simple name.
questions.rule: No clash, no hiding.

questions.q: Vehicle has a double field speed. Boat extends Vehicle and adds a String field speed holding a label such as slow. A method in Boat computes speed times 2. What goes wrong?
options: Nothing; the compiler picks the double automatically
The code quietly uses Vehicle's speed and Boat's speed together
The code compiles but multiplies the text
The name speed now means the String, so the arithmetic fails
optionExplain: The simple name refers to Boat's field.
One name means one field in a given place.
Text cannot be multiplied by 2.
Right: the hidden double is reachable only as super.speed.
questions.explain: Adding one field changed the meaning of an existing line.
questions.rule: Hiding can silently change meanings.
questions.teaches: Adding a same-named field to a subclass can change the meaning of existing lines or break them, which is the practical reason the tutorial discourages hiding.

questions.q: Subclass overrides printMethod, which Superclass also defines. Inside the override, how can it run the Superclass version?
options: By calling super.printMethod()
By calling printMethod() with no prefix
By calling Superclass.printMethod()
By calling this.printMethod()
optionExplain: Right: super reaches the parent's version.
That calls the subclass's own version again.
That form is for static methods.
this refers to the current object, so its own version runs.
questions.explain: The keyword super is the way up. The card next explains it.
questions.rule: Super followed by a dot and a member name reaches the superclass's version of an overridden method or a hidden field.

questions.q: Inside an override, the call ____.printMethod() runs the superclass's version of printMethod.
questions.explain: The word super followed by a dot reaches the parent's version.
questions.rule: super.method() calls the parent's version.

questions.q: Class Cat overrides describe from Animal. Cat's description should be Animal's description followed by the word purrs. Which body is correct?
options: return describe() + " purrs";
return super.describe() + " purrs";
return " purrs";
return Animal.describe() + " purrs";
optionExplain: describe() here calls Cat's own describe again.
Right: it reuses the parent's text and adds to it.
This drops the Animal description.
describe is an instance method, so it cannot be called on the class name.
questions.explain: An override that extends the parent's work calls super first or last.
questions.rule: Call super to extend, not replace.

questions.q: How can you tell that a use of the keyword super is a constructor call rather than a member access?
options: It is followed by a dot and then a member name such as printMethod
It appears inside an overriding method, after some other statement
It is followed by parentheses and opens a constructor
It is written in capital letters
optionExplain: That is the member form.
Members are accessed that way, not constructors.
Right: the constructor form uses parentheses.
The keyword is always lower case.
questions.explain: One keyword, two jobs, told apart by what follows.
questions.rule: Dot means member, parentheses mean constructor.
questions.teaches: The same keyword super has a member use with a dot and a constructor use with parentheses, and the two follow different rules.

questions.q: True or false: If the override prints its own line before calling super.printMethod(), the output shows the subclass line first.
questions.explain: The lines run in the order written, so the subclass line comes first.
questions.rule: Order of statements decides output order.

questions.q: Other code calls printMethod on a Subclass object, and the Subclass override calls super.printMethod() inside. Which version of printMethod does the other code start with?
options: Superclass's version only
Both versions directly from the caller, one after the other
The compiler picks at random
Subclass's override, which then calls the parent's
optionExplain: The object's own override is chosen first.
The caller reaches only the override.
There is a fixed rule.
Right: super affects only the call written with it.
questions.explain: The outside caller sees the override; the override decides to reuse the parent's code.
questions.rule: Super is a private route for the subclass.
questions.teaches: Callers outside the subclass always reach the override first; only code inside the subclass can choose to also run the superclass's version with super.

questions.q: Class Vehicle has only one constructor, which takes a String id. Class Car extends Vehicle and has an empty constructor Car() with no other code. What happens?
options: An error, because Vehicle has no no-argument constructor
It compiles, and the id is left empty
It compiles, but fails with an error when a Car is created later
It compiles, because Car has no fields
optionExplain: Right: the compiler inserts a call to super() and it cannot be satisfied.
The compiler never makes up an id.
The error is found when compiling.
Fields are not the issue.
questions.explain: The card next explains the inserted call.
questions.rule: Every constructor starts with a call to a superclass constructor, either written first or implied as the no-argument one, and the calls chain up to Object.

questions.q: A call to a superclass constructor must be the ____ line of the subclass constructor.
questions.explain: Super must come first.
questions.rule: super(...) comes first.

questions.q: Vehicle has only the constructor Vehicle(String id). Which Car constructor compiles?
options: Car() { id = "none"; super("none"); }
Car() { Vehicle("none"); }
Car() { super("none"); }
Car() { super(); }
optionExplain: super must be the first line.
A constructor is not called like a method.
Right: it calls the matching constructor on the first line.
Vehicle has no no-argument constructor.
questions.explain: Match the parent's constructor and put the call first.
questions.rule: Match the constructor; call it first.

questions.q: Class C extends B, B extends A, and A extends Object, with no explicit super calls. Creating a C object involves ____ constructors in total.
questions.explain: The constructors of C, B, A and Object all take part.
questions.rule: Constructors chain upward.
questions.teaches: Creating one object runs a constructor for every class in its chain up to Object, not only the constructor of its own class.

questions.q: True or false: If Vehicle gains a second constructor with no parameters, Car's empty constructor with no explicit super call compiles.
questions.explain: The inserted super() now finds a no-argument constructor to call.
questions.rule: A no-argument constructor satisfies the implied call.

questions.q: Account has constructors Account(String owner) and Account(String owner, double opening). SavingsAccount extends Account and has no no-argument constructor in Account to rely on. Which SavingsAccount constructor compiles?
options: SavingsAccount() { }
SavingsAccount(String n) { super(n, 0, 0); }
SavingsAccount(String n) { total = 0; super(n); }
SavingsAccount(String n, double rate) { super(n); }
optionExplain: The implied super() has no no-argument constructor to call.
No Account constructor takes three arguments.
The super call must be first.
Right: it calls a matching superclass constructor and takes an extra parameter of its own.
questions.explain: A subclass constructor may take more parameters than the superclass one and pass on only some.
questions.rule: Pass on what the parent needs.
questions.teaches: A subclass constructor may take extra parameters of its own and pass on to the superclass constructor only the ones that constructor needs.

questions.q: True or false: If Book does not override equals, two separate Book objects with the same ISBN are not equal according to equals.
questions.explain: Object's equals compares identity, so two separate objects are not equal.
questions.rule: Override equals when identity is the wrong test, and override hashCode with it so that equal objects have equal hash codes.

questions.q: Object's equals compares references with the ____ operator, written ==.
questions.explain: Identity means the same object.
questions.rule: Default equals is identity.

questions.q: Class Card has rank and suit and overrides equals to compare both fields. What else should its author do?
options: Override getClass so that it reports the rank
Override hashCode using the same fields
Nothing, since equals is enough
Override finalize to compare the cards
optionExplain: getClass cannot be overridden.
Right: equal cards must have equal hash codes.
The tutorial says to override hashCode too.
finalize has nothing to do with equality.
questions.explain: The two methods must agree.
questions.rule: equals and hashCode go together.

questions.q: Card overrides equals to compare rank and suit but keeps Object's hashCode. Two separate cards with the same rank and suit are equal by equals. What is the problem?
options: Equal cards report the same hash code, so the rule holds anyway
The compiler will refuse to compile the class
Equal cards usually report different hash codes
equals will stop working
optionExplain: The default code comes from the object itself, not its fields.
The compiler does not enforce this.
Right: the default hash code reflects identity, so it disagrees with the new equal.
equals still works.
questions.explain: Changing the meaning of equal means changing hashCode to follow.
questions.rule: hashCode must follow equals.
questions.teaches: Object's default hashCode reflects the identity of the object, so once equals is overridden to compare fields, the default hash codes disagree with the new meaning of equal.

questions.q: True or false: If Book.equals compares ISBN and title but hashCode uses only the ISBN, the rule that equal objects have equal hash codes is broken.
questions.explain: Equal books share an ISBN, so they share a hash code, and the rule holds.
questions.rule: Equal implies same hash code.

questions.q: A Lock class models physical door locks. Two locks with the same colour and size are still two different locks. What should the author do about equals?
options: Override equals to compare colour and size
Override only hashCode to use the colour
Override getClass to report the colour
Keep Object's identity-based equals
optionExplain: This would call two real locks the same.
It would break the link between the two methods.
getClass cannot be overridden.
Right: each lock is its own thing, so identity is the right test.
questions.explain: Overriding is a choice about what counts as the same thing.
questions.rule: Choose identity when each object is unique.
questions.teaches: Overriding equals is a decision about what counts as the same thing; when every object is unique, the identity-based default is the correct choice.

questions.q: A program must close a file reliably once it is finished with it. What does the tutorial recommend instead of relying on the finalize method?
options: A try-with-resources statement
Override finalize and wait for the garbage collector
Override toString to close the file
Call getClass on the file
optionExplain: Right: it closes the resource when the block ends.
The collector may run late or never.
toString has no cleanup role.
getClass reports a class, it does not close anything.
questions.explain: Cleanup should not depend on the collector. The card next gives the details.
questions.rule: Override toString for readable output, remember getClass is fixed, make clone copy referenced objects when copies must be independent, and do not rely on finalize.

questions.q: Match each Object method to what the tutorial says about it.
pairs: Returns a text form of the object
Returns the runtime class and cannot be overridden
Creates a copy, and needs Cloneable
Called by the garbage collector at an uncertain time
questions.explain: Four methods, four different jobs.
questions.rule: Match method to job.

questions.q: True or false: After the default clone copies playlist p into q, a song added through q's list also shows up in p's list, when the field refers to a list object.
questions.explain: The default copy copies the reference, so both playlists share one list.
questions.rule: Default clone shares referenced objects.

questions.q: True or false: You can override getClass in your own class to make it report a different class.
questions.explain: The tutorial says getClass cannot be overridden. Object declares it final.
questions.rule: getClass is fixed.
questions.teaches: Because getClass is final in Object, no class can change what an object reports as its runtime class.

questions.q: Playlist now overrides clone so that it also copies the songs list. A song is added through q.songs. What does p see?
options: The new song, because the lists are still shared
An error, because songs is now null
No new song, because p and q have separate lists
The new song, but only after the next garbage collection
optionExplain: The override was written to stop the sharing.
The override copies the list, it does not clear it.
Right: the override gave the clone its own list.
Collection plays no part.
questions.explain: The override decides how deep the copy goes.
questions.rule: Override clone for independent copies.

questions.q: A program opens many network connections and counts on finalize to close each one once its object is no longer used. According to the tutorial's reasoning, what is the risk?
options: finalize closes the connections twice
finalize cannot be called on objects at all
finalize always runs immediately, so connections close too early to use
The collector may run late, leaving the program short of connections
optionExplain: The risk is missing cleanup, not double cleanup.
It can be called, but not predictably.
The timing is uncertain, not immediate.
Right: late or missing cleanup can exhaust a limited resource.
questions.explain: The tutorial gives file descriptors as the example of a resource that can run out.
questions.rule: Do not tie scarce resources to finalize.
questions.teaches: A program that leaves cleanup to finalize can exhaust a limited resource, such as file descriptors, before the collector ever runs the cleanup.

questions.q: True or false: A subclass can override a method that its superclass declared final.
questions.explain: A final method cannot be overridden. The card next explains when to use it.
questions.rule: A final method blocks overriding, a final class blocks subclassing, and methods called from constructors should be final.

questions.q: A class declared ____ cannot be subclassed.
questions.explain: Final on a class blocks subclassing.
questions.rule: Final class means no subclasses.

questions.q: A class Money must stay immutable, and a subclass could add mutable fields. What is the best step according to the tutorial's reasoning?
options: Declare the class final
Declare the class abstract
Declare its constructors protected
Declare its methods static
optionExplain: Right: no subclass can then add mutable state.
An abstract class can still be subclassed.
Subclasses could still extend it.
Static methods do not prevent subclassing.
questions.explain: The tutorial names String as an immutable final class.
questions.rule: Final class protects immutability.

questions.q: Beyond the tutorial's text: Parent's constructor calls a non-final method describe. Child overrides describe to use a field that Child's own constructor sets. When new Child() runs, what can describe see in that field?
options: The value Child's constructor sets, since it runs first
The default value; Parent's constructor runs first
An error is raised before describe runs
The field of Parent instead
optionExplain: Child's constructor has not run yet.
Right: the override runs too early.
The call runs normally.
The override uses Child's field, which is not yet set.
questions.explain: This is the kind of surprise the tutorial warns of.
questions.rule: Constructors should call final methods.
questions.teaches: Beyond the tutorial's text: a superclass constructor runs before the subclass's fields are set, so an overridden method called from it can see unset values.

questions.q: True or false: If another team's class extends Report and Report is then declared final, the other team's class still compiles.
questions.explain: A final class cannot be subclassed, so the extends relation is no longer allowed.
questions.rule: Adding final can break subclasses.

questions.q: A game has a Rules class whose method scoreFor must work the same in every game variant, while designers should be free to extend Rules for new variants. What fits?
options: Declare the whole class final
Leave both open and rely on documentation to protect it
Declare scoreFor abstract
Declare scoreFor final; leave the class open
optionExplain: Designers could not extend Rules.
Nothing then protects the scoring.
Subclasses would have to write their own version.
Right: the one critical method is locked while the class stays extensible.
questions.explain: Final works on single methods as well as whole classes.
questions.rule: Lock the critical part only.
questions.teaches: Final can be applied selectively: lock the one method that carries the rule while leaving the class open for extension.

questions.q: A class contains one method marked abstract, with no body and a semicolon. What must be true of the class?
options: It must be declared abstract
It must be declared final
It must be declared public
It needs no special declaration
optionExplain: Right: a class with an abstract method is abstract.
Final and abstract do not fit together.
Access is unrelated.
The compiler requires abstract.
questions.explain: One missing body makes the class incomplete. The card next gives the rule.
questions.rule: An abstract class cannot be instantiated; a class with an abstract method must be abstract, and a subclass must implement inherited abstract methods or be abstract itself.

questions.q: An abstract method has no body; its declaration ends with a ____.
questions.explain: The semicolon stands where the braces would be.
questions.rule: No braces, a semicolon.

questions.q: GraphicObject is abstract with abstract methods draw and resize. Triangle extends it and writes draw but not resize. What must be done for the code to compile?
options: Nothing; only the first abstract method needs a body
Declare resize final in Triangle
Write resize in Triangle, or make Triangle abstract
Move draw into GraphicObject
optionExplain: Every inherited abstract method needs one.
A final method without a body is not a body.
Right: an unfinished subclass must be abstract.
That changes the superclass, not Triangle's problem.
questions.explain: A subclass finishes the job or passes it on.
questions.rule: Implement all, or stay abstract.

questions.q: Abstract class X implements interface Y but writes all of Y's methods except one. Class XX extends X and writes the remaining method. Which of X and XX can be instantiated?
options: XX only
X only
Both X and XX
Neither, since Y is an interface
optionExplain: Right: X is incomplete, and XX completes it.
X lacks one method and is abstract.
X is abstract.
XX is a normal concrete class.
questions.explain: The abstract class carries partial work, and the concrete class finishes.
questions.rule: Abstract classes can partly implement interfaces.
questions.teaches: An abstract class may implement an interface only in part, leaving the remaining methods to a concrete subclass, so shared code can sit between the interface and the final classes.

questions.q: True or false: A class declared abstract that contains no abstract methods can still be instantiated with new.
questions.explain: The keyword abstract blocks instantiation whether or not any method is abstract.
questions.rule: Abstract blocks new.

questions.q: A vending app has an abstract class Product. Sort each member by whether it belongs written in Product or left abstract for the subclasses.

items.t: A price field every product has
A method that formats the price for display
A method that prepares the item's own wrapping
A method that dispenses the item, which differs by product

questions.explain: What all subclasses do the same way belongs in the abstract class. What differs is left abstract.
questions.rule: Share what is common; leave open what differs.
questions.teaches: In an abstract class, write what every subclass does identically and leave abstract only what differs, so subclasses fill in just the gaps.

questions.q: A group of closely related classes must share fields that hold each object's own state. Which tool fits better?
options: An abstract class
An interface
A marker interface
A static method
optionExplain: Right: abstract classes can hold non-static, non-final fields.
Interface fields are constants shared by all.
A marker interface has no members.
Static methods hold no per-object state.
questions.explain: State points to a class. The card next compares the two tools.
questions.rule: Choose an abstract class to share state and code among closely related classes and an interface to give unrelated classes a common type, and combine them when both needs exist.

questions.q: Match each feature to the tool it describes.
pairs: Fields can be non-static and non-final
A class can use any number of them
A class can extend only one
Abstract class, since it is a class
questions.explain: The two tools differ in state, access and how many a class may use.
questions.rule: Compare field and count rules.

questions.q: Invoices, photos and robots are unrelated classes that must all be accepted by one print queue. Which design fits?
options: An abstract class Printable that all three extend
An interface that each of them implements
A final class Printable
A static method in each class
optionExplain: Three unrelated classes would be forced under one superclass.
Right: unrelated classes share a type through an interface.
Final classes cannot be extended.
This gives the queue no common type.
questions.explain: Unrelated classes call for a common type, not a common parent.
questions.rule: Unrelated classes, interface.

questions.q: HashMap extends the abstract class AbstractMap and implements the interface Map. Why would a library use both?
options: The interface supplies the fields, and the abstract class gives the type
An abstract class cannot be used alone
The interface is the common type; the abstract class shares code
Interfaces cannot hold method names
optionExplain: Interface fields are constants, and the type is the interface's job.
It can be used alone.
Right: each tool does the job it suits.
They hold method signatures.
questions.explain: The type and the shared code are separate needs.
questions.rule: Type from the interface, code from the abstract class.
questions.teaches: Libraries pair an interface, which defines the type for callers, with an abstract class, which supplies shared code for implementers.

questions.q: Truck already extends Vehicle. A designer plans an abstract class PrintBase for printable things and wants Truck to be printable too. What happens?
options: Truck can extend both classes if they are in the same package
Truck can extend PrintBase and silently drop Vehicle
Truck becomes an interface
Truck cannot also extend PrintBase; an interface is needed
optionExplain: Package does not change the single-parent limit.
Extending replaces nothing; two parents are not allowed.
It stays a class.
Right: a class extends only one class.
questions.explain: The single-superclass rule can decide the question.
questions.rule: One superclass only.

questions.q: A music app has Track and Podcast, which share a duration field and a method that formats it. Track and a separate Document class can both be downloaded. Which design choices fit? Select all that apply.
options: An abstract class Media holding duration and the formatting method, extended by Track and Podcast
An interface Downloadable implemented by Track and Document
An abstract class Downloadable that both Track and Document extend
Put the duration field in an interface so each Track has its own
optionExplain: Right: related classes sharing state suit an abstract class.
Right: an unrelated ability suits an interface.
Track would already extend Media, and Document is unrelated.
Interface fields are shared constants, not per-object state.
questions.explain: Shared state sits in an abstract superclass, and abilities across unrelated classes sit in interfaces.
questions.rule: Mix both tools.
questions.teaches: Real designs mix the two tools: shared state goes into an abstract superclass, and abilities that cut across unrelated classes go into interfaces.

questions.q: True or false: Every primitive number type in Java has a matching class that can hold the same value as an object.
questions.explain: Each primitive has a wrapper class, for example Integer for int. The card next shows how Java moves between the two.
questions.rule: Each primitive has a wrapper class.

questions.q: The abstract class that all numeric wrapper classes extend is called ____.
questions.explain: Byte, Short, Integer, Long, Float and Double all extend the abstract class Number.
questions.rule: Numeric wrappers extend Number.

questions.q: A reviewer lists these types from a program. Sort each as a primitive type or a wrapper class.

items.t: int
Double
byte
Long
float
Short

questions.explain: The lower-case names are the primitives; the capitalised names are the classes that wrap them.
questions.rule: Lower-case is the bare value, capitalised is the object.

questions.q: Which of these classes extend Number, according to the tutorial? Select all that apply.
options: Integer
BigDecimal
AtomicLong
String
Character
optionExplain: Right: Integer is one of the numeric wrappers under Number.
Right: BigDecimal is a further Number subclass, used for high-precision calculations.
Right: AtomicLong is a Number subclass meant for multithreaded programs.
A String holds text, and text is not a number type, so it is not under Number.
Character wraps a single char; it is a wrapper but not a numeric one, so it is not under Number.
questions.explain: Number has more subclasses than the wrappers: BigDecimal and BigInteger for high precision, AtomicInteger and AtomicLong for multithreaded programs. Character and String are not numeric types.
questions.rule: Number is wider than the six wrappers.
questions.teaches: Besides the six numeric wrappers, Number has subclasses BigDecimal and BigInteger (high-precision calculations) and AtomicInteger and AtomicLong (multithreaded applications), which this lesson does not cover.
questions.hint: Which of these hold numbers rather than text or letters?

questions.q: A coder wants an object that holds the single letter 'q'. Which wrapper class fits, and is it a Number subclass?
options: Character, which is not a Number
Character, and it extends Number
Letter, and it is a separate class
Char, and it is a Number subclass
optionExplain: Right: Character wraps char, and since it is not a numeric wrapper it is outside Number.
The name is right, but a letter is not a number, so the numeric parent does not apply.
No wrapper called Letter exists; every primitive uses a fixed wrapper name.
There is no wrapper called Char; the one for char is Character.
questions.explain: Every primitive, including char and boolean, has a wrapper, but only the numeric ones extend Number.
questions.rule: Every primitive has a wrapper; only the numeric wrappers extend Number.
questions.teaches: The wrapper for char is Character, and boolean has Boolean; the tutorial's table lists all eight pairs, while only the numeric wrappers extend Number.
questions.hint: Which primitive does 'q' belong to?

questions.q: A program runs: int count = 500; Integer boxed = count; int back = boxed; What does back hold afterwards?
options: Nothing; the code does not compile
0, because unboxing resets the value
500, as both steps keep the value
5, because only the first digit is kept
optionExplain: The compiler boxes and unboxes automatically, so this compiles.
Unboxing only reads the value inside the object; it never resets it.
Right: boxing wraps 500 and unboxing returns the same 500.
Boxing keeps the whole number; there is no digit truncation.
questions.explain: Both conversions are automatic and carry the value unchanged.
questions.rule: Boxing and unboxing preserve the value.

questions.q: You need the smallest value a byte can hold without typing the digits yourself. Where is the most natural place to look?
options: A method called on any byte variable
A constant on the Byte wrapper class
The Math class, as a method call
The println method of System.out
optionExplain: Primitives such as byte have no methods, so nothing can be called on a bare byte variable.
Right: wrapper classes hold constants for the bounds of their types.
Math offers functions such as abs and sqrt, not the limits of a type.
println prints values; it does not report type limits.
questions.explain: Type bounds live as constants on the wrapper classes. The card next lists the tutorial's three reasons to use wrappers.
questions.rule: Bounds are wrapper constants.

questions.q: Integer.MAX_VALUE and Byte.MIN_VALUE are examples of ____ that give the bounds of a data type.
questions.explain: These are constants defined by the wrapper classes.
questions.rule: Wrapper constants give type bounds.

questions.q: Which program step gives the clearest reason to use an Integer object instead of an int?
options: Counting loop passes from 0 to 9
Adding two local variables for a total
Storing a customer age in a local variable
Passing a number to an object parameter
optionExplain: A loop counter is plain arithmetic, which a primitive handles with no object.
Adding values is ordinary arithmetic, where primitives are the default.
A local variable holding a number needs nothing an object adds.
Right: when a method expects an object, a Number object is what it accepts.
questions.explain: Only the object-argument case matches one of the three reasons; the others are ordinary primitive work.
questions.rule: Wrappers earn their place when the API wants an object.

questions.q: The smallest value a byte can hold is Byte.MIN_VALUE, which equals ____.
questions.explain: A byte covers negative 128 up to 127, and Byte.MIN_VALUE gives the lower end.
questions.rule: Each wrapper names its own bounds.
questions.teaches: Each numeric wrapper class names its own bounds: Byte.MIN_VALUE is negative 128, and the upper bound of a byte, Byte.MAX_VALUE, is 127.

questions.q: A weather logger keeps the highest short reading so far and must start lower than any real reading. Which start value fits?
options: Short.MAX_VALUE
zero
Short.MIN_VALUE
Number
optionExplain: Starting at the top means no reading could ever exceed it, so the maximum never updates.
Zero fails when every reading is negative, such as winter temperatures.
Right: the lowest possible short is below or equal to every reading, so the first reading replaces it.
Number is a class, not a value to compare readings against.
questions.explain: A running maximum should start at the lowest value the type can hold.
questions.rule: Start a running maximum at the type's MIN_VALUE.
questions.teaches: Beyond the tutorial: a common use of MIN_VALUE is as the starting value when searching for a largest item, since every real value is at least as large.

questions.q: True or false: A teammate says every int in a program should become Integer, because the tutorial recommends wrappers for all numbers. The tutorial supports this.
questions.explain: The tutorial lists specific needs for wrappers; for ordinary arithmetic it keeps primitives as the default.
questions.rule: Primitives are the default; wrappers answer specific needs.

questions.q: True or false: Integer.valueOf(5).equals(Long.valueOf(5)) returns true because both objects hold the number five.
questions.explain: equals also checks that the two objects have the same type, and Integer differs from Long. The card next states the full rule.
questions.rule: equals needs matching types.

questions.q: Which Integer instance method returns the held value as a double?
options: doubleValue
toDouble
intValue
parseDouble
optionExplain: Right: doubleValue returns the value as a double.
There is no method named toDouble among the Number conversions.
intValue gives an int, not a double.
parseDouble turns a string into a double; it does not read an existing number object.
questions.explain: The xxxValue methods are named for the primitive they return.
questions.rule: xxxValue returns the named primitive.

questions.q: Long a = Long.valueOf(40); Long b = Long.valueOf(40); the expression a.equals(b) evaluates to ____.
questions.explain: Both are Long objects holding 40, so type and value match.
questions.rule: Same type and same value gives true.

questions.q: Which conditions must hold for equals on a Number to return true, per the tutorial? Select all that apply.
options: The argument is not null
The argument has the same type
The argument holds the same numeric value
The argument was stored in a collection
The argument has the same memory address
optionExplain: Right: a null argument always gives false.
Right: an object of a different wrapper type gives false.
Right: the numbers must match.
Collections play no role in equals.
Equals compares type and value; being the very same object is not required.
questions.explain: Three conditions together make equals true. For Double and Float the API documentation adds further requirements.
questions.rule: Equals checks null, type and value.
questions.teaches: For Double and Float, equals has extra requirements beyond type and value; the tutorial sends readers to the API documentation for them.

questions.q: A sensor library hands you a Double target of 3.0 and a Float reading of 3.0, and reading.equals(target) returns false. What explains it?
options: The numbers differ in the last digit
A Float can never hold three
equals only compares string contents
The wrapper types are different
optionExplain: Both show 3.0, so the digits are not the cause.
A Float can hold three; the problem is the type mismatch.
equals on a Number compares type and number, not strings.
Right: Float and Double are different types, so equals fails despite equal-looking values.
questions.explain: Different wrapper types fail equals, which is a type check before it is a value check.
questions.rule: A type mismatch makes equals false.
questions.teaches: Beyond the tutorial: to compare values across wrapper types, convert both to one primitive with a xxxValue method, such as doubleValue, and compare the primitives.

questions.q: A student writes: Integer a = 3; Integer b = 8; boolean smaller = a.compareTo(b); Which statement finds the real fault?
options: compareTo is missing from Integer
compareTo gives an int, not a boolean
Integer objects cannot be compared
The variables must be primitives first
optionExplain: Integer has a compareTo method, listed among the Number methods.
Right: compareTo returns an int, so assigning it to a boolean fails to compile.
Comparing is exactly what compareTo does.
Wrapper objects can call compareTo directly.
questions.explain: The tutorial lists compareTo with an int result, so a boolean variable cannot take it.
questions.rule: compareTo returns an int.

questions.q: Which call best reads the text 101 as a binary number?
options: Integer.parseInt of 101 with radix 2
Integer.parseInt of 101 with radix 10
Integer.toString of 101
Integer.parseInt of 101 with radix 101
optionExplain: Right: radix 2 tells the method the text is written in base 2.
Radix 10 reads the same digits as decimal one hundred one.
toString converts a number to text, the opposite direction.
A radix of 101 would name a base that does not match the text.
questions.explain: The radix argument names the base of the text. The card next explains the conversions.
questions.rule: The radix names the base of the text.

questions.q: In parseInt(String s, int radix), a radix of 16 means the string is read as a ____ number.
questions.explain: Radix 16 is hexadecimal.
questions.rule: Radix 16 is hex.

questions.q: parseInt applied to the text 101 with radix 2 returns ____.
questions.explain: Binary 101 is 1 times 4 plus 0 times 2 plus 1, which is 5.
questions.rule: Read the digits with place values in the given base.

questions.q: Per the tutorial, valueOf applied to the text 333 with radix 8 gives the decimal value ____.
questions.explain: Octal 333 equals 3 times 64 plus 3 times 8 plus 3, which is 219.
questions.rule: valueOf accepts a radix too.
questions.teaches: valueOf has a version taking a radix, so it can read octal text; unlike parseInt it returns an Integer object, here holding 219.

questions.q: A script receives colour codes as text such as 1f (hexadecimal) and needs the int value. Which call fits, and what value for 1f?
options: parseInt with radix 8, giving 15
parseInt with radix 10, giving 1
parseInt with radix 16, giving 31
toString with radix 16, giving 31
optionExplain: Radix 8 has no digit f and would not give 15.
Radix 10 does not accept the letter f as a digit.
Right: 1f in base 16 is 1 times 16 plus 15, which is 31.
toString converts numbers to text, so it cannot read the code.
questions.explain: A radix lets you read hexadecimal text such as 1f.
questions.rule: Match the radix to how the text is written.
questions.teaches: parseInt with a radix reads text in that base; a letter digit such as f (15) is only valid when the radix is above 15, so radix 16 reads 1f as 31 while radix 10 would fail.

questions.q: True or false: A call reads the text 12 with radix 10. If the radix is changed to 8, the result changes from twelve to ten.
questions.explain: Octal 12 means 1 times 8 plus 2, which is 10, so the same digits give a different number.
questions.rule: Same digits, different base, different number.

questions.q: What is the main job of the characters starting with a percent sign inside a format string?
options: They comment out the rest of the line
They mark a slot filled by an argument
They compute the percentage of a number
They repeat the previous word
optionExplain: A percent sign does not start a comment in a format string.
Right: each specifier is a slot that formats the next argument.
It is a marker for a formatted value, not a percentage calculation.
Nothing in a specifier repeats text.
questions.explain: Specifiers are slots for arguments. The card next names their parts.
questions.rule: A specifier is a formatted slot.

questions.q: Match each converter to what it prints.
questions.explain: These four converters appear in the tutorial's examples: d for integers, f for floating-point, s for strings and n for the line break.
questions.rule: Know the converter letters.

questions.q: The String name holds Ana and the int age is 31. Which call prints Ana is 31 followed by a line break?
options: printf("%d is %s%n", name, age)
printf("%n is %s%d", name, age)
printf("%s is %f%n", name, age)
printf("%s is %d%n", name, age)
optionExplain: The d converter is first but name is text, so the order of converters is wrong.
Here %n would insert a line break at the front instead of taking an argument.
f expects a floating-point number, and age is an int.
Right: %s takes the String, %d takes the int, and %n ends the line.
questions.explain: Converters must match the argument types in order.
questions.rule: Converters follow argument order and type.

questions.q: A line of output is meant to end on every operating system. The tutorial recommends ending the format string with which item?
options: A semicolon
A backslash and the letter n
The %n specifier
The converter d
optionExplain: A semicolon ends a Java statement and prints nothing.
The backslash-n escape is a fixed newline; the tutorial prefers %n.
Right: %n gives the platform-appropriate newline.
d prints an integer, not a line break.
questions.explain: The tutorial points to %n as the way to end a line in a format string.
questions.rule: Prefer %n for a line break.
questions.teaches: Different platforms use different line endings, which is why %n is the platform-appropriate newline.

questions.q: True or false: A program formats a price with printf and its Locale set to France. The decimal point in the printed number will be a comma.
questions.explain: The Locale overload changes number formatting; the tutorial's example with France prints a comma as the decimal separator.
questions.rule: Locale shapes separators.
questions.teaches: The overload that takes a Locale first switches decimal and grouping style to that region's, for example a comma instead of a point under the French locale.
questions.hint: Which overload changes the style of the numbers?

questions.q: System.out.printf("%f%n", 2.5) runs with no precision given. What does it print?
optionExplain: Right: the default is six decimal places.
Two decimals is a common choice but not the default.
f pads to its default precision, so the output is longer.
f prints a floating-point number, so it keeps a fractional part.
questions.explain: Without a precision, f shows six decimal places.
questions.rule: The default precision of f is six.

questions.q: True or false: The specifier %,d prints an integer with grouping separators such as 1,234,567.
questions.explain: The comma flag asks for locale-specific grouping separators. The card next covers all the flags and their order.
questions.rule: The comma flag groups digits.

questions.q: Match each flag or part to its effect.
questions.explain: These four are the flags in the tutorial's examples.
questions.rule: Learn each flag's single job.

questions.q: The specifier %05d applied to the value 42 prints ____.
questions.explain: A width of 5 with the zero flag pads 42 with three leading zeros.
questions.rule: Zero flag plus width pads with zeros.

questions.q: The specifier %-6d is followed directly by a bar character, with the value 42. What is printed?
options: The text 42 and the bar with no spaces
Four spaces, then 42, then the bar
The text 000042 and then the bar
42, then four spaces, then the bar
optionExplain: A width of 6 still takes six characters, so spaces fill the rest.
That is the right-justified result, which is what happens without the minus flag.
Zero padding needs the zero flag, which is not present here.
Right: the minus flag left-justifies, so the padding lands after the value and before the bar.
questions.explain: The minus flag moves the padding to the right of the value.
questions.rule: Minus left-justifies and pads on the right.
questions.teaches: With the minus flag the padding goes after the value, so text that follows lines up at the same column in every row.

questions.q: A receipt prints prices in a column. Each price must show two decimals and take nine characters, right-justified. Which specifier fits?
optionExplain: The width and precision are swapped, so this asks for width 2 and nine decimals.
Right: width 9 and precision 2 give nine columns with two decimals, right-justified.
The d converter is for integers and gives no decimals.
The minus flag would left-justify the prices, which breaks right alignment.
questions.explain: Write width first, then a point and the precision.
questions.rule: Width comes before the point, precision after it.
questions.teaches: The width counts every character, including the decimal point and the digits after it: the tutorial's 10.3 example fills ten columns in all.

questions.q: The specifier %10.3f prints pi as 3.142 in ten columns. The number of spaces before the 3 is ____.
questions.explain: The text 3.142 uses five characters, so five spaces fill the width of ten.
questions.rule: Width includes the digits and the point.

questions.q: A price held as the number 5 must print as 5.00. What kind of tool lets you state exactly how many digits to show?
options: A pattern-based formatter
The Math.abs method call
The parseInt method call
A StringBuilder reverse call
optionExplain: Right: a pattern states leading, trailing and decimal digits.
abs returns an absolute value and does not format anything.
parseInt turns text into a number, the opposite direction.
reverse flips characters and does not format numbers.
questions.explain: A pattern describes the exact digits. The card next shows how DecimalFormat reads one.
questions.rule: Patterns describe digits.

questions.q: Match each pattern symbol to its meaning.
pairs: A digit that is always shown
A digit that is not forced
questions.explain: Zero forces a digit, hash does not, the comma groups, and other symbols are literal.
questions.rule: 0 forces, # does not force.

questions.q: The value 7.5 formatted with the pattern 000.0 produces ____.
questions.explain: Three forced integer digits turn 7 into 007, and the one decimal digit stays 5.
questions.rule: Each 0 shows a digit.

questions.q: The value 2500.5 is formatted with the pattern ###,###.###. Which text results?
optionExplain: The # positions do not force digits, so no trailing zeros are added.
The comma in the pattern asks for a grouping separator.
Right: grouping appears, and the optional decimal digits show only the 5.
Leading and trailing zeros need forced 0 digits, not #.
questions.explain: A # position shows a digit only when the number has one.
questions.rule: # adds no padding.
questions.teaches: Optional # digits do not pad: in the tutorial's own example 12345.67 shows as 12,345.67 with a dollar prefix, not with a trailing zero added.

questions.q: A shop must show 1234.5 as $1,234.50, with grouping and two decimals every time. Which pattern fits?
optionExplain: The # digits after the point would drop the trailing zero and give $1,234.5.
Right: the comma groups the thousands and the two 0 digits after the point force two decimals.
There is no comma, so the grouping is missing.
This has no grouping and allows only one decimal digit.
questions.explain: Use 0 after the point to force decimals and a comma for grouping.
questions.rule: Force decimals with 0 and group with a comma.
questions.teaches: To always show two decimals, end the pattern with 0 digits after the point; the tutorial's summary uses #,##0.00 to show 1234.5 as 1,234.50.

questions.q: True or false: After a DecimalFormat with the pattern ###.## formats the double 123456.789, the double variable itself now holds 123456.79.
questions.explain: format returns a new String; the original double is untouched.
questions.rule: Formatting returns text and leaves the number alone.

questions.q: True or false: To use Math.sqrt you must first create a Math object with the new keyword.
questions.explain: All Math methods are static, so you call them on the class. The card next lists what Math offers.
questions.rule: Math methods are static.

questions.q: Math.floor(43.74) returns the value ____.
questions.explain: floor gives the largest whole number not above the argument, returned as a double.
questions.rule: floor rounds down.

questions.q: A game needs a random whole number from 0 to 5 inclusive, to pick one of six doors. Which expression does that?
options: Math.random() * 6
(int)(Math.random() * 5)
(int)(Math.random() * 7)
(int)(Math.random() * 6)
optionExplain: This stays a double and can be fractional, not a door number.
Multiplying by 5 gives 0 through 4, so the last door is never picked.
Multiplying by 7 gives 0 through 6, one door too many.
Right: the value is below 6, and the cast keeps 0 through 5.
questions.explain: Multiply by the count of outcomes, then cast to int.
questions.rule: Scale by the number of outcomes, then cast.

questions.q: Math.round is called with a double argument. What type does it return?
options: int
float
long
double
optionExplain: int is what round returns for a float argument, not for a double.
round does not return a float.
Right: round returns a long for a double argument.
ceil and floor return doubles, but round gives a whole-number type.
questions.explain: Math.round returns a whole-number type chosen by its argument.
questions.rule: round(double) gives long; round(float) gives int.
questions.teaches: round is overloaded: it returns a long when given a double and an int when given a float.

questions.q: An animation needs the sine of a 90 degree turn. Which call is correct?
options: Math.sin(Math.toRadians(90))
Math.sin(90)
Math.sin(Math.toDegrees(90))
Math.toRadians(Math.sin(90))
optionExplain: Right: toRadians converts the angle, and sin then receives radians.
sin takes radians, so 90 is read as 90 radians.
toDegrees converts the wrong way, from radians to degrees.
This takes the sine of 90 radians and then converts the result as if it were an angle.
questions.explain: Convert degrees to radians before calling sin, cos or tan.
questions.rule: Degrees need toRadians first.
questions.teaches: The inverse methods asin, acos and atan return radians as well, which is why the tutorial's demo passes their results through toDegrees to get 45 back.

questions.q: A coder changes (int)(Math.random() * 10) to (int)(Math.random() * 10 + 1). How does the range of results change?
options: It stays 0 through 9
It becomes 1 through 9
It becomes 0 through 10
It becomes 1 through 10
optionExplain: Adding 1 before the cast shifts every result up by one.
The largest result reaches 10, not 9.
The smallest result is now 1, not 0.
Right: random times 10 is below 10, adding 1 makes it below 11 and at least 1, so the cast gives 1 through 10.
questions.explain: Adding a constant shifts the whole range.
questions.rule: Scale, then shift for a different start.

questions.q: True or false: The tutorial recommends calling Math.random once per number to produce a long series of random numbers.
questions.explain: Math.random suits a single number; for a series the tutorial recommends creating a java.util.Random object and calling its methods.
questions.rule: Use Random for a series.

questions.q: Which literal holds the single letter Z as a primitive character?
options: Z
Character Z
optionExplain: Without quotes, Z would be read as a variable name.
Right: single quotes mark a char literal.
Double quotes make a String, which is an object holding text.
Character is a class name; this is not a literal.
questions.explain: A char literal sits in single quotes. The card next separates char, Character and strings.
questions.rule: Single quotes mean char.

questions.q: A single character is held by default in the primitive type ____.
questions.explain: char is the default, and Character is the wrapper for when an object is needed.
questions.rule: char first, Character when an object is required.

questions.q: Sort each situation: is the primitive char or the Character object the better fit?

items.t: A local variable that holds a first letter
A method parameter that accepts only objects
A value handed to a collection that holds objects
A loop variable stepping over letters
A variable used in a plain comparison
An argument that an API declares as an object

questions.explain: The primitive does plain work; the object is used where an object is required.
questions.rule: Object needed means Character.

questions.q: Which literal stores the Greek capital omega in a char using a Unicode escape?
optionExplain: Right: backslash, u and four hexadecimal digits write a character by its Unicode value.
The backslash is missing, so this is not an escape at all.
Without the letter u, the backslash escape does not name a Unicode value.
A forward slash starts nothing special in Java.
questions.explain: A Unicode escape is backslash, u and four hexadecimal digits.
questions.rule: Backslash-u plus four hex digits writes any Unicode character.
questions.teaches: A char can be written as a Unicode escape: backslash, the letter u and four hexadecimal digits, such as the tutorial's omega.

questions.q: A program must print the path text C:\tmp exactly, with a visible backslash. Which literal does that?
options: "C:\tmp"
"C:/tmp\t"
"C:\\tmp"
"C:\"tmp"
optionExplain: The compiler reads backslash t as a tab, so the printed text would contain a tab instead of a backslash.
This changes the path and appends a tab character.
Right: a doubled backslash inserts one backslash, so the next letter stays a letter.
Backslash-quote inserts a double quote, which is not part of the path.
questions.explain: To print a backslash, write two of them.
questions.rule: Escape the backslash itself.
questions.teaches: Even inside a path, backslash followed by t is read as a tab, so a literal backslash must be written as two.

questions.q: True or false: A Character object can be changed after creation by assigning it a new char value inside the object.
questions.explain: Character is immutable: once created, its value cannot change. Assigning a new value to a variable points it at a different value.
questions.rule: Character is immutable.

questions.q: Which call tests whether the char variable c holds a digit?
options: c.isDigit()
Character.isDigit(c)
Digit.test(c)
isDigit(c) with no class
optionExplain: A primitive char has no methods to call.
Right: the test is a static method on the Character class.
There is no class called Digit for this.
Without the class name the compiler cannot find the method.
questions.explain: Character methods are called on the class. The card next lists the common ones.
questions.rule: Call Character methods on the class.

questions.q: Match each method to what it does.
questions.explain: Names beginning is give true or false, while to methods give converted values.
questions.rule: is tests, to converts.

questions.q: Character.toUpperCase('k') returns the char ____.
questions.explain: toUpperCase returns the upper-case form of the char.
questions.rule: Convert methods return the new char.

questions.q: A condition must be true when a char c is a letter or a digit. Which expression fits?
options: Character.isLetterOrDigit(c) is the only option
Character.isLetter(c) + Character.isDigit(c)
Character.isLetter(isDigit(c))
Character.isLetter(c) || Character.isDigit(c)
optionExplain: Two tests joined by or also work, so naming one method as the only option is wrong.
True or false values cannot be added to each other.
isLetter expects a char, not the true or false answer of another test.
Right: both tests give true or false, so they combine with the or operator.
questions.explain: The tests return boolean values, so they combine with and or or.
questions.rule: Boolean tests combine with and, or.
questions.teaches: Beyond the tutorial: because each test returns true or false, several can be joined in one condition with the logical operators.

questions.q: A title checker counts capital letters. For each char c it should add one when which condition holds?
options: Character.isLetter(c)
Character.toUpperCase(c)
Character.isUpperCase(c)
Character.isLowerCase(c)
optionExplain: This counts every letter, including lower-case ones.
toUpperCase returns a char, not true or false, so it cannot serve as the condition.
Right: isUpperCase is true exactly for upper-case chars.
This would count the small letters, the opposite of the goal.
questions.explain: Choose the test that matches the property you count.
questions.rule: Pick the test that names the property.
questions.teaches: Beyond the tutorial: counting is done by running a test on each char and adding one when it returns true.

questions.q: A student writes the line Character.toUpperCase(initial); on its own and expects the variable initial to now be upper-case. What is the fault?
options: The returned char is thrown away
toUpperCase only works on Strings
The class name must be lower-case
initial must be declared as a Character first
optionExplain: Right: the method returns the converted char, and the returned value was thrown away.
The method works on a char; String has its own toUpperCase.
Class names such as Character start with a capital letter.
A plain char works fine with this static method.
questions.explain: The method returns the new char and leaves the argument alone.
questions.rule: Use the returned value.

questions.q: A String variable s holds the text cat. The line s.concat with the text x is run and its result is not stored. What does s hold afterwards?
options: catx
an error is raised
x
cat
optionExplain: That would be true only if the returned string had been stored in s.
The call is legal; it just has no lasting effect on s.
The original text is not replaced by the argument.
Right: concat returns a new string and leaves the original alone.
questions.explain: Methods that look like edits return new strings. The card next explains why.
questions.rule: Strings do not change in place.

questions.q: A String cannot be changed after it is created, a property called ____.
questions.explain: Strings are immutable, so any apparent change produces a new string.
questions.rule: Strings are immutable.

questions.q: String first holds Ada. The code runs String full = first.concat(a space and then Lovelace). What do first and full hold?
options: Both hold Ada Lovelace
first holds Ada and full holds Ada Lovelace
Both hold Ada
first holds Ada Lovelace and full holds Ada
optionExplain: The original string is not changed, so first cannot hold the longer text.
Right: first is untouched and full holds the new joined string.
full receives the new, longer string returned by concat.
This reverses the roles: the new string goes to full.
questions.explain: The new string goes to the variable you assign it to; the old one stays.
questions.rule: The returned string is the only new text.
