questions.q: A char array named letters holds h, e, l, l, o. Which statement creates a String from it?
options: new String(letters)
String(letters)
letters.toString() as a String literal
letters + String
optionExplain: Right: new String(letters) is one of the class's constructors.
Without the new keyword a constructor is not invoked.
An array does not turn into text this way.
This is not valid Java.
questions.explain: A String can be built from a char array with a constructor.
questions.rule: Literals are usual; constructors also exist.
questions.teaches: The String class has thirteen constructors; the tutorial shows one that takes a char array, though a literal is the usual way to create a string.

questions.q: To reverse a String using char arrays, put these steps in order.
items: Copy the characters of the String into a char array
Fill a second array with those characters from last to first
Build a new String from the second array
Print or return the new String
questions.explain: Because a String cannot be changed, the reversal works on arrays and ends by creating a new String.
questions.rule: Reverse by building a new String.
questions.teaches: The tutorial reverses Dot saw I was Tod this way and gets doT saw I was toD; it notes that the String method getChars can do the first copying step in one call.

questions.q: True or false: Because a String is immutable, a variable of type String cannot be made to refer to a different String after its first assignment.
questions.explain: Immutability is about the String object. A variable can be reassigned to refer to another String. This reading goes beyond the tutorial's text.
questions.rule: The object is fixed, not the variable.

questions.q: True or false: String.format prints its result to the console in the same way as printf.
questions.explain: String.format returns the formatted text as a String instead of printing it. The card next compares the two.
questions.rule: format returns a String; printf prints.

questions.q: Match each tool to its description.
pairs: A method returning a new joined String
Joins and converts other operands with toString
Returns formatted text as a String
Prints formatted text to the console
questions.explain: The first three produce or build strings; printf prints.
questions.rule: Know what each tool returns.

questions.q: int stock = 7 and the text is Stock: followed by the value. Which approach produces the String Stock: 7 without calling any conversion method yourself?
options: Call printf and read what it returns
Use concat with stock as its argument
Use plus between the text and stock
Compare the text with stock using equals
optionExplain: printf prints the text rather than returning it as a String.
concat accepts only a String argument, so an int does not fit.
Right: plus converts the int by calling toString for you.
equals asks a question; it does not build text.
questions.explain: Plus converts the non-String operand.
questions.rule: Plus converts non-Strings; concat needs a String.

questions.q: A long message is written over three source lines. Which approach is valid, since a string literal cannot span several lines?
options: Press Enter in the middle of the quotes
Split it up and end each line with a plus
Put a backslash at each line end inside the quotes
Use three separate literals with no operator
optionExplain: A line break inside a literal is not allowed.
Right: each piece is its own literal, and the plus joins them.
A backslash at a line end does not continue a Java literal.
Literals need an operator to join them.
questions.explain: Break long literals into pieces joined by plus.
questions.rule: Plus at the end of the line continues the expression.
questions.teaches: A string literal cannot span lines in source code; the tutorial breaks long text by ending each line with a plus.

questions.q: A logger must build one message with a decimal number and a name, store it in a variable, and use it in two places. Which tool fits best?
options: System.out.printf, called twice
A String literal containing percent signs only
concat with the number as its argument
String.format, storing its returned String
optionExplain: printf prints each time but gives you nothing to store.
A literal with percent signs is not filled in by itself.
concat requires a String argument, and gives no number formatting.
Right: format returns text you can keep and reuse.
questions.explain: To keep formatted text, return it with String.format.
questions.rule: Reuse needs a returned String.
questions.teaches: String.format accepts the same specifiers as printf, such as d, f and s, so one format string works with either; the difference is only print versus return.

questions.q: A line calls String.format with the format %d items and the number 5, but nothing uses the returned value. The text the console shows for that line is ____.
questions.explain: format only returns the text; without a print or a stored variable, the console shows nothing from it.
questions.rule: A returned String does nothing until it is used.

questions.q: True or false: A String holding the characters 12 can take part in arithmetic as the number twelve without any conversion.
questions.explain: Text and numbers are different types; text must be converted first. The card next shows the conversion methods.
questions.rule: Convert text before calculating.

questions.q: Float.valueOf converts a string to a Float ____, from which floatValue extracts the primitive.
questions.explain: valueOf returns a wrapper object, not a primitive.
questions.rule: valueOf gives an object; parse gives a primitive.

questions.q: The tutorial's ValueOfDemo program does these things. Put them in order.
items: Check that exactly two command-line arguments were given
Convert each argument string to a float
Do arithmetic on the two floats
Print each result
questions.explain: The program first checks the argument count, then converts, calculates and prints.
questions.rule: Check, convert, calculate, print.

questions.q: The tutorial's FPAdder exercise (from the tutorial's exercise, not the lesson text) sums the arguments 1, 1e2, 3.0 and 4.754 and prints the total with exactly two decimals. The printed text is ____.
questions.explain: The text 1e2 is read as 100, so the sum is 108.754, which prints as 108.75 with two decimals.
questions.rule: Floating-point parsing reads scientific notation.
questions.teaches: Text in scientific notation such as 1e2 is accepted by floating-point parsing and means 100; the exercise's total of 108.754 is shown as 108.75 with two decimals.

questions.q: java Adder 1 3 2 10 should print 16. Each element of the args array is a String. Which statement correctly adds one element to an int total at index i?
options: total += args[i];
total += Integer.toString(args[i]);
total += Integer.parseInt(args[i]);
total += args.length;
optionExplain: Adding text to an int total is not a numeric addition.
toString converts numbers to text, the wrong direction and also a wrong argument type.
Right: parseInt converts the text of args[i] to an int that can be added.
This adds how many arguments there are, not their values.
questions.explain: Convert each command-line String before summing.
questions.rule: Command-line arguments are text.
questions.teaches: Command-line arguments always arrive as strings, so a program that sums them must convert each one, and can handle a varying count by using args.length.

questions.q: True or false: In the tutorial's ValueOfDemo program, the code checks that both arguments are valid numbers before converting them.
questions.explain: The demo only checks that two arguments were given. Whether they are valid numbers is not checked, and the tutorial does not discuss it.
questions.rule: Count checks do not check validity.

questions.q: Which call returns a String for the int variable i?
options: String.valueOf(i)
Integer.parseInt(i)
i.toString
Integer.valueOf(i) as a String
optionExplain: Right: String.valueOf accepts the int and returns text.
parseInt goes the other way, from text to int.
A primitive has no members to call.
valueOf returns an Integer object, not text.
questions.explain: Several calls turn a number into text. The card next lists them.
questions.rule: valueOf and toString make text.

questions.q: Sort each call by the direction of conversion.

items.t: Float.parseFloat(s)
Integer.toString(i)
String.valueOf(i)
Integer.parseInt(s)
Double.valueOf(s)
Double.toString(d)

questions.explain: The parse methods and wrapper valueOf read text into numbers; toString and String.valueOf produce text.
questions.rule: parse reads text; toString writes it.

questions.q: The double d holds 12.345. Double.toString(d) is the text 12.345, and its length() is ____.
questions.explain: The text has two digits, a point and three digits: six characters.
questions.rule: The text length counts the point as well.

questions.q: The tutorial converts 858.48 to text. The point is at index 3 and the text length is 6, so the digits after the point number length minus index minus 1, which is ____.
questions.explain: Six minus three minus one is two digits after the point.
questions.rule: Convert first, then count with String methods.
questions.teaches: After converting a double to text, the tutorial finds the point with a String method and subtracts its position from the length to count digits on each side.

questions.q: A tool must report how many digits the int 40213 has. Which approach fits what you have learned?
options: Call length() directly on the int
Use Math.sqrt on the int
Convert it with parseInt and call length()
Convert with String.valueOf, then length()
optionExplain: A primitive int has no length method.
Square roots measure something else.
parseInt goes from text to number and cannot be applied to an int.
Right: the text 40213 has five characters, so its length counts the digits.
questions.explain: To use String methods on a number, convert it to text first.
questions.rule: Convert to text to use String methods.
questions.teaches: Beyond the tutorial: counting digits with length works for plain whole numbers; a leading minus sign would count as a character too.

questions.q: A coder writes int i = 5; String s = i; and the compiler rejects the second line. Which fix matches the tutorial?
options: Change it to String s = parseInt(i);
Use String s = String.valueOf(i);
Change it to int s = i.toString();
Remove the type String
optionExplain: parseInt reads text into numbers.
Right: valueOf accepts the int and returns the text.
A primitive int has no members to call.
The variable still needs a type that can hold text.
questions.explain: Convert explicitly; an int does not become text by assignment.
questions.rule: Use a conversion method.

questions.q: In a Java String, what is the index of the first character?
options: The length of the string
optionExplain: Right: indexes start at 0.
Counting from 1 is how people count, but Java starts one earlier.
A negative index is not a valid position.
The length is one past the last character.
questions.explain: Java counts from 0. The card next uses this to read characters and slices.
questions.rule: Indexes start at 0.

questions.q: For a String of length 10, the last valid index is ____.
questions.explain: Indexes run from 0 to length minus 1, so 9.
questions.rule: The last index is length minus 1.

questions.q: String word holds stationery. The call word.substring(2, 6) returns ____.
questions.explain: Index 2 is a and index 5 is o; the end index 6 is excluded, so the text is atio.
questions.rule: The end index is excluded.

questions.q: String word holds stationery, which has length 10. What does word.substring(10) return?
options: The whole String
The last character, y
An empty String
It throws an error
optionExplain: Starting at 10 skips every character.
The last character is at index 9, not 10.
Right: an index equal to the length is legal and leaves nothing to return.
Only an index greater than the length is rejected.
questions.explain: A start index equal to the length gives an empty String.
questions.rule: Index equal to length is legal for substring.
questions.teaches: The tutorial notes that substring accepts an index equal to the length and returns an empty String, but rejects anything greater.

questions.q: In an address of length 16, the @ sign is at index 4. Which call returns the part after the @ sign?
options: substring(4)
substring(5)
substring(0, 4)
substring(3)
optionExplain: This starts at the @ sign itself, so the result begins with it.
Right: starting one past the marker skips it.
This returns the part before the @ sign.
This starts at the character before the @ sign.
questions.explain: To start after a marker, use its index plus one.
questions.rule: After a marker means index plus one.
questions.teaches: The tutorial's Filename example finds the extension with substring(dot + 1), starting one past the dot.

questions.q: String word holds stationery. The call changes from substring(2, 6) to substring(2, 7). What is the new result?
options: tation
atio
ationery
ation
optionExplain: Changing only the end does not change the start at 2.
That was the result with the old end index.
That would need no end index at all.
Right: the end index 7 is excluded, so index 6, the n, is included and the text is ation.
questions.explain: Raising the end index adds characters at the end of the slice.
questions.rule: Move the end, extend the slice.

questions.q: True or false: The call s.charAt(s.length()) reads the last character of the String s.
questions.explain: The last valid index is length minus 1, so index length is out of range.
questions.rule: The last index is length minus 1.

questions.q: True or false: When indexOf does not find the requested character, it returns 0.
questions.explain: It returns minus 1, since 0 is a valid index. The card next lists the search methods.
questions.rule: Not found is minus 1.

questions.q: Match each method to its job.
pairs: Searches forward for the first occurrence
Searches backward for the last occurrence
Replaces every match of a regular expression
questions.explain: The two index methods return positions; contains returns a boolean; replaceAll takes a pattern.
questions.rule: Match the method to what it returns.

questions.q: String fruit holds banana. lastIndexOf with the char a returns ____.
questions.explain: The last a sits at index 5 of banana.
questions.rule: lastIndexOf scans from the end.

questions.q: Which String method returns a copy with leading and trailing white space removed?
options: subSequence
split
trim
replaceFirst
optionExplain: subSequence returns a range of characters, not trimmed text.
split cuts a String into an array at matches of a regular expression.
Right: trim removes white space from both ends.
replaceFirst changes the first regex match only.
questions.explain: trim cleans both ends and returns a copy.
questions.rule: trim returns a copy without end white space.
questions.teaches: trim returns a copy with leading and trailing white space removed; likewise toLowerCase and toUpperCase return copies, handing back the original String if no conversion is needed.

questions.q: A support tool only needs to know whether a message contains the word refund, not where it appears. Which call fits best?
options: contains with the text refund
replace, then compare lengths
lastIndexOf, then compare the result to 0
substring over every position
optionExplain: Right: contains returns true or false for presence.
Replacing changes the text for a question that needs no change.
This gives a position when only presence matters, and is easy to get wrong.
Trying every position is the long way round.
questions.explain: Use contains when presence is the question.
questions.rule: Presence only means contains.
questions.teaches: contains takes a CharSequence, an interface that String implements, so you can pass a String straight in.

questions.q: A Filename-style class stores the text /home/user/index, which has no period, and its filename method looks up the last period, then calls substring between the last slash and that period. What happens?
options: It returns index, as in the demo output
It returns an empty String instead
It prints -1 and carries on normally
It throws a StringIndexOutOfBoundsException
optionExplain: Without a period there is no end position, so the usual result is not possible.
An empty String needs equal start and end indexes, which is not the case.
-1 is the search result, but the code then uses it as an index.
Right: the missing period gives -1, and substring cannot take that end index.
questions.explain: A search result of minus 1 must not be used as an index.
questions.rule: Check for minus 1 before using an index.

questions.q: Which check tells you whether two Strings hold the same letters when upper and lower case are treated alike?
options: equals
equalsIgnoreCase
compareTo
startsWith
optionExplain: equals is case-sensitive.
Right: equalsIgnoreCase ignores differences in case.
compareTo returns an int about ordering, not a plain yes or no.
startsWith only tests the beginning.
questions.explain: There is a case-blind version of equals. The card next lists the comparison methods.
questions.rule: equalsIgnoreCase ignores case.

questions.q: Match each method to the kind of answer it gives.
pairs: a negative, zero or positive int
true or false for the suffix
true or false for two stretches
questions.explain: Only compareTo returns an int; the other three answer yes or no.
questions.rule: Only compareTo and compareToIgnoreCase return ints.

questions.q: String x holds cat and String y holds dog. What is the sign of x.compareTo(y), and of y.compareTo(x)?
options: Negative, then positive
Positive, then negative
Zero, then zero
Negative, then negative
optionExplain: Right: cat comes before dog, so it is less, and the swapped call is greater.
That reverses the order: it would hold if dog came before cat.
Zero means the Strings are equal, which they are not.
Swapping the operands must flip the sign.
questions.explain: Swapping the operands flips the sign.
questions.rule: compareTo is antisymmetric in sign.

questions.q: A program searches a String of length 18 for a piece of length 4 with regionMatches. The largest start index worth testing is ____.
questions.explain: The piece must fit, so the last start is 18 minus 4, which is 14.
questions.rule: A region must fit inside the String.
questions.teaches: The tutorial's search loop runs the start index up to the first length minus the second length, because the region has to fit; Eggs is found at index 6 in Green Eggs and Ham.

questions.q: A contact list must be sorted by name, ignoring upper and lower case. Names x and y are compared. Which call should the sort use?
options: x.equalsIgnoreCase(y)
x.regionMatches(y)
x.compareToIgnoreCase(y)
x.endsWith(y)
optionExplain: That answers only equal or not, which cannot order names.
regionMatches needs offsets and a length and answers true or false.
Right: it returns a negative, zero or positive int, ignoring case.
endsWith tests a suffix, not an order.
questions.explain: Ordering needs an int result; ignoring case needs the IgnoreCase version.
questions.rule: Order needs the int; only its sign counts.
questions.teaches: Only the sign of compareTo's result is meaningful, so code should test for negative, zero or positive, not for a specific number such as minus 1.

questions.q: True or false: The call equals on the Strings Apple and apple returns true, because both contain the same letters.
questions.explain: equals is case-sensitive; only equalsIgnoreCase treats the two as equal.
questions.rule: Plain equals cares about case.

questions.q: A loop must join thousands of small pieces of text into one long result. Which tool does the tutorial favour?
options: Many String concatenations in a loop
StringBuilder with append calls
A char variable for each piece
A Character object for each piece
optionExplain: Each join makes a new String, which adds up over thousands of joins.
Right: appending to a StringBuilder is more efficient for large numbers of joins.
A char holds one character only.
A Character also holds one character only.
questions.explain: Mutable text suits repeated joins. The card next gives the guidance.
questions.rule: Many joins suit StringBuilder.

questions.q: A StringBuilder created with no arguments has a capacity of ____.
questions.explain: The default empty builder has capacity 16.
questions.rule: Default capacity is 16.

questions.q: A StringBuilder is created from a String holding the five letters hello. What are its length and capacity?
options: 5 and 5
5 and 16
21 and 21
5 and 21
optionExplain: The constructor adds spare space beyond the characters.
16 is the capacity of an empty builder, not of one created from a String.
The length counts characters, not spare space.
Right: five characters, plus 16 spare spaces, gives capacity 21.
questions.explain: Created from a String, capacity is the length plus 16.
questions.rule: Capacity is length plus 16 here.

questions.q: An empty default StringBuilder gets the nine-character String Greetings appended. What are its length and capacity?
options: 9 and 9
25 and 25
9 and 16
16 and 16
optionExplain: Capacity was already 16 and does not shrink to fit.
Length is not added to capacity.
Right: the length is 9, and the capacity stays 16 since the length does not exceed it.
Length reports characters, not allocated space.
questions.explain: Capacity only grows when the length would exceed it.
questions.rule: Capacity grows only when needed.
questions.teaches: Appending does not touch capacity until the new length would exceed it; then the capacity is increased automatically.

questions.q: A coder wants the text level reversed in as few lines as possible. Which approach does the tutorial's comparison favour?
options: Build a StringBuilder, then reverse
Two char arrays and two copy loops
Call reverse directly on the String
Use concat again and again
optionExplain: Right: a StringBuilder has reverse, and printing it calls toString for you.
This works but takes more code, as the tutorial's first version shows.
String has no reverse method.
concat joins; it does not reverse.
questions.explain: A builder's own methods can replace loops over arrays.
questions.rule: Builders carry editing methods that Strings lack.
questions.teaches: The tutorial's version with reverse is shorter than the two-array version, and printing a builder with println calls its toString automatically.

questions.q: True or false: The tutorial advises replacing every String in a program with a StringBuilder.
questions.explain: The tutorial says to use String by default and StringBuilder when it gives simpler code or better performance.
questions.rule: String stays the default.

questions.q: True or false: On a StringBuilder, append adds text at the end while insert adds it at a chosen position.
questions.explain: append goes to the end; insert takes an offset. The card next lists the editing methods.
questions.rule: append is the end; insert is anywhere.

questions.q: Match each StringBuilder method to its effect.
pairs: Adds converted data at the end
Adds data before a given offset
questions.explain: These four are the core editing methods.
questions.rule: Know the four core methods.

questions.q: A StringBuilder sb holds abcde. After sb.delete(1, 3), what does sb hold?
options: ae
acde
abe
ade
optionExplain: That would remove three characters, but the end index is excluded.
That would be deleteCharAt(1), which removes one character.
That would remove indexes 2 and 3, not 1 and 2.
Right: indexes 1 and 2 (b and c) go, leaving a, d and e.
questions.explain: delete removes from start up to but not including end.
questions.rule: The end index is excluded.

questions.q: A StringBuilder holds ab. After sb.append(7) and then sb.append(true), its length is ____.
questions.explain: The int 7 adds one character and the boolean adds the four letters of true, so 2 plus 1 plus 4 is 7.
questions.rule: append converts any type to text.
questions.teaches: append is overloaded for any data type and adds the converted text, so a boolean adds the characters of its text form.

questions.q: A loop builds a list of names into a StringBuilder, each followed by a comma. Which statement removes the last comma?
options: sb.deleteCharAt(sb.length())
sb.deleteCharAt(sb.length() - 1)
sb.setLength(sb.length() + 1)
sb.delete(0, 1)
optionExplain: The last valid index is length minus 1, so this index is out of range.
Right: this removes the final character.
A larger length pads the end with null characters instead of removing anything.
This removes the first character.
questions.explain: Count from 0, so the last index is length minus 1.
questions.rule: Use length minus 1 for the last character.
questions.teaches: Removing the last character is deleteCharAt at the last valid index, length minus 1, the same indexing rule as for a String.

questions.q: A coder calls toUpperCase directly on a StringBuilder variable and the compiler rejects it. What fits the tutorial?
options: Call toString, then use the method
Rename the variable and recompile
Use StringBuffer instead, which has it
Call reverse on it first and retry
optionExplain: Right: any String method can be used on the result of toString.
The name is not the problem.
StringBuffer has the same methods as StringBuilder.
reverse does not make the method available.
questions.explain: Convert with toString to reach String methods.
questions.rule: toString opens the String methods.

questions.q: True or false: Assigning an int to a variable of type Integer needs an explicit method call to wrap it.
questions.explain: The compiler boxes it automatically. The card next lists where this happens.
questions.rule: Boxing is automatic.

questions.q: Match each primitive type to its wrapper class.
questions.explain: Most wrappers capitalise the primitive's name; char and int are the exceptions with longer names.
questions.rule: Know the wrapper names.

questions.q: Sort each situation by the conversion the compiler performs.

items.t: Assigning the char a to a Character variable
Assigning a Double to a double variable
Passing an int to a method expecting an Integer
Passing an Integer to a method expecting an int
Adding a double to a list of Double objects
Reading a Double from a list into a double

questions.explain: A primitive going into an object slot is boxed; an object going into a primitive slot is unboxed.
questions.rule: Primitive into object boxes; object into primitive unboxes.

questions.q: A loop visits Integer objects and uses the remainder operator and += on them. Why does this compile?
options: The loop converts each Integer to a String
Integer objects define their own remainder operator
The compiler unboxes them with intValue calls
The += operator boxes the int total
optionExplain: Strings are not involved in numeric remainder.
Operators work on primitive values, not on objects.
Right: the operators work on primitives, so the compiler unboxes the objects.
The total is already a primitive, and the objects need to be unboxed.
questions.explain: Operators work because the compiler unboxes first.
questions.rule: Arithmetic on wrappers means unboxing.
questions.teaches: The tutorial's sumEven example uses % and += on Integer objects; the compiler adds intValue calls so that the arithmetic works.

questions.q: A method is declared with one parameter of type Double. A caller passes the literal 21.5. Which conversion does the compiler apply?
options: Unboxing from Double to double
Autoboxing from double to Double
No conversion, because the types match
Conversion of the literal to a String
optionExplain: The literal is a primitive, so there is nothing to unbox.
Right: a primitive passed where the wrapper is expected is boxed.
The literal is a primitive double and the parameter is an object.
No text is needed anywhere in this call.
questions.explain: A primitive meeting an object parameter is boxed.
questions.rule: Method arguments box and unbox too.
questions.teaches: The tutorial's example adds the double literal 3.1416 to a list of Double objects and relies on boxing through the method call.

questions.q: A method absoluteValue(int i) is called with an Integer holding -8. If its parameter is changed to Integer and the caller passes the int -8, which conversion happens instead?
options: Unboxing, as before
A cast to a String
No conversion
Autoboxing at the call
optionExplain: Before, an object met a primitive parameter; now a primitive meets an object parameter.
Strings are not part of this.
The types still differ, so the compiler converts.
Right: a primitive passed to an object parameter is boxed.
questions.explain: Reverse the direction and you reverse the conversion.
questions.rule: The direction of the mismatch decides.

questions.q: A teammate claims that with Integer n = 5; the statement int m = n + 1; fails to compile because n is not a primitive. True or false: This code fails to compile.
questions.explain: The claim is wrong: the compiler unboxes n automatically, so n + 1 is an int and the assignment to m compiles.
questions.rule: A wrapper is unboxed automatically where a primitive is needed.
questions.teaches: Autoboxing also works in reverse in arithmetic: an Integer used in n + 1 is unboxed to an int by the compiler, so no cast or method call is needed (beyond the tutorial).

questions.q: A programmer wants one storage class that can hold apples in one program and wrenches in another, with no rewriting. Which feature is designed for this?
options: Overloading the constructor
Making every field static
Type parameters on the class
Copying the class once per item type
optionExplain: Overloading gives several constructors, but the stored item type stays fixed in the class.
Static fields are shared by the whole class and do nothing to vary the item type.
Right: a type parameter lets one definition be used with different item types.
This works but defeats the goal of one definition.
questions.explain: Type parameters let one definition serve many item types. The card next shows how they compare with ordinary parameters.
questions.rule: A type parameter is to types what a formal parameter is to values: one definition, many inputs.

questions.q: True or false: a formal parameter of a method receives a value, while a type parameter receives a type.
questions.explain: That is the comparison the tutorial draws: formal parameters take values, type parameters take types.
questions.rule: Values go to formal parameters, types go to type parameters.

questions.q: Which of these can be supplied for a type parameter when a generic class is used?
options: An array type such as String array
The primitive type int
A literal value such as 8
A method name
optionExplain: Right: a class type, an interface type, an array type or another type variable are all allowed.
Primitives are not allowed as type arguments; the wrapper Integer is used instead.
A type parameter takes types, not values.
Method names are not types, so they cannot fill a type parameter.
questions.explain: Type arguments must be non-primitive types, and arrays, interfaces and other type variables count.
questions.rule: Any non-primitive type can fill a type parameter.
questions.teaches: A type argument may be a class type, an interface type, an array type or another type variable, but never a primitive type.

questions.q: A bakery app needs a Tray class that holds cakes on one screen and loaves on another, from one definition. What stands for the item type inside Tray?
options: A formal parameter of the Tray constructor
A static constant naming the item
A field of the plain base type Object that is cast later
A type parameter such as T
optionExplain: A formal parameter carries a value, not a type.
A constant would fix one item type for every use.
This is the old approach that needs casts and gives weaker checks.
Right: T is replaced by Cake or Loaf where Tray is used.
questions.explain: The item type is the thing that varies, so it becomes a type parameter of Tray.
questions.hint: Which thing in the class changes between uses: a value or a type?
questions.rule: A type parameter is to types what a formal parameter is to values: one definition, many inputs.

questions.q: A class Crate with a type parameter T is written once. The same program uses it for Apple objects and, later, for Wrench objects. What happens?
options: The second use fails because T is fixed by the first use
Both uses work, each with its own type argument
Crate must be copied for the second type
Both uses must share the type chosen first
optionExplain: T is not fixed by one use; each use of the class supplies its own argument.
Right: each use supplies its own type argument to the same definition.
Copying is exactly what the type parameter avoids.
Different uses may choose different types.
questions.explain: A type parameter is filled separately at each use, like a formal parameter at each call.
questions.rule: Each use of a generic type picks its own type argument.

questions.q: Sort each input by whether it goes to a method's formal parameter or to generic code as a type argument.

items.t: the number 8 handed to a price method
String handed to a Box declaration
a customer name handed to a greet method
Integer in a list declaration
the text hello handed to a print method
Character as a second type argument of a Pair

questions.explain: Values such as 8 and hello travel through formal parameters; type names such as String travel as type arguments.
questions.teaches: Generic code can take several type arguments at once, in a list, just as a method can take several values.
questions.rule: A type parameter is to types what a formal parameter is to values: one definition, many inputs.

questions.q: A list is meant to hold only String values, but one line tries to add an Integer. When is it best for that mistake to be reported?
options: When the program reaches the add line during a run
When the compiler checks the add line
Only when another line later reads the item
Never, because Java converts the Integer to a String
optionExplain: This is the old behaviour for some mistakes, and it is harder to find than a compile error.
Right: an early report at the faulty line is the easiest to fix.
A late report may be far from the real cause.
Java does not convert an Integer into a String here.
questions.explain: Reporting the mistake at the faulty line, before the program runs, is the aim of generics. The card next shows how.
questions.rule: Declare the element type so the compiler, not a later run, finds wrong items and removes the need for casts.

questions.q: With a list of String, taking an item out of the list needs no ____.
questions.explain: The compiler already knows the items are Strings, so the cast is unnecessary.
questions.rule: Typed collections remove casts.

questions.q: True or false: In code that stores items as plain Object, a wrongly stored item is usually reported at the line that stored it.
questions.explain: No. The failure normally appears at the line that reads and casts the item, which may be far from the faulty add, so the cause is hard to trace.
questions.rule: Object-based errors surface late.
questions.teaches: In non-generic code the failure appears at the reading line, which can be far from the line that stored the wrong item, so tracing it is hard.

questions.q: A ticket app keeps a list of Ticket. A developer writes a line that adds the text VIP to it. What happens?
options: The program fails with an error only when the line runs
The text is converted to a Ticket automatically
The line compiles with a warning and the text is stored
The compiler reports an error at that line
optionExplain: That timing belongs to Object-based lists, not a typed list.
Java does not make a Ticket from text.
A typed list is checked, so the mismatch is an error, not a warning.
Right: text is not a Ticket, so the typed list refuses it.
questions.explain: A list of Ticket accepts only Ticket values, and the compiler enforces that at the add line.
questions.rule: Declare the element type so the compiler, not a later run, finds wrong items and removes the need for casts.

questions.q: Sam summarises generics. Which statements are wrong? Select all that apply.
options: Generic code lets you read items without casting
Compile-time errors are harder to find than run-time errors
A list of String accepts an Integer but prints a warning
The compiler checks generic code for type safety and reports violations
optionExplain: True: the compiler already knows the item type.
Wrong: the tutorial says compile-time errors are easier to fix, since run-time errors can be hard to find.
Wrong: the add is a compile-time error, not a warning.
True: that is the first benefit the tutorial lists.
questions.explain: Two statements reverse the facts: compile-time errors are the easier ones, and a wrong item is rejected, not just warned about.
questions.rule: Early errors are the cheaper errors.

questions.q: A teammate says: the compiler erases type parameters anyway, so generics add nothing. Which reply fits the tutorial's reasoning?
options: The checks run at compile time, so wrong items are caught before running
Erasure only happens in old versions of Java, so generics still help later
Generics make the program run faster, which is the real reason
Generics are only for documentation and the compiler ignores them
optionExplain: Right: the benefit comes from the compiler's checks, whatever is left at run time.
Erasure is part of how generics work, not a version quirk.
The tutorial's benefits are about checking and casts, not speed.
The compiler checks them; that is the point.
questions.explain: Erasure removes type parameters after the compiler has used them to check the code, so the benefit holds.
questions.rule: The compiler checks first; erasure comes after.
questions.teaches: Erasure happens after the compiler has done its checks, so the compile-time benefit is real even though type parameters are gone at run time.

questions.q: A shop has code that finds the cheapest item in a list of Book and the same code, copied line for line, for a list of Toy. What would let one method serve both?
options: Two overloads with different names
Storing both kinds in one list of Object
A method with a type parameter for the element type
A static field holding the current type
optionExplain: Two names still mean two copies of the logic.
This loses the element type and brings casts back.
Right: one generic method replaces the copies.
A field does not make a method work for several types.
questions.explain: A type parameter on the method lets the logic be written once. The card next explains this.
questions.rule: Write the procedure once over a type parameter instead of once per element type.

questions.q: True or false: a generic algorithm is written once and can work on collections of different element types.
questions.explain: That is the third benefit the tutorial lists for generics.
questions.rule: One algorithm, many element types.

questions.q: Which task can be written with an unbounded type parameter T?
options: Count the elements greater than a given element, using the greater-than operator
Add up all elements as numbers
Find the largest element with a greater-than test
Count the array elements that are equal to a given element, using equals
optionExplain: That operator works only on primitive numeric types, so it fails for T.
Adding as numbers needs number methods, which T does not promise.
Again the operator is not available on T.
Right: every object has equals, so no bound is needed.
questions.explain: Equality testing is something every object supports, so an unbounded T is enough.
questions.teaches: A method that needs only operations every object has, such as testing equality, can use an unbounded type parameter.
questions.rule: Write the procedure once over a type parameter instead of once per element type.

questions.q: A generic method takes a list of T and returns a list of T. It is called with a list of Double. The result holds items of type ____.
questions.explain: T is replaced by Double at that call, so the result is a list of Double.
questions.rule: T is replaced consistently in one call.

questions.q: A generic method with an unbounded type parameter T compares two T values using the greater-than operator. What happens when it is compiled?
options: It fails to compile
It compiles and works for numbers only
It compiles and fails when run with text
It compiles because every object can be compared
optionExplain: Right: the operator works only on primitive numeric types, and T may be any object.
The compiler does not check at the call whether T is a number.
The error is caught at compile time instead.
Objects cannot be compared with greater-than.
questions.explain: With no bound, the compiler allows only what every object supports, and greater-than is not one of those.
questions.rule: No bound, no extra operations.

questions.q: Sort each operation by whether an unbounded type parameter T allows it.
groups: Needs more than an unbounded T offers

items.t: store an item in a list of T
test two items with equals
test whether one item is greater than another with the greater-than operator
return an item as it was received
call intValue on an item
add two items as numbers

questions.explain: Storing, returning and equality use only what every object has; operators and number methods need help.
questions.teaches: Containers fit an unbounded type parameter, while ordering and arithmetic do not, which is why a bound exists.
questions.rule: Write the procedure once over a type parameter instead of once per element type.

questions.q: A Box class has set taking Object and get returning Object. Another team wants boxes that the compiler checks to hold only Integer. Which change helps most?
options: Add a second method that casts the result to Integer
Rename the class IntegerBox and keep Object inside
Give Box a type parameter and use it in set and get
Make the stored field final
optionExplain: A cast method still trusts the programmer, not the compiler.
Renaming changes nothing about what the compiler can check.
Right: the type parameter lets each use state its own type.
A final field cannot be reassigned but can still hold any object.
questions.explain: Replacing Object with a type variable lets the compiler check each use. The card next shows how.
questions.rule: Add a type parameter list after the class name and use it wherever the class said Object.

questions.q: In a class declared as Box with the parameter T, the letter T is called a type ____.
questions.explain: The tutorial calls T a type parameter, also known as a type variable.
questions.rule: T is a type variable.

questions.q: Given a Box of Integer variable ib, the statement ib.set(10) passes the int literal 10. Why does it compile?
options: Box of Integer accepts primitive ints directly
Autoboxing turns the int into an Integer
Integer is a subtype of int
The compiler ignores the type argument in calls
optionExplain: The type argument is Integer, an object type, not int.
Right: the compiler wraps the primitive, so it matches the expected Integer.
Subtyping does not apply between a primitive and a class.
Type arguments are checked in calls.
questions.explain: set expects an Integer, and autoboxing converts the int 10 to one.
questions.rule: Autoboxing bridges primitives and their wrapper types.
questions.teaches: Autoboxing lets an int be passed where an Integer is expected, which is why a Box of Integer can be given the literal 10.

questions.q: Put the steps of making a Crate class generic in a sensible order.
items: Write a type parameter list after the class name
Replace each Object in the field and method signatures with the type variable
Use the type variable inside the class body
Create objects using a type argument such as Fruit
questions.explain: The parameter list comes first, then the signatures change, then uses supply an argument.
questions.rule: Add a type parameter list after the class name and use it wherever the class said Object.

questions.q: A student converts Box to a generic class Box of T. The field is T and set takes T, but get still returns Object. What is wrong?
options: Callers get Object back and still need a cast
Nothing: get always returns Object in a generic class
set must return T, since it stores a T
The field must be Object so any T fits
optionExplain: Right: get should return T so callers receive the argument type.
A generic class returns the type variable where the class says so.
set stores a value and need not return one.
A T field is what makes the class generic.
questions.explain: Every Object that meant the stored item should become T, including the return type of get.
questions.rule: Convert every Object that meant the stored item.

questions.q: A generic interface Repository with the type parameter T declares find, which returns a T. A class UserRepository says it implements Repository of User. What does find return in UserRepository?
options: An Object, since the interface is generic
A T, still unresolved
A User
A Repository
optionExplain: The argument User replaces T; it does not fall back to Object.
T was given the argument User.
Right: the concrete argument User replaces T for this class.
find returns the item type, not the interface.
questions.explain: A class that implements a generic interface with a concrete argument fixes that parameter for itself.
questions.teaches: A class can implement or extend a generic type with a concrete type argument, which fixes that type parameter for the class.
questions.rule: Add a type parameter list after the class name and use it wherever the class said Object.

questions.q: The collections framework uses one letter for the type of items a list holds. Which letter is it most likely?
options: K
E
N
R
optionExplain: K is the usual letter for a key.
Right: E stands for element.
N usually marks a number.
R is not one of the tutorial's conventional letters.
questions.explain: The letters carry meaning. The card next shows the common ones.
questions.rule: Name type parameters with a single uppercase letter whose meaning matches its role.

questions.q: By convention, the type parameter for the key of a lookup table is the letter ____.
questions.explain: K stands for key.
questions.rule: K is for key.

questions.q: A method has several type parameters. T is the first. According to the tutorial's list, which letters stand for the second, third and fourth types?
options: A, B and C
E, K and N
T2, T3 and T4
S, U and V
optionExplain: These are not among the tutorial's letters.
These have other meanings: element, key and number.
The convention is single letters, not numbered names.
Right: S, U and V come after T.
questions.explain: After T the tutorial continues with S, U and V for the further types.
questions.rule: After T come S, U and V.
questions.teaches: The letters S, U and V name the second, third and fourth types when a generic definition needs more than one.

questions.q: A class Dictionary links word types to definition types. Which declaration follows the convention?
options: Dictionary with the parameters Word and Meaning
Dictionary with the parameters k and v
Dictionary with the parameters K and V
Dictionary with the parameters KEY and VALUE
optionExplain: Mixed-case names look like ordinary classes.
Lowercase letters look like ordinary variables.
Right: single capital letters for key and value.
All-capital words look like constants.
questions.explain: A single uppercase letter signals a type variable and keeps it apart from classes, variables and constants.
questions.rule: Name type parameters with a single uppercase letter whose meaning matches its role.

questions.q: A teammate names a type parameter Item. A reviewer objects. Which reason fits the tutorial?
options: A mixed-case name looks like an ordinary class and invites confusion
Compilers reject any type parameter name that is longer than one letter
Item is a reserved word in Java
Type parameters must be named T, since the compiler recognises only that letter
optionExplain: Right: single capitals prevent exactly that confusion.
The tutorial describes a convention, not a compiler error.
Item is not reserved; the concern is readability.
T is one conventional letter among several.
questions.explain: The reason for the single uppercase letter is to avoid confusion with class and interface names.
questions.rule: A type variable should not look like a class.

questions.q: Match each role to the conventional letter.
pairs: The type of keys in a lookup table
The type of items in a queue
The type of values stored with a key
A type that is meant to be a number
questions.explain: K, E, V and N cover key, element, value and number.
questions.teaches: N is the conventional letter for a type that is expected to be a number.
questions.rule: Name type parameters with a single uppercase letter whose meaning matches its role.

questions.q: In the code List of String names, the word String is known as the ...
options: type parameter
raw type
type bound
type argument
optionExplain: The parameter is the name in the declaration, such as E in the List definition.
A raw type has no argument at all.
A bound restricts allowed arguments; it is not what String is called here.
Right: it is what the type parameter is replaced with.
questions.explain: The two terms differ by position. The card next explains.
questions.rule: Parameters appear where a generic is defined; arguments appear where it is used.

questions.q: In the declaration of class Box with T, the T is a type ____.
questions.explain: A name in the declaration is a type parameter.
questions.rule: Declaration: parameter.

questions.q: True or false: Declaring a variable of the type Box of Integer creates a Box object.
questions.explain: A declaration only creates a reference variable. A separate new expression creates the object.
questions.rule: Declare, then instantiate.
questions.teaches: Declaring a variable of a parameterized type creates no object; a separate new expression does that.

questions.q: Match each piece of code to its name.
pairs: The T in class Node with T
The Circle in Node of Circle nc
Node of Circle as a whole
Writing Node of Circle in place of Node of T
questions.explain: Parameters sit in the definition; arguments sit in the use; the whole use is a parameterized type.
questions.rule: Parameters appear where a generic is defined; arguments appear where it is used.

questions.q: A teammate says: the type parameter in Box of String is String. Which correction fits the tutorial's strict usage?
options: String is a raw type; the parameter is Box
String is the type argument; the type parameter is the T in the declaration
It is correct, because the tutorial uses parameter and argument as the same word
String is a bound and Box is the argument
optionExplain: A raw type has no argument.
Right: the declaration has a parameter and the use has an argument.
The tutorial keeps them apart.
A bound is a restriction, not this.
questions.explain: Strictly, the declaration has the parameter and the use has the argument.
questions.rule: Parameters appear where a generic is defined; arguments appear where it is used.

questions.q: A class Cache is declared with two type parameters, K and V. A line uses Cache of Long and Report. How many type parameters and how many type arguments are involved?
options: One parameter in the declaration and two arguments in the use
Two parameters in the declaration and two arguments in the use
Two parameters in the declaration and one argument in the use
No arguments at all, because Long and Report are ordinary classes
optionExplain: Cache declares two parameters, K and V.
Right: one argument is supplied for each parameter.
Each parameter receives its own argument.
Classes written between the brackets are the arguments.
questions.explain: A generic type invocation supplies one argument per parameter, in order.
questions.rule: One argument for each parameter, in order.
questions.teaches: A generic type invocation supplies exactly one type argument per type parameter, in the same order.

questions.q: Since Java 7, writing new ArrayList followed by an empty pair of angle brackets lets the compiler ____ the type argument.
questions.explain: The compiler can often work out the argument from the context. The card next shows when.
questions.rule: The compiler infers it.

questions.q: True or false: the diamond is the informal name for an empty pair of angle brackets used in place of type arguments in a constructor call.
questions.explain: That is the tutorial's informal name.
questions.rule: Diamond: empty brackets.

questions.q: With the diamond, where does the compiler usually get the type arguments from?
options: The names of the fields declared inside the class being created
A global default type that the compiler applies in every case
The statement written on the line before the constructor call
The declared type of the variable receiving the new object
optionExplain: Field names carry no type argument information.
There is no such default; leaving out the information would make the type raw.
Inference uses the call and its context, not earlier code.
Right: the target type supplies them.
questions.explain: The declared type of the variable, and sometimes the constructor arguments, supply the information.
questions.rule: Context supplies the arguments.
questions.teaches: With the diamond the compiler draws the type arguments from the context, such as the declared type of the variable, and from the constructor arguments.

questions.q: A program creates objects with each construction below. Sort them by whether the created object has a parameterized type or a raw type.

items.t: new ArrayList followed by an empty pair of angle brackets
new ArrayList with no brackets at all
new HashMap of String and Integer
new HashMap with no brackets at all
new Box followed by an empty pair of angle brackets
new Box with no brackets at all

questions.explain: Only the diamond or explicit arguments keep the parameterized type; no brackets at all means raw.
questions.rule: Use the diamond when the declared type already tells the compiler the type arguments.

questions.q: A variable is declared as a Map of String and List of String and is assigned new HashMap with no brackets at all. What happens?
options: It compiles with an unchecked conversion warning
It compiles with no warning, as the compiler infers the arguments
It does not compile
It compiles and the map accepts only String keys
optionExplain: Right: the right side is a raw type.
Inference works only when the diamond is used.
The tutorial says it compiles, with a warning.
A raw HashMap is not restricted by the declared type.
questions.explain: Without the diamond, the construction is raw, and assigning it to a parameterized variable is an unchecked conversion.
questions.rule: No brackets is not the diamond.

questions.q: A variable has the declared type OrderedPair of String and Integer. It is created with new OrderedPair, the diamond, and the arguments the text Even and the int 8. What are K and V?
options: K is Object and V is Object
K is String and V is int
K is String and V is Integer
K is Integer and V is String
optionExplain: Inference does not fall back to Object here, because the declared type supplies the arguments.
Type arguments cannot be primitives.
Right: the declared type fixes them and 8 is boxed.
The order follows the declaration: key first, then value.
questions.explain: Inference handles several type parameters together, and the int 8 is boxed to match Integer.
questions.teaches: Inference with the diamond fills in several type parameters at once, and a primitive argument is boxed to fit its wrapper type.
questions.rule: Use the diamond when the declared type already tells the compiler the type arguments.

questions.q: A class Pair has two type parameters, K then V. A use is written as Pair of String and Integer. What does V stand for there?
options: String
Pair
Both String and Integer
Integer
optionExplain: String is the first argument, so it fills K.
Pair is the class itself, not an argument.
Each parameter receives one argument.
Right: arguments match parameters in order.
questions.explain: Arguments are matched to parameters by position. The card next explains.
questions.rule: Supply one type argument for each type parameter, in order, and an argument may itself be a parameterized type.

questions.q: Given the declaration Pair with type parameters K then V, in Pair of String and Integer the parameter K is replaced by ____.
questions.explain: K is first, so it takes the first argument, String.
questions.rule: First argument, first parameter.

questions.q: The interface Pair has parameters K and V. A class OrderedPair declares its own K and V and says it implements Pair with K and V. What does this tell you?
options: OrderedPair of String and Integer is also a Pair of String and Integer
OrderedPair must use String for K in every program that implements Pair
The interface Pair no longer needs type parameters
OrderedPair and Pair stay unrelated, since OrderedPair declares its own K and V
optionExplain: Right: its parameters flow through to the interface.
Its K is open; each use picks one.
The interface still has its parameters.
Implementing makes OrderedPair a subtype of the Pair it names.
questions.explain: Passing its own parameters on keeps the relationship generic.
questions.rule: A generic class can pass its parameters to what it implements.
questions.teaches: A generic class can implement a generic interface by passing its own type parameters on, so each use of the class is also a use of the interface with the same arguments.

questions.q: Match each use of Entry (parameters K then V) to what it says.
pairs: K is String and V is Integer
K is Integer and V is String
Entry of String and List of String
both arguments are the same type
questions.explain: Positions decide the roles, and the third use shows an argument that is itself parameterized.
questions.rule: Supply one type argument for each type parameter, in order, and an argument may itself be a parameterized type.

questions.q: A method accepts an Entry of String and Integer. What if a caller passes an Entry of Integer and String?
options: It is accepted, since both entries use the same two types
It is accepted with a warning
It is rejected, because the swapped arguments make a different type
It is accepted and the roles swap automatically
optionExplain: The order of arguments matters.
A mismatch is an error here, not a warning.
Right: the parameterizations differ.
The compiler never swaps roles.
questions.explain: Entry of Integer and String is a different type from Entry of String and Integer.
questions.rule: Order of arguments is part of the type.

questions.q: A store keeps a Pair whose key is a product code (text) and whose value is a list of Review objects. Which type argument fits V?
options: Review only, since a list is a raw type
A parameterized type: List of Review
List with no argument
Object, because values of different shapes need it
optionExplain: A list written with its argument is a parameterized type, not raw.
Right: an argument can itself carry arguments.
That is a raw type and gives up the checking.
Object loses the item type.
questions.explain: Arguments can be nested as deeply as needed, for example a map from String to a list of String.
questions.teaches: Nesting can go deeper than one level: a map from String to a list of String is a valid use, with the list type as the value argument.
questions.rule: Supply one type argument for each type parameter, in order, and an argument may itself be a parameterized type.

questions.q: Box is declared with a type parameter T. A variable is declared with the type Box and no angle brackets at all. This type is called ...
options: a raw type
a parameterized type
a bounded type
a wildcard type
optionExplain: Right: no type arguments means raw.
A parameterized type supplies arguments.
A bounded type restricts the allowed arguments.
A wildcard uses a question mark.
questions.explain: A generic name with no arguments has a special name. The card next gives it.
questions.rule: Name the type argument; use a raw type only where old code forces it.

questions.q: True or false: String, which is not generic, is a raw type.
questions.explain: A raw type is a generic name used with no arguments; a non-generic class is not one.
questions.rule: Only generic names can be raw.

questions.q: Why do raw types exist at all in the language?
options: Raw types run faster than parameterized types because they skip the checks at run time
They are required for generic classes that declare several type parameters at once
Library classes such as the collections predate generics, and old code uses them
They are the only way to store primitive values
optionExplain: The tutorial gives compatibility, not speed, as the reason.
Several parameters work fine with arguments.
Right: raw types keep that code working.
Raw types do not help with primitives.
questions.explain: Legacy code was written before type arguments existed.
questions.rule: Raw types are for compatibility.
questions.teaches: Raw types exist for compatibility, because many library classes, including the collections, were not generic before JDK 5.0 and old code still uses them.

questions.q: Sort each declared type by whether it is a raw type, assuming Box and List are generic and Label is not.

items.t: Box with no type argument
Box of Integer
List with no type argument
Label
List of String
Box of Box of String

questions.explain: Only a generic name used without arguments is raw.
questions.rule: Name the type argument; use a raw type only where old code forces it.

questions.q: A variable has the raw type Box, and its get method is called. What type does the result have?
options: T, the type variable the class declares
Object, so using it as a specific type needs a cast
Integer, the most common type argument used with such a box
The type of the last value stored
optionExplain: Without an argument there is no T to give back.
Right: raw types behave the pre-generics way.
Nothing tells the compiler that.
The compiler does not track stored values.
questions.explain: A raw Box returns Object values.
questions.rule: Raw means Object coming out.

questions.q: New code receives a list from an old library method whose return type is a raw List. What risk does the raw type bring?
options: The list will refuse to store any item
The list will hold only Object values of one fixed class chosen at the first use
The compiler will convert the list to a parameterized one automatically when it is used
The compiler cannot check the list's items, so a wrong item may appear only at run time
optionExplain: A raw list accepts items freely.
Nothing restricts it to one class.
No automatic conversion happens.
Right: raw types bypass generic checks.
questions.explain: Mixing old and new code is where unchecked problems start.
questions.teaches: Mixing legacy code that returns raw types with new generic code is the usual source of unchecked warnings.
questions.rule: Name the type argument; use a raw type only where old code forces it.

questions.q: True or false: assigning a raw Box to a variable of type Box of Integer draws a warning from the compiler.
questions.explain: The compiler cannot confirm the raw box holds Integers. The card next lists the cases.
questions.rule: Raw to parameterized warns.

questions.q: Match each operation to the compiler's reaction.
pairs: Box of String assigned to a raw Box variable
Raw Box assigned to a Box of Integer variable
Calling set through a raw Box reference
questions.explain: Only the raw-to-parameterized assignment and the raw call warn.
questions.rule: Parameterized to raw is silent; raw to parameterized, or a call through a raw reference, draws an unchecked warning.

questions.q: The compiler prints only a short note about unchecked operations. Which choice shows every unchecked warning?
options: Compiling with the option -Xlint:-unchecked
Adding the annotation SuppressWarnings with unchecked
Compiling with the option -Xlint:unchecked
Nothing: the note already lists every line
optionExplain: The leading minus switches the warnings off completely.
That annotation silences the warnings in a scope.
Right: it lists each unchecked warning.
The note only says details exist.
questions.explain: One option shows the details, one disables them, and the annotation hides them in a chosen scope.
questions.rule: Lint option shows; annotation hides.
questions.teaches: The option -Xlint:unchecked shows all unchecked warnings, -Xlint:-unchecked disables them completely, and the annotation SuppressWarnings with unchecked silences them in a specific scope.

questions.q: An old method returns a raw List. A new line assigns its result to a variable of type List of String. What does the compiler report?
options: An unchecked conversion warning
An error: the types differ
Nothing, because List of String is a subtype of List
An unchecked invocation warning
optionExplain: Right: raw to parameterized.
It compiles, with a warning.
The assignment goes the other way, from raw to parameterized.
That one is for calling a generic method through a raw reference.
questions.explain: Raw to parameterized assignment is an unchecked conversion.
questions.rule: Parameterized to raw is silent; raw to parameterized, or a call through a raw reference, draws an unchecked warning.

questions.q: A raw Box variable refers to a Box of String. What if the code calls set with the int 8 through the raw variable?
options: It does not compile, since 8 is not a String
It compiles and converts 8 to the text 8
It compiles with no warning at all
It compiles with an unchecked invocation warning
optionExplain: The raw reference bypasses that check.
No conversion is done.
A call through a raw reference is warned about.
Right: the check that would reject 8 is bypassed.
questions.explain: The raw reference hides the String requirement from the compiler.
questions.rule: Raw calls skip the check.

questions.q: A build prints only: Note: Example.java uses unchecked or unsafe operations. Which responses fit the tutorial? Select all that apply.
options: Recompile with the unchecked lint option to see where
Treat it as a sign the compiler cannot guarantee type safety somewhere
Ignore it, since notes never matter
Remove every generic type from the code
optionExplain: Right: the note is a hint that details are available.
Right: that is what unchecked means.
Wrong: it flags places where a run-time failure is possible.
Wrong: the problem comes from mixing raw and generic types, not from generics.
questions.explain: The note is a prompt to look closer, not a verdict.
questions.teaches: When a method returns a raw type that is assigned to a parameterized variable, the detailed warning names the type found and the type required.
questions.rule: Parameterized to raw is silent; raw to parameterized, or a call through a raw reference, draws an unchecked warning.

questions.q: In the declaration of a generic method, where does the list of type parameters go?
options: After the method name
Before the return type
After the parameter list
At the top of the class only
optionExplain: The name comes after the return type, and the list does not follow it.
Right: the list comes first, then the return type.
By then the parameter types have already used the type variables.
A class-level list belongs to the class, not to the method.
questions.explain: The position is fixed by the language. The card next shows it.
questions.rule: Declare the method's type parameters in angle brackets before the return type.

questions.q: Put the parts of a generic static method header in order.
items: public static
the type parameter list
the return type
the method name and its parameters
questions.explain: The type parameter list sits between the modifiers and the return type.
questions.rule: Declare the method's type parameters in angle brackets before the return type.

questions.q: A static generic method compare takes two Pair objects. How does the tutorial say it is usually called?
options: With the type arguments written between the class name and the method name every time
Like an ordinary method, with the types inferred from the arguments
Only through a raw reference
With a cast of both arguments to Object
optionExplain: That explicit form is legal but not usually needed.
Right: the explicit form is allowed but usually unnecessary.
Raw references are what generics avoid.
Casting would discard the type information.
questions.explain: The compiler infers the type arguments, so the call looks like any other.
questions.rule: Let inference supply the arguments.
questions.teaches: A generic method can be called with explicit type arguments written between the dot and the method name, but the tutorial treats the plain call as the usual form.

questions.q: A static method pick takes two values of the same type and returns one of them. Its type parameter list appears ____ the return type.
questions.explain: The list is written first and the return type follows it.
questions.rule: List first, then return type.

questions.q: Inside a class Box with the parameter T, a developer writes a static method with the header public static T first(T a). What is the problem?
options: A method may not return a type variable
The parameter a must be declared as Object so that any argument type is accepted
Static methods cannot take parameters
Static methods cannot use the class's T; they declare their own parameter
optionExplain: Methods can return type variables.
Nothing requires Object.
They can.
Right: T belongs to instances, not to the class as a whole.
questions.explain: A static generic method declares its own parameters before the return type.
questions.rule: Static methods declare their own parameters.

questions.q: A non-generic class Logger needs a constructor that accepts one value of any type and records a description of it. Is that possible with generics?
options: Yes: the constructor can declare its own type parameter
No: only methods can declare type parameters
Only if Logger itself becomes generic
Only if the parameter is Object
optionExplain: Right: constructors may be generic, even in a non-generic class.
The tutorial allows generic constructors.
The constructor can carry its own parameter.
Object would give up the generic type.
questions.explain: Generic constructors are allowed in generic and non-generic classes alike.
questions.teaches: The tutorial allows generic constructors, in generic and non-generic classes alike.
questions.rule: Declare the method's type parameters in angle brackets before the return type.

questions.q: True or false: because Integer is a subtype of Number, a Box of Integer can be passed to a method that takes a Box of Number.
questions.explain: Generic types do not inherit the relationship of their arguments. The card next explains.
questions.rule: Related arguments do not relate the boxes.

questions.q: For two different type arguments A and B, a Box of A and a Box of B are ____ to each other, whether or not A and B are related.
questions.explain: The tutorial says there is no relationship between them.
questions.rule: No relationship.

questions.q: Given a Box of Number, what does its add method accept?
options: Only objects whose class is exactly Number
Only a Box of Integer
Any Number, including an Integer or a Double
Nothing, because Number is abstract
optionExplain: Subtypes of Number are accepted.
add takes items, not boxes.
Right: the argument type of add is Number, and Integer and Double are Numbers.
The box accepts Number values; an abstract type does not stop that.
questions.explain: The restriction is on the box types, not on the items that fit inside a Box of Number.
questions.rule: Items follow is-a; boxes do not.
questions.teaches: A Box of Number accepts any Number in add, so the ban on passing a Box of Integer concerns the box type, not the items.

questions.q: A method takes a Crate of Fruit. Apple extends Fruit. Sort each argument by whether the call is accepted or rejected.

items.t: a Crate of Fruit
a Crate of Apple
a Crate of Object
a new Crate of Fruit made with the diamond
a Crate of Fruit stored in a variable
a Crate of Apple stored in a variable

questions.explain: Only a Crate of Fruit matches; Crate of Apple and Crate of Object are different types.
questions.rule: Related type arguments do not make related generic types: a Box of Integer is not a Box of Number.

questions.q: A method takes a Crate of Apple. What if a caller passes a Crate of Fruit, where Apple is a subtype of Fruit?
options: It is accepted, because a Fruit crate can hold an Apple
It is accepted with a warning
It is accepted only if Fruit is final
It is also rejected, since neither direction creates a relationship
optionExplain: Whether items fit does not make the crate types related.
This is a compile error, not a warning.
Finality of the argument is not the issue.
Right: the two boxes are unrelated both ways.
questions.explain: The relationship fails in both directions.
questions.rule: Unrelated both ways.

questions.q: Class Node has one type parameter. Circle and Rectangle both extend Shape. The code creates a Node of Circle in a variable nc and then assigns nc to a variable of type Node of Shape. What happens?
options: It does not compile, because the two Node types are unrelated
It compiles, since a Circle is a Shape
It compiles but then fails at run time when the node is first used
It compiles if Shape is an interface
optionExplain: Right: Circle being a Shape does not relate the nodes.
The relationship does not carry over to Node.
The check is made at compile time.
Shape being an interface changes nothing here.
questions.explain: Beyond the tutorial: if the assignment were allowed, a Rectangle could be added through the Node of Shape view into what is really a Node of Circle, so the refusal protects the nodes.
questions.teaches: Beyond the tutorial: the refusal protects the original node, because if the assignment were allowed, a Rectangle could be added through the Node of Shape view of a Node of Circle.
questions.rule: Related type arguments do not make related generic types: a Box of Integer is not a Box of Number.

questions.q: The class ArrayList of E implements List of E. Which statement is true?
options: An ArrayList of String can be used where a List of Object is expected
An ArrayList of String can be used where an ArrayList of Object is expected
An ArrayList of String can be used where a List of String is expected
An ArrayList of String cannot be used as any List
optionExplain: String being an Object does not relate the lists.
Different arguments mean unrelated types.
Right: same argument, subtype by implements.
The implements clause makes it a List of the same argument.
questions.explain: Implementing a generic interface creates subtyping for matching arguments. The card next shows how.
questions.rule: A generic type is a subtype of what it extends or implements, as long as the type argument passed along stays the same.

questions.q: An ArrayList of String is a subtype of List of ____.
questions.explain: The argument is passed along unchanged.
questions.rule: Same argument.

questions.q: The interface PayloadList has parameters E and P and extends List of E. Which type is a List of String?
options: PayloadList of Exception and String
PayloadList of String and Exception
PayloadList of Object and String
None: P must also be String
optionExplain: Here E is Exception, so it is a List of Exception.
Right: E is String, and P is free to be anything.
E is Object, which gives a List of Object.
Only E is used in the extends clause.
questions.explain: Only the parameter named in the extends clause is tied to the supertype; the other can vary.
questions.rule: Follow the extends clause.
questions.teaches: An extra type parameter that the supertype does not use, such as P in PayloadList, can vary freely without breaking the subtype relationship.

questions.q: Order these types from most specific to most general.
items: ArrayList of String
List of String
Collection of String
Object
questions.explain: Each type extends or implements the next one, with the argument String held fixed.
questions.rule: A generic type is a subtype of what it extends or implements, as long as the type argument passed along stays the same.

questions.q: A method takes a Collection of Number. A developer passes an ArrayList of Integer and says it is fine because ArrayList is a Collection and Integer is a Number. What is wrong?
options: The argument changed as well as the class, and only the class may change
ArrayList is not a Collection, because it implements only the List interface
Integer is not a Number
Collection cannot take type arguments, because it is an old interface
optionExplain: Right: the argument must stay the same.
It implements List, which extends Collection.
Integer is a Number; the argument change is the issue.
It is generic with the parameter E.
questions.explain: Both a Collection of Number and an ArrayList of Integer differ in the argument, so they are unrelated.
questions.rule: Class may widen; argument must stay.

questions.q: The interface Labeled has parameters P and E, in that order, and extends List of E. Which type is a List of String?
options: Labeled of String and Integer
Labeled of String and Object
Labeled of Integer and String
Labeled of Integer and Integer
optionExplain: Here E, the second parameter, is Integer.
Here E, the second parameter, is Object, so it is a List of Object.
Right: E, the second parameter, is String.
E is Integer, so it is a List of Integer.
questions.explain: Position in the declaration matters only through the extends clause, which names E.
questions.teaches: What counts is which parameter the extends clause passes along, not where the parameter sits in the declaration.
questions.rule: A generic type is a subtype of what it extends or implements, as long as the type argument passed along stays the same.

questions.q: True or false: the compiler can work out a generic method's type arguments from the arguments in the call.
questions.explain: Inference does exactly this. The card next lists what else it uses.
questions.rule: Arguments feed inference.

questions.q: True or false: type inference uses code that appears later in the program to decide a call's type arguments.
questions.explain: Inference uses the call's arguments and the target type, never later code.
questions.rule: No look-ahead.

questions.q: A method pick takes two values of one type T. A call passes the text d and an ArrayList of String, and both are Serializable. Which T does inference choose?
options: String, because the first argument is a String
Serializable, the most specific type that fits both
Object, because every value is an Object
ArrayList of String, because it is the longer name
optionExplain: The second argument is not a String.
Right: it is the most specific type that suits both arguments.
Object fits, but it is not the most specific type that does.
The text d is not an ArrayList.
questions.explain: Inference picks the most specific type that works for all arguments.
questions.rule: Most specific type that fits all.
questions.teaches: When arguments have different types, inference picks the most specific type that fits all of them, which here is a shared interface.
