questions.q: A generic method call assigns its result to a variable of type List of Invoice. Which pieces of information can inference use? Select all that apply.
options: The types of the arguments in the call
The declared type of the variable receiving the result
A statement written ten lines later
The name of the variable
optionExplain: Right: arguments are an input.
Right: the target type is an input.
Wrong: later code is never used.
Wrong: names carry no type information.
questions.explain: Inference works from the arguments and the target type.
questions.rule: Arguments and target only.

questions.q: According to the tutorial, in Java SE 7 the call emptyList() is passed directly as the argument of a method that takes a List of String. What happens?
options: It compiles, with T inferred as String from the method's parameter type
It compiles with an unchecked warning
It fails only at run time
It fails to compile, because T was inferred as Object
optionExplain: That is the Java SE 8 behaviour.
The tutorial reports a compile error.
The error is reported by the compiler.
Right: Java SE 7 gave no target typing for method arguments.
questions.explain: With no information, Java SE 7 chose Object and produced a List of Object.
questions.rule: Java 7 ignored the parameter type.

questions.q: A method showOrders takes a List of Order. A caller passes Collections.emptyList() directly as the argument, with no type witness. According to the tutorial, what happens in Java SE 8?
options: It fails, as in Java SE 7
It compiles, but only if a type witness is written explicitly
It compiles, since the parameter type is used as the target
It compiles and the list holds Object values
optionExplain: That was the earlier behaviour.
The witness is no longer needed in this context.
Right: Java SE 8 extended target typing to method arguments.
T is inferred as Order.
questions.explain: In Java SE 8 the target type includes the parameter type of the method being called.
questions.teaches: In Java SE 8 target typing includes method arguments, so a witness such as the explicit String form is no longer needed there.
questions.rule: Let the compiler infer type arguments from the call's arguments and target; write a type witness only when it cannot decide.

questions.q: A class MyClass has the type parameter X. One constructor declares an extra type parameter T and takes a value of type T. How many sets of type parameters can be involved when an object is created?
options: Two: the class's X and the constructor's T
One: constructors cannot declare parameters
One: T replaces X
Three: one for each field
optionExplain: Right: both are filled in.
The tutorial allows generic constructors.
They are separate parameters.
Fields do not add parameters.
questions.explain: A constructor is allowed its own parameters. The card next shows how both are filled.
questions.rule: A constructor's own type parameters are separate from the class's and are inferred from the constructor's arguments.

questions.q: True or false: a non-generic class may have a generic constructor.
questions.explain: The tutorial says constructors can be generic in both generic and non-generic classes.
questions.rule: Constructors can be generic anywhere.

questions.q: A class MyClass of X has a constructor with its own parameter T. The code writes new MyClass of Integer, passing the empty text. What is T inferred as?
options: Integer, taken from the class argument
Object, because no witness was written
It cannot be inferred and the call fails
String, taken from the argument
optionExplain: Integer fills X, not T.
Inference uses the argument.
The argument type determines T.
Right: T is inferred from the constructor argument.
questions.explain: X is written in the new expression and T is inferred from the argument.
questions.rule: X from the type; T from the argument.
questions.teaches: In such a call both parameters are filled at once: the class parameter from the written type and the constructor parameter from the argument.

questions.q: A variable is declared as MyClass of Integer. The object is created with the diamond and the empty text as the argument. Which inference is correct?
options: X and T are both Integer, since the declared type applies to both
X is Integer from the declared type; T is String from the argument
X and T are both String, since the argument applies to both
X is String and T is Integer
optionExplain: T follows the constructor's argument.
Right: each comes from its own source.
X follows the declared type.
The sources are swapped.
questions.explain: With the diamond the compiler infers both sets: the class's from the target and the constructor's from the argument.
questions.rule: A constructor's own type parameters are separate from the class's and are inferred from the constructor's arguments.

questions.q: A constructor's own parameter T is declared on one constructor of a class. What if another method of the same class uses T in its signature without declaring it?
options: It compiles, because T belongs to the class that contains the constructor
It does not compile, as T exists only for that constructor
It compiles but T is always Object
It compiles if the method is static
optionExplain: T was declared on the constructor, not the class.
Right: the scope is the constructor.
T is simply not in scope.
Being static does not extend the scope.
questions.explain: Like a generic method's parameters, the constructor's parameter does not leak out.
questions.rule: Scope is the declaring constructor.

questions.q: A class Report with the class parameter X has a constructor with the parameter T. Sort each name by which source fills it.
groups: Filled from the written or declared type

items.t: X, when the variable is declared as Report of Date
T, when the argument is the number 5
X, when the type is written after new
T, when the argument is a text
X, with the diamond and a declared target
T, with the diamond

questions.explain: The class parameter follows the type, the constructor parameter follows the argument.
questions.teaches: The diamond helps only with the class's own parameters coming from the target; the constructor's parameter is always taken from the arguments.
questions.rule: A constructor's own type parameters are separate from the class's and are inferred from the constructor's arguments.

questions.q: A method declares the type parameter U extends Number. Which call is rejected at compile time?
options: Passing an Integer
Passing a Double
Passing a value whose type is Number itself
Passing the text some text
optionExplain: Integer is a subtype of Number, so it fits.
Double is a subtype of Number, so it fits.
The bound itself is allowed.
Right: a String is not a Number.
questions.explain: The bound sets the allowed family of types. The card next shows how.
questions.rule: Put extends and a bound after a type parameter to limit the arguments and to unlock the bound's methods.

questions.q: In the declaration U extends Number, the type Number is called the upper ____.
questions.explain: The type after extends is the upper bound.
questions.rule: Bound = limit.

questions.q: A class declares NaturalNumber with the parameter T extends Integer. Which types can be used as T?
options: Only Integer, because Integer is a final class with no subtypes
Integer and Number, since Number is the bound's parent class
Any class that has an intValue method, whatever its parent
Any numeric primitive, since the boxes convert them automatically
optionExplain: Right: the bound is final, so nothing else qualifies.
Number is a supertype of Integer and fails the bound.
The bound requires a subtype, not a matching method.
Primitives are never type arguments.
questions.explain: A final bound leaves one possible type, so the bounded parameter adds little beyond the call to the bound's methods.
questions.rule: Bounds admit the bound and its subtypes.
questions.teaches: When the bound is a final class such as Integer, the type parameter can only ever be that one class, so the bound serves mainly to expose that class's methods.

questions.q: To call doubleValue on a value of type N, declare the parameter as N ____ Number.
questions.explain: The upper bound is written with extends.
questions.rule: extends Bound.

questions.q: True or false: When the bound is an interface rather than a class, the declaration uses the word implements after the parameter name.
questions.explain: Extends is used in a general sense, so it covers interfaces too.
questions.rule: One word for both.

questions.q: A media app declares Playlist with the parameter T extends Playable, where Playable is an interface. Song implements Playable. Podcast has a play method with the same shape but does not implement Playable. Which statement is correct?
options: Both compile, since both have a play method
Neither compiles, since Playable is an interface
Playlist of Song compiles and Playlist of Podcast does not
Only Playlist of Podcast compiles
optionExplain: Having matching methods is not enough.
Interfaces work as bounds with extends.
Right: the type must actually implement the bound.
Podcast does not implement Playable.
questions.explain: The bound is a type relationship, not a method shape.
questions.rule: Subtype of the bound, not merely similar.
questions.teaches: A type with matching methods does not qualify; it must actually extend or implement the bound.

questions.q: True or false: a generic method with an unbounded T can compare two T values with the greater-than operator.
questions.explain: The operator is not available on objects. The card next shows what to use instead.
questions.rule: No operator on objects.

questions.q: To make compareTo available on T, the bound is T extends ____ of T.
questions.explain: Comparable declares compareTo.
questions.rule: Bound by Comparable.

questions.q: In the loop, the test is e.compareTo(elem) greater than 0. Which elements does it count?
options: Those equal to elem
Those smaller than elem
Those that are the same object as elem
Those greater than elem
optionExplain: Equal elements give zero.
Smaller elements give a negative result.
compareTo orders values; it does not test identity.
Right: a positive result means the receiver is greater than the argument.
questions.explain: A positive compareTo result means the receiver is greater.
questions.rule: Positive means greater.
questions.teaches: A compareTo result above zero means the receiver is greater than the argument, so testing for above zero counts the greater elements.

questions.q: A method must count how many array elements are smaller than a probe, using compareTo. Which header allows this?
options: A type parameter T bounded by Comparable of T
A type parameter T with no bound
A type parameter T extends Object
An unbounded T with the less-than operator
optionExplain: Right: it guarantees compareTo.
An unbounded T has no compareTo.
Object adds no compareTo.
Operators do not work on objects.
questions.explain: Only the Comparable bound promises the method needed.
questions.rule: To order or compare generic items, bound the parameter by Comparable of itself and use compareTo, not an operator.

questions.q: True or false: if the counting method is declared with T extends Comparable of T, a caller can still pass an array of a class that does not implement Comparable.
questions.explain: The bound is checked by the compiler, so such a call is rejected at compile time.
questions.rule: Callers must satisfy the bound.

questions.q: A method max takes two values x and y of type T and returns x when x is greater than y, otherwise y. It does not compile. Which change repairs it?
options: Declare the parameters as Object so any value is accepted
Change greater-than to equals
Bound T by Comparable of T and test with compareTo
Make the method non-static
optionExplain: Object has no ordering either.
Equality does not give the larger value.
Right: object comparison needs a method, and the bound supplies it.
Static or not, the operator does not apply to objects.
questions.explain: The same repair works for any maximum or sorting task over generic items.
questions.teaches: Finding a maximum needs the same repair: bound the parameter by Comparable of itself and compare with compareTo.
questions.rule: To order or compare generic items, bound the parameter by Comparable of itself and use compareTo, not an operator.

questions.q: True or false: when a type parameter has a class bound and interface bounds, the class bound may be listed anywhere.
questions.explain: The class must come first. The card next explains.
questions.rule: Class first.

questions.q: A type parameter with bounds B1 and B2 must be a subtype of ____ of them.
questions.explain: It must satisfy every bound.
questions.rule: All bounds apply.

questions.q: T extends Shape & Drawable, where Shape is a class and Drawable is an interface. Which methods may the code call on a T value?
options: Only methods of Shape, the first bound
Methods of Shape and methods of Drawable
Only methods of Drawable, the last bound
Only methods all objects have
optionExplain: T is also known to be Drawable.
Right: T is a subtype of both.
Shape is a bound too.
Bounds add more than that.
questions.explain: A subtype of all bounds can use all their methods.
questions.rule: All bounds' methods are available.
questions.teaches: With several bounds the code can call the methods of every bound on a value of the type parameter.

questions.q: A class Report needs T to be a Chart (a class) that is also Printable and Exportable (interfaces). Which header is valid?
options: T extends Chart & Printable & Exportable
T extends Printable & Chart & Exportable
T extends Printable & Exportable & Chart
T extends Chart, Printable, Exportable
optionExplain: Right: the class comes first.
The class bound is not first.
The class bound comes last.
The ampersand joins bounds, not commas.
questions.explain: Only the first header puts the class first and joins the bounds correctly.
questions.rule: List the class bound first, then the interfaces, and remember that a type argument must satisfy all bounds.

questions.q: True or false: when all the bounds are interfaces, the rule about listing the class first does not come into play.
questions.explain: There is no class bound to place, so the rule has nothing to order.
questions.rule: No class, no ordering issue.

questions.q: Animal is a class. Pet and Trained are interfaces. Sort each header by whether it compiles.

items.t: T extends Animal & Pet
T extends Pet & Trained
T extends Pet & Animal
T extends Animal & Pet & Trained
T extends Trained & Pet & Animal
T extends Pet & Trained & Animal

questions.explain: Headers fail when the class Animal is not first.
questions.teaches: A bound list may contain several interfaces and no class at all, in any order among the interfaces.
questions.rule: List the class bound first, then the interfaces, and remember that a type argument must satisfy all bounds.

questions.q: In generic code, what does a lone question mark used as a type argument stand for?
options: The type Object
A raw type
An unknown type
Any primitive type
optionExplain: The wildcard is not simply Object.
A raw type has no argument at all.
Right: that is the wildcard.
Primitives are never type arguments.
questions.explain: The wildcard has a name and a set of places where it may appear. The card next gives them.
questions.rule: Use the wildcard for a type that is unknown and does not matter, in parameters, fields and local variables.

questions.q: True or false: a wildcard can be the type of a method parameter.
questions.explain: Parameters, fields and local variables can all use it.
questions.rule: Allowed in parameters.

questions.q: Sort each use of a wildcard by whether the tutorial allows it.

items.t: as the type of a method parameter
as the type of a field
as the type of a local variable
as the type argument when creating an object with new
as the type argument of a generic method invocation
as a supertype in an extends clause

questions.explain: Wildcards describe variables, not what you create, call or extend.
questions.rule: Not for creating, calling or extending.
questions.teaches: A wildcard is never used as a type argument for a generic method invocation or for creating an instance of a generic class, and never as a supertype.

questions.q: Which declaration uses the wildcard in a way the tutorial allows?
options: An object created with new ArrayList of question mark
A method parameter of type List of question mark
A class that extends List of question mark
A call that passes question mark as a type witness
optionExplain: Instances cannot be created with a wildcard argument.
Right: a parameter may be a wildcard type.
A wildcard cannot be a supertype.
Wildcards are not allowed as method invocation arguments.
questions.explain: Only the parameter use is permitted.
questions.rule: Use the wildcard for a type that is unknown and does not matter, in parameters, fields and local variables.

questions.q: True or false: a wildcard type used as a method's return type is rejected by the compiler as an error.
questions.explain: It can sometimes be used as a return type, though a more specific type is better practice.
questions.rule: Allowed but not preferred.

questions.q: A utility method returns the first item of a list. The author considers a wildcard return type. Which advice fits the tutorial?
options: Use a wildcard, since it is the most flexible return type
Return a raw type, which avoids wildcards
Return void and print the item
Prefer a more specific type, so callers need not deal with a wildcard
optionExplain: Flexibility for callers is the opposite of what a wildcard return gives.
A raw type loses the checking.
Returning nothing is not an answer to the design.
Right: the guidelines advise avoiding wildcard return types.
questions.explain: A wildcard in the return type pushes the work of handling it onto every caller.
questions.teaches: A wildcard return type forces the people who call the method to deal with wildcards, which is why the tutorial advises avoiding it.
questions.rule: Use the wildcard for a type that is unknown and does not matter, in parameters, fields and local variables.

questions.q: A method must total the numbers in a List of Integer, a List of Double and a List of Number alike. Which parameter type fits?
options: A List of Number written without a wildcard
A List of Object, since every item is an Object
A List of question mark extends Number
A List of Integer, since Integer is the commonest
optionExplain: Only a List of Number matches this exactly.
Only a List of Object matches.
Right: it accepts the bound and all subtypes.
Only a List of Integer matches.
questions.explain: A wildcard with a bound can cover a family of list types. The card next shows how.
questions.rule: Use question mark extends Bound for a list you only read from, when it may hold the bound or any subtype.

questions.q: A List of question mark extends Number matches a list of Number or a list of any ____ of Number.
questions.explain: The bound and everything below it matches.
questions.rule: Bound and below.

questions.q: A method has a parameter of type List of question mark extends Number and runs list.add(Integer.valueOf(1)). What happens?
options: It does not compile, since the exact element type is unknown
It compiles and adds the Integer to the end of the list
It compiles but fails at run time when the list holds Doubles
It compiles for Integer values but not for Double values
optionExplain: Right: the compiler cannot confirm an Integer fits the list.
The list might be a List of Double, which cannot hold an Integer.
The compiler refuses it instead.
Neither is accepted, because the element type is unknown.
questions.explain: A list of an unknown subtype of Number may not be able to accept the new item.
questions.rule: Extends lists are for reading.
questions.teaches: Adding an item to a list whose type is question mark extends Number is a compile-time error, because the exact element type is unknown.

questions.q: A method takes a List of question mark extends Number. Sort each argument by whether the call is accepted or rejected.

items.t: a List of Integer
a List of Double
a List of Number
a List of String
a List of Object
an ArrayList of Integer

questions.explain: Number and its subtypes qualify; String and Object do not.
questions.rule: Use question mark extends Bound for a list you only read from, when it may hold the bound or any subtype.

questions.q: The parameter is changed from List of question mark extends Number to a List of Number. What if a caller passes a List of Integer?
options: It is still accepted, because Integer is a Number
It is accepted with a warning
It is accepted only for lists of exactly three items
It is rejected, since the types are unrelated
optionExplain: Generic types do not inherit the relationship.
This is an error, not a warning.
List length has no part in typing.
Right: wildcards were what made it work.
questions.explain: Without the wildcard, only a List of Number fits.
questions.rule: No wildcard, no family.

questions.q: A method takes a List of question mark extends Shape and, for each item, calls area, a method defined in Shape. Does it compile?
options: No: the element type is unknown, so no method can be called
Yes: each item is treated as a Shape
Yes, but only for Shape itself, not subtypes
No: area must be declared in an interface
optionExplain: The unknown type is still known to be a Shape.
Right: methods of the bound are available.
Subtype objects are Shapes too.
A class bound provides methods too.
questions.explain: The bound gives every item at least the bound's methods.
questions.teaches: Items read from a list with an upper bounded wildcard can use any method defined in the bound.
questions.rule: Use question mark extends Bound for a list you only read from, when it may hold the bound or any subtype.

questions.q: True or false: a method that takes a List of Object can be called with a List of String.
questions.explain: The two list types are unrelated. The card next shows the type that does accept both.
questions.rule: Not a subtype.

questions.q: In a List of question mark, the question mark stands for an ____ type.
questions.explain: The wildcard is an unknown type.
questions.rule: Unknown.

questions.q: Which item can be added to a List of the unbounded wildcard?
options: Any Object
Only null
Any String
Nothing at all, not even null
optionExplain: The element type is unknown, so an Object may not fit.
Right: null fits any type, and nothing else is known to fit.
The list could be a List of Integer.
null is the one value allowed.
questions.explain: A List of Object takes any Object, but a List of the wildcard takes only null.
questions.rule: Wildcard lists take only null.
questions.teaches: Only null can be inserted into a list of the unbounded wildcard, while a List of Object accepts any Object.

questions.q: Which tasks suit a parameter of type List of the unbounded wildcard? Select all that apply.
options: Report how many items the list has
Empty the list with clear
Print each item using only Object operations
Add up the items as numbers
Add a new String to the list
optionExplain: Right: size does not depend on the element type.
Right: clear does not depend on the element type.
Right: Object is all that is needed.
Wrong: numbers need a bound such as Number.
Wrong: only null can be inserted.
questions.explain: The wildcard suits tasks independent of the element type.
questions.rule: Use a list of the unbounded wildcard when the code needs nothing from the element type beyond Object.

questions.q: The printList method is declared to take a List of Object. What if a caller passes a List of Integer?
options: It is accepted, because Integer is an Object
It is accepted with an unchecked warning
It is accepted and each item is printed as text
It is rejected, because the types are unrelated
optionExplain: Generic types do not follow their arguments' relationship.
This is a compile error.
The call does not compile.
Right: only a List of Object matches.
questions.explain: That is why the wildcard version was needed.
questions.rule: List of Object is narrower than it looks.

questions.q: A reflection helper accepts Class objects for any type and uses only methods that do not involve the type parameter. Which parameter type fits?
options: A Class of the unbounded wildcard
A Class of Object
A raw Class
A Class bounded by Comparable
optionExplain: Right: the tutorial notes this form is common because most Class methods do not depend on the parameter.
That accepts only Class of Object.
A raw type loses checking.
Nothing needs comparing here.
questions.explain: Where the type parameter does not matter, say so with the wildcard.
questions.teaches: Class of the unbounded wildcard is common because most Class methods do not depend on its type parameter.
questions.rule: Use a list of the unbounded wildcard when the code needs nothing from the element type beyond Object.

questions.q: A method adds Integer values to a list and should accept a List of Integer, a List of Number and a List of Object. Which parameter type fits?
options: A List of question mark extends Integer
A List of Integer
A List of question mark super Integer
A List of Double
optionExplain: That matches Integer and its subtypes.
That matches only a List of Integer.
Right: it matches Integer and its supertypes.
That accepts lists of Double only.
questions.explain: A bound can point downward as well as upward. The card next shows the lower bound.
questions.rule: Use question mark super Type when the code puts values of Type into a collection.

questions.q: True or false: question mark super Integer matches Integer and its supertypes.
questions.explain: The lower bound sets the lowest type allowed.
questions.rule: Bound and above.

questions.q: Can a single wildcard have both an upper bound and a lower bound?
options: Yes: write extends first and super second
Yes, but only for interfaces
Yes, if the bounds are the same type
No: a wildcard has one bound, either upper or lower
optionExplain: The tutorial does not allow both.
Interfaces make no difference.
Even equal bounds are not allowed together.
Right: the tutorial allows one or the other.
questions.explain: Choose the bound that matches the job.
questions.rule: One bound per wildcard.
questions.teaches: A wildcard may have an upper bound or a lower bound, but not both.

questions.q: A method adds Integer values to a list whose type is List of question mark super Integer. Sort each argument by whether it is accepted.

items.t: a List of Integer
a List of Number
a List of Object
a List of Double
a List of String
an ArrayList of Number

questions.explain: Integer and its supertypes can hold Integer values; Double and String lists cannot.
questions.rule: Use question mark super Type when the code puts values of Type into a collection.

questions.q: The addNumbers parameter is changed from question mark super Integer to question mark extends Integer. What if a caller passes a List of Number?
options: It is rejected, since Number is not a subtype of Integer
It is accepted, since a List of Number can hold Integers
It is accepted with a warning
It is accepted but adds nothing
optionExplain: Right: the bound now points the other way.
The bound is checked by type, not by what the list can hold.
This is a compile error.
The call does not compile.
questions.explain: Extends admits subtypes; super admits supertypes.
questions.rule: Extends goes down, super goes up.

questions.q: Cat extends Animal, and Animal extends Object. A method adds Cat objects to a list parameter of type List of question mark super Cat. Which arguments can it receive? Select all that apply.
options: a List of Cat
a List of Animal
a List of Object
a List of Dog, where Dog extends Animal
optionExplain: Right: Cat is the bound itself.
Right: Animal is a supertype of Cat.
Right: Object is a supertype of Cat.
Wrong: Dog is not a supertype of Cat.
questions.explain: Only the bound and its supertypes qualify.
questions.teaches: With a lower bound, the method knows exactly what it may put in (the bound type) while accepting a whole range of list types.
questions.rule: Use question mark super Type when the code puts values of Type into a collection.

questions.q: True or false: a List of question mark extends Integer is a subtype of a List of question mark extends Number.
questions.explain: Upper bounded wildcards follow the relationship of their bounds. The card next shows how.
questions.rule: Extends follows the bounds.

questions.q: Order these list types from most general to most specific.
items: List of the bare wildcard
List of question mark extends Number
List of question mark extends Integer
List of Integer
questions.explain: Each type sits under the one before it.
questions.rule: Extends wildcards follow the direction of the arguments, super wildcards run the opposite way, and the bare wildcard sits on top.

questions.q: Which type is a common supertype of every List parameterization, such as a List of Integer, a List of Number and a List of String?
options: A List of Object
A List of question mark extends Number
A List of the bare wildcard
A List of question mark super Integer
optionExplain: A List of Object is unrelated to those types.
A List of String is not covered, since String is not a Number.
Right: it sits above every parameterization of List.
A List of String is not covered, since String is not a supertype of Integer.
questions.explain: The unbounded wildcard type is the common parent.
questions.rule: The bare wildcard is the top.
questions.teaches: The common parent of unrelated parameterizations such as List of Integer and List of Number is the List of the unbounded wildcard.

questions.q: Match each list type to one wildcard type it can be assigned to.
pairs: List of question mark extends Integer
List of question mark super Number
List of question mark extends Integer
List of question mark extends Number
List of question mark super Number
List of question mark super Integer
questions.explain: Extends follows the arguments upward; super works the opposite way.
questions.rule: Extends wildcards follow the direction of the arguments, super wildcards run the opposite way, and the bare wildcard sits on top.

questions.q: A variable has the type List of question mark super Integer. What if the code assigns it a List of Number?
options: It is rejected, since Number is not a subtype of Integer
It is accepted, since a List of Number is a subtype of that type
It is accepted only with a cast
It is rejected because generic types are unrelated
optionExplain: The lower bound admits supertypes of Integer.
Right: the lower bound runs the other way.
No cast is needed.
Wildcards are exactly what creates the relationship.
questions.explain: A List of Number can hold Integers, so it fits under the lower bound.
questions.rule: Super bounds admit supertypes.

questions.q: Animal is a supertype of Dog, and Dog is a supertype of Puppy. Which assignment compiles?
options: Assigning a List of question mark extends Puppy to a List of question mark extends Dog
Assigning a List of question mark extends Dog to a List of question mark extends Puppy
Assigning a List of question mark super Puppy to a List of question mark super Dog
Assigning a List of Dog to a List of Animal
optionExplain: Right: extends follows the direction of the arguments.
The direction is reversed.
Super runs the opposite way, so a super Dog list is the subtype.
Plain parameterizations are unrelated.
questions.explain: Follow the bound's direction: extends goes with the hierarchy, super against it.
questions.teaches: With super, the list with the higher (more general) bound is the narrower type, which is the reverse of extends.
questions.rule: Extends wildcards follow the direction of the arguments, super wildcards run the opposite way, and the bare wildcard sits on top.

questions.q: A method takes a List of the bare wildcard, reads item 0 and sets it back at position 0. The compiler rejects the line. What is the likely reason?
options: Lists do not allow a set call after a get call on the same list
A List of the bare wildcard is read-only in every possible way
It cannot link the unknown type of the item read to the type the list needs
get returns an int, which cannot be written back into the list
optionExplain: Lists do allow it.
The issue is the link between read and write types.
Right: the read and write types are both unknown to it.
get returns the element type, not int.
questions.explain: The compiler tracks an unknown type but cannot link the two uses. The card next shows the fix.
questions.rule: When a capture-of error blocks code that is truly safe, route it through a private generic helper; if it is unsafe, redesign.

questions.q: By convention, a helper that captures the wildcard for a method foo is named foo____.
questions.explain: The helper takes the original name plus Helper.
questions.rule: Name plus Helper.

questions.q: A method swapFirst takes two lists, each a List of question mark extends Number, and moves items between them. It does not compile. Should it?
options: No: it is safe because both lists hold only Number objects, so any swap works
Yes: the two wildcards are captured separately and could hide different types
Yes, but only because lists cannot have their items swapped at all
No: a private helper method would make the swap type safe
optionExplain: Both hold Numbers, but possibly different subtypes.
Right: the two captures are different types.
Swapping within one list can be fine.
A helper cannot make unsafe code safe.
questions.explain: Two separate captures cannot be treated as the same type, and mixing them can break a list.
questions.rule: Two wildcards, two captures.
questions.teaches: Each wildcard in a signature is captured separately, so the compiler cannot treat two of them as the same type even when they have the same bound.

questions.q: A method reverse takes a List of the bare wildcard and must swap items inside that one list. Which private helper signature lets the compiler capture the wildcard?
options: A method taking a List of Object
A method taking a List of the bare wildcard
A method taking a raw List
A generic method taking a List of T
optionExplain: A List of Object does not accept every list.
That repeats the same problem.
A raw list loses the checking.
Right: T gives the captured type a name.
questions.explain: The helper's type parameter is what names the captured type.
questions.rule: When a capture-of error blocks code that is truly safe, route it through a private generic helper; if it is unsafe, redesign.

questions.q: True or false: adding a private helper to swapFirst, which takes two lists of question mark extends Number, makes mixing their items type safe.
questions.explain: The code is truly unsafe, so no helper can fix it; the compiler is right to refuse.
questions.rule: A helper cannot repair unsafe logic.

questions.q: Sort each task by whether a private generic helper can make it compile safely.

items.t: read an item from a List of the bare wildcard and write it back to the same list
swap two items inside one List of the bare wildcard
move an item from one List of question mark extends Number into another such list
put a Double into a List of question mark extends Number

questions.explain: A helper works when every use refers to the same unknown type.
questions.teaches: A helper applies only when all the uses involve the same unknown type, as with operations inside a single list.
questions.rule: When a capture-of error blocks code that is truly safe, route it through a private generic helper; if it is unsafe, redesign.

questions.q: A method copies items from one list into another. Which list is the in variable?
options: The destination list, because items go in
Both lists, because both are lists
The source list, because it supplies data
Neither, since both are parameters
optionExplain: The destination receives data, so it is out.
They play different roles.
Right: in variables serve data to the code.
Each parameter has a role.
questions.explain: The words in and out describe the data's direction relative to the code. The card next gives the guideline.
questions.rule: In means extends, out means super, Object-only in means the bare wildcard, and both in and out means no wildcard.

questions.q: Match each role to the wildcard the guideline gives it.
pairs: An in variable used only through Object methods
A variable that is both in and out
questions.explain: Direction decides the wildcard.
questions.rule: In means extends, out means super, Object-only in means the bare wildcard, and both in and out means no wildcard.

questions.q: A method only prints each item of a list, using methods every object has. Which parameter type does the guideline suggest?
options: A List of the unbounded wildcard
A List of question mark extends Object
A List of question mark super Object
A List of Object
optionExplain: Right: Object methods alone need no bound.
The guideline reserves the bare wildcard for this case.
A lower bound is for out variables.
That would reject most lists.
questions.explain: An in variable used only through Object methods gets the unbounded wildcard.
questions.rule: Object-only in: the bare wildcard.
questions.teaches: An in variable accessed only through Object methods gets the unbounded wildcard rather than an extends bound.

questions.q: Sort each parameter by the wildcard the guideline suggests.

items.t: a list a method reads Shape items from
a list a logger method appends Message objects to
a source list in a copy method
a destination list in a copy method
a list a method fills with Integer values
a list a method sums numbers from

questions.explain: Reading means extends; writing means super.
questions.rule: In means extends, out means super, Object-only in means the bare wildcard, and both in and out means no wildcard.

questions.q: A method both reads items from a list and adds items back into the same list. What does the guideline suggest?
options: Use extends, since it reads
Use super, since it writes
Use the bare wildcard, since both matter
Use no wildcard on that parameter
optionExplain: Extends rules out adding items.
Super limits what you can read.
The bare wildcard allows only null to be added.
Right: a variable that is both in and out gets none.
questions.explain: A wildcard would block one of the two directions.
questions.rule: Both in and out: no wildcard.

questions.q: A method mergeInto takes two source lists and one destination list. Which parameter types fit the guideline?
options: Super for both sources and extends for the destination
Extends for both sources and super for the destination
Extends for all three lists
No wildcard on any list
optionExplain: The roles are reversed.
Right: each variable is classified by its own role.
The destination is written to.
A wildcard fits the in and out roles here.
questions.explain: A method can have several in variables and out variables, each classified separately.
questions.teaches: A method can have several in variables and out variables, and each is classified separately by its own role.
questions.rule: In means extends, out means super, Object-only in means the bare wildcard, and both in and out means no wildcard.

questions.q: True or false: a new NaturalNumber can be added to a variable of type List of question mark extends NaturalNumber.
questions.explain: The list might hold a narrower type, so the add is refused. The card next explains.
questions.rule: No adding.

questions.q: A wildcard is best avoided as a ____ type, since callers would have to handle it.
questions.explain: The tutorial advises against wildcard return types.
questions.rule: Return types: be specific.

questions.q: Which operations are still allowed on a List of question mark extends Number? Select all that apply.
options: Add null
Call clear
Get an iterator and call remove
Add a new Integer
Replace item 0 with a new Double
optionExplain: Right: null fits any reference type.
Right: clear removes items without needing the element type.
Right: removing does not insert anything.
Wrong: the exact element type is unknown.
Wrong: the compiler cannot confirm a Double fits.
questions.explain: The list cannot take new items of known types, but it can still lose items.
questions.rule: Informally read-only, not strictly.
questions.teaches: An extends list still allows adding null, calling clear, getting an iterator and calling remove, and writing back items that were read from the list through wildcard capture.

questions.q: A method returns the longest words found in a text. Which return type fits the tutorial's advice?
options: A List of question mark extends String
A specific type such as List of String
A List of the bare wildcard
A raw List
optionExplain: Callers would then deal with a wildcard.
Right: callers can use it directly.
Callers would only see Object items.
A raw list loses the checking.
questions.explain: Wildcards belong on parameters; return a precise type.
questions.rule: Treat an extends list as read-only for new items, know that some changes still work, and avoid wildcard return types.

questions.q: The variable ln is a List of question mark extends NaturalNumber and actually refers to a List of EvenNumber. What if the code adds an EvenNumber?
options: It compiles, because the list really does hold only EvenNumber objects
It compiles with a warning
It fails only at run time
Still a compile-time error: the compiler knows only the wildcard type
optionExplain: The compiler checks the declared type, not the actual list.
This is an error, not a warning.
The compiler rejects it earlier.
Right: it cannot see what ln really refers to.
questions.explain: Static types decide what compiles.
questions.rule: The declared type decides.

questions.q: A colleague claims a list typed with an extends wildcard cannot change in any way. Which counter-example fits the tutorial?
options: Calling clear on it removes all the items
Calling add with a valid item
Assigning a new item to position 0
Calling size on it
optionExplain: Right: the list can still lose items.
Adding items of known type is refused.
Replacing an item is refused too.
size does not change the list.
questions.explain: Informally read-only is not strictly read-only.
questions.teaches: Informal read-only describes what cannot be stored into the list, not a promise that the list stays unchanged.
questions.rule: Treat an extends list as read-only for new items, know that some changes still work, and avoid wildcard return types.

questions.q: After compilation, what does the type parameter T of an unbounded generic class become?
options: A random class chosen at run time
The first type argument ever used
Object
Nothing: T stays in the compiled code
optionExplain: Nothing is chosen at run time.
The compiled class does not depend on uses.
Right: with no bound, Object replaces it.
Type parameters are erased.
questions.explain: Erasure fixes the compiled form once. The card next lists what it does.
questions.rule: Erasure replaces type parameters with bounds or Object, adds casts where needed, and adds bridge methods.

questions.q: Match each action of the compiler to its purpose.
pairs: with their bounds, or Object if unbounded
where needed to keep type safety
to preserve polymorphism in extended generic types
questions.explain: Each action keeps compiled code correct without type arguments.
questions.rule: Erasure replaces type parameters with bounds or Object, adds casts where needed, and adds bridge methods.

questions.q: A program creates both a Box of Integer and a Box of String. How many compiled classes correspond to these types?
options: Two, one for each of the two type arguments that are used
Three, one per argument and one shared base class
None, because generic classes are not compiled until they are used
One, since erasure creates no new classes for parameterized types
optionExplain: Erasure does not create a class per argument.
Nothing in the tutorial adds a third.
Generic classes are compiled once.
Right: the same class serves every use.
questions.explain: Because no new classes are created, generics add no runtime overhead.
questions.rule: One class for all uses.
questions.teaches: Erasure creates no new classes for parameterized types, so generics incur no run-time overhead.

questions.q: A class with the unbounded parameter T is erased so that T becomes ____.
questions.explain: Unbounded parameters become Object.
questions.rule: Unbounded: Object.

questions.q: A class has the parameter T extends Number. What if the class is erased?
options: T becomes Number
T becomes Object
T becomes Integer
T stays as it is
optionExplain: Right: the bound replaces the parameter.
Object replaces only unbounded parameters.
The bound is Number, not a particular subtype.
Erasure removes parameters.
questions.explain: The bound replaces the parameter.
questions.rule: Bound if there is one, else Object.

questions.q: Given erasure, can a running program tell a Box of Integer from a Box of String by looking at their classes?
options: Yes: each keeps its own class
Yes, but only for primitive arguments
No: both are the same erased class
Yes, if the program is compiled twice
optionExplain: No separate classes are created.
Primitives are not type arguments.
Right: the type arguments are not kept.
Compiling twice changes nothing.
questions.explain: The run-time class carries no type argument.
questions.teaches: At run time a Box of Integer and a Box of String are the same class, so the running program cannot tell them apart by type argument.
questions.rule: Erasure replaces type parameters with bounds or Object, adds casts where needed, and adds bridge methods.

questions.q: After erasure, an unbounded type parameter T is replaced by ____.
questions.explain: Without a bound, Object replaces T. The card next covers bounded cases too.
questions.rule: Unbounded becomes Object.

questions.q: Match each declaration to what the type parameter T becomes.
pairs: Node of T as a type
questions.explain: Bounded parameters become their first bound; generic names become raw types.
questions.rule: Erasure turns each type parameter into its first bound, or Object when there is none.

questions.q: A class has T extends Comparable of T and a field of type T. What is the field's type after erasure?
options: Comparable of T
The raw type Comparable
Object
T
optionExplain: The bound's argument is dropped too.
Right: the first bound, without its own type argument.
The bound exists, so it is used.
Parameters are removed.
questions.explain: Erasure leaves the bound as a raw type.
questions.rule: Bounds become raw types.
questions.teaches: The bound's own type argument is dropped as well, so a bound such as Comparable of T is erased to the raw type Comparable.

questions.q: A method has the header with T extends Shape and takes one parameter of type T. After erasure, that parameter has type ____.
questions.explain: T is replaced by its bound.
questions.rule: Bound replaces T.

questions.q: True or false: a counting method with an unbounded T that tests e.equals(elem) still works after erasure, because every class inherits equals from Object.
questions.explain: After erasure the elements are Objects, and equals is defined for every Object.
questions.rule: Equality survives erasure.

questions.q: A method has T extends Comparable of T and takes an array of T and one T. A student says the erased method takes an Object array and an Object. What is wrong?
options: T has a bound, so they become a Comparable array and a Comparable
Nothing: unbounded and bounded parameters both erase to Object arrays
The array becomes a List
The method disappears
optionExplain: Right: the array of T erases to an array of the bound.
Bounded parameters erase to their bound.
Arrays stay arrays.
Erased methods remain.
questions.explain: An array of T erases to an array of whatever T erases to.
questions.teaches: An array of T erases to an array of the bound, so the array parameter above becomes a raw Comparable array.
questions.rule: Erasure turns each type parameter into its first bound, or Object when there is none.

questions.q: After erasure, Node's setData takes an Object and MyNode's setData takes an Integer. With no extra help, how do these two relate?
options: MyNode's method overrides Node's
MyNode's method is removed
MyNode's method overloads rather than overrides
Both methods become a single method with an Object parameter
optionExplain: Overriding needs the same signature.
It stays.
Right: the signatures differ.
They keep their separate signatures.
questions.explain: Erasure changed one signature but not the other. The card next shows the fix.
questions.rule: A bridge method keeps overriding working after erasure by casting and then delegating to the real method.

questions.q: True or false: a bridge method is written by the programmer.
questions.explain: The compiler generates it; it is synthetic.
questions.rule: Compiler-made.

questions.q: A MyNode is stored in a variable of the raw type Node, and the code calls setData with the text Hello. What happens?
options: It does not compile, because the text is not an Integer and the compiler sees that
It compiles with a warning, then throws ClassCastException when it runs
It compiles and stores the text inside the node unchanged
It compiles and silently converts the text into a number
optionExplain: The raw type bypasses the check.
Right: the bridge's cast to Integer fails.
The bridge cast rejects it.
No conversion is done.
questions.explain: The raw reference hides the type, and the bridge's cast catches it at run time before MyNode's own code prints anything.
questions.rule: Raw types move errors to run time.
questions.teaches: With a raw reference, the bad argument reaches the bridge method, whose cast to Integer throws ClassCastException before the real setData body runs.

questions.q: Order the steps that lead to a bridge method.
items: The generic superclass is erased, so its method takes Object
The subclass method takes Integer, so it no longer overrides
The compiler adds a bridge method taking Object to the subclass
The bridge casts to Integer and calls the Integer method
questions.explain: The bridge restores the override and then forwards the call.
questions.rule: A bridge method keeps overriding working after erasure by casting and then delegating to the real method.

questions.q: True or false: a call to setData with an Integer through a Node of Integer variable that refers to a MyNode runs MyNode's version.
questions.explain: The bridge makes the override work, so the call reaches MyNode.
questions.rule: Bridges preserve polymorphism.

questions.q: A class Handler has the parameter T and a method handle taking T. OrderHandler extends Handler of Order and has handle taking Order. Which statements about the compiled OrderHandler are correct? Select all that apply.
options: It has a compiler-made handle method taking Object
The bridge casts its argument to Order and calls the Order version
It has only handle taking Order, so overriding is lost
The bridge appears in the source code
optionExplain: Right: that is the bridge.
Right: that is what a bridge does.
Wrong: the bridge restores overriding.
Wrong: bridges are synthetic.
questions.explain: A bridge has the erased signature of the superclass method, and it is what actually overrides it.
questions.teaches: The bridge has the same signature as the erased superclass method, so it is the method that actually overrides it.
questions.rule: A bridge method keeps overriding working after erasure by casting and then delegating to the real method.

questions.q: True or false: at run time a program can tell a List of String from a List of Number.
questions.explain: Erasure removes the arguments. The card next names such types.
questions.rule: Arguments are erased.

questions.q: Sort each type by whether it is reifiable.

items.t: int
String
List of String
List of the bare wildcard
a raw List
Map of String and Integer

questions.explain: Primitives, non-generic types, raw types and bare wildcards keep their information.
questions.rule: Non-reifiable types lose their arguments at run time, and unchecked warnings are the warning signs of heap pollution.

questions.q: Why can the running program not support instanceof with List of String?
options: List is a library interface, so instanceof cannot be applied to it
instanceof works only on arrays and cannot be used on generic types
String is a final class, so no test against it can be written
Erasure removed the type argument, so there is nothing to test
optionExplain: A list is an object.
instanceof works on classes too.
Finality is not the reason.
Right: the runtime sees only List.
questions.explain: Non-reifiable types cannot be used in an instanceof expression or as an array element type.
questions.rule: No arguments at run time, no tests on them.
questions.teaches: Non-reifiable types cannot be used in an instanceof expression or as an array element type, because the information is gone at run time.

questions.q: Which situations can lead to heap pollution? Select all that apply.
options: Mixing raw and parameterized types
Performing an unchecked cast
Calling a method on a List of String that returns a String
Assigning a String to a String variable
optionExplain: Right: such operations give unchecked warnings.
Right: it too gives an unchecked warning.
Wrong: this is fully checked.
Wrong: nothing generic is involved.
questions.explain: Operations that produce unchecked warnings are the cause.
questions.rule: Non-reifiable types lose their arguments at run time, and unchecked warnings are the warning signs of heap pollution.

questions.q: All the code of a program is compiled together and the compiler gives no warnings. What if you ask whether heap pollution can occur?
options: It can still occur through raw types
It occurs once at start up
It cannot occur
It occurs only on arrays
optionExplain: Raw type use would have produced warnings.
Nothing in clean code causes it.
Right: no warnings means no heap pollution.
Arrays are not the point.
questions.explain: Warnings flag the operations that cause it.
questions.rule: Clean compile, no pollution.

questions.q: Which situation makes heap pollution hardest to detect?
options: Separately compiled pieces, because the compiler cannot warn across them
Code with only primitive variables and no generic types in it
Code that uses a List of String in several different classes at once
Code that prints no output
optionExplain: Right: the guarantee covers code compiled together.
Primitive code has no parameterized types.
Typed code is checked.
Printing is unrelated.
questions.explain: The compiler warns only about what it can see.
questions.teaches: When code is compiled in separate pieces, the compiler cannot warn about heap pollution across the pieces.
questions.rule: Non-reifiable types lose their arguments at run time, and unchecked warnings are the warning signs of heap pollution.

questions.q: True or false: a method with a varargs parameter of a parameterized type can compile with a warning about possible heap pollution.
questions.explain: The compiler warns at the declaration. The card next explains why.
questions.rule: Generic varargs warn.

questions.q: The annotation SafeVarargs removes the warning at the method's ____.
questions.explain: It removes the declaration warning.
questions.rule: Declaration warning.

questions.q: Why does the tutorial call SuppressWarnings with unchecked and varargs less desirable than SafeVarargs?
options: It cannot be used on methods that declare varargs parameters
It makes the method unsafe
It only works on constructors
It does not suppress the warnings generated at call sites
optionExplain: It can.
It hides warnings; it does not change safety.
It is not limited to constructors.
Right: callers would still see them.
questions.explain: SafeVarargs states safety as part of the contract; the other hides the warnings in one place.
questions.rule: SafeVarargs is a contract.
questions.teaches: SuppressWarnings with unchecked and varargs is less desirable than SafeVarargs because it does not suppress warnings generated at call sites.

questions.q: Sort each method body by whether SafeVarargs would be honest.

items.t: adds each varargs element to a list
prints each varargs element
stores a List of Integer into the varargs array through an Object array alias
overwrites element 0 with a List of Integer and then reads it as a List of String

questions.explain: A body that only reads is safe; one that writes foreign items is not.
questions.rule: Use SafeVarargs only on a method whose body merely reads its generic varargs.

questions.q: faultyMethod takes a varargs of List of String. It stores a List of Integer into the varargs array through an Object[] alias, then reads the first element's first item into a String. It is called with two lists of String as arguments. Where does the ClassCastException occur?
options: At the call, when the arguments are checked against the parameter
Inside faultyMethod, where it reads the polluted element
At compile time
Nowhere: the method runs normally
optionExplain: The arguments are fine.
Right: the fault is in the method, not the call.
It compiles with a warning.
The read of the polluted element throws.
questions.explain: The callers pass valid lists; the method pollutes its own array.
questions.rule: The bug is in the method.

questions.q: Which statements about SafeVarargs are correct? Select all that apply.
options: It tells readers and the compiler that the author vouches for the method
It should be used only if the body cannot cause a ClassCastException from its varargs
It adds run-time checks that make the body safe
It can be placed on a local variable
optionExplain: Right: it asserts that the implementation is safe.
Right: it is a promise.
Wrong: it adds nothing at run time.
Wrong: it applies to methods.
questions.explain: It states safety; it does not create it.
questions.teaches: SafeVarargs also silences the unchecked warning at every call site, so a false promise hides a real heap-pollution risk (beyond the tutorial notes).
questions.rule: Use SafeVarargs only on a method whose body merely reads its generic varargs.

questions.q: True or false: a Pair of int and char is a valid parameterized type.
questions.explain: Type arguments must be object types. The card next explains.
questions.rule: No primitive arguments.

questions.q: Match each invalid type argument to a valid replacement.
questions.explain: Each primitive has a wrapper class that can serve as the argument.
questions.rule: Use wrapper types as type arguments, and obtain instances of a type parameter some way other than new.

questions.q: A generic method needs to create an object of type E. Which approach does the tutorial describe?
options: Cast a new Object to E and rely on the cast to work
Pass in a Class of E and create the instance through it by reflection
Declare E as a primitive type
Write new E followed by the diamond to let the compiler infer it
optionExplain: A cast does not create an E.
Right: the Class object stands in for the erased type.
Primitives cannot be type arguments.
new E is rejected whatever follows it.
questions.explain: The erased type cannot be instantiated, but a Class object carries the real class.
questions.rule: Pass a Class object to create instances.
questions.teaches: A workaround for creating an instance of a type parameter is to pass a Class of E to the method and create the object through it by reflection.

questions.q: To make a list that holds whole numbers, declare a List of ____, not a List of int.
questions.explain: Integer is the wrapper for int.
questions.rule: Wrapper types.

questions.q: The compiler is changed to accept new E inside a generic method. Why would the call still be impossible to run?
options: E is always an abstract class, which cannot be instantiated
new is allowed only for primitive types, never for type variables
E has no constructors
E is erased at run time, so there is no class to instantiate
optionExplain: E can be any non-primitive type.
new creates objects.
Which constructors exist depends on the argument, not on erasure.
Right: nothing remains to create from.
questions.explain: The runtime has no class for E.
questions.rule: Erased means not creatable.

questions.q: Sort each item by whether the tutorial allows it.

items.t: Box of Integer
Box of int
Map of String and Long
Map of long and String
creating a T with new T inside a generic class
passing a Class of T into a method and creating through it

questions.explain: Wrapper types and the Class workaround are fine; primitives and new T are not.
questions.teaches: The restriction on primitives applies to every position in a type argument list, so Map of long and String fails just as Map of String and long would.
questions.rule: Use wrapper types as type arguments, and obtain instances of a type parameter some way other than new.

questions.q: True or false: a generic class can declare a static field whose type is its type parameter.
questions.explain: Statics are shared by all instances. The card next explains.
questions.rule: No static T.

questions.q: A static field is shared by every instance of the ____.
questions.explain: A static field belongs to the class.
questions.rule: Static means class-wide.

questions.q: Which member of a class Cache with the parameter T is allowed?
options: A non-static field of type T
A static field of type T
A static field of type List of T
A static method returning T that uses the class's T
optionExplain: Right: each instance has its own T.
A static field cannot use the class's T.
The class's T still cannot appear in a static member.
Static methods cannot use the class's parameters.
questions.explain: Only instance members can use the class's type parameters.
questions.rule: Instance members only.
questions.teaches: Instance fields and methods may use the class's type parameters; static members, even ones that mention T inside another type such as a list, may not.

questions.q: In a class Singleton with the parameter T, which declarations fail to compile? Select all that apply.
options: private static T instance = null
public static T getInstance()
private T value
public T get()
optionExplain: Right: a static field of the parameter type.
Right: a static method cannot use the class's T.
Wrong: an instance field may use T.
Wrong: an instance method may use T.
questions.explain: Statics cannot use the class's parameter; instance members can.
questions.rule: Static members cannot use the class's type parameters.

questions.q: Suppose Java allowed a static field os in MobileDevice of T, and objects exist for Smartphone, Pager and TabletPC. How many copies of os would exist?
options: Three, one for each type argument that is used
Two, one for each pair of types
One, shared by all, so it could not be all three types
None, because static fields are erased with the type argument
optionExplain: Static fields are not copied per argument.
Nothing creates pairs.
Right: that is why the field is banned.
A static field is a single field.
questions.explain: One shared field cannot have three different types.
questions.rule: One static, many arguments.

questions.q: A class Registry with the parameter T wants to count how many Registry objects have been created. Is a static int counter allowed?
options: No: every static field of a generic class is banned
Yes, but only if it is also final
No: the counter would need to be of type T
Yes: its type does not use the class's type parameter
optionExplain: The ban is on types using the parameter.
Finality is not required.
A counter is a plain number.
Right: only types that use T are restricted.
questions.explain: The restriction targets the parameter, not statics in general.
questions.teaches: Static fields of a generic class are fine when their type does not use the class's type parameter.
questions.rule: Static members cannot use the class's type parameters.

questions.q: True or false: a program can ask at run time whether a list is an ArrayList of Integer using instanceof.
questions.explain: The type argument is gone at run time. The card next explains.
questions.rule: No instanceof on arguments.

questions.q: Storing a wrong element into an array throws an ____.
questions.explain: Arrays check element types at run time.
questions.rule: Arrays check at run time.

questions.q: Sort each expression by whether it compiles.

items.t: instanceof with ArrayList of the bare wildcard
instanceof with ArrayList of Integer
casting a List of String to an ArrayList of String
casting a List of Integer to a List of Number
creating an array of List of Integer
creating an ArrayList of Integer object

questions.explain: The bare wildcard is reifiable, and a cast the compiler already knows to be valid is fine.
questions.rule: Reifiable forms are allowed.
questions.teaches: instanceof with the unbounded wildcard is allowed because that type is reifiable, and a cast such as List of String to ArrayList of String is allowed because the compiler already knows the type arguments match.

questions.q: Which line compiles?
options: An instanceof test against ArrayList of the bare wildcard
An instanceof test against ArrayList of Integer
Creating an array whose element type is ArrayList of String
A cast of a List of Integer to a List of Number
optionExplain: Right: the bare wildcard is reifiable.
Parameterized instanceof is rejected.
Arrays of parameterized types are rejected.
Casts between parameterizations are rejected.
questions.explain: Only the wildcard test asks for nothing erased.
questions.rule: Do not test, cast to or build arrays of types whose arguments erasure removes.

questions.q: Arrays of parameterized types were allowed. An Object array of two slots holds a List of String in one slot and a List of Integer in the other. Could the runtime object to the second?
options: Yes: it throws an ArrayStoreException as soon as the second list is stored
Yes: the compiler inserts a check that compares the type arguments
No: it cannot see the type arguments, so it cannot spot the wrong list
No: arrays never check element types
optionExplain: That exception relies on run-time element types.
The compiler cannot check the Object view.
Right: erasure leaves nothing to check.
Arrays do check ordinary element types.
questions.explain: The safety net of arrays needs run-time types.
questions.rule: Arrays need run-time types.

questions.q: A program stores the number 5 into an Object array that was created as an array of String. What happens?
options: A compile-time error, since the array is typed Object
An ArrayStoreException is thrown at run time
The 5 is converted to a String
Nothing: the store succeeds
optionExplain: The compiler sees only the Object type.
Right: arrays check their real element type.
No conversion occurs.
The array rejects the wrong element.
questions.explain: Ordinary arrays have real run-time element types, which is the check erased generics lack.
questions.teaches: An ordinary array remembers its real element type at run time and refuses a mismatched store with ArrayStoreException, even when seen through an Object array.
questions.rule: Do not test, cast to or build arrays of types whose arguments erasure removes.

questions.q: True or false: a method taking a Set of String and another method of the same name taking a Set of Integer can be overloads in one class.
questions.explain: After erasure both take a Set. The card next explains.
questions.rule: Same erasure, clash.

questions.q: After erasure, print with a Set of String and print with a Set of Integer both take a ____.
questions.explain: Both become print taking a Set.
questions.rule: Erased to the same raw type.

questions.q: Which of these is allowed?
options: A type parameter in a throws clause
A generic class that extends Exception
A catch clause that catches a type parameter
A generic class that extends Throwable directly
optionExplain: Right: the tutorial allows it.
A generic class cannot extend Throwable.
Catching needs a run-time class.
Throwable is also banned as a supertype.
questions.explain: Only the throws clause may use a type parameter.
questions.rule: throws yes, catch no.
questions.teaches: A type parameter may be used in a throws clause, even though it cannot be used in a catch clause.

questions.q: Sort each declaration by whether it compiles.

items.t: a class Failure with a type parameter that extends Exception
a class Failure with no type parameter that extends Exception
a catch clause that catches a type parameter T
a method that declares throws T
print with a List of String next to print with a Set of String
print with a List of String next to print with a List of Integer

questions.explain: Generic subclasses of Throwable, catching T and same-erasure overloads are rejected.
questions.rule: Exception matching and overloading depend on run-time types, so type arguments erased away cannot tell cases apart.

questions.q: A class has convert taking a Map of String and Integer and another convert taking a Map of Long and Long. Does it compile?
options: Yes: the type arguments differ
Yes: Integer and Long are different classes
No: both erase to a method taking a Map
No: Map cannot be a parameter
optionExplain: The compiler looks at the erased signatures.
The arguments are erased before comparing.
Right: they share one erased signature.
Map can be a parameter type.
questions.explain: Different type arguments do not count as different overloads.
questions.teaches: The clash is in the erased signature, so differing only in type arguments is not enough to make two overloads distinct.
questions.rule: Exception matching and overloading depend on run-time types, so type arguments erased away cannot tell cases apart.

questions.q: A team puts related classes and interfaces into one package. Which benefit does that give?
options: The grouped types are merged into a single class file
The grouped types then run faster at run time than the same types left ungrouped
The grouped types become subclasses of one another
The types get a namespace, so their names stay apart from other packages
optionExplain: Each type is still compiled on its own; a package is not a file.
Packages organise names and access; they do not change how fast code runs.
Grouping does not create inheritance; subclassing is declared with extends.
Right: a package is a namespace, so equal simple names in different packages do not clash.
questions.rule: A package is a namespace plus an access boundary.
questions.explain: A package's main gifts are a separate namespace and access control. The card next shows both.

questions.q: A package gives its types their own ____, so two packages can each hold a type with the same simple name.
questions.rule: One package, one namespace.
questions.explain: The namespace is what keeps same-named types in different packages apart.

questions.q: Sort each situation by the package purpose it relies on.

items.t: Two vendors each ship a class called Report
A helper type meant for use only by its neighbours in one package
Your Order class and a library Order class used in one program
Keeping outside code away from internal types
Telling two Logger types apart by their package prefix
Letting types in one package share access freely

questions.rule: Names: namespace. Reach: access protection.
questions.explain: Clashing names are solved by namespaces; deciding who may reach a type is access protection. These are the two purposes of a package.

questions.q: True or false: enumerations and annotation types can belong to a package in the same way as classes and interfaces.
questions.rule: A package holds every kind of type.
questions.teaches: The tutorial says classes and interfaces as shorthand for all four kinds of type, including enumerations and annotation types.
questions.explain: They can. They are special kinds of classes and interfaces, so a package can hold all four kinds of type.

questions.q: A hospital software library has types for scheduling, billing and lab results, all in one package. A new developer wants to find the scheduling code quickly. Which package design would help most?
options: One package per area, such as scheduling, billing and labs
Types sorted by the length of their names
One package per developer who wrote the code, named after each person
Everything in the unnamed package, for easy access
optionExplain: Right: grouping related types makes the code easy to find, because others know where to look.
Name length says nothing about what a type does, so it helps nobody find code.
Authors change, but the question is about function, which is what readers search by.
The unnamed package suits only small programs and groups nothing.
questions.rule: Group by what the types are for.
questions.teaches: Grouping related types in a package also makes them easy to find, because other programmers know where to look for that kind of functionality.
questions.explain: Besides separating names, packages tell others where to look. Grouping by area makes the related code easy to locate.

questions.q: Two firms each name their package tools and each has a class Logger. One program uses both libraries. What does the namespace idea alone achieve here?
options: It separates them, because every class has a unique simple name
It fails to separate them, because the full names are identical
It separates them, because the compiler renames one package
It separates them, because the later library overrides the earlier
optionExplain: Simple names are exactly what clash; the namespace works only when package names differ.
Right: the full name tools.Logger is the same for both, so the namespace cannot tell them apart.
The compiler never renames packages for you.
Nothing overrides anything; the same full name for two types is the problem.
questions.rule: Namespaces need distinct package names.
questions.hint: Compare the full names of the two Logger classes.
questions.explain: A namespace separates names only when package names differ. Avoiding identical package names is left to convention, the topic of the naming idea.

questions.q: True or false: one source file may contain two package statements when it declares two classes.
questions.rule: One package statement per file.
questions.explain: A file has one package statement and it covers every type in the file. The card next gives the rules for the statement.

questions.q: A file named Sketch.java holds a public top-level class. That class must be named ____.
questions.rule: Public type name equals file name.
questions.explain: The public top-level type takes the file's name, minus the .java ending.

questions.q: A developer puts public class Parcel and public class Label in one file named Parcel.java. What does the tutorial's rule say about this file?
options: It breaks the rule: only one top-level type per file may be public
It breaks the rule: a source file may hold only one class of any kind at all
It is fine, because both classes share one package statement
It is fine as long as Label is declared first
optionExplain: Right: Label is also public, so it would need its own file named Label.java.
Non-public types may share the file; the limit applies only to public ones.
A shared package statement does not lift the limit on public types.
The order of the types in the file does not matter to this rule.
questions.rule: Second public type, second file.
questions.explain: At most one top-level type per file can be public. Label must either lose public or move to Label.java.

questions.q: A public enumeration named Season belongs in a file called ____ (include the file ending).
questions.rule: Same file-name rule for all kinds of type.
questions.teaches: The rule that a public type lives in a file of the same name covers enumerations and interfaces, not only classes.
questions.explain: The file-name rule applies to every kind of type. A public enumeration Season goes in Season.java, and a public interface goes in its own interface-named file.

questions.q: A file named Cafe.java contains the two lines: package cafe; public class Menu followed by an empty body. Which statement about this file is correct?
options: The file is invalid, since package names may not be lower case
The file is valid, since the package statement is first
The file is valid, since a package name is allowed to differ from the file name
The file is invalid, since a public class must sit in a file named after it
optionExplain: Lower case is the recommended style for package names.
The package statement is correctly placed, but the file still has another problem.
Package and file names are separate things; the problem is the class and file names.
Right: public class Menu needs the file Menu.java.
questions.rule: Match public type and file name.
questions.explain: The public class Menu must live in Menu.java. The file name Cafe.java does not match.

questions.q: According to the tutorial, which situations fit the unnamed package, where files have no package statement? Select all that apply.
options: A quick throwaway experiment
A first program written by a beginner
A large shared library
An application with many classes built by a team
A temporary tool used for one week
optionExplain: Right: small or temporary code is what the unnamed package suits.
Right: the tutorial says it is acceptable when you are just beginning.
A shared library needs named packages so its names stay distinct.
Larger applications should use named packages, according to the tutorial.
Right: temporary applications are named as a fit.
questions.rule: Unnamed package: small and temporary only.
questions.teaches: The tutorial advises the unnamed package only for small or temporary applications or first steps, and named packages for anything larger.
questions.explain: The tutorial limits the unnamed package to small or temporary applications and first steps; anything larger belongs in named packages.

questions.q: A company owns the domain example.com. Which package name best follows the tutorial's convention?
options: example.com.reports
com.example.reports
reports.example.com
Example.Com.reports
optionExplain: The domain is written in the original order here, but the convention reverses it.
Right: reversed domain first, lower case, then the project part.
This keeps the domain order and puts the project first, the opposite of the convention.
Capitals clash with the style of type names.
questions.rule: Reversed domain, lower case.
questions.explain: Conventional names start with the reversed domain in lower case. The card next gives the reasoning.

questions.q: A firm owns the domain tulip.example.org. Its package names should start with ____.
questions.rule: Reverse the domain, part by part.
questions.explain: The domain parts are reversed: org, then example, then tulip.

questions.q: Two teams at one firm, whose packages start with net.sample.shop, both want a package named payments. What does the tutorial suggest?
options: Let the compiler pick one of the two and rename the other package
Use capital letters in one team's name
Add a region or project name after the company prefix
Drop the company prefix for one team
optionExplain: The compiler never renames packages; this is for the people to arrange.
Capitals are against the lower-case convention and invite confusion with type names.
Right: for example net.sample.shop.north.payments and net.sample.shop.south.payments.
