Dropping the prefix removes the protection that keeps names distinct.
questions.rule: Collision inside a firm: add region or project.
questions.explain: Inside one company, extend the name with a region or project part so the packages stay distinct.

questions.q: A domain part is not a legal identifier in Java. Match each domain to the package prefix the tutorial's underscore fix would give.
questions.rule: Add an underscore to repair an illegal part.
questions.teaches: If a reversed domain contains a hyphen, a Java keyword or a part that starts with a digit, add an underscore to make it a legal name.
questions.explain: A hyphen cannot appear in an identifier, so it becomes an underscore. A keyword part gets an underscore after it. A part starting with a digit gets an underscore in front.

questions.q: A hobbyist writes a card-game library and wants to name the package javax.games.cards so that it looks official. What does the tutorial say about this?
options: It is discouraged, because java and javax are reserved for the language itself
It is required, because every games library must live under the javax prefix
It is fine, because javax is open to all authors
It is fine if the games part is lower case
optionExplain: Right: according to the tutorial, those prefixes are reserved for the Java language itself.
Nothing requires games to sit under javax.
The prefix is not open; it belongs to the platform.
Lower case does not change who owns the prefix.
questions.rule: Leave java and javax to the platform.
questions.teaches: The package prefixes java and javax are reserved for the Java language itself, so your own code must not use them.
questions.explain: Your own code should use your own reversed domain. The names starting with java and javax are reserved for the language.

questions.q: Sort each package name by whether it follows the tutorial's naming convention.

items.t: com.acme.shop
Com.Acme.Shop
javax.acme.tools
org.example.tulip.emea
acme.com.shop
net.example.maps

questions.rule: Lower case, reversed domain, no java or javax.
questions.explain: Good names are lower case, start with the reversed domain, and avoid the java and javax prefixes. Capitals, the unreversed domain and a javax prefix each break the convention.

questions.q: True or false: code outside a package can use the simple name of one of its public classes without any import or qualification.
questions.rule: Outside a package, qualify or import.
questions.explain: Outside the package the simple name is unknown unless imported. The card next gives the three routes.

questions.q: To import every type of the package pets, write import pets.____;
questions.rule: Asterisk imports a whole package.
questions.explain: The asterisk stands for all types in the package.

questions.q: A class uses five types from package charts (Bar, Pie, Line, Axis, Legend) many times each. Which route fits best, according to the tutorial?
options: Write charts.Bar and the like at every use
Import the whole package with an asterisk
Import only Bar and use qualified names for the rest
Copy the five classes into the current package
optionExplain: Repeating long qualified names becomes tedious and hard to read.
Right: many types from one package call for a package import.
Mixing routes for five busy types makes the file hard to read.
Copying duplicates code and is not one of the three routes.
questions.rule: Many types: import the package.
questions.explain: Frequent use of many types from one package is what the asterisk import is for.

questions.q: Put the three parts of a source file in the order Java requires.
items: package shop;
import pets.Dog;
public class Walker with its body
questions.rule: Package, imports, types.
questions.teaches: Import statements go after the package statement and before any type definitions.
questions.explain: The package statement comes first, then imports, then the type definitions.

questions.q: Package billing holds public classes Invoice and Payment, and Invoice uses Payment. Both files start with package billing;. What must Invoice add to use Payment by its simple name?
options: import billing.Payment;
import billing.*;
The qualified name billing.Payment at each use
Nothing: they are in the same package
optionExplain: Harmless, but not needed, since the type is already in the same package.
Also not needed; a package's own types need no import.
Qualifying works but is not required either.
Right: a simple name works for a type in the same package.
questions.rule: Same package: simple names just work.
questions.teaches: Code can use the simple name of a type that lives in its own package without any import.
questions.explain: Simple names work for types in the same package or already imported. Invoice and Payment share billing.

questions.q: Class Secret in package vault is declared without public. Code in another package writes import vault.Secret;. What would the tutorial lead you to expect?
options: Only the qualified name works for such types
The import works, since an import statement ignores access rules altogether
The import fails to give access, as only public types are usable from outside
Only the asterisk form works for such types
optionExplain: A qualified name is also just a name form and cannot widen access.
Access still applies; an import only shortens names.
Right: a type without public is package private, so outside code cannot use it under any route.
An asterisk import changes the name form, not what is accessible.
questions.rule: Routes shorten names; public grants access.
questions.explain: All three routes apply only to public types. A package-private type is usable only inside its own package.

questions.q: True or false: import java.awt.*; also makes the types of the package java.awt.color usable by simple name.
questions.rule: Name prefixes do not nest packages.
questions.explain: Each package needs its own import, whatever its name suggests. The card next explains why.

questions.q: Besides java.lang, the compiler automatically imports the ____ package of each source file.
questions.rule: Automatic: java.lang and the current package.
questions.explain: Types of the file's own package are in scope without an import.

questions.q: A file uses Car from package vehicles and Wheel from package vehicles.parts, both by simple name. Which imports does it need?
options: import vehicles.*; and import vehicles.parts.*;
import vehicles.*.*; which names every subpackage of vehicles in one line
import vehicles.*; only
import vehicles.parts.*; only
optionExplain: Right: two packages, so two imports.
This pattern is not valid; an asterisk only ends an import.
That brings in Car but not Wheel, because the parts package is a separate package.
That brings in Wheel but not Car.
questions.rule: One import per package.
questions.explain: vehicles and vehicles.parts are two unrelated packages for import purposes, so each needs its own line.

questions.q: True or false: if class Shape has a public nested class Shape.Dot, the single line import shapes.Shape.*; lets you use Shape itself by its simple name.
questions.rule: Nested types need their own import.
questions.teaches: Importing the nested classes of a class does not import the class itself, so both lines are needed to use the outer class and its nested ones.
questions.explain: That line imports the nested types only. To use Shape by its simple name as well, you also need import shapes.Shape;.

questions.q: A developer wants Cart and Card from package shop and writes import shop.Ca*; as the only import. What happens?
options: Only the first matching name is imported
The compiler reports an error, since the asterisk cannot match part of a name
Both are imported, but with a warning
Both Cart and Card are imported
optionExplain: No matching of names takes place at all.
Right: the asterisk may only stand for all types in a package.
The tutorial calls it an error, not a warning.
Wildcard patterns of this kind are not supported.
questions.rule: No partial wildcards.
questions.explain: The asterisk means all types of the package. Partial patterns are a compile error, so import the types one by one.

questions.q: Class Item lives in package shop. A file in package shop.cart, with no import lines, uses Item by its simple name. What do you expect?
options: It compiles only if the file is in the same folder as Item
It compiles, since shop.cart sits inside shop
It compiles, since both names start with shop
It fails to find Item, since the current package means shop.cart only
optionExplain: Folders are not the test; package membership and imports decide name lookup.
Package names show relation, not containment.
A shared prefix does not import anything.
Right: the file's own package is shop.cart, so Item needs an import.
questions.rule: Current package means exactly that one.
questions.teaches: Because packages do not nest, the automatic import of the current package never includes the package above it in the name.
questions.explain: The automatic import covers exactly the file's own package. Because shop.cart does not contain shop, the file needs import shop.Item;.

questions.q: Two packages that a file imports with asterisks both contain a type called Rectangle. The file declares a variable of type Rectangle by simple name. What happens?
options: The compiler reports an ambiguity error
The program fails only when it runs
The compiler uses the package imported first
The compiler uses the package imported last
optionExplain: Right: the simple name could mean either type, so it cannot be compiled.
The problem is found at compile time, not at run time.
Import order does not decide between the types.
Neither order settles it.
questions.rule: Ambiguous simple name: compile error.
questions.explain: A shared simple name is ambiguous. The card next shows how to resolve it.

questions.q: To say which Rectangle you mean when two clash, write its ____ name, which includes the package.
questions.rule: Qualify to resolve a clash.
questions.explain: The qualified name carries the package, which removes the doubt.

questions.q: A file begins with import maps.*; and import geom.*;, and both packages contain Point. It declares Point p; and the compiler complains. What is the smallest fix?
options: Delete both import lines
Write maps.Point (or geom.Point) at that use
Rename the file
Add a static import of Point
optionExplain: Removing the imports breaks every other simple name from those packages.
Right: qualifying the clashing name there resolves it, and the rest of the file stays as it is.
The file name has nothing to do with name lookup.
Static import applies to static members, not to types such as classes.
questions.rule: Qualify only the clashing name.
questions.explain: Only the clashing use needs the qualified name. The other types from both packages stay usable by simple name.

questions.q: True or false: static import works for your own constants and utility methods, and not only for those of the platform.
questions.rule: Static import is not limited to the platform.
questions.teaches: Static import works for constants and utility methods in your own packages as well as for those in the Java platform.
questions.explain: A line such as import static followed by your own constants class and an asterisk works the same as it does for Math.

questions.q: A file imports maps.* and geom.*. Only maps has a type called Line, and both have Point. What happens to the declaration Line l; by simple name?
options: Error: any two wildcard imports make every name ambiguous
Error: Line is ambiguous because geom has Point
It compiles, since only one imported package has Line
It compiles only after a static import
optionExplain: Ambiguity needs the same simple name in both packages, not just two imports.
A clash on Point does not affect an unrelated name such as Line.
Right: Line has one meaning here, so no ambiguity arises.
Static import is irrelevant for types.
questions.rule: Ambiguity is per name.
questions.explain: Ambiguity arises per name, so a name found in only one imported package stays usable.

questions.q: Sort each use of static import by whether the tutorial's reasoning supports it or warns against it.

items.t: Using a Math constant forty times in one geometry file
Wildcard static imports of five utility classes into one file
Importing the one constant a file needs repeatedly
Static-importing everything so readers must guess where each method comes from

questions.rule: Few members, often: fine. Everything: avoid.
questions.teaches: The risk of static import lies in quantity: the more members used without a class name, the harder it is for readers to tell where each one is defined.
questions.explain: Static import helps when a few members are used often. Heavy use leaves readers unable to tell which class defines a member.

questions.q: Where would you normally store the source file of public class com.acme.tools.Saw?
options: com.acme.tools/Saw.java
com/acme/tools.java
tools/Saw.java
com/acme/tools/Saw.java
optionExplain: A single directory with dots is not the layout used; each part is its own level.
The type name, not the last package part, names the file.
Only the last name part is kept; the rest of the package path is lost.
Right: each package name part becomes a directory, and the file is named after the type.
questions.rule: Package parts become directories.
questions.explain: Package parts become directories and the file carries the type's name. The card next states the layout.

questions.q: A file Z.java declares package a.b.c;. It belongs in the directory ____.
questions.rule: a.b.c is the path a/b/c.
questions.explain: Each part of the package name is one directory level.

questions.q: File Keeper.java declares package zoo.staff;, a public class Keeper, and a non-public class Badge. Which class files does compiling produce? Select all that apply.
options: zoo/staff/Keeper.class
zoo/staff/Badge.class
zoo/Keeper.class
Badge.class directly in the starting directory
optionExplain: Right: one class file for the public type, in the matching directories.
Right: a non-public type still gets its own class file.
The class file stays at the directory level that matches the full package name.
The package decides the directory, so Badge is not placed outside it.
questions.rule: One class file per type.
questions.explain: There is one class file per type, named after the type and placed in directories that match the package name.

questions.q: True or false: source files and class files must be kept under the same root directory.
questions.rule: Source and class trees can be separate.
questions.teaches: Keeping the source tree and the class tree under separate roots lets you hand out compiled classes without giving away the source code.
questions.explain: The trees may have different roots, for instance a sources folder and a classes folder. The class folder can then be shared without exposing the source.

questions.q: A developer saves Dog.java, which declares package pets;, in a folder called animals, so the path is animals/Dog.java. What does the tutorial's layout rule say?
options: Wrong: the path should mirror the package, so pets/Dog.java
Wrong: the file should be named pets.java
Fine: the folder name is free
Fine if the class is public
optionExplain: Right: the package pets maps to the directory pets.
The file is named after its top-level type, not the package.
The path is meant to mirror the package name, not to be arbitrary.
Being public does not change where the file lives.
questions.rule: Path mirrors package; file name mirrors type.
questions.explain: Directories follow the package name and the file follows the type name, giving pets/Dog.java.

questions.q: A project has mygame/server/Server.java and mygame/client/Client.java. From which directory should you run javac mygame/server/Server.java?
options: Inside the mygame/client directory
In the directory that contains mygame
Any directory, since the compiler searches the whole disk
Inside the mygame/server directory
optionExplain: Same problem, and this is the wrong subdirectory.
Right: the path starts with mygame, so it is relative to the directory holding mygame.
The compiler follows the path and class path you give it; it does not scan the disk.
The path given would then not point at an existing file.
questions.rule: Start from the directory above the package tree.
questions.teaches: When compiling with package paths, run the compiler from the directory that contains the top package directory, such as mygame.
questions.explain: A relative path begins at the top of the package tree, so you compile from the directory that contains the first package directory.

questions.q: True or false: to find class shop.cart.Cart, the class path entry should be the directory that directly contains Cart.class.
questions.rule: Class path entry is the root, not the leaf.
questions.explain: The entry is the root above the package directories. The card next explains how the search builds the rest of the path.

questions.q: Entries in a class path are separated by a semicolon on Windows and a ____ on UNIX.
questions.rule: Windows semicolon, UNIX colon.
questions.explain: The two systems use different separators for the list of roots.

questions.q: The file /srv/app/classes/org/example/tools/Saw.class holds class org.example.tools.Saw. Which class path entry lets the tools find it?
options: /srv/app/classes/org/example/tools
/srv/app/classes/org
/srv/app
/srv/app/classes
optionExplain: That is the package directory itself, so the search would add the package parts again.
That is partway down the tree; the search would then look for org/org/example/tools.
That root would need the class files under /srv/app/org/example/tools.
Right: the root of the package tree, to which the search adds org/example/tools.
questions.rule: Root plus package path equals class file directory.
questions.explain: The tools append the package path to each root, so the root must be the directory that contains the first package directory.

questions.q: True or false: you must add the Java platform's own classes and the current directory to the class path before programs can find them.
questions.rule: Defaults cover the current directory and platform classes.
questions.teaches: By default the compiler and the virtual machine already search the current directory and the archive of platform classes, so you need not add them.
questions.explain: By default the tools search the current directory and the archive holding the platform classes, so neither needs to be listed.

questions.q: The class path is /home/g/classes, but the compiled class shop.cart.Cart sits at /home/g/other/shop/cart/Cart.class. What is the smallest change that lets the tools find it?
options: Move the package statement into the class file
Rename Cart.class
Add /home/g/other to the class path
Add /home/g/other/shop/cart to the class path
optionExplain: Package declarations live in source files, and moving them does not change where files are searched.
The file name already matches its type; the location is the problem.
Right: that root plus shop/cart reaches the class file.
This points at the package directory, so the tools would append shop/cart again.
questions.rule: Add the missing root.
questions.explain: Adding the missing root makes the search reach shop/cart under it, while the other root keeps working.

questions.q: A team builds with Maven or Gradle, which usually handle the class path for them. What does the tutorial's note say about the package-to-directory rule?
options: It still applies underneath, even though the tool sets the class path
It applies only to the unnamed package
It applies only to Windows
It no longer applies, since the tool manages everything
optionExplain: Right: the tool only takes over the class path chore, and the mapping still holds.
Named packages are exactly where the rule applies.
The rule is not tied to an operating system.
The tool automates the class path; the layout rule is still what it relies on.
questions.rule: Tools hide the class path, not the layout.
questions.teaches: Modern build tools such as Maven and Gradle usually set the class path for you, but the package-to-directory rule still applies underneath.
questions.explain: Build tools set the class path for you, but package names still map to directories.

questions.q: A method meets a problem it cannot continue past. According to Java's model, what does it do?
options: It restarts from its first line and keeps trying until the problem disappears
It silently returns zero to its caller and carries on with the next task
It builds an object describing the problem and hands it over
It asks the compiler to pause the program until the programmer edits the code
optionExplain: Nothing in the model retries automatically; a restart would repeat the same failure.
Returning a plain value is the old error-code style, which this model replaces.
Right: the problem becomes an object, and that object is handed over.
The compiler works before the program runs, so it cannot be consulted during execution.
questions.explain: Java turns a problem into an object and hands it over. The card next shows what that act is called.
questions.rule: A problem becomes an object that is handed over.

questions.q: True or false: Throwing an exception means building an exception object and handing it to the runtime system.
questions.explain: That is the definition: the method creates the object and passes it to the runtime system.
questions.rule: Throwing = build the object, hand it over.

questions.q: A parsing method meets text it cannot read, builds an object describing the failure, and hands that object to the runtime system. This act is called ____ an exception.
questions.explain: The act of creating the exception object and handing it to the runtime system is called throwing.
questions.rule: Hand-over of the object is called throwing.

questions.q: A program reads a file in a loop and the loop ends because the stream reaches its end-of-stream marker, as planned. According to the tutorial's exercise, how is this classified?
options: No exception: a stream's end is normal flow
An error, because the stream has run out of data to give
A checked exception, because the read had to stop early
A compile error, because the loop never ends with a throw
optionExplain: Right: nothing disrupted the normal flow, so there is no exceptional event.
An error means a serious outside failure; a planned stop is not a failure.
A checked exception is still an exceptional event; here nothing exceptional happened.
Compile errors are about the source code; this is ordinary behavior at run time.
questions.explain: An exception is an event that disrupts normal flow. Reaching a planned end of input does not disrupt anything, so nothing is thrown.
questions.hint: Ask whether anything unexpected happened.
questions.rule: Expected, planned events are not exceptions.

questions.q: True or false: A method throws an exception only when a quantity is zero, and otherwise divides. When the quantity passed in is 5, no exception object is built and the method runs through normally.
questions.explain: The throw is guarded by the check. With a false check the throw never runs, so there is no exception event.
questions.rule: No error event, no exception object.

questions.q: A library method fails because a settings key is missing. Why is handing the caller an exception object more informative than handing back the number minus one?
options: A number cannot be returned from a method that has failed, so only objects can signal it
Objects are faster for the runtime system to compare than plain numbers are
The caller no longer needs to know that anything failed once an object exists
The object has a type and can carry details such as a message
optionExplain: A number can be returned; the trouble is how little it says.
Speed is not the point; the point is the information carried.
The caller still has to learn of the failure; the object helps it do so.
Right: an object can carry several facts, while a bare number carries one.
questions.explain: Because the thrown thing is an object, it can describe the problem by type and by extra data such as a message, which an error number cannot do well.
questions.rule: An object can say more than a number.
questions.teaches: Because an exception is an object, it can carry extra information such as an error message, not only its type.

questions.q: Method a calls b, b calls c, and c throws an exception. In which order does the runtime system look for a handler?
options: a, then b, then c
c, then b, then a
Only in a, because it started everything
Only in c, and the program ends if c has none
optionExplain: That is the order of the calls, but the search goes the other way.
Right: from the method that failed back toward the first caller.
The search covers every method on the chain, not just the first.
The search continues past c to the callers.
questions.explain: The search runs backward along the chain of calls. The card next gives the full rule.
questions.rule: Search runs from the failing method outward.

questions.q: Put these steps in the order they happen when a method throws an exception that a caller can handle.
items: A method throws an exception object
The runtime system checks the failing method for a handler
The runtime system checks the caller of that method
A matching handler catches the exception
questions.explain: The throw comes first, then the search starts at the failing method and moves outward until a matching handler catches it.
questions.rule: Search outward from the failing method.

questions.q: start calls loadUser, and loadUser calls readFile. readFile throws an exception. start and readFile each have a handler whose type matches; loadUser has none. Which handler catches the exception?
options: The handler in start, because it is the outermost
Both handlers, one after the other
The handler in readFile, because the failing method is searched first
Neither, because loadUser in the middle has no handler
optionExplain: The outermost is searched last, not first.
One handler catches it; the search ends there.
Right: the failing method is searched first, and it has a matching handler.
A method without a handler is just passed through.
questions.explain: The search begins at readFile. It finds an appropriate handler there and stops.
questions.rule: The nearest matching handler wins.

questions.q: True or false: In a chain where the failing method has a handler for an unrelated type and a caller has a matching handler, the program ends because the failing method already has a handler.
questions.explain: A handler of an unrelated type is not appropriate. The search moves on to the caller, whose handler catches the exception.
questions.rule: A handler of the wrong type does not count.

questions.q: In the same chain, both the handler in readFile and the handler in start match the thrown type. Which handlers run?
options: Only the one in readFile; the search stops there
Both, starting with readFile and then moving on to start
Only start's, since the outermost method has the final say
Neither, because two matching handlers cancel each other out
optionExplain: Right: the first appropriate handler found catches the exception, and the search ends.
One thrown exception is caught once, not once per matching handler.
The nearest match is chosen, not the outermost.
More than one match does not produce a conflict; the first found wins.
questions.explain: The runtime takes the first appropriate handler it meets, so a nearer matching handler hides farther ones.
questions.rule: First match, nearest first.
questions.teaches: The search stops at the first appropriate handler it meets, so a nearer handler shadows a farther one of the same type.

questions.q: A company passes an expense claim from clerk to manager to director. Each person deals only with certain claim categories. A travel claim reaches the director, who handles only equipment claims. What is the closest match in Java?
options: An exception caught by the first method on the chain that has any handler at all
A checked exception that the compiler rejected before the program ran
A handler that catches every type of exception thrown anywhere in the program
A thrown exception that no handler on the stack matches, so the program ends
optionExplain: The clerk and manager did not deal with the claim, just as a handler of the wrong type does not.
The compiler works before the program runs; this chain exhausted at run time.
The director handles only one category, so it is not a catch-all.
Right: every stage was passed through, none was appropriate, and the chain is exhausted.
questions.explain: Having handlers is not the same as having an appropriate handler. When the whole stack has none of a matching type, the program ends.
questions.rule: Matching type, not mere presence, ends the search.
questions.teaches: An exception is unhandled when no handler on the stack matches its type; a handler of some other type does not rescue the program.

questions.q: A method calls a constructor that can throw a checked exception. The method neither catches it nor mentions it. What happens?
options: It compiles and fails only if the exception occurs
The compiler rejects the code
It compiles with a warning and runs normally
The runtime system adds a handler automatically
optionExplain: The compiler checks this before any run.
Right: the requirement is enforced at compile time.
A warning is not enough; the code is invalid.
The runtime system never adds code.
questions.explain: Checked exceptions must be dealt with in the source. The card next states the requirement.
questions.rule: Checked exceptions must be dealt with in the source.

questions.q: True or false: A method can satisfy the requirement by naming the exception in a throws clause instead of catching it.
questions.explain: Specifying the exception is one of the two allowed options.
questions.rule: Catch it or specify it.

questions.q: void save(String name) { new FileWriter(name); } fails to compile because the FileWriter constructor can throw an IOException, which is checked. To satisfy the requirement by specifying it, add a ____ clause naming IOException before the opening brace.
questions.explain: Either wrap the call in try with a catch for IOException, or add throws IOException after the parameter list and before the brace.
questions.rule: The throws clause sits after the parameter list.

questions.q: A reviewer says this compiles because it has a try statement: try { new FileReader(path); } finally { count = count + 1; } and the enclosing method has no throws clause. What is wrong with the claim?
options: Nothing; any try statement satisfies the requirement by itself
The println call inside finally throws its own checked exception, which is the real problem
A finally block is not a handler, so nothing is caught or specified
FileReader may only be used inside a catch block of an enclosing try
optionExplain: The requirement needs a handler for the exception, not merely a try.
println is not the problem here.
Right: only a catch handler for the exception counts as catching it.
FileReader can be used anywhere; the exception is what needs handling.
questions.explain: The try must provide a handler for the exception. A finally block alone provides cleanup, not handling, so the call is left unhandled and unspecified.
questions.rule: A try counts only with a catch for that exception.
questions.teaches: A try statement meets the requirement only through a catch handler for the exception; a try with just a finally block does not.

questions.q: True or false: Method readName declares throws FileNotFoundException. main calls readName with no try and no throws clause. This compiles, because readName already specified the exception.
questions.explain: Specifying passes the duty to the caller: main now faces the requirement itself, so the code does not compile.
questions.rule: A throws clause hands the duty to the caller.

questions.q: A weather app calls a method declared to throw a checked exception only when the network is down. On the tester's machine the network stays up throughout, and the call has no handler and no throws clause. What does the tester see?
options: A compile error, even though the exception never occurs there
The app runs normally because no exception ever occurs on that machine
The app runs, then ends when the network happens to drop
A runtime warning on the first call, then normal operation
optionExplain: Right: the compiler checks what might be thrown, not what is thrown in one run.
The check does not depend on one run's behavior.
The code never gets to run in the first place.
The rule is applied by the compiler, not at run time.
questions.explain: The requirement is about code that might throw, so it is enforced whether or not the exception happens in a particular run.
questions.rule: Might throw is enough to trigger the requirement.
questions.teaches: Because the compiler checks code that might throw, a violation is reported even in programs where the exception would never occur.

questions.q: Which of these is the compiler most likely to force a programmer to handle or declare?
options: A null passed by mistake to a method
A hardware fault in the middle of a read
A bug that indexes past the end of an array
A missing file whose name a user typed in
optionExplain: That is a programming bug, which is not enforced.
That is an outside failure, usually beyond recovery, and is not enforced.
Another programming bug; the compiler does not enforce it.
Right: an anticipated, recoverable condition is the kind the compiler enforces.
questions.explain: The compiler enforces conditions a program can plan for. The card next sorts the three kinds.
questions.rule: The compiler enforces the plannable conditions.

questions.q: Match each kind of exceptional condition with the description that fits it.
pairs: Anticipated condition the application can recover from
Outside condition the application usually cannot recover from
Inside condition that usually points to a programming bug
questions.explain: The three kinds differ by where the problem comes from and whether recovery is realistic.
questions.rule: Checked, error, runtime: three kinds.

questions.q: Sort these cases by whether the compiler requires the code to catch or specify them.

items.t: A user-supplied file name points to no file
A class extends Exception but not RuntimeException
A logic bug calls a method with null
A disk fault interrupts a read
A subclass of RuntimeException is thrown
A subclass of Error is thrown

questions.explain: Checked exceptions are those not descending from Error or RuntimeException. The rest are unchecked.
questions.rule: Not under Error or RuntimeException means checked.

questions.q: A method receives null for an argument it cannot accept. Why is throwing NullPointerException, which needs no throws clause, a reasonable way to report this?
options: Null values are fatal to the whole program and must stop it
The caller used the method incorrectly, which is a bug to fix, not to recover from
A throws clause cannot name NullPointerException, so a declaration is impossible
Checked exceptions can only be thrown by the Java runtime system, not by application code
optionExplain: Nothing fatal is implied; the point is about who can fix the problem.
Right: misuse of a method is the sort of internal programming error runtime exceptions stand for.
A throws clause may name it; it is just not required.
Any code may throw a checked exception; the choice depends on recovery.
questions.explain: A caller that passes an unacceptable argument has a bug, and handling it at run time would not repair that bug.
questions.rule: Misuse of a method is a bug, not a recoverable condition.
questions.teaches: Throwing a runtime exception, such as for a null argument, is the usual way for a method to report that its caller used it incorrectly.

questions.q: True or false: If a custom exception class changes its parent from Exception to RuntimeException, methods that throw it no longer have to catch or specify it.
questions.explain: The class becomes a runtime exception, hence unchecked, and the requirement no longer applies to it.
questions.rule: A class's ancestry decides whether it is checked.

questions.q: A method throws a RuntimeException on some path. It compiled with no handler and no throws clause, and a run reaches that path with no handler anywhere on the stack. What happens?
options: The compiler stops it before the run, because the throw is not declared anywhere
The exception is ignored at run time because it is an unchecked exception
The program compiled but ends at run time because no handler was found
The runtime system converts it into a checked exception and asks for a handler
optionExplain: The compiler did not require handling, so it let the code through.
Unchecked exceptions are still thrown and still searched for.
Right: the missing compile-time duty does not remove the run-time search.
Exceptions do not change kind while the program runs.
questions.explain: Unchecked exceptions are exempt from the compile-time requirement only. At run time an unhandled one still ends the program.
questions.rule: Exempt from the compiler is not exempt from the run time.
questions.teaches: Being exempt from Catch or Specify only removes the compile-time duty; an uncaught unchecked exception still terminates the program.

questions.q: True or false: A try block on its own, with nothing after it, is enough to handle an exception thrown inside it.
questions.explain: Handling is done by the catch blocks attached to the try. The card next shows the pieces.
questions.rule: The try marks the code; catch blocks handle.

questions.q: What is the job of a try block?
options: To enclose code that might throw so handlers can be attached to it
To stop any exception from being thrown by the statements inside the block
To list the exceptions a method can throw to the callers of that method
To close files that were opened inside it
optionExplain: Right: it marks the region that the attached handlers cover.
The exception is still thrown; the try only sets up how it is dealt with.
Listing exceptions for callers is the job of a throws clause.
Closing resources is done by finally or try-with-resources.
questions.explain: The try block fences off risky code; the handlers named after it say what to do.
questions.rule: Try fences, catch handles.

questions.q: A method needs a variable named reader to stay visible to a cleanup block placed after the try. A common pattern is to declare it before the try and set it to ____.
questions.explain: Declaring it before the try keeps it in scope for later blocks, and null is the starting value until the try assigns it.
questions.rule: Declare before the try, start with null.

questions.q: A try block holds statement A and then statement B. A throws an exception that a handler catches. What happens to B?
options: It runs after the handler finishes, and then execution carries on
It runs before the handler does, since it follows A in the block
It runs only if the handler prints a message about the failure
It is skipped, because the rest of the try block is abandoned once the exception is thrown
optionExplain: Control does not go back into the try block after a handler runs.
Statements run in order; the throw interrupts that order.
What the handler does has no effect on the abandoned statements.
Right: once an exception is thrown, execution leaves the try block for the handler.
questions.explain: A throw ends the try block's normal flow at that statement. Later statements in the block do not run.
questions.rule: A throw abandons the rest of the try block.
questions.teaches: When a statement in a try block throws, the remaining statements of that block are skipped and control moves to a handler.

questions.q: True or false: If a variable is declared inside the braces of the try block, a cleanup block placed after the try can still refer to it.
questions.explain: A variable declared inside the try block is out of scope after it. This is why the tutorial's example declares the variable before the try.
questions.rule: Declare what cleanup needs before the try.

questions.q: Two statements in one try block throw the same exception type, and a team wants a different message for each. Which layout allows that?
options: Add a second catch block of the same type after the first
Give each statement its own try block and its own catch
Wrap both in one try and use one catch that prints a message
Move one statement before the try and ignore its exception
optionExplain: The first matching handler takes every object of that type, so the second never gets one.
Right: separate try blocks make the source of the failure clear to each handler.
One handler cannot tell which statement failed.
A checked exception cannot be ignored by moving it out.
questions.explain: Because the first matching handler wins, two handlers of the same type cannot split the work. Smaller try blocks can.
questions.rule: Separate try blocks give separate handlers.
questions.teaches: Handlers can tell failures apart only by exception type or by being attached to different try blocks.

questions.q: Which of these can be the parameter type of a catch block?
options: Any class whose name ends in Exception
String, so the message can be read
Any class that inherits from Throwable
Any type that has a method named getMessage
optionExplain: The name is irrelevant; the ancestry decides.
A String is not Throwable.
Right: the parameter must be a Throwable type.
Having a method is not enough; the type must descend from Throwable.
questions.explain: The parameter's type must be in the Throwable family. The card next shows how a handler is picked.
questions.rule: The parameter type must inherit from Throwable.

questions.q: True or false: Code may sit between the end of a try block and the first catch block, provided that code does not throw.
questions.explain: Catch blocks go directly after the try block, with no code between.
questions.rule: Catch follows try directly.

questions.q: try { read(); } catch (FileNotFoundException e) { A } catch (IOException e) { B }. read() throws an EOFException, which is a subclass of IOException and not of FileNotFoundException. Which block runs?
options: B, since the EOFException object fits the IOException parameter but not the first one
A, because it is written first in the list of handlers
Both, A first and then B, since both are written there
Neither, since the exact class EOFException is not named
optionExplain: Right: EOFException fits IOException but not FileNotFoundException.
Being first matters only if it matches.
One handler is chosen.
Subclass objects match a superclass parameter.
questions.explain: The runtime goes down the handlers in order and takes the first that can accept the object: A cannot, B can.
questions.rule: Subclass objects fit superclass parameters.

questions.q: True or false: If a thrown NullPointerException matches neither of two handlers written for IOException and FileNotFoundException, the search for a handler continues in the calling methods.
questions.explain: Handlers that do not fit are passed over, and the search moves outward along the call stack.
questions.rule: No match here means the search goes on.

questions.q: A catch block has the parameter type IOException. Which thrown objects does it accept? Select all that apply.
options: An IOException
A FileNotFoundException, a subclass of IOException
An EOFException, another subclass of IOException
A NullPointerException
optionExplain: Right: the type itself always fits its own parameter.
Right: a subclass object can be assigned to a superclass parameter.
Right: this is also a subclass of IOException.
A NullPointerException is not in the IOException family, so it does not fit.
questions.explain: A superclass parameter accepts any object of the superclass and its subclasses.
questions.rule: One handler for a general type covers its family.
questions.teaches: Because a subclass object fits a superclass parameter, one handler for a general type catches the whole family below it.

questions.q: A hospital desk could send every patient to one general ward instead of checking for specialist wards. In Java terms, what does a single handler for a very general exception type cost?
options: The compiler refuses to compile any handler written for such a general type
The handler runs more slowly than a specific one, because it examines more cases
The handler can no longer receive checked exceptions, only the unchecked ones
The handler must inspect the exception to learn what happened
optionExplain: Nothing in the rules forbids a general handler.
Speed is not the cost the tutorial describes.
A general type still accepts the checked exceptions below it.
Right: a general handler receives many kinds of problem, so it must work out which one it has.
questions.explain: A narrow handler knows what went wrong from its type. A broad one has to examine the object, and may also catch problems nobody planned for.
questions.rule: Narrow handlers know what happened; broad ones must ask.
questions.teaches: A very general handler must inspect the exception object to learn what happened, and it may also catch unanticipated exceptions.

questions.q: Two exception types need exactly the same logging response. Which approach repeats the least code?
options: Two catch blocks that have identical bodies, one for each type
One catch clause listing both types separated by a vertical bar, with a single body
A catch of Exception, whatever else that also happens to cover
Two try blocks around the same statement, each with its own catch
optionExplain: That works but repeats the body.
Right: one block serves both types.
It is shorter, but it also catches types you never meant to handle.
Extra try blocks do not remove the duplicated handler code.
questions.explain: A newer form of catch lets one block cover several types. The card next shows its shape.
questions.rule: One block can list several types.

questions.q: In a catch clause that handles several types, the types are separated by the vertical ____ character.
questions.explain: The separator is the vertical bar, written |.
questions.rule: Types are separated by a vertical bar.

questions.q: Which catch clause is written correctly to handle IOException and SQLException in one block?
options: catch (IOException, SQLException ex)
catch (IOException || SQLException ex)
catch (IOException | SQLException ex)
catch (IOException) (SQLException) ex
optionExplain: A comma is not the separator for catch types.
Two bars form the logical-or operator, which is not used here.
Right: the types are joined by a vertical bar, followed by one parameter name.
A single parameter list holds both types; they are not two separate clauses.
questions.explain: A multi-catch uses one pair of parentheses, the types joined by one bar, and a single parameter name.
questions.rule: One bar between types, one parameter.

questions.q: In this handler, what goes wrong: catch (IOException | SQLException ex) { ex = new IOException('x'); log(ex); }
options: The multi-catch parameter is implicitly final and cannot be assigned
SQLException cannot be listed next to IOException in one clause because they differ
The block must end with a throw statement whenever it catches several types
Multi-catch cannot call a method such as log from inside its block
optionExplain: Right: assignment to ex is not allowed in this form.
Listing different types together is exactly what the form is for.
Nothing requires a throw at the end.
Calling methods is allowed; only reassignment is blocked.
questions.explain: The implicit final stops any assignment to the parameter inside the block.
questions.rule: Do not reassign the multi-catch parameter.

questions.q: True or false: If the two exception types need different recovery, they should still share one multi-catch block to avoid duplicated code.
questions.explain: Sharing makes sense when the response is the same. Different recovery needs separate handlers.
questions.rule: Share only when the response is the same.

questions.q: A multi-catch block logs the exception it caught and then rethrows it with throw ex. Given that the parameter is implicitly final, is the rethrow allowed?
options: No, because a final parameter cannot be used at all inside the block
No, because a multi-catch block is required to end quietly
Yes, but only if the clause lists only one exception type
Yes, because final blocks reassignment, not use
optionExplain: Final restricts assignment, not use.
No rule makes a handler end quietly.
Rethrow does not depend on how many types are listed.
Right: reading the parameter and throwing it back is not an assignment to it.
questions.explain: The tutorial's own multi-catch sample logs the exception and rethrows it. Final blocks only new assignments.
questions.rule: Final blocks assignment, not use.
questions.teaches: A handler may log an exception and rethrow it with a throw statement, because the final parameter can still be used.

questions.q: A try is followed first by catch (Exception e) and then by catch (ArithmeticException a). According to the tutorial's exercise, what happens?
options: It compiles, and ArithmeticException goes to the second block that names it
It does not compile; the first handler makes the second unreachable
It compiles, and both blocks run when an ArithmeticException is thrown
It compiles but the second block is used for all errors
optionExplain: The first block would take the object, so the second could never run.
Right: Exception already accepts every ArithmeticException.
Only one handler runs per exception.
The second block is for ArithmeticException only, and it is never reached.
questions.explain: A broad handler first hides the specific one. The card next explains why.
questions.rule: A broad handler first hides later ones.

questions.q: True or false: A catch for Exception placed before a catch for ArithmeticException makes the second block unreachable.
questions.explain: ArithmeticException is a subclass of Exception, so the first handler accepts every object the second was meant for.
questions.rule: Broad before specific hides the specific.

questions.q: Arrange these catch blocks so that more specific types come before more general ones. FileNotFoundException is a subclass of IOException, which is a subclass of Exception.
items: catch (FileNotFoundException e)
catch (IOException e)
catch (Exception e)
questions.explain: Each block must come before any block for one of its ancestors: FileNotFoundException, then IOException, then Exception.
questions.rule: Subclasses before superclasses.

questions.q: A student writes catch (IOException e) { A } and then catch (FileNotFoundException e) { B }, and says it is fine because the two types are different. What is the flaw?
options: Two catch blocks may not share the parameter name e in one try statement
FileNotFoundException can only be caught when it stands on its own
FileNotFoundException is a subclass of IOException, so B is unreachable and the compiler rejects it
IOException is an unchecked exception and cannot be caught
optionExplain: Each block has its own parameter; the same name is fine.
It can be caught together with others, in the right order.
Right: different is not the same as unrelated; the first handler accepts the subclass, so B can never run and the compiler rejects it.
IOException is checked and can be caught.
questions.explain: FileNotFoundException is a subclass of IOException, so B is unreachable and the compiler rejects it. The question is not whether the names differ but whether one type is an ancestor of the other.
questions.rule: Check ancestry, not names.

questions.q: True or false: With the FileNotFoundException handler written first and the IOException handler second, a thrown FileNotFoundException runs both blocks.
questions.explain: Only the first fitting handler runs, so the FileNotFoundException block runs alone and the IOException block still serves other I/O exceptions.
questions.rule: Only one handler runs.

questions.q: Which pair of catch blocks can be written in either order without making one unreachable?
options: IndexOutOfBoundsException and IOException
Exception and ArithmeticException, in either order
IOException and FileNotFoundException, in either order
Throwable and Exception, in either order
optionExplain: Right: neither is a subclass of the other, so they never compete for the same object.
ArithmeticException is a subclass of Exception.
FileNotFoundException is a subclass of IOException.
Exception is a subclass of Throwable.
questions.explain: Order matters only when one type is an ancestor of the other.
questions.rule: Unrelated types can go in any order.

questions.q: Four handlers are written in turn: Exception, RuntimeException, IOException and Throwable. In a hierarchy where Throwable is the parent of Exception, which one, placed first, would hide the most of the others?
options: Exception, since it is the most widely used handler type in practice
RuntimeException, since it is the type that is thrown most often
IOException, since it handles all input and output problems in Java
Throwable, since it accepts all of the others and errors as well
optionExplain: It accepts the other two exception handlers but not errors or the Throwable one.
It covers only the runtime branch.
It covers only the I/O branch.
Right: Throwable sits above both Error and Exception.
questions.explain: A handler's reach is its type plus everything below it, and Throwable is the top of the tree.
questions.rule: Reach equals the type plus all its subclasses.
questions.teaches: A catch for Throwable would accept errors as well as exceptions, so it is broader than a catch for Exception.

questions.q: A try block contains a return statement. Does the code in the matching finally block still run?
options: No, a return leaves the method at once and skips whatever follows
Yes, finally stops the return from skipping the cleanup
Only if the returned value happens to be an object reference
Only if an exception was thrown somewhere before the return
optionExplain: Leaving through a return is one of the exits finally covers.
Right: the finally block runs when the try block exits, including through a return.
The type of the returned value does not matter.
An exception is not needed; any exit triggers finally.
questions.explain: Finally is tied to leaving the try block, not to errors. The card next states the promise.
questions.rule: Finally runs on every exit from try.

questions.q: True or false: A finally block runs only when an exception occurs in the try block.
questions.explain: It runs when the try block exits in any way, normal exits included.
questions.rule: Finally runs on normal exits too.

questions.q: Sort these events by whether the finally block is expected to run.

items.t: The try block completes normally
An exception is thrown and caught
A return statement inside the try block executes
A break statement leaves the try block
The JVM exits while try code is running
The JVM exits while catch code is running

questions.explain: Every way of leaving the try block triggers finally, with the exception of the JVM itself exiting.
questions.rule: Only a JVM exit can skip finally.

questions.q: A finally block closes a writer that is assigned inside the try block. The failure happened while creating the writer, before the assignment. What should the finally block do before calling close?
options: Nothing, because finally runs only after every assignment has succeeded
Assign the variable again, in case the value was lost on the way
Check that the variable is not null, since an early failure leaves it unassigned and null
Rethrow the exception to the caller before doing anything else
optionExplain: Finally runs on every exit, including the early failure.
Re-assigning would repeat the failing operation.
Right: after an early failure the variable still has its starting value of null.
Rethrowing is unrelated to whether the variable holds an object.
questions.explain: Finally runs even for failures that happen before the work is set up, so it must cope with unset variables.
questions.rule: Check for null before closing.
questions.teaches: Because finally runs after early failures too, a variable assigned inside the try may still be null there, so cleanup code must check it before use.

questions.q: True or false: If the first statement of a try block is System.exit(0), the matching finally block is certain to run.
questions.explain: The finally block may not execute if the JVM exits while the try or catch code is running.
questions.rule: The JVM exiting can skip finally.

questions.q: A developer must close a file reliably in code that follows this tutorial's advice for closing files. The tutorial recommends a ____ statement rather than a finally block.
questions.explain: For closing a file or recovering other resources, the tutorial recommends try-with-resources over finally.
questions.rule: Prefer try-with-resources to close resources.
questions.teaches: For closing files and similar resources, the tutorial advises try-with-resources rather than a finally block.

questions.q: A try-with-resources statement declares a, then b. Both are resources. Which is closed first?
options: b, the one declared last
a, the one declared first
They close together in no fixed order
Neither, until the program ends
optionExplain: Right: resources close in the reverse order of their creation.
That would be creation order.
The order is fixed: the reverse of creation.
Resources close when the statement ends.
questions.explain: Closing runs backward through the declarations. The card next gives the full rule.
questions.rule: Close in reverse order of creation.

questions.q: True or false: Any object whose class implements AutoCloseable can be declared as a resource in a try-with-resources statement.
questions.explain: AutoCloseable is the interface the statement requires, and Closeable extends it.
questions.rule: AutoCloseable qualifies an object as a resource.

questions.q: Put the events of a try-with-resources statement with resources a then b in order.
items: Resource a is opened
Resource b is opened
The body runs
Resource b is closed
Resource a is closed
questions.explain: Resources open in declaration order, the body runs, and they close in the reverse order.
questions.rule: Open in order, close in reverse.

questions.q: True or false: When the body of a try-with-resources statement throws, the catch block attached to the statement runs before the resources are closed.
questions.explain: Catch and finally blocks of the statement run after the resources have been closed.
questions.rule: Resources close before catch and finally run.

questions.q: A resource's close method declares that it can throw IOException. The method that uses this resource in try-with-resources has no catch block. What must it do to compile?
options: Nothing, since the closing is carried out by the runtime system itself
Declare the resource variable as final inside the parentheses
Use a finally block to close the resource a second time
Specify IOException in its throws clause, since close can throw it
optionExplain: The compiler still sees the close call that can throw.
Declaring something final does not affect exceptions.
The statement already closes it; a second close is not the cure.
Right: the implicit close call is covered by Catch or Specify like any other call.
questions.explain: Closing can fail, so a checked exception from close must be caught or specified.
questions.rule: Close can throw too.
questions.teaches: The automatic close can throw its declared checked exception, so the enclosing method must catch or specify that exception.

questions.q: A BufferedReader named br wraps a FileReader named fr, and fr is declared first. Why is the reverse closing order, br first, a sensible fit?
options: Readers must be closed in alphabetical order of their variable names
The wrapper closes before what it wraps, since it was created last
The runtime system picks the closing order at random each time
Closing fr first would also close br at the very same moment
optionExplain: No alphabetical rule exists.
Right: closing the outer layer first mirrors how the layers were built.
The order is fixed by declaration, not random.
Nothing in the rules says one closes the other.
questions.explain: Reverse order undoes the setup like unwrapping layers: the last built is the first taken apart.
questions.rule: Last opened, first closed.
questions.teaches: Reverse closing order means a wrapper resource is closed before the resource it wraps, undoing the construction in reverse.

questions.q: A body throws exception A. Closing a resource in a finally block throws exception B. Which does the caller receive?
options: A, because it was the first exception to be thrown in the method
Both, packed together into one array that the caller receives
B, because the exception thrown from the finally block replaces A and A is lost
Neither, since the two exceptions cancel each other out
optionExplain: The later exception from finally takes over.
Only one propagates.
Right: with finally-based closing the body's exception is lost.
Exceptions do not cancel each other.
questions.explain: In the finally style the second failure wins. The card next shows what try-with-resources does instead.
questions.rule: In finally, the close exception can replace the body exception.

questions.q: True or false: With try-with-resources, an exception thrown while closing is suppressed when the body also threw.
questions.explain: The body's exception propagates and the close exception is attached to it as suppressed.
questions.rule: The body's exception wins; close exceptions are suppressed.

questions.q: Match each situation with its outcome.
pairs: Body throws and close throws, with a finally-based close
The close exception propagates and the body exception is lost
Body throws and close throws, with try-with-resources
The body exception propagates and the close exception is suppressed
Call getSuppressed on the main exception
questions.explain: The two styles differ in which exception survives, and suppressed ones are read from the main exception.
questions.rule: Try-with-resources keeps the body's exception.

questions.q: In a finally block, br.close() throws and the next line fr.close() is skipped. Why does leaving fr unclosed matter, given that its object will later be garbage collected?
options: Garbage collection frees memory, not the system's hold on the file
Garbage collection runs only when the whole program is ending, so the file stays open
Unclosed readers are not garbage collected at any point of the run
The next call to close would throw an error complaining about fr
optionExplain: Right: the operating system still counts the file as in use.
Collection happens during the run; the issue is what it frees.
The object can be collected; what stays held is the resource.
No later call is implied by the leak.
questions.explain: A leak concerns the operating system resource, which the garbage collector does not release.
questions.rule: The garbage collector frees memory, not files.
questions.teaches: The garbage collector reclaims memory but not operating-system resources, so an unclosed file stays in use even after its object is unreachable.

questions.q: True or false: A try-with-resources body throws exception A and closing the resource throws exception B. The caller receives A, with B attached as a suppressed exception.
questions.explain: The body's exception propagates and the close exception is suppressed, readable with getSuppressed.
questions.rule: Body exception propagates; close exceptions are attached.

questions.q: A support team wants to log every problem, including failures during closing, for a method that uses try-with-resources. Which approach fits?
options: Add a finally block that closes the resource a second time and logs the result
Catch Exception and ignore what it carries
Declare every exception with throws and log nothing
Catch the main exception and read its suppressed ones with getSuppressed
optionExplain: A second close would not reveal the earlier failures.
Ignoring the exception loses the information.
Logging needs a place where the exception is actually caught.
Right: getSuppressed gives the array of close failures attached to the main exception.
questions.explain: The close failures are not lost; they hang on the primary exception until someone reads them.
questions.rule: Read close failures with getSuppressed.
questions.teaches: getSuppressed returns an array of the suppressed Throwable objects, one for each close failure attached to the primary exception.

questions.q: True or false: When the try block completes normally, the finally block is skipped because nothing went wrong.
questions.explain: Finally runs after a normal completion as well. The card next traces both paths.
questions.rule: Finally runs on both paths.

questions.q: Put these steps in order for a try block that throws an exception matched by the first catch block, with a finally block after it.
items: An exception is thrown in the try block
The first matching catch block runs
The finally block runs
Execution continues after the finally block
questions.explain: The throw ends the try block, the matching handler runs, finally runs, and flow continues.
questions.rule: Throw, catch, finally, continue.

questions.q: What does this print? try { print 1; int[] a = new int[2]; a[2] = 5; print 2; } catch (ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException e) { print 3; } finally { print 4; } print 5; (Here print writes its number.) Write the numbers separated by spaces: ____
questions.explain: Trace the exception: statement 2 is skipped, the handler prints 3, finally prints 4, and the code after it continues.
questions.rule: Trace try, then catch, then finally, then what follows.

questions.q: Same code, but the assignment is changed to a[1] = 5, a valid index. Write the numbers it prints, separated by spaces: ____
questions.explain: With no exception the try block runs to its end, the catch block is skipped, finally still runs, and the code after it continues.
questions.rule: No exception: skip catch, still run finally.

questions.q: Same code with a[2] = 5, but the only catch block is for NumberFormatException. What happens in this method?
options: 1 and 5 print, since an exception that no handler here matches is ignored
1 prints, then 4 from finally, and the exception moves up; 5 is skipped
1 prints and the finally block is skipped because no catch block matched
1 and 3 print, since the handler for the other type runs anyway
optionExplain: An unmatched exception is not ignored; it leaves the method.
Right: nothing here matches, so finally runs and the search for a handler goes on in the callers.
Finally runs even when no catch block matches.
The handler is for a different type, so it does not run.
questions.explain: Finally runs on the way out even when no handler in this method fits, and the exception then moves on.
questions.rule: Finally runs even if no catch here matches.
questions.teaches: The finally block runs even when no catch block in the method matches the exception; the exception then continues up the call stack.

questions.q: A student expects the message about closing the writer when the file cannot be created, reasoning that finally runs on every exit. What is wrong with the expectation?
options: Finally does not run after an exception that a catch block has handled, so no message appears
The IOException handler closes the writer first, so finally has nothing left to close
Finally does run, but the writer is still null, so the not-open branch is taken
The writer is closed by the runtime system before the finally block starts
optionExplain: Finally runs after a caught exception.
The handler in the example only reports the problem.
Right: the failure came before the assignment, so there is nothing to close.
The runtime does not close anything on its own.
questions.explain: Finally ran, but the variable it checks was never assigned.
questions.rule: Check what actually exists before you clean it up.

questions.q: A try block opens file A into variable a and then opens file B into variable b. Opening B fails. The finally block closes a and b, each guarded by a null check. Which closes happen?
options: Only a is closed, since b is null and its guard skips it
Both are closed, because finally closes everything that it names
Neither, since an exception skips the finally block entirely
Only b is closed, because the failure involved b
optionExplain: Right: a was assigned before the failure, b was not.
Closing something never created is not possible, hence the guard.
Finally runs after the exception.
b was never opened, so there is nothing to close.
questions.explain: A failure partway through leaves some resources open and others never created, so each needs its own check.
questions.rule: Guard each cleanup step separately.
questions.teaches: A failure partway through the try block leaves some resources open and others never created, so cleanup must check each variable separately.

questions.q: Where does the throws clause go in a method declaration?
options: Before the return type, at the start of the header
After the closing brace of the method body
Inside the parameter list, after the last parameter
After the parameter list, before the opening brace
optionExplain: The return type comes first in the header, then the name.
The body ends at the closing brace; the clause belongs to the header.
Parameters describe inputs, not exceptions.
Right: it sits between the parameter list and the body.
questions.explain: The clause is part of the header, between the parameters and the body. The card next shows when to use it.
questions.rule: The throws clause sits between parameters and body.

questions.q: When a throws clause lists several exceptions, they are separated by ____.
questions.explain: The list is comma-separated.
questions.rule: Comma-separated list after throws.

questions.q: Sort these exceptions by whether a method that does not catch them must list them in its throws clause.

items.t: IOException thrown by a FileWriter constructor
A custom class that extends Exception
IndexOutOfBoundsException from a list lookup
NullPointerException from a null argument
A subclass of RuntimeException

questions.explain: Checked exceptions must be listed. Unchecked ones may be listed for documentation but the compiler does not require it.
questions.rule: Checked: list it. Unchecked: optional.

questions.q: Callers of a method read its header. What is the status of the exceptions in a throws clause for those callers?
options: Comments that the compiler ignores completely when it checks calls
Part of its interface, as much as its parameters and return value are
Private details of the method body that callers cannot depend on
Guesses about what might fail in some future version of the method
optionExplain: The compiler checks them, so they are far from ignorable.
Right: callers must know which exceptions to expect in order to decide how to respond.
Callers depend on them, so they are public, not private.
They are a firm contract, not a guess.
questions.explain: The declared exceptions tell callers what they must be ready to catch or declare.
questions.rule: Declared exceptions are part of the method's contract.
questions.teaches: The exceptions a method can throw are part of its public interface, as much as its parameters and return value.

questions.q: True or false: A method that catches the IOException inside its own try and catch must also declare it in a throws clause.
questions.explain: Once the method catches the exception, the requirement is satisfied by the catch, so no declaration is needed.
questions.rule: Caught here means nothing to declare.

questions.q: A shared utility method reads a file chosen by its caller. One application using it wants to show a dialog if the file is missing, and another wants to write to a log and quit. Which design lets both work?
options: Catch the exception in the utility and show a dialog to the user
Catch the exception in the utility and then quit the whole program
Declare the exception with throws so each caller handles it
Catch the exception in the utility and discard it without a trace
optionExplain: That suits the first application but would force a dialog on the second.
That suits the second application but would shut down the first.
Right: the decision stays with the callers, who know what they need.
Discarding it hides the problem from both.
questions.explain: The utility cannot know every caller's preferred response, so passing the exception up serves all of them.
questions.rule: Declare when callers differ in how they should respond.
questions.teaches: Declaring a checked exception lets different callers handle the same failure in different ways.

questions.q: Which of these may follow the throw keyword?
options: An instance of Throwable or a subclass of it
A text message that describes the problem in plain words
Any object at all, since every object can be thrown
An integer error code
optionExplain: Right: a throwable object is the only kind of argument.
Text can be carried inside an exception object, but is not itself thrown.
Only Throwable objects can be thrown.
A number is not a Throwable.
questions.explain: Throw needs a throwable object. The card next shows how it is used.
questions.rule: Only a Throwable can be thrown.

questions.q: True or false: A throw statement takes exactly one argument.
questions.explain: The argument is a single throwable object.
questions.rule: One throwable object per throw.

questions.q: A method must reject a null name by throwing NullPointerException. Which statement does that correctly?
options: throw NullPointerException;
throws new NullPointerException();
throw 'null name';
throw new NullPointerException();
optionExplain: That names the class, not an object.
Throws belongs in method headers, not as a statement.
Text is not a throwable object.
Right: the keyword throw followed by a newly created object.
questions.explain: Create the exception object with new and throw it in the same statement.
questions.rule: throw followed by new and the class.

questions.q: In a stack's pop method, why is the emptiness check placed before the lines that remove the top item?
options: Because a throw statement has to be the first line of every method
So the failure is reported before the stack has been changed in any way
Because removing an item from an empty stack cannot be written
Because exceptions can only be thrown at the start of a method
optionExplain: A throw can appear anywhere a statement can.
Right: nothing is modified when the check fails, because the throw ends the method first.
It could be written; it would just misbehave.
Exceptions may be thrown from the middle of a method too, as the condition shows.
questions.explain: Guarding first keeps the object consistent: a failed call leaves the stack as it was.
questions.rule: Check first, change second.
questions.teaches: Checking the condition and throwing before any change is made leaves the object in its earlier state when the call fails.

questions.q: If pop threw a checked exception instead of the unchecked EmptyStackException, the method would need a ____ clause or a catch block.
questions.explain: A checked exception that is not caught must be specified with a throws clause.
questions.rule: Checked and not caught means declare it.

questions.q: A ticket machine method contains if (stock == 0) { throw new SoldOutException(); }. SoldOutException extends Exception, and the method has no throws clause and no try. What happens?
options: It compiles, since the programmer wrote the throw deliberately and knows the risk
It compiles, and the machine ignores the exception when it is thrown
A compile error, since the checked exception is neither caught nor specified
It compiles, but only when the variable stock is declared as final
optionExplain: Deliberate throws are still subject to the requirement.
Exceptions are not ignored at run time, and the question is about compile time.
Right: the throw is a place where Catch or Specify applies.
The kind of variable has nothing to do with it.
questions.explain: Writing the throw yourself does not exempt it. A checked exception needs a catch or a throws clause.
questions.rule: A checked throw needs a catch or a throws clause.
questions.teaches: A throw statement for a checked exception is itself subject to Catch or Specify, even when you wrote it deliberately.

questions.q: Which class is the direct parent of both Error and Exception?
options: Throwable
RuntimeException
Closeable
Exception
optionExplain: Right: both branches begin directly under Throwable.
RuntimeException is below Exception, not above Error.
Closeable concerns resources, not exceptions.
Exception is a sibling of Error, not their parent.
questions.explain: There is one common root for everything throwable. The card next draws the tree.
questions.rule: Throwable is the root of the family.

questions.q: Match each branch with what it stands for.
pairs: Serious failures in the JVM, such as a linking failure
Problems that are not serious system failures and that programs handle
Incorrect use of an API, such as dereferencing null
questions.explain: Error is the hard failure branch; Exception is the handled-problem branch; RuntimeException marks API misuse inside Exception.
questions.rule: Three branches, three meanings.

questions.q: Arrange these classes from the most general to the most specific.
items: Throwable
Exception
RuntimeException
NullPointerException
questions.explain: Throwable is the root, Exception is one branch, RuntimeException is within it, and NullPointerException is a particular runtime exception.
questions.rule: General above specific.

questions.q: An application needs to signal that a user's uploaded file is malformed. Which branch is the normal home for such an exception?
options: Error, since a malformed file is a broken input that the program cannot repair
Throwable itself, so that anything can catch it
RuntimeException, since every bad input is an API misuse
Exception, since applications normally throw Exception objects
optionExplain: Error stands for hard system failures such as one that stops the JVM.
Throwable itself is not the tutorial's choice for application problems.
The tutorial advises against subclassing RuntimeException in most applications.
Right: Error is reserved for serious system failures, not for this.
questions.explain: A malformed file is a problem the application can reasonably handle, so it belongs under Exception.
questions.rule: Application problems belong under Exception, not Error.
questions.teaches: Applications normally throw Exception objects; Error is reserved for serious system failures such as one that prevents the JVM from running.

questions.q: True or false: If a class extends RuntimeException, a method that throws it must catch it or list it in a throws clause.
questions.explain: RuntimeException classes are unchecked, so the compiler does not require either.
questions.rule: RuntimeException branch means unchecked.

questions.q: A library defines class DiskFullException extends IOException. Is DiskFullException checked or unchecked?
options: Unchecked, because the name suggests a hardware problem on the machine
Checked, since IOException is under Exception, not RuntimeException
