Unchecked, because new classes start as unchecked
Neither, because it has to extend Throwable directly
optionExplain: The name does not decide it; ancestry does.
Right: a subclass takes the checked status of its ancestry.
No such default exists.
Any descendant of Throwable can be thrown; a direct child is not required.
questions.explain: IOException is a checked exception, so its subclasses are checked as well, unless they also fall under RuntimeException or Error.
questions.rule: Check the ancestry, not the name.
questions.teaches: A subclass inherits the checked status of its ancestry, so a new subclass of a checked exception is itself checked.

questions.q: A handler catches an IOException and throws a new exception of a different class. What keeps the original reachable for later handlers?
options: Nothing, since the original is always passed along automatically
Calling getStackTrace on the new exception
Passing the original to the new exception as its cause
Catching the new exception in the same method
optionExplain: Nothing links them unless the code does.
The trace shows calls, not the earlier exception.
Right: the cause link is how the original stays attached.
Where it is caught does not create the link.
questions.explain: The link must be created on purpose. The card next shows how.
questions.rule: The cause must be passed on purpose.

questions.q: Match each Throwable member with its purpose.
pairs: Returns the exception that caused this one
Sets the cause of an exception
Returns an array of frames describing the call history
Creates an exception that carries both
questions.explain: The four members cover reading, setting and creating a cause, plus access to the call history.
questions.rule: Cause: get, set, or pass at creation.

questions.q: A higher-level handler holds a ReportException and wants the IOException that caused it. It calls the ____ method on the ReportException.
questions.explain: getCause returns the exception recorded as the cause of the current one.
questions.rule: getCause reads the link.

questions.q: A team wants trace information written to a file rather than to the screen. Which tool does the tutorial show for this?
options: The logging API, using a file handler for the records
Calling getCause repeatedly until it returns the file
Rethrowing the exception from the main method of the program
Catching Error instead of Exception in every handler
optionExplain: Right: the tutorial's example sends diagnostic output to a file through the logging facilities.
getCause follows exception links, not output destinations.
Rethrowing from main does not write anything.
The exception branch has no effect on where output goes.
questions.explain: The logging classes can attach a file handler, so each frame of a trace can be recorded persistently.
questions.rule: Logging can send trace output to a file.
questions.teaches: The java.util.logging classes can send stack trace information to a file through a file handler instead of printing it to the screen.

questions.q: True or false: If a new exception is created with the original as its cause, the original is lost once the new one is thrown.
questions.explain: The original stays reachable through getCause, which is the point of chaining.
questions.rule: Chained exceptions keep the original reachable.

questions.q: A support agent re-files a customer's ticket under a new number but forgets to link the old ticket. Which mistake in Java does this match?
options: Catching an exception with the wrong parameter type in the catch block
Declaring an exception in a throws clause that is never thrown
Closing a resource twice in the same cleanup block
Throwing a new exception without the original as its cause
optionExplain: That sends the exception to the wrong handler, a different slip.
That adds noise, but does not lose the earlier story.
That concerns cleanup, not tracing a cause.
Right: the next person sees the new problem but cannot find the one that led to it.
questions.explain: Without the link, the information about what really failed is lost to everyone downstream.
questions.rule: Keep the link to the earlier problem.
questions.teaches: Without a cause link, the information about the original failure is not available to the handler that receives the new exception.

questions.q: A library can fail in three related ways, and its authors want callers to be able to catch all three with one handler. What helps most?
options: Three unrelated exception classes, one for each failure
A common base class for the three exceptions
Making each of them a subclass of Error
Putting each failure in a different package
optionExplain: Unrelated classes need three handlers.
Right: a handler for the base type accepts every subclass.
Error is for serious system failures, and it would not help grouping.
Separating packages does not group them.
questions.explain: A shared parent lets one handler cover the family. The card next gives the full guidance.
questions.rule: A common base class groups related exceptions.

questions.q: True or false: The tutorial advises ending the name of every class that inherits from Exception with the word Exception.
questions.explain: The suffix makes code easier to read, and it applies to direct and indirect subclasses.
questions.rule: Name subclasses of Exception ending in Exception.

questions.q: Which situations favor writing your own exception class, according to the tutorial's questions? Select all that apply.
options: The platform has no exception type that represents the failure
Users of your package would gain from telling your exceptions from other vendors' exceptions
Your code throws several related exceptions that callers may want to catch together
An existing platform class already describes the failure and users can reach it
optionExplain: Right: a missing type is a reason to write one.
Right: distinguishing yours from others' is a reason.
Right: related exceptions share a base class.
With an existing, reachable class that fits, reuse it.
questions.explain: Any yes to the four questions justifies a new class. A fitting, reachable platform class points the other way.
questions.rule: One yes is enough to write your own.

questions.q: True or false: For a new failure condition, the tutorial's four questions are all answered no. They ask about a type the platform lacks, telling your exceptions apart from other vendors' exceptions, several related exceptions, and a self-contained package. In that case the tutorial suggests using an existing exception class.
questions.explain: With no reason to write a new class, reuse the platform's.
questions.rule: No to all four means reuse.

questions.q: Why does the tutorial make LinkedListException extend Exception, rather than a specialized platform class such as IOException?
options: Specialized classes cannot have subclasses of their own
Only Exception has a constructor that takes a message
The other candidates were too specialized or unrelated
IOException is unchecked and so it cannot be extended
optionExplain: Specialized classes can have subclasses.
Other classes can carry messages too.
Right: Exception is the nearest class that fits without implying a different kind of problem.
IOException is checked and can be extended.
questions.explain: A parent should fit what its children represent. A specialized parent would suggest, for example, an I/O problem where there is none.
questions.rule: Choose a parent that fits all its children.
questions.teaches: A new base exception should extend the nearest platform class that fits all its children; specialized or unrelated classes would misdescribe the failures.

questions.q: A payments package defines a class for a declined card that extends Exception. By the tutorial's convention, its name should be DeclinedCard followed by the word ____.
questions.explain: Every class inheriting from Exception, directly or indirectly, ends its name with Exception.
questions.rule: The name ends in Exception.
questions.teaches: The naming suffix applies to every class that inherits from Exception, directly or indirectly, whatever domain the class serves.

questions.q: According to the tutorial, how should the choice between checked and unchecked be made for a new exception?
options: By whether a client can reasonably recover from it
By whether the author wants to avoid writing throws clauses
By how often the exception is likely to occur
By whether the exception comes from the Java runtime
optionExplain: Right: recoverable means checked, not recoverable means unchecked.
The tutorial warns against exactly that motive.
Frequency plays no role in the rule.
Origin does not decide it; recoverability does.
questions.explain: The test is about what the caller can do. The card next gives the full argument.
questions.rule: Recoverable means checked.

questions.q: True or false: According to the tutorial, making all of your exception classes extend RuntimeException is a good way to spare the users of your classes extra work.
questions.explain: The tutorial says this sidesteps the intent of the requirement and can cause problems for the people who use your classes.
questions.rule: Do not choose unchecked to avoid declarations.

questions.q: Using the tutorial's rule, sort these failures by the kind of exception that fits.

items.t: A caller can retry with another file name
A caller can fall back to default settings when a file is missing
A caller can prompt the user again after bad input
A caller passes null for a required argument
A caller reads past the end of a list because of a logic error
A caller divides by zero because of a flaw in its own logic

questions.explain: Where the caller has a sensible recovery, the exception is checked. Where only a bug fix helps, it is unchecked.
questions.rule: Recovery possible: checked. Only a fix helps: unchecked.

questions.q: A library author lists a runtime exception in a throws clause even though no one requires it. Is that allowed?
options: No, the compiler rejects any unchecked exception in a throws clause
No, a throws clause may only hold exceptions from the java.io package
Yes, but only if the exception is first wrapped in a checked one
Yes, listing it is allowed and can document it, though the compiler does not require it
optionExplain: The compiler allows it.
The clause may name any exception.
Wrapping is not required.
Right: the compiler does not demand it, and the author may still include it.
questions.explain: Not being required to catch or declare an unchecked exception does not forbid doing so.
questions.rule: Unchecked exceptions may be caught or declared, but need not be.
questions.teaches: Runtime exceptions may still be caught or listed in throws clauses voluntarily; the compiler just does not require it.

questions.q: A recoverable condition, such as a taken seat on a booking page, is made an unchecked exception so that nobody has to write throws. What is the likely effect on the people who call the method?
options: They gain a guarantee that the exception cannot occur in any of their calls
The compiler will not remind them to handle it, so they may not notice
They are forced to catch it at the very first call they write
The exception can no longer be caught by any handler
optionExplain: Hiding it from the signature does not prevent it.
Right: the duty has moved to them without a warning.
Unchecked exceptions are not forced on callers.
Unchecked exceptions can still be caught.
questions.explain: A checked exception shows up in the signature and forces a decision. Hiding it removes both.
questions.rule: Unchecked hides the exception from the signature.

questions.q: A booking package defines SeatTakenException extends RuntimeException. Customers can pick another seat when it is thrown. What does the tutorial's reasoning say about this choice?
options: It is correct, because every exception in a booking system is a programming error
It is correct, because unchecked exceptions are always faster
It is questionable, since a recoverable condition was made unchecked
It is required, because custom classes must extend RuntimeException
optionExplain: A taken seat is not a bug; the customer can recover.
Speed is not part of the tutorial's rule.
Right: callers are not prompted to handle a failure they could recover from.
Nothing forces custom classes to extend RuntimeException.
questions.explain: Recoverable means checked by the rule. Choosing unchecked to avoid declarations makes the package's users pay.
questions.rule: Recoverable failures belong in checked exceptions.
questions.teaches: Choosing unchecked to avoid declaring shifts the cost from the author of a method to everyone who calls it.

questions.q: A five-step file-reading method needs a failure check after each step. What is the main difficulty when the checks are written as nested error-code tests?
options: The few lines of real work are buried in checks
The checks make each step run in a different thread
The checks cannot detect failures in the first step
The checks make memory allocation impossible
optionExplain: Right: the main logic is hard to see.
Nesting does not change threads.
They can detect it; they just clutter the code.
Allocation still works; the code is simply harder to read.
questions.explain: Checks interleaved with work hide the work. The card next shows the alternative.
questions.rule: Checks nested around work bury the work.

questions.q: True or false: According to the tutorial, exceptions remove the need to detect and handle errors.
questions.explain: The tutorial says they do not remove that work; they only help you organize it.
questions.rule: Exceptions organize error work; they do not remove it.

questions.q: Match each style with its description.
pairs: A check after every step, nested around the real work
Main steps together in a try block with separate catch blocks
Someone must still decide how to respond to each failure
questions.explain: The two styles lay the same duties out differently, and neither removes the need to respond.
questions.rule: Same duties, different layout.

questions.q: Some programmers skip the error-code checks because they clutter the code. What does the tutorial say this leads to?
options: Programs that run faster and carry no extra risk at all
Programs that handle errors by themselves
Programs that cannot be compiled
Programs that crash, since failures go unhandled
optionExplain: Skipping checks adds risk and the tutorial does not describe a speed benefit.
Errors do not handle themselves.
The code compiles; the problem shows at run time.
Right: skipped checks leave errors unhandled, which can bring the program down.
questions.explain: Clutter tempts people to drop checks, and the dropped checks hide failures. Exceptions give an organized way to keep them.
questions.rule: Skipped checks lead to crashes.
questions.teaches: When error-code checks are skipped to avoid clutter, failures go unhandled and programs can crash, which is a reason to prefer exceptions.

questions.q: True or false: If a sixth step is added to the file-reading method written with exceptions, the normal flow can stay in the same try block and only a new catch block may be needed.
questions.explain: The normal path stays in order, and the error handling for the new step is added in its own catch block.
questions.rule: New step: new line in try, maybe a new catch.

questions.q: A recipe lists its steps in order, and a troubleshooting section after the recipe covers what to do if the sauce splits or the oven fails. Which part of a Java method does the troubleshooting section resemble?
options: The try block, which holds the main steps of the work
The catch blocks, which hold the responses apart from the main steps
The throws clause, which names the exceptions in the method header line
The finally block, which runs after each step of the work
optionExplain: The main steps correspond to the try block.
Right: the failures are handled in one place rather than between the steps.
The throws clause lists exceptions; it does not hold responses.
Finally runs once at the end, not for specific failures.
questions.explain: Handlers can live apart from the steps they protect, because an exception carries control to them.
questions.rule: Handlers sit apart from the steps.
questions.teaches: Because an exception carries control to its handler, the handler can be written apart from the failing step instead of between steps.

questions.q: Method a calls b, b calls c, and c fails. Only a can decide what to do. With exceptions, what must b do?
options: Check an error code that c returned and pass that code on to a
Catch the exception and restart c
Nothing beyond declaring the exception, if it is checked
Terminate the program
optionExplain: That is the error-code style that exceptions replace.
A restart is not part of the model.
Right: b ducks the exception and a handles it.
The program ends only if no handler is found.
questions.explain: Middle methods may just let the exception pass. The card next shows how.
questions.rule: Middle methods only duck.

questions.q: Put these events in order as a checked exception travels up the chain.
items: readFile throws an exception
method3 passes it up without handling it
method2 passes it up without handling it
method1's handler catches it
questions.explain: The exception moves backward through the callers until it reaches a method with a matching handler.
questions.rule: The exception climbs to the method that handles it.

questions.q: A method named middle calls a method that declares throws IOException, and middle itself has no try and no catch. What must the header of middle say so that it compiles?
options: It must declare throws IOException
Nothing, since the exception is handled somewhere above
It must declare throws RuntimeException
It must be declared final
optionExplain: Right: middle ducks the exception by declaring it.
The compiler checks each method, not the whole chain.
That would not cover IOException.
Final concerns overriding, not exceptions.
questions.explain: Each method must itself catch or specify a checked exception that passes through it.
questions.rule: Each middle method declares what passes through.

questions.q: True or false: If the exception were a runtime exception, method2 and method3 would still have to list it in their throws clauses.
questions.explain: Unchecked exceptions need no declaration, so the middle methods would not have to list it.
questions.rule: Unchecked passes through without declarations.

questions.q: method2 wants to report a higher-level failure to method1 but keep the details of what went wrong in readFile. What can it do?
options: Catch it and print nothing at all, so that method1 never hears of it
Declare the exception and also catch it, so as to do both
Replace it with an error code returned by method2 to method1
Catch it and throw a new one that has the original as its cause
optionExplain: That would hide the failure.
Doing both is not meaningful; a method either lets it pass or takes control.
Error codes are the style exceptions replace.
Right: chaining lets it translate the error without losing the story.
questions.explain: A middle method is free to catch and rethrow a different exception, and chaining preserves the original.
questions.rule: Middle methods can translate errors and keep the cause.
questions.teaches: A method in the middle of a chain may catch an exception and throw a different one with the original attached as its cause.

questions.q: A field worker finds a safety problem. Only the safety officer decides what to do, and the worker's supervisor and the supervisor's manager pass the report along. What cost to the managers matches the throws clauses in Java?
options: They must investigate the safety problem themselves before reporting
Each must formally pass the report along without acting on it
They must each keep a private copy of the report
They must each change the report's wording before passing it on
optionExplain: That would be handling it, not passing it.
Right: the middle methods carry the exception in their declarations.
No copy is needed; the same exception object is passed along.
Changing the report is not part of passing it along.
questions.explain: The cost of ducking is the declaration: the middle methods must mention the exception even when they do nothing else with it.
questions.rule: Passing along costs a declaration.
questions.teaches: Methods that only pass a checked exception along still carry it in their declarations, so their own callers must handle or declare it as well.

questions.q: A handler is written for IOException. Which of these thrown objects will it receive?
options: Only an object of exactly the class IOException and no other
Only objects whose message contains the word file
A FileNotFoundException, because it is a subclass of IOException
Nothing, since handlers cannot take library classes
optionExplain: A superclass handler also accepts subclass objects.
Messages play no role in matching.
Right: a handler for a general type receives the subclasses too.
Library classes are ordinary types for handlers.
questions.explain: Handlers receive a whole family at once. The card next shows what that gives you.
questions.rule: A general handler receives its subclasses.

questions.q: Sort these handlers by whether they catch one specific case or a group of cases.

items.t: A handler for FileNotFoundException, which has no subclasses
A handler for IOException
A handler for Exception
A handler for a superclass of several I/O exceptions

questions.explain: A class with no subclasses catches just itself. A class with subclasses catches the whole family.
questions.rule: Superclass handler means group.

questions.q: A program reads a file the user chose. If it is missing, the program should ask for another name. For any other I/O trouble it should print a message and stop. Which handlers, in order, fit?
options: FileNotFoundException to ask again, then IOException to report and stop
IOException first and then FileNotFoundException placed after it as a second block
Exception only, asking again whatever the failure turns out to be
FileNotFoundException only, ignoring every other I/O problem
optionExplain: Right: the narrow handler comes first for the special response, the group handler after it for the rest.
The group handler first would take the missing-file case too.
That treats every failure as a missing file.
Other I/O trouble would be left unhandled.
questions.explain: Use the specific type for the special response and the group type for the remainder, with the specific one first.
questions.rule: Specific first, group after.

questions.q: A handler for IOException calls printStackTrace on the exception. Where does the trace go by default, and how can it go elsewhere?
options: To a file named after the exception class, and to no other destination
To the user's screen only, with no option to redirect it to another stream
To the caller of the method, as a returned value
To standard error by default, or standard output if System.out is passed
optionExplain: No such file is chosen automatically.
The tutorial's example shows a way to send it to System.out.
printStackTrace prints; it does not return anything.
Right: the plain call writes to System.err, and a call that is given System.out writes there instead.
questions.explain: The inspection tool writes a trace for the programmer, and a stream argument chooses the destination.
questions.rule: printStackTrace(System.out) changes the destination.
questions.teaches: printStackTrace writes to the standard error stream by default, and passing System.out sends the trace to standard output instead.

questions.q: True or false: A handler for Exception around a block of code also catches a runtime exception that nobody anticipated.
questions.explain: Exception sits high in the hierarchy and accepts runtime exceptions too, which is why such a handler is discouraged outside simple report-and-exit cases.
questions.rule: A catch of Exception receives unplanned problems too.

questions.q: A web page shows the same apology for any of five related failures that all extend one parent class. Which handler fits best, according to the tutorial's guidance?
options: Five separate handlers, one per class, each with the same apology
A handler for the common parent, since all five are handled in the same way
A handler for Exception, to be sure nothing is missed
A handler for Throwable, so errors are included too
optionExplain: That repeats the same code without a reason.
Right: when every member of a group gets the same response, a group type fits.
That would also catch unrelated problems.
That is even broader and would include serious system failures.
questions.explain: Choose a group type when all its members need the same treatment and nothing unrelated falls under it.
questions.rule: A shared response fits a shared parent.
questions.teaches: A group type fits when all of its members are handled the same way, because one handler on the common parent then covers them all.

questions.q: A text editor runs a spell checker in the background. Which setup lets the checker read the editor's in-memory document most directly?
options: The checker is a separate process that reads the editor's memory
No setup can do it, because documents cannot be seen by two activities
The checker is a process on another machine linked by a socket
The checker is a thread inside the editor's own process, sharing its memory
optionExplain: Each process has its own private memory space, so a separate process cannot simply read it.
Threads in one process do see the same objects; that is what makes sharing efficient.
A socket carries messages between systems; it does not give shared access to memory.
Threads of one process share its memory, so the document object is directly visible to both.
questions.explain: Threads inside one process share its memory and files, while separate processes keep private memory and need IPC. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: A process has private memory and talks to other processes through IPC, while the threads inside one process share its memory and files.

questions.q: True or false: Every process contains at least one thread.
questions.explain: The tutorial says threads exist within a process and every process has at least one.
questions.rule: A process has private memory and talks to other processes through IPC, while the threads inside one process share its memory and files.

questions.q: Two programs on one computer must exchange a large result. Each program runs as its own process. What does the tutorial name as the way they communicate?
options: Reading each other's variables, since both run on the same computer
Sharing the process's memory the way threads do
Creating a thread in each, which then shares the two memory spaces
Inter-process communication, for example through pipes or sockets
optionExplain: Private memory spaces mean one process cannot read the other's variables directly.
Two processes by definition do not share one memory space; threads inside one process do.
Threads share the memory of their own process only; they do not merge two processes' memory.
IPC is the tutorial's name for communication between processes, on one system or across systems.
questions.explain: Separate processes have private memory, so they need an explicit channel such as a pipe or a socket.
questions.rule: A process has private memory and talks to other processes through IPC, while the threads inside one process share its memory and files.

questions.q: A Java program needs to run an external converter that must have its own memory space. Which tool does the tutorial name for creating another process?
options: A new Thread object with its own memory space
The sleep method on the main thread
A Runnable passed to the main thread
A ProcessBuilder object, which creates and starts a new process
optionExplain: A Thread lives inside a process and shares that process's memory.
Sleep pauses a thread; it creates no process.
A Runnable is a task for a thread, not a process.
The tutorial names ProcessBuilder for creating processes, though it calls multiprocess applications beyond its scope.
questions.explain: Processes, unlike threads, are created through a ProcessBuilder.
questions.teaches: Most Java Virtual Machines run as a single process, and a Java application can create further processes with a ProcessBuilder object, which the tutorial treats as beyond its scope.
questions.rule: A process has private memory and talks to other processes through IPC, while the threads inside one process share its memory and files.

questions.q: A game has a download manager and a renderer. Sort each situation by what it describes.

items.t: A loader and a renderer both update one shared list of textures
A launcher and a game each have their own memory and talk through a pipe
Two workers read the same open file handle owned by the program
A server on one machine and a client on another exchange data over a socket
A background timer and the main loop see the same score variable

questions.explain: Sharing memory and open files marks threads within a process; a pipe or socket marks communication between processes.
questions.teaches: Sharing is decided by where the activities live: inside one process they share everything of that process, across processes they share nothing unless a channel carries data.
questions.rule: A process has private memory and talks to other processes through IPC, while the threads inside one process share its memory and files.

questions.q: True or false: If a thread and the activity it shares data with were moved into two separate processes, one could no longer change the other's variables directly.
questions.explain: Separate processes have private memory spaces, so they would need IPC to exchange data; threads of one process share memory.
questions.rule: Shared memory belongs to threads of one process, not to separate processes.

questions.q: One core, three programs: a browser, a music player and a download all seem to progress together. What best explains this?
options: The core divides itself into three smaller cores for the moment
Each program is quietly moved onto a different computer
Two of them are frozen until the third one finishes completely
The operating system rotates short turns among them, switching quickly
optionExplain: A core is physical hardware; the operating system does not split it, it shares its time.
Nothing moves to another machine; the one processor is shared.
Frozen programs would not seem to progress; slicing keeps all of them moving.
Time slicing shares one core's time among many threads, switching quickly.
questions.explain: The operating system shares one core among many threads by time slicing. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: Time slicing lets one core share its time among many threads, and every Java program begins with the main thread.

questions.q: True or false: A computer needs several processors or cores before it can run more than one thread concurrently.
questions.explain: Concurrency is possible on a single core through time slicing; extra cores only let more threads run at the same instant.
questions.rule: Time slicing lets one core share its time among many threads, and every Java program begins with the main thread.

questions.q: On a machine with one core, the operating system shares processor time among threads using a technique called time ____.
questions.explain: The technique is time slicing: each thread gets a short turn.
questions.rule: Time slicing lets one core share its time among many threads, and every Java program begins with the main thread.

questions.q: A program's own code creates no threads except main. Which statement about its threads does the tutorial support?
options: The application's threads are all created by the user pressing keys
The application has exactly one thread, so it cannot be doing anything concurrently
The application has no thread at all until the program calls start
It also has system threads doing housekeeping tasks, in addition to its main thread and any it creates
optionExplain: Threads are created by the program and the system, not by user keystrokes.
System threads exist beside main, so more than one thread is normally alive.
Every application begins with at least the main thread; start is for further threads.
The tutorial notes that Java applications have system threads in addition to the programmer's main thread.
questions.explain: Besides main, system threads run housekeeping tasks.
questions.teaches: Even a program that creates no threads of its own has system threads running tasks such as memory management and signal handling.
questions.rule: Time slicing lets one core share its time among many threads, and every Java program begins with the main thread.

questions.q: A kitchen has one cook (one core) preparing soup, bread and a salad by working a few minutes on each in turn. In this lesson's terms, what does the cook's rotation resemble?
options: Three cores running three threads at the same instant
Three separate processes, each with private kitchens
Time slicing on a single core, sharing its time among the tasks
A deadlock, because no dish ever finishes first
optionExplain: There is one cook, so only one dish is worked at a time; that is not simultaneous execution.
All dishes share one kitchen and one cook; no private environments exist.
Each dish gets short turns, so all progress, though only one is worked at any instant.
Dishes finish normally; rotating turns is not a permanent blockage.
questions.explain: One worker rotating among tasks is time slicing; several workers at once is multiple cores.
questions.teaches: Progress on several tasks at once need not mean simultaneous work: it can be one worker alternating quickly.
questions.rule: Time slicing lets one core share its time among many threads, and every Java program begins with the main thread.

questions.q: The same program with three busy threads is run first on one core and then on three cores. What does the tutorial's account lead you to expect?
options: Both runs are identical, since the threads share the same time slices
The program fails on one core because concurrency needs several cores
Only the main thread runs on three cores; the others wait
Up to three run at once on three cores, one at a time on one core
optionExplain: Time slicing explains the single core; extra cores add real parallel execution.
Concurrency works on one core through time slicing.
Nothing in the account limits extra cores to the main thread.
Multiple cores allow more threads to run simultaneously, and a single core runs one at an instant.
questions.explain: More cores allow more threads to execute simultaneously.
questions.rule: Time slicing lets one core share its time among many threads, and every Java program begins with the main thread.

questions.q: You want some code to run on a new thread. Which sequence gets it running there?
options: Pass the class to sleep so that it runs after a pause
Put the code in a run method and call join on a new Thread
Mark the class synchronized so that it runs on its own thread
Put it in a run method, wrap that in a Thread, and call start
optionExplain: Sleep pauses the calling thread; it does not run a task elsewhere.
Join makes the caller wait for a thread to finish; it does not launch anything.
Synchronized controls access to an object; it does not create threads.
Start is the call that launches the thread, which then executes run.
questions.explain: A Runnable supplies run, and Thread.start launches it on a new thread. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: Put the task in a Runnable, hand it to a Thread, and call start so that the new thread executes run.

questions.q: The Runnable interface declares a single method, which holds the thread's code and is named ____.
questions.explain: The one method of Runnable is run.
questions.rule: Put the task in a Runnable, hand it to a Thread, and call start so that the new thread executes run.

questions.q: Put the steps for running a task on its own thread in order.
items: Write a class implementing Runnable with the task in run
Create an instance of that class
Pass the instance to the Thread constructor
Call start on the Thread
questions.explain: The task is written first, wrapped in a Thread, and only start launches it.
questions.rule: Put the task in a Runnable, hand it to a Thread, and call start so that the new thread executes run.

questions.q: According to the tutorial, how do Thread's static methods differ from its instance methods?
options: Static methods affect every thread at once; instance methods affect only main
Static methods work before start; instance methods only after it
Static ones concern the calling thread; instance ones manage a given Thread
Static methods run on a new thread; instance methods run on the caller
optionExplain: Static methods concern the calling thread, not all threads.
The tutorial draws no before-or-after-start distinction.
The tutorial draws exactly this line, which later matters for sleep and interrupt.
Neither kind of method creates a thread by itself.
questions.explain: Static: about the caller. Instance: managing a particular Thread object.
questions.teaches: Thread has static methods that act on the thread invoking them and instance methods that other threads invoke to manage a given Thread object.
questions.rule: Put the task in a Runnable, hand it to a Thread, and call start so that the new thread executes run.

questions.q: A shop wants the same cleaning task run by three threads at once. How does keeping the task in a separate Runnable help?
options: Runnable makes the three threads share one processor core
Runnable guarantees the three threads cannot interfere with each other
The task must be copied into three new classes, one for each thread
One Runnable can be handed to several Thread objects, so each runs the same task code
optionExplain: Runnable has nothing to do with how cores are shared.
Separate objects do not protect shared data; interference comes up later.
No copying is needed; the same class can be given to several Threads.
Separating the task from the thread is the flexibility the tutorial points to.
questions.explain: A task object is independent of the thread that runs it.
questions.teaches: Because the task is separate from the thread, one task class can be handed to several Thread objects, each started on its own.
questions.rule: Put the task in a Runnable, hand it to a Thread, and call start so that the new thread executes run.

questions.q: main builds a Thread from a Runnable whose run prints a line, then main ends without ever calling start on that thread. What does the tutorial's account predict?
options: The line is printed once, as soon as the Thread is created
The line is printed when main ends, as a final step
Never: construction only creates the Thread object, and the task runs once start is called
The line is printed twice, once by each thread
optionExplain: Creating the Thread does not execute the task.
Nothing in the account runs the task at the end of main.
Construction creates the Thread object; start is what makes a new thread execute run.
Without start there is no second thread to print.
questions.explain: No start, no new thread, no run.
questions.rule: Put the task in a Runnable, hand it to a Thread, and call start so that the new thread executes run.

questions.q: A class Beeper extends Thread and overrides run. Which call starts a new thread that executes that run?
options: Declaring the Beeper class final
Creating a Beeper object and calling join on it
Creating a Beeper object and passing it to sleep
Creating a Beeper object and calling start on it
optionExplain: Final prevents subclassing; it has no bearing on starting threads.
Join waits for a thread to finish; it does not launch one.
Sleep pauses the calling thread and does not start another.
Start is the call that launches the thread; it then executes run.
questions.explain: Both idioms start threads with start. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: Subclassing Thread works for simple cases, but Runnable is more general because the task stays free to extend another class.

questions.q: True or false: In the Thread-subclass idiom, threads are started with start, the same call as in the Runnable idiom.
questions.explain: Both idioms use Thread.start; the new thread then executes run.
questions.rule: Subclassing Thread works for simple cases, but Runnable is more general because the task stays free to extend another class.

questions.q: A class InvoiceMailer already extends a class Mailer, and its main work must run on a thread. Which idiom can it use?
options: Extend Thread as well, listing both classes after extends
Copy Mailer into Thread so that both are one class
Neither idiom, because a class with a superclass cannot run on a thread
Implement Runnable, since a Runnable class may extend another class
optionExplain: A class cannot also descend from Thread while descending from Mailer; the tutorial notes the task class must descend from Thread.
Nothing in the tutorial suggests rewriting the class hierarchy.
The Runnable idiom exists exactly for classes that extend something else.
The Runnable idiom leaves the task free to have its own superclass.
questions.explain: Runnable keeps the superclass slot free.
questions.rule: Subclassing Thread works for simple cases, but Runnable is more general because the task stays free to extend another class.

questions.q: Beyond the tutorial: Thread implements Runnable, so a Thread object can be passed to the constructor of another Thread. What does that make possible?
options: Two threads that share one stack for their local variables
Automatic joining of the inner thread by the outer one
A guarantee that the inner thread starts first
A Thread object used as the task of the outer thread, whose run it executes
optionExplain: Threads never share a stack; nothing in the idiom changes that.
No waiting is arranged just by nesting objects.
Nesting gives no ordering guarantee.
A Thread object can fill the Runnable slot, but it only becomes a thread of its own if its own start is called.
questions.explain: Because Thread implements Runnable, it can be used wherever a Runnable is accepted.
questions.teaches: Beyond the tutorial: since Thread implements Runnable, a Thread object can be passed wherever a Runnable is expected, and then only its run is used as a task.
questions.rule: Subclassing Thread works for simple cases, but Runnable is more general because the task stays free to extend another class.

questions.q: A team wrote forty small tasks as subclasses of Thread. They now want a pool of reusable worker threads to run the tasks. Why would Runnable have made this move easier?
options: A Runnable makes the pool unnecessary
Runnable tasks start themselves without any thread at all
Subclasses of Thread cannot override run
A Runnable is only a task, so a worker thread can run it
optionExplain: Pools and Runnables serve different purposes; one runs the other.
A Runnable still needs a thread to run in; the executor supplies one.
They can; that is the whole idiom.
The executor material later shows tasks given to executors as Runnable objects, because the task is separate from the thread.
questions.explain: Separating the task from the thread lets something else decide which thread runs it.
questions.teaches: A task written as a Runnable can later be handed to an executor and run by whatever worker thread it chooses, because the task is not tied to one Thread object.
questions.rule: Subclassing Thread works for simple cases, but Runnable is more general because the task stays free to extend another class.

questions.q: A student summarises the two idioms. Which statements are wrong according to the tutorial? Select all that apply.
options: Both idioms start a thread by calling start
Thread's own run method already does useful work, so subclasses need not override it
A class that extends Thread can also extend a second class
The lesson prefers Runnable because it separates the task from the thread
optionExplain: Correct: this is true of both idioms.
Wrong: Thread's run does nothing, so the subclass supplies the work.
Wrong: the task class must descend from Thread, which blocks a different superclass.
Correct: this is the stated reason for preferring it.
questions.explain: Statements two and three contradict the tutorial: Thread's run is empty and the task class is tied to Thread.
questions.rule: Subclass to override run; use Runnable for flexibility.

questions.q: Thread A of a two-thread program calls Thread.sleep(2000). What is paused?
options: Nothing; sleep only schedules a message for later
Both threads, since they belong to one process
Every program on the machine, until the time passes
Only thread A, leaving the processor free for other threads
optionExplain: Sleep really suspends the calling thread.
Sleep acts on the caller only, not on the process.
Other programs can use the processor during the sleep.
Sleep suspends the thread that calls it, so others can use the processor.
questions.explain: Sleep suspends the thread that calls it. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: Thread.sleep pauses only the calling thread for about the requested time, and its InterruptedException must be caught or declared.

questions.q: Thread.sleep can throw a checked exception named ____ when another thread interrupts the sleeper.
questions.explain: The checked exception is InterruptedException; the caller must catch or declare it.
questions.rule: Thread.sleep pauses only the calling thread for about the requested time, and its InterruptedException must be caught or declared.

questions.q: A status checker must poll a server every 30 seconds, pausing with sleep(30000) between checks. What does the tutorial's account of timing imply?
options: Exactly 30 seconds each time, because sleep takes a precise number
At least 30 and never more than 31 seconds
About 30 seconds apart, though the exact gap may vary
As often as the server happens to answer
optionExplain: The tutorial says you cannot assume the thread sleeps for exactly the period.
No such bound is promised.
Sleep times are limited by the operating system, so they are approximate.
The sleep call, not the server, sets the pause.
questions.explain: Treat sleep as approximate.
questions.rule: Thread.sleep pauses only the calling thread for about the requested time, and its InterruptedException must be caught or declared.

questions.q: A developer replaces sleep(1000) with sleep(1000, 500000), hoping for a more exact pause. What does the tutorial's account predict?
options: A pause exact to the nanosecond, since the finer form exists
No promise, since both forms are limited by the operating system
A pause that cannot be interrupted, because the finer form is protected
A compile error, because only one form may be used per program
optionExplain: The extra argument does not remove the operating system's limits.
The limit on precision comes from the operating system, whichever form is used.
Both forms respond to interrupts.
Both forms are available.
questions.explain: A finer unit in the call is not a finer clock.
questions.teaches: The nanosecond form of sleep does not escape the operating system's timing limits, so it does not make the pause any more exact.
questions.rule: Thread.sleep pauses only the calling thread for about the requested time, and its InterruptedException must be caught or declared.

questions.q: A helper method pause() in a class calls Thread.sleep(500) and fails to compile with an unreported-exception error. Which changes make it compile? Select all that apply.
options: Wrap the sleep call in a try block that catches InterruptedException
Add throws InterruptedException to pause's declaration
Mark pause as synchronized
Change the call to sleep(500, 0)
optionExplain: Catching handles the checked exception where it arises.
Declaring passes the obligation to callers, which is allowed.
Synchronization has no effect on checked exceptions.
The other form throws the same checked exception.
questions.explain: A checked exception must be caught or declared; declaring only moves the obligation to the callers of pause.
questions.teaches: Declaring throws InterruptedException moves the obligation to every caller, so somewhere up the call chain the exception must be caught or declared again.
questions.rule: Thread.sleep pauses only the calling thread for about the requested time, and its InterruptedException must be caught or declared.

questions.q: A loop prints a line after each 4-second sleep, and main only declares the exception. During the second sleep another thread interrupts main. What happens to the remaining lines?
options: The sleep ends early and printing carries on as before
The interrupt waits until the loop finishes, then takes effect
The interrupt is ignored because main has no catch clause
Sleep throws, the loop is left, and no more lines are printed
optionExplain: Sleep does not quietly resume; it throws the exception.
The interrupt acts on the sleep in progress.
A missing catch means the exception propagates; it is not ignored.
An interrupt during sleep makes sleep throw, and nothing catches it inside the loop.
questions.explain: An uncaught InterruptedException ends the code that was sleeping.
questions.rule: Thread.sleep pauses only the calling thread for about the requested time, and its InterruptedException must be caught or declared.

questions.q: A worker thread runs an endless loop of calculations written without any thought for cancellation. Another thread calls interrupt on it. What happens to the loop?
options: It restarts its loop from the beginning
It stops at once, because interrupt terminates a thread
It pauses until the interrupter resumes it
It keeps going; its code never checks for or responds to an interrupt
optionExplain: Nothing restarts the loop.
Interrupt asks; it does not terminate by force.
Interrupt does not pause a thread.
An interrupt works only if the thread supports its own interruption.
questions.explain: An interrupt is a request that the target must honour. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: Interrupt only asks; the interrupted thread must be written to notice the request and respond.

questions.q: True or false: An interrupt is sent by calling interrupt on the Thread object of the thread to be interrupted.
questions.explain: The sender calls interrupt on the target's Thread object.
questions.rule: Interrupt only asks; the interrupted thread must be written to notice the request and respond.

questions.q: A report thread should stop when the user closes the window. Which design matches the tutorial's model?
options: The window code calls interrupt, which destroys the report thread wherever it is
The window calls interrupt, and the report thread checks and returns
The report thread calls interrupt on the window thread to ask it to close
Nothing is done, because an interrupt cannot be used to end work
optionExplain: Interrupt does not destroy a thread.
Both halves are needed: the signal and the cooperative response.
The signal must go to the thread that should stop.
Ending work is the most common use.
questions.explain: Send the signal to the target, and write the target to respond.
questions.rule: Interrupt only asks; the interrupted thread must be written to notice the request and respond.

questions.q: A thread runs one long calculation with no checks. Another thread interrupts it after a minute. When does the interrupt change what the loop does?
options: Immediately, as the processor stops the loop
At the next time slice, when the operating system takes the thread off the core
Only if the loop's own code checks for interrupts
When the loop ends, because the interrupt is stored as a result
optionExplain: Nothing forces the loop to stop.
Time slicing does not read interrupts.
Without checks in its code the thread does not notice the signal.
The signal does not become a result.
questions.explain: A thread that does not call blocking methods must look for interrupts itself.
questions.teaches: A thread that goes a long time without a blocking call must look for interrupts on its own, otherwise it reacts only when it next happens to check.
questions.rule: Interrupt only asks; the interrupted thread must be written to notice the request and respond.

questions.q: A factory controller thread must stop when a supervisor thread asks. Match each job to who does it.
pairs: The supervisor calls interrupt on the controller's Thread object
The controller's own code, which must be written to check
The programmer of the controller, who may let it stop or do something else
questions.explain: The sender only raises the signal; noticing and responding belong to the target's code.
questions.teaches: The same interrupt can be answered in different ways by different threads, and the sender cannot dictate which: it only raises the signal.
questions.rule: Interrupt only asks; the interrupted thread must be written to notice the request and respond.

questions.q: True or false: If the downloader's code is changed so that it returns when it notices an interrupt, the same interrupt call from main can now end the download.
questions.explain: Once the target supports its own interruption, the same signal has an effect.
questions.rule: Changing the target changes what the signal does.

questions.q: A loop sleeps four seconds, then prints a message, over and over. Another thread interrupts it halfway through a sleep. What should the loop's code expect?
options: The program is stopped by the operating system
The sleep call keeps sleeping and reports the interrupt afterwards
The message is printed twice to make up for the lost time
The sleep call ends early by throwing InterruptedException
optionExplain: The operating system does not stop the program for this.
Sleep cancels and returns at once when interrupted.
Nothing makes up lost time.
Blocking methods such as sleep respond to an interrupt by throwing.
questions.explain: Sleep reacts to an interrupt right away. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: If a thread calls blocking methods often, handle InterruptedException by returning from run.

questions.q: To support interruption in a loop that sleeps, catch InterruptedException and then ____ from run.
questions.explain: Returning from run ends the thread's task.
questions.rule: If a thread calls blocking methods often, handle InterruptedException by returning from run.

questions.q: Put these events in order for a thread that sleeps in a loop, is interrupted, and handles it by returning.
items: The thread calls sleep
Another thread calls interrupt on it
Sleep throws InterruptedException
The catch block returns from run
questions.explain: The signal arrives during sleep, which throws, and the catch ends the task.
questions.rule: If a thread calls blocking methods often, handle InterruptedException by returning from run.

questions.q: A thread has the catch block but, by mistake, it contains only a comment and no return. After an interrupt during sleep, what does the loop do?
options: It ends anyway, because the exception always ends the thread
It carries on, since nothing in the catch ended the loop
It throws the exception again out of run
It skips the remaining sleeps but continues printing
optionExplain: A caught exception does not end the thread by itself.
Catching handles the exception; without a return the loop proceeds as before.
Nothing rethrows it.
Later sleeps run normally; nothing cancels them.
questions.explain: The catch block is where the response is chosen.
questions.teaches: Catching InterruptedException does not itself stop anything: the thread ends only if the catch block makes it end, for example by returning.
questions.rule: If a thread calls blocking methods often, handle InterruptedException by returning from run.

questions.q: A supermarket checkout thread waits one second between scanning items using sleep. A manager thread wants it to finish immediately. Which design uses the tutorial's pattern?
options: The manager calls sleep on the checkout thread so it stops
The manager shortens the sleep time, and the thread ends after that
The manager calls start again on the checkout thread
The manager interrupts, and the checkout code catches and returns
optionExplain: Sleep pauses the caller; it cannot be aimed at another thread.
A shorter pause does not end the task.
Start launches a thread; it does not end one.
The signal wakes the sleeping thread through an exception that its own code handles.
questions.explain: The pattern is interrupt, exception, catch, return.
questions.teaches: Sleep is called by the thread that wants to pause itself; to cut another thread's sleep short, you call interrupt on it instead.
questions.rule: If a thread calls blocking methods often, handle InterruptedException by returning from run.

questions.q: The sleep in the message loop is lengthened from 4000 to 8000 milliseconds. Another thread interrupts the loop one second into a sleep. When is InterruptedException thrown?
options: After the full eight seconds, once the sleep is over
Never, because a longer sleep cannot be interrupted
About one second in, not after the full eight seconds of the sleep
At the start of the next loop pass, after the sleep ends normally
optionExplain: Sleep does not wait out its time once interrupted.
Any sleep can be interrupted.
Sleep cancels and returns at once when interrupted, however long it was meant to last.
The exception comes from the sleep that was interrupted.
questions.explain: An interrupted sleep ends immediately, whatever its length.
questions.rule: If a thread calls blocking methods often, handle InterruptedException by returning from run.

questions.q: A thread runs a loop that calls a long calculation 500 times and does not sleep or wait. Another thread interrupts it. How can the loop learn of the interrupt?
options: It cannot, since only sleeping threads can be interrupted
By waiting for the calculation to throw InterruptedException
By calling join on itself after each calculation
By calling Thread.interrupted between calculations
optionExplain: Any thread can be sent an interrupt; it has to look for it itself.
A calculation that does not block does not throw that exception.
Join waits for another thread to end; it is not a check for interrupts.
The static method reports whether an interrupt has been received.
questions.explain: A thread that never blocks must poll for interrupts itself. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: A thread that rarely blocks should poll Thread.interrupted between units of work, and may throw InterruptedException to centralise the handling.

questions.q: True or false: Thread.interrupted is a static method that returns true if an interrupt has been received.
questions.explain: The lesson names Thread.interrupted as the polling call for threads that rarely block.
questions.rule: A thread that rarely blocks should poll Thread.interrupted between units of work, and may throw InterruptedException to centralise the handling.

questions.q: Put the steps of one pass through a polling loop in order.
items: Do one unit of heavy work
Test Thread.interrupted
If the test is true, return from run
If the test is false, go on to the next unit
questions.explain: Work, then check, then either leave or continue.
questions.rule: A thread that rarely blocks should poll Thread.interrupted between units of work, and may throw InterruptedException to centralise the handling.

questions.q: Code running in thread A calls Thread.interrupted. Whose interrupt status does it report?
options: The main thread's, whichever thread calls it
The most recently started thread's
Thread A's own, since the static method concerns the calling thread
A combined flag for every running thread
optionExplain: Nothing ties the answer to main.
Start order plays no part.
As a static method it concerns the thread that invokes it.
There is one status per thread, not a shared one.
questions.explain: Static Thread methods concern the calling thread.
questions.teaches: Because Thread.interrupted is static, it reports the status of the thread that calls it, not of a thread you name; to look at another thread, an instance method is needed.
questions.rule: A thread that rarely blocks should poll Thread.interrupted between units of work, and may throw InterruptedException to centralise the handling.

questions.q: A recalculation thread works through 10,000 spreadsheet cells with heavy formulas and does not block. Which placements of the interrupt check let it react within a reasonable time? Select all that apply.
options: After each cell is recalculated
After every batch of ten cells
Once, after all 10,000 cells are done
Once, before the loop begins
optionExplain: Frequent checks give a quick response.
Checking per small batch still reacts quickly.
The check would run only when the work is already over.
Nothing would be noticed after the loop started.
questions.explain: The response is only as quick as the next check.
questions.teaches: How often a thread checks decides how soon it can respond to an interrupt: checks spread through the work give prompt responses, a single check at the end gives none.
questions.rule: A thread that rarely blocks should poll Thread.interrupted between units of work, and may throw InterruptedException to centralise the handling.

questions.q: A student writes: for each job, call crunch(job); and after the loop ends, test Thread.interrupted and return if it is true. What is wrong?
options: Thread.interrupted is not a static method and cannot be called here
A run method is not allowed to use return
Each job needs a sleep before it can be interrupted
The check comes only after all the work, far too late
optionExplain: It is a static method of Thread, as the lesson says.
Returning from run is the normal way to end the thread's task.
A thread that never sleeps can still poll.
Polling has to happen between units of work to be useful.
questions.explain: Put the check inside the loop, between units of work.
questions.rule: A thread that rarely blocks should poll Thread.interrupted between units of work, and may throw InterruptedException to centralise the handling.

questions.q: True or false: After Thread.interrupted returns true for a thread, calling it again at once, with no new interrupt, returns true again.
questions.explain: That call clears the status, so a repeat returns false unless a new interrupt arrives. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: Interrupt sets the flag, Thread.interrupted reads and clears it, and isInterrupted reads it without clearing.

questions.q: Match each call to its effect on the interrupt status.
pairs: Sets the interrupt status of thread t
Returns the current thread's status and clears it
Returns the status of thread t and leaves it unchanged
questions.explain: Interrupt sets, the static method reads and clears, the instance method only reads.
questions.rule: Interrupt sets the flag, Thread.interrupted reads and clears it, and isInterrupted reads it without clearing.

questions.q: A monitor thread wants to peek at whether worker w has been interrupted, without disturbing the flag. Which call fits?
options: w.join()
Thread.interrupted()
w.interrupt()
w.isInterrupted()
optionExplain: Join waits for the worker to end and does not report the flag.
The static call would read the monitor's own flag, and it clears the status.
That call sets the flag instead of reading it.
The instance method reads the flag and leaves it as it is.
questions.explain: Use isInterrupted to look without changing.
questions.rule: Interrupt sets the flag, Thread.interrupted reads and clears it, and isInterrupted reads it without clearing.

questions.q: A sleeping thread is interrupted, and sleep throws InterruptedException. Inside the catch block, what does isInterrupted() report for that thread, by convention?
options: true, because the interrupt has not yet been handled
false, since the throw cleared the status
true, until Thread.interrupted is called
An exception is thrown again by the query
optionExplain: The status was cleared when the exception was thrown.
The convention is that the throw clears the flag.
The catch block sees the status already cleared.
Querying the flag throws nothing.
questions.explain: A method that throws InterruptedException clears the status.
questions.teaches: By convention, a method that exits by throwing InterruptedException clears the interrupt status as it throws, so the catch block finds the flag already false.
questions.rule: Interrupt sets the flag, Thread.interrupted reads and clears it, and isInterrupted reads it without clearing.

questions.q: A helper library method catches InterruptedException from sleep, ignores it and carries on. Its caller later polls Thread.interrupted to decide whether to stop. What goes wrong?
options: The poll throws InterruptedException itself
The poll always returns true afterwards
The throw cleared the flag, so the poll finds nothing
Nothing; the library keeps the flag set for the caller
optionExplain: Polling returns a boolean; it does not throw.
The flag was cleared, so the poll returns false.
Swallowing the exception hides the interrupt from later polling.
Nothing restores the flag unless the code does so.
questions.explain: Do not hide an interrupt that others may need to see.
questions.teaches: Code that catches InterruptedException and carries on hides the interrupt from any later polling, because the throw has already cleared the status.
questions.rule: Interrupt sets the flag, Thread.interrupted reads and clears it, and isInterrupted reads it without clearing.

questions.q: True or false: If thread T calls Thread.interrupted and gets false, no other thread can set T's flag afterwards.
questions.explain: Another thread may call interrupt on T at any moment, so a false reading can be followed by a set flag.
questions.rule: A false reading is true only for the moment it was taken.

questions.q: Main starts a worker thread and then needs the worker's finished output. Which call in main fits?
options: worker.start() a second time
Thread.sleep(1)
worker.interrupt()
worker.join(), which waits until the worker terminates
optionExplain: Starting does not wait, and a finished task is not what main needs.
A short sleep does not tell main when the worker is done.
That sends a stop request; it does not wait for anything.
Join pauses main until the worker terminates.
questions.explain: To wait for a thread, join it. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: t.join() pauses the caller until thread t terminates, and a timed version limits how long it waits.

questions.q: Calling t.____() pauses the current thread until the thread t terminates.
questions.explain: Join is the waiting call.
questions.rule: t.join() pauses the caller until thread t terminates, and a timed version limits how long it waits.

questions.q: A launcher must print a message only after a download thread has finished. Put the steps in order.
items: Main starts the download thread
Main calls join on the download thread
The download thread terminates and join returns
Main prints the finished message
questions.explain: The message comes after join returns, which is after termination.
questions.rule: t.join() pauses the caller until thread t terminates, and a timed version limits how long it waits.

questions.q: Thread A is waiting inside b.join() when thread C interrupts A. What does the tutorial say happens?
options: Join keeps waiting, since only sleep can be interrupted
Thread b is stopped, because the interrupt travels to it
Join exits with InterruptedException, and A resumes
Join returns normally, as if b had finished
optionExplain: Join responds to interrupts just as sleep does.
The interrupt acts on the waiting thread A, not on b.
Like sleep, join responds to an interrupt by exiting with that exception.
It exits with an exception, which is not a normal return.
questions.explain: Join, like sleep, can be cut short by an interrupt.
questions.teaches: Like sleep, join exits with InterruptedException when the waiting thread is interrupted, so the caller must handle or declare that exception and cannot assume the joined thread has ended.
questions.rule: t.join() pauses the caller until thread t terminates, and a timed version limits how long it waits.

questions.q: A build tool starts a compile thread and calls t.join(30000). Control returns to the tool. How should the tool treat the return?
options: The thread has certainly finished, since join never returns early
The thread has been interrupted by the join call
The thread has been restarted for another 30 seconds
It may still be running; a timed join can time out
optionExplain: A timed join returns after its period whether or not the thread has finished.
Join waits; it does not interrupt.
Join does not restart anything.
Only an untimed join, or a timed one that ended early, implies termination.
questions.explain: After a timed join, check whether the thread is still alive.
questions.teaches: After a timed join returns, the caller should check whether the thread is still running (the lesson uses isAlive for this), because the return alone does not show that it terminated.
questions.rule: t.join() pauses the caller until thread t terminates, and a timed version limits how long it waits.

questions.q: True or false: If main's call to worker.join() is changed to worker.join(2000), main may continue while the worker is still running.
questions.explain: The timed form returns after the period even when the worker has not finished.
questions.rule: A timed join may return with the thread still alive.

questions.q: Main starts a slow worker, wants to check on it every second, and wants to cancel it after a limit. Which combination suits?
options: sleep(1000) in a loop, restarting the worker each time
An untimed join, then interrupt after it returns
Interrupt right after start, then join
A timed join in a loop, then interrupt at the limit
optionExplain: Restarting does not cancel; and sleep does not observe the worker.
An untimed join returns only once the worker has ended, so there is nothing left to cancel.
The worker would be asked to stop before it did any work.
Timed joins give regular check-ins, and interrupt asks the worker to stop.
questions.explain: Check in with timed joins; cancel with interrupt. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: Main polls with a timed join and isAlive, interrupts when patience runs out, then waits fully with an untimed join.

questions.q: True or false: In SimpleThreads, main calls join with no time limit only after it has interrupted the message thread.
questions.explain: The timed join is used while waiting; the untimed one follows the interrupt.
questions.rule: Main polls with a timed join and isAlive, interrupts when patience runs out, then waits fully with an untimed join.

questions.q: Put the events of a SimpleThreads run with a short patience in order.
items: Main starts the message thread
Main keeps printing waiting notes between timed joins
Patience runs out and main interrupts the message thread
The message thread's sleep throws and it prints that it was not done
Main's untimed join returns and main prints its closing line
questions.explain: Start, wait in small steps, interrupt, thread reacts, main finishes.
questions.rule: Main polls with a timed join and isAlive, interrupts when patience runs out, then waits fully with an untimed join.

questions.q: In SimpleThreads every output line starts with the name of the thread that printed it. Which expression supplies that name inside the printing code?
options: Thread.sleep().getName()
Thread.currentThread().getName()
Thread.currentThread().getPriority()
Thread.interrupted().getName()
optionExplain: Sleep is a pause, and it returns nothing to ask for a name.
currentThread gives the thread running this code, and getName reads its name.
That returns the priority number, not the name.
That call returns a boolean, which has no name.
questions.explain: Thread.currentThread() names the thread running the code.
questions.teaches: Thread.currentThread() returns the Thread object of the code that is running, and getName on it lets output be labelled by thread.
questions.rule: Main polls with a timed join and isAlive, interrupts when patience runs out, then waits fully with an untimed join.

questions.q: After the interrupt, main calls join with no time limit. What does that last call rely on?
options: That join can force the thread to end
That the thread has already ended before the interrupt
That the thread supports interruption and ends soon
That main's own flag has been cleared
optionExplain: Join only waits; it ends nothing.
Then no interrupt would have been needed.
Without its cooperation the untimed join could wait indefinitely.
Main's own flag has no part in this wait.
questions.explain: An untimed join is safe only if the target will actually finish.
questions.teaches: The final untimed join is safe only because the message thread has been written to respond to the interrupt and finish soon; against a thread that ignores interrupts it could wait indefinitely.
questions.rule: Main polls with a timed join and isAlive, interrupts when patience runs out, then waits fully with an untimed join.

questions.q: With a patience of 2 seconds, the message thread prints ____ of its four messages before it is interrupted.
questions.explain: Its first message comes after a four-second sleep, so an interrupt at about two seconds ends the sleep before any message is printed.
questions.rule: Interrupt arrives during the first sleep, before the first message.

questions.q: True or false: When two threads share a field, the Java runtime automatically stops them from interfering with each other.
questions.explain: Preventing interference takes synchronization written by the programmer; sharing alone brings the risk. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: Shared fields make communication cheap but invite interference and inconsistency, which synchronization prevents at the cost of possible contention.

questions.q: True or false: Thread interference and memory consistency errors are the two kinds of error the tutorial links to sharing data between threads.
questions.explain: These are the two named errors, and synchronization is the tool against both.
questions.rule: Shared fields make communication cheap but invite interference and inconsistency, which synchronization prevents at the cost of possible contention.

questions.q: A shopping cart object is guarded so only one thread uses it at a time, and customers slow down when many arrive together. Which term from the tutorial names this slowdown?
options: Time slicing
Thread interference
Memory consistency error
Thread contention
optionExplain: Slicing is the operating system sharing a core, not competition for a guarded object.
Interference is mixed-up steps and lost updates, not waiting.
That is an inconsistent view of data, not a slowdown from waiting.
Contention is threads competing for one resource, being slowed or suspended.
questions.explain: Contention is the cost of guarding a shared resource.
questions.rule: Shared fields make communication cheap but invite interference and inconsistency, which synchronization prevents at the cost of possible contention.

questions.q: Which of these does the tutorial describe as a form of contention? Select all that apply.
options: Starvation
Livelock
Thread interference
Memory consistency error
optionExplain: Named as a form of contention, treated under liveness.
Also named as a form of contention.
This is an error from interleaved steps, not a form of contention.
This is an inconsistent view of data, not a form of contention.
questions.explain: Starvation and livelock are forms of contention; interference and inconsistency are the errors synchronization prevents.
questions.teaches: Starvation and livelock, met in the liveness section, count as forms of contention, so contention is the umbrella for the slowdowns that synchronization can cause.
questions.rule: Shared fields make communication cheap but invite interference and inconsistency, which synchronization prevents at the cost of possible contention.

questions.q: A team lets 20 threads update one shared tally with no coordination, because coordination slows threads down. What does the tutorial's account say they risk?
options: Nothing, because slower threads are the only danger
Wrong results from interference or stale views
Only a compile error, which the compiler will report
Only a shorter run time, with no other effect
optionExplain: Contention is a cost of the remedy; the errors are a cost of skipping it.
Dropping synchronization removes the remedy but leaves the errors it prevents.
Interference does not show up as a compile error.
Speed gained this way may come with wrong results.
questions.explain: Skipping synchronization trades contention for errors.
questions.teaches: Avoiding synchronization does not avoid the problems it guards against: it removes the remedy and leaves the errors, so the choice is between contention and incorrectness, not between cost and no cost.
questions.rule: Shared fields make communication cheap but invite interference and inconsistency, which synchronization prevents at the cost of possible contention.

questions.q: A guarded resource is wanted at the same moment by 2 threads. The number rises to 20. What does the tutorial's description lead you to expect?
options: Fewer errors, since more threads check each other
Interference gets worse because the lock fails
More threads slowed or suspended by contention for the resource
No change, since contention depends on core count only
optionExplain: Extra threads do not add protection.
The lock keeps working; the cost is waiting.
Contention is the runtime slowing or suspending threads that compete for the resource.
Contention comes from competing for one resource.
questions.explain: More competitors for one guarded resource means more waiting.
questions.rule: Shared fields make communication cheap but invite interference and inconsistency, which synchronization prevents at the cost of possible contention.

questions.q: Thread A runs c++ once and thread B runs c-- once on a shared int c that starts at 0. Which final values of c are possible?
options: Only 0 or 1
Only 0, because the two cancel out
Only 1 or minus 1, never 0
0, 1 or minus 1, by timing
optionExplain: Minus 1 is possible if B stores last after both retrieved 0.
That holds only when the steps do not interleave.
Without interleaving the result is 0.
If the steps interleave, either update may overwrite the other.
questions.explain: Interleaved steps make the outcome depend on timing. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: A compound statement such as c++ is several steps, and if threads interleave them an update can be lost.

questions.q: Put the three steps of c++ in order.
items: Retrieve the current value of c
Increase the retrieved value by 1
Store the result back in c
questions.explain: The statement is a retrieve, a computation and a store.
questions.rule: A compound statement such as c++ is several steps, and if threads interleave them an update can be lost.

questions.q: Both threads retrieve 0 first. Then A stores 1 and later B stores minus 1. The final value of c is ____.
questions.explain: B stored last, overwriting A's 1, so A's update is lost and c ends at minus 1.
questions.rule: A compound statement such as c++ is several steps, and if threads interleave them an update can be lost.
