questions.q: c is 5. Thread A and thread B each run c++ once, with their steps interleaved. What are the possible final values?
options: Only 7, since two increments always add two
6 or 7, depending on how the steps interleave
Only 6, since interference cannot occur here
optionExplain: Interleaving can make both threads store 6.
Both retrieve 5 and both store 6, or the steps do not overlap and c reaches 7.
The steps can interleave, and each thread may end with 6 or the sum may reach 7.
Both threads store a value of at least 6, so 5 cannot be the result.
questions.explain: Two increments can end up counted once.
questions.teaches: Interference can lose an update even when both threads do the same operation, so two increments can end as one.
questions.rule: A compound statement such as c++ is several steps, and if threads interleave them an update can be lost.

questions.q: Which of these statements are read-modify-write operations that interleaving could break? Select all that apply.
options: seats = seats - 1
total = total + price
visits++
limit = 100
optionExplain: It reads seats, subtracts and stores a value computed from the old one.
It reads total, adds and stores a result computed from the old value.
It retrieves, increments and stores, like c++.
It only stores a constant and reads no earlier value.
questions.explain: The danger pattern is a store that depends on an earlier read of the same shared value.
questions.teaches: The dangerous pattern is read-modify-write: a statement that reads a shared value and then writes back something computed from it.
questions.rule: A compound statement such as c++ is several steps, and if threads interleave them an update can be lost.

questions.q: A teammate says: We ran the two-thread counter test 1000 times and saw no wrong total, so the class is safe. What is the flaw?
options: A test with two threads proves nothing about one thread
The total can only be wrong if the test runs fewer than 1000 times
Interference only happens at program start, before tests begin
Passing runs do not prove interference cannot happen on another run
optionExplain: The claim concerns several threads; what fails is the inference from passing runs.
The count of runs does not decide it.
Interference can happen whenever steps interleave.
The tutorial notes these bugs are unpredictable and hard to detect.
questions.explain: Many clean runs do not prove the absence of interference.
questions.rule: A compound statement such as c++ is several steps, and if threads interleave them an update can be lost.

questions.q: True or false: Thread A increments a shared int. B is started independently, with no synchronization or join between A and B. B is guaranteed to see the new value.
questions.explain: Nothing in that setup creates a guarantee that B sees A's write. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: Without a happens-before relationship between a write and a later read, the reader has no guarantee of seeing the write.

questions.q: True or false: If the increment and the print ran in the same thread, it would be safe to assume the output is 1.
questions.explain: Within one thread, later statements see earlier writes.
questions.rule: Without a happens-before relationship between a write and a later read, the reader has no guarantee of seeing the write.

questions.q: A corrector thread sleeps 1 second and then sets a shared static message to the right text. Main sets the message to a wrong text at once, sleeps 2 seconds, and prints it. By the tutorial's reasoning, is the right text guaranteed to be printed?
options: Yes, because one second is shorter than two seconds
Yes, because the write happens earlier by the clock
No, because no happens-before link joins the write and the read
No, because sleep stops other threads from writing
optionExplain: Shorter sleeps do not create a happens-before relationship.
Clock order is not the same as happens-before.
Timing alone gives no guarantee of visibility.
Sleep pauses only the calling thread.
questions.explain: Only a happens-before relationship guarantees visibility.
questions.rule: Without a happens-before relationship between a write and a later read, the reader has no guarantee of seeing the write.

questions.q: A developer fixes a stale-read bug by adding a long sleep before the read. According to the tutorial's reasoning, is the fix sound?
options: No, because sleeping threads cannot read shared fields
Yes, any delay longer than the write guarantees visibility
Yes, but only if the sleep is longer than one second
No, because a delay creates no happens-before relationship at all
optionExplain: Sleeping threads can read after waking; the problem is the missing guarantee.
Elapsed time does not create a guarantee.
No length of sleep creates the guarantee.
Only the listed actions or synchronization create the guarantee.
questions.explain: Waiting is not a happens-before link.
questions.teaches: A long enough delay between a write and a read does not create a happens-before relationship, so waiting does not make the write visible by guarantee.
questions.rule: Without a happens-before relationship between a write and a later read, the reader has no guarantee of seeing the write.

questions.q: An admin thread turns on a debugEnabled setting, yet worker threads keep logging as if it were off for a long time. Which explanation fits the tutorial?
options: The admin thread wrote the value into the wrong thread
No happens-before link guarantees workers see the write
The workers must be sleeping, since awake threads see every write
Boolean settings cannot be shared between threads
optionExplain: Writes go to the shared field, not to a thread.
This is the kind of inconsistent view the tutorial describes.
Being awake gives no guarantee.
Shared fields of any type can be seen by several threads.
questions.explain: A change that seems to take effect late is the mark of a missing guarantee.
questions.teaches: A memory consistency error can look like a change that takes effect late or not at all for some threads, which is different from a lost update.
questions.rule: Without a happens-before relationship between a write and a later read, the reader has no guarantee of seeing the write.

questions.q: Sort each symptom by which error it points to.

items.t: Two threads add one at the same time and only one add is counted
A reader thread never sees a flag that a writer thread set
The retrieve, increase and store steps of two updates mix together
A thread reads a counter after another wrote it and gets the old value

questions.explain: Mixed-up steps point to interference; a stale view of a finished write points to a memory consistency error.
questions.rule: Without a happens-before relationship between a write and a later read, the reader has no guarantee of seeing the write.

questions.q: Thread W computes a value into a shared field and ends. Main then calls W.join() and reads the field. What may main rely on?
options: It sees the value only if the field is declared inside main
It may see an old value, since join gives no visibility
It sees the value only if W slept at least once
It sees W's value, since join returned after W ended
optionExplain: Where the field is declared does not decide it.
Join does create a visibility guarantee when it returns after termination.
Sleeping plays no part in the guarantee.
The join return creates a happens-before link from W's work to main.
questions.explain: Join returning after termination makes the thread's work visible. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: Writes made before start are visible to the new thread, and writes by a finished thread are visible to the thread whose join on it returns.

questions.q: When a thread ends and another thread's ____ on it returns, everything the ended thread did is visible afterwards.
questions.explain: Join is one of the two actions the tutorial names.
questions.rule: Writes made before start are visible to the new thread, and writes by a finished thread are visible to the thread whose join on it returns.

questions.q: In a program, main sets a static message to a wrong text, sleeps 2 seconds, then prints it. A corrector thread sleeps 1 second and sets the correct text. Which change guarantees main sees the corrector's write?
options: Make main sleep ten seconds instead of two
Make the corrector sleep for less time
Print the message twice
Have main join the corrector
optionExplain: More waiting creates no guarantee.
Shorter sleeps change timing, not visibility.
Repeating the read adds no guarantee.
Join returning after the corrector terminates makes its write visible.
questions.explain: Use join, or another happens-before action, instead of timing.
questions.rule: Writes made before start are visible to the new thread, and writes by a finished thread are visible to the thread whose join on it returns.

questions.q: Main starts workers A and B, each writing its own result field, then joins A and B before reading both fields. Which statements hold? Select all that apply.
options: A's write is visible to main after join on A returns
B's write is visible to main after join on B returns
Main would see both results even if it never joined
Main sees the results only if A and B each slept first
optionExplain: Join on A creates the link for A's work.
Join on B does the same for B.
Without a join there is no guarantee.
Sleeping plays no part.
questions.explain: Each join covers the thread it waits for.
questions.teaches: A coordinator can start several workers, join each, and then safely read what each wrote, because every join creates the link for its own thread.
questions.rule: Writes made before start are visible to the new thread, and writes by a finished thread are visible to the thread whose join on it returns.

questions.q: Main starts a worker and, after the call to start, writes a new value into a shared field. The worker reads that field. Is the worker guaranteed to see the new value?
options: Yes, because the worker was started by main
No, start only covers writes made before the call to start
Yes, because starting a thread makes all fields shared
No, because a worker may never read a field main wrote
optionExplain: Being started by main gives no guarantee for later writes.
The start guarantee extends to statements before the call.
Fields are shared anyway; visibility is the question.
Workers can read fields; the issue is the guarantee.
questions.explain: Start orders only the writes made before it.
questions.teaches: The guarantee from start covers only writes made before the call; a write made after start has no guarantee of being seen by the new thread.
questions.rule: Writes made before start are visible to the new thread, and writes by a finished thread are visible to the thread whose join on it returns.

questions.q: True or false: If main calls worker.join(1000) and the call returns because 1000 milliseconds passed while the worker is still running, everything the worker has done so far is guaranteed visible to main.
questions.explain: The guarantee comes when join returns because the thread terminated, not when a timeout ends the wait.
questions.rule: Join gives visibility when it returns after termination.

questions.q: A counter has increment and value, both synchronized. Thread A is inside increment. Thread B calls value on the same counter. What happens to B?
options: B is skipped and its call returns zero
B reads at once and may see a half-updated value
B waits until A leaves increment and the lock is released
B and A swap places in the middle of the call
optionExplain: Calls are not skipped; they wait.
That would be interleaving, which synchronization prevents.
Synchronized calls on one object do not interleave.
Threads do not swap places inside a method.
questions.explain: Synchronized calls on one object take turns. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: Synchronized methods of one object run one thread at a time, and each exit makes its changes visible to later calls.

questions.q: True or false: Two calls to synchronized methods on the same object cannot interleave.
questions.explain: While one thread runs a synchronized method, the others wait.
questions.rule: Synchronized methods of one object run one thread at a time, and each exit makes its changes visible to later calls.

questions.q: A class Stock has a private int units, an add method that does units += n, and a get method that returns units. Several threads use one Stock. What is the fix in the tutorial's style?
options: Declare only add synchronized, since readers change nothing
Declare the units field final
Declare both add and get synchronized
Declare the whole class synchronized
optionExplain: A reader outside the synchronized methods has no happens-before link to the writes.
A final field cannot be changed after construction, so add could not work.
Both write and read must pass through synchronized methods to get ordering and visibility.
Synchronized applies to methods and statements, not to a class declaration.
questions.explain: Guard readers and writers alike.
questions.rule: Synchronized methods of one object run one thread at a time, and each exit makes its changes visible to later calls.

questions.q: A class synchronizes increment but leaves value unsynchronized. A reader calls value right after another thread's increment has finished. What can the tutorial promise?
options: The reader sees the new count, since increment has finished
Nothing: only later synchronized calls get the link
The reader is blocked until increment is called again
The reader sees the new count only after a sleep
optionExplain: Finishing is not enough; the link runs to later synchronized calls.
The reader may see a stale count.
An unsynchronized method does not wait for the lock.
Sleeping does not create the link.
questions.explain: The visibility link runs between synchronized methods.
questions.teaches: Synchronizing only the writing methods leaves readers uncovered: the link from a synchronized method's exit reaches later synchronized calls, so a reader that is not synchronized can see stale data.
questions.rule: Synchronized methods of one object run one thread at a time, and each exit makes its changes visible to later calls.

questions.q: Two threads use bank account objects with synchronized deposit methods. Match each situation to what happens.
pairs: Both threads call deposit on the same account
The threads call deposit on two different accounts
Neither waits: each account has its own lock
One thread calls deposit and the other calls an unsynchronized method of the same account
Neither waits: the unsynchronized method asks for no lock
questions.explain: Blocking is per object and only among synchronized calls.
questions.teaches: The blocking applies to calls on the same object, so work on different objects goes ahead in parallel.
questions.rule: Synchronized methods of one object run one thread at a time, and each exit makes its changes visible to later calls.

questions.q: True or false: If decrement is left unsynchronized, a call to decrement can still run in the middle of a synchronized increment on the same object.
questions.explain: An unsynchronized method does not ask for the lock, so nothing holds it back.
questions.rule: Only synchronized methods are held back by the lock.

questions.q: An object visible to several threads has an int field changed by a setter and read by a getter. What does the tutorial's strategy say?
options: Make both the setter and the getter synchronized
Synchronize the setter only, since readers change nothing
Synchronize neither; threads sort it out themselves
Synchronize the constructor instead
optionExplain: All reads and writes of the variable go through synchronized methods.
A reader that skips the lock gets no visibility guarantee.
Nothing sorts it out without synchronization.
Constructors cannot be synchronized.
questions.explain: Guard every access, not just the writes. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: Route every access to shared changeable state through synchronized methods, read final fields freely, and do not let this escape from a constructor.

questions.q: True or false: Adding the synchronized keyword to a constructor is a syntax error.
questions.explain: The tutorial says constructors cannot be synchronized.
questions.rule: Route every access to shared changeable state through synchronized methods, read final fields freely, and do not let this escape from a constructor.

questions.q: A class Profile has a final field id, a changeable field status, and a constructor. Sort each member by what the strategy says.

items.t: A getter returning the final field id
The constructor itself
A getter returning the changeable status
A setter changing status
A method that reads the final field createdAt
A method that increments a changeable hits count

questions.explain: Final fields and constructors need no synchronized methods; changeable state does.
questions.rule: Route every access to shared changeable state through synchronized methods, read final fields freely, and do not let this escape from a constructor.

questions.q: Beyond the tutorial: a class must record every new instance in a shared list. How can it avoid exposing half-built objects?
options: Add this inside the constructor, and synchronize the constructor
Build it first, then add it outside the constructor
Add this at the first line of the constructor, to be early
Make the list final so that it cannot be changed
optionExplain: Constructors cannot be synchronized.
The object is complete before any other thread can reach it through the list.
Early registration makes the half-built object reachable.
A final reference to a list does not stop other threads from using the object.
questions.explain: Publish an object only after construction finishes.
questions.teaches: Beyond the tutorial: one way to avoid leaking this is to build the object completely and register it afterwards, for example in a factory method.
questions.rule: Route every access to shared changeable state through synchronized methods, read final fields freely, and do not let this escape from a constructor.

questions.q: A Settings class holds final values loaded from a file and one changeable theme string that users toggle. Which methods need to be synchronized under the strategy?
options: All getters and setters, including those for final values
Only the constructor
None, since the theme is a string
Only the theme getter and setter
optionExplain: Final fields may be read without synchronized methods.
Constructors cannot be synchronized.
A changeable field still needs guarded access.
Final values are safe to read; changeable state needs guarded access.
questions.explain: Synchronize what can change.
questions.teaches: A class can mix both kinds of state, so the cost of synchronization falls only on the methods that touch changeable data.
questions.rule: Route every access to shared changeable state through synchronized methods, read final fields freely, and do not let this escape from a constructor.

questions.q: A teammate sketches a class shared by threads. Which lines break the tutorial's strategy? Select all that apply.
options: Line 1: the constructor is declared synchronized to protect initialisation
Line 2: the constructor ends with allInstances.add(this) on a shared static list
Line 3: getName returns a final field and is not synchronized
Line 4: setLevel and getLevel are both synchronized
optionExplain: Constructors cannot be synchronized; this is a syntax error.
The object leaks before construction is finished.
Fine: final fields can be read without synchronized methods.
Fine: reads and writes of changeable state are guarded.
questions.explain: Lines 1 and 2 break the strategy; lines 3 and 4 follow it.
questions.rule: No synchronized constructors, no early leaks.

questions.q: Thread A is inside a synchronized method of object X when an uncaught exception ends the method. What happens to X's lock?
options: It is released as the method exits, even through the exception
It stays held until the program ends
It stays held until A calls notify
It passes to the thread started first
optionExplain: The lock is released even when the return is caused by an uncaught exception.
Nothing keeps a lock after the method has exited.
Notify is not needed to release a lock on exit.
Locks are not handed on by start order.
questions.explain: Exit, normal or not, releases the lock. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: A synchronized method owns its object's lock, or the Class object's lock if static, until it returns or fails.

questions.q: Match each term to what it means for an intrinsic lock.
pairs: A thread takes the lock before using the object's fields
The span from acquiring the lock until releasing it
Suspend while another thread owns the lock
questions.explain: A thread acquires, owns until it releases, and others block meanwhile.
questions.rule: A synchronized method owns its object's lock, or the Class object's lock if static, until it returns or fails.

questions.q: Class Sensor has synchronized instance methods and a static synchronized method calibrate. Thread A is running inside s1.read(). Which thread is blocked?
options: A thread that calls Sensor.calibrate()
A thread that calls s1.read(), since it needs the same lock A owns
A thread that calls s2.read() on another Sensor
No thread, since A is the only one running
optionExplain: A static synchronized method uses the Class object's lock, a different lock.
It needs the same lock that A owns.
Another object has its own lock.
Other threads that need the lock block.
questions.explain: Each object, and each Class object, has its own lock.
questions.rule: A synchronized method owns its object's lock, or the Class object's lock if static, until it returns or fails.

questions.q: True or false: While a thread owns an object's intrinsic lock, another thread calling an unsynchronized method of that object is blocked.
questions.explain: Only threads that try to acquire the lock block; an unsynchronized method does not ask for it.
questions.teaches: Owning a lock holds back only the threads that try to acquire it, so unsynchronized methods of the same object still run.
questions.rule: A synchronized method owns its object's lock, or the Class object's lock if static, until it returns or fails.

questions.q: A hotel class has a static synchronized method openBooking and an instance synchronized method checkIn on Room objects. Which pairs of calls can run at the same time? Select all that apply.
options: openBooking in one thread, checkIn on room 101 in another
checkIn on room 101 in one thread, checkIn on room 102 in another
checkIn on room 101 in two threads
openBooking in two threads
optionExplain: One needs the Class object's lock, the other room 101's lock.
Two instances have two locks.
Both need room 101's lock, so one waits.
Both need the Class object's lock, so one waits.
questions.explain: Calls conflict only when they need the same lock.
questions.teaches: Calls on distinct instances use distinct locks, so they never exclude each other even when they run the same method.
questions.rule: A synchronized method owns its object's lock, or the Class object's lock if static, until it returns or fails.

questions.q: Sort each synchronized member by which lock it acquires.
groups: The lock of the Class object

items.t: A synchronized instance method called on sensor1
A static synchronized method declared in Sensor
Another synchronized instance method called on sensor1
Another static synchronized method declared in Sensor

questions.explain: Instance methods use the object's lock; static methods use the Class object's lock.
questions.rule: A synchronized method owns its object's lock, or the Class object's lock if static, until it returns or fails.

questions.q: A method updates two fields and then calls a slow method on another object. You want the lock held briefly and no foreign call made under it. Which design does the tutorial favour?
options: A synchronized block around the two updates only
Make the whole method synchronized
Put the slow call inside the block so it is protected
Drop the locking, since the call is slow anyway
optionExplain: The block names the lock and leaves the foreign call outside.
That would hold the lock during the slow call as well.
Calling another object's methods while holding the lock is the thing to avoid.
The fields still need protection.
questions.explain: Lock around the shared updates, not around foreign calls. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: A synchronized statement locks a named object around only the lines that need it, keeping calls to other objects outside.

questions.q: Unlike a synchronized method, a synchronized statement must ____ the object that provides the lock.
questions.explain: The block has to name its lock object.
questions.rule: A synchronized statement locks a named object around only the lines that need it, keeping calls to other objects outside.

questions.q: In record(int v), a block synchronized on this contains total += v and count++, and the line history.add(v) comes after the block. Which statement is right?
options: All three lines run under the lock, because they are in one method
Only total changes under the lock; count and history do not
total and count change under the lock; history.add runs without it
None of the lines hold the lock, since the method is not synchronized
optionExplain: The block, not the method, defines the locked region.
Both statements inside the block are under the lock.
Only the code inside the block holds the lock.
The block takes the lock of this.
questions.explain: The braces of the block mark the guarded lines.
questions.rule: A synchronized statement locks a named object around only the lines that need it, keeping calls to other objects outside.

questions.q: A class has a synchronized method m() and another method n() containing a block synchronized on this. Can two threads run m() and the block of n() on one object at the same time?
options: No, both use the object's intrinsic lock
Yes, because one is a method and the other a block
Yes, but only when the block is smaller
No, but only because n() was written after m()
optionExplain: Synchronized methods and blocks on this take the same lock.
The kind of construct does not matter; the lock does.
Size has no effect on which lock is used.
Order of writing is irrelevant.
questions.explain: Locks, not constructs, decide who waits.
questions.teaches: A block synchronized on this takes the same lock as the object's synchronized methods, so the block and those methods exclude one another.
questions.rule: A synchronized statement locks a named object around only the lines that need it, keeping calls to other objects outside.

questions.q: True or false: In a method that checks its arguments and then updates shared fields, the argument check can be placed before the synchronized block.
questions.explain: The check touches only the arguments, so it need not hold the lock.
questions.teaches: Work on local values need not hold the lock, so a block can begin where the shared state is first touched.
questions.rule: A synchronized statement locks a named object around only the lines that need it, keeping calls to other objects outside.

questions.q: Which of these uses of synchronized statements is a problem? Select all that apply.
options: A block guards only the first of two fields that must change together
Two methods guard the same data with blocks on two different objects
A block leaves a logging call to another object outside it
A block names this and shares the lock with synchronized methods
optionExplain: The second change is left unprotected, so a reader may see a mixed state.
The two blocks use different locks, so they do not exclude each other.
Fine: foreign calls are better kept outside the lock.
Fine: they exclude one another as intended.
questions.explain: Guard together what changes together, and under one lock.
questions.rule: A synchronized statement locks a named object around only the lines that need it, keeping calls to other objects outside.

questions.q: An object has two counters that no code ever uses together. Updates to both go through methods synchronized on this. What is the drawback?
options: Updating one counter blocks updating the other
The counters may lose updates in single-threaded use
The code cannot be compiled with two counters
Each counter is updated twice by every call
optionExplain: Both updates need the same lock, so they take turns needlessly.
Single-threaded use has no interference.
Compilation is not the problem.
Nothing doubles the updates.
questions.explain: One lock for unrelated fields serialises needlessly. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: Independent fields may be guarded by separate lock objects so their updates can overlap, but only if interleaving them is certainly safe.

questions.q: True or false: With separate lock objects, one thread updating c1 and another updating c2 can proceed at the same time.
questions.explain: Each update takes only its own lock.
questions.rule: Independent fields may be guarded by separate lock objects so their updates can overlap, but only if interleaving them is certainly safe.

questions.q: A class holds hits and misses counters, each guarded by its own lock object. Two threads both call recordHit at the same moment. What happens?
options: They run at once and may lose updates
They take turns on the hits lock
One of them takes the misses lock instead
Both wait for the misses lock
optionExplain: They share one lock, so they cannot run their updates at once.
Both need the lock of the hits counter.
recordHit uses the hits lock.
The misses lock is not involved.
questions.explain: Same counter, same lock, turns taken.
questions.rule: Independent fields may be guarded by separate lock objects so their updates can overlap, but only if interleaving them is certainly safe.

questions.q: A new method resetBoth sets rain to zero under lockRain, releases it, then sets wind to zero under lockWind. Another thread reads both fields in between. What can that reader see?
options: Only a state where both are zero, because resets are quick
Only the old values, since the reader holds a lock
A state where rain is zero but wind has not yet been reset to zero
An error from the compiler, since two locks cannot be used
optionExplain: Speed of the reset gives no guarantee.
The reader holds no lock that the resets need.
No single lock covers both fields, so the reader can see the halfway state.
Two lock objects are allowed.
questions.explain: Separate locks cannot make a two-field change appear at once.
questions.teaches: With separate locks no single lock covers both fields, so an operation that needs them to change together is not protected.
questions.rule: Independent fields may be guarded by separate lock objects so their updates can overlap, but only if interleaving them is certainly safe.

questions.q: Sort each pair of shared values by whether separate locks might be safe.

items.t: Two click counters, one for each of two unrelated buttons
A bank balance and a transaction count that must always match
Cache hit and miss counters that are never read together
A start time and an end time that are compared with each other

questions.explain: The deciding question is whether any operation relates the two values.
questions.teaches: What decides is whether any operation relates the values, not whether they are different kinds of data.
questions.rule: Independent fields may be guarded by separate lock objects so their updates can overlap, but only if interleaving them is certainly safe.

questions.q: True or false: If the two lock objects in Gauges are replaced by the single lock this, updates to rain and wind exclude one another.
questions.explain: Both updates would then need the same lock and take turns.
questions.rule: One shared lock serialises all the updates it guards.

questions.q: In one thread, synchronized method a() calls synchronized method b() of the same object. What happens when b() is reached?
options: It proceeds at once, because the thread already owns the lock
It blocks forever, waiting for itself
It must release the lock and queue up again
An error is thrown for double locking
optionExplain: A thread may acquire a lock it already owns.
This is what would happen without reentrant locks.
Nothing in the model requires releasing.
Re-acquiring an owned lock is allowed.
questions.explain: A thread is never blocked by its own lock. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: A thread may acquire an intrinsic lock it already owns, so synchronized code can call other synchronized code on the same lock.

questions.q: True or false: A thread can acquire a lock that is owned by another thread.
questions.explain: Another thread's ownership blocks it; only its own lock can be re-acquired.
questions.rule: A thread may acquire an intrinsic lock it already owns, so synchronized code can call other synchronized code on the same lock.

questions.q: A Cart class has synchronized addItem(), which calls synchronized recalculate() on this. Thread T1 is inside addItem and owns the lock. Thread T2 now calls recalculate(). What happens?
options: T1 blocks at recalculate because T2 asked first
T1 continues into recalculate; T2 waits for the lock
T2 enters recalculate, because it is a different method
Both threads enter, since the methods differ
optionExplain: T1 is not blocked by itself, and T2 did not hold the lock.
T1 re-acquires its own lock, while T2 must wait.
Both methods need the same lock.
The lock is per object, not per method.
questions.explain: Owner continues, others wait.
questions.rule: A thread may acquire an intrinsic lock it already owns, so synchronized code can call other synchronized code on the same lock.

questions.q: Synchronized m1 calls an unsynchronized helper, which calls synchronized m2 on the same object, all in one thread. What happens at m2?
options: It blocks, because the helper broke the chain of calls
It proceeds only if the helper is also synchronized
It proceeds; reentrancy holds on indirect paths
It blocks for a moment and then continues
optionExplain: An unsynchronized helper does not release the lock.
The helper being unsynchronized does not matter.
The thread still owns the lock at that point.
No waiting arises for a lock the thread owns.
questions.explain: Ownership belongs to the thread, not to a single call.
questions.teaches: Reentrancy covers indirect calls: however long the chain between two synchronized sections, the thread keeps the lock it owns.
questions.rule: A thread may acquire an intrinsic lock it already owns, so synchronized code can call other synchronized code on the same lock.

questions.q: True or false: A synchronized method that calls itself recursively on the same object blocks itself on the second call.
questions.explain: The thread already owns the lock, so each nested call re-acquires it.
questions.teaches: A recursive synchronized method works because each nested call re-acquires a lock the thread already owns.
questions.rule: A thread may acquire an intrinsic lock it already owns, so synchronized code can call other synchronized code on the same lock.

questions.q: Which situations let the calling thread go on without waiting? Select all that apply.
options: Calling a synchronized method of the object it is already inside
Calling a synchronized method of an object whose lock another thread owns
Calling a synchronized method of another object whose lock nobody owns
Calling a synchronized method of the same object after another thread took the lock
optionExplain: It already owns that lock.
That lock is not free, so it blocks.
The lock is free, so it can be acquired.
The lock is no longer free, so it blocks.
questions.explain: A thread waits only for locks that another thread owns.
questions.rule: A thread may acquire an intrinsic lock it already owns, so synchronized code can call other synchronized code on the same lock.

questions.q: True or false: The statement c++ on an int field is executed by the virtual machine as one indivisible step.
questions.explain: It breaks into a retrieve, an increment and a store, so it is not atomic. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: Single reads and writes of references and most primitives are atomic, but compound actions such as c++ are not, and atomicity alone does not guarantee visibility.

questions.q: A read or write of a variable declared ____ is atomic even when the variable is a long or a double.
questions.explain: Volatile makes reads and writes atomic for every type.
questions.rule: Single reads and writes of references and most primitives are atomic, but compound actions such as c++ are not, and atomicity alone does not guarantee visibility.

questions.q: Which fields have atomic reads and writes? Select all that apply.
options: A reference variable
An int field
A long field that is not volatile
A long field declared volatile
optionExplain: Reads and writes of references are atomic.
Most primitives, including int, are covered.
long and double are excluded unless volatile.
Volatile makes its reads and writes atomic.
questions.explain: Everything except non-volatile long and double.
questions.rule: Single reads and writes of references and most primitives are atomic, but compound actions such as c++ are not, and atomicity alone does not guarantee visibility.

questions.q: Where does the tutorial say to find atomic methods that do not rely on synchronization?
options: Some classes of java.util.concurrent, not the core language itself
Static methods of the Thread class
Wait and notify on every object
The synchronized keyword on constructors
optionExplain: Some of them offer atomic methods without synchronization.
Thread's static methods concern the calling thread.
Those coordinate threads and do not make updates atomic.
Constructors cannot be synchronized.
questions.explain: The high-level concurrency classes offer atomic methods.
questions.teaches: Beyond the tutorial: the java.util.concurrent.atomic classes provide these single-variable atomic operations.
questions.rule: Single reads and writes of references and most primitives are atomic, but compound actions such as c++ are not, and atomicity alone does not guarantee visibility.

questions.q: A writer sets an int field ready to 1, and a reader loops until it sees 1. Writes of int are atomic. Why might the reader still fail to see 1?
options: Writes of int are not atomic, so the value is corrupted
Atomic means indivisible; it does not guarantee other threads see the write
Readers can only see values written before they started
The write is atomic only if the reader holds a lock
optionExplain: Writes of int are atomic; the value is not corrupted.
Atomicity does not remove the risk of memory consistency errors.
Visibility is not decided by when a reader starts.
Atomicity does not depend on the reader.
questions.explain: Atomic does not mean visible.
questions.teaches: Atomic means indivisible, not visible: a perfectly atomic write may still go unseen by another thread without a happens-before link.
questions.rule: Single reads and writes of references and most primitives are atomic, but compound actions such as c++ are not, and atomicity alone does not guarantee visibility.

questions.q: A teammate says: c++ is a single statement, so it is atomic and needs no protection. What is the flaw?
options: Statements can be atomic only inside synchronized methods
The statement is atomic but too slow for threads
A statement can hide several steps, such as retrieve, increase and store
The statement is atomic only for long variables
optionExplain: Atomicity is not limited to synchronized code.
Speed is not the issue.
Simple expressions can describe complex actions.
Longs are the exception, not the rule.
questions.explain: Count the steps, not the statements.
questions.rule: Single reads and writes of references and most primitives are atomic, but compound actions such as c++ are not, and atomicity alone does not guarantee visibility.

questions.q: Thread A writes 7 to a volatile int v. Later, thread B reads v. What does the tutorial promise about B?
options: It sees the latest change to v and the code that led to it
It may see an older value, as with any shared field
It is blocked until A releases a lock
It sees the value only if B declares v volatile too
optionExplain: A volatile write is visible to later reads.
That is the risk volatile removes.
Volatile involves no lock.
The variable is declared once, for all threads.
questions.explain: Volatile writes are visible to later readers. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: A write to a volatile variable happens before later reads of it, so readers also see what the writer did earlier.

questions.q: True or false: A write to a volatile variable happens before every later read of that same variable.
questions.explain: This is the guarantee the tutorial states.
questions.rule: A write to a volatile variable happens before later reads of it, so readers also see what the writer did earlier.

questions.q: A loader fills fields a, b and c of a config object, then sets a volatile boolean loaded to true. A reader sees loaded true and reads a, b and c. According to the tutorial, what will it see?
options: Only loaded, because volatile covers only that variable
The filled values, as earlier effects are visible too
Only c, the last field written before the flag
Values only if a, b and c are volatile too
optionExplain: The tutorial says more than the variable itself is visible.
A volatile read sees what led up to the write.
All earlier effects are visible, not only the last.
They need not be volatile themselves.
questions.explain: A volatile read brings the writer's earlier work into view.
questions.rule: A write to a volatile variable happens before later reads of it, so readers also see what the writer did earlier.

questions.q: How does the tutorial compare simple atomic access, such as volatile, with synchronized code?
options: It is slower but needs no care
It is the same in cost and care
It is more efficient but needs more care
It is always better and can replace all synchronization
optionExplain: The trade runs the other way round.
The tutorial describes a trade-off.
Whether the effort pays off depends on the application.
Memory consistency errors still need attention.
questions.explain: Cheaper, but the programmer carries more of the burden.
questions.teaches: Simple atomic access is more efficient than going through synchronized code but needs more care from the programmer, and whether it pays off depends on the size and complexity of the application.
questions.rule: A write to a volatile variable happens before later reads of it, so readers also see what the writer did earlier.

questions.q: A worker loop polls a stop flag that another thread sets. Declaring the flag ____ lets the worker see the change.
questions.explain: A volatile write is visible to later reads of the flag.
questions.teaches: In a case like this, a flag written by one thread and read by others can be made visible by declaring it volatile, without any lock.
questions.rule: A write to a volatile variable happens before later reads of it, so readers also see what the writer did earlier.

questions.q: True or false: Declaring a shared counter volatile makes c++ from two threads safe from lost updates.
questions.explain: Beyond the tutorial's wording, the guarantees cover individual reads and writes, and c++ is a retrieve, an increment and a store, whose steps from two threads can still interleave.
questions.rule: Volatile does not turn compound actions into atomic ones.

questions.q: Thread P owns lock A and waits for lock B. Thread Q owns lock B and waits for lock A. What is this situation called?
options: Deadlock
Reentrant synchronization
Thread interference
Time slicing
optionExplain: Each thread is blocked forever, waiting for the other.
Reentrancy concerns a thread re-acquiring its own lock.
Interference is mixed-up steps on shared data, not waiting.
Slicing is the operating system sharing a core.
questions.explain: A cycle of threads waiting for each other's locks is deadlock. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: Liveness is timely progress, and deadlock, its most common failure, leaves threads blocked forever waiting for one another.

questions.q: A concurrent application's ability to execute in a timely manner is called its ____.
questions.explain: Liveness is the term for timely execution.
questions.rule: Liveness is timely progress, and deadlock, its most common failure, leaves threads blocked forever waiting for one another.

questions.q: Which situation is a deadlock?
options: Two threads wait forever, each for a lock the other holds
One thread runs slowly because it gets fewer time slices
A thread loops quickly and finishes its task late
A thread finishes and releases its lock for the next
optionExplain: Both are blocked and neither can release what the other needs.
Slowness is not blocking forever.
It is making progress, only slowly.
Releasing a lock is the opposite of deadlock.
questions.explain: Deadlock means blocked forever, in a cycle.
questions.rule: Liveness is timely progress, and deadlock, its most common failure, leaves threads blocked forever waiting for one another.

questions.q: True or false: A single thread calling synchronized methods on one object can deadlock itself.
questions.explain: Locks are reentrant, so a thread is not blocked by a lock it already owns; deadlock involves two or more threads.
questions.teaches: Deadlock involves two or more threads; because locks are reentrant, a lone thread cannot block itself on a lock it owns.
questions.rule: Liveness is timely progress, and deadlock, its most common failure, leaves threads blocked forever waiting for one another.

questions.q: Which situation resembles a deadlock?
options: A driver waits at a red light that will turn green in a minute
Two drivers meet in a one-lane alley and each waits for the other
Two drivers keep swerving left and right and still block each other
A driver queues behind a slow truck on an open road
optionExplain: The wait ends by itself, so it is not deadlock.
Each waits on the other and neither can ever move.
They keep moving; deadlocked threads are blocked.
The truck will move on; the wait is not circular.
questions.explain: Deadlock is circular, permanent waiting.
questions.teaches: In deadlock the waiting is circular and permanent; waiting that ends by itself is only slowness or contention.
questions.rule: Liveness is timely progress, and deadlock, its most common failure, leaves threads blocked forever waiting for one another.

questions.q: True or false: If each thread released its first lock before asking for the second, the circular wait of this deadlock could not form.
questions.explain: A thread that holds nothing while it waits cannot be part of a cycle of waiting.
questions.rule: Deadlock needs threads that hold a lock while waiting for another.

questions.q: Both bow methods are synchronized, and each calls bowBack on the other friend. Thread 1 runs alphonse.bow(gaston) while thread 2 runs gaston.bow(alphonse). What is the likely outcome?
options: Both threads block forever, each holding the lock the other needs
Both print and finish quickly
One thread throws an exception and ends
The second thread is skipped
optionExplain: Each waits for a lock the other holds.
That needs one bow to finish before the other starts.
Nothing throws; the threads wait.
Threads are not skipped; both start.
questions.explain: Holding one lock while waiting for another can deadlock. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: Deadlock arises when each thread holds one object's lock and, while holding it, calls a synchronized method of another object whose lock the other thread holds.

questions.q: Put the events of the bowing deadlock in order.
items: Thread 1 enters alphonse.bow and holds Alphonse's lock
Thread 2 enters gaston.bow and holds Gaston's lock
Thread 1 calls gaston.bowBack and waits
Thread 2 calls alphonse.bowBack and waits
questions.explain: Each thread takes its own friend's lock first and then waits on the other's.
questions.rule: Deadlock arises when each thread holds one object's lock and, while holding it, calls a synchronized method of another object whose lock the other thread holds.

questions.q: Account objects have a synchronized send(Account to) that calls to.receive(this), also synchronized. Thread 1 runs a.send(b) while thread 2 runs b.send(a). What can happen?
options: They cannot, since send and receive are different methods
They can deadlock, like the bowing friends
They cannot, since the accounts have different names
They deadlock only if a third thread joins in
optionExplain: The locks, not the method names, decide.
Each holds one account's lock and waits for the other's.
Names play no part in locking.
Two threads are enough.
questions.explain: Two threads and two locks taken in opposite order can deadlock.
questions.rule: Deadlock arises when each thread holds one object's lock and, while holding it, calls a synchronized method of another object whose lock the other thread holds.

questions.q: True or false: If only the thread running alphonse.bow(gaston) is started, with no second thread, it completes.
questions.explain: Gaston's lock is free when bowBack is called, so the single thread gets it and finishes.
questions.teaches: The same code that deadlocks with two overlapping threads completes with one, so deadlock comes from the interaction of timing and lock ownership, not from one method alone.
questions.rule: Deadlock arises when each thread holds one object's lock and, while holding it, calls a synchronized method of another object whose lock the other thread holds.

questions.q: Beyond the tutorial: threads X and Y both lock A first and then lock B. Could they deadlock the way the friends did?
options: Yes, any two threads using two locks can deadlock
Yes, because both lock A first
No, since neither holds B while waiting for A
No, but only because locks are reentrant
optionExplain: The friends deadlocked because they took the locks in opposite orders.
Sharing the first lock creates a queue, not a cycle.
The thread holding A can always go on to take B, so no cycle forms.
Reentrancy concerns one thread; it plays no part here.
questions.explain: A cycle of waiting needs opposite orders.
questions.teaches: Beyond the tutorial: when every thread takes the locks in the same order, no cycle of waiting can form, so the circular wait of the friends does not arise.
questions.rule: Deadlock arises when each thread holds one object's lock and, while holding it, calls a synchronized method of another object whose lock the other thread holds.

questions.q: A student lists causes of the bowing deadlock. Which listed causes are wrong? Select all that apply.
options: Both bow calls run at the same time on separate threads
The println inside bow blocks forever
The two Friend objects share a single lock
Each thread holds its own friend's lock while asking for the other's
optionExplain: Correct cause: the overlap is needed.
Wrong: printing is not what blocks; the lock requests do.
Wrong: each object has its own lock, which is why each thread holds a different one.
Correct cause: this is the hold-and-wait.
questions.explain: The cause is hold-and-wait on two separate locks, not printing or a shared lock.
questions.rule: Deadlock arises when each thread holds one object's lock and, while holding it, calls a synchronized method of another object whose lock the other thread holds.

questions.q: One thread keeps calling a synchronized method that takes a long time. Other threads need the same object briefly but often find it taken. What problem is this?
options: Starvation
Deadlock
Thread interference
A memory consistency error
optionExplain: Greedy long holds deny the others regular access.
No cycle of threads waiting for each other exists here.
Synchronization prevents mixed-up steps; the issue is waiting.
The others do get a consistent view when they get in; they get in rarely.
questions.explain: Long holds by one thread can starve the rest. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: Starvation means a thread rarely gets the shared resource it needs because other threads hold it for long stretches.

questions.q: True or false: According to the tutorial, starvation is more common than deadlock.
questions.explain: The tutorial says starvation and livelock are much less common than deadlock.
questions.rule: Starvation means a thread rarely gets the shared resource it needs because other threads hold it for long stretches.

questions.q: A job thread keeps a print queue locked for minutes at a time, again and again. A status thread that needs the queue for a moment seldom gets in. Which change addresses the cause?
options: Make the status thread sleep longer between tries
Shorten the time the job thread holds the lock
Start a second job thread to share the work
Declare the queue volatile
optionExplain: Sleeping does not stop the long holds.
Greedy long holds are the cause the tutorial names.
More long holders add more competition.
Volatile concerns visibility, not how long a lock is held.
questions.explain: Starvation is cured at the greedy holder.
questions.rule: Starvation means a thread rarely gets the shared resource it needs because other threads hold it for long stretches.

questions.q: A method spends 10 ms updating shared fields and 5 s on slow input and output. Which restructuring lowers the risk of starving other threads?
options: Hold the lock for the shared updates only
Hold the lock for the whole method, so the work stays together
Hold the lock for the input and output only
Remove the lock and let threads sort it out
optionExplain: Shorter holds leave other threads more chances to get in.
A long hold is what starves others.
That would lengthen the hold and leave the fields unprotected.
Shared updates still need protection.
questions.explain: Hold locks only as long as the shared work needs.
questions.teaches: Holding a lock only for the work that needs it, as a synchronized statement allows, leaves less time for other threads to be starved.
questions.rule: Starvation means a thread rarely gets the shared resource it needs because other threads hold it for long stretches.

questions.q: Sort each situation by whether it is starvation.

items.t: One thread holds a busy resource for long stretches and others rarely get it
A thread waits a short time and then gets its turn
A thread calling a long synchronized method over and over blocks the others each time
Two threads each hold a lock the other needs

questions.explain: Starvation is uneven, repeated denial of access; a brief wait or a circular wait is something else.
questions.teaches: Brief waits and circular waits are different problems from starvation, which is about repeated, uneven denial of access.
questions.rule: Starvation means a thread rarely gets the shared resource it needs because other threads hold it for long stretches.

questions.q: True or false: If the greedy thread is changed to call the long synchronized method only now and then, the other threads are blocked less often.
questions.explain: Fewer long holds mean fewer chances to find the lock taken.
questions.rule: Fewer long holds, less starvation.

questions.q: Two people in a corridor each step aside for the other, then each steps aside again, over and over without passing. Which problem is this?
options: Deadlock
Thread interference
Livelock
Time slicing
optionExplain: Deadlocked threads are blocked; these people keep moving.
Interference is mixed-up steps on shared data.
They keep responding to each other and do not get past.
Slicing is the operating system sharing a core.
questions.explain: Constant mutual reaction without progress is livelock. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: In livelock the threads stay active, responding to each other, but make no progress; in deadlock they are blocked.

questions.q: Match each liveness problem to its description.
pairs: Threads are blocked forever waiting for one another
Threads keep responding to each other and make no progress
A thread rarely gets access to a resource that greedy threads hold
questions.explain: Each problem blocks progress in a different way.
questions.rule: In livelock the threads stay active, responding to each other, but make no progress; in deadlock they are blocked.

questions.q: Two threads, on seeing a conflict, each back off and retry at the same moment, again and again, without ever succeeding. Both stay busy. Which problem is this?
options: Deadlock
Livelock
Starvation
A memory consistency error
optionExplain: Deadlocked threads are blocked, not busy.
They keep reacting to each other but make no progress.
No greedy thread is holding a resource for long.
The issue is a pattern of reactions, not stale data.
questions.explain: Busy but stuck is livelock.
questions.rule: In livelock the threads stay active, responding to each other, but make no progress; in deadlock they are blocked.

questions.q: Which observations match livelock rather than deadlock? Select all that apply.
options: The threads are active and reacting to each other
No thread makes real progress
Each thread is blocked forever on a lock
One thread holds a lock for long stretches while others rarely get it
optionExplain: Livelocked threads are not blocked.
Both problems share this.
That describes deadlock.
That describes starvation.
questions.explain: Livelock is activity without progress.
questions.teaches: Because livelocked threads stay active, they use processor time while achieving nothing, whereas deadlocked threads sit blocked.
questions.rule: In livelock the threads stay active, responding to each other, but make no progress; in deadlock they are blocked.

questions.q: Beyond the tutorial: two threads retry in lockstep and collide every time. Which change would most plausibly break the pattern?
options: Make both retry faster
Make both retry at the same fixed time
Add the synchronized keyword to the retry
Let each wait a random time
optionExplain: Faster identical retries repeat the same collisions.
Identical timing keeps the lockstep.
Locking does not change the matching reactions.
Different responses stop the mirror-image cycle.
questions.explain: Break the symmetry of the responses.
questions.teaches: Beyond the tutorial: because livelock comes from threads reacting identically to one another, making the responses differ, for example with a random wait, can break it.
questions.rule: In livelock the threads stay active, responding to each other, but make no progress; in deadlock they are blocked.

questions.q: True or false: In the corridor picture, if Gaston stood still while Alphonse stepped aside, they would stop blocking each other.
questions.explain: One of them no longer reacts, so the mirrored cycle ends.
questions.rule: Livelock needs both sides to keep reacting.

questions.q: Thread B must not go on until thread A sets a flag to true. Which approach wastes the most processor time?
options: B runs an empty loop that keeps testing the flag
B suspends until A signals that the flag changed
B is started only after A has finished, using join
B sleeps for a long time and then checks once
optionExplain: The loop uses the processor on every pass while nothing changes.
A suspended thread uses no processor time.
B does not run at all until A is done.
A long sleep leaves the processor free.
questions.explain: Spinning burns processor time while waiting. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: A guarded block waits for a condition before going on, and spinning in an empty loop to do so wastes processor time.

questions.q: True or false: A guarded block is a block that waits for a condition to become true before it goes on.
questions.explain: The guard polls a condition that must hold before the block can proceed.
questions.rule: A guarded block waits for a condition before going on, and spinning in an empty loop to do so wastes processor time.

questions.q: Sort each way of waiting by whether it wastes processor time.

items.t: An empty while loop that tests a flag
Suspending until another thread signals
Calling join on a thread
A tight loop that keeps re-reading a variable

questions.explain: Loops that keep testing use the processor; suspended threads do not.
questions.rule: A guarded block waits for a condition before going on, and spinning in an empty loop to do so wastes processor time.

questions.q: A thread spins on a plain boolean field that another thread sets to true. Beyond wasted time, what is the tutorial-based worry?
options: The field is deleted when the loop starts
Without happens-before, no guarantee of seeing it
The spinner is blocked until the other thread ends
The other thread cannot write a boolean field
optionExplain: Nothing deletes the field.
Visibility still needs a guarantee.
A spinning thread is running, not blocked.
Writes of booleans are allowed.
questions.explain: A spin on a plain field also lacks a visibility guarantee.
questions.teaches: A spin on a plain field has no guarantee of ever seeing the other thread's change, because nothing links the write to the read.
questions.rule: A guarded block waits for a condition before going on, and spinning in an empty loop to do so wastes processor time.

questions.q: A kitchen display thread should show an order only after the cook thread marks it ready. Which design avoids burning processor time?
options: The display thread loops re-checking the order status continually
The display thread shows every order at once, before it is ready
The display thread suspends until the cook signals
The cook thread runs the display code itself and ends
optionExplain: That is busy waiting.
This breaks the condition instead of waiting for it.
Suspension wastes nothing while the order is not ready.
This avoids coordination by merging the work.
questions.explain: Wait by suspending and be woken by a signal.
questions.teaches: Coordination should suspend the waiting thread and wake it by a signal rather than make it keep asking.
questions.rule: A guarded block waits for a condition before going on, and spinning in an empty loop to do so wastes processor time.

questions.q: True or false: If more threads spin on the same condition, more processor time is wasted.
questions.explain: Each spinning thread uses processor time on every pass.
questions.rule: Each spinner adds to the waste.

questions.q: A thread must pause until another thread sets a flag, without wasting processor time. Which pair of calls does the tutorial recommend?
options: wait in a loop in the waiter, notifyAll in the setter
sleep in the waiter, and join in the thread that sets the flag
interrupt in the waiter, and start in the thread that sets the flag
wait in the setter, and notifyAll in the waiter
optionExplain: The waiter suspends, and the setter wakes it after changing the condition.
Sleep and join do not signal a changed condition.
Neither call coordinates on a condition.
The roles are reversed: the waiter must be the one to wait.
questions.explain: The waiter waits; the changer notifies. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: Inside a synchronized method, wait in a loop that re-tests the condition, and have the other thread set the condition and call notifyAll.

questions.q: After changing the condition, the second thread calls ____ to wake all threads waiting on the lock.
questions.explain: notifyAll wakes every thread waiting on that lock.
questions.rule: Inside a synchronized method, wait in a loop that re-tests the condition, and have the other thread set the condition and call notifyAll.

questions.q: Put the steps of a guarded wait in order.
items: The waiter, inside a synchronized method, tests the condition and finds it false
It calls wait, which releases the lock and suspends it
Another thread acquires the lock, sets the condition and calls notifyAll
The waiter reacquires the lock and returns from wait
It tests the condition again before going on
questions.explain: The cycle is test, wait, signal, wake, and test again.
questions.rule: Inside a synchronized method, wait in a loop that re-tests the condition, and have the other thread set the condition and call notifyAll.

questions.q: wait throws InterruptedException, and the tutorial's joy example has an empty catch block. Why is that acceptable there?
options: Interrupts cannot reach a thread that is in wait
An empty catch block cancels the interrupt for good
The exception is thrown only when notifyAll is called
The condition matters, and the loop re-tests it
optionExplain: A waiting thread can be interrupted; that is why the exception exists.
The block does not undo anything.
It signals an interrupt, not a notification.
The guard loop makes the wake-up reason unimportant.
questions.explain: The loop turns any wake-up into a re-check.
questions.teaches: wait can throw InterruptedException, which the tutorial's guard may ignore because the loop re-tests the condition anyway.
questions.rule: Inside a synchronized method, wait in a loop that re-tests the condition, and have the other thread set the condition and call notifyAll.

questions.q: A mail room has several clerk threads waiting for a parcel, and one delivery thread. Which clerk code is correct?
options: synchronized take: if (empty) wait();
synchronized take: while (empty) wait();
take, not synchronized: while (empty) wait();
synchronized take: while (empty) { }
optionExplain: After a wake-up the parcel may already be taken, so an if is not enough.
The loop makes each woken clerk re-check, so one that finds no parcel waits again.
wait needs the caller to own the lock.
That spins instead of waiting.
questions.explain: Use while, not if, and hold the lock.
questions.teaches: With several waiters, one notifyAll can wake several of them although only one parcel is available; the loop makes the others go back to waiting.
questions.rule: Inside a synchronized method, wait in a loop that re-tests the condition, and have the other thread set the condition and call notifyAll.

questions.q: A student writes: void waitForJoy() { if (!joy) { wait(); } use(); } Which mistakes does the code contain? Select all that apply.
options: The method is not synchronized, so wait runs without owning the lock
The condition is tested with if instead of a loop
The code tests a condition at all
The code calls wait
optionExplain: wait needs the intrinsic lock of the object.
After a wake-up the condition may not hold.
Testing the condition is the point of a guard.
Calling wait is the right way to suspend.
questions.explain: Two mistakes: no lock, and an if in place of a loop.
questions.rule: Inside a synchronized method, wait in a loop that re-tests the condition, and have the other thread set the condition and call notifyAll.

questions.q: True or false: In a producer-consumer pair sharing one slot, the producer may deliver a new message before the consumer has taken the previous one.
questions.explain: The coordination rule forbids it: the producer waits until the slot has been emptied. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: A shared object with a full-or-empty flag, synchronized put and take, wait loops and notifyAll lets one thread hand data to another in turn.

questions.q: True or false: In Drop, the flag empty starts out true.
questions.explain: Initially there is nothing to take, so empty is true.
questions.rule: A shared object with a full-or-empty flag, synchronized put and take, wait loops and notifyAll lets one thread hand data to another in turn.

questions.q: Put the steps of a successful put, called while empty is true, in order.
items: The producer calls put and finds no need to wait
put sets empty to false
put stores the message
put calls notifyAll to wake waiting threads
questions.explain: put changes the state, stores the data and then signals.
questions.rule: A shared object with a full-or-empty flag, synchronized put and take, wait loops and notifyAll lets one thread hand data to another in turn.

questions.q: Why does take also call notifyAll, even though it only removes the message?
options: To wake the consumer itself, so that it reads the message again
To clear the message so that it can be collected
To wake a producer waiting in put, now that the slot is empty
To stop the producer from calling put again
optionExplain: The consumer is already running.
Notification does not clear anything.
Each method frees the other kind of thread.
The producer needs to be woken, not stopped.
questions.explain: Each side signals the other when it changes the state.
questions.teaches: Both methods call notifyAll because each one changes the state that the other kind of thread is waiting for: take frees the producer and put frees the consumer.
questions.rule: A shared object with a full-or-empty flag, synchronized put and take, wait loops and notifyAll lets one thread hand data to another in turn.

questions.q: Instead of writing a new class like Drop for real code, what does the tutorial recommend?
options: Look in the Collections Framework for a ready class
Copy Drop and add a larger array for the messages
Remove the synchronization to make the hand-off faster
Use sleep loops in place of wait and notifyAll
optionExplain: A blocking queue from java.util.concurrent can replace the hand-written Drop.
The tutorial says Drop only demonstrates guarded blocks.
Without it the hand-off would be unsafe.
Busy loops are what guarded blocks avoid.
questions.explain: Prefer a standard class to a hand-written hand-off.
questions.teaches: A blocking queue from java.util.concurrent can replace a hand-written Drop: its put blocks when the queue is full and its take blocks when it is empty.
questions.rule: A shared object with a full-or-empty flag, synchronized put and take, wait loops and notifyAll lets one thread hand data to another in turn.

questions.q: The producer is changed so that it does not send the DONE marker. The consumer takes until it sees DONE. What happens after the four messages?
options: The consumer ends by itself after four messages
The consumer repeats the last message forever
The producer is woken to send DONE for it
The consumer waits in take for good
optionExplain: It stops only when it sees DONE.
take returns messages that were put, not copies.
Nothing makes the producer send it.
Without the marker it has no way to know the stream has ended.
questions.explain: The DONE marker tells the consumer to stop.
questions.rule: A shared object with a full-or-empty flag, synchronized put and take, wait loops and notifyAll lets one thread hand data to another in turn.

questions.q: Several threads read a configuration object that is not modified after it is built. Which statement is most accurate?
options: No inconsistent state exists, as its state does not change
They must still lock it, because reads can interfere with each other
They see a different copy each, since threads do not share objects
They can see it half-updated while the program starts up
optionExplain: An immutable object has only one state to observe.
Reads interfere only when something changes the data.
Threads of one process do share objects.
After construction nothing updates it.
questions.explain: No changes after construction, no inconsistent view. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: Immutable objects need no protection from interference or inconsistent views, and their extra object creation is often cheaper than feared.

questions.q: True or false: An immutable object's state cannot change after it is constructed.
questions.explain: This is the definition the tutorial gives.
questions.rule: Immutable objects need no protection from interference or inconsistent views, and their extra object creation is often cheaper than feared.

questions.q: A team hesitates to make a Point class immutable, because every move would create a new Point. Which tutorial argument answers the worry?
options: New objects are free, so the cost does not exist
The cost is often overestimated and offset
Mutable objects cannot be used with threads at all
Point objects are too small to matter to anyone
optionExplain: The tutorial calls the cost overestimated, not zero.
Less garbage-collection overhead and no protective code balance the cost.
They can, with the protection the tutorial describes.
Size is not the tutorial's argument.
questions.explain: The cost is real but often smaller than the savings.
questions.rule: Immutable objects need no protection from interference or inconsistent views, and their extra object creation is often cheaper than feared.

questions.q: An immutable Price object must produce a lowered price. What should its applyDiscount method do?
options: Change the stored amount in place and return nothing
Throw an exception, since a price cannot be lowered
Return a new Price and leave the original unchanged
Change the amount and lock the object for readers
optionExplain: That would make the object mutable.
Producing a new value is allowed.
Operations on immutable objects yield new objects.
Locking does not make a changing object immutable.
questions.explain: Immutable means new object, not changed object.
questions.teaches: Operations on an immutable object produce new objects instead of changing the old one, so every holder of the old object still sees the old state.
questions.rule: Immutable objects need no protection from interference or inconsistent views, and their extra object creation is often cheaper than feared.

questions.q: Sort each concern by whether immutability removes it.

items.t: A reader seeing half of an update
Two threads losing each other's updates to one object
The cost of creating replacement objects
The need to allocate memory for each new version

questions.explain: No updates means no half-updates or lost updates; replacements still cost something to create.
questions.teaches: Immutability removes update problems by removing updates, and it pays for that in object creation, a cost the tutorial argues is often modest.
questions.rule: Immutable objects need no protection from interference or inconsistent views, and their extra object creation is often cheaper than feared.

questions.q: A colleague makes four claims about immutable objects. Which does the tutorial contradict? Select all that apply.
options: Creating a new object is so costly that immutability is too expensive
Immutable objects can still be corrupted by thread interference
Immutable objects need extra code to protect them from corruption
An immutable object's state is fixed once it is constructed
optionExplain: The tutorial says the cost is often overestimated.
The tutorial says they cannot be.
The tutorial lists not needing such code as a saving.
This agrees with the tutorial.
questions.explain: The tutorial favours immutable objects on all three disputed points.
questions.rule: Immutable objects need no protection from interference or inconsistent views, and their extra object creation is often cheaper than feared.

questions.q: Thread T reads a colour with two separate synchronized getter calls. Between the two calls another thread changes the colour. What does T hold?
options: A mix of a value from the old state and a value from the new
Two values from the old state, since each getter is synchronized
Two values from the new state, since the setter runs last
Nothing, because the second call fails with an exception
optionExplain: Each call was safe alone, but the pair spans two states.
Synchronization does not freeze the object between calls.
The first value was read before the change.
The call succeeds; the values just do not match.
questions.explain: Two synchronized calls are not one synchronized step. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: Synchronizing each method does not make a sequence of calls atomic; a caller that needs related values together must hold the object's lock across the calls.

questions.q: True or false: Making each getter synchronized guarantees that two calls in a row return values from the same state.
questions.explain: Another thread can change the object between the two calls.
questions.rule: Synchronizing each method does not make a sequence of calls atomic; a caller that needs related values together must hold the object's lock across the calls.

questions.q: A reader runs: int rgb = color.getRGB(); String name = color.getName(); with both getters synchronized. What fixes the possible mismatch?
options: Declare the two local variables final
Synchronize on color around both
Call getName before getRGB
Make getRGB static
optionExplain: Final locals change nothing about the object.
Holding color's lock across both calls blocks set in between.
The order does not remove the gap between calls.
A static method would lose access to the object's fields.
questions.explain: Lock the object across the whole sequence.
questions.rule: Synchronizing each method does not make a sequence of calls atomic; a caller that needs related values together must hold the object's lock across the calls.

questions.q: Put the events that produce a mismatched pair in order.
items: The reader calls getRGB and gets the old colour
Another thread calls set with a new colour and name
The reader calls getName and gets the new name
The reader now holds a colour and name that do not match
questions.explain: The gap between the two calls is where the other thread slips in.
questions.teaches: The window for a mismatch is the gap between the calls, however short it is, and only a lock held across both calls closes it.
questions.rule: Synchronizing each method does not make a sequence of calls atomic; a caller that needs related values together must hold the object's lock across the calls.

questions.q: A BankAccount has synchronized getBalance and getOverdraftLimit. A report thread computes available funds from the two results, while another thread updates both values. What is the risk?
options: The getters fail, since two synchronized calls cannot be used together
The sum is always right, since each getter is synchronized
The numbers may come from different states
The update thread cannot run while the report thread is awake
optionExplain: Each call works; the combination is the problem.
Synchronized getters do not protect the pair.
Combining two getter results is a multi-call sequence.
Awake threads are not excluded.
questions.explain: Any computation that combines several getters needs one lock.
questions.teaches: Any computation that combines the results of several getter calls is a multi-call sequence, and it needs one lock held across all of them to see a single state.
questions.rule: Synchronizing each method does not make a sequence of calls atomic; a caller that needs related values together must hold the object's lock across the calls.

questions.q: True or false: If SynchronizedRGB were replaced by an immutable version, a caller reading getRGB and getName in two calls, both calls on the same immutable object, could still see a mismatched pair.
questions.explain: No call can change an immutable object, so both calls see the same state.
questions.rule: Immutability closes the gap between calls.

questions.q: Which design makes a class Temperature immutable under the tutorial's strategy?
options: A final class with a private final field and no setter
A public field with a comment asking callers not to change it
A private field with a synchronized setter
A non-final class with final fields
optionExplain: It follows the first three rules.
Nothing enforces the comment.
A setter makes the object changeable.
