Subclasses could still override methods.
questions.explain: No setters, final private fields, no overriding. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: For an immutable class provide no setters, make all fields final and private, and prevent overriding, for example with a final class.

questions.q: The tutorial says to make all fields final and ____.
questions.explain: Fields should be final and private.
questions.rule: For an immutable class provide no setters, make all fields final and private, and prevent overriding, for example with a final class.

questions.q: Class Point has public int x and y and a method setX. Which changes are needed to make it immutable under the strategy? Select all that apply.
options: Make x and y private and final
Remove setX
Declare the class final
Add the synchronized keyword to setX
optionExplain: Rule two: fields private and final.
Rule one: no setters.
Rule three: prevent overriding.
A synchronized setter still changes the object.
questions.explain: Remove setters, lock down the fields, and block overriding.
questions.rule: For an immutable class provide no setters, make all fields final and private, and prevent overriding, for example with a final class.

questions.q: Why does the third rule matter even when all fields are final and private?
options: Final fields can be changed by any subclass constructor
A subclass could override and change behaviour
Private fields are visible to every subclass
Subclasses make the class run more slowly
optionExplain: Final fields cannot be reassigned after construction.
Overriding can undo what the fields promise.
Subclasses cannot see private fields.
Speed is not the concern.
questions.explain: Allowing overriding allows changing behaviour.
questions.teaches: A subclass can add changing behaviour by overriding methods, so allowing overriding can undo the immutability that the fields seem to promise.
questions.rule: For an immutable class provide no setters, make all fields final and private, and prevent overriding, for example with a final class.

questions.q: Beyond the tutorial's wording: a class has a private constructor, private final fields, no setters, and a static method of(int v) that returns new instances. Does it follow the third rule?
options: No, only a final class can follow the third rule
No, because factory methods allow overriding
Yes, but only if the class is also synchronized
Yes, it is the private-constructor alternative
optionExplain: The tutorial names the private constructor approach as another way.
Factory methods that return new instances do not allow overriding.
Synchronization plays no part in this rule.
Outside classes cannot extend a class whose only constructor is private.
questions.explain: A private constructor is another way to block subclassing.
questions.teaches: A class whose only constructor is private cannot be extended by outside classes, so factory methods give a way to control instances without declaring the class final.
questions.rule: For an immutable class provide no setters, make all fields final and private, and prevent overriding, for example with a final class.

questions.q: True or false: If the class is final but one of its fields is public and not final, it is still immutable under the strategy.
questions.explain: The second rule is broken, and any code can change the public field.
questions.rule: All the rules must hold together.

questions.q: A class stores in a field the list object that its constructor received. The caller keeps its own reference and later adds an element. What has happened to the class's state?
options: It changed, since the class shares the caller's list
It stayed the same, since the field is private
It stayed the same, since the constructor ran only once
It was copied automatically when the constructor ran
optionExplain: Both references lead to the same mutable object.
Private hides the field name, not the object it refers to.
The list itself can still change afterwards.
Java does not copy objects on assignment.
questions.explain: A shared mutable object leaks control. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: Keep no reference to a mutable object that outsiders can reach: copy on the way in and copy on the way out.

questions.q: True or false: A String field of an immutable class needs no copy of the object it refers to.
questions.explain: A String is itself immutable, so sharing it is safe.
questions.rule: Keep no reference to a mutable object that outsiders can reach: copy on the way in and copy on the way out.

questions.q: A getter that would expose an internal mutable array should return a ____ of it.
questions.explain: Returning a copy keeps the original out of outsiders' hands.
questions.rule: Keep no reference to a mutable object that outsiders can reach: copy on the way in and copy on the way out.

questions.q: A field is declared final and refers to a mutable list. Does final make the list's contents safe from change?
options: Yes, final stops every change to the object it refers to
Yes, but only for lists of numbers
No, final fixes the reference, not the list contents
No, because final fields cannot refer to objects at all
optionExplain: Final applies to the reference only.
The type of the elements does not matter.
The object it refers to can still change.
Final fields may refer to objects.
questions.explain: Final protects the reference, not the referred object.
questions.teaches: Final fixes which object a field refers to, not the state of that object, so a final field holding a mutable object does not by itself make the class immutable.
questions.rule: Keep no reference to a mutable object that outsiders can reach: copy on the way in and copy on the way out.

questions.q: A constructor receives a mutable Point object, but the class needs only its x and y numbers. What is the simplest way to follow the fourth rule?
options: Keep the Point in a private field and trust the caller
Keep the Point and synchronize every method
Keep the Point in a public field so callers can see it
Copy the numbers into final fields; keep no Point
optionExplain: The caller could still change it.
Locking does not stop the caller's own reference from changing it.
That exposes it further.
No reference to the mutable object remains.
questions.explain: Store values, not the mutable object.
questions.teaches: When only some values of an external object are needed, storing those values in final fields avoids holding the mutable object at all.
questions.rule: Keep no reference to a mutable object that outsiders can reach: copy on the way in and copy on the way out.

questions.q: A class meant to be immutable holds a private final int array. Which parts break the fourth rule? Select all that apply.
options: The constructor stores the caller's array in the field
A getter returns a clone of the array
A method set(index, value) writes into the array
A method getLength returns the array's length
optionExplain: The caller keeps a reference and can change it.
Fine: a copy is handed out.
This modifies the referred object.
Fine: a number reveals nothing changeable.
questions.explain: Storing the caller's array and modifying the array both break the rule.
questions.rule: Keep no reference to a mutable object that outsiders can reach: copy on the way in and copy on the way out.

questions.q: In an immutable colour class, what should invert do?
options: Return a new object holding the inverted values
Change the stored values and return nothing
Change the stored values and lock the object
Throw an exception, since inverting is not possible
optionExplain: The original stays unchanged and the new object carries the result.
That would make the object mutable.
Locking does not make it immutable.
Producing a new value is possible.
questions.explain: Immutable operations return new objects. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: Remove setters, make the class and fields final, and let operations such as invert return new objects instead of modifying the old one.

questions.q: Match each part of the SynchronizedRGB conversion to what the tutorial does with it.
pairs: Removed, since it changes the object arbitrarily
Kept, but now returns a new object
questions.explain: Each part is handled by one of the rules.
questions.rule: Remove setters, make the class and fields final, and let operations such as invert return new objects instead of modifying the old one.

questions.q: Code runs: ImmutableRGB c = new ImmutableRGB(10, 20, 30, label); c.invert(); and then reads c.getRGB(). Which colour values does c hold?
options: 245, 235, 225, since invert was called on c
10, 20, 30, since the result was discarded
0, 0, 0, since invert resets the object
The call fails to compile, since the result is unused
optionExplain: invert does not change c.
invert returns a new object and leaves c alone.
Nothing resets the object.
Ignoring a return value is allowed.
questions.explain: Calling invert without using the result does nothing visible.
questions.rule: Remove setters, make the class and fields final, and let operations such as invert return new objects instead of modifying the old one.

questions.q: True or false: ImmutableRGB needs its check that colour values are between 0 and 255 only in the constructor.
questions.explain: Values never change after construction, so a valid object stays valid.
questions.teaches: Since no method can change the values afterwards, validating once in the constructor guarantees that every existing object is valid for its whole life.
questions.rule: Remove setters, make the class and fields final, and let operations such as invert return new objects instead of modifying the old one.

questions.q: Beyond the tutorial: a shared immutable Config object must change when an admin edits it. Using the invert pattern, how can all threads come to use the new settings?
options: Change the fields of the existing Config in place
Create a new Config and keep the old one in use
Create a new Config and publish the shared reference
Make the Config class non-final so that edits are allowed
optionExplain: That would make it mutable.
Nothing then uses the new settings.
The old object stays as it was, and the reference to the new one must be made visible.
That removes the guarantees.
questions.explain: Replace the object, then publish the new reference.
questions.teaches: Beyond the tutorial: replacing an immutable object with a new one moves the changeable part to the shared reference, which other threads must be able to see, for example through a volatile field.
questions.rule: Remove setters, make the class and fields final, and let operations such as invert return new objects instead of modifying the old one.

questions.q: True or false: With ImmutableRGB, if thread A calls invert, thread B holding the same object sees its colour flip.
questions.explain: invert returns a new object and leaves the original, which B holds, unchanged.
questions.rule: Immutable objects never flip under a reader.

questions.q: Which group does the tutorial present as the higher-level concurrency features?
options: Locks, executors, collections, atomics, ThreadLocalRandom
synchronized, wait, notify, volatile and join
Pipes, sockets, ProcessBuilder, IPC and JVM flags
Runnable, Thread subclasses, sleep, interrupt, join and start
optionExplain: These are the five features the lesson goes on to cover.
These are the low-level tools met earlier.
These concern processes, not the higher-level thread tools.
These belong to the basic thread objects section.
questions.explain: Five tools make up the higher-level set. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: Reach for the java.util.concurrent tools when low-level threads and locks are not enough, especially in large, multi-core applications.

questions.q: Match each higher-level tool to what the tutorial says it does.
pairs: Support locking idioms that simplify many concurrent applications
Provide a high-level API for launching and managing threads
Make large collections easier to manage and can greatly reduce synchronization
Support lock-free operations on single variables with volatile-like memory effects
questions.explain: Each tool targets a different cost of low-level coordination.
questions.rule: Reach for the java.util.concurrent tools when low-level threads and locks are not enough, especially in large, multi-core applications.

questions.q: A server for thousands of simultaneous clients must make good use of many cores. Which level of tool does the tutorial point to?
options: The higher-level concurrent objects
Only the low-level thread API, written by hand
Only larger sleep times between tasks
Starting the server as a process per client
optionExplain: They are meant for massively concurrent applications.
The low-level API suits basic tasks.
Pausing does not use cores better.
That concerns processes, not the thread tools.
questions.explain: Big concurrent workloads call for the higher-level tools.
questions.rule: Reach for the java.util.concurrent tools when low-level threads and locks are not enough, especially in large, multi-core applications.

questions.q: Which feature does the tutorial describe as providing thread pool management suited to large-scale applications?
options: The synchronized keyword on methods
Executor implementations
ThreadLocalRandom
The volatile modifier on fields
optionExplain: It guards state, not pool management.
Executors give the pool management for large-scale use.
It generates random numbers with less contention.
It affects visibility of one variable.
questions.explain: Executors bring thread pool management.
questions.teaches: Executor implementations in java.util.concurrent provide thread pool management suitable for large-scale applications.
questions.rule: Reach for the java.util.concurrent tools when low-level threads and locks are not enough, especially in large, multi-core applications.

questions.q: True or false: A small utility that starts one background thread to print a message needs the higher-level tools.
questions.explain: The tutorial calls the low-level API adequate for very basic tasks.
questions.teaches: The higher-level tools are chosen by need, not because they are newer: a very basic task is served well enough by the low-level API.
questions.rule: Reach for the java.util.concurrent tools when low-level threads and locks are not enough, especially in large, multi-core applications.

questions.q: Sort each item by where it belongs.

items.t: synchronized methods
wait and notifyAll
Executors
Concurrent collections
Thread.start
Lock objects

questions.explain: The older primitives are part of the language and Thread; the executors, collections and locks come from the concurrent packages.
questions.rule: Reach for the java.util.concurrent tools when low-level threads and locks are not enough, especially in large, multi-core applications.

questions.q: A thread wants a lock but would rather do something else if it cannot get it at once. What can a Lock object do that synchronized code cannot?
options: Back out when the lock is not available
Allow two threads to own the lock together
Release itself when the thread ends
Make the thread run faster by raising its priority
optionExplain: tryLock returns instead of waiting.
Only one thread can own a Lock at a time.
A Lock is never released automatically; the thread must call unlock, so this is not a Lock feature.
Locks do not change priority.
questions.explain: Backing out is the advantage of Lock objects. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: A Lock object behaves like an intrinsic lock but can give up: tryLock and lockInterruptibly let a thread back out of acquiring.

questions.q: The Lock method that backs out if the lock is not immediately available is ____.
questions.explain: tryLock returns at once, or after a timeout if one is given.
questions.rule: A Lock object behaves like an intrinsic lock but can give up: tryLock and lockInterruptibly let a thread back out of acquiring.

questions.q: Match each need to the Lock feature that meets it.
pairs: Give up at once if the lock is taken
Wait a limited time and then give up
Give up if interrupted while waiting for the lock
questions.explain: Each way of backing out has its own method.
questions.rule: A Lock object behaves like an intrinsic lock but can give up: tryLock and lockInterruptibly let a thread back out of acquiring.

questions.q: Why does the tutorial's Safelock example release its locks in finally blocks?
options: Because finally blocks are the only place a Lock can be released
Because finally blocks wake up waiting threads automatically
So the locks are released on every path, including a failed second tryLock or an exception
Because Lock objects cannot be released in the code that acquired them
optionExplain: Locks can be released elsewhere, but finally is the safe place.
Finally does not wake any thread.
A Lock is released by an explicit call, which must run even on failure.
They can; the example does exactly that.
questions.explain: Release explicit locks in finally (idiom, beyond the tutorial's wording).
questions.teaches: Unlike a synchronized method, a Lock is released by an explicit call, so the call belongs in a finally block that runs even when an exception occurs.
questions.rule: A Lock object behaves like an intrinsic lock but can give up: tryLock and lockInterruptibly let a thread back out of acquiring.

questions.q: A thread waits for the lock of a shared resource but should give up after two seconds and report that the resource is busy. Which fits?
options: A synchronized block, which gives up after two seconds
tryLock with a two-second timeout
lockInterruptibly, which gives up after two seconds
An empty loop that counts for two seconds
optionExplain: A synchronized block waits until the lock is free.
A bounded wait followed by a report.
It backs out on an interrupt, not on a timer.
That wastes processor time and does not acquire anything.
questions.explain: A timeout turns an endless wait into a decision.
questions.teaches: A bounded wait for a lock lets the caller report failure or do something else instead of blocking with no limit.
questions.rule: A Lock object behaves like an intrinsic lock but can give up: tryLock and lockInterruptibly let a thread back out of acquiring.

questions.q: True or false: If another thread owns the lock, a call to lock.tryLock() with no arguments blocks the caller until the lock is released.
questions.explain: It backs out at once instead of waiting.
questions.rule: tryLock does not wait for an unavailable lock.

questions.q: Two threads each need locks A and B. Which strategy avoids deadlock by not waiting while holding one lock?
options: Try both with tryLock, releasing anything held on failure
Take A and then wait for B for as long as it takes
Take B and then A in one thread, and A and then B in the other
Take neither lock and let the threads sort it out
optionExplain: No thread waits while holding a lock.
That is hold-and-wait, the deadlock pattern.
Opposite orders invite a cycle of waiting.
The shared data would be left unprotected.
questions.explain: Do not wait while holding a lock. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: Acquire all needed locks with tryLock, and if any attempt fails, release what you hold and back out instead of waiting.

questions.q: Put the steps of impendingBow in order.
items: Call tryLock on its own lock
Call tryLock on the bower's lock
If only one lock was obtained, release it
Return true only if both locks were obtained
questions.explain: Try both, repair a partial result, then report.
questions.rule: Acquire all needed locks with tryLock, and if any attempt fails, release what you hold and back out instead of waiting.

questions.q: True or false: In Safelock, a thread that obtains its own lock but fails to obtain the other friend's lock keeps its own lock while it waits.
questions.explain: It releases the lock it holds and backs out.
questions.rule: Acquire all needed locks with tryLock, and if any attempt fails, release what you hold and back out instead of waiting.

questions.q: Beyond the tutorial: why might each bowing thread pause for a random short time before its next attempt?
options: To give the operating system time to delete unused locks
To keep the threads from retrying in lockstep
To make tryLock succeed more slowly and so more safely
To let the garbage collector release the Friend objects
optionExplain: Locks are not deleted by waiting.
Different timings break the mirrored pattern.
The pause does not change what tryLock does.
The pause has nothing to do with collection.
questions.explain: Backing off at different times breaks the symmetry.
questions.teaches: Beyond the tutorial: a random pause before each attempt helps keep the two threads out of lockstep, the pattern that would turn backing out into livelock.
questions.rule: Acquire all needed locks with tryLock, and if any attempt fails, release what you hold and back out instead of waiting.

questions.q: Two robots each need a hammer and a saw. A robot picks up the hammer, but the saw is already taken. Following the Safelock idea, what should it do?
options: Keep the hammer and wait for the saw
Take the saw from the other robot
Put down the hammer and retry
Stop working for good
optionExplain: This is hold-and-wait, as in the deadlock.
Nothing in the model allows taking an owned resource.
It stops holding one resource while wanting another.
Backing out is followed by another attempt.
questions.explain: Release what you hold when the rest is unavailable.
questions.teaches: Releasing the first resource when the second is unavailable breaks the hold-and-wait part of a deadlock.
questions.rule: Acquire all needed locks with tryLock, and if any attempt fails, release what you hold and back out instead of waiting.

questions.q: A student rewrites impendingBow. Which versions break the Safelock design? Select all that apply.
options: Calls the blocking lock method on its own lock and then on the bower's lock
Calls tryLock on both and releases any lock it got if one failed
Bows even when the second tryLock failed
Unlocks both locks in a finally block after bowing
optionExplain: Waiting while holding a lock brings back the deadlock.
This is the tutorial's design.
The model requires both locks before bowing.
This is the tutorial's design.
questions.explain: Keep both rules: try rather than wait, and bow only with both locks.
questions.rule: Acquire all needed locks with tryLock, and if any attempt fails, release what you hold and back out instead of waiting.

questions.q: A large application has to run 500 short tasks. Which approach does the tutorial suggest for managing the threads?
options: Pass the tasks to an executor that manages the threads
Create a Thread subclass for each task and start them all
Run all tasks inside one synchronized method
Give every task a larger sleep time
optionExplain: Executors separate thread management from the application.
This ties each task to its own thread.
Locking serialises the tasks without managing threads.
Pausing does not manage threads.
questions.explain: Let an executor own the threads. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: Hand tasks to an executor with execute instead of creating threads yourself, so thread management lives in one place.

questions.q: True or false: Calling e.execute(r) must create a brand-new thread for r.
questions.explain: The executor may reuse a worker thread or queue r until a worker is free.
questions.rule: Hand tasks to an executor with execute instead of creating threads yourself, so thread management lives in one place.

questions.q: Put the life of a task under an executor in order.
items: The application creates a task as a Runnable
The application passes the task to the executor with execute
The executor starts a thread, reuses a worker or queues the task
The task's run method executes
questions.explain: The application hands over the task, and the executor decides how it gets a thread.
questions.rule: Hand tasks to an executor with execute instead of creating threads yourself, so thread management lives in one place.

questions.q: Beyond the tutorial: a Thread object is itself a Runnable. If one is passed to execute, what should you expect?
options: The Thread starts itself and the executor is bypassed
The executor refuses it because it is not a Runnable
It runs as a plain task on a worker
The Thread gives its priority to the executor
optionExplain: Nothing in execute starts the passed object as a thread.
A Thread implements Runnable, so it is accepted.
The Thread fills the Runnable slot only.
Priority plays no part.
questions.explain: A Thread passed to an executor is just a task.
questions.teaches: Beyond the tutorial: since Thread implements Runnable, it can be passed to execute, but it then serves only as a task, which defeats the point of letting the executor manage threads.
questions.rule: Hand tasks to an executor with execute instead of creating threads yourself, so thread management lives in one place.

questions.q: A photo app creates a new thread for every thumbnail request and slows badly under load. What does the executor idea offer?
options: A guarantee that every thumbnail is made at the same speed
Threading policy can change without touching task code
A rule that each task now needs its own synchronized method
A way to avoid writing the thumbnail code
optionExplain: Executors make no such guarantee.
The executor can be replaced to change how threads are used.
Nothing of the kind is required.
The tasks still have to be written.
questions.explain: Separate the task from the threading policy.
questions.teaches: Because the application only hands over tasks, the executor can be changed to change the threading policy without changing the task code.
questions.rule: Hand tasks to an executor with execute instead of creating threads yourself, so thread management lives in one place.

questions.q: True or false: If the executor is replaced by a different implementation, every line that calls execute must be rewritten.
questions.explain: The calls use the same interface, so they stay as they are.
questions.rule: The interface hides the threading policy.

questions.q: A task must compute a number that the caller reads later. Which executor feature suits it?
options: submit with a Callable, which returns a Future
execute with a Runnable, which returns the number
scheduleAtFixedRate, which hands back the number
Subclassing Thread and returning from run
optionExplain: A Callable can return a value, retrieved through the Future.
A Runnable returns nothing.
It repeats a task; it is not for one result.
A run method returns nothing.
questions.explain: Results come back through a Future. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: Use execute for plain Runnables, submit when you want a Future or a result, and a scheduled executor for delayed or repeating tasks.

questions.q: True or false: ExecutorService is a subinterface of Executor.
questions.explain: It extends Executor with life-cycle management and submit.
questions.rule: Use execute for plain Runnables, submit when you want a Future or a result, and a scheduled executor for delayed or repeating tasks.

questions.q: A monitor must run a check every 10 seconds, indefinitely. Which method fits?
options: scheduleAtFixedRate
schedule with a ten-second delay
submit with a Callable
execute with a Runnable
optionExplain: It runs a task repeatedly at defined intervals.
It runs a task once after the delay.
It hands in a task to run once.
It launches a task once.
questions.explain: Repeating work needs a repeating schedule method.
questions.rule: Use execute for plain Runnables, submit when you want a Future or a result, and a scheduled executor for delayed or repeating tasks.

questions.q: How are variables that refer to executors typically declared?
options: With the name of the executor class that was created
As Thread variables, since executors manage threads
With one of the three executor interface types
As Runnable variables, since executors run tasks
optionExplain: Class types are not the typical choice.
An executor is not a Thread.
The tutorial says interface types, not executor classes.
An executor is not itself a task.
questions.explain: Declare by interface.
questions.teaches: Variables that refer to executor objects are typically declared with one of the three interface types, not with an executor class type.
questions.rule: Use execute for plain Runnables, submit when you want a Future or a result, and a scheduled executor for delayed or repeating tasks.

questions.q: Match each job in a small shop's software to the best executor feature.
pairs: Compute an invoice total and hand it back
submit with a Callable on an ExecutorService
Send a reminder once, ten minutes from now
questions.explain: Results need submit, one delay needs schedule, repetition needs a fixed-rate or fixed-delay method.
questions.teaches: schedule accepts a Runnable or a Callable, so even a delayed task can return a value.
questions.rule: Use execute for plain Runnables, submit when you want a Future or a result, and a scheduled executor for delayed or repeating tasks.

questions.q: True or false: Tasks that ignore interrupts can still be stopped promptly by an immediate shutdown.
questions.explain: Prompt shutdown relies on tasks handling interrupts correctly.
questions.rule: Shutdown needs interrupt-aware tasks.

questions.q: A server creates a new thread for every request, and a spike brings far more requests than the system can handle. What does the tutorial say may happen?
options: It may suddenly stop responding to all requests
It answers the extra requests faster than before
It answers only the first request and ignores the rest
It slows down only the extra requests
optionExplain: Thread overhead can exceed what the system can sustain.
More threads do not make the system faster.
Nothing selects the first request.
The overload can affect every request.
questions.explain: Unbounded thread creation can collapse the service. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: A fixed thread pool runs tasks on a set number of reusable workers and queues the rest, so heavy load slows the service instead of collapsing it.

questions.q: A thread pool is made of ____ threads, each of which can run many tasks one after another.
questions.explain: Worker threads are reused for many tasks.
questions.rule: A fixed thread pool runs tasks on a set number of reusable workers and queues the rest, so heavy load slows the service instead of collapsing it.

questions.q: A fixed pool has 3 workers and receives 8 tasks at once. The number of tasks waiting in the internal queue is ____.
questions.explain: Three run and the other five wait.
questions.rule: A fixed thread pool runs tasks on a set number of reusable workers and queues the rest, so heavy load slows the service instead of collapsing it.

questions.q: Match each Executors factory method to what it creates.
pairs: A pool with a set number of threads, extra tasks queued
An expandable pool, suited to many short-lived tasks
An executor that runs one task at a time
questions.explain: Each factory method makes a ready-made executor of one kind.
questions.teaches: The Executors factory methods build ready-made pools, and ThreadPoolExecutor and ScheduledThreadPoolExecutor exist for cases where none of them fits.
questions.rule: A fixed thread pool runs tasks on a set number of reusable workers and queues the rest, so heavy load slows the service instead of collapsing it.

questions.q: A call centre has 5 phone lines and 100 callers at once. Which statement best matches graceful degradation?
options: Every caller is cut off until the lines are free for all
Callers wait longer but each gets served
Extra lines appear without limit as callers arrive
Only the first five callers ever get served
optionExplain: That is the collapse the pool avoids.
Service slows under overload instead of failing for everyone.
That is unbounded growth.
Queued callers are served in turn.
questions.explain: Queue the excess instead of multiplying the threads.
questions.teaches: A pool's size is a limit you choose, and the queue absorbs demand beyond it, so overload makes service slower instead of failing.
questions.rule: A fixed thread pool runs tasks on a set number of reusable workers and queues the rest, so heavy load slows the service instead of collapsing it.

questions.q: True or false: If a worker in a fixed pool of four ends while still in use, the pool carries on with three workers.
questions.explain: The pool replaces the worker automatically.
questions.rule: A fixed pool keeps its set number of threads.

questions.q: Sort each need by the pool that suits it.

items.t: A steady limit on how many threads run at once
Many short-lived tasks arriving at unpredictable times
The thread count must not exceed a chosen number
The pool may expand as demand grows

questions.explain: A fixed pool caps the thread count; a cached pool expands for many short tasks.
questions.rule: A fixed thread pool runs tasks on a set number of reusable workers and queues the rest, so heavy load slows the service instead of collapsing it.

questions.q: A job can be split into smaller, similar pieces, again and again, and the machine has many cores. Which tool does the tutorial offer?
options: The fork/join framework
A ScheduledExecutorService
A guarded block with notifyAll
A volatile flag read by every core
optionExplain: It is built for work that splits recursively and for multiple processors.
It runs tasks after delays or at intervals.
It coordinates two threads over a condition.
It shares one value; it does not divide work.
questions.explain: Recursive splitting plus many cores suggests fork/join. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: Split work recursively until pieces are small enough to run directly, run them in a ForkJoinPool, and let idle workers steal queued tasks.

questions.q: Match each fork/join term to its role.
pairs: A task that returns a result
A task that returns no result
The pool that runs the tasks, with work stealing
Passes a task to the pool to run
questions.explain: Two task types, one pool, one way in.
questions.rule: Split work recursively until pieces are small enough to run directly, run them in a ForkJoinPool, and let idle workers steal queued tasks.

questions.q: A task prints every file name in a folder tree, splitting the work by subfolder. Nothing is returned. Which base class fits?
options: RecursiveAction
RecursiveTask
ScheduledExecutorService
ThreadLocalRandom
optionExplain: It is the type for tasks that return no result.
It is the type for tasks that return a result.
It is an interface for timing tasks.
It generates random numbers.
questions.explain: No result means RecursiveAction.
questions.rule: Split work recursively until pieces are small enough to run directly, run them in a ForkJoinPool, and let idle workers steal queued tasks.

questions.q: According to the tutorial, ____, introduced in Java SE 8, sorts large arrays using fork/join.
questions.explain: The tutorial names Arrays.parallelSort as a library use of fork/join.
questions.teaches: Parts of the standard library use fork/join internally, for example Arrays.parallelSort in Java SE 8, which the tutorial says sorts large arrays faster than sequential sorting on multiprocessor systems.
questions.rule: Split work recursively until pieces are small enough to run directly, run them in a ForkJoinPool, and let idle workers steal queued tasks.

questions.q: A task counts the words in a very long text. Put its logic in order.
items: If the range of the text is small enough, count its words directly
Otherwise split the range in two
Run both halves and wait for their results
Add the two counts together and return the sum
questions.explain: Direct work for small pieces, otherwise split, wait, combine.
questions.teaches: A RecursiveTask combines the partial results after waiting for both pieces, so splitting is followed by a combining step.
questions.rule: Split work recursively until pieces are small enough to run directly, run them in a ForkJoinPool, and let idle workers steal queued tasks.

questions.q: True or false: If a task's compute method does the whole work directly without ever splitting, the pool spreads that work across all cores.
questions.explain: One unsplit task is one piece of work on one worker.
questions.rule: Without splitting there is nothing for other workers to take.

questions.q: A student writes the logic as: if my work is large enough, do it directly; otherwise split it in two. What is wrong?
options: Splitting in two is not allowed; pieces must be split in three
Work may never be done directly inside a task
The test is reversed: small work is done directly
Nothing; the order of the cases does not matter
optionExplain: The tutorial splits into two pieces.
Direct work is the base case.
Splitting stops when pieces are small enough.
The condition decides when splitting stops.
questions.explain: Small enough means do it; otherwise split.
questions.rule: Split work recursively until pieces are small enough to run directly, run them in a ForkJoinPool, and let idle workers steal queued tasks.

questions.q: In ForkBlur, a task's segment length is below the threshold. What does compute do?
options: It blurs the segment directly
It splits the segment into three parts
It waits for another task to finish
It returns a result to the pool
optionExplain: Small segments are done without splitting.
The segment is halved, and only when it is large.
A direct blur needs no waiting.
ForkBlur is a RecursiveAction and returns nothing.
questions.explain: Below the threshold, work directly. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: Below the threshold a task works directly; at or above it, the task splits in half and runs both halves with invokeAll.

questions.q: ForkBlur extends ____ because it writes into an array and returns no result.
questions.explain: RecursiveAction is the type for tasks without a result.
questions.rule: Below the threshold a task works directly; at or above it, the task splits in half and runs both halves with invokeAll.

questions.q: With a threshold of 100,000, a task has a segment of 300,000 pixels. Each of the two pieces it creates holds ____ pixels.
questions.explain: Splitting in half gives two pieces of 150,000.
questions.rule: Below the threshold a task works directly; at or above it, the task splits in half and runs both halves with invokeAll.

questions.q: When ForkBlur reads neighbouring pixels, what is the job of the Math.min and Math.max calls?
options: They choose which of two tasks runs first
They keep neighbour indexes inside the array
They make the blur window wider at the edges
They make the threshold smaller for small images
optionExplain: Task order is not decided there.
Clamping prevents reads outside the array.
The window stays the same width.
The threshold is a fixed field.
questions.explain: Clamp indexes at the ends of the data.
questions.teaches: The direct blur clamps each neighbour index with Math.min and Math.max, so pixels near the ends of the array do not read outside it.
questions.rule: Below the threshold a task works directly; at or above it, the task splits in half and runs both halves with invokeAll.

questions.q: With the same threshold of 100,000, an image has 250,000 pixels. How many pieces are blurred directly?
options: 4 pieces of 62,500 pixels
2 pieces of 125,000 pixels
8 pieces of 31,250 pixels
1 piece of 250,000 pixels
optionExplain: 250,000 splits into 125,000 twice, and each of those splits into 62,500 twice.
125,000 is not below the threshold, so each splits again.
Splitting stops as soon as a piece is below the threshold.
That is not below the threshold, so it splits.
questions.explain: Halve until below the threshold.
questions.teaches: The number of direct pieces follows from halving until each piece is below the threshold, not from the number of cores.
questions.rule: Below the threshold a task works directly; at or above it, the task splits in half and runs both halves with invokeAll.

questions.q: True or false: Lowering the threshold to 1,000 produces more and smaller tasks.
questions.explain: Splitting continues until pieces are below the lower limit.
questions.rule: A lower threshold means more, smaller tasks.

questions.q: A worker should wait for jobs when none are available, and a producer should wait when the buffer is full. Which standard collection fits?
options: BlockingQueue
ConcurrentHashMap
ConcurrentSkipListMap
A plain array shared by both threads
optionExplain: It blocks or times out on a full add or an empty retrieve.
It is a map, not a queue of jobs.
It is a sorted map for approximate matches.
An array neither blocks nor orders access.
questions.explain: Waiting on empty or full is what a blocking queue does. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: Use the concurrent collections instead of hand-made locking: queues that block, and maps with atomic conditional operations.

questions.q: Match each collection to its description.
pairs: A first-in-first-out queue that blocks or times out when full or empty
A map with atomic add-if-absent and remove-if-present operations
questions.explain: Each name points to a familiar collection or interface.
questions.rule: Use the concurrent collections instead of hand-made locking: queues that block, and maps with atomic conditional operations.

questions.q: Several threads register a user id only if it is absent from a shared map. Which interface offers that as one atomic operation?
options: BlockingQueue
ConcurrentMap
Executor
Lock
optionExplain: It is a queue, not a map.
It defines add-if-absent as an atomic operation.
It launches tasks and holds no data.
It guards code; it does not define map operations.
questions.explain: Atomic conditional map operations come from ConcurrentMap.
questions.rule: Use the concurrent collections instead of hand-made locking: queues that block, and maps with atomic conditional operations.

questions.q: True or false: A consumer that removes an object from a BlockingQueue can rely on seeing the fields the producer set before it added the object.
questions.explain: Adding an object happens before later access to or removal of it.
questions.teaches: These collections create a happens-before relationship between adding an object and later accessing or removing it, so what the producer did before the add is visible to the consumer.
questions.rule: Use the concurrent collections instead of hand-made locking: queues that block, and maps with atomic conditional operations.

questions.q: A hotel cache keyed by room number must reserve a room only if nobody holds it. Which approach is safer?
options: Call get, test the result, then call put as three separate steps
Call put first and undo it if somebody else had the room
Use the map's atomic add-if-absent operation as one step
Skip the test, since a map keeps one value per key
optionExplain: Another thread can reserve the room between the calls.
Another thread may see the wrong reservation meanwhile.
One atomic step leaves no gap for another thread.
A later put would overwrite an earlier reservation.
questions.explain: Close the gap with a single atomic operation.
questions.teaches: A check followed by a separate put is a multi-call sequence that other threads can interleave with; the atomic conditional operation closes that gap.
questions.rule: Use the concurrent collections instead of hand-made locking: queues that block, and maps with atomic conditional operations.

questions.q: True or false: If a program calls get on a ConcurrentHashMap and then, in a separate call, puts a value based on the result, the two calls together form one atomic step.
questions.explain: Only the single atomic operations are atomic; two separate calls can be interleaved.
questions.rule: Atomicity belongs to single operations, not to sequences of them.

questions.q: Many threads increment a shared counter and no update may be lost. Which versions does the tutorial show as thread-safe? Select all that apply.
options: Synchronized increment and value methods
A plain int with c++ in an ordinary method
An AtomicInteger updated with incrementAndGet
A plain int updated by only one thread at a time by luck
optionExplain: The tutorial shows this version as thread-safe.
This suffers interference.
The tutorial shows this version as thread-safe.
Luck is not a safe strategy.
questions.explain: Both a synchronized counter and an atomic counter avoid lost updates. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: Replace a plain shared variable by an atomic variable and update it with its atomic methods instead of locks.

questions.q: AtomicCounter keeps its value in an ____ and updates it with incrementAndGet.
questions.explain: AtomicInteger supplies the atomic update methods.
questions.rule: Replace a plain shared variable by an atomic variable and update it with its atomic methods instead of locks.

questions.q: A counter has: private int visits; void visit() { visits++; } int total() { return visits; }. Which rewrite makes it safe without synchronized?
options: AtomicInteger visits, with incrementAndGet() and get()
Keep the int and add a comment asking threads not to overlap
Make visits an AtomicInteger but do a get and then a separate set
Make visits final and keep visits++ as it is
optionExplain: Both operations use the atomic methods.
Comments do not stop interleaving.
Two separate calls are not one atomic step.
A final int cannot be incremented.
questions.explain: Use the atomic update method, not two calls.
questions.rule: Replace a plain shared variable by an atomic variable and update it with its atomic methods instead of locks.

questions.q: True or false: compareAndSet has the same memory consistency features as the get and set methods of an atomic variable.
questions.explain: The tutorial gives compareAndSet and the simple atomic arithmetic methods the same features as get and set.
questions.teaches: compareAndSet and the simple atomic arithmetic methods have the same memory consistency features as get and set.
questions.rule: Replace a plain shared variable by an atomic variable and update it with its atomic methods instead of locks.

questions.q: A statistics class has two counters that must stay equal at all times. Would two AtomicIntegers be enough?
options: Yes, because every atomic variable is linked to the others
No, updating the pair is not one atomic step
Yes, because atomic variables lock the whole class
No, because atomic variables cannot be used in pairs
optionExplain: Atomic variables are independent of each other.
A rule tying two variables together needs more than two atomic variables.
They involve no lock.
They can be used in any number.
questions.explain: Atomic variables cover single variables.
questions.teaches: Atomic variables make single operations on single variables safe; a rule that ties two variables together needs a lock or another design.
questions.rule: Replace a plain shared variable by an atomic variable and update it with its atomic methods instead of locks.

questions.q: An AtomicInteger starts at 5. Two threads each call incrementAndGet once, at the same time. The final value is ____.
questions.explain: Each atomic increment is counted, so the value ends at 7.
questions.rule: Atomic increments cannot lose each other.

questions.q: Many threads need random numbers at a high rate. Which does the tutorial prefer?
options: ThreadLocalRandom.current()
Math.random() shared by all the threads
Thread.sleep() between the draws
A synchronized block around Math.random()
optionExplain: It causes less contention than the shared alternative.
This is the choice the tutorial moves away from.
Pausing does not produce numbers.
Locking increases contention.
questions.explain: Prefer ThreadLocalRandom for concurrent use. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: In multi-threaded code, take random numbers from ThreadLocalRandom.current() rather than Math.random() to reduce contention.

questions.q: To get the generator you call ThreadLocalRandom.____().
questions.explain: The static current method returns the generator.
questions.rule: In multi-threaded code, take random numbers from ThreadLocalRandom.current() rather than Math.random() to reduce contention.

questions.q: Which expression draws an int for use in a worker thread, in the tutorial's style?
options: ThreadLocalRandom.getRandom().nextInt(4, 77)
ThreadLocalRandom.current().nextInt(4, 77)
new ThreadLocalRandom().nextInt(4, 77)
ThreadLocalRandom.nextInt(4, 77)
optionExplain: The generator is obtained with current, not with a method of that name.
current() first, then a method on the result.
The tutorial gets the instance with current, not with new.
nextInt is called on the instance from current, not on the class.
questions.explain: Call current(), then the method.
questions.rule: In multi-threaded code, take random numbers from ThreadLocalRandom.current() rather than Math.random() to reduce contention.

questions.q: True or false (beyond the tutorial, from the API docs): ThreadLocalRandom.current().nextInt(4, 77) can return 77.
questions.explain: The upper bound of nextInt(origin, bound) is exclusive, so results run from 4 to 76.
questions.teaches: Beyond the tutorial (API docs): nextInt(origin, bound) includes the origin and excludes the bound; the tutorial only shows the call nextInt(4, 77).
questions.rule: In multi-threaded code, take random numbers from ThreadLocalRandom.current() rather than Math.random() to reduce contention.

questions.q: A parallel simulation runs many ForkJoinTasks, each needing random numbers. Which choice suits it?
options: One Math.random() source shared through a synchronized method
A volatile int that the tasks increase to make numbers
ThreadLocalRandom, meant for threads or ForkJoinTasks
A single thread that makes numbers for all tasks one by one
optionExplain: Sharing and locking raise contention.
That is not a random generator.
The tutorial names both uses.
That creates a bottleneck.
questions.explain: ThreadLocalRandom suits fork/join tasks too.
questions.teaches: Per the tutorial, ThreadLocalRandom is for random numbers from several threads or ForkJoinTasks, with less contention than Math.random(); beyond the tutorial, funnelling every task through one synchronized source makes them queue on its lock.
questions.rule: In multi-threaded code, take random numbers from ThreadLocalRandom.current() rather than Math.random() to reduce contention.

questions.q: True or false: If two threads both call Math.random() heavily, the tutorial's reasoning says they may compete with each other.
questions.explain: The tutorial prefers ThreadLocalRandom because it causes less contention.
questions.rule: A shared source invites contention.

questions.q: A class extends Thread but does not override run. When start is called on an instance, the new thread executes a run method that ____.
questions.explain: Thread's own run method does nothing, so the subclass must override it to give the thread work.
questions.rule: A Thread subclass needs its own run.

questions.q: True or false: If the interrupt check in a polling loop is moved to the start of each pass instead of the end, an interrupt that arrives during the first unit of work is noticed only after that unit finishes.
questions.explain: The check runs once per pass, so the first chance to see the signal is the start of the next pass.
questions.rule: A poll sees an interrupt only when the check runs.

questions.q: The shared c is 10 and two threads each run c++ once with interleaved steps. If one update is lost, c ends at ____.
questions.explain: Both threads retrieved 10 and stored 11, so one increment is lost and c ends at 11.
questions.rule: A lost update leaves the count short.

questions.q: True or false: If the thread that increments counter and the thread that prints it are replaced by one thread doing both in that order, the stale-read problem disappears.
questions.explain: Within one thread, a later statement sees the earlier write.
questions.rule: Within a single thread, source order is enough.

questions.q: Under the tutorial's strategy (all reads and writes of a shared object's variables go through synchronized methods, except final fields), if a final field becomes non-final with a setter, can its getter stay unsynchronized?
questions.explain: Once the field can change, reads and writes of it must go through synchronized methods.
questions.rule: Only final fields escape the rule.

questions.q: Sensor's calibrate method is changed from static synchronized to non-static synchronized. A thread is inside s1.read(), and another thread now calls s1.calibrate(). What happens?
options: It blocks, since both need s1's lock
The second thread runs at once, since the methods differ
The second thread uses the Class object's lock instead
The first thread is interrupted to let it in
optionExplain: Both are instance methods of s1, so they share its lock.
Different methods on one object still share the object's lock.
Only static methods use that lock.
Locks do not interrupt their owners.
questions.explain: Instance methods of one object share one lock.
questions.rule: A synchronized method owns its object's lock, or the Class object's lock if static, until it returns or fails.

questions.q: In addName, the call that adds the name to a separate list is moved inside the synchronized block. What changes?
options: The updates to lastName and nameCount become atomic only now
Another object's method now runs under the lock
The block no longer needs to name a lock object
The lock is released earlier than before
optionExplain: They were already protected by the block.
The tutorial warns this can cause liveness problems.
A synchronized statement must name its lock.
Moving the call inside lengthens the hold; it does not shorten it.
questions.explain: Keep foreign calls outside the lock.
questions.rule: A synchronized statement locks a named object around only the lines that need it, keeping calls to other objects outside.

questions.q: True or false: If a shared int field is changed to a non-volatile long field, its reads and writes are still guaranteed to be atomic.
questions.explain: Reads and writes of long and double are atomic only when the variable is volatile.
questions.rule: long and double need volatile for atomic access.

questions.q: True or false: If the second bow thread is started only after the first bow has completed, the bowing deadlock does not occur.
questions.explain: The two bows then do not overlap, so neither waits for a lock the other holds.
questions.rule: Deadlock needs overlapping threads.

questions.q: The thread that sets the condition forgets to call notifyAll. A waiter is suspended in wait. What does the tutorial's account lead you to expect?
options: The waiter wakes after a short time by itself
The waiter finds the condition true and goes on
The waiter stays suspended; nothing wakes it
The setter is blocked until the waiter finishes
optionExplain: Nothing in the account wakes it.
It never gets to test the condition.
Wait suspends the thread until another thread issues a notification.
The setter has done its work and moves on.
questions.explain: A change without a notification leaves waiters suspended.
questions.rule: Inside a synchronized method, wait in a loop that re-tests the condition, and have the other thread set the condition and call notifyAll.

questions.q: True or false: If an immutable Price class gains a public setter, the guarantee that readers cannot see it in an inconsistent state still holds.
questions.explain: With a setter the object is no longer immutable, so the guarantee is gone.
questions.rule: The benefits depend on there being no changes.

questions.q: True or false: If the constructor copies the caller's list but the getter returns the internal list itself, outsiders can still change the class's contents.
questions.explain: The getter leaks the original, so a copy is needed on the way out as well.
questions.rule: Copy in and copy out.

questions.q: True or false: If an application grows from a few threads into a massively concurrent design on a many-core machine, the tutorial points toward the higher-level tools.
questions.explain: Massively concurrent applications on multi-core systems are the stated reason for them.
questions.rule: Scale and cores call for higher-level tools.

questions.q: True or false: Beyond the tutorial, if the random pauses in BowLoop were removed and both threads retried at the same instants, backing out with tryLock could keep repeating failed attempts.
questions.explain: Retrying in lockstep can repeat the collision, which is the livelock pattern.
questions.rule: Backing out needs varied timing to make progress.

questions.q: In Java's regular expression API, how do you get a Pattern object?
options: Write new Pattern and pass the expression
Call matcher on the input string
Call Pattern.compile with the expression
Call the compile method on a Matcher
optionExplain: A constructor is the usual way to make an object, but Pattern hides its constructors.
matcher is called on a Pattern, and it produces a Matcher, not a Pattern.
Right: Pattern has no public constructors, so compile is the way in.
The Matcher is made from a Pattern, so it cannot be the source of one.
questions.explain: Pattern offers no public constructor, so the static compile method is the entry point. The card next shows how the three classes fit together.
questions.rule: Compile the expression into a Pattern, ask it for a Matcher on your input, and let the Matcher do the searching.

questions.q: Match each class or method to its job.
pairs: The engine that applies a pattern to input
The static way to obtain a Pattern
questions.explain: Pattern holds the compiled expression, Matcher runs it on input, and the exception reports a malformed expression. compile is the single route to a Pattern.
questions.rule: Pattern holds, Matcher runs, the exception reports.

questions.q: You must print every number found in one receipt line. Put the steps in order.
items: Compile the expression with Pattern.compile
Ask the Pattern for a Matcher on the receipt text
Call find in a loop
Print group inside the loop
questions.explain: The expression must be compiled first, because the Matcher is made from the Pattern. The loop runs find, and group reads the match found by the latest find.
questions.rule: Compile, get a Matcher, loop on find, read the match.

questions.q: A program runs Pattern.compile of [0-9]+ and matcher on the input no digits here (no digit appears in it), then loops while find returns true, printing group each time. What happens?
options: The text null is printed
A PatternSyntaxException is thrown at compile
An empty line is printed once
Nothing is printed; no exception
optionExplain: group is only read after a successful find, so there is nothing to print.
That exception reports a malformed expression, and this one is well formed.
find returns false at once, so the loop body never runs and nothing is printed.
Right: the expression is valid, and a search that finds nothing is a normal result.
questions.explain: The expression is well formed, so compile succeeds. find returns false because the input has no digit, so the loop body never runs.
questions.rule: A valid expression that finds nothing is a result, not an error.

questions.q: According to the tutorial, PatternSyntaxException is unchecked. A method calls Pattern.compile on a string typed by a user and has no try block and no throws clause. What follows?
options: It does not compile, because the exception must be handled
It compiles, and a bad expression fails at run time
It compiles, and a bad expression is silently ignored
It compiles only if the method is declared static
optionExplain: That would be true for a checked exception, which the tutorial says this is not.
Right: unchecked exceptions do not need a declaration, so the risk moves to run time.
Nothing is ignored; compile throws the exception when the expression is malformed.
Declaring a method static has no bearing on whether an exception must be handled.
questions.explain: An unchecked exception needs no catch or throws clause, so the code compiles. A malformed expression then throws at run time, so code that takes user patterns should catch it.
questions.rule: Unchecked means the compiler will not remind you to catch it.
questions.teaches: Because PatternSyntaxException is unchecked, the compiler will not force you to handle it; the failure shows up at run time unless you catch it.

questions.q: True or false: A program calls Pattern.compile on the text (abc and then, as a separate step, creates a Matcher on some input. The syntax error is reported when the Matcher starts searching.
questions.explain: The error is raised by Pattern.compile, before any Matcher exists, because the expression is checked when it is compiled.
questions.rule: A bad expression fails at compile, before any searching starts.
questions.teaches: A syntax error surfaces at Pattern.compile, so no Matcher is ever created for a malformed expression.

questions.q: The expression foo is searched in the input foo. Which start and end indexes are reported?
options: Start 0, end 3
Start 0, end 2
Start 1, end 3
Start 1, end 4
optionExplain: Right: the text fills cells 0 to 2, and the end index sits after the last cell.
This counts the index of the last character instead of the position after it.
Counting usually begins at 1 in everyday life, but these indexes begin at 0.
This shifts both numbers up by one.
questions.explain: Indexes start at 0, and the end index is the position after the last matched character. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: A match covers its start index up to but not including its end index, so its length is end minus start.

questions.q: A match that starts at index 4 and ends at index 7 is ____ characters long.
questions.explain: Length is end minus start, so 7 minus 4 is 3.
questions.rule: Length equals end minus start.

questions.q: The expression foo is searched in the input xx foo yy (two x characters, a space, foo, a space, two y characters). Which range is reported for the match?
options: Start 3, end 5
Start 3, end 6
Start 2, end 6
Start 4, end 7
optionExplain: This takes the index of the last character as the end.
Right: x is 0, x is 1, the space is 2, so foo starts at 3 and ends after cell 5.
This counts the space as part of the match.
This shifts both numbers up by one.
questions.explain: Three characters come before foo, so the match starts at index 3. It is three long, so it ends at 6.
questions.rule: Count the cells before the match for the start, then add the length.

questions.q: The expression aa is searched with a find loop in the input aaaa. It reports ____ matches in total.
questions.explain: The first match uses cells 0 and 1. The search resumes at index 2, finds the second pair, and then the input is used up.
questions.rule: Matches from one search sit side by side, never overlapping.

questions.q: A reader runs the tutorial's test harness from an IDE run configuration that has no terminal attached, so System.console returns null. According to the tutorial, what does the program do?
options: It reads the expression from a pop-up dialog
It treats the input as empty and reports no match
It throws a PatternSyntaxException
It prints No console and exits
optionExplain: The harness only knows how to prompt through the console.
It never reaches the matching step without a console.
No expression is compiled, so no syntax exception can occur.
Right: with no console the harness cannot prompt, so it reports that and stops.
questions.explain: The harness asks for each expression and input through the console. When System.console returns null, it prints No console and exits.
questions.rule: The harness needs a console to prompt for the expression and the input.
questions.teaches: The tutorial's test harness depends on System.console; when none is attached, as in some IDE runs, it prints No console and exits instead of searching.

questions.q: A booking system stores a slot as a start minute and an end minute, counted the same way as match indexes. Match each slot to its length.
questions.explain: Length is end minus start. A slot whose start equals its end holds nothing, just as a match can have the same start and end.
questions.rule: Length is end minus start, and equal numbers mean an empty range.
questions.teaches: A range whose start equals its end is empty; the same idea lets a regex match consume no characters.

questions.q: The expression cat. is searched in the input cats. What happens?
options: It does not match, because the input has no dot after cat
It matches, because the dot stands for any one character
It matches only the three letters cat
It throws a PatternSyntaxException because of the dot
optionExplain: This reads the dot as a literal, but in an expression a bare dot is special.
Right: the dot accepts s, so cats matches from 0 to 4.
The dot still has to consume one character, so the match includes the s.
The dot is a valid metacharacter, so the expression is well formed.
questions.explain: A bare dot is a metacharacter meaning any one character. The card next shows how to turn that off.
questions.rule: A metacharacter keeps its special meaning unless you escape it with a backslash or enclose it between \Q and \E.

questions.q: True or false: According to the tutorial, characters such as @ and # have no special meaning in an expression, in any position.
questions.explain: The tutorial names @ and # as characters that are never special, so they need no escape.
questions.rule: Only characters on the metacharacter list can be special.

questions.q: A log contains the text a+b, and you want to find exactly that text. Which expression does it?
options: a+b
a.b
a\+b
ab+
optionExplain: The plus here repeats the a, so this matches aab or aaab but not a+b.
The dot matches any character, so this matches axb but not the plus.
Right: the backslash makes the plus an ordinary character, so only a+b matches.
The plus here repeats the b, which is a different pattern altogether.
questions.explain: Escaping the plus turns it from a quantifier into an ordinary character. The other forms either repeat a letter or accept any character.
questions.rule: Escape the metacharacter you mean literally.

questions.q: The expression is \Qcat.\E. Which description of its results is correct?
options: It matches neither, because \Q needs a closing \E at the very end
It matches both cat. and cats
It matches cats but not cat.
It matches the text cat. but not the text cats
optionExplain: The \E closes the quote here, so the expression is complete.
That would need the dot to stay special, but the quote switches it off.
This has the roles reversed: the quoted dot is a real dot.
Right: inside the quoted section the dot is a plain dot.
questions.explain: Everything between \Q and \E is taken literally, so the dot must be a real dot. The text cat. matches from 0 to 4, and cats has no dot.
questions.rule: Quoted text is matched exactly as written.

questions.q: The expression is a\Q.*\Eb. Which input does it match as a whole?
options: axxb
ab
a.b
a.*b
optionExplain: This treats .* as the usual any-characters pattern, but it sits inside the quote.
This lets .* match nothing, but the quoted text is required exactly.
The quoted text is two characters long, a dot and a star, and only one is present.
Right: only the middle part is quoted, so it needs a literal dot and a literal star between a and b.
questions.explain: The quote covers only the dot and the star, so those two characters must appear exactly. The a and the b outside the quote are ordinary here.
questions.rule: A quote can cover just part of an expression.
questions.teaches: \Q and \E can quote only a section in the middle of an expression; the text outside the quote keeps its normal meaning.

questions.q: A tool turns a file name into a search pattern, so the file name must be matched literally. Sort each character by whether it needs an escape first.

items.t: g

questions.explain: Dot, question mark, dollar sign and vertical bar are on the metacharacter list, so they need an escape. @, # and ordinary letters or digits are never special.
questions.rule: Escape every character that is on the metacharacter list.
questions.teaches: To match arbitrary text literally, escape each character that appears on the metacharacter list; characters outside it need nothing.

questions.q: Which input does the expression [bcr]at match?
options: hat
cat
bcrat
at
optionExplain: h is not in the set b, c, r, so the first character fails.
Right: c is one of the listed first letters.
A class matches one character, so only one of b, c or r may come before at.
The class needs one character in front of at, and this input has none.
questions.explain: The class stands for exactly one of b, c or r, followed by at. The card next shows how classes are built.
questions.rule: A class matches one character from its set: a caret negates, a hyphen spans a range, nesting joins, && intersects, and && with a negated class subtracts.

questions.q: In the class [a-c], the hyphen means an inclusive ____.
questions.explain: A hyphen between two characters spans everything from the first to the last, both included.
questions.rule: A hyphen between two characters is an inclusive range.

questions.q: You need one digit that is not 3, 4 or 5 (the input is a single character). Which class does it?
optionExplain: This excludes 3, 4 and 5 but also accepts letters and symbols.
A nested class makes a union, so this accepts every digit and everything not in 345.
This is the intersection with 345, which keeps only 3, 4 and 5.
Right: the intersection keeps the digits, and the negated nested class removes 3, 4 and 5.
questions.explain: Subtraction is an intersection with a negated class. Only the first option limits the result to digits and also removes 3, 4 and 5.
questions.rule: To subtract, intersect with a negated class.

questions.q: The expression is [^bcr]at. Which one input of sat, rat and at matches?
options: rat and sat
sat and at
sat only
All three
optionExplain: r is listed in the negated set, so rat is excluded.
at has no first character, and a class always needs one.
Right: s is allowed, r is excluded, and the class needs a character before at.
Both rat (r is excluded) and at (no first character) fail.
questions.explain: A negated class still consumes one character. rat fails because r is excluded, at fails because nothing precedes it, and sat matches.
questions.rule: A negated class still needs exactly one character.

questions.q: Match each class to a flat class that describes the same set.
questions.explain: Each nested form can be rewritten by listing the remaining ranges side by side. Subtraction removes the named letters from the range.
questions.rule: A union or subtraction can be rewritten as a flat class of ranges.
questions.teaches: Different class expressions can describe the same set of characters, so a union or subtraction can be flattened into one list of ranges.

questions.q: Room codes are one letter from A to F followed by one digit from 1 to 9, but rooms with the letter C are closed. Which expression matches an open room code as a whole input?
optionExplain: The caret is not at the start of the class, so it does not subtract C, and C stays allowed.
Adding C to the set makes C allowed, the opposite of the goal.
Right: the first class takes A to F without C, the second takes one digit.
This intersects with C, which would keep only the closed letter.
questions.explain: Each class matches one character, so two classes in a row match a letter and a digit. The letter class subtracts C by intersecting with a negated class.
questions.rule: Chain classes for each position, using subtraction inside the class that needs it.
questions.teaches: Each class in a pattern covers one character position, so you can chain a letter class and a digit class, using subtraction only where it is needed.

questions.q: Which expression matches exactly one decimal digit?
options: \d
\D
\s
\w
optionExplain: Right: \d is the shorthand for a digit.
The capital letter is the opposite, any character that is not a digit.
This is a whitespace character such as a space or a tab.
This accepts digits but also letters and the underscore.
questions.explain: \d is the predefined class for one digit. The card next lists the others.
questions.rule: Use \d, \s and \w, with capitals for the opposites, and write each backslash twice inside a Java string.

questions.q: Match each shorthand to what it stands for.
pairs: Any character except letters, digits and underscore
questions.explain: The lower-case letters name the sets; the capital negates the set.
questions.rule: Lower case names a set, capital negates it.

questions.q: A Java string literal holds the expression \d. Counting the source text between the quotes, it contains ____ backslash characters.
questions.explain: Each backslash of the expression must be doubled in Java source, because a backslash in a string literal is itself an escape.
questions.rule: Double every regex backslash inside a Java string.

questions.q: The expression \w+ is searched with a find loop in the input café au lait, where the fourth letter of the first word is an accented e. What text does the first match contain?
options: café
caf
c
café au
optionExplain: This treats the accented letter as a word character, but the tutorial's class covers ASCII letters, digits and underscore.
Right: the accented letter is outside [a-zA-Z_0-9], so the first run ends before it.
The plus lets the match continue through caf, so it takes more than one letter.
A space ends a run of word characters, so a match cannot cross it.
questions.explain: With the class [a-zA-Z_0-9], the accented e ends the run after caf. The second match is au and the third is lait.
questions.rule: The word class is limited to ASCII letters, digits and underscore.

questions.q: Which of these characters does \s match? Select all that apply.
options: A tab
A carriage return
A form feed
An underscore
A comma
optionExplain: Right: a tab is one of the whitespace characters.
Right: carriage return is part of the whitespace class.
Right: form feed is also listed, along with the vertical tab.
The underscore is a word character, not whitespace.
A comma is a punctuation mark, not whitespace.
questions.explain: The class is the same as [ \t\n\x0B\f\r]: space, tab, newline, vertical tab, form feed and carriage return.
questions.rule: \s covers six whitespace characters, not only the space.
questions.teaches: \s is equivalent to the class [ \t\n\x0B\f\r], so it also covers the vertical tab, form feed and carriage return.

questions.q: A colleague wants to flag any character in a phone number field that is not a digit and writes \W for it. Which statement finds the problem?
options: \W is correct, because W stands for wrong character
\W must be written \w to flag bad characters
\W skips letters and underscores; \D is the non-digit class
\W is correct but must be typed with one backslash in Java source
optionExplain: The capital letter negates its own lower-case set only, here the word class.
\w would flag exactly the letters and digits, which is nearly the reverse.
Right: \W is the opposite of \w, not of \d.
The doubling rule is true, but the real flaw is that \W is the wrong set.
questions.explain: Each capital letter negates only its own set. \W is the opposite of the word class, so a letter or an underscore in the field would not be flagged, while \D flags every non-digit.
questions.rule: Negate the exact set you mean: \D for digits, \W for word characters.
questions.teaches: The opposite of \d is \D, not \W; each capital shorthand negates only its own lower-case set.

questions.q: Which expression matches the text abab as a whole input?
options: ab{2}
optionExplain: The class matches one character, so this matches only two characters.
The 2 repeats only the b, giving abb.
This is two a characters then two b characters, aabb.
Right: the group is repeated twice.
questions.explain: To repeat the two-letter unit ab, it needs parentheses. The card next explains how far a quantifier reaches.
questions.rule: A quantifier repeats only the single element before it, so use parentheses to repeat a longer piece.

questions.q: Match each quantifier to its meaning.
questions.explain: The question mark allows zero or one, the star zero or more, the plus at least one, and braces give explicit limits.
questions.rule: Question mark, star, plus and braces set how many times X may occur.

questions.q: A product code is two capital letters followed by three to five digits, and the whole input must be exactly a code. Which expression fits?
optionExplain: This allows only three digits, not three to five.
This allows extra letters and demands exactly five digits.
This allows only one letter, and two digits would pass.
Right: two letters, then a run of three to five digits.
questions.explain: Each quantifier repeats the element before it. {2} fixes the letter count and {3,5} lets the digit run vary.
questions.rule: Put the count right after the element it controls.

questions.q: The expression a{3} is searched with a find loop in seven a characters. Which matches are reported?
options: One match: 0 to 7
Two matches: 0 to 3 and 3 to 6
Three matches: 0 to 3, 3 to 6 and 6 to 7
Two matches: 0 to 3 and 4 to 7
optionExplain: The count is exactly three, so the match cannot take all seven.
Right: the leftover seventh a is too short for another match.
The last match would have only one a, but three are required.
The second search starts at index 3, where the first ended.
questions.explain: The first match takes three, the second takes the next three, and one a is left, which cannot satisfy a count of three.
questions.rule: A leftover shorter than the count produces no match.

questions.q: True or false: The expression a{3,6} is searched with a find loop in eight a characters. It reports two matches, one of six a characters and one of two.
questions.explain: The first match takes six. The two left over are fewer than the minimum of three, so there is no second match.
questions.rule: Every match must still reach the minimum count.
questions.teaches: A later match must still meet the minimum count; a leftover shorter than the minimum ends the search.

questions.q: A chat tool should flag the laughter hahaha (ha three times in a row). A developer writes ha{3} and tests it on hahaha. Which statement finds the problem?
options: ha{3} is correct, since 3 applies to the whole word
A class such as [ha]{3} is the fix
ha{3} repeats only the a; (ha){3} is needed
The braces need a comma, as in ha{3,}
optionExplain: A quantifier reaches only the single element before it, here the a.
A class matches one character at a time, so it would also match aaa or hhh.
Right: the 3 attaches to the single element before it.
A comma changes the meaning to at least three, but the scope problem would remain.
questions.explain: The pattern ha{3} means h followed by aaa, so it fails on hahaha. Putting ha in parentheses lets the 3 repeat the pair.
questions.rule: To repeat a multi-character unit, group it.
questions.teaches: A character class cannot repeat a fixed multi-character sequence, because it matches one character at a time; only a group repeats a whole sequence.

questions.q: How many matches does a find loop report for the expression a* on the empty input?
options: One
None
Two
The search throws an exception
optionExplain: Right: a* allows zero repeats, so it matches the empty string once.
