There is no a, but a* does not need one.
The empty input has just one position.
An empty input is allowed, and the expression is well formed.
questions.explain: Zero repeats satisfy a*, so the empty string matches at index 0. The card next shows more cases.
questions.rule: A quantifier that allows zero repeats can match nothing, so it may report empty matches wherever the element is absent.

questions.q: True or false: The expression a+ reports a match on the empty input.
questions.explain: The plus needs at least one a, and an empty input has none.
questions.rule: A plus cannot match nothing.

questions.q: The expression a* is searched with a find loop in the input bab. It reports ____ matches in total.
questions.explain: Matches are: empty at 0, a at 1 to 2, empty at 2, and empty at 3, the position after the last character.
questions.rule: Count the empty positions as well as the real matches.
questions.hint: List the match at each position from left to right.

questions.q: The input is bab. How many matches are reported for a followed by a question mark, a followed by a star, and a followed by a plus, in that order?
options: 1, 1 and 1
2, 2 and 1
4, 1 and 1
4, 4 and 1
optionExplain: Only a+ reports just the single a; the others add empty matches.
The empty positions are 0, 2 and 3, so there are more than two matches.
a* allows zero repeats, so it reports empty matches just like a?.
Right: the first two allow zero repeats and report empty matches at positions 0, 2 and 3.
questions.explain: a? and a* both allow zero repeats, giving empty matches at 0, 2 and 3 plus the a at 1. a+ needs a real a, so it reports only that.
questions.rule: Only a quantifier with a zero minimum reports empty matches.

questions.q: A find loop searches the one-character input b with the expression a{0,}. It reports ____ matches.
questions.explain: A count with minimum zero behaves like *. The input b has an empty position at 0 and another at 1, so there are two empty matches.
questions.rule: An input of n characters has n plus 1 positions for empty matches.
questions.teaches: A count of at least zero behaves like a star, and an input of n characters offers n plus 1 positions for empty matches.

questions.q: A form check calls find with the expression \d* to learn whether a text field contains a digit. Which choice is the correct expression for that check?
optionExplain: The star allows zero digits, so find succeeds even on a field with letters only.
The question mark also allows zero digits, so it succeeds on any text.
Right: the plus needs at least one digit, so find succeeds only if one exists.
This looks for non-digits, the opposite of the goal.
questions.explain: With find, an expression that can match nothing succeeds on every input. Using + forces at least one digit.
questions.rule: When presence matters, use a quantifier with a minimum of one.
questions.teaches: When you only test whether find succeeds, an expression that can match nothing always succeeds, so require at least one repeat when presence matters.

questions.q: Which kind of quantifier tries the shortest text first and extends it one character at a time?
options: Reluctant
Greedy
Possessive
All three work the same way
optionExplain: Right: it starts with as little as possible.
A greedy quantifier starts with as much as possible.
A possessive quantifier also takes as much as possible and does not give back.
They accept the same counts but search in different orders.
questions.explain: The three flavors differ in where they start and whether they back off. The card next explains each.
questions.rule: Greedy takes the most and gives back, reluctant takes the least and adds, possessive takes the most and never gives back.

questions.q: Match each flavor to how it behaves.
pairs: Takes as much as possible, then gives back if needed
Takes as little as possible, adding one character at a time
Takes as much as possible and never gives back
questions.explain: The three flavors differ in their starting point and in whether they can give text back.
questions.rule: Greedy gives back, reluctant adds, possessive holds on.

questions.q: In the text cut [x] and [y] end, you want [x] and [y] as two separate matches. Which expression does that?
optionExplain: The greedy star runs to the last closing bracket and returns one long match.
The possessive star swallows the closing brackets and cannot give one back, so nothing matches.
Right: the reluctant star stops at the first closing bracket each time.
This is greedy too, so it also returns one long match.
questions.explain: Only the reluctant form stops at the earliest closing bracket. The greedy ones overshoot, and the possessive one has no text left for the closing bracket.
questions.rule: Use the reluctant form to stop at the first possible end.

questions.q: The input is foo1foo2. How many matches does a find loop report for the greedy expression .*foo and for its reluctant version, in that order?
options: 1 and 2
1 and 1
2 and 1
2 and 2
optionExplain: Right: the greedy form takes foo1foo as one match; the reluctant one finds foo and 1foo.
The reluctant form stops early, so it finds two matches here.
This swaps the two: it is the greedy form that takes the long match.
The greedy form takes as much as possible up to the last foo, so it finds one match.
questions.explain: The greedy star runs on to the last foo, giving foo1foo at 0 to 7. The reluctant star ends at the first foo, giving foo at 0 to 3 and 1foo at 3 to 7.
questions.rule: Greedy finds the longest, reluctant the shortest.

questions.q: True or false: The expression a*+b finds no match in the input aaab.
questions.explain: The possessive star takes aaa, and nothing needs to be given back, since the b is not an a. The whole text aaab matches.
questions.rule: Possessive fails only if the rest needs text it already took.
questions.teaches: A possessive quantifier fails only when the rest of the expression needs text it has already taken; if the rest needs different characters, it works as usual.

questions.q: The text is ID=7;ID=8; and a colleague wants each assignment as its own match, sees ID=.*; return one long match, and proposes ID=.*+; as the fix. What happens with the proposal?
options: A PatternSyntaxException from the compiler call
Two matches, one for each ID assignment in the text
The same single long match as before the change
No match at all, nothing is left for the semicolon
optionExplain: The construct is valid syntax, so the expression compiles.
Possessive does not stop early; it takes everything and holds it.
A possessive quantifier never gives text back, so the semicolon cannot match.
Right: .*+ takes every remaining character and cannot return one for the semicolon.
questions.explain: Possessive is not a stronger greedy. It is the reluctant form (ID=.*?;) that stops at each first semicolon and gives one match per assignment.
questions.rule: Pick reluctant to stop early; possessive can only hold on.
questions.teaches: Making a quantifier possessive does not shorten a greedy match; to get separate matches per assignment you need the reluctant form.

questions.q: How many capturing groups does groupCount report for the expression ((A)(B(C)))?
optionExplain: Counting only the inner pairs misses the outer group.
Right: each of the four opening parentheses starts a group.
Group 0 stands for the whole match but is not counted by groupCount.
The nested groups each count separately.
questions.explain: Each opening parenthesis starts a capturing group, and group 0 is not included in the count. The card next shows the numbering.
questions.rule: Count opening parentheses from left to right for group numbers; group 0 is the whole match, and groupCount leaves it out.

questions.q: Group number ____ stands for the entire match.
questions.explain: Group 0 is the whole expression's match, and groupCount does not count it.
questions.rule: Group 0 is the whole match.

questions.q: The expression (\w+)@(\w+)\.com is applied to the input mia@shop.com. What does group(2) return?
options: shop
mia
mia@shop.com
shop.com
optionExplain: Right: the second opening parenthesis starts the group after the at sign.
This is group 1, the first opening parenthesis.
This is group 0, the whole match.
The dot and com sit outside the second group.
questions.explain: Group 1 is the user part, and group 2 is the part between the at sign and the dot. The dot com text is outside both groups.
questions.rule: Number groups by their opening parentheses.

questions.q: True or false: For the expression (a)(?:b(c))(d), groupCount returns 3.
questions.explain: The groups are (a), (c) and (d). The (?: group does not capture, so it is not counted.
questions.rule: A (? group is not counted.

questions.q: The expression ((A)(B(C))) is applied to the input xABC, and the match is found at index 1. What do start(3) and end(3) return?
options: 2 and 3
0 and 2
1 and 4
2 and 4
optionExplain: The end index is the position after the last character, so it is 4.
The indexes refer to the whole input, not to positions inside the match.
Group 3 starts after the A, not at the beginning of the match.
Right: group 3 is BC, which sits at cells 2 and 3 of the whole input.
questions.explain: Group 3 covers B and C. In the input xABC they occupy cells 2 and 3, so the range is 2 to 4.
questions.rule: Group indexes are positions in the whole input.
questions.teaches: start(n) and end(n) report positions in the whole input string, not positions relative to the match or to the enclosing group.

questions.q: A date expression is ((\d{4})-(\d{2}))-(\d{2}), applied to 2026-10-11. Which call returns the day, 11?
options: group(3)
group(4)
group(2)
group(1)
optionExplain: This is the month, 10, since the outer group added a number.
Right: the day group is the fourth opening parenthesis.
This is the year, 2026.
This is the outer group, 2026-10.
questions.explain: The outer group takes number 1, the year 2, the month 3 and the day 4. Wrapping some parts in an extra group moved the day's number from 3 to 4.
questions.rule: Adding a group in front shifts the numbers of the groups after it.
questions.teaches: Wrapping parts of an expression in an extra group shifts the numbers of the later groups, because numbers follow opening parentheses and not meaning.

questions.q: Which input does the expression (\d\d)\1 match as a whole?
optionExplain: Right: the second pair repeats the first pair.
The second pair differs from the first.
Four digits are needed: a pair and its repeat.
The repeat needs the full pair, two digits, not one.
questions.explain: The \1 must repeat the exact two digits captured by the group. The card next shows how.
questions.rule: A backreference \n matches the exact text that group n captured, not just anything the group could match.

questions.q: True or false: In the expression (\d\d)\1, the \1 matches any two digits.
questions.explain: The \1 matches only the exact two digits that group 1 captured.
questions.rule: A backreference repeats the captured text, not the pattern.

questions.q: You want to find doubled words separated by a single space, such as go go or is is. Which expression fits?
optionExplain: The second word may be any word, not the same one.
There is no group 1 to refer back to, so nothing matches.
This has no space between the two copies, so it fails on go go.
Right: the group captures a word, and \1 demands the same word again.
questions.explain: The group stores the first word. The space comes next, and \1 then matches the same word again.
questions.rule: Capture the first copy in a group, then refer back to it.

questions.q: The expression is (\d)(\d)\2\1. Which one input does it match as a whole?
optionExplain: Right: 1 then 2, then a repeat of the second digit, then a repeat of the first.
The third digit would have to be 2, but it is 1.
The third digit would have to be 1, but it is 2.
The third digit would have to be 2, but it is 3.
questions.explain: The backreferences come in reverse order: \2 first, then \1. So the digits read a, b, b, a.
questions.rule: Backreferences can come in any order.

questions.q: The expression is ((\d)\d)\2. Which inputs does it match as a whole? Select all that apply.
optionExplain: Right: group 1 is 12, group 2 is 1, and \2 repeats the 1.
Right: the third digit repeats the first, 2.
This would need \1, which repeats the whole outer group, to follow.
The third digit would have to be 1, the text of group 2.
Right: the third digit repeats the first, 1.
questions.explain: Group 2 is the inner (\d), so \2 repeats only the first digit. Any three digits of the form a, b, a match.
questions.rule: Use the number of the exact group whose text you want repeated.
questions.teaches: With nested groups, \2 repeats only the inner group's text, not the outer group's.

questions.q: Forum markup looks like [b]bold[/b] and [i]slanted[/i]. Which expression matches a tag pair only when the closing name equals the opening name?
optionExplain: The closing name may differ from the opening one, so [i]x[/b] would match.
Right: the group captures the opening name, and \1 demands the same name in the closing tag.
There is no group 1 to refer to, so no tag pair is matched.
Both names are captured but never compared, so mismatched pairs still match.
questions.explain: A backreference lets the closing tag be checked against the opening tag. A plain \w+ accepts any name, so it cannot pair them.
questions.rule: Use a backreference when one part must equal another.
questions.teaches: Backreferences can pair an opening marker with its closing marker, which no fixed pattern can do.

questions.q: You search the text The doggie plays for the word dog on its own. Which expression avoids matching inside doggie?
options: \bdog\b
dog
^dog$
dog\B
optionExplain: Right: the boundary after dog fails when another letter follows.
A plain dog also matches the first three letters of doggie.
This requires the whole line to be dog.
The non-boundary form matches only when dog is followed by more word characters.
questions.explain: A word boundary on each side keeps the match from being part of a longer word. The card next explains boundaries.
questions.rule: Use ^ and $ to pin lines, \b to pin whole words, and \G to continue exactly where the last match stopped.

questions.q: Match each boundary matcher to what it marks.
pairs: The end of the previous match
questions.explain: Each matcher names a place in the input rather than a character.
questions.rule: Boundary matchers name places, not characters.

questions.q: The expression \bit\b is searched in the input: it sit it's item it. It reports ____ matches.
questions.explain: The standalone it at the start, the it in it's (the apostrophe ends the word) and the last it match. The it in sit and item sits inside longer words.
questions.rule: A word boundary needs a non-word character or an edge beside it.

questions.q: The expression \Gdog is searched in the input dogdog dog. How many matches does a find loop report?
options: None
One
Three
Two
optionExplain: The first match is allowed, since the search starts there.
\G also allows a match that starts exactly where the last one ended, and the second dog does.
The third dog follows a space, so it does not start where the second ended.
Right: the second dog starts at 3 where the first ended, but the third is after a space.
questions.explain: The first dog starts the search at 0. The second starts at 3, exactly at the end of the first. The third begins at 7 after a space, so \G fails there.
questions.rule: \G allows only matches that continue without a gap.

questions.q: The expression ^dog\w* is searched in each line. Which lines does it match? Select all that apply.
options: dogblahblah
dog
hotdog
dog (two spaces, then dog)
a dog
optionExplain: Right: dog starts the line, and the \w* takes the rest of the word.
Right: \w* may match nothing, so exactly dog is enough.
The line starts with hot, so dog is not at the beginning.
The two leading spaces block the caret, because ^ anchors at the very start.
The line starts with a, so the caret fails.
questions.explain: The caret pins only the start. The \w* afterwards is free and can be empty, so any line beginning with dog matches.
questions.rule: A caret pins the start but leaves the end free unless you add a dollar sign.
questions.teaches: Pinning only the start with ^ leaves the end free: ^dog\w* accepts dog followed by any number of word characters, including none.

questions.q: A form must accept a field only if the whole line is digits. The check uses find. Which expression is right?
options: \b\d+\b
optionExplain: Right: both anchors force the digits to fill the entire line.
This succeeds on 12a, because find only needs some digits somewhere.
This succeeds on 12a, since only the start is pinned.
This succeeds on 12-34, because the hyphen is a word boundary.
questions.explain: Anchors at both ends turn a search into a whole-line check. Without the dollar sign, trailing letters are allowed.
questions.rule: Anchor both ends to check a whole line.
questions.teaches: Anchoring both ends turns find into a whole-line check; anchoring one end, or using word boundaries, still lets stray characters through.

questions.q: How can you make the expression dog also match DOG?
options: Compile it with the MULTILINE flag
Add the CASE_INSENSITIVE flag
Compile it with the LITERAL flag
Write it as DOG instead
optionExplain: That flag changes how ^ and $ behave across lines, not case.
Right: that flag ignores case.
That treats the pattern as plain text but does not ignore case.
That matches the upper-case form only, not both.
questions.explain: A flag passed to compile changes the matching rules. The card next lists the flags.
questions.rule: Pass flags to compile joined with the or operator, or embed their letter forms such as (?i) in the expression.

questions.q: Match each flag to its effect.
pairs: The dot also matches line terminators
Ignores whitespace and # comments in the expression
questions.explain: Each flag changes one rule of matching.
questions.rule: Each flag switches one matching rule.

questions.q: The input is ab, then a newline, then cd. Which flag lets the expression ab.cd match all of it?
options: MULTILINE
CASE_INSENSITIVE
DOTALL
COMMENTS
optionExplain: This changes ^ and $, not the dot.
This changes how letters are compared, not what the dot accepts.
Right: the dot then matches the newline between b and c.
This ignores whitespace in the expression itself, not in the input.
questions.explain: By default the dot does not match a line terminator. DOTALL removes that limit, so the dot can take the newline.
questions.rule: DOTALL lets the dot cross line breaks.

questions.q: True or false: On the input DOG dog Dog, the plain expression dog finds one word, while the same expression with the embedded flag (?i) at its start finds all three.
questions.explain: Without a flag, case matters, so only dog matches. With (?i) at the start, DOG, dog and Dog all match.
questions.rule: An embedded flag has the same effect as the matching compile flag.

questions.q: Which expression ignores case and also lets ^ match at the start of every line?
options: (?i)(?m)dog
(?x)^dog
(?is)^dog
(?im)^dog
optionExplain: This sets the flags but has no caret, so nothing is pinned to line starts.
The x flag handles whitespace and comments, not case or lines.
The s flag lets the dot match line terminators, not the caret.
Right: several embedded flags can sit in one group.
questions.explain: i is CASE_INSENSITIVE and m is MULTILINE, so (?im) turns on both at once. The caret then matches after each line break.
questions.rule: Letters combine inside one (?...) group.
questions.teaches: Several embedded flags can be combined in one group, as in (?im).

questions.q: Code compiles a.b with Pattern.LITERAL | Pattern.DOTALL, hoping to match the three-character text a, newline, b. What is wrong?
options: LITERAL makes the dot a plain dot, and DOTALL has no effect
DOTALL needs the embedded (?s) form instead
The flags cannot be combined with the or operator
LITERAL matches a, newline, b only if CASE_INSENSITIVE is added
optionExplain: Right: with LITERAL only the case flags still apply.
The compile flag works, but LITERAL switches off special meanings.
Combining flags with the or operator is the standard way.
The case flags do not turn the dot back into a wildcard.
questions.explain: LITERAL treats the whole expression as plain text, so the dot must be a real dot. Of the other flags, only the two case flags still apply, so DOTALL changes nothing.
questions.rule: With LITERAL, only the case flags still matter.
questions.teaches: When LITERAL is set, only CASE_INSENSITIVE and UNICODE_CASE still have an effect; other flags are ignored.

questions.q: True or false: Pattern.matches called with the expression for one digit and the input 12 returns true.
questions.explain: The method tests the whole input, and 12 is two characters, not one digit. The card next explains whole-input matching.
questions.rule: The static and String shortcuts test whole inputs or split text, and quote turns user text into a literal pattern.

questions.q: The static method ____ returns a pattern string that matches its argument literally.
questions.explain: quote wraps the text so every metacharacter in it is matched as an ordinary character.
questions.rule: quote turns text into a literal pattern.

questions.q: Which expression passed to split cleanly cuts the text red , green,blue into red, green and blue, whatever spaces surround each comma?
options: \s,\s
optionExplain: This leaves a trailing space on red and a leading space on green.
This demands exactly one space on each side, which fails at green,blue.
This splits at every comma and every space, producing empty pieces in between.
Right: optional spaces on both sides of the comma are part of the delimiter.
questions.explain: The delimiter must absorb the optional spaces. \s* allows zero or more on each side, so the pieces come out clean.
questions.rule: Put the surrounding noise inside the delimiter expression.

questions.q: True or false: Pattern.compile(Pattern.quote("a.b")).matcher("axb").matches() returns true.
questions.explain: The quoted pattern matches only the exact text a.b, so axb fails. Without quote, the dot would accept the x.
questions.rule: A quoted pattern matches only the exact text.

questions.q: What does String.replace("aa", "b") produce when called on the text aaa?
options: ab
bb
ba
b
optionExplain: This would replace the last two a characters, but the scan starts at the left.
Only one occurrence of aa fits in three characters.
Right: it replaces literal occurrences scanning from the start, so the first two a characters become b.
The leftover a stays in the result.
questions.explain: String.replace works on literal text from the start. The first aa is replaced, and the lone a that remains stays as it is.
questions.rule: String.replace is literal and scans from the start.
questions.teaches: String.replace replaces literal text, scanning from the left, without overlapping: aa in aaa becomes b followed by the leftover a.

questions.q: A search box passes whatever the user typed, for instance the text cost (USD, straight into Pattern.compile, and the call throws an exception. What best fixes it?
options: Add the CASE_INSENSITIVE flag
Wrap the typed text in Pattern.quote
Use matches instead of find
Double the backslashes in the typed text first
optionExplain: The flag changes case rules and leaves the unbalanced parenthesis in place.
Right: quote makes the parenthesis an ordinary character.
The expression is rejected at compile, before either method is used.
There are no backslashes to double, and doubling is a Java string rule.
questions.explain: The error comes from treating user text as an expression. quote makes the whole text literal, so the unbalanced parenthesis no longer matters.
questions.rule: Quote any user text you want matched literally.
questions.teaches: Text typed by users can be a malformed expression, so quote it when you mean it as plain text.

questions.q: The expression is foo and the input is foobar. Which methods return true?
options: matches only, since foo is in the input
find only, since foo appears inside it
lookingAt and find, not matches
All three methods
optionExplain: matches needs the entire input to be foo, and the input has bar after it.
lookingAt also returns true, because foo is at the start.
Right: the input starts with foo and contains it, but it is not only foo.
matches fails because bar is left over.
questions.explain: The three methods differ in how much of the input must match. The card next sets them out.
questions.rule: Use matches when all the input must fit, lookingAt when the start must fit, and find to look anywhere.

questions.q: Match each method to the rule it enforces.
pairs: The match must begin at the start of the input
Searches forward for the next match
Resets, then searches from a given index
questions.explain: The methods differ in how much of the input must match and where the search starts.
questions.rule: Whole input, prefix, anywhere.

questions.q: The expression is [A-Z]{2}. Sort each call by whether it returns true or false.

items.t: lookingAt() on NY2026
find() on NY2026
matches() on NY2026
matches() on NY
lookingAt() on 2026NY
find() on 2026NY

questions.explain: lookingAt needs the letters at the start, matches needs nothing else in the input, and find accepts them anywhere.
questions.rule: Decide how much of the input must fit, and where.

questions.q: The expression is \d, the input is a1b2c3, and the code calls find(2) on a fresh matcher. Afterward, start() returns ____.
questions.explain: find(int) resets the matcher and begins at the given index. The characters from index 2 are b, 2, c and 3, so the first digit is at index 3.
questions.rule: find(int) searches from the index you give it.
questions.hint: Index 2 holds the letter b.

questions.q: A find loop uses \bdog\b on the input dog dog dog doggie dogg. Which statements are true? Select all that apply.
options: Three matches are found
The third match starts at index 8
For every match, end minus start is 3
doggie is matched, since it begins with dog
The second match ends at 3
optionExplain: Right: doggie and dogg are not whole words.
Right: the first two dog words take cells 0 to 6 plus spaces, so the third begins at 8.
Right: each match is the three-letter word dog.
The boundary after dog fails when more letters follow.
The second match is 4 to 7, so it ends at 7.
questions.explain: Each match is the three-letter word, so its length is end minus start. The starts are 0, 4 and 8.
questions.rule: end minus start gives the length of any match.
questions.teaches: Because end minus start is the length of every match, a find loop can report match lengths without reading the matched text.

questions.q: A file name is accepted if it starts with IMG_ followed by digits, and anything may follow, such as .png. Which method and expression check that?
options: lookingAt with IMG_\d+
matches with IMG_\d+
find with IMG_\d+
lookingAt with \d+
optionExplain: Right: lookingAt pins the match to the start and allows the rest.
This rejects IMG_12.png, because the extension is left over.
This also accepts old_IMG_1.png, where the prefix is not at the start.
This accepts names starting with digits and never checks for IMG_.
questions.explain: Prefix checks fit lookingAt. matches is too strict for names with extensions, and find would let the pattern sit anywhere.
questions.rule: Use lookingAt for prefix checks.
questions.teaches: lookingAt is the right tool for a prefix check where the rest of the text is free; matches is too strict and find too loose.

questions.q: You must change every run of digits in the text room 12 and 345 into the symbol #. Which method fits?
options: replaceAll
replaceFirst
lookingAt
appendTail
optionExplain: Right: it replaces every match.
This replaces only the first run, 12.
This only tests whether the input starts with a match.
This copies leftover text and does not replace matches by itself.
questions.explain: One call that swaps every match is replaceAll. The card next covers the other methods.
questions.rule: Use replaceAll or replaceFirst for a fixed replacement, and find with appendReplacement and appendTail when each replacement needs logic.

questions.q: To copy the text after the final match into the result, call ____.
questions.explain: appendTail copies everything after the last match once the loop has finished.
questions.rule: appendTail copies the leftover text.

questions.q: You must replace each number in a line with a text that differs per match. Put the steps in order.
items: Create a Matcher and an empty StringBuffer
Call find in a loop
Call appendReplacement inside the loop
Call appendTail after the loop
questions.explain: The loop gives you one chance per match to compute the replacement. appendTail then adds the text after the last match.
questions.rule: Loop with appendReplacement, then finish with appendTail.

questions.q: What does replaceAll with the expression cat and the replacement dog produce on the text concatenate cat?
options: concatenate dog
condogenate cat
condogenate dog
concatenate cat
optionExplain: This would need word boundaries around cat.
replaceAll changes every match, including the last word.
Right: the expression has no boundaries, so it also matches inside concatenate.
The text contains cat twice, so something is replaced.
questions.explain: The cat inside concatenate is a match as well, so both occurrences change. \bcat\b would replace only the whole word.
questions.rule: Add word boundaries to replace whole words only.

questions.q: Code runs: Matcher m on the expression \d and the input a1b2c3, with a counter n starting at 0. In a loop, while m.find(), it adds 1 to n and calls m.appendReplacement(sb, a bracket, n, a bracket). After the loop it calls appendTail. What does sb hold?
optionExplain: The counter grows with each match, so the numbers differ.
Right: each match is replaced by its own counter value.
Each replacement is built at the time of its match, not at the end.
The letters between the matches are copied too.
questions.explain: appendReplacement runs once per match, so the replacement can be computed each time. The letters between matches are copied along.
questions.rule: The loop lets each replacement be computed.
questions.teaches: Because appendReplacement runs once per match, each replacement can be computed from loop state, which a fixed replaceAll string cannot do.

questions.q: A program replaces the word PRICE in a template with the user's text, which may contain a dollar sign or a backslash. What should it do with the user's text?
options: Pass it unchanged, since replacement text is literal
Pass it through quoteReplacement first
Pass it through Pattern.quote
Use replaceFirst instead
optionExplain: A dollar sign in the replacement can refer to a group, and a bad one throws an exception.
Right: that escapes backslash and dollar in the replacement.
quote protects the pattern side, not the replacement side.
The number of replacements does not change how the replacement text is read.
questions.explain: The replacement has its own special characters. quoteReplacement makes them literal, while Pattern.quote does the same job for the expression.
questions.rule: Quote the pattern with quote, quote the replacement with quoteReplacement.
questions.teaches: quote protects the pattern side and quoteReplacement protects the replacement side; they are not interchangeable.

questions.q: A user types an unbalanced expression into a search box. Which exception does Pattern.compile throw?
options: IOException
NullPointerException
IllegalArgumentException
PatternSyntaxException
optionExplain: This signals a problem reading or writing data, not a bad expression.
This signals a missing object, and the expression is present.
This signals a bad argument value in general, not a malformed expression.
Right: it reports a malformed expression.
questions.explain: The class name says it: a syntax problem in the pattern. The card next shows what the exception tells you.
questions.rule: Catch PatternSyntaxException around compile for expressions you do not control, and use getDescription and getIndex to report the problem.

questions.q: Match each method of PatternSyntaxException to what it returns.
pairs: The position of the error in the expression
A multi-line report with a caret under the error
questions.explain: Each method answers one question about the fault: what, where, which expression and a full report.
questions.rule: Description says what, index says where.

questions.q: A test program catches PatternSyntaxException e from compiling the text *abc and prints e.getDescription(). Which message does the tutorial's wording suggest?
options: An unclosed group of parentheses
An illegal escape sequence
A dangling metacharacter
No error is reported at all
optionExplain: There is no parenthesis in this expression.
There is no backslash in this expression.
Right: the star has nothing before it to repeat.
A quantifier with nothing before it is not valid.
questions.explain: The star needs an element before it. With none, the compiler reports a dangling metacharacter, as in the tutorial's ?i) example.
questions.rule: A quantifier with nothing before it is a dangling metacharacter.

questions.q: True or false: A valid expression that matches nothing in the input makes find throw a PatternSyntaxException.
questions.explain: The exception is about malformed syntax, found when compiling. A valid expression with no match just makes find return false.
questions.rule: No match is a result, not an error.

questions.q: Which of these expressions are malformed, so that compile fails? Select all that apply.
options: *abc
a*
(?i)abc
+x
abc+
optionExplain: Right: the star has nothing before it to repeat.
A star after a is valid, and it may repeat the a zero or more times.
The embedded flag is written correctly with both parentheses.
Right: the plus has nothing before it to repeat.
A plus after c repeats the c, which is valid.
questions.explain: A quantifier needs an element in front of it. *abc and +x start with a quantifier, so they are malformed.
questions.rule: A quantifier cannot come first.
questions.teaches: A quantifier placed where nothing precedes it, not only a missing parenthesis, produces the dangling metacharacter error.

questions.q: An application reads search patterns, one per line, from a settings file at start-up. Which design handles a bad line best?
options: Compile each line in try, report the index, skip it
Let the exception end the program at the first bad line
Test each line first with Pattern.matches before compiling it
Catch Exception around the loop and print nothing at all
optionExplain: Right: one bad line does not stop the rest, and the user learns where the fault is.
One faulty line would block every other pattern.
matches runs the expression and needs a valid one, so it fails the same way.
The user would not learn which line failed or why.
questions.explain: Patterns from a file are outside your control. Catching the exception at compile time, and using its description and index, gives a useful report.
questions.rule: Catch at compile for patterns you do not control.
questions.teaches: Validate externally supplied patterns by compiling each one inside try and catch, and report the index so the faulty line can be fixed.

questions.q: A character has the code point 1F600, with five hex digits. Which escape names it in an expression?
optionExplain: Right: the braced form takes any number of digits.
This is four digits followed by an extra 0.
Without braces this is not the braced form.
The \p form names a property, not a code point.
questions.explain: Five digits do not fit the four-digit escape. The card next shows the form that does.
questions.rule: Use \uFFFF for a code point written with four hex digits, and \x{...} when it may need more.

questions.q: The escape \u must be followed by exactly ____ hexadecimal digits.
questions.explain: The four-digit form can reach only code points up to FFFF.
questions.rule: \u takes exactly four hex digits.

questions.q: The musical G clef has code point 1D11E. Which expression matches that single character?
options: \u1D11E
\x1D11E
optionExplain: This is code point 1D11 followed by the letter E.
Without braces this reads two digits, 1D, then 11E.
Right: the braces allow the five digits.
The \p form names a property, not a code point.
questions.explain: Only the braced form can name a five-digit code point. The \u form would stop after four digits and treat the last one as an ordinary character.
questions.rule: Use braces for code points above FFFF.

questions.q: What happens when the expression \u41, with only two digits after \u, is compiled?
options: It matches the letter A, code point 41
A PatternSyntaxException is thrown
It matches the plain text u41 as written
It compiles but then never matches anything
optionExplain: The code point 41 is A, but the short form is not accepted.
Right: the escape requires exactly four digits.
The backslash makes it an escape, not a plain u.
A malformed escape is a syntax error, not a silent failure.
questions.explain: The four-digit rule is strict. A shorter form is a syntax error, so use \x{41} or \u0041.
questions.rule: \u wants four digits, not fewer.

questions.q: True or false: The expression \x{6771} matches the same single character as \u6771.
questions.explain: The braced form accepts any number of digits, including four, so it names the same code point.
questions.rule: \x{...} covers every code point, not only the large ones.
questions.teaches: \x{...} is not limited to supplementary characters; with four digits it names the same code point as \u does.

questions.q: A chat filter in Java source must detect the grinning face, code point 1F600. Which string literal holds a working expression?
optionExplain: The four-digit form cuts the code point short.
In Java source, a single backslash before x is not a valid string escape.
The \p form names a property such as a script or category, not a code point.
Right: the doubled backslash becomes one, and the braces allow five digits.
questions.explain: Two rules combine. The code point has five digits, so use the braced form, and the Java string needs each backslash doubled.
questions.rule: Combine the braced form with doubled backslashes in Java source.
questions.teaches: In Java source the braced code point form needs a doubled backslash, and a single one in a string literal is a compile error.

questions.q: Which expression matches exactly one upper-case letter, in any language?
options: \P{gc=Lu}
[A-Z]
\p{gc=Lu}
\w
optionExplain: The capital P negates, matching anything that is not an upper-case letter.
This covers only the English capital letters.
Right: the general category Lu is the upper-case letters.
This matches ASCII letters, digits and the underscore, in either case.
questions.explain: The tutorial lets you match by category. The card next shows how.
questions.rule: Use \p{...} with a script, block or category name to match by property, and \P{...} for the opposite.

questions.q: Match each expression to what it matches.
pairs: Any character that is not a letter
A character of the Hiragana script
questions.explain: \p picks characters with the property, and \P picks those without it.
questions.rule: Small p includes, capital P excludes.

questions.q: To match one character that is NOT an upper-case letter, change \p{gc=Lu} to \____{gc=Lu}.
questions.explain: The capital P negates the property test.
questions.rule: Capital P negates.

questions.q: True or false: Pattern.matches with the expression \p{IsL}+ and the input ab7 returns true.
questions.explain: The plus lets the letter test repeat, but the 7 is not a letter, so the whole input does not match.
questions.rule: Each \p tests one character, and the quantifier repeats it.

questions.q: Which characters does \P{gc=Lu} match?
options: Only lower-case letters, the opposite kind of letter
Anything that is not an upper-case letter
Only upper-case letters, the characters that have it
Only characters that are not letters of any kind
optionExplain: The negation is not limited to the other kind of letter.
Right: it negates the property, so everything outside the category matches.
Those are the characters that have the property.
Lower-case letters are letters but not upper-case, so they match too.
questions.explain: The property test splits all characters into those with it and those without. The negated form takes every one without it.
questions.rule: A negated property matches everything outside the category.
questions.teaches: \P{gc=Lu} means lacks the upper-case property, so it matches lower-case letters, digits and symbols alike; it is not the opposite kind of letter.

questions.q: A form accepts a one-word name made only of letters from any script. Which check fits best?
options: Pattern.matches("\\w+", name)
Pattern.matches("\\p{Lu}+", name)
Pattern.matches("\\p{L}+", name)
Pattern.matches("\\P{L}+", name)
optionExplain: This accepts digits and the underscore, and rejects accented letters.
This accepts upper-case letters only.
Right: the category L covers letters of every script, and the plus repeats it.
This accepts only characters that are not letters.
questions.explain: The category L is independent of script, unlike \w, which the tutorial defines as ASCII letters, digits and the underscore.
questions.rule: Use a category when the characters come from any script.
questions.teaches: A category such as \p{L} accepts letters from any script and nothing else, whereas \w accepts digits and the underscore and misses non-ASCII letters.

questions.q: Which set of parts makes up a collections framework?
options: Containers, iterators and comparators
Lists, sets, maps and queues
Interfaces, implementations, algorithms
Classes, packages, libraries and modules
optionExplain: These are names of things in the library, but they are not the three parts of the architecture.
These are three kinds of interface, which are only one of the three parts.
Right: these are the three parts the tutorial names.
These are general code-organisation words and say nothing about collections.
questions.explain: A framework combines contracts (interfaces), data structures that obey them (implementations) and reusable procedures (algorithms). The card next explains it.
questions.rule: A collections framework is interfaces, implementations and algorithms working together, so code written against an interface can swap implementations and reuse algorithms.

questions.q: Match each part of a collections framework to what it provides.
pairs: Abstract data types that hide the representation
Reusable functionality such as sorting, usable on many implementations
questions.explain: Interfaces are the contracts, implementations are the structures that obey them, and algorithms are the shared procedures.
questions.rule: Interfaces are contracts, implementations are structures, algorithms are procedures.

questions.q: Sort each item into the framework part it belongs to.

items.t: A class that stores elements in a resizable array
A method that sorts any list it is given
A class that stores elements in a hash table
A method that finds the smallest element of any collection
A method that shuffles the elements of any list
A class that stores elements in linked nodes

questions.explain: Implementations are the data structures themselves. Algorithms are methods that operate on whatever implementation they are handed.
questions.rule: A data structure is an implementation; a procedure that works on any of them is an algorithm.

questions.q: True or false: Because every implementation of an interface obeys the same contract, all of them perform equally well.
questions.explain: The contract fixes behaviour, not speed. The tutorial presents interchangeable implementations as a way to tune a program, which only makes sense if their performance differs.
questions.teaches: Interfaces guarantee what operations do, not how fast they run, so swapping implementations is a tuning tool and the right choice still has to be judged or measured.
questions.rule: A collections framework is interfaces, implementations and algorithms working together, so code written against an interface can swap implementations and reuse algorithms.

questions.q: A method depends only on a collection interface. A team replaces the implementation it is given with another that obeys the same interface. What happens to the method?
options: It keeps working, because it never depended on the representation
It must be rewritten for the structure of each new implementation
It works only when the new class comes from the same package
It compiles but returns the elements in a random order
optionExplain: Right: depending on the interface is exactly what makes implementations interchangeable.
That would be true only if the method used implementation-specific details instead of the interface.
The package has no bearing: any class that obeys the interface qualifies.
Nothing about swapping implementations randomises results; ordering is set by each interface's contract.
questions.explain: Interface-based code is insulated from the representation, so swapping implementations is a tuning choice rather than a rewrite.
questions.rule: Code that depends on the interface survives a change of implementation.

questions.q: A music app defines a Playlist contract with add, remove and play-next. Two classes store tracks differently, and one routine removes repeated tracks from any playlist. Which mapping onto the three framework parts fits?
options: The routine is the interface and the contract is the algorithm, since the routine states what is allowed
The two classes are algorithms and the routine an implementation, because the classes do the work
All three are implementations, because each of them is made of code that runs
Contract is interface, classes are implementations, routine is an algorithm
optionExplain: This swaps the roles: the contract lists operations, and the routine is a procedure that runs.
Storing data is what an implementation does; an algorithm is a procedure over a collection.
Interfaces are abstract and the routine is a shared procedure, so they are not implementations.
Right: this mirrors the interface, implementation and algorithm roles.
questions.explain: The three-part split can be used to read any library: what is promised, what stores the data, and what reusable procedures exist.
questions.teaches: The same three-way reading (contract, storage, reusable procedure) lets you analyse a library from any domain, not only collections.
questions.rule: A collections framework is interfaces, implementations and algorithms working together, so code written against an interface can swap implementations and reuse algorithms.

questions.q: Which core interface is not part of the Collection tree?
options: Set
Map
Queue
List
optionExplain: Set extends Collection, so it is in the tree.
Right: Map sits at the root of its own tree.
Queue extends Collection, so it is in the tree.
List extends Collection, so it is in the tree.
questions.explain: Collection holds elements; a Map holds key-to-value pairs, so it was kept separate. The card next explains it.
questions.rule: Collection roots one tree and Map roots a separate one, and each interface adds one rule about duplicates, order or keys.

questions.q: Match each interface to its defining rule.
pairs: Ordered, duplicates allowed, access by position
Each key maps to at most one value
Holds elements before processing, usually first in first out
questions.explain: Each branch of the hierarchy is named for one rule about duplicates, order or keys.
questions.rule: Know the one rule that sets each interface apart.

questions.q: A method only needs to loop over a group of customer names. It does not care about order or duplicates. Which parameter type gives callers the most freedom?
options: List
Collection
Set
Map
optionExplain: Requiring a List forces callers who hold a Set to copy their data first.
Right: it is the most general type and accepts any Set, List or Queue.
A Set parameter rejects callers who hold a List, and adds a no-duplicates promise the method does not need.
A Map holds pairs, so it cannot stand in for a plain group of names.
questions.explain: Choose the least specific interface that still gives you what the method uses.
questions.rule: Take the most general interface that does the job.

questions.q: A Map cannot be passed to a method that expects a ____ , because Map is outside that tree.
questions.explain: Map has its own root, so it is not a Collection and a Map variable cannot be passed where a Collection is required.
questions.teaches: A Map can still hand you collections: its keys, values or entries can each be seen as a collection, which is how data crosses between the two trees.
questions.rule: Collection roots one tree and Map roots a separate one, and each interface adds one rule about duplicates, order or keys.

questions.q: A program keeps ticket numbers in a Set. The rule changes: the same ticket number may be sold twice and the sale order matters. Which interface fits the new rule?
options: SortedSet
Map
Set
List
optionExplain: A SortedSet orders by value and still refuses duplicates.
A Map would need a key for each entry, and it also refuses duplicate keys.
That is the old rule: it would drop the second sale of the same number.
Right: a List allows duplicates and keeps their order.
questions.explain: When the duplicate or order rule changes, the interface that expresses the rule changes.
questions.rule: Pick the interface whose rule matches the data.

questions.q: A help desk handles tickets in the order received and removes each ticket once handled. Which interface expresses that way of working?
options: Queue
Set
SortedMap
List
optionExplain: Right: a Queue holds elements before processing and typically serves the oldest first.
A Set expresses no duplicates, not a processing order.
A SortedMap pairs keys to values in key order, which is not about arrival.
A List could hold tickets, but it does not say they are consumed from the head.
questions.explain: Some interfaces are chosen for how elements are consumed rather than how they are looked up.
questions.teaches: Queue and Deque are chosen for how elements are consumed (from a head), not for lookup by value or position.
questions.rule: Collection roots one tree and Map roots a separate one, and each interface adds one rule about duplicates, order or keys.

questions.q: True or false: Naming the element type of a collection lets the compiler reject inserts of the wrong type.
questions.explain: Specifying the element type moves a whole class of mistakes from run time to compile time. The card next explains it.
questions.rule: Declare a collection with its element type so the compiler, not a failing run, finds wrong insertions.

questions.q: According to the tutorial, what is the benefit of declaring the element type of a collection?
options: The collection runs faster because it skips internal type checks
The collection can then hold elements of any type without further checks
The compiler checks insertions, so wrong types are caught at build time
The collection becomes unmodifiable once its element type is declared
optionExplain: The tutorial's point is about catching mistakes, not about speed.
It does the reverse: it restricts the elements to the named type.
Right: that is the stated advantage.
Element typing says nothing about whether the collection can change.
questions.explain: Static checking turns a run-time surprise into a compile-time error.
questions.rule: Name the element type so the compiler can check it.

questions.q: A developer declares a List of Integer called scores and writes scores.add of the text value high. What happens?
options: The program compiles and throws an error when the line runs
The text is converted to a number automatically
The element is stored and later reads return text
The compiler reports an error
optionExplain: That would be the outcome without an element type; the declared type makes the check happen earlier.
No automatic conversion from text to a number happens here.
The declared element type prevents the insertion in the first place.
Right: a text value does not match the declared element type.
questions.explain: The declared type is part of what the compiler enforces on every call to add.
questions.rule: A typed collection rejects wrong inserts at compile time.

questions.q: True or false: Once the element type is declared, no wrong-typed element can get into the collection by any route.
questions.explain: The check is made by the compiler, and the tutorial's section on wrappers notes that it can be defeated, for example through raw types.
questions.teaches: Compile-time checking has gaps: older code that uses raw types can slip a wrong element in, which is why the tutorial offers checked wrappers as a run-time safety net.
questions.rule: Declare a collection with its element type so the compiler, not a failing run, finds wrong insertions.

questions.q: A developer adds the wrong type to a typed list. Put the stages in the order they happen.
items: Developer writes a call that adds a wrong-typed element
The compiler checks the call against the declared element type
The compiler reports an error
The program is never built and never runs the faulty line
questions.explain: With element types the mistake is stopped at the second stage, long before anything can run.
questions.rule: Typed collections fail early.

questions.q: A team stores items in a collection declared without an element type, and a bug report says a number was found where text was expected, only in production. Which tutorial advice would have moved the discovery earlier?
options: Switch to a faster implementation of the same collection interface
Declare the element type so the compiler checks each insertion
Wrap the collection so that every call to it is synchronized
Replace the collection with a plain array of objects
optionExplain: Speed is unrelated to when the type error is noticed.
Right: the check then happens at compile time.
Synchronization concerns threads, not element types.
The tutorial does not suggest this, and arrays do not give the same compile-time guard for every collection operation.
questions.explain: Production-only type errors are what untyped collections tend to produce; compile-time typing prevents them.
questions.teaches: Without an element type, a wrong insertion may stay hidden until much later code uses the element, which makes the cause hard to trace.
questions.rule: Declare a collection with its element type so the compiler, not a failing run, finds wrong insertions.

questions.q: A collection cannot support an operation you call. What does the framework expect it to do?
options: Silently ignore the call and carry on
Return null and leave the data unchanged
Throw UnsupportedOperationException
Convert itself to a different implementation
optionExplain: A silent no-op would hide a bug; the framework asks for an exception.
Return values are not used to signal unsupported operations.
Right: that is the framework's way of saying the operation is not supported.
Collections never swap their own implementation to satisfy a call.
questions.explain: An exception makes the failure loud instead of letting the program continue with wrong assumptions. The card next explains it.
questions.rule: Modification operations are optional, and calling one the collection does not support throws UnsupportedOperationException.

questions.q: True or false: According to the tutorial, the general-purpose implementations support all the optional operations.
questions.explain: The tutorial says every general-purpose implementation of the Java platform supports all optional operations, so exceptions arise mainly with special collections.
questions.rule: General-purpose collections support everything; special ones may not.

questions.q: A list is created with Arrays.asList on an array of three names. A program calls set on index 0, then add of a fourth name. Which call fails?
options: add, because the list has a fixed size
set, because the list is read-only
Both fail, because the list is backed by an array
Neither fails, because every list supports add
optionExplain: Right: add is unsupported and throws UnsupportedOperationException.
set is supported: it only replaces an element and does not change the size.
Being backed by an array limits size changes but still allows replacing elements.
Optional operations mean some lists do not support add.
questions.explain: A fixed-size list keeps its length, so only size-changing calls are refused.
questions.rule: Fixed-size lists allow set but refuse add and remove.

questions.q: Why did the designers make operations optional instead of defining a separate interface for each variant?
options: To avoid extra interfaces for variants such as immutable or fixed-size
To let implementations leave out documentation of what they support
To make every collection thread-safe by default without wrappers
To prevent the framework from offering sorting algorithms at all
optionExplain: Right: this is the reason the tutorial gives.
The tutorial requires implementations to document which operations they support.
Optional operations have no link to thread safety.
Sorting is unaffected; it is not an optional-operation matter.
questions.explain: Each new variant would double the interface count, so one interface with optional operations was chosen.
questions.teaches: The cost of the choice is that support is checked when the call runs, not when the program compiles, so documentation is essential.
questions.hint: Think how many interfaces immutable, fixed-size and append-only versions of each type would need.
questions.rule: Modification operations are optional, and calling one the collection does not support throws UnsupportedOperationException.

questions.q: A method receives a List and calls add on it. A caller passes a list that came from Arrays.asList. Which statement predicts the result?
options: The code does not compile, because that kind of list has no add method at all
The call quietly adds the element to the backing array and grows it
It throws UnsupportedOperationException at run time although the code compiled
The call succeeds and the list silently turns into a resizable ArrayList
optionExplain: The type is List, so add exists at compile time; support is a run-time matter.
An array cannot grow, so no such quiet addition occurs.
Right: support is only discovered when the call runs.
A list never changes its class to accommodate a call.
questions.explain: Because optional operations are not part of the type, the compiler cannot warn you.
questions.rule: Unsupported operations fail at run time, not compile time.

questions.q: A service hands out collections to clients. Sort the situations by whether UnsupportedOperationException is a plausible result.

items.t: add on a list that wraps a fixed-size array
remove on a read-only view given to clients
size on any collection
contains on a fixed-size list
add on a general-purpose ArrayList
set on a general-purpose ArrayList

questions.explain: Only size-changing or write calls on restricted collections can be refused. Read calls and general-purpose collections do not raise it.
questions.teaches: The exception belongs to restricted views and special collections, so a service that exposes read-only collections should tell clients which writes are refused.
questions.rule: Modification operations are optional, and calling one the collection does not support throws UnsupportedOperationException.

questions.q: A Set of String already contains the word blue. What does add of blue return?
options: true, because the element is now in the set
false, because the set did not change
It throws an exception, because duplicates are refused
null, because there is nothing new to return
optionExplain: The element was in the set before the call; true means the collection was modified.
Right: add reports whether the collection changed.
Duplicates are quietly refused by returning false, not with an exception.
add returns a boolean.
questions.explain: A Set refuses a duplicate by not changing and saying so. The card next explains it.
questions.rule: add returns whether the collection changed, and remove takes out one instance and reports whether anything was removed.

questions.q: In the Collection interface, what does remove(o) do when the object occurs several times?
options: It removes every instance of the object
It removes the object only if it appears once
It removes the last instance of the object
It removes a single instance of the object
optionExplain: Removing all instances needs removeAll with a one-element collection.
Several occurrences do not block the call.
The tutorial describes one instance, without naming the last.
Right: it removes one instance.
questions.explain: remove is a single-instance operation, and its result tells you whether anything went.
questions.rule: remove takes out one instance.

questions.q: A List already holds the word cat once. After one more call to add with cat, the List holds cat ____ times.
questions.explain: A List allows duplicates, so the second cat is stored and add returns true. The list then holds the word twice.
questions.rule: A List stores duplicates; a Set refuses them.

questions.q: True or false: A call to remove on a collection that does not contain the object throws an exception.
questions.explain: remove returns false when nothing was removed; it does not throw for an absent element.
questions.teaches: The boolean result of remove is the only signal of absence, so code that must know whether something was removed should check it.
questions.rule: add returns whether the collection changed, and remove takes out one instance and reports whether anything was removed.

questions.q: A list holds 5, 7, 5. After one call to remove with the value 5, the list holds ____ copies of 5.
questions.explain: One call removes a single instance, so one 5 is left. Two calls would be needed to remove both.
questions.rule: One remove call removes one instance.
questions.hint: Think how many instances a single call takes out.

questions.q: A signup form stores email addresses in a Set. The code must tell the user when an address was already registered. Which approach uses only what this card covers?
options: Call remove first, and treat a true result as already registered
Call size before and after add and compare nothing else
Call add and treat a false result as already registered
Catch an exception thrown by add for duplicates
optionExplain: That would delete the existing address as a side effect.
Possible, but it ignores the return value the interface provides for this purpose.
Right: add returns false when the set already had the element.
A Set does not throw for duplicates; it returns false.
questions.explain: The return value of add is a built-in duplicate detector for sets.
questions.teaches: The return value of add can double as a membership test in one step, which saves a separate contains call.
questions.rule: add returns whether the collection changed, and remove takes out one instance and reports whether anything was removed.

questions.q: Which call removes every instance of the value x from the collection c?
options: c.removeAll(Collections.singleton(x))
c.remove(x)
c.retainAll(Collections.singleton(x))
c.containsAll(Collections.singleton(x))
optionExplain: Right: removeAll with a one-element set removes all matches.
remove deletes only one instance.
retainAll keeps only x, which does the opposite.
containsAll only tests; it changes nothing.
questions.explain: A singleton set is a convenient one-element argument for a bulk operation. The card next explains it.
questions.rule: addAll, removeAll, retainAll and clear change the target, and removeAll with a singleton removes every instance of one value.

questions.q: Match each bulk operation to its effect on the target collection.
pairs: Adds every element of the other collection
Removes the elements that appear in the other collection
Keeps only the elements that appear in the other collection
Tests whether every element of the other collection is present
questions.explain: Each bulk operation takes a whole collection as its argument; only containsAll leaves the target unchanged.
questions.rule: Three bulk operations change the target; containsAll only tests.

questions.q: A list holds 1, 2, 3, 4. A program calls retainAll with a collection holding 2 and 4. What is the list afterwards?
optionExplain: That would be the result of removeAll with the same argument.
retainAll changes the list whenever some elements are absent from the argument.
No reordering or appending takes place.
Right: only elements also found in the argument are kept.
questions.explain: retainAll is an intersection with the argument, applied to the target in place.
questions.rule: retainAll keeps the overlap.

questions.q: To remove all null elements from the collection c, call c.removeAll(Collections.____(null)).
questions.explain: singleton builds an immutable one-element set; removing it removes every null.
questions.teaches: remove(null) would delete only one null, whereas removeAll with a singleton of null clears all of them in one call.
questions.rule: addAll, removeAll, retainAll and clear change the target, and removeAll with a singleton removes every instance of one value.

questions.q: True or false: If removeAll is called twice in a row with the same argument, the second call returns true as well.
questions.explain: After the first call nothing matching remains, so the second call changes nothing and returns false.
questions.rule: The result reports a change, so a repeated call reports none.

questions.q: A report must show the customers common to two lists while keeping both original lists intact. Which approach respects that?
options: Call retainAll on the first list directly
Copy the first list, then call retainAll on the copy
Call removeAll on the second list with the first as argument
Call clear on the first list afterwards
optionExplain: That would change the first list, which must stay intact.
Right: the bulk operation changes only the copy.
That changes the second list and gives the difference, not the overlap.
Clearing destroys the data the report needs to keep.
questions.explain: Because bulk operations are mutative, you protect an original by working on a copy.
questions.teaches: Copy through a conversion constructor before a destructive bulk operation to get a nondestructive version.
questions.rule: addAll, removeAll, retainAll and clear change the target, and removeAll with a singleton removes every instance of one value.

questions.q: A program must delete every element that fails a test while walking through a collection. Which traversal tool is needed?
options: A for-each loop with a call to remove inside
An explicit Iterator calling remove
A for-each loop with a break
Any of them, since all three allow removal
optionExplain: for-each cannot remove elements, and trying to change the collection during it is unreliable.
Right: the Iterator can remove the current element safely.
A break stops the loop but removes nothing.
Only the Iterator supports removal during traversal.
questions.explain: Only the Iterator carries a remove operation tied to the element just returned. The card next explains it.
questions.rule: Prefer aggregate operations to read or transform, for-each for plain loops, and an Iterator when you must remove while walking.

questions.q: Match each traversal method to a feature the tutorial gives it.
pairs: Preferred in JDK 8, built from streams and lambdas
Concise, but hides the iterator and cannot remove
Can remove the current element during traversal
questions.explain: Each method has one distinguishing trait: expressiveness, brevity or the ability to remove.
questions.rule: Know each method's distinguishing trait.

questions.q: A method must print the names in a List of Person, one per line, with no changes to the list. Which tool does the tutorial prefer in JDK 8?
options: An Iterator with hasNext and next
A for loop using get and an index
An Enumeration
Aggregate operations on a stream
optionExplain: It works, but the tutorial prefers aggregate operations in JDK 8.
This is not among the three ways the tutorial lists.
The tutorial does not list this among the three ways.
Right: the tutorial prefers streams with lambda expressions.
questions.explain: Aggregate operations are the tutorial's first choice for expressing a read-only pass.
questions.rule: Prefer streams for read-only passes in JDK 8.

questions.q: True or false: A for-each loop over a collection can be used to filter it by removing unwanted elements.
questions.explain: for-each hides the iterator, so there is nothing to call remove on; the tutorial says it cannot be used for filtering.
questions.teaches: for-each is syntax over an iterator the program cannot reach, which is why filtering needs the explicit Iterator instead.
questions.rule: Prefer aggregate operations to read or transform, for-each for plain loops, and an Iterator when you must remove while walking.

questions.q: Two lists must be walked side by side, taking one element from each in step. Which tool does the tutorial point to?
options: Explicit Iterators, one per list
One for-each loop nested inside another
A single stream pipeline over both lists
The clear operation on each list
optionExplain: Right: iterating over multiple collections in parallel is a stated reason to use Iterators.
Nested loops produce every pairing instead of walking in step.
A stream has one source, so it cannot step two collections together in this way.
clear empties the list and walks nothing.
questions.explain: Stepping through two collections together needs control over each walk, which only explicit Iterators give.
questions.rule: Use Iterators to walk several collections in step.

questions.q: A teammate passes a lambda to a stream filter that appends each element to an outside list as a side effect. According to the tutorial, what risk does this create?
options: The stream will refuse to run because the lambda has side effects
The source collection will be emptied after the pipeline finishes
The code can break if the pipeline later runs as a parallel stream
The lambda will be converted into an Iterator by the compiler
optionExplain: A stream runs it; the danger is in unreliable results.
Aggregate operations do not modify the source collection.
Right: the tutorial warns that lambdas should avoid side effects for this reason.
No such conversion exists.
questions.explain: Side effects that rely on order or single-threaded execution can fail when processing is split across threads.
questions.teaches: A lambda that works on a serial stream can still be wrong, because correctness under parallel execution is a separate question.
questions.rule: Prefer aggregate operations to read or transform, for-each for plain loops, and an Iterator when you must remove while walking.

questions.q: During an iteration over a collection, which way of removing the current element is safe?
options: Calling remove on the collection with the same element
Calling clear on the collection and refilling it
Calling add on the collection to keep the size equal
Calling remove on the Iterator itself
optionExplain: Other modifications during iteration give unspecified behaviour.
That is also a modification from outside the iterator.
Adding is another outside modification, which is not safe.
Right: this is the only safe way the tutorial names.
questions.explain: The iterator knows its position, so only it can remove without confusing the traversal. The card next explains it.
questions.rule: Call next first, then remove at most once per next, and make no other change to the collection while the loop runs.

questions.q: Put these calls in a valid order for removing one element with an Iterator.
items: Call hasNext and find it true
Call next and receive the element
Test the element
Call remove on the Iterator
questions.explain: remove always acts on the element that the most recent call to next returned, so next must come first.
questions.rule: next first, then remove.

questions.q: A loop calls it.remove() twice in a row after a single call to next. What happens on the second call?
options: It removes the element that came before the removed one
It throws an exception, since remove is allowed once per next
It removes nothing and quietly returns false to the caller
It removes the next element and moves the cursor past it
optionExplain: remove works only on the element last returned by next.
Right: the rule is one remove per call to next.
remove returns nothing; it throws when misused.
Moving on is the job of next, not remove.
questions.explain: Each remove is tied to the element that next just returned.
questions.rule: At most one remove per next.

questions.q: True or false: An Iterator for a collection that does not support removal may throw an exception when remove is called.
questions.explain: Iterator.remove is an optional operation, so a collection can refuse it; the exception raised is UnsupportedOperationException.
questions.teaches: Iterator.remove is itself one of the optional operations, so safe in the tutorial's sense does not mean always available.
questions.rule: Call next first, then remove at most once per next, and make no other change to the collection while the loop runs.

questions.q: A loop over a List calls list.remove on the list itself whenever it meets a bad element, instead of calling remove on the Iterator. What does the tutorial say about the outcome?
options: It works, because the list also has a remove method
It throws the same exception on the very first removal
The behaviour is unspecified, so the loop may fail
It works only for the first bad element it meets
optionExplain: The list has remove, but using it inside the loop is the unsafe route.
The tutorial calls it unspecified, which does not promise a particular exception.
Right: changing the collection by any other route during iteration is unspecified.
No such guarantee is given, even for the first one.
questions.explain: Unspecified means no promise: it may skip elements, fail, or appear to work.
questions.rule: Other changes during iteration are unspecified.

questions.q: A program keeps a Map of user names to sessions and must drop every entry whose session is expired while looping over the keys. Which pattern follows the tutorial's rule?
options: Iterate the key view and call remove on that iterator
Loop over the key view with for-each and call remove on the map
Collect the expired keys and call put with null values for them
Call clear on the key view each time an expired session is found
optionExplain: Right: removal through the iterator is the safe route, and it writes through to the Map.
That modifies the map from outside the iteration, which is unspecified.
put with null keeps the entries rather than dropping them.
clear would remove every entry, not just the expired ones.
questions.explain: Views write through to the map, so the same Iterator.remove rule works for filtering a map.
questions.teaches: Iterator.remove on an iterator of a map's key view removes the entry from the map itself, so the rule extends to maps.
questions.rule: Call next first, then remove at most once per next, and make no other change to the collection while the loop runs.

questions.q: A legacy method needs a String array. You hold a Collection of String called c. Which call produces one?
options: c.toArray(new String[0])
c.toArray()
c.asArray()
(String[]) c
optionExplain: Right: the typed form returns an array of the argument's type.
This form returns an array of Object, not of String.
The Collection interface has no such method.
A collection is not an array, so a cast cannot turn it into one.
questions.explain: The typed form of toArray is how you pick the result's element type. The card next explains it.
questions.rule: toArray() gives an Object array, and passing an array of the wanted type gives an array of that type.

questions.q: True or false: Calling toArray with no argument creates a new array of type Object.
questions.explain: The no-argument form returns an Object array whose length equals the number of elements.
questions.rule: No argument means an Object array.

questions.q: To get an array of Integer from a Collection of Integer called nums, call nums.toArray(new ____[0]).
questions.explain: The argument's type fixes the type of the result, so an Integer array argument yields an Integer array.
questions.rule: The argument's type picks the result type.

questions.q: True or false: Replacing an element slot in the array returned by toArray changes the contents of the collection.
questions.explain: toArray creates a new array, so putting a different object in a slot of the array leaves the collection as it was.
questions.teaches: The array is a separate snapshot of the element references: reassigning a slot affects only the array, so toArray is a copy, not a view.
questions.rule: toArray() gives an Object array, and passing an array of the wanted type gives an array of that type.

questions.q: A Collection of String holds 3 elements. A program calls toArray with a String array of length 0. How long is the array returned?
options: 0, the same as the argument
1, since only one array is created
3, the same as the collection
The call fails because the argument is too short
optionExplain: The argument only supplies the type, here; the new array gets the collection's length.
The count of arrays created has no bearing on the length.
Right: the new array has the collection's length.
A short argument is acceptable; the method creates a new array when needed.
questions.explain: The supplied array fixes the type; the collection fixes the length.
questions.rule: Length comes from the collection, type from the argument.

questions.q: An older payroll routine expects an Employee array. A newer module has a Collection of Employee called staff. Which call hands the routine what it needs?
options: Employee[] list = staff.toArray();
staff.toArray(new Employee[0])
staff.toArray(Object.class)
Collections.sort(staff)
optionExplain: toArray() produces an Object array, so assigning it to an Employee array is a type mismatch.
Right: it produces an array whose type is Employee.
toArray takes an array argument, not a class.
Sorting reorders a list; it does not convert anything to an array.
questions.explain: The same bridge works for any element type: pass an empty array of that type.
questions.teaches: An empty array is enough as the type argument, so you do not need to size the array yourself.
questions.rule: toArray() gives an Object array, and passing an array of the wanted type gives an array of that type.

questions.q: A List of words with repeats is copied into a Set. What happens to the repeats?
options: All repeats are kept in order
The copy fails with an exception
Only the last copy of each word is dropped
Each word is kept once
optionExplain: Keeping repeats in order is what a List does.
Copying a collection with repeats into a Set is allowed; repeats are simply dropped.
A Set keeps one copy of each, not removing only the last.
Right: a Set cannot hold duplicates.
questions.explain: A Set ignores any element equal to one it already has. The card next explains it.
