questions.rule: A Set is a Collection without duplicates: use HashSet for speed, TreeSet for value order and LinkedHashSet for insertion order.

questions.q: Match each Set implementation to its main trait.
pairs: Hash table, no ordering guarantee, best performing
Sorted by element value, substantially slower
Remembers insertion order at a small cost
questions.explain: The three differ in order and speed, and the choice follows from which you need.
questions.rule: Pick the Set implementation by the order you need.

questions.q: A tool reads postcodes with repeats and must print each distinct postcode in ascending order. Which approach fits?
options: Copy them into a HashSet and iterate
Copy them into a LinkedHashSet and iterate
Copy them into a TreeSet and iterate
Copy them into a List and iterate
optionExplain: A HashSet removes repeats but guarantees no order.
That keeps first-seen order, which need not be ascending.
Right: TreeSet removes repeats and iterates in value order.
A List would keep the repeats.
questions.explain: Value order is the job of TreeSet.
questions.rule: TreeSet gives value order.

questions.q: True or false: A HashSet and a TreeSet holding exactly the same elements are equal to each other.
questions.explain: The tutorial gives Set a stronger equals contract: two Set instances are equal if they hold the same elements, whatever their implementation types.
questions.teaches: Set equality depends only on the elements held, so implementation classes and iteration order do not matter.
questions.rule: A Set is a Collection without duplicates: use HashSet for speed, TreeSet for value order and LinkedHashSet for insertion order.

questions.q: The words i came i saw i left are added to a TreeSet of String. What does printing the set show?
options: 4 distinct words: [came, i, left, saw]
6 distinct words: [came, i, i, i, left, saw]
4 distinct words: [i, came, saw, left]
3 distinct words: [came, i, saw]
optionExplain: Right: four distinct words, in alphabetical order.
Repeats are not kept in a Set.
That is first-seen order, which belongs to a LinkedHashSet.
The word left is also a distinct word and is kept.
questions.explain: TreeSet sorts as it stores, so the printed order is the sorted order.
questions.rule: TreeSet iterates in sorted order.

questions.q: To remove duplicates from a Collection c while keeping the order of first occurrences, write new ____(c).
questions.explain: A LinkedHashSet drops repeats and remembers insertion order, so the first occurrences keep their order.
questions.teaches: Converting through a LinkedHashSet is a one-line way to deduplicate and keep order, and it can be wrapped in a generic method that returns the same element type.
questions.rule: A Set is a Collection without duplicates: use HashSet for speed, TreeSet for value order and LinkedHashSet for insertion order.

questions.q: Which bulk operation turns s1 into the intersection of s1 and s2?
options: s1.addAll(s2)
s1.removeAll(s2)
s1.containsAll(s2)
s1.retainAll(s2)
optionExplain: That produces the union.
That produces the difference, removing the shared elements.
That only tests for a subset and changes nothing.
Right: it keeps only the elements that are also in s2.
questions.explain: Intersection means keeping what both sets share. The card next explains it.
questions.rule: containsAll is subset, addAll is union, retainAll is intersection and removeAll is difference, and each changes the set it is called on.

questions.q: Match each operation on s1 and s2 to its set-algebra name.
questions.explain: The bulk operations map one-to-one onto the standard set operations.
questions.rule: Each bulk operation is a set operation.

questions.q: s1 holds 1, 2, 3, 4 and s2 holds 3, 4, 5. After s1.removeAll(s2), s1 holds ____ elements.
questions.explain: The elements 3 and 4 are shared and are removed, which leaves 1 and 2.
questions.rule: removeAll leaves only what s2 lacks.

questions.q: True or false: s1.removeAll(s2) and s2.removeAll(s1) give the same result for any two sets.
questions.explain: Asymmetric difference depends on the order of the operands: with 1, 2 and 2, 3 the first call leaves 1 and the second leaves 3.
questions.teaches: Asymmetric difference depends on operand order, whereas the symmetric difference treats both sets alike.
questions.rule: containsAll is subset, addAll is union, retainAll is intersection and removeAll is difference, and each changes the set it is called on.

questions.q: s1 holds 1, 2 and s2 is empty. What does s1.retainAll(s2) do to s1?
options: It leaves s1 exactly as it was before the call
It empties s1, since nothing in s1 is also in s2
It throws an exception because s2 is empty
It copies the elements of s2 into s1 instead
optionExplain: That is the effect of removeAll with an empty set, not retainAll.
Right: intersection with an empty set is empty.
An empty argument is legal.
retainAll never adds elements.
questions.explain: Changing the second set changes the result; an empty set makes retainAll empty the target.
questions.rule: retainAll with an empty set empties the target.

questions.q: Put these steps in order to find the words that occur exactly once, using the result of add.
items: Make two empty sets, uniques and dups
For each word, call add on uniques
If add returned false, add the word to dups
After the loop, call removeAll on uniques with dups
questions.explain: A false from add marks a repeat. Removing the repeats from uniques afterwards leaves words seen once.
questions.teaches: Combining the return value of add with removeAll finds the single-occurrence items in one pass, with no counting.
questions.rule: containsAll is subset, addAll is union, retainAll is intersection and removeAll is difference, and each changes the set it is called on.

questions.q: What does indexOf return when the element is not in the list?
options: Zero
Minus one
null
It throws an exception
optionExplain: Zero is a valid index, the first position.
Right: minus one signals absence.
indexOf returns an int, which cannot be null.
Absence is reported by a value, not by an exception.
questions.explain: A negative index cannot be a real position, so minus one is a safe signal. The card next explains it.
questions.rule: A List keeps elements in position, allows duplicates, and its set and remove by index return the old element.

questions.q: The set method replaces an element and returns the ____ element.
questions.explain: set hands back the element it replaced, which is why swapping can be done with get and set.
questions.rule: set and remove by index return the old element.

questions.q: names holds Ann, Bob, Ann. A program calls remove with the object Ann. What does the list hold afterwards?
options: Bob
Ann, Bob
Ann, Bob, Ann
Bob, Ann
optionExplain: Both copies would be gone only with a bulk removal.
That would mean the last occurrence was removed.
The list changes, since the object is present.
Right: the first occurrence is removed.
questions.explain: On a List, removing an object takes out its first occurrence.
questions.rule: remove of an object removes the first occurrence.

questions.q: True or false: A LinkedList and an ArrayList holding the same elements in the same order are equal lists.
questions.explain: List equality depends only on the elements and their order, not on the implementation class.
questions.teaches: Equality for lists compares order as well as contents, so the same elements in a different order are not equal.
questions.rule: A List keeps elements in position, allows duplicates, and its set and remove by index return the old element.

questions.q: A list holds A, B, C. A program calls addAll at index 1 with a collection that returns X then Y. What does the list hold?
options: A, X, Y, B, C
X, Y, A, B, C
A, B, C, X, Y
A, Y, X, B, C
optionExplain: Right: the new elements go in at the index, in the order the collection's iterator returns them.
Index 1 is not the start of the list.
That is the result of addAll without an index, which appends.
The elements are inserted in the iterator's order, not reversed.
questions.explain: The index form of addAll inserts, shifting later elements along.
questions.rule: addAll with an index inserts in iterator order.

questions.q: A seating plan is a List of names. Put these steps in order to swap the people in seats i and j.
items: Read the name at seat i into a temporary variable
Set seat i to the name read from seat j
Set seat j to the temporary variable
questions.explain: Reading both values before overwriting either avoids losing one, and only get and set are needed.
questions.teaches: A swap written with only get and set works on any List, which is why such algorithms are called polymorphic.
questions.rule: A List keeps elements in position, allows duplicates, and its set and remove by index return the old element.

questions.q: A list has 4 elements. How many valid cursor positions does its ListIterator have?
optionExplain: Three would count only the gaps between four elements.
Four would count one position per element, but the cursor sits between elements.
Right: the cursor can sit before the first element, between each pair, and after the last.
There are only the gaps and the two ends, which make 5.
questions.explain: Positions are gaps, and n elements have n plus 1 gaps counting both ends. The card next explains it.
questions.rule: The cursor sits between elements, and remove and set act on whichever element next or previous returned last.

questions.q: Which of these does ListIterator add to a plain Iterator? Select all that apply.
options: previous, for backward traversal
set, to overwrite the last returned element
nextIndex, to report the cursor position
hasNext, to test whether more elements remain
next, to return the following element
optionExplain: Right: walking backward is new in ListIterator.
Right: Iterator has no way to replace an element.
Right: position queries are new.
Iterator already has hasNext.
Iterator already has next.
questions.explain: ListIterator keeps everything Iterator has and adds backward movement, set, add and position queries.
questions.rule: The cursor sits between elements, and remove and set act on whichever element next or previous returned last.

questions.q: On the list A, B, C a ListIterator starts at the beginning and next is called once. After that, nextIndex returns ____ .
questions.explain: The cursor has crossed A, so it sits between A and B, and the next element has index 1.
questions.rule: nextIndex is the index next would return.

questions.q: True or false: Immediately after the last element has been returned by next, nextIndex equals the size of the list.
questions.explain: At the end, the cursor is past the last element, and nextIndex is defined as the size there. previousIndex is minus one at the start.
questions.teaches: The two ends are marked by previousIndex minus one and nextIndex equal to size, so no separate bounds check is needed.
questions.rule: The cursor sits between elements, and remove and set act on whichever element next or previous returned last.

questions.q: On the list A, B, C a ListIterator is created at index 3. It calls previous twice, then remove. What does the list hold?
options: A, B
B, C
A, B, C
A, C
optionExplain: That would remove C, which previous returned first rather than last.
That would remove A, which previous has not yet returned.
remove acts on the last returned element, so the list changes.
Right: the second previous returned B, so remove deletes B.
questions.explain: remove always removes the element returned by the most recent next or previous.
questions.rule: remove acts on the last element returned.

questions.q: A search loop reads: for (ListIterator it = list.listIterator(); it.hasNext(); ) { if (it.next().equals(target)) print(it.next()); }. What is wrong?
options: hasNext must be replaced by hasPrevious in a forward loop
The second next moves on, so it prints the following element
print cannot be called from inside the body of an if statement
equals cannot be called on the object that next returns
optionExplain: hasNext is correct for a forward walk.
Right: each call to next advances the cursor.
Nothing prevents calls inside a loop.
The result of next is an ordinary object, so equals is allowed.
questions.explain: The tutorial's own indexOf and replace snippets repeat this slip; store the result of next once if you need it twice.
questions.rule: Call next once and keep the result.

questions.q: A playlist is a List of track names. Put these steps in order to replace every occurrence of a track with several new tracks while walking with a ListIterator.
items: Call next and compare the track with the one to replace
On a match, call remove to delete it
Call add once for each new track, in the order wanted
Continue the loop with hasNext
questions.explain: add inserts before the cursor, so the new tracks land where the old one was, in the order added, and the loop carries on after them.
questions.teaches: Because add inserts before the cursor, the new tracks are not visited again by the same loop.
questions.rule: The cursor sits between elements, and remove and set act on whichever element next or previous returned last.

questions.q: A list holds A, B, C, D, E, F. What does subList with arguments 1 and 4 contain?
options: B, C, D, E
A, B, C, D
B, C, D
A, B, C
optionExplain: That would include index 4.
The range starts at index 1, not 0.
Right: index 1 is included and index 4 is excluded.
That would be the view of the first three, from 0 to 3.
questions.explain: The end index is excluded, as in a for loop that stops before reaching it. The card next explains it.
questions.rule: subList is a live window with an included start and an excluded end; use it briefly and copy it if you need an independent list.

questions.q: True or false: In subList(from, to), the element at index to is not part of the view.
questions.explain: The range is half-open: the start is included and the end is excluded.
questions.rule: subList is from inclusive, to exclusive.

questions.q: To remove the elements at positions 2, 3 and 4 of a list, call list.subList(2, ____).clear().
questions.explain: The end index is excluded, so removing positions 2 to 4 needs an end of 5.
questions.rule: The end index is one past the last position wanted.

questions.q: A list holds A to F. The sublist from 2 to 5 is searched for D with indexOf. What is returned?
options: 1, the position in the sublist
3, the position in the whole list
minus one, since D is outside the range
4, the end of the range
optionExplain: Right: indexes are relative to the sublist, whose first element is C.
That would be the index in the backing list, not in the sublist.
D is inside the range 2 to 4.
The end index plays no part in the answer.
questions.explain: To convert a sublist index to a backing-list index, add the from index.
questions.teaches: The index returned by a sublist search must be translated by adding the from index to find the position in the backing list.
questions.rule: subList is a live window with an included start and an excluded end; use it briefly and copy it if you need an independent list.

questions.q: A sublist is made. The program then adds an element directly to the original list, not through the sublist, and reads the sublist. What does the tutorial say about the result?
options: Its behaviour is undefined
The sublist shows the new element
The sublist keeps showing its old contents
The original list rejects the addition
optionExplain: Right: structural changes made outside the sublist leave it undefined.
A view is not guaranteed to reflect outside structural changes.
No such stable snapshot is promised; a view is not a copy.
The original list accepts the addition; it is the sublist that suffers.
questions.explain: A view is only trustworthy while no one else restructures the backing list.
questions.rule: Do not keep a sublist while the backing list changes.

questions.q: A card game must deal the last n cards of a deck list into a new hand and remove them from the deck. Put the steps in a safe order.
items: Take a view of the last n cards with subList
Copy the view into a new list
Clear the view
Return the new list as the hand
questions.explain: Clearing before copying would empty the view, and with it the data to be copied, since the view writes through.
questions.teaches: Because a view writes through, you must copy it before clearing it, or the copy has nothing left to hold.
questions.rule: subList is a live window with an included start and an excluded end; use it briefly and copy it if you need an independent list.

questions.q: True or false: On an empty queue, poll throws an exception.
questions.explain: poll is the special-value form for removal, so it returns null; remove is the one that throws. The card next explains it.
questions.rule: Each queue operation has a throwing form (add, remove, element) and a special-value form (offer, poll, peek).

questions.q: Match each Queue method to its role.
pairs: Insert, throws if capacity is exceeded
Insert, returns false instead of throwing
Remove the head, returns null if empty
Examine the head, throws if empty
questions.explain: The throwing forms and the special-value forms come in matched pairs.
questions.rule: Every operation has a throwing form and a special-value form.

questions.q: A worker loop should stop quietly as soon as the queue is empty, without exception handling. Which removal fits?
options: remove, and catch the exception at the end
element, and stop when it returns null
poll, and stop when it returns null
add, and stop when it returns false
optionExplain: It works, but it forces exception handling the loop wanted to avoid.
element throws on an empty queue, and it does not remove the head.
Right: poll signals an empty queue with null.
add inserts rather than removes.
questions.explain: Special-value forms suit loops that expect to run out.
questions.rule: Use poll or peek when emptiness is normal.

questions.q: element returns the head of the queue without removing it, and throws ____ when the queue is empty.
questions.explain: element and remove both throw NoSuchElementException on an empty queue; element leaves the head in place.
questions.teaches: element and peek read the head without removing it, so they differ from remove and poll in whether the queue changes, not only in how failure is reported.
questions.rule: Each queue operation has a throwing form (add, remove, element) and a special-value form (offer, poll, peek).

questions.q: A queue is bounded and already full. A producer changes its code from add to offer. What changes for a call that cannot fit?
options: It blocks the producing thread until space becomes free
It returns false instead of throwing IllegalStateException
It silently discards the oldest element to make room
It throws NoSuchElementException instead of IllegalStateException
optionExplain: Queue does not define blocking operations.
Right: offer reports the failure with a value.
Neither form removes elements to make room.
That exception belongs to removal and examination of an empty queue.
questions.explain: Switching to the special-value form changes how failure is reported, not whether it happens.
questions.rule: offer is intended mainly for bounded queues.

questions.q: A queue implementation allows null elements. A loop calls poll until it gets null, to drain it. What risk does the tutorial's advice point to?
options: The loop will run forever because a full queue never drains
poll will throw an exception once the queue has been drained
The queue will refuse to store any element after the null
The loop may stop early at a stored null while elements remain
optionExplain: A full queue is not the issue; the null return is.
poll signals empty with null and does not throw.
Storing remains possible; the problem lies in reading.
Right: null then means both empty and a real element.
questions.explain: Using null as a signal is only safe when null cannot be an element.
questions.teaches: Avoiding null elements keeps null free to mean empty, which is why the tutorial advises against inserting null even where an implementation allows it.
questions.rule: Each queue operation has a throwing form (add, remove, element) and a special-value form (offer, poll, peek).

questions.q: In a FIFO queue, which element does remove return?
options: The element that was added last
The smallest element by value
The element that was added first
A random element
optionExplain: That would be last in, first out, like a stack.
Value order belongs to a priority queue.
Right: first in, first out.
No queue policy picks at random.
questions.explain: FIFO serves elements in the order they arrived. The card next explains it.
questions.rule: The head is whatever remove or poll would return, and the queue's ordering policy decides which element that is.

questions.q: True or false: In a priority queue, the head is the element that was added first.
questions.explain: A priority queue orders by value, so the head is the first element by that ordering, whenever it was added.
questions.rule: Priority queues order by value, not arrival.

questions.q: A queue is loaded by add with 3, 2, 1, 0 in that order, then drained with remove. If it is FIFO, the first number removed is ____ .
questions.explain: FIFO returns the oldest element first, which here is the 3 that was added first.
questions.rule: FIFO removes the oldest element first.

questions.q: Which statements does the tutorial make about queue ordering? Select all that apply.
options: Every implementation must specify its ordering properties
A new element is placed at the head in every queue
Every queue removes elements in the order they were added
The head is the element remove or poll would return, whatever the ordering
optionExplain: Right: the ordering is part of what each implementation documents.
In a FIFO queue it goes at the tail.
Priority queues are the stated exception.
Right: head is defined by removal, not by arrival.
questions.explain: Head is a role defined by the removal operations, so it works for any ordering policy.
questions.teaches: Head is defined by what remove and poll return, so the term still makes sense for a priority queue where arrival order does not matter.
questions.rule: The head is whatever remove or poll would return, and the queue's ordering policy decides which element that is.

questions.q: A routine copies 5, 1, 4 into a PriorityQueue with natural ordering and drains it with remove into a list. If the PriorityQueue is replaced by a FIFO LinkedList, what does the list hold?
options: 5, 1, 4, the original order
1, 4, 5, sorted order
4, 1, 5, reversed order
The list is empty
optionExplain: Right: a FIFO queue returns elements in arrival order.
Sorting needs a value-ordered queue, which has been removed.
A FIFO queue does not reverse.
Draining a queue moves its elements across; it does not lose them.
questions.explain: The ordering policy of the queue, not the draining loop, produces the sorting.
questions.rule: A value-ordered queue drains in sorted order; a FIFO queue drains in arrival order.

questions.q: An emergency room must treat patients by severity, whatever their arrival time. Which queue policy does the tutorial's description suggest?
options: A FIFO queue, so earlier arrivals go first
A bounded queue, so only severe cases fit
A queue allowing null elements for unknown cases
A priority queue, ordered by a severity comparator
optionExplain: That serves by arrival and ignores severity.
Bounding limits the count, not the order.
Null elements do not affect ordering and are discouraged.
Right: elements are ordered by value or a supplied comparator.
questions.explain: When service order is a property of the items, a value-ordered queue expresses it.
questions.teaches: A priority queue needs some ordering for its elements, either natural ordering or a comparator, to know what its head is.
questions.rule: The head is whatever remove or poll would return, and the queue's ordering policy decides which element that is.

questions.q: Which interface lets you insert and remove elements at both ends?
options: Queue
Deque
SortedSet
Set
optionExplain: A Queue inserts at the tail and removes from the head; it is not double-ended.
Right: Deque is the double-ended queue.
A SortedSet keeps order by value and is not about ends.
A Set is defined by having no duplicates, not by its ends.
questions.explain: The name Deque comes from double-ended queue. The card next explains it.
questions.rule: A Deque works at both ends, so the same structure serves as a queue or as a stack depending on which ends you use.

questions.q: Match each Deque method to what it does.
pairs: Inserts at the tail, throws if capacity is exceeded
Inserts at the head, returns false on failure
Removes the tail, returns null if empty
Examines the head, throws if empty
questions.explain: Each name combines an action with an end, and the add, remove and get forms throw while the offer, poll and peek forms return a value.
questions.rule: Action plus end gives the method name.

questions.q: A deque is used as a stack: three items A, B, C are pushed on by addFirst in that order. Which call takes off the most recently added item?
options: removeLast
removeFirst
getLast
pollLast
optionExplain: That takes A, the earliest item, which is queue behaviour.
Right: addFirst puts C at the front, so removeFirst takes it.
That examines A without removing anything.
That removes A, the earliest item.
questions.explain: A stack inserts and removes at the same end.
questions.rule: Same end in and out gives a stack.

questions.q: When a deque's capacity is restricted, the tutorial says to prefer offerFirst and offerLast over ____First and addLast.
questions.explain: The offer forms report failure by returning false instead of throwing an exception.
questions.teaches: On a capacity-restricted deque the offer forms are preferred, because a full deque is an expected condition that a return value reports without exception handling.
questions.rule: A Deque works at both ends, so the same structure serves as a queue or as a stack depending on which ends you use.

questions.q: True or false: Calling removeFirst on an empty deque returns null.
questions.explain: removeFirst is a throwing form, so an empty deque makes it throw an exception. pollFirst is the form that returns null.
questions.rule: remove throws; poll returns null.

questions.q: A text editor keeps its history with the newest entry at the front. Undo must take the newest entry, and when the history is too long the oldest entry must be dropped. Which pair of calls does this need?
options: removeFirst for both undo and dropping the oldest
removeLast for both undo and dropping the oldest
getFirst to undo and getLast to drop the oldest
removeFirst for undo, removeLast to drop the oldest
optionExplain: That would drop the newest entry instead of the oldest.
That would undo the oldest entry instead of the newest.
The get methods examine without removing, so nothing would be taken off.
Right: the two ends serve two different jobs.
questions.explain: Using one end for stack-like undo and the other for queue-like dropping is exactly what a double-ended structure allows.
questions.teaches: A single deque can behave as a stack at one end and a queue at the other at once, which neither Stack nor Queue can do.
questions.rule: A Deque works at both ends, so the same structure serves as a queue or as a stack depending on which ends you use.

questions.q: A Map holds the key cat with the value 2. What does put of the key cat with the value 5 do?
options: It replaces the value, leaving one entry for cat
It adds a second entry for the key cat holding the value 5
It throws an exception because the key cat already exists
It ignores the call and keeps the existing value of 2
optionExplain: Right: each key maps to at most one value.
A Map cannot hold duplicate keys.
put on an existing key is allowed and updates the value.
put overwrites; it does not skip existing keys.
questions.explain: A key identifies one entry, and putting it again updates that entry. The card next explains it.
questions.rule: A Map holds each key once, put on an existing key replaces its value, and get gives null when the key has no mapping.

questions.q: True or false: A Map can contain two entries with the same key if their values differ.
questions.explain: A Map cannot contain duplicate keys, and each key maps to at most one value.
questions.rule: Keys are unique in a Map.

questions.q: A frequency program counts the words a, b, a using get and put. When it finishes, the value stored for a is ____ .
questions.explain: The first a stores 1; the second a finds 1 and puts 2, replacing the earlier value.
questions.rule: Counting uses get to find the old value and put to replace it.

questions.q: True or false: A HashMap and a TreeMap holding the same key-value mappings are equal.
questions.explain: Two Map objects are equal if they represent the same mappings, regardless of implementation type, in the way Sets are.
questions.teaches: Map equality depends on the mappings only, so the implementation class and the iteration order do not affect it.
questions.rule: A Map holds each key once, put on an existing key replaces its value, and get gives null when the key has no mapping.

questions.q: A frequency program is changed only by replacing the HashMap constructor with a TreeMap constructor. What changes in the output?
options: The counts change, because a TreeMap counts differently
The program no longer compiles, since the variable is a Map
The keys print in sorted order, and the counts stay the same
The keys print in the order they were first inserted
optionExplain: Counts come from the program logic, not the map class.
A Map variable accepts any Map implementation.
Right: only the key order is affected.
That is LinkedHashMap behaviour.
questions.explain: Swapping the implementation changes iteration order and speed, not the stored mappings.
questions.rule: The implementation chooses the iteration order.

questions.q: Which of these tasks are best modelled by a Map? Select all that apply.
options: Keeping visitors in arrival order, repeats allowed
Holding a collection of unique tags with no extra data
Counting how many times each page has been visited
Looking up a country's currency from its name
optionExplain: That is a List, since there is no key and repeats must be kept.
That is a Set, since no value goes with each tag.
Right: each page is a key with a count as its value.
Right: the name is a unique key with a currency as value.
questions.explain: A Map fits data that pairs a unique key with a value.
questions.teaches: Reach for a Map when each item has a unique identifier and a piece of data attached to it, and for a Set or List when the items stand alone.
questions.rule: A Map holds each key once, put on an existing key replaces its value, and get gives null when the key has no mapping.

questions.q: Which view of a Map may contain duplicate elements?
options: keySet
entrySet
None of them, since all views are Sets
values
optionExplain: Keys are unique in a Map, so the key set has no duplicates.
Each entry has a distinct key, so the entries are distinct.
values is a Collection, not a Set.
Right: two keys can map to the same value.
questions.explain: Only the values can repeat. The card next explains it.
questions.rule: Iterate and edit a map through its views: removal through a view changes the map, but there is no way to add through one.

questions.q: Match each Map view to what it contains.
pairs: A Collection of the values, repeats possible
questions.explain: The three views cover the keys, the values, and the pairs.
questions.rule: keySet, values, entrySet.

questions.q: To delete every entry whose value is the word closed from the map called tickets, call tickets.____().removeAll(Collections.singleton(closed)).
questions.explain: The values view writes removal through to the map, so every entry with that value is removed.
questions.rule: Remove entries by value through the values view.

questions.q: True or false: Calling add on the keySet view of a Map adds a new entry to the map.
questions.explain: Views do not support adding, because a key alone has no value. New entries are made with put or putAll.
questions.teaches: A view cannot add because it holds only part of an entry (a key or a value), so adding always goes through put.
questions.rule: Iterate and edit a map through its views: removal through a view changes the map, but there is no way to add through one.

questions.q: Map m1 has keys a, b, c and map m2 has keys b, c, d. A program runs m1.keySet().retainAll(m2.keySet()). Which entries does m1 hold afterwards?
options: Those for a only
Those for b and c
Those for a, b, c and d
None, since the views are copies
optionExplain: That would be the keys not in m2, the result of removeAll.
Right: only keys also in m2 are kept, and the removal writes through.
retainAll never adds keys, and m1 cannot gain d.
The views are backed by the map; they are not copies.
questions.explain: A key view is live, so intersecting it narrows the map itself.
questions.rule: Bulk operations on a key view change the map.

questions.q: A map pairs each student with a tutor. Which expression gives the students who are not anyone's tutor?
options: A copy of the values, with removeAll of the key set
The key set, with retainAll of the values, on the map itself
A copy of the key set, with removeAll of the values
The entry set, with clear called on it
optionExplain: That finds tutors who are not themselves students in the map.
That would keep only students who are tutors, and it would damage the map.
Right: from all students remove those who appear as tutors.
That would delete every entry.
questions.explain: Combining the key view and the values view answers questions about relationships inside one map.
questions.teaches: Key set minus values (on a copy) finds the entries that never appear on the value side, a pattern for questions such as who manages nobody.
questions.rule: Iterate and edit a map through its views: removal through a view changes the map, but there is no way to add through one.

questions.q: A program must store several phone numbers per person, but the framework has no multimap. What does the tutorial suggest?
options: A Map from each person to a List of numbers
A List of Maps with one number each
A Set that allows duplicate keys
A Map that accepts the same key several times
optionExplain: Right: the value of each key is itself a list.
That scatters one person's numbers across many maps, losing the grouping by key.
Sets hold elements without keys and refuse duplicates.
A Map cannot have duplicate keys.
questions.explain: A list-valued map turns one key into many values. The card next explains it.
questions.rule: For several values per key, store a list as the value and create the list the first time a key is used.

questions.q: Put the steps for adding a word to the anagram map in order.
items: Sort the letters of the word to make the key
Call get on the map with that key
If the result is null, put a new empty list under the key
Add the word to the list
questions.explain: Creating the list before adding is the step that makes the structure work.
questions.rule: Create the list on first use.

questions.q: In the anagram map the words cat and act share the key made from their sorted letters, which is ____ .
questions.explain: Sorting the letters of cat or act gives a, c, t, so the key is act.
questions.rule: Anagrams share the same sorted-letters key.

questions.q: True or false: A stream pipeline can build a Map from keys to Lists of elements without a hand-written loop.
questions.explain: The tutorial shows Collectors.groupingBy producing a Map from each classifier result to a List, for example employees by department.
questions.teaches: groupingBy is the stream version of the multimap pattern: it makes and fills the lists for you.
questions.rule: For several values per key, store a list as the value and create the list the first time a key is used.

questions.q: A program does this for a new key: List l = m.get(key); l.add(word); with no check. What happens?
options: A NullPointerException, because get returned null
The list is created automatically and the word added
The word is added to a shared default list for new keys
The call is ignored without any error being reported
optionExplain: Right: no list exists yet for a new key.
A Map does not create values by itself.
There is no default list.
Calling add on a null reference is an error, not a no-op.
questions.explain: The null check followed by put is the creation step.
questions.rule: Check for null and create the list.

questions.q: A school must record, for each student, the set of clubs joined, with no club listed twice for a student. Beyond the tutorial's List technique, which value type suits this?
options: A List of clubs under each student
A Map from club to student under each student
A Set of clubs under each student
An array of fixed size under each student
optionExplain: A List would permit the same club twice.
That adds a layer of keys the task does not need.
Right: a Set refuses repeats, so each club appears once per student.
A fixed size cannot grow as a student joins more clubs.
questions.explain: The value in a multimap can be any collection, chosen by the rule you need.
questions.teaches: Beyond the tutorial: the value type of a multimap is a design choice, and a Set suits cases where repeats under one key must be avoided.
questions.rule: For several values per key, store a list as the value and create the list the first time a key is used.

questions.q: Collections.sort is called on a List of objects whose class does not implement Comparable. What happens?
options: The elements are sorted by their hash codes
It throws ClassCastException
The list is left unchanged without an error
The elements are sorted in the order they were created
optionExplain: The sort never falls back to hash codes.
Right: the elements cannot be compared.
A failed sort reports the problem with an exception.
Creation order is not recorded by the objects.
questions.explain: Sorting needs an ordering, and Comparable is how a class supplies one. The card next explains it.
questions.rule: Implement Comparable so compareTo gives the natural ordering, and compare the most significant field first, using later fields only on a tie.

questions.q: Match each class to its natural ordering.
questions.explain: Each library class defines the ordering that is most natural for its values.
questions.rule: Library classes come with a natural ordering.

questions.q: In the Name class, x is Anna Smith and y is Zed Smith. x.compareTo(y) returns a ____ number.
questions.explain: The last names tie, so the first names decide, and Anna comes before Zed, so the result is negative.
questions.rule: Negative means the receiver comes first.

questions.q: True or false: compareTo returns exactly minus one, zero or one.
questions.explain: It returns a negative integer, zero or a positive integer; the negative or positive value can be any size.
questions.teaches: Callers must test the sign of the result, not compare it with minus one or one, because any negative or positive integer is allowed.
questions.rule: Implement Comparable so compareTo gives the natural ordering, and compare the most significant field first, using later fields only on a tie.

questions.q: The Name class is changed to compare first names before last names. In which order do Karl Ng, Tom Rich, Jeff Smith and John Smith sort?
options: Karl Ng, Tom Rich, Jeff Smith, John Smith
Tom Rich, Karl Ng, John Smith, Jeff Smith
John Smith, Jeff Smith, Karl Ng, Tom Rich
Jeff Smith, John Smith, Karl Ng, Tom Rich
optionExplain: That is the original last-name-first order.
That reverses the alphabetical order of first names.
Jeff comes before John in alphabetical order.
Right: the first names decide, in alphabetical order.
questions.explain: Whichever field is compared first becomes the main sort key.
questions.rule: The first field compared is the main sort key.

questions.q: A Version class has major, minor and patch numbers. Which compareTo logic follows the tutorial's pattern for multi-part values?
options: Add the three numbers together and compare the sums
Compare patch first, then minor, and major last
Compare major, then minor on a tie, then patch on a tie
Compare only the major number and ignore the rest
optionExplain: Different versions can have equal sums, such as 1.2.0 and 0.3.0.
That puts the least significant part in charge.
Right: most significant first, and continue only on a tie.
Versions that differ only in the minor number would count as equal.
questions.explain: The same most-significant-first rule applies however many parts a value has.
questions.teaches: With any number of parts, comparison continues part by part until a difference is found or the parts run out, in which case the objects are equal in order.
questions.rule: Implement Comparable so compareTo gives the natural ordering, and compare the most significant field first, using later fields only on a tie.

questions.q: An Employee class has a natural ordering by name. How can you sort a list of employees by hire date instead?
options: Pass a Comparator for hire date to Collections.sort
Change the natural ordering and recompile every time
Call shuffle until the dates line up
Sort twice with the natural ordering
optionExplain: Right: a comparator supplies an alternative ordering.
A comparator avoids exactly this kind of change.
Shuffling is random and does not sort.
The natural ordering is by name, so repeating it will not order by date.
questions.explain: A Comparator lets one class have many orderings. The card next explains it.
questions.rule: A Comparator supplies an ordering from outside the class; reverse it by swapping arguments, and compare ints explicitly instead of subtracting.

questions.q: To reverse a comparison, ____ the two arguments instead of negating the result.
questions.explain: Swapping arguments is always safe, whereas negation can fail for the smallest int.
questions.rule: Reverse by swapping.

questions.q: Match each comparator body for strings a and b to the order it produces.
pairs: Compare the length of a with the length of b, explicitly
Compare the length of b with the length of a, explicitly
questions.explain: Which argument is on which side decides the direction of the order.
questions.rule: Argument order decides direction.

questions.q: True or false: Negating the result of compareTo is a safe way to reverse an ordering.
questions.explain: compareTo may return the smallest negative int, and negating it yields the same value, so the sign does not flip.
questions.teaches: The sign of compareTo is the contract, not the exact number, so reversing by negation can fail at one extreme value.
questions.rule: A Comparator supplies an ordering from outside the class; reverse it by swapping arguments, and compare ints explicitly instead of subtracting.

questions.q: A comparator returns x minus y for ints. For x equal to 2,000,000,000 and y equal to minus 2,000,000,000, what sign does it report?
options: Positive, which correctly says x is larger
Zero, since the two numbers cancel each other
The call throws an exception when the overflow occurs
Negative, which wrongly says x is smaller than y
optionExplain: That is what the mathematics says, but a 32-bit int cannot hold 4,000,000,000.
They are opposite in sign, not equal in size to cancel out.
Integer arithmetic wraps silently; it does not throw.
Right: the difference overflows and wraps around to a negative value.
questions.explain: Overflow turns a correct-looking comparison into a wrong answer.
questions.rule: Do not subtract ints to compare them.

questions.q: A scheduler compares tasks by an int priority that may be any int, with return t1.priority minus t2.priority. What is the flaw, and what is the fix?
options: The tasks must implement Comparable instead, so remove the comparator
The subtraction can overflow, so compare the two priorities explicitly
The order must be negated, so return the opposite sign
Nothing is wrong, because priorities are small in practice
optionExplain: A comparator is fine; the flaw is in its body.
Right: explicit comparison avoids overflow.
The sign is not the issue; the arithmetic can overflow.
The stem says any int is possible, which makes overflow possible.
questions.explain: An ordering that is wrong only for extreme values produces subtle sorting bugs.
questions.teaches: An overflowing comparator can break transitivity, so a sort may misbehave only for some data, which makes the bug hard to reproduce.
questions.rule: A Comparator supplies an ordering from outside the class; reverse it by swapping arguments, and compare ints explicitly instead of subtracting.

questions.q: Two different employees hired the same day are added to a TreeSet ordered only by hire date. What happens to the second?
options: It is kept and placed after the first
It is treated as a duplicate and dropped
It replaces the first employee
An exception tells the programmer of the clash
optionExplain: A sorted set keeps one element per equal ordering position.
Right: the ordering says the two are equal.
Replacement is not how a set handles an equal element; the original stays.
No error is raised; the loss is silent.
questions.explain: The ordering, not equals, decides duplicates in a sorted set. The card next explains it.
questions.rule: An ordering used by a sorted set or map should call two objects equal only when equals does, so break ties with a unique field.

questions.q: True or false: Sorting a List with a comparator that treats some elements as equal removes those elements from the list.
questions.explain: Sorting only reorders; elements that compare as equal simply stay in the list.
questions.rule: Ties are harmless when sorting a List.

questions.q: A seniority comparator compares hire dates first and, when they tie, the unique employee ____ .
questions.explain: A unique tiebreak means only truly identical employees compare as equal.
questions.rule: Break ties with a unique field.

questions.q: Which of these are rules the tutorial gives for classes used as set elements or map keys? Select all that apply.
options: equals should throw an exception for a null argument
Do not change an element or key while it is stored in a Set or Map
Override hashCode whenever equals is overridden
hashCode may differ between two equal objects
optionExplain: equals returns false for null; compareTo is the one that throws.
Right: changes corrupt the collection, which is why immutability helps.
Right: equal objects must have equal hash codes.
Equal objects must have equal hash codes.
questions.explain: These rules keep hash-based and sorted collections consistent.
questions.teaches: Immutable element classes are safest, because a field changed after insertion can leave an element in the wrong place in a set or map.
questions.rule: An ordering used by a sorted set or map should call two objects equal only when equals does, so break ties with a unique field.

questions.q: A TreeSet uses a comparator on last name only and receives Ana Smith then Bo Smith. How many elements does it hold, and how many if first names are added as a tiebreak?
options: Two, then two
One, then one
Two, then one
One, then two
optionExplain: Without the tiebreak the comparator says the two are equal.
The tiebreak makes the two compare differently.
Adding a tiebreak cannot reduce the number of distinct elements.
Right: the tie hides Bo, and the tiebreak separates them.
questions.explain: Making the ordering finer keeps elements that a coarser ordering merged.
questions.rule: A finer ordering keeps more elements.

questions.q: A TreeSet of strings is built with a case-insensitive comparator. Foo is added, then foo. What does the set hold?
options: One element, because the comparator treats them as equal
Two elements, because the strings differ in case
Zero elements, because the clash cancels both of them out
An exception is thrown to report the clash between them
optionExplain: Right: the comparator decides what counts as a duplicate.
equals would separate them, but the TreeSet follows the comparator.
A clash keeps the first element; it removes nothing.
No exception is thrown; the second add simply returns false.
questions.explain: In sorted collections the comparator redefines equality for that collection.
questions.teaches: A comparator can be used deliberately to merge elements that are different under equals, such as strings differing only in case.
questions.rule: An ordering used by a sorted set or map should call two objects equal only when equals does, so break ties with a unique field.

questions.q: True or false: In subSet(from, to) on a SortedSet, the element equal to to is included.
questions.explain: The range is half-open: from is included and to is excluded. The card next explains it.
questions.rule: Sorted collections give ordered iteration and live, half-open range views whose ends are values, not positions.

questions.q: Match each SortedSet method to what it returns.
pairs: Elements greater than or equal to x
The ordering used, or null for natural ordering
questions.explain: The sorted set methods are defined by position in the order, not by index.
questions.rule: Range views are cut at values.

questions.q: A SortedSet of lowercase words is held in dictionary. Which call removes every word beginning with t?
options: dictionary.headSet("t").clear()
dictionary.tailSet("t").clear()
dictionary.subSet("t", "u").clear()
dictionary.first().clear()
optionExplain: That clears all words before t.
That clears t and every word after it.
Right: the range from t up to but not including u covers every word starting with t.
first returns a single word, which has no clear method.
questions.explain: A half-open range between a letter and the next letter selects the words starting with that letter.
questions.rule: Use from-inclusive, to-exclusive ranges.

questions.q: True or false: A subSet view of a sorted set remains valid after other code adds elements to the backing set.
questions.explain: The endpoints are values in the element space, not positions, so the view stays valid, unlike a sublist of a list.
questions.teaches: Because the ends are values, a sorted-set view can be kept for a long time, whereas a list sublist should be short-lived.
questions.rule: Sorted collections give ordered iteration and live, half-open range views whose ends are values, not positions.

questions.q: A SortedSet s was built with a reverse-order comparator. A program stores it in a variable of type Collection and calls new TreeSet with that variable. Which ordering does the new set use?
options: The same reverse ordering as s, copied from its comparator
No ordering at all, since a TreeSet is unordered by default
It fails to compile because Collection and SortedSet differ
Natural ordering, since the Collection constructor is chosen
optionExplain: Only the constructor taking a SortedSet would keep it.
A TreeSet is always ordered.
A Collection argument is accepted by that constructor.
Right: the static type picks the constructor, and it ignores any comparator.
questions.explain: Overload selection happens at compile time, from the declared type.
questions.rule: The static type of the argument picks the constructor.

questions.q: An event log is a SortedMap keyed by timestamp. Which call gives a view of the events from 10:00 up to but not including 11:00?
options: headMap(t1100)
subMap(t1000, t1100)
tailMap(t1000)
subMap(t1100, t1000)
optionExplain: That includes every event before 11:00, including those before 10:00.
Right: it includes the first key and excludes the second.
That includes every event from 10:00 onward, including 11:00 and later.
The ends are reversed.
questions.explain: SortedMap views follow the same half-open rule as SortedSet views.
questions.teaches: The ideas of range views, half-open ends and value endpoints carry over from SortedSet to SortedMap, so one set of rules covers both.
questions.rule: Sorted collections give ordered iteration and live, half-open range views whose ends are values, not positions.

questions.q: Which part of a stream pipeline produces a result that is not a stream?
options: The source
An intermediate operation
The terminal operation
The lambda expression
optionExplain: The source supplies the elements; it is a collection, array or similar.
Intermediate operations each produce another stream.
Right: it ends the pipeline with a value, a collection or nothing.
A lambda is behaviour passed to an operation, not a pipeline part.
questions.explain: Intermediate steps stay inside the stream world; the terminal step leaves it. The card next explains it.
questions.rule: A pipeline is a source, zero or more intermediate operations that each yield a stream, and a terminal operation that produces the result.

questions.q: Put the parts of a pipeline in the order they appear.
items: The source, such as a collection
Zero or more intermediate operations
One terminal operation
questions.explain: A pipeline starts from a source, transforms through intermediate steps and ends with one terminal step.
questions.rule: Source, intermediates, terminal.

questions.q: Sort each operation into the kind it is.

items.t: filter
mapToInt
average
forEach
collect
count

questions.explain: filter and mapToInt return streams, so the pipeline goes on. average, forEach, collect and count end it.
questions.rule: Operations that return a stream are intermediate.

questions.q: True or false: In roster.stream().filter(p).mapToInt(f).average().getAsDouble(), getAsDouble is a stream operation.
questions.explain: The pipeline ends at average, which returns an OptionalDouble. getAsDouble is called on that result, not on a stream.
questions.teaches: The terminal operation hands back an ordinary object, so what you call on it afterwards is outside the pipeline.
questions.rule: A pipeline is a source, zero or more intermediate operations that each yield a stream, and a terminal operation that produces the result.

questions.q: In a pipeline that averages the ages of male members, the filter step is removed. Whose ages are averaged now?
options: The ages of every element from the source
Only the age of the first element of the source
No ages, so the result is empty
The ages of female members only
optionExplain: Right: with no filter nothing is excluded.
Nothing limits the stream to one element.
The stream still carries every element to the average step.
Removing a filter does not invert it.
questions.explain: Each intermediate operation narrows or transforms what flows on to the next step.
questions.rule: Intermediate operations shape what the terminal operation sees.

questions.q: For orders.stream().filter(paid).mapToInt(total).sum(), which choice identifies the parts correctly?
options: Source orders, intermediates filter and mapToInt, terminal sum
Source orders, intermediates filter and sum, terminal mapToInt
Source filter, intermediate mapToInt, terminal orders
No source, because stream creates the data
optionExplain: Right: sum is the only step that ends the pipeline.
sum cannot be intermediate since it returns a number.
orders is the collection, so it is the source.
A stream carries data; it does not create it from nothing.
questions.explain: Naming the three parts is the first step in reading any pipeline.
questions.teaches: Reading a pipeline starts by finding the one operation that returns a non-stream value, which is the terminal operation.
questions.rule: A pipeline is a source, zero or more intermediate operations that each yield a stream, and a terminal operation that produces the result.

questions.q: True or false: In a for-each loop, the program rather than the library drives the iteration.
questions.explain: A for-each loop is external iteration: the code controls the traversal step by step. The card next explains it.
questions.rule: With aggregate operations you state what happens to each element and the library controls how the traversal runs.

questions.q: Match each term to its description.
pairs: Your code drives the loop, with an iterator or for-each
You supply behaviour and the library drives the traversal
Behaviour passed as a parameter to an operation
Carries values through a pipeline without storing them
questions.explain: The contrast is who drives the traversal and where the behaviour lives.
questions.rule: Internal iteration hands control of traversal to the library.

questions.q: Which of these snippets is internal iteration?
options: A for-each loop that prints each person
An Iterator with a while loop over hasNext and next, printing each person
roster.stream().forEach with a lambda that prints each person
An index loop from 0 to size minus one, calling get and printing each person
optionExplain: This is for-each, where your code loops.
Here your code calls hasNext and next itself, which is external iteration.
Right: only the action is supplied, and the library loops.
An index loop is external iteration too.
questions.explain: If you write the loop, it is external iteration.
questions.rule: No loop in your code means internal iteration.

questions.q: True or false: External iteration can only proceed sequentially.
questions.explain: Because your code takes each step in turn, the library cannot split the work, whereas internal iteration can be divided into subproblems.
questions.teaches: Handing the traversal to the library is what makes parallel execution possible, since the library can split the work without changing your behaviour code.
questions.rule: With aggregate operations you state what happens to each element and the library controls how the traversal runs.

questions.q: A pipeline is switched from stream to parallelStream with the lambdas unchanged. What is the library now free to do?
options: Rewrite the lambdas automatically so that they run faster
Split the work, run parts on several threads and combine the results
Remove the filter step if it seems to slow the processing down
Modify the source collection so that it matches the final result
optionExplain: The library does not alter your lambdas.
Right: internal iteration allows this.
Changing what the pipeline computes is not permitted.
Aggregate operations do not modify the source.
questions.explain: Because the library owns the traversal, how it runs can change without your behaviour code changing.
questions.rule: The library may parallelise internal iteration.

questions.q: A team must delete every item that fails a check from a collection in place. Which tool does the earlier material point to?
options: A stream with a filter and forEach
A for-each loop calling remove on the collection
parallelStream with a filter
An Iterator calling remove
optionExplain: Aggregate operations produce results; they leave the source collection unchanged.
for-each hides the iterator, so it cannot remove safely.
Parallel execution does not change the source either.
Right: aggregate operations do not change the source, while Iterator.remove does.
questions.explain: Choose the tool by what must change: use a stream to compute a result and an Iterator to edit in place.
questions.teaches: Aggregate operations compute new results, so editing the original collection in place still calls for an Iterator or a classic bulk operation.
questions.rule: With aggregate operations you state what happens to each element and the library controls how the traversal runs.

questions.q: Terminal operations such as sum, count and average that combine a stream into one value are called ____ operations.
questions.explain: A reduction combines the contents of a stream into a single result. The card next explains it.
questions.rule: reduce folds a stream into one value from an identity and an accumulator that returns a new partial result each time.

questions.q: In a reduce call whose identity is 0 and whose accumulator adds its two arguments, the 0 is the ____ .
questions.explain: The identity is the initial value of the reduction.
questions.rule: reduce starts from its identity.

questions.q: Numbers 2, 3 and 4 are reduced with identity 1 and an accumulator that multiplies its two arguments. What is the result?
optionExplain: That adds the numbers instead of multiplying them.
That would follow from an identity of 0, which would zero every product.
Right: 1 times 2, times 3, times 4.
The identity is only the starting point; each element is then multiplied in.
questions.explain: The identity must suit the operation: 1 for products, 0 for sums.
questions.rule: Pick an identity that fits the accumulator.

questions.q: True or false: For an empty stream, reduce with identity 0 and addition returns 0.
questions.explain: The identity serves as the default result when there are no elements.
questions.teaches: The identity is also the answer for an empty stream, which is another reason it must fit the operation.
questions.rule: reduce folds a stream into one value from an identity and an accumulator that returns a new partial result each time.

questions.q: The sum of ages 20, 30 and 40 is computed with reduce, but the identity is changed from 0 to 10 in a serial stream. What is the result?
optionExplain: Right: the reduction starts at 10 instead of 0.
That is the result with identity 0.
The elements are still added to the starting value.
That would drop the identity and one element.
questions.explain: A wrong identity shifts every result by the same amount.
questions.rule: The identity is the starting value.

questions.q: A pipeline builds a List of names with reduce, where each accumulator call copies the list so far and appends one name. What is the drawback, and what does the tutorial suggest?
options: It loses some of the names, so use filter instead
It sorts the names in place, so use shuffle instead
It throws an exception at once, so use an Iterator
It makes a new list for every element, so use collect
optionExplain: The names are kept; the cost is the repeated copying.
Nothing is sorted by this approach.
The code runs; it simply does a lot of avoidable work.
Right: collect mutates one container instead.
questions.explain: Mutating a single container is cheaper than creating a fresh one at every step.
questions.teaches: The cost of reduce on collections grows with the number of elements, since each step copies what came before.
questions.rule: reduce folds a stream into one value from an identity and an accumulator that returns a new partial result each time.

questions.q: Which terminal operation is designed to gather stream elements into a List?
options: reduce
collect
filter
average
optionExplain: reduce builds a new value each step, which the tutorial calls inefficient for collections.
Right: collect accumulates into a mutable container.
filter is an intermediate operation.
average combines numbers into one value.
questions.explain: Containers are the job of collect. The card next explains it.
questions.rule: Use collect to accumulate into a mutable container, and groupingBy with a downstream collector to group and reduce in one pass.

questions.q: Match each part of the three-argument collect to its job.
pairs: Adds one element to a container
questions.explain: The three parts build, fill and join containers.
questions.rule: Supplier builds, accumulator fills, combiner joins.

questions.q: Which expression produces a Map from department to the List of employees in it?
options: employees.stream().collect(Collectors.toList())
employees.stream().collect(Collectors.groupingBy(Employee::getDepartment))
employees.stream().reduce(0, Integer::sum)
employees.stream().forEach(Employee::getDepartment)
optionExplain: That gives one List of employees, with no grouping.
Right: groupingBy classifies by the function given.
That counts elements and fits neither the types nor the goal.
forEach returns nothing, so no Map results.
questions.explain: The classifier function chooses the keys of the result Map.
questions.rule: groupingBy builds a Map from classifier results to Lists.

questions.q: True or false: Used as a downstream collector, Collectors.averagingInt gives a Double for each group, whereas average on a primitive stream gives an OptionalDouble.
questions.explain: The downstream collector produces the final value stored in each group, so there is no Optional wrapper.
questions.teaches: A downstream collector fixes the type of the Map's values, so the same average appears as a plain Double inside a grouped result.
questions.rule: Use collect to accumulate into a mutable container, and groupingBy with a downstream collector to group and reduce in one pass.

questions.q: A pipeline uses groupingBy of Person::getGender with downstream Collectors.mapping of Person::getName and toList. What do the Map's values hold?
options: Lists of Person objects
The count of people in each group
A single name per gender
Lists of names
optionExplain: That would be the result without the mapping step.
Counting would need a counting collector.
toList keeps all the names in each group.
Right: mapping turns each Person into a name before toList gathers them.
questions.explain: The downstream collector transforms what each group stores.
questions.rule: The downstream collector decides what each group holds.

questions.q: A pipeline groups orders by country and uses summingInt of the order total as the downstream collector. The result is a Map from country to ____ .
questions.explain: summingInt produces an Integer total for each group.
questions.teaches: Swapping the downstream collector changes the Map's value type without changing the grouping, which makes grouping and reducing one reusable pattern.
questions.rule: Use collect to accumulate into a mutable container, and groupingBy with a downstream collector to group and reduce in one pass.

questions.q: True or false: Switching a pipeline from a serial to a parallel stream is guaranteed to make it faster.
questions.explain: The tutorial says parallelism is not automatically faster; it depends on the amount of data, the cores and the application. The card next explains it.
questions.rule: Ask for parallel execution with parallelStream or parallel; the runtime splits and combines, but speed is not guaranteed and parallel forEach is unordered.

questions.q: Streams are ____ by default, and you request parallel execution with parallelStream or parallel.
questions.explain: A stream runs in serial unless you ask for parallel execution.
questions.rule: Serial is the default.

questions.q: A parallel pipeline must print the numbers of a list in the list's order. Which terminal operation fits?
options: forEachOrdered
forEach
peek
filter
optionExplain: Right: it keeps the encounter order, possibly at some cost in parallelism.
In a parallel stream forEach does not preserve the order.
peek is for side effects such as debugging and promises no order.
filter is an intermediate operation and does not print anything.
questions.explain: Order and parallel speed pull in opposite directions.
questions.rule: Use forEachOrdered when parallel output must keep order.

questions.q: True or false: To use a parallel stream on a collection, you must first wrap the collection in a synchronized wrapper.
questions.explain: Parallel streams work with non-thread-safe collections as long as the collection is not modified during the operation.
questions.teaches: Parallel streams avoid shared mutable state by splitting the data and combining partial results, so a synchronized wrapper would only add contention.
questions.rule: Ask for parallel execution with parallelStream or parallel; the runtime splits and combines, but speed is not guaranteed and parallel forEach is unordered.

questions.q: The same pipeline using parallelStream().forEach(print) is run twice on the same list. What can be said about the two outputs?
options: They are identical, since the list is the same
The second run is always faster
They may list the elements in different orders
The second run prints nothing, since the stream is used up
optionExplain: Same data does not fix the order of parallel processing.
The tutorial makes no such claim.
Right: parallel forEach does not preserve order and can vary between runs.
Each run builds a new stream from the list.
questions.explain: Parallel execution makes the processing order the runtime's decision.
questions.rule: Parallel forEach order can change between runs.

questions.q: A concurrent reduction by the runtime needs certain conditions. Which of these must hold? Select all that apply.
options: The stream is ordered and the collector lacks UNORDERED
The stream is parallel
The collector has the CONCURRENT characteristic
The stream is unordered or the collector is UNORDERED
The source collection is a synchronized wrapper
optionExplain: That combination fails the third condition, so no concurrent reduction takes place.
Right: a concurrent reduction is a parallel technique.
Right: the collector must allow concurrent accumulation.
Right: ordering would otherwise force coordination.
The source collection does not need to be synchronized.
questions.explain: Three conditions must hold together for the runtime to accumulate into one shared container.
questions.teaches: groupingByConcurrent and toConcurrentMap exist because groupingBy and toMap merge maps by key, which is expensive on parallel streams.
questions.rule: Ask for parallel execution with parallelStream or parallel; the runtime splits and combines, but speed is not guaranteed and parallel forEach is unordered.

questions.q: True or false: Intermediate operations such as filter start processing as soon as they are called.
questions.explain: They are lazy and run only when a terminal operation starts. The card next explains it.
questions.rule: Keep lambdas stateless and free of side effects, leave the source alone, and remember nothing runs until the terminal operation starts.

questions.q: An operation that is evaluated only when its value is required is called ____ .
questions.explain: Intermediate operations are lazy; an eager algorithm is evaluated immediately.
questions.rule: Intermediate operations are lazy.

questions.q: Which lambda passed to map is stateful and risky?
options: a lambda that returns the element's age plus one
a method reference to the getName getter method
a lambda that tests whether the gender is MALE
a lambda that adds each element to an outside set
optionExplain: This uses only its argument, so it is stateless.
A method reference to a getter has no hidden state.
It only reads its argument.
Right: it changes a collection outside the lambda, so results depend on shared state.
questions.explain: A lambda that reads or writes outside variables is stateful.
questions.rule: Prefer lambdas that use only their arguments.

questions.q: True or false: A lambda that adds elements to its own source collection is safe as long as the stream is serial.
questions.explain: Interference is a problem regardless: the tutorial's example uses a serial pipeline and still gets ConcurrentModificationException.
questions.teaches: Modifying the source breaks the pipeline even without threads, so interference is a separate hazard from parallel execution.
questions.rule: Keep lambdas stateless and free of side effects, leave the source alone, and remember nothing runs until the terminal operation starts.

questions.q: A pipeline is stream().filter(a).peek(print) with no terminal operation. What is printed?
options: Every element that passes the filter
Nothing, since no terminal operation has run
Every element of the source
An exception warns that the terminal operation is missing
optionExplain: That needs a terminal operation to trigger processing.
Right: laziness means nothing is processed yet.
The filter would still apply, and the stream would not run at all.
No exception is thrown; the pipeline is simply never executed.
questions.explain: Adding a terminal operation is what starts the work.
questions.rule: Nothing runs until the terminal operation.

questions.q: A map lambda appends each element to a shared ArrayList. It looks fine serially. The pipeline is switched to a parallel stream. What should the team expect?
options: The list is filled in exactly the same order as before
The compiler refuses to build the parallel version at all
The list order and possibly its contents become unpredictable
The list is filled only once and then locked automatically
optionExplain: Parallel threads reach elements in the runtime's order.
The code compiles; the hazard shows up at run time.
Right: several threads update shared state in an unplanned order.
No automatic locking is applied to the list.
questions.explain: Making the list thread-safe stops corruption but not the varying order.
questions.teaches: A synchronized list protects against corrupted data but not against a different order on each run, so stateful lambdas still give unreliable results in parallel.
questions.rule: Keep lambdas stateless and free of side effects, leave the source alone, and remember nothing runs until the terminal operation starts.

questions.q: The default general-purpose implementation of Set is ____ .
questions.explain: HashSet is the usual starting point for a Set. The card next explains it.
questions.rule: Start from the default implementation behind the interface you need, and change it only when measurement says to.

questions.q: Match each kind of implementation to what it is.
pairs: In java.util.concurrent, built for high concurrency
Adds or restricts the behaviour of another collection
Small implementations from static factory methods
Skeletons for building your own collection
questions.explain: The kinds differ in purpose, not in the interfaces they implement.
questions.rule: Know what each kind is for.

questions.q: A program must be safe when several threads use one collection. Which advice does the tutorial give?
options: Use a synchronization wrapper or a concurrent implementation
Use any general-purpose implementation, since they are synchronized
Use a fail-fast iterator and ignore other precautions
Declare the variable as an implementation type
optionExplain: Right: general-purpose implementations are not synchronized.
They are not synchronized, so users do not pay for it.
A fail-fast iterator only reports illegal modification; it does not make access safe.
Declaring a type does not add thread safety.
questions.explain: Thread safety is added on top of the general-purpose classes, not built in.
questions.rule: General-purpose collections are not synchronized.

questions.q: True or false: A fail-fast iterator throws an exception on illegal concurrent modification instead of behaving unpredictably.
questions.explain: That is the tutorial's description of fail-fast.
questions.teaches: Fail-fast reporting turns a hidden inconsistency into a visible error, but it does not prevent the concurrent modification.
questions.rule: Start from the default implementation behind the interface you need, and change it only when measurement says to.

questions.q: A variable is declared with the interface type List, and the object is created as an ArrayList. A test shows poor speed and the constructor is changed to LinkedList. What else must change?
options: Nothing else, because the code uses only the List interface
Every call to add, which must now become a call to addFirst
The type of the variable, which must become LinkedList
The imports, which must be rewritten for every method
optionExplain: Right: the declaration ties the code to the interface only.
The List interface already has add; nothing forces a change.
The List variable accepts either implementation.
Nothing about the other methods depends on the implementation class.
questions.explain: Interface-typed code keeps the implementation a one-line decision.
questions.rule: Declare with the interface type.

questions.q: A reviewer insists LinkedList is faster for inserts, so it should be used everywhere. What does the tutorial advise instead?
options: Accept the claim, since asymptotic speed always decides
Switch every collection to a Set to avoid the question
Measure with the real application before deciding
Use an abstract implementation, which is the fastest
optionExplain: The tutorial says asymptotic descriptions have limits.
A Set does not offer the List operations the code may need.
Right: this is the tutorial's own caution.
Abstract implementations are skeletons, not speed choices.
questions.explain: Measurement settles a speed argument that theory cannot.
questions.teaches: Constant factors and real usage patterns can outweigh the neat growth rates, so a measurement beats a rule of thumb.
questions.rule: Start from the default implementation behind the interface you need, and change it only when measurement says to.

questions.q: True or false: TreeSet is the fastest general-purpose Set.
questions.explain: HashSet is the best performing, and TreeSet is substantially slower. The card next explains it.
questions.rule: Use HashSet by default, TreeSet for sorted needs and LinkedHashSet for insertion order, and size a HashSet at about twice the expected number of elements.

questions.q: A rule of thumb sets a HashSet's initial capacity to about ____ the expected number of elements.
questions.explain: The tutorial suggests about twice the expected size, with the default load factor.
questions.rule: Capacity about twice the expected size.

questions.q: A HashSet will hold about 1,000 elements and be iterated often. Which initial capacity does the rule of thumb suggest?
options: 16, the default
About 2,000
Exactly 1,000
optionExplain: The default would force many growth steps for 1,000 elements.
Right: roughly twice the expected size.
A huge capacity wastes space and slows iteration over empty buckets.
That is the expected size, not twice it.
questions.explain: Twice the size leaves room without waste.
questions.rule: Aim at about twice the size.

questions.q: True or false: The time to iterate a LinkedHashSet depends on its initial capacity.
questions.explain: Unlike a HashSet, a LinkedHashSet iterates through its linked list, so capacity does not affect iteration time.
questions.teaches: The linked list through the hash table is why LinkedHashSet iteration cost follows the number of entries alone.
questions.rule: Use HashSet by default, TreeSet for sorted needs and LinkedHashSet for insertion order, and size a HashSet at about twice the expected number of elements.

questions.q: A HashSet is created with an initial capacity of 1,000,000 but holds only 10 elements. What is the effect on iteration?
options: It is fast, because a bigger table is always faster
It is unaffected, because only entries are visited
It throws an exception because the set is too empty
It is slow, because iteration also walks the empty buckets
optionExplain: Iteration cost grows with capacity.
Capacity counts for a HashSet but not for a LinkedHashSet.
A sparse table is allowed.
Right: the cost is linear in entries plus capacity.
questions.explain: Oversizing trades iteration speed for fewer growth steps.
questions.rule: Do not oversize a HashSet that is iterated often.

questions.q: A service oversizes a set to avoid growth but also iterates it constantly, and it needs no sorting. Which choice keeps iteration cost down?
options: HashSet with the same capacity
TreeSet with the same capacity
LinkedHashSet, whose iteration ignores capacity
CopyOnWriteArraySet, because it iterates safely
optionExplain: Iteration there pays for the empty buckets.
