TreeSet has no capacity parameter to set.
Right: iteration follows entries, not capacity.
It copies on every change and is aimed at rarely modified sets, not at avoiding sparse tables.
questions.explain: When two needs pull in different directions, a different implementation can remove the conflict.
questions.teaches: Choosing between implementations can remove a tuning problem altogether, as LinkedHashSet does by being immune to capacity in iteration.
questions.rule: Use HashSet by default, TreeSet for sorted needs and LinkedHashSet for insertion order, and size a HashSet at about twice the expected number of elements.

questions.q: Which Set suits a combination of flags such as BOLD and ITALIC taken from an enum?
options: EnumSet
TreeSet
CopyOnWriteArraySet
LinkedHashSet
optionExplain: Right: it is built for enum values and replaces bit flags.
It would work but is not the specialised, high-performance choice.
It is built for rarely changed sets shared among threads, not for flags.
It keeps insertion order, which flags do not need.
questions.explain: A bit vector represents a small fixed universe of values very compactly. The card next explains it.
questions.rule: Use EnumSet for sets of enum values and CopyOnWriteArraySet for rarely changed, often iterated sets that several threads share.

questions.q: Match each Set to its description.
pairs: Bit-vector set for the values of one enum type
Copies its array on each change, no locking
questions.explain: The special-purpose sets trade generality for a specific strength.
questions.rule: Match the set to its special strength.

questions.q: An event-handler list is read on every event by many threads, changes only a few times a day, and must hold no duplicates. Which Set fits?
options: EnumSet
TreeSet
HashSet
CopyOnWriteArraySet
optionExplain: Handlers are not enum values.
Sorting is not needed, and it is not built for concurrent iteration.
It is not synchronized, so concurrent modification and iteration are unsafe.
Right: iteration is safe without locking, and rare changes are cheap enough.
questions.explain: Read-heavy shared sets are where copy-on-write pays off.
questions.rule: Copy-on-write suits read-mostly sets.

questions.q: True or false: In a CopyOnWriteArraySet, add takes time proportional to the size of the set.
questions.explain: Each change copies the whole array, so the cost grows with the size.
questions.teaches: The cost of each write is linear in the set's size, which is why the structure is attractive only when writes are rare.
questions.rule: Use EnumSet for sets of enum values and CopyOnWriteArraySet for rarely changed, often iterated sets that several threads share.

questions.q: Many threads add elements to a CopyOnWriteArraySet all the time. What happens to its performance?
options: It improves, because the threads share the copies
It gets poor, because every add copies the whole array
It stays constant, since no locks are needed for the writes
It fails outright, because the set is read-only
optionExplain: Each change makes its own full copy.
Right: write-heavy use defeats the design.
Avoiding locks does not avoid copying.
The set accepts changes; they are just expensive.
questions.explain: The cost model decides which workloads suit it.
questions.rule: Do not use copy-on-write for write-heavy sets.

questions.q: Sort each situation by the Set that suits it better.

items.t: Weekdays on which a shop is open
Permissions drawn from a fixed list of enum values
Listeners registered at startup and notified thousands of times
A subscriber list read on every message and changed a few times a day
Text styles chosen from an enum
A registry of callbacks that is iterated constantly by many threads

questions.explain: A small fixed universe of enum values calls for EnumSet. A shared, read-mostly collection calls for copy-on-write.
questions.teaches: The two special sets answer different questions: how small and fixed the set of possible values is, and how often the set changes compared with how often it is read.
questions.rule: Use EnumSet for sets of enum values and CopyOnWriteArraySet for rarely changed, often iterated sets that several threads share.

questions.q: True or false: ArrayList offers constant-time positional access.
questions.explain: That is one of the main reasons the tutorial calls it the usual choice. The card next explains it.
questions.rule: Start with ArrayList, and consider LinkedList only for frequent front insertions or interior deletions during iteration, after measuring.

questions.q: Match each List implementation to its trait.
pairs: Constant-time positional access, usually the fastest
Cheap insertion at the front, linear positional access
Safe iteration during modification, copies on write
Synchronized legacy class, use through List
questions.explain: Each List implementation trades something for something else.
questions.rule: ArrayList is the default; others have niches.

questions.q: A program reads items by index many times and changes the list rarely. Which implementation does the tutorial favour?
options: LinkedList
ArrayList
CopyOnWriteArrayList
Vector
optionExplain: Positional access there is linear time.
Right: positional access is constant time.
It is for lists that are iterated often and shared across threads, not for index reads.
It is a synchronized legacy class that the tutorial does not recommend as a default.
questions.explain: Index-heavy reading is exactly what an array handles best.
questions.rule: Index reads favour ArrayList.

questions.q: Which statements does the tutorial support about LinkedList? Select all that apply.
options: Positional access takes linear time
It is usually faster than ArrayList in practice
Positional access is faster than in ArrayList
It implements Queue and has addFirst and removeLast
optionExplain: Right: it must follow the links to the position.
The tutorial says ArrayList is usually faster.
ArrayList has constant-time positional access.
Right: it offers those extra operations.
questions.explain: LinkedList has niche strengths and several extra operations.
questions.teaches: LinkedList doubles as a Queue and a Deque, which is a reason to pick it that has nothing to do with List performance.
questions.rule: Start with ArrayList, and consider LinkedList only for frequent front insertions or interior deletions during iteration, after measuring.

questions.q: A loop calls get(i) for every index i of a LinkedList of n elements. What does this cost overall?
options: About n steps, since each get is constant
About one step, since the list is cached
About log n steps, since the list is sorted
About n times n steps, since each get is linear
optionExplain: That is true for an ArrayList, not a LinkedList.
The tutorial describes no such caching.
A LinkedList is not a search tree.
Right: n calls each take linear time.
questions.explain: A hidden linear cost inside a loop makes the whole loop quadratic.
questions.rule: Do not index into a LinkedList in a loop.

questions.q: A teammate wants LinkedList because front insertion is constant time. What does the tutorial advise?
options: Measure the application with both implementations first
Accept it, since constant time always beats linear time
Use Vector, since it is synchronized and well tested
Use a plain array, since lists are slow in general
optionExplain: Right: ArrayList is usually faster, so verify the claim.
Constant factors can outweigh the growth rate.
Synchronization is not the question here.
The tutorial does not suggest abandoning lists.
questions.explain: A rule of thumb is a hypothesis to test with real data.
questions.teaches: Asymptotic arguments and real performance can disagree, so the nominally better structure needs a measurement before it replaces the default.
questions.rule: Start with ArrayList, and consider LinkedList only for frequent front insertions or interior deletions during iteration, after measuring.

questions.q: True or false: A TreeMap iterates its keys in sorted order.
questions.explain: TreeMap is the SortedMap implementation, so its views iterate in key order. The card next explains it.
questions.rule: Pick HashMap for speed, TreeMap for key order and LinkedHashMap for insertion order or cache-style eviction through removeEldestEntry.

questions.q: To limit a LinkedHashMap's size automatically, override the method removeEldest____ .
questions.explain: removeEldestEntry is called when a new mapping is added and decides whether the eldest goes.
questions.rule: Override removeEldestEntry to evict.

questions.q: A LinkedHashMap subclass overrides removeEldestEntry to return size() greater than 100. The 101st distinct key is put. What results?
options: The size becomes 101 and nothing is removed
The put throws an exception because the limit is reached
The size stays at 100 and the eldest entry is removed
The newest entry is discarded instead of the eldest
optionExplain: The override returns true at size 101, which triggers removal.
The map evicts quietly; it does not throw.
Right: the override trims the map back to 100.
The method removes the eldest entry.
questions.explain: The test runs after each addition, keeping the map at the limit.
questions.rule: size() greater than the maximum keeps it at the maximum.

questions.q: True or false: With the default insertion order, a LinkedHashMap with removeEldestEntry evicts the least recently read entry.
questions.explain: In insertion order the eldest is the oldest inserted. Reads count only when access order is turned on.
questions.teaches: A least-recently-used cache needs access order enabled as well, because it makes each lookup move the key to the end.
questions.rule: Pick HashMap for speed, TreeMap for key order and LinkedHashMap for insertion order or cache-style eviction through removeEldestEntry.

questions.q: A LinkedHashMap is in access order and holds a, b, c in that order of use. The program looks up a. Which key is now the eldest?
options: a
c
None, since lookups do not change the order in an access-order map
b
optionExplain: A lookup moves a to the end, away from the eldest position.
c is now second from the end, not the eldest.
In access order, lookups reorder the keys.
Right: a moved to the end, so b is now the oldest by use.
questions.explain: In access order, using a key refreshes it.
questions.rule: Access order moves a used key to the end.

questions.q: A web app caches the 50 most recently used rendered pages, where both reads and writes count as use. Which design follows the tutorial's pieces?
options: A TreeMap, evicting the entry with the smallest key
An access-order LinkedHashMap that overrides removeEldestEntry
A HashMap, evicting an arbitrary key when it is full
A LinkedHashMap in insertion order with no override
optionExplain: Key order is unrelated to how recently a page was used.
Right: access order tracks use and the override evicts.
A HashMap has no usage order to guide eviction.
Nothing would evict old pages, and reads would not count.
questions.explain: Access order plus an eviction rule is a cache recipe.
questions.teaches: Combining the two LinkedHashMap features gives a bounded cache that discards the entry unused for longest.
questions.rule: Pick HashMap for speed, TreeMap for key order and LinkedHashMap for insertion order or cache-style eviction through removeEldestEntry.

questions.q: True or false: A WeakHashMap compares its keys by reference using ==.
questions.explain: That description fits IdentityHashMap; a WeakHashMap is about weak references to keys. The card next explains it.
questions.rule: Use EnumMap for enum keys, WeakHashMap for entries that should vanish with their keys, IdentityHashMap for reference-based keys and ConcurrentHashMap for shared maps.

questions.q: Match each map to its distinguishing feature.
pairs: Entries can be collected when the key is unreachable elsewhere
Compares keys with == rather than equals
Retrievals never block, atomic operations such as putIfAbsent
questions.explain: Each special map changes one rule of ordinary map behaviour.
questions.rule: Each special map changes one rule.

questions.q: A scheduling program maps each value of a Day enum to a list of tasks. Which Map does the tutorial prefer to an array indexed by the enum?
options: IdentityHashMap
WeakHashMap
EnumMap
TreeMap
optionExplain: It compares by reference, which does not help with enum keys.
It lets entries vanish, which a schedule must not do.
Right: it has array-like speed with the Map interface.
It works but is not the specialised, array-like choice.
questions.explain: EnumMap is the array-like option for enum keys.
questions.rule: Prefer EnumMap to an array indexed by an enum.

questions.q: True or false: An entry in a WeakHashMap stays until it is removed explicitly.
questions.explain: An entry can be garbage-collected once its key is no longer referenced outside the map, without any remove call.
questions.teaches: A WeakHashMap makes the key's reachability decide the entry's life, which fits registries that should clean themselves up.
questions.rule: Use EnumMap for enum keys, WeakHashMap for entries that should vanish with their keys, IdentityHashMap for reference-based keys and ConcurrentHashMap for shared maps.

questions.q: Two separate objects that are equal under equals are used as keys in an IdentityHashMap. How many entries does it hold?
options: Two, since the keys are different objects
One, since the keys are equal
None, since the keys clash
An exception is thrown for the second key
optionExplain: Right: it compares by reference.
That is HashMap behaviour, which uses equals.
A clash would not empty the map.
No exception is thrown; the keys are simply different.
questions.explain: Reference comparison treats equal-looking objects as different keys.
questions.rule: IdentityHashMap compares keys with ==.

questions.q: A debugger attaches notes to live objects, and some of those objects have badly written equals methods. Which Map avoids trouble?
options: IdentityHashMap, since it never calls equals on keys
HashMap, since it uses equals to find keys
TreeMap, since it sorts the keys by their natural order
EnumMap, since it is the fastest map for small key sets
optionExplain: Right: bad equals methods cannot affect it.
A faulty equals can corrupt lookups in a HashMap.
The keys would need an ordering, and equals problems can still surface.
It needs enum keys, which these objects are not.
questions.explain: Reference identity is robust against faulty equality code.
questions.teaches: The tutorial notes IdentityHashMap protects against spoof attacks from perverse equals methods, which is a reason beyond speed to choose it.
questions.rule: Use EnumMap for enum keys, WeakHashMap for entries that should vanish with their keys, IdentityHashMap for reference-based keys and ConcurrentHashMap for shared maps.

questions.q: True or false: PriorityQueue permits null elements.
questions.explain: PriorityQueue does not permit null; LinkedList is the queue that does. The card next explains it.
questions.rule: Pick LinkedList or ArrayDeque for plain FIFO or double-ended use, PriorityQueue for value order and a BlockingQueue when threads must wait for each other.

questions.q: Match each implementation to its description.
pairs: Heap ordered by natural ordering or a comparator, no nulls
Bounded FIFO that makes threads wait when full or empty
questions.explain: Each implementation answers a different combination of ordering, bounds and thread behaviour.
questions.rule: Match ordering, bounds and blocking to the need.

questions.q: A producer thread and a consumer thread share a bounded buffer. The producer must wait when it is full and the consumer when it is empty. Which fits?
options: A PriorityQueue
An ArrayDeque
A BlockingQueue such as ArrayBlockingQueue
A LinkedList
optionExplain: It is not thread-safe and does not block.
It is not thread-safe and does not block.
Right: blocking queues provide exactly that waiting.
It is not thread-safe and does not block.
questions.explain: Waiting for space or elements is the feature of the BlockingQueue family.
questions.rule: Waiting between threads needs a BlockingQueue.

questions.q: True or false: A PriorityQueue's iterator visits elements in priority order.
questions.explain: Its iterator is not guaranteed to follow any particular order. For ordered traversal sort the result of toArray.
questions.teaches: The heap keeps only the head reliably ordered, so a loop that prints a priority queue's iterator output can look unsorted.
questions.rule: Pick LinkedList or ArrayDeque for plain FIFO or double-ended use, PriorityQueue for value order and a BlockingQueue when threads must wait for each other.

questions.q: A program needs a Deque that can hold a null element. What does that rule out among the Deque implementations?
options: LinkedList, which forbids null, leaving ArrayDeque
ArrayDeque, which forbids null, leaving LinkedList
Both, since no Deque implementation allows null
Neither, since every Deque implementation allows null
optionExplain: LinkedList permits null.
Right: LinkedList is the one that permits null.
LinkedList is a Deque that permits null.
ArrayDeque forbids null.
questions.explain: A new requirement can rule out the default choice.
questions.rule: ArrayDeque forbids null, LinkedList permits it.

questions.q: A scheduler holds tasks that may run only after their delay has expired, and the worker should take the one that expires first. Which queue does the tutorial describe for that?
options: SynchronousQueue, which holds tasks until a consumer arrives
ArrayBlockingQueue, which orders tasks by their arrival
PriorityQueue, because a delay is a kind of priority
DelayQueue, whose head is the earliest to expire
optionExplain: It has zero capacity and hands over directly; it does not time anything.
It orders by arrival and does not wait for expiry.
It has no notion of waiting for a delay to pass.
Right: elements can be taken only after their delay expires.
questions.explain: Time-based release is a feature of DelayQueue alone.
questions.teaches: DelayQueue needs elements that implement the Delayed interface, so each element reports how long until it may be taken.
questions.rule: Pick LinkedList or ArrayDeque for plain FIFO or double-ended use, PriorityQueue for value order and a BlockingQueue when threads must wait for each other.

questions.q: The static factory methods that create wrappers are in the class named ____ .
questions.explain: Collections, with an s, holds the wrapper factories; Collection is the interface. The card next explains it.
questions.rule: Wrap with the Collections factory methods to add thread safety, read-only access or run-time type checks, and keep no stray reference to the backing collection when the guarantee matters.

questions.q: Match each wrapper to its effect.
pairs: Rejects wrong-typed insertions at run time with ClassCastException
questions.explain: Each factory adds or removes one capability from the list it wraps.
questions.rule: Wrappers add or restrict one capability.

questions.q: A class keeps a private list and must give clients a read-only view while it continues to edit the list. Which should its getter return?
options: Collections.synchronizedList(list), then return that wrapper
A new ArrayList holding the same elements as the list
Collections.unmodifiableList(list), keeping list private
list itself, but declared with the type Collection
optionExplain: That adds locking but still lets clients modify the list.
A copy is not a live view, and the tutorial's technique is the wrapper.
Right: clients get read-only access and the class keeps full access.
A Collection variable still allows modification through add and remove.
questions.explain: A read-only wrapper over your private list is the tutorial's second use of unmodifiable wrappers.
questions.rule: Return the wrapper, keep the backing list.

questions.q: True or false: Iterating over a synchronized list needs no extra synchronization, because every call is already synchronized.
questions.explain: Iteration is many calls, and they must be composed into one atomic operation by synchronizing on the wrapper.
questions.teaches: A wrapper makes single calls atomic but not sequences of calls, so compound actions such as iteration need an outer lock.
questions.rule: Wrap with the Collections factory methods to add thread safety, read-only access or run-time type checks, and keep no stray reference to the backing collection when the guarantee matters.

questions.q: A program iterates over the key view of a map obtained from Collections.synchronizedMap. On which object should its synchronized block lock?
options: The synchronized map itself
The key view
The backing HashMap
No lock, since the map is already synchronized
optionExplain: Right: the tutorial says to synchronize on the map, not on the view.
The tutorial warns that the view is the wrong lock.
Going around the wrapper defeats its protection.
Iteration still needs a lock.
questions.explain: All access, including iteration, must use the same lock, which is the wrapper.
questions.rule: Lock on the wrapper, not on its views.

questions.q: Older code inserts a number into your List of String through a raw type, and the failure shows up much later. Which wrapper turns it into an immediate error?
options: A synchronized wrapper
An unmodifiable wrapper
A fixed-size list from Arrays.asList
A checked wrapper such as checkedList
optionExplain: Locking does not check types.
It would refuse every insertion, not only the wrong ones.
Fixed size is unrelated to element type.
Right: it throws ClassCastException at the point of insertion.
questions.explain: Generics are checked at compile time and can be bypassed; the checked wrapper repeats the check at run time.
questions.teaches: Compile-time generics checking can be defeated by raw types, and a checked wrapper is the run-time safety net that closes the gap.
questions.rule: Wrap with the Collections factory methods to add thread safety, read-only access or run-time type checks, and keep no stray reference to the backing collection when the guarantee matters.

questions.q: Which call creates a list of 1,000 placeholder values without a loop?
options: Arrays.asList(1000)
Collections.nCopies(1000, null) wrapped in new ArrayList
Collections.singleton(null)
Collections.emptyList()
optionExplain: That would not build 1,000 elements.
Right: nCopies supplies the values and the ArrayList makes them modifiable.
That is a set with one element.
That is an empty list.
questions.explain: nCopies is a repetition factory. The card next explains it.
questions.rule: Arrays.asList is a fixed-size writable view, and nCopies, singleton and the empty constants are immutable.

questions.q: Match each factory to what it returns.
pairs: A fixed-size list view of the array
An immutable list of n references to x
questions.explain: Each factory fills a small, specific need.
questions.rule: Each convenience factory serves a narrow need.

questions.q: A method takes a Collection of purchases, and a tourist bought nothing. Which argument avoids creating a new object?
options: new HashSet()
Collections.emptySet()
null
Collections.singleton(null)
optionExplain: That creates a new object each time.
Right: it is a shared immutable empty collection.
The method may not accept null, and the tutorial's idiom is the empty constant.
That is a set holding one null element, not an empty set.
questions.explain: An immutable empty constant stands for no values.
questions.rule: Use the empty constants for no values.

questions.q: True or false: Calling set on a list returned by Collections.nCopies replaces an element.
questions.explain: The list is immutable, so every modification is refused.
questions.teaches: An immutable list can be turned into a modifiable one by copying it, for example with the ArrayList conversion constructor.
questions.rule: Arrays.asList is a fixed-size writable view, and nCopies, singleton and the empty constants are immutable.

questions.q: A program wraps a String array in Arrays.asList, then assigns a new value to array element 1 and reads list.get(1). What does it see?
options: The old value, since the list copied the array
An exception, since the array was changed behind the list
null, since the link is broken by the change
The new value, since the list is a view of the array
optionExplain: asList does not copy; it views.
Changing the array behind the list is allowed.
The view stays linked.
Right: changes write through in both directions.
questions.explain: A view stays in step with the thing it views.
questions.rule: Arrays.asList writes through both ways.

questions.q: Sort each list by whether set can replace one of its elements.

items.t: Arrays.asList on a String array
A new ArrayList built from Collections.nCopies
The list returned by Collections.nCopies itself
Collections.emptyList()
A list made by Collections.unmodifiableList
A new ArrayList built from Arrays.asList

questions.explain: A fixed-size view allows set, immutable results refuse it, and copying into an ArrayList gives a list that can be changed.
questions.teaches: Copying through an ArrayList constructor turns any of these into an ordinary modifiable list, and it also breaks the write-through link to an array.
questions.rule: Arrays.asList is a fixed-size writable view, and nCopies, singleton and the empty constants are immutable.

questions.q: True or false: Sorting a mail list by date and then by sender with Collections.sort keeps each sender's mail in date order.
questions.explain: The sort is stable, so the second sort does not reorder messages from the same sender. The card next explains it.
questions.rule: Collections.sort is fast and stable, so sort first by the secondary key and then by the primary key to get a two-level order.

questions.q: A sort in which equal elements keep their relative order is called ____ .
questions.explain: Collections.sort is stable.
questions.rule: Stable sorts keep ties in their earlier order.

questions.q: A staff list must be ordered by department and, within each department, by name. Using two stable sorts, which order of passes gives that?
options: Sort by name first, then sort by department
Sort by department first, then sort by name
Sort by department twice
Shuffle, then sort by department
optionExplain: Right: the last pass is the main key, and ties keep the name order.
That leaves names as the main key, scattering departments.
The second pass adds nothing and names are never ordered.
Shuffling destroys the name order that the last pass was meant to keep.
questions.explain: With stable sorts the last pass is the main key and the earlier pass orders the ties.
questions.rule: Sort by the secondary key first, then the primary key.

questions.q: True or false: A quicksort is generally faster than the merge sort in Collections.sort and is also stable.
questions.explain: The tutorial says quicksort is generally faster but is not stable and does not guarantee n log n.
questions.teaches: The designers traded a little raw speed for stability and a guaranteed n log n bound, which suits repeated sorting.
questions.rule: Collections.sort is fast and stable, so sort first by the secondary key and then by the primary key to get a two-level order.

questions.q: The inbox is sorted by date and then by sender. What could happen to one sender's messages if the second sort were not stable?
options: They would be removed from the list
They would be sorted by date automatically
They could end up out of date order
They would be grouped under a different sender
optionExplain: Sorting never removes elements.
Only a stable pass preserves that earlier order.
Right: ties could be shuffled by the second pass.
Sender is the key being sorted on, not something that changes.
questions.explain: Without stability the first sort's work is lost among equal keys.
questions.rule: Stability keeps the earlier order among ties.

questions.q: A library list is sorted by title and then by author. In what order does the result appear?
options: By title, with each title's books in author order
By author, with each author's books in the original order
In the original order
By author, with each author's books in title order
optionExplain: That would result from sorting by author first.
The title sort set the order within authors before the author sort began.
Both sorts change the order.
Right: the last sort is the main key and stability keeps the titles ordered.
questions.explain: The same reasoning applies in any domain with two sort keys.
questions.teaches: A stable sort lets you build a multi-key ordering one key at a time, which is simpler than writing one comparator that covers all keys.
questions.rule: Collections.sort is fast and stable, so sort first by the secondary key and then by the primary key to get a two-level order.

questions.q: True or false: Collections.shuffle can be used to destroy any ordering in a List.
questions.explain: shuffle is the opposite of sort: it randomises the order. The card next explains it.
questions.rule: Use shuffle to randomise, reverse, fill and swap to rearrange or reset, and copy to overwrite a destination that is at least as long as the source.

questions.q: Match each Collections algorithm to its effect.
pairs: Reverses the order of the elements
Overwrites every element with one value
Exchanges the elements at two positions
Copies a source list over a destination list
questions.explain: Each routine operation changes a list in one simple way.
questions.rule: Know what each routine operation does.

questions.q: A destination list has 5 elements and a source has 3. After Collections.copy(destination, source), what is true of the destination's last two elements?
options: They are removed, so the list has 3 elements
They are unchanged
They are replaced by copies of the last source element
They cause an exception, since the lists differ in size
optionExplain: copy does not shrink the destination.
Right: copy only overwrites as many elements as the source has.
No filling takes place.
Only a destination shorter than the source is a problem.
questions.explain: The destination keeps everything beyond the source's length.
questions.rule: copy overwrites only as many as the source holds.

questions.q: True or false: Collections.copy appends the source elements to the end of the destination.
questions.explain: copy overwrites existing elements starting from the beginning and needs a destination at least as long as the source. addAll is the way to append.
questions.teaches: Copy and append are different jobs: copy overwrites in place, and appending is addAll's task.
questions.rule: Use shuffle to randomise, reverse, fill and swap to rearrange or reset, and copy to overwrite a destination that is at least as long as the source.

questions.q: A list holding 1, 2, 3 has reverse applied twice. What does it hold?
options: 3, 2, 1, the reversed order
2, 1, 3, a partly reversed order
1, 2, 3, the original order
An empty list, since the changes cancel
optionExplain: That is the result after one reversal.
reverse always reverses the whole list.
Right: two reversals cancel.
Reversal rearranges elements; it never removes them.
questions.explain: Applying an operation and its inverse restores the starting state.
questions.rule: Reversing twice restores the list.

questions.q: A tester wants to check that a routine does not depend on the order of its input list. Which Collections algorithm helps generate many inputs?
options: shuffle, applied to copies of the data
fill, applied to copies of the data
copy, applied to copies of the data
binarySearch, applied to copies of the data
optionExplain: Right: the tutorial lists generating test cases as a use of shuffle.
fill makes all elements equal, removing the variety the test needs.
copy duplicates the same order.
binarySearch finds an element; it creates no new orders.
questions.explain: Random orderings expose hidden order assumptions.
questions.teaches: Shuffling the same data many times is a cheap way to test whether code secretly relies on input order.
questions.rule: Use shuffle to randomise, reverse, fill and swap to rearrange or reset, and copy to overwrite a destination that is at least as long as the source.

questions.q: For the sorted list 1, 3, 5, what does binarySearch return for the key 4?
options: Minus 3
Minus 1
optionExplain: Right: 4 would be inserted at index 2, and the result is minus 2 minus 1.
That is the insertion point, but a missing key returns a negative number.
That is the result for a key smaller than every element.
A nonnegative result would mean the key was found.
questions.explain: A negative result flags absence and encodes where the key belongs. The card next explains it.
questions.rule: A nonnegative result is the index of the key; a negative result n means not found, and the insertion point is minus n minus one.

questions.q: binarySearch needs the list to be ____ in ascending order before the call.
questions.explain: The algorithm halves the range using the order, so the list must be sorted.
questions.rule: Sort before you binarySearch.

questions.q: binarySearch on the sorted list 10, 20, 30, 40 for the key 25 returns ____ .
questions.explain: 25 belongs at index 2, so the result is minus 2 minus 1, which is minus 3.
questions.rule: Result is minus insertion point minus one.

questions.q: True or false: A binarySearch result of 0 means the key was not found.
questions.explain: Zero is a valid index, so the key is at the first position. Absence is signalled by negative results.
questions.teaches: Using minus one as the offset keeps an insertion point of 0 distinguishable from an index of 0, which is why a missing key at the front returns minus one.
questions.rule: A nonnegative result is the index of the key; a negative result n means not found, and the insertion point is minus n minus one.

questions.q: The key 4 is inserted into the sorted list 1, 3, 5 using the add-at-minus-pos-minus-one idiom. What does the list hold afterwards?
optionExplain: That would put it at index 0.
That would append it, leaving the list unsorted.
Right: the key goes in at index 2, keeping the list sorted.
The key was absent, so the idiom adds it.
questions.explain: Converting the negative result back to an index gives the position that keeps order.
questions.rule: add at minus pos minus one keeps the list sorted.

questions.q: A sorted list of timestamps has a new timestamp searched, and binarySearch returns minus 6. At which index should the new timestamp be inserted?
options: Minus 5
optionExplain: That forgets to subtract one.
Right: minus the result, minus one, is 6 minus 1.
That adds one instead of subtracting it.
An index cannot be negative.
questions.explain: Undoing the encoding is a fixed calculation.
questions.teaches: The same formula works at either end: a result of minus the list size, minus one, means the key is larger than every element and belongs at the end.
questions.rule: A nonnegative result is the index of the key; a negative result n means not found, and the insertion point is minus n minus one.

questions.q: Which Collections algorithm counts how many times an element appears in a collection?
options: disjoint
max
fill
frequency
optionExplain: It tests whether two collections share elements.
It returns the largest element.
It overwrites every element.
Right: it counts occurrences.
questions.explain: The name says what is measured. The card next explains it.
questions.rule: frequency counts occurrences, disjoint tests for no overlap, and min and max find extremes by natural ordering or a Comparator.

questions.q: Match each algorithm to its job.
pairs: Tests that two collections share nothing
questions.explain: Each is a one-call query about a collection.
questions.rule: One call answers each query.

questions.q: Which call tells you whether two guest lists contain no person in common?
options: Collections.frequency(listA, listB)
Collections.max(listA, listB)
Collections.disjoint(listA, listB)
listA.retainAll(listB)
optionExplain: frequency counts one element, not whole collections.
max finds an extreme; it does not compare collections for overlap.
Right: it returns true when there is no overlap.
It changes listA and does not answer a yes-or-no question.
questions.explain: disjoint is a read-only test, unlike retainAll.
questions.rule: disjoint tests overlap without changing anything.

questions.q: True or false: min with a Comparator returns the smallest element according to that comparator, which can differ from the smallest by natural ordering.
questions.explain: The comparator defines what smallest means for that call.
questions.teaches: The Comparator form lets you find extremes by any attribute, such as shortest string or cheapest product, without sorting.
questions.rule: frequency counts occurrences, disjoint tests for no overlap, and min and max find extremes by natural ordering or a Comparator.

questions.q: A Product class is not Comparable and has a price. How do you find the cheapest product in a collection called products?
options: Collections.min(products, byPrice) with a Comparator on price
Collections.min(products), relying on a natural ordering
Collections.frequency(products, cheapestProduct) to count it
Collections.disjoint(products, byPrice)
optionExplain: Right: the Comparator form supplies the ordering the class lacks.
The products have no natural ordering, so this would fail.
That counts an element you do not yet know.
disjoint compares two collections, not a collection with a comparator.
questions.explain: Supply an ordering whenever the elements do not have a natural one.
questions.teaches: A Comparator is also the answer for classes you cannot or do not want to make Comparable.
questions.rule: frequency counts occurrences, disjoint tests for no overlap, and min and max find extremes by natural ordering or a Comparator.

questions.q: True or false: The built-in collections keep their contents after the program ends.
questions.explain: They live in main memory, which is one reason to write a persistent collection. The card next explains it.
questions.rule: Write a custom collection only for a need the built-ins do not meet, and extend the abstract class that matches your storage so you write only the core methods.

questions.q: Match each reason for a custom collection to the tutorial's example.
pairs: A collection that fronts an external database
A List representing a range of integers
A bag built on a HashMap
A legacy collection API made to fit the framework
questions.explain: Each reason names a need the built-in classes do not meet.
questions.rule: A custom collection answers a need the built-ins lack.

questions.q: A collection will be backed by a plain array and needs fast positional access. Which abstract class and core methods fit?
options: AbstractSequentialList, supplying listIterator and size
AbstractMap, supplying entrySet
AbstractQueue, supplying offer and poll
AbstractList, supplying get and size
optionExplain: That class is for sequential storage such as a linked list.
The data is a list, not key-value pairs.
The data is accessed by position, not by queue operations.
Right: random-access storage is what AbstractList is for.
questions.explain: Match the abstract class to how the storage is accessed.
questions.rule: Random access means AbstractList; sequential access means AbstractSequentialList.

questions.q: True or false: A class that extends AbstractList and implements only get and size will accept calls to add, as in the tutorial's array-backed example.
questions.explain: Without further code add and remove are unsupported, which makes the collection fixed-size or read-only.
questions.rule: Skip add and remove for a fixed-size collection.

questions.q: A company has an old Inventory class with its own methods and wants framework algorithms to work on it. Which reason category from the tutorial describes this?
options: Persistent, since inventory records are stored long term
Adapter, presenting a legacy API as a framework collection
High-performance, since the framework algorithms then run faster
Convenience, since a wrapper class saves typing for callers
optionExplain: Persistence is about surviving program restarts, not about fitting an old API.
Right: an adapter lets the old API be used inside the framework.
Nothing here is about speed.
Convenience is about a handy shape such as a range of integers.
questions.explain: Naming the reason clarifies what the design must do.
questions.teaches: An adapter keeps the old class intact and wraps it, so existing code keeps working while new code gets the framework interfaces.
questions.rule: Write a custom collection only for a need the built-ins do not meet, and extend the abstract class that matches your storage so you write only the core methods.

questions.q: True or false: A class extending AbstractList that implements only get and size is a usable read-only List.
questions.explain: AbstractList supplies the rest of the List behaviour, so a read-only list needs only those two. The card next explains it.
questions.rule: Extend the abstract class that matches your storage, implement its few core methods, and optimise only after measuring.

questions.q: Put the tutorial's process for a custom implementation in order.
items: Choose the abstract class that fits the storage
Implement its abstract methods
Test and debug the implementation
Optimise only if needed, measuring each override
questions.explain: Optimisation comes last and only on evidence.
questions.rule: Choose, implement, test, then optimise if measured.

questions.q: In the array-backed list, what should set(index, element) return?
options: The new element
The element that was previously at that index
The size of the array
Nothing, since set returns void
optionExplain: That is what the caller passed in.
Right: set returns the old value, as in List.
size is a separate method.
List.set returns the old element.
questions.explain: The List contract fixes what set returns.
questions.rule: set returns the old element.

questions.q: True or false: Overriding toArray to clone the underlying array can make it faster than the version AbstractList provides.
questions.explain: AbstractList walks the list element by element, whereas the data already sits in an array that can be cloned in one step.
questions.teaches: An inherited method that is correct for every list may be slow for yours, because only you know the storage.
questions.rule: Extend the abstract class that matches your storage, implement its few core methods, and optimise only after measuring.

questions.q: An array-backed list is wrapped around array a. A program calls set at index 0 with a new value, then reads a[0]. What does it see?
options: The old value, because the list copied the array
null, because the array was cleared
An exception, because the list is fixed-size
The new value, because the list writes through
optionExplain: The class holds the array itself, not a copy.
set does not clear the array.
Fixed size forbids add and remove, but set is supported.
Right: the list is a view, not a copy.
questions.explain: A view has no storage of its own.
questions.rule: A view writes through to its source.

questions.q: A RangeList extends AbstractList to present the integers 1 to n without storing them. Which methods does it need?
options: get, returning the index plus one, and size, returning n
get and set, with an internal array of n integers
iterator and size, as for AbstractCollection or AbstractSet
offer, peek and poll, as for AbstractQueue implementations
optionExplain: Right: values can be computed on demand.
The point is to avoid storing the values.
AbstractList wants get and size, and supplies iterators itself.
Those belong to queues, not lists.
questions.explain: A collection need not store its elements if they can be computed from the index.
questions.teaches: A collection can be a computation rather than a container, since get only has to return a value for the index.
questions.rule: Extend the abstract class that matches your storage, implement its few core methods, and optimise only after measuring.

questions.q: An old method returns a Vector, and a new method expects a List. What conversion is needed?
options: Arrays.asList on the Vector
Collections.list on the Vector
None, since Vector already implements List
new Hashtable built from the Vector
optionExplain: That converts an array, not a Vector.
That converts an Enumeration.
Right: it can be passed directly.
That makes a Hashtable, which is a Map.
questions.explain: Retrofitting made the old classes members of the framework. The card next explains it.
questions.rule: Arrays go through Arrays.asList, Vector and Hashtable pass straight in, and an Enumeration goes through Collections.list.

questions.q: Match each old type to the way it enters new code.
questions.explain: Two types are already collections, and two need a conversion call.
questions.rule: Know which old types need a conversion.

questions.q: An old method returns a Foo array called result, and newMethod takes a List. Which call is right?
options: newMethod(result)
newMethod(Collections.list(result))
newMethod(new Vector(result))
newMethod(Arrays.asList(result))
optionExplain: An array is not a List, so it cannot be passed directly.
Collections.list converts an Enumeration.
That is the backward direction and does not take an array.
Right: asList views the array as a List.
questions.explain: An array needs asList to look like a List.
questions.rule: Wrap an array with Arrays.asList.

questions.q: True or false: Vector and Hashtable were retrofitted to implement List and Map, which is why they need no conversion.
questions.explain: The tutorial says they now implement the framework's interfaces.
questions.teaches: Retrofitting an old class onto a new interface is a way to join the new framework without breaking old callers.
questions.rule: Arrays go through Arrays.asList, Vector and Hashtable pass straight in, and an Enumeration goes through Collections.list.

questions.q: An old method returns an Enumeration instead of a Vector, and the new method takes a Collection. What call is needed?
options: None, since every old type is already a Collection
Collections.list on the Enumeration
Arrays.asList on the Enumeration
The Enumeration constructor of ArrayList
optionExplain: Enumeration is not a collection type.
Right: it builds a list from the Enumeration.
asList takes an array.
The tutorial uses Collections.list for this case.
questions.explain: Changing the old type changes the conversion.
questions.rule: Enumeration goes through Collections.list.

questions.q: Sort each situation by whether a conversion call is needed before passing the old value to code expecting a collection.

items.t: A String array to a List parameter
An Enumeration to a Collection parameter
A Vector to a List parameter
A Hashtable to a Map parameter
An integer array to a List parameter
A Vector to a Collection parameter

questions.explain: Arrays and Enumerations are not collections, so they need a conversion. Vector and Hashtable already are.
questions.teaches: The test is whether the old type already implements the target interface; if it does, passing it needs no conversion.
questions.rule: Arrays go through Arrays.asList, Vector and Hashtable pass straight in, and an Enumeration goes through Collections.list.

questions.q: An old method wants a Vector, and you have a Collection called c. Which expression supplies it?
options: Collections.list(c)
c.toArray()
new Vector(c)
Arrays.asList(c)
optionExplain: That converts an Enumeration into a list.
That produces an array, not a Vector.
Right: the constructor copies the collection into a Vector.
asList takes an array and produces a List.
questions.explain: A collection-taking constructor is the bridge to Vector. The card next explains it.
questions.rule: Use toArray for arrays, a constructor for Vector and Hashtable, and Collections.enumeration for an Enumeration.

questions.q: Match each backward conversion to the call.
questions.explain: Each old type has one recognised conversion.
questions.rule: Each old type has one conversion.

questions.q: To pass a Map called m to an old method that expects a Hashtable, call new ____ (m).
questions.explain: The Hashtable constructor accepts a map and copies its mappings.
questions.rule: Use the Hashtable constructor.

questions.q: True or false: Collections.enumeration is a static factory method, whereas new Vector(c) is a constructor call.
questions.explain: The conversions come in both forms: constructors for Vector and Hashtable, and a static factory for Enumeration.
questions.teaches: The conversions are not uniform: some use constructors and some use static methods, so each one has to be remembered by its target type.
questions.rule: Use toArray for arrays, a constructor for Vector and Hashtable, and Collections.enumeration for an Enumeration.

questions.q: An old routine needs a String array. A program passes c.toArray() instead of c.toArray(new String[0]). What mismatch occurs?
options: It supplies an Object array, which is not a String array
It supplies a Vector, which the routine cannot read
It supplies an empty array, which has no elements
It supplies a List, which the routine can read
optionExplain: Right: the no-argument form returns Object[].
toArray returns an array, never a Vector.
The array has the collection's length.
toArray returns an array.
questions.explain: The argument decides the array type.
questions.rule: Pass a typed array to get a typed array.

questions.q: A new payments module returns a Collection of String, and a legacy printer takes an Enumeration. Which direction is this, and which call bridges it?
options: Backward, with Collections.enumeration(c)
Upward, with the call Collections.list(c)
Backward, with the constructor new Vector(c)
Upward, with the call Arrays.asList(c)
optionExplain: Right: new code feeds old code, and enumeration builds the old type.
Upward means old feeding new, and list converts an Enumeration into a list.
The printer wants an Enumeration, not a Vector.
asList takes an array, and the direction is wrong too.
questions.explain: First name the direction, then pick the conversion for the target type.
questions.teaches: Naming the direction first (old feeding new, or new feeding old) tells you whether the target type is a collection or a legacy type, which narrows the choice of call.
questions.rule: Use toArray for arrays, a constructor for Vector and Hashtable, and Collections.enumeration for an Enumeration.

questions.q: A method only needs to loop over a group of strings. Which parameter type serves callers best?
options: ArrayList of String
List of String
Collection of String
HashSet of String
optionExplain: That demands a specific implementation and rejects other collections.
That rejects callers holding a Set or a Queue.
Right: it accepts any List, Set or Queue of strings.
That demands one implementation and also forces no-duplicates.
questions.explain: The more general the parameter type, the more callers can use the method. The card next explains it.
questions.rule: Accept the most general interface that does the job and return the most specific interface you can promise.

questions.q: Parameters should be interface types, not ____ types.
questions.explain: Interface types keep callers free of any particular implementation.
questions.rule: Take interfaces, not implementations.

questions.q: A method builds its result in key order on every call and returns it as a map. Which return type does the tutorial's advice favour?
options: Map
SortedMap
TreeMap
Object
optionExplain: It is true but hides the sorted order callers could use.
Right: the most specific interface that is always true.
It is an implementation type, which the tutorial advises against exposing.
That throws away all the useful structure.
questions.explain: A specific return interface gives callers more.
questions.rule: Return the most specific interface.

questions.q: True or false: A method that returns an ImageList, a List with an extra indexImage operation, should still accept general Collection arguments.
questions.explain: The tutorial says to accept general types on input even when returning specialised ones.
questions.teaches: Input and output follow different rules: be generous in what you accept and precise in what you promise.
questions.rule: Accept the most general interface that does the job and return the most specific interface you can promise.

questions.q: A method takes an ArrayList parameter, and a caller holds a LinkedList. What happens?
options: It compiles without trouble, since both are kinds of list
It compiles and converts the list automatically at run time
It runs, but with noticeably worse speed than before
The call does not compile, so the caller must copy
optionExplain: The parameter type is the specific class ArrayList.
No automatic conversion exists.
The mismatch is found at compile time, not as a speed problem.
Right: an implementation parameter rejects other implementations.
questions.explain: A concrete parameter type forces copying on callers.
questions.rule: A concrete parameter type shuts out other implementations.

questions.q: An API method takes a List of String but only counts the distinct words in it. Which change widens the set of callers without changing the result?
options: Take an ArrayList of String instead
Take a Map of String to String instead
Take a Collection of String instead
Return a List instead of a Set
optionExplain: That narrows the callers further.
That changes the meaning of the input.
Right: the method does not depend on order, so a Collection suffices.
That changes the return, not the parameter.
questions.explain: Ask what property of the type the method really uses.
questions.teaches: A good test for a parameter type is to ask which operations the method actually calls, and to pick the least specific interface that offers them.
questions.rule: Accept the most general interface that does the job and return the most specific interface you can promise.

questions.q: A team designs a date library so that code is easy to read and hard to misuse. Which set of goals fits best?
options: Short names, public setters on every field, and one class that holds every kind of value
Lenient methods that accept null quietly, shared objects anyone may edit, and hidden defaults
Predictable methods, chainable calls, values that cannot change, and room for user extensions
A closed design with fixed behavior, many constructors, and silent repair of bad input
optionExplain: Setters invite accidental changes and one huge class is harder to read, so misuse becomes easier.
Quiet leniency hides bugs, and editable shared objects are unsafe, so misuse becomes harder to spot.
These goals match the clear, fluent, immutable and extensible principles that this API follows.
A closed design blocks extension, and silent repair of bad input hides mistakes instead of exposing them.
questions.explain: A date API that is clear, fluent, immutable and extensible is easiest to read and hardest to misuse. The card next shows what each word promises.
questions.rule: Expect Date-Time methods to be predictable, chainable, safe against null, and open to adjusters and queries you write yourself.

questions.q: True or false: According to the tutorial, most Date-Time methods accept and return null so that calls can be chained.
questions.explain: The opposite holds: most methods neither accept nor return null, and that is what lets one call feed the next.
questions.rule: Chaining rests on avoiding null.

questions.q: A form handler calls LocalDate.parse on a text field that is null by mistake. Which outcome fits the clear principle?
options: The call returns today's date so the page keeps working without any error
The call returns null and later code is expected to test for it
The call returns a date at the epoch, which makes the error easy to spot later
A NullPointerException is thrown at that call, so the bug appears at once
optionExplain: A silent fallback would hide the bug, which is the opposite of clear.
Most methods do not return null, and passing the problem along hides where it began.
A made-up default date would look like real data and is not what the tutorial describes.
Failing at once is what clear means here: the mistake is reported where it happens.
questions.explain: The tutorial says a null argument typically makes a Date-Time method throw NullPointerException, which makes misuse visible straight away.
questions.rule: A bad argument fails where it is passed.

questions.q: Why does the fluent style depend on the rule that most methods neither accept nor return null?
options: Each result can feed the next call safely, so a chain needs no null checks
Null values compare slowly, so a chain with null in it would run slowly
A null in the middle of a chain would silently change the original object
Chained calls are only allowed on classes that cannot be subclassed
optionExplain: A chain is only safe if no link hands back null, which is what the rule gives.
The concern is safety of the next call, not speed of comparison.
Nothing is changed in the original; the next call would simply fail on null.
Chaining is not restricted that way; it works because each call returns a usable value.
questions.explain: If every call returns a usable value, the next call can run without a guard. That is why the no-null rule is what makes long chains safe, not only neat.
questions.rule: No null results, so no guards inside a chain.
questions.teaches: The no-null rule is what makes a long chain safe: with no null results, no call in the middle needs a guard, so fluent style is a consequence of that rule and not only a matter of neat naming.

questions.q: Which statements about the four principles are accurate? Select all that apply.
options: Clear: a null argument usually makes a method fail at once
Fluent: most methods avoid null, which makes chaining safe
Extensible: only the library authors can add new adjusters
Clear: every method accepts null and picks a sensible default
optionExplain: Failing at the call is what clear means here; the tutorial says typically.
Because most results are usable, one call can feed the next.
Users can write their own adjusters and queries; that is the point of extensible.
Clear methods reject null rather than hiding it behind a default.
questions.explain: Clear and fluent are about failing early and chaining safely, and both claims are worded with most or typically. Extensible means users can add rules.
questions.rule: Most, not all; users can extend.

questions.q: A team builds a recipe-scaling library. Cooks must be able to add a rounding rule of their own, such as nearest quarter cup, without editing the library. Which Date-Time principle are they copying?
options: Clear: every method has a well-defined meaning
Extensible: the library accepts rules that the user writes
Fluent: calls can be chained into one line
Immutable: values cannot change after creation
optionExplain: Clear is about predictable methods, not about letting users add rules.
Extensible is the principle that lets users supply their own rules, as with custom adjusters and queries.
Fluent concerns readable chains, which a rounding rule does not need.
Immutable concerns values staying fixed, not user-written rules.
questions.explain: A user-supplied rule that plugs into the library is extensibility. The same idea lets Date-Time users write adjusters and queries.
questions.rule: Extensible means users can plug in their own rules.
questions.teaches: Extensibility works through a small agreed shape: the library defines what a rule looks like, and the user supplies one that fits, so the library never needs to know about each user's rule.

questions.q: True or false: Calling plusDays on a LocalDate changes that same object.
questions.explain: A LocalDate never changes after it is created; plusDays returns a different object. The card next explains why.
questions.rule: Changes produce new objects.

questions.q: Because Date-Time objects cannot be altered once created, the API has no ____ methods.
questions.explain: A setter would change an existing object, which immutable classes do not allow. The with, plus and minus methods return copies instead.
questions.rule: No setters on immutable values.

questions.q: Sort each name by whether it fits the immutable design of the API.
groups: Does not fit: would change an object in place

items.t: plusWeeks
withYear
minusDays
setDayOfMonth
setYear
setMonth

questions.explain: Methods that start with plus, minus or with return copies. A set method would edit an existing object, so immutable classes do not offer one.
questions.rule: Copies in, no edits in place.

questions.q: Why can one LocalDate object be shared by many threads without locking?
options: Each thread automatically receives its own private copy of the object
The runtime locks each date object for as long as any thread is reading its value
Nothing can modify it, so every thread that reads it sees the same value
Date objects are stored only in memory that one thread can reach
optionExplain: Nothing is copied when a reference is shared; all threads see the same object.
No such locking exists; the safety comes from the object itself.
With no way to change the object, readers cannot disagree and no lock is needed.
Objects can be reached by many threads; they are safe because they never change.
questions.explain: Thread safety comes from immutability: sharing is safe because no thread can alter the value, and a change by one holder makes a new object the others do not see.
questions.rule: Cannot change, so safe to share.
questions.teaches: Immutability gives thread safety without locks: a change by one holder creates a different object that other holders never see, so sharing one value among threads cannot cause disagreement.

questions.q: A programmer writes LocalDate due = LocalDate.of(2024, Month.JUNE, 30); then due.minusDays(2); and later uses due as the moved deadline. What goes wrong?
options: minusDays returned a new date that was discarded, so due still holds 30 June
minusDays only works on LocalDateTime, so the call has no effect
due must first be converted to a LocalDateTime before its value may be moved
June has too few days for minusDays to apply
optionExplain: The result of a change must be kept, for example in a new variable or by reassigning due.
minusDays exists on LocalDate and works; the issue is the discarded result.
Converting to LocalDateTime is not needed: LocalDate has minusDays and it works; the problem is the discarded result.
June has plenty of days; the amount of days is not the problem.
questions.explain: Because the object is immutable, the line computes a new date and drops it. Keeping the result, as in due = due.minusDays(2), fixes it.
questions.rule: Keep what the call returns.

questions.q: A banking class Money is immutable and has a method add that returns a new Money. Which statement keeps a running balance correctly?
options: balance.add(fee);
Money.add(balance, fee);
balance.setAmount(fee);
balance = balance.add(fee);
optionExplain: The returned Money is discarded, so balance is unchanged.
A static call with a discarded result also leaves balance unchanged.
An immutable class has no setter to call.
Reassigning the variable to the returned value keeps the new total.
questions.explain: With immutable values you rebind the variable to the result. Any other reference to the old object keeps the old amount.
questions.rule: Reassign the variable to the returned value.
questions.teaches: With immutable types the usual idiom is to rebind the variable to the result, as in x = x.change(); any other reference to the earlier object keeps the earlier value.

questions.q: True or false: The java.time.format package holds the tools for converting values to text and back.
questions.explain: Formatting and parsing sit in java.time.format. The card next maps all five packages.
questions.rule: Formatting has its own package.

questions.q: Match each package to its purpose.
pairs: converting values to text and back
questions.explain: Each subpackage has one specialised job, and the core package keeps the classes most programs use.
questions.rule: One package, one job.

questions.q: A framework author needs constants that name date fields, such as day of week or month of year. Which package defines those building blocks?
options: java.time.format
java.time.zone
java.time.temporal
java.time.chrono
optionExplain: Formatting converts to and from text; it does not define the fields.
Zone rules and offsets are about time zones, not field constants.
The temporal package defines the fields and units that date classes are built from.
Chrono is about alternative calendars, not the generic field constants.
questions.explain: Fields and units, together with querying and adjusting, belong to java.time.temporal.
questions.rule: Fields and units live in temporal.

questions.q: A developer converts a LocalDateTime to a ZonedDateTime for Asia/Tokyo and asks which package to import ZoneId from. What is the best answer?
options: java.time.zone, because every class that deals with zones is declared in that package
java.time.format, because zones are mostly about display
java.time.temporal, because zones are low-level fields
java.time itself, since the everyday zone classes are declared in the core package
optionExplain: The zone package holds rule classes; the three everyday zone classes are in the core package.
Formatting is a separate concern; ZoneId is not declared there.
Zones are not low-level field definitions; ZoneId is a core class.
Beyond the tutorial: ZonedDateTime, ZoneId and ZoneOffset are declared in java.time, so ordinary zone work needs no import from java.time.zone.
questions.explain: The tutorial says most developers need only ZonedDateTime, ZoneId and ZoneOffset from the zone area. Beyond the tutorial, those three are declared in java.time itself.
questions.rule: Everyday zone classes sit in the core package.
questions.teaches: Beyond the tutorial: ZonedDateTime, ZoneId and ZoneOffset are declared in java.time itself, so ordinary zone work needs no import from java.time.zone, which holds the rule classes.

questions.q: Sort each task by where you would first look.

items.t: Create a date for a birth day
Represent a point on the timeline as an instant
Store the span between two moments as a duration
Turn a date into text with a custom pattern
Read the daylight saving rules of a zone
Define your own calendar system

questions.explain: Dates, instants and durations are core classes. Text conversion, zone rules and new calendars are specialised jobs with their own packages.
questions.rule: Core first, subpackage for special jobs.

questions.q: A graphics toolkit keeps basic shapes in one package, and puts image file conversion, color profiles and a plugin interface in three subpackages. Which Date-Time package plays the role of image file conversion?
options: java.time.format
java.time.zone
java.time.chrono
java.time
optionExplain: File conversion turns values into another representation and back, as formatting does for dates.
Zone rules are not a conversion to text; they match color profiles better.
Alternative calendars match a second kind of content, not file conversion.
The core package matches the basic shapes, not the conversion step.
questions.explain: Converting between internal values and text is the job of java.time.format, just as converting between images and files is a separate toolkit package.
questions.rule: Conversion gets its own package.
questions.teaches: A common library layout is a small core package plus subpackages for specialised jobs, so a newcomer can learn the core first and open a subpackage only when a task needs it.

questions.q: Building a LocalDate from the numbers 2024, 3 and 15 uses LocalDate.____(2024, 3, 15).
questions.explain: Of builds a value from parts you supply. The card next sets out all three creation prefixes.
questions.rule: Of builds from parts.

questions.q: Match each prefix to what it does.
pairs: builds a value from parts and checks them
converts an object of another type
reads a string into a value
questions.explain: The three static factory prefixes differ in their input: parts, another object, or text.
questions.rule: The prefix tells you the input.

questions.q: True or false: LocalDate.of(2024, Month.FEBRUARY, 30) rolls over and returns 1 March 2024.
questions.explain: Of checks that its parts form a real date. There is no 30 February, so the call fails with an exception instead of rolling over.
questions.rule: Of validates; it does not repair.

questions.q: To read the text 2024-03-15 into a LocalDate, call LocalDate.____ with that text.
questions.explain: Parse reads a string into a value. With one argument it expects the ISO layout.
questions.rule: Parse is for text.

questions.q: LocalDate.from(zonedDateTime) converts a ZonedDateTime to a LocalDate. What does the result keep?
options: The whole value, because from never loses anything
The time and zone, with the date dropped
Nothing, because from only works between values of the same class and type
Only the year, month and day, because a LocalDate holds no time or zone
optionExplain: The tutorial says from may lose information, and a LocalDate has no room for a time.
A LocalDate holds only a date, so it keeps the date part.
From exists to convert between different classes.
From keeps only what the target type can hold, which is why the tutorial says it may lose information.
questions.explain: A LocalDate has fields for year, month and day only, so a conversion into it keeps those and drops the rest.
questions.rule: From keeps what the target can hold.
questions.teaches: From converts by keeping only what the target type can hold, so information is lost one-way: you cannot rebuild the original time and zone from the resulting LocalDate.

questions.q: A new immutable class Money follows the Date-Time naming habit. Which method name suits creating a Money from an amount and a currency code that the caller supplies?
options: Money.of(amount, code)
Money.parse(amount, code)
Money.from(amount, code)
Money.toCode(amount, code)
optionExplain: Of is the habit for building a value from parts you supply.
Parse is for reading one string, not two supplied parts.
From converts an object of another type, not loose parts.
To converts an existing value to another type; it is not a creator.
questions.explain: Reading a method name by its prefix works across any class that follows the habit, so the parts-in case gets of.
questions.rule: Read the prefix to learn the input.
questions.teaches: Beyond the tutorial: the same prefix vocabulary is used by many other libraries, so seeing of, from or parse on an unfamiliar class often tells you what kind of creation it is before you read its documentation.

questions.q: Which method name would you guess gives you the same date with only the day of the month replaced by a new value?
options: setDayOfMonth
withDayOfMonth
getDayOfMonth
isDayOfMonth
optionExplain: Immutable classes have no set methods.
With returns a copy with one element changed.
Get reads the current day; it does not replace it.
Is asks a yes-or-no question; it does not produce a date.
questions.explain: A copy with one element replaced is a with method. The card next lists the whole instance vocabulary.
questions.rule: Pick the prefix by what you want back: a part, an answer, a replaced value, a shifted value, another type, or a richer combination.

questions.q: Match each prefix to what the call gives back.
pairs: a yes-or-no answer about the state
a copy with one element replaced
the value converted to another type
questions.explain: Each prefix names the kind of result, so you can predict a method's job from its first word.
questions.rule: The prefix names the result.

questions.q: The date is 2024-03-15. Which call produces 2024-03-22?
options: plusDays(7)
withDayOfMonth(7)
minusDays(7)
atTime(7, 0)
optionExplain: Plus shifts by an amount: seven days after 15 March is 22 March.
With replaces the day of month by 7, giving 2024-03-07.
Minus shifts backward and gives 2024-03-08.
At combines the date with a time and produces a date-time, not a later date.
questions.explain: Plus adds an amount and with sets a field, so only plusDays(7) moves 15 March to 22 March.
questions.rule: Plus shifts, with replaces.

questions.q: The date is 2024-03-31. What do withDayOfMonth(30) and plusDays(30) give, in that order?
optionExplain: Plus moves forward by 30 days, so it cannot land on the same day as with.
This swaps the two results: with stays in March and plus reaches April.
With replaces the day with 30, staying in March; plus moves forward 30 days, which reaches 30 April.
With replaces the day with 30, not 1.
questions.explain: With changes one field to a value and keeps the others, while plus shifts the whole date by an amount, so the same number 30 gives different dates.
questions.rule: With sets a field, plus moves the date.

questions.q: Which pair of calls turns a date into a date-time, and a date-time into a date?
options: toLocalDateTime on the date, then atDate on the date-time
withTime on the date, then getDate on the date-time
plusTime on the date, then isDate on the date-time
atTime on the date, then toLocalDate on the date-time
optionExplain: The prefixes are swapped: reaching a richer type uses at, converting down uses to.
With replaces a field and get returns a part; neither changes the type.
Plus shifts by an amount and is gives a yes-or-no answer; neither changes the type.
At adds what you supply to reach a richer type, and to converts toward a simpler type.
questions.explain: At combines the value with something you supply, so its result is richer, while to converts the value into another type that may hold less.
questions.rule: At enriches, to converts.
questions.teaches: The prefixes have a direction: at goes toward a richer type by adding what you supply, while to converts toward a different type that may hold less.

questions.q: A class Recipe is immutable and follows the Date-Time naming habit. Which calls would you expect to return a new Recipe? Select all that apply.
options: withServings(6)
plusIngredient(egg)
getServings()
isVegan()
toShoppingList()
optionExplain: With returns a copy with one element replaced, so a new Recipe.
Plus returns a copy with something added, so a new Recipe.
Get reads a part of the state, so it returns a number, not a Recipe.
Is answers a yes-or-no question, so it returns a boolean.
To converts to another type, so it returns a shopping list, not a Recipe.
questions.explain: On an immutable class, with, plus and minus give back the same type as a changed copy, while get, is and to give back something else.
questions.rule: With, plus, minus keep the type.
questions.teaches: On an immutable class the with, plus and minus families are the ones that return a new object of the same type, while get, is and to hand back something different.

questions.q: A server records the exact moment each order arrived so the orders can be compared with one another. Which kind of time fits best?
options: A year, month and day only
A clock reading with no date
A point on a continuous timeline
A recurring month and day
optionExplain: This drops the exact moment, so two orders on the same day would look equal.
Without a date, orders on different days cannot be compared.
Comparing exact moments needs one continuous timeline, which is machine time.
A recurring date has no year and cannot order separate events.
questions.explain: Exact moments that must be compared belong on a continuous timeline. The card next calls this machine time.
questions.rule: Choose machine time for stamping and comparing moments, and human time for what people read on a calendar and a clock.

questions.q: Machine time is measured from an origin called the ____.
questions.explain: The timeline is counted from the epoch, with nanosecond resolution.
questions.rule: Machine time counts from the epoch.

questions.q: Sort each item by the kind of time it uses.

items.t: Birthday printed on a card
Library opening hours
Wedding date
Timestamp used to order database events
Instant a sensor reading was taken
Nanoseconds between two log entries

questions.explain: Items that people read off a calendar or clock are human time. Items used to stamp, order or measure between moments are machine time.
questions.rule: Calendar and clock readings are human; stamps are machine.

questions.q: A shop's opening time is stored as 09:00, a human-time reading. The shop now opens branches in several zones and must compare when each opened on the same day. What is needed?
options: Nothing, because 09:00 means exactly the same moment in every zone where it is read
A zone or offset, or a conversion to instants, because bare readings fix no moment
A longer clock reading with more decimal places
A different epoch for each branch
optionExplain: 09:00 in two zones are different moments, so the readings do not compare.
A reading such as 09:00 names a different moment in each zone, so comparing needs more information.
More decimals add precision but still give no zone.
The epoch is one fixed origin; changing it per branch would make instants incomparable.
questions.explain: A human reading with no zone does not name one moment. Adding a zone, or converting to machine time, makes comparison possible.
questions.rule: Readings need a zone to name a moment.
questions.teaches: A human-time reading without a zone does not fix a moment, so comparing readings from different places needs a zone or a conversion to machine time.

questions.q: A developer says: machine time and human time describe different events, so an Instant and a ZonedDateTime can not refer to the same moment. What is wrong with this claim?
options: Nothing is wrong, because the two classes belong to separate packages
Instants cannot represent events that happen in the future, only the past
A ZonedDateTime stores machine time in nanoseconds only, with no calendar fields
They are two views of one timeline, so a single moment can be held by either
optionExplain: Packages do not decide what a class can represent; both name moments on the timeline.
An Instant can be any point on the timeline, past or future.
A ZonedDateTime holds human fields plus a zone; the nanoseconds are only its precision.
A ZonedDateTime can be converted to an Instant because each maps to an exact moment.
questions.explain: The split is about viewpoint, not about different events. A ZonedDateTime and an Instant can describe the same moment.
questions.rule: Two views, one timeline.

questions.q: A music program stores each note's position as a count of samples from the start of the track, while the printed score shows bars and beats. Which one resembles machine time, and why does it suit calculation?
options: The sample count: a plain count from an origin, so no calendar rules are needed
The bars and beats: they form a continuous count from an origin, like the epoch
Neither: music has no equivalent of machine time
Both are machine time because both are numbers
optionExplain: Like time since the epoch, a count from an origin can be added and compared directly.
Bars and beats are structured units, like human time, and need rules to convert.
A count from a starting point is exactly the shape of machine time.
Being numbers does not make bars and beats a continuous count from an origin.
