questions.explain: A single count from an origin is easy to add and compare. Structured units need rules, such as month lengths and leap years for dates.
questions.rule: A plain count is easy; structured units need rules.
questions.teaches: Machine time can be a plain count from an origin, which makes arithmetic simple, while human time is built from calendar fields whose lengths follow rules such as month lengths and leap years.

questions.q: You must store the day a person was born, with no clock time and no zone. Which class holds exactly that?
options: Instant
LocalDateTime
ZonedDateTime
LocalDate
optionExplain: An Instant is a point on the timeline with nanosecond resolution, far more than a birth day.
A LocalDateTime adds a time of day that a birth date does not need.
A ZonedDateTime adds both a time and a zone, neither of which is needed.
A LocalDate holds year, month and day and nothing else.
questions.explain: A birth date is a date only. The card next shows how to match needs to classes.
questions.rule: List the parts you need, then take the class that holds exactly those parts.

questions.q: Match each need to the class that holds it.
pairs: A month of a particular year
Hour, minute and second with no date
questions.explain: Each class holds a specific set of parts, so naming the parts you need names the class.
questions.rule: Name the parts, then the class.

questions.q: Put the tutorial's selection questions in the order you would ask them.
items: Do I need human time or machine time?
Does the value need a time zone?
Do I need a date and a time, or only a date?
If a date, do I need month, day and year, or only some of them?
questions.explain: The tutorial starts with the human or machine decision, then narrows by zone, date or time, and finally which date parts.
questions.rule: Broad choice first, parts last.

questions.q: A ticket app stores a concert start of 20:00 on 14 February 2025 in Berlin, and travelers elsewhere will convert it. Which class suits the stored value?
options: LocalDateTime
ZonedDateTime
LocalTime
MonthDay
optionExplain: It holds date and time but no zone, so the Berlin meaning would be lost.
It holds the date, the time and the Berlin zone, so others can convert it.
It holds only a time of day, so the date would be lost.
It holds a recurring month and day with no year or time.
questions.explain: The value needs a date, a time and a zone, which is exactly what ZonedDateTime holds.
questions.rule: Match the parts to the class.

questions.q: A credit card expiry of 08/27 names only a month and a year. The class that holds exactly that is ____.
questions.explain: An expiry names a month of a year. A class with exactly those two parts avoids inventing a day.
questions.rule: Do not invent parts you do not have.
questions.teaches: When a value names only a month of a year, YearMonth holds it without an invented day, while a LocalDate would force you to make up a day that the data never stated.

questions.q: A warehouse records when each pallet crossed a scanner. Scanners are in several countries. The manager wants to order all scans on one timeline and print each scan in its own country's local time. Which classes suit the two jobs? Select all that apply.
options: Instant, for storing and ordering the scans
ZonedDateTime, for printing each scan in its zone
MonthDay, for printing the scan moment
LocalTime, for ordering scans across days
optionExplain: An Instant is one point on the machine timeline, so scans from any country sort together.
A ZonedDateTime shows the same moment as a local reading in a chosen zone.
MonthDay has no year, time or zone, so it cannot show a moment.
A time of day without a date cannot order scans that happen on different days.
questions.explain: Store the moment once as machine time, then convert it to a zoned reading when you show it to people in a place.
questions.rule: One stored moment, many views.
questions.teaches: Two classes can do two jobs on the same moment: store it as machine time, and convert it to a zoned human reading only at display time.

questions.q: DayOfWeek.FRIDAY.plus(3) gives the constant ____.
questions.explain: Three days after Friday is Saturday, Sunday, then Monday, wrapping around the week. The card next shows the enums in detail.
questions.rule: Days of the week wrap around.

questions.q: With an English locale and the day MONDAY, match each text style to what getDisplayName prints.
questions.explain: FULL is the complete name, SHORT an abbreviation, NARROW a single letter.
questions.rule: Style decides how much of the name appears.

questions.q: Month.FEBRUARY.maxLength() returns ____.
questions.explain: maxLength reports the largest number of days the month can have, which for February is 29.
questions.rule: maxLength is the maximum, not this year's length.

questions.q: DayOfWeek.MONDAY.plus(10) gives the constant ____.
questions.explain: Ten days is one full week plus three days, and three days after Monday is Thursday.
questions.rule: Seven days return to the same weekday.

questions.q: A calendar header prints month initials with the NARROW style in an English locale. Which statement about this header is accurate?
options: Several months share a letter, so the header alone cannot identify a month
Each month gets a unique letter because there are fewer months than letters
NARROW prints the month number instead of a letter
NARROW is defined only for days of the week
optionExplain: NARROW is one letter, and in English January, June and July all give J.
Fewer months than letters does not mean initials differ; J starts three months.
NARROW prints a single-letter name, not a number.
It is defined for months as well, as the August example shows.
questions.explain: Single letters cannot separate twelve months, so NARROW is best where context already tells the reader which month is meant.
questions.rule: NARROW is short, not unique.
questions.teaches: NARROW is meant for tight spaces and is not unique: January, June and July all give J in English, so use it only where context disambiguates.

questions.q: A night-shift rota starts on a Wednesday and repeats a task every 10 days. Using the wrap-around idea, on which weekday does the task next fall?
options: WEDNESDAY
FRIDAY
SATURDAY
SUNDAY
optionExplain: Ten is not a multiple of seven, so the weekday changes.
This adds only two days after the full week, but ten days leaves three.
Ten days is one week plus three days, and three days after Wednesday is Saturday.
This adds four days after the week, but ten days leaves three.
questions.explain: The weekday after n days equals the weekday after n modulo 7 days, so ten days behaves like three.
questions.rule: Reduce large steps by sevens.
questions.teaches: Wrap-around is arithmetic modulo seven: plus(n) behaves like plus(n mod 7), so a large step can be reduced to a small one before you count.

questions.q: 2024-09-02 is a Monday. Which date is the next Friday after it?
optionExplain: This is the Thursday, one day before Friday.
This is the Saturday, one day after Friday.
Friday follows Monday by four days, so the next Friday after 2 September is 6 September.
This is the Monday of the following week.
questions.explain: Counting forward from a weekday to another is what the next adjuster does. The card next shows how.
questions.rule: A LocalDate is a calendar day only: ask it for its weekday with getDayOfWeek and move it with with and an adjuster.

questions.q: True or false: A LocalDate stores the time of day as well as the date.
questions.explain: A LocalDate holds only year, month and day. For a time of day you need LocalTime or LocalDateTime.
questions.rule: Date only.

questions.q: LocalDate.of(2024, Month.JULY, 4).getDayOfWeek() returns the DayOfWeek constant ____.
questions.explain: getDayOfWeek gives the weekday as a constant, and 4 July 2024 was a Thursday.
questions.rule: Weekday comes back as a constant.

questions.q: Put the steps in order to find the next Wednesday after a LocalDate called date.
items: Create or obtain the starting LocalDate
Build the adjuster with TemporalAdjusters.next and DayOfWeek.WEDNESDAY
Pass the adjuster to the with method of the date
Keep the returned new LocalDate in a variable
questions.explain: The date and the adjuster exist first, with applies one to the other, and the new date must be kept because the original does not change.
questions.rule: Adjuster, with, keep the result.

questions.q: 2024-05-16 is a Thursday. Which date does date.with(TemporalAdjusters.next(DayOfWeek.THURSDAY)) give for that date?
optionExplain: This would keep the same date; next does not include the starting date.
This is the following day, which is a Friday, not a Thursday.
This goes backward; next looks forward.
Next looks strictly after the starting date, so from a Thursday it moves a full week.
questions.explain: Beyond the tutorial: next excludes the starting date, so on a matching weekday it jumps a whole week. A variant that includes the starting date is nextOrSame.
questions.rule: Next means strictly after.
questions.teaches: Beyond the tutorial: next looks strictly after the starting date, so on a date that already has the requested weekday it jumps a full week; nextOrSame is the variant that keeps the date.

questions.q: A school rule says report cards are due on the first Monday after term ends. Term ends on Friday 2024-12-20. Which date results from the same idea?
optionExplain: From a Friday, the first Monday after is three days later, 23 December.
This is the second Monday after, one week too late.
The term end date itself is a Friday, not a Monday.
This is the Saturday directly after term ends.
questions.explain: The rule is next(MONDAY) applied to the end date, which gives the first Monday after it.
questions.rule: First weekday after a date is next.
questions.teaches: A rule such as first Monday after is a reusable adjuster object: the same next(MONDAY) works on any LocalDate, so a rule can be stored in a variable and applied to many dates.

questions.q: The class that knows both a year and a month, and so can report how many days February has in 2023, is ____.
questions.explain: The length of a month depends on the year, so you need a class with both. The card next shows it.
questions.rule: Month length needs a year.

questions.q: Match each class to what it holds.
pairs: a month and a day, no year
a year, a month and a day
questions.explain: The classes differ only in which parts of a date they keep.
questions.rule: Parts decide the class.

questions.q: YearMonth.of(2024, Month.FEBRUARY).lengthOfMonth() returns ____.
questions.explain: 2024 is a leap year, so its February has 29 days.
questions.rule: A year decides February's length.

questions.q: MonthDay.of(Month.FEBRUARY, 29) is asked isValidYear for four years. For which years does it return true? Select all that apply.
optionExplain: 2024 is a leap year, so 29 February exists.
2023 is not a leap year, so there is no 29 February.
2028 is a leap year, so 29 February exists.
2025 is not a leap year, so there is no 29 February.
questions.explain: A month-day of 29 February exists only in leap years, so only 2024 and 2028 give true.
questions.rule: Feb 29 needs a leap year.

questions.q: A person was born on 29 February and an app stores a MonthDay. What does isValidYear let the app do?
options: Change the stored birthday to 28 February automatically in non-leap years
Add a year to the birthday so it becomes valid
Detect years where the birthday does not exist and pick a fallback date
Convert the birthday into an Instant for comparison
optionExplain: isValidYear only answers a question; it never changes the stored value.
MonthDay has no year to add, and nothing is changed by the check.
isValidYear answers in advance whether the stored month and day exist in a given year.
A MonthDay has no year or time, so it cannot become an instant.
questions.explain: The check gives a yes or no, and what to show in a non-leap year is the app's decision.
questions.rule: The check informs; you decide the fallback.
questions.teaches: isValidYear lets a program learn in advance in which years a recurring date does not exist, so it can choose a fallback date instead of failing.

questions.q: A subscription bills on day 31 of each month. Which class helps the app learn how many days a particular month has, so it can choose a fallback day?
options: MonthDay
YearMonth
Year
Instant
optionExplain: MonthDay can check one stored day against a year, but it does not report month lengths.
Its lengthOfMonth gives the exact length of a month in a given year.
A Year can test leap years but does not give the length of an arbitrary month.
An Instant has no calendar months at all.
questions.explain: YearMonth reports how long each month is, which is what choosing a fallback day needs.
questions.rule: YearMonth gives month lengths.
questions.teaches: Two tools guard against a day that does not exist: YearMonth reports the length of a specific month, and MonthDay checks a specific day against a year.

questions.q: The class that holds a time of day such as 09:30, with no date, is called ____.
questions.explain: A LocalTime holds a time of day with no date. The card next shows what Local means.
questions.rule: Time of day only.

questions.q: True or false: A LocalDateTime stores a time zone along with the date and time.
questions.explain: Local means no zone is stored. For a zone you use ZonedDateTime or OffsetDateTime.
questions.rule: Local means no zone.

questions.q: LocalDateTime.of(2024, Month.OCTOBER, 31, 22, 5).plusHours(3) prints ____ (write it as it would print).
questions.explain: Three hours after 22:05 on 31 October is 01:05 on 1 November; hours carry into the next day and month.
questions.rule: Time arithmetic carries into the date.

questions.q: Sort each item by whether a LocalDateTime holds it.

items.t: Year
Minute
Nanosecond
Day of month
Time zone identifier
Offset from UTC
Daylight saving rules

questions.explain: A LocalDateTime is a date plus a time. Anything about zones, offsets or daylight saving rules is outside it.
questions.rule: Date and time, nothing about place.

questions.q: A meeting is stored as the LocalDateTime 2024-07-10T09:00 for Paris. A colleague in Tokyo reads the same stored value. What does it tell the colleague about the zone?
options: It is Paris time, because the stored value remembers its creator
It is Tokyo time, because it is read in Tokyo
Nothing, because the value carries no zone
It is UTC, because that is the default for Local classes
optionExplain: The value stores no creator or place.
Where a value is read does not change what it stores.
A LocalDateTime has no zone, so the value does not say whether 09:00 means Paris or Tokyo.
Local classes have no default zone stored; the value is just a reading.
questions.explain: Without a zone the same text can mean different moments, so shared values need a zone or offset.
questions.rule: Local values do not name a moment.

questions.q: A school's lessons start at 10:00 on every campus every school day. The timetable system needs one value for the recurring start and another for the lesson on 12 March 2025. Which pair of classes fits?
options: LocalTime for the recurring start, LocalDateTime for the specific lesson
LocalDate for the recurring start, Instant for the specific lesson on that day
LocalDateTime for both, with the date left blank
MonthDay for the recurring start, LocalTime for the lesson
optionExplain: A time of day that repeats is a LocalTime, and one dated occurrence is a LocalDateTime.
A date does not hold a time of day, and an Instant would fix a zone-free school time to a moment.
A LocalDateTime always holds a date; it cannot be left blank.
MonthDay holds a month and a day, not a time of day.
questions.explain: A pattern that repeats daily needs only a time of day, while one occurrence needs a date as well.
questions.rule: Pattern is time, occurrence is date-time.
questions.teaches: LocalTime can describe a pattern that repeats every day, while LocalDateTime pins down one occurrence of it on a specific date.

questions.q: Which of these is a time zone identifier in the usual region/city form?
options: Asia/Tokyo
UTC plus nine
GMT-08
optionExplain: Asia/Tokyo names a region and a city, the usual form of a zone identifier.
This is an offset from UTC, not an identifier.
This describes an offset in words and is not an identifier.
This resembles an offset, not a region/city identifier.
questions.explain: Identifiers name a region and a city. The card next separates them from offsets.
questions.rule: Use a ZoneId when a place's rules matter and a ZoneOffset when only a fixed distance from UTC matters.

questions.q: Match each term to its meaning.
pairs: a named zone that carries rules
a zone identifier in region/city form
questions.explain: A ZoneId names a place with rules; a ZoneOffset is only a number of hours and minutes from UTC.
questions.rule: Name with rules versus a fixed number.

questions.q: Code stores a zone offset as a whole number of hours in an int variable. Which offset breaks that code?
optionExplain: This is a whole number of hours and fits.
This offset has a 45-minute part and cannot be stored as whole hours.
This is a whole number of hours and fits.
This is zero hours and fits.
questions.explain: Some zones use offsets such as +05:30 and +05:45, so whole-hour storage loses information.
questions.rule: Offsets are not always whole hours.

questions.q: ZoneOffset.of with the text +05:30 has a total of ____ seconds.
questions.explain: Five and a half hours is 5.5 times 3600 seconds, which is 19800.
questions.rule: Convert hours and minutes to seconds.

questions.q: New York is five hours behind UTC in winter. Does the identifier America/New_York have a single fixed offset all year?
options: Yes, because an identifier always maps to the same offset for the whole year
Yes, because only a ZoneOffset can change
No, because the identifier changes name in summer
No: its rules shift the offset when daylight saving time starts and ends
optionExplain: If that were true, ZoneId would need no rules; the rules exist because offsets change.
A ZoneOffset is the fixed one; the ZoneId is where the changing rules live.
The identifier stays the same; its rules give a different offset.
A ZoneId carries rules, and those rules can change the offset during the year.
questions.explain: The identifier stays America/New_York, but the offset it gives depends on the moment, because daylight saving rules apply.
questions.rule: A ZoneId maps a moment to an offset.
questions.teaches: A ZoneId maps a moment to an offset through its rules, so one identifier gives different offsets in January and July, while a ZoneOffset is already the single answer.

questions.q: A call app lets a user choose either Europe/Paris or +01:00 for a weekly call that must stay at 09:00 local Paris time all year. Which should the app store?
options: The offset +01:00, since offsets never change
Both as one text, so either can be used
The identifier Europe/Paris, so daylight saving changes are applied
Neither, since zones cannot describe a weekly call that repeats on a schedule
optionExplain: An offset is fixed, so the call would drift an hour from Paris clocks in summer.
Storing both does not remove the choice, and the fixed offset cannot follow the rules.
The identifier carries rules, so the call keeps its local clock time through the year.
Zones describe the place whose clock the call follows, so they suit it well.
questions.explain: A fixed offset records a fixed distance from UTC, while a named zone keeps following the local clock, including daylight saving changes.
questions.rule: Store the zone for local clock time, the offset for a fixed distance.
questions.teaches: Store the zone identifier when you mean local clock time in a place, and an offset when you mean a fixed distance from UTC, for example in a timestamp that has already been converted.

questions.q: True or false: OffsetDateTime knows when a region switches to daylight saving time.
questions.explain: An OffsetDateTime holds only a fixed offset, so it cannot know when the switch happens. The card next shows which class can.
questions.rule: Offsets have no rules.

questions.q: Match each class to the parts it combines.
questions.explain: The id or offset it carries decides whether a class can use zone rules.
questions.rule: Id brings rules; offset does not.

questions.q: Sort each statement by the class it describes.

items.t: Holds a ZoneId
Uses zone rules for daylight saving
Handles gaps and overlaps
Holds only a fixed ZoneOffset
Suits timestamps that track absolute offsets from UTC
Used by XML and network formats to carry date-times

questions.explain: ZonedDateTime is the one with an identifier and rules. The offset classes keep a fixed offset and suit storage and transfer formats.
questions.rule: Rules mean ZonedDateTime.

questions.q: A teammate says: OffsetDateTime is the more precise class, because it has an offset while ZonedDateTime has only a name. What is wrong with this claim?
options: Nothing is wrong, because an offset is always more precise than a name could be
A ZonedDateTime also has an offset and adds the rules the offset classes lack
OffsetDateTime has no offset, only a zone id
ZonedDateTime cannot be converted to an Instant
optionExplain: A ZonedDateTime holds the offset as well, so it has everything the offset class has.
The overview table shows ZonedDateTime with both a zone offset and a zone id.
The name says it: OffsetDateTime holds an offset, not an identifier.
Both zone-aware classes can be converted to an Instant.
questions.explain: The difference is the rules, not the offset. ZonedDateTime carries an offset and rules, while OffsetDateTime carries the offset only.
questions.rule: Zoned adds rules; it does not drop the offset.

questions.q: Clocks in New York move forward on 10 March 2024 at 2:00, so local 02:30 does not exist that day. What happens when the local time 02:30 is given to ZonedDateTime for America/New_York and to OffsetDateTime with offset -05:00?
options: ZonedDateTime moves it forward to 03:30; the offset class keeps 02:30
Both keep 02:30, because the clock reading given is always honored as stated
Both throw an exception, because the time does not exist
ZonedDateTime keeps 02:30; the offset class moves it to 03:30
optionExplain: Beyond the tutorial: the zone rules let ZonedDateTime repair a gap, while a fixed offset has no rules to consult.
Only the offset class keeps it; ZonedDateTime consults its rules and moves the time out of the gap.
The offset class accepts any time with its fixed offset, and ZonedDateTime adjusts rather than failing.
This reverses the roles: the rules belong to the zoned class.
questions.explain: A gap is a rule-based fact, so only a class with rules can notice it. The offset class has none and keeps the reading as given.
questions.rule: Only rules can see a gap.
questions.teaches: Beyond the tutorial: for a local time inside a gap, ZonedDateTime moves the value forward to the first valid time (03:30 here), while an offset class keeps 02:30 with its fixed offset because it has no rules to consult.

questions.q: A device sends only a time of day and its fixed distance from UTC, with no date, for example 14:20 at +02:00. Which class holds that value?
options: OffsetDateTime
ZonedDateTime
LocalTime
OffsetTime
optionExplain: This needs a date as well, which the device does not send.
This needs a date and a zone identifier, neither of which is sent.
This holds the time but drops the offset the device provides.
It combines a LocalTime with a ZoneOffset and has no date.
questions.explain: A clock time with an offset and no date is an OffsetTime.
questions.rule: No date plus an offset gives OffsetTime.
questions.teaches: OffsetTime exists for data that has a clock time and an offset but no date; without the date, you cannot tell on which day a later or earlier clock reading falls.

questions.q: A plane leaves Los Angeles at 7:30 p.m. and flies 10 hours 50 minutes to Tokyo, whose clock is 16 hours ahead of Los Angeles in July. What does the Tokyo clock read at arrival?
options: 6:20 a.m. on the next day
3:30 a.m. on the same day
8:40 a.m. on the same day
10:20 p.m. on the next day
optionExplain: This adds only the flight time and ignores the 16-hour difference between the clocks.
This subtracts the 16-hour zone difference instead of adding it, and skips the flight time.
This subtracts the flight time and ignores the zone difference.
Adding the flight to 7:30 p.m. gives 6:20 a.m. in Los Angeles, which is 16 hours later on Tokyo's clock: 10:20 p.m. the next day.
questions.explain: Clocks in different zones read different times for one moment, so both the flight time and the zone difference matter. The card next shows the calls.
questions.rule: Convert the departure to the arrival zone with withZoneSameInstant, then add the travel time, so the arrival reads on the destination clock.

questions.q: The method withZoneSame____ keeps the moment and changes the zone.
questions.explain: withZoneSameInstant keeps the same instant and shows it on the clock of another zone.
questions.rule: Same instant, new clock.

questions.q: Put the steps of the flight example in order.
items: Build the departure ZonedDateTime from the local date-time and the departure zone
Convert the departure to the arrival zone with withZoneSameInstant
Add the flight time with plusMinutes
Format the arrival for display
questions.explain: You convert onto the destination clock first, add the travel time, then format the result.
questions.rule: Convert, add, format.

questions.q: A flight leaves Paris at 06:00 on 10 July 2024 (UTC+2) and lasts 9 hours. Los Angeles is UTC-7 on that date. What does the Los Angeles clock read at arrival?
options: 15:00 on 10 July
06:00 on 10 July
21:00 on 9 July
13:00 on 10 July
optionExplain: This adds the flight to 06:00 without adjusting for the zone difference.
06:00 in Paris is 04:00 UTC; 9 hours later is 13:00 UTC, which is 06:00 in Los Angeles.
This subtracts the flight time instead of adding it.
This is the arrival in UTC, not the Los Angeles clock.
questions.explain: Convert the departure to the arrival clock, then add the flight time: the two zone shifts and the 9 hours combine to the same clock digits.
questions.rule: Check the moment in UTC, then read it in the target zone.

questions.q: The same Paris flight at 06:00 and 9 hours now lands in Tokyo (UTC+9) instead of Los Angeles. What does the Tokyo clock read at arrival?
options: 13:00 on 10 July
04:00 on 10 July
22:00 on 10 July
15:00 on 10 July
optionExplain: This is the arrival in UTC, not Tokyo's clock.
This is the departure moment in UTC, not the arrival on Tokyo's clock.
06:00 in Paris is 04:00 UTC; 9 hours later is 13:00 UTC, which is 22:00 in Tokyo.
This adds the flight to the departure clock and ignores the zone difference.
questions.explain: Only the arrival zone changed, so the moment is the same and just the final clock reading differs.
questions.rule: Same moment, different clock.

questions.q: The example asks the arrival zone's rules whether daylight saving time applies at the arrival instant. Why is the question given an instant instead of the clock reading shown to passengers?
options: A moment is unambiguous, while a clock reading can occur twice or not at all
An instant is shorter to write down than a clock reading
Clock readings are not accepted by zone rules, which only work with whole dates
Instants always fall in standard time, so the answer is easier to compute
optionExplain: Around a daylight saving change a clock reading can fall in an overlap or a gap, while an instant names exactly one moment.
Length of text has nothing to do with the reason.
The rules could be given a local time; the issue is that the local time may be ambiguous.
Instants can fall in daylight saving time as well; the rules decide.
questions.explain: Asking about an instant removes doubt about gaps and overlaps, so the answer is exact.
questions.rule: Ask rules about instants, not readings.
questions.teaches: The daylight saving question takes an instant instead of a clock reading because a local reading near a transition can be ambiguous, while an instant names exactly one moment.

questions.q: A concert streams live and starts at 20:00 on 15 July 2024 in Sydney (UTC+10). A fan wants the start on the clock in Chicago (UTC-5 on that date). What does Chicago's clock read?
options: 15:00 on 15 July
05:00 on 15 July
01:00 on 15 July
05:00 on 16 July
optionExplain: This subtracts only Chicago's offset from the Sydney clock reading, skipping the Sydney offset.
20:00 in Sydney is 10:00 UTC, which is 05:00 in Chicago on the same calendar day.
This subtracts 19 hours, which is not the difference between the zones.
The time is right but the date is a day too late.
questions.explain: Convert the stored moment to the viewer's zone; the viewer's clock is the stored moment seen through that zone.
questions.rule: One stored moment, one view per zone.
questions.teaches: Showing one event in many zones needs the moment stored once and converted at display time, because the same instant produces a different clock reading in each zone.

questions.q: The class meant for stamping an event with a point on the machine timeline is called ____.
questions.explain: An Instant is one point on the machine timeline, so stamps from any country sort together. The card next explains it.
questions.rule: Instants stamp moments.

questions.q: True or false: An Instant before 1970-01-01T00:00:00Z has a negative value.
questions.explain: Values count from the epoch, so an instant before it is negative and one after it is positive.
questions.rule: The epoch is zero.

questions.q: Instant.ofEpochSecond(3600).toString() prints ____.
questions.explain: 3600 seconds is one hour after the epoch, and the Z marks UTC.
questions.rule: Seconds from the epoch map to UTC time.

questions.q: The instant 2024-03-15T23:30:00Z is read in Tokyo, which is UTC+9. The local date shown is ____ (write it as year-month-day).
questions.explain: Nine hours after 23:30 on 15 March is 08:30 on 16 March, so Tokyo is already on the next day.
questions.rule: A zone can change the date.

questions.q: A ZonedDateTime can be converted to an Instant directly, but a LocalDateTime cannot. Why?
options: A LocalDateTime has too little precision to hold an instant
A local reading belongs to a different moment in each zone, so it names no single instant
A LocalDateTime is stored in a different calendar than an Instant
Instants cannot be created from any date-time class
optionExplain: Precision is not the issue; the zone is missing.
Only a value that includes a zone or offset maps to exactly one moment.
Both use the ISO calendar; the zone is what is missing.
Zoned and offset classes do convert to an Instant.
questions.explain: 11:30 on a date is a different moment in Paris and in Tokyo, so a local value cannot decide one instant by itself.
questions.rule: A moment needs a zone or offset.
questions.teaches: A local date-time cannot become an Instant on its own because the same clock reading belongs to different moments in different zones; adding a zone or offset is what fixes the moment.

questions.q: A parcel tracker compares two scan instants. Scan a is 2024-03-15T12:30:00Z and scan b is 2024-03-15T10:00:00Z. What does a.until(b, ChronoUnit.MINUTES) return?
optionExplain: This is the size of the gap but ignores the direction from a to b.
The unit is minutes and the result is a whole number, not hours.
The two instants differ, so the result is not zero.
b is 150 minutes before a, so measuring from a to b is negative.
questions.explain: until measures from the first instant to the argument, in the chosen unit, and the sign shows the direction.
questions.rule: Positive if later, negative if earlier.
questions.teaches: until measures from this instant to the argument in one chosen unit and is positive when the argument is later and negative when it is earlier.

questions.q: When text cannot be parsed into a date, Date-Time code throws a ____.
questions.explain: A failed parse raises DateTimeParseException. The card next lists both exceptions.
questions.rule: Parse failure has its own exception.

questions.q: True or false: LocalDate.parse with a single text argument accepts the layout 15/03/2024.
questions.explain: With one argument, parse expects the ISO layout year-month-day. Another layout needs a formatter as a second argument.
questions.rule: One argument means ISO.

questions.q: A formatter uses the pattern MMM dd yyyy with an English locale. Which input text does it accept?
optionExplain: Dd requires two characters, so a one-digit day is rejected.
The text is in ISO layout, which does not match this pattern.
Dd demands two characters for the day, and the text provides 03.
The day comes first in this text, but the pattern puts the month first.
questions.explain: A pattern must match the text letter for letter in order and width.
questions.rule: Match order and width.

questions.q: LocalDate.of(2024, Month.MARCH, 5).format with the pattern dd/MM/yyyy gives ____.
questions.explain: Both dd and MM write two characters, so the 5th of March becomes 05/03/2024.
questions.rule: Doubled letters pad to two characters.

questions.q: Several threads format dates using one shared DateTimeFormatter. What synchronization does the tutorial's description imply is needed?
options: A lock around every call to format, held while the call runs
One separate formatter for each thread that formats dates
A lock around parse calls only, since format does not share state
None, because the formatter is immutable and thread-safe
optionExplain: The formatter is thread-safe, so no lock is needed.
This would work but is unnecessary; one shared instance is safe.
Both parse and format are safe with a shared immutable formatter.
An object that cannot change can be used by many threads at once.
questions.explain: Thread safety follows from immutability, which is why the tutorial suggests a shared static constant.
questions.rule: Immutable formatter, shared safely.
questions.teaches: Because a formatter holds no changing state, one instance can be used by many threads at the same time, so there is no need to create one per call or to synchronize around it.

questions.q: A genealogy program reads dates typed as 1921.03.03, meaning year, month and day separated by dots. Which pattern reads that text?
options: yyyy.MM.dd
dd.MM.yyyy
MM.dd.yyyy
yyyy-MM-dd
optionExplain: The pattern lists the fields in the order they appear, with the dots as literal separators.
This expects the day first, which does not match the text.
This expects the month first, which does not match the text.
This uses hyphens, but the text has dots.
questions.explain: A pattern is read left to right against the text, so field order and separators must both match.
questions.rule: Order and separators must match.
questions.teaches: Literal characters in a pattern, such as dots or slashes, must appear in the text as well; they are part of the layout, not decoration.

questions.q: True or false: The java.time.temporal package is mainly aimed at framework and library writers.
questions.explain: It holds low-level building blocks that frameworks use across many classes. The card next maps them out.
questions.rule: Temporal is low-level.

questions.q: Match each interface to its role.
pairs: framework for objects that can add and subtract units
names a part such as month of year
names a measure such as hours
questions.explain: Fields name parts of a value, units name measures of an amount, and Temporal and its read-only form are the objects themselves.
questions.rule: Field for parts, unit for measures.

questions.q: Sort each field by whether a LocalDate supports it.

items.t: DAY_OF_WEEK
MONTH_OF_YEAR
DAY_OF_YEAR
CLOCK_HOUR_OF_DAY
MINUTE_OF_HOUR
NANO_OF_DAY

questions.explain: A LocalDate has year, month and day fields only. Anything about hours, minutes or nanoseconds of the day is not supported.
questions.rule: Date fields only for a date.

questions.q: Which call returns true?
options: Instant.now().isSupported(ChronoUnit.YEARS)
Instant.now().isSupported(ChronoUnit.MONTHS)
LocalDateTime.now().isSupported(ChronoUnit.MONTHS)
LocalDate.now().isSupported(ChronoField.CLOCK_HOUR_OF_DAY)
optionExplain: An Instant does not support years.
An Instant does not support months.
A LocalDateTime has a date part, so it supports months.
A LocalDate has no clock fields.
questions.explain: Support depends on what the class holds: a date-time holds months, an instant does not.
questions.rule: Support follows content.

questions.q: Why does Instant reject months and years as units while accepting seconds and hours?
options: Months and years are too large for a timeline value to hold
Months and years vary in length with the calendar, while hours and seconds are fixed
Instant stores its seconds as plain text, which cannot represent calendar months or years
Months and years are only used by the legacy Date class
optionExplain: Instant can hold distant dates; the issue is the unfixed length.
A pure timeline point has a fixed number of seconds for an hour but none for a month.
Instant is a numeric point; the storage format is not the reason.
They are standard Date-Time units and appear on LocalDate and others.
questions.explain: A month is 28 to 31 days and a year 365 or 366, so a timeline point cannot say how many seconds a month holds without a calendar.
questions.rule: Fixed-length units fit a timeline.
questions.teaches: A timeline point supports only units of fixed length: an hour is always 3600 seconds, but a month or year varies with the calendar, so it needs a date class that knows the calendar.

questions.q: A reusable helper must accept both LocalDate and ZonedDateTime arguments and read a field from either. Which parameter type suits it?
options: LocalDate
String
Object
TemporalAccessor
optionExplain: This accepts only dates and would reject a ZonedDateTime.
This would make callers convert to text and lose type safety.
This accepts anything, including values that have no fields to read.
It is the read-only interface that these classes share, so the helper accepts any of them.
questions.explain: Application code declares concrete types, but a library function meant for many classes accepts the shared interface.
questions.rule: Concrete types for apps, interfaces for libraries.
questions.teaches: Application code names concrete types, but a reusable function that must work with many temporal classes accepts the shared interface, which is why adjusters and queries take interface parameters.

questions.q: Which call most likely gives the last day of the month for a LocalDate called d?
options: d.lastDayOfMonth()
d.with(TemporalAdjusters.lastDayOfMonth())
d.set(TemporalAdjusters.lastDayOfMonth())
d.adjust(lastDay)
optionExplain: LocalDate has no such method; adjusters are applied through with.
With applies an adjuster and returns the new date.
Immutable classes have no set method.
There is no adjust method taking a bare name; adjusters go through with.
questions.explain: Adjusters come from TemporalAdjusters and are applied with with. The card next lists them.
questions.rule: To land on a calendar landmark, pass the matching TemporalAdjusters method to with.

questions.q: Predefined adjusters are static methods of the class named Temporal____, in the plural.
questions.explain: The plural TemporalAdjusters class holds the ready-made adjusters; the singular TemporalAdjuster is the interface.
questions.rule: Plural class, singular interface.

questions.q: For the date 2024-09-10, match each adjuster to the date it gives.
questions.explain: September 2024 ends on the 30th, its first Monday is the 2nd, and its last Friday is the 27th.
questions.rule: Read the landmark from the calendar.

questions.q: A ZonedDateTime holds 2024-05-15 at 14:30 in Asia/Tokyo. What does with(TemporalAdjusters.lastDayOfMonth()) give?
options: 2024-05-31 at 00:00 in Asia/Tokyo
2024-05-31 at 14:30 in Asia/Tokyo
2024-05-15 at 14:30 in Asia/Tokyo
optionExplain: The time of day is kept, not reset to midnight.
The zone is kept; it is not changed to UTC.
The adjuster changes only the date and keeps the time and zone.
The date does move to the last day of the month.
questions.explain: A date adjuster applied to a ZonedDateTime keeps its time and zone.
questions.rule: Adjusters change the date only.

questions.q: Today is 2024-06-20. What is the date of the first Tuesday of next month, built by applying two adjusters in turn?
optionExplain: firstDayOfNextMonth gives 1 July, a Monday, and firstInMonth with TUESDAY then gives 2 July.
This is the first day of next month, a Monday, so the second step is missing.
This is the first Tuesday after today, in June, not in next month.
This is the second Tuesday of July, not the first.
questions.explain: Each adjuster returns a new date that the next one takes as input, so adjusters combine by chaining with calls.
questions.rule: Chain adjusters with calls.
questions.teaches: Adjusters compose by chaining: each with call returns a new date that the next adjuster takes as input, so simple landmarks combine into more specific rules.

questions.q: A gardening club plants on the first Saturday after New Year's Day. Today is 2024-12-05, and 1 January 2025 is a Wednesday. Which planting date results from chaining adjusters?
optionExplain: This is New Year's Day itself, a Wednesday, so the second step is missing.
This is the next Saturday after today, in December, not after New Year's Day.
This is the second Saturday of the year, one week late.
firstDayOfNextYear gives 1 January 2025, and next with SATURDAY then gives 4 January.
questions.explain: The rule splits into firstDayOfNextYear followed by next(SATURDAY), and the first step's result feeds the second.
questions.rule: Break a rule into landmark steps.
questions.teaches: A scheduling rule stated in words can be split into landmark steps, one adjuster per step, and each step's output becomes the next step's input.

questions.q: A company pays staff on the 15th and the last day of each month, moving earlier when that day is a weekend. Where would this repeatable rule best live?
options: Copied into each place that needs a payday
In a comment above each date calculation
In one reusable class written once
In a new setter on LocalDate
optionExplain: Copies drift apart and make the rule hard to change.
A comment documents a rule but does not apply it.
One class that every date calculation can call keeps the rule in a single place.
LocalDate is immutable and has no setters, and you cannot add methods to it.
questions.explain: A rule used in many places is best written once. The card next shows the adjuster form.
questions.rule: Encode a repeated date rule once in an adjustInto method, then apply it with with.

questions.q: A custom adjuster must implement the single method named ____.
questions.explain: TemporalAdjuster has one method, adjustInto, which receives a Temporal and returns an adjusted one.
questions.rule: One method: adjustInto.

questions.q: Put the steps of the payday rule in order.
items: Read the day of the month of the input date
Choose the 15th if the day is before 15, otherwise the last day of the month
If the chosen day is a Saturday or Sunday, move back to the previous Friday
Return the input with the chosen date applied
questions.explain: The rule picks a target day first, corrects for weekends, and returns the result as a new value.
questions.rule: Pick target, fix weekend, return.

questions.q: Under the payday rule, the date 2024-11-16 gives ____ (year-month-day). The 30th of November 2024 is a Saturday.
questions.explain: The day is after the 15th, so the target is 30 November, a Saturday, which moves back to Friday 29 November.
questions.rule: Target day, then weekend fix.

questions.q: In the tutorial's logic, what does 2024-08-15 give? The 31st of August 2024 is a Saturday.
optionExplain: The rule does not keep the starting date when it is the 15th; it takes the month-end branch.
The rule never chooses the day after the 15th.
This is the month end before the weekend correction.
The day is not before 15, so the target is the last day, 31 August, a Saturday, which moves back to Friday 30 August.
questions.explain: The comparison is strictly before 15, so a date on the 15th goes to the month-end branch.
questions.rule: Test the boundary day.

questions.q: A teammate says: my adjuster changes the date object it receives, so the original date is edited in place. What is wrong with this claim?
options: Nothing is wrong, because adjusters are the only tools that are allowed to edit dates in place
Date-Time values are immutable, so the adjuster returns a new value and leaves the input
Adjusters can edit only the time, not the date
The original is edited only when the adjuster is a predefined one
optionExplain: No Date-Time tool edits an immutable value; every change produces a new one.
The adjustInto method returns an adjusted temporal; the input is not edited.
Date adjusters change the date and return a new value.
Predefined adjusters also return new values.
questions.explain: Because the value types are immutable, an adjuster computes and returns a new value.
questions.rule: Adjusters return new values.

questions.q: A shop ships orders on the next Monday, Wednesday or Friday after the order date. Which design uses the tutorial's approach?
options: Subclass LocalDate and override its constructor so that it picks the shipping day
Add a setShipDay method to LocalDate that edits the date
A class implementing adjustInto that picks the earliest of the three days
Call next for each weekday and always keep the last result
optionExplain: LocalDate is not meant to be subclassed this way, and the tutorial uses an interface.
Immutable classes have no setters, and you cannot add methods to LocalDate.
A rule that chooses among several candidate days is custom logic, and the adjuster form lets every caller reuse it.
The last result would be the latest day, not the earliest.
questions.explain: Choosing the earliest of several candidates is logic the predefined set does not express, so it belongs in a custom adjuster.
questions.rule: Custom logic goes in adjustInto.
questions.teaches: A rule that chooses the earliest of several candidate dates is itself a good candidate for a custom adjuster, because the predefined set moves to one landmark and does not compare several.

questions.q: Which task suits a query rather than an adjuster?
options: Moving a date to the end of its month
Finding out whether a date falls on a family birthday
Shifting a date forward by a week
Replacing the year of a date with another year
optionExplain: This produces a different date, which is an adjuster's job.
A yes-or-no answer is information about the date, which is what a query returns.
This also produces a different date.
This changes the date, which is the job of with or an adjuster.
questions.explain: A query answers a question about a value. The card next contrasts it with adjusters.
questions.rule: Use an adjuster to get a different date, and a query to get information about a date.

questions.q: Match each term to its meaning.
pairs: gives back information about a temporal
reports the smallest unit an object can represent
the method you write for a custom query
questions.explain: An adjuster changes the date it returns; a query reports a result of any type.
questions.rule: Adjuster returns a date, query returns an answer.

questions.q: Year.now().query(TemporalQueries.precision()) reports ____.
questions.explain: A Year can represent only whole years, so its smallest unit is years.
questions.rule: Precision follows content.

questions.q: Which pair of precision results is correct for a LocalDateTime and for a YearMonth, in that order?
options: Days and Years
Nanos and Days
Seconds and Months
Nanos and Months
optionExplain: A LocalDateTime holds more than days, and a YearMonth holds months, not only years.
A YearMonth holds months, not days.
A LocalDateTime reports Nanos, because it can hold a fraction of a second.
A LocalDateTime can hold nanoseconds, while a YearMonth holds only whole months.
questions.explain: Precision reports the smallest unit the object can hold, so richer objects report finer units.
questions.rule: More parts, finer precision.

questions.q: The tutorial's FamilyVacations query reads only the month and day of the date it receives. What does that allow?
options: The same query can run on any temporal that has those fields
It can change the date to the nearest vacation day
It works only on Instant, which holds every field
It must be rewritten for each class that holds a date
optionExplain: A query takes a read-only TemporalAccessor, and it works for any type that supplies the fields it reads.
A query reads and does not change anything.
An Instant has no month or day fields, so such a query does not suit it.
Reading only shared fields is what avoids rewriting it for each class.
questions.explain: Because the parameter is the read-only interface and the query reads shared fields, many classes can use it.
questions.rule: Read shared fields, reuse across classes.
questions.teaches: A query takes a read-only TemporalAccessor, so the same query can run on many classes as long as they support the fields it reads.

questions.q: A store writes a custom adjuster to answer whether an order date is a public holiday. What is wrong with that design?
options: Nothing is wrong, because adjusters are allowed to return any type of result, including a Boolean
Adjusters are not allowed to read the day of the month
An adjuster must return a temporal, while a yes-or-no answer is information for a query
Queries are required for every date calculation
optionExplain: An adjuster returns a temporal; a Boolean answer is not one.
Adjusters may read fields; the problem is the return type.
Choose by what the call gives back: a temporal from an adjuster, a result of any type from a query.
Queries and adjusters have different jobs, and neither is required for all calculations.
questions.explain: A yes-or-no answer is a result, not a changed date, so it should be written as a query.
questions.rule: Match the tool to the return type.
questions.teaches: Choose by return type: an adjuster hands back a temporal of the same kind, while a query can hand back a result of any type, such as a Boolean or a unit.

questions.q: A Duration of one day is added to a moment. How much later is the result?
options: 23 hours in summer and 25 hours in winter
Exactly 24 hours
Whatever the length of the local calendar day
One calendar date later, at the same clock time
optionExplain: That describes a calendar day across daylight saving changes, which is not a Duration.
A Duration is an exact length of time, and one day as a Duration is 24 hours.
A Duration does not follow the local calendar.
That describes adding a Period, which follows the calendar.
questions.explain: A Duration counts exact time. The card next sets it beside Period.
questions.rule: Use Duration for exact elapsed time and Period for calendar-based amounts.

questions.q: Match each amount to what it measures.
pairs: time-based amounts in seconds and nanoseconds
date-based amounts in years, months and days
questions.explain: Duration is machine-based and Period is human-based, and their printed forms start with PT and P.
questions.rule: Duration for seconds, Period for calendar.

questions.q: Sort each item by the amount class that suits it.

items.t: Time between two log entries
Length of a ninety-minute film
A thirty-second timeout
A person's age in years, months and days
A lease of six months
Three weeks of notice counted on a calendar

questions.explain: Exact elapsed time is a Duration. Amounts counted in calendar units such as months and weeks are a Period.
questions.rule: Clock length versus calendar length.

questions.q: Clocks in New York move forward at 2:00 a.m. on 10 March 2024. A ZonedDateTime reads 2024-03-09 at 12:00 in New York. What does adding Duration.ofDays(1) give?
optionExplain: That is what adding a Period of one day gives, following the calendar.
This would be 23 hours later, but a Duration adds exactly 24 hours.
That night has only 23 clock hours, so 24 exact hours after noon lands at 13:00 the next day.
That is two calendar days later, but only one day was added.
questions.explain: A Duration adds exact hours, and the missing hour on the clocks shifts the clock reading by one hour.
questions.rule: Duration is exact, the clock may shift.

questions.q: Clocks in New York move back on 3 November 2024. Starting from 2024-11-02 at 12:00 in New York, what do adding Period.ofDays(1) and Duration.ofDays(1) give, in that order?
options: 3 November at 12:00, then 3 November at 11:00
3 November at 11:00, then 3 November at 12:00
3 November at 12:00, then 3 November at 12:00
3 November at 13:00, then 3 November at 12:00
optionExplain: The calendar day is 25 hours long, so the exact 24 hours land an hour earlier on the clock.
This swaps the two results: the Period follows the calendar, the Duration is exact.
The two differ because the day is not 24 hours long.
The extra hour is a repeated hour, not a missing one, so the Duration lands earlier, not later.
questions.explain: When clocks go back, a calendar day lasts 25 hours, so 24 exact hours reach only 11:00 on the clock.
questions.rule: The difference flips direction when clocks go back.
questions.teaches: The two behave differently in the opposite direction when clocks go back: a calendar day then lasts 25 hours, so a 24-hour Duration lands one hour earlier on the clock than a Period of one day.

questions.q: A parking meter sells 90 minutes, and a gym membership runs for one month. Which pairing of amount classes fits?
options: Both as Durations, since both are lengths of time
Both as Periods, since both count units
The parking time as a Period, the membership as a Duration
The parking time as a Duration, the membership as a Period
optionExplain: A month has no fixed number of seconds, so a Duration does not fit the membership.
Ninety minutes is a fixed clock length, which is a Duration's job.
This swaps them: the meter is exact time and the membership is calendar time.
Ninety minutes is a fixed length of time, while a month is counted on the calendar.
questions.explain: Pick Duration when the length is fixed by the clock and Period when it is fixed by the calendar.
questions.rule: Clock-fixed or calendar-fixed?
questions.teaches: Choose Duration when the length is fixed by the clock, as for a parking meter, and Period when it is fixed by the calendar, as for a monthly membership, whose length in seconds varies.

questions.q: From 2024-01-15 to 2024-03-20, which result describes the gap as a calendar amount in months and days?
options: 2 months and 5 days
65 months
5 months and 2 days
1 month and 35 days
optionExplain: From 15 January, two months reach 15 March, and five more days reach 20 March.
65 is the number of days in the gap, not months.
The numbers are swapped: the gap is 2 months and 5 days.
The months and days are not split this way; Period reports 2 months and 5 days.
questions.explain: A calendar amount is split into months and days. The card next shows the tools.
questions.rule: Take a Period for a calendar-style answer in years, months and days, or ChronoUnit.between for one total in a single unit.

questions.q: True or false: ChronoUnit.DAYS.between returns years, months and days together.
questions.explain: ChronoUnit.between returns one number in a single unit. Years, months and days together come from Period.
questions.rule: One unit versus three.

questions.q: Period.between(2024-01-15, 2024-03-20).getMonths() returns ____.
questions.explain: The period is 2 months and 5 days, so getMonths returns 2.
questions.rule: Read the part you need.

questions.q: What does Period.between(later, earlier) give if the arguments are swapped, with later 2024-03-20 and earlier 2024-01-15?
options: The same period of 2 months and 5 days
A negative period of 2 months and 5 days
An error, because the start must be earlier
A period of 0 days
optionExplain: The sign flips when the start is later than the end.
The sign follows the direction: the end comes before the start.
Swapping is allowed and gives negative values.
The dates differ, so the period is not zero.
questions.explain: Measuring from a later date to an earlier one reverses the direction, so the amounts are negative.
questions.rule: Direction decides the sign.

questions.q: What does ChronoUnit.MONTHS.between(2024-01-15, 2024-03-20) return?
optionExplain: The method returns a whole number, not a fraction.
It counts only complete months, and the third month is not complete.
It counts only whole months in the gap and drops the leftover 5 days.
65 is the number of days, not months.
questions.explain: Beyond the tutorial: ChronoUnit.between counts whole units and drops any remainder.
questions.rule: Between counts whole units.
questions.teaches: Beyond the tutorial: ChronoUnit.between counts only whole units and drops the remainder, so the months result is 2 even though the gap is 2 months and 5 days.

questions.q: A library charges a fine for each overdue day. A book due on 2024-05-10 is returned on 2024-06-12. Which tool and result fit?
options: Period.between, reading only its days part, giving 2
Period.between, giving 1 month and 2 days
ChronoUnit.MONTHS.between, giving 33
ChronoUnit.DAYS.between, giving 33
optionExplain: The days part of a Period is only what is left after whole months, so it understates the total overdue days.
This is a correct calendar breakdown, but a per-day fine needs one total in days, not months and days.
That would count whole months, and the total of 33 is a number of days, not months.
A fine per day needs one total in days, and 10 May to 12 June is 33 days.
questions.explain: When a rate is per unit, you need one total in that unit, not a years-months-days breakdown. The days part of a Period holds only the remainder after whole months.
questions.rule: Rates need one total.
questions.teaches: When a charge is per unit, use a single-unit total such as DAYS.between, because the days part of a Period is only what remains after whole months and years are taken out.

questions.q: A test needs today's date to be the same on every run. Which approach fits best?
options: Run the test only on one day of the week
Set the computer's date by hand before each run
Round the date to the nearest week
Give the code a clock whose time does not move
optionExplain: This does not make the date identical on each run.
This is fragile and affects everything else on the machine.
Rounding does not make the date the same on every run.
A fixed clock returns the same instant every time, so the test is repeatable.
questions.explain: Repeatable tests need a controllable source of time. The card next introduces Clock.
questions.rule: Give now a Clock when the result must not depend on the machine's own clock and zone.

questions.q: A clock whose time stands still is created with Clock.____.
questions.explain: Clock.fixed takes an Instant and a ZoneId and always returns that instant.
questions.rule: Fixed means time stands still.

questions.q: A clock is fixed at 2024-01-15T20:00:00Z in the zone Asia/Tokyo, which is UTC+9. What does LocalDate.now(clock) return?
optionExplain: That is the UTC date, but the clock reads in Tokyo.
At 20:00 UTC it is already 05:00 on 16 January in Tokyo.
Tokyo is ahead of UTC, so it cannot be behind.
Nine hours cannot move the date two days.
questions.explain: The zone of the clock decides which calendar date the same instant shows.
questions.rule: The clock's zone decides the date.

questions.q: The same instant is used, but the clock's zone is changed from Asia/Tokyo to UTC. LocalDate.now(clock) then returns ____ (year-month-day).
questions.explain: At 20:00 UTC the UTC date is still 15 January; changing the zone changes the calendar reading but not the instant.
questions.rule: Same instant, different zone, possibly different date.

questions.q: Which statements about Clock are accurate? Select all that apply.
options: Clock is abstract, so you obtain one from factory methods
A fixed clock always returns the same instant
Clock.systemUTC reads the default zone of the machine
Passing a Clock is required for every call to now
optionExplain: Clock cannot be created directly; factories such as systemUTC and fixed provide instances.
Clock.fixed makes time stand still, which suits tests.
systemUTC reads UTC, not the machine's default zone.
The no-argument now still exists and uses the system clock and default zone.
questions.explain: A Clock is an abstract source of time obtained from factories. Fixed clocks never advance, and passing one is optional.
questions.rule: Optional, abstract, built by factories.

questions.q: A billing job charges a late fee if today is after the due date, and the team must test the first day of a new month without waiting for it. What design makes that testable?
options: Pass the clock into the job and use a fixed clock set to the chosen date
Call the no-argument now inside the job and change the computer's clock before each run
Store the due date as text and compare text
Run the job daily until the right date arrives
optionExplain: Receiving the clock as an input lets a test supply any date it needs.
This makes the test depend on the machine and is hard to repeat.
This does not remove the need to know today's date.
Waiting makes the test slow and unreliable.
questions.explain: Making the clock an input turns time into a parameter that a test can control.
questions.rule: Make time an input.
questions.teaches: Passing the clock in as a parameter, instead of calling the no-argument now inside the logic, is what makes time-dependent code testable, because a test can then supply any moment it needs.

questions.q: A date in the Thai Buddhist calendar must become an ISO LocalDate. Which call is the most likely?
options: LocalDate.parse(thaiDate)
LocalDate.from(thaiDate)
LocalDate.at(thaiDate)
LocalDate.toIso(thaiDate)
optionExplain: Parse reads a string, not a date object.
From converts another date type into a LocalDate.
At combines the object it is called on with another; it is not a static converter.
There is no such method; conversion follows the from convention.
questions.explain: Converting between date types uses from. The card next walks through both directions.
questions.rule: Convert with from in either direction, and treat the ISO LocalDate as the common form between calendars.

questions.q: To convert an ISO date to a MinguoDate, call MinguoDate.____ with the ISO date.
questions.explain: Each non-ISO date class has a static from method that accepts a temporal such as a LocalDate.
questions.rule: From converts.

questions.q: The tutorial's output shows ISO year 1996 as Thai Buddhist year 2539. Using the same difference, which Thai Buddhist year matches ISO 2024?
optionExplain: This subtracts 543 instead of adding it.
The years differ between calendars, so the number changes.
The Thai year is the ISO year plus 543, and 2024 plus 543 is 2567.
This is the Thai year for 1996, not for 2024.
questions.explain: A fixed difference between two calendars can be found from one matching pair and then applied to other years.
questions.rule: Find the offset from one pair.

questions.q: True or false: Converting a LocalDate to a MinguoDate changes which day the date names.
questions.explain: The same day is shown with a different numbering; converting back gives the original LocalDate.
questions.rule: Numbering changes, the day does not.

questions.q: A MinguoDate named m must become a ThaiBuddhistDate. Which route works?
options: ThaiBuddhistDate.from(m), because from accepts any date-like value
ThaiBuddhistDate.parse(m), because parse accepts date objects
It is impossible, because only an ISO date can be converted
Add 543 to its year number by hand and rebuild the date
optionExplain: The from method takes a TemporalAccessor, so one non-ISO date can be converted to another directly.
Parse reads a string, not a date object.
from accepts any date-like value, not only ISO dates.
This is error-prone, and the conversion method exists for this purpose.
questions.explain: Since from accepts any temporal that can supply a date, conversion between two non-ISO calendars needs no ISO code from you.
questions.rule: From accepts any date-like value.
questions.teaches: Because from accepts any date-like value, you can convert directly between two non-ISO calendars without writing ISO code; the day is the same and only its numbering changes.

questions.q: A museum catalog stores dates as ISO values but prints Thai Buddhist dates for visitors from Thailand. A teammate suggests storing the Thai year instead. What is the better design?
options: Store both years in two columns and update the columns separately by hand
Store the Thai year, since visitors from Thailand are the main users of the catalog
Store text such as the printed Thai date
Keep ISO values for storage and convert for display, so sorting stays uniform
optionExplain: Two copies can drift apart and the day is the same anyway.
Arithmetic and sorting then depend on a calendar most tools do not expect.
Text is hard to sort and compute with.
The day is identical in both calendars, so one stored form with a display conversion avoids two sets of numbers.
questions.explain: The calendar is a way of showing a day, not a different day, so conversion at the edge keeps the stored data simple.
questions.rule: Store in one calendar, convert for display.
questions.teaches: Keeping one calendar for storage and converting for display keeps sorting and arithmetic consistent, because the calendar only changes how a day is numbered, not which day it is.

questions.q: The old java.util.Date corresponds most closely to the java.time class ____.
questions.explain: Both a Date and an Instant are points on the UTC timeline, independent of zone. The card next gives the bridges.
questions.rule: Date is a moment, like Instant.

questions.q: Match each legacy item to its closest java.time counterpart.
pairs: GregorianCalendar with its date fixed at 1970-01-01
questions.explain: The mapping is approximate, but each legacy class has a nearest modern partner.
questions.rule: Nearest partner, not an exact twin.

questions.q: A java.util.Date called d becomes an Instant with d.____().
questions.explain: Date.toInstant bridges to java.time, and Date.from(Instant) goes back.
questions.rule: Date to Instant is toInstant.

questions.q: A service converts a Date to an Instant with toInstant and back with Date.from. What do you expect from the round trip?
options: A moment shifted by the machine's offset from UTC when it is converted back
A moment rounded to the nearest day
An exception, because Date cannot be converted
An equal moment, because both are zone-independent UTC timeline points
optionExplain: Neither type applies an offset; both count from the epoch.
Neither type stores a day, so no rounding to a day happens.
The bridge methods exist for exactly this conversion.
Neither side involves a zone, so nothing about the moment is lost.
questions.explain: Date and Instant both describe a moment independent of zone, so the trip needs no zone choice.
questions.rule: No zone involved, no loss of the moment.
questions.teaches: The Date to Instant to Date trip involves no zone choice and so keeps the moment, whereas a trip through ZonedDateTime requires you to choose a zone for the human reading.

questions.q: A teammate says: a GregorianCalendar set to 00:00 is a safe way to store a date-only value, so no change is needed. According to the tutorial, what is the flaw?
options: Midnight does not occur on some dates in some countries at daylight saving changes
GregorianCalendar can store only times, never dates
Midnight is stored in nanoseconds only, a unit that date classes cannot use at all
A date-only value must always be stored as an Instant
optionExplain: That is why LocalDate is the proper class for date-only values.
It stores both; the flaw is about midnight not existing on some dates.
The tutorial gives no such reason.
LocalDate is the date-only class; an Instant would add a moment.
questions.explain: A date-only value should not depend on a clock time that may not exist, so use LocalDate.
questions.rule: Dates should not hide in midnight.

questions.q: A company is replacing a mutable Customer class with an immutable one, but a plugin still calls the old setters. Which strategy parallels the tutorial's advice for legacy dates?
options: Delete the plugin because old code cannot be bridged to the new immutable class
Make the new class mutable again so both work
Add conversion at the edge so the plugin keeps working, and rewrite it later
Rewrite everything at once before any release
optionExplain: The tutorial offers bridges precisely so old code can keep working.
This loses the benefits that motivated the change.
Bridging at the boundary keeps old code running, and rewriting removes the bridge in time.
The tutorial offers a gradual route as the easiest.
questions.explain: The tutorial's easiest route is a bridge, with rewriting as the long-term cleanup.
questions.rule: Bridge first, rewrite where you can.
questions.teaches: Migration works best through thin conversion code at the boundary, so the inside can be rewritten step by step while old callers keep working.

questions.q: A programmer reads an item from a list with a cast to String. Who vouches that the item really is a String?
questions.explain: A cast is an assertion by the programmer, verified once at run time. The card next shows what a declared type changes.
options: The programmer, whose claim is checked only at run time
The compiler, which has proved it from the list's contents
The list class, which accepts only Strings by design
The JVM, which checks every item when it is added
optionExplain: Right: the cast is the programmer's assertion, and it is tested only at the moment the line executes.
The compiler cannot see what a raw list holds, so it trusts the cast.
A raw list stores any object, so it has no such design.
The JVM does not check an item at the time it is added to a raw list.
questions.rule: State the element type in the declaration so the compiler guarantees it at every use and no cast is needed.

questions.q: True or false: With an element type declared on a list variable, the compiler checks every use of that variable, not only one line.
questions.explain: The declared type is a guarantee that holds wherever the variable is used, which is what replaces the single-point cast.
questions.rule: State the element type in the declaration so the compiler guarantees it at every use and no cast is needed.

questions.q: A list variable declared as holding Double rejects a String added to it at ____ time, before the program runs.
questions.explain: The compiler knows the declared element type at every use, so the wrong add is reported while compiling.
questions.rule: State the element type in the declaration so the compiler guarantees it at every use and no cast is needed.

questions.q: Method A adds an Integer to a raw list. Much later, method B reads the list's items with a cast to String. Where does the ClassCastException appear?
questions.explain: The cast is the first place the wrong item is tested, which can be long after it was stored.
options: In method A at the add, because the Integer is refused there
In method B at the cast, far from the faulty add
At compile time, because the cast is suspicious
Nowhere, because the cast silently converts the Integer
optionExplain: A raw list accepts the Integer, so the add succeeds.
Right: the failure shows up where the bad item is read, so the cause is far from the symptom.
The compiler accepts any cast between Object-derived types it cannot disprove.
A cast to an unrelated type fails; it does not convert.
questions.teaches: A cast reports the error where the item is read, not where the wrong item was stored, so the compile-time check also finds the bug at its source.
questions.rule: State the element type in the declaration so the compiler guarantees it at every use and no cast is needed.

questions.q: A public method returns a raw list of orders, and its comment says the items are Order objects. Callers cast every item. What changes if the return type becomes a List of Order?
questions.explain: A declared element type in a signature is documentation that the compiler enforces.
options: Callers still cast, but each cast is now guaranteed to fail at run time
Nothing, since the comment still carries the claim for every reader
The claim joins the signature, so the compiler checks it and callers drop their casts
The method stops compiling because a typed list cannot be returned
optionExplain: A correct cast does not fail; the point is that the casts are no longer needed.
A comment is not checked by anything, so the situation does change.
Right: the type turns a note into a contract the compiler checks on both sides of the call.
Returning a parameterized list is allowed.
questions.teaches: A declared element type in a method signature turns a documentation comment into a contract checked on both the caller's side and the method's own side.
questions.rule: State the element type in the declaration so the compiler guarantees it at every use and no cast is needed.

questions.q: A field holds a raw list. One method adds a Date to it, and another reads items with a cast to String. The field is redeclared as a List of String. Which results follow? Select all that apply.
questions.explain: The declaration lets the compiler find the Date add and remove the need for the cast.
options: The line adding a Date is rejected at compile time
The line adding a Date still compiles and fails when it runs
The casts in the reading method become unnecessary
Each remaining cast now fails at run time
optionExplain: Right: a Date does not fit the declared element type, and the compiler reports it.
The declared type is checked while compiling, so the add no longer reaches run time.
Right: the reading line gets a String directly from the typed list.
The casts that remain are not failing; they are redundant.
questions.rule: State the element type in the declaration so the compiler guarantees it at every use and no cast is needed.

questions.q: True or false: Using a generic class with ten different type arguments makes the compiler produce ten separate compiled versions of the class.
questions.explain: The tutorial says a generic is compiled once. The card next shows what that means.
questions.rule: Formal type parameters stand in the definition and actual type arguments replace them at each use, without any copy of the code being made.

questions.q: Match each term to its meaning.
questions.explain: The tutorial pairs type parameters and arguments with the familiar value parameters and arguments of methods.
pairs: The placeholder named in the generic's definition
The real type supplied at a use of the generic
A generic with its arguments supplied, such as List of Integer
The placeholder in a method definition that each call fills with a value
questions.rule: Formal type parameters stand in the definition and actual type arguments replace them at each use, without any copy of the code being made.

questions.q: A definition Cache of K and V has a method lookup taking a K and returning a V. What does lookup take and return in Cache of String and Integer?
questions.explain: Each formal parameter is replaced by the argument in its position.
options: It takes an Integer and returns a String
It takes a String and returns a String
It takes an Object and returns an Object
It takes a String and returns an Integer
optionExplain: The arguments are matched to the parameters in order, so K is String, not Integer.
V is the second parameter, so the result is Integer, not String.
Substituting the arguments gives exact types; the Object picture belongs to the raw type.
Right: K is replaced by String and V by Integer, in the order they were declared.
questions.rule: Formal type parameters stand in the definition and actual type arguments replace them at each use, without any copy of the code being made.

questions.q: True or false: In a generic Crate of E, a method may return a parameterized type built from E, such as an Iterator of E.
questions.explain: The tutorial's own List does this: next returns an E and iterator returns an Iterator of E.
questions.teaches: A formal type parameter can be used wherever an ordinary type could, including inside other parameterized types, subject to restrictions given later in the fine print.
questions.rule: Formal type parameters stand in the definition and actual type arguments replace them at each use, without any copy of the code being made.

questions.q: A program uses one generic class with thirty different type arguments instead of three. What must hold for the code inside the generic class?
questions.explain: Because there is one class, nothing in it can vary with the type argument at run time.
options: It may check which type argument is in use and branch on it
It must be recompiled for each new type argument that appears
It must behave the same for every type argument, since one class file serves them all
It runs faster, because each argument has its own tuned copy
optionExplain: The argument is not present at run time for the code to inspect.
Compiling once is the point; no recompilation per argument happens.
Right: one class file serves all arguments, so its body cannot depend on which argument was chosen.
No tuned copies exist, so no speedup comes from the number of arguments.
questions.teaches: Since the one compiled class cannot vary with the type argument, later fine-print rules forbid anything that would need the argument at run time, such as static use and instanceof tests.
questions.rule: Formal type parameters stand in the definition and actual type arguments replace them at each use, without any copy of the code being made.

questions.q: A colleague describes generics in four statements. Which are wrong according to the tutorial? Select all that apply.
questions.explain: The expansion picture is a helpful intuition about signatures, but the tutorial warns that no expansion takes place.
options: List of Integer is a parameterized type
The compiler writes a separate IntegerList class on disk for it
E in a List definition is a formal type parameter
Generics are expanded into copies in memory, like C++ templates
optionExplain: This statement is accurate: a generic used with an argument is a parameterized type.
The tutorial says there are no copies in source, binary, disk or memory.
This statement is accurate: E is the placeholder in the definition.
The tutorial names this as a difference from C++ templates.
questions.rule: Formal type parameters stand in the definition and actual type arguments replace them at each use, without any copy of the code being made.

questions.q: A list of Circle is assigned to a variable declared as a list of Shape, and Circle is a subtype of Shape. What does the compiler do?
questions.explain: This is the hardest part of generics for many readers. The card next gives the reason.
options: It rejects the assignment at compile time
It accepts the assignment with an unchecked warning
It accepts the assignment silently
It accepts it and checks each add at run time
optionExplain: Right: related element types do not make the two list types related.
