No warning applies, because the assignment is refused outright.
Intuition says a list of Circle is a list of Shape, but the compiler does not follow it.
No such run-time check exists; the protection is at compile time.
questions.rule: A generic of a subtype is not a subtype of the generic of the supertype, because a shared writable list could be corrupted through the wider view.

questions.q: Put these steps in order, pretending a list of String could be assigned to a list of Object variable.
questions.explain: Both names reach one list, so a value added through the wider name is later read through the narrower one.
items: A list of String is assigned to a list of Object variable
An Object is added through the Object variable
The String variable's list is read at that position
A plain Object lands in a String variable
questions.rule: A generic of a subtype is not a subtype of the generic of the supertype, because a shared writable list could be corrupted through the wider view.

questions.q: Truck is a subtype of Vehicle. A list of Truck is not a ____ of a list of Vehicle, so passing it to a parameter of the latter type does not compile.
questions.explain: Subtyping of the arguments does not carry over to the generic types.
questions.rule: A generic of a subtype is not a subtype of the generic of the supertype, because a shared writable list could be corrupted through the wider view.

questions.q: A program views a List of Driver as a List of Person (assume this were allowed) and adds a non-driver. The Driver list is a copy of the registry's list. Is the registry's own list affected?
questions.explain: The risk lies in writing through a wider view of a shared list; a copy is not shared.
options: Yes, because both names still refer to one shared list
Yes, because the compiler links the copy back to the original
Yes, but only the declared type of the original changes
No, because the addition lands in the copy and the original is never touched
optionExplain: A copy is a separate list, so it is not shared with the registry.
Nothing links a copy to its original after copying.
Declared types do not change when a copy is modified.
Right: the non-driver goes into the copy, and the registry's list is never touched.
questions.teaches: The danger comes from writing through a wider view of a shared list; with a copy, the original list is untouched.
questions.rule: A generic of a subtype is not a subtype of the generic of the supertype, because a shared writable list could be corrupted through the wider view.

questions.q: A generic Box of T has a set method taking a T and a get method returning a T. Integer is a subtype of Number. Can a Box of Integer be passed where a Box of Number is expected?
questions.explain: The aliasing argument works for every generic whose methods take the parameter.
options: Yes: Box is not a collection, so the rule does not apply
No: set on the Number view could store a Double
Yes: Integer objects cannot be changed
No: the rule applies only to List and Set
optionExplain: The argument concerns any generic with a method that accepts the type parameter, not only collections.
Right: any generic with a method taking its parameter has the same hazard as the list.
The Integer values may be fixed, but the Box can be handed a different Number.
The reasoning rests on set, which Box has, so it reaches beyond lists and sets.
questions.teaches: The invariance rule concerns every generic class with a method that takes its type parameter, not only collections.
questions.rule: A generic of a subtype is not a subtype of the generic of the supertype, because a shared writable list could be corrupted through the wider view.

questions.q: True or false: If the assignment of a list of String to a list of Object were allowed but the Object view were only ever read from, an Object could not end up in a String variable through that view.
questions.explain: The harm needed a write through the wider view. The compiler still bans the assignment for all code, which is why read-only forms need their own, safer syntax.
questions.rule: A generic of a subtype is not a subtype of the generic of the supertype, because a shared writable list could be corrupted through the wider view.

questions.q: A method receives a Collection of question mark, a collection of unknown element type. Which operation inside it is the compiler most likely to allow?
questions.explain: Reads are safe as Object; writes need a value known to fit. The card next explains why.
options: Reading an item into a variable of type Object
Adding a String to the collection
Adding a new Object to the collection
Reading an item into a variable of type String
optionExplain: Right: whatever the unknown type is, its items are Objects.
The element type may not be String, so a String might not fit.
The element type may be narrower than Object, so a plain Object might not fit.
The items might not be Strings, so assigning them to String is unsafe.
questions.rule: With a wildcard type you can read items as the bound (Object when unbounded) but can add only null, so use extends for a structure the method only reads.

questions.q: Match each parameter type to what a method can do with it.
questions.explain: The wildcard trades the ability to add for the ability to accept many parameterizations.
pairs: Any collection; read as Object, add only null
Collection of question mark extends Shape
Shapes or subtypes; read as Shape, add only null
Only this exact type; Shapes can be read and added
Fits every type, so it can be added to a wildcard collection
questions.rule: With a wildcard type you can read items as the bound (Object when unbounded) but can add only null, so use extends for a structure the method only reads.

questions.q: A method has a parameter list of type List of question mark extends Animal. Which statements inside it compile? Select all that apply.
questions.explain: Reads give the bound; the only value known to fit an unknown subtype is null.
options: Animal a = list.get(0);
list.add(new Dog());
list.add(null);
Dog d = list.get(0);
optionExplain: Right: every item is an Animal or a subtype.
The list might hold Cats, so a Dog may not fit.
Right: null belongs to every type.
The items might be Cats, so assigning them to Dog is not safe.
questions.rule: With a wildcard type you can read items as the bound (Object when unbounded) but can add only null, so use extends for a structure the method only reads.

questions.q: A method takes a Map of String to question mark extends Person. Which put call inside it compiles?
questions.explain: A wildcard in one type argument leaves the other arguments exact.
options: put("id7", new Person())
put("id7", null)
put("id7", new Driver())
put(7, null)
optionExplain: The value type may be a narrower subtype, so a plain Person may not fit.
Right: the key type String is fixed and null fits any value type.
The value type may be another Person subtype, so a Driver may not fit.
The key type is exactly String, so an integer key is wrong even with a null value.
questions.teaches: A wildcard in one type argument of a multi-parameter generic loosens only that argument; the other arguments, such as the key type, stay exact.
questions.rule: With a wildcard type you can read items as the bound (Object when unbounded) but can add only null, so use extends for a structure the method only reads.

questions.q: A method copyAll takes two parameters, both declared as List of question mark. It tries to add each item read from the first list to the second. What happens?
questions.explain: Two wildcards are two unrelated unknowns.
options: It compiles, since both lists share the same unknown element type
It compiles and fails at run time when the element types differ
Compile error: each wildcard is a separate unknown, so no value is known to fit the second list
It compiles only when both parameters are given the same list object
optionExplain: The two unknowns are independent; nothing says they match.
The check is made at compile time, so the failure never reaches run time.
Right: each wildcard is a separate unknown, so the items read cannot be shown to fit the target.
The compiler judges the declared types, not which objects the caller passes.
questions.teaches: Two wildcards are unrelated unknowns, so moving items between wildcard-typed lists needs a named type parameter that links them.
questions.rule: With a wildcard type you can read items as the bound (Object when unbounded) but can add only null, so use extends for a structure the method only reads.

questions.q: True or false: If a parameter changes from List of question mark extends Shape to List of Shape, a caller holding a List of Circle can still call the method.
questions.explain: A list of Circle is not a list of Shape, so the narrower declaration refuses it. The extends wildcard is what admitted the subtype lists.
questions.rule: With a wildcard type you can read items as the bound (Object when unbounded) but can add only null, so use extends for a structure the method only reads.

questions.q: A method takes a list and returns its first item, typed to match the list's element type. Which signature idea fits best?
questions.explain: Linking the parameter to the result is the clue. The card next names this.
options: A wildcard list parameter with a return type of Object
A raw list parameter with a return type of Object
Two separate type parameters, one for each position
A type parameter T in both the list and the return type
optionExplain: The result would lose the element type and need a cast.
A raw type drops the checking the declaration exists for.
Two unrelated parameters do not say the result matches the list.
Right: the same T links the argument to the result.
questions.rule: Use a type parameter on a method where it relates several types, and use a wildcard where it would appear only once.

questions.q: A type parameter that links one argument type to the return type expresses a ____ between them.
questions.explain: The tutorial calls such a link a dependency, and it is what justifies naming a type parameter.
questions.rule: Use a type parameter on a method where it relates several types, and use a wildcard where it would appear only once.

questions.q: Sort each method by whether its design needs a named type parameter or is served by a wildcard.
questions.explain: A name is needed when two places must agree on a type; a wildcard is enough when the type is used once and its identity does not matter.

items.t: Returns the same element type as the list it receives
Copies items from a source list into a destination list of matching element type
Adds the items of an array of T to a collection of T
Prints every item of any collection
Counts how many items a list holds, whatever the element type
Checks whether a collection holds all items of another collection of any element type

questions.rule: Use a type parameter on a method where it relates several types, and use a wildcard where it would appear only once.

questions.q: A generic array-to-collection copier has a type parameter T and takes an array of T and a Collection of T. A call passing a Number array and a Collection of String fails. What if the collection argument changes to a Collection of Object?
questions.explain: The failure was a conflict between two constraints, and loosening one resolves it.
options: It compiles, with T inferred as Number
It still fails, because the array's type is fixed
It compiles, with T inferred as Object
It compiles only if the array is also changed to Object
optionExplain: Number cannot work, since the collection's element type must equal T exactly.
The array may be viewed as an array of a supertype, so its fixed element type does not block the call.
Right: Object is a supertype of Number, so a single T satisfies both arguments.
No change to the array is needed once T can move up to Object.
questions.teaches: A failing call can be fixed by loosening one argument's type, since inference can move T up to a common supertype that satisfies every argument.
questions.hint: Ask which single type T would satisfy both arguments.
questions.rule: Use a type parameter on a method where it relates several types, and use a wildcard where it would appear only once.

questions.q: A class keeps a static field recording every list ever drawn, where each list holds some subtype of Shape. Which declaration for the field fits?
questions.explain: Wildcards are not limited to method parameters.
options: A List of List of question mark extends Shape
A List of List of Shape, fixed to a single shape type
A flat List of Shape holding every drawn item
A raw List with no type arguments given at all
optionExplain: Right: the wildcard sits inside the outer list's argument, so lists of Circle and lists of Rectangle both fit.
Lists of Circle are not lists of Shape, so they would be refused.
This describes one flat list of shapes, not a record of lists.
A raw list would work, but it gives up the checking the declaration should provide.
questions.teaches: Wildcards can also appear in fields, local variables and nested type arguments, not only in method signatures.
questions.rule: Use a type parameter on a method where it relates several types, and use a wildcard where it would appear only once.

questions.q: A colleague rewrites a copy method with a List of T destination and a List of question mark extends T source as a generic method with a second type parameter S that extends T, used for the source. Which comments are accurate? Select all that apply.
questions.explain: A single-use type parameter is a wildcard in disguise, and the tutorial prefers the wildcard.
options: The two forms accept the same calls
S appears only once, so a wildcard is clearer
S is needed because the return type depends on it
T and S must always be the same type
optionExplain: Right: the extra name adds no accepted calls.
Right: a parameter used once is better written as a wildcard.
The method returns nothing, so no return type depends on S.
S may be a subtype of T, so the two need not match.
questions.rule: Use a type parameter on a method where it relates several types, and use a wildcard where it would appear only once.

questions.q: A legacy method returns a raw Collection and its documentation promises it holds only Part objects. You assign the result to a Collection of Part. What does the compiler do?
questions.explain: Interoperation is allowed but flagged. The card next shows the directions.
options: It rejects the assignment as a type error
It inserts a check of every item at the assignment
It accepts the assignment silently
It accepts it with an unchecked warning
optionExplain: Rejecting it would make legacy code unusable from generic code.
No check of the contents is made at that point.
Silence would hide a claim the compiler cannot verify.
Right: the compiler allows it for interoperability but flags that it cannot verify the contents.
questions.rule: Treat each unchecked warning at a generic and legacy boundary as a claim you must be able to justify from the legacy method's documented contract.

questions.q: Sort each operation by whether it draws an unchecked warning.
questions.explain: Warnings mark the places where the compiler is asked to trust the contents of raw data.

items.t: Assign a legacy method's raw result to a collection of Part
Pass a raw collection to a parameter declared as collection of Part
Add an item through a raw collection variable
Pass a collection of Part to a legacy raw parameter
Add a Part to a variable of type collection of Part
Read a Part from a variable of type collection of Part

questions.rule: Treat each unchecked warning at a generic and legacy boundary as a claim you must be able to justify from the legacy method's documented contract.

questions.q: The library method Rates.load returns a raw List, and its documentation promises only Double values. Which response to the unchecked warning on assigning it to a List of Double is best?
questions.explain: The programmer takes responsibility for the boundary.
options: Ignore it, since the warning means the compiler proved safety
Check the contract promises Double, and record why it is safe
Add a cast to List of Double to silence the compiler's concern
Remove the declared type so the warning disappears
optionExplain: A warning means the compiler could not prove safety.
Right: safety depends on the legacy method's documented contract, so the author must check and justify it.
A cast to a parameterized type is itself unchecked and does not verify anything.
A raw variable only hides the claim, and gives up the checking for the rest of the code.
questions.rule: Treat each unchecked warning at a generic and legacy boundary as a claim you must be able to justify from the legacy method's documented contract.

questions.q: True or false: Using generics in my own code is pointless if I must call legacy code, because the boundary voids the guarantees.
questions.explain: The guarantees are lost only at the boundary; the rest of the code stays more consistent than it would be without generics.
questions.teaches: Mixing generic and legacy code voids guarantees only at the boundary, so converting your own code is still worthwhile.
questions.rule: Treat each unchecked warning at a generic and legacy boundary as a claim you must be able to justify from the legacy method's documented contract.

questions.q: A payments library changes its method from taking a raw Collection to taking a Collection of Rule. Other teams' old code still passes raw collections. What should those teams expect?
questions.explain: Converting a library to generics does not break old source, but it adds warnings.
options: Their code still compiles, with unchecked warnings about the raw arguments
Their code stops compiling until it is converted to generics
Their code fails with an exception at each of those calls
Their code is unaffected and gets no new warnings at all
optionExplain: Right: the old calls keep working, but the compiler now flags the unverified contents.
The raw argument is still accepted, only flagged.
The call itself does not fail; only a wrong item read later could.
The raw argument meets a parameterized parameter, which is the warned direction.
questions.teaches: Converting a library method to generics does not break callers' source; raw callers still compile and receive unchecked warnings.
questions.rule: Treat each unchecked warning at a generic and legacy boundary as a claim you must be able to justify from the legacy method's documented contract.

questions.q: True or false: A reviewer writes: the assignment drew only a warning, so the compiler has checked that the legacy list holds only Double values. This reasoning is correct.
questions.explain: The warning says the compiler could not check the contents. Safety rests on the documented contract.
questions.rule: Treat each unchecked warning at a generic and legacy boundary as a claim you must be able to justify from the legacy method's documented contract.

questions.q: A List of String variable and a raw List variable refer to one list. An Integer is added through the raw variable. When does the first failure occur?
questions.explain: The trouble surfaces at the read. The card next shows the translation.
options: At compile time, as an error on the raw add
At run time, when an item is read as a String
At run time, at the moment of the raw add
Never, since erasure removes the types entirely
optionExplain: The raw add draws only a warning, not an error.
Right: the add succeeds, and the bad item is caught by the cast on the read.
The list itself accepts any object, so the add does not fail.
Erasure inserts casts, so the types still matter at the read.
questions.rule: An unchecked warning marks a place where the casts erasure inserts may fail later, so code without such warnings is type safe, and code with them fails safely at a cast.

questions.q: A List of String variable and a raw List variable refer to one list. An Integer is added through the raw variable, and later the first item is read into a String variable. Order these events.
questions.explain: The warning comes first at compile time; the failure comes last, at the cast.
items: The compiler warns about the add through the raw variable
The compiler erases the type arguments and inserts a cast to String at the read
The program runs and the Integer sits in the list unnoticed
The read executes the cast to String
A ClassCastException is thrown
questions.rule: An unchecked warning marks a place where the casts erasure inserts may fail later, so code without such warnings is type safe, and code with them fails safely at a cast.

questions.q: A List of Integer is aliased by a raw List, and a String is added through the raw one. Reading the first item through the List of Integer into an Integer variable throws a ____ at the inserted cast.
questions.explain: The translated read casts to Integer, and a String fails that cast.
questions.rule: An unchecked warning marks a place where the casts erasure inserts may fail later, so code without such warnings is type safe, and code with them fails safely at a cast.

questions.q: A wrong item is added through a raw variable, but the program does not read that position through the parameterized type. What happens?
questions.explain: A polluted list is harmless until something reads it through the typed view.
options: A ClassCastException at the add
A compile-time error at the raw variable
No exception; the item sits unnoticed
A ClassCastException when the program ends
optionExplain: The add through a raw variable is not checked.
The raw add compiled with a warning, not an error.
Right: the check happens only at a cast, and no cast runs.
Nothing checks the list when the program ends.
questions.teaches: Failures are deferred to the first cast, so a polluted list can sit unnoticed, and a quiet run does not show that a warning was harmless.
questions.rule: An unchecked warning marks a place where the casts erasure inserts may fail later, so code without such warnings is type safe, and code with them fails safely at a cast.

questions.q: A build tool reports a module compiled with no unchecked warnings. What does the generics design goal about unchecked warnings let you conclude about that module's generics?
questions.explain: Zero unchecked warnings is the signal for type safety.
options: Its generic code is correct but slower than raw code
Its generic code is checked again each time it runs
Its generic code may still fail at casts it cannot predict
Its generic code is type safe, so its casts should hold
optionExplain: Speed is not what the goal is about.
The run time does not repeat the compile-time check.
The goal is meant to rule out that failure for such code.
Right: the goal is that a program free of unchecked warnings is type safe.
questions.teaches: Compiling without any unchecked warnings is the signal that the generic type system's guarantees hold for that code.
questions.rule: An unchecked warning marks a place where the casts erasure inserts may fail later, so code without such warnings is type safe, and code with them fails safely at a cast.

questions.q: True or false: A List of String and a raw List refer to one list, and an Integer is added through the raw one. If the first item is then read into an Object variable instead of a String variable, a ClassCastException is still thrown at that read.
questions.explain: Erasure inserts casts only where needed, and an Object target needs none. The wrong item would pass unnoticed.
questions.rule: An unchecked warning marks a place where the casts erasure inserts may fail later, so code without such warnings is type safe, and code with them fails safely at a cast.

questions.q: True or false: At run time, a list created as an ArrayList of String and one created as an ArrayList of Integer report different classes.
questions.explain: Both report the same class. The card next shows what follows from that.
questions.rule: A generic class is one run-time class, so run-time questions about the type argument (instanceof, reliable casts, static use) have no answer.

questions.q: Asking an ArrayList of String and an ArrayList of Integer for their run-time classes gives the ____ Class object.
questions.explain: All instances of a generic class share one run-time class.
questions.rule: A generic class is one run-time class, so run-time questions about the type argument (instanceof, reliable casts, static use) have no answer.

questions.q: A generic class Counter of T declares a static int named created, increased in the constructor. The program builds a Counter of String and a Counter of Integer. How many created variables exist?
questions.explain: Statics are shared across all parameterizations.
options: None, because static fields are not allowed in generic classes
Two, one for each type argument
One, shared by both, because there is a single run-time class for Counter
One for each object created
optionExplain: A static field that does not use T is allowed.
Separate copies would need separate classes, which do not exist.
Right: statics belong to the single run-time class.
One per object describes an instance field.
questions.rule: A generic class is one run-time class, so run-time questions about the type argument (instanceof, reliable casts, static use) have no answer.

questions.q: A generic method declares T badCast taking a T t and an Object o, and returns the result of casting o to T. What does the compiler do?
questions.explain: Casts to type variables and to parameterized types are unchecked.
options: It compiles with an unchecked warning
It compiles with no warning
It rejects the cast as an error
It adds a check of the object's type argument at run time
optionExplain: Right: T does not exist at run time, so the cast cannot check what it claims.
A cast to a type variable is not verifiable, so the compiler warns.
The cast is legal, so no error is raised.
No such run-time check exists.
questions.teaches: A cast to a type variable compiles with an unchecked warning, because at run time it cannot check anything about T.
questions.rule: A generic class is one run-time class, so run-time questions about the type argument (instanceof, reliable casts, static use) have no answer.

questions.q: A method receives an Object that is a list and must decide whether it holds Strings or Dates. What is possible given one shared run-time class?
questions.explain: To act on a type argument at run time, the program has to carry it explicitly or look at the items.
options: Cast to a List of String and see whether it compiles
Test with instanceof against a List of String
Compare the list's class with a List of String class
Inspect an element, or have the caller pass the type
optionExplain: The cast compiles with a warning but proves nothing about the contents.
The test against a parameterized type is illegal.
The list's class is the same as any other list's.
Right: the list does not carry its argument, so the information must be found in the data or passed in.
questions.teaches: To use a type argument at run time a program must carry it explicitly or inspect the items, since the list object does not hold it.
questions.rule: A generic class is one run-time class, so run-time questions about the type argument (instanceof, reliable casts, static use) have no answer.

questions.q: A programmer adds each of these to a generic class Cache of V. Which compile without error? Select all that apply.
questions.explain: Statics are shared by all parameterizations, so they cannot depend on a type parameter.
options: A static int field named hits
A static field of type V named latest
A static method with a parameter of type V
An instance method with a parameter of type V
optionExplain: Right: it does not use the type parameter.
A static variable may not refer to the type parameter.
A static method may not refer to the class's type parameter.
Right: instance members may use the type parameter.
questions.rule: A generic class is one run-time class, so run-time questions about the type argument (instanceof, reliable casts, static use) have no answer.

questions.q: An array of List of String is created, and through an Object view a List of Integer is stored in it. At which point does the array object itself object?
questions.explain: The array's check cannot see the type argument. The card next shows the consequence.
options: At the store, because the item is not a List of String
It does not: the run-time check sees only a List
At creation, because the element type is parameterized
At the declaration of the variable
optionExplain: The arguments do not exist at run time, so the check cannot tell.
Right: the check at run time cannot see the type arguments, so the store passes.
Creation is the thing the language bans, not something the array can refuse.
Declaring the variable is legal.
questions.rule: Arrays of wildcard-only lists can be created, but arrays of type variables or of lists with named arguments cannot.

questions.q: True or false: Declaring a variable whose type is an array of List of String is legal, but creating such an array object is not.
questions.explain: The restriction is on array objects. Array types may be declared.
questions.rule: Arrays of wildcard-only lists can be created, but arrays of type variables or of lists with named arguments cannot.

questions.q: Sort each array expression by whether it is allowed.
questions.explain: Only element types that exist fully at run time, or the unbounded wildcard form, can have arrays created.

items.t: An array of List of question mark, size 5
An array of String, size 5
A variable of type array of List of String, assigned null
An array of List of String, size 5
An array whose element type is the type variable T, size 8
An array of Map of String to Integer, size 3

questions.rule: Arrays of wildcard-only lists can be created, but arrays of type variables or of lists with named arguments cannot.

questions.q: An array a of List of question mark (a list of unknown element type) is created, and a List of Integer is stored in a[0]. The programmer wants to read the first item of a[0] as a String. What must be written on the read line?
questions.explain: With an unknown element type the item comes back as an Object, so reading it as a String needs an explicit cast.
options: An explicit cast to String
Nothing; the array supplies the type
A cast to List of String
A call that reads the array's type argument
optionExplain: Right: the element type is unknown, so the item is an Object and the cast must be written out.
With an unknown element type the item is an Object, so something must convert it.
The array holds lists of unknown element type, not a typed list.
Type arguments are not available at run time.
questions.teaches: An array of List of ? is allowed, but reading from it needs an explicit cast.
questions.rule: Arrays of wildcard-only lists can be created, but arrays of type variables or of lists with named arguments cannot.

questions.q: A generic Stack of E needs an internal array of E, and the line that creates it with E as the element type is an error. Which direction does the tutorial point to for obtaining the array's type?
questions.explain: A type that does not exist at run time must be supplied some other way.
options: Using instanceof on E
Passing the type in as a class literal
Casting the Object array to E without any check
Reading E from a static field
optionExplain: A type variable cannot be tested at run time.
Right: a class literal acts as a run-time type token that the program can use.
An unchecked cast would silence the compiler but would not supply the array's type.
Static members cannot refer to the type parameter.
questions.teaches: Because a type variable is missing at run time, code that needs the real type, such as for building an array, must receive it explicitly as a class literal.
questions.rule: Arrays of wildcard-only lists can be created, but arrays of type variables or of lists with named arguments cannot.

questions.q: True or false: If creating an array of List of String were allowed, the run-time store check would refuse a List of Integer stored into it.
questions.explain: The store check sees only the List class, so the store passes. That is why the creation is refused.
questions.rule: Arrays of wildcard-only lists can be created, but arrays of type variables or of lists with named arguments cannot.

questions.q: A utility method must return a collection of whatever class the caller names, such as employees or invoices, with the right element type. Which parameter gives the compiler that element type?
questions.explain: A value that names the type can also type the result. The card next shows how.
options: A plain Object
A String holding the class name
A Class object for the wanted class
No parameter; the return type decides
optionExplain: An Object carries no information about the wanted type.
A String has no type argument for the compiler to use.
Right: the Class object carries a type argument that the compiler can use.
Without an argument naming the class, the compiler has nothing to infer from.
questions.rule: Pass the class literal as a Class of T argument so the compiler fixes T and the run-time object can still make instances of it.

questions.q: The class literal String.class has the type Class of ____.
questions.explain: The type parameter of Class is the type the Class object stands for.
questions.rule: Pass the class literal as a Class of T argument so the compiler fixes T and the run-time object can still make instances of it.

questions.q: A method loadAll takes a Class of T and returns a List of T. A caller writes a List of Invoice variable and assigns loadAll called with Customer.class. What happens?
questions.explain: The literal's type argument fixes the result type.
options: It compiles, since both are business classes
It compiles and fails with a ClassCastException
It compiles, with an unchecked warning only
Compile error: the result is a List of Customer
optionExplain: Related meaning does not matter; the types are checked exactly.
The mismatch is caught earlier, at compile time.
Nothing here is unchecked.
Right: the literal binds T to Customer, so the result type is a List of Customer.
questions.rule: Pass the class literal as a Class of T argument so the compiler fixes T and the run-time object can still make instances of it.

questions.q: Compared with passing a factory object (an object with a make method, written as an anonymous class or a factory class per type), which burdens does passing a class literal remove at each call? Select all that apply.
questions.explain: The token replaces per-type helper code without losing typing.
options: Writing an anonymous class at the call
Declaring a factory class for each element type
Casting each element of the returned collection
Declaring a type parameter on the method
optionExplain: Right: the class literal already exists for every class.
Right: no per-type helper class is needed.
The factory version was also typed, so no casts were removed.
Both versions declare a type parameter.
questions.teaches: A class literal exists for every class, so it replaces per-type factory code, such as anonymous classes or one factory class per type, at no cost in typing.
questions.rule: Pass the class literal as a Class of T argument so the compiler fixes T and the run-time object can still make instances of it.

questions.q: Which sentence best explains why a Class of T argument can do something a bare type variable T cannot?
questions.explain: The two roles complement each other.
options: A Class object is faster than a type variable
A Class of T is checked by instanceof, but T is not
The Class object exists at run time; T does not
T has no static type for the compiler to use
optionExplain: Speed is not the reason.
instanceof does not test type arguments.
Right: T guides the compiler, and the Class object supplies the run-time ability.
T does serve the compiler as a static type.
questions.teaches: T serves compile-time typing and the Class object serves run-time ability, so passing both gives code that is typed and still able to make objects.
questions.rule: Pass the class literal as a Class of T argument so the compiler fixes T and the run-time object can still make instances of it.

questions.q: True or false: If the tutorial select method took a raw Class and returned a raw Collection, a caller could still receive a Collection of EmpInfo without a cast or warning.
questions.explain: A raw return type is untyped, so the caller must cast or accept an unchecked warning.
questions.rule: Pass the class literal as a Class of T argument so the compiler fixes T and the run-time object can still make instances of it.

questions.q: A TreeSet of String is being built. A comparator written for Object works on any object. Which constructor parameter type lets the TreeSet use it?
questions.explain: A comparator for a wider type can order narrower items. The card next names the pattern.
options: Comparator of question mark super E
Comparator of E
Comparator of question mark extends E
A raw Comparator
optionExplain: Right: the comparator may be for E or any supertype of E.
An exact match refuses the Object comparator.
An extends bound admits narrower comparators, not wider ones.
Raw would work but drops the checking.
questions.rule: Use question mark super T on a parameter that only consumes values of T, and question mark extends T on one that only produces them.

questions.q: True or false: A sink of Object can be used where a sink of question mark super String is expected.
questions.explain: Object is a supertype of String, so a sink of Object satisfies the super bound.
questions.rule: Use question mark super T on a parameter that only consumes values of T, and question mark extends T on one that only produces them.

questions.q: A method copyInto takes a source list of Integer and a destination, and it only adds Integer values to the destination. The destination may be a list of Integer, Number or Object. Which destination parameter type accepts all three?
questions.explain: A destination that is only written to takes super.
options: List of question mark extends Integer
List of Integer
List of question mark
List of question mark super Integer
optionExplain: Extends admits only Integer and its subtypes.
An exact type admits only the first.
The bare wildcard would not allow adding Integer values at all.
Right: Integer, Number and Object are all Integer or a supertype of it.
questions.rule: Use question mark super T on a parameter that only consumes values of T, and question mark extends T on one that only produces them.

questions.q: A class Foo implements Comparable of Object. A max method whose bound is T extends Comparable of T rejects a collection of Foo. Why?
questions.explain: Using super in the bound accepts Foo.
options: Foo cannot be compared to any other object at all
Foo is not Comparable of Foo, which is demanded
Max needs a numeric type such as Integer or Double
Comparable of Object is not a real interface here
optionExplain: Foo can compare to any object, including other Foos.
Right: the exact bound asks for Comparable of Foo, but Foo only offers a wider comparison.
Nothing in the bound is about numbers.
Comparable of Object is a legitimate parameterization.
questions.teaches: A Comparable bound should use super: every Foo can be compared to Foo through its Object comparison, so Comparable of question mark super T accepts it.
questions.rule: Use question mark super T on a parameter that only consumes values of T, and question mark extends T on one that only produces them.

questions.q: Match each use to the wildcard the producer or consumer rule suggests.
questions.explain: A comparator consumes the items it compares, so the same rule applies beyond collections.
pairs: A list the method only reads from
A list the method only writes to
A list the method both reads and writes
The exact type T, with no wildcard
A comparator that orders T items
Question mark super T, since a comparator consumes items
questions.teaches: The producer or consumer test applies to any generic interface, such as a comparator that consumes the items it compares.
questions.rule: Use question mark super T on a parameter that only consumes values of T, and question mark extends T on one that only produces them.

questions.q: True or false: A method writeAll takes a parameter of type sink of question mark super String. A call passing a sink of String, rather than a sink of Object, still compiles.
questions.explain: The super bound includes T itself, so String is an acceptable supertype of String.
questions.rule: Use question mark super T on a parameter that only consumes values of T, and question mark extends T on one that only produces them.

questions.q: A set of unknown element type really holds Strings at run time. A generic method addToSet takes a set of T and a value of T. Does passing that set and the text abc compile?
questions.explain: The compiler works from declared types. The card next shows a similar call that does compile.
options: No: the compiler cannot guarantee abc fits
Yes, but with an unchecked warning attached
Yes: the set holds Strings, so abc fits there
No: Strings cannot be added to sets
optionExplain: Right: the compiler judges the declared types, and the unknown type might not be String.
No warning path exists; the call is refused.
The compiler cannot see the run-time contents.
Strings can be added to sets whose element type is String.
questions.rule: A wildcard-typed value can be passed to a generic method that works for every element type, because the compiler captures the unknown type; a separate value cannot be tied to it.

questions.q: True or false: The compiler decides whether a call with a wildcard-typed set is allowed from the set's declared type, not from the objects it holds at run time.
questions.explain: Compile-time checking uses declared types only.
questions.rule: A wildcard-typed value can be passed to a generic method that works for every element type, because the compiler captures the unknown type; a separate value cannot be tied to it.

questions.q: A variable u has the type Set of question mark. Sort each call by whether it is accepted.
questions.explain: Passing the whole structure through works because it ties no separate value to the unknown type. By the same reasoning, calls that insert a given value are refused.

items.t: unmodifiableSet applied to u
A generic method that only wraps its set argument in a read-only view, applied to u
A generic method that only returns its set argument unchanged, applied to u
addToSet applied to u and a String
addToSet applied to u and an Integer
Any generic method that inserts a caller-supplied value into its set argument, applied to u and a String

questions.rule: A wildcard-typed value can be passed to a generic method that works for every element type, because the compiler captures the unknown type; a separate value cannot be tied to it.

questions.q: A method addToSet takes a Set of T and a value of T, and unmodifiableSet takes a Set of question mark extends T. Why is unmodifiableSet accepted with a set of wildcard while addToSet is not?
questions.explain: Mismatch needs a second place that mentions T.
options: unmodifiableSet is declared as a static method
unmodifiableSet ties no separate value to T
addToSet changes the set's run-time class
unmodifiableSet has no type parameter of its own
optionExplain: Static methods get no special treatment.
Right: with one argument carrying T, nothing is left that could mismatch.
Adding does not change the run-time class.
It does have a type parameter T, which is what capture fills in.
questions.teaches: Safety depends on whether the signature relates a separate value to the element type; with only one argument carrying T there is nothing to mismatch.
questions.rule: A wildcard-typed value can be passed to a generic method that works for every element type, because the compiler captures the unknown type; a separate value cannot be tied to it.

questions.q: A generic method describe takes a set of T and an example value of T and only prints them. It is called with a set of wildcard and the text abc. Does the call compile?
questions.explain: Calls are judged from the method's declared types.
options: Yes: printing is a harmless operation
Yes: the body only prints and never inserts abc
No: the signature ties abc to the unknown type
No: describe may not take two parameters
optionExplain: Safety of printing is not what the check tests.
The compiler does not look inside the body to decide.
Right: the compiler checks the signature, not what the body does.
Two parameters are fine; the link to T is the issue.
questions.teaches: The compiler judges a call from the method's signature, so any signature tying a separate value to the element type is refused even if the body never inserts it.
questions.rule: A wildcard-typed value can be passed to a generic method that works for every element type, because the compiler captures the unknown type; a separate value cannot be tied to it.

questions.q: True or false: A method addToSet takes a Set of T and a value of T. If the set were declared as a Set of String instead of a Set of question mark, the call addToSet with that set and the text abc would compile.
questions.explain: With an exact element type, T is String and abc fits.
questions.rule: A wildcard-typed value can be passed to a generic method that works for every element type, because the compiler captures the unknown type; a separate value cannot be tied to it.

questions.q: An old method containsAll took a raw Collection and returned false when the elements differed. A new version takes a Collection of E, where E is the class's type parameter. What breaks?
questions.explain: A stricter parameter rejects calls that used to work. The card next gives the fix.
options: Nothing, since generics are only checked at run time
Old binaries throw an error when they are loaded
Callers become slower once the new version is used
Callers with another element type stop compiling
optionExplain: The check is made at compile time.
The stricter signature affects source, not the loading of binaries.
Speed is not the issue.
Right: the new parameter is stricter than the old contract.
questions.rule: When generifying a published method, keep every call it used to accept, keep its erasure identical, and do not narrow return types.

questions.q: Match each rule to what it protects.
questions.explain: Each rule protects one group of existing users: source callers, old binaries and old subclasses.
pairs: Calls the old method accepted still compile
Old compiled code still finds the method
questions.rule: When generifying a published method, keep every call it used to accept, keep its erasure identical, and do not narrow return types.

questions.q: An original method returns Object. A generic version with the bound T extends Comparable of question mark super T would erase to return Comparable. Adding ____ as the first bound restores the original erasure.
questions.explain: A type parameter with several bounds erases to its first bound.
questions.rule: When generifying a published method, keep every call it used to accept, keep its erasure identical, and do not narrow return types.

questions.q: The JDK's max takes a Collection of question mark extends T rather than a Collection of T. Why does that wildcard fit?
questions.explain: Compatibility and flexibility are separate fixes in one signature.
options: The method only writes to the collection, so extends applies
It was needed to keep the erasure the same
The method only reads from the collection, so extends applies (the producer rule)
Collections of T cannot be passed to methods
optionExplain: Writing would call for super, not extends.
The first bound fixes the erasure, and the wildcard leaves it unchanged.
Right: the producer rule gives extends for a read-only parameter.
A Collection of T can be passed to a method.
questions.teaches: Compatibility fixes, such as the first bound, and flexibility fixes, such as the extends wildcard, can appear together in one library signature.
questions.rule: When generifying a published method, keep every call it used to accept, keep its erasure identical, and do not narrow return types.

questions.q: A published class Invoice has a method copy declared to return Document. A library update changes it to return Invoice. A third party's class Receipt extends Invoice and overrides copy with the return type Document. What happens to Receipt?
questions.explain: Narrowing a return type in a published class can break outside subclasses.
options: It stops compiling: Document is not a subtype of Invoice
It compiles, but its copy method is ignored by callers
It compiles unchanged and overrides the method correctly
It runs, with a warning about covariant returns
optionExplain: Right: the override's return type must now fit the narrowed one, and a supertype does not.
Its source no longer compiles, so it never reaches the point of being ignored.
An override must be compatible with the new return type, and Document is wider.
The compiler reports an error, not a warning.
questions.teaches: An override returning the old, wider type is rejected once the base method's return type is narrowed, so third-party subclasses must change.
questions.rule: When generifying a published method, keep every call it used to accept, keep its erasure identical, and do not narrow return types.

questions.q: True or false: A method written fresh today, with no existing binaries, must still list Object as its first bound to preserve erasure.
questions.explain: The first bound matters for matching an old signature. With no old signature, no match is needed.
questions.rule: When generifying a published method, keep every call it used to accept, keep its erasure identical, and do not narrow return types.

questions.q: In the classic workflow, what does the compiler produce from your Java source file?
questions.explain: The compiler output is a file of bytecode that the java command runs. The card next shows the whole cycle.
options: A shorter text file with the comments removed
A class file containing bytecode
A copy of the JDK folder
A program that needs no Java tools at all
optionExplain: Compilers translate the code; they do not just trim the text, so the result is not readable source.
Right: javac writes a file ending in .class that holds bytecode.
The JDK is the toolset that includes the compiler; it is not the compiler's output.
The result is bytecode, which still needs the java command to run.
questions.rule: javac turns source into bytecode.

questions.q: The command that compiles Java source code into bytecode is called ____.
questions.explain: javac is the compiler from the JDK; it takes the full file name with the .java suffix.
questions.rule: Compile with javac.

questions.q: Put these steps in the classic order for a new file Notes.java.
questions.explain: You must have a source file before compiling, and a class file must exist before the java command can run it.
items: Write Notes.java in a plain text editor
Compile it with javac Notes.java
Run it with java Notes
questions.rule: Write, compile, then run.

questions.q: True or false: According to the tutorial, every Java program must pass through a separate javac step before it can run.
questions.explain: The tutorial says Java SE 11 and later can run a .java file directly, merging compile and run into one step. A merged step still compiles; it does not skip checking the code.
questions.rule: The separate compile step is the classic path, not the only one.
questions.teaches: Beyond the tutorial: merging steps does not remove compilation, so mistakes in the source are still caught before the program runs.

questions.q: Ivy compiles Counter.java, then edits a message in the source and saves it. She does not run javac again and types java Counter. What is expected from the classic cycle?
questions.explain: The java command runs the existing Counter.class, which was built from the earlier source. Only compiling again updates the class file.
options: The new message appears, because java notices the edit
A syntax error is reported for the edited line
The old message appears, because the class file is unchanged
The program refuses to start until it is renamed
optionExplain: java runs bytecode, not source, so it cannot see the edit in the classic cycle.
Syntax checking is done by javac when it compiles; java does not compile in this cycle.
Right: the class file still holds the old compiled code until javac runs again.
Names matter for finding the class, but an edit to the text does not change the name.
questions.rule: After editing the source, compile again before running.

questions.q: A tester's machine has only run-time tools (a JRE) and no compiler. Which file should you hand over so they can run your program?
questions.explain: Bytecode in the .class file is what the run-time tools execute, so no compiler is needed on the tester's side. Beyond the tutorial: the tester also needs the class file in a place where java can find it.
options: Counter.java, so the tester can compile it
The text editor you used to write it
Nothing, because java can only run code on the author's machine
Counter.class, the compiled bytecode
optionExplain: Compiling needs javac, which a JRE does not have.
The editor plays no part in running a program.
The run-time tools run bytecode on any machine that has them.
Right: bytecode runs with run-time tools alone.
questions.rule: Running needs bytecode and run-time tools; compiling needs the JDK.
questions.teaches: Beyond the tutorial: because compiling and running are separate, a finished class file can be sent to machines that have no compiler.

questions.q: True or false: when javac reports a syntax error, it still creates a class file that you can try to run.
questions.explain: According to the tutorial, errors stop the .class file from being created. The card next sorts the errors by step.
questions.rule: No class file after a compile error.

questions.q: Match each mistake to what it gets wrong.
questions.explain: Each mistake breaks a different rule from the tutorial: the compiler wants the suffix, the launcher wants the class name, and so on.
pairs: Gave a file name instead of the class name
Variable used before it is initialized
questions.rule: Each error has one specific fix.

questions.q: Sort each problem by the step where it shows up.
questions.explain: Compile-step problems involve javac and the source; run-step problems involve java, the class file and the entry point.

items.t: A missing semicolon on line 7
A variable read before it is initialized
javac typed with a name that lacks .java
javac reports an undeclared variable
java cannot find the class file in the current directory
java given Report.class instead of Report
A class with no main method
A stale CLASSPATH hiding the class

questions.rule: Compile problems concern source and javac; run problems concern the class and java.

questions.q: Lena compiled Tracker.java successfully in the folder project/src. She then opened a new prompt in the folder project and typed java Tracker, which reports that it cannot find the class. What does the tutorial suggest first?
questions.explain: java searches the current directory first, so the prompt must be in the folder holding Tracker.class. A good compile says nothing about where your prompt is.
options: Change to project/src, confirm with dir or ls, then rerun
Reinstall the JDK, then compile the file once more
Add .java to the end of the java command and run it again
Rewrite the source file to add a missing semicolon at line 1
optionExplain: Right: the class file is in project/src, and java looks in the current directory first.
The compile worked, so the JDK is not the problem.
java wants the class name; adding .java is a different mistake from the card.
A syntax error would have stopped the compile, which succeeded.
questions.rule: Run java from the folder that holds the class file.
questions.teaches: The dir or ls command lists the files in the current folder, so you can confirm the .class file is there before running java.

questions.q: Ana's program compiles with no errors, but when started the JVM reports there is no method to begin execution. Which description fits?
questions.explain: The compiler checks syntax and meaning; the start point is needed only when launching. So the compile can succeed while the program cannot run.
options: A semantic error, and no class file was created
A PATH problem, so javac is missing
A run-step problem: the class needs a main method
A CLASSPATH problem with the compile step
optionExplain: Semantic errors stop the class file from being created, but here the compile worked.
If javac were missing, the compile itself would not have happened.
Right: the tutorial says the JVM starts at a main method, and without one the program cannot run.
CLASSPATH concerns finding classes at run time, and the compile here succeeded.
questions.rule: Compiling well does not mean the program has a start point.
questions.teaches: Beyond the tutorial: a clean compile only shows the code is valid, not that the class is an entry point you can run.

questions.q: Raj's log reads: Step 1, javac Hello.java succeeded. Step 2, he typed java Hello.class and got an error. Which step went against the tutorial?
questions.explain: Compiling with the full file name was right. Running needs the class name without the suffix.
options: Step 1, because javac wants the name without any suffix
Step 2, because java wants a class name, not a file name
Both steps, because each command used a file name
Neither step; the failure came from a missing semicolon
optionExplain: javac wants the full file name including .java.
Right: the run command takes Hello, without .class.
Step 1 matches the rule, so only one step is wrong.
A syntax error would have stopped the compile in step 1, which succeeded.
questions.rule: javac takes a file name; java takes a class name.

questions.q: True or false: since JDK 11, the java command can compile and run a single source file in one step.
questions.explain: The tutorial says the launcher compiles the source and keeps the result in memory. The card next gives the conditions.
questions.rule: The launcher can compile in memory.

questions.q: When the java launcher runs a source file, the compiled classes are kept ____ rather than saved as class files.
questions.explain: The tutorial says the launcher compiles the file and holds the compiled classes in memory.
questions.rule: Source launch compiles in memory.

questions.q: Dev's file Shop.java defines class Helper (no main method) first, and class App (with main) second. He launches the file directly. What does the tutorial's rule predict?
questions.explain: The rule is that the first class defined in the file must contain main. Here the first class is Helper, which has none.
options: App runs, because the launcher searches for any main method
Both classes run in order
Shop runs, because the launcher uses the class named like the file
The launch fails because the first class has no main method
optionExplain: The tutorial ties the entry point to the first class, not to a search of the whole file.
The launcher starts one program entry point, not every class.
The file name does not choose the entry class under this rule.
Right: put the class with main first.
questions.rule: The first class in the file must hold main.

questions.q: True or false: launching a source file that uses only core JDK classes such as Scanner needs a classpath setting.
questions.explain: Core JDK classes need no classpath setup. The classpath tells the launcher where to find classes that are not part of the JDK.
questions.rule: Classpath is for non-JDK classes.
questions.teaches: Beyond the tutorial: your own team's jar of helper classes is also outside the JDK, so by the same reasoning it would need the classpath.

questions.q: Kofi wants a Unix tool he can run as ./greet by launching a source file like a script. Which items does the tutorial's recipe include? Select all that apply.
questions.explain: The recipe is a first line naming java and a source version, a file name without .java, and execute permission. Compiling first is not part of it.
options: A first line giving the java location and a source version
Saving the file as greet.java
Making the file executable with chmod +x
Saving the file as greet, with no .java extension
Compiling it with javac first
optionExplain: Right: that first line tells the system which program runs the file.
The tutorial says the file must not have a .java extension.
Right: execute permission lets the file run like a script.
Right: the extensionless name is required.
No class file is needed because the launcher compiles in memory.
questions.rule: Shebang line, no .java extension, execute permission.
questions.teaches: Beyond the tutorial: the first line works because the operating system hands the file to the program it names, which then compiles and runs it.

questions.q: Under JDK 22, Main.java in the folder work uses a class Person declared in package model. The file Person.java sits in work itself, not in work/model. What is expected?
questions.explain: The tutorial requires each file's directory path to match its package name, so Person.java in the wrong folder is not found.
options: The launcher finds Person anywhere in the folder tree under work
The launcher cannot find Person; its path must match the package
The launch works only if Person is also copied into the JDK folders
Main runs normally, but Person is skipped without any message
optionExplain: The tutorial ties lookup to the directory path matching the package.
Right: Person.java would need to be in work/model.
Core JDK folders are not where your own source goes.
A missing class is a failure, not a quiet skip.
questions.rule: Directory path must match the package name.

questions.q: True or false: in JShell, every statement you type must end with a semicolon.
questions.explain: The tutorial says missing semicolons are added automatically. The card next explains snippets and commands.
questions.rule: JShell adds missing semicolons.

questions.q: Match each JShell command to what it does.
questions.explain: Each command starts with a slash and does one job in managing the session.
pairs: Shows variables with type and value
Shows everything entered in the session
questions.rule: Slash commands manage the session.

questions.q: In JShell, Sam defined a method grade that treats 80 as a pass, and now wants the pass mark to be 85. What is the approach the tutorial shows?
questions.explain: Defining a method again with the same name replaces it, and the up arrow brings back earlier input for editing; /edit suits larger changes.
options: Run /reset and retype everything first
Define a second class that wraps the old one
Enter the method again with 85, replacing the old definition
Exit JShell, because definitions cannot change
optionExplain: That discards all snippets; nothing requires it for one change.
Wrapping adds clutter; redefinition is direct.
Right: a new definition replaces the old one.
Definitions can change within a session.
questions.rule: Redefine a snippet to replace it.

questions.q: True or false: /reload restarts the session and replays the earlier history, while /reset discards the snippets without replaying.
questions.explain: That is the tutorial's contrast. The -quiet option on /reload replays without showing output, though errors still appear.
questions.rule: Reload replays history; reset does not.
questions.teaches: Reload can run with -quiet so the replay hides normal output, but errors still show.

questions.q: Rae wants her own wording for the message after a method is created, so she tries to edit the built-in normal feedback mode. What does the tutorial say about this?
questions.explain: Only custom modes can be modified. She can create one with /set mode, copying normal, then change its text with /set format.
options: It works, since normal is the default mode of JShell
It works only inside a startup script that she loads
It fails because silent mode locks all other modes
Only a custom mode can be edited, so she should create one
optionExplain: Being the default does not make a mode editable.
Startup scripts do not change which modes are editable.
Silent mode is a feedback level, not a lock.
Right: create a custom mode, copying an existing one, then adjust it.
questions.rule: Make a custom mode; do not edit the built-in ones.
questions.teaches: A custom mode can start as a copy of an existing mode, so you change only the pieces you want.

questions.q: In JShell, /-n reruns an earlier input counting back from the latest one. Slash commands such as /list and /vars are not counted; only ____ are counted.
questions.explain: The tutorial notes that commands are not counted when /-n counts back, so only snippets (statements, declarations and expressions you entered) are counted.
questions.rule: /-n counts back through snippets only, not commands.
questions.teaches: Because commands are skipped, /-n always points at code you entered, so running /list or /vars in between does not shift the count.

questions.q: Roughly how often does a new Java feature release appear today?
options: Every two to three years, once the planned features are ready
Every six months, on a fixed calendar rhythm
Once a year, in the autumn
Whenever the language architects decide a release is ready
optionExplain: This was the older pattern, which is why it feels familiar, but it describes Java before 2017.
Right: since 2017 the platform ships feature releases on a six-month schedule, in March and September.
A yearly cycle sounds tidy, but the schedule has two releases a year, not one.
This is close to the old, readiness-driven approach, which the time-based schedule replaced.
questions.explain: Today's rhythm is two feature releases a year, although a guess based on older habits is understandable. The card next shows how the change came about.
questions.rule: Feature releases now follow a calendar.

questions.q: Since 2017, Java feature releases arrive on a time-based schedule about every ____ months.
questions.explain: The tutorial gives six months, with feature releases in March and September.
questions.rule: Six months, March and September.

questions.q: A small team dreads upgrading its JDK because past upgrades were big, risky projects. Using the tutorial's reasoning about the release rhythm, which plan fits best?
options: Skip every release and plan one large migration every ten years
Wait until a release has been out for two or three years, then migrate
Hold upgrades until the whole team can review everything by hand
Run automated tests against each new release so every step stays small
optionExplain: A single huge migration recreates the disruptive event the tutorial says the rhythm helps avoid.
Waiting for the old two-to-three-year interval misreads the schedule, which now delivers releases every six months.
Manual review of everything keeps upgrades slow and heavy; the tutorial points to automated testing instead.
Right: automated tests on each release make each upgrade a routine, small step.
questions.explain: The tutorial says upgrades can be tested automatically in pipelines, avoiding one disruptive event. Small regular steps follow from that.
questions.rule: Test each new release automatically to keep upgrades small.
questions.hint: What does the tutorial say pipelines can do with upgrades?

questions.q: Match each Java release to what the tutorial says about it.
pairs: Came in 2017, the year time-based releases began
questions.explain: The tutorial ties releases to dates and to notable changes, from the language to the runtime.
questions.rule: Releases carry dates, and not all headline work is syntax.
questions.teaches: A release can be notable for runtime work, such as the G1 improvements in Java 12, and not only for new syntax such as var.

questions.q: True or false: Suppose one planned feature is unfinished when a March release is due. Under a time-based model, the calendar date, not that feature, is what sets the timing of the release.
questions.explain: Time-based means the date comes first, which is the contrast the tutorial draws with the old readiness-driven releases. What then happens to the unfinished feature is not stated in the tutorial.
questions.rule: Time-based means the calendar sets the release.

questions.q: A manager asks how many years a given Java release will receive security fixes. The only source available is the tutorial's release-cadence section. What is the sound answer?
options: The tutorial gives no support periods, so another source is needed
Six years, since releases come every six months
Two to three years, as in the older release interval
One release cycle, because each release replaces the last
optionExplain: Right: the section covers the rhythm and its benefits, not maintenance periods.
This invents an arithmetic link between release frequency and support, which the tutorial never makes.
The old interval described how often features came, not how long anything was supported.
This guesses a support rule the tutorial does not state.
questions.explain: A schedule of when features arrive is a different matter from how long a release is maintained.
questions.rule: A release schedule does not tell you support length.
questions.teaches: A release schedule says when features arrive, not how long a release is maintained; the tutorial leaves support lifetimes out, so another source is needed.

questions.q: What does it mean when a Java feature is released as a preview?
options: It is final and will stay unchanged in every release that follows it
It is hidden from developers until the feature is completely finished
It is shared for feedback and may change before it becomes standard
It is a feature that is already scheduled to be removed later
optionExplain: Final features are the standard ones; a preview is the stage before that.
The point of a preview is the opposite of hiding: developers get to try it.
Right: previews are released to collect feedback and can change before being finalized.
Removal is not what preview means; the intent is to refine and often finalize the feature.
questions.explain: A preview is shared early so that developers can respond, which is why it can still be altered. The card next sets out the term.
questions.rule: A preview invites feedback and may still change.

questions.q: Preview features are released to gather ____ from developers before they become standard.
questions.explain: The tutorial gives feedback as the purpose of previews.
questions.rule: Previews exist to collect feedback.

questions.q: Match each term to what the tutorial says about it.
pairs: Released for feedback and may change before it is finalized
A time-based build published at jdk.java.net
Brings language features, many starting as previews
Expected to remain for a long time
questions.explain: Each term names a different stage or channel, and keeping them apart avoids mixing up what may change with what is meant to last.
questions.rule: Keep preview, early-access, Amber and standard apart.

questions.q: Nadia reads that a language feature in the current release is a preview. She plans a weekend prototype with it. Which expectation matches the tutorial?
options: Details may change before it is finalized, so the prototype may need edits later
The feature is final, so the prototype will compile unchanged in every later release
The feature disappears as soon as feedback has been given
Only the platform team is allowed to run previews
optionExplain: Right: the tutorial says preview features may change before they are finalized.
This treats a preview as standard, but only standard features are expected to remain.
Feedback is meant to improve a feature, and the tutorial does not say previews vanish after it.
Previews are released so that developers can try them, not just the platform team.
questions.explain: Because a preview may change before it is finalized, her prototype could need edits when the final form arrives.
questions.rule: Expect previews to move.

questions.q: A lead must choose how to use two things: a long-lived billing module and a throwaway experiment to give feedback on a new language idea. Which pairing follows the tutorial's distinction?
options: Preview features for billing, since previews are supported longest
Preview features for both, since feedback matters most in production
Standard features for the experiment, since previews cannot be tried
Standard features for billing and a preview for the experiment
optionExplain: The tutorial says standard features, not previews, are expected to remain for a long time.
Production code is where change is costly, so putting previews there inverts the tutorial's contrast.
Previews are released precisely so developers can try them, so they can be tried.
Right: long-lived code fits features expected to stay, and an experiment fits something open to change.
questions.explain: Standard features are expected to last, which suits long-lived code, while previews invite experiments and feedback.
questions.rule: Long-lived code suits standard features; experiments suit previews.
questions.teaches: Stability needs and feedback goals call for different choices, so the contrast of may change versus expected to remain can weigh risk (how a team should decide is beyond the tutorial).

questions.q: True or false: Java 8 was the last release to add major features, and later releases mostly fix bugs.
questions.explain: Later releases kept adding features, from language to runtime and tooling. The card next shows the tutorial's evidence.
questions.rule: Java has kept adding substantial features since Java 8.

questions.q: Match each goal to a feature the tutorial groups under it.
pairs: Safer work with non-Java code and data
questions.explain: The tutorial lists features since Java 8 by the purpose they serve.
questions.rule: Features are grouped by purpose.

questions.q: A developer reads that average G1 pauses fell to about 60 percent of Java 8's in the tutorial's benchmark. Her service uses a 4 GB heap and hand-tuned collector flags. What is the sound reading of the figure?
options: She will see exactly a 60 percent average pause on her own service, whatever her heap
It is a measured pattern for a 16 GB heap without tuning, so her result may differ
It is meaningless, because the benchmark compared different Java versions with each other
It applies only to ZGC and the tutorial says nothing about the G1 collector here
optionExplain: This treats one setup's result as a guarantee, which the stated conditions do not support.
Right: the conditions are part of the evidence, so her different heap and tuning mean her result needs checking.
Comparing versions is the whole point of the benchmark, so this dismisses it for no good reason.
The tutorial reports the 60 percent figure for Parallel and G1, not for ZGC.
questions.explain: The benchmark used a 16 GB heap and no tuning, so those conditions limit how far its numbers carry.
questions.rule: Benchmark figures belong to their setup.
questions.teaches: A benchmark number is tied to its setup, such as heap size and tuning, so applying it elsewhere is a hypothesis to test.

questions.q: A team runs a latency-critical service with a 128 GB heap and has memory to spare. Based on the tutorial benchmark, which choice fits?
options: Parallel, because it has the lowest footprint of all the collectors at 128 GB
G1, because its pauses stayed sub-millisecond at 128 GB with no extra footprint
ZGC, which kept sub-millisecond pauses at 128 GB but needs a higher footprint
Any collector, because pause times in Java 17 are identical for all of them
optionExplain: The tutorial says Parallel's overhead is similar to G1's, not the lowest of all.
The sub-millisecond result at 128 GB is reported for ZGC, not G1.
Right: low latency at a large heap is ZGC's strength in the benchmark, and a higher footprint is its price.
The benchmark shows ZGC pauses far below the others, so pauses are not identical.
questions.explain: ZGC kept sub-millisecond pauses at 128 GB, and the tutorial notes it pays for that with a larger footprint.
questions.rule: ZGC trades memory footprint for low pauses.

questions.q: A service runs on Java 8 with Parallel and moves to Java 17, where G1 is the default. Which statements follow from the tutorial footprint discussion? Select all that apply.
options: Footprint means native memory used by the collector structures
In Java 17, G1 overhead is roughly double its Java 8 level
Choosing ZGC would reduce footprint compared with G1
In Java 17, Parallel overhead is similar to G1 overhead, so the switch should not change memory use significantly
In the benchmark, G1 overhead dropped from about 10 percent to about 5 percent
optionExplain: Right: this is how the tutorial defines footprint.
The tutorial reports a drop, not a doubling.
The tutorial says ZGC has the higher footprint, as the cost of low latency.
Right: since Parallel and G1 have similar overhead in Java 17, a switch between them should not change memory use significantly.
Right: this is the benchmark's reported change for G1, which the tutorial calls relatively favorable.
questions.explain: Footprint is native memory used by collector structures, and the tutorial says Parallel overhead is similar to G1 overhead in Java 17. It also reports G1 overhead falling from about 10 to about 5 percent, and ZGC costing more footprint.
questions.rule: Footprint is a separate dimension from pause time.
questions.teaches: Pause time and footprint are separate dimensions, so a collector can win on one and lose on the other, and a single headline figure cannot settle a choice.

questions.q: A new language feature is released in a JDK version labelled as a preview feature. What does that label most likely tell you?
questions.explain: Preview means the team considers the feature complete enough to try, but it may still change after feedback. The card next shows the details.
options: It is complete as designed, but it may still change before it is permanent
It is an unfinished sketch that the JDK team knows does not work
It is permanent already, but only for paying customers of the JDK
It is a bug fix that is switched on automatically in every program
optionExplain: Right: a preview is believed fully specified and implemented, with room to change after feedback.
Plausible because previews feel risky, but the tutorial says they are believed to be fully specified and implemented.
Sounds like a licence tier, but preview is about stability of the design, not who may use it.
Previews are off by default and need switches, so they are not applied automatically.
questions.rule: Preview means try it and tell us, not finished forever.

questions.q: Only the ____ version of a feature is covered by the platform's long-term compatibility rules.
questions.explain: According to the tutorial, preview versions may change between rounds, so compatibility promises begin at the final version.
questions.rule: Compatibility promises start at the final version.

questions.q: A developer wants to publish a library to a public repository such as Maven Central. The library's code uses a language feature that is in preview in the JDK they build with. What does the tutorial advise?
