questions.explain: The tutorial warns that artifacts built with preview features run only on the specific Java feature release they were built for, so publishing them to a wide audience causes breakage.
options: Publish it, because any later JDK runs preview-built code
Do not distribute it, because it runs only on the release it was built for
Publish it only after removing the compile warning
Publish it, since a repository check confirms the feature is final
optionExplain: Seems natural because newer JDKs are usually friendly to old code, but preview-built output is tied to one feature release.
Right: such artifacts are bound to one feature release, so wide distribution is discouraged.
The warning only reports preview use; hiding it would not make the output portable.
Repositories do not check this, and the feature stays in preview regardless of publishing.
questions.rule: Do not distribute preview-built artifacts.

questions.q: True or false: a program compiled with a feature that is in preview in JDK 16 is guaranteed to run unchanged on JDK 17.
questions.explain: It is not guaranteed. Preview-built output is bound to its feature release, and feedback may have changed the feature by the next release, so code often has to be recompiled and sometimes edited.
questions.rule: Preview-built code is tied to its release; moving on means rebuilding.
questions.teaches: Upgrading the JDK means recompiling preview-based code, and the source may need edits if feedback changed the feature in between.

questions.q: Dana tries a preview feature and finds one rule awkward for her use case. According to the tutorial, how should she try to influence the feature?
questions.explain: Preview exists to gather feedback, and the tutorial points to the mailing list that the feature's JEP designates rather than social networks.
options: Send feedback to the mailing list named in the feature's JEP
Stay silent, since only final features can be changed
Post about it on social networks and wait
Rewrite the feature in her own project and ship that
optionExplain: Right: each JEP designates a mailing list for feedback on its feature.
Silence misreads preview: feedback is exactly what changes a feature before it is final.
Social posts are easy to make, but the tutorial says feedback belongs on the designated mailing list.
A private copy would not change the JDK feature, and the tutorial does not suggest it.
questions.rule: Send preview feedback to the mailing list named by the JEP.
questions.teaches: Each feature's JEP names its own feedback mailing list, so reporting is a defined step in the preview process.

questions.q: A new garbage collector appears in a JDK release, but it is not yet considered production-ready. How would you expect it to be enabled?
questions.explain: Features not yet production-ready are usually hidden behind explicit options. The card next shows the tutorial's three kinds and their switches.
options: It is on by default, and you switch it off if it causes problems
By unlocking experimental options, then adding its own option
By adding a requires line for it to a module descriptor file
By compiling the program with the compiler preview switch turned on
optionExplain: Unfinished features are not on by default, so there would be nothing to disable.
Right: this is the two-step pattern for experimental JVM features.
Module requires lines apply to modules, not to JVM collectors.
Preview switches concern the compiler and language or API features, not a collector in the JVM.
questions.rule: Experimental JVM features need an unlock plus their own option.

questions.q: Match each kind of nonfinal feature to what the tutorial says it mainly covers.
questions.explain: The three labels stage different parts of the platform: language and API features, the JVM, and new APIs and tools.
pairs: New Java language or API features
Potentially new APIs and JDK tools
questions.rule: Preview is language and API, experimental is JVM, incubating is APIs and tools.

questions.q: A modular application wants to use an incubating module called jdk.incubator.sample (an invented name). What does the tutorial say to do in its module descriptor?
questions.explain: Incubating modules must be requested explicitly, and in a modular application that means a requires or requires transitive directive.
options: Declare requires for the incubating module
Compile with the preview switch for the language
Pass the unlock option for experimental VM features
Nothing, because incubating modules are always resolved
optionExplain: Right: modular applications declare requires or requires transitive for the incubating module.
Preview concerns language and API features, not incubator modules.
That option belongs to experimental JVM features, a different kind.
Incubating modules are requested explicitly, so they are not picked up on their own.
questions.rule: Incubating modules are requested with requires, or --add-modules on the classpath.

questions.q: True or false: every experimental JDK feature goes through the same JEP 12 process as preview features.
questions.explain: The tutorial says no JEP governs experimental features; their process is an established HotSpot convention. JEP 12 governs preview features.
questions.rule: Preview has JEP 12; experimental follows a HotSpot convention.
questions.teaches: Experimental features are not governed by any JEP; their handling is an established HotSpot convention.

questions.q: A phone maker has three channels: a beta toggle for new app features, a hidden developer option for new hardware behaviour, and a separate labs app where each new interface must be added by hand. Which JDK kind best matches the labs app?
questions.explain: The labs app mirrors incubating modules, which sit in their own namespace and must be requested explicitly.
options: Preview features
Experimental features
Final features
Incubating modules
optionExplain: The beta toggle is the closer match: a switch for new language or API features.
The hidden developer option fits experimental VM options better.
Final features need no special request at all.
Right: incubating modules are separate and need an explicit request.
questions.rule: Incubating means separate and explicitly requested.
questions.teaches: The same idea holds for all three kinds: nothing unfinished is switched on without an explicit request from the developer.

questions.q: A language feature changed its syntax between two preview releases. What would drive such a change?
questions.explain: Previews exist so that developer experience can reshape a feature. The card next gives the tutorial's examples.
options: Developers leaving feedback after trying the preview
A rule that syntax is renamed after every release
Compiler vendors voting to change the names
Nothing, because previews cannot change once released
optionExplain: Right: feedback from developers is what drives changes between preview rounds.
No such renaming schedule is described; changes respond to feedback.
The tutorial describes JDK feedback processes, not vendor votes.
Preview features may change, which is the point of the label.
questions.rule: Feedback shapes previews.

questions.q: Put the stages of switch expressions in the order the tutorial gives them.
questions.explain: Switch expressions previewed in Java 12, again in Java 13, and became final in Java 14.
items: First preview in Java 12
Second preview in Java 13
Final feature in Java 14
questions.rule: Switch expressions: Java 12 preview, 13 preview, 14 final.

questions.q: A developer on JDK 16 compiles a sealed interface Shape that lists Circle and Square after permits, using the ordinary compile command with no preview switch. What does the tutorial say happens?
questions.explain: Sealed classes were in preview in JDK 16, so permits is not available without enabling preview.
options: It compiles silently
It compiles but warns
It compiles and ignores the permits clause
It fails because permits needs preview
optionExplain: Silent success would mean preview was unnecessary, which contradicts the tutorial.
The warning appears when preview is enabled, not when it is off.
Nothing in the tutorial suggests the clause is quietly dropped.
Right: without preview, permits is not available on JDK 16 and compilation fails.
questions.rule: Without the preview switch, preview syntax fails to compile.

questions.q: On JDK 16, a developer compiles the sealed Shape code with preview enabled and sees a warning. She then starts the program with the ordinary run command. What should she expect?
questions.explain: The tutorial states that running the classes also requires preview to be enabled.
options: It runs, since the compiled classes carry what they need
It runs after printing the warning again
It fails, because the run also needs preview enabled
It runs only on JDK 17
optionExplain: Plausible because compilation succeeded, but the tutorial says running needs preview too.
The warning belongs to compilation, and running without the switch is the problem.
Right: preview must be enabled at run time as well as compile time.
JDK 17 made sealed classes final, but this program was built for JDK 16 with preview.
questions.rule: Preview must be switched on at both compile time and run time.

questions.q: True or false: early access builds of work such as Project Loom follow the same regular preview feedback process as preview features.
questions.explain: The tutorial says such novel features may be unstable, so they do not use the regular feedback process. Each early access page names its own feedback list.
questions.rule: Early access builds sit outside the regular preview process.
questions.teaches: Each early access download page documents its limitations and names the mailing list for feedback on that build.

questions.q: Match each situation to the channel that best fits it.
questions.explain: The less final a channel is, the more a program built on it can break.
pairs: Run a service for years in production
Try a nearly finished language feature and report feedback
Test a novel project feature that may break between builds
Evaluate a new JDK tool API in its own namespace
questions.rule: Choose the channel by how much change you can tolerate.
questions.teaches: Choosing a channel is a risk decision: the less final the channel, the shorter the life of code written against it.

questions.q: A class has a non-static field called ticks. Two objects are created from it, and the ticks of the first object is changed. What happens to the ticks of the second object?
options: It changes too, because the field belongs to the class
It is unchanged: every object has its own copy
It is reset to zero, so that both objects agree
The program stops with a compile error
optionExplain: That describes a static field, which has one shared copy.
Right: a field declared without static belongs to each object separately.
Java does not reset one object because another changed.
Nothing here is a compile error; changing a field on one object is normal.
questions.explain: Without static, every object carries its own value. The card next names this kind and its three neighbours.
questions.rule: Each object has its own copy unless the field is static.

questions.q: True or false: A parameter such as args in main is classed by the tutorial as a field.
questions.explain: The tutorial counts parameters as variables, not fields. Fields are the ones that belong to a type, leaving out local variables and parameters.
questions.rule: Parameters are variables, not fields.

questions.q: A class declares static int games = 0; and int points; and its constructor runs games = games + 1. Three objects are created. Which statement is true afterwards?
options: games is a separate copy in each object, holding 1 in each
points is one shared copy, because every object has the same field name
games holds 3 only inside the constructor, because it is a local variable
games is one shared copy holding 3, and each object has its own points
optionExplain: That would be an instance variable; static removes the per-object copies.
Having the same name does not share the field; without static each object has its own.
A local variable is declared inside a method body; this one is declared in the class.
Right: the static field has one copy that every constructor call updates; points is an instance variable.
questions.explain: static gives exactly one copy of games, updated by all three constructor calls, while points exists once per object.
questions.rule: static means one copy for the whole class.

questions.q: Adding the keyword ____ to the declaration static int numGears = 6; makes the class variable a constant whose value does not change.
questions.explain: A static field with final is a constant: one copy, never changed.
questions.rule: static final makes a constant.
questions.teaches: Adding final to a class variable makes it a constant whose value never changes, which the tutorial writes with static and final together.

questions.q: Suppose static is removed from games in class Score, where int games = 0; and the constructor runs games = games + 1, and three objects are created. What does each object's games hold?
options: 1 in every object, because each has its own copy starting at 0
3 in every object, because they still share the count
0 in every object, because a constructor cannot change a field
1, 2 and 3 in the three objects, in creation order
optionExplain: Right: without static, every object starts its own copy at 0 and the constructor adds 1 once.
Sharing needs static; without it the copies are separate.
A constructor can assign fields; here each copy goes from 0 to 1.
That would need one shared counter to read from; separate copies cannot see each other.
questions.explain: Removing static turns the counter into an instance variable, so each object counts only its own constructor call.
questions.rule: No static means one copy per object.

questions.q: True or false: The declaration int count = 0; on its own is enough to tell you that count is a local variable.
questions.explain: The same text can be a field when written in a class body and a local variable when written inside a method. Position decides the kind.
questions.rule: Where it is written decides the kind.

questions.q: A constructor header reads Library(String owner). What is owner, according to the tutorial's list of kinds?
options: A class variable, since it is declared once in the header
An instance variable, since it will be stored in each Library object
A parameter, which is a variable but not a field
A local variable, since the constructor is a method-like body
optionExplain: Class variables use static in the class body, not a constructor header.
It is named in the header, so it is a parameter; it becomes a field only if the body copies it into one.
Right: owner is named in a signature, so it is a parameter.
Parameters are their own kind; local variables are declared inside the body.
questions.explain: The tutorial lists parameters as their own kind and notes that they also appear in constructors and exception handlers, not only in methods.
questions.rule: A name in a signature is a parameter.
questions.teaches: Parameters are also used by constructors and exception handlers, not only by methods.

questions.q: Which of these is not a legal Java variable name?
options: total_2
$price
2ndPlace
_x
optionExplain: Digits and underscores are allowed after the first character.
A dollar sign is allowed at the start, although it is discouraged.
Right: a name may not start with a digit.
An underscore is allowed at the start, although it is discouraged.
questions.explain: Names start with a letter, a dollar sign or an underscore. The card next gives the full rules.
questions.rule: A name may not start with a digit.

questions.q: True or false: In Java, the names speed and Speed refer to the same variable.
questions.explain: Names are case-sensitive, so the two differ.
questions.rule: Names are case-sensitive.

questions.q: A static final field holds the number of seats in a hall. Which name follows the tutorial's convention?
options: MAX_SEATS
maxSeats
max_seats
MaxSeats
optionExplain: Right: constants are written in capitals with underscores between words.
Camel case is for ordinary variables, not for constants.
The underscore is used only in capitals for constants.
Capitalising each word without underscores matches neither the camel case nor the constant style.
questions.explain: A static final field is a constant, so the convention is capital letters with underscores.
questions.rule: Constants: capitals with underscores.

questions.q: The tutorial advises against the dollar sign in your own names. Why might you still meet it in code you did not write?
options: It is needed to separate two words in a long name
The compiler requires it for every static field
It marks a constant in the same way as capitals
Some names are generated automatically and use it
optionExplain: Words are separated by camel case, not by a dollar sign.
No such rule exists; static fields are marked by the keyword.
Constants are marked by capitals and underscores.
Right: the tutorial notes that auto-generated names may contain a dollar sign.
questions.explain: The dollar sign is legal, and tools that generate code use it, but your own names should leave it out.
questions.rule: Legal does not mean recommended.
questions.teaches: Names generated automatically by tools may contain a dollar sign, even though your own names should avoid it.

questions.q: A teammate wrote the four declarations given as options. Which of them depart from the tutorial conventions? Select all that apply.
options: (a) int gearRatio;
(b) static final int numGears = 6;
(c) int s;
(d) int current_gear;
optionExplain: This is camel case for an ordinary variable, as recommended.
A constant should be NUM_GEARS, in capitals with underscores.
A cryptic abbreviation; the tutorial prefers a full word such as speed.
The underscore is meant for constants; an ordinary variable uses camel case, currentGear.
questions.explain: Only gearRatio is fully conventional. The other three compile, but they break the advice on constants, full words and underscores.
questions.rule: Style rules are about readers, not the compiler.

questions.q: A programmer writes an ordinary instance field as int SPEED; with no static or final. What is the best description of this?
options: It fails to compile, because capitals are reserved for constants
It compiles, but readers will take it for a constant
It compiles and becomes final automatically
It compiles, and the compiler warns that the name should be lower case
optionExplain: Capitals are a convention only; the compiler does not check them.
Right: capitals are a signal to readers, not a keyword.
Only the final keyword makes a field unchangeable.
The compiler does not check naming style, so it gives no such warning.
questions.explain: Writing a name in constant style does not change what the variable is; it only misleads anyone who trusts the style.
questions.rule: Style signals the intent but does not enforce it.
questions.teaches: The capital-letter style is only a signal to human readers; the final keyword, not the spelling, is what prevents change.

questions.q: Which of these is not one of Java's eight primitive types?
options: char
String
boolean
long
optionExplain: char is a primitive holding one 16-bit Unicode character.
Right: String is a class in java.lang, although it is used as if it were built in.
boolean is a primitive for true and false.
long is a primitive, the 64-bit whole-number type.
questions.explain: Eight keywords name the primitives, and String is not among them. The card next lists all eight.
questions.rule: String is a class, not a primitive.

questions.q: Match each whole-number type to its size.
questions.explain: Each whole-number type has twice the bits of the one before it: 8, 16, 32 and 64.
questions.rule: byte 8, short 16, int 32, long 64.

questions.q: A program stores the number of students in a class, at most 40, using the tutorial's default whole-number type. Which declaration does that?
options: boolean students = true;
double students = 31.0;
long students = 31L;
int students = 31;
optionExplain: boolean holds true or false, not a count.
double is the default decimal type, not a whole-number type.
long works for larger values but is not the default.
Right: int is the default whole-number type.
questions.explain: Default choices keep code predictable: int for whole numbers and double for decimals.
questions.rule: Default: int for whole numbers, double for decimals.

questions.q: According to the tutorial, how can Java SE 8 or later code treat an int as an unsigned number?
options: Call the unsigned helper methods in the Integer class
Use a char instead, since char cannot be negative
Declare the variable with a type called uint
It is not possible; int is always signed
optionExplain: Right: the tutorial names methods such as Integer.compareUnsigned for unsigned work.
char is for characters; the tutorial does not offer it as an unsigned int.
The tutorial names no such type; the primitives are the eight keywords.
int is signed in storage, but SE 8 added library methods for unsigned use.
questions.explain: The int type itself stays signed, but Integer methods let you treat its 32 bits as 0 up to 4,294,967,295.
questions.rule: Unsigned work goes through Integer and Long methods.
questions.teaches: Java SE 8 added methods in the Integer and Long classes, such as compareUnsigned and divideUnsigned, so int can stand for 0 to 4,294,967,295.

questions.q: A program must hold an exact money amount such as 19.99. Which choice does the tutorial recommend?
options: float, because it is the smallest decimal type
double, because it is the default decimal type
The BigDecimal class
char, with one character per digit
optionExplain: Floating-point types should not hold precise values such as currency.
Default does not mean exact; double is also floating point.
Right: the tutorial points to java.math.BigDecimal for precise values.
char holds a single Unicode character, not a number type for arithmetic.
questions.explain: Floating-point values are approximations; for exact amounts the tutorial recommends BigDecimal.
questions.rule: Exact amounts: BigDecimal, not float or double.

questions.q: A kiosk counts waiting print jobs, from 0 to 50000. Which of char and short can hold 50000?
options: Both, since each is 16 bits
Only short, because it is a number type and char is not
Only char, whose range is 0 to 65,535
Neither; both would need int
optionExplain: Both are 16 bits, but short is signed and so tops out at 32,767.
char is a 16-bit unsigned range and can hold the number, though it is meant for characters.
Right: short stops at 32,767, while char covers 0 up to 65,535.
char's range reaches 65,535, which includes 50000.
questions.explain: Size alone does not give range: short is signed, char is not.
questions.rule: Check the range, not just the bit count.
questions.teaches: char is a 16-bit type with range 0 to 65,535, so it can hold counts that short (up to 32,767) cannot, though it exists for characters.

questions.q: True or false: The tutorial gives boolean a precise size of exactly one bit.
questions.explain: The tutorial says the size of boolean is not precisely defined; it only holds true or false.
questions.rule: boolean has two values, but no stated size.

questions.q: A class has an int field that no code ever assigns. What does it hold?
options: null
Whatever was left in memory
Nothing; reading it is a compile error
optionExplain: Right: fields get a default, and for int it is zero.
null is the default for objects such as String, not for primitives.
The compiler sets a defined default; nothing is left over.
That is the rule for local variables, not for fields.
questions.explain: Fields are initialised for you. The card next gives the full list and one exception.
questions.rule: Fields get defaults.

questions.q: A whole-number literal with the suffix ____ is of type long.
questions.explain: A whole-number literal is long when it ends with L or l, and the tutorial prefers uppercase because lowercase l looks like the digit 1.
questions.rule: Suffix L means long.

questions.q: Which of these are valid declarations? Select all that apply.
options: int count = 1_000_;
long step = 15_L;
int mask = 0b1010_0101;
double ratio = 2._75;
optionExplain: Underscores between digits are allowed.
An underscore may not end a number.
An underscore may not come before the L suffix.
Underscores may separate digits of a binary literal too.
An underscore may not sit beside a decimal point.
questions.explain: Underscores are fine only between digits, not at an end, beside a decimal point or before a suffix.
questions.rule: Underscores go between digits, nowhere else.

questions.q: A programmer needs a char literal for a character that is hard to type on their keyboard. Which method does the tutorial name?
options: Using the 0x prefix on a char variable name
Writing the character name in double quotes
Writing the decimal code after a dollar sign
A Unicode escape: backslash, u, four hex digits
optionExplain: 0x is a prefix for whole-number literals, not a way of naming characters.
Double quotes make a String literal, not a char.
Dollar signs have no such meaning in literals.
Right: the tutorial shows an escape such as the one for the character with code 0108.
questions.explain: A Unicode escape lets any code unit be written with plain keys.
questions.rule: Unicode escapes can stand for characters you cannot type.
questions.teaches: Char and String literals can hold a Unicode escape, a backslash followed by u and four hex digits; the tutorial adds that such escapes also work outside literals, even in identifiers.

questions.q: What happens when this code is compiled? class Box { int w; void show() { int h; System.out.println(w + h); } }
options: It compiles and prints 0, since both are int
Compile error: h is read before it has a value
Compile-time error, because the field w has no value
It compiles and prints null
optionExplain: Only the field w gets a default; the local h does not.
Right: a local variable has no default, so reading it unassigned is an error.
Fields get defaults, so w is fine.
int values are never null, and a local is not defaulted anyway.
questions.explain: Fields are defaulted but locals are not, so the compiler stops at h.
questions.rule: Fields have defaults; locals do not.

questions.q: Which of these assignments is not allowed, according to the tutorial's description of the null literal?
options: String name = null;
int stock = null;
Object item = null;
String[] rows = null;
optionExplain: String is a class, a reference type, so null is allowed.
Right: null can go to reference types but not to primitives.
Any reference type can be set to null.
An array variable refers to an array object and can be null.
questions.explain: null marks that an object is unavailable, so it only fits reference types.
questions.rule: null is for objects, not for primitives.
questions.teaches: The null literal can be assigned to any reference type but not to a primitive; its main use is to show that an object is unavailable.

questions.q: An array is created to hold 10 integers. What is the index of its last element?
optionExplain: That would be the eleventh element.
Index 1 is the second element.
That is beyond the end by two.
Right: counting starts at 0, so ten elements run from 0 to 9.
questions.explain: Indexing begins at 0. The card next states this and the length rule.
questions.rule: The first index is 0.

questions.q: True or false: After the declaration int[] data; the variable data already refers to an array that can hold values.
questions.explain: A declaration only says the variable will refer to an array. new, or a braces list, creates it.
questions.rule: Declaring is not creating.

questions.q: A String array has 6 elements, indexed from 0. The last valid index is ____.
questions.explain: Six elements occupy indexes 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5.
questions.rule: Last index is length minus one.

questions.q: Which of these is a valid declaration of an array variable?
options: int[] marks;
int[10] marks;
int marks[10];
array int marks;
optionExplain: Right: the size is not part of the type, so the brackets are empty.
A size does not belong in the declaration.
Size is not part of a declaration in either bracket position.
Java has no array keyword; brackets mark an array type.
questions.explain: Size belongs to creation, not to the type.
questions.rule: Brackets in a declaration stay empty.
questions.teaches: The size is not part of an array's type, so a declaration has empty brackets; the length is given only when the array is created.

questions.q: int[] odd = {1, 3, 5, 7}; and later code needs room for a fifth value. What does the fixed-length rule imply?
options: Assigning odd[4] makes the length 5 automatically
odd.length changes when a value is added with a method call
A new, larger array is created and the values moved
The braces shortcut can be repeated to extend the same array
optionExplain: The length cannot grow by assigning.
Arrays have no way to grow; length is set at creation.
Right: the length is set at creation, so a bigger array means a new one.
The shortcut creates a new array each time it is used.
questions.explain: No operation lengthens an existing array, so growth means a new array and copying.
questions.rule: Fixed length means copy into a bigger array.

questions.q: A weather app keeps 7 daily temperatures as decimals and must set the fourth day's value to 21.5. Which code does that?
options: double[] temps = new double[7]; temps[4] = 21.5;
double temps = new double[7]; temps[3] = 21.5;
double[] temps = new double[7]; temps[3] = 21.5;
double[] temps = new double[3]; temps[7] = 21.5;
optionExplain: Index 4 is the fifth day.
Without brackets the variable is a single double, not an array.
Right: seven slots of double, and the fourth day has index 3.
The array is too short, and 7 is not a valid index of it.
questions.explain: The same array patterns work for double, and the index is one less than the day number.
questions.rule: Element type is free; the index still starts at 0.
questions.teaches: The fourth day has index 3, so an array of seven elements uses indexes 0 to 6.

questions.q: A method copies the range from index 1 up to index 3 of the array 10, 20, 30, 40, 50. Which values does a typical Java range copy return?
optionExplain: Right: the first index is included and the last index is left out.
That starts at index 0, not 1.
That starts at index 2 and ends one element later than the range asked for.
That would include index 3, which the range stops before.
questions.explain: Java ranges include the start and exclude the end. The card next shows the exact tool.
questions.rule: Range copies include the start and exclude the end.

questions.q: True or false: System.arraycopy creates the destination array for you.
questions.explain: The destination must already exist. Arrays.copyOfRange is the tool that creates and returns a new array.
questions.rule: arraycopy fills an existing array.

questions.q: int[][] grid = { {1, 2}, {3, 4, 5}, {6} }; What are grid.length and grid[1].length?
options: 2 and 3
3 and 2
6 and 3
3 and 3
optionExplain: grid has three rows, not two.
grid[1] is the second row, which has three values.
Six counts all values, but length counts the rows.
Right: three rows, and the second row holds 3, 4 and 5.
questions.explain: The outer length counts rows; each row's length is read separately, which is why jagged arrays work.
questions.rule: Outer length counts rows; each row has its own length.

questions.q: A program wants the position of a value in an int array whose values are in no particular order. What does the tutorial say binarySearch needs?
options: The array must hold no repeated values
The array must be sorted
The array must be two-dimensional
The array must have been created with the braces shortcut
optionExplain: No such condition is given.
Right: the tutorial says it finds a value's index in a sorted array.
It works on a one-dimensional sorted array.
How it was created does not matter.
questions.explain: Sort first, for example with Arrays.sort, then search.
questions.rule: binarySearch needs a sorted array.
questions.teaches: binarySearch is meant for a sorted array, so an unordered array should be sorted (for example with Arrays.sort) before it is searched.

questions.q: src holds 4, 5, 6, 7, 8 and dst is created as new int[4]. After System.arraycopy(src, 1, dst, 0, 2) the value dst[1] is ____.
questions.explain: Two elements are copied from src position 1: the values 5 and 6, into dst positions 0 and 1. dst[1] is 6.
questions.rule: Source start, then destination start, then count.

questions.q: Data holds 10, 20, 30, 40, 50, 60, 70, 80. A developer wants the values at indexes 3, 4 and 5 and calls Arrays.copyOfRange(data, 3, 5). What is wrong, and what fix gives the three values?
options: The start is excluded, so only indexes 4 and 5 come back; use 2 and 5
The end is excluded, so only two values come back; use 3 and 6
Nothing is wrong; both ends are included
The result has no fixed length; use System.arraycopy
optionExplain: The start is included, not excluded.
Right: index 5 is left out, so the end must be 6.
The end index is excluded, so index 5 is missing.
The result has a fixed length, namely end minus start.
questions.explain: From is included and to is excluded, so the number of values is to minus from.
questions.rule: Ask for the index after the last one you want.
questions.teaches: The length of the copy is to minus from, so choose to as one past the last index wanted.

questions.q: Inside a method, var count = 12; is written. What type does count have?
options: A type decided later, which can change as the program runs
The type var
Object, the most general type
int, inferred from the literal 12
optionExplain: var does not make a changing type.
var is not a type; it asks the compiler to infer one.
The compiler infers the specific type from the value.
Right: the initializer is an int literal, so count is an int.
questions.explain: The compiler reads the initializer and fixes the type. The card next states the full rule.
questions.rule: var infers a fixed type from the initializer.

questions.q: True or false: After var total = 10; the variable total can later hold the text hello.
questions.explain: The type is inferred once, as int, and then fixed. var is not a changing type.
questions.rule: The inferred type stays fixed.

questions.q: Which declaration compiles inside a method body?
options: var c = 4.5;
var a;
var b = null;
var[] d;
optionExplain: Right: the initializer is a double literal, so the type can be inferred.
No initializer means no way to infer a type.
null alone has no type, so the compiler has nothing to infer from.
Still no initializer, so there is nothing to infer from.
questions.explain: var needs a typed initializer at the declaration.
questions.rule: No initializer, or only null, means no var.

questions.q: In a method, strings is a List of String. In the loop header for (var element : strings), what type is inferred for element?
options: List of String, the type of strings itself
Object, because var always picks the widest type
String, from the type of the list's items
Nothing; var cannot appear in a for statement
optionExplain: The loop variable stands for one item, not the whole list.
var picks the specific inferred type.
Right: the loop variable gets the element type of the list.
The tutorial's example uses var in a for statement.
questions.explain: var also works in a for statement, where the loop variable takes its type from the iterated collection. The tutorial's example for a try-with-resources works the same way.
questions.rule: var also works in for headers and try-with-resources.
questions.teaches: Besides ordinary local declarations, the tutorial's examples use var in a for statement and in a try-with-resources statement, inferring the type from the collection or resource.

questions.q: Class Report contains the four lines given as options. Which lines fail to compile because of var? Select all that apply.
options: (a) var title = 7; as a field
(b) void show(var copies) { }
(c) var n = 2; inside show
(d) the class name Report
optionExplain: var is not allowed for fields.
var is not allowed for method parameters.
This is a local variable with an initializer, which is allowed.
The class name has nothing to do with var.
questions.explain: var is limited to local variables; fields and parameters need explicit types.
questions.rule: Only local variables may use var.

questions.q: A payment method declares var fee; and then sets it in both branches of an if-else, to 0 for members and 5 for others. Does it compile?
options: Yes, but fee can then hold only the values 0 or 5, nothing else
Yes; both branches give an int, so the compiler infers int
No; the type is inferred at the declaration, which has no initializer
No; var is not allowed for a variable that is named fee
optionExplain: It does not compile, so no such restriction arises.
The compiler decides at the declaration, not from later assignments.
Right: assigning later does not help, since the type is chosen at the declaration.
The name has no effect; the missing initializer is the fault.
questions.explain: Inference happens at the declaration, so every path assigning later still leaves the declaration without a type.
questions.rule: Inference needs the initializer at the declaration itself.
questions.teaches: The compiler infers a type at the point of declaration only, so assignments that come later cannot supply one, even when every path assigns the same type.

questions.q: What value does 2 + 3 * 4 have in Java?
optionExplain: Right: the multiplication runs before the addition.
That adds first, which multiplication's higher precedence prevents.
That would multiply the whole sum, which needs parentheses.
That adds all three numbers and ignores the operator.
questions.explain: Multiplication binds tighter than addition. The card next gives the full order.
questions.rule: Multiplication binds tighter than addition.

questions.q: True or false: x += 5 has the same effect as x = x + 5.
questions.explain: A compound assignment joins an operator with =, so it expands to the longer form.
questions.rule: x op= y means x = x op y.

questions.q: int n = 7; int m = n++ * 2; After these lines, what are n and m?
options: n is 8 and m is 16
n is 7 and m is 14
n is 7 and m is 16
n is 8 and m is 14
optionExplain: That multiplies the new value, which is the prefix behaviour.
Postfix does change n; the increment happens.
That mixes both mistakes.
Right: postfix gives the original 7 to the multiplication and then raises n to 8.
questions.explain: Postfix x++ yields the original value, which is 7, so m is 14; afterwards n has become 8.
questions.rule: Postfix yields the old value, prefix the new.

questions.q: int r = 100 / 10 % 4 * 3; The value of r is ____.
questions.explain: Division, remainder and multiplication share a row, so they run left to right: 100 / 10 is 10, 10 % 4 is 2, and 2 * 3 is 6.
questions.rule: Same-row operators go left to right.
questions.teaches: Associativity is part of the answer: grouping the same operators differently, as in 100 / (10 % 4) * 3, gives 150 instead of 6.

questions.q: int k = 4; int j = k-- - 1; gives j = 3. If k-- is changed to --k, what is the new value of j?
options: 3, because the change happens afterwards in both cases
2, because prefix uses the decreased value 3
4, because the decrement is ignored
5, because the minus signs cancel
optionExplain: Prefix changes k before its value is used.
Right: --k yields 3, and 3 - 1 is 2.
The decrement is applied; it is the value used that differs.
They do not cancel; one is a decrement and one is subtraction.
questions.explain: Prefix yields the new value; postfix the original.
questions.rule: Prefix before use, postfix after use.

questions.q: True or false: In a pay formula, int pay = base + bonus / 10; and int pay = base + (bonus / 10); give the same value.
questions.explain: Division already binds tighter than addition, so the parentheses do not change the value; the tutorial still recommends them for readability.
questions.rule: Matching parentheses document intent without changing results.
questions.teaches: Parentheses can also change the result: (base + bonus) / 10 differs from base + bonus / 10, so add them where they match the intent.

questions.q: In the expression flag1 && flag2, flag1 is false. What happens to flag2?
options: It is evaluated first, to make sure it is safe
It is skipped, since the result is settled
It is evaluated anyway and then ignored
The program stops with a compile error
optionExplain: Evaluation goes left to right, so flag1 comes first.
Right: false AND anything is false.
The tutorial says the second operand is evaluated only when needed.
Nothing is wrong with the code; the operator simply stops early.
questions.explain: Short-circuiting skips the right side when the left side settles the result. The card next names it.
questions.rule: The left side can settle && and skip the right.

questions.q: The ternary operator takes ____ operands.
questions.explain: The ternary has a condition and two values, so three operands.
questions.rule: Condition, value if true, value if false.

questions.q: int a = 0; boolean r = (a != 0) && (++a != 0); After this line, what is a?
options: 1, because ++a runs first
The code fails to compile
2, because both sides increase it
0, because ++a is skipped
optionExplain: Evaluation goes left to right, and the left side already settles the result.
The code is valid Java; short-circuit evaluation is a run-time rule, not a compile-time error.
Only one increment exists, and it is skipped.
Right: the left side is false, so the right side is never evaluated.
questions.explain: Because a != 0 is false, && skips the right side, including its increment.
questions.rule: A skipped operand has no side effects.

questions.q: True or false: If s holds null, then s instanceof String is true.
questions.explain: The tutorial states that null is an instance of no type, so instanceof gives false for it.
questions.rule: instanceof is false for null.
questions.teaches: null is not an instance of any type, so instanceof returns false for it rather than failing.

questions.q: int a = 0; boolean r = (a != 0) || (++a != 0); What are a and r afterwards?
options: a is 1 and r is true
a is 0 and r is true
a is 0 and r is false
a is 1 and r is false
optionExplain: Right: the left side is false, so || evaluates ++a, which gives 1, and 1 != 0 is true.
r can be true only if the right side ran, which also changes a.
The left side is false, so || must still look at the right side.
After ++a, the test 1 != 0 is true.
questions.explain: || skips its right side only when the left side is true. Here the left side is false, so the right side runs.
questions.rule: || skips the right side when the left is true.

questions.q: Which task fits the ternary operator, according to the tutorial's advice?
options: Running several statements in one of two branches
Updating a running total and printing a log line when a flag is set
Choosing between two badge texts for a score
Calling a method that changes stored data in one branch only
optionExplain: The ternary yields a value; several statements need a block.
That needs statements and side effects, so an if-else is clearer.
Right: a compact choice of two values with no side effects.
A side-effecting call is the case the tutorial steers away from.
questions.explain: The ternary suits a choice between two values; anything with side effects reads better as if-else.
questions.rule: Ternary for values, if-else for actions.
questions.teaches: The ternary produces a value, so it fits where a value is needed, such as an assignment; work that changes things belongs in an if-else.

questions.q: Which line, written inside a method, is a valid statement?
options: x;
optionExplain: An addition produces a value but is not a complete instruction.
A bare variable name is not a statement.
Right: an increment followed by a semicolon is an expression statement.
A bare literal is not a statement.
questions.explain: Only certain expressions become statements. The card next explains the three kinds of statement.
questions.rule: Only some expressions make statements.

questions.q: Match each term to its meaning.
questions.explain: Each term names a different unit: a value, a variable declaration, a group, and a steering statement.
questions.rule: Expression yields a value; statement does a job; block groups statements.

questions.q: n is a double. What is the type of the expression (n = 5)?
options: double, the type of the left operand
int, because 5 is an int literal
boolean, because it looks like a comparison
It has no type, because it is a statement
optionExplain: Right: an assignment gives a value of its left operand's type.
The type follows the left operand, not the literal.
A single = is an assignment, not a comparison.
It is an expression, and so has a value and a type.
questions.explain: The tutorial's own example, cadence = 0, is an int expression for the same reason.
questions.rule: An assignment has the type of its left side.

questions.q: All variables are ints. Which expression gives the same result however its parts are grouped?
options: x + y / z
(x + y) / z
x / y + z
x * y * z
optionExplain: Mixing addition and division makes the result depend on order.
The parentheses show that regrouping would change the result.
Mixed division and addition again depends on order.
Right: the tutorial notes that order does not matter for multiplication.
questions.explain: Chains of multiplication can be grouped in any way, while mixed addition and division cannot.
questions.rule: Order matters when operators are mixed.
questions.teaches: The tutorial notes that the order of evaluation does not matter for a chain of multiplications but does matter once addition and division are mixed.

questions.q: A tester says: 0.1 * 3 is 0.3 in mathematics, so a double check a == 0.3 on that product must be true. What is the flaw?
options: A double cannot be compared with a decimal literal
Floating-point rounding can make it false
The check needs = instead of ==
The product is an int, which cannot equal 0.3
optionExplain: Comparison is allowed; the trouble is rounding.
Right: the tutorial warns that floating-point arithmetic can surprise.
A single = would assign rather than compare.
0.1 is a double, so the product is a double.
questions.explain: Doubles store decimals approximately, so equality with an exact-looking literal may fail.
questions.rule: Do not trust floating-point equality.

questions.q: Each line ends with a semicolon. Which are valid expression statements? Select all that apply.
options: price * qty;
discount = 5;
list.clear();
new Order();
qty + 1;
optionExplain: A product is a value, not a complete instruction.
An assignment qualifies.
A method invocation qualifies.
Object creation qualifies.
A sum alone does not qualify.
questions.explain: Assignments, increments and decrements, method invocations and object creation can stand as statements. Plain arithmetic cannot.
questions.rule: Only four kinds of expression make statements.
questions.teaches: Only assignments, uses of ++ or --, method invocations and object creation qualify as expression statements.

questions.q: A do-while loop's test is false the very first time it is checked. How many times does its body run?
options: 0 times
1 time
2 times
It depends on the body
optionExplain: That is true of a while loop, which tests first.
Right: a do-while tests at the bottom, so the body runs once before the first test.
Nothing makes it run a second time when the test is false.
The test alone decides repetition here.
questions.explain: The test comes after the body in a do-while. The card next compares it with while.
questions.rule: A do-while body runs once before its first test.

questions.q: True or false: The body of a while loop can run zero times.
questions.explain: A while loop tests first, so if the test is false at the start the body is skipped.
questions.rule: while tests before the body.

questions.q: int n = 0; do { n = n + 3; } while (n == 0); After the loop, n is ____.
questions.explain: The body runs once, making n 3. The test n == 0 is then false, so the loop ends.
questions.rule: A do-while body runs before its first test.

questions.q: After the loop for (int i = 0; i != 3; i++) { } ends, a later line in the same method uses i. What happens?
options: It compiles and i is 3
It compiles and i is 0, because the loop resets it afterwards
It compiles but i is undefined at runtime, as in some languages
It fails to compile; i exists only inside the loop
optionExplain: The loop variable is not available after the loop.
Nothing resets it; it simply is not in scope.
Java reports the problem at compile time.
Right: a variable declared in the initialization is scoped to the loop.
questions.explain: Declaring the counter in the for header limits its lifetime to the loop, which the tutorial says reduces errors.
questions.rule: A for counter lives only in its loop.
questions.teaches: A variable declared in the initialization part of a for loop is scoped to the loop, which limits its lifetime and reduces errors.

questions.q: int[] v = {3, 8, 3, 5}; int c = 0; for (int x : v) { if (x != 3) { continue; } c++; } leaves c at 2. What if continue is replaced by break?
options: c is 1, because the loop stops at the first 8
c is 2, because break also skips only one pass
c is 0, because break skips the first 3
c is 4, because break counts every item
optionExplain: Right: the first 3 counts, then 8 triggers break and ends the loop.
break ends the whole loop, not one pass.
The first value, 3, is counted before the 8 is reached.
Only values equal to 3 are counted.
questions.explain: continue skips one iteration; break leaves the loop altogether.
questions.rule: continue skips a pass; break ends the loop.

questions.q: Nested loops search a grid for 9. Inside the inner loop, if (grid[r][c] == 9) { break; } runs. The outer loop still keeps going with the next row. Without leaving the method, which fix stops both loops?
options: Replace break with continue
Add a second plain break after the inner loop's closing brace
Label the outer loop and use a labeled break
Remove the inner loop's braces
optionExplain: continue only skips to the next pass of the inner loop.
That would stop the search after the first row even when 9 is not found.
Right: it ends the labeled outer statement and resumes after it.
That changes the structure without stopping the outer loop.
questions.explain: A plain break leaves only the innermost loop; a labeled break can reach the outer one.
questions.rule: A label lets break reach an outer loop.

questions.q: A shop checks each order (outer loop) and each of its items (inner loop). If any item is out of stock, the whole order is skipped and the next order is processed. Which statement in the inner loop does that?
options: break, which ends the inner loop and still processes the order
A plain continue, which skips only that item
A labeled continue naming the outer loop
return, which leaves the method after the first bad order
optionExplain: The order would still be processed afterwards.
The remaining items would still be checked, and the order not skipped.
Right: it skips the rest of the current order and starts the next one.
That would also drop all later orders.
questions.explain: A labeled continue skips the current iteration of the labeled outer loop.
questions.rule: Labeled continue jumps to the next pass of an outer loop.
questions.teaches: A labeled continue skips the current iteration of the outer loop that carries the label, just as a labeled break ends that outer loop.

questions.q: In a classic switch on an int, case 1 has no break, and the selector is 1. What runs?
options: Case 1 and the code below it, until a break
Nothing, because a break is required
Only the default section, since no break exists
Only the statements of case 1
optionExplain: Right: execution falls through.
A break is not required; it only stops the run.
default runs only when no case matches.
Without a break, execution continues past the end of case 1.
questions.explain: Without break, the run continues into later labels. The card next names this fall-through.
questions.rule: Without break, execution falls through.

questions.q: True or false: A switch statement may use a selector of type long.
questions.explain: The allowed selectors are byte, short, char, int, their wrappers, enums and String. boolean, long, float and double are not allowed.
questions.rule: Selector: small integers, enums or String.

questions.q: int m = 2; int t = 0; switch (m) { case 1: t += 1; case 2: t += 10; case 3: t += 100; break; case 4: t += 1000; } What is t afterwards?
optionExplain: That would need a break after case 2.
Case 1 does not match, so 1 is never added.
The break after case 3 stops the run before case 4.
Right: case 2 matches, falls through into case 3, and the break then stops.
questions.explain: Match at case 2, fall through to case 3, stop at its break.
questions.rule: Trace from the matching label to the next break.

questions.q: String cmd = "STOP"; switch (cmd) { case "stop": run = false; break; default: run = true; } Does the stop case match?
options: Yes, because switch ignores letter case
No; matching works like equals, which is case-sensitive
No, because String selectors are not allowed
Yes, but only if the case is followed by a break statement
optionExplain: A String selector is matched like an equals call, which is case-sensitive.
Right: STOP and stop differ, so default runs.
String selectors are allowed since Java SE 7.
A break has no effect on whether a label matches.
questions.explain: The tutorial's own month example lowercases the input first so that capitalisation does not matter.
questions.rule: String labels match like equals.
questions.teaches: A String selector is compared with each label as if by the equals method, so matching is case-sensitive, which is why the tutorial's example converts the input to lowercase first.

questions.q: String cmd = null; switch (cmd) { case "go": run = true; break; default: run = false; } If cmd is null, the switch throws a ____ (give the exception name).
questions.explain: The tutorial says a null selector makes the switch throw a NullPointerException, so the default section is never reached. It advises guarding against null selectors.
questions.rule: Guard against a null selector.

questions.q: Which task is a poor fit for a switch statement, according to the tutorial's comparison with if-then-else?
options: Mapping a weekday number from 1 to 7 to its name
A grade letter from score bands such as 90 and above
Mapping a command String such as go or stop to an action
Mapping the constants of an enum to display texts
optionExplain: Exact whole-number values suit a switch.
Right: a switch matches exact labels, while if-then-else handles ranges.
String selectors are allowed.
Enumerated types are allowed selectors.
questions.explain: A switch needs a label for each value, so ranges are better handled by conditions.
questions.rule: Exact values: switch. Ranges: if-then-else.
questions.teaches: A switch matches single values against fixed labels, so a range such as a score band would need a label for every value; if-then-else expresses ranges directly.

questions.q: A block inside a switch that is used as a value must hand back its result. Which keyword does Java use for that?
options: return
break
result
yield
optionExplain: return leaves a method, and is ambiguous inside a switch.
break ends a switch statement but supplies no value.
Java has no such keyword.
Right: yield supplies the value of the enclosing switch expression.
questions.explain: A special keyword exists for this job. The card next explains why return will not do.
questions.rule: yield gives the value of a switch expression.

questions.q: True or false: With arrow labels, the code of the next label also runs after a match.
questions.explain: Only the code to the right of the matched arrow runs; there is no fall-through.
questions.rule: Arrow labels do not fall through.

questions.q: A switch expression on an enum Level with the constants LOW, MEDIUM and HIGH has an arrow label for each of the three, and no default. Does it compile?
options: Yes, because all constants are covered, so it is exhaustive
No, because enums cannot be selectors in a switch expression
Yes, if a break follows each label
No, because every switch needs a default
optionExplain: Right: covering every constant is enough for an enum.
The tutorial uses enums to explain exhaustiveness.
Arrow labels need no break.
A default is not needed when every enum constant has a label.
questions.explain: Exhaustive means every possible value is covered, and for an enum that means every constant.
questions.rule: All enum constants covered means no default needed.

questions.q: A switch expression over an enum has a label for every constant. Later a new constant is added to the enum and the enum is recompiled, but the class holding the switch is not. According to the tutorial, what does the compiler-added hidden default do when the new constant arrives?
options: It runs the first label
It silently does nothing, as an unmatched value normally does
It throws an error instead of carrying on
It converts the new constant to an int
optionExplain: The hidden default never picks a label for you; running an arbitrary label would hide the mistake.
That is what an ordinary non-exhaustive statement does, not the hidden default.
Right: the compiler adds a hidden default that fires only in this situation, and it reports the problem as an error.
No conversion happens; an enum constant stays an enum constant, and the default only reports the problem.
questions.explain: The hidden default turns a silent failure into a loud error.
questions.rule: An exhaustive switch over an enum gets a hidden error-throwing default.
questions.teaches: According to the tutorial, a switch expression over an enum gets a hidden default that throws an error, and it fires only if a constant was added to the enum without the switch being recompiled. The tutorial names IncompatibleClassChangeError; later JDK versions throw MatchException (beyond the tutorial).

questions.q: String r = switch (n) { case 1: yield "one"; case 2: return "two"; default: yield "other"; }; Which case fails to compile, and why?
options: case 1, because yield needs braces
default, because default must come first
case 2: return cannot supply the switch's value
None; return and yield are interchangeable
optionExplain: yield needs no braces here; a colon label may be followed directly by a yield statement.
default can come last; its position does not decide whether the code compiles.
Right: the tutorial uses yield for this purpose.
They are not; return is ambiguous inside a switch.
questions.explain: Inside a switch expression, return is ambiguous, so the value must be given with yield.
questions.rule: Use yield, not return, for the value.

questions.q: True or false: A switch expression on an int selector has labels for 1, 2 and 3 only, and no default. It compiles.
questions.explain: An int can take many more values than three, so the expression is not exhaustive and does not compile. The default label is how it becomes exhaustive.
questions.rule: For int selectors, default makes the expression exhaustive.
questions.teaches: Exhaustive means every possible selector value is covered. Among the selector types in this card, only an enum with every constant listed can omit default; an int selector needs one.

questions.q: Sort each description into the form it belongs to.

items.t: May leave some selector values unhandled
Unmatched value silently does nothing
Must cover every possible selector value
Can be assigned to a variable
Uses yield to give a value from a block
Does not produce a value directly

questions.explain: A switch statement runs code and need not be exhaustive; a switch expression gives a value and must be exhaustive.
questions.rule: Statement: acts. Expression: yields a value and is exhaustive.

questions.q: Which call turns the text 42 into a primitive int?
options: Integer.valueOf(text)
Integer.toString(text)
Integer.parseInt(text)
String.valueOf(text)
optionExplain: It reads the text but returns an Integer object, not a primitive int.
toString goes from a number to text, the opposite direction.
Right: parseInt reads the text and returns a primitive int.
String.valueOf turns values into text, so it does not read numbers from text.
questions.explain: Parsing returns a primitive, while valueOf returns an object. The card next sets out both families.
questions.rule: A parse method returns a primitive.

questions.q: The abstract class that numeric wrappers such as Integer and Double extend is named ____.
questions.explain: Number is the common parent of the numeric wrapper classes, which is why they share methods such as intValue.
questions.rule: Numeric wrappers extend Number.

questions.q: A form field holds the text ff, which is a hexadecimal number. Which call gives the int 255?
options: Integer.parseInt(text)
Integer.parseInt(text, 16)
Integer.parseInt(text, 8)
Integer.toString(text, 16)
optionExplain: With no radix the text is read as decimal, so the letters f cannot be digits.
Right: radix 16 reads ff as 15 times 16 plus 15, which is 255.
Radix 8 allows only digits 0 to 7, so ff is not valid octal text.
toString converts a number to text, so it cannot read the text ff.
questions.explain: Hexadecimal is radix 16, so the radix argument must say 16; without it the text is read as decimal.
questions.rule: Pass the radix that matches the text.
questions.hint: Hexadecimal digits run 0 to 9 and then a to f.

questions.q: True or false: The call Integer.parseInt applied to the text 1010, with no radix argument, returns the int 10.
questions.explain: Without a radix the text is read as decimal, so the result is one thousand and ten. Only radix 2 makes it 10.
questions.rule: No radix means decimal.

questions.q: An Integer object holds 5 and a Long object holds 5. According to the tutorial's rule for equals, what does the Integer's equals method return when given the Long?
options: true, because the numeric values are the same
true, because the Long is converted to Integer first
An error, because the types differ
false, because the types differ
optionExplain: Matching values seem enough, but the rule also demands the same type.
No automatic conversion takes place inside equals.
Mixed types are allowed as an argument; the call just reports false.
Right: the argument is not an Integer, so the result is false.
questions.explain: The rule needs a non-null argument of the same type with the same numeric value. The types differ, so the answer is false even though the numbers match.
questions.rule: equals checks type as well as value.
questions.teaches: Wrapper equals compares the type as well as the number, so equal-looking values of different wrapper types are not equal.

questions.q: Several threads update one shared counter. Which Number subclass does the tutorial name for use in multithreaded code?
options: AtomicInteger
BigDecimal
Short
Float
optionExplain: Right: the tutorial names AtomicInteger and AtomicLong for multithreaded use.
BigDecimal is named for high-precision math, not for sharing between threads.
Short is an ordinary wrapper with no special thread support in the tutorial.
Float is an ordinary wrapper with no special thread support in the tutorial.
questions.explain: The tutorial lists AtomicInteger and AtomicLong for multithreaded use, and BigDecimal and BigInteger for high-precision math. It does not cover them further.
questions.rule: Number has subclasses beyond the plain wrappers.
questions.teaches: Number also has subclasses beyond the plain wrappers: AtomicInteger and AtomicLong for multithreaded code, BigDecimal and BigInteger for high-precision math.

questions.q: True or false: Math.round called with a double argument returns a double.
questions.explain: It returns a whole-number type, long, not a double. The card next lists the return types of the Math methods.
questions.rule: round returns long for a double.

questions.q: In a printf format string, the specifier ____ produces the platform's line break.
questions.explain: The n converter writes whatever line break the platform uses, which is why the tutorial prefers it to a backslash-n escape.
questions.rule: Prefer the n specifier for line breaks.

questions.q: Which DecimalFormat pattern shows the value 5.5 as 005.50?
optionExplain: Optional digits show only what is needed, giving 5.5.
Right: three required integer digits and two required decimals give 005.50.
One required digit on each side gives 5.5, with no padding.
The decimals are forced, giving 5.50, but the integer part gets no leading zeros.
questions.explain: Zeros are required digits, so three zeros before the dot force leading zeros and two after force the trailing zero. Hash signs are optional digits and add nothing.
questions.rule: Zero forces a digit; hash leaves it optional.
questions.hint: Which symbol forces a digit to appear?

questions.q: True or false: A raffle program multiplies Math.random() by 50, and the product can be exactly 50.0.
questions.explain: Random is at least 0.0 and below 1.0, so the scaled product is at least 0.0 and below 50.0. The upper bound is excluded.
questions.rule: Scaling keeps the lower bound and the excluded upper bound.

questions.q: Math.floor applied to the double -2.5 returns the double ____.
questions.explain: Floor gives the largest whole number not above the argument. For a negative number that is further from zero, so -3.0.
questions.rule: floor moves toward the smaller number, even for negatives.
questions.teaches: Math.ceil of -2.5 gives -2.0 and Math.round of -2.5 gives -2, so the rounding methods can give different results for the same input.

questions.q: A simulation needs a long series of random numbers. According to the tutorial, what is suggested?
options: Call Math.random again and again
Create a Random object and call it
Format each value with DecimalFormat
Use Math.rint on a seed value
optionExplain: It works, but the tutorial points to a better tool for a series.
Right: the tutorial recommends a java.util.Random instance for a series.
DecimalFormat only formats numbers that already exist.
rint rounds a value; it does not produce random numbers.
questions.explain: For a series, the tutorial points to a java.util.Random object and its methods rather than repeated Math.random calls.
questions.rule: Use a Random object for a series.
questions.teaches: Beyond the tutorial: a Random object can be created with a seed, so the same seed gives the same series.

questions.q: How many bits does a Java char hold?
optionExplain: Eight bits is the size of a byte, and would hold only 256 values.
Right: 16 bits cover 0000 to FFFF.
32 bits is the size of an int, which can hold any code point but is not what char uses.
64 bits is the size of a long, far more than a single character needs.
questions.explain: A char is a 16-bit value. The card next explains what that range covers and what lies beyond it.
questions.rule: A char is 16 bits.

questions.q: The static Character method ____ tests whether a char is a digit.
questions.explain: isDigit is one of the static helpers; others test for letters, white space, and upper or lower case.
questions.rule: Character has static test methods.

questions.q: Match each need to the Character method that fits it.
pairs: Check that a typed character is a number
Turn a typed q into Q
Skip spaces and tabs between fields
Turn a char into a one-character String
questions.explain: Each helper does one job: isDigit classifies, toUpperCase converts, isWhitespace finds spaces and tabs, and toString makes a one-character String.
questions.rule: Pick the helper by the job: test, convert or wrap.

questions.q: The tutorial's release table lists Java SE 8 with Unicode 6.2 and Java SE 11 with Unicode 10.0. A team on Java SE 8 needs characters first added in Unicode 10.0. What does the table imply?
options: Every Java release recognizes all characters
The char type must be replaced by byte
A newer release such as Java SE 11 is needed
Each such character needs its own escape
optionExplain: The table pairs each release with a version, so support is not the same everywhere.
byte is smaller than char and holds fewer values, so it cannot help.
Right: only releases that list Unicode 10.0 or later cover those characters.
Escape sequences insert listed special characters; they do not add Unicode support.
questions.explain: Each Java release is tied to a Unicode version, so characters added later need a release that lists that version or a newer one, such as Java SE 11.
questions.rule: Unicode support depends on the Java release.
questions.teaches: The Unicode version a program can rely on depends on the Java release, as the tutorial's table pairs each release with a version.

questions.q: According to the tutorial, which type can hold the code point U+1F600, which is above FFFF, as a single value?
options: A char variable
A byte variable
A Character object
An int variable
optionExplain: char covers only 0000 to FFFF, the Basic Multilingual Plane.
byte is only eight bits, far too small.
Character wraps a char, so it has the same 16-bit limit.
Right: an int can hold any Unicode code point.
questions.explain: A char stops at FFFF, and a Character wraps a char. An int can hold any code point, including supplementary ones.
questions.rule: Use int for code points above FFFF.

questions.q: A literal holds a folder path typed with single backslashes, and one backslash is followed by the letter t. According to the escape table, what does the compiler insert for that pair?
options: A tab
A backslash and a t
A newline
A carriage return
optionExplain: Right: backslash t is the tab escape, so the path is silently changed.
It would only appear this way if the backslash were doubled.
Newline is backslash n, a different letter.
Carriage return is backslash r, a different letter.
questions.explain: A backslash followed by t is the tab escape, so a single backslash cannot stand for itself in a path. Two backslashes insert one backslash.
questions.rule: Double a backslash to keep it.
questions.teaches: Doubling backslashes is needed only in source literals; a path typed by a user at run time contains single backslashes unchanged.

questions.q: True or false: calling toUpperCase on a String variable changes the text stored in that variable.
questions.explain: A String cannot change; the call returns a new String and leaves the original alone. The card next explains this.
questions.rule: String methods return new Strings.

questions.q: String.format works like printf but ____ the formatted text as a String instead of printing it.
questions.explain: format is the static partner of printf, and handing back a String lets you store and reuse the text.
questions.rule: format returns; printf prints.

questions.q: A String variable w holds the text plan. The code calls w.concat with the string literal et and ignores the result, then runs w = w.concat with the string literal s. What does w hold at the end?
options: planets
planet
plans
plan
optionExplain: That needs both results to be kept, but the first was thrown away.
That is the first call's result, which was never stored.
Right: only the assigned concat is kept, giving plan followed by s.
The second call is assigned, so w does change.
questions.explain: The first concat builds a new String that is discarded, so w is unchanged. The second is assigned, so w becomes plans.
questions.rule: Only an assigned result is kept.
questions.hint: Which of the two calls has its result stored?

questions.q: A class Point has a toString method that returns the text P(1,2). For a Point p, the statement System.out.println with the string literal At plus a space, then plus p, prints the line At followed by ____.
questions.explain: When plus meets an operand that is not a string, it uses that object's toString, so the text P(1,2) is appended.
questions.rule: Plus calls toString on non-string operands.

questions.q: True or false: For a String of length 5, the call charAt(5) returns its last character.
questions.explain: Indexes start at 0, so the last valid index is length minus one, which is 4. Index 5 is beyond the end.
questions.rule: The last index is length minus one.

questions.q: On Java SE 17 a team writes a multi-line message as a text block. According to the tutorial, which opening is valid?
options: Triple quote, then a line break, then text
Triple quote, then text on the same line
One quote mark, then a line break, then text
Triple quote only, after the final line
optionExplain: Right: the delimiter is followed by a line terminator and the text begins below it.
The text cannot start on the delimiter's line.
A single quote opens an ordinary literal, which cannot span lines.
Opening and closing delimiters are not interchangeable; the opening comes first.
questions.explain: The opening triple quote must be followed by a line terminator, though spaces may sit between them. The text then starts on the next line.
questions.rule: The opening delimiter ends its line.
questions.teaches: A text block's opening delimiter must be followed straight away by a line terminator (spaces may sit between), so text cannot start on that line.

questions.q: What does substring(3, 6) return for the text sunrise?
options: rise
unr
ris
ise
optionExplain: That runs from index 3 to the end, which is substring(3).
That starts at index 1, not 3.
Right: indexes 3, 4 and 5 are r, i and s.
That is substring(4, 7); it starts at index 4, not 3.
questions.explain: The end index is excluded, so characters 3, 4 and 5 are returned. The card next states this rule.
questions.rule: The end index is excluded.

questions.q: When indexOf finds no match it returns ____.
questions.explain: A missing match is reported by -1, which cannot be a valid index.
questions.rule: No match gives -1.

questions.q: A String f holds report.v2.pdf. Which expression returns pdf?
options: f.substring(f.indexOf('.') + 1)
f.substring(f.lastIndexOf('.') + 1)
f.substring(f.lastIndexOf('.'))
f.substring(0, f.lastIndexOf('.'))
optionExplain: indexOf finds the first dot, so this returns v2.pdf.
Right: the last dot is at index 9, so this starts at p and returns pdf.
This starts at the dot itself, giving .pdf.
This returns the part before the last dot, report.v2.
questions.explain: lastIndexOf finds the final dot at index 9, and adding 1 starts just after it. indexOf would find the first dot instead.
questions.rule: lastIndexOf finds the final dot; add 1 to skip it.
questions.hint: Which dot marks the extension, the first or the last?

questions.q: A file is named README, with no dot. What does f.substring(f.lastIndexOf('.') + 1) return when no check for -1 is made?
options: An empty string
An error is thrown
README, the whole name
optionExplain: That is what the tutorial's example returns, but only because it checks for the missing dot.
The result is a String, not an index.
Start index 0 is valid, so no error occurs.
Right: -1 plus 1 is 0, and substring from 0 returns the whole string.
questions.explain: lastIndexOf returns -1, adding 1 gives 0, and substring from 0 returns the entire string. This is why the tutorial's example tests for a missing dot.
questions.rule: Check for -1 before slicing.
questions.teaches: Without a -1 check, the arithmetic turns a missing dot into a start index of 0, so substring returns the whole name instead of an empty extension.

questions.q: Match each replacement method to what it changes.
pairs: Every occurrence of that literal text
Every match of a regular expression
questions.explain: Replace works on literal text, replaceAll on every regular-expression match, and replaceFirst on only the first match.
questions.rule: Match the method to its scope: every literal, every pattern match, or just the first.

questions.q: A log viewer only needs to know whether a line mentions the word ERROR, not where. According to the tutorial, which method fits best?
options: indexOf
compareTo
contains
regionMatches
optionExplain: indexOf would work, but it computes a position that this job does not need.
compareTo orders two strings; it does not search inside one.
Right: contains answers only yes or no, which is all the job needs.
regionMatches compares chosen regions, which is more setup than the job needs.
questions.explain: The tutorial suggests contains when you want to know only whether a sequence is present. It takes a CharSequence, and since String implements that interface, a String can be passed.
questions.rule: Use contains when only presence matters.
questions.teaches: contains accepts a CharSequence, and String implements that interface, so a String can be passed to it directly.

questions.q: True or false: A StringBuilder created from the five-character text hello has a capacity of exactly 5.
questions.explain: A builder made from a String gets the characters plus 16 extra slots, so capacity is 21. The card next explains length and capacity.
questions.rule: Capacity can exceed length.

questions.q: A new empty StringBuilder starts with a capacity of ____ characters.
questions.explain: An empty builder has capacity 16, and it grows automatically when more room is needed.
questions.rule: Empty builder capacity is 16.

questions.q: A StringBuilder holds marathon. After delete(2, 5), what does it hold?
options: maathon
mahon
mathon
marhon
optionExplain: That removes only the r at index 2.
Right: r, a and t at indexes 2, 3 and 4 are removed, leaving mahon.
That removes only r and a, stopping one index early.
That removes the a at index 3 and the t, which does not match the range.
questions.explain: Delete removes indexes 2, 3 and 4, which are r, a and t, leaving ma followed by hon. The end index is excluded.
questions.rule: delete removes start through end minus one.
questions.hint: Which indexes are removed: 2 up to but not including 5.

questions.q: A builder holds abcdef. According to the tutorial, what does setLength(3) do?
options: Raises the capacity to 3
Adds three null characters
Removes the first three characters
Cuts the content to abc
optionExplain: setLength changes the content length, not the capacity.
Null characters are added only when the new length is larger than the old one.
Truncation removes characters from the end, not the start.
Right: the trailing characters def are truncated, leaving abc.
questions.explain: A new length smaller than the current one truncates the trailing characters. A larger length would add null characters at the end instead.
questions.rule: setLength truncates or pads.
questions.teaches: setLength truncates trailing characters when the new length is smaller, and adds null characters when it is larger.

questions.q: True or false: According to the tutorial, for joining a few strings in one expression on Java SE 9 and later, appending to a StringBuilder is faster than plain string concatenation.
questions.explain: The tutorial says Java SE 9 optimized plain concatenation, which now outperforms appending. A builder is chosen when it makes code simpler.
questions.rule: On Java SE 9 and later, plain concatenation wins for simple joins.
