questions.q: Several threads write log lines into one shared text buffer. According to the tutorial, which class fits?
options: StringBuilder, the usual choice
String, since it never changes
StringBuffer, whose methods are synchronized
StringBuilder with bigger capacity
optionExplain: It is the default, but its methods are not synchronized.
A String cannot be edited, so it cannot serve as a growing shared buffer.
Right: synchronization makes StringBuffer thread-safe.
Capacity affects room, not thread safety.
questions.explain: StringBuffer has the same API as StringBuilder but its methods are synchronized, making it thread-safe. The tutorial says to use it only when thread safety is needed.
questions.rule: Choose StringBuffer only for thread safety.
questions.teaches: StringBuffer has the same API as StringBuilder but synchronized methods; use it only when thread safety is needed.

questions.q: True or false: You can add an int value directly to a list whose elements are Integer objects.
questions.explain: The compiler creates the Integer for you. The card next names this autoboxing.
questions.rule: Primitives convert to their wrappers automatically.

questions.q: Match each primitive type to its wrapper class.
questions.explain: Two names differ from the primitive: char pairs with Character and int with Integer. The others only capitalize.
questions.rule: Each primitive has one matching wrapper.

questions.q: Given Integer count = 5; and int next = count + 1; what does the compiler do with count?
options: It boxes the number 1 into an Integer
It unboxes count to an int
It rejects adding to an Integer
It turns count into a String
optionExplain: The sum is assigned to an int, so no boxing is needed.
Right: arithmetic works on primitives, so count is unboxed.
The tutorial shows Integer objects used in arithmetic, so this compiles.
Text conversion happens with plus only when a String is involved.
questions.explain: The addition needs a primitive, so the compiler unboxes count to an int. The result is an int and assigned to an int, so nothing is boxed.
questions.rule: A wrapper in arithmetic is unboxed.
questions.hint: Is the addition done on objects or on primitives?

questions.q: Mia says an Integer object works with the percent operator because Integer defines its own remainder operator. According to the tutorial, what really happens?
options: The compiler inserts intValue calls
Integer overloads the operator
The program converts to String
The compiler rejects it
optionExplain: Right: intValue calls unbox each Integer so the operator works on ints.
Java classes cannot redefine operators like this; the work is done by the compiler.
No String conversion is involved in arithmetic.
The tutorial shows such code compiling.
questions.explain: The tutorial explains that the compiler inserts intValue calls so the operators work on primitive ints. The conversion is done by the compiler, not by operators inside Integer.
questions.rule: The compiler writes the unboxing calls.
questions.teaches: Operators such as the remainder and compound plus-assignment work on Integer objects because the compiler inserts intValue calls.

questions.q: Sort each operation: does the compiler box a primitive or unbox a wrapper?

items.t: Assigning a char value to a Character variable
Passing a Double object to a method that takes a double
Passing a long value to a method that takes a Long
Assigning a Boolean object to a boolean variable
Adding an int value to a list of Integer objects

questions.explain: Boxing makes an object from a primitive; unboxing extracts the primitive. Collections hold objects, so adding an int to a list of Integer needs boxing.
questions.rule: Primitive to wrapper is boxing; wrapper to primitive is unboxing.
questions.teaches: Reading an element back with get and adding it to an int unboxes it, so boxing and unboxing both occur around a collection.

questions.unitTitle: Objects, Classes, Interfaces, Packages and Inheritance (dev.java)
questions.q: True or false: An object keeps its state in fields and offers its behavior through methods.
questions.explain: This is how Java objects are described: fields hold the state and methods expose the behavior. The card next explains why the methods matter.
questions.rule: Fields hold state; methods expose behavior.

questions.unitTitle: Objects, Classes, Interfaces, Packages and Inheritance (dev.java)
questions.q: A class is the ____ from which individual objects are created.
questions.explain: The tutorial calls a class the blueprint, and each object made from it is an instance.
questions.rule: A class is a blueprint; objects are its instances.

questions.unitTitle: Objects, Classes, Interfaces, Packages and Inheritance (dev.java)
questions.q: A LibraryCard object stores how many books its owner has borrowed, and the library allows at most 5. Which design follows data encapsulation?
options: Make the count open to any code and trust staff to keep it at 5 or below
Offer a borrow method that checks the limit before raising the count
Keep a note on the card telling staff to stop at the fifth book
Let every class compute its own copy of the count when it needs one
optionExplain: Open access lets any code set the count to 9, so the object cannot guard its own state.
Right: with all changes passing through a method, the object can refuse a sixth book, just like the gear method refusing a seventh gear.
A note depends on people reading it; the object itself still accepts any value.
Separate copies can disagree, and none of them is guarded by the object that owns the state.
questions.explain: Encapsulation puts the rule inside the object by routing every change through a method that can say no.
questions.rule: Put the validity check in the method that changes the state.
questions.hint: Which option lets the object itself refuse a bad value?

questions.unitTitle: Objects, Classes, Interfaces, Packages and Inheritance (dev.java)
questions.q: A team rewrites how the setGear method of a Bicycle class checks its limits but keeps the method name and parameters unchanged. According to the tutorial benefits of objects, which statements hold? Select all that apply.
options: Code that calls setGear need not know how the check works
Callers must all be rewritten because the internals moved
A different object offering the same methods could replace this one
The change ruins modularity because objects can no longer be maintained alone
optionExplain: Right: information hiding means users of an object see only its methods, not the implementation.
Callers depend on the method, not on its inside, so they stay as they are.
Right: the tutorial's pluggability benefit is that a problematic object can be swapped for another, like a bolt in a machine.
Independent maintenance is exactly what modularity offers, so changing one object's inside supports it.
questions.explain: Callers see only the methods, so the inside can change and the object can be swapped without touching them.
questions.rule: Callers depend on methods, so the inside is free to change.
questions.teaches: Because callers depend only on a method's name and parameters, its inside can be rewritten or the whole object replaced without changing any caller; this is an inference from the tutorial's information hiding and pluggability benefits.

questions.unitTitle: Objects, Classes, Interfaces, Packages and Inheritance (dev.java)
questions.q: A learner writes a class Thermostat with a field and two methods, then asks the Java launcher to run it as a program and gets an error about a missing main method. Which reading fits the tutorial's description of a class?
options: Every class needs a main method before it may have fields
The error means the fields were declared with the wrong type
Methods of a class may only be called by the class itself
Thermostat is a blueprint; another class must create and use its objects
optionExplain: The tutorial's Bicycle class has fields and methods but no main, so main is not a precondition for fields.
The message is about starting a program, not about field types.
Objects communicate by calling each other's methods, so outside code can call them.
Right: like Bicycle, it is not a complete application, and a separate class (like BicycleDemo) creates and uses its objects.
questions.explain: A blueprint class describes objects; a different class must supply the entry point that creates and uses them.
questions.rule: A blueprint class needs a separate class to put its objects to work.
questions.teaches: Beyond the tutorial: the class that you ask the Java launcher to start is the one that must declare the main method, which is why the usage class holds it and the blueprint class does not.

questions.unitTitle: Objects, Classes, Interfaces, Packages and Inheritance (dev.java)
questions.q: True or false: In Java a class may have several direct superclasses, but a superclass may have only one subclass.
questions.explain: It is the other way round: exactly one direct superclass, any number of subclasses. The card next shows how this fits with extends and implements.
questions.rule: One direct superclass, unlimited subclasses.

questions.unitTitle: Objects, Classes, Interfaces, Packages and Inheritance (dev.java)
questions.q: Match each Java word to what it does.
pairs: Names the one superclass a class builds on
Adopts an interface and its contract
Group of related methods with empty bodies
Namespace grouping related classes and interfaces
questions.explain: Extends points to one superclass, implements adopts a contract, an interface lists method signatures, and a package groups names.
questions.rule: Four words, four jobs.

questions.unitTitle: Objects, Classes, Interfaces, Packages and Inheritance (dev.java)
questions.q: Kettle is declared to implement Switchable, which lists turnOn and turnOff, but the Kettle code defines only turnOn. According to the tutorial, what happens at build time?
options: It builds, and turnOff gets an empty body by default
It builds, and turnOff fails only when someone calls it
The build fails because every interface method must be present
It builds if Kettle and Switchable share one package
optionExplain: The tutorial says nothing of default bodies; the interface bodies are empty, and the class must supply its own.
The check happens when compiling, not when the method is called.
Right: the compiler enforces the contract by requiring every interface method in the class.
Packages group names; they do not relax the contract.
questions.explain: Implementing an interface is a formal commitment, and the compiler refuses a class that leaves part of it out.
questions.rule: Implement every method of the interface, as public methods.
questions.hint: Who checks the contract, and when?

questions.unitTitle: Objects, Classes, Interfaces, Packages and Inheritance (dev.java)
questions.q: Sort each statement by the mechanism it describes.

items.t: The class receives fields and methods from a superclass
The source file does not repeat the inherited code
A class has exactly one direct superclass of this kind
The compiler checks that every listed method is present
The methods in the interface have empty bodies
The class commits to a set of behavior

questions.explain: Extends brings in existing state and behavior from one superclass; implements brings in a list of methods that the class must then supply.
questions.rule: Extends brings code in; implements demands code be written.
questions.teaches: Beyond the tutorial: a class has one superclass but may implement more than one interface, which is how Java lets a class take on several contracts.

questions.unitTitle: Objects, Classes, Interfaces, Packages and Inheritance (dev.java)
questions.q: A large payroll program has two different classes both called Report, one for billing and one for staff records. Which tutorial idea gives a way to keep them apart?
options: Make one Report a subclass of the other
Put each Report in its own package, a namespace for its group
Declare both Report classes to implement the same interface
Give each Report class a public main method
optionExplain: A subclass relation shares code; it does not separate two unrelated names.
Right: a package is a namespace grouping related classes, as folders group files, so each group has its own space.
An interface is a contract of methods and does nothing to separate names.
A main method is an entry point and has no bearing on naming.
questions.explain: Packages exist to organise large programs, so related types live together in a namespace of their own.
questions.rule: Use packages to organise types into namespaces.
questions.teaches: Beyond the tutorial: two classes with the same simple name can exist in different packages, and code tells them apart by the package name.

questions.q: Which header is a valid class declaration?
options: public class Ship extends Vessel implements Sailing, Tracked
public class Ship implements Sailing extends Vessel
public class Ship extends Vessel, Hull
public class ship() extends Vessel implements Sailing, Tracked
optionExplain: Right: one superclass after extends, then a comma-separated list of interfaces after implements.
The extends clause has to come before the implements clause, so this order does not compile.
A class can extend only one superclass, so a comma list after extends is not allowed.
A class name takes no parentheses, and by convention it starts with a capital letter.
questions.explain: The parts appear in a fixed order: name, then extends, then implements. The card next shows the full order.
questions.rule: Class header order: name, extends, implements.

questions.q: True or false: A class can extend only one superclass but may implement several interfaces.
questions.explain: The extends clause names a single parent. The implements clause takes a comma-separated list.
questions.rule: One parent, many interfaces.

questions.q: In the class below, which name is a parameter? class Counter { int total; void add(int amount) { int next = total + amount; total = next; } }
options: total
next
amount
add
optionExplain: total is declared in the class body outside any method, so it is a field.
next is declared inside the method body, so it is a local variable.
Right: amount is declared in the signature of add, so it is a parameter.
add is the method name, not a variable.
questions.explain: A parameter is declared in the method signature, between the parentheses. Here that is amount.
questions.rule: Parameters live in the signature.

questions.q: Sort each item: is it declared directly in the class body, or inside a method?
groups: Declared directly in the class body

items.t: The cadence field of a Bicycle class
A constructor of Bicycle
Another method of Bicycle
The parameter speed in a method signature
A loop counter i declared in a for loop
A local variable total in a method

questions.explain: Constructors, fields and methods sit directly in the class body. Parameters and locals belong to a method, so they exist only while it runs.
questions.rule: Class body: constructors, fields, methods. Method: parameters and locals.
questions.teaches: An instance field lives as long as its object, while parameters and local variables live only for one method call, so they are separate from the object state.

questions.q: Making fields private and offering public methods such as getters is common practice called ____.
questions.explain: The tutorial names this encapsulation: the class hides its fields and offers controlled access through methods.
questions.rule: Private fields, public methods: encapsulation.
questions.teaches: Encapsulation lets the class change how it stores a value later without breaking any code that calls its public methods.

questions.q: A Thermostat class stores a target temperature in a field. Changes must be checked to stay between 5 and 30 degrees. Which design fits the common practice?
options: A public field target that other classes can assign directly, with no checking at all
A private field target with a public method that checks the value, then stores it
A local variable target declared inside the constructor of the class and kept there
A public constructor that other classes call again whenever target changes
optionExplain: Any class could then store 100, and the Thermostat has no chance to reject it.
Right: the method sits between outside code and the field, so it can reject values outside the range.
A local variable disappears when the constructor ends, so it cannot hold state for the object.
Calling a constructor creates a new object; it does not change the existing one.
questions.explain: A public setter method can run a check before assigning the field. A public field cannot, because any class could assign any value directly.
questions.rule: Private field plus a method lets the class guard its state.
questions.teaches: Because outside code goes through a method, the class can check or refuse a change before it reaches the field, which a public field cannot do.

questions.q: True or false: Two methods in one class can share a name and a parameter list if their return types differ.
questions.explain: The compiler does not use the return type to tell methods apart. The card next shows what it does use.
questions.rule: Return type does not separate methods.

questions.q: The name of a method together with its parameter types is called its ____.
questions.explain: That pair is the signature; the return type and modifiers are not part of it.
questions.rule: Signature = name + parameter types.

questions.q: A class already declares double convert(int cents). Which extra method can be added to the same class without a compile error?
options: int convert(int amount)
String convert(int cents)
void convert(int cents)
double convert(long n)
optionExplain: Parameter names do not count and the type list is still one int, so the signature matches.
The return type differs but the parameter list is the same, so the signatures clash.
void is a different return type, but the signature convert with one int is unchanged, so it clashes.
Right: the parameter type long differs from int, so this is a valid overload.
questions.explain: A new method must differ from the existing one in parameter types or count. Only the long version does.
questions.rule: Change parameters, not just the return type.

questions.q: In what ways can a method hand control back to its caller? Select all that apply.
options: Its last statement finishes
A return statement runs
An exception is thrown
It calls another overload with the same name
optionExplain: Right: reaching the end of the body returns control, which is how void methods usually finish.
Right: return ends the method immediately, with a value unless the method is void.
Right: a thrown exception leaves the method as well.
A call to another method runs that method, and the first method continues afterwards.
questions.explain: A method returns when its last statement finishes, when a return statement runs, or when an exception is thrown, whichever comes first. Calling an overload does not by itself end the method.
questions.rule: Three exits: end of body, return, exception.
questions.teaches: A method gives control back when its last statement finishes, a return statement runs, or an exception is thrown, whichever comes first.

questions.q: A student writes this class and says it compiles because the return types differ: class Tally { int add(int a) { return a; } long add(int b) { return b; } }. What is wrong with the claim?
options: Both methods have the same signature, so differing return types do not separate them
Overloaded methods must have identical return types in every case, so one of them must change
A class may not declare two methods whose names both start with the same word add
The parameter names a and b would have to be spelled the same in both methods
optionExplain: Right: the name add and the single int parameter match, and the return type is not part of the signature.
Overloads with different parameters may return different types; the problem here is the matching parameters.
A class can declare many methods with the same name when their parameter lists differ.
Parameter names play no role in the signature, so renaming them would not fix or cause anything.
questions.explain: Both methods have the signature add with one int parameter. Return types and parameter names are outside the signature.
questions.rule: Same name and same parameter types means a clash.

questions.q: True or false: A Greeter class can declare void greet(String name) and String greet(String name, int times), even though their return types differ.
questions.explain: The parameter lists differ in number, so the signatures differ and the return types are free to differ. The rule is about identical parameter lists.
questions.rule: Different parameter lists allow different return types.
questions.teaches: Return type is not part of the signature, so two methods with the same name and parameter list that differ only in return type are a compile-time error.

questions.q: Which declaration is a constructor of a class named Ticket?
options: public void Ticket() { }
public int Ticket() { return 0; }
public Ticket(int seat) { }
public create(int seat) { }
optionExplain: With void in front this is an ordinary method that happens to share the class name.
A return type of int makes this an ordinary method.
Right: it carries the class name and has no return type.
It has no return type but its name is not the class name, so it is not valid.
questions.explain: A constructor uses the class name and names no return type. The card next gives the full rules.
questions.rule: Class name, no return type.

questions.q: True or false: A constructor declaration states a return type before its name.
questions.explain: Constructors have no return type at all, not even void.
questions.rule: No return type on a constructor.

questions.q: A class Sensor has no constructor and no extends clause. What happens with the statement new Sensor()?
options: It fails to compile because every class must declare at least one constructor of its own
It compiles; the default constructor calls the no-argument constructor of Object
It compiles only if Sensor has a main method
It compiles but no constructor runs at all, so the fields stay uninitialized
optionExplain: Writing one is optional, since the compiler provides a default.
Right: the compiler-supplied constructor takes no arguments and calls the parent's, here Object's.
A main method has nothing to do with creating an object.
The default constructor does run, and it initializes the object.
questions.explain: The compiler adds a no-argument default constructor, which calls the no-argument constructor of Object.
questions.rule: No constructor written: the compiler supplies one.

questions.q: Class Base declares only the constructor Base(int id). Class Child extends Base and declares no constructor, so it does not compile. Which changes make it compile? Select all that apply.
options: Add a no-argument constructor to Base
Write a Child constructor that explicitly calls Base(int) with an int argument
Give Child a private field
Declare Child as public
optionExplain: Right: the default constructor of Child can then call it.
Right: the tutorial says a constructor can explicitly use a superclass constructor, which replaces the failing implicit call.
A field does not affect which parent constructor runs.
The access of the class does not change how its constructor reaches the parent's.
questions.explain: Child's default constructor calls a no-argument Base constructor. Either give Base one, or give Child a constructor that explicitly calls an existing Base constructor.
questions.rule: The parent needs a usable constructor for the child to call.
questions.teaches: Beyond the tutorial: the explicit call is written as super with arguments, such as super(5), as the first statement of a Child constructor.

questions.q: Sort each description: does it fit a constructor or an ordinary method?

items.t: Shares its name with the class
Runs as part of evaluating the new operator
Declares no return type, not even void
Declares void or a type before its name
Called on an existing object with the dot operator
Its name starts with a lowercase verb by convention

questions.explain: Constructors share the class name, lack a return type and run via new. Ordinary methods have a return type or void and are called on an existing object.
questions.rule: Constructors are named after the class and run with new.

questions.q: True or false: The class Pack { Pack(int a) { } Pack(int b) { } } compiles because the two parameter names differ.
questions.explain: Names do not count. Both constructors take one int, so the compiler cannot tell them apart and reports an error.
questions.rule: Overloads differ by types or count, not names.

questions.q: True or false: If a method adds 1 to its int parameter, the caller's int variable also increases by 1.
questions.explain: A primitive argument is copied, so the caller's variable is untouched. The card next explains the copying.
questions.rule: Primitives are copied.

questions.q: The variables named in a method declaration are parameters; the actual values passed at the call are called ____.
questions.explain: Parameters appear in the declaration, arguments appear in the call.
questions.rule: Parameter in the declaration, argument in the call.

questions.q: With class Box { int size; } and void grow(Box b) { b.size = b.size + 10; }, the caller runs Box x = new Box(); x.size = 5; grow(x);. What is x.size afterwards?
options: 5, because arguments are always copied in full
10, because the method starts from zero
The code does not compile, since grow cannot change a Box
15, because the field of the shared object changed
optionExplain: Only the reference is copied, not the object, so the object changes.
The method adds 10 to the current size of 5, not to zero.
Changing an accessible field through a parameter is allowed.
Right: the copied reference points to the same Box, so size becomes 15.
questions.explain: The method got a copy of the reference to the same Box, so changing its field changes what the caller sees.
questions.rule: A reference copy still points to the same object.

questions.q: The method void swapIn(Box b) { b = new Box(); b.size = 99; } is called with a Box x whose size is 5. After the call, x.size is ____.
questions.explain: The method reassigns its local copy of the reference, so the new Box with size 99 is never seen by the caller. The caller's Box still has size 5.
questions.rule: Reassigning the parameter does not move the caller's variable.

questions.q: The method int total(int... nums) adds up its arguments. Which calls are valid? Select all that apply.
options: total()
total(7, 8, 9)
total(new int[] {1, 2})
total(3.5)
optionExplain: Right: zero values are allowed, and nums becomes an empty array.
Right: a comma-separated list of ints fits the varargs parameter.
Right: because the parameter is an array inside, an int array can be passed directly.
3.5 is a double, which does not match the int type of the parameter.
questions.explain: A varargs parameter accepts none, one or many values, or an array. A decimal number is not an int.
questions.rule: Varargs take a list or an array.
questions.teaches: A varargs parameter must be the last parameter in the method parameter list.

questions.q: The method void zero(int[] data) { data[0] = 0; } is called with the array a, which holds 7 and 8 in that order. What does a[0] hold afterwards?
options: It does not compile
optionExplain: Right: the copied reference leads to the same array, so element 0 is overwritten.
7 would only remain if the method had worked on a private copy of the array.
8 is the second element and the method does not touch it.
Passing an array to an int array parameter is fine.
questions.explain: Arrays are reference types, so the method works on the caller's array and the change is visible.
questions.rule: Arrays behave like other references.
questions.teaches: Reassigning the parameter inside the method, as in data = new int[3], would leave the caller variable a untouched.

questions.q: After the single line Cup c; and nothing else, what does the variable c refer to?
options: An empty Cup with default fields
A Cup made by its no-argument constructor
No object yet
The Cup class itself
optionExplain: No object has been allocated, so there are no fields to have defaults.
A constructor only runs through the new operator.
Right: only new creates an object, so c refers to nothing until assigned.
A variable of type Cup refers to Cup objects, not the class.
questions.explain: Declaring a reference variable does not create an object. The card next shows the three steps.
questions.rule: Declaring does not create.

questions.q: The operator that allocates memory, runs a constructor and returns a reference is called ____.
questions.explain: That is the new operator, the instantiation step.
questions.rule: new = instantiation.

questions.q: The class Lamp has a boolean field on, false at first. The code is Lamp a = new Lamp(); Lamp b = a; b.on = true;. What does a.on hold afterwards?
options: false, since only b was changed
true, because a and b refer to the same Lamp
It depends on when the garbage collector runs
The code does not compile, since b is not created with new
optionExplain: a and b would only be separate if a second Lamp had been created with new.
Right: one object, two references, one on field.
The collector affects when memory is freed, not what a live object holds.
Assigning an existing reference to another variable is allowed.
questions.explain: Both variables hold references to the same Lamp, so the field change shows through either one.
questions.rule: Two references to one object share its state.

questions.q: True or false: Given two Lamp objects a and b created by two separate new expressions, setting b.on to true also changes a.on.
questions.explain: Each object has its own copy of its instance fields, so the separate Lamp objects do not share on.
questions.rule: Separate objects, separate instance fields.

questions.q: True or false: After Tank t1 = new Tank(); Tank t2 = t1; t1 = null; the Tank object is eligible for garbage collection.
questions.explain: t2 still refers to the Tank, so it is still reachable. It becomes eligible only after t2 is dropped too.
questions.rule: All references must be gone.

questions.q: After the statement int h = new Box(4, 6).height; the program keeps no variable for the new Box, so it holds no ____ to it and the Box is eligible for garbage collection.
questions.explain: The field was read straight from the new expression. Nothing refers to the object afterwards.
questions.rule: No remaining reference means eligible.
questions.teaches: Reading a field or calling a method straight on a new expression leaves the object with no reference once the statement ends, so it becomes eligible for collection at that point.

questions.q: A class has a field row and a constructor Seat(int row) { row = row; }. What does this constructor do to the field?
options: It sets the field of the object to the value of the argument that was passed
It fails to compile because the name row is declared twice in the same scope
It sets both the field and the parameter to the same value
It assigns the parameter to itself and leaves the field unchanged
optionExplain: That is what the author intended, but the field is hidden by the parameter.
A parameter may share a name with a field; that is shadowing.
Only the parameter is touched.
Right: both sides of the assignment are the parameter, so the field keeps its default.
questions.explain: The plain name row means the parameter, so the statement assigns the parameter to itself. The card next shows how to reach the field.
questions.rule: Plain name = parameter when it shadows.

questions.q: True or false: Writing this.x in a constructor refers to the field named x of the object being created.
questions.explain: this stands for the current object, so this.x is its field x even if a parameter is also named x.
questions.rule: this.x reaches the field.

questions.q: In class Dial { int level; void set(int level) { ____ = level; } } the blank must name the field so that the parameter is stored in it.
questions.explain: this.level is the field; plain level is the parameter.
questions.rule: this.level fixes the shadowing.

questions.q: Put these events in order for new Seat(3), with constructors Seat(int row) { this(row, 1); } and Seat(int row, int col) that assigns both fields.
items: The one-argument constructor starts running
It reaches the call this with row and 1
The two-argument constructor assigns both fields
Control returns to the one-argument constructor
questions.explain: The one-argument constructor starts, passes control to the two-argument one, which finishes its assignments before control returns.
questions.rule: Chained constructors run the called one to completion first.
questions.teaches: Beyond the tutorial: after the constructor named by this finishes, control returns to the calling constructor, which then runs its remaining statements.

questions.q: Under JDK 21, a constructor reads Seat(int row) { System.out.println(row); this(row, 1); }. According to the tutorial, what is the problem?
options: The this call must be the first statement before JDK 25
this with arguments cannot be used inside constructors of a class at all
System.out.println is not allowed to appear inside constructor bodies at all
The constructor needs a return type
optionExplain: Right: the tutorial states the first-statement rule for versions before JDK 25.
It is allowed; its purpose is to reuse another constructor.
Printing is an ordinary statement and is fine anywhere a statement can appear.
Constructors never state a return type.
questions.explain: Before JDK 25 the call to another constructor of the same class has to be the first statement.
questions.rule: Before JDK 25, this(...) comes first.

questions.q: True or false: In class Tank { int capacity; void set(int capacity) { this.capacity = capacity; } int read() { return capacity; } }, the plain name capacity in read refers to the field.
questions.explain: The parameter hides the field only inside set. In read there is no parameter of that name, so the simple name reaches the field.
questions.rule: Shadowing lasts only within the parameter's scope.
questions.teaches: A parameter shadows a field only inside its own method; other methods of the class can use the plain field name.

questions.q: A field has no access modifier at all. Which code can use it?
options: Only the declaring class
Every class in the whole program, whichever package it is in
Classes in the same package
Subclasses in any package
optionExplain: That describes private, which is stricter.
That describes public, which is wider.
Right: package-private opens the member to the class itself and its package.
Subclasses in other packages need protected or public.
questions.explain: No modifier means package-private. The card next gives the table.
questions.rule: No modifier = package-private.

questions.q: Match each modifier to who can use the member.
pairs: Package plus subclasses in other packages
questions.explain: private is own class only, none adds the package, protected adds subclasses in other packages, public is everyone.
questions.rule: Each level widens the audience of the one before.

questions.q: A helper method in package billing is called by other classes in billing but must be hidden from all other packages. Which is the most restrictive level that works?
options: private
no modifier
public
protected
optionExplain: It would block the other classes of billing that need to call it.
Right: package-private serves exactly the classes of billing.
It is more open than needed, since all packages could call it.
It also admits subclasses in other packages, which is wider than needed.
questions.explain: private would block the other billing classes; no modifier lets the package in but nothing more.
questions.rule: Pick the narrowest level that works.

questions.q: A package-private method in a superclass is not reachable by a subclass in another package. Changing its modifier to ____ is the narrowest change that gives that subclass access.
questions.explain: Protected adds subclasses in other packages to the audience, without opening the member to everyone.
questions.rule: protected = package plus subclasses.

questions.q: A review of class Account { public double balance; } makes comments. Which comments agree with the tutorial? Select all that apply.
options: Any class can change balance directly, so the Account cannot protect it
Fields should usually be private, with methods giving access
Java forbids public fields
A constant would also have to be private
optionExplain: Right: public means every class can read and write the field.
Right: the tutorial's guidance is to start from private.
Java allows public fields; the tutorial only discourages them.
The tutorial makes an exception for constants, which may be public.
questions.explain: The tutorial favors private fields with accessors, because public fields tie code to one implementation and limit later changes.
questions.rule: Hide fields, expose methods.

questions.q: A constant TAX_RATE is read by many classes in a program and keeps one value. Which access level fits the tutorial's guidance?
options: private, with every class using a getter method to read it
protected, so that only subclasses see it
no modifier, so that only its own package can use it
public, since constants are the accepted exception
optionExplain: That works but adds a method for a value that never changes; the tutorial permits public here.
Classes that are not subclasses could not read it.
Other packages could not read it, though many classes need to.
Right: the tutorial advises against public fields except for constants.
questions.explain: The tutorial accepts public fields for constants. A value that never changes leaves nothing for other code to depend on in a fragile way.
questions.rule: Constants are the exception to private-by-default.
questions.teaches: Public is safe for a constant because nobody can change it; the risk of public access comes from state that can change.

questions.q: True or false: A field declared static exists once for the whole class, not once per object.
questions.explain: A static field is shared. The card next shows how it is used.
questions.rule: static = one shared copy.

questions.q: A constant is declared with the modifiers static and ____.
questions.explain: static final: one shared copy that cannot be reassigned.
questions.rule: Constants are static final.

questions.q: With class Ticket { static int issued; int number; Ticket() { issued++; number = issued; } }, three tickets are created in a row. What is Ticket.issued afterwards?
options: 3, because all three constructors updated the same variable
1, since the last ticket resets it
0, since it is only a template
It does not compile, since a constructor cannot change a static field
optionExplain: Right: one shared variable, incremented three times.
Nothing resets a static field; each constructor adds to the same value.
Static fields keep their value; they are not templates.
Constructors can use class variables; instance code may reach class members.
questions.explain: issued is shared and incremented by each constructor call, so it ends at 3. The numbers of the individual tickets are 1, 2 and 3.
questions.rule: A class variable counts across all objects.

questions.q: True or false: A class method int count() { return number; } that reads the instance field number compiles, because every method can read every field.
questions.explain: A class method has no current object, so it cannot reach instance fields directly. It would need an object reference.
questions.rule: Static code needs an object for instance members.

questions.q: Which can a class method use directly, without an object reference? Select all that apply.
options: A class variable
Another class method
An instance variable
this
optionExplain: Right: class variables are shared and need no particular object.
Right: class methods can call each other directly.
An instance variable belongs to a particular object, which a class method does not have.
this stands for the current object, and class methods have none.
questions.explain: Class methods have direct access to class variables and class methods only. Instance variables and this need an object.
questions.rule: Static reaches static.

questions.q: Library declares public static final int LIMIT = 10 and App was compiled using it. Library is changed to 20 and only Library is recompiled. What might App still use?
options: 20, since constants are read when the program runs
0, since the old constant was removed
10, the value copied in when App was compiled
Nothing, because it fails to start
optionExplain: That would happen for a value looked up at run time, but compile-time constants are inlined.
Replacing the value does not give a default of zero.
Right: the tutorial says the compiler inlines such constants.
The program starts; it can use the stale copy.
questions.explain: For compile-time constants of primitives or Strings the compiler copies the value into dependent classes, so App may still hold 10 until it is recompiled.
questions.rule: Changing a compile-time constant means recompiling dependents.
questions.teaches: Compile-time constants of primitive or String type are copied into the classes that use them, so those classes must be recompiled when the value changes.

questions.q: Class Outer has a private int count. A non-static class declared inside Outer reads count. Does this compile?
options: No, private members are visible only to the methods of Outer itself, not to nested classes
Yes, a nested class can use private members of its enclosing instance
Only if count is made public
Only if the nested class is itself declared as static
optionExplain: This is the common first guess, but the nested class is part of Outer's code for access purposes.
Right: reaching private members of the outer class is one reason to nest a class.
Making it public is unnecessary.
A static nested class actually has less direct access to the outer instance.
questions.explain: A nested class is a member of Outer and can reach even its private members. The card next explains the inner and static kinds.
questions.rule: Nested code can reach private outer members.

questions.q: True or false: A static nested class can read an instance field of its outer class directly by its simple name.
questions.explain: A static nested class is tied to the class, not an instance, so it needs an object reference to reach instance fields.
questions.rule: Static nested needs an object reference.

questions.q: A Garden class has a private int plants. Its helper class Row must know the plants of the particular Garden it belongs to. Which form fits?
options: A static nested class of Garden
A top-level class with a public field
A static method of Garden
An inner class of Garden
optionExplain: It has no enclosing instance, so it would need an explicit Garden reference.
That would expose the field and lose the tie to one Garden.
A method is not a class, and it has no instance of its own.
Right: each inner instance is tied to one Garden and can read its private fields.
questions.explain: The helper depends on a particular outer object, which is what an inner class is tied to.
questions.rule: Needs the outer instance: inner class.

questions.q: In class Box { int x = 1; class Inner { int x = 2; void show(int x) { System.out.println(x); } } }, the call show(3) on an Inner prints ____.
questions.explain: The parameter x is the innermost declaration, so it hides the Inner field and the Box field.
questions.rule: Innermost name wins.
questions.teaches: To reach a shadowed field, qualify it: this.x names the inner class field and Box.this.x names the outer one.

questions.q: A static nested class Helper reads the instance field outerField of Outer by its simple name and the compiler rejects it. Which changes fix this? Select all that apply.
options: Pass an Outer object to Helper and read the field through that reference
Make Helper a non-static inner class
Declare Helper private
Rename outerField
optionExplain: Right: through a reference, a static nested class may use instance fields.
Right: an inner class is tied to an outer instance, so the simple name works.
Access level of the class does not change whether an instance is available.
Renaming does not provide an Outer object.
questions.explain: The static nested class needs a reference to an Outer object, or it should be an inner class so that it has one.
questions.rule: Give it an Outer object, or make it inner.

questions.q: Sort each helper: does it fit an inner class or a static nested class?

items.t: An iterator that walks the data of one specific list object
A helper that needs the private fields of the outer object
A click handler that reads state of its window object
A small record of values that never touches outer instance data
A calculation helper working only on its own arguments
A lookup table that does not depend on any instance

questions.explain: A helper that depends on one outer object fits inner; one that uses only its own data fits static nested.
questions.rule: Depends on an outer object?
questions.teaches: A static nested class is named through the outer class, as in Outer.Nested, and it cannot use the outer instance members directly.

questions.q: True or false: Java can declare a class and create an object of it in one expression without ever giving the class a name.
questions.explain: That is an anonymous class. The card next shows its form.
questions.rule: Anonymous = declared and created at once.

questions.q: A local variable used by a local class must be final or ____ final.
questions.explain: Effectively final means never reassigned after initialization.
questions.rule: final or effectively final.

questions.q: A method void check(int len) declares a local class Rule whose method compares n == len, and later the method runs len = 7;. What happens?
options: It fails: len is no longer effectively final
It compiles and the class Rule sees the new value 7 when it runs
It compiles but the class Rule keeps seeing the old value of len
It compiles only if the class Rule is itself made static in some way
optionExplain: Right: len is captured, and the later assignment breaks the effectively final condition.
Capturing a variable that changes is exactly what the rule prevents.
Java does not keep silent copies of changed variables for this; it refuses the code.
Static does not change the capture rule.
questions.explain: Reassigning len means it is no longer effectively final, so the local class cannot capture it and compilation fails.
questions.rule: Captured locals must not be reassigned.

questions.q: True or false: If the line len = 7; is deleted from the method, the local class Rule may use len.
questions.explain: With no reassignment len stays effectively final, so the capture is allowed.
questions.rule: Remove the reassignment and the capture works.

questions.q: Which of these may the body of an anonymous class declare? Select all that apply.
options: A field
An extra method beyond the interface methods
A constructor
An instance initializer block
optionExplain: Right: anonymous classes may declare fields.
Right: extra methods are allowed, even if code outside cannot name the type.
Anonymous classes cannot declare constructors.
Right: an instance initializer block is allowed in place of a constructor.
questions.explain: Fields, extra methods and instance initializers are allowed. A constructor is not, since the class has no name.
questions.rule: No name, no constructor.
questions.teaches: A constructor must carry the class name, and an anonymous class has no name, so it cannot declare one.

questions.q: Inside a method, a helper type must be created several times with different constructor arguments. Which form fits?
options: An anonymous class
A lambda expression
A local class
An enum
optionExplain: It cannot declare a constructor and is meant for a single use.
A lambda gives no constructor or named type.
Right: a local class has a name and constructors, so many instances can be created.
An enum fixes its instances, so arguments could not vary per call.
questions.explain: An anonymous class has no name or constructor, so it suits one-off use. A local class has both.
questions.rule: More than one instance: local class.
questions.teaches: An anonymous class has no name, so code cannot create further instances of it by name; repeated creation with different constructor arguments needs a named class.

questions.q: Which statement about creating new instances of an enum type is correct?
options: It is allowed if the enum declares a public constructor for outside code to call
Only the constants in its declaration exist; no others can be created
It is allowed through a subclass that is written elsewhere in the program
It is allowed with new, but only inside the same file as the enum
optionExplain: Enum constructors do not make new instances available to outside code.
Right: the compiler knows all instances, which are exactly the declared constants.
An enum cannot have named subclasses.
new cannot be used for an enum anywhere.
questions.explain: The constants are the only instances. The card next explains what an enum is.
questions.rule: Only the listed constants exist.

questions.q: True or false: According to the tutorial, enum values are compared with ==.
questions.explain: Because each constant is a single instance, == works.
questions.rule: Compare constants with ==.

questions.q: With enum Size { SMALL, MEDIUM, LARGE }, the value of Size.LARGE.ordinal() is ____.
questions.explain: Ordinals start at 0 in declaration order: SMALL 0, MEDIUM 1, LARGE 2.
questions.rule: ordinal counts from 0.

questions.q: True or false: A switch expression over Size that lists only SMALL and LARGE, with no default branch, compiles.
questions.explain: A switch expression must cover every constant, and MEDIUM is missing, so the compiler reports an error.
questions.rule: Switch expressions must be exhaustive.

questions.q: A release removes the constant MEDIUM from Size. Which problems can follow? Select all that apply.
options: Code that refers to Size.MEDIUM no longer compiles
A file that stored the text MEDIUM no longer matches a constant
== stops working between the remaining constants
values() returns null
optionExplain: Right: this is the compile-error case the tutorial names.
Right: this is the inconsistency case, since stored values refer to a constant that is gone.
The remaining constants are still single instances, so == is fine.
values() returns an array of the constants that remain.
questions.explain: Code naming MEDIUM stops compiling, and stored text MEDIUM no longer matches any constant. Equality checks on remaining constants are unaffected.
questions.rule: Removing a constant breaks users and stored data.

questions.q: An app saves Size names as text and later turns text back into constants with valueOf. After a release removes a constant, an old file still holds its name. When does the problem show up?
options: At compile time, when the file is saved by the program
Never, because valueOf returns the nearest matching constant instead
At compile time, when the app starts up for the first time
When the old file is read and valueOf finds no matching constant
optionExplain: Text in a file is not checked by the compiler.
Nothing makes valueOf guess a nearby constant.
Compilation happens before any file is read.
Right: the stored value is inconsistent with the enum, and only running code can notice.
questions.explain: Compilation sees no problem because the text is data. The mismatch appears when the old file is read at run time.
questions.rule: Stored data fails at run time, not compile time.
questions.teaches: Beyond the tutorial: valueOf throws an exception when the text matches no constant, so the mismatch shows up while the program runs.

questions.q: A task needs one block of code to run when it finishes, passed to other code. Which is the lightest fit?
options: A lambda expression
A local class with a constructor
A static nested class
An enum constant
optionExplain: Right: a lambda expresses one unit of behavior compactly.
A constructor and name are more than a single behavior needs.
A whole separate type is heavier than needed.
Enum constants are fixed instances, not a way to pass behavior.
questions.explain: One unit of behavior to pass along is the lambda case. The card next lists the cases.
questions.rule: One behavior to pass: lambda.

questions.q: Match each construct to the situation the tutorial gives for it.
pairs: One unit of behavior passed to other code
One-off object that needs fields or extra methods
Named type created more than once inside a method
Helper in the outer class with no need for an outer instance
questions.explain: Each construct has its own best case; the pairs follow the tutorial's rules.
questions.rule: Match need to construct.

questions.q: A one-off object must implement an interface and also keep a counter field across calls. Which construct fits?
options: A lambda expression
A static nested class used from many places
An anonymous class
An inner class with a constructor argument
optionExplain: A lambda cannot declare fields, so it cannot keep the counter.
A heavier form made for wider reuse than this one-off.
Right: it can declare the field and suits a single use.
This works but is heavier than a one-off needs.
questions.explain: A lambda has no fields. An anonymous class can declare a field and is used once.
questions.rule: Needs a field, used once: anonymous.

questions.q: A functional interface is an interface with exactly ____ abstract method.
questions.explain: A lambda can implement an interface with a single abstract method.
questions.rule: Functional interface = one abstract method.
questions.teaches: A lambda can stand in wherever a functional interface is expected, so a type with more than one abstract method needs a class form instead.

questions.q: True or false: Picking a lambda as the lightest construct for an object that needs two named methods and a field follows the tutorial rules.
questions.explain: A lambda suits a single behavior and offers no fields or extra methods, so the tutorial points to a class form here.
questions.rule: Lambda: no fields, no extra methods.

questions.q: Sort each need: is a lambda enough, or does it call for a class form?

items.t: Run an action on every element of a list
Run an action when an error occurs in a process
Pass one comparison rule to a sort method
Create several instances with different constructor arguments
Keep a counter field between calls
Add a second helper method next to the interface method

questions.explain: Needs for state, extra methods or several instances call for a class form.
questions.rule: State, methods or several instances mean a class.
questions.teaches: Beyond the tutorial: the choice turns on state, extra methods and instance count, not on how long the behavior is, so a long block of behavior can still be a lambda.

questions.unitTitle: Using Records to Model Immutable Data (dev.java)
questions.q: A class holds two int values and must be immutable, with accessors and sensible equals, hashCode and toString. Which Java feature is meant to remove most of the hand-written code?
options: An interface with default methods
A record declaration listing the two values
An abstract class with two protected fields
An enum with two constants
optionExplain: Default methods add behavior to interfaces but do not create fields or constructors.
Right: a record declares the values once and the compiler derives the rest.
An abstract class still needs fields, constructor and methods written by hand, and protected fields are not immutable.
An enum models a fixed set of constants, not freely created data values.
questions.explain: Records exist to cut the boilerplate of immutable data classes. The card next shows what the compiler derives.
questions.rule: A record header replaces the boilerplate of an immutable data class.

questions.unitTitle: Using Records to Model Immutable Data (dev.java)
questions.q: The parenthesised list in a record header declares its ____, from which the compiler derives fields and accessors.
questions.explain: Each entry in the header is a component; the compiler makes a private final field and a same-named accessor for it.
questions.rule: Components drive everything the compiler generates.

questions.unitTitle: Using Records to Model Immutable Data (dev.java)
questions.q: A record Reading has components double value and String unit. Sort these body members by whether the compiler accepts them.
groups: Not allowed in a record body

items.t: a static field with an initializer
a static initializer block
an overriding toString method
an extra instance field int count
an instance field initializer
an instance initializer block

questions.explain: Static state and methods are fine, and generated methods may be overridden. Extra instance state in any form is not allowed, because the components must fully describe the record.
questions.rule: Static members yes, extra instance state no.

questions.unitTitle: Using Records to Model Immutable Data (dev.java)
questions.q: A record Basket has a component List of String items. Which statements about its generated accessor items() are correct?
options: It is created by the compiler with the same name as the component
The final field makes the list contents impossible to change
You may write your own version that returns a copy of the list
It returns the stored list itself, so a caller can still change its contents
A record may not declare its own accessor
optionExplain: Right: one same-named accessor per component is generated.
Final fixes which list the field refers to, not what the list holds, so contents can still be changed.
Right: the tutorial names a defensive copy as a common reason to write your own accessor.
Right: the generated accessor hands back the stored reference, so a mutable list is exposed.
The tutorial says you may write your own accessor.
questions.explain: A final field protects the reference only. For a mutable component, copy on the way in, on the way out, or both.
questions.rule: Immutable fields do not make mutable components immutable.
questions.teaches: Beyond the tutorial: final prevents reassigning a field but does not freeze the object it refers to, which is why records with mutable components still need copies.

questions.unitTitle: Using Records to Model Immutable Data (dev.java)
questions.q: A record Seat has components int row and int seat. A developer adds a third component, char block, and changes nothing else in the record. Which result follows?
options: equals and hashCode must be rewritten by hand so that they include the new block component
The old two-argument constructor still exists alongside a new three-argument constructor
The generated members include block, and callers of the old two-argument constructor no longer compile
toString stays as it was, because it is not regenerated when the header changes
optionExplain: The tutorial says the compiler regenerates these methods, so they cannot go stale.
The canonical constructor is derived from the header, so the header change replaces it; no extra overload appears.
Right: the derived methods follow the header, and the canonical constructor now needs three arguments.
toString is also generated from the components, so it follows the header too.
questions.explain: Everything generated tracks the header, which keeps the record consistent. The cost is that the constructor signature changes.
questions.rule: Change the header and the generated members change with it.
questions.teaches: Beyond the tutorial: adding a component changes the canonical constructor signature, so existing call sites that pass the old argument list stop compiling.

questions.unitTitle: Using Records to Model Immutable Data (dev.java)
questions.q: True or false: when a record needs to check its input, you must give up the generated constructor and assign every field by hand.
questions.explain: A compact constructor lets you add a check and still have the fields assigned for you. The card next shows how.
questions.rule: Validation does not force you to write all assignments.

questions.unitTitle: Using Records to Model Immutable Data (dev.java)
questions.q: A compact canonical constructor is written without a ____ list, and the compiler assigns the fields after your code runs.
questions.explain: The compact form omits the parameter list; the components act as implicit parameters.
questions.rule: Compact means no parameter list.

questions.unitTitle: Using Records to Model Immutable Data (dev.java)
questions.q: A record Playlist has components String name and List of String tracks. Which addition lets callers create a playlist from only a name, starting with no tracks, while keeping the canonical constructor's checks?
options: A constructor taking the name that assigns this.name and leaves tracks unassigned
A constructor taking the name that calls this(name, List.of())
A second record named Playlist with a single component
A static field holding an empty list that all instances share by assignment
optionExplain: Every field must be assigned and the constructor must delegate, so this does not compile.
Right: delegation to the canonical constructor supplies the empty list and runs the same checks.
A second declaration with the same name is a duplicate, not a constructor.
Instance fields beyond the components are not allowed, so assigning to one from a constructor is not possible.
questions.explain: Additional constructors must call the canonical one, which keeps validation in one place.
questions.rule: Extra constructors delegate with this(...).

questions.unitTitle: Using Records to Model Immutable Data (dev.java)
questions.q: A record Span has components int start and int end. Its compact constructor reads: Span { if (end != 0 && end == start) throw new IllegalArgumentException(); this.start = start; } Which statement finds the real problem?
options: Compact constructors are not allowed to throw exceptions of any kind
A compact constructor must repeat the record parameter list in brackets
The condition has to be checked after the field has been assigned, not before
A compact constructor may not assign this.start itself; the compiler does that
optionExplain: Throwing is the normal way to reject bad input in a constructor, compact or not.
A compact constructor has no parameter list by definition.
Assignment order is not the issue; the compiler assigns the fields after the body.
Right: direct field assignment is not allowed in the compact form. Reassign the parameter, or use the explicit form.
questions.explain: In the compact form you work on the parameters and the compiler stores them. Writing to the field yourself is rejected.
questions.rule: Compact: change parameters, never fields.
questions.hint: Look at the last statement of the body.

questions.unitTitle: Using Records to Model Immutable Data (dev.java)
questions.q: Match each description to the constructor form it describes.
pairs: No parameter list; the compiler assigns fields after your code
Full parameter list; you assign every field yourself
Must begin by calling this(...) on the canonical constructor
Takes all components and copies them when you write none
questions.explain: Each form differs in who assigns the fields and whether delegation is required.
questions.rule: Know who assigns the fields in each form.

questions.unitTitle: Using Records to Model Immutable Data (dev.java)
questions.q: A record Roster has a component List of String names, and its compact constructor reassigns names to List.copyOf(names). According to the tutorial, List.copyOf gives an unmodifiable copy that rejects null elements. A caller passes a list containing a null element. What happens?
options: The record is created and holds a copy with the null element removed
The record is created and the null element is kept in its list
Creation is rejected, because the copy step refuses the null element
The null element is replaced by an empty string in the copy
optionExplain: Nothing in the copy step filters elements out.
A copy that rejects null elements cannot keep one.
Right: the rejection happens inside the constructor, so no Roster with bad data ever exists.
No component of the copy step substitutes values.
questions.explain: Work done in the canonical constructor runs for every creation path, so invalid input is refused before an object exists.
questions.rule: Checks and copies in the canonical constructor guard every path.
questions.teaches: Beyond the tutorial: because the record holds its own copy, later changes the caller makes to the original list do not reach the record.

questions.unitTitle: Using Records to Model Immutable Data (dev.java)
questions.q: Data objects are sent as bytes between programs and rebuilt on the other side. Which property would make a rebuilt object safer to trust?
options: Rebuilding skips all constructors for speed
Rebuilding runs the same validation as normal creation
Rebuilding copies fields without any checks
Rebuilding is only allowed for mutable objects
optionExplain: Skipping constructors also skips their checks, which makes trust harder.
Right: the same checks on incoming data keep invalid states out.
Unchecked copying lets bad data in.
Mutability does not make rebuilding safer.
questions.explain: Checking incoming data the same way as new data is safer. The card next shows how records handle it.
questions.rule: Validate rebuilt data like new data.

questions.unitTitle: Using Records to Model Immutable Data (dev.java)
questions.q: True or false: according to the tutorial, deserializing a record invokes its canonical constructor, so validation written there also applies to deserialized data.
questions.explain: The tutorial states that deserialization always goes through the canonical constructor.
questions.rule: Deserialization runs the canonical constructor.

questions.unitTitle: Using Records to Model Immutable Data (dev.java)
questions.q: Put these steps in a sensible order for finding the customer with the most orders, using the approach from the tutorial. Assume the local record is declared once the map exists, and that mapping the entries to the record needs the record to be declared first.
items: Build a Map from customer to order count with a stream
Declare a local record pairing a customer with a count
Map each Map.Entry to the local record through its constructor
Take the maximum using a comparator on the count
Read the customer name from the winning record
questions.explain: The map comes first, then the record gives its entries meaningful names, then the maximum and the result read by name.
questions.rule: Count, name the pair, then compare.

questions.unitTitle: Using Records to Model Immutable Data (dev.java)
questions.q: If several states share the highest city count, the tutorial's maximum computation reports ____ of them.
questions.explain: The tutorial points out that ties are not handled: a single state is returned.
questions.rule: A maximum picks one winner.
questions.teaches: Beyond the tutorial: to report every tied state, first find the highest count, then keep every record whose count equals it, rather than taking a single maximum.

questions.unitTitle: Using Records to Model Immutable Data (dev.java)
questions.q: A record Percent has a component int value, and its canonical constructor rejects any value above 100. A tampered byte stream for a serialized Percent claims the value 250. What does deserialization do?
options: It creates the Percent with 250, since bytes bypass checks
It clamps the value to 100
It ignores the stream and returns a default Percent
It fails, because the canonical constructor runs and rejects 250
optionExplain: For records the tutorial says the canonical constructor is invoked, so the check runs.
No code in the record clamps values; the constructor rejects instead.
Nothing in the tutorial describes falling back to a default record.
Right: the check applies to deserialized data, so the tampered value is refused.
questions.explain: Because the canonical constructor is always used, the invariant holds even for data from outside.
questions.rule: Records enforce their checks on incoming bytes too.
questions.teaches: Beyond the tutorial: a tampered or corrupt stream cannot produce an invalid record, which is why validation in the canonical constructor protects data crossing a trust boundary.

questions.q: A class Truck extends class Vehicle. Which of these does Truck not receive from Vehicle?
options: Vehicle's public methods
Vehicle's protected fields
Vehicle's constructors
Vehicle's public nested classes
optionExplain: Public methods are inherited.
Protected fields are inherited, whatever the package.
Constructors are not members of a class, so they are not passed down.
Public nested classes are members and are inherited.
questions.explain: Guessing is fair here. Constructors are the one item that is not inherited. The card next shows the full rule.
questions.rule: A subclass inherits the members that access rules let it see, never constructors, from exactly one direct superclass.

questions.q: True or false: A class that names no superclass is still a subclass of Object.
questions.explain: When no superclass is named, the class automatically extends Object, which is why every class inherits the Object methods.
questions.rule: Every class except Object has a direct superclass.

questions.q: Class Account is in package bank and has: a private field balance, a protected method audit, a public method getBalance and a package-private method note. Class Savings extends Account but lives in package app. Which statements are legal inside a Savings method?
options: balance = 0;
audit();
note();
getBalance();
optionExplain: Private members are not inherited directly, so the name balance is not available.
Protected members are inherited in every package.
Package-private members are inherited only inside the same package, and Savings is in a different one.
Public members are inherited in every package, and this accessor is also the route to the private field.
questions.explain: Public and protected members reach Savings from any package; private and package-private ones do not, here.
questions.rule: Package position matters only for package-private members.
questions.hint: Which two access levels cross package borders?

questions.q: Class Account is in package bank and has a private balance, a protected audit, a public getBalance and a package-private note. Class Savings extends Account and is also in package bank. Besides audit and getBalance, which other member can Savings code use by simple name?
options: Neither, since the package makes no difference
balance, the private field
Both note and balance
note, the package-private method
optionExplain: The package of the subclass decides about package-private members, so it does matter.
Private members stay out of reach, whichever package the subclass lives in.
Only one of the two becomes visible, because balance is private.
Inside the same package the package-private method is inherited too.
questions.explain: Moving the subclass into the superclass's package adds package-private members to what it inherits; private ones stay hidden.
questions.rule: Package-private members are inherited only inside the same package.

questions.q: True or false: Class Parent has a private field secret and a public nested class Peek whose method returns secret. A Child of Parent, in another package, can read secret by using Peek.
questions.explain: A nested class can reach every private member of its enclosing class, and a public nested class is inherited, so the subclass gets indirect access.
questions.rule: Private data can be reached indirectly, through members that are inherited.
questions.teaches: A private field is not inherited directly, but an inherited public or protected nested class has full access to it, giving the subclass an indirect route.
questions.hint: Both accessor methods and nested classes can expose private members.

questions.q: A hobby club wants a Member to be several things at once. Sort each idea: does Java allow it, or does it forbid it?

items.t: Member implements Chef and Driver, two interfaces
A variable of type Chef holds a Member object
A Member object has the types Member, Chef and Driver
Member extends Cook and Racer, two classes
Member extends one class Person and also implements Chef and Driver

questions.explain: One class cannot extend two classes, which avoids clashes over fields and constructors. Types are different: an object may have many interface types, because interfaces carry no fields.
questions.rule: Many types, one class parent.
questions.teaches: Java's ban on several superclasses guards state such as fields; having many interface types at once is safe because interfaces do not hold object fields.

questions.q: Class Dog extends class Animal. The line Animal a = new Dog(); is followed by Dog d = a; What happens?
options: The second line fails to compile
Both lines compile and then run without a problem
It compiles, but it fails when the program runs
It compiles, and afterwards d holds the value null
optionExplain: The compiler cannot be sure that a holds a Dog, so it needs an explicit cast.
That would let any Animal be treated as a Dog.
A cast would compile and might fail at run time, but with no cast the compiler stops first.
Nothing in the language turns a failed assignment into null.
questions.explain: A fair guess either way. The card next shows why the compiler refuses.
questions.rule: Upcast freely, and downcast only with an explicit cast guarded by instanceof, because the runtime checks the real type.

questions.q: Assigning a Dog object to a variable of type Animal is called ____ and needs no cast.
questions.explain: Moving up the hierarchy is safe, since every Dog is an Animal.
questions.rule: Up is implicit, down needs a cast.

questions.q: Put the steps of a safe downcast in order. The variable pet has type Animal and holds some object.
items: Hold the object in an Animal variable
Test with instanceof Dog
Cast to Dog inside the guarded branch
Call a method that only Dog has
questions.explain: The test comes before the cast, and the Dog-only call comes after it, because the Animal type does not offer that method.
questions.rule: Test first, cast second, use third.

questions.q: Shape s = new Shape(); Square q = (Square) s; where Square extends Shape. What happens if the first line is changed to Shape s = new Square();?
options: It runs: the cast succeeds
It still throws an exception at run time
It stops compiling
It compiles, but q becomes null
optionExplain: The object is really a Square, so the runtime check passes.
That was the result for the plain Shape object, but the object is now a Square.
The cast was already legal to compile in both versions.
A successful cast hands back the same object.
questions.explain: The runtime check looks at the real object, not at the variable type. With a Square inside, the cast passes.
questions.rule: The object, not the variable, decides.

questions.q: Triangle and Square are sibling subclasses of Shape, so a Triangle is not a Square. Code: Object o = new Triangle(); / if (o instanceof Square) { Square q = (Square) o; } / Triangle u = (Triangle) o; Which statements about it are right?
options: The instanceof branch is skipped, because o holds a Triangle
The cast inside the branch cannot fail, because of the test
The line Triangle u = (Triangle) o; throws at run time
The line Triangle u = (Triangle) o; compiles and works, since the object is a Triangle
optionExplain: The object is a Triangle, so the test for Square is false.
Inside a true instanceof test the cast cannot fail.
The object really is a Triangle, so this cast passes.
The cast is explicit and the object has that type, so it compiles and runs.
questions.explain: The test for Square is false for a Triangle, so the branch is skipped. A cast guarded by instanceof is safe, and the final cast works because the object is a Triangle.
questions.rule: Check the compile rule and the runtime fact separately.

questions.q: True or false: Interface Playable is implemented by class Song. The line Playable p = new Song(); is followed by Song s = p; and this compiles without a cast.
questions.explain: Casting rules do not depend on whether the variable type is a class or an interface: the compiler cannot tell that p holds a Song, so a cast is needed.
questions.rule: Interface-typed variables need a cast to go back to a class.
questions.teaches: The upcast and downcast rules apply to interface types as well: a variable of interface type may reference any implementing object, but returning to the class type needs an explicit cast.

questions.q: Class Pet has an instance method sound returning dots. Class Cat extends Pet and redefines sound to return meow. What does Pet p = new Cat(); p.sound() return?
options: A run-time exception
dots
A compile-time error
meow
optionExplain: Nothing about the call can fail at run time.
That would be the answer if the variable type chose the method.
Redefining an instance method with the same signature is allowed.
The method of the object's own class runs, even through a Pet variable.
questions.explain: A fair guess. The card next shows what decides the version.
questions.rule: Instance methods are overridden and chosen by the object; static methods are hidden and chosen by the class named in the call.

questions.q: True or false: The annotation Override must be present for a subclass method to override a superclass method.
questions.explain: It is optional. It is recommended because the compiler then reports an error if no matching superclass method exists.
questions.rule: Add Override to catch mistakes early.

questions.q: Superclass Base has a protected method int size(). Which subclass declarations are legal overrides of it?
options: protected int size()
public int size()
private int size()
public long size()
optionExplain: Same name, parameters, return type and access, so it overrides.
More access than protected is allowed, so this overrides.
This gives less access than protected, which is not allowed.
long is not a subtype of int, so the return type does not match.
questions.explain: The exact match and a wider access are legal. Less access and an unrelated return type fail.
questions.rule: Same signature, same or wider access.

questions.q: Light and its subclass Lamp both declare a static method kind. In Light it returns light and in Lamp it returns lamp. What do the calls Light.kind() and Lamp.kind() return, in that order?
options: lamp, then lamp
lamp, then light
light, then lamp
light, then light
optionExplain: The Lamp version would run for the Light call only if kind were overridden by an object.
The versions would be swapped, but each call names its own class.
Each call runs the version of the class named in it.
Lamp has its own version, which Lamp.kind() reaches.
questions.explain: Hidden static methods are chosen by the class named in the call.
questions.rule: Static: look at the class name in the call.

questions.q: Sort each situation: does it compile, or is it a compile-time error?
