items.t: Subclass instance method has the same signature as a superclass instance method
Subclass static method has the same signature as a superclass static method
Subclass makes a protected method public
Subclass static method has the same signature as a superclass instance method
Subclass instance method has the same signature as a superclass static method
Subclass makes a public method protected

questions.explain: Matching kinds override or hide. Mixing static and instance is an error, and so is giving less access.
questions.rule: Same kind, same or wider access.

questions.q: Class Parser has a method Number parse(). Class IntParser extends it and declares Integer parse(). With Parser p = new IntParser();, what type does the compiler see for the expression p.parse()?
options: Integer, because the object is one
Object
Number, as Parser declares
The line does not compile
optionExplain: The compiler works from declared types, not from what the object will be.
Number is more specific than Object, and Number is the declared return type.
The compiler uses the declared type of the variable, so it sees the return type declared in Parser, although an Integer arrives at run time.
A covariant return is legal, so the declaration compiles.
questions.explain: A covariant return is legal, but a caller using the superclass type only knows the superclass return type.
questions.rule: Callers see declared types.
questions.teaches: Covariant overriding narrows the return type only for callers who use the subclass type; through a superclass variable the compiler still sees the superclass return type. (Reasoned from the tutorial rules, beyond its text.)

questions.q: Class Tractor has an instance method describe returning tractor. Interface Hauler has a default describe returning hauler. Class Ox extends Tractor implements Hauler and declares nothing. What does new Ox().describe() return?
options: hauler
tractor
A compile-time error
Both, joined together
optionExplain: That would be right if the default beat the class method.
The method from the class takes precedence over an interface default.
There is no conflict to resolve: one source is a class.
A call runs exactly one method.
questions.explain: A fair guess. The card next gives the precedence rule.
questions.rule: A class method beats a default, an overridden default is ignored, and any other clash must be resolved by overriding.

questions.q: If a superclass instance method and an interface default share a signature, the ____ method is used.
questions.explain: A method inherited from a class is preferred to a default method.
questions.rule: Class methods win.

questions.q: Unrelated interfaces Printer and Scanner each declare a default start(). Class Combo implements both and declares nothing. What happens?
options: Printer's start is used because it is named first
The compiler reports an error
Scanner's start is used because it is named last
Both start methods run in turn
optionExplain: Order in the implements list gives no priority.
Two independent defaults conflict, so Combo must override start.
Order does not decide in either direction.
A call runs one method, and here none is chosen automatically.
questions.explain: Independent defaults with one signature force the class to decide.
questions.rule: Conflicts need an explicit override.

questions.q: Interface Scanner extends Printer and overrides its default start(). Class Combo implements both Scanner and Printer and declares nothing. What happens?
options: It is undefined which is used
Printer's start is used
The compiler reports an error
Scanner's start is used
optionExplain: The more specific default wins by rule, so the choice is not left undefined.
Printer's version is the overridden candidate, which is disregarded.
Scanner start overrides Printer start, so there is no conflict to report.
Scanner's default already overrides Printer's, so the overridden one is ignored.
questions.explain: Because Scanner extends Printer, its start overrides Printer start, so there is no conflict.
questions.rule: The more specific default wins.

questions.q: True or false: Two interfaces each declare a static method with the same name. A class implementing both must override it to avoid a compile-time error.
questions.explain: Static interface methods are not inherited, so they do not clash inside the class.
questions.rule: Static interface methods stay with their interface.
questions.teaches: Since static interface methods are not inherited, two of them with one name cannot conflict in an implementing class.

questions.q: True or false: Interface Alpha has a default hello(). Interface Beta declares an abstract hello(). A class implementing both compiles without declaring hello(), since the default supplies a body.
questions.explain: A default clashing with an abstract method is a compile-time error. The class must override hello().
questions.rule: Even the abstract clash needs an override.
questions.teaches: A default does not satisfy an abstract method of the same signature from another interface; the class must write its own version.

questions.q: Class Manager extends Staff and overrides describe. After Staff s = new Manager(); which describe runs for s.describe()?
options: The Staff version
Both, Staff first
The Manager version
None: it does not compile
optionExplain: That would require the variable type to decide.
One call runs one method; super would be needed for the second.
The object is a Manager, so its version runs.
The assignment and the call are both legal.
questions.explain: A fair guess. The card next names this rule.
questions.rule: The object's class chooses the instance method, super reaches the parent version, and constructors chain upward starting with a super call.

questions.q: The rule that the JVM runs the method of the object's actual class is called virtual method ____.
questions.explain: Virtual method invocation is the tutorial's name for choosing the method by the real object.
questions.rule: The object decides.

questions.q: Class Parent has only a constructor Parent(int n). Class Child extends Parent and declares a constructor Child() with an empty body. What happens when this is compiled?
options: A compile-time error
It compiles, and n is zero
It compiles, and Parent is skipped
A run-time exception
optionExplain: The compiler inserts super(), but Parent has no no-argument constructor.
Nothing passes a value for n.
Constructors chain upward, so the Parent constructor cannot be skipped.
The problem is found before the program runs.
questions.explain: An inserted super() needs a matching no-argument constructor.
questions.rule: Call super with arguments yourself when needed.

questions.q: Classes A, B extends A and C extends B each have a no-argument constructor that prints its own letter, and none calls super explicitly. What does new C() print?
options: CBA, bottom class first
ABC
Only C, the last class
BC, without A
optionExplain: The chain starts at the top, not the bottom.
Each inserted super() runs first, so output starts at the top of the chain.
Parents are not skipped; each constructor first runs its superclass constructor, so A and B also print.
A also runs, since the chain reaches Object through A.
questions.explain: Constructors run from the top ancestor down.
questions.rule: Chain goes up; bodies run top first.

questions.q: Which of these fail to compile?
options: class Sub extends String
A subclass overriding a method marked final in its parent
A subclass method calling super.show() inside its own show
A constructor whose first statement is super(7), where the parent has Parent(int)
optionExplain: String is a final class, so it cannot be subclassed.
A final method cannot be overridden.
Calling the parent's version through super is allowed.
This is the normal form of a superclass constructor call.
questions.explain: The first two break final. The other two are normal uses of super.
questions.rule: final stops subclassing or overriding.

questions.q: Class A has a field name set to A. Class B extends A, declares its own name set to B and a method both returning name followed by super.name. What does new B().both() return? Answer with the two letters: ____
questions.explain: The subclass field hides the inherited one but both exist; the plain name gives B and super.name reaches A.
questions.rule: Hiding does not remove the parent's field.
questions.teaches: A hidden field is still part of the object, reachable through super, so hiding is not replacing (reasoned from the tutorial, beyond its text).

questions.q: True or false: Two separate objects of a class that does not override equals, with identical field values, are reported equal by equals.
questions.explain: Default equals uses identity, so only the very same object is equal to itself. The card next explains the default.
questions.rule: Default equals means same object.

questions.q: True or false: The default equals method on Object tests identity, like the == operator.
questions.explain: Unless overridden, equals is true only when both references point to the same object.
questions.rule: Default equals means same object.

questions.q: Class Ticket overrides equals so that two tickets with the same id are equal. Nothing else is overridden. What else should be done?
options: Override getClass so it returns the ticket id
Make Ticket implement the AutoCloseable interface
Override finalize so it compares the ticket ids
Override hashCode to match equals
optionExplain: getClass is final and cannot be overridden.
AutoCloseable is about releasing resources, not equality.
finalize is a cleanup callback and is discouraged.
Objects that are equal must have equal hash codes, and the inherited hashCode does not know about ids.
questions.explain: Changing equality changes what hashCode must do.
questions.rule: equals and hashCode go together.

questions.q: Sort each item for a class you write: is it a sensible thing to override or write, or something to avoid or that is impossible?

items.t: toString, to print a readable description
equals, when two objects with the same ISBN should be equal
hashCode, after overriding equals
getClass, to report a different class
finalize, to close files

questions.explain: toString, equals and hashCode are the usual overrides. getClass is final, and finalize is deprecated and unreliable.
questions.rule: Override what describes your objects; do not override getClass or lean on finalize.

questions.q: Class Order has a field address holding a reference to an Address object, and implements Cloneable using the default clone. After copy = (Order) original.clone(), code changes the street through copy.address. What happens to original.address's street?
options: It stays the same, since the copy is complete and separate
It changes too, as both share one Address
It becomes null
The clone call throws an exception
optionExplain: A complete copy would need clone overridden to copy the Address as well.
The default clone copies the reference, not the Address it points to.
Nothing resets the original.
Cloneable is implemented, so no exception is thrown.
questions.explain: The default clone is shallow; to separate the objects, override clone to copy referenced objects as well.
questions.rule: Copied references share.
questions.teaches: Beyond the tutorial: an independent copy needs the referenced Address copied as well, which the default clone does not do.

questions.q: Which statement about an abstract class is correct?
options: It must contain at least one abstract method inside
It cannot be created with new, but can be extended
It can be created with new when it has fields
It cannot have any fields, only methods
optionExplain: An abstract class may have no abstract methods at all.
Instantiation is blocked; subclassing is the point.
Fields do not change the ban on instantiation.
Abstract classes can hold non-static, non-final fields.
questions.explain: A fair guess. The card next lists what an abstract class can contain.
questions.rule: Share code and state among related classes with an abstract class; describe behavior for any class with an interface.

questions.q: True or false: A class that contains an abstract method must itself be declared abstract.
questions.explain: A class with an incomplete method cannot be instantiated, so the language requires abstract on it.
questions.rule: Abstract method means abstract class.

questions.q: Invoice and Receipt are closely related, share a customer field and a method that totals tax, and each prints differently. What fits best?
options: A final class holding both kinds of document together
An interface that carries the customer field as state
Two unrelated classes with copied code in each of them
An abstract class sharing the field and method
optionExplain: A final class cannot be subclassed.
Interface fields are public static final, so they cannot hold per-object state.
Copying code is what inheritance avoids.
Shared state and code among related classes favors an abstract class.
questions.explain: Shared fields and code point to an abstract class.
questions.rule: State plus related classes: abstract class.

questions.q: Sort each declaration: does it compile, or is it an error? Abstract class Base declares an abstract method run.

items.t: Abstract class Mid extends Base and does not implement run
Concrete class Leaf extends Base and implements run
Abstract class Plain declares no abstract methods
Concrete class Mid2 extends Base and does not implement run
The statement new Base();

questions.explain: A subclass must implement inherited abstract methods or be abstract itself. Abstract classes cannot be instantiated.
questions.rule: Concrete means complete.

questions.q: True or false: Interface Payable declares pay(). Abstract class Employee implements Payable without writing pay(). A concrete class Intern extends Employee, also without pay(), and compiles.
questions.explain: Intern is concrete, so it must implement pay(). Only abstract Employee may leave it out.
questions.rule: The first concrete class must finish the job.
questions.teaches: Beyond the tutorial: if the concrete subclass still lacks an implementation, the compiler reports the error there, at compile time rather than run time.

questions.q: Two teams build one product. Team A writes code that calls methods, and team B writes the code behind them. What can they share so that neither has to read the other's source?
options: A list of method signatures and return types
A copy of team B's full source code for team A to study
One class that both teams are allowed to edit
The names of team B's private variables
optionExplain: Right: signatures and return types are what callers need and what implementers must supply.
This works but defeats the purpose, since team A would then depend on how team B's code works.
Shared editing couples the teams tightly; a contract is meant to let them work apart.
Private variables are internal details that callers have no use for.
questions.explain: A shared description of the method names, inputs and results is enough for A to write calls and for B to write the bodies. The card next names this description.
questions.rule: Share the promise, not the code.

questions.q: True or false: According to the tutorial, an interface is a reference type like a class, and it acts as a contract between the code that calls methods and the code that supplies them.
questions.explain: The tutorial introduces an interface as a reference type like a class and uses the word contract for the agreement between the code that calls methods and the code that supplies them.
questions.rule: An interface is a reference type used as a contract.

questions.q: A weather company publishes an interface WeatherFeed with the method double temperatureIn(String city), and many apps call it. Next month the company moves its data from files to a database but still implements WeatherFeed. What do the apps need?
options: To be rewritten, since the storage they rely on has changed
To rename their calls, as new storage needs new method names
Nothing: they rely on signatures, not on how data is stored
The database driver code, to keep calling the same methods
optionExplain: The apps never touched the storage; they only called the published method.
Method names belong to the interface, which did not change, so no renaming is needed.
Right: the implementation is private to the company and may change behind an unchanged interface.
The apps call methods only; any driver is the company's own internal concern.
questions.explain: Callers depend on the published signature, and the company may change its implementation while it still implements the same interface.
questions.rule: Callers depend on the signature, not on the implementation.
questions.hint: Which part of the interface do the apps rely on?

questions.q: Makers of guidance software call a car's turning and braking methods without knowing how each car's ____ carries them out.
questions.explain: The callers know only the published methods. How each car turns or brakes is the implementation, which differs between makers.
questions.rule: Many implementers can sit behind one interface.
questions.teaches: A new implementer can be added later without touching the caller, because the caller never named a particular class.

questions.q: True or false: Given an interface Shape that declares double area();, the statement Shape s = new Shape(); creates an object that follows the contract.
questions.explain: According to the tutorial, an interface cannot be instantiated. It is implemented by classes, and objects come from those classes.
questions.rule: An interface is a contract, not an object; only implementing classes are instantiated.
questions.hint: Who supplies the method bodies?

questions.q: A fire-safety interface Alarm declares void ring(); and void silence();. A concrete class Bell implements Alarm and gives a body only for ring. According to the tutorial, what must Bell do?
options: Nothing more, since methods that nobody calls need no body
Add a comment above silence to mark it as intentionally empty
Declare silence as static, which removes the duty to implement it
Give silence a body too, because every declared method needs one
optionExplain: The duty covers every declared method, whether or not it gets called.
A comment is not a body; the class still lacks an implementation.
Static methods in an interface are separate members; this would not turn an abstract method into an optional one.
Right: all declared methods need bodies in a concrete implementing class.
questions.explain: A concrete class that implements an interface must supply a body for every method the interface declares, so Bell needs a body for silence as well.
questions.rule: A concrete implementer supplies every declared method.
questions.teaches: Beyond the tutorial: a class may leave an interface method unimplemented only if the class is declared abstract; otherwise it is a compile-time error.

questions.q: A Java interface declares the line int MAX = 10; with no modifiers. What is MAX?
options: An instance variable that each implementing object holds separately
A constant that is implicitly public, static and final
A package-private variable that implementers may reassign
A private field visible only inside the interface
optionExplain: Instance variables belong to classes; an interface holds constants instead.
Right: constants in an interface are implicitly public, static and final.
Reassigning is blocked because the constant is final, and it is also public.
A private constant would be of no use to the implementers that need to read it.
questions.explain: Fields in an interface are constants. The card next lists which modifiers are implied.
questions.rule: Interface fields are constants.

questions.q: A constant declared in an interface is implicitly public, static and ____.
questions.explain: Final is implied, so the value cannot change after it is set.
questions.rule: Interface constants are public static final.

questions.q: Class Taxi must extend the class Vehicle and also meet the interfaces Billable and Trackable. Which declaration has the right shape?
options: class Taxi extends Vehicle implements Billable, Trackable
class Taxi implements Billable, Trackable extends Vehicle
class Taxi extends Vehicle, Billable implements Trackable
class Taxi implements Billable extends Trackable, Vehicle
optionExplain: Right: one parent class after extends, then a comma-separated implements list.
The implements clause must follow the extends clause, not precede it.
A class extends only one class, and an interface goes in implements, not extends.
This swaps the clauses and treats a class as a second parent of the interface Trackable.
questions.explain: The extends clause comes first, and the implements clause follows it with interfaces separated by commas.
questions.rule: Extends first, then implements with a comma-separated list.

questions.q: Which of these members can have a method body inside an interface? Select all that apply.
options: An abstract method signature
A default method
A constant declaration
A static method
A private instance method
A nested type
optionExplain: An abstract signature ends with a semicolon and has no body.
Right: a default method must have a body.
A constant holds a value, not a method body.
Right: a static method has a body.
Right: a private instance method has a body, and exists to share code among default methods.
A nested type is a member type, not a method, so it has no method body.
questions.explain: Bodies appear only in default, static and private methods. An abstract signature ends with a semicolon.
questions.rule: Bodies live in default, static and private methods.
questions.teaches: According to the tutorial, private interface methods (from Java SE 9) hold code shared by default methods, and a private interface method can be neither default nor abstract.

questions.q: In package shop, the file declares interface Discount { int apply(int price); } with no public modifier. A class in package web tries to use Discount. According to the tutorial, what is the situation?
options: Discount is usable anywhere because its method is implicitly public
Discount is usable from web if web's class extends it
Discount is not accessible from web, only from inside shop
Discount is usable from web if apply is marked abstract
optionExplain: Implied public applies to the methods; the interface itself still needs the public keyword for wider access.
Extends does not widen access, and a class would implement an interface, not extend it.
Right: without public the interface is limited to its own package.
Abstract is already implied for such a method and has no effect on access.
questions.explain: Without public, an interface is accessible only within its own package. The implied public on its methods does not change that.
questions.rule: No public on the interface means package-only access.

questions.q: interface Metric { static double toKm(double miles) { return miles * 1.609; } double value(); } and a class Run implements Metric. According to the tutorial, to what does the static method toKm belong?
options: Each Run object, as an inherited instance method
The interface itself, not the implementing objects
Run alone, which must override it to use it
The first class that happens to call it
optionExplain: Instance methods belong to objects; static ones do not.
Right: static interface methods belong to the interface.
Overriding applies to instance methods; static methods are not handed down to the implementing objects.
Ownership is fixed by the declaration, not by who calls it first.
questions.explain: Static methods belong to the interface itself, not to the objects of implementing classes.
questions.rule: A static interface method belongs to the interface.
questions.teaches: A static interface method is called through the interface name, as in Metric.toKm(5.0), not through a Run object.

questions.q: A library's interface Reader is implemented by 200 classes written by other teams. The library owner adds a new abstract method to Reader. What do you expect?
options: All 200 classes get an empty version automatically
Only the classes that call the method need changes
Nothing happens until someone calls the method
Each of the 200 classes now lacks a required body
optionExplain: An abstract method comes without a body, so nothing is filled in for the classes.
Calling is not the issue; every concrete implementer is missing a required body.
The missing body is a problem in the class itself, whether or not the method is ever called.
Right: each implementer now lacks a body for the new abstract method.
questions.explain: Each implementing class must supply the new body, so adding an abstract method breaks them. The card next shows safer options.
questions.rule: A new abstract method breaks existing implementers.

questions.q: Adding a ____ method to an existing interface gives implementers a body without requiring changes in their classes.
questions.explain: A default method carries its own body, so existing implementers inherit it.
questions.rule: Default methods add behavior safely.

questions.q: interface Logger declares void log(String message), and 30 classes implement it. The team wants a method logAll that calls log once for each message in a list. Which addition keeps all 30 classes compiling?
options: A default method logAll whose body calls log for each message
An abstract method logAll, with a note asking teams to add it
A protected method logAll that the 30 classes may override
A constant named logAll holding the list of messages
optionExplain: Right: the default body uses log, so no implementer needs changes.
An abstract method forces all 30 classes to add a body, which breaks them.
The tutorial lists interface methods as public or private, so a protected method is not an option.
A constant is a value, not a method that performs the looping.
questions.explain: A default method supplies the body itself, using only log, which every implementer already has.
questions.rule: Give the new method a body as default, built from existing methods.

questions.q: Interface Base has a default method String label(). A child interface Strict extends Base and redeclares the method as String label(); with no body. A class Item implements Strict and gives no label method. What happens?
options: Item inherits Base's label, since defaults cannot be undone
Item gets an automatic empty label from the compiler
Item is accepted, and calling label returns nothing
Item lacks a required body, so it must write label
optionExplain: A child interface may redeclare a default method as abstract, which cancels the inherited body.
No such empty version is supplied for an abstract method.
An abstract method has no body to return anything, so Item cannot be accepted as it stands.
Right: Strict made label abstract, so a concrete implementer must supply it.
questions.explain: Redeclaring the default method as abstract in the child makes implementers write it, so Item is missing a required body.
questions.rule: A child can turn an inherited default back into an abstract method.
questions.teaches: According to the tutorial, a child interface can leave an inherited default method alone, redeclare it as abstract so implementers must write it, or redefine it with a new default body.

questions.q: True or false: According to the tutorial, adding a default method to an interface is safe even when a class implementing it also gets a method with the same signature from another interface.
questions.explain: The tutorial says a default method must not clash with methods from other interfaces that a class implements, so the clash is a problem to avoid.
questions.rule: A new default method must not clash with another interface's method.

questions.q: interface Invoice has two default methods, totalWithTax and totalWithDiscount, which both need the same rounding code. Which design keeps the rounding code inside the interface and hidden from clients?
options: A public abstract method round, which every implementer must supply
A private method round with a body, called by both defaults
A protected method round, inherited by implementing classes
A constant ROUND, holding the rounding code
optionExplain: This adds a duty for every implementer and exposes the helper.
Right: a private method with a body is shared by the defaults and is hidden from clients.
The tutorial lists private and public interface methods, not protected ones.
A constant holds a value, not code that performs rounding.
questions.explain: A private interface method can hold shared code for default methods without being part of the public contract.
questions.rule: Shared default code can sit in a private interface method.
questions.teaches: Because the private helper is hidden from clients and implementers, it can be changed later without breaking any caller.

questions.q: In a method declared as static Priced pick(Priced a, Priced b), the type Priced is an interface. What can the arguments be?
options: Only objects of a class literally named Priced
Only objects whose classes share one named parent
Any value, as interface parameters carry no type check
Any objects whose classes implement Priced
optionExplain: Priced is an interface, so no object is created from it directly.
The classes may have unrelated parents; what they share is the interface.
Interface names are types, so the compiler checks what is passed.
Right: any object whose class implements the interface is accepted.
questions.explain: An interface-typed parameter accepts objects whose classes implement the interface. The card next explains why.
questions.rule: Interface-typed parameters accept implementers.

questions.q: True or false: A variable declared with an interface type can refer to any object, whether or not its class implements that interface.
questions.explain: According to the tutorial, an object assigned to an interface-typed variable must be an instance of a class that implements the interface.
questions.rule: Only implementers fit an interface-typed variable.

questions.q: Classes Song and Podcast both implement the interface Playable. A program runs Playable item = new Podcast(); and later item = new Song();. What is true?
options: The second assignment fails, since item already holds a Podcast
Both assignments are fine, as each class implements Playable
Both work only if Song extends Podcast
Both fail, since a variable cannot have an interface type
optionExplain: A variable can be reassigned to another object of a fitting type.
Right: each class implements Playable, so each object fits.
The classes do not need to be related by inheritance; the shared interface is enough.
Interface names are types and can be used for variables.
questions.explain: Both classes implement Playable, so both objects fit the variable, one after the other.
questions.rule: A variable of interface type can hold any implementer.

questions.q: interface Sized { boolean biggerThan(Sized other); } and class Box implements Sized has the extra method int volume(). Inside Box.biggerThan(Sized other), the code calls other.volume(). Why is it rejected?
options: The type Sized has no volume method, so a cast to Box is needed
Parameters of interface type cannot be read at all
volume must be marked static to be called on another object
Only the first parameter of a method may have an interface type
optionExplain: Right: the compiler sees Sized, and only a cast to Box reaches volume.
Interface-typed parameters can be read through the interface's methods.
Static would change what kind of member volume is and would not fix the type problem.
Any parameter may have an interface type.
questions.explain: The parameter is typed Sized, which offers only the interface's methods. In the tutorial, the matching example casts to the class before calling its own method.
questions.rule: Interface type exposes interface methods only.
questions.teaches: According to the tutorial, an interface-typed parameter exposes only the interface's methods, so the code casts it to the implementing class before calling a class-specific method such as getArea.

questions.q: True or false: Interface Relatable declares isLargerThan(Relatable other), and class Rectangle implements it by casting other to Rectangle and comparing width times height. According to the tutorial, a method that compares two Relatable objects this way gives meaningful results when the two come from different implementing classes.
questions.explain: The comparison is written for one class, here through the cast to Rectangle. The tutorial notes it works only when both objects are of the same class, even though both implement Relatable.
questions.rule: Same interface does not guarantee comparable objects.

questions.q: class Pet extends Animal implements Trainable, Showable. Which statements describe a Pet object? Select all that apply.
options: It can be used where a Pet is expected
It can be used where an Animal is expected
It can be used where a Trainable or a Showable is expected
It can hold only the type of the first interface it lists
It has only the type Pet, because interfaces are not types
optionExplain: Right: Pet is the object's own class.
Right: Animal is its superclass, so it has that type too.
Right: an interface it implements is also a type for the object.
Nothing limits the object to the first listed interface.
The tutorial says defining an interface defines a reference type.
questions.explain: A Pet object has the type of its own class, of its superclass, and of each interface it implements.
questions.rule: An object can have several types at once.
questions.teaches: Passing a Pet to a method that expects a Trainable lets that method call only the Trainable methods, even though the object is more than that.

questions.q: A container class stores its content as Object, so every read needs a cast. Which change lets the compiler check element types and remove the casts?
options: Give the class a type parameter and use it instead of Object
Rename the class so that its name ends with the word Generic
Store the content in an array of Object instead of one field
Mark the read method final so that its return type cannot change
optionExplain: Right: a type parameter lets each use of the class say what it holds, and the compiler checks it.
A name has no effect on type checking; only type parameters carry element types.
An Object array still holds anything and still needs casts on read.
final stops overriding, not the Object return type, so casts stay.
questions.explain: Replacing Object with a type parameter is what generics are for. The card next shows the vocabulary.
questions.rule: A type parameter replaces Object to get checks and drop casts.

questions.q: In the declaration of a generic class, a placeholder such as T is called a type ____.
questions.explain: T is the type parameter, also called a type variable. The concrete type supplied later is the type argument.
questions.rule: Declaration side: parameter. Use side: argument.

questions.q: A class Pair is declared with type parameters K and V. Code declares a variable of type Pair with String and Integer supplied for them. What do String and Integer count as here?
options: Type parameters, because they sit inside the angle brackets
Type arguments, the concrete types supplied for K and V
A raw type, because no new class was written for them at all
Type variables, because they can vary at run time
optionExplain: The brackets alone do not decide it; K and V are the parameters, and what fills them is an argument.
Right: K and V are the parameters; String and Integer are the arguments that replace them.
A raw type is a generic name with no arguments, the opposite of this case.
Type variable is another name for a parameter such as K, and nothing varies at run time.
questions.explain: The names K and V belong to the declaration. String and Integer are the arguments given at the use.
questions.rule: Parameter in the declaration, argument at the use.

questions.q: True or false: A generic class can be given the type argument int, because an int value is converted to Integer automatically.
questions.explain: Autoboxing converts values, not type arguments. The argument must be a non-primitive type, so the wrapper Integer is written.
questions.rule: Write the wrapper class as the type argument.
questions.teaches: A type argument must be a non-primitive type; autoboxing converts values passed in, but the argument itself is written as the wrapper, such as Integer.

questions.q: Sort each use by whether it is a raw type.

items.t: A Map variable declared with no type arguments
A Map variable declared with String and Integer
An ArrayList variable declared with no type arguments
A String variable
A Set variable declared with no type arguments
An Integer variable

questions.explain: Raw means a generic name used without arguments. String and Integer are not generic, so they are not raw.
questions.rule: Only a generic name without arguments is raw.
questions.teaches: A non-generic class such as String is not a raw type even though it takes no type arguments; rawness needs a generic name used bare.

questions.q: A generic method compares two values of type T with the greater-than operator and fails to compile. Which fix does the tutorial point to?
options: Cast both values to int before comparing them, as numbers
Bound T by Comparable of T and call its method
Declare the method static so that T becomes a primitive type
Replace T with Object, because Object supports comparison
optionExplain: A cast to int fails for most object types and discards the point of a generic method.
Right: the bound promises a compare method, and the body can use it.
static has no effect on T, which can never be a primitive.
Object has no ordering operator or comparison method of this kind.
questions.explain: Operators like greater-than work only on primitives, so objects must be compared through a method the bound supplies. The card next shows the syntax.
questions.rule: Bound the parameter to gain the methods you need.

questions.q: In a bounded type parameter, the keyword written after the parameter name and before the bound is ____.
questions.explain: The form is parameter, extends, bound, and extends also covers implementing an interface.
questions.rule: Write: name extends bound.

questions.q: A utility totals values of type T by calling doubleValue on each one. A caller passing a String must fail at compile time. What does the declaration need?
options: No bound, because doubleValue exists on every object
A bound of String, because the caller must not pass one
A bound of Number, so that doubleValue is available
A bound of Object, since every class extends it
optionExplain: doubleValue is not defined on Object, so an unbounded T cannot call it.
Bounding by String would accept only Strings, the opposite of the goal.
Right: Number supplies doubleValue and excludes String.
Object admits every type, so a String would compile, and Object lacks doubleValue.
questions.explain: The bound both restricts the arguments and makes the method callable.
questions.rule: A bound restricts callers and unlocks methods.

questions.q: True or false: A type parameter may be bounded by the interface Serializable followed by the class Number, because the order of several bounds does not matter.
questions.explain: When one of the bounds is a class, it must come first. Listing the interface first is a compile-time error.
questions.rule: With several bounds, a class bound goes first.
questions.teaches: With multiple bounds, any class must be listed first and interfaces after it; the reverse order is rejected at compile time.

questions.q: A method has a type parameter bounded by Number. Sort each argument type by whether a call is accepted.

items.t: Integer
Double
Float
String
Object

questions.explain: A bound admits the bound and its subtypes. Object is a supertype of Number, so it is rejected like String.
questions.rule: A bound admits the type and its subtypes only.
questions.teaches: A supertype of the bound, such as Object, is rejected just like an unrelated type; the bound admits only itself and its subtypes.

questions.q: A class Shelf has type parameter T. One of its methods declares its own type parameter U. Where can U be used?
options: Anywhere inside Shelf, like T
Only inside the method that declares it
In every method of every class in the program
Only in static methods of Shelf
optionExplain: Class parameters cover the class; a method's own parameter does not leave the method.
Right: the scope of a method type parameter is that method only.
Scope never extends past the declaring method, let alone to other classes.
Both static and non-static methods can declare their own parameters, and scope is still the method.
questions.explain: Method type parameters are local to their method, while class type parameters apply throughout the class.
questions.rule: Class parameter: whole class. Method parameter: that method.

questions.q: A variable is declared as a map from String to a list of String. It is initialised with new HashMap and no angle brackets at all after the class name. What does the tutorial say happens?
options: It compiles silently, because the declared type supplies the arguments
It fails with an error, because HashMap is not a generic class at all
It compiles with an unchecked warning, as the call names a raw type
It compiles and the compiler infers Object for both arguments, quietly
optionExplain: Inference from the declared type needs the diamond; without it nothing is inferred.
HashMap is generic; the problem is how it is written here, not what it is.
Right: with no brackets the constructor refers to the raw HashMap, so the assignment is an unchecked conversion.
Object would be used only if inference ran, and without the diamond it does not run.
questions.explain: Omitting the diamond leaves a raw type. The card next separates the diamond from inference.
questions.rule: No diamond means raw type and a warning.

questions.q: Match each term to its meaning.
pairs: Type arguments written out before a method name
Empty angle brackets on a constructor call
The type expected from where an expression appears
The compiler choosing type arguments that make a call valid
questions.explain: Inference is the process, the diamond and witness are two ways to write or omit arguments, and the target type is one source of information.
questions.rule: Inference is the process; witness, diamond and target type are its terms.

questions.q: A generic method named emptyBox returns a Box of T and takes no arguments. A statement assigns emptyBox() to a variable of type Box of Integer, with no witness. How does the compiler pick T?
options: From the method name, which hints at an empty box
From the target type, which supplies Integer
It uses Object and reports an error
From code later in the program that reads the box
optionExplain: Names are never used for inference.
Right: the assignment target is Box of Integer, so T is Integer.
Object would be chosen only if nothing else constrained T, and here the target does.
Inference looks at the call and its target type, not at code that follows.
questions.explain: With no arguments to examine, the assignment target is the information that settles T.
questions.rule: The assignment target can settle a type argument.

questions.q: True or false: In Java SE 8, according to the tutorial, an empty-list generic call can be passed directly to a method whose parameter is a list of String, with no type witness.
questions.explain: In Java SE 8 the target type also covers method arguments, so the parameter type supplies String. In Java SE 7 the compiler chose Object, and a witness was needed.
questions.rule: Since Java SE 8, a method parameter can be a target type.
questions.teaches: Before Java SE 8 a method argument was not used as a target, so an empty-list call passed directly was inferred as list of Object and needed an explicit witness; Java SE 8 uses the parameter type.

questions.q: Two overloads exist: submit taking a Runnable, and submit taking a Callable of T. A call passes a lambda with no parameters whose body is the value 42. Which overload is chosen?
options: The Runnable one, because its method is shorter
The Callable one, because the lambda yields a value
Neither, because a lambda cannot be passed to overloads
The call is ambiguous and never compiles
optionExplain: Method length plays no role; Runnable's run returns nothing, so a value-returning lambda does not fit.
Right: the lambda returns a value, which fits Callable and not Runnable.
Lambdas can be passed to overloaded methods; the compiler resolves the target type.
The shape of the lambda body separates the two cases, so the call is not ambiguous.
questions.explain: The compiler pairs overload resolution with inference, and a value-returning lambda matches Callable.
questions.rule: A value-returning lambda selects the value-returning interface.
questions.teaches: The shape of the lambda body, whether it produces a value, takes part in choosing among overloads, so the lambda's type is settled together with the choice of method.

questions.q: Which of these does the compiler use when inferring type arguments of a method call? Select all that apply.
options: The types of the arguments
The type the result is assigned to
A statement written later that reads the result
The most specific type that fits all arguments
The name of the method
optionExplain: Right: the argument types are the first source.
Right: the assignment or return target helps decide.
Later code is not consulted; inference uses only the invocation and its target.
Right: when several types fit, the most specific one that works for every argument is taken.
A method's name is irrelevant to which type arguments are inferred.
questions.explain: Inference works from the call itself and its target, not from what happens afterwards.
questions.rule: Arguments, target type, most specific fit.

questions.q: True or false: Because Integer is a subtype of Number, a list of Integer can be passed to a method whose parameter is a list of Number.
questions.explain: Generic types with different arguments are unrelated, whatever the relation between the arguments. The card next shows the wildcard that does allow this.
questions.rule: Subtype relations between arguments do not carry over.

questions.q: A wildcard written with the keyword ____ matches a given type and its subtypes.
questions.explain: An upper bounded wildcard uses extends; a lower bounded wildcard uses super and admits supertypes.
questions.rule: extends: the type and subtypes. super: the type and supertypes.

questions.q: A method must print every element of any list, whatever the element type, using only methods from Object. Which parameter type fits?
options: A list of Object, because every class extends Object
A list with an unbounded wildcard
A list with a lower bounded wildcard on Object
A raw list, the only form that accepts every list
optionExplain: A list of Object accepts only lists declared exactly so; a list of String is unrelated to it.
Right: every list of some type is a subtype of the unbounded wildcard type, and Object methods suffice.
A lower bounded wildcard on Object matches Object and its supertypes, which means only a list of Object.
The unbounded wildcard also accepts every list, so a raw list is not the only way, and it gives up checking.
questions.explain: The unbounded wildcard is the tutorial's tool when only Object functionality is needed.
questions.rule: Object-only work: use the bare wildcard.

questions.q: True or false: Through a variable whose type is a list with an unbounded wildcard, code may add the string hello to the list.
questions.explain: The element type is unknown, so no non-null value is known to fit. Only null can be added, while a list of Object accepts any object.
questions.rule: Unknown element type: only null can be added.
questions.teaches: Through a list of unknown element type, only null can be added, which is why a list of Object and a list with an unbounded wildcard are not interchangeable.

questions.q: A method appends Double readings to the end of a list. Callers hold a list of Double, a list of Number and a list of Object, and no list of String. Which parameter type accepts all three?
options: A list with an upper bounded wildcard on Double
A list of Number
A list with a lower bounded wildcard on Double
A list with an unbounded wildcard
optionExplain: extends on Double admits Double and its subtypes, which would exclude Number and Object.
A list of Number would accept only lists declared exactly as Number.
Right: super on Double admits Double and its supertypes, which are Number and Object.
The bare wildcard would also accept a list of String, and appending a Double to it must be refused.
questions.explain: The supertypes of Double are exactly the element types the callers hold, and a Double fits every one of them.
questions.rule: Supertype family: use super.
questions.teaches: Adding a Double through a lower bounded wildcard is safe because whatever the unknown element type is, it is Double or a supertype of Double, and a Double belongs to every one of those types.

questions.q: A method takes a list with an upper bounded wildcard on Number. Sort each argument by whether it is accepted.

items.t: A list of Integer
A list of Double
A list of Float
A list of Number
A list of String
A list of Object

questions.explain: The wildcard admits Number and its subtypes. String is unrelated and Object is a supertype, so both are rejected.
questions.rule: extends admits the bound and subtypes, not supertypes.

questions.q: True or false: According to the tutorial's advice, the source list of a copy method should use super and the destination list should use extends.
questions.explain: It is the other way round: the source supplies data, so it is extends, and the destination receives data, so it is super. The card next gives the reasoning.
questions.rule: Source: extends. Destination: super.

questions.q: Match each situation to the tutorial's recommended form.
pairs: A variable that only supplies data to the code
A variable that only receives data
An in variable needing only Object methods
A variable both read and written
questions.explain: The role of the variable, not the type, decides the form.
questions.rule: In: extends. Out: super. Object-only: bare. Both: none.

questions.q: A method reorders a playlist: it reads a Track from a list and writes a Track back into the very same list. Which parameter type follows the tutorial's advice?
options: A list of Track, with no wildcard
A list with an upper bounded wildcard on Track
A list with a lower bounded wildcard on Track
A list with an unbounded wildcard
optionExplain: Right: the list is both an in and an out variable, so the tutorial advises no wildcard.
extends suits a variable that is only read; writing a Track back would be refused.
super suits a variable that is only written; reading would then give only Object.
The bare wildcard allows reading Objects and writing null, which fits neither job.
questions.explain: One variable that does both jobs gets the exact type.
questions.rule: Both in and out: no wildcard.

questions.q: A variable has the type list with an upper bounded wildcard on Number. Which operations are still permitted on it? Select all that apply.
options: Adding null
Calling clear
Adding the Integer 5
Taking an iterator and calling remove
Adding a new Double 2.5
optionExplain: Right: null belongs to every type, so adding it is safe.
Right: clearing does not depend on the element type.
The unknown type might be Double, so an Integer is not known to fit.
Right: removing through an iterator does not insert anything.
The unknown type might be Integer, so a Double is not known to fit.
questions.explain: Operations that insert a typed value are refused, while those that insert nothing or only null are allowed.
questions.rule: extends blocks typed inserts, not removal.
questions.teaches: An extends wildcard blocks inserting typed values but still permits adding null, clear, and removing through an iterator, so calling it read-only is only informal.

questions.q: A method takes two lists, each typed with an upper bounded wildcard on Number, and copies element 0 of the second into the first. A developer adds a private capture helper hoping this makes it compile safely. Why can the helper not make this safe?
options: The lists may hold different types, so one element could be wrong
Helper methods may not declare type parameters, so the unknown type cannot be named
A captured wildcard is read-only in every case, so nothing can be written into it
Capture works only for public helpers, so a private helper is never given the type
optionExplain: Right: capture names one unknown type per list, and two lists can have different ones, so the code is unsafe.
Helpers can declare type parameters; that is exactly how capture is used.
Writing back elements that were read from the same list is allowed through a helper.
Visibility does not matter; the tutorial's helper is private.
questions.explain: A helper fixes code that is safe but unprovable, such as writing back to the same list. Mixing two independently unknown types is genuinely wrong.
questions.rule: A helper fixes safe code, not unsafe code.
questions.teaches: A capture helper can name one unknown type, so it fixes a safe operation on a single list, but it cannot make two lists with independently unknown types compatible.

questions.q: After compilation, what does the type parameter T of an unbounded generic class become in the compiled code?
options: A new class generated for each type argument used
The first type argument seen at any call site
A hidden marker kept so that the JVM can check it
The type Object
optionExplain: The tutorial says no new classes are created for parameterized types.
Erasure does not look at call sites to choose a replacement.
Erasure removes the parameter information rather than keeping a marker.
Right: an unbounded type parameter is replaced with Object.
questions.explain: Erasure replaces an unbounded T with Object. The card next adds bounds, casts and bridges.
questions.rule: Unbounded T becomes Object.

questions.q: After erasure, a type parameter that has bounds is replaced by its ____ bound.
questions.explain: A bounded parameter becomes its first bound; with no bound it becomes Object.
questions.rule: First bound, else Object.

questions.q: A generic class Slot declares T with two bounds: the class Number first, then the interface Serializable. What type does a field of type T have in the compiled class?
options: Object
Serializable
Both types at once
Number
optionExplain: Object is used only when there is no bound.
Only the first bound is used, and Serializable is the second.
A field has one type, so erasure picks the first bound alone.
Right: the first bound is the class Number.
questions.explain: Erasure uses the first bound, which is why the class bound comes first.
questions.rule: The erased type is the first bound.

questions.q: Which of these types are reifiable? Select all that apply.
options: The primitive type int
A list of String
A list with an unbounded wildcard
A list of Number
A raw list
optionExplain: Right: primitives are fully known at run time.
Its argument is erased, so a list of String cannot be told from a list of Number.
Right: an unbounded wildcard invocation has no argument to lose.
Its argument is erased in the same way as a list of String.
Right: a raw type already has no argument.
questions.explain: A type is reifiable when nothing about it was erased; parameterized types with real arguments are not.
questions.rule: Real arguments are lost; bare ones are not.
questions.teaches: Primitives, non-generic types, raw types and unbounded wildcard invocations are reifiable, while parameterized types with real arguments are not.

questions.q: A generic interface Handler has a method handle taking T. A class EmailHandler implements Handler for String and defines handle taking String. Code stores an EmailHandler in a raw Handler variable and calls handle with the Integer 5. What happens at run time?
options: The call is ignored quietly, because the types differ
The compiler refuses the call before the program starts
handle receives 5 and runs normally as an Integer
A ClassCastException arises in the bridge cast
optionExplain: Nothing in Java silently skips a method call for a type mismatch.
A raw call compiles, with an unchecked warning, so the failure comes later.
The real handle takes a String, so an Integer cannot be passed to it.
Right: the erased bridge method takes Object, casts it to String and fails.
questions.explain: The raw variable lets the wrong argument through the compiler. The bridge method that casts it fails at run time.
questions.rule: A bad value fails inside the bridge cast.
questions.teaches: Raw access skips the compile-time check, so the failure shows up at run time inside the bridge method's cast, which is why bridge methods can appear in stack traces.

questions.q: True or false: A developer suppresses every unchecked warning in a class, so heap pollution cannot occur there.
questions.explain: Suppression hides the warning but does not remove the unchecked operation that causes pollution. The no-pollution guarantee applies to code that compiles with no warnings.
questions.rule: Hidden warnings are not absent warnings.

questions.q: Inside a generic class with type parameter T, which statement does the compiler reject?
options: Declaring a local variable whose type is T
Passing a T value to another method
Calling a method on a T value that is declared with a bound
Creating a new object with new T
optionExplain: Using T as a variable type is the normal use of a type parameter.
Values of type T can be passed around like any other values.
With a bound, the bound's methods are available on T values.
Right: the real type is unknown at compile time, so new T is an error.
questions.explain: Instantiating a type parameter is forbidden because the actual type is not known. The card next lists the other bans.
questions.rule: new T is rejected.

questions.q: Match each forbidden construct to the reason the tutorial gives.
pairs: Creating an instance with new T
The actual type is unknown at compile time
A static field of type T
One field is shared by instances that may use different arguments
An array of a parameterized type
The wrong-element check that arrays rely on would be lost
Overloads taking a list of String and a list of Integer
Both erase to the same raw signature
questions.explain: Each ban traces back to missing run-time type information or to a single shared slot.
questions.rule: Each ban has a reason.

questions.q: Inside a generic class with type parameter T, sort each statement by whether the compiler accepts it.

items.t: An instance field of type T
A static method declaring its own type parameter U
An instanceof test against a list with an unbounded wildcard
A static field of type T
An instanceof test against a list of String
A call to new T

questions.explain: Instance fields and per-method parameters do not need a shared or run-time type. The three rejected forms each need the real argument at run time or at class level.
questions.rule: Instance and method scope are fine; class-level and run-time uses are not.

questions.q: Which of these is allowed in generic code?
options: A generic class that extends Exception
A catch block whose parameter type is a type parameter
A throws clause that names a type parameter
A generic class that extends Throwable indirectly
optionExplain: Extending Exception extends Throwable, which a generic class may not do.
A method cannot catch an instance of a type parameter.
Right: a type parameter may appear in a throws clause.
Throwable is banned directly and indirectly.
questions.explain: Catching and extending Throwable are banned, but declaring a thrown type parameter is permitted.
questions.rule: throws may name T; catch and Throwable subclassing may not.
questions.teaches: A type parameter may appear in a throws clause, even though catching it and subclassing Throwable are banned, so a method can leave the thrown exception type to the caller.

questions.q: A class declares one method show taking a list of String and a second method show taking a set of String. What happens?
options: Compile error, because both methods have the same name
Compile error, because overloads may not use generic parameter types
It compiles, because the erased parameter types List and Set differ
It compiles but fails when one of them is called
optionExplain: Overloading by parameter type is normal; the name alone is not the issue.
Generic parameter types are fine in overloads; only erased-identical signatures clash.
Right: after erasure the signatures are show with List and show with Set, which are distinct.
Distinct erased signatures cause no run-time failure.
questions.explain: The ban applies only when the erased signatures coincide. Changing one list to a set removes the clash.
questions.rule: The ban applies only when erasure makes the signatures identical.
questions.teaches: Generic overloads are accepted when their erased raw types differ, so the compile error depends on the erased signature, not on the use of type arguments.

questions.q: True or false: A developer reasons that an ArrayList of Integer and an ArrayList of String are different classes at run time, so an instanceof test against an ArrayList of Integer can tell them apart, and this reasoning is correct.
questions.explain: Erasure removes the type argument, so both are the same ArrayList at run time. The test is rejected unless it uses an unbounded wildcard.
questions.rule: At run time both are plain ArrayList.

questions.q: True or false: An interface with one abstract method and two default methods can be the type of a lambda.
questions.explain: Default methods have a body, so they do not count as the abstract method a lambda must implement. The card next shows exactly what is counted.
questions.rule: A lambda can only be written where the target type is an interface with exactly one abstract method, and the lambda supplies the body of that method.

questions.q: An interface with exactly one ____ method is called a functional interface.
questions.explain: The count that matters is the number of abstract methods. Default and static methods do not change it.
questions.rule: Count only abstract methods.

questions.q: Sort each interface by whether a lambda can be written for it.
groups: Can be the type of a lambda
Cannot be the type of a lambda

items.t: Greeter: one abstract method greet and one default method
Shape: abstract methods area and perimeter
Marker: no methods at all
Parser: one abstract method parse and a static method of
Task: one abstract method run and two default methods
Door: abstract methods open and close

questions.explain: Exactly one abstract method is needed, whatever else the interface holds. Two abstract methods or none rule the lambda out.
questions.rule: One abstract method, any number of default or static methods.

questions.q: A developer reasons: my interface Audit declares a method log that takes a String, a default method flush, and a static method create. That is three methods, so Audit is not functional and a lambda cannot implement it. Which step of the reasoning is wrong?
options: Assuming Audit needs the FunctionalInterface annotation before a lambda is allowed for it
Counting flush and create, which are not abstract methods
Reaching the number three, since Audit declares fewer methods than that
Leaving out create, which a lambda for Audit would have to implement as well
optionExplain: The annotation is optional; the shape alone makes an interface functional, so this is not the faulty step.
Right: only log lacks a body, so only one method counts and the conclusion fails.
Audit does declare three methods, so the count is right; the mistake lies in which of them count toward the single abstract method.
Static methods have bodies already; a lambda implements only the single abstract method, so nothing is missing.
questions.explain: Only log is abstract. The default and static methods are not counted, so Audit is functional and a lambda can implement log.
questions.rule: Default and static methods do not count.

questions.q: True or false: If an interface marked with the FunctionalInterface annotation gains a second abstract method, the compiler reports an error.
questions.explain: The annotation asks the compiler to verify that the interface stays functional. A second abstract method breaks that, and every lambda using the interface would also break.
questions.rule: The annotation turns a silent shape change into a compile error.

questions.q: Interface Greeter declares one abstract method greet that takes a String, and a default method greetLoudly whose body calls greet and upper-cases the result. A lambda is assigned to a Greeter variable. A caller invokes greetLoudly on that variable. Which code runs for greetLoudly?
options: The lambda, because a lambda replaces every method of its interface
Nothing, because default methods cannot be called on a lambda
The lambda, once it is given a second parameter for greetLoudly
The interface default body, which then calls the lambda
optionExplain: A lambda implements one method only; it has no way to replace the others.
Default methods are callable on any instance of the interface, and a lambda is such an instance.
A lambda has the parameters of the abstract method; adding parameters would not target a different method.
Right: the interface's default code runs and reaches the lambda through greet.
questions.explain: The lambda supplies only the single abstract method. For a default method, the code written in the interface runs, and that code calls back into the lambda for greet.
questions.rule: A lambda fills in the abstract method; default methods keep the interface's own code.
questions.teaches: Calling a default method on a lambda runs the code defined in the interface, and a lambda cannot override a default method.

questions.q: True or false: A lambda may change a local variable of its enclosing method as long as the variable is not declared final.
questions.explain: The compiler rejects a lambda that modifies an outer local. The card next explains the rule and the term effectively final.
questions.rule: Copy the parameter list from the single abstract method, add the arrow and a body, drop what the compiler can infer, and only read outside locals that are effectively final.

questions.q: A local variable that is not changed after its initialization, even without the final keyword, is called ____ final.
questions.explain: The compiler treats such a variable as final in the compiled code, so a lambda may read it. The source code is not changed.
questions.rule: Unchanged after initialization means effectively final.

questions.q: A method declares int limit = 5 and does not assign to it again. A lambda in the method reads limit. A later edit adds the line limit = 6 after the lambda. What happens to the lambda?
options: It still compiles and reads 5, the value at the time of creation
It compiles and reads 6, the newest value of limit
It no longer compiles, because limit is not effectively final
It compiles, and fails only when the lambda is called
optionExplain: Capturing a value does not excuse a later assignment; the compiler checks effective finality first.
A lambda cannot see later changes; the rule exists so that no changing variable is shared.
Right: the extra assignment makes limit not effectively final, which is a compile-time error.
The check is made when compiling, not when the lambda runs.
questions.explain: Effective finality depends on the whole method: one assignment after initialization ends it. The lambda only reads limit, but it no longer compiles.
questions.rule: One later assignment anywhere removes effective finality.
questions.teaches: Beyond the tutorial: a single later assignment anywhere in the method ends effective finality, so even a lambda that only reads the variable is rejected.

questions.q: Put these steps in order for writing a lambda that tests whether an Integer is even.
items: Identify the target type: a Predicate of Integer
Find its single abstract method: test, taking an Integer and returning boolean
Copy the parameter block: one Integer named n
Add the arrow and a body checking that n divided by 2 leaves remainder 0
Drop the type and the parentheses, leaving only n before the arrow
questions.explain: Type first, then the method, then the parameter block copied from it, then the body, and shortening last, because inference needs the type.
questions.rule: Type, method, parameters, body, then shorten.

questions.q: Which of these are valid shortened parameter forms? Select all that apply.
options: One parameter written as s with no parentheses
Two parameters written as a, b with no parentheses
No parameters written as empty parentheses
No parameters written with nothing before the arrow
Two parameters written as (a, b) with their types left out
optionExplain: Right: a single parameter may drop its parentheses and its type.
Two parameters need the parentheses; without them the form is not a lambda.
Right: a lambda for Runnable must keep the empty pair.
Something must stand before the arrow; zero parameters are written as empty parentheses.
Right: the types are inferred, and the parentheses stay because there are two parameters.
questions.explain: Types can be inferred, so they may go. Parentheses may go only for exactly one parameter. Zero parameters need empty parentheses.
questions.rule: Parentheses go only when there is exactly one parameter.

questions.q: A method builds and returns a Supplier of Integer from a local int named start, set once to 7 and left unchanged. The caller runs the supplier after the method has returned. What does the supplier give?
options: 7, since the lambda took the value of start earlier
An error, because start no longer exists after the method returns
0, because local variables reset when their method ends
The current value of start, read from the finished method
optionExplain: Right: the value is captured and travels with the lambda.
The variable is gone, but the lambda never needs it, only the copied value.
Locals are not reset; the lambda holds the value it captured.
There is no live variable to read after the method ends; the lambda holds a copied value.
questions.explain: A lambda captures the value of start, not the variable itself. The value 7 travels with the lambda, so it works after the method has finished.
questions.rule: A lambda keeps the captured value.
questions.teaches: A lambda captures the value of a local variable, not the variable itself, so the value stays available after the creating method has ended.

questions.q: You need a lambda that takes a customer name and says whether it is empty. Which standard interface fits best?
options: Supplier
Consumer
Predicate
Function
optionExplain: A Supplier takes no argument, but this lambda receives a name.
A Consumer returns nothing, but a yes-or-no answer is needed.
Right: a Predicate takes a value and returns a boolean.
A Function could return a boolean, but the interface made for boolean results is the Predicate.
questions.explain: The lambda takes a value and returns a yes-or-no answer. The card next names the interface built for that shape.
questions.rule: Choose the family by shape: nothing in and a value out is a Supplier, a value in and nothing out is a Consumer, a value in and a boolean out is a Predicate, and a value in and a result out is a Function.

questions.q: Match each interface to its shape.
pairs: takes a value, returns a boolean
takes a value, returns a result
questions.explain: Each family is defined by what goes in and what comes out.
questions.rule: Shape decides the family.

questions.q: A lambda that receives an order and sends it to a printer, returning nothing, implements a ____.
questions.explain: A value goes in and nothing comes out, which is the Consumer shape; its method is accept.
questions.rule: Value in, nothing out is a Consumer.

questions.q: A list of names comes from List.of. Code calls removeIf on it with a Predicate that matches at least one name. According to the tutorial, what happens?
options: The matching names are replaced by null
The matching names are removed and the list shrinks
A new filtered list is returned and the original stays
An exception, because this list cannot be modified
optionExplain: removeIf removes elements; it does not null them, and an immutable list refuses changes anyway.
That is the outcome on a modifiable list, but a list from List.of cannot change size.
removeIf returns a boolean and acts on the collection itself; it builds no new list.
Right: a mutating method on an immutable list fails with an exception.
questions.explain: removeIf changes the collection, and a list from List.of cannot be changed, so an exception is thrown.
questions.rule: removeIf needs a collection that can shrink.
questions.teaches: removeIf takes a Predicate and changes the collection, so it fails on collections that cannot change, such as lists from List.of or Arrays.asList.

questions.q: According to the tutorial, boxing costs performance. In which setting would switching from a Predicate of Integer to IntPredicate matter least?
options: A loop that tests ten million numbers in memory
A numeric filter inside a large in-memory sort
A test run once before a slow database call
A tight inner loop that runs on every frame of a game
optionExplain: Ten million tests multiply the boxing cost, so the switch could help a lot.
A sort calls the filter many times, so boxing adds up.
Right: the tutorial says boxing is negligible beside database or network calls.
A frame loop is a hot path, where the boxing cost is felt.
questions.explain: Boxing cost is small beside a slow call. In a hot path the saving can add up, but next to a database call it is lost in the noise.
questions.rule: Primitive versions pay off in hot paths.

questions.q: According to the tutorial, a Function may take and return any of: the generic type, int, long or double. The number of specialized Function variants this gives, with every input paired with every output, is ____.
questions.explain: Four choices for the input times four for the output give 16 combinations.
questions.rule: Primitive Function variants cover every input and output pairing.
questions.teaches: Function has 16 primitive-specialized combinations, and they are named by what they return: apply, applyAsInt, applyAsLong and applyAsDouble.

questions.q: What does the method reference String::length stand for when it is assigned to a function from String to int?
options: A call to a static method named length of the String class
A lambda taking a string s and returning s.length()
A constructor that creates a String of a given length
A fixed string whose length is read each time it runs
optionExplain: It looks like a static call, but length is an instance method, so it is not one.
Right: the string arrives as the argument and length is called on it.
Constructor references end in new; this one names length.
A fixed object would have to appear before the colons; here a type does.
questions.explain: A type name followed by an instance method name means the receiver arrives as an argument. The card next names this kind.
questions.rule: To read a method reference, look at the target functional interface and rebuild the lambda: a type before the colons with an instance method means the first argument is the receiver, an object before them means the receiver is fixed.

questions.q: Match each method reference to its kind.
questions.explain: The text before the colons shows the kind: a type with a static method, a type with an instance method, an object, or a class with new.
questions.rule: Look at what stands before the colons and what follows.

questions.q: A Function from User to String is set to User::getName. Written as a lambda with parameter u, the body is u.____
questions.explain: The user arrives as the first argument and getName is called on it.
questions.rule: Unbound: the first argument is the receiver.

questions.q: Variable a is a Supplier of an ArrayList of String set to ArrayList::new. Variable b is a Function from Integer to an ArrayList of String, also set to ArrayList::new. What does this show?
options: The second line fails to compile, because ArrayList has a single constructor
Both call the no-argument constructor and the Integer is dropped
The reference picks the constructor with the most parameters available
The target type sets the arguments, so each calls its own constructor
optionExplain: ArrayList has several constructors, so the second line compiles.
The Integer is an argument the target type passes on; it is not ignored.
Selection follows the arguments supplied, not the longest parameter list.
Right: the arguments come from the functional interface, so the same text can select different constructors.
questions.explain: The target interface decides how many arguments are passed. ArrayList has a constructor taking an initial capacity (general Java knowledge, beyond the tutorial), so b can call it while a calls the no-argument one.
questions.rule: Read a constructor reference through its target type.
questions.teaches: The same constructor reference text can call different constructors, because the number and types of arguments come from the target functional interface.

questions.q: Sort each reference by whether the object is fixed in the reference (bound) or arrives as the first argument (unbound).
groups: Bound: object fixed in the reference
Unbound: object arrives as first argument

items.t: System.out::println
greeting::length, where greeting is a local String
names::add, where names is a local list of String
String::toUpperCase
User::getName
String::indexOf

questions.explain: An object expression before the colons fixes the receiver. A type name before them means the receiver arrives as the first argument.
questions.rule: Object before the colons: bound. Type before the colons: unbound.

questions.q: A Comparator of String has one abstract method taking two Strings and returning an int. A lambda with parameters a and b has the body a.compareToIgnoreCase(b), an instance method of String. Which method reference stands for it?
options: String::new
a::compareToIgnoreCase, with a fixed in advance
String::compareToIgnoreCase
Comparator::compare
optionExplain: new would create Strings and does not call compareToIgnoreCase.
a is a lambda parameter, not an object existing before the reference, so it cannot be fixed in advance.
Right: the first string is the receiver and the second is the argument.
That names the comparator's own method, not the String method the body calls.
questions.explain: The type name before the colons makes the first argument the receiver. The second argument is then passed to the method.
questions.rule: Unbound: first argument is the receiver, the others are the arguments.
questions.teaches: With two parameters, an unbound reference uses the first as the receiver and passes the remaining ones as the method's arguments.

questions.q: True or false: f2.compose(f1) applies f2 first and then f1.
questions.explain: The name compose puts the function that runs first inside the call. The card next explains the order.
