questions.rule: Chain predicates with and, or and negate, run consumers one after the other, and join functions with andThen or compose, which both run the inner function first.

questions.q: To require that two predicates both pass, call the ____ method on the first one and give it the second.
questions.explain: and joins two tests so that both must be true; or needs only one, and negate flips a single test.
questions.rule: and needs both, or needs one, negate flips.

questions.q: The function doubler multiplies a number by 2, and cutTen subtracts 10. What does doubler.andThen(cutTen) give when applied to 100?
optionExplain: 180 is the result when cutTen runs first, which is what compose on doubler would do.
200 skips cutTen, but andThen applies the second function too.
Right: 100 doubled is 200, then 10 is subtracted.
90 skips the doubling, but both functions are applied.
questions.explain: andThen runs doubler first, giving 200, then cutTen, giving 190. The other order, doubler.compose(cutTen), would give 180.
questions.rule: andThen runs the receiver first.

questions.q: True or false: f1.andThen(f2) is type-correct when f1 maps a String to an Integer and f2 maps a Double to a String.
questions.explain: The Integer produced by f1 must fit the input type of f2, and an Integer is not a Double. The chain is rejected.
questions.rule: The first result type must fit the second input type.

questions.q: A method takes a Function from String to String that cleans each name, and for some customers no cleaning is wanted. Which ready-made function returns its input unchanged?
options: A Predicate joined to itself with and
A Consumer chained twice
A function built with compose on itself
Function.identity()
optionExplain: A Predicate returns a boolean, not the input.
A Consumer returns nothing, so it cannot supply the cleaned name.
Composing a cleaning function with itself cleans twice; it does not leave the input alone.
Right: identity is the function provided for exactly this purpose.
questions.explain: Function.identity is a static factory that returns a function giving back its input. According to the tutorial it works for any valid type.
questions.rule: Function.identity is the do-nothing function.
questions.teaches: Function.identity() is a static factory returning a function that gives back its input unchanged, and it works for any type.

questions.q: In a shop application, audit is a Consumer that records an order and mail is a Consumer that sends it. They are chained so that audit runs first, then mail. When the combined consumer receives an order, what happens?
options: Mail runs first, because the last one added goes first
Mail receives whatever audit returns
Only audit runs, since chaining replaces mail
Audit runs first, then mail receives that same order
optionExplain: The first consumer runs first, as the tutorial describes.
Audit returns nothing, so there is nothing for mail to receive.
Chaining adds the second consumer; it does not drop it.
Right: both see the same order, in the order chained.
questions.explain: Consumers return nothing, so nothing can be passed along. The tutorial says the second consumer receives the same input as the first.
questions.rule: A chained consumer gives both the same input.
questions.teaches: In a chained consumer both consumers receive the same original input, because a consumer returns nothing that could be passed on.

questions.q: True or false: When compare(a, b) returns a positive number, the comparator ranks a after b.
questions.explain: Positive means the first argument is larger. The card next gives the full contract.
questions.rule: A comparator returns negative, zero or positive for first smaller, equal or larger, with opposite signs when the arguments are swapped, and for integers it should use Integer.compare rather than subtraction.

questions.q: If compare(x, y) returns a negative number, then compare(y, x) must return a ____ number.
questions.explain: The two results must have opposite signs.
questions.rule: Swapping the arguments flips the sign.

questions.q: Two int sensor readings r1 and r2 must be ordered in a comparator lambda. Which body does the tutorial recommend?
options: Return r1 minus r2
Return Integer.compare of r1 and r2
Return 1 whenever r1 and r2 are not the same value
Return the quotient of r1 divided by r2
optionExplain: Subtraction seems to work but has corner cases, which the tutorial warns about.
Right: it is the safe way to compare two ints.
A constant 1 for any difference breaks the opposite-sign rule when the arguments are swapped.
Division can fail on zero and does not give a negative, zero or positive ranking by order.
questions.explain: Integer.compare follows the contract for every pair of ints, while subtraction has corner cases.
questions.rule: Use Integer.compare for ints.

questions.q: A comparator body returns the first int minus the second. The first value is 2000000000, the second is minus 2000000000, and the first is truly larger. The difference 4000000000 does not fit in an int. What sign can the returned int have?
options: Positive, because the true difference is positive
Zero, since the overflow is discarded
Negative, because the overflowed value wraps around
None, because Java throws an exception on int overflow
optionExplain: That would hold only without overflow; the real int result wraps.
Overflow does not discard the value; it wraps to another number.
Right: the wrapped result is negative here, which breaks the ranking.
Java does not throw on plain int arithmetic overflow; it wraps silently.
questions.explain: Int arithmetic wraps around when it overflows, so the result can be negative even though the first value is larger. The comparator then says the opposite of the truth.
questions.rule: Subtraction can overflow and flip the sign.
questions.teaches: Beyond the tutorial: int subtraction wraps around on overflow, so a difference that is truly positive can come out negative.

questions.q: Words are compared by length in a comparator. Sort each pair of results by whether the comparator follows the contract.

items.t: compare(a, b) returns 5 and compare(b, a) returns -5
compare(a, b) returns 1 and compare(b, a) returns 1
compare(a, b) returns 0 for two different words of equal length
compare(a, b) returns -1 and compare(b, a) returns 0
compare(a, b) returns -30 and compare(b, a) returns 2
compare(a, b) returns 3 and compare(b, a) returns 7

questions.explain: Only the sign matters, and swapping the arguments must flip it. A zero for two different words of equal length is allowed, but equal signs, or a zero opposed to a nonzero, break the contract.
questions.rule: Opposite signs on swap; the size of the number does not matter.
questions.teaches: Only the sign of a comparator's result matters, so 5 and minus 5 are as valid as 1 and minus 1, while the same sign for swapped arguments breaks the contract.

questions.q: A list of people is sorted by last name, and two people with the same last name should then be ordered by first name. Which Comparator method expresses the fallback?
options: comparing
thenComparing
reversed
nullsFirst
optionExplain: comparing starts an ordering from a key; it does not chain a fallback onto an existing one.
Right: thenComparing is consulted only when the earlier comparator returns zero.
reversed flips the whole order and adds no tie-break.
nullsFirst handles null values and has no role in tie-breaking.
questions.explain: The second ordering applies only when the first returns zero. The card next names the method for that.
questions.rule: Build a comparator from a key function with comparing, break ties with thenComparing, flip it with reversed, and wrap with nullsFirst or nullsLast when keys may be null.

questions.q: Match each Comparator tool to what it does.
pairs: orders by a primitive int key without boxing
is consulted only when the earlier comparator returns zero
places null values at the end
questions.explain: Each tool has one job: key extraction without boxing, tie-breaking, null placement, and flipping.
questions.rule: One tool, one job.

questions.q: Words are sorted with comparingInt on String::length followed by thenComparing with naturalOrder. Put the words pear, fig, plum and kiwi in the resulting order.
items: fig
kiwi
pear
plum
questions.explain: Length decides first: fig has 3 letters, the others have 4. Among 4-letter words the natural order of strings breaks the tie: kiwi, pear, plum.
questions.rule: The second comparator only breaks ties.

questions.q: Users are sorted with comparing on a getNickname key, and some users have a null nickname. What does the tutorial say can happen, and what fixes it?
options: A NullPointerException can occur; wrap with a nulls helper
Nulls sort first on their own, so no change is needed here
The sort quietly skips the null users and leaves them in place
A compile error is reported; the nickname key must be made final
optionExplain: Right: null keys can throw, and the wrappers handle them.
Nothing in the tutorial gives nulls a default place; comparing them can throw.
The sort does not skip elements; every element is compared.
Null keys are a runtime matter, and the compiler does not check them.
questions.explain: Comparing a null can throw a NullPointerException. The tutorial's fix is to wrap the comparator with nullsFirst or nullsLast.
questions.rule: Wrap with nullsFirst or nullsLast when nulls can occur.
questions.teaches: nullsFirst and nullsLast replace a hand-written null-checking comparator: they wrap the comparator that orders the non-null values.

questions.q: Employees are ordered by department with comparing, then by name with thenComparing, and reversed is called on the whole result. The employees are Ana and Bo in Sales and Cy in Admin. Without reversed the order is Admin Cy, Sales Ana, Sales Bo. What order does the reversed comparator give?
options: Sales Ana, Sales Bo, Admin Cy
Admin Cy, Sales Bo, Sales Ana
Admin Cy, Sales Ana, Sales Bo
Sales Bo, Sales Ana, Admin Cy
optionExplain: This flips only the department and keeps names ascending, but reversed flips the whole order.
This flips only the names and keeps departments ascending.
This is the unchanged order, as if reversed had no effect.
Right: this is exactly the opposite of the original order.
questions.explain: reversed gives the opposite of the combined order, so it flips every step of the chain at once: the departments and the names.
questions.rule: reversed flips the whole chain.
questions.teaches: Calling reversed on a chained comparator flips the whole combined order, every key at once, not only the last step.

questions.q: True or false: the compiler rejects an instanceof test that cannot succeed, such as testing a String variable against the type Integer.
questions.explain: A String variable can hold only a String, and the two types are unrelated, so the check is impossible and does not compile. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: Impossible matches are compile errors.

questions.q: Every pattern match has a matched target, a pattern and a ____.
questions.explain: The result is what the match reports; for a type pattern it is a new typed variable, for a regular expression it is the start and end positions.
questions.rule: Target, pattern, result.

questions.q: A class Money has a long field named cents, and its equals method takes a parameter o of type Object. Which equals body correctly uses an instanceof pattern?
options: return o instanceof Money && cents == m.cents;
if (o instanceof Money) { return cents == m.cents; } return false;
return o instanceof Money m && cents == m.cents;
return o instanceof Money m && cents == o.cents;
optionExplain: It declares no variable m, so m.cents has nothing to refer to and does not compile.
The test declares no variable, so m is undefined in the branch; a cast would be needed.
The pattern declares m, and the and operator runs the second part only after the match succeeded, so m is a Money there.
o has the static type Object, which has no field named cents, so o.cents does not compile.
questions.explain: The pattern variable m replaces the cast and is safe to use on the right of the and operator.
questions.rule: Declare the variable in the pattern, use it after the test.

questions.q: True or false: Method B compiles, where method A is static void a(Object o) { if (!(o instanceof String s)) { return; } System.out.println(s.length()); } (which compiles) and method B is identical to A except that its if body prints a message instead of returning.
questions.explain: In B the if branch can finish normally, so execution can reach the last line without a match, and s is not in scope there. A pattern variable stays in scope after the if only when the branch always leaves.
questions.rule: Scope after the if depends on the branch always leaving.

questions.q: Object o holds some value. Which condition compiles and uses the pattern variable s only where the match succeeded?
options: o instanceof String s || s.isEmpty()
!(o instanceof String s) && s.isEmpty()
s.isEmpty() && o instanceof String s
o instanceof String s && s.isEmpty()
questions.teaches: Beyond the tutorial: the compiler allows a pattern variable only where the match is known to have succeeded, so using it before the test, after an or, or under a negation fails.
optionExplain: After an or, the right side runs when the match failed, so s has no value there.
Under the negation the right side runs only when the match failed, so s is unusable.
s is used before the test that declares it, so it is not yet in scope.
The right side of and runs only when the match succeeded, so s is a String there.
questions.explain: Only the right side of and is guaranteed to run after a successful match.
questions.rule: Use the variable only where success is guaranteed.

questions.q: A method receives an Object and must return 1 for a String and 2 for an Integer, using one switch. What should the case labels hold?
options: Constant values of String and Integer
Type patterns such as String s and Integer i
An instanceof expression inside each label
Class names ending in a dot and the word class
optionExplain: Constants select by value, not by the type of the selector.
A type pattern in a case label tests the selector's type, which is what pattern matching for switch adds.
An instanceof test belongs in an if statement; a label is not a boolean expression.
A class literal is a value, and labels do not test types that way.
questions.explain: Type patterns in case labels branch on the selector's type. The card next shows the details.
questions.rule: Case labels can hold type patterns.

questions.q: In a switch, a boolean expression added after a type pattern with the word ____ is called a guard.
questions.explain: The word when introduces the guard; the combined label is a guarded case label.
questions.rule: Type pattern, then when, then a boolean expression.

questions.q: In a switch over an Object, which case label matches only a String of exactly 3 characters?
options: case String s && s.length() == 3:
case s.length() == 3:
case String s if s.length() == 3:
case String s when s.length() == 3:
optionExplain: The and operator does not join a pattern and a condition in a label; the word when does.
A label cannot be a bare boolean condition, and s would not be declared.
If is not the keyword for a guard in a case label.
A type pattern followed by when and a boolean expression forms a guarded case label.
questions.explain: The guard needs the word when after the pattern.
questions.rule: Pattern, when, condition.

questions.q: Consider: int describe(Object o) { switch (o) { case String s when s.isEmpty(): return 1; case String s: return 2; case Integer i: return 3; default: return 0; } } A String variable named word holds three letters. What does describe(word) return?
options: A compile error because String appears in two labels
questions.teaches: Beyond the tutorial: a label whose guard is false does not match, so the switch goes on to test the later labels.
optionExplain: The guard of the first label is false for word, so that label is skipped and the plain String label matches.
The guard s.isEmpty() is false for word, so the first label does not match.
The default label is used only when no other label matches, and the String label matches.
The same type may appear in several labels when a guard separates them; this code is valid.
questions.explain: A false guard means no match for that label, not a failure of the switch.
questions.rule: A false guard moves on to the next label.

questions.q: Sort each type: was it in the tutorial's list of selector types before type patterns, or not?

items.t: byte
Integer
String
an enum type
long
Long
double

questions.explain: The tutorial lists byte, short, char, int, their four wrappers, String and enums, and says long was not accepted. Long, double and similar types are not in that list.
questions.rule: Before type patterns, selectors came from a short fixed list.

questions.q: With record Point(int x, int y) and an Object o, what does o instanceof Point(int a, int b) do when o is a Point?
options: Compares o with a new Point built from the values a and b
Casts o to Point and leaves a and b without any values
Declares a and b and fills them from its components
Tests only the type and ignores the names a and b
optionExplain: The names a and b are new variables, not values to compare against.
The variables are given values from the record, not left empty.
A record pattern takes the record apart and binds each component to a pattern variable.
The names matter: they are the variables you then use.
questions.explain: Record patterns deconstruct. The card next shows the rules.
questions.rule: A record pattern binds the components.

questions.q: Match each element of the test of o against Point(int x, int y) with its role.
pairs: x and y filled from the accessors on success
questions.explain: The same three elements as in any pattern match: the object under test, the pattern, and what the match produces.
questions.rule: Target, pattern, result.

questions.q: A record is declared as Range(int low, int high). Which pattern compiles and takes an Object o apart when it is a Range?
options: Range(int lo)
Range(var lo, var hi)
Range(int lo, int hi, int step)
Range(String lo, String hi)
optionExplain: It gives one pattern for two components; one pattern per component is needed.
One pattern per component, and var lets the compiler use each component type.
It gives three patterns for two components.
String is unrelated to the int components, so this does not compile.
questions.explain: The pattern must fit the components: the right count and compatible types.
questions.rule: One fitting pattern per component.

questions.q: Records are Point(int x, int y) and Line(Point from, Point to). The nested pattern Line(Point(int x1, int y1), Point(int x2, int y2)) declares ____ pattern variables in total. Give a number.
questions.teaches: With nesting, the variables come from the innermost patterns, so the count is the total of all the leaf type patterns.
questions.explain: Each Point pattern declares two variables, and there are two of them, so four variables in all; the Line level adds none of its own.
questions.rule: Nested patterns bind variables at the leaves.

questions.q: A record is declared as Box(CharSequence content). Which patterns compile? Select all that apply.
options: Box(String s)
Box(var c)
Box(Integer i)
Box(CharSequence c)
Box(String s, String t)
questions.teaches: A component pattern with a narrower type, such as String, makes the record pattern match only when the component has that type, which lets a switch branch on a component's type.
optionExplain: String extends CharSequence, so it is a permitted narrower type.
var takes the component type, so it fits.
Integer is unrelated to CharSequence, so this fails like an impossible instanceof check.
The same type as the component is allowed.
The record has one component, so two patterns do not fit.
questions.explain: Component patterns must be var or a type related to the declared component type, with one per component.
questions.rule: Component types: var, the same type or a subtype.

questions.q: Given record Counter(int n), a teammate says if (o instanceof Counter(Integer n)) is fine because an int boxes to an Integer automatically. What is wrong with this reasoning?
options: Records forbid components of primitive types in any pattern
The pattern must list the canonical constructor's parameter names
A pattern may only name Integer after the keyword var
Record patterns apply no boxing, so an int needs int or var
optionExplain: The tutorial says type patterns in record patterns may use primitive types.
Only the types and the count must fit the constructor signature; the names are your own.
The keyword var stands in for the type; it does not combine with Integer.
The tutorial states record patterns do not support boxing or unboxing, so Integer does not fit an int component.
questions.explain: According to the tutorial, automatic boxing does not happen in record patterns, so the pattern type must fit the component type.
questions.rule: No boxing or unboxing in record patterns.

questions.unitTitle: Refactoring from the Imperative to the Functional Style (dev.java)
questions.q: In a loop that sends each of the numbers 0 to 4 to a printer using an index variable, which part is ceremony rather than essence?
options: The numbers 0 to 4 that are being visited
The printing that is done with each number
Declaring and raising the index variable
The fact that exactly five values are visited
optionExplain: The values are what the loop is about, so they belong to the essence.
The action is the purpose of the loop, so it is essence.
Right: the index handling only drives the loop and says nothing about which values or which action.
How many values are visited follows from the range, which is part of the essence.
questions.explain: The index machinery is mechanics, while the range and the action are the point. The card next separates the two.
questions.rule: Index handling is ceremony; values and action are essence.

questions.unitTitle: Refactoring from the Imperative to the Functional Style (dev.java)
questions.q: In the tutorial's terms, a for loop that you step yourself is an ____ iterator, while forEach on a stream is an internal one.
questions.explain: With a for loop your code controls the stepping, which makes the iterator external. With forEach the stream does the stepping.
questions.rule: For loop: external iterator. Stream forEach: internal iterator.

questions.unitTitle: Refactoring from the Imperative to the Functional Style (dev.java)
questions.q: A developer is asked to fix a bug in one report class that contains an index loop, and the class has twenty other untouched loops. According to the tutorial, what is the best approach?
options: Convert all twenty-one loops now so the class stays consistent
Convert the loop being fixed and check it with existing tests
Leave every loop alone because refactoring is too risky to try
Convert the untouched loops first, then fix the bug afterwards
optionExplain: The tutorial warns against a blanket rewrite; touching code you were not asked to change adds risk without a trigger.
Right: refactoring is advised when you fix a bug or enhance code, one change at a time with a check.
The tutorial does not say to avoid refactoring; it says to do it when you are already working on the code.
Changing untouched code first reverses the advice, which ties a refactor to code you are fixing or enhancing.
questions.explain: The tutorial links refactoring to an occasion, a bug fix or an enhancement, and asks for verification after each change.
questions.rule: Refactor the code you are touching, then verify.
questions.hint: Which loop is the developer already working on?

questions.unitTitle: Refactoring from the Imperative to the Functional Style (dev.java)
questions.q: Sort each part of a counting loop into essence or ceremony for a loop that prints the integers 1 to 6.

items.t: The values 1 to 6 to be visited
The action printed for each value
Declaring the index variable
Testing the index against the limit
Raising the index after each pass
The decision to print every value

questions.explain: Values and action describe what happens; declaring, testing and raising the index only drive the loop. Streams hide the second group, unless the task itself needs the index.
questions.rule: Essence is values plus action; ceremony is index handling.
questions.teaches: Beyond the tutorial: what counts as essence depends on the task; if the action needed the position of each value, the index would become part of the essence.

questions.unitTitle: Refactoring from the Imperative to the Functional Style (dev.java)
questions.q: An accountant describes two ways to total a stack of receipts. Which instruction is in the declarative spirit that the tutorial calls functional?
options: Pick up the top receipt, add its amount to a running sum, then take the next
Start at receipt zero and keep an index until the stack ends
Open the drawer, read each amount aloud and write it down in order
Give me the total of all these receipts
optionExplain: This spells out the steps and the running state, which is the imperative how.
This manages an index by hand, which is the external stepping the tutorial calls ceremony.
This lists the procedure step by step, so it says how rather than what.
Right: it states the result wanted and leaves the method to the person doing it.
questions.explain: The first instruction states what is wanted; the others describe how to do it.
questions.rule: Declarative says what; imperative says how.
questions.teaches: Beyond the tutorial: the same imperative versus declarative contrast appears outside streams, for example when a database query states the rows wanted instead of the loop that finds them.

questions.unitTitle: Refactoring from the Imperative to the Functional Style (dev.java)
questions.q: Which call visits the numbers 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5 and nothing else?
options: IntStream.range(1, 5)
IntStream.rangeClosed(1, 10)
IntStream.rangeClosed(0, 5)
IntStream.rangeClosed(1, 5)
optionExplain: This stops before 5, so it gives 1 through 4.
This includes 6, so it gives 1 through 6.
This starts at 0 and stops before 5, giving 0 through 4.
Right: rangeClosed includes both of its ends, giving 1 through 5.
questions.explain: One factory includes its end and the other excludes it. The card next states which is which.
questions.rule: rangeClosed includes its end; range excludes it.

questions.unitTitle: Refactoring from the Imperative to the Functional Style (dev.java)
questions.q: A loop starts at 0 and continues while its index is below 8. It maps to IntStream.____(0, 8).
questions.explain: The end value 8 is excluded, which is the behaviour of range. rangeClosed would visit 8 as well.
questions.rule: Excluded end: range.

questions.unitTitle: Refactoring from the Imperative to the Functional Style (dev.java)
questions.q: A loop starts k at 3, continues while k is at most 6, and calls log with k. Which stream version does the same work?
options: IntStream.rangeClosed(3,6).forEach(k gives log(k))
IntStream.range(3, 6).forEach(k gives log(k))
IntStream.rangeClosed(4, 6).forEach(k gives log(k))
IntStream.rangeClosed(3, 7).forEach(k gives log(k))
optionExplain: Right: the loop visits 3, 4, 5, 6 and rangeClosed(3, 6) does the same.
This stops before 6, so the final pass with 6 is missing.
This starts at 4 and drops the first value 3.
This runs one pass too many, with 7.
questions.explain: At-most means the end value is visited, so the closed version with the same two numbers fits.
questions.rule: At-most test: rangeClosed with the same bounds.

questions.unitTitle: Refactoring from the Imperative to the Functional Style (dev.java)
questions.q: A loop runs its index from 0 while the index is below a count n, and rangeClosed is not used. If n is 0, how many times does IntStream.range(0, n).forEach run its action?
options: Once, with the value 0
Zero times
An exception is thrown for an empty range
Twice, once for the start and once for the end value
optionExplain: That would be true of rangeClosed(0, 0), which includes its end, but range excludes it.
Right: with equal ends there is nothing to visit, just as the loop never enters its body.
Beyond the tutorial: an empty range is allowed and gives an empty stream, so nothing is thrown.
Visiting both ends is the behaviour of rangeClosed, and even rangeClosed(0, 0) would give one pass, not two.
questions.explain: range(0, 0) holds no values, which matches a loop whose test fails at once.
questions.rule: Equal ends in range give no passes.
questions.teaches: Beyond the tutorial: when the two arguments of range are equal the stream is empty, matching a loop that never enters its body.
questions.hint: Is the end value visited by range?

questions.unitTitle: Refactoring from the Imperative to the Functional Style (dev.java)
questions.q: A scheduling tool has six loops. Sort each by the factory that matches it: range for an excluded end, rangeClosed for an included end.

items.t: Seat number from 0 while seat is below 40
Hour from 1 while hour is at most 24
Row from 0 while row is below the height
Year from 2020 while year is at most 2025
Day from 1 while day is at most 31
Slot from 0 while slot is below 8

questions.explain: A below test excludes the end and fits range. An at-most test includes it and fits rangeClosed.
questions.rule: Read the comparison in the loop test to choose the factory.
questions.teaches: Beyond the tutorial: range gives end minus start values, while rangeClosed gives end minus start plus one, which is a quick check on a conversion.

questions.unitTitle: Refactoring from the Imperative to the Functional Style (dev.java)
questions.q: A colleague rewrites a loop that runs i from 1 while i is at most 100 and logs i, as IntStream.range(1, 100).forEach(i gives log(i)), and says it is equivalent. What is wrong?
options: range always starts at 0 whatever its first argument is
forEach cannot be called on an IntStream at all
The end value 100 is excluded, so the last call is lost
range includes both of its ends, so an extra pass happens
optionExplain: The first argument is the first value visited, so the start is fine.
forEach exists on IntStream and runs the action for each value.
Right: range stops before its second argument, so 100 is never logged.
range excludes its end, so a pass is lost rather than added.
questions.explain: At-most 100 needs rangeClosed(1, 100), or range(1, 101).
questions.rule: Check whether the end value must be visited.

questions.unitTitle: Refactoring from the Imperative to the Functional Style (dev.java)
questions.q: Which IntStream method takes a seed, a test and a step as its three arguments?
options: IntStream.range
IntStream.iterate
IntStream.concat
IntStream.rangeClosed
optionExplain: range takes only a start and an end.
Right: iterate takes a starting seed, a predicate for continuing and an operator for the next value.
concat joins two streams and has no seed or step.
rangeClosed takes only a start and an inclusive end.
questions.explain: Only one of these builds values from a rule. The card next shows the mapping.
questions.rule: iterate takes seed, test and step.

questions.unitTitle: Refactoring from the Imperative to the Functional Style (dev.java)
questions.q: Match each part of a stepped loop with its place in the stream version.
questions.explain: The three header parts become the three arguments of iterate, while break needs the two-argument form plus takeWhile.
questions.rule: Header parts map onto iterate arguments.

questions.unitTitle: Refactoring from the Imperative to the Functional Style (dev.java)
questions.q: A loop starts n at 10, continues while n is below 40 and adds 10 each pass, calling show with n. Which stream version matches?
options: iterate with seed 10, step add 10, test n below 40, then forEach show
iterate with seed 10 and step add 10 only, then forEach show
iterate with seed 10, test n below 40, step add 10, forEach show
range with 10 and 40 as its arguments, then forEach show
optionExplain: The test and the step are swapped, so the arguments no longer match the order seed, test, step.
Without a test the stream is endless, so it never stops at 40.
Right: seed, then test, then step is the order of the three-argument iterate and gives 10, 20, 30.
range steps by one, so it would also show 11, 12 and so on.
questions.explain: The seed 10, the test below 40 and the step 10 each fill one argument.
questions.rule: Seed, test, step in that order.
questions.hint: Which argument is the predicate?

questions.unitTitle: Refactoring from the Imperative to the Functional Style (dev.java)
questions.q: A countdown loop starts t at 60, continues while t is above 0 and subtracts 15 each pass. Which values does the matching iterate version produce?
optionExplain: Right: the step subtracts 15 and the test above 0 stops before 0 is reached.
The test requires t above 0, so 0 does not pass.
The seed itself, 60, is the first value produced.
The step subtracts, so the values fall, not rise.
questions.explain: iterate emits the seed first, then applies the step while the test keeps passing.
questions.rule: The step can subtract as well as add.
questions.teaches: Beyond the tutorial: the step operator is any int-to-int rule, so iterate also covers countdowns, not only upward loops.

questions.unitTitle: Refactoring from the Imperative to the Functional Style (dev.java)
questions.q: Put the steps in order for converting a loop that starts at 0, adds 3 and breaks when the value exceeds 20.
items: Build an endless stream from a seed of 0 and a step adding 3
Add takeWhile keeping values at most 20
Finish with forEach for the action
questions.explain: The endless stream is created first, takeWhile cuts it at the first failing value, and forEach is the action.
questions.rule: Source, cut-off, action.
questions.teaches: Beyond the tutorial: the endless stream from the two-argument iterate would never finish if no limit such as takeWhile were added before a terminal step.

questions.unitTitle: Refactoring from the Imperative to the Functional Style (dev.java)
questions.q: A loop starts i at 0, adds 3 and breaks when i exceeds 20. A rewrite uses iterate with seed 0, step add 3 and takeWhile with the predicate i above 20. What happens?
options: The stream ends at once as 0 fails the test
It produces 0, 3, 6 and on up to 18, like the loop does
It produces 21, 24 and every later value that follows
It fails to compile because iterate needs three arguments
optionExplain: Right: takeWhile stops at the first value that fails, and 0 is not above 20.
That needs the keep-going predicate, i at most 20, not the break condition.
takeWhile takes values from the start; it does not skip ahead to the large ones.
The two-argument iterate is valid; the problem lies in the predicate.
questions.explain: takeWhile needs the condition to keep going, the opposite of the break test.
questions.rule: Negate the break test for takeWhile.

questions.unitTitle: Refactoring from the Imperative to the Functional Style (dev.java)
questions.q: A loop prints only the names whose length is 4. Which stream operation takes the place of the if inside the loop?
options: map
count
filter
forEach
optionExplain: map changes each element and does not choose which ones continue.
count returns a number of elements and does not pass any on.
Right: filter lets elements pass when its test gives true.
forEach performs an action but does not choose elements.
questions.explain: The if decides which elements are used. The card next names the stream counterpart.
questions.rule: An if that selects becomes filter.

questions.unitTitle: Refactoring from the Imperative to the Functional Style (dev.java)
questions.q: Which statements match the tutorial? Select all that apply.
options: forEach is available on a Collection
forEach is available on a Stream
filter is available directly on a Collection
filter is available on a Stream
The enhanced for loop is built on an index counter
optionExplain: Right: the tutorial converts a plain foreach into forEach called straight on the collection.
Right: forEach also exists on streams, so stream then forEach works.
The tutorial says filter lives only on streams, so a collection needs stream first.
Right: filter is an intermediate operation on streams.
The tutorial describes it as sugar over an iterator, not an index counter.
questions.explain: forEach exists on both Collection and Stream, while filter is a stream operation.
questions.rule: forEach on both; filter only on streams.

questions.unitTitle: Refactoring from the Imperative to the Functional Style (dev.java)
questions.q: A loop goes over orders and, for each order whose total is above 100, calls flag with the order. Which version matches the tutorial?
options: orders.stream().filter(total above 100).forEach(flag)
orders.filter(total above 100).forEach(flag) directly
orders.stream().forEach(total above 100).filter(flag)
orders.forEach(total above 100, flag) in one call here
optionExplain: Right: stream gives the pipeline, filter holds the test, forEach holds the action.
filter is not available directly on a collection, so this does not compile.
forEach ends the pipeline, so filter cannot follow it, and the test and action are in the wrong places.
forEach takes one action; it has no separate test position.
questions.explain: The selecting if becomes filter on a stream; the action stays in forEach.
questions.rule: stream, filter, forEach.

questions.unitTitle: Refactoring from the Imperative to the Functional Style (dev.java)
questions.q: Sort each operation into intermediate (more can follow it) or terminal (it ends the pipeline).

items.t: filter
map
takeWhile
forEach
findFirst
count

questions.explain: The tutorial names forEach and findFirst as terminal operations after intermediate ones such as filter. map and takeWhile also return streams; count ends the pipeline with a number.
questions.rule: Intermediate operations chain; a terminal one ends the pipeline.
questions.teaches: Beyond the tutorial: operations that return another stream are called intermediate, those that produce the final result are terminal, and a pipeline ends with exactly one terminal operation.

questions.unitTitle: Refactoring from the Imperative to the Functional Style (dev.java)
questions.q: A list holds Ann, Bob, Cleo and Dean. The pipeline calls stream, filter with length equal to 4, then forEach to print. What is printed?
options: Ann then Bob
Cleo then Dean
Ann, Bob, Cleo and Dean
Nothing, because filter needs map first
optionExplain: Ann and Bob have three letters, so the test discards them.
Right: only Cleo and Dean have four letters, and they stay in their original order.
This would be the output with no filter, so the test is ignored.
filter needs no map; it works on its own before forEach.
questions.explain: The test keeps four-letter names and leaves their order alone.
questions.rule: filter keeps the passing elements in order.
questions.teaches: Beyond the tutorial: the elements that pass filter keep their original order, so the output follows the order of the list.

questions.unitTitle: Refactoring from the Imperative to the Functional Style (dev.java)
questions.q: True or false: A filter step can change the elements it passes on, for example by converting them to uppercase.
questions.explain: filter only decides which elements continue and leaves them unchanged. Changing elements is a job for map, covered next.
questions.rule: filter selects; it does not transform.

questions.unitTitle: Refactoring from the Imperative to the Functional Style (dev.java)
questions.q: A loop converts every name to uppercase before printing it. Which stream operation does the converting?
options: map
filter
forEach
count
optionExplain: Right: map applies a function to each element and passes on the results.
filter chooses elements and leaves their values unchanged.
forEach performs an action at the end and does not hand on new values.
count only returns how many elements remain.
questions.explain: A conversion turns each element into another one. The card next names the operation.
questions.rule: A conversion in a loop becomes map.

questions.unitTitle: Refactoring from the Imperative to the Functional Style (dev.java)
questions.q: Wherever a loop body transforms data, the functional style uses the ____ operation.
questions.explain: The tutorial's rule is that transformation inside a loop calls for map.
questions.rule: Transformation: map.

questions.unitTitle: Refactoring from the Imperative to the Functional Style (dev.java)
questions.q: A loop goes over names, skips those whose length is not 4, and prints the uppercase form of the rest. Put the stream version in order.
items: Call stream on the collection of names
Apply filter keeping names of length 4
Apply map converting each name to uppercase
Finish with forEach printing each result
questions.explain: The source comes first, then selection, then transformation, then the terminal action.
questions.rule: stream, filter, map, forEach.

questions.unitTitle: Refactoring from the Imperative to the Functional Style (dev.java)
questions.q: With names Mia, Noah, Liam and Zoe, one pipeline applies filter with length 4, then map to uppercase, then forEach printing. A second swaps the first two steps. What does the second print?
options: Nothing, because uppercase letters change the length
MIA, NOAH, LIAM and ZOE
NOAH and LIAM, the same as the first
An error, because map must come last
optionExplain: Uppercasing does not change how many letters a name has.
The length test still discards Mia and Zoe after the swap.
Right: uppercasing keeps each length, so the same two names pass the test.
A map can be followed by another intermediate step such as filter.
questions.explain: The swap is safe here only because the transformation leaves the property tested by the filter untouched.
questions.rule: Swapping filter and map is safe only if the test ignores what map changes.
questions.teaches: Beyond the tutorial: the order of filter and map matters whenever map changes what the test reads, because each step sees the values produced by the step before it.
questions.hint: Does uppercasing change the length?

questions.unitTitle: Refactoring from the Imperative to the Functional Style (dev.java)
questions.q: A loop converts Celsius readings to Fahrenheit (times 9, divide by 5, add 32) and prints only readings whose Celsius value is above 30. A rewrite does map to Fahrenheit first, then filter with value above 30. What is the flaw?
options: map cannot change numbers, since it only works on text values
The filter tests Fahrenheit values, so wrong readings pass
filter must be placed after forEach to see every value
Nothing is wrong, since map keeps all of the values equal
optionExplain: map can apply any function, including arithmetic.
Right: each step sees the output of the step before it, so filter should come first.
forEach ends the pipeline, so nothing can follow it.
map changes the values, so the later test no longer sees the Celsius numbers.
questions.explain: A reading of 10 Celsius is 50 Fahrenheit, which would pass a test of above 30.
questions.rule: Filter on the original value before map changes it.
questions.teaches: Beyond the tutorial: a predicate in filter tests whatever value reaches it, so a map before it changes what is being tested.

questions.unitTitle: Refactoring from the Imperative to the Functional Style (dev.java)
questions.q: True or false: map decides which elements continue down the pipeline.
questions.explain: map produces one result for each element and keeps them all. Choosing which elements continue is the job of filter.
questions.rule: filter chooses; map converts.

questions.unitTitle: Refactoring from the Imperative to the Functional Style (dev.java)
questions.q: True or false: In a stream version of a line counter, the count operation can take the place of the counter variable.
questions.explain: count returns how many elements reach the end of the pipeline, so no counter variable is needed. The card next shows the whole pipeline.
questions.rule: count replaces a manual counter.

questions.unitTitle: Refactoring from the Imperative to the Functional Style (dev.java)
questions.q: Match each part of the imperative line counter with its stream counterpart.
pairs: While loop reading lines one at a time
If the line contains the word
questions.explain: The stream supplies the lines and the stepping, filter replaces the if, and count replaces the counter.
questions.rule: Source, filter, count.

questions.unitTitle: Refactoring from the Imperative to the Functional Style (dev.java)
questions.q: A path variable names a text file and marker holds a String. Which pipeline counts the lines that contain marker?
options: Files.lines(path).map(line has marker).count()
Files.lines(path).count().filter(line has marker)
Files.readLine(path).filter(line has marker).count()
Files.lines(path).filter(line has marker).count()
optionExplain: map turns each line into true or false and keeps every one, so count returns the total number of lines.
count ends the pipeline with a number, so filter cannot follow it.
The tutorial uses Files.lines to get a stream; there is no such stream-returning readLine on Files.
Right: filter keeps matching lines and count counts them.
questions.explain: Selection belongs in filter before the final count.
questions.rule: filter first, count last.
questions.hint: Which step chooses lines and which step counts them?

questions.unitTitle: Refactoring from the Imperative to the Functional Style (dev.java)
questions.q: You must count the files in a folder whose names end in .txt. According to the tutorial, what is the first question to ask?
options: Whether the JDK or a library gives a stream of the folder
Whether the folder is small enough to loop over by hand
Whether the files can be sorted before they are counted
Whether a counter variable can be declared outside the loop first
optionExplain: Right: if a stream exists, filter and count apply as they do for lines.
Size is not the tutorial's test; it asks about a stream source.
Sorting is not part of the advice for this counting task.
A counter variable belongs to the loop style the lesson is replacing.
questions.explain: Finding a stream source is the first step of the conversion.
questions.rule: Ask first whether a stream over the resource exists.
questions.teaches: Beyond the tutorial: Files.list returns a stream of the entries in a directory, so the same filter and count pipeline can answer the folder question.

questions.unitTitle: Refactoring from the Imperative to the Functional Style (dev.java)
questions.q: True or false: When neither the JDK nor a library offers a stream over a resource, filter and count can still be applied directly to the resource.
questions.explain: filter and count are stream operations, so the pipeline needs a stream source first. Until one is found, the loop stays as it is.
questions.rule: No stream source, no pipeline.
questions.teaches: Beyond the tutorial: when no source exists, an imperative loop can first fill a collection, and the later steps can then use stream on that collection.

questions.unitTitle: Refactoring from the Imperative to the Functional Style (dev.java)
questions.q: A loop starts at 0, adds 5 each pass and leaves with break once the value exceeds 40. Which stream operation takes the place of the break?
options: filter
limit of fixed size
takeWhile
forEach
optionExplain: filter drops values but does not end an endless stream.
A fixed-size limit is not the tutorial's mapping for a break.
Right: takeWhile ends the stream at the first value that fails its predicate.
forEach runs the action and does not stop the stream.
questions.explain: Leaving a loop early is a cut-off in the stream. The card next gives the full mapping.
questions.rule: A break becomes takeWhile.

questions.unitTitle: Refactoring from the Imperative to the Functional Style (dev.java)
questions.q: Match each loop cue with the stream operation the tutorial links it to.
pairs: Index over a range with included end
If choosing which values to use
questions.explain: Each cue has its own counterpart in the tutorial's mapping.
questions.rule: One cue, one operation.

questions.unitTitle: Refactoring from the Imperative to the Functional Style (dev.java)
questions.q: A loop runs i from 1 while i is at most 50 and, when i is a multiple of 7, prints i plus 1. Which pipeline matches?
options: rangeClosed(1, 50), filter multiples of 7, map plus 1, forEach
range(1, 51), filter multiples of 7, map plus 2, forEach print
rangeClosed(1, 50), map plus 1, filter multiples of 7, forEach print
rangeClosed(1, 50), filter multiples of 7, forEach print, map plus 1
optionExplain: Right: the closed range includes 50, and the test reads the original i before it is changed.
This range has the right numbers, but the change of plus 2 prints values that differ from the loop.
Adding 1 first means the test reads i plus 1, which selects different numbers.
forEach ends the pipeline, so map cannot follow it.
questions.explain: Range cue, selecting if, transformation and print give four steps in that order.
questions.rule: Source, filter, map, terminal.
questions.hint: Which value should the multiple-of-7 test see?

questions.unitTitle: Refactoring from the Imperative to the Functional Style (dev.java)
questions.q: Starting at 1, a pipeline uses iterate with a step that doubles the value, then takeWhile keeping values below 50. It passes ____ values to forEach.
questions.explain: The values are 1, 2, 4, 8, 16 and 32. The next one, 64, fails the test and ends the stream.
questions.rule: takeWhile stops at the first failing value.
questions.teaches: Beyond the tutorial: the step operator may apply any int-to-int rule, such as doubling, so iterate is not limited to adding a constant.

questions.unitTitle: Refactoring from the Imperative to the Functional Style (dev.java)
questions.q: A loop goes over orders and counts those from 2025 whose total is above 100. Which operations appear in the matching pipeline? Select all that apply.
options: stream on the collection
filter for the year and total
map to uppercase
count at the end
takeWhile for a break
iterate with a seed
optionExplain: Right: the orders are a collection, so stream is the source.
Right: the year and total tests select orders, which is the job of filter.
Nothing in the loop transforms an order, so map is not needed.
Right: counting matches is done by count.
There is no break in this loop.
There is no stepped numeric sequence, so iterate is not needed.
questions.explain: The cues are a collection source, a selecting if and a counter, giving stream, filter and count.
questions.rule: Match cues one at a time.
questions.teaches: Beyond the tutorial: two conditions can sit in one filter predicate joined by and, or in two filter steps one after the other.

questions.unitTitle: Refactoring from the Imperative to the Functional Style (dev.java)
questions.q: True or false: According to the tutorial, every loop should be converted as soon as one of its cues is recognised.
questions.explain: The tutorial advises refactoring opportunistically, when fixing a bug or making an enhancement, and checking behaviour after each change.
questions.rule: Refactor opportunistically and verify.

questions.q: A developer puts an annotation on a method. What is the direct effect of the annotation on how that method's own logic runs?
options: It inserts extra statements into the method before it runs
It describes the method without changing its logic
It makes the compiler optimise the method more heavily
It blocks other classes from calling the method directly
optionExplain: Code insertion sounds plausible because annotations look like commands, but an annotation is information, not a statement.
It carries information about the method for readers such as tools, while the method's logic stays as written.
Optimisation hints are a different feature; an annotation does not tune the compiler by itself.
Access control is done with access modifiers, not with an annotation's presence.
questions.explain: Annotations are metadata, so they describe the method rather than alter its logic. The card next shows who reads them.
questions.rule: An annotation informs readers; it does not change the logic.

questions.q: An annotation is written with the ____ sign followed by its name.
questions.explain: The at sign tells the compiler that an annotation follows, and the next token is its name.
questions.rule: An annotation begins with an at sign.

questions.q: An annotation type Level has exactly one element, named value, of type int. Which use applies it with the value 3 using the shortcut the tutorial describes?
options: @Level(3)
@Level 3
@Level = 3
@Level[3]
optionExplain: The name value is dropped and the number sits in parentheses, which is the shortcut for a lone value element.
Parentheses are needed whenever a value is given; without them the 3 is just a stray token.
The equals form is only meaningful inside parentheses, as in a named element, so this is not valid.
Square brackets are used for array element values inside parentheses, not as an application syntax.
questions.explain: Because the only element is named value, its name can be omitted and the value goes in parentheses.
questions.rule: A lone element named value may be written without its name.
questions.hint: Which spelling leaves out the element name but keeps the parentheses?

questions.q: True or false: an annotation type whose only element is named size can be applied as @Limit(10), leaving the name out.
questions.explain: The shortcut depends on the element's name. Only an element called value may be left unnamed, so size must be written as size equals 10.
questions.rule: The unnamed shortcut applies only to an element called value.

questions.q: Sort each example by who reads the annotation: tools before the program runs, or the program while it runs.
groups: Read by tools before the program runs
Read by the program while it runs

items.t: A deployment tool writes an XML file from annotated classes
The compiler warns about a call to a deprecated method
A generator creates helper classes from annotations in source
The compiler rejects a method that wrongly claims to override
A running program asks a class which annotations it carries
A running framework reads annotations to configure a request

questions.explain: Compiler checks, code generation and deployment files all happen before the program starts. Only the last two items are read by the running program itself.
questions.rule: Ask who reads an annotation, and when.
questions.teaches: An annotation's purpose does not decide whether the running program can read it; that also depends on how long the annotation is kept, which is controlled separately.

questions.q: A team wants an annotation they define to be readable by code while the program runs. Where is that choice made?
options: On the type's definition, using another annotation
In a compiler flag that applies to every annotation
At each place where the annotation type is applied
In the name chosen for the annotation type itself
optionExplain: The type's definition carries a meta-annotation that says how long the annotation is kept.
A flag is a plausible build setting, but the keep-length is a property of each annotation type, not a global switch.
Use sites supply element values, not the keeping policy, so every use would otherwise differ.
Names have no meaning to the compiler beyond identification, so a name cannot hold a policy.
questions.explain: The choice is stored on the annotation type itself, using another annotation. The card next names it.
questions.rule: The keeping policy belongs to the annotation type.

questions.q: An annotation type is declared like an interface, with an @ placed before the keyword ____.
questions.explain: The declaration reads at sign interface, followed by the type name and its elements.
questions.rule: Declare annotation types with at sign interface.

questions.q: An annotation Audited is read by a monitoring library through reflection while the application is running. Which retention setting fits?
options: SOURCE, since it is kept in the source code
CLASS, because the compiler keeps it
RUNTIME, because the JVM keeps it
DOCUMENTED, since it shows in Javadoc
optionExplain: Source-only annotations are dropped when the code is compiled, so nothing remains to read at run time.
The compiler keeps it, but the JVM ignores it, so the running application cannot see it.
The JVM keeps RUNTIME annotations and runtime code can query them.
Documented is a separate meta-annotation, not a retention value.
questions.explain: Only RUNTIME is kept by the JVM and visible to running code. SOURCE disappears after compilation, and CLASS is ignored by the JVM.
questions.rule: Choose RUNTIME when running code must read the annotation.

questions.q: Match each meta-annotation to the job it does.
pairs: Sets how long the annotation is kept
Limits the places it may be applied
Makes it appear in generated Javadoc
Lets a subclass pick it up from its superclass
questions.explain: Each meta-annotation sets one aspect: lifetime, placement, Javadoc visibility and inheritance.
questions.rule: One meta-annotation, one aspect.

questions.q: True or false: an annotation marked Inherited, placed on a method of a base class, is also seen on the overriding method in a subclass.
questions.explain: According to the tutorial Inherited applies only to class declarations, so a method annotation is not carried to an overriding method.
questions.rule: Inherited works on classes only.

questions.q: A style checker needs an annotation LocalNote that developers place only on local variables and that is used only while compiling. Which settings fit?
options: Target METHOD with Retention RUNTIME
Target LOCAL_VARIABLE with Retention SOURCE
Target TYPE with Retention CLASS
Target FIELD with Retention RUNTIME
optionExplain: Methods are not local variables and RUNTIME keeps more than a compile-only checker needs.
LOCAL_VARIABLE limits placement to what the checker needs and SOURCE is enough for a compile-time tool.
TYPE covers classes and interfaces, not local variables.
FIELD covers fields, not locals, and RUNTIME is unneeded for a compile-time tool.
questions.explain: Target and Retention are independent: one says where, the other says how long. Local variables plus compile-time use means LOCAL_VARIABLE with SOURCE.
questions.rule: Pick placement and lifetime separately.
questions.teaches: Placement (Target) and lifetime (Retention) are chosen separately, so the narrowest fitting value of each can be picked for a given job.

questions.q: A method needs the same annotation type applied twice, once for month-end and once for Friday evening. What must be arranged for that to compile?
options: Nothing; the annotation can be written twice as it stands
A second copy of the annotation type with another name
A compiler flag that allows duplicate annotations
A repeatable declaration naming a container annotation
optionExplain: Writing it twice feels natural, but without the marking the compiler reports an error.
Copying the type does avoid repeats of one type, but it is not the mechanism the language offers.
Compiler flags do not turn on repeating; the type itself must be marked.
The type is marked repeatable and names a container that holds the repeats.
questions.explain: The language does not allow repeating by default. The annotation type must be declared repeatable with a container. The card next gives the details.
questions.rule: Repeating needs a Repeatable marking and a container.

questions.q: True or false: according to the tutorial, repeating an annotation type that is not marked Repeatable causes a compile-time error.
questions.explain: The Repeatable marking, with its container, is what permits more than one use of the same type on a declaration.
questions.rule: No Repeatable marking, no repeats.

questions.q: A class Office carries two Alert annotations. Which call returns both of them according to the tutorial?
options: getAnnotation with the Alert class
getAnnotationsByType with the Alert class
getAnnotation with the Office class
getAnnotationsByType with the String class
optionExplain: This call works only when one instance is present, so with two uses it does not return both.
It returns all repeated instances of the Alert type in one go.
The argument must be the annotation type, not the class that carries it.
The argument must name the annotation type being asked about, and String is unrelated.
questions.explain: getAnnotationsByType returns every repeated instance at once. getAnnotation is only for a single instance.
questions.rule: Use getAnnotationsByType to read repeats.
questions.hint: One call is meant for the single-instance case only.

questions.q: Which of these places can carry a type annotation according to the tutorial? Select all that apply.
options: A new expression that creates an object
A type cast
An implements clause
A line comment in the source
The text inside a string literal
optionExplain: Object creation uses a type, so it can be annotated.
A cast names a type, so the use can be annotated.
The interface named after implements is a type use.
A comment is not part of the program, so nothing can be annotated there.
String content is data, not a use of a type.
questions.explain: Type annotations go wherever a type is used: an object creation, a cast, an implements clause or a throws clause. A line comment holds no type use, and neither does the text inside a string literal.
questions.rule: Type annotations attach to uses of a type.
questions.teaches: Beyond the tutorial: because a type annotation attaches to a type use, it can also sit on a type argument, such as the element type of a list, which a declaration annotation cannot reach.

questions.q: A team marks a parameter with a NonNull-style type annotation but compiles with no checker module. What does the tutorial's description imply about the compile?
options: The compiler will warn about every null use anyway
No null warnings come from the annotation by itself
The compiler refuses to compile the parameter
The annotation is erased and the parameter is rejected
optionExplain: The compiler has no built-in type checking for this, so it does not warn about null from the annotation alone.
The warning is produced by a checker module, which is absent here, so the annotation alone yields no warning.
Refusing to compile would need a rule in the compiler, and none is described.
Erasing the annotation and rejecting the parameter are both unrelated to how the tutorial describes checkers.
questions.explain: The annotation only declares intent. Warnings about possible null use come from a checker plugged into the compiler, so none appears here.
questions.rule: A type annotation needs a checker to take effect.
questions.teaches: The same annotated source can behave differently depending on which checker modules are plugged in, since the checking is in the checker and not in the annotation.

questions.q: A method deep inside a program meets a problem it cannot fix. What does the Java runtime do first?
options: It searches the callers for code able to handle it
It ends the whole program right away, before looking anywhere
It restarts the failing method again from its first line
It skips the failing statement and carries on regardless
optionExplain: Right: it searches the call stack for a handler, starting at the failing method.
Ending is only the last outcome, and only when nobody can handle the problem.
Nothing in the mechanism repeats the method; restarting would hit the same problem.
Skipping would hide the problem; the normal flow is interrupted instead.
questions.explain: The runtime starts looking for code that can deal with the problem, beginning in the failing method and moving back through its callers. The card next shows the details.
questions.rule: Look for a handler along the call stack.

questions.q: Creating an exception object and handing it to the runtime system is known as ____ the exception.
questions.explain: That act is called throwing. The runtime then searches for a handler.
questions.rule: Creating the object and handing it over is throwing.

questions.q: Method main calls report, and report calls format. Format throws an exception of type T. Report has a handler only for an unrelated type U. Main has a handler for T. Which handler receives the exception?
options: Report's handler, because it sits closer to the failing code
Both handlers, one after the other, report first and then main
Neither, because a handler must sit in the failing method itself
Main's handler, the first one whose type matches
optionExplain: Nearness alone does not decide; the type must match, and U does not match T.
One thrown object goes to one handler; the search stops at the match.
Handlers in callers are exactly what the call stack search is for.
Right: report's handler is skipped for its type, and main's handler matches T.
questions.explain: The runtime checks format, then report, then main. Report's handler is for U, which does not match T, so it is skipped. Main's handler matches and catches it.
questions.rule: Only a handler whose type matches can catch.

questions.q: True or false: A handler declared for IOException can receive a thrown FileNotFoundException, which is a subclass of IOException.
questions.explain: According to the tutorial, a handler fits when the thrown type can be assigned to the handler's type. A subclass object can be assigned to its parent type, so the broader handler matches.
questions.rule: A handler matches by assignability, so a parent type catches its subclasses.
questions.teaches: A handler matches when the thrown object can be assigned to its declared type, so a handler for a parent type also catches objects of its subclasses.

questions.q: In a hotel, a porter reports a flooded room to a floor supervisor, who reports to the duty manager. The porter and the duty manager are both allowed to resolve flooding. By the runtime's search order, who deals with it?
options: The duty manager, who has the most authority
The floor supervisor, because every report passes through that role
The porter, because the search begins where the problem occurred
Whoever answers first, since order does not matter
optionExplain: Authority is not the criterion; the search goes outward from the failure and stops at the first match.
The supervisor is only checked if the porter has no matching handler, and being on the path does not make a handler.
Right: the failing method is checked first, so a matching handler there catches it.
Order matters: the search runs in reverse call order.
questions.explain: The search starts at the place where the problem occurred and goes outward. A matching handler in the failing method wins over any handler in a caller.
questions.rule: The failing method is checked first.
questions.teaches: The search begins in the failing method itself, so a matching handler there takes priority over any handler in its callers.
questions.hint: Where does the search begin?

questions.q: True or false: If no method on the call stack has a handler whose type matches, the exception is ignored and execution resumes after the failing statement.
questions.explain: With no match the thread ends. In the main thread that ends the program, so nothing resumes after the failing statement.
questions.rule: No matching handler means the thread ends.

questions.q: A program asks the user for a file name and opens that file. The user types a name that does not exist. What kind of problem is this?
options: An internal bug that the programmer needs to go and fix
A failure outside the program that it cannot foresee
A condition the program can expect and recover from
A problem that the compiler quietly ignores
optionExplain: A typo by a user is not a bug in the code; the code can handle it.
The file name is input the program asks for, so it is foreseeable.
Right: a well-written application expects bad names and can ask again.
The compiler does not ignore this one; code that may throw it must handle or declare it.
questions.explain: It is a problem the application can foresee and recover from, for example by asking again. The card next names this kind.
questions.rule: Recoverable conditions are checked exceptions.

questions.q: Match each term to its meaning.
pairs: A condition a well-written application should expect and recover from
A problem outside the application that it usually cannot recover from
A problem inside the application, usually a bug
Errors and runtime exceptions taken together
questions.explain: Each term names a kind by who is expected to foresee or fix the problem, with unchecked covering two of them.
questions.rule: Checked is recoverable, error is external, runtime is a bug.

questions.q: Sort these situations by whether the catch or specify requirement applies to the exception involved.

items.t: A user supplies a name of a file that does not exist
A disk or memory malfunction that no application code could repair
A list is read at an index beyond its end
A call passes null to a method that forbids it
Opening a file for writing may fail with an IOException
A stack is asked to remove an item when it is empty

questions.explain: A missing file is checked because a program can recover. A hardware malfunction is an error, and null or a bad index are runtime exceptions. Those last two kinds are exempt.
questions.rule: Only checked exceptions fall under the requirement.

questions.q: The class RuntimeException is a subclass of Exception. A method throws a new object of the plain class Exception, which is not under RuntimeException or Error. Does the catch or specify requirement apply?
options: Yes, since plain Exception is in neither exempt branch
No, because every subclass of Exception is unchecked by definition
No, because the method throws it on purpose
Yes, but only when the method also catches an Error
optionExplain: Right: checked means every exception except those in the Error and RuntimeException branches, and this one is neither.
Only the RuntimeException branch below Exception is unchecked; other subclasses and Exception itself are checked.
Intent plays no role; the compiler looks at the type.
Error is a separate branch and has no bearing on this exception.
questions.explain: Only Error, RuntimeException and their subclasses are exempt. The plain Exception class is outside those branches, so it is checked.
questions.rule: Being an Exception does not make it unchecked.
questions.teaches: Exception itself is checked: of the types under Throwable, only the Error branch and the RuntimeException branch of Exception are exempt.

questions.q: A method has neither a try nor a throws clause and calls a library routine whose documentation says it throws a checked exception only when a disk is physically pulled out during a write. What does the compiler do?
options: It accepts the code, because such an event is so rare
It rejects the code: the checked exception is not handled
It accepts the code but gives a warning when it runs
It rejects the code only if the disk is removed while running
optionExplain: Rarity is not part of the rule; the type alone triggers the requirement.
Right: the requirement is applied to the type at compile time, however rare the case.
The rule is a compile-time one, not a run-time warning.
Compilation happens before any disk is pulled, so the condition is never tested then.
questions.explain: The compiler decides by the exception's type, not by how rare the event is. A checked type that is neither caught nor declared is a compile error.
questions.rule: The compiler checks the type, not the probability.
questions.teaches: The catch or specify check depends only on the exception's type, never on how likely the event is, so a rare checked exception still has to be handled or declared.
questions.hint: Does the compiler read the documentation about rarity?

questions.q: True or false: An exception that is exempt from the catch or specify requirement cannot be caught with a catch block.
questions.explain: Exempt means the compiler does not force you to handle it. The tutorial notes that an application can still catch a runtime exception, though fixing the cause makes more sense.
questions.rule: Exempt does not mean uncatchable.

questions.q: A try block throws an exception, and a matching catch block handles it. A finally block follows the catch. When does the finally block run?
options: Only when no exception was thrown at all
Only when the catch block throws a second time
Only when no catch block matched the exception
Whether or not an exception was thrown
optionExplain: It also runs after an exception has been caught.
Rethrowing is not the trigger; finally runs on every exit from the try.
It runs when a catch matched and also when none did.
Right: finally runs when the try block exits in any way.
questions.explain: Finally runs whenever the try block exits, with or without an exception. The card next shows the details.
questions.rule: Finally runs on every exit from try.

questions.q: In one catch clause that handles several unrelated exception types in the same way, the types are separated by a ____.
questions.explain: Multi-catch lists the alternatives separated by a vertical bar.
questions.rule: Multi-catch uses a vertical bar, and the types must be unrelated.

questions.q: A method has a try block, then a catch block for IOException, then a catch block for FileNotFoundException. FileNotFoundException is a subclass of IOException. What happens when this is compiled?
options: It compiles, and the second catch handles missing files
It compiles, and both catch blocks run for a missing file
It fails to compile, because the second catch can never run
It fails to compile, because two catch blocks cannot follow one try
optionExplain: The first catch matches first, so the second never gets a chance.
Only one catch block runs for a thrown exception.
Right: the broader type came first, which makes the narrower catch unreachable.
Several catch blocks may follow one try; the problem is their order.
questions.explain: The first catch already covers every FileNotFoundException, so the second can never run. The compiler rejects a broader type placed before a narrower one.
questions.rule: Narrow catch blocks go first.

questions.q: True or false: A resource in try-with-resources must implement Closeable, and implementing only AutoCloseable is not enough.
questions.explain: The requirement is AutoCloseable. Closeable extends it, so Closeable types qualify, and so do other AutoCloseable types.
questions.rule: A resource needs AutoCloseable.
questions.teaches: Closeable extends AutoCloseable: Closeable.close declares IOException while AutoCloseable.close declares Exception, and an implementation may narrow what its close method throws.

questions.q: A try-with-resources statement declares a sound card first and a recording stream second, then has a catch block. The body throws an exception, and both closes succeed. Put the events in order.
items: The body throws an exception
The recording stream is closed
The sound card is closed
The catch block runs
questions.explain: The body ends abruptly, the resources close in reverse order of creation, and only then does the catch block run.
questions.rule: Resources close before catch or finally runs.
questions.teaches: Any catch or finally attached to a try-with-resources runs only after all its resources have been closed.

questions.q: A method has a try block that ends with a return statement, followed by a finally block that prints a message. The try block throws no exception. What happens when the method is called?
options: The message prints, and then the method returns
The method returns, and the message never prints
The message prints only if a catch block exists
The compiler rejects a finally after a return
optionExplain: Right: return in try does not skip finally.
This is the very case finally exists to cover.
A catch block is not needed for finally to run.
A return inside try with a finally after it is allowed.
questions.explain: Finally runs whenever the try block exits, and that includes leaving through return. The message prints, then the method returns.
questions.rule: Finally runs even when try returns.

questions.q: Which statements about finally and try-with-resources agree with the tutorial? Select all that apply.
options: Finally runs when the try block leaves by return
Finally runs when the try block throws an exception that no catch handles
Finally is guaranteed even if the JVM exits during the try block
An exception thrown from finally is attached to the earlier one as suppressed
optionExplain: Correct: leaving through return is one of the exits finally covers.
Correct: finally runs on abrupt exits too, before the exception moves on.
Wrong: if the JVM exits during try or catch, finally may not run.
Wrong: in a plain finally the new exception replaces the earlier one; suppression is a try-with-resources feature.
questions.explain: Finally runs after a return in try and after an unhandled exception. It is not guaranteed if the JVM exits, and when finally throws, the earlier exception is lost.
questions.rule: Finally is strong but not absolute.

questions.q: A library method hits a failure it cannot sensibly handle, since only its callers know what to do. What is the usual approach in Java?
options: Catch it itself and print a message to the console
Declare it in the method header so callers decide
Return normally and hope that nobody notices it
End the whole program from inside the method
optionExplain: A printed message cannot give callers a say in the response.
Right: a declared exception lets a caller that knows more decide what to do.
Hiding the failure leaves callers unaware of it.
A library that ends the program takes the decision away from its users.
questions.explain: The method passes the problem up by declaring it, so a caller with more knowledge handles it. The card next shows how.
questions.rule: Declare what you cannot handle.

questions.q: Put the parts of a method header that declares an exception in the order they appear.
items: Return type and method name
Parameter list
The word throws and the exception types
Opening brace of the body
questions.explain: The throws clause comes after the parameter list and before the opening brace of the body.
questions.rule: Throws sits after the parameters and before the body.

questions.q: A method archive takes a String name and calls code that can throw IOException, a checked exception. The method has neither a try statement nor a throws clause. Which change makes it compile and leaves the handling to its callers?
options: Add throws IOException before the parameter list
Add a catch block for NullPointerException
Add throws IOException after the parameter list
Add throws Error after the parameter list
optionExplain: The clause belongs after the parameter list, not before it.
A different type does not cover IOException, so the error remains.
Right: the clause after the parameters satisfies the catch or specify requirement.
Listing Error does not cover IOException, which is a different type.
questions.explain: A throws clause naming IOException after the parameter list declares the exception, so the method no longer needs to catch it.
