questions.rule: Uncaught checked exceptions go in a throws clause.

questions.q: A program logs a stack trace and builds a long message with a costly formatting call, but the logger may discard the message. According to the tutorial, how can the cost be avoided?
options: Build the message first and store it in a field for later
Catch the exception twice so that the second copy is cheaper
Turn the exception into an Error before it is logged
Pass a supplier, so building waits until it is logged
optionExplain: Building first pays the cost even when the message is dropped.
Catching twice adds work and does not defer anything.
The kind of throwable has no effect on the cost of formatting.
Right: a supplier is called only when the message is actually logged.
questions.explain: Passing a supplier delays building the message until the logger decides to log it. If the message is discarded, the work is never done.
questions.rule: Defer building messages that may be discarded.
questions.teaches: Logging with a supplier defers the costly message building until the logger actually writes the message.
questions.hint: Think of when the work gets done.

questions.q: In a delivery app, a layer catches a database timeout and throws OrderFailedException, which only has a message constructor. Later, developers see no trace of the timeout. Which Throwable feature lets them attach the timeout as the cause after the object exists?
options: initCause
getCause
getStackTrace
throws
optionExplain: Right: initCause sets the cause on an existing exception.
It reads the cause that is already set; it cannot set one.
It reads the call history; it does not attach a cause.
It is a header clause, not a method of the exception.
questions.explain: Throwable offers constructors and a method named initCause for setting the cause. Getting the cause back is getCause.
questions.rule: A cause can be set by constructor or by initCause.
questions.teaches: Besides constructors, Throwable has an initCause method for setting the cause of an existing exception, which helps when a class lacks a cause constructor.

questions.q: Sort these descriptions by whether they belong to the throw statement or the throws clause.

items.t: Raises an exception object at that point in the code
Takes one Throwable object as its argument
Lists exception types separated by commas
Appears in the method header
Is optional for unchecked exceptions
Would be used to signal an empty stack

questions.explain: Throw is an action inside code that raises one Throwable object. Throws is a declaration in the header that lists types.
questions.rule: Throw raises; throws declares.

questions.q: A team debates writing its own exception classes. Which situations match the reasons the tutorial gives? Select all that apply.
options: A platform class already names the problem exactly
Users should be able to tell these exceptions apart from other vendors'
The class should extend Error so that it looks serious
The package throws several related exceptions that belong in one family
optionExplain: Wrong: when the platform fits, the tutorial says a platform class is probably enough.
Correct: telling them apart from other packages' exceptions is a stated reason.
Wrong: Error is for severe system failures, and the tutorial advises extending Exception.
Correct: related exceptions are a stated reason for their own hierarchy.
questions.explain: The tutorial gives four reasons: no fitting platform type, telling your exceptions apart from others', several related exceptions, and a self-contained package. A fitting platform class or a wish to look serious is not among them.
questions.rule: Write a custom class only for the listed reasons.

questions.q: Your method can fail in a way the caller could fix by trying again with different input. How should that failure be modelled?
options: As an unchecked exception, to keep the header short
As a checked exception, so callers must plan for it
As an Error, so that it stops the program
As any type, since the choice has no effect on callers
optionExplain: Short headers are tempting, but this hides a recoverable case from callers.
Right: a recoverable failure belongs in the interface so callers decide how to respond.
Errors are for failures callers usually cannot recover from.
The choice changes what the compiler demands of every caller.
questions.explain: A failure the caller can recover from should be visible in the method's interface. The card next gives the tutorial's rule.
questions.rule: Recoverable failures belong in the interface.

questions.q: True or false: According to the tutorial, making a custom exception extend RuntimeException only to avoid writing throws clauses is a recommended practice.
questions.explain: The tutorial says this shortcut avoids compiler errors but defeats the purpose of the rule and can cause problems for users of your classes.
questions.rule: Do not pick unchecked only to dodge throws.

questions.q: Sort these failures by how the tutorial's guideline would classify them.

items.t: A user enters an expired coupon code and can type another
A loop reads past the end of an array because of a counting slip
A partner service refuses a request that can be retried later
A method gets null for an argument it requires
A backup file is missing and another location can be tried
A division by zero comes from a missing guard

questions.explain: Where a client can reasonably recover, the exception is checked. Where it is a programming error the client cannot repair at run time, it is unchecked.
questions.rule: Recoverable means checked; a bug means unchecked.

questions.q: True or false: According to the tutorial, a handler for the plain Exception class is the best default, because it covers every case.
questions.explain: Broad handlers are acceptable mainly for simple cases such as printing a message and exiting. Otherwise handlers should be as specific as possible, because general ones catch errors the programmer never anticipated.
questions.rule: Prefer specific handlers over broad ones.
questions.teaches: Handlers should be as specific as possible, because a very general handler such as one for Exception also catches errors the programmer never anticipated.

questions.q: A setup script checks a result code after each of twelve steps, with nested if statements, and the real work is hard to see. By the tutorial's reasoning, what do exceptions improve here?
options: They make each step of the script run noticeably faster
They remove the need to handle any failure at all
They let callers choose which steps get skipped
They keep main flow apart from error handling
optionExplain: Speed is not the claim; the gain is in how the code is organized.
Failures still need handlers; the handling moves elsewhere.
Skipping steps is not what exceptions provide; they interrupt the flow at the failure.
Right: the steps read as one clear path, and the handlers deal with failures separately.
questions.explain: With exceptions, the normal flow of the steps can be written plainly, while error handling lives in separate handlers.
questions.rule: Exceptions separate normal flow from error handling.
questions.teaches: Exceptions let normal logic be written without error checks mixed into each step, and intermediate methods can pass an exception up so that only one method handles it.

questions.q: A colleague reasons: A caller can fix a null argument by passing something else, so by the recovery rule NullPointerException ought to be checked. What is wrong with this reasoning?
options: Null is not a problem in Java, so nothing can go wrong
A bug is fixed in the code, not recovered from
Unchecked exceptions are only meant for hardware faults
The recovery rule applies only to custom exception classes
optionExplain: Null can cause a NullPointerException, so it is a problem.
Right: a coding mistake is fixed by changing the code, which is why the tutorial treats such cases as unchecked.
Hardware faults are errors; runtime exceptions cover internal bugs too.
The rule is stated for exceptions in general, not only custom ones.
questions.explain: The tutorial counts a null passed in by mistake as a programming error. Fixing the code is the remedy, not recovery at run time, so an unchecked exception fits.
questions.rule: A bug is fixed in the code, not recovered from.
questions.hint: What is the remedy for a bug?

questions.q: Which statement about Collection and Map in the Java Collections Framework is correct?
options: Map extends Collection and adds a key to each element it holds
Collection and Map are separate hierarchies, not directly related
Collection extends Map and treats every element as a map key
Both extend Iterable, which is the single root of the framework
optionExplain: It sounds natural that a map is a bigger collection, but Map does not extend Collection.
Right: the tutorial says the two hierarchies are not directly related.
Treating elements as keys is a plausible idea, but Collection does not extend Map.
Iterable sits above Collection only, and the tutorial says it is not even part of the framework.
questions.explain: The two main categories are independent trees. The card next shows how queues and iterators fit around them.
questions.rule: Collection and Map are separate roots.

questions.q: The root interface of the category that stores key and value pairs is ____.
questions.explain: Map is the root of the key and value category; Collection is the root of the other main category.
questions.rule: Map is the root for key and value pairs.

questions.q: A ticketing app stores booked seats, where each seat number identifies exactly one customer, and it must look up a customer by seat number. Which category does the framework structure point to?
options: A List from the Collection hierarchy
A Queue, because seats are served in turn
An Iterator, because seats are visited one by one
A Map, because a seat number identifies one customer
optionExplain: A List gives positions, but the need here is lookup by an identifying key, which is the job of a map.
A Queue models arrival order, which is not what a seat number lookup needs.
An Iterator walks over a collection; it does not store anything.
Right: a key that identifies one value is the defining use of a Map.
questions.explain: Retrieval by a key that identifies each object is the sign of the Map category.
questions.rule: Lookup by an identifying key points to Map.

questions.q: True or false: Because Collection extends Iterable, the iterator method is available on a List, a Set and a Queue.
questions.explain: Iterable declares iterator(), and every interface under Collection inherits it. Queues and stacks can therefore be iterated.
questions.rule: iterator() is inherited down the Collection hierarchy.
questions.teaches: The iterator method is declared once, on Iterable, and inherited by every interface below Collection, so List, Set and Queue need no separate declaration.

questions.q: Sort each interface by the hierarchy it belongs to.

items.t: List
Queue
Set
SortedMap
NavigableMap
Deque

questions.explain: List, Set, Queue and Deque descend from Collection. SortedMap and NavigableMap descend from Map.
questions.rule: Queue and Deque live under Collection; sorted maps live under Map.

questions.q: A teammate wants to pass a Map to a method that expects a Collection of String, reasoning that a map is a larger collection. What does the framework structure say about this?
options: It fails, because the two hierarchies are unrelated
It works, because Map extends Collection
It works if the map is first wrapped in an Iterator
It fails, because Collection extends Map instead
optionExplain: Right: with no direct relationship, a Map is not accepted where a Collection is required.
This is the natural guess, but Map does not extend Collection.
An Iterator walks over a collection and is not a conversion tool.
The relationship is not reversed either; neither extends the other.
questions.explain: The two hierarchies share no inheritance, so a Map cannot stand in for a Collection.
questions.rule: Convert with a view of keys, values or entries instead.
questions.teaches: A map is not a collection; to treat its parts as collections you use views of its keys, values or entries, which the Maps section covers.

questions.q: True or false: For a last-in first-out structure in new single-threaded code, the tutorial recommends the Stack class.
questions.explain: The tutorial lists Stack as a legacy class and points to ArrayDeque. The card next gives the full replacement list.
questions.rule: Stack is legacy; use ArrayDeque.

questions.q: Match each legacy class to the tutorial's suggested replacement.
questions.explain: Each legacy type has a modern counterpart; the choice between HashMap and ConcurrentHashMap depends on concurrency.
questions.rule: Each legacy class has a named replacement.

questions.q: A script stores exactly seven weekday names that stay fixed and are only printed. Following the tutorial's advice about arrays, what is reasonable?
options: Use Vector, because it is the oldest list type in the JDK
Use Hashtable, because the names are fixed and unique
Keep a simple array, because it already fits the need
Use a collection, since arrays are discouraged in new code
optionExplain: Vector is a legacy class, and age is not a reason to choose it.
Hashtable is a legacy key and value class and a poor match for a plain sequence.
Right: the tutorial says to keep a mastered simple solution when it fits.
The tutorial does not discourage arrays; it lists what collections add.
questions.explain: A fixed, small need that an array meets does not call for a collection.
questions.rule: Keep an array when it already fits.

questions.q: Which of these are advantages of a collection over an array, according to the tutorial? Select all that apply.
options: It tracks how many elements it holds
It can refuse certain elements such as null
Most JDK collections can be extended to add operations
It is always faster to read than an array
optionExplain: Right: a collection knows its size without a separate counter.
Right: a collection can reject elements such as null.
Right: collections are objects, so most JDK collections can be extended, which is not possible with an array.
The tutorial makes no such speed claim; the listed advantages are about features.
questions.explain: The advantages are features: size tracking, flexible capacity, element control, membership tests, set operations, and extensibility.
questions.rule: Collections add features, not speed.
questions.teaches: Because a collection is an object, most JDK collections can be extended to add operations, which is not possible with an array.

questions.q: A game keeps an undo stack used by one thread. Later the same stack must be shared by many threads. Which pairing fits the tutorial's guidance for the two stages?
options: Stack first, then Vector once the stack is shared
ArrayDeque for both, since it is already thread-safe
ArrayDeque first, then BlockingQueue implementations
Hashtable first, then ConcurrentHashMap for sharing
optionExplain: Stack and Vector are the legacy pair the tutorial advises avoiding in new code.
ArrayDeque is the non-concurrent choice; the tutorial does not call it thread-safe.
Right: ArrayDeque replaces Stack when thread safety is not needed, and the tutorial points to BlockingQueue implementations for a thread-safe stack or queue.
Hashtable and ConcurrentHashMap are key and value types, not stacks.
questions.explain: The right implementation depends on whether concurrent access is needed, and the answer changes when that condition changes.
questions.rule: Re-check the implementation when the concurrency condition changes.
questions.teaches: For a thread-safe stack or queue, the tutorial advises looking at BlockingQueue implementations; ArrayDeque is the choice when thread safety is not needed.

questions.q: Which collection interface promises that the same element cannot appear twice?
options: Set
List
Collection
Iterable
optionExplain: Right: forbidding duplicates is the one promise Set adds.
A List keeps every addition, including repeats, in the order added.
A plain Collection can hold equal elements, even the same instance twice.
Iterable only allows looping and says nothing about contents.
questions.explain: Uniqueness is the defining promise of Set. The card next shows what the other interfaces add.
questions.rule: Set means no duplicates.

questions.q: Match each interface to what it adds.
pairs: Ascending order by a comparison rule
questions.explain: Each interface contributes one main promise to the level above.
questions.rule: Each interface adds a distinct promise.

questions.q: A club registry must refuse repeat sign-ups and also list members in sign-up order. Which of List, Set, SortedSet and NavigableSet promises both on its own?
options: List, because it keeps insertion order
Set, because it forbids duplicates
SortedSet, because it keeps a stable order
None of them promises both on its own
optionExplain: List keeps order but allows duplicate entries.
Set forbids duplicates but promises no insertion order.
SortedSet is ordered by a comparison rule, not by arrival time.
Right: uniqueness comes from Set, insertion order from List, and the sorted types order by comparison.
questions.explain: Uniqueness and insertion order are promised by different interfaces, so no single one covers both.
questions.rule: Match each need to the interface that promises it.

questions.q: True or false: A SortedSet that was given a Comparator uses that Comparator even when its elements implement Comparable.
questions.explain: The tutorial says a Comparator may be used even for Comparable elements, to sort differently from compareTo.
questions.rule: A supplied Comparator can override natural order.
questions.teaches: A Comparator can override the order that compareTo defines, so the same element type can be sorted in a different order.

questions.q: A program iterates a Set of five strings, adds a sixth string, and iterates again. Which expectation fits the tutorial?
options: The first five keep their positions and the sixth comes last
No order is promised, so code should not depend on one
Elements appear in alphabetical order because strings are Comparable
The new string replaces the oldest element in the set
optionExplain: That describes a List; a plain Set promises no insertion order.
Right: the tutorial warns that a consistent order, where it appears, is incidental.
Alphabetical order is what a SortedSet gives, not a plain Set.
A Set only refuses duplicates; it does not replace an existing element with a new one.
questions.explain: A Set promises uniqueness, not order, so a program should not rely on one.
questions.rule: Do not rely on Set iteration order.

questions.q: A reviewer reads this about a leaderboard: scores is a Set of Integer, so scores.get(0) returns the best score. Which flaw does the hierarchy reveal?
options: get takes a key rather than an index, as a map does
Set has no index operations; those belong to List
Set cannot hold Integer values at all
get is a method that only a SortedSet provides
optionExplain: Taking a key is how a map works, and Set is not a map.
Right: Set adds nothing beyond Collection, and index operations are what List adds.
A Set can hold any element type, including Integer.
SortedSet adds first and last, not an index lookup.
questions.explain: Positions exist only where an interface adds them, and Set adds no operations at all.
questions.rule: Only List adds index operations.
questions.teaches: Index-based operations come from List alone; the sorted forms add first, last or navigation but no position lookup, and a plain Set offers none of these.

questions.q: The Collection method retainAll performs the set operation called ____ (compare union and complement).
questions.explain: retainAll keeps only the elements that also appear in the argument, which is intersection. The card next covers all four bulk methods.
questions.rule: retainAll is intersection.

questions.q: Match each Collection method to the set operation it models.
questions.explain: The four bulk methods mirror the four basic set operations.
questions.rule: Bulk methods mirror set operations.

questions.q: A Collection of String called tags holds red, green and blue. What does tags.removeAll(other) do when other holds green and pink?
options: Removes green and pink from tags in one step
Throws an exception, since pink is absent from tags
Keeps only green and removes the rest of tags
Removes green only, because pink is not in tags
optionExplain: Pink was never in tags, so there is nothing to remove for it.
Absent elements are not errors for removeAll.
Keeping only the shared elements is retainAll, not removeAll.
Right: removeAll removes only elements that are present in both collections.
questions.explain: removeAll removes what the two collections share, so missing elements have no effect.
questions.rule: removeAll removes only shared elements.

questions.q: A program copies a three-element collection into a String array of length five by calling toArray with that array. Afterwards, the cell at index 3 holds ____.
questions.explain: With room to spare, toArray fills the given array in place and puts null in the cell right after the last element.
questions.rule: A big enough array is filled and returned.
questions.teaches: When the array argument is large enough, the returned array is the very same object that was passed in, so the argument and the result are one array.

questions.q: True or false: containsAll returns true when the argument collection is empty.
questions.explain: Inclusion asks whether every element of the argument is present; with no elements, nothing fails the test.
questions.rule: Empty argument means included.

questions.q: A student calls scores.contains(userObject) on a Collection of Integer. The code compiles, so the student concludes it is a valid search. Which statement fits the tutorial?
options: It compiles, but can never be true for a non-Integer
Compiling proves the check can find the object
It will not compile unless the argument is an Integer
It always throws ClassCastException
optionExplain: Right: contains takes any type, so a mismatched check compiles but cannot succeed; an IDE may warn.
The compiler accepts the call, which does not make the search meaningful.
The tutorial says it does compile, which is why an IDE warning matters.
An exception is possible in some implementations, but the tutorial presents it as possible, not certain.
questions.explain: The method signature is permissive, so the type safety of a membership check rests on the programmer.
questions.rule: A compiling contains call can still be pointless.
questions.teaches: Because contains accepts any type, a mismatched check compiles; an IDE may warn, and some implementations throw ClassCastException instead of returning false.

questions.q: True or false: Calling the list's own remove method inside a for-each loop over that same list is a safe way to delete elements.
questions.explain: Changing the collection directly during iteration can throw ConcurrentModificationException. The card next shows safe alternatives.
questions.rule: Do not change the collection directly during iteration.

questions.q: To delete the element most recently returned by next(), you call the iterator's ____ method.
questions.explain: The iterator's remove deletes the element last returned by next().
questions.rule: Use the iterator's remove, not the collection's.

questions.q: Put these steps in the order one pass of an iterator loop takes to delete the negative numbers from a list.
items: Check hasNext() to see whether another element exists
Call next() to get the element
Test whether the element is negative
Call remove() on the iterator
questions.explain: An iterator loop checks, advances, tests, then removes the element just returned.
questions.rule: Check, advance, test, then remove through the iterator.

questions.q: Which iterator can be expected to throw UnsupportedOperationException from remove()?
options: The iterator of an ArrayList
The iterator of a LinkedList
The iterator of an immutable collection
The iterator of a HashSet
optionExplain: The tutorial names ArrayList iterators as supporting remove.
The tutorial names LinkedList iterators as supporting remove.
Right: an immutable collection has nothing it may remove, so its iterator refuses.
The tutorial names HashSet iterators as supporting remove.
questions.explain: Support for remove depends on the collection behind the iterator.
questions.rule: Iterator removal depends on the collection.
questions.teaches: The Iterator interface lets an implementation refuse remove, so support depends on the collection the iterator came from.

questions.q: True or false: A for-each loop that calls remove on the very list it is looping over can throw ConcurrentModificationException even when only one thread is involved.
questions.explain: The tutorial says a direct change during iteration can throw this exception, and that it can occur in single-threaded code.
questions.rule: Direct changes during iteration can throw.

questions.q: A class Playlist wraps an array of songs and implements Iterable by supplying an iterator, but it is not a Collection. A teammate says it cannot be used in a for-each loop. What is the right response?
options: Correct, because for-each needs a Collection
Correct, unless Playlist also implements Map
Wrong, because for-each only needs an Iterable
Wrong, but only if Playlist is a record
optionExplain: For-each accepts any Iterable, not only collections.
Map has nothing to do with for-each.
Right: Iterable is the requirement, which is why the tutorial's own Range class works in for-each.
The tutorial uses a record from Java 16 on and a plain class before; either works.
questions.explain: For-each depends on Iterable, so a custom class qualifies once it supplies an iterator.
questions.rule: Implement Iterable to use for-each.
questions.teaches: The for-each loop works on any Iterable, so your own class qualifies once it supplies an iterator; a record (Java 16 and later) or a plain class both work.

questions.q: A list holds A, B, C, D, E. Which elements does subList(1, 3) contain?
options: B and C
A and B
B, C and D
A, B and C
optionExplain: Right: the range starts at index 1 and stops before index 3.
Counting would start at index 0, but the start index here is 1.
The end index is not included, so D is left out.
This treats the arguments as a count of three elements, which they are not.
questions.explain: The start is included and the end is excluded. The card next shows more index operations.
questions.rule: Start is included, end is excluded.

questions.q: When the element is absent, indexOf returns ____.
questions.explain: indexOf and lastIndexOf signal a missing element with -1.
questions.rule: Absent means -1.

questions.q: A list of String holds ant, bee, cat, dog. After add(1, elk) and then remove(3), what does the list hold?
options: ant, elk, cat, dog
ant, elk, cat
ant, elk, bee, cat
ant, elk, bee, dog
optionExplain: This removes bee, which would be index 2 after the insert.
This treats add(1, elk) as replacing bee, so the list stays four long and remove(3) then takes dog.
This removes dog, the last element, rather than index 3.
Right: after the insert the list is ant, elk, bee, cat, dog; index 3 is cat, which is removed.
questions.explain: Each operation shifts the elements after it, so index 3 means something different after the insert.
questions.rule: Re-count the indexes after each insert or remove.

questions.q: True or false: Calling set(element) on a ListIterator before next() or previous() has been called replaces the first element.
questions.explain: set replaces the last element returned by next() or previous(); with neither called, it throws IllegalStateException.
questions.rule: ListIterator.set needs a prior next or previous.
questions.teaches: ListIterator.set works on the last element returned by next() or previous(), so it throws IllegalStateException if neither has been called.

questions.q: A program creates a view with subList(0, 2) of a list and calls set(0, Z) on the view. Afterwards, list.get(0) returns ____.
questions.explain: A sublist is a view, so a change made through it shows in the original list.
questions.rule: Writes through a view reach the original.

questions.q: A list of several Staff objects, whose class does not implement Comparable, is sorted with sort(null). Which outcome and remedy fit the tutorial?
options: It sorts by insertion order, so nothing needs to change
ClassCastException; pass a Comparator for Staff
NullPointerException, because null is not a valid argument
A compile error, because sort has no overload that accepts null
optionExplain: Insertion order is the list's existing order, not the result of a sort.
Right: null asks for natural order, which needs Comparable; supplying a Comparator fixes it.
The tutorial says null is accepted and means natural order.
The call compiles; the failure is at run time.
questions.explain: A null comparator means natural order, so elements must be Comparable.
questions.rule: Pass a Comparator when elements are not Comparable.
questions.teaches: List has no no-argument sort, so even natural order is requested with an argument, and the tutorial prefers Comparator.naturalOrder() over null.

questions.q: Which Set implementation does the tutorial present as the main one, wrapping a HashMap internally?
options: TreeSet
HashSet
LinkedHashSet
NavigableSet
optionExplain: TreeSet is the sorted implementation, not the main general one.
Right: HashSet is the main implementation and uses a HashMap as its delegate.
LinkedHashSet adds a linked list on top of the set idea.
NavigableSet is an interface, not an implementation.
questions.explain: HashSet is the default Set. The card next sets it beside LinkedHashSet and TreeSet.
questions.rule: HashSet is the main Set.

questions.q: Match each Set implementation to what the tutorial says it offers.
pairs: Main implementation, iteration order not guaranteed
questions.explain: Each implementation answers a different order need.
questions.rule: Pick the implementation for the order you need.

questions.q: A TreeSet holds 10, 20, 30, 40. What do floor(30) and lower(30) return, in that order?
options: 20 and 20
30 and 30
20 and 30
30 and 20
optionExplain: floor allows an equal element, so it returns 30, not 20.
lower never returns an equal element, so the second result is 20.
This swaps the two behaviours.
Right: floor may match 30 itself, and lower returns the greatest strictly smaller element, 20.
questions.explain: floor and ceiling include an equal element; lower and higher do not.
questions.rule: floor and ceiling may match; lower and higher may not.

questions.q: A TreeSet holds 10, 20, 30, 40. The call descendingSet().first() returns ____.
questions.explain: The descending view lists 40, 30, 20, 10, so its first element is the original greatest.
questions.rule: The descending view reverses first and last.
questions.teaches: descendingSet returns a NavigableSet in reverse order, so its first element is the original greatest and its navigation methods work in reverse.

questions.q: True or false: Adding 35 through the headSet(30) view of a TreeSet holding 10, 20, 30, 40 throws an IllegalArgumentException.
questions.explain: A range view remembers its bounds, and 35 is not below 30, so the add through the view is illegal.
questions.rule: A view refuses elements outside its bounds.

questions.q: A shop keeps price points 5, 10, 20, 50 in a TreeSet. A customer has a budget of 15. Which call finds the highest price point that does not exceed the budget?
options: floor(15)
ceiling(15)
higher(15)
first()
optionExplain: Right: floor returns the greatest element less than or equal to the argument, here 10.
ceiling returns the lowest element at or above 15, which is 20 and over budget.
higher returns the lowest element above 15, also 20.
first returns the lowest price point, 5, which ignores the budget.
questions.explain: Neighbour queries answer limit questions without scanning the whole set.
questions.rule: Use floor for the largest value not above a limit.
questions.teaches: floor fits the question of the largest value not above a limit, and ceiling the smallest value not below one; both give null when no element qualifies.

questions.q: Which call returns a list whose elements can be replaced but whose size cannot change?
options: List.of(a, b, c)
List.copyOf(existing)
Arrays.asList(array)
Set.of(a, b, c)
optionExplain: List.of makes an unmodifiable list, so replacing fails too.
copyOf also gives an unmodifiable list.
Right: the wrapper over an array allows replacement but not adding or removing.
Set.of makes an unmodifiable set.
questions.explain: Arrays.asList sits between modifiable and unmodifiable. The card next compares all the options.
questions.rule: Arrays.asList is replace-only.

questions.q: Sort each way of getting a collection by whether it is independent of the collection it came from or tied to it.

items.t: List.copyOf(original)
Set.copyOf(original)
Arrays.asList(array)
Collections.unmodifiableList(original)
Collections.unmodifiableSet(original)

questions.explain: Copies are snapshots; array wrappers and unmodifiable wrappers are windows on what they wrap.
questions.rule: Copies are independent, wrappers are windows.

questions.q: A class keeps a list of config names that its owner may add to later. It hands callers a read-only list that must not reflect those later additions. Which call fits?
options: Collections.unmodifiableList(names)
names itself
List.copyOf(names)
Arrays.asList(names.toArray())
optionExplain: The wrapper is a view, so later additions would show through it.
Returning the list itself lets callers modify it.
Right: copyOf gives an independent unmodifiable snapshot.
This list lets callers replace elements, so it is not read-only.
questions.explain: A snapshot needs a copy; a read-only view shows later changes.
questions.rule: Copy for a snapshot, wrap for a window.

questions.q: A developer casts the result of List.of(1, 2, 3) to ArrayList to call ensureCapacity. What does the tutorial say about this?
options: It may fail, since the returned class is not an ArrayList
It works, because List.of builds an ArrayList inside
It works only for lists of three or fewer elements here
It works, but only when Set.of is used in its place
optionExplain: Right: the concrete class is unspecified and is not ArrayList, so only the interface can be relied on.
The tutorial says the concrete class is not ArrayList.
Size does change the concrete class, but never to the ArrayList the code assumes.
Set.of does not return a list at all.
questions.explain: The factory methods promise an interface, not a class.
questions.rule: Rely on the interface, not the concrete class.
questions.teaches: The concrete class returned by List.of and Set.of varies with the number of elements and is neither ArrayList nor HashSet, so casting to a class is unsafe.

questions.q: True or false: If an owner adds an element to a list after handing out Collections.unmodifiableList of it, the element shows up through the wrapper.
questions.explain: The wrapper does not copy the data; it is backed by the original, so later changes to the original show through.
questions.rule: Wrappers show later changes to the original.

questions.q: A teammate says Arrays.asList returns an unmodifiable list, so it is safe to hand out to prevent any change. Which correction fits the tutorial?
options: Correct, since adding and removing throw exceptions
Wrong, because it also allows adding through the iterator
Correct, since all modifications throw UnsupportedOperationException
Wrong, because elements can still be replaced
optionExplain: Replacement is allowed, so some change is still possible.
The tutorial says adding or removing through the iterator throws too.
Replacement is the exception to that claim.
Right: replacing elements, even with null, is allowed, so the list is only restricted.
questions.explain: Unmodifiable means no change at all; Arrays.asList permits replacement.
questions.rule: Restricted is not the same as unmodifiable.
questions.teaches: Arrays.asList has a third status besides modifiable and unmodifiable: replace-only, with a fixed size and no adds or removes, even through its iterator.

questions.q: What does Collections.max throw when it is given an empty collection?
options: ClassCastException
NoSuchElementException
NullPointerException
IndexOutOfBoundsException
optionExplain: That exception concerns elements that cannot be compared, not an empty input.
Right: with no elements there is no maximum to return.
The collection is empty, not null, so there is no null to dereference.
There is no index involved in max.
questions.explain: An empty input has no extreme to return. The card next lists the helpers and their failures.
questions.rule: Empty input has no min or max.

questions.q: To make Collections.shuffle repeatable, you pass it a ____ instance created with a fixed seed.
questions.explain: Supplying a Random makes the shuffle repeatable.
questions.rule: Pass a Random for repeatable shuffles.

questions.q: A list holds A, B, C, D. After Collections.swap(list, 0, 3), the element at index 0 is ____.
questions.explain: swap exchanges the elements at the two indexes, so D moves to index 0 and A to index 3.
questions.rule: swap exchanges two indexes only.

questions.q: A list holds Ticket objects whose class does not implement Comparable. Which call finds the ticket with the highest priority?
options: Collections.max(tickets)
Collections.max(tickets, byPriority) with a Comparator
tickets.max()
Collections.sort(tickets) then reading the last one, without a Comparator
optionExplain: Without a Comparator, non-Comparable elements cause a ClassCastException.
Right: with a Comparator the elements need not be Comparable.
List has no max method of its own in the tutorial.
Sorting without a Comparator needs Comparable too.
questions.explain: A Comparator supplies the ordering the elements lack.
questions.rule: A Comparator removes the Comparable requirement.
questions.teaches: Beyond the tutorial: a class has only one natural order through Comparable but can have many Comparators, so the Comparator chosen decides which property counts as the extreme.

questions.q: True or false: Wrapping a list with synchronizedList makes a for-each loop over it safe without any extra synchronization.
questions.explain: The wrapper protects individual calls; iterating or streaming over it must be synchronized by hand, or race conditions can occur.
questions.rule: Synchronize the loop, not just the calls.

questions.q: A developer must move the element at index 1 to index 4 of a list. Which combination does the tutorial describe for this?
options: Collections.swap(list, 1, 4) on the two indexes
Collections.reverse(list) on the whole list
Collections.shuffle(list) with a fixed Random
rotate over subList(1, 5) with distance -1
optionExplain: swap exchanges two elements, so the old index 4 element would land at index 1.
Reversing the list changes every position.
Shuffling is random, not a targeted move.
Right: rotating a sublist moves the element at its start to its end, leaving the others in order.
questions.explain: rotate on a sublist view shifts a range with wrap-around.
questions.rule: rotate on a subList moves one element.
questions.teaches: Combined with subList, rotate removes the element at fromIndex and inserts it at toIndex minus one, which moves a single element while the others keep their order.

questions.q: True or false: Calling poll on an empty queue throws an exception.
questions.explain: poll returns null when the queue is empty; remove is the method that throws. The card next lays out all the pairs.
questions.rule: poll returns null, remove throws.

questions.q: Match each Queue method to what it does when the queue is empty or full.
questions.explain: Each operation comes as a throwing version and a special-value version.
questions.rule: Throwing and special-value pairs.

questions.q: A worker loop must stop quietly when its task queue becomes empty, without any try and catch. Which call fits?
options: poll()
remove()
element()
add(task)
optionExplain: Right: poll returns null on an empty queue, which the loop can test.
remove throws NoSuchElementException on an empty queue.
element also throws when the queue is empty.
add inserts, it does not take a task out.
questions.explain: A special-value method lets the loop test for emptiness without exceptions.
questions.rule: Use poll for an empty-tolerant take.

questions.q: The Deque method with First in its name that examines the head and throws on an empty deque is ____.
questions.explain: getFirst examines the head and throws on an empty deque, as element does in Queue; peekFirst returns null instead.
questions.rule: Match behaviour: examine and throw is getFirst.
questions.teaches: The examine method is called element() in Queue but getFirst() or getLast() in Deque, and the peek forms return null instead of throwing.

questions.q: A program pushes A, then B, then C onto an empty ArrayDeque used as a stack, and then calls pop twice. The element still held is ____.
questions.explain: pop removes C and then B, so only A remains: a stack gives back the most recent element first.
questions.rule: LIFO: last in is first out.

questions.q: A triage system stores Patient objects in a PriorityQueue created with no Comparator, and Patient does not implement Comparable. What happens, and what fixes it?
options: Patients leave in insertion order; nothing needs to change
NoSuchElementException; call offer instead of add
ClassCastException; pass a Comparator that ranks by severity
The head is the largest patient; reverse the Comparator
optionExplain: Insertion order is for a plain queue, not a priority queue.
That exception is about taking from an empty queue.
Right: without a way to compare, the priority queue cannot order its elements.
The head is the least element under the ordering, not the largest.
questions.explain: A PriorityQueue needs an ordering from Comparable or a Comparator.
questions.rule: A priority queue needs an ordering.
questions.teaches: The head of a PriorityQueue is the least element under its ordering, so the Comparator decides what next means.

questions.q: True or false: In a map, two different keys can be bound to the same value.
questions.explain: Keys must be unique, but values need not be, so one value can sit under several keys. The card next draws the consequences.
questions.rule: Keys are unique, values may repeat.

questions.q: Match each part of a map to how it behaves.
pairs: Form a Set, with no duplicate keys
Also form a Set, with no duplicate pairs
A view: changing its value changes the map
questions.explain: Keys and entries cannot repeat, values can, and entries are views of the map.
questions.rule: Keys and entries are set-like; values are not.

questions.q: A map holds student IDs as keys and grades as values, with three students graded B. Which statement is correct?
options: The values must hold B only once, like the keys
Each grade may appear once as a key, while IDs repeat as values
Values may repeat B three times, while each ID is a key once
The keys may hold an ID twice if the grades differ
optionExplain: Values form a plain Collection, which allows repeats.
This reverses the roles of keys and values.
Right: values may repeat, while keys form a Set with no duplicates.
A key is bound to only one value, so it cannot appear twice at all.
questions.explain: The key rule is about uniqueness of keys, not values.
questions.rule: Keys are unique; values may repeat.

questions.q: A program must map each author to all of that author's books. The framework has no multimap type. What does the tutorial suggest?
options: Bind each author to a list of books
Allow the same author key to appear several times
Use an IdentityHashMap so that equal keys differ
Use a Set of authors with no values
optionExplain: Right: making each value a list imitates a multimap.
Keys are unique, so repeating an author key replaces the earlier entry.
IdentityHashMap compares keys by reference and is meant for very specific cases, not for this.
A set holds no values, so the books would have nowhere to go.
questions.explain: A single value can itself be a collection, which lets one key stand for many items.
questions.rule: Imitate a multimap with a list as the value.
questions.teaches: Without a built-in multimap, bind each key to a list of values, so one key effectively holds several items.

questions.q: True or false: Calling setValue on an entry taken from a map changes the value stored in the map.
questions.explain: Entries are views of the map, so changing an entry's value changes the map; only the key cannot be changed.
questions.rule: Setting an entry's value changes the map.

questions.q: A developer stores residents by city, writing one entry per resident with the city as the key and the resident's name as the value. What does the key rule predict about the result?
options: Every resident is kept, since values may repeat
The map refuses the second resident with an exception
Residents are merged into one sorted value
Only the last resident for each city is kept
optionExplain: Values may repeat, but that does not let one key hold several of them.
The tutorial does not describe an exception for storing under an existing key.
Nothing in the map rules merges values.
Right: each key is bound to one value, so later residents replace earlier ones unless the value is a list.
questions.explain: One key means one value, so grouping needs a collection as the value.
questions.rule: One key holds one value; make the value a collection to group.
questions.teaches: A key's single value can itself be a collection, which is why grouping code builds a map from a key to a list.

questions.q: A map holds apple to 3. What does put of apple to 5 return?
options: null
true
optionExplain: 5 is the new value, but put reports what was there before.
Right: put returns the value previously bound to the key.
null is returned only when the key was not present.
put does not return a boolean.
questions.explain: put hands back the replaced value. The card next gives the other map operations.
questions.rule: put returns the previous value.

questions.q: When the key was not already in the map, put returns ____.
questions.explain: A new key had no previous value, so put returns null.
questions.rule: New key means put returns null.

questions.q: A map holds a to 1 and b to 2. What does remove("a", 2) do?
options: Removes a and returns its value 1
Returns false and leaves the map unchanged
Removes a and returns true as the result
Removes b, since 2 matches that value
optionExplain: The pair is removed only when both key and value match.
Right: a is bound to 1, not 2, so nothing is removed and the result is false.
It would return true only if the value matched.
The key given is a, not b.
questions.explain: The two-argument remove needs both parts to match.
questions.rule: remove(key, value) is conditional on both.

questions.q: Which statements about removing elements through a map's views are true? Select all that apply.
options: Removing a key from keySet removes that pair from the map
Removing a value from values removes only the first matching pair
Removing a value from values removes every pair with that value
Removing from entrySet has no effect on the map
optionExplain: Right: the key set is backed by the map.
Right: only the first match goes, and which one that is cannot be predicted when values repeat.
Only the first matching pair is removed, not all of them.
The views are backed by the map, so removal passes through.
questions.explain: Views write through to the map, but values() removal is limited to one match.
questions.rule: values() removal takes one match only.
questions.teaches: Beyond the tutorial: to remove every pair with a given value in one call, the values collection offers removeAll and removeIf, which also write through to the map.

questions.q: A map has the key x bound to null. After putIfAbsent of x with the value 9, get of x returns ____.
questions.explain: putIfAbsent treats a null binding like an absent key, so it replaces the null with the new value.
questions.rule: putIfAbsent also repairs null values.

questions.q: A program must raise every price in a large price map by ten percent. Which loop does the tutorial's guidance favour?
options: Loop over keySet and call get for each key
Loop over values and call put for each
Call containsValue for each price
Loop over entrySet and set each entry's value
optionExplain: Looping over keys and calling get does an extra lookup per key, which the tutorial calls much less efficient.
values() holds no keys, so put cannot be called.
containsValue only tests presence.
Right: entrySet hands over key and value together.
questions.explain: entrySet gives both parts at once, and its entries are views of the map.
questions.rule: Loop over entrySet to work with pairs.
questions.teaches: Entries from entrySet are views of the map, so setValue on an entry updates the map without another put call.

questions.q: Which Map method is the best fit for adding a new empty list under a key only when that key has no list yet?
options: computeIfAbsent
putIfAbsent
merge
replace
optionExplain: Right: the lambda runs only when the key is missing, so the list is created on demand.
putIfAbsent works but needs the empty list created up front, even if unused.
merge combines an old and a new value, which is a different job.
replace acts only when the key is already present.
questions.explain: Creating the value only when needed is the point of computeIfAbsent. The card next compares the compute and merge methods.
questions.rule: computeIfAbsent creates values on demand.

questions.q: Match each method to the condition under which it acts.
pairs: Only if the key is present
Only if the current value equals old
Only if the key has a non-null value
Only if the key is absent or bound to null
questions.explain: Each method guards a different case.
questions.rule: Each method guards one condition.

questions.q: A map holds cat bound to 2. After merge of cat with 1 and Integer::sum, the value bound to cat is ____.
questions.explain: The key has a non-null value, so merge calls the function with the old value 2 and the new value 1, and stores 3.
questions.rule: merge combines old and new for an existing key.

questions.q: True or false: computeIfAbsent called for a missing key with a lambda that returns null leaves that key bound to null.
questions.explain: A null result means no mapping: the key stays absent, because these methods never store a null value.
questions.rule: A null result leaves or makes the key absent.
questions.teaches: The compute methods and merge never store a null value: a null result removes the key or leaves it absent.

questions.q: A developer calls computeIfAbsent for the key title with a lambda returning an empty String, then appends a word to the returned String, expecting the map's value to grow. Why does the map not change?
options: The method returns null for an absent key, so there is nothing to append to
computeIfAbsent only works when the values are Integer objects
A String is immutable, so appending makes a new String
The lambda ran twice and the two results cancelled each other
optionExplain: It returns the new value bound to the key.
It works with any value type.
Right: computeIfAbsent only helps when the value is a mutable aggregate such as an ArrayList.
The lambda runs once, and only if the key is absent.
questions.explain: Appending to an immutable value cannot change what the map holds.
questions.rule: Use merge for immutable values.

questions.q: Two stock maps map item names to counts. They must be combined so that counts of shared items add up. Which call per entry of the second map does the tutorial's practice suggest?
options: putAll with the second map into the first
computeIfAbsent with a function that adds counts per item
merge on the first map with a function that adds counts
replaceAll on the first map for each item
optionExplain: putAll overwrites the values of shared keys instead of adding them.
computeIfAbsent runs only for missing keys, so shared items would not be added.
Right: merge binds missing items and combines the counts of shared items.
replaceAll rewrites existing values without bringing in new items.
questions.explain: merge handles both cases, absent and present, in one call.
questions.rule: merge combines maps value by value.
questions.teaches: merge can combine two whole maps: call it on one map for each entry of the other, with a function that adds the values of shared keys.

questions.q: True or false: ceilingKey can return a key equal to its argument, but higherKey cannot.
questions.explain: ceiling and floor may match the given key, while higher and lower return strictly greater or strictly smaller keys. The card next sets out all four.
questions.rule: ceiling and floor may match; higher and lower may not.

questions.q: Match each NavigableMap key method to the key it returns.
pairs: Greatest key less than or equal to the argument
Greatest key strictly less than the argument
Lowest key greater than or equal to the argument
Lowest key strictly greater than the argument
questions.explain: The four methods differ in direction and in whether an equal key may be returned.
questions.rule: Direction and equality distinguish the four.

questions.q: A TreeMap holds keys 10, 20, 30, 40. What do ceilingKey(25) and lowerKey(30) return, in that order?
options: 30 and 20
20 and 20
30 and 30
20 and 30
optionExplain: Right: the lowest key at or above 25 is 30, and the greatest key strictly below 30 is 20.
The first result looks downward, which is floor behaviour.
lower excludes 30 itself, so the second result is 20.
This swaps both behaviours.
questions.explain: ceiling looks up, lower looks down and excludes an equal key.
questions.rule: ceiling goes up, lower goes down strictly.

questions.q: Which statement about navigableKeySet() on a TreeMap is correct?
options: It returns a detached copy of the keys, not backed by the map
It is only available on a SortedMap, not on a NavigableMap
It returns the keys in descending order, like descendingKeySet
It returns the same object as keySet(), so no cast is needed
optionExplain: The key set views are backed by the map.
It belongs to NavigableMap, not to SortedMap.
Descending order comes from descendingKeySet.
Right: for a TreeMap, keySet() and navigableKeySet() give the same object, and the second avoids a cast.
questions.explain: navigableKeySet is a convenience that returns the already-navigable key view.
questions.rule: navigableKeySet saves the cast.
questions.teaches: navigableKeySet returns the same object as keySet on a TreeMap, but typed as a NavigableSet, so you do not need a cast.

questions.q: True or false: According to the tutorial, a descendingKeySet view of a TreeMap supports removing keys but does not support adding them.
questions.explain: The tutorial says the descending views support removal but not addition, so adding a key through the view is refused.
questions.rule: Descending views: remove yes, add no.

questions.q: A scheduler stores start time as key and job as value in a TreeMap. Which call returns the first job starting at or after a given time, keeping the job in the map?
options: higherKey(time)
ceilingEntry(time)
pollFirstEntry()
floorEntry(time)
optionExplain: higherKey excludes an exact match and returns only a key, not the job.
Right: ceilingEntry gives the lowest entry at or above the time, with its job, and removes nothing.
pollFirstEntry removes the earliest entry and ignores the given time.
floorEntry looks at or before the time, the wrong direction.
questions.explain: Choose the direction, whether an exact match counts, and whether you need the key or the whole entry.
questions.rule: Entry forms return key and value together.
questions.teaches: The Entry forms of the navigation methods return both key and value, while the Key forms return only the key, so a lookup of the job needs an Entry method.

questions.q: True or false: Changing a key object after it has been stored in a HashMap is safe as long as you keep a reference to the same object.
questions.explain: The tutorial shows that a mutated key can no longer retrieve its value, even through the same reference. The card next walks through the cases.
questions.rule: A mutated key can lose its value.

questions.q: The tutorial calls using mutable map keys an ____.
questions.explain: The tutorial uses the word antipattern for mutable keys.
questions.rule: Mutable keys are an antipattern.

questions.q: A map holds Key objects, whose equals and hashCode use their text: K1 with text a bound to 1, and K2 with text b bound to 2. K1's text is then changed to b. According to the tutorial, what does a lookup with K1 return?
options: 1, the value originally bound to it
2, the value bound to the other key
null for both keys, since nothing matches
An exception, because the key changed
optionExplain: Its own value becomes unreachable once the key changes.
Right: the mutated key now matches the other key, so the lookup returns that key's value.
The other key still works; only the mutated pair is affected.
The tutorial describes wrong results, not an exception.
questions.explain: After mutation the key matches the other key, not its own entry.
questions.rule: A mutated key may find another key's value.

questions.q: An element already in a HashSet is mutated. Which symptom does the tutorial's example show?
options: The mutation is rejected with an exception at once
The set removes the duplicate element by itself
The set size drops by one after the mutation
One object appears twice, as first and last element
optionExplain: Nothing blocks the mutation.
The set does not clean itself up after a mutation.
The tutorial reports a repeated object, not a smaller set.
Right: the output shows one object turning up more than once.
questions.explain: A mutated element can break the guarantee that a set holds no duplicates.
questions.rule: Mutating a set element can break uniqueness.
questions.teaches: In the tutorial's set example, the output shows the first and last elements as the same object, which a set should not allow.

questions.q: True or false: After a stored key was mutated to a text no other key uses, a lookup with a new key holding the original text finds the original value.
questions.explain: The tutorial says looking up the original value also fails, so the pair is effectively lost.
questions.rule: Mutation can leave the pair unreachable.

questions.q: A team stores User objects in a HashSet, where equals and hashCode use the email field. Users will later be allowed to change their email. Which advice fits the tutorial?
options: Avoid mutating stored objects; prefer an unmodifiable key type
Mutate the email freely, since the object stays the same one
Switch to a LinkedHashSet, which tolerates this mutation
Call clear on the set before each mutation, then re-add
optionExplain: Right: the best choice is an unmodifiable key type, and mutation after insertion should be avoided.
The same object does not protect against the failure.
The tutorial does not claim any set variant tolerates mutation.
Clearing the set is not a remedy the tutorial offers.
questions.explain: The tutorial's advice is about the stability of whatever equals and hashCode read.
questions.rule: Keep what equals and hashCode read stable.
questions.teaches: Beyond the tutorial: a common remedy is to key the container by a stable immutable identifier, such as a user ID, and keep changeable data in the value.

questions.q: In the usual textbook table of operation costs for ArrayList and LinkedList, which operation is constant for LinkedList but linear for ArrayList?
options: Reading the middle element
Adding at the end
Inserting at the beginning
Reading the first element
optionExplain: Reading the middle is the reverse: constant for ArrayList, linear for LinkedList.
Adding at the end is constant for both.
Right: ArrayList must shift every element, while LinkedList only relinks nodes.
Reading the first element is constant for both.
questions.explain: Front insertion is where the table favours LinkedList. The card next shows why the table is only a first guide.
questions.rule: Front insertion favours LinkedList in theory.

questions.q: Match each operation to its cost in the tutorial's textbook table.
pairs: Constant for ArrayList, linear for LinkedList
Linear for ArrayList, constant for LinkedList
questions.explain: The table favours ArrayList for indexed reads and LinkedList for front insertion.
questions.rule: Learn the table, then test it.

questions.q: A job repeatedly reads elements by index from the middle of a list of 100,000 items. Which type does the textbook cost table favour?
options: LinkedList, because it keeps references to both ends
Either, since both are linear
ArrayList, because middle reads are constant
LinkedList, because middle reads are constant
optionExplain: Keeping both end references helps end access, not the middle.
Only LinkedList is linear for middle reads.
Right: ArrayList reads by index in constant time, while LinkedList walks from the nearer end.
The table gives middle reads as linear for LinkedList.
questions.explain: Indexed reads suit the array-backed list.
questions.rule: Indexed reads favour ArrayList.

questions.q: Which structures does the tutorial say suffer from pointer chasing in the same way as LinkedList? Select all that apply.
options: Trees
Tries
Hash maps, to a lesser extent
Plain arrays of primitives
optionExplain: Right: reference-based trees follow pointers from node to node.
Right: tries are reference-based too.
Right: the tutorial includes hash maps, to a lesser extent.
An array of primitives sits in one block of memory, so it does not chase references.
questions.explain: Pointer chasing is a cost of reference-based structures in general.
questions.rule: Reference-based structures pay for pointer chasing.
questions.teaches: Pointer chasing is not specific to LinkedList: any reference-based structure, such as trees, tries, skip lists and, less so, hash maps, pays for it.

questions.q: True or false: According to the tutorial, absolute benchmark times from one machine can be expected unchanged on another machine.
questions.explain: The tutorial warns that absolute numbers differ between machines; only relative comparisons on the same machine are meaningful.
questions.rule: Compare options on the same machine.

questions.q: A teammate reads that a benchmark on someone else's machine took 0.5 ms to iterate 1,000 linked elements by index, and concludes that their own program will also take 0.5 ms. What is the best response?
options: Wrong: figures depend on the machine, so measure there
Correct, because the benchmark used the same JDK
Correct, because 1,000 elements cost the same everywhere
Wrong, because LinkedList iteration is constant time
optionExplain: Right: the tutorial warns that absolute numbers differ and tells readers to benchmark their own workload.
A shared JDK does not fix the hardware, which the tutorial says matters.
The cost depends on the machine and the layout, not only the count.
Indexed iteration over a LinkedList is quadratic, not constant.
questions.explain: Benchmark figures describe a pattern, and the ratio carries over better than the milliseconds.
questions.rule: Reuse the pattern, not the figures.
questions.teaches: A measured figure transfers at best as a ratio; judge by relative comparisons you run on your own hardware.

questions.q: True or false: Looping over a LinkedList by index is about as fast as looping with its iterator.
questions.explain: Indexed access walks the nodes each time, so the loop is quadratic. The card next gives the tutorial's measured gap.
questions.rule: Do not loop over a LinkedList by index.

questions.q: The tutorial advises iterating over a LinkedList with an ____ instead of by index.
questions.explain: An iterator follows the node references once, instead of walking from the end for each index.
questions.rule: Use an iterator for LinkedList.

questions.q: A program prints each of 1,000 names held in a LinkedList once. Which loop does the tutorial support?
options: An index loop calling get(i)
An index loop calling get(i) over a reversed copy
A while loop that calls remove(0) each time
A for-each loop, which uses the iterator
optionExplain: Each get(i) walks the nodes again, which makes the loop quadratic.
Reversing does not remove the repeated walks.
This empties the list and is not a read-only pass.
Right: for-each uses the iterator, which follows the nodes once.
questions.explain: Iterate with the structure's own cursor.
questions.rule: Prefer iterators on linked structures.

questions.q: Why does the tutorial suggest Stream.toList() when copying a LinkedList into an array-based list?
options: It sorts the elements on the way into the copy
It gives an unmodifiable list sized correctly at once
It keeps the same nodes, so nothing is copied over
It returns a modifiable view of the LinkedList itself
optionExplain: Nothing in the description sorts the elements.
Right: the result is unmodifiable and avoids repeated growth, since the size is known up front.
It copies into an array-based list; the nodes do not carry over.
The result is a separate, unmodifiable list, not a view.
questions.explain: Allocating once at the right size avoids growth steps.
questions.rule: toList copies once, at the right size.
questions.teaches: Stream.toList() returns an unmodifiable list, so the copy cannot be changed afterwards, and it allocates the array at the correct size up front.

questions.q: True or false: Creating an ArrayList with the expected size avoids the growth steps that a default-capacity ArrayList goes through.
questions.explain: A full ArrayList grows by a factor of 1.5 and copies its contents; pre-sizing avoids those steps, although they are rare and cheap on average.
questions.rule: Pre-size when the size is known.

questions.q: A log viewer appends new lines at the end of a list and reads old lines back by index. A teammate proposes LinkedList because it inserts quickly. What do the benchmarks suggest?
options: Accept, since LinkedList wins every insertion benchmark
Reject: ArrayList reads by index and appends cheaply
Accept, because LinkedList reads the middle fastest
Reject, because ArrayList cannot append
optionExplain: ArrayList beat LinkedList on almost every insertion benchmark.
Right: indexed reads are constant for ArrayList, and appending is cheap for it too.
LinkedList reads the middle slowest.
ArrayList appends at the end cheaply.
questions.explain: Look at the whole mix of operations, not one fast operation.
questions.rule: Judge the mix of operations.
questions.teaches: A workload's mix of operations decides the choice: indexed reads need ArrayList, and only insertion at the front gives LinkedList a clear win.

questions.q: Which extra cost does each element of a LinkedList carry that an ArrayList element does not?
options: A spare slot reserved for future growth of the list
A copy of the element kept for iteration
A counter of how often it was read
A Node object with previous, next and item references
optionExplain: Spare slots are an ArrayList trait, and LinkedList has none.
No copies are kept for iteration.
No access counters exist in the description.
Right: every element sits in a Node, which adds references and an object header.
questions.explain: The linked structure pays per element in node overhead. The card next puts numbers on it.
questions.rule: LinkedList pays a Node per element.

questions.q: Match each one-element list to its approximate size in the tutorial.
questions.explain: List.of is lightest, a trimmed ArrayList next, then LinkedList, then a default ArrayList.
questions.rule: Small lists differ a lot in size.

questions.q: A service keeps 100,000 mutable lists, each with one or two names. Which creation reduces memory, according to the tutorial?
options: An ArrayList created with initial capacity 2
new LinkedList, since it has no unused capacity
A default ArrayList, since it grows as needed
List.of for each, even though names must change later
optionExplain: Right: capacity 2 takes 48 bytes for zero to two elements.
A LinkedList costs 56 bytes for one element, more than a capacity-2 ArrayList.
The default ArrayList reserves more space than needed here.
List.of lists cannot be modified, so they do not fit mutable lists.
questions.explain: Pre-sizing to the real need saves memory per list.
questions.rule: Pre-size small lists.

questions.q: True or false: After many removals, an ArrayList shrinks its backing array automatically to fit the remaining elements.
questions.explain: An ArrayList does not shrink by itself; trimToSize releases the excess.
questions.rule: ArrayList does not shrink by itself.
questions.teaches: An ArrayList never shrinks its backing array automatically, so many removals can leave a large, mostly empty array until trimToSize is called.

questions.q: If the single element in a list will not change after creation, the lightest option in the tutorial's comparison is ____.
questions.explain: List.of takes about 26 bytes for one element, at the price of being unmodifiable.
questions.rule: Immutable small lists are the lightest.

questions.q: A teammate argues that LinkedList saves memory because it has no unused capacity. What does the tutorial's data say for a list of 1,000 elements?
options: The argument holds, since unused slots are the main memory cost in a list
The argument fails, but only when the heap is larger than 32 GB or so
The argument fails: node overhead is larger, about 24 KB against 5 KB
The argument holds for single-element lists but not for larger ones
optionExplain: Unused slots are real, but the node cost is larger.
The 32 GB figure is about when measurements are exact, not about the winner.
Right: the Node object adds about 24 bytes per element.
For a single element, LinkedList (56 bytes) is also heavier than a trimmed ArrayList.
questions.explain: Count all costs, not one cost.
questions.rule: Weigh per-element overhead, not just unused capacity.
questions.teaches: Beyond the tutorial: node overhead is paid for every element, so the gap between LinkedList and ArrayList grows with the list length, while the unused slots of an ArrayList stay a fraction of its size.

questions.q: Which List implementation does the tutorial present as the default choice?
options: LinkedList
Vector
ArrayList
List.of
optionExplain: LinkedList is preferable only for end-focused work.
Vector is a legacy class.
Right: it wins on most operations and on memory.
List.of makes unmodifiable lists, which is a special case.
questions.explain: The default is the array-backed list. The card next gives the exceptions.
questions.rule: ArrayList is the default List.

questions.q: Match each need to the structure the tutorial points to.
pairs: ArrayList, pre-sized if the size is known
LinkedList is the one exception to the default
questions.explain: Each need has a named structure; the default list is ArrayList.
questions.rule: Match the structure to the task.

questions.q: A playlist of 20,000 songs is built once, read by index, and rarely changed. The size is known in advance. What does the tutorial point to?
options: A pre-sized ArrayList
A LinkedList from the JDK
A Stack from the JDK
A Hashtable from the JDK
optionExplain: Right: ArrayList suits indexed reads, and pre-sizing avoids growth.
LinkedList is slow for indexed reads.
Stack is a legacy class and not for indexed reads.
Hashtable is a legacy key and value class.
questions.explain: Indexed reads and a known size both point to a pre-sized ArrayList.
questions.rule: Default plus pre-size.

questions.q: Even though LinkedList implements Queue and Deque, the tutorial recommends ____ for double-ended queues.
questions.explain: ArrayDeque is the tutorial's recommendation for double-ended queues, even though LinkedList also implements Queue and Deque.
questions.rule: Prefer ArrayDeque for double-ended queues.
questions.teaches: The tutorial notes that ArrayDeque is array-backed and does not accept null elements, while LinkedList does, so replacing a LinkedList that stores nulls needs care.

questions.q: A library returns a LinkedList of 1,000 results. The program will iterate it many times and access elements randomly, can afford extra memory, and the source will not change. What does the tutorial suggest?
options: Keep it as it is and keep looping over it by index
Wrap it in Collections.synchronizedList to gain speed
Convert it to a Stack and pop each result in turn
Copy it into an array-based list, e.g. Stream.toList()
optionExplain: Indexed loops on a LinkedList are quadratic.
Synchronization is about threads, not speed.
Stack is a legacy class and does not address the problem.
Right: the copy costs little and pays back with repeated iteration or random access.
questions.explain: A choice is not only made at creation; you can change representation when usage justifies it.
questions.rule: Copy when you iterate repeatedly.
questions.teaches: The copy is justified when you iterate repeatedly or access randomly, can afford the extra memory, and the source is not modified during iteration.

questions.q: A list of 10 words is mapped with a function that returns the length of each word. How many values does the mapping produce?
options: 10 values, one length for each word
One value, the sum of all the lengths
Fewer than 10, because words with equal lengths merge into one value
As many values as there are different lengths
optionExplain: Right: a mapping produces exactly one output per input, in the same order.
Adding lengths together is a reduction; a mapping leaves each element on its own.
Merging equal results is what a grouping does; a mapping is one-to-one.
Counting different lengths would need a grouping step, not a one-to-one mapping.
questions.explain: A mapping changes values, not how many there are. The card next names the three kinds of step.
questions.rule: Map keeps the count.

questions.q: True or false: a filter step can change how many elements a stream holds.
questions.explain: A filter keeps or drops elements with a yes-or-no test, so the count can shrink. The elements that pass are untouched, so their type stays the same.
questions.rule: Filter changes the count, map changes the type.

questions.q: A shop wants the total price of all items that cost more than 20 euros from a list of Item objects. Which order of steps matches map-filter-reduce?
options: Reduce to one total first, then filter that total to keep values above 20
Filter items above 20, map kept items to prices, then reduce by adding
Map every item to its price, add all the prices, then filter the items by cost
Filter the items, map the whole result into one total, then reduce each single price
optionExplain: A total has no individual items left to test, so the filter has to come before the reduction.
Right: filter picks the items, map extracts the number, reduce combines the numbers into one result.
Adding the prices first leaves nothing to filter, and the test would apply to items that no longer exist.
A map is one-to-one, so it cannot produce one total, and a reduction needs many values to combine.
questions.explain: The filter must see the items, the map extracts the price, and the reduction ends the pipeline with one result.
questions.rule: Filter and map prepare the values; reduce ends the pipeline.

questions.q: According to the tutorial, why were map and filter placed on Stream rather than directly on Collection?
options: Collections are immutable, so they cannot hold values that were mapped
Interfaces in the JDK cannot gain new methods once they are released
Each step would build a whole intermediate collection and work eagerly
Collections hold only primitive values and cannot hold objects
optionExplain: Collections can be mutable; the problem is the cost of building extra collections, not immutability.
The tutorial gives a cost reason; it does not claim that existing interfaces cannot change.
Right: mapping 1,000 cities would create 1,000 integers and filtering another collection, and eager work cannot stop early when a first match settles the answer.
Collections hold objects of any type; this is not the reason given.
questions.explain: On a collection, every step would store its full result before the next step starts. A stream passes elements through without storing them.
questions.rule: Steps on a stream avoid intermediate collections.
questions.teaches: If map and filter returned collections, each step would build a whole intermediate collection and work eagerly, even when one match could already settle the answer; putting them on Stream avoids this.

questions.q: A reporting tool turns three requests into stream steps. Match each request to the kind of step it needs.
pairs: Keep only the rows from March
questions.explain: Choosing rows is filtering, changing each value is mapping, and combining many values into a single one is reducing.
questions.rule: Aggregations such as highest, total or count are reductions.
questions.teaches: According to the tutorial, count, sum, minimum, maximum and average are all reductions: each combines many elements into one value.

questions.q: True or false: according to the tutorial, side effects such as changing an outside variable from inside a stream operation can be avoided.
questions.explain: The tutorial advises avoiding such side effects and says this is possible. Building a list is the job of a reduction, not of a step that changes outside state.
questions.rule: Build results by reducing, not by changing outside state.

questions.q: A programmer maps a list of 5 names to upper case and filters those that start with A, then ends the statement with no further call. What happens when this line runs?
options: Five names are processed and the result is thrown away
An exception is thrown because the pipeline is incomplete
A list of the matching names is created in memory
No element is processed, because nothing triggers the work
optionExplain: Processing happens only after a terminal operation; map and filter alone start nothing.
The code compiles and runs; an unfinished pipeline is legal but does nothing.
A list needs a collecting terminal operation, which is missing.
Right: map and filter only add steps, so without a terminal operation no data is processed.
questions.explain: Intermediate operations are lazy. The card next names the call that starts the work.
questions.rule: No terminal operation, no work.

questions.q: An operation that returns another stream and processes no data is called an ____ operation.
questions.explain: Intermediate operations such as map and filter return a stream and add a step. Terminal operations return something else and start processing.
questions.rule: Intermediate adds a step; terminal starts the run.

questions.q: The words red, green and blue pass through step A (prints A and the word, keeps all), then step B (prints B and the word, keeps all), then a terminal collect. In which order do the prints appear?
options: A red, B red, A green, B green, A blue, B blue
A red, A green, A blue, B red, B green, B blue
B red, A red, B green, A green, B blue, A blue
B red, B green, B blue, A red, A green, A blue
