optionExplain: Right: each element goes through the whole pipeline before the next element enters.
This runs each step over all elements before the next step, which is how a collection method would work, not a stream.
Step B comes after step A in the pipeline, so an element cannot reach B first.
Both the step order and the element-by-element flow are wrong here.
questions.explain: Elements are pulled through the pipeline one by one, so the prints interleave: step A and step B for red, then for green, then for blue.
questions.rule: One element completes the pipeline before the next starts.

questions.q: According to the tutorial, why should a method not receive a stream that was created elsewhere?
options: Streams are not thread-safe, so a second method would cause a race
The receiver cannot tell whether the stream has already been used
A stream copies its source on every call, which wastes a lot of memory
A stream cannot be declared as the type of a parameter
optionExplain: The tutorial's reason is about single use, not thread safety.
Right: a used stream throws IllegalStateException, and the receiving code cannot tell from the object whether it is already used.
A stream does not store or copy data; this is not the concern raised.
Streams can be passed as parameters; the advice is about trust, not about what the compiler allows.
questions.explain: A stream carries no marker the receiver can rely on, so the safe habit is to create and consume it in one place.
questions.rule: Create and consume a stream on the spot.
questions.teaches: Streams should not be stored in fields or local variables or handed to other methods, because the receiver cannot know whether the stream has already been operated on.

questions.q: A bakery line bakes, slices and bags each loaf, like a lazy pipeline that works one element at a time. Put the first two loaves' events in the order such a pipeline produces them.
items: Bake loaf 1
Slice loaf 1
Bag loaf 1
Bake loaf 2
Slice loaf 2
Bag loaf 2
questions.explain: Each loaf finishes the whole line before the next one starts, so no tray of half-finished loaves builds up between steps.
questions.rule: No batch of half-processed elements is stored between steps.
questions.teaches: According to the tutorial, because elements are pulled through one at a time, some pipelines need not visit every element: a first match can end the run early.

questions.q: True or false: because intermediate operations are lazy, calling count on a stream also processes no data until some later call starts the work.
questions.explain: count is a terminal operation, so it starts the processing at once. Laziness belongs to intermediate operations.
questions.rule: Terminal operations run the pipeline.

questions.q: A program holds a Map of String to Integer and calls stream directly on the map. What does the language do?
options: It streams the entries as key and value pairs
It streams only the keys of the map, as a set
It does not compile, since Map has no stream method
It streams only the values of the map, as a collection
optionExplain: Entries are reachable through entrySet, but the map itself has no stream method.
Keys are reachable through keySet, not directly on the map.
Right: a map offers views such as keySet, entrySet and values, and you stream one of those.
Values are reachable through the values method, not directly on the map.
questions.explain: A Map is not a Collection, so it has no stream method of its own. The card next lists the sources that do work.
questions.rule: Stream a view of a map, not the map.

questions.q: The call IntStream.range with 1 and 5 produces the numbers 1, 2, 3 and ____ .
questions.explain: range excludes the upper bound, so it stops at 4. rangeClosed with 1 and 5 would include 5.
questions.rule: range excludes the upper bound; rangeClosed includes it.

questions.q: A tester needs 100 repeatable die rolls from 1 to 6 as an IntStream. Which Random call fits?
options: An unseeded Random calling ints with 100, 1 and 6
An unseeded Random calling ints with 100, 1 and 7
A seeded Random calling ints with 100, 1 and 6
A seeded Random calling ints with 100, 1 and 7
optionExplain: This is neither repeatable nor able to produce a 6.
Without a seed the sequence differs on every run, so it is not repeatable.
The seed gives repeatability, but the exclusive bound 6 means no roll of 6 appears.
Right: the seed makes the sequence repeat, and the upper bound is exclusive, so 7 allows a 6.
questions.explain: A seeded Random always produces the same sequence, which helps tests. The lower bound is inclusive and the upper bound exclusive.
questions.rule: Seed for repeatability; the upper bound is exclusive.
questions.hint: Check both the seed and which number the upper bound excludes.

questions.q: According to the tutorial, why is Pattern.splitAsStream better than String.split when a pipeline follows the split?
options: split builds a whole array first, wasted if the pipeline stops early
split cannot take a regular expression, so it cannot split text
splitAsStream returns the pieces already sorted in natural order
split returns a List, while splitAsStream returns a plain array
optionExplain: Right: the array holds every piece before the pipeline starts, which wastes memory and sometimes CPU.
split does take a regular expression; the difference lies elsewhere.
The pieces come in text order, not sorted.
split returns an array, and splitAsStream returns a stream; neither returns what this option states.
questions.explain: Array-based splitting finishes all the work first. The stream version hands pieces on as the pipeline asks for them.
questions.rule: Prefer a stream source over building an array first.
questions.teaches: String.split and Pattern.split build an intermediate array, wasted memory and CPU when the pipeline stops early or does not need it, while splitAsStream avoids that array.

questions.q: A new-developer checklist matches each data source to the stream source the tutorial offers. Match them.
pairs: Lines of a local text file
Lines of an HTTP response body
A body handler that supplies lines
The values stored in a Map
values on the map, then stream
questions.explain: Each source has its own pattern: Files.lines for files, a lines body handler of the HTTP client for responses, chars for letters, and a map view for map content.
questions.rule: Match the pattern to the data.
questions.teaches: The HTTP Client of JDK 11 can supply a response body as a stream of lines, so a large download need not be held fully in memory.

questions.q: A reviewer checks four stream creations. Which ones have a problem? Select all that apply.
options: Stream.iterate from 1, doubling each time, followed directly by a terminal sum with no limit
Files.lines opened inside a try-with-resources block and then filtered
A stream builder that has built one stream is asked to build a second stream
IntStream.rangeClosed with 1 and 3, followed by mapToObj
optionExplain: Problem: an infinite stream needs a short-circuiting operation such as limit, or the run does not end.
Fine: this is the pattern the tutorial shows for closing file-backed streams.
Problem: a builder cannot be used again, and reuse throws IllegalStateException.
Fine: mapToObj converts the primitive numbers into objects.
questions.explain: Infinite sources need a cut-off, and builders are single use. The other two lines follow the tutorial's patterns.
questions.rule: Limit infinite streams; use a builder once.

questions.q: True or false: the same method reference String::length can be used with both map and mapToInt.
questions.explain: It fits both, because the reference only needs a string to turn into a length. The difference is the kind of stream you get back. The card next explains why that matters.
questions.rule: Same function, different stream kind.

questions.q: Which call on a stream of strings gives an IntStream of their lengths?
options: map with String::length
mapToInt with String::length
filter with String::length
boxed with String::length
optionExplain: map gives a stream of Integer objects, not an IntStream.
Right: mapToInt produces the primitive stream.
filter needs a yes-or-no test, not a length function.
boxed takes no function; it turns primitives into objects.
questions.explain: mapToInt is the mapping that produces a primitive IntStream; map produces a stream of objects.
questions.rule: mapToInt returns an IntStream.

questions.q: To compute the average word length of a list of words, map the words with ____ and then call average.
questions.explain: average exists on primitive streams, so the words must first become numbers with a mapToInt, mapToLong or mapToDouble call.
questions.rule: Numeric terminal operations need a primitive stream.

questions.q: Why does the count operation return a long and not an int?
options: count also works on infinite streams, so it needs a larger type
long arithmetic is faster than int arithmetic
A stream can hold more elements than the int maximum
Streams of strings need extra room for the characters
optionExplain: An infinite stream never finishes counting, so the type does not help.
The tutorial gives no speed reason; the reason is range.
Right: some sources are huge, and flatMap can multiply the number of elements.
The count is about elements, not about the characters in them.
questions.explain: A count may exceed the largest int, for instance when flatMap turns each element into many.
questions.rule: count is a long.
questions.teaches: count returns a long because a stream can hold more elements than an ArrayList or an int can count, for example from a huge source or a flatMap that multiplies elements.

questions.q: A quiz app filters an IntStream of scores to those above 100 and calls max. No score passes the filter. The call returns an empty ____ .
questions.explain: On a primitive stream, max returns an optional result, because an empty stream has no maximum. That is why the call does not return a plain int.
questions.rule: min, max and average return optional results.
questions.teaches: min, max and average on primitive streams return optional results, because an empty stream has no minimum, maximum or average.

questions.q: A fitness app has Workout objects with an int minutes field. Which pipelines correctly compute the total minutes? Select all that apply.
options: Stream the workouts, mapToInt with Workout::minutes, then sum
Stream the workouts, map with Workout::minutes, then sum
Stream the workouts, mapToInt with Workout::minutes, then summaryStatistics and read the sum
Stream the workouts, filter with Workout::minutes, then sum
optionExplain: Right: mapToInt gives an IntStream, which has sum.
A stream of Integer objects has no sum; the numeric operations belong to primitive streams.
Right: summaryStatistics computes count, min, max, sum and average in one pass.
filter needs a yes-or-no test, and the result would still be a stream of workouts.
questions.explain: Total minutes need a primitive stream, either with sum or by reading the sum from the statistics.
questions.rule: Go through a primitive stream for numeric aggregates.

questions.q: Each of three countries holds a list of cities. A pipeline over the countries must produce one flat stream of all the cities. Which step does that?
options: filter
limit
distinct
flatMap
optionExplain: A filter keeps or drops whole countries; it cannot open the lists inside them.
limit cuts the stream short; it does not open the lists inside the elements.
distinct removes duplicates; it does not open the lists inside the elements.
Right: flatMap turns each country into a stream of its cities and merges them into one stream.
questions.explain: A flat stream of inner elements needs a step that maps each outer element to a stream and merges the results. The card next names it.
questions.rule: flatMap flattens streams of streams.

questions.q: True or false: the function given to flatMap must return a stream for each element.
questions.explain: flatMap merges the streams the function returns, so each element must map to a stream, which may be empty.
questions.rule: flatMap function returns a stream.

questions.q: A list holds the strings 4, an empty string, 9 and abc. A pipeline turns each string into an int when parsing works and drops it otherwise, using flatMap with empty streams. What numbers come out?
options: 4 and 9
An exception on the empty string stops the pipeline
4, 0, 9, 0, because failed parses become zero
4, 9 and abc
optionExplain: Right: good strings produce one number, bad strings produce an empty stream and vanish.
The function catches the failure and returns an empty stream, so nothing is thrown.
No zero is created; a failed parse yields an empty stream, which contributes nothing.
abc cannot be parsed, so it is dropped rather than passed on.
questions.explain: Returning an empty stream for bad input removes it silently, so only the numbers 4 and 9 remain.
questions.rule: An empty stream removes the element.

questions.q: According to the tutorial, how should you combine four existing streams into one?
options: Call Stream.concat with four arguments
Use flatMap over a stream of the four streams
Chain three concat calls, which create no extra streams
Call mapMulti on each stream in turn
optionExplain: Stream.concat takes exactly two arguments.
Right: flatMap over a stream of streams creates only one stream for the whole join.
Each concat call creates an intermediate stream, so chaining is the costly way.
mapMulti emits values for an element; it does not join separate streams.
questions.explain: concat joins two streams and makes a stream for each join. For more than two, flatMap over the streams is cheaper.
questions.rule: concat for two, flatMap for many.
questions.teaches: Stream.concat takes exactly two streams and each join creates an intermediate stream, so for more streams the tutorial advises flatMap over a stream of streams.

questions.q: A mapMulti lambda receives a number n and a consumer. It calls the consumer with n, and then calls it again with n plus 100. The input stream holds 1 and 2. The output stream holds ____ elements.
questions.explain: Each input element produces two emitted values, so two elements give four. A lambda may call the consumer any number of times.
questions.rule: Each consumer call emits one element.
questions.teaches: A mapMulti lambda may call its consumer any number of times per element, so it can act like a filter (zero calls), a map (one call) or a flatMap (many calls).

questions.q: Sort each situation by the tool that suits it better according to the tutorial.

items.t: A function already returns a stream for each element
Merging many existing streams into one
Dropping bad strings without creating a stream per element
Emitting a value only when parsing succeeds, with no stream
The code must run on Java SE 15
An element should produce a few values through a consumer

questions.explain: flatMap suits functions that already return streams and code from before Java SE 16. mapMulti suits emitting values through a consumer without stream creation.
questions.rule: Streams in hand mean flatMap; values to emit mean mapMulti.

questions.q: A stream of the integers 1, 2, 3 and so on has no end. Which pipeline can produce a result?
options: sorted followed by limit 3
Both can produce a result
distinct followed by limit 3
Neither can produce a result
optionExplain: sorted must see every element before emitting the first, so on an endless stream it never emits.
One of the two cannot finish, because one of them waits for the end of the stream.
Right: distinct passes each new element on at once, so limit can cut the stream after three.
distinct emits as it goes, so a result is possible.
questions.explain: An operation that passes elements on at once can be cut short; one that must see everything cannot. The card next compares them.
questions.rule: sorted waits for all elements.

questions.q: To pick the integers 3 to 8 from 1, 2, 3 and so on, call skip(2) and then limit(____ ).
questions.explain: After skipping two, the stream starts at 3, and limit counts from there: six elements give 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8.
questions.rule: limit counts after the skip.

questions.q: A report pages through ordered results with 20 rows per page. Page 3 must show rows 41 to 60. Which calls produce page 3?
options: skip(20) then limit(40)
skip(40) then limit(60)
limit(60) then skip(60)
skip(40) then limit(20)
optionExplain: This skips only 2 pages of 20 and then takes 40 rows, which gives rows 21 to 60.
limit counts after the skip, so 60 rows follow the skipped 40, giving rows 41 to 100.
This takes 60 rows and then skips all 60, leaving nothing.
Right: skip 40 rows, then take the next 20.
questions.explain: The skip count is the number of rows before the page, and the limit is the page size, because limit counts from the stream that skip produced.
questions.rule: skip the rows before, limit to the page size.

questions.q: Elements 5, 8, 2 and 9 arrive in this order. dropWhile is applied with the test: the element is less than 6. Which elements are passed on?
options: 8, 2 and 9
8 and 9
2 only
5 and 2
optionExplain: Right: 5 is dropped, 8 fails the test and opens the door, and after that everything passes, including the 2.
This treats dropWhile like a filter, which would also drop the 2, but dropWhile only drops at the start.
The 2 passes only because it comes after the door opened; the 8 and 9 pass as well.
These are the elements dropWhile removes or never reaches, not the ones it passes.
questions.explain: dropWhile stops dropping at the first element that fails its test and then lets all later elements through, whatever they are.
questions.rule: Once dropWhile opens, it stays open.
questions.teaches: Unlike filter, dropWhile tests only until the first failure, and takeWhile stops at the first failure; so on an infinite ordered stream takeWhile can finish, while filter would keep searching.

questions.q: A list of several Pet objects, whose class does not implement Comparable, is streamed and sorted with sorted() and no argument. When the pipeline runs, it throws ____ .
questions.explain: Natural order needs Comparable elements. Without it, a Comparator must be supplied, or the sort fails at run time.
questions.rule: sorted without a Comparator needs Comparable elements.
questions.teaches: Calling sorted with no argument on elements that do not implement Comparable throws ClassCastException when the stream runs (with several elements to compare), so a Comparator has to be supplied.

questions.q: True or false: applying skip(2) and then limit(8) to the integers 1, 2, 3 and so on produces a stream that ends at 10.
questions.explain: After the skip the stream starts at 3, and limit counts eight elements from there: 3 to 10. The tutorial notes that on unordered streams takeWhile and dropWhile give no such reliable result.
questions.rule: limit counts after the skip.

questions.q: One stream comes from an ArrayList of strings and another from a HashSet of the same strings. Which statement about their order is likely?
options: Both streams are ORDERED alike
Only the list stream is ORDERED
Only the HashSet stream is ORDERED
Neither stream is ORDERED
optionExplain: A HashSet does not keep a defined encounter order, so its stream is not ORDERED.
Right: lists have an order that matters, sets do not.
The set is the unordered one, not the list.
A list has a defined order, so its stream carries ORDERED.
questions.explain: Order is a property of the source. The card next lists this and five more characteristics.
questions.rule: Lists are ordered, sets are not.

questions.q: Match each characteristic to what it says about the stream.
pairs: The number of elements is known
questions.explain: Each characteristic describes one property of the elements or of the stream's size, set when the stream is created.
questions.rule: Characteristics describe order, content and size.

questions.q: Strings from a list pass through distinct and then a filter. Which characteristic does the filtered stream have?
options: SORTED
SIZED
DISTINCT
SUBSIZED
optionExplain: Nothing in the pipeline sorts the strings, so SORTED is absent.
distinct erases SIZED, and the filter erases it too.
Right: distinct sets it, and a filter only removes elements, which cannot create duplicates.
Both distinct and filter erase SUBSIZED.
questions.explain: Removing elements cannot create duplicates, so filtering keeps DISTINCT, but it makes the count unknown.
questions.rule: Filter keeps DISTINCT and erases SIZED.

questions.q: Why is a stream from a HashSet SIZED but not SUBSIZED?
options: A HashSet may hold null elements, which blocks exact sizes
A HashSet cannot report its size, so the stream is not sized
A HashSet stream is parallel by default, which blocks sized splits
Elements can share one cell, so the half sizes are unknown
optionExplain: Null elements are about NONNULL, not about splitting sizes.
A HashSet reports its size, which is why the stream is SIZED.
Whether a stream is parallel is chosen by the caller, not by the source.
Right: the count after splitting cannot be known without counting, while an ArrayList splits a compact array into parts of known size.
questions.explain: SIZED knows the total, but SUBSIZED needs the count of each half after splitting, which a bucket array cannot give cheaply.
questions.rule: SUBSIZED needs known half sizes.
questions.teaches: A HashSet stream is SIZED but not SUBSIZED because several elements can share one array cell, so the sizes of the two halves are unknown without counting.

questions.q: A stream starts from a collection and is SIZED and SUBSIZED. Sort each operation by what it does to those two characteristics.

items.t: map to another type
sorted
flatMap
filter
distinct

questions.explain: Mapping and sorting keep the number of elements, so the count stays known. Filtering, distinct and flatMap change the number in ways that cannot be known in advance.
questions.rule: Operations that change the count unpredictably erase SIZED.
questions.teaches: Filter, distinct and flatMap change the count unpredictably, so they erase SIZED and SUBSIZED even for a SIZED source, which makes later parallel splitting less predictable.

questions.q: True or false: after you map a stream from a list of strings to their lengths, the new stream is still SIZED.
questions.explain: Mapping keeps the number of elements, so SIZED survives. It erases SORTED, DISTINCT and NONNULL, because the mapped values need not have those properties.
questions.rule: Map keeps SIZED; it erases SORTED, DISTINCT and NONNULL.

questions.q: The numbers 8, 3 and 2 are reduced with subtraction. Computed left to right, (8-3)-2 is 3. A parallel run splits the data and computes 8-(3-2). What does the parallel run give?
options: 3, the same as the sequential run
optionExplain: Right: 3-2 is 1, and 8-1 is 7, which differs from 3.
The grouping changes the arithmetic, so the result differs from the sequential one.
This is not what either grouping produces.
Reversing the signs does not match either grouping.
questions.explain: Subtraction gives different answers for different groupings, which is a problem for parallel runs. The card next names the property that prevents this.
questions.rule: Groupings must not change the result.

questions.q: An operator for which every way of splitting the data gives the same result is called ____ .
questions.explain: Associativity means that grouping does not matter, so parallel splitting is safe.
questions.rule: Associative operators are safe to split.

questions.q: Which operator is a safe choice for a parallel reduce over integers?
options: Subtract the second value from the first
Take the larger of the two values
Take the average of the two values
Divide the first value by the second
optionExplain: (10-4)-3 is 3 but 10-(4-3) is 9, so subtraction depends on grouping.
Right: the maximum of a group is the same however the values are grouped.
Averaging 1 and 3 and then averaging that with 5 gives 3.5, but averaging 1 with the average of 3 and 5 gives 2.5, so grouping changes the result.
Division also changes with grouping: (8 divided by 4) divided by 2 is 1, but 8 divided by (4 divided by 2) is 4.
questions.explain: Only the maximum gives the same result for every grouping. The others change when the grouping changes.
questions.rule: Test an operator by regrouping the same values.

questions.q: A reduce call has the identity 0, an accumulator and a combiner, and it sums the lengths of strings. Which description fits?
options: The accumulator adds two partial sums, and the combiner maps a string to its length
The combiner maps each string to its length, while the accumulator is left optional
The accumulator adds a string's length to the partial sum; the combiner adds two sums
Both functions receive only strings, and each adds the lengths of its two strings
optionExplain: The roles are swapped: the accumulator handles one element, and the combiner merges two results.
The accumulator is the step that sees the elements; the combiner merges partial results.
Right: the accumulator fuses the mapping and the adding, and the combiner merges the parts of a parallel run.
The combiner receives partial results, which are numbers, not strings.
questions.explain: The three-argument form fuses mapping into the reduction: one function handles an element, the other merges two results.
questions.rule: Accumulator takes an element; combiner merges two results.
questions.teaches: Beyond the tutorial: in the three-argument form the result type may differ from the element type (strings in, an integer out), which the two-argument form with one operator on the element type cannot do.

questions.q: A team reduces a stream of words using string concatenation as the operator and the empty string as the identity. Which statements are true? Select all that apply.
options: Concatenation is associative, so different splits give the same text
The empty string works as an identity, because joining it to a word leaves the word unchanged
The word x would also be a valid identity
Concatenation is not safe, because splitting the data changes the order of the words
optionExplain: Right: (a joined to b) joined to c equals a joined to (b joined to c).
Right: an identity leaves every other value unchanged, and the empty string does so for concatenation.
An identity must leave every value unchanged; x would add a letter to every result.
Splitting does not reorder the words, because the parts are merged in order, so the text stays the same.
questions.explain: An identity leaves every other value unchanged, and concatenation passes the regrouping test.
questions.rule: An identity leaves other values unchanged.
questions.teaches: Beyond the tutorial: associative does not mean commutative; concatenation depends on order yet is safe, because an ordered stream merges its parts in encounter order.

questions.q: True or false: if a reduction passes a hundred tests with random data, the operator is proven to be associative.
questions.explain: Passing tests does not prove it, because an untried counterexample may exist. A single differing result, however, proves the operator is not associative.
questions.rule: Tests can disprove, not prove.

questions.q: A stream is empty. Which call returns true?
options: anyMatch with any predicate
findFirst, tested for a present value
max, tested for a present value
allMatch with any predicate
optionExplain: With no element to match, anyMatch has nothing to find and returns false.
An empty stream gives an empty Optional, so the test is false.
An empty stream has no maximum, so the Optional is empty.
Right: nothing fails the predicate, so allMatch holds for an empty stream.
questions.explain: An operation that asks whether all elements pass has nothing to disprove on an empty stream. The card next lists all three match calls.
questions.rule: allMatch on empty is true.

questions.q: On an empty stream, noneMatch returns ____ .
questions.explain: With no elements, no element matches, so noneMatch is true. The predicate is never invoked.
questions.rule: noneMatch on empty is true.

questions.q: A parallel pipeline filters orders and needs any one matching order, with no preference. Which terminal operation is cheaper than findFirst?
options: findAny
anyMatch
count
toList
optionExplain: Right: findAny returns one element and does not enforce encounter order, so it avoids that cost in parallel.
anyMatch answers only yes or no, so it gives you a boolean and no order object to work with.
count returns a number, not an element.
toList reads every element and builds a list; you only need one.
questions.explain: findFirst enforces order, which is expensive in parallel. If order does not matter, findAny is the cheaper choice.
questions.rule: Use findAny when order does not matter.

questions.q: Why can Stream.toList be more efficient than collecting into an ArrayList when the stream knows its size?
options: It skips the terminal operation
It can allocate an array of exactly the right size
It sorts the elements while copying them
It shares the source list's memory without copying
optionExplain: A terminal operation is still needed; toList is one.
Right: an ArrayList grows by copying into larger arrays, but a known size allows one exact array.
Sorting is not part of toList.
The result holds its own copy; sharing memory with the source is not what the tutorial describes.
questions.explain: A known size lets the implementation avoid growing and copying a backing array.
questions.rule: Known size allows an exact allocation.
questions.teaches: Stream.toList, when the stream knows its size, can allocate an array of exactly the right size, which makes it more efficient than growing an ArrayList; the tutorial recommends it for immutable lists.

questions.q: A library streams book ids. In which situations must the pipeline still read every element before it can answer? Select all that apply.
options: anyMatch for overdue books, when no book is overdue
anyMatch for overdue books, when the first book is overdue
allMatch for returned books, when every book is returned
findFirst, when the second book matches
optionExplain: Right: a false result from anyMatch needs the whole stream.
The first book decides the answer, so the stream can stop.
Right: a true result from allMatch needs every element to pass.
The match is found at the second element, so the stream can stop there.
questions.explain: A search can stop when it finds the deciding element. An answer that rests on absence, or on all elements passing, needs the whole stream.
questions.rule: Absence and universal truth need a full scan.
questions.teaches: Early stopping depends on the data: an empty result from find, false from anyMatch, and true from allMatch or noneMatch all need the whole stream.

questions.q: True or false: adding each element to a list declared outside the stream with forEach is the pattern the tutorial recommends for gathering results.
questions.explain: The tutorial calls this a bad pattern: it captures an outside variable and is unsafe in parallel. It recommends a collector or Stream.toList.
questions.rule: Collect results; do not push them out with forEach.

questions.q: The words tree, sun, moon and tree are collected once with toList and once with toSet. How many elements does each result hold?
options: toList 3 and toSet 3
toList 4 and toSet 4
toList 4 and toSet 3
toList 3 and toSet 4
optionExplain: A list keeps duplicates, so it holds all four words.
A set drops duplicates, so it cannot hold both copies of tree.
Right: the list keeps all four words, and the set keeps each distinct word once.
A list cannot hold fewer elements than the stream delivers.
questions.explain: A set holds each value once, while a list keeps every element. The card next introduces the collectors.
questions.rule: toSet drops duplicates.

questions.q: True or false: Collectors.joining works on a stream of integers.
questions.explain: joining works only on streams of strings. Map the integers to strings first, or use another approach.
questions.rule: joining needs strings.

questions.q: A teacher has the marks 35, 62, 48 and 90 and wants two groups: marks of 50 or more and the rest. Which collector fits?
options: joining the marks into one text
counting the marks into one number
toSet over all of the marks
partitioningBy with the pass test
optionExplain: joining builds a string and needs strings, not marks.
counting gives a single number and no groups.
toSet gathers the marks into one set with no split.
Right: partitioningBy splits elements by a yes-or-no test into a true group and a false group.
questions.explain: A yes-or-no test that splits the elements into two groups is what partitioningBy is for.
questions.rule: Two groups from a test: partitioningBy.

questions.q: Marks are partitioned by a pass test, with counting passed as a second collector that processes each group. What is the result type?
options: A map from Boolean to Long
A map from Boolean to a list of marks
A map from Integer to Long
A map from String to Long
optionExplain: Right: the keys are true and false, and each group is replaced by its count, a Long.
A list per group is the default result, but the second collector replaces each list with a count.
The keys of partitioningBy are the booleans true and false, not integers.
The keys are true and false, not strings.
questions.explain: A collector placed inside another collector, called a downstream collector, processes each group's values and replaces the list.
questions.rule: The downstream collector replaces each group's list.
questions.teaches: partitioningBy has an overload that takes a downstream collector, which processes each group's values, so counting can replace each list with a number.

questions.q: An attendee list is joined with the separator comma, the prefix open bracket and the suffix close bracket. For an empty stream of names the result is ____ .
questions.explain: joining handles empty and one-element streams correctly, with no stray separator. With no names, only the prefix and the suffix remain.
questions.rule: joining copes with empty streams.
questions.teaches: Beyond the tutorial: joining copes with empty and one-element streams, adding no stray separator.

questions.q: True or false: after boxed turns an IntStream into a stream of Integer objects, the stream accepts a collector.
questions.explain: IntStream has no collect method that takes a collector, but a stream of Integer objects does. Boxing the numbers first is the way round the limit.
questions.rule: Box a primitive stream before collecting.

questions.q: The words ant, bee and tiger are collected with toMap, using the word length as key and the word as value, and no third argument. What happens?
options: The last word with each length replaces the earlier one
An IllegalStateException is thrown
The first word with each length is kept
Each key maps to a list of its words
optionExplain: Keeping the last value would silently lose data; toMap does not do that by default.
Right: ant and bee share the key 3, and without a merge function a duplicate key is an error.
Keeping the first value would also hide the clash; toMap does not do that by default.
Building lists is what groupingBy does, not toMap.
questions.explain: toMap protects you from silent overwrites by failing on a duplicate key. The card next shows the alternatives.
questions.rule: toMap rejects duplicate keys by default.

questions.q: groupingBy with counting as the downstream collector builds a ____ that shows how many elements share each key.
questions.explain: Each key holds the number of elements in its group, which is a histogram of the classifier's values.
questions.rule: groupingBy plus counting is a histogram.

questions.q: A school has a list of students, each with a grade letter. It wants the number of students per grade. Which call fits?
options: toMap with the grade as key and the student as value
partitioningBy using the grade letter as the test
groupingBy on the grade, plus counting downstream
groupingBy on the grade with no second argument
optionExplain: Many students share a grade, so toMap would throw on the first duplicate.
partitioningBy splits by a yes-or-no test, not by many grade values.
Right: the classifier picks the grade and counting turns each group into a number.
This builds a list of students per grade, not a number.
questions.explain: A key shared by many elements calls for groupingBy, and a count per key calls for counting as the downstream collector.
questions.rule: Shared keys: groupingBy; counts: counting.

questions.q: Words apple (5 letters), avocado (7) and banana (6) are collected with toMap: first letter as key, length as value, and a merge function that adds the two values. What is the map?
options: An exception is thrown
a to 5 and b to 6
a to 7 and b to 6
a to 12 and b to 6
optionExplain: The merge function resolves the clash, so no exception occurs.
This would keep only the first value for a, which is not what an adding merge function does.
This would keep only the last value for a, which is not what an adding merge function does.
Right: apple and avocado share the key a, so the merge function adds 5 and 7.
questions.explain: A merge function receives the existing value and the new value for the same key and returns what to keep. It can compute a total, not only join strings.
questions.rule: The merge function decides what a clash becomes.
questions.teaches: A merge function combines the existing and the new value of a clashing key, so it can compute totals and not only join strings.

questions.q: An HR tool must find the most common first name among employees. Put the steps in order.
items: Group the employees by first name with counting as downstream collector
Stream the entry set of the resulting map
Take max with a comparator on the entry values
Open the Optional result
questions.explain: The histogram comes first, the entries are streamed because a map has no stream method, the maximum needs a comparator on the values, and the result is an Optional.
questions.rule: Histogram, entries, maximum, open.
questions.teaches: max on the entries returns an Optional because a histogram of an empty stream has no entries, so the extraction must handle absence.

questions.q: True or false: toMap without a merge function throws IllegalStateException when two elements produce the same key.
questions.explain: toMap rejects duplicate keys by default. groupingBy, by contrast, gathers elements that share a key into one group.
questions.rule: Shared keys: groupingBy, or toMap with a merge function.

questions.q: In a collector, the component that merges two containers filled by different parts of a parallel run is called the ____ .
questions.explain: Each parallel part fills its own container, and the combiner merges them. The card next names all four components.
questions.rule: Combiner merges containers.

questions.q: Match each collector component to its job.
pairs: Adds one element to the container
Merges two containers from parallel parts
Turns the container into the final result
questions.explain: The four parts split the work: create, add, merge and finish. The finisher is the only optional one.
questions.rule: Create, add, merge, finish.

questions.q: Which approach turns the result of toList into an unmodifiable list without writing a collector from scratch?
options: collectingAndThen with toList and an unmodifiable finisher
teeing with toList used twice, then merging the two lists
groupingBy with the identity function as classifier and toList
partitioningBy with a test that every element passes
optionExplain: Right: collectingAndThen applies a finisher to another collector's result.
teeing merges two results over the same data; it is not a way to post-process a single result.
groupingBy builds a map, not an unmodifiable list.
partitioningBy builds a map from true and false, not a list.
questions.explain: collectingAndThen exists to apply a function to a collector's finished result.
questions.rule: collectingAndThen post-processes a result.

questions.q: A joining-like collector accumulates strings in a buffer and calls toString in its finisher. Which characteristics fit it?
options: IDENTITY_FINISH only
None of them
CONCURRENT and UNORDERED
UNORDERED only
optionExplain: The finisher is not the identity, so IDENTITY_FINISH does not apply.
Right: it keeps order, has a real finisher, and is not safe for concurrent use, so its set of characteristics is empty.
The buffer is not safe for concurrent access, and order matters, so neither applies.
The collector preserves encounter order, so it is not UNORDERED.
questions.explain: Each characteristic is a promise. A joining-like collector cannot make any of the three.
questions.rule: Declare only the promises you can keep.
questions.teaches: Beyond the tutorial: a joining-like collector declares no characteristics, while a toSet-like collector adds UNORDERED because a set does not preserve encounter order.

questions.q: An online shop streams order totals as doubles. In one pass it needs the number of orders and their sum, then the average as the sum divided by the count. Which design fits?
options: Read the stream twice, once for the count and once for the sum
Store the totals in a field, then loop over the field again
teeing with counting, summingDouble and a dividing BiFunction
groupingBy on the totals with counting as downstream
optionExplain: Two reads fail for a stream, which is single use, and waste a pass.
Storing data in a field defeats the one-pass pipeline and adds outside state.
Right: teeing runs both collectors over the same data in one pass, and the BiFunction combines the two results.
groupingBy builds a histogram of totals, which does not give a sum or an average.
questions.explain: teeing gives both results to a merging function, so a derived value such as an average can be computed in one pass.
questions.rule: Two results, one pass: teeing.
questions.teaches: The BiFunction of teeing receives both collectors' results, so derived values such as an average can be formed from them.

questions.q: True or false: the combiner of a collector is needed when the stream runs sequentially.
questions.explain: The combiner merges containers filled by parallel parts. A sequential run fills one container, so there is nothing to merge.
questions.rule: Combiner is for parallel runs.

questions.q: What does Optional.of do when it is given null?
options: It returns an empty Optional
It returns zero
It returns an Optional holding null
It throws NullPointerException
optionExplain: Turning null into an empty Optional is the job of ofNullable, not of.
Optional does not return numbers.
A nonempty Optional never holds null.
Right: of requires a non-null value and rejects null.
questions.explain: There are two creation methods that wrap a value, and they treat null differently. The card next compares them.
questions.rule: of rejects null.

questions.q: Match each Optional factory method to what it does.
pairs: Wraps a value, which must not be null
Wraps a value, or gives an empty Optional for null
questions.explain: empty never wraps, of wraps a certain value, and ofNullable handles the uncertain case.
questions.rule: Pick the factory by how sure you are of the value.

questions.q: A configuration lookup returns an Optional of String. The code needs the value, or a default text that takes an expensive database call to build. Which call is best?
options: orElseGet with a supplier that makes the default
get, then a null test on the result
isPresent followed by get on the Optional
orElse with the expensive call as its argument
optionExplain: Right: the supplier runs only when the Optional is empty.
get never returns null for an empty Optional: it throws NoSuchElementException, so the null test never helps.
This pattern still ends in get, which the tutorial advises avoiding where alternatives exist.
The argument of orElse is always evaluated, so the expensive call runs even when a value exists.
questions.explain: orElse builds its default every time; orElseGet builds it only when needed.
questions.rule: Expensive default: orElseGet.
questions.hint: Which call evaluates its argument only when needed?

questions.q: A collector returns a map from year to an Optional of top pair, and some values are empty. According to the tutorial, how should the empty values be handled?
options: Keep them, because Optional values in maps are the idiomatic result
Drop the empty ones with flatMap, map and Optional.stream, then toMap
Call get on every value and let the exceptions pass up the call chain
Replace the empty ones with null so that later code can test them
optionExplain: The tutorial calls empty optionals sitting in a map an antipattern.
Right: Optional.stream gives nothing for an empty value, so flatMap removes those entries, and toMap rebuilds the map.
get throws NoSuchElementException for the empty values.
Null is what Optional exists to avoid.
questions.explain: Optional.stream is the bridge that lets Stream.flatMap remove empty results.
questions.rule: Drop empties with stream and flatMap.
questions.teaches: Leaving empty Optionals as map values is an antipattern; the tutorial cleans them out with flatMap over the entries, using map and Optional.stream, and rebuilds the map with toMap.

questions.q: Sort each use of Optional by whether it follows the tutorial's advice.

items.t: The return type of a method that looks up a user by id
The result of max on a stream of orders
A field of a class holding a nickname
A parameter of a method that sets a discount
An element inside a list of results
The return type of a cache lookup that may find nothing

questions.explain: Optional is meant for return values that may be absent. Fields, parameters and elements of collections are outside its purpose, and it is also not serializable.
questions.rule: Optional is for return values.
questions.teaches: Beyond the tutorial: Optional is not serializable and discourages identity-sensitive operations, which is one more reason to keep it out of fields and collections.

questions.q: A reviewer reads four code decisions about Optional. Which break the tutorial's rules? Select all that apply.
options: A method returns null where an Optional of the result was possible
A class stores an Optional of String as a field
A method returns an Optional of Customer built from findFirst and map
Code uses ofNullable on a value that might be null
optionExplain: Break: the tutorial says not to use null for an optional variable or return value.
Break: Optional is for return values, not for fields.
Fine: this is the pattern the tutorial shows for a lookup.
Fine: ofNullable is the method for a value that may be null.
questions.explain: Return null instead of an Optional and store an Optional in a field are both against the advice. The other two lines follow it.
questions.rule: No null returns, no Optional fields.

questions.q: True or false: adding parallel to a pipeline makes it faster whenever the machine has several cores.
questions.explain: Parallel work has overhead for splitting and merging, and it depends on the source and the work per element. The card next lists what to check.
questions.rule: Parallel is not automatically faster.

questions.q: Match each source to what the tutorial says about splitting it.
pairs: The middle is easy to find and the halves are predictable
Finding the middle means walking half the list
The bucket array is hard to split evenly
Each element may depend on the previous ones
questions.explain: Good splitting is fast and even. Arrays and ranges do well, while linked and generated sources do not.
questions.rule: Splitting must be fast and even.

questions.q: A busy web server holds 50 records in a LinkedList. A developer wants to add parallel to a stream over them, although no performance requirement is unmet. According to the tutorial's rules, what should the team do first?
options: Add parallel now, because it can only help the throughput
Replace the list with a HashSet to improve the splitting
Hold off without a measured need; measure before changing
Wrap the list in a synchronized collection before streaming it
optionExplain: Parallel adds overhead and takes threads from request handling, so it may hurt.
HashSet is also hard to split evenly, so this does not fix the problem.
Right: the first rule is not to optimise for its own sake, and the last is to measure instead of guessing.
The problem is not thread safety of the list; synchronization adds more overhead.
questions.explain: With no unmet requirement there is nothing to fix, and any change must be measured under production-like conditions.
questions.rule: Need first, measurement second.

questions.q: Why can the elements of a parallel stream be processed in any order?
options: The stream shuffles its elements first, to balance the load between threads
The merge step sorts the partial results by their hash codes
Splitting divides the data into three parts that finish at random
Idle threads steal queued tasks from other threads, so no fixed order
optionExplain: The stream does not shuffle data; the order comes from how tasks are scheduled.
Merging combines partial results; it does not sort by hash code.
The tutorial describes splitting into two parts, and the order issue lies in scheduling.
Right: work stealing keeps all threads busy, and as a result no fixed processing order exists.
questions.explain: The common pool has a queue per thread, and idle threads take tasks from the others.
questions.rule: Work stealing makes order arbitrary.
questions.teaches: The Fork/Join pool uses work stealing: idle threads take tasks from the queues of other threads, which keeps all threads busy but means elements may be processed in any order.

questions.q: A library app runs a parallel stream that adds each overdue book title to a plain ArrayList declared outside the stream. Which outcomes can happen? Select all that apply.
options: Some titles go missing from the list
Different runs give different results
An ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException is thrown
The compiler rejects the code
optionExplain: Possible: several threads write into a list that is not thread-safe, so updates are lost.
Possible: the outcome depends on how the threads happen to interleave.
Possible: the tutorial reports that this exception may occur.
The code compiles; the problem appears only at run time.
questions.explain: Changing external state from parallel threads is a race condition, and the tutorial calls it an antipattern.
questions.rule: Share no mutable state between threads.
questions.teaches: With a non-thread-safe collection filled from a parallel stream, results vary between runs, elements go missing, and an ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException may occur.

questions.q: True or false: limit depends on encounter order, which makes it costly in a parallel stream.
questions.explain: limit, skip and findFirst depend on encounter order, which a parallel run must preserve, and that preservation costs extra work.
questions.rule: Order-dependent operations cost more in parallel.

questions.q: Which Stream method applies a custom intermediate operation that is written as a Gatherer?
options: gather
reduce
collect
flatMap
optionExplain: Right: gather is the intermediate operation that takes a Gatherer.
reduce is a terminal operation that combines elements.
collect applies a Collector, which is a terminal operation.
flatMap is a fixed operation; it does not accept a Gatherer.
questions.explain: Collectors serve terminal operations, and gatherers serve intermediate ones. The card next shows the parts of a gatherer.
questions.rule: gather applies a Gatherer.

questions.q: Match each part of a gatherer to its job.
pairs: Creates the mutable state once per run
Runs after the last element and returns nothing
Merges two states in a parallel run
questions.explain: The integrator is the core, the initializer and finisher bracket the run, and the combiner serves parallel runs.
questions.rule: Initialize, integrate, finish; combine if parallel.

questions.q: A limit-like gatherer has pushed its third element, which is its limit. What should its integrator return?
options: true, because the last push succeeded
false, to tell upstream to stop
Nothing, because integrators have no return value
The number of elements pushed
optionExplain: Returning true asks for more elements and wastes work after the limit.
Right: false tells upstream that no more elements are wanted.
An integrator returns a boolean.
The return value is a boolean, not a count.
questions.explain: Returning false is how an integrator interrupts the stream once its work is done.
questions.rule: false means stop.

questions.q: According to the tutorial, what is the advice for writing the integrator of a new gatherer?
options: Make it greedy from the start, because it is always faster
Avoid integrators that need state, and use the finisher instead
Start plain, then make the integrator greedy once all works
Write the integrator in a parallel style before anything else
optionExplain: A greedy integrator never stops the stream by itself, and breaking that promise can cause failures.
Stateful gatherers are supported with an initializer.
Right: a greedy integrator allows optimisations, but the tutorial advises making the integrator greedy only after everything works.
The tutorial does not recommend starting with the parallel form.
questions.explain: Greedy is a promise that the integrator never stops the stream on its own. A plain integrator is safe to start with.
questions.rule: Plain first, greedy later.
questions.teaches: A greedy integrator promises never to stop the stream by itself, which lets the API optimise; a non-greedy integrator that behaves greedily still works but misses those optimisations.

questions.q: A dropWhile-like gatherer for log lines keeps a box holding a flag, false at the start. Put the steps of one run in order.
items: The initializer creates a box with the flag set to false
The integrator receives the first line and sees the flag is false
The line still matches the drop condition, so nothing is pushed
A later line fails the condition, so the flag turns true and the line is pushed
Every following line is pushed without testing the condition
questions.explain: State is created first. While lines match, they are dropped. The first non-matching line flips the flag, and after that everything flows through. A plain mutable box suffices because a sequential gatherer does not share its state.
questions.rule: State remembers that the door has opened.
questions.teaches: The tutorial notes that a small mutable holder, such as a box class with a boolean, is enough for the state of a sequential gatherer; atomics are unnecessary because the state is not shared.

questions.q: True or false: after an integrator returns false, the API may call it again with the next element.
questions.explain: Once the integrator returns false it is not called again, so it must not return true after returning false.
questions.rule: false ends the integrator's calls.

questions.q: The elements 1, 2, 3 and 4 pass through fold with addition, and separately through scan with addition. How many elements does each emit?
options: fold emits 4 and scan emits 1
Both emit 4
Both emit 1
fold emits 1 and scan emits 4
optionExplain: The roles are swapped: fold reduces everything to one element.
fold reduces to a single element, so it does not emit four.
scan pushes each running total, so it emits more than one element.
Right: fold gives only the final total, while scan pushes every intermediate result.
questions.explain: Both combine elements left to right, but only one of them shows the steps along the way. The card next describes the five ready-made gatherers.
questions.rule: fold: one result; scan: every step.

questions.q: windowFixed(3) over seven elements ends with a last window that holds ____ element(s).
questions.explain: Seven elements split into windows of 3, 3 and 1. The last window may be shorter than the window size.
questions.rule: The last fixed window may be shorter.

questions.q: A sensor app wants the average of every three consecutive readings, with overlapping groups. Which gatherer should feed the averaging step?
options: windowSliding(3)
windowFixed(3)
fold
scan
optionExplain: Right: windowSliding gives overlapping windows that move one element at a time.
windowFixed makes disjoint groups, so the readings do not overlap.
fold produces one value for the whole stream, not groups.
scan emits running totals, not groups of readings.
questions.explain: Overlap is the defining feature of sliding windows. Fixed windows never share elements.
questions.rule: Overlapping windows: windowSliding.

questions.q: What does the first argument of mapConcurrent control?
options: The number of elements in each window that is produced
The maximum number of mapping calls active at once
The index of the first element that the mapping starts at
The number of upstream elements to skip before mapping
optionExplain: Window sizes belong to the window gatherers.
Right: mapConcurrent maps elements with virtual threads, one per element, and the argument limits how many are active.
mapConcurrent maps every element; it does not choose a start.
Skipping elements is done by skip, not by mapConcurrent.
questions.explain: The mapping calls may overlap in time, so a limit on how many run at once is needed.
questions.rule: maxConcurrency limits active threads.
questions.teaches: mapConcurrent maps elements on virtual threads, one per element, and its maxConcurrency argument limits how many are active at once.

questions.q: A stateless gatherer upper-cases each log line and must add one closing marker line after the last line. The marker is pushed from the ____ .
questions.explain: The finisher runs once after the last upstream element and receives the downstream, so it can push a final element. A gatherer needs no state to use one.
questions.rule: A finisher can add a final element.
questions.teaches: A gatherer does not need state to use a finisher: a stateless mapping gatherer can push a final marker element from its finisher after the last upstream element.

questions.q: True or false: in a parallel stream, a sequential gatherer forces the whole pipeline, including the steps before and after it, onto one thread.
questions.explain: Steps before the gatherer still run in parallel, the gatherer itself runs on one thread, and steps after it can run in parallel again.
questions.rule: Only the sequential gatherer is single-threaded.

questions.q: A Java method must hand a text buffer to a C function. Where does the buffer have to live?
options: Anywhere on the heap, since the garbage collector tracks it for C code too
Outside the heap, in off-heap memory
Inside a static final field so that it is never moved
In a Java String object, which C code can read directly
optionExplain: A reasonable guess, but the collector does not manage memory on behalf of C code.
Right: the tutorial says arguments passed to a C function must be in off-heap memory.
Pinning in a field sounds safe, but a Java field still lives in the managed heap.
C code expects raw bytes, not a Java object layout.
questions.explain: C code reads raw memory it is given, so the data has to sit outside the managed heap. The card next explains how Java describes such memory.
questions.rule: C function arguments live off-heap.

questions.q: Which facts does a value layout such as JAVA_BYTE state about a memory access? Select all that apply.
options: The size of the access in bytes
The byte order of the access
Which arena owns the memory
The Java type that the access produces
Which thread may perform the access
optionExplain: Right: the layout fixes how many bytes are read or written.
Right: JAVA_BYTE uses the hardware's native order, and the layout carries that choice.
Tempting because arenas matter nearby, but ownership belongs to the segment's arena, not to the layout.
Right: the layout ties the access to a Java type, byte for JAVA_BYTE.
Thread rules come from the arena kind, not from the layout.
questions.explain: A value layout encodes size, byte order, bit alignment and Java type. It says nothing about ownership or threads, which belong to the arena.
questions.rule: A value layout describes how to interpret bytes, not who owns them.

questions.q: A program copies the Java String ok into a native segment using an arena's allocateFrom method. It then calls get with JAVA_BYTE and offset 0. What does it get?
options: The byte for o, which is 111
The number 2, the length of the string
A zero byte, because text starts after a header
An exception, because a String needs a char layout
optionExplain: Right: allocateFrom stores the text as UTF-8 bytes, and offset 0 is the first byte.
A length prefix is a common design elsewhere, but a C string has none.
The segment holds the string bytes from offset 0, with no header.
The access reads a single byte, so JAVA_BYTE fits the stored data.
questions.explain: The string becomes a null-terminated UTF-8 C string starting at offset 0, so the first byte is the code for o.
questions.rule: Offsets count bytes from the start of the segment.

questions.q: A native segment holds the C string ok created by allocateFrom. What does get with JAVA_BYTE and offset 2 return?
options: 107, the code for the next letter
An exception, since offset 2 lies beyond the two characters
The number 2, the string length
0, the null terminator that allocateFrom adds
optionExplain: Nothing follows the two letters except the terminator.
The segment is longer than the text, so the offset is inside it.
Offsets are positions, not lengths.
Right: the tutorial says the string is stored null-terminated, so a two-letter text takes three bytes.
questions.explain: A null-terminated C string needs one extra zero byte after its characters. The segment for ok therefore has three bytes, and offset 2 is the zero.
questions.rule: A C string takes one byte more than its characters.
questions.teaches: A string stored by allocateFrom is null-terminated, so its segment is one byte longer than the text and the last byte is zero.

questions.q: A teammate holds sensor readings in an ordinary Java byte array and wants a C function to process them. A heap segment can wrap that array. According to the tutorial's rule about C arguments, what should the teammate do?
options: Pass the heap segment straight to the C function
Copy them into a native segment first
Make the array static so it cannot move
Call the C function twice so the data is cached
optionExplain: Wrapping looks like a shortcut, but the tutorial requires off-heap memory for C arguments.
Right: native segments are backed by off-heap memory, so they can be handed to C.
A static field still lives on the managed heap.
Calling twice changes nothing about where the bytes live.
questions.explain: Heap segments give Java a segment-style view of heap data, but C arguments have to be off-heap. A copy into a native segment is the step that bridges the two.
questions.rule: Copy heap data into a native segment before native code sees it.
questions.teaches: A heap segment is a Java-side view of heap data and is not a way to give that data to C; the data must be copied into a native segment first.

questions.q: True or false: If the arena that allocated a native segment is closed, the segment can still be read as long as the garbage collector has not run.
questions.explain: Off-heap memory is not tied to the collector. Once the arena scope ends, the segment is invalid, and reading it throws an exception.
questions.rule: Validity follows the arena scope, not the garbage collector.

questions.q: A method allocates a native segment in an arena that is closed by try-with-resources, and returns the segment. A caller reads it. What happens?
options: It returns the stored values until the garbage collector runs
It silently returns zeros
It throws IllegalStateException
It waits until another arena allocates memory
optionExplain: Memory is not freed lazily here; the arena ends the scope at once.
Zeros would hide a bug, and the API reports the error instead.
Right: the tutorial says access after the scope is closed throws IllegalStateException.
Nothing waits; validity is decided by the arena scope.
questions.explain: Closing the arena invalidates all its segments, so later access fails loudly. The card next lists the arena kinds.
questions.rule: A closed arena invalidates its segments.

questions.q: Match each arena kind to what the tutorial says about it.
pairs: Only the owner thread may access its segments
Any thread can access and any thread can close it
Managed by the garbage collector; close throws
questions.explain: Confined is single-owner, shared is multi-thread, automatic leaves release to the collector, and global never releases.
questions.rule: Arena kind decides threads and lifetime.

questions.q: Four worker threads must read one lookup table copied into native memory. The main thread will free the table after the workers finish. Which arena fits?
options: A confined arena created by the main thread, with segments given to the workers
A shared arena that the main thread closes
The global arena, closed by the main thread
An automatic arena closed by the main thread
optionExplain: Only the owner thread may access a confined arena's segments, so workers would fail.
Right: many threads can use its segments and the main thread can close it.
The global arena never frees memory, and its close throws.
The collector manages an automatic arena, and calling close throws.
questions.explain: The need is sharing among threads plus an explicit release point. Only the shared arena provides both.
questions.rule: Several threads plus explicit release means a shared arena.

questions.q: Arena extends the ____ interface, which is why an arena can allocate a segment and copy a String into it with allocateFrom.
questions.explain: Allocation methods such as allocateFrom come from SegmentAllocator, and Arena inherits them, so one object both allocates and controls lifetime.
questions.rule: An arena is also an allocator.
questions.teaches: Arena extends SegmentAllocator, so the object that bounds the lifetime of segments is the same object that allocates them.

questions.q: True or false: Thread A creates a confined arena and allocates a segment, then passes the segment to thread B, which reads it. B can read it because it holds a reference to the segment.
questions.explain: The thread restriction belongs to the confined arena, not to the variable that refers to the segment. Only the owner thread may access it, so B's read fails. A shared arena would allow B.
questions.rule: A reference does not grant access; the arena kind does.
questions.teaches: The thread restriction travels with the arena, so handing a segment reference to another thread does not make it accessible; choose a shared arena at creation instead.

questions.q: A developer wants memory freed at the end of a block and writes: try (Arena a = Arena.global()) { use(a); }. What is wrong with this plan?
options: The global arena has no owner thread, so the block cannot start
Try-with-resources only accepts confined arenas
Close throws UnsupportedOperationException; nothing is freed
The global arena frees memory after one thread finishes
optionExplain: Lacking an owner thread does not stop the block from starting.
The statement accepts anything closable; the problem is what close does here.
Right: the global arena cannot be closed, so the plan fails and nothing is freed.
Nothing in the tutorial lets a thread finishing release global memory.
questions.explain: Global means never deallocated, and close throws UnsupportedOperationException. Choose a confined or shared arena if the memory must be released at a known point.
questions.rule: Global memory is never released.

questions.q: A C struct holds two int members. Instead of calculating byte offsets by hand, what does the FFM API offer?
options: A layout object that describes the members
An annotation that turns a Java record into native memory
Automatic conversion of any Java class into a segment
A subclass of MemorySegment for each struct
optionExplain: Right: a MemoryLayout describes complex native types such as C structures.
Annotations are not the mechanism the tutorial describes.
The API does not infer native layouts from Java classes.
Segments are not subclassed per struct; layouts describe the shape.
questions.explain: A MemoryLayout captures member types and arrangement, so you name fields rather than count bytes. The card shows how.
questions.rule: Describe structure with a layout.

questions.q: Calling MemoryLayout.____ with the member layouts returns a StructLayout.
questions.explain: structLayout takes the member layouts in order and returns a StructLayout.
questions.rule: structLayout builds a struct description.

questions.q: A 40-byte segment feeds a slicing allocator, and the code requests four slices of 8 bytes each in a row. At which byte offset does the third slice begin?
optionExplain: Three slices of 8 bytes would end at 24, but the third slice starts earlier, after the first two.
That is where the second slice starts.
Right: each slice starts right after the previous one, so the third begins after 8 plus 8 bytes.
The first slice starts at 0; the allocator moves forward.
questions.explain: Slices are consecutive and contiguous, so offsets go 0, 8, 16, 24. The third request starts at 16.
questions.rule: Slicing allocators hand out the next free bytes.

questions.q: A tutorial call looks like numeratorHandle.set(fraction1, 0, 1). What is the role of the 0?
options: The index of the struct within a sequence of fractions
The base offset, allowing extra offset computation
The value that gets written into the field
The thread that owns the segment, as an id
optionExplain: A sequence index would need its own meaning; here 0 is a base offset.
Right: it is added to the position the handle already knows, which allows further offset computation.
The value is the last argument, 1.
Threads are not passed to a VarHandle call.
questions.explain: The three arguments are segment, base offset and value. The base offset is where extra offset computation is injected into the handle.
questions.rule: set takes segment, base offset, value.
questions.teaches: A VarHandle call carries a base offset argument, which allows additional offset computation to be injected into the handle.

questions.q: A warehouse segment holds 100 item records of 8 bytes each. To get record 7 as its own slice, call asSlice(____, 8).
questions.explain: Record 7 starts after seven records of 8 bytes, at 7 times 8, which is 56. A slicing allocator could only hand out the next free record, but asSlice can start anywhere.
questions.rule: Record i starts at i times the record size.
questions.teaches: Record number i of a table of equal-sized records starts at i times the record size, so asSlice with that offset reaches any record directly, which a forward-only slicing allocator cannot do.

questions.q: True or false: Calling asSlice with offset 40 and size 16 on a 48-byte segment returns the last 8 bytes, cut off at the end.
questions.explain: According to the tutorial, a slice is returned only when its size stays within the original segment's bounds. This request reaches byte 56, which is past the end, so no slice is returned.
questions.rule: A slice never extends past its parent segment.

questions.q: To call the C function strlen from Java with the FFM API, which object gives Java code access to foreign functions?
options: A Thread instance
A ClassLoader for the C library
The Runtime object
The native Linker
optionExplain: Threads run code but do not link to native symbols.
Class loaders load Java classes, not C functions.
Runtime manages the process, not native linking.
Right: the tutorial says the linker gives Java code access to foreign functions.
questions.explain: The Linker is the entry point for calls in both directions. The card next lists the full sequence.
questions.rule: The Linker connects Java and native code.

questions.q: Put the tutorial's downcall steps in order.
items: Copy the argument into off-heap memory
Obtain the native linker
Locate the function address
Describe the signature with a FunctionDescriptor
Build the downcall method handle
Invoke the handle
questions.explain: Arguments are prepared first, then the linker finds the function, the descriptor says how to call it, and only then is the handle built and invoked.
questions.rule: Prepare, link, locate, describe, build, invoke.

questions.q: A company library named imgfilter was loaded earlier with System.loadLibrary. Java code now needs the address of its function blur. Which lookup fits?
options: Linker.defaultLookup, which covers every loaded library
SymbolLookup.loaderLookup, for libraries loaded by System.loadLibrary
SymbolLookup.libraryLookup, which is only for libraries already loaded by System
FunctionDescriptor.of, which searches for symbols
optionExplain: It covers the standard C library only, so blur would not be found.
Right: this lookup is meant for exactly that situation.
libraryLookup loads a named library itself, with an arena controlling the lookup.
A descriptor describes a signature and finds nothing.
questions.explain: System.loadLibrary registers the library with the class loader, and loaderLookup searches those libraries.
questions.rule: Match the lookup to how the library gets loaded.

questions.q: In the tutorial's strdup example the pointed-to string is described as a sequence layout of Long.MAX_VALUE elements of the layout ____.
questions.explain: The pointer refers to a null-terminated byte string, which the tutorial models as a sequence of bytes of very large length because its real length is not known in advance.
questions.rule: A C string is a run of bytes.
questions.teaches: According to the tutorial, strdup's pointer return and argument are modeled as pointers to a null-terminated byte string, written as a sequence layout of Long.MAX_VALUE bytes.

questions.q: A downcall handle for C int abs(int j) has the type taking an int and returning an int. The call uses invokeExact, and the argument is the literal -5. Which line satisfies the exactness rule?
options: long r = (long) handle.invokeExact(-5);
int r = (int) handle.invokeExact(-5L);
Object r = handle.invokeExact(-5);
int r = (int) handle.invokeExact(-5);
optionExplain: A long result does not match the handle's int return.
A long argument does not match the handle's int parameter.
Without a cast to int, the call site returns Object, which does not match.
Right: argument int and result cast to int give a call-site type equal to the handle's.
questions.explain: invokeExact compares the call site's argument types and return type with the handle's type. Only the int in, int out form matches.
questions.rule: With invokeExact, cast the result to the exact return type.
questions.teaches: An exact invocation fixes both argument and return types at the call site, so a wider, boxed or uncast type breaks it even when the value would fit.

questions.q: True or false: The descriptor FunctionDescriptor.of(JAVA_LONG, ADDRESS) for strlen would also be correct on a 32-bit x86 platform.
questions.explain: According to the tutorial, size_t is JAVA_LONG on 64-bit x64 but JAVA_INT on 32-bit x86, so the return layout changes. Linker.canonicalLayouts shows what your platform uses.
questions.rule: Check layouts against the platform.

questions.q: A C function needs a callback that compares two items. How can Java code supply it?
options: Pass a Java Comparator object straight to the C function
Wrap a Java method as a native function pointer
Copy the compiled class file into a native segment
Serialize a lambda and pass the bytes
optionExplain: C cannot call into a Java object without a native function pointer.
Right: the tutorial calls the wrapper an upcall stub.
Bytes of a class file are not executable native code.
A serialized object is data, not a callable pointer.
questions.explain: C needs a real function pointer, and the FFM API can produce one from a Java method. The card next shows the steps.
questions.rule: Java callbacks become function pointers.

questions.q: The function pointer given to qsort is created by Linker.____ from a method handle and a function descriptor.
questions.explain: upcallStub takes the method handle, descriptor, arena and options, and returns a segment that serves as the function pointer.
questions.rule: upcallStub makes the callback pointer.

questions.q: A class Sorter has a static method byAge taking two MemorySegment values and returning int. How does Java obtain its MethodHandle for an upcall stub?
options: Linker.nativeLinker().defaultLookup().find with the name byAge
findStatic with Sorter.class, byAge and a MethodType
Linker.upcallStub called with only the name of the class Sorter
A new FunctionDescriptor built for a method named byAge
optionExplain: A symbol lookup searches native symbols, and byAge is a Java method.
Right: findStatic takes the class, method name and method type.
upcallStub needs a method handle, so one must exist first.
A descriptor describes the signature and does not locate the Java method.
questions.explain: findStatic locates the Java method as a MethodHandle. That handle then goes into upcallStub together with the descriptor.
questions.rule: findStatic yields the handle for upcallStub.

questions.q: True or false: The arena passed to upcallStub determines how long the stub stays valid, and with an automatic arena the garbage collector decides when that ends.
questions.explain: Every native object needs a scope. The arena given to upcallStub is the scope of the stub, and an automatic arena leaves its release to the collector.
questions.rule: The stub's arena is the stub's lifetime.
questions.teaches: The arena passed to upcallStub bounds the lifetime of the function pointer, and an automatic arena leaves its release to the garbage collector.

questions.q: A hypothetical C function takes a pointer to a callback with one int parameter, to report progress. Which pieces does Java need to provide the callback? Select all that apply.
options: A static Java method with a matching int parameter
A MethodHandle for that method, such as one from findStatic
A slicing allocator over the array being processed
A call to Linker.upcallStub with a FunctionDescriptor and an arena
A call to captureCallState with errno
optionExplain: Right: the callback body is ordinary Java.
Right: upcallStub works from a method handle.
Slicing divides segments and plays no part in building a callback.
Right: that call produces the function pointer.
That option captures errno after a downcall and is unrelated to callbacks.
questions.explain: The recipe is the same for any callback: a static Java method, a handle, a descriptor and an upcallStub. Only the method and its descriptor change.
questions.rule: The upcall recipe fits any callback shape.
questions.teaches: The upcall recipe does not depend on qsort: any C function that expects a callback pointer is served by a static method, a method handle, a descriptor and upcallStub.

questions.q: A developer passes a Java int array directly as the first argument to a qsort downcall handle. Which tutorial step was skipped?
options: Creating a second upcall stub dedicated to the array data
Calling invokeExact twice
Closing the arena before calling qsort
Copying the array into an off-heap memory segment
optionExplain: The array is data, so no stub is involved.
Repeating the call does not move data off-heap.
