Closing first would invalidate the memory rather than prepare it.
Right: qsort needs native memory, so the ints are copied into a segment first.
questions.explain: Arguments to C must be off-heap. The tutorial copies the ints into a native segment and, after sorting, copies them back.
questions.rule: Copy in before the call, copy out after.

questions.q: A C function allocates a buffer and returns a pointer to it. What does the FFM API give Java for that pointer?
options: A zero-length memory segment
A copy of the buffer in a Java byte array
A segment sized to the buffer automatically
A null reference until the buffer is freed
optionExplain: Right: the runtime does not know the size, so the segment has zero length.
The API does not copy memory behind a returned pointer.
The JVM cannot learn the size from a bare pointer.
The pointer is represented, not hidden behind null.
questions.explain: A bare pointer carries no size, so the API uses a zero-length segment. The card next shows how to use one.
questions.rule: A returned pointer has unknown size.

questions.q: True or false: Reading a byte from a zero-length segment throws IndexOutOfBoundsException.
questions.explain: The JVM cannot validate an access to memory of unknown size, so the access is refused.
questions.rule: Zero-length means unreadable until reinterpreted.

questions.q: A malloc call returned the zero-length segment p. To read 32 bytes through an arena that will run a cleanup action, call p.____(32, arena, cleanup).
questions.explain: The three-argument overload of reinterpret gives the segment a size, associates it with the arena and registers the cleanup action.
questions.rule: reinterpret adds size, arena and cleanup.

questions.q: A struct stored in a native segment contains a pointer member. Java reads that pointer value out of the segment. According to the tutorial, what kind of segment does it get?
options: A zero-length segment
A segment as long as the struct
A heap segment
No segment, only a Java long
optionExplain: Right: the tutorial lists pointers read from a segment among those represented as zero-length segments.
Nothing ties the pointed-to memory to the struct's size.
Heap segments wrap Java arrays, not native pointers.
The API keeps a segment so that the pointer can be passed on to native code.
questions.explain: Besides returned pointers, the API also represents pointers passed by native code to an upcall and pointers read from a segment as zero-length segments.
questions.rule: Any pointer of unknown extent is zero-length.
questions.teaches: Pointers passed by native code to an upcall and pointers read out of a segment are also represented as zero-length segments, not only pointers returned from downcalls.

questions.q: A graphics library returns a pointer to a texture buffer and offers a release function taking that pointer. Java does not read the texture bytes. What does the tutorial's reasoning suggest?
options: Call reinterpret with a guessed size so the buffer can be freed
Copy the buffer into a heap segment before releasing it
Pass the zero-length segment to the release function unchanged
Wrap the pointer in a confined arena to free it automatically
optionExplain: Guessing a size risks the corruption the tutorial warns about, and it is unnecessary.
Copying wastes work when Java never reads the bytes.
Right: zero-length segments are mainly meant to be passed to other native functions.
An arena does not know how to release library memory without a cleanup action.
questions.explain: Reinterpret is for when Java itself accesses the memory. Handing a returned pointer back to native code needs no size.
questions.rule: Pass pointers back unchanged when Java does not read them.
questions.teaches: reinterpret is needed only when Java reads or writes the memory; to hand a pointer back to native code, the zero-length segment is enough.

questions.q: True or false: If reinterpret is given a size larger than the real allocation, the JVM detects this when reinterpret is called and throws an exception.
questions.explain: The JVM cannot check the size, which is why reinterpret is restricted. An oversized segment can lead to out-of-bounds access, a JVM crash or silent memory corruption.
questions.rule: reinterpret trusts the caller.

questions.q: True or false: A Java catch block for IOException is how code reads the errno value that a failed C function left behind.
questions.explain: A native failure does not raise IOException on its own. The downcall handle must be created with an option that captures errno. The card next shows which one.
questions.rule: errno must be captured by the handle.

questions.q: Match each item to what it does.
pairs: Grants warning-free native access to all class-path code
Grants it to code in module com.shop
Grants it for an executable JAR, with ALL-UNNAMED only
Turns an errno value into readable text
questions.explain: The flag has two forms, one for the class path and one for named modules. The manifest route is limited to ALL-UNNAMED.
questions.rule: Flags grant access per module or for the class path.

questions.q: A modular application has modules com.shop and com.pay, and both call restricted FFM methods. Which launch option silences warnings for both?
options: --enable-native-access=ALL-UNNAMED
A manifest line Enable-Native-Access: com.shop,com.pay
--enable-native-access=com.shop only
--enable-native-access=com.shop,com.pay
optionExplain: That covers class-path code, not named modules.
The manifest attribute does not accept module names.
That leaves com.pay still producing warnings.
Right: a comma-separated list covers several modules.
questions.explain: Named modules need the command-line flag with module names, separated by commas.
questions.rule: List several modules with commas.

questions.q: According to the tutorial, why is creating a downcall handle a restricted operation?
options: The linker cannot check that the descriptor matches the function
It always opens a network connection to fetch the library from its vendor
It requires the owner thread of a confined arena to be the caller
It deallocates the Java heap
optionExplain: Right: a wrong descriptor makes the native call unsafe, and the linker cannot detect it.
Handles are created locally and do not involve a network.
Thread ownership is an arena rule, not the reason here.
Creating a handle does not touch the heap.
questions.explain: A descriptor is a promise about a C signature. Because the linker cannot check it, the call is inherently unsafe.
questions.rule: The descriptor is a promise the linker cannot check.
questions.teaches: Creating a downcall handle is restricted because the linker cannot verify that the function descriptor matches the real target function.

questions.q: A team ships an executable JAR started with java -jar and wants to silence native-access warnings for its class-path code without changing the launch command. What does the tutorial allow?
options: Add Enable-Native-Access: ALL-UNNAMED to the manifest
A manifest attribute Enable-Native-Access naming their module
A manifest attribute holding the list of restricted methods
Nothing; only the command-line flag works
optionExplain: Right: an executable JAR can declare that attribute.
Module names cannot be used in this attribute.
The attribute takes ALL-UNNAMED, not a list of methods.
The manifest attribute is the alternative the tutorial describes.
questions.explain: The manifest route exists for executable JARs, so no command-line flag is needed. It is limited to ALL-UNNAMED.
questions.rule: Manifest grants only ALL-UNNAMED.
questions.teaches: The manifest attribute works only with the value ALL-UNNAMED, so granting access to individual named modules requires the command-line flag.

questions.q: True or false: according to the tutorial, if no --enable-native-access option is given, a call to a restricted FFM method fails to run.
questions.explain: According to the tutorial, using a restricted method makes the runtime print a warning, not refuse the call. The option exists to avoid that warning.
questions.rule: No flag means a warning, not a block.

questions.q: What does the tool jextract take as its input to generate Java bindings?
options: Compiled Java class files
Java source files with annotations
Only a compiled shared library
C header files
optionExplain: Class files are output of Java compilation, not of this tool's input.
The tool does not read annotated Java source.
A library alone has no declarations to read.
Right: it reads headers and generates bindings that use the FFM API.
questions.explain: Headers contain the declarations jextract needs. The card next lists its options.
questions.rule: jextract starts from headers.

questions.q: Match each jextract option to its meaning.
pairs: Name of the generated header class
Writes all encountered symbols to a file for filtering
questions.explain: Each option controls one aspect of generation, from package name to filtering.
questions.rule: Know the four basic options.

questions.q: Without --header-class-name, jextract run on the header sensors.h names the header class ____.
questions.explain: The default name comes from the header file name, so foo.h gives foo_h and sensors.h gives sensors_h.
questions.rule: Default header class: file name plus _h.

questions.q: For the -l option, a value that starts with the character ____ is treated as a path to the library rather than a library name.
questions.explain: The leading colon is the signal that the rest of the value is a path, as in a colon followed by /usr/lib/libGL.so.1. A bare value is a name.
questions.rule: A leading colon marks a path.
questions.teaches: For the -l option, a value that starts with a colon is a path to the library; any other value is treated as a library name.

questions.q: A project includes a huge system header but calls only two of its functions. Which approach limits what jextract generates?
options: Edit the system header on disk and delete other declarations
Use --include-function once for each of the two functions
Pass -D with the two function names as macros
Run jextract with --version first
optionExplain: Editing system files is fragile; the tool offers filters.
Right: once any include filter is present, unmatched symbols are omitted.
Macros define preprocessor values and do not select symbols.
--version prints version information and exits.
questions.explain: Include filters switch jextract to an include-only mode, so only symbols that match a filter are generated.
questions.rule: Include filters turn generation into an allow list.
questions.teaches: As soon as any --include option is given, jextract omits every symbol that does not match one of the filters.

questions.q: True or false: If you filter out a typedef that a struct you kept depends on, jextract skips the struct and still generates everything else.
questions.explain: According to the tutorial, jextract reports the missing dependency, stops and generates nothing. Keep the needed declaration or drop the struct as well.
questions.rule: Missing dependencies stop generation.

questions.q: A program adds one month to 31 January. Which statement fits best?
options: Every year gives the same February date, since months have fixed lengths
The result is always an error, because February has no 31st
The outcome depends on whether the year is a leap year
The answer ignores the year and only looks at the day number
optionExplain: Month lengths are not fixed: February varies.
Adding a month is allowed; the tutorial only says results differ.
Right: February length changes with leap years, so the result can differ.
The year matters because February has 28 or 29 days.
questions.explain: February has a different length in leap years, which is why month arithmetic is subtle. The card next lists what else makes time hard.
questions.rule: Date and time arithmetic depends on calendar and zone rules, so the API uses the ISO calendar by default and takes locale text from CLDR and zone rules from TZDB.

questions.q: The default calendar of the Date Time API is based on the Gregorian system and is called ____.
questions.explain: ISO-8601 is the default calendar and the de facto world standard, according to the tutorial.
questions.rule: Default calendar: ISO-8601.

questions.q: A scheduling tool shows wrong local times after a government announced a daylight saving change on short notice. Which data source holds the zone changes the API relies on?
options: CLDR, the Unicode locale data
The java.time.chrono package
The ISO-8601 calendar definition
TZDB, the Time-Zone Database
optionExplain: CLDR is about locale text such as names in many languages, not zone rules.
java.time.chrono offers other calendars, not zone rules.
The ISO calendar defines dates, not zone rule changes.
Right: TZDB records zone changes worldwide since 1970.
questions.explain: Zone rules, including daylight saving changes, come from TZDB, so the tool needs current TZDB data.
questions.rule: Zone rules come from TZDB; locale text from CLDR.

questions.q: Beyond the tutorial: in the ISO calendar, what does LocalDate.of(2023,1,31).plusMonths(1) give?
options: 2023-03-03, spilling over into March
2023-02-28, the last valid day of February
An exception, because 31 February does not exist
2023-02-31, kept as an invalid date
optionExplain: Spilling over is what some older APIs did; java.time clamps instead.
Right: month arithmetic clamps to the last valid day of the target month.
The method does not fail; it adjusts to a valid date.
A LocalDate always holds a valid date, so 31 February cannot exist.
questions.explain: Month arithmetic in java.time keeps the result valid by moving to the last day of the shorter month.
questions.rule: Adding months clamps the day to the target month's length.
questions.teaches: Beyond the tutorial: adding a month to a day that does not exist in the target month gives that month's last day, so leap years change the answer for 29 to 31 January.

questions.q: Sort each need by the outside data source the API relies on.

items.t: Month names in many languages
A government moving the start of daylight saving
Localized text for hundreds of languages
Zone changes recorded since 1970
Whether a region skipped daylight saving this year
Day names in the user's language

questions.explain: CLDR supplies text for locales; TZDB supplies zone rules and their history.
questions.rule: Text from CLDR, zones from TZDB.
questions.teaches: Beyond the tutorial: because zone rules change, a program running on old zone data can give wrong local times, so the zone data must be kept up to date.

questions.q: True or false: A Thai Buddhist date cannot be handled by the JDK at all, because java.time only supports the ISO calendar.
questions.explain: The ISO calendar is the default, but java.time.chrono provides other calendars such as Hijrah and Thai Buddhist, and you can build your own.
questions.rule: ISO is the default, not the only calendar.

questions.q: True or false: A LocalDate has a setter that changes the stored day of the month in place.
questions.explain: The API has no set methods; changes produce new objects. The card next explains this design.
questions.rule: No set methods.

questions.q: Match each design principle with its meaning.
pairs: Methods behave as expected; null normally causes NullPointerException
Calls chain because methods reject null and do not return it
A change returns a new object, so sharing across threads is safe
You may define your own adjusters, queries or calendars
questions.explain: Each principle names one property: predictable methods, chainable calls, unchanging objects and room to add your own.
questions.rule: Clear, fluent, immutable, extensible.

questions.q: What does this code print? LocalDate d = LocalDate.of(2024, 3, 10); d.plusDays(5); System.out.println(d);
options: It does not compile, because plusDays needs an assignment
optionExplain: That would be the value of the returned object, which was thrown away.
Nothing subtracts days here.
The statement compiles; the returned value is ignored.
Right: plusDays returns a new object and d is unchanged.
questions.explain: Because LocalDate is immutable, d still holds 10 March. To use the result, assign it: d = d.plusDays(5).
questions.rule: Keep the returned object.

questions.q: Two threads read the same LocalDate stored in a shared field, and neither can reassign the field. What does immutability give them?
options: They must copy it first, because reading can alter it
They get the same value only if they call now() themselves
They can read it without locks, since its value cannot change
They are blocked until one thread finishes with it
optionExplain: Reading never alters an immutable object.
now() is unrelated to sharing an existing object.
Right: an object that cannot change needs no locking for reads.
Immutable objects need no blocking.
questions.explain: The tutorial calls the API thread-safe because of immutability; this is the practical consequence.
questions.rule: Immutable objects can be shared freely.
questions.teaches: Beyond the tutorial: because an immutable object can never change, you can pass or return it without making a defensive copy.

questions.q: True or false: A call chain such as a.plusDays(1).plusHours(2) is safe to write because most methods in the API return null when they have nothing to add.
questions.explain: The fluent principle says most methods never return null, which is why chaining is safe. The reasoning given is the opposite of the claim.
questions.rule: Fluent methods do not return null.
questions.teaches: Chaining only works because each call returns a usable object; a call that could return null would break the chain on its first use.

questions.q: Sort each item by the package it belongs to.

items.t: ChronoUnit
DateTimeFormatter
TemporalField
The rules for parsing text
ChronoField
The rules for formatting a date as text

questions.explain: Fields and units belong to the temporal package, while formatting and parsing belong to the format package.
questions.rule: Know the package by its job.

questions.q: Which prefix suggests that a method returns a copy with exactly one element changed?
options: with
to
at
get
optionExplain: Right: with is the immutable counterpart of a setter.
to converts to another type.
at combines with another object.
get returns a part of the state, not a copy.
questions.explain: In an immutable API a setter becomes a with method that returns a new object. The card next lists all prefixes.
questions.rule: The prefix tells the kind of operation: of validates, from converts, with replaces one element, plus and minus shift, is asks, to converts type and at combines.

questions.q: Match each prefix with its purpose.
pairs: Creates an instance, mainly validating inputs
Converts from another type, possibly losing information
questions.explain: Each prefix has one fixed meaning across classes.
questions.rule: Learn prefix meanings once.

questions.q: A developer needs a boolean answer to whether a date falls before another date. Which prefix family should the method name start with?
options: to
at
get
is
optionExplain: to converts to another type, so it does not answer a yes-or-no question.
at combines the object with another object; it does not answer a yes-or-no question.
get returns a part of the state rather than answering a condition.
Right: is methods query the object's state.
questions.explain: A yes or no question about state is the job of an is method, such as isBefore or isLeap.
questions.rule: is asks a question.
questions.hint: Which prefix queries state?

questions.q: Sort each prefix by what the call returns.
groups: A new object of the same type
Something else, such as text, a boolean or a part

items.t: plus
minus
with
is
get
format
to

questions.explain: plus, minus and with return changed copies; the other prefixes return a different kind of value (to returns another type).
questions.rule: Copies come from plus, minus and with.
questions.teaches: Beyond the tutorial: because plus, minus and with return new objects, you can chain them in a row, each step working on the result of the one before.

questions.q: Someone has a LocalDate and a LocalTime and wants a combined value. Which prefix should they look for first, following the naming convention?
options: of
with
plus
at
optionExplain: of is a static factory that validates inputs, not an instance method that combines.
with changes one element of a same-type copy.
plus adds an amount of time.
Right: at combines the object with another object.
questions.explain: Combining two different kinds of objects is the job of at. A naming guess like this can guide your search.
questions.rule: Search by prefix.
questions.teaches: Beyond the tutorial: a method name guess from the prefix is a good way to search the documentation, but the documentation decides the exact meaning.

questions.q: Which comparison of of and from is correct according to the tutorial?
options: Both do the same job, but from is the older spelling
of converts other types, while from validates its inputs
of is an instance method and from is a static factory
of validates inputs, while from converts and may lose data
optionExplain: They differ in purpose, not age.
This swaps the two meanings.
Both are described as static factories.
Right: of validates; from converts, possibly with a loss.
questions.explain: Telling of and from apart helps you predict whether a call can drop information.
questions.rule: from may lose information.

questions.q: Which class is best for the date on which a person was born, when people celebrate on the same calendar date wherever they are?
options: LocalDate
Instant
ZonedDateTime
Duration
optionExplain: Right: a calendar date without time or zone.
Instant is a point on the machine timeline.
ZonedDateTime adds time and zone that a birthday does not need.
Duration is an amount of time, not a date.
questions.explain: A birth date needs year, month and day only. The card next gives the full method for choosing.
questions.rule: Pick the class from two questions: human or machine time, and which parts (zone, date, time) you need.

questions.q: Machine time counts continuously from an origin called the ____.
questions.explain: The tutorial defines machine time as a count from the epoch with nanosecond resolution.
questions.rule: Machine time starts at the epoch.

questions.q: A web server must log when each request arrived so that logs from several servers can be compared on one timeline. Which class fits?
options: LocalDate
Instant
LocalDateTime
MonthDay
optionExplain: LocalDate drops the time of day.
Right: Instant is a point on the timeline, suitable for timestamps.
LocalDateTime has no zone, so the same value can mean different moments on different servers.
MonthDay holds only month and day.
questions.explain: Timestamps are machine time, so Instant is the suitable choice.
questions.rule: Timestamp means Instant.

questions.q: Match each class with what it holds.
questions.explain: The names of the date-only and time-only classes tell their content.
questions.rule: The class name names its parts.
questions.teaches: Beyond the tutorial: a type that omits a part cannot be wrong about it, so MonthDay can describe a yearly anniversary that has no fixed year.

questions.q: True or false: A Duration stores separate fields for days, hours and minutes.
questions.explain: The tutorial says a Duration keeps seconds and nanoseconds and only offers methods that report days, hours and minutes. The claim assumes separate stored fields.
questions.rule: Duration stores seconds and nanoseconds.

questions.q: A museum wants to print the opening time shown on a door sign, 09:30, with no date and no zone. Following the card's method, which class is the best fit?
options: Instant
OffsetTime
LocalTime
YearMonth
optionExplain: Instant is a machine timeline point.
OffsetTime carries a fixed offset that the sign does not need.
Right: human time of day with no zone or date.
YearMonth holds a year and month, not a time.
questions.explain: Choosing means listing what you need (time only, no zone) and picking the class with exactly that.
questions.rule: Choose the smallest class that has what you need.
questions.teaches: Beyond the tutorial: choosing the class with the fewest parts that still meets the need avoids storing guessed values, such as an invented day or zone.

questions.q: True or false: In the DayOfWeek enum, Monday has the integer value 1.
questions.explain: DayOfWeek numbers days from 1 for Monday to 7 for Sunday. The card next shows how to use the constants.
questions.rule: Monday is 1.

questions.q: Adding 3 days to DayOfWeek.MONDAY gives ____.
questions.explain: Monday plus three days is Thursday, according to the tutorial.
questions.rule: plus moves forward through the week.

questions.q: A roster program stores a shift on DayOfWeek.FRIDAY and must find the day 3 days later. Which result is expected?
options: SATURDAY
SUNDAY
An exception because the week ends
MONDAY
optionExplain: Saturday is only one day after Friday.
Sunday is two days after Friday.
The enum arithmetic wraps around the week, so no exception occurs.
Right: Friday plus 3 wraps past Sunday to Monday.
questions.explain: Counting from Friday: Saturday, Sunday, Monday. The enum wraps around.
questions.rule: Enum arithmetic wraps.

questions.q: What does Month.APRIL.maxLength() return?
optionExplain: 28 is February's usual length, not April's.
Right: April has at most 30 days.
31 belongs to months such as January.
29 is the maximum for February only.
questions.explain: maxLength reports the longest a month can ever be. Only February differs from its usual length (29 rather than 28).
questions.rule: maxLength is a maximum.
questions.teaches: Beyond the tutorial: of the twelve months only February has a maximum length different from its normal length, because only its length changes between years.

questions.q: A calendar header needs one-letter column heads for weekdays in a tight space. Which TextStyle matches the tutorial's description?
options: FULL
SHORT
NARROW
STANDALONE
optionExplain: FULL is the complete name.
SHORT is an abbreviation, usually longer than one letter.
Right: NARROW gives a short form, typically one letter.
STANDALONE variants are for languages where wording changes when a name appears alone.
questions.explain: Choosing the style follows the space available.
questions.rule: NARROW suits tight spaces.
questions.teaches: Beyond the tutorial: narrow names can repeat within one week in a language (for example, two weekdays can share the same first letter), so they suit labels but not unique identification.

questions.q: Which statements about the enums agree with the tutorial? Select all that apply.
options: Use constants such as Month.SEPTEMBER instead of raw integers
Month values run from 1 for January to 12 for December
DayOfWeek values run from 0 for Monday to 6 for Sunday
getDisplayName ignores the user's locale
optionExplain: Right: constants are more readable and type safe.
Right: the numbering matches ISO numbering.
DayOfWeek starts at 1 for Monday.
getDisplayName takes a Locale precisely to produce locale-specific names.
questions.explain: The enums use ISO numbering starting at 1, and display names depend on the locale.
questions.rule: Start counting at 1.

questions.q: Which class stores only a year and a month, such as 2024-09?
options: YearMonth
MonthDay
LocalTime
Year
optionExplain: Right: YearMonth is a month within a specific year.
MonthDay holds a month and a day.
LocalTime holds a time of day.
Year holds only the year.
questions.explain: The name names the parts. The card next introduces all four date-only classes.
questions.rule: Choose the date class that holds exactly the parts you need: LocalDate, YearMonth, MonthDay or Year.

questions.q: Year.isLeap on 2012 returns ____.
questions.explain: The tutorial's example shows 2012 is a leap year.
questions.rule: isLeap answers true or false.

questions.q: A payment card shows an expiry as month and year only, for example 09/27. Which class suits storing it?
options: LocalDate
MonthDay
YearMonth
Year
optionExplain: LocalDate would need an invented day.
MonthDay holds a month and a day, so the year of the expiry would be lost.
Right: it holds year and month with no day.
Year holds only a year, so the month of the expiry would be lost.
questions.explain: Choosing the class with exactly the parts you need avoids inventing a day.
questions.rule: Do not invent missing parts.

questions.q: What does MonthDay.of(Month.FEBRUARY, 29).isValidYear(2016) return?
options: false
An exception, because 29 February is not a real date
It depends on the user's time zone
true
optionExplain: false would hold for a non-leap year such as 2010.
The method only checks validity and does not throw for this.
These classes carry no zone.
Right: 2016 is a leap year, so 29 February exists.
questions.explain: Because February 29 exists only in leap years, isValidYear gives true for leap years such as 2016. Century years such as 1900 are not leap years unless divisible by 400.
questions.rule: Feb 29 needs a leap year.
questions.teaches: Beyond the tutorial: leap years are usually every fourth year, but century years such as 1900 are not leap years unless divisible by 400.

questions.q: A city plans a yearly festival on 29 February. Which statement fits what the card says about MonthDay?
options: The festival falls on 28 February in every other year automatically
The festival date exists only in years where isValidYear is true
MonthDay cannot represent a leap-day date
The festival date is valid in every year
optionExplain: The class does not choose substitute days for you.
Right: isValidYear tells which years contain the day.
MonthDay can represent 29 February; it just is not valid in every year.
February 29 is not valid in 2010, so it is not valid in every year.
questions.explain: Check validity per year, and decide your own substitute rule.
questions.rule: Check isValidYear.
questions.teaches: Beyond the tutorial: a type that can represent a date does not decide what your business rule does when that date is missing in a year, so you must choose the substitute day yourself.

questions.q: Sort each type by whether it holds a year.

items.t: LocalDate
YearMonth
Year
MonthDay
LocalTime
DayOfWeek

questions.explain: LocalDate, YearMonth and Year contain a year; MonthDay, LocalTime and DayOfWeek do not.
questions.rule: Know which part each type lacks.

questions.q: A cinema lists showtimes such as 19:30 with no date. Which class fits best?
options: LocalTime
Instant
LocalDateTime
ZonedDateTime
optionExplain: Right: a time of day with no date or zone.
Instant is a point on the machine timeline.
LocalDateTime adds a date that is not needed.
ZonedDateTime adds a date and zone that are not needed.
questions.explain: A showtime is a clock reading. The card next explains the two Local time classes.
questions.rule: LocalTime and LocalDateTime hold local clock values with no zone, so they name a clock reading, not a moment on the timeline.

questions.q: Conceptually, a LocalDateTime is a LocalDate combined with a ____.
questions.explain: The tutorial describes LocalDateTime as a LocalDate combined with a LocalTime.
questions.rule: Date plus time.

questions.q: A university notice says: the entrance test starts on 3 July at 10:00 in the hall, by the hall's own clock. Which class fits best?
options: Instant
LocalDateTime
LocalTime
OffsetTime
optionExplain: Instant would pin one world moment, which the notice does not.
Right: a date and a time with no zone.
LocalTime loses the date.
OffsetTime has a fixed offset and no date.
questions.explain: A date and clock reading with no zone is a LocalDateTime.
questions.rule: Date plus time, no zone.

questions.q: True or false: beyond the tutorial, adding one hour to a LocalDateTime of 2024-05-01T23:30 gives 2024-05-02T00:30.
questions.explain: A LocalDateTime holds date and time together, so time arithmetic that passes midnight carries into the next date.
questions.rule: Time arithmetic carries into the date.
questions.teaches: Beyond the tutorial: adding hours to a LocalDateTime that passes midnight carries into the next date, because date and time are stored together.

questions.q: Servers in Tokyo and Paris each store LocalDateTime 2024-05-01T12:00 for an event. What is true about those two stored values?
options: They name the same moment because the readings match
They differ by the nanosecond count
They are equal as values but name different moments
They are not allowed, because LocalDateTime needs a zone
optionExplain: The matching reading does not fix a moment without a zone.
There is no hidden nanosecond difference.
Right: equal readings in different zones are different moments.
LocalDateTime is zone-free by design.
questions.explain: The values are equal because they hold the same reading, but each places a different moment on the timeline.
questions.rule: Equal reading is not an equal moment.
questions.teaches: Beyond the tutorial: comparing or ordering LocalDateTime values from different places is only meaningful if you know the zone each one was recorded in.

questions.q: A developer says: a flight departure should be stored as LocalDateTime, because LocalDateTime knows the departure airport's daylight saving rules. What is wrong?
options: LocalDateTime cannot store times of day at all
Daylight saving applies only to dates and not to times
LocalDateTime stores a zone but no daylight saving rules
LocalDateTime holds no zone or daylight saving data
optionExplain: It stores both a date and a time.
Daylight saving affects clock readings, which is why zones matter.
It stores neither a zone nor rules.
Right: zone and daylight saving data need a zoned class.
questions.explain: For flights, the tutorial's example uses a ZonedDateTime.
questions.rule: Zones need a zoned class.

questions.q: Which of these can account for the one-hour gap when clocks move forward for daylight saving?
options: ZonedDateTime
OffsetDateTime
OffsetTime
LocalDate
optionExplain: Right: ZonedDateTime uses zone rules.
OffsetDateTime holds only a fixed offset.
OffsetTime holds only a fixed offset.
LocalDate has no time at all.
questions.explain: Handling a gap needs zone rules. The card next compares the zoned classes.
questions.rule: Use ZonedDateTime when zone rules such as daylight saving matter, and OffsetDateTime or OffsetTime when only a fixed offset from UTC is needed.

questions.q: Match each class or type with what it combines or means.
pairs: How a zone's offset changes over time
questions.explain: The zoned class uses a ZoneId and rules; the offset classes use a fixed ZoneOffset.
questions.rule: Zone id means rules; offset means fixed.

questions.q: A database column stores each event timestamp as a LocalDateTime plus its absolute offset from UTC, with no need for daylight saving logic. Which class matches that purpose?
options: ZonedDateTime
LocalDateTime
OffsetDateTime
OffsetTime
optionExplain: ZonedDateTime carries a zone id and rules that the column does not need.
LocalDateTime has no offset.
Right: it holds a date, time and fixed offset.
OffsetTime has an offset but no date, so it cannot hold an event timestamp.
questions.explain: The tutorial names database timestamps with absolute offsets as a use for OffsetDateTime.
questions.rule: Fixed offset: OffsetDateTime.

questions.q: A ZonedDateTime reads 2024-03-10T09:00 in Asia/Tokyo (+09:00). What local time results from withZoneSameInstant for Asia/Kolkata (+05:30)?
optionExplain: Keeping the clock reading would change the moment, not keep it.
Right: same moment, 3.5 hours earlier on the local clock.
Kolkata is behind Tokyo, so the clock reading is earlier, not later.
That is 12.5 hours behind, which is not the difference.
questions.explain: Tokyo is 3 hours 30 minutes ahead of Kolkata, so the same moment reads 05:30 there.
questions.rule: withZoneSameInstant keeps the moment.
questions.teaches: Beyond the tutorial: withZoneSameInstant keeps the moment and changes the displayed clock fields, whereas a method that keeps the clock fields and changes the zone, withZoneSameLocal, moves the moment.

questions.q: A recurring meeting is held every Monday at 09:00 in New York, a zone that changes its offset for daylight saving. Which class lets you compute each week's moment correctly?
options: OffsetDateTime with a fixed offset of -05:00
LocalTime only, kept as 09:00 each week
OffsetTime with a fixed offset of -05:00
ZonedDateTime with zone America/New_York
optionExplain: A fixed offset stays the same and would drift from New York's clock after a change.
LocalTime has no date or zone.
A fixed offset cannot follow the change.
Right: zone rules adjust the offset across the change.
questions.explain: Only a class with zone rules follows a zone's changes, so the meeting stays at 09:00 local.
questions.rule: Rules follow the zone's changes.
questions.teaches: Beyond the tutorial: a fixed offset is a snapshot of one moment's difference from UTC, so storing only the offset loses the zone name needed for future dates.

questions.q: True or false: An OffsetDateTime with offset +01:00 knows the daylight saving rules of Paris, so it shows correct Paris time in July.
questions.explain: An OffsetDateTime holds a fixed offset only and has no access to ZoneRules, so it cannot adjust for Paris daylight saving.
questions.rule: No rules in offsets.

questions.q: What sign does an Instant before 1970-01-01T00:00:00Z have, if it is expressed as a count from the epoch?
options: Negative
Positive
Zero
It cannot be represented
optionExplain: Right: before the epoch means a negative value.
Positive values come after the epoch.
Zero is the epoch itself.
Instants before the epoch are allowed.
questions.explain: The epoch is the zero point, so earlier moments are negative. The card next covers Instant.
questions.rule: An Instant is a zone-free point on the timeline; add a zone to get human date fields.

questions.q: Instant values count from the reference point called the ____.
questions.rule: Count from the epoch.

questions.q: A token must expire exactly 1 hour after it was issued, and the check compares the current time with the expiry. Which type is the better fit for storing issue and expiry points?
options: LocalDate
Instant
MonthDay
LocalTime
optionExplain: LocalDate has no time of day.
Right: Instant supports plus and comparison on a timeline.
MonthDay holds only a month and day.
LocalTime loses the date and zone, so expiry across midnight cannot be compared.
questions.explain: Machine points on the timeline are Instants; plus adds the hour and isBefore compares.
questions.rule: Use Instant for time stamps.

questions.q: The same Instant is 2024-03-10T22:00:00Z. In a zone at +09:00, which calendar date results?
options: 10 March 2024
9 March 2024
11 March 2024
12 March 2024
optionExplain: That is the date in UTC, not at +09:00.
This would be a zone behind UTC.
Right: 22:00 plus 9 hours is 07:00 the next day.
Nine hours does not cross two midnights.
questions.explain: The date of an Instant depends on the zone you choose.
questions.rule: The date depends on the zone.
questions.teaches: The same Instant gives different calendar dates in different zones, so a date is only defined after choosing a zone.

questions.q: Put the steps in order to display a stored Instant as local text for a reader in another country.
items: Take the stored Instant
Choose the reader's ZoneId
Convert to a ZonedDateTime or LocalDateTime for that zone
Format the result with a DateTimeFormatter
questions.explain: The zone must be chosen before the calendar fields exist, and formatting works on the converted object.
questions.rule: Choose the zone before the fields.
questions.teaches: Beyond the tutorial: store and compare timestamps as Instants and convert to a zone only at the edge, when showing them to a person.

questions.q: True or false: According to the tutorial, calling plus with 3 months on an Instant is a supported way to move it three months later.
questions.explain: An Instant cannot add months; convert it to a zoned or local type for calendar arithmetic. (The tutorial also lists days as unsupported, but the Java documentation treats a day as exactly 24 hours for an Instant, so this question avoids days.)
questions.rule: No months on Instant.

questions.q: True or false: LocalDate.parse can read a text like 2024-02-09 without any formatter argument.
questions.explain: With one argument it uses the ISO local date format. The card next explains formatters.
questions.rule: Default is ISO_LOCAL_DATE.

questions.q: In a DateTimeFormatter pattern, the letters ____ stand for a day of month that must be two characters, zero-padded.
questions.explain: dd is the padded form; d allows one digit.
questions.rule: dd pads, d does not.

questions.q: With an English-language locale, which pattern parses the text Sep 5 2021?
options: MMM dd yyyy
mmm d yyyy
MMM d yyyy
MM d yyyy
optionExplain: dd requires two characters, so the one-digit day fails.
Lower case mmm is not the month letter; pattern letters are case-sensitive.
Right: MMM reads the abbreviation and d accepts one digit.
MM expects a numeric month, not text like Sep.
questions.explain: Match the pattern to the text: abbreviation, one-digit day, four-digit year.
questions.rule: Pattern letters must match the text.

questions.q: In a pattern, which letters stand for the month and for the minute?
options: Lower mm for month, upper MM for minute
Both mean month, and case is ignored
Both mean minute, and case is ignored
Upper MM for month, lower mm for minute
optionExplain: This swaps the meanings: upper case MM is the month and lower case mm is the minute.
The tutorial says pattern letters are case-sensitive.
Case is not ignored: upper case MM and lower case mm are different letters with different meanings.
Right: pattern letters are case-sensitive and MM and mm differ.
questions.explain: Because letters are case-sensitive, MM is the month and mm the minute.
questions.rule: Case changes the meaning.
questions.teaches: Beyond the tutorial: in a pattern, upper case MM means the month number while lower case mm means the minute of the hour, so swapping the case produces wrong values without an obvious error.

questions.q: With an English-language locale, the text 7 Jan 2020 is parsed with a formatter built from MMM d yyyy. What happens?
options: The date is read as 7 January 2020
The result is null
The day and month are swapped silently
A DateTimeParseException is thrown
optionExplain: The pattern expects the month first.
Parsing signals failure with an exception, not null.
No silent swap occurs; the parse fails.
Right: the text order does not match the pattern.
questions.explain: Pattern order matters, so you catch DateTimeParseException when text may be wrong.
questions.rule: Mismatch means exception.
questions.teaches: Beyond the tutorial: the text must follow the pattern in order and shape, so each expected input layout needs its own pattern.

questions.q: True or false: A team creates a new DateTimeFormatter for every call because the class is not safe to share across threads.
questions.explain: The tutorial describes DateTimeFormatter as immutable and thread-safe, and says it can be kept in a static constant.
questions.rule: Formatters can be shared.

questions.q: Which one is a read-only view of a temporal object, without add and subtract methods?
options: Temporal
TemporalAccessor
TemporalAmount
TemporalUnit
optionExplain: Temporal adds add and subtract.
Right: TemporalAccessor is the read-only version.
TemporalAmount is Period or Duration.
TemporalUnit measures an amount.
questions.explain: The card next lays out the roles in the package.
questions.rule: Fields name parts, units name measures, amounts such as Period and Duration are applied to temporal objects, and isSupported tells what an object can do.

questions.q: The enum ChronoUnit implements the interface ____.
questions.explain: ChronoUnit implements TemporalUnit and ChronoField implements TemporalField.
questions.rule: Enums implement the interfaces.

questions.q: Generic code receives a LocalTime and wants to read MONTH_OF_YEAR. What should it do first?
options: Read the field and hope it is zero
Convert the value to a Period
Call isSupported with MONTH_OF_YEAR
Declare the variable as Temporal
optionExplain: A time of day has no month, so reading may fail.
Period is an amount, not a conversion target.
Right: isSupported asks whether the object can answer.
The tutorial advises concrete types in application code, not Temporal.
questions.explain: A LocalTime has no date fields, so isSupported would be false.
questions.rule: Check support before reading.

questions.q: True or false: Reading an unsupported field from a temporal object would silently return zero.
questions.explain: Beyond the tutorial: an unsupported field throws an exception, so isSupported is the safe check.
questions.rule: Check isSupported.
questions.teaches: Beyond the tutorial: reading a field that an object does not support throws an UnsupportedTemporalTypeException rather than returning a default.

questions.q: Match each type with its role.
pairs: Constants naming parts such as DAY_OF_YEAR
Read-only access to a temporal value
questions.explain: Each type has one role in field, unit, amount and access.
questions.rule: Know each role.
questions.teaches: Beyond the tutorial: field, unit and amount are three separate roles: a field names a part, a unit measures, and an amount such as Period or Duration holds a size.

questions.q: Sort each item by whether it names a part to read or a measure of amount.

items.t: DAY_OF_WEEK
MINUTE_OF_HOUR
NANO_OF_DAY
DAYS in ChronoUnit
Duration
Period

questions.explain: Fields name parts; units and amounts are for measuring.
questions.rule: Fields are parts; units measure.

questions.q: Which predefined tool would you reach for to find the last Wednesday of a month?
options: A predefined TemporalAdjuster
A Duration of one week
A predefined TemporalQuery
A DateTimeFormatter pattern
optionExplain: Right: adjusters move a date by a rule.
Duration measures time, not dates.
A query returns information.
A formatter turns objects into text.
questions.explain: The card next shows adjusters and queries.
questions.rule: Adjusters return a changed temporal; queries return information about it.

questions.q: You apply a TemporalAdjuster to a date by calling the method ____.
questions.explain: The tutorial applies adjusters through with().
questions.rule: Use with.

questions.q: An app needs the last day of the month for the date 15 October 2000. Which result should the lastDayOfMonth adjuster give?
options: 1 October 2000
31 October 2000
30 October 2000
1 November 2000
optionExplain: That would be the first day.
Right: October has 31 days.
October has 31 days, not 30.
That moves into the next month.
questions.explain: lastDayOfMonth keeps the month and sets the day to its last.
questions.rule: Adjusters keep the type.

questions.q: A payday rule: the 15th and the last day of each month, with a weekend payday moved to the previous Friday. From 20 November 2024, the next payday is on 30 November 2024, a Saturday. Which date results?
options: 30 November 2024
2 December 2024
29 November 2024
15 November 2024
optionExplain: 30 November is a Saturday, so the rule moves it.
Moving forward is not the rule.
Right: Saturday moves back to Friday the 29th.
15 November is before the starting date.
questions.explain: The custom adjuster applies the 15th or end-of-month payday, then the weekend rule.
questions.rule: Weekend moves to Friday.
questions.teaches: Beyond the tutorial: the order of the rules matters in a custom adjuster; here the payday date is chosen first and the weekend shift is applied afterwards, because shifting first could change which payday is picked.

questions.q: A calendar app has a method that returns true when a date falls in a school holiday. Which tool describes it?
options: A TemporalAdjuster implementing adjustInto
A TemporalAmount
A ChronoUnit
A TemporalQuery implementing queryFrom
optionExplain: It does not change the date.
TemporalAmount is Period or Duration.
ChronoUnit measures amounts.
Right: it asks a question and returns information.
questions.explain: A query returns an answer without changing the object.
questions.rule: Query answers, adjuster changes.
questions.teaches: Beyond the tutorial: you can tell adjusters and queries apart by what they return: an adjuster gives back a temporal of the same kind, a query gives back some other kind of answer.

questions.q: True or false: To use the method isFamilyBirthday as a query in a lambda expression, its class must implement TemporalQuery.
questions.explain: The tutorial says isFamilyBirthday does not implement TemporalQuery but can still be used in a lambda expression.
questions.rule: Lambdas can use plain methods.

questions.q: A stopwatch measures how long a task took, between two Instants. Which class fits best?
options: Duration
Period
MonthDay
YearMonth
optionExplain: Right: a time-based amount for machine time.
Period is date-based.
MonthDay holds a month and day.
YearMonth holds a year and month.
questions.explain: Elapsed machine time suits Duration. The card next compares the options.
questions.rule: Use Duration for elapsed machine time, Period for calendar amounts, and between when one total in one unit is needed.

questions.q: A Duration is stored in seconds and ____.
questions.explain: The tutorial says a Duration uses seconds and nanoseconds.
questions.rule: Duration: seconds plus nanos.

questions.q: A form must show a person's age as years, months and days from a birth date. Which tool gives the three parts?
options: Duration
Period
ChronoUnit.DAYS.between
Instant.until
optionExplain: Duration has no years, months or days.
Right: Period holds years, months and days.
between gives one total in days only.
Instant does not work with calendar units.
questions.explain: Period offers getYears, getMonths and getDays.
questions.rule: Period gives the parts.

questions.q: For 10 January 2024 to 25 March 2024, Period.between gives 2 months and 15 days. How many days does ChronoUnit.DAYS.between give for the same dates?
options: 60 days
74 days
75 days
106 days
optionExplain: That is the time until 10 March only.
Counting is off by one day.
Right: 31 days to 10 February, 29 more to 10 March (2024 is a leap year), plus 15.
That is far more than the span.
questions.explain: between gives the total days; Period gives parts. The total includes the leap day, which the parts do not show.
questions.rule: Total versus parts.
questions.teaches: Beyond the tutorial: ChronoUnit.DAYS.between counts the actual days, so the 75 includes the leap day 29 February 2024 that the Period of 2 months and 15 days hides.

questions.q: On the day daylight saving begins in a zone, a program adds Duration.ofDays(1) to a ZonedDateTime in that zone and, separately, Period.ofDays(1). What is true of the two results?
options: The Duration adds exactly 24 hours; the Period adds a calendar day
Both add exactly 24 hours, whatever the zone rules say
The Period adds exactly 24 hours; the Duration adds a calendar day
Both ignore the zone and give the same local clock time
optionExplain: Right: Duration is exactly 24 hours; Period accounts for local time.
Period can differ from 24 hours on such a day.
This swaps the two classes.
Period takes the zone into account for zoned values.
questions.explain: On a daylight saving change day a local day is not 24 hours, so the two give different results.
questions.rule: Duration is exact time; Period is calendar time.
questions.teaches: On a daylight saving change day a calendar day is not 24 hours long, which is why a Period of one day and a Duration of one day give different clock times on a zoned value.

questions.q: True or false: for a ZonedDateTime at 12:00 on the day before the spring clock change, adding Duration.ofDays(1) gives 12:00 on the next day.
questions.explain: A one-day Duration is exactly 24 hours and ignores daylight saving, so after the clock moves forward the local time reads 13:00.
questions.rule: Duration ignores DST.

questions.q: True or false: LocalDate.now() without arguments depends on the default time zone.
questions.explain: The no-argument version uses the system clock and default zone. The card next shows how to choose another Clock.
questions.rule: now() uses the default zone.

questions.q: Match each Clock factory with its behaviour.
pairs: A clock in the UTC zone
A clock shifted from a base clock by a Duration
questions.explain: Each factory builds a clock with one behaviour.
questions.rule: One factory, one behaviour.

questions.q: A unit test checks that a coupon is expired after 31 December 2024. The test should not depend on the real date. Which Clock fits?
options: The system UTC clock
A clock offset by a Duration from the system clock
The default clock with no argument
A fixed clock set to a chosen Instant
optionExplain: The UTC clock still advances with real time.
An offset clock still moves with the base clock.
The default clock reads the real time.
Right: a fixed clock always returns the same instant.
questions.explain: A fixed clock makes the result repeatable.
questions.rule: Fixed clock, repeatable test.

questions.q: Why might a team pass a Clock into a service, rather than let the service call now() on its own?
options: The service then runs noticeably faster in production
Tests can inject a fixed clock; system time stays alone
The service stops using time zones when it reads dates
The service can no longer read the date from a clock
optionExplain: Passing a Clock adds no speed; the reason is control over time, not performance.
Right: the clock becomes a replaceable input.
Zones still apply: every Clock carries a zone, so the service still uses one.
The service reads dates from the clock it was given, so reading still works.
questions.explain: A clock given as an input can be replaced in tests.
questions.rule: Inject the clock.
questions.teaches: Beyond the tutorial: giving code its Clock as an input, instead of calling now() inside it, lets a test control time without touching the system clock.

questions.q: A tester wants a clock that runs but keeps reading exactly 2 hours ahead of another clock. Which factory matches?
options: Clock.offset with a Duration of 2 hours
Clock.fixed with an Instant 2 hours ahead
Clock.systemUTC read twice for each call
Clock.systemDefaultZone, which reads the default zone
optionExplain: Right: offset shifts a base clock by a Duration.
A fixed clock does not advance, so it would not keep running.
The UTC clock gives no shift, however often it is read.
It reads the system time in the default zone and applies no two-hour shift.
questions.explain: Offset keeps time moving but moves it by a Duration.
questions.rule: Offset shifts, fixed freezes.
questions.teaches: A clock produced by offset keeps advancing with its base clock and only shifts the reading, whereas a fixed clock stops time.

questions.q: True or false: A Clock.fixed clock moves forward as real time passes, but starts at the chosen instant.
questions.explain: A fixed clock always returns the same instant, so time does not advance.
questions.rule: Fixed does not advance.

questions.q: Which call converts a Hijrah or Japanese date back into an ISO LocalDate?
options: LocalDate.from
LocalDate.parse
LocalDate.of
LocalDate.plusDays
optionExplain: Right: from converts another temporal object to a LocalDate.
parse reads text, not another calendar's date object.
of builds a date from year, month and day numbers, not from another date object.
plusDays adds days to a LocalDate.
questions.explain: The card next shows conversion in both directions.
questions.rule: Use the target type's from method to convert between calendars; both directions may throw DateTimeException.

questions.q: Converting between calendars can throw a ____ if the date cannot be converted.
questions.explain: The tutorial says both from methods throw DateTimeException.
questions.rule: Conversion can fail.

questions.q: A program holds a JapaneseDate and needs the ISO date to store in a database. Which call should it make?
options: JapaneseDate.from with the LocalDate
LocalDate.from with the JapaneseDate
DateTimeFormatterBuilder alone
Instant.EPOCH
optionExplain: That is the opposite direction.
Right: LocalDate.from converts a non-ISO date to ISO.
The builder only formats text.
EPOCH is a fixed instant.
questions.explain: Non-ISO to ISO uses LocalDate.from.
questions.rule: Target type's from.

questions.q: After converting an ISO date to a Thai Buddhist date and back, what should the result be?
options: The following day
A different month
The original date
An Instant
optionExplain: Conversion does not shift the day.
The month stays the same day.
Right: conversion only changes the calendar naming, so the round trip returns the original date.
The result is a LocalDate.
questions.explain: A calendar conversion relabels a day without moving it.
questions.rule: Relabel, not shift.
questions.teaches: Beyond the tutorial: converting between calendars relabels the same day in a different numbering system; it is not date arithmetic, so no days are added.

questions.q: Put the steps of the tutorial's round trip in order.
items: Start with a LocalDate
Convert it to a date of another chronology
Format it as text using a formatter built for that chronology
Parse the text back into a LocalDate
questions.explain: The round trip goes ISO, chronology, text, ISO.
questions.rule: The round trip ends where it began.
questions.teaches: Beyond the tutorial: because a round trip returns to the starting date, comparing the result with the original is a handy check that a custom format and parse pair agree.

questions.q: True or false: Because java.time.chrono is a separate package, a Japanese date cannot be turned into an ISO date.
questions.explain: LocalDate.from converts a non-ISO date to a LocalDate.
questions.rule: Conversion works both ways.

questions.q: Which of these is a problem the tutorial attributes to the old Calendar class?
options: It is mutable, so it is unsafe in multithreaded code
It is immutable, so each change needs a new object
It stores only nanoseconds, so dates are impossible
It has no month field, so months cannot be set
optionExplain: Right: mutability is one of the three listed problems.
Immutability is the property of java.time.
Nanosecond storage is a property of Instant.
Calendar has months, with unusual numbering.
questions.explain: The card next lists the drawbacks and conversions.
questions.rule: Use the conversion methods at the boundary with old code: toInstant, toZonedDateTime, Date.from, GregorianCalendar.from and toZoneId.

questions.q: Match each legacy conversion method with what it returns.
questions.explain: Each method moves between an old type and a new type.
questions.rule: Know the direction.

questions.q: Old code returns a TimeZone, and new code needs the zone rules type. Which call bridges them?
options: toInstant on the TimeZone
Date.from on the TimeZone
toZoneId on the TimeZone
toZonedDateTime on the TimeZone
optionExplain: toInstant is on Date and Calendar.
Date.from takes an Instant.
Right: TimeZone.toZoneId gives a ZoneId.
toZonedDateTime belongs to GregorianCalendar.
questions.explain: The named method for TimeZone is toZoneId.
questions.rule: TimeZone to ZoneId.

questions.q: Why must you supply a zone when turning an Instant into a ZonedDateTime?
options: An Instant is mutable, so it cannot convert safely
An Instant has no zone, so you must supply one
A ZonedDateTime cannot hold an offset beside its zone
The epoch changes with the zone, so a zone is needed
optionExplain: An Instant is immutable, so mutability is not the reason.
Right: the Instant lacks zone information, so the zone must come from you.
A ZonedDateTime holds a zone and an offset.
The epoch is fixed at 1970-01-01T00:00:00Z, whatever the zone.
questions.explain: The tutorial notes an Instant carries no zone.
questions.rule: Supply the zone.
questions.teaches: Beyond the tutorial: a java.util.Date also has no zone inside it, since it is a point on the timeline, even though printing it shows the default zone's clock.

questions.q: Which statements about moving old objects to java.time agree with the tutorial? Select all that apply.
options: Date.toInstant converts a Date to an Instant
GregorianCalendar.from takes a ZonedDateTime
Date.from takes a ZonedDateTime directly
Calendar objects are immutable
optionExplain: Right: this is a listed conversion.
Right: it converts back to a GregorianCalendar.
The tutorial lists Date.from taking an Instant.
Calendar is mutable, which is a listed drawback.
questions.explain: The tutorial's table pairs methods with the types they take and return.
questions.rule: Check argument types.
questions.teaches: Beyond the tutorial: when only one direction has a named method, check the argument type of each method, since Date.from takes an Instant and GregorianCalendar.from takes a ZonedDateTime.

questions.q: True or false: The call Date.from(zonedDateTime) is the listed way to convert a ZonedDateTime to a Date.
questions.explain: The listed method takes an Instant. Convert the ZonedDateTime to an Instant first.
questions.rule: Date.from takes an Instant.

questions.q: Old code stores a date of birth by setting a calendar to midnight on that day. Which java.time type is the better choice?
options: LocalDate
Instant
Duration
OffsetTime
optionExplain: Right: a date without time or zone.
Instant is a moment, not a date.
Duration is an amount of time.
OffsetTime holds a time and an offset but no date, so it cannot hold a birth date.
questions.explain: The card next lists mappings. The tutorial also points out that midnight can be missing.
questions.rule: Try the conversions first; otherwise map the purpose: moment to Instant, calendar with zone to ZonedDateTime, time of day to LocalTime, date to LocalDate.

questions.q: Code that sets a calendar to 1970-01-01 only to hold a time of day should use ____.
questions.explain: The fake date is just a holder, so LocalTime is the match.
questions.rule: Time of day: LocalTime.

questions.q: A legacy method keeps a shop's closing time by creating a GregorianCalendar for 1970-01-01 at 18:30. Which replacement fits?
options: ZonedDateTime on 1 January 1970
LocalTime of 18:30
Instant at the epoch
Period of 18 hours 30 minutes
optionExplain: That keeps the fake date and adds a zone.
Right: only a time of day is needed.
That is a moment at midnight UTC.
Period is date-based and not a time of day.
questions.explain: Map what the old object was used for.
questions.rule: Match the purpose.

questions.q: Why is storing a date as a calendar at midnight flawed, according to the tutorial?
options: Midnight always has two different readings in a year
A calendar cannot hold hours at all
Midnight does not exist on some days when DST starts
Midnight is stored with the wrong epoch value in files
optionExplain: The tutorial reports a missing midnight in some countries, not two readings.
A calendar can hold hours.
Right: a missing midnight makes the stored value unreliable.
The epoch is not involved.
questions.explain: A date needs no time of day, so LocalDate avoids the problem.
questions.rule: Do not fake dates with midnight.
questions.teaches: Beyond the tutorial: a LocalDate has no time of day, so it cannot be affected by a missing midnight or a daylight saving shift.

questions.q: Sort each old usage by the java.time type that replaces it.

items.t: A calendar at midnight used as a date
A calendar set to 1970-01-01 used as a time of day
A Date used as a point on the timeline
A GregorianCalendar with a zone and fields

questions.explain: Date-only and time-only uses map to Local types; moment and zoned uses map to Instant or ZonedDateTime.
questions.rule: Map by purpose.
questions.teaches: Beyond the tutorial: choosing the replacement by purpose rather than by class name avoids copying old workarounds, such as midnight-as-date, into new code.

questions.q: True or false: Every old Calendar method has an exact replacement in java.time, so code can be converted one line at a time.
questions.explain: The tutorial says there is no one-to-one replacement, so most code needs rewriting unless the conversion methods are enough.
questions.rule: No one-to-one mapping.

questions.q: A ZonedDateTime for 2024-03-10T22:00Z is shown in a zone at +09:00. What happens to the calendar date compared with UTC?
options: It moves forward to 11 March
It stays 10 March
It moves back to 9 March
It becomes a MonthDay
optionExplain: Right: 22:00 plus 9 hours passes midnight.
The clock reading changes by 9 hours, which here crosses midnight.
A zone ahead of UTC moves the reading forward, not back.
Showing a zone does not change the type to MonthDay.
questions.explain: A zone ahead of UTC reads later, so 22:00Z becomes 07:00 on the next day.
questions.rule: A zone shifts the human reading of a point on the timeline.

questions.q: A Duration measured from a start point to an end point that comes before the start has a sign that is ____ (positive, negative or zero).
questions.explain: The tutorial says a Duration can be negative, which happens when the end comes before the start.
questions.rule: Duration can be negative.

questions.q: True or false: You get a Pattern object by calling a public constructor of the Pattern class.
questions.explain: Pattern has no public constructors; you call the static method compile instead. The card next shows how.
questions.rule: Patterns come from compile, not from a constructor.

questions.q: Which class is the compiled form of a regular expression?
options: Matcher
PatternSyntaxException
String
Pattern
optionExplain: A Matcher applies a compiled pattern to input; it is not the compiled form itself.
This class reports an error in a pattern; it holds no compiled expression.
The regex text is a String, but the compiled form is a separate class.
Right: compile turns the regex text into a Pattern.
questions.explain: A Pattern is the compiled representation; a Matcher is the engine that uses it on an input.
questions.rule: Pattern is compiled; Matcher is the engine.

questions.q: To get a Matcher for a Pattern named p and an input text s, you call p.____(s).
questions.explain: The Pattern method matcher takes the input and returns a Matcher for it.
questions.rule: Ask the Pattern for a Matcher.

questions.q: A program calls Pattern.compile on the text a(b, whose opening parenthesis is left unclosed. What happens?
options: javac rejects the line as an error in the source
A Pattern is made that never matches any input
A checked exception forces a try block here
PatternSyntaxException is thrown when it runs
optionExplain: The text is only a String to javac, so the compiler accepts it.
A malformed pattern is reported, not turned into an empty matcher.
PatternSyntaxException is unchecked, so no try block is required.
Right: the exception is unchecked and appears when compile runs.
questions.explain: The regex text is a String until compile examines it, so the error is found while the program runs.
questions.rule: Syntax errors in a regex appear at run time.
questions.teaches: Beyond the tutorial: javac does not read regex text, so a malformed pattern passes compilation and fails only when compile runs.

questions.q: A tool must flag every character of a product code that is not an uppercase letter. Which regex finds one such character?
options: \P{Lu}
\p{Lu}
\p{IsL}
optionExplain: Right: capital P matches one character outside the category.
This is the code point of a single letter U, not a category.
This matches an uppercase letter, the opposite of what is wanted.
This matches any letter, so it would flag lowercase and uppercase alike.
questions.explain: Backslash capital P reverses the property, so it matches digits, spaces, lowercase letters and symbols.
questions.rule: Capital P negates a property.
questions.teaches: Beyond the tutorial: a negated category also flags digits and spaces, not just punctuation, because it matches everything outside the category.

questions.q: True or false: A regex written for Python is guaranteed to work unchanged in java.util.regex.
questions.explain: The tutorial lists many regex flavors and says Java's is most similar to Perl's, so syntax differences between flavors are possible.
questions.rule: Check a pattern against the Java flavor.

questions.q: True or false: The regex cat. fails to match the input cats, because the input contains no dot.
questions.explain: The dot is a metacharacter that stands for any one character, so it matches the s. The card next explains this.
questions.rule: Dot means any character.

questions.q: A match of foo in the input foo starts at index 0, and its end index is ____.
questions.explain: The end index is one past the last matched character, so a three-character match starting at 0 ends at 3.
questions.rule: End index is exclusive.

questions.q: A price list contains 3.50 and 3x50. A developer changes a regex from 3.50 to 3\.50. For which input does the result change from a match to no match?
options: 3.50, because the new regex rejects a real dot
3x50, because only a real dot is now accepted
Neither input, because the dot already meant a dot
Both inputs, because the backslash breaks the pattern
optionExplain: The escaped dot is still a real dot, so 3.50 keeps matching.
Right: before the change the dot matched x; afterwards it must be a dot.
The unescaped dot meant any character, so it matched the x in 3x50.
The backslash only changes the dot's meaning; the pattern stays valid.
questions.explain: An unescaped dot accepts any character, so 3.50 matched 3x50 too. Escaping it makes the match literal.
questions.rule: Escape a dot to match a real dot.

questions.q: The regex aa is applied to the input aaa by repeated searching. How many matches are found?
options: Two, at 0 to 2 and 1 to 3
Three, one for each a
One, at 0 to 2
None, since aaa is not the text aa
optionExplain: Overlapping matches are not reported.
Each match needs two a characters, so three cannot occur.
Right: the next search starts at index 2, where only one a remains.
The regex can match part of the input, not only the whole of it.
questions.explain: The first match ends at 2, and the next search starts there. One a is left, which is too short for aa.
questions.rule: Each search resumes at the previous end index.
questions.teaches: Beyond the tutorial: overlapping matches are never reported, because each search resumes at the previous match's end index.

questions.q: An email address pattern is built for the text user@site.com. Sort each character by whether it must be escaped to be read literally.

items.t: The dot before com
The at sign
The plus sign in user+tag
The digit 7
The dollar sign
The letter u

questions.explain: The dot, plus and dollar are metacharacters. According to the tutorial the at sign is never special, and letters and digits are ordinary.
questions.rule: Escape only true metacharacters.
questions.teaches: Beyond the tutorial: in a pattern for user@site.com, only the dots need escaping; the at sign is already literal.

questions.q: True or false: Each character in the tutorial's metacharacter list is special in every position of every pattern.
questions.explain: The tutorial says these characters are not always special; it depends on context.
questions.rule: Context decides what is special.

questions.q: Which input does the regex [bcr]at match in full?
options: bcrat
at
bcr
cat
optionExplain: The class picks one letter, so three letters before at cannot match.
The class needs one character before at, so at alone is too short.
The pattern needs at after the class character.
Right: c is in the class and at follows.
questions.explain: The class stands for exactly one of b, c or r, so the whole input has three characters. The card next explains it.
questions.rule: One class, one character.

questions.q: Match each class with the characters it accepts.
pairs: Any character except a, b and c
The letters a to d and m to p
The letters a to z except b and c
questions.explain: Caret negates, nesting joins, and the double ampersand intersects or subtracts.
questions.rule: Know the four combining forms.

questions.q: A seat-row field must hold one digit from 0 to 9 other than 3, 4 or 5. Which class accepts exactly those digits?
optionExplain: Right: the intersection keeps the digits and removes 3, 4 and 5.
This accepts any character that is not 3, 4 or 5, including letters.
This is two classes in a row, so it needs two characters.
A union with negated classes accepts almost every character, not only digits.
questions.explain: Subtraction is an intersection with a negated class, so only digits outside 3, 4 and 5 stay.
questions.rule: Subtract with and-and plus a negated class.

questions.q: Which single characters does the class [a^b] accept?
options: Only a and b, since the caret is ignored
a, b or the caret itself
Any character except a and b
None, because the class is malformed
optionExplain: The caret is not ignored; it stays in the set.
Right: not first, the caret is an ordinary member.
Negation only happens when the caret comes first.
The class is valid; the caret is just a character.
questions.explain: The caret negates only at the start of the brackets. Elsewhere it is one of the listed characters.
questions.rule: Only a leading caret negates.
questions.teaches: Beyond the tutorial: a caret that is not the first character inside the brackets is an ordinary character of the set.

questions.q: A tool reads hex-style codes with the class [a-f0-9&&[^b]]. Sort each single character by whether the class accepts it.

items.t: a
c
b
g
B

questions.explain: The class keeps a to f and 0 to 9 but removes b. The letter g is outside the ranges, and capital B is outside the lowercase range.
questions.rule: Ranges are case sensitive.
questions.teaches: Beyond the tutorial: ranges are case sensitive, so capital letters need their own range such as A-F.

questions.q: True or false: The regex [abc] matches the three-character input abc as a whole.
questions.explain: A class matches exactly one character, so [abc] matches a single letter and the whole input needs a longer pattern.
questions.rule: One class, one character.

questions.q: Which string literal in Java source holds a regex that matches one digit?
optionExplain: A single backslash before d is not a legal escape in a Java string, so javac rejects it.
This class matches the letter d, not a digit.
Right: the doubled backslash reaches the regex engine as one backslash.
Slashes are not regex delimiters in Java.
questions.explain: The string literal needs two backslashes so that the regex contains one. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: Type backslash twice in source.

questions.q: Match each shorthand with its meaning.
pairs: A character that is not a letter, digit or underscore
questions.explain: Lowercase shorthands select a kind of character; the capital form selects everything else.
questions.rule: Capital reverses.

questions.q: The shorthand ____ matches one character that is not a digit.
questions.explain: Backslash capital D is the reverse of backslash d, which is the same as the class 0 to 9.
questions.rule: Capital D is a non-digit.

questions.q: Which regex accepts one digit or one underscore as a single character?
options: \w
optionExplain: This needs a digit followed by an underscore, two characters.
The reversed shorthand accepts letters and symbols too.
Right: a class can list a shorthand together with other characters.
This also accepts letters, not only digits and underscores.
questions.explain: Putting the shorthand inside brackets lets it share a set with other characters.
questions.rule: Shorthands also work inside classes.
questions.teaches: Beyond the tutorial: predefined classes can be used inside square brackets, as in a class holding a digit shorthand and an underscore.

questions.q: Each item is the text between the quotation marks of a Java string literal that is meant to hold a regex. Sort the items by whether javac accepts them.

items.t: \d
\W
\w

questions.explain: A single backslash before d, w or W is an illegal escape in a Java string. The doubled form is a legal escaped backslash.
questions.rule: Double the backslash in source.
questions.teaches: Beyond the tutorial: javac rejects a lone backslash before most letters in a string literal, so the mistake shows up at compile time rather than at run time.

questions.q: True or false: When a program reads a regex that the user types at a console prompt, every backslash typed must also be doubled.
questions.explain: Doubling is a Java source rule for string literals. Text read at run time already holds the characters as typed.
questions.rule: Doubling is for literals only.

questions.q: Which input does the regex ab+ match in full?
options: abab
bbbb
aab
abbb
optionExplain: The plus repeats only b, so the pair ab cannot repeat.
The pattern starts with an a, which this input lacks.
The pattern allows one a only, not two.
Right: one a followed by one or more b.
questions.explain: The plus applies to b alone. The card next shows how to repeat a longer piece.
questions.rule: The quantifier binds to the element before it.

questions.q: Match each quantifier form with the number of repeats it allows.
questions.explain: Question mark, star and plus are shorthands for common counts; braces give exact bounds.
questions.rule: Know the six forms.

questions.q: Product codes are two uppercase letters followed by exactly three digits, like AB123. Which regex accepts a code when the entire input must match it, and rejects anything longer or shorter?
optionExplain: Right: exactly two letters, then exactly three digits.
This needs one letter and five digits.
This also accepts three letters before the digits.
The open upper bound lets longer digit runs through.
questions.explain: Braces with one number fix the count, so the code length is fixed.
questions.rule: Use exact counts for fixed formats.

questions.q: The regex ab{2} is changed to (ab){2}. Which input is matched in full by the new regex but not by the old one?
options: abb
abab
aabb
bbab
optionExplain: The old regex already matches this, since only b repeats.
Right: the group makes the whole pair ab repeat twice.
Neither regex accepts two a characters at the start.
Neither regex accepts input that begins with b.
questions.explain: Without the group, braces repeat only b. With it, the pair ab repeats.
questions.rule: A group lets a quantifier repeat many characters.

questions.q: The regex a* finds ____ matches, counting zero-length ones, in the input bcd.
questions.explain: Each of the four positions (before b, between letters, and after d) gives a zero-length match, since there is no a to take.
questions.rule: Zero-length matches occur between characters.
questions.teaches: Beyond the tutorial: an input with no matching letter still yields zero-length matches for a star, and the count equals the input length plus one.

questions.q: A signup form accepts usernames matched in full by [a-z]{3,6}. Sort each input by whether the whole input is accepted.

items.t: abc
abcdef
wxyz
ab
abcdefg
ABCD

questions.explain: The count must be between three and six, and the letters must be lowercase.
questions.rule: Bounds limit length when the whole input must match.
