questions.teaches: Beyond the tutorial: when the whole input must match, the upper bound rejects longer input, while a search for a part would still find a six-letter piece inside a longer word.

questions.q: True or false: A developer wants to require at least one digit in the input and writes the pattern \d* for a whole-input check. The empty input is then rejected.
questions.explain: The star allows zero repeats, so the empty input matches. Use the plus form to demand at least one.
questions.rule: Star cannot demand presence.

questions.q: The regex a.*b is applied to the input axbxbq. Which part does the first match cover?
options: axbxb
axb
xbxb
axbxbq
optionExplain: Right: by default the star takes as much as possible, up to the last b.
This stops at the first b, which is the reluctant behavior.
The match must begin with an a.
The match must end at a b, and q is not one.
questions.explain: The star takes everything it can, then backs off only as far as needed. The card next names this style.
questions.rule: Default quantifiers take the most.

questions.q: Put the steps of the greedy pattern .*foo on the input xfooxxxxxxfoo in order.
items: The star takes the whole input
The pattern foo fails at the end of the input
The star gives back one character at a time
The rightmost foo is found and the match ends
questions.explain: A greedy quantifier grabs everything, then backtracks until the rest of the pattern fits.
questions.rule: Greedy takes all, then backs off.

questions.q: The input is (red) and (blue). Which regex finds (red) and (blue) as two separate matches?
optionExplain: This matches the whole input as one match.
The possessive star swallows the closing parenthesis and no match remains.
Right: the reluctant star stops at the first closing parenthesis.
This is still greedy, so it matches the whole input.
questions.explain: Reluctant takes as little as it can, so each match ends at the nearest closing parenthesis.
questions.rule: Reluctant finds the nearest end.

questions.q: True or false: Changing the pattern .*foo to .*+foo does not change the result on the input xfoo.
questions.explain: The possessive version takes all of xfoo and cannot give any back, so foo has nothing left and no match is found.
questions.rule: Possessive can remove a match.

questions.q: True or false: The regex \d++x matches the input 123x.
questions.explain: The possessive digits take 123 and the x that follows is exactly what the pattern needs next, so nothing has to be given back.
questions.rule: Possessive fails only if something must be returned.
questions.teaches: Beyond the tutorial: a possessive quantifier still succeeds when the rest of the pattern matches what follows it; it fails only when it would have had to give characters back.

questions.q: Fields are separated by semicolons in the input one;two;three. Which regex matches only the first field and its semicolon?
optionExplain: The greedy star runs to the last semicolon and matches one;two;.
Right: the reluctant star stops at the first semicolon.
The greedy plus also runs to the last semicolon.
The possessive star takes the whole input and leaves no semicolon.
questions.explain: The reluctant form grows one character at a time, so the first semicolon ends the match.
questions.rule: Use reluctant to stop at the first delimiter.
questions.teaches: Beyond the tutorial: a negated class such as a class listing every character except the semicolon, followed by a star, reaches the same result without any backing off.

questions.q: In the regex (a)(b(c)), the number of capturing groups, not counting group 0, is ____.
questions.explain: There are three opening parentheses, so three groups. The card next shows how they are numbered.
questions.rule: Count opening parentheses.

questions.q: In the regex ((A)(B(C))), which group number belongs to the part (B(C))?
optionExplain: Group 1 is the outermost parentheses.
Group 2 is (A), the first inner group.
Right: its opening parenthesis is the third from the left.
Group 4 is (C), the innermost.
questions.explain: Numbers follow the order of opening parentheses: outer, (A), (B(C)), (C).
questions.rule: Number by opening parenthesis.

questions.q: The regex (\d+)-(\d+)-(\d+) fully matches the input 12-345-6. Calling group(2) on the Matcher returns ____.
questions.explain: The second pair of parentheses captured the middle run of digits.
questions.rule: Group n is the nth opening parenthesis.

questions.q: The regex (\d\d)\1 is changed to apply to different inputs. Which inputs does it match in full? Select all that apply.
optionExplain: Right: the second pair repeats the captured 45.
The second pair is 46, which differs from the captured 45.
Right: the captured 11 repeats.
The second pair is 54, which differs from the captured 45.
questions.explain: A backreference needs the same text again, not just any two digits.
questions.rule: A backreference repeats the captured text.

questions.q: The regex (a)|(b) is applied to the input b with find, and the search succeeds. What does group(1) return?
options: a
b
An empty string
null
optionExplain: The first alternative did not match, so it captured nothing.
The letter b was captured by group 2.
A group that did not take part gives null, not an empty string.
Right: group 1 took no part in the match.
questions.explain: Only the second alternative matched, so group 2 holds b and group 1 holds nothing.
questions.rule: A group that did not take part gives null.
questions.teaches: Beyond the tutorial: a group that took no part in the match returns null from group(n), not an empty string.

questions.q: An editor should flag a repeated word such as is is. Which regex, searched with find, is best suited to that?
optionExplain: This matches any two words, repeated or not.
This captures a word but never checks the second one.
This matches any single word and trailing spaces.
Right: the backreference demands the same word again.
questions.explain: Only a backreference compares the second word with the first.
questions.rule: Backreferences detect repetition.
questions.teaches: Beyond the tutorial: a backreference search can match inside longer words, so the text this isle contains a hit on is is unless the pattern also uses word boundaries.

questions.q: True or false: The call groupCount on a Matcher for the pattern (a)(b) returns 3, because group 0 is counted.
questions.explain: groupCount does not count group 0, so it returns 2 for this pattern.
questions.rule: groupCount excludes group 0.

questions.q: True or false: The regex dog finds a match inside the input hotdog.
questions.explain: Plain text matches wherever it occurs. Boundary matchers, shown next, restrict where a match may sit.
questions.rule: Plain text matches anywhere.

questions.q: Match each boundary construct with the position it tests.
pairs: The end of the previous match
questions.explain: Each construct names a position and consumes no characters.
questions.rule: Boundaries test positions.

questions.q: A search must succeed only when a whole line holds lowercase letters and nothing else, with at least one letter. Which regex does that?
optionExplain: Text before the letters is not ruled out.
This also accepts trailing whitespace.
Right: both ends are pinned, so the line holds only letters.
Text after the letters is not ruled out.
questions.explain: Caret and dollar together stop the pattern from matching a part of the line.
questions.rule: Pin both ends for a whole-line test.

questions.q: How many matches does the regex \Bcat find in the input cat concat?
optionExplain: The concat word contains a cat that is not at a word edge.
Right: only the cat inside concat sits at a non-boundary.
The first cat starts at a word boundary, so it is excluded.
There are only two occurrences of cat in the input.
questions.explain: The backslash capital B needs a position that is not a word edge, which the first cat lacks.
questions.rule: Capital B excludes word edges.

questions.q: The regex \b finds ____ matches, counting zero-length ones, in the input ab cd.
questions.explain: Each word has a start and an end boundary: positions 0, 2, 3 and 5.
questions.rule: Boundaries are zero-length matches.
questions.teaches: Beyond the tutorial: each word contributes two boundaries, its start and its end, and each is reported as a zero-length match.

questions.q: A parser reads the input 1,2,3,x,4, and uses the regex \G\d, with repeated find calls. How many matches does it report?
options: Three, stopping at the x
Four, skipping the x
Five, one for each digit
One, covering the whole list
optionExplain: Right: after 3, the next match must start at x, which fails.
The match cannot skip over the x; it stops at the gap.
Each match covers a digit and its comma, and the chain stops at the x, so five digit matches cannot occur.
Each match covers one digit and one comma, so the list gives several matches, not one.
questions.explain: Backslash G requires each match to start where the last one ended. The matches 1, 2 and 3 (each with its comma) chain together, and the search stops at x because no digit follows the third comma.
questions.rule: G chains matches together.
questions.teaches: Beyond the tutorial: once a search with backslash G fails to continue from the previous end, it stops; it never skips ahead to later matches.

questions.q: True or false: The regex \bdog\b finds no match in the input dog-house.
questions.explain: The hyphen is not a word character, so a boundary lies between g and the hyphen. The word dog is found.
questions.rule: Punctuation makes a word edge.

questions.q: True or false: By default, Pattern.compile of the text dog matches the input DOG.
questions.explain: Matching is case sensitive unless a flag changes it. The card next lists the flags.
questions.rule: Case matters by default.

questions.q: Match each flag with its effect.
pairs: Ignores case, assuming US-ASCII by default
Lets the dot match line terminators
Caret and dollar also match at line terminators
Ignores pattern whitespace and hash comments
questions.explain: Each flag changes one reading rule of the pattern.
questions.rule: Flag names describe the change.

questions.q: Which regex makes cat match the input CaT without passing a second argument to compile?
options: (?s)cat
(?i)cat
(?m)cat
(?x)cat
optionExplain: The s flag is DOTALL, which affects the dot, not case.
Right: the embedded i flag is CASE_INSENSITIVE.
The m flag is MULTILINE, which affects caret and dollar.
The x flag is COMMENTS, which affects whitespace.
questions.explain: The embedded form of CASE_INSENSITIVE is (?i), written at the start of the regex.
questions.rule: (?i) means ignore case.

questions.q: The regex is the letter a, then the embedded flag for ignoring case, then the letter b. Which input does it match in full?
options: AB
Ab
Ba
aB
optionExplain: The a before the flag is still case sensitive.
The a before the flag is still case sensitive.
The letters are in the wrong order for this regex.
Right: the flag affects only what follows it.
questions.explain: The embedded flag takes effect where it appears, so the first letter stays case sensitive.
questions.rule: An embedded flag works from where it appears.
questions.teaches: Beyond the tutorial: an embedded flag affects only the part of the pattern after it, so a flag in the middle leaves the earlier part unchanged.

questions.q: A long date regex is spread over several lines, with explanations after hash signs. Which flag lets the engine skip the whitespace and the comments?
options: COMMENTS
DOTALL
CANON_EQ
LITERAL
optionExplain: Right: it ignores pattern whitespace and hash-to-end-of-line text.
This changes only what the dot matches.
This compares canonical character forms.
This reads the whole pattern as plain text, comments included.
questions.explain: COMMENTS lets a long pattern be laid out and explained.
questions.rule: Use COMMENTS for readable layouts.
questions.teaches: Beyond the tutorial: with COMMENTS on, a real space in the target text must be escaped with a backslash in the pattern, since plain spaces are ignored.

questions.q: True or false: Compiling the regex a.b with LITERAL and DOTALL together lets the dot match any character, so the input axb matches.
questions.explain: LITERAL makes every pattern character plain text, so the dot is an ordinary dot and the other flags become superfluous.
questions.rule: LITERAL overrides special meaning.

questions.q: True or false: The String method replace treats its first argument as a regular expression.
questions.explain: replace takes plain text. The card next compares it with the regex-reading methods.
questions.rule: replace is literal.

questions.q: Match each method with its job.
pairs: Makes pattern text that matches a string literally
Returns the text between the matches
Tests whether the whole input matches
Returns the regex it was compiled from
questions.explain: These four methods cover quoting, splitting, whole-input testing and reading back the source.
questions.rule: Know each method's job.

questions.q: Using the String method replace to change the text aa into b inside aaa produces ____.
questions.explain: replace works from left to right on plain text: the first two a characters become b and one a remains.
questions.rule: replace goes left to right.

questions.q: The String method split is called with a comma regex on the text a,b,, (two commas at the end). How many strings come back?
optionExplain: Right: the trailing empty strings are removed.
Split with limit zero would remove both trailing empty strings, so one cannot remain.
This would keep both trailing empty strings, which needs a negative limit.
The text has only four fields at most.
questions.explain: With no limit, split uses a limit of zero and drops trailing empty strings, leaving a and b.
questions.rule: Limit zero removes trailing empties.
questions.teaches: Beyond the tutorial: passing a negative limit keeps trailing empty strings, so splitting the same text with limit minus one gives four parts.

questions.q: A search box stores the text a user typed, such as 1+1=2, in a variable named text and must find that text literally. Which call builds a suitable pattern?
options: Pattern.compile(text)
Pattern.compile(Pattern.quote(text))
Pattern.compile("[" + text + "]")
Pattern.compile(text, Pattern.DOTALL)
optionExplain: The plus is read as a quantifier here, so the text is not found literally.
Right: quote turns the typed text into a literal pattern.
This matches a single character from the listed set.
A flag about the dot does not remove the special meaning of the plus.
questions.explain: quote protects every metacharacter at once, which is handy when the text comes from a user.
questions.rule: Quote user text before searching.
questions.teaches: Beyond the tutorial: the replacement side has its own helper, Matcher.quoteReplacement, so user text needs quote in the pattern and quoteReplacement in the replacement.

questions.q: True or false: The String method matches, given the regex backslash d, returns true for the input 7a because the input contains a digit.
questions.explain: String matches tests the whole input, and the input has two characters while the regex covers one.
questions.rule: matches needs a whole-input match.

questions.q: Pattern cat is applied to the input catalog. Which Matcher call returns false?
options: lookingAt()
find()
matches()
find(0)
optionExplain: The input starts with cat, so this returns true.
The input contains cat, so this returns true.
Right: the whole input is longer than cat.
Searching from index 0 finds cat, so this returns true.
questions.explain: Only matches requires the pattern to cover everything. The card next compares all three.
questions.rule: matches is the strict one.

questions.q: Match each Matcher method with what it does.
pairs: Succeeds only if the whole input fits
Succeeds if the match begins at the start
Finds the next matching part anywhere
Gives the offset after the last matched character
questions.explain: Three study methods differ in where and how much they require; end reports a position.
questions.rule: Know the three study methods.

questions.q: The pattern is \d+ and the input is room 42. Which Matcher call returns true on a fresh Matcher?
options: matches()
lookingAt()
None, because the digits are not at the start
find()
optionExplain: The input holds letters, so the whole input does not fit.
The input starts with r, not a digit.
find searches anywhere, so the digits are found.
Right: digits occur later in the input.
questions.explain: find looks anywhere in the input, so it succeeds on the digits 42.
questions.rule: find searches anywhere.

questions.q: A Matcher for cat on the input cat has called find twice; the first returned true and the second returned false. What does a later call to start() do?
options: Throws an IllegalStateException
Returns minus one
Returns 0, the last start
Returns the length of the input
optionExplain: Right: there is no current match.
Java does not report absence with minus one here.
The failed search leaves no match to report.
The method reports a match position, not the input length.
questions.explain: After find fails there is no previous match, so asking for its start is an error.
questions.rule: Index methods need a current match.
questions.teaches: Beyond the tutorial: calling start() or end() when no match exists throws an IllegalStateException.

questions.q: A website needs a Matcher method for each job. Sort each job by the best method.

items.t: Check that a whole postcode field is valid
Count how often a word occurs in an essay
Locate each phone number inside a paragraph
Confirm a username holds only letters
List every date in a log file
Reject a code that has stray text after it

questions.explain: Validation needs the whole input to fit; searching needs a hit anywhere.
questions.rule: Validate with matches, search with find.
questions.teaches: Beyond the tutorial: validating with find lets junk around a valid part pass, so whole-input checks should use matches.

questions.q: True or false: After a Matcher finds cat in the input cat, end() returns 2, the index of the letter t.
questions.explain: end() gives the offset just after the last matched character, so it returns 3.
questions.rule: end is exclusive.

questions.q: Pattern a, input banana, replacement o. What does replaceAll give?
options: bonana
bonono
ooooo
banano
optionExplain: This is the result of replaceFirst.
Right: each a in banana is replaced by o, giving bonono.
Only the letter a is replaced, not every letter.
Only the last letter would change, which does not match the method.
questions.explain: replaceAll swaps every match. The card next compares it with replaceFirst.
questions.rule: All matches are replaced.

questions.q: Put the steps of a manual replacement loop in order.
items: Create a Matcher and a result buffer
Call find in a loop
Call appendReplacement for each match
After the loop call appendTail
questions.explain: The loop builds the output piece by piece, and appendTail adds the leftover text.
questions.rule: Loop, replace each, then add the tail.

questions.q: The regex \d+ is used with replaceAll("#") on the input a1b22c333. The result is ____.
questions.explain: Each run of digits is one match, so three runs give three hash signs.
questions.rule: One run, one match.

questions.q: The pattern (\d+) is used with the replacement [$1] and replaceAll on the input a1b22. What is the result?
optionExplain: The dollar-one is not kept as text.
Only the pattern text, not the whole input, would remain.
Right: dollar-one inserts the text captured by group 1.
Group 1 holds the digits, so the brackets are not empty.
questions.explain: In a replacement string, dollar followed by a group number inserts the captured text.
questions.rule: Dollar-n inserts group n.
questions.teaches: Beyond the tutorial: in a replacement string, a dollar sign followed by a group number inserts the text captured by that group.

questions.q: A template reads Cost: PRICE. A program calls replaceAll with the pattern PRICE and the user-typed replacement $5. What is the risk?
options: An exception, since $5 names a group
It inserts the text $5 exactly as the user typed it
Only the first PRICE is replaced, and the others stay
The result is Cost: 5, because the dollar sign is dropped
optionExplain: Right: there is no group 5, so the call fails.
The dollar sign is special, so the typed text is not inserted as it stands.
replaceAll replaces every match.
The dollar sign is not silently dropped.
questions.explain: The replacement treats dollar as a group reference. Matcher.quoteReplacement makes the text literal.
questions.rule: Quote replacement text from users.
questions.teaches: Beyond the tutorial: unquoted user text with a dollar sign in a replacement can throw an exception when it names a group that does not exist.

questions.q: True or false: A loop calls find and appendReplacement but omits the appendTail call. The built result is the same as replaceAll.
questions.explain: Without appendTail the text after the last match is missing, so the result is shorter than the replaceAll output.
questions.rule: appendTail adds the rest.

questions.q: True or false: Pattern.compile must be wrapped in a try block or declared, because PatternSyntaxException is a checked exception.
questions.explain: It is unchecked, so no handling is forced. The card next lists what it can tell you.
questions.rule: Unchecked means optional handling.

questions.q: Match each PatternSyntaxException method with what it returns.
pairs: The position of the error in the pattern
A multi-line text with description, index, pattern and a marker
questions.explain: Each method exposes one piece of the error report.
questions.rule: Four methods, four pieces.

questions.q: A search box passes the text a user types straight to Pattern.compile, and the user types [a-z. Which response helps the user most?
options: Let the exception end the program
Declare it in a throws clause so the compiler is satisfied
Catch the exception and show getDescription and getIndex
Search for the typed text as plain characters instead
optionExplain: A typo would crash the tool.
The compiler never required it, and the user still sees no message.
Right: the user sees what is wrong and where.
Silently changing the meaning hides the mistake.
questions.explain: Catching the unchecked exception turns a typo into feedback.
questions.rule: Catch it where the pattern comes from users.
questions.teaches: Beyond the tutorial: PatternSyntaxException extends IllegalArgumentException, so a catch for IllegalArgumentException around compile also covers it.

questions.q: The pattern *abc starts with a quantifier that has nothing before it. The index that getIndex reports is ____.
questions.explain: As in the tutorial's ?i)foo example, a dangling metacharacter at the very start is reported at index 0.
questions.rule: A dangling metacharacter is reported where it sits.
questions.teaches: Beyond the tutorial: a quantifier with nothing before it, such as a leading star, is reported as a dangling metacharacter in the same way as the leading question mark.

questions.q: A teammate says: if my code compiles the user's pattern without PatternSyntaxException, I know it finds what the user wants. What does this overlook?
options: The compiler would reject any pattern that the user could mean
A well-formed pattern can still match different text than intended
A checked exception is hidden inside the same compile call and must be caught
Only patterns that are compiled with flags can count as valid
optionExplain: Valid patterns compile normally.
Right: the exception checks syntax, not meaning.
The exception is unchecked.
Flags only change how a pattern is read; whether it is well-formed does not depend on them.
questions.explain: Syntax and meaning are separate: a valid regex such as digits-or-nothing can still accept the wrong input.
questions.rule: Valid is not the same as correct.
questions.teaches: Beyond the tutorial: a syntactically valid pattern can still be wrong in meaning, and only trying it on sample inputs reveals that.

questions.q: True or false: calling getClass on a variable whose declared type is an interface returns the Class object of that interface.
questions.explain: getClass reports the real runtime class of the object, which is a concrete class that implements the interface. The card next shows how.
questions.rule: getClass reports the runtime class, not the declared type.

questions.q: The method inherited from Object that returns an object's actual runtime class is called ____.
questions.explain: Every object has getClass because it is declared in Object.
questions.rule: getClass comes from Object.

questions.q: A variable named items is declared as Collection but holds a new ArrayList. What does items.getClass describe?
options: The Collection interface, because that is the declared type
The ArrayList class, because that is what the object really is
The Object class, because every object descends from it
Nothing, because the call does not compile on an interface type
optionExplain: Tempting since the declared type is what the compiler sees, but getClass is resolved at run time on the actual object.
The object was created from ArrayList, and getClass reports exactly that.
Object is a superclass of everything, but getClass does not report the top of the hierarchy.
Every reference type inherits getClass from Object, so the call compiles.
questions.explain: The runtime class of the object decides the result, whatever the variable's declared type is.
questions.rule: Declared type does not change what getClass returns.

questions.q: True or false: for a normal JDK class such as String, getClassLoader returns null, which signals the bootstrap loader and not a problem.
questions.explain: According to the tutorial, JDK classes sit in the bootstrap loader, and its result is null.
questions.rule: A null loader marks a bootstrap-loaded JDK class.
questions.teaches: Beyond the tutorial: because null is a valid answer here, code that calls a method on the result of getClassLoader must check for null first, or it hits a NullPointerException for JDK classes.

questions.q: Sort each class by the loader a normal compiled run would report for its Class object.

items.t: java.util.HashMap
java.lang.Integer
An Invoice class you compiled and ran from your classpath
A Cart class in your own application
java.util.List
A Receipt class written in your project

questions.explain: JDK types come from the bootstrap loader and report null; classes you wrote report the application loader.
questions.rule: JDK classes report null; your own classes do not.
questions.teaches: Beyond the tutorial: a null loader is a hint, not proof of a JDK class, because JDK classes outside the base module can come from the platform loader, which is not null.

questions.q: True or false: when you call a static method through reflection, the tutorial passes the Class object of the declaring type as the first argument to invoke.
questions.explain: A static method has no target object, so the tutorial passes null in that position. The card next shows the pattern.
questions.rule: Static methods get null as the target.

questions.q: By the tutorial's convention, the target argument passed to invoke for a static method is ____.
questions.explain: Instance methods take the target object there; static methods have no target, so null is used.
questions.rule: Static call: invoke(null, arguments).

questions.q: A Method named rev stands for the static method Collections.reverse, which takes a List named names. Which call performs the reversal?
options: rev.invoke(names)
rev.invoke(names, null)
rev.invoke(null, names)
rev.invoke(null, Collections.class)
optionExplain: This treats names as the target object, which is how an instance method is called, so the argument list would be missing.
This swaps the two positions, so null becomes the argument and the list becomes the target.
Right: the target slot holds null because the method is static, and the list follows as the argument.
The Class object lands in the argument position where the list belongs, so the argument type does not fit.
questions.explain: The first slot is the target, which a static method does not have, and the arguments follow.
questions.rule: invoke(target or null, arguments...).

questions.q: One catch of ReflectiveOperationException can handle which of these failures? Select all that apply.
options: NoSuchMethodException when the name or parameter types do not match
IllegalAccessException when the member may not be used
NumberFormatException when text is not a valid number
ArithmeticException when a division by zero happens
IllegalStateException when an object is in the wrong state
optionExplain: Right: the tutorial lists it as one of the reflection failures covered.
Right: it is the other failure the tutorial names under that parent type.
It is a runtime exception from parsing, unrelated to reflection lookups.
It comes from arithmetic, not from looking up or accessing members.
It is a general runtime exception that the reflection parent type does not cover.
questions.explain: Since Java 7 the reflection-specific failures share one parent, so a single catch is enough.
questions.rule: Catch ReflectiveOperationException for lookup and access failures.
questions.teaches: Catching only the shared parent hides which failure happened, so log the exception type or message if you need to tell a missing method from a forbidden one.

questions.q: A test helper must run every public no-argument method of an object whose name starts with check. Which design fits the tutorial's advice?
options: Take the first matching method that getMethods returns and run only that one
Assume the methods come back in alphabetical order and number the results by it
Use a stream with a lambda that calls invoke and silently ignore any exceptions
Loop over every match, invoke each one, and catch the reflection exception
optionExplain: The order is not guaranteed, so the first match may differ between JDK builds and some checks would be skipped.
Method order is unspecified, so numbering by assumed order may give different results elsewhere.
A lambda cannot throw the checked exceptions of invoke without awkward wrapping, which is why the tutorial uses a plain loop.
A loop handles checked exceptions naturally and does not depend on any order.
questions.explain: The tutorial uses for-each because of checked exceptions and warns that method order is not guaranteed.
questions.rule: Loop, catch, and do not rely on method order.
questions.teaches: Beyond the tutorial: collect the matches and sort them by name before running them if you want the same output on every JDK.

questions.q: True or false: no code can change a private final field of an object after it is created.
questions.explain: Reflection can do it in the right conditions, which the card next sets out.
questions.rule: Deep reflection can reach private state when conditions allow.

questions.q: Deep reflection into a package works only when that package's module is ____ to your module.
questions.explain: The tutorial says the module must be open to yours for deep reflection to succeed.
questions.rule: Deep access needs an open package.

questions.q: A class Ticket has a private final field named seat, and its package is open to your code. Ticket is then rewritten as a record with a component named seat. What happens to code that reflectively overwrites seat on an existing object?
options: It still works as before, because the package is open to the caller
It works only if the field is first made non-final by other code
It fails, since deep reflection cannot change a record's properties
It works for static fields of the record but not for instance fields
optionExplain: The open package is needed, but the tutorial says records block the change anyway.
Finality was not the obstacle in the tutorial, where a private final field was changed; the record itself is the obstacle.
According to the tutorial, converting to a record means deep reflection can no longer change its properties.
Records have no such static and instance split in the tutorial's account; the block applies to the properties.
questions.explain: An open package is necessary but not enough here: the record stops the change.
questions.rule: An open package does not rescue a record.

questions.q: A colleague says: reflection changed a private final field in our own class, so the same code will also work on private fields inside a JDK module. What is the flaw?
options: Reflection cannot touch private fields in any class, so the demo must be wrong
Final fields can be changed only in classes that you wrote yourself
Reflection works on public methods only, so private fields are out of reach
It depends on the package being open, and a JDK package is not open by default
optionExplain: The tutorial's own demo changes a private field, so this is false.
Nothing in the tutorial ties the change to who wrote the class; the module setting is what matters.
Shallow access is limited to public members, but deep access goes further.
Module encapsulation decides, and the add-opens option exists for the case when it is not open.
questions.explain: Your own class worked because nothing closed it off, but deep reflection must pass module boundaries. Beyond the tutorial: JDK packages are not open to application code by default.
questions.rule: Check the module before assuming deep access works.
questions.teaches: Beyond the tutorial: code that works in a plain classpath demo may fail once the same class sits in a named module whose package is not open to the caller.

questions.q: True or false: opening a package for reflection costs the module author nothing, since only the caller's code is affected.
questions.explain: Once outside code depends on field names and types, the author cannot change them freely without breaking that code, which is why authors usually refuse.
questions.rule: Opening a package exposes internals.
questions.teaches: Beyond the tutorial: a module can open a package only to named modules, which limits the exposure to the callers it trusts.

questions.q: Sort each mistake by when the problem shows up.

items.t: Calling a method that is not declared, written directly in source
Passing a misspelled method name as a String to a lookup
Reflectively writing a field of a package that is not open
Using a variable that was never declared

questions.explain: Direct source is checked by the compiler; names held in Strings and module openness are checked only when the program runs.
questions.rule: Reflection moves checks from compile time to run time.
questions.teaches: Beyond the tutorial: a typo in a String name is invisible to the compiler, so code that uses reflection needs tests that actually run each lookup.

questions.q: A program must create an object from a class name it reads from a text file while running. Which Java feature is designed for jobs like this?
questions.explain: Reflection is the feature that inspects and uses types at run time. The card next shows its uses and costs.
options: Operator overloading
Static imports
Reflection
Method overloading
optionExplain: Java has no operator overloading, and it would not help to find a class by name.
Static imports shorten names of members known at compile time; they do not look classes up from text.
Reflection can examine and create types that are only known at run time, such as a class named in a file.
Overloading chooses among methods with the same name at compile time; it cannot create an object from text.
questions.rule: Use reflection when ordinary code cannot do the job, because it is slower, can be blocked, and exposes internals.

questions.q: True or false: According to the tutorial, reflection should be chosen whenever it is available, because reflective calls run faster than ordinary calls.
questions.explain: The tutorial says the opposite: reflective operations are slower because some JVM optimizations cannot be applied, so plain code is preferred when it can do the job.
questions.rule: Prefer plain code when it can do the job.

questions.q: A pricing service calls the method getDiscount of a class it already knows, many thousands of times a second. A developer proposes reaching that method through reflection. What fits the tutorial's advice?
questions.explain: A known class and a hot path are the cases where the tutorial's advice to avoid reflection applies most strongly.
questions.rule: Known at compile time means call it directly.
options: Call it directly, since the class is known and reflection adds overhead
Use reflection, because reflected calls skip checks and therefore run faster than direct calls
Use reflection, because it keeps the discount data safely private from other code
Use reflection, because the tutorial names it the preferred way to call known methods
optionExplain: The class is known at compile time and the call is frequent, so plain code is better and faster.
Reflection does the opposite: dynamic resolution blocks some JVM optimizations.
Reflection can reach private members, which exposes data rather than protecting it.
The tutorial recommends avoiding reflection when an operation can be done without it.

questions.q: Which of these are costs the tutorial attaches to reflection? Select all that apply.
questions.explain: Slower dynamic resolution and module restrictions are named costs; reaching private members is a risk, not an inability.
questions.rule: Dynamic resolution costs speed; modules can restrict access.
questions.teaches: Beyond the tutorial: caching a Method or Field object instead of looking it up on every call removes part of the lookup cost.
options: Some JVM optimizations cannot be applied
Reflection cannot read private fields at all
A module can refuse reflective access to its internals
Reflected code has to be recompiled for every call
optionExplain: Right: types resolved dynamically block some optimizations.
Reflection can reach private members; that is part of the risk, not a limit.
Right: modules can block reflective access, a design consideration the tutorial stresses.
Nothing is recompiled per call; the overhead comes from dynamic resolution.

questions.q: A tool uses reflection to read a private field inside a vendor library. The vendor ships a new release that reorganizes that class. What does the tutorial's warning about internals suggest for the tool?
questions.explain: The tutorial says reflection can break portability and change behavior when the platform is upgraded, since it bypasses abstractions.
questions.hint: Is a private field something the vendor promised to keep?
options: It may break, since reflection bypasses the abstraction the vendor promised
It keeps working, since private fields are part of the library's public contract
It keeps working, because reflection updates itself to match the new layout
It fails at compile time, because reflective code is checked against the library
optionExplain: Private members are not a promise, so a tool that depends on them can break when the library changes.
Private fields are exactly what a vendor may change freely.
Reflection looks things up as they are at run time; it does not adjust the tool's assumptions.
Reflective lookups happen at run time, so a mismatch shows up then, not at compile time.
questions.rule: Use reflection when ordinary code cannot do the job, because it is slower, can be blocked, and exposes internals.

questions.q: A team lists jobs for their code. Sort each job by whether reflection suits it or plain code is the better choice.
questions.explain: The first three need to find or inspect types that are unknown when the code is written. The last three use members known at compile time.
questions.rule: Reflection is for what is unknown at compile time.
questions.teaches: Beyond the tutorial: tools often do both, reflecting once to discover members and then calling them through ordinary interface code, so the reflection cost is paid once.

items.t: A debugger that must show the private members of any class
A test tool that calls every discoverable method of classes it has never seen
A loader that builds objects of classes named in a settings file
Calling a known public getter of a class you wrote
Adding two integer variables
Calling a known method inside a loop that runs constantly

questions.q: Which expression gives the Class object that represents the primitive type double?
questions.explain: Primitives are reached through the class literal. The card next shows the other routes.
options: double.getClass()
double.class
Class.forName with the text double
new Class of double
optionExplain: A primitive has no methods, so this does not compile.
A class literal works on primitive type names and needs no instance.
forName cannot be used for primitive names.
Class objects are made by the JVM, not by calling a constructor.
questions.rule: Use getClass() for an object, a class literal for a type known at compile time, and forName for a name held as text.

questions.q: True or false: Calling getClass() on an int variable returns the Class for int.
questions.explain: Primitives are not objects, so a method cannot be called on them. The Class for int comes from int.class or Integer.TYPE.
questions.rule: getClass() is for reference types only.

questions.q: A method receives a parameter declared as Object named item. It must report the runtime class of whatever object arrived. Which expression does that?
questions.explain: getClass() reports what the object is at run time, while a class literal names a type fixed in the source.
options: Object.class
Class.forName(item)
Void.TYPE
item.getClass()
optionExplain: Object.class is the Class for Object itself, whatever item holds.
forName needs a text name, not an object.
Void.TYPE is the Class for void, unrelated to item.
getClass() on the variable returns the class of the actual object.
questions.rule: Use getClass() for an object, a class literal for a type known at compile time, and forName for a name held as text.

questions.q: According to the tutorial, Class.forPrimitiveName returns ____ when it is given text that is not a primitive name, such as banana.
questions.explain: It returns null for a string that is not a primitive name, and throws NullPointerException if it is given null.
questions.rule: forName throws for a missing name; forPrimitiveName returns null.
questions.teaches: The two lookups signal a missing result differently: forName throws ClassNotFoundException, while forPrimitiveName returns null, so one needs a catch and the other a null check.

questions.q: A variable declared with the interface type Set refers to a HashSet object. What does getClass() on that variable return?
questions.explain: The object decides the answer, not the variable's declared type.
options: The Class for HashSet
The Class for Set
The Class for Object
null, because interfaces have no Class
optionExplain: getClass() reports the runtime class, here HashSet.
The declared type of the variable does not matter to getClass().
Object is a superclass of HashSet, not its runtime class.
Interfaces do have Class objects, and this call concerns the object's class anyway.
questions.rule: Use getClass() for an object, a class literal for a type known at compile time, and forName for a name held as text.

questions.q: A tool author needs a Class object in four different situations. Match each situation to the expression that fits.
questions.explain: Each route fits what you already hold: an instance, a type name in the source, or only text. TYPE bridges from a wrapper to its primitive.
questions.rule: Pick the route by what you already hold.
questions.teaches: Beyond the tutorial: a class literal is checked by the compiler, so a typo in the type name is caught earlier than a typo in text given to forName.
pairs: An object is held in a variable and you need its runtime class
The primitive long is known when writing the code
The class name exists only as text read at run time
The primitive double, starting from its wrapper class

questions.q: A class declares one public and one private nested class. Which call would be expected to reveal the private one?
questions.explain: Declared forms see every access level. The card next shows the whole family.
options: getDeclaredClasses()
getClasses() on the same class
getSuperclass() on the same class
getInterfaces() on the same class
optionExplain: The Declared form lists member classes of any access, declared in the class itself.
The plain form returns public member classes only.
getSuperclass() returns the parent class, not nested classes.
getInterfaces() returns interfaces the class lists, not nested classes.
questions.rule: Methods with Declared in the name look only at the class itself at any access level, and an anonymous class has a null declaring class but a non-null enclosing class.

questions.q: True or false: getSuperclass() called on the Class for Object returns null.
questions.explain: Object has no parent, so there is nothing to return.
questions.rule: No superclass means null.

questions.q: Class Report extends Document and implements Printable. Document implements Serializable. According to the tutorial, what does getInterfaces() on the Class of Report return?
questions.explain: Inherited interfaces are not listed; you would walk up with getSuperclass() to find them.
questions.rule: getInterfaces() shows direct interfaces only.
options: Printable and Serializable
Only Serializable
Only Printable
No interfaces, since they must come from a parent
optionExplain: Serializable is inherited from Document, so it is not listed.
Serializable belongs to Document, not to Report.
getInterfaces() lists only what the class itself implements directly.
Report lists Printable itself, so the list is not empty.

questions.q: According to the tutorial, calling getInterfaces() on the Class of an array type shows which interfaces?
questions.explain: Array classes fit the same model as other classes.
questions.rule: Arrays extend Object and implement Cloneable and Serializable.
questions.teaches: Beyond the tutorial: getSuperclass on an array class returns Object, which completes the picture of arrays as ordinary classes.
options: Cloneable and Serializable
Comparable and Iterable
List and Serializable
None, because arrays are not classes
optionExplain: Arrays extend Object and implement Cloneable and Serializable.
Arrays do not implement Comparable or Iterable.
Arrays do not implement List; they implement Cloneable and Serializable.
Array types do have Class objects and these interfaces.

questions.q: The nested class Line in Order is changed from public to private, and Audit stays private. What does getClasses() on Order then list for Order's own nested classes?
questions.explain: Changing the access changes what the plain form can see, while getDeclaredClasses() would still list both.
questions.hint: Which access level does the plain form report?
options: Both of them, because they are still members of Order
Only Audit, because it was private before the change
Both of them, plus the nested classes of Object
None, since getClasses() reports public ones only
optionExplain: Membership is not enough; the plain form needs public access.
Audit was never public, so it was never listed.
Object adds no nested classes here; the plain form adds public ones only.
With no public member class left, nothing from Order itself appears.
questions.rule: Methods with Declared in the name look only at the class itself at any access level, and an anonymous class has a null declaring class but a non-null enclosing class.

questions.q: A plug-in loader inspects classes. Sort each call by whether the tutorial says it gives null or gives a class.
questions.explain: Null means there is no such class: Object has no parent, and anonymous and top-level classes are not members of another class. An anonymous class still has an enclosing class.
questions.rule: Null is an answer, not a failure.
questions.teaches: Beyond the tutorial: getEnclosingClass returns null for a top-level class, so a null from it means the class is not nested at all.

items.t: getSuperclass() on the Class for Object
getDeclaringClass() on an anonymous class
getEnclosingClass() on an anonymous class written inside Menu
getSuperclass() on the Class for String
getDeclaringClass() on a public nested member class
getDeclaringClass() on a top-level class

questions.q: What does getName() return for the Class of a one-dimensional int array?
questions.explain: Arrays use a coded form. The card next shows the code table.
options: int[]
I
[I
java.lang.int
optionExplain: int[] is how the source writes it; getName() uses a coded form for arrays.
Without the bracket it would name the element type alone, which is not an array name.
A bracket marks the array and I is the code for int.
There is no class named java.lang.int.
questions.rule: Simple and canonical names follow the source, the type name exists even for anonymous classes, and getName encodes arrays with brackets and letter codes.

questions.q: Match each primitive type to the letter getName() uses for it inside an array name.
questions.explain: Z is boolean and J is long because the letters B and L are already taken by byte and by reference types (the reason is beyond the tutorial).
questions.rule: Boolean is Z and long is J.

questions.q: For a two-dimensional array of byte, getName() returns two opening brackets followed by the letter ____.
questions.explain: Byte is B. Two brackets show two levels of nesting.
questions.rule: One bracket per dimension, then the element code.

questions.q: A program prints names of arbitrary classes, including lambda classes. According to the tutorial, which call can return null for a lambda class?
questions.explain: Only the canonical name is missing for lambda and anonymous classes.
questions.rule: Canonical name can be null.
questions.teaches: Beyond the tutorial: the name of a lambda class contains compiler-generated text, so it is fine to print but unwise to parse.
options: getTypeName() on the lambda's Class
getName() on the lambda's Class
getSimpleName() on the lambda's Class
getCanonicalName()
optionExplain: Lambda classes do have a type name, the compiler generated one.
For a non-array class getName() matches getTypeName(), so it exists.
The tutorial reports the declaring class name for a lambda, though it may vary.
Lambda classes have no canonical name.

questions.q: Put the pieces of the getName() text for the Class of a two-dimensional String array in order.
questions.explain: Brackets come first, one per dimension, then L, the name, and a closing semicolon.
questions.rule: Brackets, L, name, semicolon.
items: Two opening square brackets
The letter L
java.lang.String
A semicolon

questions.q: A reviewer says Class.forName with the text D returns the Class for double, because D is the code for double in array names. What is wrong with that claim?
questions.explain: For the Class of double use double.class, Double.TYPE, or forPrimitiveName where it exists.
questions.rule: Codes live inside array names.
questions.teaches: According to the tutorial, Class.forName does accept an array name written with the codes, so the text bracket D gives the Class for an array of double.
options: D is the code for float, not for double, so the result differs
Letter codes exist only in array names, and forName rejects primitives
forName only accepts simple names, so it rejects any fully qualified text
forName returns the wrapper class Double, not the primitive double
optionExplain: D is the code for double; float is F.
Codes are part of array-name syntax; a bare code is not a name forName accepts.
forName takes fully qualified names, and it does accept array names with codes.
forName fails for primitive names; it does not return a wrapper for them.

questions.q: A reflected modifiers value is a single int. What does each bit of that int stand for?
questions.explain: The int packs flags into bits. The card next shows how to decode it.
options: One modifier, such as public
One parameter of the member that was reflected
One annotation placed on the member reflected
One character of the name of the member
optionExplain: Each bit is a flag that is set when the modifier applies.
Parameters are described by other objects, not by modifier bits.
Annotations are read through different methods.
The name is returned as text, not packed into the modifier int.
questions.rule: Read modifiers with getModifiers() and decode the int with Modifier, or call accessFlags() on newer platforms for a readable set.

questions.q: True or false: The class Modifier has static methods that decode the int returned by getModifiers().
questions.explain: Modifier is the intended tool, so you rarely read bits by hand.
questions.rule: Decode with Modifier.

questions.q: Code runs int m = String.class.getModifiers(). Which check does the tutorial's description of String lead you to expect to be true?
questions.explain: The tutorial's example reports String as final and non-abstract.
questions.hint: Which keyword stops other classes from extending String?
options: Modifier.isAbstract(m)
Modifier.isPrivate(m)
Modifier.isStatic(m)
Modifier.isFinal(m)
optionExplain: String is final but not abstract, so this check is false.
String is a public class, not private.
Static is a bit that belongs to nested members, and String is a top-level class.
String is final and not abstract.
questions.rule: Read modifiers with getModifiers() and decode the int with Modifier, or call accessFlags() on newer platforms for a readable set.

questions.q: A developer reflects on the interface Collection and finds abstract reported although the source did not write that keyword. Why?
questions.explain: What reflection reports is the compiled class.
questions.rule: Reflection shows the compiled class.
questions.teaches: A reflected modifier set describes the compiled class, which can carry modifiers the source never wrote, so reflected output may not match the source text exactly.
options: getModifiers() invents abstract for any type with methods
The compiler adds abstract to every interface
Every library type is abstract
The JVM marks a type abstract when it is not final
optionExplain: Reflection reports what the compiled class has; it does not invent flags.
The compiler adds the abstract modifier to interfaces.
String is not abstract, so library types are not all abstract.
A non-final class is not marked abstract for that reason.

questions.q: A program calls accessFlags(), which according to the tutorial arrived in Java SE 20, on a platform older than that. What should be expected?
questions.explain: Check the platform release before relying on newer reflection methods.
questions.hint: Where does the tutorial say accessFlags() begins?
options: It works, but returns an empty set of flags
It quietly falls back to getModifiers() instead
The method is missing; use getModifiers() instead
It is available on every release of the platform
optionExplain: Nothing in the tutorial suggests an empty fallback; the method is simply not there.
There is no automatic fallback; you must choose the older API.
A method added in SE 20 is absent from earlier releases.
The tutorial ties accessFlags() to Java SE 20.
questions.rule: Read modifiers with getModifiers() and decode the int with Modifier, or call accessFlags() on newer platforms for a readable set.

questions.q: A constants class declares: public static final int LIMIT = 5. For the Field of LIMIT, which checks on getModifiers() are true? Select all that apply.
questions.explain: One int can have several bits set, so public, static and final all report true.
questions.rule: One int, many bits.
questions.teaches: A constant-like field reports public, static and final at once, because one modifier int can have several bits set.
options: Modifier.isAbstract(modifiers)
Modifier.isStatic(modifiers)
Modifier.isPrivate(modifiers)
Modifier.isPublic(modifiers)
Modifier.isFinal(modifiers)
optionExplain: A field cannot be abstract.
Right: the field is declared static.
The field is declared public, so private is false.
Right: the field is declared public.
Right: the field is declared final.

questions.q: You need the Field object for a private field of a class. Which call is meant for that?
questions.explain: Declared forms see all access levels. The card next shows the four lookups.
options: getDeclaredField(name)
getField(name) on the same Class
getFields() on the same Class
getSuperclass() on the same Class
optionExplain: The Declared form sees private fields of the class itself.
The plain form returns public fields only.
getFields() also returns public fields only, as an array.
getSuperclass() returns a parent class, not a field.
questions.rule: Declared lookups see every access level of one class; plain lookups see the public fields of the class and its parents.

questions.q: True or false: getFields() returns private fields declared in the class.
questions.explain: getFields() returns public fields only, including inherited ones.
questions.rule: Plain lookups are public only.

questions.q: Class Shape has a private field color and a public field sides, and extends Figure, which has a public field id and a private field secret. Which call returns exactly sides and id?
questions.explain: Combine the two axes: own or inherited, any access or public only.
questions.rule: Public and inherited use the plain form.
options: Shape.class.getDeclaredFields()
Figure.class.getDeclaredFields()
Shape.class.getFields()
Shape.class.getField with the name secret
optionExplain: That returns color and sides, Shape's own fields at every access level.
That returns id and secret, Figure's own fields.
getFields() gives public fields of Shape and of its parents.
secret is private, so a plain lookup cannot find it.

questions.q: In a generic class Box of T, a field is declared as T item. What do getType() and getGenericType().getTypeName() give for it?
questions.explain: The generic view shows the declaration, not the arguments of one object.
questions.rule: Reflection shows declarations.
questions.teaches: A Field records the declaration, not any particular use, so a Field alone cannot tell you whether one Box object holds strings or numbers.
options: T, then Object
Object, then Object
String, then T
Object, then T
optionExplain: The erased type is Object and the generic form keeps T, not the other way round.
The generic form keeps the name T.
No type argument such as String is stored in the field.
getType() is erased to Object; the generic type shows the declaration as written.

questions.q: The field balance in Account is changed from private to public. What changes for getField(balance)?
questions.explain: Access level, not inheritance alone, decides what the plain lookups see.
questions.hint: Which access level do the plain forms accept?
options: It still fails, because balance is not inherited
It now succeeds, since the field is public
It returns null instead of throwing
It now returns every public field
optionExplain: Plain lookups cover the class itself as well as parents.
Plain lookups find public fields of the class itself too.
A missing field leads to NoSuchFieldException, not null; here the field would be found.
The singular form returns one Field, the one you named.
questions.rule: Declared lookups see every access level of one class; plain lookups see the public fields of the class and its parents.

questions.q: A class Car extends Vehicle. Sort each field by whether getFields() on Car finds it.
questions.explain: getFields() keeps public fields of Car and of its parents. Private, protected and package-level fields are left out.
questions.rule: Plain lookups mean public.
questions.teaches: getFields keeps public fields only, so protected and package-level fields are left out along with private ones, even though code in the same package could use them.

items.t: A public field wheels declared in Car
A private field vin declared in Car
A public field brand declared in Vehicle
A protected field fuel declared in Car
A package-level field tag declared in Car
A public field tires declared in a grandparent class of Vehicle

questions.q: Field.get needs the object passed in. Why?
questions.explain: The Field is shared, so the instance travels with each call. The card next shows the details.
options: So that reflection can copy the object before reading it
A Field belongs to the Class and is shared by all instances
Because a Field stores the value held by exactly one instance
So that access checks know which caller is asking for the value
optionExplain: Reflection reads the value in place; nothing is copied.
One Field serves every instance, so you say which instance to read.
A Field holds no value; it describes the field.
Access checks look at the caller, not at the object you pass.
questions.rule: Pass the instance to get and set, use setAccessible(true) to pass access checks, and expect records and static final fields to stay unwritable.

questions.q: True or false: setAccessible(true) turns a private field into a public one.
questions.explain: It only suppresses the access checks; the declared visibility stays private.
questions.rule: setAccessible skips checks, it does not change visibility.

questions.q: Person has a private int age. From another class, code has Field f = Person.class.getDeclaredField("age") and a Person p. Which sequence reads the age without an access exception?
questions.explain: Two steps: suppress the check, then pass the instance.
questions.rule: Suppress, then read with the instance.
options: f.getInt(p) with no other call
f.setAccessible(true); then f.getInt(null)
Person.class.getField("age") then f.getInt(p)
f.setAccessible(true); then f.getInt(p)
optionExplain: Without setAccessible the private access fails.
null stands for no instance, which a non-static field cannot be read from.
getField finds public fields only, so private age is not found.
The check must be suppressed first, then the instance is passed.

questions.q: A field is declared as Integer age (a wrapper) instead of int age. Code that used f.getInt(p) successfully now runs against it. What happens, according to the tutorial?
questions.explain: Choose the accessor by the field's declared type.
questions.rule: Match the accessor to the declared type.
questions.teaches: The primitive accessors check the declared type exactly, so boxing does not bridge int and Integer; for a wrapper field use get and cast.
options: It returns the unboxed value of the Integer field
It returns 0 if the Integer in the field is null
It throws an exception, as the accessor matches primitives
It fails to compile, because the field type is a wrapper
optionExplain: Boxing does not bridge the two types here.
No special null handling is described; the type mismatch throws.
The primitive accessors match primitive fields.
The mismatch is found while running, not while compiling.

questions.q: The class User is rewritten as a record with the same component name, and a program calls setAccessible(true) and then Field.set on that component. What happens?
questions.explain: Records are one place where setAccessible(true) does not help.
questions.hint: Look at the final-field exceptions in the card.
options: The write still fails with IllegalAccessException
The write succeeds, because setAccessible(true) removes all checks
The write succeeds but prints a warning
The write is ignored silently
optionExplain: Record fields cannot be modified through reflection, even after setAccessible(true).
For ordinary final fields it does suppress the check; records are the exception.
The warning belongs to ordinary final fields from JDK 26; for records the write fails.
The failure is an exception, not a silent skip.
questions.rule: Pass the instance to get and set, use setAccessible(true) to pass access checks, and expect records and static final fields to stay unwritable.

questions.q: After setAccessible(true), which of these fields can be changed reflectively, according to the tutorial?
questions.explain: setAccessible(true) removes access and final checks for ordinary instance fields, but record fields and static final fields stay unwritable.
questions.rule: Records and static final fields stay unwritable.

items.t: A private final instance field of an ordinary class
A private non-final instance field
An instance field of a record
A static final field

questions.q: A mapping library fills private fields of application classes with setAccessible(true). The application is packaged as a named module that does not open its packages. What should be expected?
questions.explain: The module declaration decides whether framework-style reflection can work.
questions.rule: Closed modules refuse setAccessible.
questions.teaches: Frameworks that fill private fields from outside depend on the application opening its packages, so the module declaration is part of making reflection-based libraries work.
options: setAccessible fails unless the package is opened
It succeeds, because named modules are open to reflection by default
It succeeds, but only for fields that are declared final
It succeeds and also turns the private fields into public ones
optionExplain: A named module is closed to reflection by default.
The default for a named module is closed.
The final check is separate from the module check.
setAccessible never changes visibility.

questions.q: You want the Method for List.get, which takes an int index. Which parameter type should the lookup pass?
questions.explain: Lookups need the declared types. The card next shows the exact-match rule.
options: int.class
Integer.class
Number.class
Object.class
optionExplain: The method is declared with the primitive int, and the lookup must match it exactly.
Integer.class names the wrapper and throws NoSuchMethodException here.
Number is not the declared type.
Object is for erased type parameters, not for a declared int.
questions.rule: Name the method and give the exact erased parameter types; use Declared forms for own methods at any access, plain forms for public ones including inherited.

questions.q: True or false: getMethods() returns private methods declared in the class.
questions.explain: getMethods() returns public methods, including inherited ones. getDeclaredMethods() is the one that reaches private methods.
questions.rule: Plain forms mean public.

questions.q: According to the tutorial's note on type erasure, which call locates the add method of a List of String?
questions.explain: Erasure removes the type argument before reflection sees the method.
questions.rule: Erased means Object.
options: getMethod("add", String.class)
getMethod("add", Object.class)
getMethod("add", List.class)
getMethod("add", Class.class)
optionExplain: String is erased away, so this lookup fails.
After erasure the parameter is Object.
The parameter is not a list.
Class is the type of a Class object, not of the element.

questions.q: Which are reasons the tutorial gives for not storing parameter names in class files by default? Select all that apply.
questions.explain: The default keeps files small and avoids exposing names; javac -parameters opts in.
questions.rule: Names need javac -parameters.
questions.teaches: Parameter names are optional metadata, so code that relies on them, such as a framework matching names, needs the library compiled with javac -parameters.
options: Class files stay smaller
Parameter names cannot be represented in the class file format
The JVM uses less memory
Names such as secret or password would be exposed
optionExplain: Right: omitting names saves space.
The format can hold them; the compiler option javac -parameters stores them.
Right: less data for the JVM to keep.
Right: sensitive names stay out of the file.

questions.q: A class User overrides toString, and getMethods() on it is printed. What if the toString override is deleted from User?
questions.explain: Public inherited methods are part of getMethods(), unless a subclass overrides them.
questions.hint: Where does the inherited version live?
options: The list loses toString altogether, as no class declares it
The list shows two toString methods, one from each class
getMethods() throws an exception for the missing method
Object's toString appears in the list instead
optionExplain: toString is still inherited from Object, so it stays.
The overridden version replaces Object's; with no override only Object's remains.
Nothing in this change throws.
Without an override the inherited public method from Object is listed.
questions.rule: Name the method and give the exact erased parameter types; use Declared forms for own methods at any access, plain forms for public ones including inherited.

questions.q: A class declares send with a parameter of type CharSequence. A lookup passes String.class for that parameter. The lookup throws ____.
questions.explain: Lookup needs the declared parameter type exactly; String is not the same type as CharSequence, so no method is found.
questions.rule: Exact types, no subtyping.
questions.teaches: Beyond the tutorial: to find a method declared with a supertype parameter, pass that supertype class in the lookup, since subtypes are never tried.

questions.q: A method called through reflection throws an IOException inside its body. What does the caller of invoke receive?
questions.explain: Failures arrive wrapped. The card next shows how to unwrap them.
options: An InvocationTargetException holding the IOException
The IOException itself, thrown straight through invoke
A NullPointerException, since the target was missing
An IllegalAccessException, since the access check failed
optionExplain: Reflection wraps whatever the invoked method throws.
The original exception is inside the wrapper, not thrown directly.
No target is missing here; the service object is passed in.
Access is not the problem in this case.
questions.rule: Pass the target first, then the arguments, cast the returned Object, and unwrap InvocationTargetException to see the real failure.

questions.q: When invoking a static method through Method.invoke, the first argument, the target, is ____.
questions.explain: A static method belongs to the class, so no instance is needed and null stands in for the target.
questions.rule: Static means null target.

questions.q: Put the steps in order to call a private instance method reflectively from another class.
questions.explain: You need the Class to find the Method, the access check must be suppressed before invoking, and invoke comes last.
questions.rule: Find, unlock, invoke.
items: Get the Class of the object
Look up the method with getDeclaredMethod
Call setAccessible(true) on the Method
Call invoke with the object and the arguments

questions.q: A static method ends with a varargs parameter of type OpenOption. A caller wants to invoke it with no varargs values. What is passed for that parameter?
questions.explain: Reflection sees the method as compiled, with the varargs parameter as an array.
questions.rule: Varargs is an array.
questions.teaches: invoke treats a varargs parameter as an ordinary array parameter, because reflection sees the method as the compiler produced it.
options: Nothing at all
An empty array of OpenOption
null
A single OpenOption.class value
optionExplain: The parameter still needs a value; invoke counts every parameter.
A varargs parameter is an array to invoke.
A null array is not the empty array the method expects.
That is a Class object, not an array of options.

questions.q: What if a private method is invoked from another class without calling setAccessible(true)?
questions.explain: Access is checked at the call unless it was suppressed.
questions.hint: Which exception does the card name for non-visible methods?
options: It runs normally
It throws InvocationTargetException
It throws NoSuchMethodException
It throws IllegalAccessException
optionExplain: Reflection does not bypass access on its own.
That wrapper is for exceptions thrown inside the method.
The method was found by getDeclaredMethod; the problem is access.
Visibility rules still apply to reflection.
questions.rule: Pass the target first, then the arguments, cast the returned Object, and unwrap InvocationTargetException to see the real failure.

questions.q: A test harness runs this and the log shows only a generic message when a service method fails: try { m.invoke(service, 5); } catch (InvocationTargetException e) { log(e.getMessage()); }. Which change reports the real failure?
questions.explain: Unwrap before reporting.
questions.rule: Unwrap, then report.
questions.teaches: The wrapper hides the real failure behind a generic exception, so a harness that reports method failures should report the target exception.
options: Log the result of e.getClass()
Call m.getExceptionTypes() and log it
Log the result of e.getTargetException()
Wrap invoke in a second InvocationTargetException
optionExplain: That prints the type of the wrapper, not what failed.
That lists exceptions the method declares, not the one thrown.
getTargetException returns the exception thrown by the service method.
Wrapping again hides the failure further.

questions.q: Which reflective call creates an object by running a chosen constructor with arguments?
questions.explain: Constructor objects create instances. The card next shows lookup and exceptions.
options: Class.getInstance
Constructor.newInstance
Method.invoke on the Class
Field.set on the Class
optionExplain: Class has no method with that name for this job.
A Constructor object can be run with arguments to create an instance.
Method.invoke runs methods, not constructors.
Field.set writes a field value.
questions.rule: Look up the constructor by its exact parameter types and call Constructor.newInstance, avoiding the deprecated Class.newInstance.

questions.q: True or false: getConstructors() includes constructors inherited from the superclass.
questions.explain: Constructors are not inherited, so each class lists only its own.
questions.rule: No inherited constructors.

questions.q: Class Ticket has only a private constructor that takes an int. Which steps create an instance from another class?
questions.explain: Match the lookup form to the access, and the types to the signature.
questions.hint: Which lookup form sees private constructors?
options: getConstructor(int.class), then newInstance with a number
Class.newInstance(), then set the int field afterwards
getDeclaredConstructor(int.class), setAccessible(true), newInstance
getDeclaredConstructor() with no types, then newInstance with a number
optionExplain: getConstructor finds public constructors only.
Class.newInstance is deprecated, needs a visible no-argument constructor, and Ticket has none.
The Declared form finds private constructors, setAccessible(true) skips the check, and the types must match.
No-argument lookup does not match a constructor taking an int.
questions.rule: Look up the constructor by its exact parameter types and call Constructor.newInstance, avoiding the deprecated Class.newInstance.

questions.q: Which are reasons the tutorial gives for avoiding Class.newInstance()? Select all that apply.
questions.explain: Three limits are named: no arguments, bypassed checking, and visibility.
questions.rule: Prefer Constructor.newInstance.
questions.teaches: Beyond the tutorial: getDeclaredConstructor().newInstance() is the usual replacement, and it reports constructor failures as InvocationTargetException.
options: It can call only the no-argument constructor
It cannot create objects of the String class
It passes on checked exceptions, bypassing compile-time checking
It requires the constructor to be visible
It always returns null
optionExplain: Right: no parameters can be passed.
Nothing in the tutorial says that.
Right: callers are not forced to handle them.
Right: a private constructor is out of reach.
It returns the new object.

questions.q: What if the lookup targets an abstract class's constructor and newInstance is called?
questions.explain: InstantiationException marks classes that cannot be instantiated, such as abstract classes and interfaces.
options: InstantiationException is thrown
A subclass is created automatically
NoSuchMethodException is thrown
The call returns null
optionExplain: An abstract class cannot be instantiated.
Reflection does not invent subclasses.
The constructor exists; the class is the problem.
A failure is reported as an exception, not as null.
questions.rule: Look up the constructor by its exact parameter types and call Constructor.newInstance, avoiding the deprecated Class.newInstance.

questions.q: A framework logs constructor failures. Match each exception to the situation it reports.
questions.explain: Each exception points to a different stage of creating the object.
questions.rule: Exception type tells the stage.
questions.teaches: Beyond the tutorial: all four exceptions extend ReflectiveOperationException, so one catch covers them when you do not need to tell the stages apart.
pairs: No constructor with those parameter types exists
The constructor body itself threw an exception
The class is abstract or an interface
The constructor is private and not made accessible

questions.q: Which reflective helper creates an array whose element type is chosen while the program runs?
questions.explain: The Array class builds arrays at run time. The card next shows how.
options: Class.getComponentType
Array.getLength
Array.newInstance
Class.forName with the element type name
optionExplain: getComponentType reports the element type of an existing array class; it creates nothing.
getLength reads the length of an existing array.
Array.newInstance takes the element type and length and returns a new array.
forName returns a Class object, not an array.
questions.rule: Use Array.newInstance when the element type or length is known only at run time, and Array.get, set, and getLength to work with the result.

questions.q: True or false: The length of an array is part of its type.
questions.explain: The length is read from each array object with Array.getLength; the type records only the component type and dimensions.
questions.rule: Length belongs to the object, not the type.

questions.q: Array.newInstance(String.class, 4) creates a one-dimensional array. Array.getLength on it returns ____.
questions.explain: The second argument is the length.
questions.rule: newInstance(type, length).

questions.q: What does getComponentType() return for the Class of a two-dimensional int array, written int[][]?
questions.explain: One level is peeled off for each call.
questions.rule: Components of int[][] are int[].
questions.teaches: For an array class getComponentType removes one dimension, so a two-dimensional array reports a one-dimensional array class as its component.
options: The Class for int[]
The Class for int
The Class for Integer
The Class for int[][]
optionExplain: The components of a two-dimensional array are one-dimensional arrays.
That would be the answer for a one-dimensional array.
Wrapper classes are not involved.
The array is not a component of itself.

questions.q: An array is created with Array.newInstance(int.class, 10). What happens if the code then calls Array.get on it with index 10?
questions.explain: Bounds are checked even through reflection.
questions.hint: What is the last valid index of a length-10 array?
options: It returns 0, the default value of an int slot
It returns null, since no element exists there
The array grows so that it can hold index 10
ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException is thrown
