optionExplain: Defaults exist only for valid positions.
An out-of-range read is an error, not a null.
Array lengths cannot change after creation.
Valid indexes run from 0 to 9, and an index at or beyond the length throws.
questions.rule: Use Array.newInstance when the element type or length is known only at run time, and Array.get, set, and getLength to work with the result.

questions.q: A utility must copy an array of any element type into a new array of the same shape, without knowing the type when it is compiled. Describe how it could create the target array.
questions.rule: Ask the source for its type, then build.
questions.teaches: Beyond the tutorial: System.arraycopy copies between arrays of any type without reflection, so reflection is needed only to create the target.
questions.a: It asks the source array's Class for its component type with getComponentType, reads the length with Array.getLength, and calls Array.newInstance with that type and length. It then copies each element with Array.get and Array.set.

questions.q: Why does the Array class have methods such as getDouble and setDouble?
questions.explain: Typed accessors avoid boxing. The card next shows their rules.
options: To access primitive elements without boxing
Because Array.get cannot read double elements at all
To resize an array that has become too short
To convert an array of numbers into a list
optionExplain: Typed methods skip the boxing that get and set perform.
Array.get can read them; it boxes the value.
Array lengths cannot change.
Nothing here converts arrays to lists.
questions.rule: Choose the typed accessor that matches the element type or widens into it, and avoid one that would narrow the value.

questions.q: True or false: Array.setInt can store an int value into a long array.
questions.explain: An int widens to long without losing precision, so the store is allowed.
questions.rule: Widening is allowed.

questions.q: Given long[] big, int[] small and float[] f, each of length 3 and created reflectively, which call completes without an exception?
questions.explain: Narrowing a long or a float into an int array is rejected, and index 3 is outside a length-3 array. Only the widening store succeeds.
options: Array.setLong(small, 0, 8L)
Array.setFloat(small, 0, 1.5f)
Array.setInt(big, 0, 8)
Array.set(small, 3, 8)
optionExplain: That would narrow a long into an int array.
That would narrow a float into an int array, which is rejected.
An int widens into a long array and index 0 is valid.
Index 3 is outside a length-3 array.
questions.rule: Choose the typed accessor that matches the element type or widens into it, and avoid one that would narrow the value.

questions.q: Array.setFloat(f, 0, 2.5f) works on a float array, but the same call on an int array fails. Why?
questions.explain: The typed setters allow only identity or widening conversions, and a float cannot widen to an int.
questions.rule: Typed setters follow widening.
questions.teaches: Beyond the tutorial: because float widens to double, Array.setFloat is accepted on a double array.
options: Typed setters cannot write into arrays of int at all
A float would narrow into an int, which typed setters reject
setFloat accepts only float arrays, never a wider element type
Index 0 is out of range for an array of int
optionExplain: Typed setters do work on int arrays, for example setInt with an int value.
Right: the typed setters allow widening only, and a float does not fit an int without narrowing.
A float widens into a double array, so setFloat is not limited to float arrays.
Index 0 is valid in any array that has at least one element.

questions.q: Array.setInt on a long array is allowed. What happens if the code instead calls Array.setLong(small, 0, 8L), where small is an int array created reflectively?
questions.explain: Widening is the allowed direction.
questions.hint: Which direction loses precision?
options: It is rejected, because narrowing is not allowed
It stores 8, because the number fits in an int
It silently truncates the value to fit the array
It converts the array into a long array first
optionExplain: Narrowing is not allowed through the typed setters.
The check looks at the types, not at whether the number would fit.
The tutorial calls this call illegal, not silently truncating.
An array's type cannot change.
questions.rule: Choose the typed accessor that matches the element type or widens into it, and avoid one that would narrow the value.

questions.q: A data-import tool stores readings through Array methods. Sort each call by whether it is allowed.
questions.explain: Narrowing into an int array (two cases) and a bad index each cause rejection; widening and exact matches are allowed.
questions.rule: Check type and bounds.
questions.teaches: Beyond the tutorial: a rejected typed access throws IllegalArgumentException for a type problem and ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException for a bounds problem, so the exception type shows which check failed.

items.t: setInt into a long array
setLong into an int array
setFloat into an int array
setDouble with a double into a double array
setInt at an index equal to the array length
getInt on an int array at a valid index

questions.q: Which Class method returns an enum's constants without needing any instance?
questions.explain: A dedicated method lists enum constants. The card next shows the enum APIs.
options: getEnumConstants()
getInterfaces()
getDeclaredClasses()
getSuperclass()
optionExplain: getEnumConstants() lists the constants in declaration order.
getInterfaces() lists interfaces.
getDeclaredClasses() lists nested types.
getSuperclass() returns the parent class.
questions.rule: Use isEnum and getEnumConstants to list the constants of a Class, expect compiler-generated members, and do not expect to create new constants.

questions.q: True or false: Reflection can create a new enum constant by invoking the enum's private constructor.
questions.explain: Enums cannot gain constants at run time, even reflectively; the attempt fails.
questions.rule: Enum constants cannot be added.

questions.q: enum Level has constants LOW and HIGH, declared in that order. What does Level.class.getEnumConstants()[1] give?
questions.explain: Declaration order decides the positions.
options: LOW
null
The Class object for Level
HIGH
optionExplain: LOW is at index 0, the first constant declared.
The array holds both constants, so index 1 is not empty.
The array holds constants, not the Class.
Constants come back in declaration order, so index 1 is the second one.
questions.rule: Use isEnum and getEnumConstants to list the constants of a Class, expect compiler-generated members, and do not expect to create new constants.

questions.q: An enum constructor written in source takes one String parameter. How many parameters does the reflected constructor show?
questions.explain: Reflection shows the compiled constructor.
questions.rule: Enum constructors gain name and index.
questions.teaches: What reflection shows is the compiled constructor, which carries two extra parameters added by the compiler, so reflected signatures of enum constructors differ from the source.
options: One parameter, matching the source
Three parameters
Two parameters, counting only the compiler's additions
Zero parameters, since enums hide their constructors
optionExplain: One is the count in source, but the reflected list is longer.
The compiler adds the constant's name and index to the one written parameter.
Name and index alone make two; the written parameter adds one more.
The constructor takes parameters; it is not empty.

questions.q: An enum has constants RED and GREEN and no other fields. According to the tutorial's output, what does getDeclaredFields() list?
questions.explain: Constants are fields, and the compiler adds one more.
options: Only RED and GREEN, the two declared constants
RED, GREEN, and a public instance field named ordinal
RED, GREEN, and a private static array named $VALUES
Nothing, since enum types contain no fields at all
optionExplain: The compiler also generates the array field.
No such instance field is described.
One public static field per constant, plus the private static array holding them.
Constants are implemented as fields.
questions.rule: Use isEnum and getEnumConstants to list the constants of a Class, expect compiler-generated members, and do not expect to create new constants.

questions.q: A form generator builds drop-downs from any enum. Match each reflective call to what it provides.
questions.explain: Together they let a generator test a type and list its choices.
questions.rule: Test with isEnum, list with getEnumConstants.
questions.teaches: A form generator can combine a field type's isEnum and getEnumConstants to build a drop-down for any enum without naming it in code.
pairs: Whether this Class is an enum type
Whether this field is one of the constants
get(null) on a constant's static field
The constant, read without an instance

questions.q: Which reflective call tells whether a Class is a record?
questions.explain: A dedicated test exists. The card next shows the record API.
options: isRecord()
isEnum()
isArray()
isRecordComponent()
optionExplain: isRecord() was added for records in Java SE 16.
isEnum() asks about enums.
isArray() asks about array classes.
No such method on Class is described in the tutorial.
questions.rule: Use RecordComponent for metadata and getDeclaredFields for fields; read freely, but create a new record instead of modifying one.

questions.q: True or false: A RecordComponent has a method that returns the Field object of its component.
questions.explain: It does not; use getDeclaredFields() on the record class to get the fields.
questions.rule: Fields come from getDeclaredFields.

questions.q: A tool needs the private Field behind the component x of a record Point. Which approach does the tutorial point to?
questions.explain: Use the class for fields and the component for metadata.
options: Call getField on the component object itself
Call getDeclaredFields() on Point and pick x
Call getAccessor().getField() on the component
Call Point.class.getFields() and pick the field x
optionExplain: The component has no such method.
RecordComponent offers no field getter, so you go through the class.
getAccessor returns a Method, which has no field getter.
getFields() returns public fields only, and record fields are private.
questions.rule: Use RecordComponent for metadata and getDeclaredFields for fields; read freely, but create a new record instead of modifying one.

questions.q: After setAccessible(true), a program calls xField.getInt(p) and then xField.set(p, 9) on a record's int field x. What results?
questions.explain: Records are read-only through reflection.
questions.rule: Read yes, write no.
questions.teaches: Reflection on a record is read-only: private fields can be read once access is granted but never written, unlike an ordinary private final field, which setAccessible(true) unlocks.
options: Both calls succeed once access has been granted
Both calls throw IllegalAccessException as well
Reads work, writes throw IllegalAccessException
getInt throws an exception, but set succeeds
optionExplain: Writing a record field is refused even after access is granted.
Reading works after setAccessible(true); only the write is refused.
Reading is allowed once access is granted; writing is refused.
The directions are reversed: the read works and the write fails.

questions.q: Point is changed from a record to an ordinary class with a private final int x, and the same setAccessible(true) then set is used on x. According to the tutorial, what happens?
questions.explain: The record rule is special; ordinary final fields behave differently.
questions.hint: Which kinds of field stay unwritable?
options: The write fails, exactly as it does for records
The write succeeds only if x is declared static
The write succeeds only if x is declared public
The write succeeds, as the final check is suppressed
optionExplain: Records are singled out because their fields stay unwritable.
Static fields are the other unwritable case.
Public is not required; setAccessible suppresses the checks.
Ordinary instance fields can be written after setAccessible(true), though JDK 26 adds a warning; records are the exception.
questions.rule: Use RecordComponent for metadata and getDeclaredFields for fields; read freely, but create a new record instead of modifying one.

questions.q: To get a changed copy of a record reflectively, put these steps in order.
questions.explain: Components and accessors give the old values, and the constructor builds the new record.
questions.rule: Rebuild, do not modify.
questions.teaches: Beyond the tutorial: the canonical constructor takes the component types in order, so its parameter types can be collected with getType on each component.
items: List the record components
Call each accessor to read its value
Swap in the new value for the one component
Invoke the canonical constructor with the values

questions.q: Which call returns only the annotations written directly on an element?
questions.explain: Declared forms look at the element only. The card next shows the family.
options: getAnnotations()
isAnnotationPresent(type)
getDeclaredAnnotations()
getModifiers()
optionExplain: The plain form may include inherited annotations.
isAnnotationPresent answers yes or no for one type; it returns no annotations.
The Declared form leaves out inherited annotations.
getModifiers() returns modifier bits, not annotations.
questions.rule: Use the Declared forms for annotations written on the element, the plain forms to include inherited ones, and getAnnotationsByType for repeatable annotations.

questions.q: True or false: Field, Method, Constructor, and Class all implement AnnotatedElement.
questions.explain: AnnotatedElement is the shared interface for reading annotations.
questions.rule: One interface for all four.

questions.q: Audit is an inheritable annotation, and User carries it. Admin extends User and has no annotation of its own. Which call on the Class of Admin finds Audit?
questions.explain: Choose the plain form when inheritance should count.
questions.rule: Plain includes inherited.
options: getDeclaredAnnotation(Audit.class)
getAnnotation(Audit.class)
getDeclaredAnnotations()
getInterfaces()
optionExplain: The Declared form returns only annotations written on Admin.
The plain form includes inherited annotations.
That lists annotations written on Admin, and there are none.
getInterfaces() lists interfaces, not annotations.

questions.q: A field carries three repeated Validator annotations. At the class-file level, what does the field itself carry, according to the tutorial?
questions.explain: Calling value() on the container reaches the repeats.
questions.rule: Repeats live in a container.
questions.teaches: A framework that reads only with getAnnotation(Validator.class) misses the repeats, since the field holds the container and not the individual Validators.
options: One container annotation, Validators, that holds all three
Three separate Validator annotations stored side by side
No annotations at all, since repeated ones are discarded
One Validator annotation that holds the other two inside it
optionExplain: Repeats are wrapped in a container.
They are wrapped, not stored separately.
They are kept inside the container.
The container is a separate annotation type.

questions.q: According to the tutorial, an inheritable annotation is placed on an enum type. Could a subtype of that enum inherit it?
questions.explain: The inheritance rule stops at final types.
questions.hint: What does inheritance require?
options: Yes, if the annotation is marked as inheritable
Yes, but only when read through getDeclaredAnnotations()
No, since enums cannot carry annotations of any kind
No, since an enum is final and cannot be extended
optionExplain: The tutorial excludes enums and records from inheritance.
The Declared form never shows inherited annotations.
Enums can carry annotations; they just do not pass them on.
Inheritance needs a subtype, and enums cannot be extended.
questions.rule: Use the Declared forms for annotations written on the element, the plain forms to include inherited ones, and getAnnotationsByType for repeatable annotations.

questions.q: Match each call to what it gives.
questions.explain: Four calls, four questions: what is present, what is written here, what repeats, and is this one there.
questions.rule: Match the call to the question.
pairs: All annotations present, including inherited ones
Only annotations written on the element
Repeated annotations unwrapped from their container
A yes-or-no test for one annotation type

questions.q: A validation framework supports a Range annotation that may be repeated on a field. Which call collects every Range without dealing with the container?
questions.explain: Repeatable annotations are read with getAnnotationsByType.
questions.rule: Repeats: getAnnotationsByType.
questions.teaches: Because the unwrapping happens inside getAnnotationsByType, framework code needs no knowledge of the container annotation type.
options: getAnnotation(Range.class)
isAnnotationPresent(Range.class)
getDeclaredAnnotation(Range.class)
getAnnotationsByType(Range.class)
optionExplain: That looks for one Range, but the field holds the container.
That only answers whether one is present.
That also looks for a single Range type.
It unwraps the container and returns the repeats directly.

questions.q: A service method is marked with an annotation that names another class. When the method is called through the factory, what is meant to run?
questions.explain: The annotation names the stand-in. The card next shows the mechanism.
options: The named class's intercept method, in place of the service call
The service method first, then the named class's method afterwards
Both methods at once, each on its own separate thread
Nothing, because annotations cannot affect how calls run
optionExplain: The interceptor stands in front of the service and may call it.
The interceptor replaces the call; it decides whether the service runs.
Nothing in the design starts threads.
Annotations are read by the factory, which then acts on them.
questions.rule: Read the annotation's class attribute, build that interceptor, and let it decide whether and how the real method runs.

questions.q: True or false: In the tutorial's design, the annotation names the interceptor class through an attribute.
questions.explain: The factory reads that attribute to know which interceptor to create.
questions.rule: The annotation carries the class.

questions.q: Put the factory's steps in order.
questions.explain: The service and the method must exist before the annotation can be checked on that method, and the result comes last.
questions.rule: Create, locate, check, run.
items: Create the service object with its no-argument constructor
Locate the method from its name and the classes of the arguments
Check whether the method carries the interceptor annotation
Run the interceptor or the service method and return the result

questions.q: A service method message is declared with a CharSequence parameter, and the factory builds its lookup from the runtime class of a String argument. What happens?
questions.explain: Exact types again.
questions.rule: Runtime argument classes must equal declared types.
questions.teaches: Because the lookup uses exact types taken from the argument values, a factory built this way works only when the arguments' runtime classes equal the declared parameter types.
options: It finds the method, because String implements CharSequence
It finds the method but then skips the interceptor
The lookup fails, since String differs from CharSequence
It returns null instead of finding the method
optionExplain: Implementing an interface does not make the types equal for lookup.
A method that is found would still be intercepted.
Lookup matches the declared type exactly.
A failed lookup throws an exception rather than returning null.

questions.q: An interceptor is written to insist on exactly one String argument and to throw otherwise before it calls the service. What happens when a call arrives with two arguments?
questions.explain: The interceptor guards the service, and its check runs before the call.
questions.hint: Where does the validation sit?
options: It runs the service method anyway and then throws
It runs the service method with a null argument
It removes the annotation and retries the call
It throws an exception and the service is not run
optionExplain: The check sits before the call, so the service is not reached.
No default argument is supplied.
Annotations are not changed at run time.
The check comes before the call.
questions.rule: Read the annotation's class attribute, build that interceptor, and let it decide whether and how the real method runs.

questions.q: A payment service must refuse calls from users who are not logged in. Which interceptor abilities, listed in the tutorial, let an interceptor do this? Select all that apply.
questions.explain: Security checks and the choice to call or skip the service are both named abilities.
questions.rule: The interceptor holds the veto.
questions.teaches: Because the interceptor is the only code that calls the service method, it holds the veto: a refusal there protects the service without editing the service.
options: Decide whether the service method runs at all
Change the declared return type of the service
Enforce security rules
Rewrite the annotation's attribute at run time
optionExplain: Right: it can refuse and skip the call.
The interceptor can change the returned value, not the declared type.
Right: security rules beyond validation are named.
Nothing in the design changes annotations.

questions.q: In dependency injection, who creates the collaborator objects a class needs?
questions.explain: The factory builds and wires objects. The card next shows how.
options: A framework or factory
The class itself, in its own constructor
The compiler, at the moment the code is built
The garbage collector, whenever memory is free
optionExplain: Injection moves object creation out of the class and into a factory.
That is the style injection replaces.
The compiler does not create run-time objects for you.
The garbage collector reclaims objects; it does not create them.
questions.rule: Construct through the factory, check the Singleton annotation for reuse, then set every Inject field with an instance obtained from the same factory.

questions.q: True or false: In the tutorial's factory, injected fields are still null when the bean has been constructed and nothing more.
questions.explain: The factory sets them afterwards, in a second step.
questions.rule: Construct first, inject second.

questions.q: Mailer has a field marked Inject of type Smtp, and Smtp is marked Singleton. Mailer is not a singleton. The application asks the factory for two Mailer objects. How many Smtp instances do they share?
questions.explain: The singleton rule is applied per class, at every request.
questions.hint: Which class carries the Singleton mark?
options: Two Mailer objects, one Smtp shared by both
Two Mailer objects, each with its own Smtp
One Mailer object, since the factory reuses everything
Two Mailer objects and no Smtp until set by hand
optionExplain: Each Mailer is new, and each asks the factory for an Smtp, which returns the registered one.
The Singleton rule applies when the factory builds the field value.
Only marked classes are reused.
The factory fills Inject fields itself.
questions.rule: Construct through the factory, check the Singleton annotation for reuse, then set every Inject field with an instance obtained from the same factory.

questions.q: Two threads both find no registered instance, both build one, and both call putIfAbsent. What does the tutorial say the factory does to return the real singleton?
questions.explain: Read the registry after the atomic insert.
questions.rule: After putIfAbsent, call get.
questions.teaches: Even with an atomic registry, a lost race leaves a surplus instance that was built and discarded, so construction code in a singleton should tolerate running more than once.
options: It uses the value putIfAbsent returned
It calls get on the map afterwards
It builds a third instance and keeps that
It stops the other thread
optionExplain: That value may not be the one stored.
The returned value may not be the stored one.
A further instance would add to the problem.
The tutorial leaves threads running; it reads the map again.

questions.q: What if a constructor takes a CharSequence and the caller passes a String to the factory's getInstanceOf?
questions.explain: Match types exactly.
questions.hint: Which type does the lookup use?
options: It works, because String implements CharSequence
It works, but returns null for the bean
NoSuchMethodException, as lookup needs exact types
It throws IllegalAccessException on the constructor
optionExplain: Implementing the interface does not make the types match.
A failed lookup throws; it does not return null.
The types are taken from the arguments, so they must equal the declared ones.
Access is not the problem; no constructor matches.
questions.rule: Construct through the factory, check the Singleton annotation for reuse, then set every Inject field with an instance obtained from the same factory.

questions.q: Beyond the tutorial: a team decides where to place the Singleton mark. Sort each class by whether sharing one instance fits.
questions.explain: The tutorial presents a singleton as a fit for a shared service such as one wrapping a database. Objects holding per-user state need their own instances.
questions.rule: Share services, not state.
questions.teaches: Beyond the tutorial: a singleton fits shared services that wrap an outside resource, while objects that hold per-user state need separate instances, so the mark is placed by how an object is used.

items.t: A client that wraps one remote REST server
A shopping cart for each customer
A service that wraps the database
A report holding one user's current filters

questions.q: A private method is reached through reflection in one program and through a method handle in another. When does each approach check whether the caller may access it?
options: Both check on each call, so the cost is the same
Reflection checks on each call; a handle checks when it is made
Reflection checks once; a handle checks on each call
Neither checks, since private members can be reached by any caller
optionExplain: Only reflection works this way; the tutorial says handles are checked at creation.
Right: this is the difference the tutorial draws between the two approaches.
This reverses the roles of the two approaches.
Private members are still protected; the check happens, just at a different time.
questions.explain: Reflection re-checks on each call, while a handle is checked when it is made. The card next shows why that matters.
questions.rule: Handles are checked at creation.

questions.q: A method handle checks the caller's access only at the moment the handle is ____.
questions.explain: The check happens at creation, so later callers are not checked again.
questions.rule: Checked once, at creation.

questions.q: A utility class builds a handle to its own private method using a lookup that can reach private members, then returns that handle from a public method to any caller. What is the consequence?
options: Callers get an error, because access is re-checked at every call by the JVM
Nothing changes, because a private method stays private whoever holds a handle
Callers may invoke it only from code in the utility class's own package
Any caller can invoke the private method, since the check was done earlier
optionExplain: That is how reflection behaves; handles skip the per-call check.
This assumes the check follows the caller, but the handle keeps the access it was created with.
Nothing ties the handle to a package after creation.
Right: the handle keeps the creator's access, so exposing it exposes the method.
questions.explain: The access check was done when the class built the handle, so every holder can invoke the private method.
questions.rule: A leaked handle carries its creator's reach.

questions.q: A program asks the lookup from MethodHandles.publicLookup for a handle to a private method of a public class. According to the tutorial's description of that lookup, what happens?
options: The lookup cannot give a handle to the private method
The handle is found, because the class itself is public
The handle is found but can be called only from the same class
The handle is found, and access is then checked on each call instead
optionExplain: Right: the lookup's access level is limited to public members, so the private method is out of its reach.
A public class does not make its private members findable.
The tutorial describes no such call restriction; the issue is what the lookup can find.
Handles are not checked per call; the limit applies when finding.
questions.explain: The public lookup finds only public members of public classes in unconditionally exported packages, so a private method is outside what it can find.
questions.rule: A public lookup reaches public members only.

questions.q: Match each task to the piece the tutorial names for it.
pairs: Turn a Method object into a handle
Turn an untransformed handle back into a Method
List the members of a class
Find only public members of public classes
questions.explain: Lookup.unreflect goes from reflection to handles, reflectAs goes back, and listing members stays with reflection.
questions.rule: Convert between the two only where the tutorial allows.
questions.teaches: Beyond the tutorial: because reflectAs works only on unadapted handles, the result of an adapter such as insertArguments cannot be turned back into a Method.

questions.q: True or false: A method type is written with the parameter types first and the return type last.
questions.explain: The return type comes first. The card next shows how types and finders fit together.
questions.rule: Return type first.

questions.q: Match each lookup method with what it finds.
pairs: A way to write a static field
questions.explain: Each finder targets one kind of member.
questions.rule: Pick the finder by member kind.

questions.q: A class Temps has a static method named toKelvin that takes a double and returns a long. Which MethodType matches what findStatic needs?
options: methodType(double.class, long.class)
methodType(long.class, long.class, double.class)
methodType(long.class, double.class)
methodType(Temps.class, double.class)
optionExplain: This puts the parameter first and reads as a method returning double.
It adds a second parameter that the method does not have.
Right: long is the return type, then double is the only parameter.
The class is not the return type; findStatic takes the class as a separate argument.
questions.explain: The return type comes first, so the type is long first, then double.
questions.rule: Return type first, then parameters.

questions.q: A handle was found for a method that takes an Object and returns a String. Code passes a variable of declared type String and calls invokeExact, then changes the call to invoke. According to the tutorial, what happens?
options: Both calls succeed, because every String is also an Object and Java widens it
Both calls fail, because the handle names Object and the code names String
invokeExact adapts the types for you while invoke demands an exact match
invokeExact fails on the mismatch; invoke adapts the types and can succeed
optionExplain: Widening does not help invokeExact, which requires the exact type.
invoke applies asType, so it can bridge the gap.
This swaps the two methods' behaviour.
Right: exact versus adapting is the difference between the two.
questions.explain: invokeExact needs an exact match, which a String argument for an Object parameter is not, while invoke adapts types first.
questions.rule: invoke adapts; invokeExact does not.

questions.q: Which statements about field handles and array handles agree with the tutorial? Select all that apply.
options: findGetter takes the field's type instead of a MethodType
arrayLength needs a Lookup object to be created
A getter handle for an instance field needs an instance of the owning class when invoked
findStaticSetter is meant for instance fields
According to the tutorial, VarHandles are generally more suitable for fields
optionExplain: Right: field finders work from the field's type.
Array handles are preset on MethodHandles and need no Lookup.
Right: an instance field belongs to an object, so one must be supplied.
The static variants are for static fields.
Right: the tutorial points to VarHandles for fields.
questions.explain: Field finders take the field type, instance getters need an instance, and the tutorial prefers VarHandles for fields. Array handles need no Lookup.
questions.rule: Field finders use a field type; arrays need no Lookup.
questions.teaches: Beyond the tutorial: a VarHandle offers access modes such as volatile reads and atomic compare-and-set, which plain getter and setter handles do not.

questions.q: You hold a handle that takes a price and a quantity. You want one that takes only a quantity, with the price fixed at 5. Which idea fits best?
options: Pre-bind the price argument ahead of time
Write a new method and look up a fresh handle for it
Convert the result of every call to a different type
Wrap the call so that it always catches an exception
optionExplain: Right: pre-binding is what the tutorial offers for this.
It works but gives up the point of adapting an existing handle.
Converting the result does not remove the price argument.
Exception handling does not change the arguments.
questions.explain: Fixing the leading argument ahead of time leaves callers only the rest. The card next names the adapter.
questions.rule: Pre-binding leaves fewer arguments.

questions.q: Match each adapter with what it does.
pairs: Converts the handle to a new type
Passes the result through another handle
questions.explain: Each adapter changes one aspect of the handle.
questions.rule: One adapter, one change.

questions.q: A handle describes a method that takes a String name and then an int count. A caller wants to pass the int first and the String second. Which adapter fits?
options: insertArguments, which fixes a leading argument in advance
filterReturnValue, which transforms the result afterwards
permuteArguments, with a new type and an index array
catchException, which supplies a handler for one failure
optionExplain: That removes an argument instead of changing order.
That works on the result, not the arguments.
Right: it reorders arguments using a new type and index array.
That deals with exceptions, not argument order.
questions.explain: permuteArguments takes a new MethodType and an index array to reorder arguments.
questions.rule: Reordering uses permuteArguments.

questions.q: A handle has its first argument fixed by insertArguments. A caller then supplies that first argument again as well. According to the tutorial, the call fails with a ____.
questions.explain: The adapted handle no longer has that parameter, so the extra argument causes a WrongMethodTypeException.
questions.rule: Do not pass pre-bound arguments again.

questions.q: A target handle takes a String and returns an int. You wrap it with catchException to handle IllegalArgumentException. Which handler shape does the tutorial describe?
options: It takes only the original String and returns void in all cases
It takes the String first, then the exception, and returns an int
It takes the exception first, then the String, and returns an int
It takes only the exception and returns a String to the caller
optionExplain: The handler must receive the exception and return the target's type.
The exception comes first, not second.
Right: exception, then original arguments, with the target's return type.
It must also receive the original arguments and return an int.
questions.explain: The handler returns the target's return type and takes the exception first, then the original arguments.
questions.rule: Handler: exception first, then the original arguments.
questions.teaches: According to the tutorial, tryFinally uses a cleanup handler that returns the target's type and takes a Throwable, then the target's result, then the original arguments.

questions.q: True or false: A handle wrapped by catchException for IllegalArgumentException also intercepts a NullPointerException thrown by the target, because the wrapper surrounds the whole call.
questions.explain: The handler is for one exception type; other types still propagate.
questions.rule: One handler, one exception type.

questions.q: A service must handle 20000 concurrent requests, and each request spends most of its time waiting for a database reply. Which thread design fits best?
options: One platform thread per request, each backed by an operating system thread
One virtual thread per request, sharing a few platform threads
A single platform thread that runs the requests one after another
A pool of eight virtual threads that all requests queue for
optionExplain: Tempting because it is the classic design, but thousands of heavy platform threads cost a lot of memory and start-up time.
A virtual thread is cheap, and a platform thread moves on to other work while one waits, so this suits mostly-waiting tasks.
This avoids thread cost, but one waiting request would hold up every other.
Queuing for a small virtual-thread pool throws away the cheapness that virtual threads offer.
questions.explain: Many requests that mostly wait suit one cheap thread each. The card next shows how virtual threads make that affordable.
questions.rule: Mostly-waiting tasks suit one virtual thread each.

questions.q: When a virtual thread blocks, it is ____ from its platform thread, which then runs a different virtual thread.
questions.explain: The block makes the virtual thread unmount, and the platform thread under it is free for other virtual threads.
questions.rule: Blocking unmounts a virtual thread.

questions.q: Sort each job by whether the tutorial would call virtual threads a good fit or a poor fit.

items.t: Fetching 5000 web pages and waiting for each reply
Holding chat connections that mostly wait for messages
Calling several remote services for each incoming request
Multiplying very large matrices in a tight loop
Computing checksums over gigabytes held in memory
Running a physics simulation on every core

questions.explain: The first three spend their time waiting on the network. The others keep the processor busy with no waiting to hide.
questions.rule: Waiting favours virtual threads; computing does not.

questions.q: According to the tutorial, how did virtual threads reach their final form?
options: Introduced in Java 17, previewed in Java 18, final in Java 19
Introduced in Java 21, previewed in Java 22, final in Java 23
Introduced in Java 8, previewed in Java 11, final in Java 17
Introduced in Java 19, previewed in Java 20, final in Java 21
optionExplain: These releases are too early; the final version came later than Java 19.
These releases are too late; the feature was already final in Java 21.
Java 8 predates the feature by a long way.
This matches the tutorial: JEP 425 in Java 19, preview in Java 20 and final in Java 21.
questions.explain: The tutorial dates virtual threads from Java 19 and gives Java 21 as the release that finalized them, so code written for earlier JDKs may lack them.
questions.rule: Final in Java 21, per the tutorial.
questions.teaches: Beyond the tutorial: in Java 20 a program had to enable preview features to use virtual threads, whereas Java 21 needs no such flag.

questions.q: A team resizes uploaded photos by looping over pixel data, using the processor all the time with no waiting. They plan one virtual thread per photo on an 8-core machine. What is the likely outcome?
options: Throughput scales well beyond eight photos at once, since each virtual thread adds capacity
Little gain, since a computing thread never blocks and so keeps its platform thread busy
Failure, since virtual threads cannot run computation at all
A large gain, since computing threads are unmounted to make room for others
optionExplain: Virtual threads add no processing capacity; the eight cores still limit the work.
The tutorial calls CPU-intensive work a poor fit, because a thread unmounts only when it blocks and computing threads keep their platform threads.
They can run computation; they just bring little benefit for it.
Unmounting is tied to blocking, and this work never blocks.
questions.explain: Cheap blocking is the source of the gain. Work that never blocks has nothing to hide, so the cores remain the limit; the tutorial suggests parallel streams or fork-join tasks.
questions.rule: No blocking, no gain.
questions.teaches: Beyond the tutorial: with CPU-bound work, many more runnable threads than cores adds scheduling overhead without finishing the work sooner.

questions.q: A developer must run 10000 short tasks on virtual threads. What does the tutorial recommend for supplying the threads?
options: Create a pool of 200 virtual threads and queue the tasks for it
Give every task its own virtual thread without pooling
Convert the tasks to platform threads first, then pool those
Create ten virtual threads and recycle each one 1000 times
optionExplain: Pools are a reflex from platform threads, but here they only add overhead.
Virtual threads are cheap enough to create per task, which is what the tutorial advises.
This brings back the cost that virtual threads were meant to avoid.
Recycling is pooling by another name, with the same overhead.
questions.explain: The tutorial calls pooling a tool for platform threads. The card next shows what to do instead.
questions.rule: One virtual thread per task.

questions.q: True or false: a virtual thread is an instance of Thread, so isVirtual can tell it from a platform thread.
questions.explain: The designers reused the Thread API. A virtual thread is a Thread, and isVirtual reports which kind it is.
questions.rule: Virtual threads reuse the Thread API.

questions.q: A program calls setPriority with the value 1 on a virtual thread. According to the tutorial, which statements are true?
options: The call is ignored
The thread is still a daemon thread
The thread keeps normal priority
The thread moves into a new thread group
The program fails with an exception
optionExplain: True: the tutorial says calls to setPriority on a virtual thread are ignored.
True: all virtual threads are daemon threads, and nothing the program calls changes that.
True: all virtual threads have normal priority, so the requested value 1 has no effect.
False: virtual threads all belong to one thread group, and there is no API to place them elsewhere.
False: the calls are ignored, not rejected.
questions.explain: Daemon status, priority and thread group are fixed for virtual threads, so the setter has no effect.
questions.rule: Daemon, normal priority, one group: fixed.

questions.q: A program has six Callable tasks, each returning a String, and runs them on a virtual-thread-per-task executor. According to the tutorial, how can it collect the results?
options: Create one thread per task with a builder, and read each return value after join
Avoid blocking calls, since Future.get is not allowed on virtual threads
Call invokeAll with the list of tasks, then call get on each Future
Pass the tasks to a ThreadFactory, whose threads return the results
optionExplain: A Thread object has no return value, and the tutorial says only the executor route handles tasks that return results.
The reverse is true: blocking is cheap on virtual threads, so Future.get is fine.
Right: invokeAll runs same-type tasks and returns Futures, and the blocking get calls are acceptable.
A ThreadFactory only makes unstarted threads, which cannot return values.
questions.explain: Results come from the executor's Futures. Since blocking is cheap on virtual threads, calling get on each Future is an acceptable way to collect them.
questions.rule: Executor, invokeAll, then get.
questions.teaches: Blocking Future.get is acceptable with virtual threads, and invokeAll runs a list of same-type tasks and returns futures from which each result can be read.

questions.q: A team's database accepts 20 connections. Their plan: 'Create a pool of 20 virtual threads, and all 5000 requests must queue for it, so the database cannot be overloaded.' According to the tutorial, what is wrong with the plan?
options: It pools the threads instead of limiting the database itself
It uses too few threads, since a pool should have one thread per core
It uses virtual threads, which cannot talk to a database
It should use platform threads, as a pool of virtual threads is unsafe
optionExplain: Right: the tutorial says to guard the resource itself, and a connection pool may already do that, rather than pool the virtual threads.
The size is not the problem; the idea of pooling virtual threads is.
Virtual threads can block on database calls cheaply; that is a main use case.
Nothing in the tutorial calls pooled virtual threads unsafe; it calls pooling unhelpful.
questions.explain: The limit belongs at the database. The tutorial notes that a database connection pool may already provide it, so tasks simply block cheaply while waiting for a connection.
questions.rule: Limit the resource, not the threads.
questions.teaches: Beyond the tutorial: 5000 virtual threads parked on a connection wait are cheap, so the backlog can simply wait in the threads instead of in a separate task queue.

questions.q: On JDK 21, as many virtual threads as there are carrier threads sleep for a long time inside a synchronized method, and then later virtual threads with almost no work stay stuck waiting. What is the likely cause?
options: Virtual threads may not enter synchronized methods at all
The heap is full of virtual thread stacks that were never freed
The sleeping threads are pinned and hold every carrier thread
Sleeping is forbidden on virtual threads, so they are stuck
optionExplain: They can enter synchronized code; the trouble is what happens when they block there.
Virtual threads are light, and the symptom is starvation rather than memory.
A pinned virtual thread cannot unmount when it blocks, so it holds its carrier, and the carriers run out.
Sleeping is allowed; blocking is cheap when the thread is not pinned.
questions.explain: Pinning plus blocking is the trap. The card next explains it.
questions.rule: Pinned and blocked holds the carrier.

questions.q: A virtual thread is mounted on a ____ thread, and by default there is one of these per CPU core.
questions.explain: Carrier threads are the platform threads that virtual threads are mounted on. By default there is one per core.
questions.rule: Carriers run virtual threads.

questions.q: Sort each situation by whether the tutorial says the virtual thread is pinned.

items.t: Running inside a synchronized block
Calling a native method
Calling a foreign function
Running a plain loop outside any synchronized code
Holding a ReentrantLock instead of using synchronized
Blocked on a Semaphore acquire outside synchronized code

questions.explain: Pinning comes from synchronized code and from native or foreign calls. ReentrantLock is the tutorial's replacement, and ordinary code outside those cases does not pin.
questions.rule: Synchronized and native code pin.

questions.q: On JDK 21 with four carriers, four virtual threads each sleep for a minute inside a synchronized method. Ten more virtual threads that only print a line are then started. According to the tutorial, what happens to the ten?
options: They run at once, since a new carrier is started for each pinned thread
They fail with an error, since the pinned threads hold all locks
They wait until a carrier becomes free, although they have almost no work
They run on the pinned virtual threads' own stacks
optionExplain: JDK 21 starts no extra carrier in this case, so the premise fails.
They are not rejected; they just cannot be scheduled yet.
Right: all four carriers are held by pinned, blocked threads, so the others wait.
A virtual thread needs a carrier to run, and these carriers are taken.
questions.explain: With every carrier held by a pinned, blocked thread, nothing else can be mounted until one finishes.
questions.rule: Starved carriers stall other virtual threads.
questions.teaches: According to the tutorial, the JDK 21 scheduler may add a carrier for some blocking operations, such as many file input and output calls and Object.wait, but a sleep inside synchronized gets no such help.

questions.q: On JDK 21, class A has a synchronized method that adds an item to an in-memory list. Class B has a synchronized method that waits many seconds for a remote reply. According to the tutorial, which needs changing?
options: Both, since every synchronized method pins and must be replaced
Neither, since pinning is harmless on JDK 21
Only A, since in-memory work is the case that needs a lock
Only B, as the blocking call inside synchronized is the problem
optionExplain: Pinning happens in both, but the tutorial says that around brief in-memory work it is harmless and can stay.
Pinning is harmless only until a pinned thread blocks, which B does.
In-memory guarding is the case the tutorial says to leave alone.
Right: B blocks while pinned and holds its carrier, so a ReentrantLock is the fix if you control the source.
questions.explain: Pinning matters only when the pinned thread blocks. A holds its carrier briefly, while B holds it for seconds.
questions.rule: Fix pinning where it blocks.

questions.q: A service used a pool of 50 threads, each caching one 2-megabyte buffer in a thread-local variable. It now uses one virtual thread per request, with 100000 requests live at once, each filling its own thread-local buffer. Buffers could then take up to ____ megabytes at once.
questions.explain: Each live thread holds its own copy, so 100000 times 2 megabytes gives 200000 megabytes, against 100 megabytes before.
questions.rule: Thread-local memory grows with live threads.
questions.teaches: Beyond the tutorial: sharing one thread-safe object across virtual threads, or borrowing a buffer only while it is needed, ties memory to use instead of to thread count.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the tutorials as a whole
questions.q: Which description of the order of the five lessons is closest to the truth?
options: Annotations are taught early, because a label is simpler than a class
Language Basics comes last, because operators are the hardest topic
Annotations come last, as they label what earlier lessons teach
Classes and Objects comes first, because every program is a class
optionExplain: A label looks small, but it can only be attached to something that already exists.
Operators are taught in the middle, as parts used inside classes.
Annotations attach to declarations, so classes, fields and methods have to be taught first.
The first lesson teaches a program; the lesson on classes comes after the concepts.
questions.explain: Annotations label declarations, so they come after the lessons that teach declarations. The card next shows the whole chain.
questions.rule: The order follows what each lesson needs from the one before.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the tutorials as a whole
questions.q: Put the five lessons in the order the tutorials teach them.
items: Getting Started: write, compile and run a first program
Object-Oriented Programming Concepts: objects, classes, inheritance, interfaces, packages
Language Basics: variables, types, operators, control flow
Classes and Objects: declaring classes and creating objects
Annotations: metadata attached to declarations
questions.explain: A program first, then concepts, then the parts, then full declarations, then labels on declarations.
questions.rule: Program, concepts, parts, declarations, labels.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the tutorials as a whole
questions.q: A reader has finished Language Basics but cannot yet write a class with a constructor and private fields. Which lesson fills the gap next?
options: Annotations, which attaches metadata to existing declarations
Getting Started, which shows one class with a main method
Classes and Objects, which shows how to declare classes and objects
Object-Oriented Programming Concepts, which explains why objects bundle state
optionExplain: Annotations label declarations; they do not teach how to write them.
The first lesson shows a single class but not constructors or access levels.
Right: declaring classes, constructors and fields is the subject of the fourth lesson.
The concept lesson gives the reasons behind classes, while the declaring syntax is taught later.
questions.explain: Constructors and private fields are declaration details, which the fourth lesson covers after the concept lesson and the language basics.
questions.rule: Match the missing skill to the lesson that teaches it.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the tutorials as a whole
questions.q: True or false: The concept lesson teaches its ideas with working code as well as prose.
questions.explain: Lesson 2 shows a Bicycle class, a demo class that creates two bicycle objects, and an interface with an implementing class. Code illustrates the ideas there.
questions.rule: Concepts and syntax mix across lessons.
questions.teaches: Even the concept lesson shows working code, such as a Bicycle class and a demo that makes two objects, so the move from ideas to syntax is gradual and does not switch at a lesson boundary.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the tutorials as a whole
questions.q: What if a reader who has finished only the first two lessons opens Annotations to learn about the Override label?
options: The reader can follow the idea, as it rests on subclasses and methods
The lesson is unreadable, since each lesson is a strict prerequisite for the one after it
The reader must first finish Language Basics, since Override is a kind of operator
The reader should return to Getting Started, since annotations are compiled like programs do
optionExplain: Right: Override marks a method that replaces an inherited one, which needs only the ideas of subclass and method.
The chain is advice about order, not a lock; much of a later lesson can be followed early.
Override is an annotation, not an operator.
Annotations are not programs; they label declarations.
questions.explain: Where a later idea rests only on ideas already met, the reader can go ahead; the chain describes the usual order, not a requirement.
questions.rule: The chain is a default order, not a rule for every topic.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the tutorials as a whole
questions.q: A cooking course teaches boiling an egg, kitchen concepts, knife skills, full recipes and plating. Why does plating come last?
options: Plating is the hardest skill, and difficulty alone fixes the order
Plating finishes a dish, so it needs the recipes to exist first
Plating needs no earlier lesson, so its place is arbitrary
Plating uses only knife skills, so it follows that lesson directly
optionExplain: Difficulty can matter, but the better reason is what plating acts on.
Right: a lesson that decorates or labels earlier work belongs after that work, as annotations come after declarations.
A lesson that finishes earlier work has a clear place after it.
Plating acts on the whole finished dish, not on one skill.
questions.explain: Plating acts on finished dishes, just as annotations act on declarations, so both come after the work they act on.
questions.rule: To test a lesson order, ask what each lesson acts on; a lesson that labels or finishes earlier work belongs after that work.
questions.teaches: To test the order of any course, ask what each lesson acts on; a lesson that labels or finishes earlier work belongs after that work.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the tutorials as a whole
questions.q: Which is the strongest one-sentence statement of what the five Java lessons are about?
options: They are the opening tutorials in Oracle's series of Java lessons
They cover programs, objects, variables, classes and annotations
They explain the Java language and platform to a beginner
They lead a reader from a first program to writing classes
optionExplain: That names the kind of material, not what it does.
That lists contents instead of saying what the whole is about.
That is so general that it would fit nearly any Java tutorial.
Right: it says what the lessons do together and fits all five.
questions.explain: A strong statement says what the whole does and covers every part. The card next shows how to tell the three weaker kinds apart.
questions.rule: State what the whole does, not its type or contents.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the tutorials as a whole
questions.q: The statement of what a whole work is about, in a sentence or short paragraph, is its ____.
questions.explain: The card calls this statement the unity of the work.
questions.rule: The unity is what the whole is about, briefly.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the tutorials as a whole
questions.q: Which sentence is the best unity for the Annotations lesson alone?
options: It is one of the tutorial lessons in Oracle's series of Java lessons
It shows how to attach metadata to declarations and who reads it
It lists Override, Deprecated, SuppressWarnings, Retention, Target and more
It is a lesson about programming in the Java language and tools
optionExplain: That names the type of material, not what the lesson does.
Right: it says what the lesson does and each section fits under it.
That is a list of contents, and it does not say what the lesson is for.
That is so broad that it fits every lesson in the series.
questions.explain: The second option says what the lesson does: it attaches information to declarations and says who acts on it.
questions.rule: Say what the part does, not what type it is or what it contains.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the tutorials as a whole
questions.q: True or false: A unity statement doubles as a test, because every part of the work should be explainable as serving it.
questions.explain: If a lesson cannot be explained under the sentence, the sentence is too narrow or the lesson has been misread.
questions.rule: Check a unity by fitting every part under it.
questions.teaches: A unity statement can be tested for coverage: take each part in turn and check that it serves the sentence; a part that does not fit means the sentence or the reading of that part needs revising.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the tutorials as a whole
questions.q: What if two readers write different one-sentence unities for the five lessons, and each sentence fits all five?
options: At least one reader is wrong, since a work has exactly one correct unity
Neither can be used, since a unity must quote the lessons
Both can be sound, because several wordings can cover every part
The longer sentence wins, since it holds more detail
optionExplain: Different wordings can both pass the fit test, so there is no single correct form.
A unity is the reader's own words, not a quotation.
Right: the test is coverage and fit, not a single fixed wording.
Length does not make a statement better; fit does.
questions.explain: The fit test accepts any wording under which all parts can be explained, so two readers may differ and both be right.
questions.rule: Unities are tested by fit, so more than one can pass.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the tutorials as a whole
questions.q: A baking book has chapters on ovens and tools, on doughs, on fillings and on finishing touches. Which unity passes the coverage test best?
options: It teaches baking from kitchen set-up to a finished item
It is a cookbook for people who want to bake at home every week
It lists ovens, doughs, fillings and glazes in four short groups
It teaches how to make pastry dough, with a list of pastries
optionExplain: Right: every chapter, from tools to finishing, fits under it.
That names the kind of book and says nothing about what it does.
That lists contents and omits the tools chapter and the idea of finishing.
That fits the dough chapter but leaves the oven, filling and finishing chapters unexplained.
questions.explain: Only the first sentence has a place for all four chapters.
questions.rule: A statement that fits some parts but not others fails the coverage test.
questions.teaches: A statement can sound right and still fail, because it fits some chapters and leaves others unexplained; the coverage test rejects it.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the tutorials as a whole
questions.q: True or false: A reader must wait for a lesson to state its goal before knowing what question it answers.
questions.explain: Readers can formulate the question from titles, headings and exercises. The card next shows how.
questions.rule: Formulate the question yourself.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the tutorials as a whole
questions.q: Match each lesson to the question it answers.
pairs: How do I write, build and run a first program?
Which building blocks (variables, types, operators, control flow) make up the code inside a method?
How do I declare a class and create objects from it?
How do I attach metadata about code that tools can read?
questions.explain: Each lesson's title and sections point to one main question.
questions.rule: One lesson, one main question.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the tutorials as a whole
questions.q: Which is the most precise question for the section on declaring your own annotation type?
options: What is Java, and who created the language?
What are annotations, and where are they used?
How do I define an annotation type with elements?
Why do programmers like to use metadata in programs?
optionExplain: That is far wider than this section.
That is the question of the opening section, not of this one.
Right: it names the task and the details the section covers.
That asks about opinion, which the section does not discuss.
questions.explain: A precise question names the task and the details the section works through.
questions.rule: Make the question as narrow as the section.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the tutorials as a whole
questions.q: The main question of Classes and Objects asks how to declare classes and create objects. Which is a subordinate question that one of its sections would answer?
options: How do I install the JDK on my computer?
What does an annotation element look like in a declaration?
How do I print text to the screen in a program?
What does the new operator do to create an object?
optionExplain: That belongs to the setup in the first lesson.
That belongs to the annotations lesson.
That belongs to the first program in Getting Started.
Right: it is a smaller question inside the lesson's main question.
questions.explain: A subordinate question stays inside the main question; the other options belong to other lessons.
questions.rule: Section questions nest inside the main question.
questions.teaches: A lesson's main question breaks into subordinate questions, each answered by one section; a candidate that belongs to another lesson is not subordinate.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the tutorials as a whole
questions.q: True or false: If, while studying a section, you find that it answers a different question from the one you wrote down, the sound move is to revise the question.
questions.explain: A formulated question is a working guess about the section, so what the section actually answers corrects it.
questions.rule: Revise questions when the text shows a better one.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the tutorials as a whole
questions.q: Lesson 1 lists ten buzzwords about Java and points to an outside paper without defining them. What question does that list answer?
options: None of its own; it points on, so note it as open
What does each buzzword mean, with an example of each one?
How does each buzzword make programs run faster than before?
How do I install the JDK on my machine at home?
optionExplain: Right: a list that only names claims answers no question by itself.
The list gives no meanings or examples.
The list makes no claim about speed for each word.
Installing is covered in a different section.
questions.explain: Where a section only names items or points elsewhere, there is no answer to record; marking it open is more honest than inventing one.
questions.rule: Not every section answers a question; mark the ones that do not as open.
questions.teaches: Some sections list or point and answer no question of their own; note them as open instead of inventing a question and an answer.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the tutorials as a whole
questions.q: True or false: The order in which a lesson presents topics must match the order in which the ideas depend on one another.
questions.explain: Authors sometimes use a word before explaining it. The card next shows how a reader tracks the real dependencies.
questions.rule: Page order and dependency order can differ.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the tutorials as a whole
questions.q: Match each idea to the earlier idea it rests on.
pairs: A class as a blueprint for objects
A subclass changing an inherited method
An interface with one abstract method
questions.explain: Each later construct stands on a concept taught earlier.
questions.rule: Name the idea underneath.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the tutorials as a whole
questions.q: A reader wants to understand a static nested class. Put the ideas in the order each one needs the previous one.
items: What a class is
How a class holds fields and methods
A class declared inside another class
A nested class that does not need an enclosing object
questions.explain: Class, then members, then nesting, then the static nested form that drops the need for an enclosing object.
questions.rule: Climb the joints one at a time.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the tutorials as a whole
questions.q: True or false: When the Hello World program is first met, its modifiers public and static are explained in full.
questions.explain: The first lesson names them as modifiers, but access levels and class-level members are taught later in Classes and Objects.
questions.rule: Forward use is an open joint.
questions.teaches: Tutorials may use a term before fully explaining it. Treat the use as an open joint, note it, and close it when the lesson that explains it arrives.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the tutorials as a whole
questions.q: A reader writes: Annotations rest on control flow, because they decide which statements run. What is wrong with this joint?
options: They rest on loops only, since only loops can be annotated in a program
The joint is right, but control flow is taught in Lesson 4 and not in Lesson 3
They label declarations, not the statements that run
They rest on nothing at all, since metadata needs no earlier idea to stand on
optionExplain: Loops are statements and are not what annotations label.
The joint itself is the error, and control flow is taught in Lesson 3.
Right: annotations are metadata about declarations, so they rest on classes and methods.
Annotations need declarations to attach to.
questions.explain: The error is in the joint: annotations describe code and do not steer it, so they stand on declarations.
questions.rule: Find the joint by asking what the idea actually acts on.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the tutorials as a whole
questions.q: A music course uses the word chord in Lesson 2 and defines it only in Lesson 3, with no note about it. What does the joint idea suggest the reader does?
options: Wait for the publisher to reorder the lessons of the course
Mark chord as an open joint and revisit it after Lesson 3
Use the everyday meaning of the word and keep on reading
Skip Lesson 2 and begin with Lesson 3 instead of it
optionExplain: Waiting stops the reading for no gain.
Right: the reader notices what must be known and closes the gap when it is taught.
The everyday sense may not match the course's technical sense.
Skipping loses the content of Lesson 2 that the later lesson builds on.
questions.explain: A forward use without a signpost is still an open joint, so note it and keep going.
questions.rule: Ask what you must already know to follow the sentence.
questions.teaches: When a text gives no signpost for a forward use, the reader's own question of what must be known to follow a sentence finds the joint.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the tutorials as a whole
questions.q: In which lesson is a bicycle first presented as an object with state such as speed and gear?
options: Lesson 1
Lesson 2
Lesson 3
Lesson 5
optionExplain: The first lesson runs a greeting program.
Right: the concept lesson introduces state and behavior through the bicycle.
Language Basics studies variables and operators.
Annotations come last and label existing code.
questions.explain: The bicycle appears as an idea in the second lesson. The card next shows what each later lesson adds to it.
questions.rule: The same example grows from lesson to lesson.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the tutorials as a whole
questions.q: Match each lesson to what it adds to the bicycle.
pairs: The idea of state, behavior and a blueprint
Typed fields with defaults and range tests
Private fields, a constructor and called methods
An Override label checked by the compiler
questions.explain: Each lesson adds one layer to the same example.
questions.rule: One lesson, one layer.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the tutorials as a whole
questions.q: A learner traces a Thermostat whose target must stay between 5 and 30, using an if test. Which lesson supplies that tool?
options: Lesson 1, because it shows how to run a program
Lesson 2, because it introduces objects and classes
Lesson 5, because it labels existing declarations
Lesson 3, because if is a decision statement
optionExplain: Running a program does not teach decisions.
The concept lesson explains objects, not statements.
A label cannot keep a value in range.
Right: the range check is a decision, which Language Basics covers.
questions.explain: A range check is a decision statement, taught in Language Basics.
questions.rule: Match the added layer to the lesson that supplies it.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the tutorials as a whole
questions.q: True or false: If the Bicycle class relied only on default field values, a new bicycle would start in gear 1.
questions.explain: An int field defaults to zero, and the lesson's class sets the gear to 1 itself.
questions.rule: Tracing shows which values the author chose.
questions.teaches: Tracing a field across lessons shows a design choice: the class sets the gear to 1 explicitly, because the default of 0 for an int is not a real gear.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the tutorials as a whole
questions.q: What if a subclass spells a method speedup in lower case, intending to replace speedUp, and marks it with Override?
options: The compiler reports an error: nothing is overridden
It compiles, and the new method runs when speedUp is called by other code
It compiles, and the label is ignored when the program runs
The program prints a warning when it runs and then goes on running
optionExplain: Right: Override asks the compiler to check, and a misspelt name fails the check.
Names are case sensitive, so the new method is a different method.
The compiler acts on the label before the program runs.
The problem is caught at build time, not at run time.
questions.explain: The compiler reads Override and finds no inherited method with that name, so the build stops.
questions.rule: Override turns a quiet typo into a build error.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the tutorials as a whole
questions.q: Lesson 3 uses plain numbers and strings, not any bicycle code. A reader wants the bicycle in its control-flow section. What is the sound move?
options: Conclude the bicycle cannot be traced through that lesson at all
Wait until a lesson shows a bicycle with an if test
Write a small bicycle gear check with an if test
Replace the bicycle with the lesson's own example, whatever it is
optionExplain: A missing example in the text does not stop the reader from writing one.
Waiting hands the work to the author, who may never supply it.
Right: tracing is a method the reader applies, so the reader can supply the missing step.
Dropping the bicycle loses the thread across lessons.
questions.explain: The reader writes the missing step and tests it, which keeps the example continuous.
questions.rule: When the text lacks your example, write the step yourself.
questions.teaches: Tracing is something the reader does, not something the text must supply; when a lesson lacks your example, write and test the missing step yourself.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the tutorials as a whole
questions.q: A program needs exactly the seven days of the week as named values. Which construct fits best?
options: An enum type
A class with seven int fields
A lambda expression
An annotation type
optionExplain: Right: a fixed set of named constants known in advance is the enum's purpose.
Seven separate fields hold values but do not make a closed set of named choices.
A lambda packages behavior, not named values.
An annotation labels code; it does not hold program values.
questions.explain: A fixed, known set of named values is what an enum is for. The card next shows the other matches between needs and constructs.
questions.rule: Match the construct to the need.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the tutorials as a whole
questions.q: Match each need to the construct that meets it.
pairs: A fixed set of named constants
A promise the compiler checks every implementing class keeps
Information about code that tools can read
A short action handed to other code
questions.explain: Each construct has a stated purpose, and the need points to it.
questions.rule: Need first, construct second.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the tutorials as a whole
questions.q: Sort these needs by whether the answer is code that runs or a label that only describes code.
groups: Code that runs with the program
Label read by the compiler or tools

items.t: Compare a score to pick a letter grade
Record which engineer reviewed a method
Mark a method so the compiler warns when others call it
Repeat a step for each element of an array
Hand a small action to a sorting method
Ask the compiler to confirm a method really overrides

questions.explain: Grading, looping and passing an action are behavior. Recording a reviewer, warning about use and checking an override are information about code.
questions.rule: Behavior runs; metadata describes.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the tutorials as a whole
questions.q: Inside a method, a program turns a day number from 1 to 7 into a name, and separately turns a score into a letter grade by ranges. Which pairing fits?
options: An if chain for the day name and a switch for the grade ranges
A switch for both, since a switch is the more general form
A switch for the day name and an if chain for the grades
An if chain for both, since a switch handles only numbers
optionExplain: The pairing is reversed: ranges are awkward for a switch.
A switch tests single values, so it is not the more general form.
Right: a switch compares one expression with single values, while ranges need conditions.
A switch handles other types too, such as strings and enums, but ranges need an if chain.
questions.explain: Matching single values suits a switch; testing ranges calls for an if chain.
questions.rule: Need-first reasoning works inside a method as well.
questions.teaches: Need-first choice applies inside a method too: a switch compares one expression with single values, while ranges and conditions need an if chain.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the tutorials as a whole
questions.q: What if the set of possible values is not fixed in advance, and users add new categories while the program runs?
options: An enum no longer fits: its constants are fixed when compiled
An enum still fits, since constants can be added while the program runs
A lambda fits, since a lambda can hold any kind of value
An annotation fits, since an annotation stores the categories for the program
optionExplain: Right: the enum's reason for existing, a fixed known set, no longer holds.
Enum constants are fixed when the program is compiled.
A lambda holds behavior, not categories.
An annotation labels code and is not a store for run-time data.
questions.explain: When the need changes from a fixed set to an open one, the construct that matched the old need stops matching.
questions.rule: Recheck the need when a condition changes.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the tutorials as a whole
questions.q: A sorting call needs a short comparison action; later the same action must keep a count of its own calls in a field. What does need-first reasoning suggest?
options: Keep the lambda, since lambdas can declare fields of their own
Switch to an enum, since a count is a fixed set of values
Move to an annotation, since a count is information about code
Move to an anonymous class, since the new need is a field
optionExplain: A lambda expresses one unit of behavior and has no fields of its own.
A count changes as calls happen, so it is not a fixed set of constants.
An annotation does not run or keep counts.
Right: a class form is the next simplest construct that can hold a field.
questions.explain: The new requirement, state in a field, is met by the next simplest construct that can hold it.
questions.rule: A choice is not permanent; repeat the match when needs grow.
questions.teaches: A construct chosen today may fail when a requirement is added; recheck the need and step up to the next simplest construct that meets it.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the tutorials as a whole
questions.q: True or false: A message saying a class could not be found means the compiler rejected the source.
questions.explain: That message comes from the launcher when it runs the program. The card next shows how to place each message.
questions.rule: The reporting stage tells you where to look.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the tutorials as a whole
questions.q: Sort these messages by the stage that reports them.

items.t: A semicolon is expected at line 7
A local variable might not have been initialized
A repeated annotation without the repeatable marking is refused
The launcher cannot find or load the class
The class has no main method of the required form
With the tutorial's JDK 8 launcher, the class was run with its file extension typed after the name

questions.explain: The compiler finds problems in the source; the launcher finds problems in locating and starting a class.
questions.rule: Compiler messages come with source lines; launcher messages concern classes.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the tutorials as a whole
questions.q: javac finishes silently and HelloWorldApp.class appears, yet the java command run from another folder cannot find the class. Which check comes first?
options: Go to the folder with the class file and check the classpath
Rewrite the source file from scratch and compile it again
Add a semicolon on the line the launcher names in its message
Mark the main method with Override to help the launcher
optionExplain: Right: a class file exists, so the problem is where the launcher looks.
The source compiled, so rewriting it fixes nothing.
The launcher names no source line; this is not a syntax error.
Override has nothing to do with locating a class.
questions.explain: A class file exists, so the compile stage passed, and the fault lies in the folder or the classpath.
questions.rule: Class file present: look at location and name.
