questions.unitTitle: Reading the tutorials as a whole
questions.q: Put these steps of handling a failed attempt in order.
items: Note which stage printed the message
Use the line number or class name in the message to find the cause
Change one thing
Rebuild and run again
questions.explain: Place the stage, locate the cause, make one change, then retest.
questions.rule: Stage, cause, one change, retest.
questions.teaches: Make one change per attempt, because with several changes you cannot tell which one fixed the problem or caused a new one.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the tutorials as a whole
questions.q: What if the program builds cleanly, runs with no message, and prints 5 where 6 is expected?
options: The launcher failed, so check the classpath setting
No stage reported a problem, so trace the code by hand
The compiler hid an error, so rebuild with the warnings turned on
The main method has the wrong form, so correct it
optionExplain: A launcher failure would print a message and stop.
Right: a wrong result with no message is a logic error, and only checking the code finds it.
A clean build means the compiler found nothing to refuse.
A wrong main form would stop the program from starting.
questions.explain: Stage placement works only when something reports; silence points to the logic, which you trace yourself.
questions.rule: No message means the stages cannot help; trace the logic.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the tutorials as a whole
questions.q: A spreadsheet rejects one formula the moment it is typed, pointing at the faulty part, and accepts another that gives a wrong total. How do these map to the Java stages?
options: The first is like a compile error, the second like a logic error
Both are like launcher errors, because both appear on the screen at once
The first is like a logic error; the second is like a compile error
Neither maps, since spreadsheets have no stages to compare with
optionExplain: Right: a gate before use catches some errors with a location, and others pass the gate.
Only one of them came with a message about the cause.
The wrong total passed the gate, as a logic error does.
Any process with a check before use has the same split.
questions.explain: The rejected formula is caught at the gate with a location; the wrong total passes the gate and shows only in the result.
questions.rule: Gate errors come located; errors that pass the gate need testing.
questions.teaches: Any process with a check before use has the same split: errors caught at the gate come with a location, and errors that pass it are found by checking the results.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the tutorials as a whole
questions.q: True or false: A reader should decide whether a lesson is right or wrong before being able to say what it claims.
questions.explain: Judging what you cannot yet state risks judging a misreading. The card next shows the order that avoids it.
questions.rule: Understand before judging.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the tutorials as a whole
questions.q: Put these reading tasks in the order they are done on a new lesson.
items: Skim the headings and summary to see what the lesson covers
State the unity in a sentence and outline the parts
Fix the key terms and what they mean
Find the key sentences and the reasoning behind them
Judge what holds and what is missing
questions.explain: Inspect, structure, terms, claims, then judgment.
questions.rule: Inspect, structure, content, judgment.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the tutorials as a whole
questions.q: You open a new Oracle lesson on generics with little time. Which step comes first?
options: Skim the title, headings and summary to see what it covers
List every key term and define each one
Decide which sections look weak
Write a full outline of the subsections before looking at anything
optionExplain: Right: inspecting first shows whether and how deeply to read.
Terms are fixed after the structure shows which words matter.
Judgment comes last.
An outline needs the skim to show what the sections are.
questions.explain: A skim comes first because it decides how much effort the lesson deserves.
questions.rule: Inspect before analysing.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the tutorials as a whole
questions.q: Why does stating the unity and outline come before hunting for key terms?
options: Terms cannot be found until the examples have all been compiled and run
They show what the lesson is about, so the weighty words stand out
Terms are defined inside the outline, so the outline replaces the lesson
An outline fixes the spelling of the terms used in the lesson text
optionExplain: Terms can be read from the text; compiling is not required.
Right: the structure tells you where the weight lies.
An outline summarises parts and does not define terms.
Spelling is fixed by the text, not by an outline.
questions.explain: Knowing the unity and parts points to the words the lesson leans on most.
questions.rule: Structure tells you which words matter.
questions.teaches: Structure guides term-hunting: words that appear in the unity and the headings are the likely key terms.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the tutorials as a whole
questions.q: What if you have used the lesson's topic at work for years and the lesson is short?
options: You may judge at once, because experience replaces understanding the lesson
You must repeat every step in full, because the order of steps is strict
Steps can merge and go fast, but understanding still comes before judging
You should skip the lesson, because nothing in it can be new to you
optionExplain: Experience may speed the reading, but it does not show what this lesson says.
The groups are not strictly chronological, and short lessons can merge steps.
Right: the steps can be quick, yet the rule of understanding before judging holds.
You cannot know it adds nothing until you have read it.
questions.explain: Familiar and short material shortens the steps without removing the order between understanding and judging.
questions.rule: Merge steps if you like; keep understanding before judgment.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the tutorials as a whole
questions.q: A chemistry lab handout is read for the first time. Which tasks belong to the structure group, before judging?
options: State in a sentence what the experiment sets out to show
Decide whether the method is the best one available
List the handout's main sections and how they connect
Mark the apparatus words the handout uses in a special way
Write down the question the experiment answers
optionExplain: Right: the unity is a structure task.
Comparing with other methods is judgment, which comes last.
Right: the outline is a structure task.
This is a content task (terms), which follows the structure.
Right: the question the handout answers is a structure task.
questions.explain: Purpose, parts and question are structure tasks. Marking special words belongs to the content group, and comparing methods is judgment.
questions.rule: Structure fixes purpose, parts and question.
questions.teaches: Structure tasks establish purpose, parts and question; marking special words is the content group, and comparing the method with others is judgment.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the tutorials as a whole
questions.q: True or false: A word that means one thing in everyday speech keeps that meaning when a Java lesson uses it as a technical word.
questions.explain: Lessons often give everyday words a fixed technical sense. The card next shows how to find and settle them.
questions.rule: Technical use can differ from everyday use.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the tutorials as a whole
questions.q: Match each word to the sense the lessons give it.
pairs: A namespace grouping related classes and interfaces
A variable that holds part of an object's state
Zero or more statements inside braces
A group of methods with empty bodies a class promises to implement
questions.explain: Each word has a fixed sense in the lessons that differs from casual use.
questions.rule: Fix one sense per word.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the tutorials as a whole
questions.q: A new lesson uses raw type and type parameter, neither of which you have met. What is the sound first move?
options: Note both as likely terms and see how the lesson uses them
Read on and rely on the everyday meaning of each of the two words
Skip them, since only the keywords of the language count as terms
Memorise the two words and move on to judging the whole lesson
optionExplain: Right: the lesson's own use fixes the meaning.
The everyday sense can mislead for a technical word.
Terms include non-keywords such as package and field.
A word has to be understood before it can be judged.
questions.explain: Terms are settled from the lesson's own sentences, not from casual meaning.
questions.rule: Let the lesson's own use fix the meaning.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the tutorials as a whole
questions.q: True or false: In the lessons, a parameter is a kind of variable but is not a field.
questions.explain: The lessons list fields, local variables and parameters as different kinds of variable, with a parameter belonging to a method signature.
questions.rule: A term's meaning includes what it is not.
questions.teaches: Terms are fixed in contrast sets: part of what a parameter means is that it is neither a field nor a local variable, so noting the contrasts keeps meanings from blurring.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the tutorials as a whole
questions.q: What if a word the lesson leans on heavily is not defined anywhere in the lesson itself?
options: Treat the guess as final, since the author must have meant it that way
Stop reading the lesson, since a lesson with a gap in it is unusable
Mark it provisional, test it on later uses, and check the API reference
Ask the compiler what the word means, by compiling the lesson's examples
optionExplain: A guess left untested can mislead.
One undefined word rarely makes the whole lesson unreadable.
Right: a provisional meaning is tested against further use and a reference.
The compiler checks code, not the meanings of words in a lesson.
questions.explain: An undefined word gets a provisional meaning that later sentences and the API reference can confirm or correct.
questions.rule: Provisional meaning, then test.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the tutorials as a whole
questions.q: A recipe step says to fold the egg whites into the batter. A reader notes: fold means to bend something over itself. What is the weakness of the note?
options: It should list the ingredients instead of defining a word of the recipe
Verbs cannot be terms, so no note about a verb is needed at all
It treats the word as having several contrasting meanings at once
It takes the everyday sense without checking the recipe's own use
optionExplain: Defining the word is the right kind of note; the sense is the issue.
Verbs can be terms too when used in a special sense.
The note gives one everyday sense rather than several.
Right: the recipe's own use fixes the sense.
questions.explain: The recipe's use, gently combining egg whites with the batter, fixes the sense, and the note skipped that evidence.
questions.rule: Take the meaning from the use in context.
questions.teaches: A word can be a term whatever its part of speech; the evidence for a special sense is the source's own use of it in context.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the tutorials as a whole
questions.q: True or false: Reading all five lessons once is enough to show that a reader understands them.
questions.explain: Reading shows exposure, while understanding shows in what you can do without the page. The card next shows what a finished understanding looks like.
questions.rule: Test understanding by doing, not by having read.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the tutorials as a whole
questions.q: Which of these show a finished understanding of the lessons?
options: Stating in a sentence what the lessons are about
Reciting the headings of every section in order
Choosing a suitable construct for a described need
Having read each page twice
Placing an error message at the compile or run stage
optionExplain: Right: stating the unity can be done without the page.
Reciting headings shows memory of labels, not of what they mean.
Right: choosing from a need shows use of the ideas.
Rereading shows effort, not ability.
Right: placing a message at its stage shows use of the pipeline.
questions.explain: Understanding shows in tasks done without the page: stating the unity, choosing a construct, placing an error.
questions.rule: Do the task without the page.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the tutorials as a whole
questions.q: A reader says she understood the else-if chain in Language Basics. Which check best supports that?
options: She rereads the section a second time, more slowly
She predicts the grade for a score of 76, then runs it
She copies the example into her notes word for word
She recalls that the section had a table of grades in it
optionExplain: Rereading shows effort but does not test the ability.
Right: predicting and then checking shows that she can use the rule that only the first true branch runs.
Copying shows the example was seen, not that it was used.
Recalling the table shows memory of a layout.
questions.explain: A prediction followed by a run tests whether she can use the rule, which is what understanding means here.
questions.rule: Predict, then check by running.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the tutorials as a whole
questions.q: True or false: A topic the lessons do not mention counts as a mistake the lessons made.
questions.explain: A mistake is a false or misleading claim; a topic left out is a gap.
questions.rule: A gap is not an error.
questions.teaches: A gap, something the lessons leave undone, is different from an error, something they state wrongly; naming a gap tells you what to read next, and only an error is a ground for disagreement.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the tutorials as a whole
questions.q: What if, in a later lesson, you find a statement that conflicts with these notes about launching applications over the web?
options: Check which Java version each source describes before deciding
Trust the notes, since they were read first and are condensed
Trust the newer lesson, since newer text always wins over older text
Conclude that both are wrong because they disagree with each other
optionExplain: Right: the lessons were written for JDK 8 and the technology changed later, so the version decides.
Reading order does not decide what is correct.
Newer is not automatically right; the notes may describe their own version correctly.
Two sources can both be right about different versions.
questions.explain: The notes describe JDK 8 and some web launch technology was later removed, so a conflict may reflect version, not error.
questions.rule: Check the version before calling a source wrong.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the tutorials as a whole
questions.q: A reader writes: The Annotations lesson is incomplete because I find its examples dull. What is wrong with this judgment?
options: Lessons with examples cannot be incomplete, whatever else is missing
A lesson may be judged only after it has been read at least twice
Dull examples are taste, not a named gap in what the lesson covers
Annotations lessons are outside what can be judged by a reader
optionExplain: Having examples does not prevent gaps.
The number of readings is not the test; naming a specific gap is.
Right: a gap is a specific thing left undone, not a feeling.
Any lesson can be judged once it is understood.
questions.explain: A specific gap names something the lesson set out to cover and did not; a taste does not.
questions.rule: Name the gap; do not report a feeling.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the tutorials as a whole
questions.q: A friend has finished a different tutorial lesson, on interfaces and inheritance. Using this unit's steps, describe what they should be able to do to show finished understanding, and one question about what the lesson leaves out.
questions.a: They should state in a sentence what the lesson is about and outline its sections; give the question it answers; explain its key terms, such as superclass and interface, with what each contrasts with; trace one example (for instance a bicycle) through it; choose between an interface and a subclass for a described need; and predict the result of a short program before running it. For completeness they should name a specific gap, for example a topic the lesson names but does not cover, and say whether it is a gap or an error.
questions.rule: Turn the steps into tasks that can be done without the page.
questions.teaches: A finished understanding is a checklist of performances drawn from the reading steps, applied lesson by lesson and ended with a question about gaps.
